*Shìtíhuányīn* (Shakra Devānām Indra) went to his location and spoke to him, saying:
'Why are you troubled, worried, and groaning?'
He responded by striking his thigh, saying:
'There are strange disasters and portents.'
*Shìtíhuányīn* recited verses (*jì*) for him, saying:
'All conditioned phenomena are impermanent; those that are born must surely perish.
Life inevitably leads to death; extinction (*miè*) is the highest happiness.'
The *Tiānzǐ* said:
'I have not heard this.'
*Shìtíhuányīn* said:
'All kindness and love entail separation.'
The *Tiānzǐ* said:
'How can I not harbor worry?
Now, all the various five desires (*wǔ yù*) in this heavenly palace are destined for separation.
When my life ends, I will be born in a sow's womb in the city of *Luóyuè*.
What I will eat is filth.
I am about to be killed by butchers.
I am worried precisely because I foresee this.'
At that time, *Shìtíhuányīn* spoke to the *Tiānzǐ*, saying:
'You should now take refuge in the Buddha, the Dharma, and the Sangha.
The reason for this is
the Buddha spoke a verse:
'Those who take refuge in the Buddha do not proceed to the Three Evil Paths;
They receive blessings among humans and *tiān*, and afterward attain the realm of *Nièpán*.'
The *Tiānzǐ* clasped his hands and spoke thus:
'World-Honored One (*Shìzūn*), the All-Knowing,
whose penetrating sight observes [all things].
May I be rescued and saved.
I now take refuge in the Buddha, take refuge in the Dharma, and take refuge in the *Bǐqiū Sēng* (Monastic Sangha).'
Consequently, he did not enter the sow's womb.
He was born into the house of the foremost elder (*zhǎngzhě*) in the city of *Luóyuèqí*.
Seeing this, [the *Tiānzǐ*] was unable to contain his joy.
There was a celestial maiden (Tīannǚ).
She sat upon a single lotus flower, one hundred *yóuxún* in length and width.
This flower was uniquely wonderful, surpassing all others.
All necessities of life that she desired emerged from the flower instantly upon thought.
Movement and rest followed her body.
Mùlián (Maudgalyāyana) asked,
“What good deeds did you perform to receive such retribution?”
The celestial maiden replied,
“After Kānèfó (Kāśyapa Buddha) attained Nirvāṇa,
a complete set of his *shèlì* (relics) was preserved.
Together with the Buddha’s disciples, a seven-jeweled stūpa was constructed.
It was forty *lǐ* high and wide.
At that time, I was a woman, and I went out and saw the image within the jeweled stūpa.
Feelings of faith and reverence arose, and I contemplated the Buddha's merits.
I removed the flower from my head and offered it to the image.”
In the Heaven of Zìzài Tiānwáng (Īśvara, the Sovereign Heavenly King), there was a jeweled maiden named Shànkǒu (Good Mouth).
From a single utterance, she manifested hundreds of thousands of entertaining sounds.
From each and every one of those sounds,
hundreds of thousands of sounds again emerged.
Disciples of the Buddha, you should know that
a single sound from Shànkǒu
gives rise to immeasurable sounds,
which, according to their needs, enable all beings to attain enlightenment.
In a past age,
in the Kingdom of Jūsàluó (Kośala), there was a man who played the zither,
named Lùniú (Deer Ox).
While traveling and resting in the wilderness, there appeared six great celestial palaces.
Celestial maidens came and spoke to Lùniú, saying,
“*Ājiù* (Uncle/Brother-in-law), *ājiù*, please play the zither for us;
we shall sing and dance.”
Lùniú strummed the zither, and the six heavens sang and danced.
The verses of the first song were:
If men and women bestow excellent and wonderful clothing in charity,
because of the condition of giving clothes, their rebirth is especially distinguished.
They bestow superb objects that never diminish, and are born in heaven according to their wishes.
See me residing in my palace, riding through the void and traveling.
My celestial body is like a heap of gold, superior among hundreds of celestial maidens.
Observing this merit and virtue, it is the best among dedications (Pāriṇāmanā).
The remaining celestial maidens’ words were similarly simple. Lùniú also performed the *lǐ* (salutation).
After the salutation was complete, the celestial beings suddenly vanished.
Within Yánfútí (Jambudvīpa),
there are sixteen great kingdoms, eighty-four thousand cities, eight kings, and four Sons of Heaven (Tīanzǐ).
To the east is the Kingdom of Jìn (Jin), whose Son of Heaven governs a prosperous people.
To the south is the Kingdom of Tiānzhú (India), whose Son of Heaven’s land has many famous elephants.
To the west is the Kingdom of Dà Qín (Roman Empire/Syria), whose Son of Heaven’s land is rich in gold, precious stones, and jade.
To the north is the Kingdom of Yuèzhī (Yuezhi/Kushana), whose Son of Heaven’s land has fine horses.
Among the eighty-four thousand cities,
there are six thousand four hundred types of people,
ten thousand types of sounds and noises,
fifty-six thousand myriad hills and settlements.
There are six thousand four hundred types of fish,
four thousand five hundred types of birds,
two thousand four hundred types of beasts,
ten thousand types of trees,
eight thousand types of grasses,
seven hundred forty types of assorted medicinal herbs,
forty-three types of assorted incense,
one hundred twenty-one types of jewels,
and seven true jewels.
In the sea, there are two thousand five hundred kingdoms.
One hundred eighty kingdoms eat the five grains.
Two thousand three hundred twenty kingdoms eat fish, turtles, and soft-shelled turtles.
There are five kings.
One king rules over five hundred cities.
The first king is named Sīlí.
His kingdom entirely serves the Buddha and does not serve any evil deities.
The second king is named Jiāluó.
His land produces the seven jewels.
The third king is named Bùluó.
His land produces forty-three types of incense and white *liúlí* (lapis lazuli/beryl).
The fourth king is named Shéyē.
His land produces *bìbō* (long pepper) and black pepper.
The fifth king is named Nàpō.
His land produces white pearls and seven-colored *liúlí*.
The cities of these five great kingdoms are mostly inhabited by short, dark-skinned people, and are sixty-five hundred thousand *lǐ* apart.
Beyond this point, there is only seawater, with no inhabitants.
It is one hundred forty *wàn lǐ* (1.4 million *lǐ*) away from Mount Tiěwéishān (Cakravāda).
The place where Yībā Juémó (Angulimāla) killed people is eighty thousand ten *lǐ* east of the Kingdom of Shèwèi (Śrāvastī).
The place where the Buddha converted him is also the same location.
The Kingdom of Jūyīnàjié (Kuśinagara) is one thousand *lǐ* southeast of the Kingdom of Jiāwéiluó (Kapila).
The Kingdom of Wángshě (Rājagṛha) is two thousand two hundred *lǐ* southeast of the Kingdom of Jiāwéiluówèi (Kapilavastu).
The place where the Buddha attained the Way is two hundred *lǐ* southeast of Wángshěchéng (Rājagṛha City).
The Kingdom of Wéiyēlífu (Vaiśālī) is one thousand eight hundred *lǐ* east of the Kingdom of Jiāwéiwèi (Kapilavastu).
The Kingdom of Nà’nǚ (Nāgarī) is three *lǐ* south of Wéiyēlíchéng (Vaiśālī City), to the west of the road.
The Kingdom of Jūshǎnmí (Kauśāmbī) is one thousand two hundred *lǐ* southwest of the Kingdom of Jiāwéiluówèi.
The Kingdom of Yèbō (Yavā) is one thousand two hundred eighty *lǐ* east of the Kingdom of Jiāwéiluówèi.
The Kingdom of Nàn (Nanda) is three thousand two hundred *lǐ* east of the Kingdom of Jiāwéiluówèi.
The Kingdom of Shèwèi is five hundred *lǐ* west of Jiāwéiluówèi.
The Kingdom of Bōluónà (Vārāṇasī) is nine hundred sixty *lǐ* west of the Kingdom of Jiāwéiwèi.
The place where the Buddha turned the Wheel of the Dharma is twenty *lǐ* north of the Kingdom of Bōluónà.
The tree is named Xiāngjìng (Fragrant Purity).
It is also the place where Māra was subjugated.
The Kingdom of Bōluónàsī (Vārāṇasī) is one thousand four hundred *lǐ* south of the Kingdom of Shèwèi.
In between, the Héngshuǐ (Ganges River) flows southeast.
Mount Qíshéjuéshān (Gṛdhrakūṭa) has five hundred peaks.
The Buddha recited sūtras on the central peak.
The Kingdom of Wángshě is below the central peak.
Question:
Cities such as Shěpótí (Śrāvastī), Jiāpíluópó (Kapilavastu),
and Bōluónàchéng (Vārāṇasī City)
all have royal residences for various kings.
Why is this city alone named Wángshě (King’s Residence)?
Answer:
Some people say
that the King of Mójiātuó (Magadha) had a son with one head, two faces, and four arms.
People at the time considered this inauspicious.
The king tore his body and head apart and discarded them in the wilderness.
A *luóchànǚguǐ* (Rākṣasī ghost) named Líluó
put his body back together and nursed him.
Later, he grew into a man of great strength and annexed all the surrounding kingdoms.
He captured eighteen thousand kings and confined them among these five mountains.
With his mighty power, he governed Yánfútí.
Therefore, these mountains were named Wángshěchéng (Rājagṛha City).
Furthermore, others say:
The city where the King of Mójiātuó originally lived suffered a fire.
It burned, and then it was rebuilt, and this happened seven times.
The people of the kingdom were exhausted by the effort.
The king gathered wise men and asked for advice, and some said,
“It would be appropriate to change location.”
The king saw that these five mountains encircled the area like a city wall.
He immediately built palaces and resided there.
Therefore, it is named Wángshěchéng.
Furthermore, in ancient times,
this kingdom had a king named Pósu (Vasu).
He grew weary of the world, left home, and became an ascetic (*xiānrén*).
At that time, household Brāhmaṇas (*póluómén*) and the renunciate ascetics debated together.
The household Brāhmaṇas said,
“In heaven worship (*tiānsì*), it is proper to kill living beings and eat meat.”
The renunciate ascetics said, “It is not proper.”
They disputed back and forth.
The renunciate Brāhmaṇas said,
“Here is a great king who left home to become an ascetic—do you trust him or not?”
The household Brāhmaṇas conceded.
The renunciate ascetics said,
“We shall take this man as our witness.
We will question him on a later day.”
The household Brāhmaṇas went first to Pósu.
They said to the ascetic Pósu,
“Tomorrow we will hold the debate.
You must support me.”
The renunciate ascetics asked,
“Is it proper to kill living beings and eat meat during heaven worship?”
The ascetic Pósu said,
“It is proper to kill living beings and eat meat.
Since this creature dies during heaven worship, it will be reborn in heaven.”
The renunciate ascetics said,
“You are utterly wrong!
You have told a great lie!” They spat at him and said,
“Sinful man, perish!”
At that moment, the ascetic Pósu
immediately sank into the ground up to his ankles.
This was the first opening of the great gate of sin.
The renunciate ascetics said,
“You ought to speak the truth.
If you still lie,
your body will sink into the ground.”
Pósu said,
“I know that killing sheep and eating their meat for the sake of heaven is not a sin.”
Immediately, he sank up to his knees.
In this way, he gradually sank up to his waist, and then up to his neck.
The renunciate ascetics said,
“Your lie has brought you immediate retribution in this life.
If you speak the truth again, even though you have sunk into the ground, I can bring you out and enable you to escape sin.”
Pósu reflected:
“I am a respected man and should not use two kinds of speech.
Moreover, the Four Védas (*wéituó*) praise the methods of worshiping Heaven.
What does it matter if I die alone?”
With a single mind, he declared,
“It is not sinful to kill living beings and eat meat during heaven worship.”
Thereupon, his whole body fell into the ground.
From that time onward, the methods of the ascetic Pósu were frequently used.
Sheep were slaughtered during heaven worship.
When the knife was brought down, people would say, “Pósu is killing you.”
Pósu’s son was named Guǎngchē.
He succeeded to the throne and became king.
He also grew weary of the ways of the world but was unable to leave home.
He thought thus:
“My father left home but sank into the ground alive.
If I govern the world, I will commit great sins again.
How should I conduct myself now?”
At that time, a voice in the void said,
“If you travel and see a rare and unusual place that is difficult to encounter, you should build a dwelling there and reside in it.”
Not long after,
the king went out hunting and saw a deer running as fast as the wind.
The king pursued it, but none of his hundred officials and attendants could keep up.
Ahead, he saw five mountains surrounding the area, steep and firm.
The ground was beautiful, there was the fragrance of celestial flowers, and he heard the music of celestial entertainment.
This place was rare and he had never seen it before.
“I should properly build my dwelling and reside here.”
He immediately abandoned his original city and resided among these mountains.
From that time onward, they dwelt there successively, hence the name Wángshěchéng.
There was a wealthy and noble elder
named Jiālántuó.
He regretted that his park had been given to the Nirgranthas (Níjiàn),
and that he could not offer it to the Buddha and the Sangha.
Lying down, his mat was uncomfortable (He could not sleep peacefully).
There was a great ghost general
named Bànshī.
Receiving the spiritual decree of the Buddha,
he immediately summoned the Yakṣas (Yuèchā) to drive out the Nirgranthas (Níjiàn).
"Naked and shameless, you should not stay here."
The Ghost General obeyed the command,
beating the Nirgranthas (Níjiàn) and dragging away their possessions.
The Nirgranthas (Níjiàn), terrified, fled and said:
"What kind of evil people are these, so violent and harmful?"
The Ghost General replied:
"The Elder Jiālántuó intends to use the Bamboo Park to build a Vihāra (Jīngshè) for the Buddha.
The great ghost general Bànshī ordered us to expel your group."
The next day, the Nirgranthas (Níjiàn) collectively censured the Elder.
The Elder was inwardly pleased, thinking, "My wish is fulfilled!"
He answered the Nirgranthas (Níjiàn):
"These ghosts and spirits are violent and harbor wrath; I fear they will certainly cause harm.
It is better to abandon this place and seek safety elsewhere."
The Nirgranthas (Níjiàn), resentful and hateful, all departed that very day.
The Elder repaired and erected the Vihāra (Jīngshè).
Monks' cells, sitting mats, and all adornments were fully completed.
He went to the place beneath the trees and invited the Buddha and the Sangha.
The Savior of the Multitude (Zhòng Yòu) accepted the offering, staying there to teach and deliver sentient beings.
Everyone was joyful and delighted.
Xūdáduō reported to the Buddha (Fó), saying:
The people within the city of Śrāvastī (Shèwèi chéng) mostly believe in heterodox teachings.
The Tathāgata (Rúlái) is immensely compassionate; I only pray that you would favor us with your presence and come to Śrāvastī (Shèwèi chéng).
The Buddha (Fó) said,
They have no monastery (jīngshè). How can I go?
Xūdá (Xūdá) said,
Your disciple wishes to build one and requests your permission.
The World-Honored One (Shìzūn) remained silent.
I request that you send Śāriputra (Shèlìfú) to instruct us regarding the pattern and plan.
Immediately, he commanded Śāriputra (Shèlìfú) to go with him to inspect the entire area, but there was no suitable location.
Only the grove of Prince Jeta (Tàizǐ Qítuó yuán) had flat ground, lush trees and forests, and a moderate distance [from the city].
Xūdá (Xūdá) reported this to the Prince.
The Prince laughed and said,
You want it for enjoyment.
After urgent pleading repeated several times,
The Prince said,
If you can cover the ground with gold such that there are no empty spaces between the pieces, then I will give it to you.
Xūdá (Xūdá) replied,
Yes. I shall respectfully pay the price.
Prince Jeta (Tàizǐ Qítuó) said,
I was just joking.
Xūdá (Xūdá) said,
A Prince should not speak falsehoods! And they immediately filed a lawsuit together.
At that time, a god from the Śuddhāvāsa Heaven (Shǒutuóhuì Tiān) transformed into a person, descended, and acted as a judge, stating,
Indeed, it is the law for a Prince (Tàizǐ) not to speak falsehoods.
Since the price has already been settled,
it is not appropriate to retract [the promise].
Thus, the judgment was made to give the land to him.
Then he commanded men and elephants to carry the gold out.
In the area of eighty *qǐng* [acres],
it was about to be filled in a short time.
A small piece of land remained, and Xūdá (Xūdá) pondered,
From which storehouse can I find enough gold?
Jeta (Qítuó) asked, saying,
Are you finding the price too high and abandoning it?
He replied, Not at all.
Jeta (Qítuó) thought,
The Buddha (Fó) must possess great virtue, seeing that this man treats treasure so lightly.
He immediately instructed Xūdá (Xūdá), saying, The land of the grove belongs to you.
The trees and forest belong to me.
I will offer them to the Buddha (Fó) myself. So Xūdá (Xūdá) proceeded with the construction work.
The Six Teachers (Liùshī) heard of this and went to report to the King (Guówáng).
The Elder Xūdá (Zhǎngzhě Xūdá) bought Jeta’s Grove (Qítuó yuán) and intends to erect a monastery (jīngshè) for Gautama (Qútán).
Allow my disciples to compete with them in magical arts.
If the Śramaṇa (Shā mén) wins, then allow the building to proceed.
If he loses, he should not be allowed to build.
The King (Wáng) summoned Xūdá (Xūdá) and questioned him, saying,
These Six Teachers (Liùshī) now say,
You bought the grove intending to build a monastery (jīngshè) for Gautama (Qútán).
They request to engage with the Śramaṇa’s (Shā mén) disciple,
to compete in their magical skills.
If he wins, permission will be given to establish the monastery (jīngshè).
But if he loses, he will not be allowed to build.
Xūdá (Xūdá) returned home, put on dirty clothes, and was distressed and unhappy.
At that time, Śāriputra (Shèlìfú), when the time came the next day, donned his robe, carried his bowl, and arrived at Xūdá’s (Xūdá) house.
He immediately asked him, saying,
Why are you unhappy?
Xūdá (Xūdá) answered fully.
These Six Teachers (Liùshī) have been ascetics for a long time, possess deep commitment, and the magical arts they have learned are unmatched by anyone.
I now want to know if Your Eminence's skills are capable of competing with them.
Śāriputra (Shèlìfú) said,
Even if these multitudes of Six Teachers (Liùshī),
filled Jambudvīpa (Yánfútí) and were as numerous as a bamboo forest,
they could not move a single hair on my foot.
What do they wish to compete in? Let them choose freely.
Xūdá (Xūdá) was overjoyed, changed into new clothes, bathed with fragrant water, and so on.
He immediately went and reported to the King (Wáng),
I have questioned him, and he permits them to choose whatever they wish.
The King (Wáng) informed the Six Teachers (Liùshī),
I now permit you to compete in the arts with the Śramaṇa (Shā mén).
The Six Teachers (Liùshī) announced to the people of the country,
Seven days from now, we will compete in the arts with the Śramaṇa (Shā mén) outside the city.
In the country of Śrāvastī (Shèwèi guó), there were eighteen *yì* people.
The custom of that country was to beat a drum to assemble the crowd.
If the copper drum was beaten, eight *yì* people would gather.
If the silver drum was beaten, fourteen *yì* people would gather.
If the golden drum was sounded, everyone would assemble.
When the seven-day period was complete, they went to the open, flat ground and struck the golden drum.
Everyone gathered.
The followers of the Six Teachers (Liùshī) numbered three *yì* people.
At that time, the people laid out high seats for the King (Guówáng) and the Six Teachers (Liùshī).
Then Xūdá (Xūdá) laid out a high seat for Śāriputra (Shèlìfú).
At that moment, Śāriputra (Shèlìfú) was sitting under a tree, entering various meditations (chán dìng).
And he reflected thus:
This gathered multitude has long practiced heterodoxy, they are arrogant and self-exalted, viewing all beings as grass and weeds. By what virtue should I subdue them?
Having thought this over, he immediately made a vow, saying,
If, throughout countless kalpas (jié), I have been compassionate and filial toward my parents, and reverent toward Śramaṇas (Shā mén) and Brāhmaṇas (Póluómén),
then, as I first enter the assembly, may all the great multitude perform prostrations to me.
The Six Teachers (Liùshī) saw that the crowd had gathered, but Śāriputra (Shèlìfú) had not yet arrived alone.
They reported to the King (Wáng), saying,
Gautama's (Qútán) disciple knows he has no skill.
Now that the assembly is gathered, he is afraid and will not come.
The King (Wáng) informed Xūdá (Xūdá),
The time for the competition has arrived.
The Buddha’s (Fó) disciple should come to debate.
Then Xūdá (Xūdá) went to where Śāriputra (Shèlìfú) was, knelt, and reported, saying,
Great Virtuous One, the great multitude has gathered.
Please come to the assembly.
Then Śāriputra (Shèlìfú) arose from meditation (chán dìng),
readjusted his robe,
placed his sitting cloth (níshī tán) on his left shoulder,
and walked slowly and majestically, like a lion king, toward the great assembly.
At that moment, the crowd, including the Six Teachers (Liùshī), suddenly stood up, like grass bending in the wind, and performed prostrations unconsciously.
Then Śāriputra (Shèlìfú) ascended the seat that Xūdá (Xūdá) had prepared.
Among the assembly of the Six Teachers (Liùshī) was a disciple named Raurakṣa (Láodùchā).
He was skilled in magical illusions.
In front of the great multitude, he conjured a tree.
It naturally grew tall and wide, sheltering the assembly, its dense branches and leaves flourishing, bearing diverse flowers and fruits.
Everyone exclaimed,
This transformation was surely made by Raurakṣa (Láodùchā)!
Then Śāriputra (Shèlìfú) used his spiritual power to create a swirling hurricane,
which blew the tree up by its roots, threw it to the ground, and shattered it into fine dust.
Everyone said that Śāriputra (Shèlìfú) had won.
Again, Raurakṣa (Láodùchā) conjured a pond.
The four sides of the pond were faced with the seven treasures.
Various flowers grew in the pond water.
Śāriputra (Shèlìfú) then transformed into a great white elephant with six tusks.
On each tusk were seven lotus flowers.
On each flower were seven celestial maidens.
The elephant majestically proceeded to the edge of the pond.
It swallowed the water entirely, and the pond immediately vanished.
Again, Raurakṣa (Láodùchā) created a mountain.
It was adorned with the seven treasures, and numerous ponds, trees, flowers, and fruits flourished.
Śāriputra (Shèlìfú) then transformed into a Vajrapāṇi (Jīngāng Lìshì).
He pointed at it from afar with the Vajra Scepter (Jīngāng chǔ).
The mountain immediately shattered, leaving nothing behind.
Raurakṣa (Láodùchā) then created a ten-headed dragon.
It rained various treasures from the empty sky.
Thunder and lightning shook the ground, startling the great assembly.
Śāriputra (Shèlìfú) then transformed into a Golden-Winged Garuḍa King (Jīnchì Niǎo Wáng).
It tore the dragon apart and consumed it.
Raurakṣa (Láodùchā) created an ox.
Its body was immense, fat, strong, with thick legs and sharp horns; it pawed the ground, roared loudly, and charged forward with a sudden burst.
Śāriputra (Shèlìfú) then transformed into a lion.
It tore the ox apart and ate it.
Raurakṣa (Láodùchā) then changed his body into a Yakṣa ghost (Yèchā guǐ).
His form was tall and enormous, fire burned on his head.
His eyes were red as blood, his four tusks were long and sharp, fire issued from his mouth and eyes, and he leaped and ran forward.
Then Śāriputra (Shèlìfú) transformed himself into Vaiśravaṇa King (Píshāmén Wáng).
The Yakṣa (Yèchā) was terrified and immediately wanted to retreat, but fire arose on all four sides, leaving him no place to go.
Only near Śāriputra (Shèlìfú) was it cool and free of fire.
Immediately, he submitted, throwing his five limbs to the ground (prostrating).
He begged for mercy and rescue; having developed a humiliated heart, the fire immediately extinguished.
The crowd all shouted,
Śāriputra (Shèlìfú) has won.
Raurakṣa (Láodùchā) has lost.
Then Śāriputra (Shèlìfú) ascended into the empty sky, displayed the four majestic postures, and performed eighteen transformations.
Having performed these transformations, he withdrew his spiritual power and sat down on his original seat.
The great assembly present, seeing his spiritual power, all felt great joy.
Then Śāriputra (Shèlìfú) immediately taught the Dharma to them, and according to their karmic dispositions, they each attained the path [of enlightenment].
The three *yì* disciples of the Six Teachers (Liùshī) left home under Śāriputra (Shèlìfú) to study the Path.
The Elder Xūdá (Zhǎngzhě Xūdá) went with Śāriputra (Shèlìfú) to draw the plans for the monastery (jīngshè).
Holding the end of the measuring string in his hand,
Śāriputra (Shèlìfú) was pleased and smiled.
Xūdá (Xūdá) asked, saying,
Venerable One, why do you smile?
He replied,
You have just started preparing this ground,
but palaces have already been completed for you in the Six Desire Heavens (Liù Yùtiān).
He immediately loaned him the spiritual eye, and Xūdá (Xūdá) saw everything.
He asked Śāriputra (Shèlìfú),
In these Six Desire Heavens (Liù Yùtiān), which place is the most enjoyable?
Śāriputra (Shèlìfú) said,
In the Fourth Heaven, desire is scarce and contentment is known.
There is always a Bodhisattva (Púsà) who is one lifetime away from Buddhahood (Yīshēng Bǔchù Púsà),
who comes to be born there, and the Dharma instruction is never interrupted.
Xūdá (Xūdá) said,
I shall definitely be born in the Fourth Heaven.
As soon as he finished speaking, the other palaces completely vanished.
He took hold of the rope again.
At that moment, Śāriputra (Shèlìfú) looked distressed and worried.
Xūdá (Xūdá) immediately asked the Venerable One (Zūn zhě) why he looked worried.
He replied,
Do you see the ants now on this ground?
In the past, during the time of Vipassī Buddha (Pípóshī Fó),
you also erected a monastery (jīngshè) on this very ground for that World-Honored One (Shìzūn).
Yet these ants are still being born within this place.
Even up to the time of Kāśyapa Buddha (Jiāshè Fó), it was likewise.
For ninety-one kalpas (jié), they have received the same kind of body.
He finished erecting the monastery (jīngshè) and built a dwelling for the Buddha (Fó).
He used wonderful sandalwood (zhāntán) to make fragrant plaster.
There were twelve hundred separate rooms for dwelling.
A total of one hundred and twenty separate places were constructed, and when the *ghaṇḍī* (qiánzhì) was struck, the work was finished.
He then reported to the King (Wáng),
I only request, O Great King (Dàwáng), that you send an envoy to invite the Buddha (Fó).
The King (Wáng) immediately sent an envoy to Rājagṛha (Wángshě Chéng) to invite the Buddha (Fó) and the Saṅgha (Sēng).
We pray that the World-Honored One (Shìzūn) will graciously come to Śrāvastī (Shèwèi).
The Buddha (Fó), surrounded before and behind by the Four Assemblies,
emitted a great radiance, shook heaven and earth, and arrived at the country of Śrāvastī (Shèwèi guó).
The rest houses they passed through, they all stopped at them.
Along the way, the number of people saved was limitless.
Gradually, they approached the border of Śrāvastī City (Shèwèi chéng).
Everyone gathered in a great crowd, carrying various offerings to welcome the World-Honored One (Shìzūn).
When the World-Honored One (Shìzūn) arrived in the country, he emitted a great light, illuminating the entire Three-Thousand Great-Thousand Worlds (Sānqiān Dàqiān Shìjiè).
His toe pressed the ground.
The earth all shook.
The musical instruments in the city sounded without being played.
The blind could see, the deaf could hear, the mute could speak, and the hunchbacked could straighten.
Those afflicted by chronic illness, crippledness, or deformities all became whole.
All the people, men and women, old and young, witnessed these auspicious signs.
Eighteen hundred million people were all gathered.
At that time, the *Shìzūn*, prescribing medicine according to the ailment, preached the marvelous Dharma for them.
Each attained the path.
Kūnlún Shān
is the center of the continent of Yánfú Dì.
The mountain is entirely gemstones.
All around it are five hundred caves.
The caves are all gold.
Five hundred *Luóhàn* constantly dwell there.
Ānòu Dà Quán
surrounds the outside of the mountain. Inside the mountain, a river runs through the flat ground.
On the river banks are four golden animal heads.
Water flows out of their mouths.
Each winds around once and returns to its four directions, entering the four great seas.
That which issues from the elephant’s mouth
is the Huáng Hé.
The spring is twenty-five *yóuyán* square in each dimension.
It is twenty-one *lǐ* deep.
Within the spring is a golden platform.
The platform is one *yóuyán* square.
On the platform is a golden lotus flower.
Its stem is made of the seven treasures.
The *Rúlái*, accompanied by five hundred *Luóhàn*, constantly preaches the precepts therein on the fifteenth day of the month.
The great earth has ten great mountain kings.
One is Xuě Shān Wáng.
Two is Xiāng Shān Wáng.
Three is Kēlíluó Shān Wáng.
Four is Xiānshèng Shān Wáng.
Five is Yóugāntuó Shān Wáng.
Six is Mǎ'ěr Shān Wáng.
Seven is Nímíntuóluó Shān Wáng.
Eight is Zhuójiāluó Shān Wáng.
Nine is Sùhuì Shān Wáng.
Ten is Xūmí Shān Wáng.
The Buddha, while in Shèwèi Chéng, addressed the *Bǐqiū*.
There are eight reasons why the great earth shakes.
This earth is sixty-eight thousand *yóuyán* deep.
It is supported by water.
The water relies on space (the void).
Or sometimes, when the wind in space moves, the water also moves.
When the water moves, the earth greatly shakes.
This is the first shaking.
If a *Bǐqiū* attains divine power and freedom to act as they wish,
seeing the earth as if in their palm, they can cause the earth to greatly shake.
This is the second shaking.
If, again, various *Tiān* possess great divine power and great might,
they can cause the earth to move strenuously.
This is the third shaking.
If, again, a *Púsà* is in Dōushuài Tiān,
and is about to descend the divine spirit to be born, at this time the earth shakes.
This is the fourth shaking.
If the *Púsà* knows himself to be in the mother's womb, the earth greatly shakes.
This is the fifth shaking.
If the *Púsà* knows that when ten months are complete they are to emerge from the mother's womb, the earth greatly shakes.
This is the sixth shaking.
If the *Púsà* leaves home and sits at the *Dàochǎng*,
subduing the demonic enemy and finally achieving complete enlightenment,
the earth greatly shakes.
This is the seventh shaking.
If the *Rúlái* enters the realm of Nirvāṇa without remainder,
and achieves *Pōnièpán*,
this is the eighth shaking.
In the past, there was a Buddha named Shīzǐ Hǒu Gǔyīn Wáng.
His kingdom was named Qiān Guāngmíng.
A tree was formed of the seven treasures.
The tree emitted the sounds of emptiness, signlessness, aimlessness, non-arising, non-possession, and non-grasping of characteristics.
These were the sounds of the various Dharmas.
There was a miraculous medicinal tree.
Its name was Mótúoqí Zhǔyàn.
All poisons in the world were prevented from spreading recklessly.
There was a great divine snake, one hundred and twenty *zhàng* long.
The snake traveled seeking food.
There was a black-headed creature, fifty *zhàng* long.
The creature walked along the road and encountered the snake.
Just as the snake was about to raise its head to strike down the great creature,
the snake smelled the medicinal fragrance, lowered its head, and wanted to flee.
The snake’s body got entangled in the medicinal tree.
Its body immediately broke in the middle, dividing into two sections.
The head half survived and managed to run away.
The tail half immediately rotted and stank.
When all poisons smelled this snake stench,
all evil poisonous vapors dissipated and vanished.
On the peak of Xuě Shān is a King of Medicine Tree.
Its name is "Not arising from the root, nor not arising from the root."
It spans six hundred and eighty myriad *yóuxún* in extent.
Its base reaches the boundary of the vajra (diamond).
When this tree sprouts roots,
all trees in Yánfú Tí sprout roots.
When it sprouts stems, and when it sprouts branches, leaves, flowers, and fruits,
all trees in Yánfú Tí likewise sprout branches, leaves, flowers, and fruits.
The tree's root can generate the stem.
The stem can generate the root.
Therefore, it is named "Not arising from the root, nor not arising from the root."
It can grow everywhere,
except in the deep pits of the hells
and in the water sphere, where it cannot grow.
Formerly, there was a king.
The king was named Wùliè. In his kingdom was a tree named Xiūbōtíhuán.
Its circumference was five hundred and sixty *lǐ*.
The circumference of its lower roots was eight hundred and forty *lǐ*.
It was four thousand *lǐ* high.
Its branches spread out in the four directions, covering a circumference of two thousand *lǐ*.
The tree bore five types of fruit.
The trunk had five sides (faces).
On one side, the king of the branch kingdom and the various palace courtesans jointly ate its fruit.
The second side was jointly eaten by the high ministers and all officials.
The third side was jointly eaten by the common people.
The fourth side was jointly eaten by the various *Shāmén* and Daoist priests.
The fifth side was jointly eaten by flying birds, insects, and beasts.
The fruits were all as large as a two-*dòu* jar.
Their flavor was like honey.
The tree had no keeper.
The fruit was naturally divided, and beings did not encroach upon each other's share.
People at that time all lived to be eighty-four thousand years old.
People at that time had nine types of illness.
One is cold.
Two is heat.
Three is hunger.
Four is thirst.
Five is defecation.
Six is urination.
Seven is sexual desire.
Eight is overeating.
Nine is old age.
Women, when they reached five hundred years of age,
would then marry.
Among humans there is a fragrance.
Its name is Dàxiàngzàng.
It originated from a dragon fight.
If one pellet is burned,
it produces great brilliant light, and fine clouds cover the top.
Its taste is like sweet dew.
For seven days and seven nights, it sends down rain of fragrant water.
If it touches a person's body, the body turns golden.
If it touches clothes, palaces, or storied pavilions,
they also all turn golden.
If any sentient being hears this fragrance,
they will feel joy and pleasure for seven days and seven nights.
All sicknesses are extinguished, and there are no unjust misfortunes.
They move far away from hearts filled with terror and harm.
They turn devotedly towards Great Compassion and universally contemplate all sentient beings.
When I know this about them, I preach the Dharma for them,
enabling immeasurable sentient beings to attain non-retrogression.
Niútóu Zhāntán Xiāng
arises from Lígòu Shān.
If one smears it on the body,
fire cannot burn it.
South of Xūmí Shān there is a great tree.
It is four thousand *lǐ* high.
Various Bōchā birds constantly dwell upon it.
The tree is usually motionless.
There was a small bird.
Its shape resembled a quail or an owl.
When it landed upon the tree,
the tree immediately shook and trembled.
The Bōchā birds asked the Tree Spirit,
"Are you ignorant?
Our bodies are large and heavy, yet you do not move.
When the small bird comes, you instead shake and tremble."
The Spirit replied,
"Although this bird is small,
it has eaten a vajra (diamond) from the bottom of the sea.
The vajra is an object
such that wherever it falls, there is nothing it cannot shatter and disperse.
This is why I am greatly terrified and cannot remain calm."
In Shèwèi Guó there was a royal garden.
A poisonous tree grew there.
Men and women who came to stroll and rest beneath it
sometimes suffered splitting headaches,
sometimes suffered pain in the waist and spine,
or sometimes died beneath the tree.
The gardener
employed a long-handled axe,
more than one *zhàng* long,
and chopped it down from afar.
Before ten days had passed,
it grew back just as it was before.
This happened many times.
The branches and leaves immediately
rounded out as before.
The marvel of the tree
caused everyone who saw it
to feel nothing but joy.
Not knowing the taboo,
they all came and suffered this fate.
The gardener's relatives
greedily enjoyed the shade of the tree
and all perished.
The gardener was left standing alone,
mourning day and night.
He wept sorrowfully as he walked.
Someone asked him.
A wise man told him:
"You must exhaust its root."
Just as he was about to dig up the root,
he was again afraid of certain death.
He went further and contemplated,
left home, and studied the Way.
The Buddha said:
If you cut down a tree without destroying the root, although cut, it will grow back again.
If you cut off desire without destroying its source, sorrow will arise frequently again.
When the mind awakens and overcomes blame.
Immediately, one obtains the first fruition (of stream entry).
Furthermore, there are four great rivers.
They flow out from the Great Lake Ānòu and proceed toward the great sea.
The first is named Gānggā.
The second is named Xīntóu.
The third is named Bǔchā.
The fourth is named Sītuó.
That Gānggā flows out from the mouth of a golden elephant.
It encircles the lake once and flows toward the Eastern Sea.
That Xīntóu flows out from the mouth of a silver ox.
It encircles the lake once and flows toward the Southern Sea.
That Bǔchā flows out from the mouth of a lapis lazuli horse.
It encircles the lake once and flows toward the Western Sea.
That Sītuó flows out from the mouth of a crystal lion, encircles the lake once, and flows toward the Northern Sea.
Those four great rivers,
each have four rivers as their dependencies (tributaries).
Only those that are vast and possess names are mentioned here.
However, those four rivers each have five hundred dependencies.
Together there are two thousand rivers,
finally flowing toward the great sea.
The one flowing west is named Héng.
The one flowing south is named Yéyún.
There are two flowing east.
One is named Shālù.
One is named Āyíyuè.
The one flowing north is named Mò.
All flow into and inundate the sea.
Since heaven and earth were established, the rain falls and the rivers inundate, yet the water [of the sea] neither increases nor decreases.
They shed their former names
and merge to become the water of a single sea.
The Buddha traveled in Wúshèng Guó.
Regularly on the fifteenth day of the month,
He spoke the precepts for the various Śrāmaṇas and sat in meditation.
The Buddha remained silent, without speaking.
Ānán said,
"[We are] sitting in meditation."
Then the World-Honored One said,
"Among the Śrāmaṇas,
there is one who harbors evil conduct and is rebellious.
It is not something that the lowly and despicable can uphold.
The pure and the foul contradict each other.
I will not speak."
Mùlián entered concentration and observed (him).
Immediately he said to him,
"Get up! This is not the place where a mundane person like you should sit."
[The man] refused to rise at that moment, so [Mùlián] pulled his arm and made him leave, saying, "You possess no supreme virtue.
Your heart harbors the six corruptions.
How dare you, with a foul and polluted body,
sit upon the seat of celestial fragrance?
You are an outcast.
You are not a Śrāmaṇa!"
The Buddha instructed the Śrāmaṇas:
"Observe that great ocean; it possesses eight kinds of virtues.
Its vastness is immense and shoreless.
Its depth has an unmeasurable bottom.
Entering gradually, it becomes gradually deeper, without obstruction beforehand.
This is the first virtue.
The tide does not fail its time.
This is the second virtue.
The sea contains all treasures, there is nothing it does not encompass.
The sea does not tolerate foul, decaying corpses.
This is the third virtue.
The sea holds many valuables.
Nothing sought is unobtainable.
This is the fourth virtue.
Under the entire sky, there are five great rivers.
They flow into the sea.
All shed their former names,
merging to become a single sea.
This is the fifth virtue.
The five rivers and ten thousand streams, along with falling rain, continually inundate it.
Yet the water in the sea remains as it was, never increasing or decreasing.
This is the sixth virtue.
The sea has many fish, whose bodies are massive and towering.
The first fish is four thousand *lǐ* long.
The second fish is eight thousand *lǐ* long.
The third fish is twelve thousand *lǐ* long.
The fourth fish is sixteen thousand *lǐ* long.
The fifth fish is twenty thousand *lǐ* long.
The sixth fish is twenty-four thousand *lǐ* long.
The seventh fish is twenty-eight thousand *lǐ* long.
This is the seventh virtue.
The seawater is uniformly salty, the same near the edge and in the middle. This is the eighth virtue."
The Bright Moonlight Maṇi pearl,
is mostly found within dragon brains.
If a sentient being has merit and virtue,
they naturally obtain it.
Just as in the Hells (Dìyù),
instruments for punishing transgressions spontaneously arise.
This jewel is also named the Wish-Fulfilling Pearl (Rúyì Zhū).
It constantly emits all kinds of treasures,
clothing and drink, according to one's desires.
He who obtains this pearl,
poison cannot harm.
Fire cannot burn it.
Some say:
This was held by Dìshì.
When Jīngāng fought with the Āxiūluó,
fragments fell down onto Yánfútí.
Others say:
The relics (shèlì) of ancient Buddhas of the past,
when the Dharma was extinguished completely,
transformed into this pearl in order to provide benefit.
Within the great sea there are four precious pearls.
All treasures are born from them.
If these four pearls did not exist,
all treasures would gradually become extinguished.
The minor Nāga deities cannot see them.
Only Suōjiāluó Lóngwáng secretly places them deep within the treasure treasury.
This deep treasure treasury has four names.
The first is named Assembly of Accumulated Treasures.
The second is named Inexhaustible Treasure Treasury. The third is named Far Burning.
The fourth is named Assembly of All Adornments.
Within the great sea,
there are four brightly burning and shining great jewels.
The first is named Sun Treasury Bright Light Great Jewel.
The second is named Away-from-Drought Bright Light Great Jewel.
The third is named Fire Pearl Bright Light Great Jewel.
The fourth is named Utterly Without Remainder Bright Light Great Jewel.
If these four jewels were not in the great sea,
the Four Continents and the Jīngāngwéi Shān (Vajra Enclosing Mountain),
and even the realm of Neither-Perception-Nor-Nonperception would all be flooded and submerged.
The Sun Treasury Bright Light
is able to transform the seawater into curds.
The Away-from-Drought Bright Light
is able to transform the sea curds into ghee.
The Fire Pearl Bright Light
is able to ignite the sea ghee.
The Utterly Without Remainder Bright Light Great Jewel
is able to burn the sea ghee until it is eternally and utterly exhausted.
In Yánfútí,
a child, having been born and fallen to the ground,
up until three years of age,
how much milk does it drink from the mother's embrace?
Mílè answered,
"It drinks one hundred and eighty *hú* (bushels) of milk,
excluding the four parts (quarters) consumed while in the mother's womb."
In Dōngfúyúdài (Eastern Continent),
a child, having been born and fallen to the ground,
up until three years of age,
drinks one thousand eight hundred *hú* of milk.
In Xījūyění (Western Continent),
a child, having been born and fallen to the ground,
up until three years of age,
drinks eight hundred and eighty *hú* of milk.
In Běiyùdānyuè (Northern Continent),
a child, having been born and fallen to the ground,
sits at the roadside.
Passersby offer a finger, and the child sucks it.
In seven days, they become an adult.
That land has no milk.
Intermediate state (Zhōngyīn) sentient beings ingest and inhale the wind.
Sentient beings in Yánfútí have a lifespan of one hundred years.
Sentient beings in Dōngfúyúdài have a lifespan of two hundred and fifty years.
Sentient beings in Xījūyění have a lifespan of five hundred years.
People in Běiyùdānyuè have a lifespan of one thousand years.
Intermediate state sentient beings have a lifespan of seven days.
The face of the people of Yánfútí is wide above and narrow below.
The face of the people of Dōngfúyúdài is perfectly round.
The face of the people of Xījūyění is narrow above and wide below.
The face shape of the people of Yùdānyuè is perfectly square.
The facial appearance of Intermediate state sentient beings
is like that of the Parinirmita-vaśavartin (Tāhuà Zìzài Tiān) heaven.
Běi Yùdān is called “The World.”
Its perimeter, width, and length
are each four hundred thousand *lǐ*.
There are various kinds of mountains.
On both banks of its rivers,
there are various kinds of trees and various kinds of flowers.
In the water, there are boats,
made of the four treasures.
The bathing pool is named Nánduō.
Its water is cool and moist.
The sand at the bottom is all gold.
All around it, there are steps,
made of the four treasures.
Gold steps have silver railings; silver steps have gold railings.
Lapis lazuli steps have crystal railings;
crystal steps have lapis lazuli railings.
There are various kinds of lotus flowers.
If the flower is broken,
the juice that comes out is like milk and tastes sweet like honey.
Its light shines forty *lǐ*.
Its fragrance is also smelled for forty *lǐ*.
East of the pool, there is a river
named Yǐwèi.
South of the pool, there is a river
named Xiūjié.
West of the pool, there is a river
named Dàtǔ.
North of the pool, there is a river
named Shànzhǒng.
The waters of these rivers all have flowering trees,
formed by the four treasures.
East of the pool, there is a garden
named Xiánshàng.
Its railings, balustrades, and rows of trees are also formed by the four treasures.
Fragrant trees in the garden produce various kinds of scents.
There are clothing trees,
and there are garland/necklace trees.
They produce various kinds of clothing, covers, and adornments.
There are music trees,
producing various kinds of music.
The trees are seven *lǐ* tall.
There are also those six, five, four, three, and two *lǐ* tall.
South of the pool, there is a garden pavilion
named Yǔxián.
West of the pool, there is a garden pavilion
named Luóyuè.
North of the pool, there is a garden pavilion
named Chángyǒuhuá (Always Having Flowers).
What the trees produce,
and their relative heights,
are also like the Eastern Garden.
In the Northern Continent, the trees twist and form intersecting paths.
Heavenly beings are upon them.
Males and females are in separate places.
There is pure, clean polished rice
that grows automatically without being planted.
It produces all flavors.
If they wish to engage in sexual activity,
the intention arises, and they look at each other without speaking.
The man then walks ahead,
and the woman follows behind.
They go to a garden pavilion and enjoy each other's company.
Sometimes for two or three days,
sometimes up to seven days.
When they feel satisfied, they leave,
and they are not attached to one another.
When a woman becomes pregnant,
she gives birth in seven or eight days.
She carries the child and places it in the middle of the four crossroads.
If someone comes from the four directions,
they give the child milk that flows from their finger joint and feed it.
After seven days pass,
due to its own virtue and merit,
it immediately grows up
like a person in Yánfú [Jambudvīpa] aged twenty,
or twenty-five.
All around the four directions,
there is water named Ānòuduōluó.
In the deep night, clouds arise and rain down water of eight flavors,
like human food and drink.
The ground is as if coated with oil, and dust does not rise.
Grass and trees are perpetually present.
Flowers and fruits are all fragrant,
like when perfume is being heated.
There are gusty winds that sweep and clean the Xiánshàng garden pavilions.
The Yīlán wind arises,
blowing fallen flowers up to people's knees.
The people of this world all enter the gardens to play and enjoy themselves, without any attachments.
When people want to eat,
they take the pure, clean polished rice,
and light a fire underneath it using the light of a Yànwèizhū (Flame-Flavor Pearl).
When the rice is cooked, they arrive from the four directions and all eat it.
The food is also inexhaustible.
There is a tree named Xiàngdōu.
Its branches twist and meet overhead like a dense canopy.
The people settle and dwell upon it.
Males and females are in separate places.
People's teeth and hair are dark blue, eight inches long.
People's complexions are the same, and their height and size are equal.
They all live for a thousand years.
When they die, they are born into the various heavens of the Desire Realm.
When the lifespan in heaven ends,
they are born into a great, wealthy, and noble family in Yánfútí.
When they relieve themselves (urinate or defecate),
the ground splits open to receive it, and once received, it closes again.
When they die, they are adorned with fine clothes, and there is no weeping or crying.
They are placed in the middle of the four crossroads.
A Yùzhē bird picks it up and places it outside the Northern Continent.
The Tathāgata [Rúlái], long ago, in a distant *kalpa*,
practiced the Bodhisattva path
and was the king of a great country.
When his father and mother passed away,
he ceded the kingdom to his younger brother
and left alone to seek the Way.
He saw a Brāhmaṇa [Póluómén]
whose surname was Qútán.
He followed him to receive instruction,
and consequently shared his surname.
He entered the deep mountains
to contemplate the Way through meditation.
He begged for food and returned to the kingdom.
The people of the country did not recognize him
and called him Little Qútán.
He established a monastery [jìngshě]
himself in a sugarcane garden outside the city.
There were five hundred great bandits
who robbed and stole government property.
They passed by the edge of the garden.
The next day, footsteps traced the route, and they consequently arrested the Bodhisattva.
They pierced his body with a wooden stake and set him up under a large tree, his blood flowing onto the ground.
The Elder Qútán flew over and asked,
"What severe crime have you committed to suffer this?"
The officials released their crossbows, shot, and killed him.
The Elder Qútán wept, and his tears moistened the coffin.
He took the blood-soaked earth to make mud balls
and carried them back to the monastery.
He placed them in two vessels, left and right, and said:
"If this devotee is truly sincere,
the heavenly spirits should transform this blood into humans."
Ten months later, the left immediately became a male,
and the right immediately became a female.
Their surname was Qútán.
The male was named Shěyí.
During the time of Bǎofó [Ratnabuddha] in the Bhadrakalpa [Xiánjié], he was also called Shìjiā [Śākya].
This is the one who exceeded the lifespan of five million years. The Buddha was in the country of Mójiětí [Magadha],
under the Yuánjí Tree at the Shànshèng Bodhimaṇḍa (place of enlightenment).
His virtue and power subdued Māra [Mó].
He converted two merchants.
Only Dìngguāng Rúlái [Dīpaṅkara Tathāgata],
bowing to my Buddha name, said,
"You, in ninety-one future *kalpas*,
shall attain Buddhahood.
Your name shall be Shìjiāwén [Śākyamuni].
The ten titles shall be complete,
just as they are for me now."
Since that time,
I have accumulated merit and practiced diligently.
I maintained the six *pāramitās* (degrees) and the four immeasurables [sìděng] without tiring.
My reward for merit was flawless, and my great vow bore fruit.
Ultimately, the Bodhisattva.
Resided in Dōu Shuài Tiān.
He questioned the devas and discussed,
asking which clan the Bodhisattva should manifest birth into.
The celestial son Zhǒng Yīng asked,
"Into which lineage shall the person filling the vacancy in one lifetime descend?"
He replied,
"Among the lineages that possess sixty virtues,
I shall descend into them. Only the Shì family has long cultivated the root of virtue."
The people of Jiā Wéi Luó Wèi.
High and low are harmonious and mutually supportive.
The country is rich, the people are happy, and they yearn for the Single Vehicle.
Moreover, Bái Jìng Wáng is naturally benevolent and virtuous.
His consort is of the Qú Tán Shì clan.
Gentle, loyal, and good, she guards her body, mouth, and mind.
For five hundred lifetimes, she has already been the Bodhisattva's mother.
When the Queen was sleeping peacefully,
the Bodhisattva transformed and mounted a white elephant,
crowned with the essence of the sun,
and entered her womb.
Her body and mind were peaceful and joyful, like profound meditation.
She went to the Wú Yōu Shù.
She sent an emissary to inform the King.
At that time, in the Wú Yōu Lín, there were ten types of auspicious signs.
First, it suddenly became vast.
Second, earth and stone transformed into Vajra.
Third, jeweled trees stood in rows.
Fourth, decorated with incense.
Fifth, filled with floral garlands.
Sixth, various treasures flowed forth.
Seventh, lotus flowers grew in the ponds.
Eighth, devas, nāgas, and yakṣas stood with palms joined.
Ninth, celestial maidens offered reverence.
Tenth, all Buddhas emitted light, universally illuminating the grove.
The King was greatly delighted.
The Queen’s body was light and supple.
She harbored no thoughts of the Three Poisons.
All those who were ill were certainly cured by her touch.
When the ten months were complete, and the time for delivery arrived,
there were thirty-two auspicious signs.
First, the trees in the royal gardens naturally bore fruit.
Second, blue lotuses the size of chariot wheels emerged from the dry ground.
Third, withered trees bloomed.
Fourth, vehicles of the Seven Jewels arrived.
Fifth, hidden treasures in the ground naturally surged forth.
Sixth, famous perfumes and beautiful flowers spread throughout near and far.
Seventh, five hundred lions from the Xuě Shān stood guard at the city gates.
Eighth, five hundred white elephants all stood before the palace.
Ninth, fine rain moistened the air with fragrance.
Tenth, hundred-flavored foods were provided to the hungry and thirsty.
On the eighth day of the fourth month, when the morning star appeared,
the Queen desired to stroll in the gardens and wandered beneath the Lián Pí Shù.
The Three Thousand Worlds shook six times.
The constellation Fèi Sù fell, and the tree immediately bent a branch.
The mother immediately reached up and grasped it.
All the devas scattered flowers.
He was born from her right flank.
His body was sixteen feet tall.
He immediately walked seven steps.
Jeweled flowers supported his feet.
He raised his hand, paused, and said,
"In the heavens above and the earth below, only I am honored."
"The Three Realms are all suffering; what joy is there?"
Shì and Fàn attended him.
The Four Kings received him onto a golden dais.
Nāgas poured fragrant water for his bath.
Five hundred blue-clad attendants each gave birth to a strong man.
White mares bore colts.
Yellow ewes bore lambs.
Seven days later, the mother died.
She was born into Dāo Lì Tiān.
Since the Crown Prince was young and required care,
at that time, there was one who spoke, saying,
"Only Dà Ài Dào is the Crown Prince's maternal aunt."
"She is pure and without a husband, and thus able to raise him."
At that time, Bái Jìng Wáng
went to Dà Ài Dào and asked her to breastfeed him.
Ài Dào complied.
A Brahmacārī from the Xuě Shān named Ā Yí Tóu Qí
saw the Crown Prince and lamented sorrowfully, shedding tears.
The King asked the reason.
He replied,
"I look up and congratulate the Great King
for giving birth to this divine person."
"Yesterday, heaven and earth greatly shook;
this was precisely the reason."
"According to my physiognomy method,
the Crown Prince possesses the Thirty-Two Marks."
"First, the body is gold colored."
"Second, a fleshy protuberance on the crown."
"Third, the hair is deep blue."
"Fourth, a white curl of hair between the eyebrows."
"Fifth, light emanates from the crown like sunlight."
"Sixth, eyelashes are deep blue."
"Seventh, blinking together, both upper and lower lids."
"Eighth, forty teeth in the mouth."
"Ninth, teeth are white and even."
"Tenth, square jaws."
"Eleventh, a broad and long tongue."
"Twelfth, when closed, the mouth fills the hall."
"Thirteenth, lion chest."
"Fourteenth, the body is square and upright."
"Fifteenth, long arms."
"Sixteenth, long fingers."
"Seventeenth, full heels."
"Eighteenth, feet are stable, flat, and straight."
"Nineteenth, internal and external grasping."
"Twentieth, palms are soft when joined."
"Twenty-first, patterns of a thousand-spoked wheel on the hands."
"Twenty-second, patterns of a thousand-spoked wheel on the feet."
"Twenty-third, genitals retracted like a horse."
"Twenty-fourth, calves like a deer."
"Twenty-fifth, collarbones like a chain."
"Twenty-sixth, hairs curl to the right."
"Twenty-seventh, one hair per pore."
"Twenty-eighth, skin and hair are fine and soft."
"Twenty-ninth, impervious to dust or water."
"Thirtieth, the chest bears the symbol Wàn Zì."
"One whose body possesses these marks,
if they remain at home,
will become a Cakravartin,
and the Seven Jewels will arrive spontaneously."
"If they leave home, they will become a Self-Awakened Buddha."
"I grieve that my years are already late;
I shall not behold the rise of the Buddha."
"This is why I weep."
The King bestowed rich rewards upon him.
He instructed Dà Ài Dào,
"Apply deep respect and protection to the Crown Prince."
The Crown Prince, at the age of seven, rode a sheep cart,
guided and followed by the assembled Shì,
and went to visit the writing master.
The master’s name was Xuǎn Yǒu.
The Crown Prince asked,
"Master, what writing method do you have to teach?"
He replied,
"I have the methods of Fàn and Qū Liú.
I can teach them to you."
The Crown Prince said,
"There are sixty-four types of unusual scripts.
Why mention only two?"
The Master said,
"I wish to hear their names."
The Crown Prince replied,
"Fàn Shū, Qū Liú Shū,
Hù Zhòng Shū,
Jí Jiān Shū,
Lóng Guǐ Shū,
Qián Dá Pó Shū,
Ā Xū Lún Lù Lún Shū,
Tiān Cháng Shū,
Zhuǎn Shù Shū,
Guān Kōng Shū — which script do you wish to teach me with?"
The Master could not understand
and could only offer praise.
The Crown Prince, for the sake of the children,
differentiated the roots and branches
and encouraged them to initiate the mind for the Way. When the Crown Prince reached seventeen years of age,
the King prepared to take a consort for him.
He screened several thousand candidates.
Finally, he obtained the daughter of a minor king,
whose surname was Qú Tán Shì,
named Qú Yī, the daughter of Bō Xū Fú.
She was unmatched in beauty, pure like a lotus flower.
Eight kingdoms competed to propose marriage, but none had yet been permitted.
The King summoned him to appear.
"We shall now contract a marriage between the Crown Prince and your daughter."
Shàn Jué was worried.
"If I do not grant permission, I will certainly be conquered."
"If I grant permission, the eight kingdoms will become resentful enemies."
The daughter said,
"The kingdom of Bái Jìng Wáng
has the superior martial arts
and is feared by all other kingdoms."
The King ordered the country,
"Seven days from now,
the Crown Prince shall demonstrate his skills."
"Those who are capable should assemble." Diào Dá struck and killed an elephant.
The Crown Prince threw it outside the city wall.
In astronomy, geography, and eighty thousand different skills,
none could surpass the Crown Prince.
Diào Dá wrestled briefly with the Crown Prince.
The Crown Prince grabbed him and threw him into the air three times, but he was unharmed.
Next, they shot at drums.
Diào Dá shot and hit a drum.
But he could not overcome the difficulty of the forty *lǐ* drum.
The Crown Prince drew his bow, and the bow became soft and broke.
He asked, "Is there another bow that I may use?"
The King replied,
"The bow used by my late grandfather was uniquely extraordinary, without equal, and no one has been able to use it."
"It is kept in the Celestial Temple."
It was retrieved and given to the Crown Prince.
None of the members of the Shì could even lift it.
The Crown Prince used it to shoot and hit the hundred *lǐ* drum.
The arrow plunged into the ground, causing a spring to spontaneously well up, reaching as far as the Tiě Wéi Shān.
The Three Thousand Worlds shook six times.
Immediately thereafter, Qú Yī
was made the Crown Prince's First Consort.
Following worldly customs, they manifested mutual enjoyment. Furthermore, he took the daughter of the elder Yí Shī
named Yē Wéi Tán.
became the second Fūrén.
He also married the daughter of an elder (Zhǎngzhě) of the Shìzhǒng clan.
Her name was Lùyě.
She became the third Fūrén.
The Tàizǐ was supposed to become a Fēixíng Huángdì (Chakravartin).
Three seasonal Diàn were built.
Sixty thousand Cǎinǚ were provided.
Luóyún (Rāhula) disappeared from heaven, transformed, manifested, and was born.
Afterwards, the Tàizǐ went out the East City Gate.
The Wáng commanded that the roads be meticulously cleared and prepared,
ensuring nothing was unclean.
Established by the miraculous power of the Tàizǐ,
the gods transformed into an Lǎorén.
His hair was white and his teeth were falling out.
His eyes were dim and his ears were deaf.
He leaned on a staff and walked hunched over.
The Tàizǐ knew, but deliberately asked:
"Who is this person?"
The Yùzhě replied:
"This is called an Lǎorén."
The Tàizǐ said:
"Human life flows away and is difficult to regain.
Not only is this true for humans, but it is true for all under heaven."
He turned his carriage around and returned to the Gōng, feeling sorrowful and unhappy.
Later, he went out the South City Gate.
He encountered a Jírén.
With a swollen belly and emaciated body, he lay beside the road.
He asked the Yùzhě.
He replied:
"A Bìngrén."
The Tàizǐ said:
"All things are impermanent; having a body entails suffering.
I am naturally subject to this too."
He immediately returned into the Gōng.
Afterwards, he went out the West City Gate.
He saw a Sǐrén.
His family was weeping bitterly.
The Yùzhě said:
"A Sǐrén.
Where there is life, there is death.
It is like having winter after spring.
All beings and things are subject to this."
The Tàizǐ said:
"Death is truly painful!
The Jīngshén suffers greatly!
When I look upon the deceased,
the form decays and the body transforms,
yet the Shén is not extinguished.
I cannot bear to accept rebirth through death again,
traveling back and forth through the Wǔdào and exhausting my Jīngshén."
He turned his carriage around and returned.
Then, on another day,
he went out the North City Gate.
He saw a Shā mén.
His clothes were neat and tidy, and he held a Fǎqì in his hand.
The Yùzhě said:
"This is called a Bǐqiū.
He has abandoned desires and passions.
His heart delights in all things.
He seeks to save the beings of the Shífāng."
The Tàizǐ said:
"Excellent!
This is what I delight in.
If I do not renounce the Wángwèi and leave home,
this would not be fitting."
Immediately, during the quiet night, he entered the King's Gōngdiàn.
A light shone far and wide.
The Fùwáng awoke and arose.
He immediately informed his Fù, saying:
"The Zhūtiān encourage and assist me.
I must leave home now."
The Fùwáng wept sorrowfully, asking:
"What are your aspirations?
When will you return?"
The Tàizǐ desired four Yuàn:
First, not to age.
Second, to be without illness.
Third, not to die.
Fourth, not to be separated.
"If the Fùwáng can grant these four Yuàn,
I will not leave home again."
The Wáng said:
"From antiquity until now, no one has achieved these."
His sorrow and grief intensified.
He immediately commanded five hundred Shìzǐ, who were strong and brave,
to guard the four gates overnight.
The sound of the city gates opening and closing could be heard forty *lǐ*.
Qiúyí (Yaśodharā) felt suspicious and did not leave his side.
The Tàizǐ reflected that the Dào is pure and it is inappropriate to stay at home.
He ought to reside in the mountains and forests, refining his spirit and practicing Chán.
His age at that time was twenty-nine.
It was after midnight on the seventh day of the fourth month.
Qiúyí experienced five Mèng at that time.
She immediately woke up in alarm.
The Tàizǐ asked her.
She replied:
"I dreamt that Mount Xūmí collapsed,
the bright moon fell to the ground,
the pearl's radiance suddenly vanished,
my hair fell out by itself,
and someone stole my Gài."
The Púsà knew that the dream concerned himself.
He said, "Mount Xūmí has not collapsed.
The bright moon continues to shine.
The pearl's radiance is not extinguished.
Your hair has not fallen out.
The Sǎngài still remains.
Just sleep peacefully
and do not worry about loss."
That night, he observed the Jìnǚ; their hundred joints were all void.
They were like a Bājiāo tree.
(There was) nasal mucus and tears in their eyes.
Musical instruments lay scattered everywhere.
He looked at his wife.
He clearly saw her form and body,
(seeing) the brains, marrow, skull, heart, liver, intestines, and stomach.
Externally it is a leather bag, internally filled with foul filth.
It is merely borrowed temporarily.
When it must be returned, it cannot be held onto for long.
The Sānjiè offer no peace; only the Dào can be relied upon.
The Zhūtiān of the Yùjiè resided in the sky.
The Fǎxíng Tiānzǐ
spoke to the Tàizǐ from afar:
"The time has arrived!
The Fóxīng has just appeared."
He called for Chēní (Chandaka) to rise.
He saddled Kǎnzhí (Kaṇṭhaka).
The Sì Tiānwáng, along with countless Yèchā, Lóng, and others,
all put on armor.
They came from the four directions.
They bowed their heads in reverence.
The Zhūtiān, fearing there might be obstacles,
immediately sent a Yànshén.
It entered the Gōng and enchanted everyone to sleep.
All the men and women in the city slept deeply.
Peacocks and all the other birds lay tiredly asleep.
Chēní wept sorrowfully.
The door lock would not open.
Four Sìshén lifted the Mǎ's hooves.
He vaulted out of the Gōngchéng.
Dìshì (Indra) led the way in front.
He emitted a great, pure light and proceeded to the Fóshù.
The next morning, they reported and asked.
[They] did not know his location.
The King immediately pursued his tracks.
He advanced to Wángtián.
Distantly, he saw the Crown Prince (Tàizǐ).
A tree bent its branches
to shade him above.
The King himself was startled and enlightened.
Without realizing it, he dismounted his horse and performed a ceremony.
The Crown Prince bowed and said,
"I have just arrived here.
Why should Your Majesty condescend to visit?"
[The King] followed the thought of the Crown Prince,
unable to abandon his feelings.
Returning, he summoned the great ministers.
"You gentlemen fondle your sons and embrace your grandsons,
mutually enjoying comfort.
I only have one son,
and I see him separated, living in the mountains.
Take five of your sons and younger brothers,
pursue him, and attend to him.
If he returns halfway,
I will exterminate your clans."
The Crown Prince removed his jeweled clothes and entrusted them to Chēnì.
[He instructed him] to return and report to his royal father,
and to tell Qiúyí,
"Once I achieve the Way (Dào), I shall return.
Do not forget this oath."
Chēnì received the instructions [and departed].
Tears fell like rain.
The white horse knelt down deeply
and licked the feet of the Bodhisattva (Púsà).
[Chēnì] returned the objects to the Royal Capital (Wángdū).
Sighing, he fell to the ground.
Qiúyí embraced the horse:
"The Crown Prince rode upon you;
why have you suddenly returned alone?"
Sweet fruits and beautiful springs—nothing was lacking.
The Bodhisattva thought to himself:
desiring to become a Śramaṇa (Shāmé), he went to the mountainside and waterside.
The Heavenly King (Tiānwáng) knew his mind
and descended holding a knife.
The Bodhisattva shaved his own head and hair.
Dìshì received the hair.
Only the fleshy protuberance (ròují) remained.
He became a great Śramaṇa.
He reached the side of the Nílián water (river).
He dwelt quietly and peacefully.
He encountered a hunter (lièshī)
whose body was wearing Dharma robes, looking like a Śramaṇa.
The Crown Prince asked,
"What is the name of these Dharma robes?"
He replied, "Kāṣāya (Jiāshā)."
"The deer, believing [me] to be studying the Way,
their hearts without fear,
come and attach themselves to me.
I kill them sequentially
and use [their meat] to support myself."
The Crown Prince felt even greater compassion.
He requested [to exchange] the clothes he was wearing
and traded with him.
The hunter said,
"Your Majesty grew up in the deep palace;
your body and flesh are delicate and soft,
having never endured cold hardship.
I fear [my coarse robes] will damage Your Majesty's body.
Moreover, they are impure."
The Crown Prince said,
"These are the symbolic vestments (biāoshì) of the sages and worthies.
Just trade them; there is no harm."
[He said,] "I will naturally wash and cleanse them."
All the heavenly beings (zhūtiān) offered him food,
but he rejected and refused to accept it.
Advancing forward, he arrived at the kingdom of Mójié.
The people saw him
and thought he was Dìshì, Fànwáng, or other heavenly beings.
The Crown Prince knew what they were thinking,
so he sat beneath a tree.
Píngshā Wáng
immediately went out with his ministers to visit the Daoist (Dàoshì).
Distantly, [Píngshā Wáng] saw the radiant appearance
and asked, "What divinity (shén) is this?
From what kingdom have you come?
What is your name?"
The Crown Prince replied,
"I originated east of Xiāngshān and north of Xuěshān.
The kingdom's name is Jiāwéi.
My father's name is Báijìng.
My mother's name is Móyē."
Píngshā asked,
"Surely you are Xīdá (Siddhārtha)?"
He replied, "It is so."
The King immediately bowed at his feet and said,
"Your features are brilliant and manifest.
You ought to rule the four directions
and be the Cakravartin (Zhuǎnlún Shèngdì).
The four seas look up eagerly,
hoping the divine treasures will arrive.
Why have you abandoned your heavenly position
and exiled yourself to the mountain wilderness?"
He replied,
"Being born entails death; there are four grave pains:
namely, birth, old age, sickness, and death—which cannot be escaped.
The body is a vessel of suffering;
worry and fear are limitless.
If one is in a respected and favored position,
then arrogance arises.
Seeking pleasure creates suffering for the world.
Because I am weary of this,
I have entered the mountains."
For six years, he labored diligently in hardship,
eating one sesame seed and one grain of rice daily.
He sat in the lotus position (jiéjiā fūzuò) and did not sway.
Wind, rain, thunder, and lightning did not change him throughout the four seasons.
He never once raised a hand to shield himself.
People found this strange.
They took grass and wood and threw it into his ears and nose,
but he did not reject or discard it.
His body was wasted and thin,
yet only his golden complexion became more evident,
his bright light shining far.
When the six years were completed,
he thought to himself,
"If I am so emaciated
when I go to the Buddha Tree (Fóshù),
later generations will ridicule me,
saying that I achieved the Way (Dào) through starvation.
I would rather eat soft food,
restore my body,
and then attain the Way."
At that time, there was the daughter of a village elder (zhǎngzhě nǚ).
She had married and given birth to a son.
Her heart was greatly joyous.
She milked a thousand cows, letting them drink and recirculating the milk.
She took the refined milk and made a porridge (mí).
She intended to offer it to the Tree Spirit (Shùshén).
She sent a maidservant to sprinkle water and sweep.
The maidservant saw the Buddha (Fó) but did not recognize him.
She returned and reported to her mistress, saying,
"Under the tree there is a spirit, upright, wondrously excellent."
The woman heard this and was delighted.
She intended to take the porridge away.
The porridge jumped out of the cauldron by more than a *zhàng* (ten feet),
and could not be taken.
The woman found this very strange.
A heavenly being in the air said,
"There is a Great Bodhisattva.
He has already risen from his seat.
You originally made a vow.
You should first feed him.
Only then will he attain Right Enlightenment (Zhèngjué)."
The woman heard the words of the heavenly being.
She immediately took the milk porridge
and filled a golden bowl (bō) with it.
She went to the side of the Nílián water.
The Bodhisattva, using his spiritual power (shéntōng lì),
entered the water to bathe.
The Tusita Heaven Sons (Dōushuài Tiānzǐ)
took heavenly robes (tiānyī) and Kāṣāya,
and respectfully offered them to the Bodhisattva.
He immediately took them and put them on.
He resided by the Nílián water.
The daughter of the village elder offered the milk porridge.
The Bodhisattva ate it.
His strength gradually replenished.
He went toward the Buddha Tree.
On the left side of the road was a person
named Jíxiáng.
He was cutting fresh, lush grass,
which was soft, smooth, and untangled.
The Bodhisattva said to Jíxiáng,
"I desire to have this grass for a seat."
The earth then greatly trembled.
All the heavenly beings magically created eighty thousand lion thrones (shīzǐ zhī zuò) beneath the Buddha Tree.
Each of the Heaven Sons saw the Bodhisattva sitting alone on his own seat.
Those with little merit and virtue (fú dé) still saw him sitting on the grass.
Sentient beings in the Three Realms (Sānjiè) saw the Bodhisattva sitting beneath the Buddha Tree, emitting great light,
which obscured the Demon Palace (Mógōng).
Bōxún (Māra), while lying asleep, dreamed of thirty-two changes:
his palace became dark, entering an evil path;
his pond water dried up;
his musical instruments were broken;
the heads of his Yakṣas (Yèchā) and frightening ghosts all fell to the ground;
the heavenly beings abandoned him and did not obey his commands.
[Bōxún] gathered all his great ministers and described what he had seen in his dream.
He raised all his weapons and armor,
and summoned his thousand sons.
Five hundred of his sons,
led by Dǎoshī, believed in and delighted in the Bodhisattva.
The other five hundred sons,
led by Èmù, followed Māra to cause chaos.
[They prepared] to subdue him.
Māra had four daughters:
the first named Yùfēi,
the second named Yuèbǐ,
the third named Kuàiguān,
and the fourth named Jiàncóng.
They went to the Bodhisattva,
using enticing words and creating allurements
of thirty-two kinds.
Their appearance, demeanor, lips, and tongue were seductive; the palace maidens carefully watched, wishing to serve at his side day and night.
He answered:
"Although your form is beautiful, your heart is not upright.
You are leather sacks filled with filth.
Why have you come here?
Go, I have no use for you."
The three jade maidens transformed into old crones.
Unable to revert themselves, they immediately returned to Mó's (Māra's) location. Mó's evil power grew even stronger.
He summoned eighteen billion followers,
who transformed into diverse shapes:
lions, bears, human bodies with insect heads, and bodies of snakes and vipers.
They carried mountains and spat fire,
producing thunder and lightning,
holding up spears and halberds.
Bódìsà's (Bodhisattva's) joyful heart remained utterly unmoved.
The demon soldiers could not approach him.
At that moment, Bódìsà slowly raised the curl of white hair (báiháo) between his eyebrows.
He directed it towards Ābǐ Yù (Avīci Hell),
allowing the sinners to see it.
The white hair streamed forth in a torrent, as large as a carriage wheel.
The fire instantly went out temporarily.
They recalled the sins they had committed in previous lives,
their hearts became cool and pure, and they invoked Námó Fó (Namo Buddha).
Because of this causation, if their suffering was completed,
they ought to be reborn among humans.
Mó saw this phenomenon,
became haggard and distressed,
and retreated back to his palace.
The báiháo then moved on,
reaching the Sixth Heaven.
Upon seeing the white hair aperture,
various jeweled lotus flowers appeared.
The Qī Fó (Seven Buddhas of the Past) were present upon the flowers.
In this way, the báiháo reached up to the Formless Heavens (Wúsè Tiān),
illuminating everything like a crystal mirror.
Eighty-four thousand celestial maidens
looked upon Bōxún's (Māra's) body,
finding his appearance
like withered wood, and instead gazed only upon the light of Bódìsà's báiháo mark.
Countless celestial sons and celestial maidens
generated the Bodhi mind (Bódítí Xīn).
The Demon King (Mówáng) once again challenged Fó (Buddha).
Fó used the power of wisdom and stretched out his hand to press the ground.
Immediately, the earth shook.
Mó and his officials and subordinates
all tumbled down head over heels.
Having completely subdued the demonic enemies,
he immediately attained perfect enlightenment (Zhèngjué).
Accompanied by tens of millions of followers,
he entered Luóyuèchéng (Rājagṛha).
Those who saw him from afar
raised their hands in praise.
Some said, "Welcome!"
Others said, "It is the Sun and Moon!"
Some took refuge in him,
and others greeted him,
asking, "Is this a deity?
Is this Dìshì (Indra)?"
The multitude followed him closely.
Píngshā Wáng (King Bimbisāra) was on a high tower,
and immediately asked his attendants,
"What is the reason for this?"
One minister said,
"The Śākya son (Shìzǐ) left home and wandered outside.
Perhaps he intends to plot against the state.
We should go and execute him."
The King said,
"If this son had succeeded to the throne and become a Cakravartin (Zhuǎnlún Shèngwáng),
we would all have been his ministers and assistants.
But since he left home to study the Way and attained Buddhahood,
I wish to be his foremost disciple.
When he first preaches the Dharma,
I desire to be immediately present at his side."
The King brought food and drink
and went to the Eastern Mountain to await him.
He immediately went forward and bowed at his feet,
declaring, "I am Píngshā Wáng, the ruler of Mójí Guó (Magadha).
I am he."
Fó said,
"I knew you previously.
Why must you show respect?"
The King then requested,
"I now present a humble offering,
to express my sincere heart.
I hope you will accept it."
Fó silently accepted.
The King said,
"If you attain the unsurpassable Way (Wúshàng Dào),
I wish to be the first to be delivered [by you]."
At that time, Ālán's (Ālāḷa Kālāma's) disciples,
seeing the World-Honored One (Shìzūn) from afar,
told their teacher,
"There is a person today
who is exceedingly handsome and distinguished.
He has passed through the teacher's gate,
and must surely be seeking to become a disciple."
Ālán then spoke a gāthā (verse):
"I observe the form of this gentleman coming from afar, complete and faultless.
He belongs to the King's world;
he will ultimately not submit to [our] lineage."
Ānán (Ānanda) asked about the funeral rites.
Fó said,
"The method of my burial
shall be like that of a Zhuǎnlún Shèngwáng (Cakravartin).
First, bathe the body with scented water,
wrap the body in linen (jiébèi).
Next, wrap it with five hundred layers of white cotton sheeting.
Place it within a golden coffin.
Pour sesame oil over it.
Then place the golden coffin inside an iron outer coffin.
A sandalwood outer coffin
should then be wrapped around that.
Pile up fragrant firewood and cover it thickly on top,
and then perform the cremation (shēwéi).
When the firewood is exhausted and the fire is extinguished,
collect the relics (shèlì).
At the junction of the four highways,
establish a stūpa and a shrine,
raising banners and streamers.
This will cause those who see it to remember and long for [me].
This will bring great benefit."
Fó said,
"There are four kinds of people for whom stūpas should be erected:
First, the Rúlái (Tathāgata);
second, the Pìzhī Fó (Pratyekabuddha);
third, the Shēngwén (Śrāvaka/Arhat);
and fourth, the Zhuǎnlún Wáng (Cakravartin).
For all of them, offerings of incense, flowers, banners, parasols, music, and enjoyment should be made."
Fó arranged a bed seat
between the twin Śāla trees,
having his head oriented south and his face directed towards the north.
The reason for this
is that when the Buddha Dharma (Fófǎ) spreads,
it will long abide in the north.
Fó himself folded his Saṃghāṭi (Sēngjiālī),
