lay down on his right side like a king of lions,
and lay with his feet overlapped.
Ānán further asked,
"How many types of burial are there in the world of Yánfútí (Jambudvīpa)?"
Fó said,
"Innumerable.
In this land of ours,
there are water burials, fire burials, and stūpa/tomb burials.
The funeral rites of the people of Zhèndàn Guó (China/the Eastern Land) are as follows:"
Carved carriages and carts made of gold, silver, and precious jewels,
flying celestial maidens, musicians, bells, and chanting
are used to please the departed.
The clothes worn by the body
are richly placed in the coffin and outer coffin.
Exquisite perfumes diffuse their fragrance.
Thousands and millions of people escort [the body] to the mountains and wilderness.
The burial place is highly adorned.
People who witness it are all greatly pleased.
Regarding the border kings of Zhèndàn
and the people they govern:
when they wish to bury someone, they construct and hold the coffin and outer coffin,
placing them inside a stone chamber.
When illness strikes, they open [the chamber] to look upon the bones,
wash them, and pray for blessings so that the illness may be cured.
There are also those whose lives end who have no coffin or outer coffin.
They simply take the corpse
and place it on a high pavilion.
When there is urgent sickness,
they bring the body down and recite incantations and prayers
in order to seek blessings and protection.
Fó said, "When those who study my Dharma wish to cultivate blessings,
they must diligently practice vigor (jīngjìn),
perform the Liù Bōluómì (Six Pāramitās),
and guard and uphold the Shí Shàn (Ten Good Deeds).
Then they may achieve rebirth in heaven
and advance toward the unsurpassable Way (Wúshàng Dào)."
The Buddha (Fó) was at the city of Kušinagara (Jūshīnà Chéng), the birthplace of the Malla (Lìshì), beside the Ajitavati River (Āyíluóbátí Hé), between the twin Śāla trees (Suōluó Shuāngshù).
Together with eighty billion hundred thousand great Bhikṣus (Bǐqiū).
Surrounding him both front and back.
On the fifteenth day of the second month, when he was about to enter Nirvāṇa (Nièpán),
by the Buddha’s divine power, a great voice issued forth,
reaching even the summit of existence (Yǒudǐng).
According to the types of sounds [in each realm],
he universally announced to all:
"Today, the Tathāgata (Rúlái),
out of compassion for sentient beings,
acts as their refuge.
The Greatly Awakened World-Honored One (Dàjué Shìzūn) is about to enter Nirvāṇa.
If any sentient being has any doubt,
they may all ask now."
When this, the final questioning, occurred in the morning,
the Buddha emitted various lights from his face,
universally illuminating the great thousandfold world
and extending even to the ten directions.
For sentient beings in the six realms,
those who encountered this light
had their sinful stains and afflictions completely eliminated.
Sentient beings who saw and heard this felt great anxiety and sorrow.
They simultaneously raised their voices,
weeping and wailing sorrowfully.
The great earth, mountains, and seas all shook.
At that time, people collectively said,
"Hurry to the Buddha’s location!
Urge the Tathāgata
not to enter Parinirvāṇa (Bōnièpán)!
Stay in the world for one Kalpa (jié)!"
The great disciples, such as Kátyāyana (Jiāzhānyán),
upon encountering the Buddha's light,
trembled and shook, unable to control themselves.
They raised their voices and cried out, experiencing various kinds of suffering.
Furthermore, there were eighty hundred thousand Bhikṣus,
and six billion Bhikṣuṇīs (Bǐqiūní),
all of whom were Arhats (Āluóhàn).
Their hairs stood on end, and blood appeared all over their bodies,
like the Palāśa flowers (Bōluóshā Huá).
Furthermore, there were one hundred million times the sands of the Ganges Bodhisattvas (Púsà),
whose positions equaled the Ten Stages (Shí Zhù).
Two times the sands of the Ganges Upāsakas (Yōupósài).
Three times the sands of the Ganges Upāsikās (Yōupóyí).
Four times the sands of the Ganges Licchavis (Líshē).
Five times the sands of the Ganges Elders (Zhǎngzhě).
Six times the sands of the Ganges Kings.
Seven times the sands of the Ganges Royal Consorts.
Eight times the sands of the Ganges heavenly maidens, and so forth.
Even the Buddhas and disciples in the ten directions,
and the great assembly in the six paths,
seeing the sign of Nirvāṇa,
wept and wailed sorrowfully, unable to control themselves.
In the assembly, there was also a son of a craftsman from Kuśi City (Jūshī Chéng),
named Cunda (Chúntuó).
He bowed to the Buddha along with fifteen people and said:
"We only pray, World-Honored One (Shìzūn),
and the assembly of Bhikṣus,
that you compassionately accept our final offering.
From now on, we
will be without a master, without relatives, without rescue, and without protection.
Poor, hungry, and distressed,
we wish to seek future sustenance from the Tathāgata.
We only pray that you compassionately accept our small offering,
and then enter Nirvāṇa."
The Buddha said:
"I shall now, for your sake,
eradicate and cut off poverty.
The unsurpassed Dharma rain (Fǎyǔ) shall shower upon your body-field,
causing the sprouts of Dharma (Fǎ Yá) to grow.
I shall cause you to perfect the Dāna Pāramitā (Tán Bōluómì)."
At that time, the assembly rejoiced,
and praised him in unison, saying,
"Rare indeed is Cunda!
The Buddha has accepted your offering!
You are truly a son of the Buddha!"
The Buddha said:
"Cunda,
now is exactly the time.
The Tathāgata is immediately about to enter Parinirvāṇa."
A second and a third time, he spoke in the same manner.
Cunda raised his voice and wailed,
and then addressed the great assembly,
"Let us now together
cast our five limbs upon the ground
and unanimously urge the Buddha,
'Do not enter Parinirvāṇa!'"
The Buddha instructed Cunda:
"Do not weep loudly and disturb your own mind.
I enter Nirvāṇa today
because of my deep compassion for you and all others.
Why is this?
It is the nature of all Buddhas, and conditioned things (Yǒuwéi) are likewise impermanent.
Quickly prepare the offering you wish to give;
it should not be delayed."
The Buddha again emitted five-colored lights from his face,
illuminating Cunda’s body.
Cunda, carrying the food offerings,
quickly went to the Buddha’s location.
Grieved, sorrowful, and disappointed,
he still wished the Buddha would compassionately remain alive for one Kalpa.
The Buddha said, "If you wish me to remain long,
you should now present the final perfection of Dāna Pāramitā."
All Bodhisattvas, devas, humans, and mixed beings
proclaimed in unison, though from different mouths:
"How wonderful, Cunda!
You have achieved great merit!
We lack virtue,
and the offerings we set forth have been wasted."
The World-Honored One, desiring to satisfy the hopes of all beings,
materialized countless Buddhas
from every single pore upon his body.
Each of these Buddhas had countless Bhikṣu Saṅghas (Bǐqiū Sēng),
and they all appeared and accepted the offering.
Śākyamuni Tathāgata (Shìjiā Rúlái)
himself accepted what Cunda had presented.
The prepared rice porridge offering carried by Cunda
filled eight measures (hú) of the Magadha (Mójiātuó) standard.
By the Buddha’s divine power,
the entire great assembly was fully satisfied. He then lay down on his right side as if ill,
like any other sick person.
He addressed Kāśyapa Bodhisattva (Jiāshè Púsà):
"These sentient beings,
who do not know the profound language of the Mahāyāna (Dàshèng) Vaipulya (Fāngděng) teachings,
will believe
that the Tathāgata is truly ill.
I now manifest lying on the lion couch between the twin Śāla trees, intending to enter Nirvāṇa.
This causes great sorrow and suffering among the disciples who have not yet attained Arhatship (Āluóhàn Guǒ), and the Mallas (Lìshì).
It causes the devas, humans, Asuras (Āxiūluó), and others to make great offerings.
Furthermore, I cause people
to wrap my body
place me in a coffin made of seven treasures filled with perfumed oil,
with one thousand pieces of fine cloth,
stack fragrant wood,
and burn it with fire.
However, two pieces of the cloth
cannot be burned:
one piece closest to the body,
and the second piece outermost.
For the sake of sentient beings,
the Śarīra (Shèlì) will be distributed
and divided into eight portions.
Although all Śrāvaka (Shēngwén) disciples say,
'The Tathāgata has entered Nirvāṇa,'
you should know that the Tathāgata
ultimately does not enter Nirvāṇa.
Why?
Because the Tathāgata eternally abides and does not change.
If you desire to hear the True Dharma (Zhèngfǎ),
you should abandon greed and lust,
observe and uphold my teachings,
and diligently practice the Way.
This is the final will and testament of the Buddha.
You should all exercise caution regarding it."
"You Bhikṣus,
observe the Buddha's dignified appearance.
It is difficult to see.
After a hundred million four thousand years,
the next appearance will be that of Maitreya Buddha (Mílè Fó)."
When the Buddha approached Nirvāṇa,
the great earth trembled violently.
All devas and humans were shocked and terrified.
In all dark and shadowy places,
where the light of the sun and moon
did not reach,
they all received a great illumination
and were able to see each other.
The devas scattered flowers and incense.
When the Buddha passed away (Mièdù),
the Kings of the Six Desire Heavens (Liù Yù Tiānwáng),
the deity Kumbhīra (Jīnpíluó Shén),
the Vajrapāṇi (Mìjì Lìshì),
the Buddha's mother Māyā (Fómǔ Móyé),
and the spirits of the Twin Śāla Tree Grove (Shuāngshù Suōluó Yuán Shén),
each composed verses of praise (gāthas).
The Bhikṣus mourned sorrowfully,
sighing individually, saying,
"How quickly the Tathāgata passed away!
Living beings suffer prolonged decline; the Eye of the World is extinguished."
Anuruddha (Ānàlǜ) instructed the Bhikṣus:
"Stop, stop! Do not grieve!
The devas are above.
They might take offense and blame us."
The Bhikṣus asked,
"How many devas are above?"
He replied,
"They fill the void; how can they be counted or measured?
They are all circling in the sky,
wringing their hands, wailing sorrowfully,
beating their breasts, leaping up, sighing, and saying:
'How quickly the Tathāgata passed away!
Living beings suffer prolonged decline; the Eye of the World is extinguished.'
Where is the Bhikṣu Ānanda (Ānán) now?"
"He is outside the Śāla Grove,
twelve Yojanas (Yóuxún) from here,
being disturbed and confused by sixty-four thousand billion Māras (Mó).
These Māra crowds have all transformed themselves
into the image of the Tathāgata,
speaking various Dharmas and making various manifestations."
Ānanda thought:
What was never seen before.
By whom was this made?
Perhaps it was not **Shìjiā** (Śākyamuni)?
Wishing to utter this speech,
it did not proceed from the intention (of the speaker).
**Ānán** suffered great distress.
He was unable to come.
The Buddha spoke the great **Tuóluóní** mantra.
**Wénshū** received it.
He went to **Ānán**’s place.
And recited it for the demons.
The demon kings and others roused the **Pútí** mind.
**Wénshū** immediately returned with **Ānán** to the Buddha’s residence, along with all the **Mòluó** people.
They gathered various offerings.
After another whole day, they took the Buddha’s **Shèlì**.
And placed them upon a couch.
All the **Mòluó** youths lifted the couch.
But none of them could manage it.
**Ānàlǜ** said:
“You all stop for now.
The Devās wish to keep him for seven days,
so that all people may have the opportunity to make offerings.”
The **Rúlái** three times extended a golden arm from inside the golden coffin.
He asked **Ānán**, approaching him:
“Have the roads been leveled, swept, and incense burned?”
“How is it, **Ānán**?
The teachings I have delivered, both earlier and later,
the **Fāngděng Dàchéng** texts,
have you received all of them?”
**Ānán** replied:
“Only the Buddha knows this.”
The Buddha said: “It is so.
These scriptures are now concluded.”
After seven days, the **Mòluó** youths lifted the four corners, bearing the burden.
“You may hold the banners and canopies.
Burn incense and scatter flowers.
Perform various music and guide the procession before and after.
Proceed slowly and calmly.
Enter the city's east gate.
Traverse all the streets and alleys.
Exit the city's north gate.
Cross the **Xīliánchán** River.
Arrive at **Tiānguān** Monastery.”
The **Mòluó** envoys
piled up the fragrant wood.
The fire burned, but did not ignite (the pyre).
**Ānàlǜ** said:
“The Devās intend to extinguish the fire.”
**Jiāshè**, leading five hundred disciples, was returning from **Bōbō** country.
He wished to see the Buddha’s body.
**Jiāshè** met a **Nígān**.
Who held a **Mantuóluó** flower in his hand.
He asked:
“Do you know if my teacher is still here?”
The man replied:
“He has been extinguished for seven days now.
I obtained this flower from that place.”
**Jiāshè** was displeased.
The five hundred disciples lamented bitterly and wailed,
unable to control themselves.
They sobbed and said:
“How swiftly the **Shànshì** entered **Nièpán**!”
At that time, **Bánántuó** said:
“Stop weeping for now.
We may perhaps attain liberation
through the **Móhēluó** (great Dharma).”
**Jiāshè** urged the **Bǐqiū**s:
“Quickly, take hold of your robes and bowls,
and go to the city of **Jūshī**.”
When he saw the **Shèlì**,
he asked **Ānán**:
“May I see the **Shìzūn**’s **Shèlì**?”
He replied:
“It is wrapped in cotton cloth.
Bound in white felt.
Placed inside a golden coffin.
Hidden within an iron sarcophagus.
Covered with fragrant kindling.
It is about to be burned, so it is difficult to see.”
**Jiāshè** requested three times.
The reply was the same as before.
He then went forward to the fragrant pyre.
The Buddha stepped on the heavily sealed coffin and revealed both his feet. The wheel marks beneath the feet displayed various wondrous colors.
He immediately asked **Ānán**.
**Ānán** replied:
“Women are soft-hearted.
When they came forward to worship the Buddha earlier,
their tears fell, and they touched them with their hands.”
**Jiāshè** performed the worship.
The great assembly bowed together.
They circled the trees three times.
Each person raised a verse of praise.
The fragrant pyre, which had not burned naturally anywhere else, burst into an extremely fierce blaze.
It was difficult to stop the fire.
The spirit of the **Suōluó** trees extinguished it with their power.
When the Buddha entered **Bō Nièpán**,
Lady **Móyé** was in the heavens.
The five signs of decay appeared:
First, the flowers on her head wilted.
Second, sweat poured from beneath her armpits.
Third, the light around her neck vanished.
Fourth, both her eyes frequently blinked.
Fifth, she felt unhappy in her former seat.
She also had five dreams:
First, **Xūmí** Mountain collapsed.
And the waters of the four oceans dried up.
Second, **Luóchà**s ran wildly, gouging out people's eyes.
Third, the Devās lost their jewel crowns and their bodies lacked light.
Fourth, the pearl banner poles fell, losing the **Rúyì** pearl.
Fifth, a lion bit her body, causing pain like a knife cut.
Having had these dreams, she immediately woke up startled.
“This is not auspicious.
In the past, when I was in the palace of King **Báijìng**,
during an afternoon nap,
I had a rare dream:
I saw a Heavenly Son.
His body was golden yellow.
He rode upon a white elephant king.
Followed by many Heavenly Sons.
Playing wonderful music.
He looked at the essence of the sun,
and entered my right flank.
My body and mind were peaceful and joyful.
Immediately thereafter, I became pregnant.
Prince **Xīdá** illuminated the world.
Now these five dreams are extremely terrifying.
This must be the sign of my son's **Nièpán**.”
At that time, after **Ānàlǜ** had completed the funeral rites for the Buddha,
he ascended to **Dāolì** Heaven.
And informed **Móyé** with a verse.
**Móyé** was breathless for a long time. With her relatives, she descended between the twin trees.
She saw the **Sēnggāli** (robe), the bowl, and the staff.
Grasping them, she wailed loudly.
She fainted and then revived, saying:
“My son’s merit transcended Devās and humans.
Now these objects are empty and without an owner.”
The Buddha used his spiritual power to make all the coffin lids open naturally.
The Buddha rose, joining his palms together.
He emitted a great brilliant light.
He greeted his mother, saying:
“It is a great condescension for you to come down from afar.
All compounded phenomena are naturally thus.
I pray you, do not weep.”
Although **Ānán** restrained himself,
he addressed the Buddha:
“Sentient beings in later ages will certainly ask me:
‘What did the Buddha speak of just before entering extinction?’
How shall I answer them?”
The Buddha informed **Ānán**:
“You shall reply:
‘The Buddha had already entered **Nièpán**.
When Lady **Móyé** descended,
the **Rúlái**, for the sake of later unfilial sentient beings,
emerged from the golden coffin, joined his palms in greeting,
and spoke the verses of respect mentioned above.’”
This sūtra is named: *The Sūtra of the Meeting Between Mother and Son When the Buddha Was Approaching Nièpán*.
Receive and uphold it thus.
The **Rúlái** wandered in the **Miàolè** World.
Wishing to reveal his wisdom and extensively deliver the boundless masses.
With his disciples, **Púsà**s, **Fànshì Tiānlóng** (Brahmā, Śakra, Devās, and Nāgas).
They gathered in the vihāra.
He emitted the light sound of the **Wànzì** (Svāstika).
Pure, penetrating far and wide.
The great sound of the five kinds of Dharma:
First is the sound of the **Dàchéng** that delivers people.
Second is the sound that delivers people beyond self and others.
Third is the sound that delivers people without reference to the **Yuánjué** path.
Fourth is the sound of wholesome upaya that delivers people without severing conceptual attachments.
Fifth is the sound of expounding the Dharma that delivers people, allowing them to enter birth and death while resolving their burdensome defilements.
There was a king named **Chùliú**.
With all his people,
he went to the Buddha, paid homage, and said:
“For a long time we have heard that the **Rúlái**
proclaims the Way and teaches transformation,
saving and liberating (beings) from birth and death,
without limit.
Yet we and our family members are still drifting in the cycle of birth and death.
We have not yet received liberation.
We pray, Venerable One, condescend to teach us, that we may understand the clear Dharma.”
The heavens and the earth shook, and they practiced the **Púsà** conduct.
What is called the Secret of Mind (Xīnmì)?
The four practices (Sìxíng) are pure, not losing spiritual powers (shéntōng), establishing the boundless actions of great compassion (Dà'āi).
By means of spiritual powers, transforming and manifesting everything universally.
Thereby completing the path of truth—the chamber of wisdom.
Observing all phenomena (fǎ).
This is the correct spiritual penetration (zhèngtōng) that universally governs everything.
Regarding the true Dharma (zhēnfǎ), wisdom, spirit, and wisdom-penetration all manifest the multitude of forms.
Explaining and clarifying all forms.
Explaining and clarifying all the Dharma of the Buddhas' paths.
Opening and transforming all sentient beings (zhòngshēng) in the ten directions.
Causing them to enter the Dharma laws (Fǎlǜ).
Reaching Avaivartika (Āwéiyán).
Turning (expounding) all Dharma.
These are the actions of the Bodhisattva's (Púsà's) Secret of Mind (Xīnmì). The Bodhisattva dwells in this Vajra Samādhi (Jīngāng Sānmèi).
With a single sound, something is proclaimed.
All sentient beings, each according to their type, attain understanding.
Manifesting a single form.
All sentient beings individually see various forms and appearances while remaining in one place.
The body does not move or change.
[The Bodhisattva] is able to make sentient beings see [him] individually according to their direction.
Proclaiming one Dharma,
be it sphere or entrance.
All sentient beings hear it, each according to their fundamental understanding. The Buddha (Fó), with a single sound, expounds the Dharma.
Sentient beings, following their types, each attain understanding.
All believe the World-Honored One (Shìzūn) speaks their language.
Sentient beings, individually according to what they understand,
universally receive, practice, and obtain benefit.
Some have fear and dread,
or joy,
or generate revulsion,
or cut off doubt.
This is the spiritual power (shénlì)—the non-shared Dharma and the characteristics of all phenomena.
Practicing without attachment or clinging.
Establishing the Victorious Precious Banner.
Sending forth a great sound.
If those who delight in hearing about generosity attain liberation (jiětuō),
they immediately hear the Tathāgata (Rúlái) speaking of the benefits of generosity.
Similarly, those who delight in precepts and wisdom, and so forth, are also like this.
When speaking the Mahāyāna Dharma (Dàshèng Fǎ), there is no sentient being who does not attain liberation.
The Buddha, with one word, speaks of all Dharma.
Sentient beings of the great thousand [worlds] (dàqiān zhòngshēng), using measureless sounds, simultaneously ask difficult questions.
All are distinct and different.
In a single instant of thought,
[He] answers with a single sound,
causing all to attain awakening and understanding.
In the kingdom of Suíluórán guó, there was a Póluómén Wáng (Brahmin King).
Named Āqídá.
He was intelligent and extremely wise.
He went to Ānánbǐnchǐguǎng and engaged in extensive discussion. When the talk concluded,
he asked Xūdáduō, saying,
“Is there any divine person worthy of reverence in this land?”
He replied, “There is.
Prince Xīdá Tàizǐ left home and attained Buddhahood.
His distinguishing marks and excellence are revered by devas and humans.”
Āqídá immediately ordered his carriage
and went to Qíhuán to behold the Buddha’s majestic spirit.
Respect arose spontaneously in his heart.
He immediately rose and spoke to the Buddha,
“I wish that the Buddha and the Saṅgha
would favor me by staying for the three months of the summer retreat.”
The Buddha said,
“My assembly here is vast,
and you hold different views and beliefs.”
The King said,
“I do not consider the number to be too many.”
This happened up to three times.
The Buddha and five hundred Bhikkhus accepted the invitation simultaneously
and traveled to his kingdom.
The cities and villages were impoverished and narrow, and the people were poor and lacked faith.
It was difficult to obtain alms food.
There was no Vihāra (monastery) previously.
North of the city was a forest.
The branches and leaves were lush and dense.
The ground was flat and spacious.
He stayed there temporarily with the assembly.
The Buddha instructed the Bhikkhus,
“You all should know
that this town is impoverished and narrow, the people are mostly faithless, and alms food is hard to acquire.
If you wish
to observe the retreat here, then stay;
if not, follow your own wishes.”
At that time, Shèlìfú went alone to Āmújiāmòjiā shān,
accepting the invitation of Tiāndìshì and the Asura maiden.
He was offered food of the devas as offerings.
At that time, there was a Māra (Heavenly Demon)
who confused the King’s mind,
causing him to return to the palace and indulge recklessly in the five desires:
First, precious ornaments;
second, female music;
third, clothing and food;
fourth, honor and benefit;
fifth, sexual desire.
He returned and entered the inner palace,
instructing the gatekeepers,
“Within three months, regardless of rank,
no external affairs, great or small, shall be reported.”
He forgot the offering and also did not make regular offerings.
After six full days, the offerings stopped.
The Bhikkhus found obtaining alms food extremely difficult and bitter.
Then Dàmùlián spoke to the Buddha,
“There is a tree called Yùyánfú.
I wish to retrieve its fruit to offer to the great assembly.
There are Hēlìlè Lín
and Āmólè Lín.
Yùdānyuē has naturally growing fine rice.
The food of the Dāolì Tiān has the Xiūtuó wèi (Amrita flavor).
I wish to gather all of these to offer to the great assembly.
There is also the sweet flavor of the earth.
With one hand, I could
hold all sentient beings,
and with the other hand, turn the earth over,
allowing the Bhikkhus to take and eat it themselves.
I beg that you grant permission.”
The Buddha said,
“You possess great divine powers yourself,
but the retribution for the Bhikkhus’ past evil actions is ripe and cannot be deflected.
I will not allow any of it.”
In this kingdom, there was clean water and beautiful grass.
There were people from Bōluó guó
who followed the water and grass to herd horses,
wishing them to grow fat, and they arrived at this spot.
The horsemen believed in the Buddha, and their hearts were pure.
They spoke to the Bhikkhus, saying,
“We know the Saṅgha is starving, and all the food is gone.
We only have horse fodder barley.
Can you eat it?”
The Bhikkhus spoke to the Buddha.
The Buddha said,
“The horses belong to the horsemen. If they can feed the horses good grass and salted water,
then this barley is naturally available and should be accepted.”
There were five hundred horses.
Each horse ate two *shēng* a day.
They divided half of it to give to the Bhikkhus. There was one excellent horse
that ate four *dǒu* a day.
They offered half of its portion to the Buddha. Ānán took the Buddha’s portion along with his own portion
and carried them into the settlement.
Before a certain woman,
he praised the Buddha’s merits,
saying, “Due to a small karmic connection,
the assembly is observing the retreat here.
Can you make dried rice for us?”
The woman said,
“My family has many tasks.
I cannot manage to make it.”
Another woman nearby heard this
and said to Ānán,
“Bring the barley; I will make the rice for you.
If there are other kind, wise, and observant Bhikkhus,
I will also make it for them.”
The woman immediately made the rice and gave it to Ānán.
Ānán’s reverence for the Buddha was profound, and he thought thus:
“The Buddha is of royal descent
and has always eaten fine dishes.
This coarse and foul rice cannot benefit his body.”
He offered water and presented the rice.
When he saw the Buddha eating it,
he was overcome with tears and choked up with sorrow.
The Buddha knew his intent
and wished to comfort him.
“Can you eat it?”
Ānán replied,
“I can accept it and eat it.”
The taste was extraordinary.
In truth, the devas had added flavor to it.
His joy was immeasurable, and his sorrow and choking immediately ceased.
He fully recounted the story of the two women.
The Buddha said,
“The first woman, if she had made the rice,
would have become the first principal consort of a Zhuǎnlún Wáng.
As for the woman who made it without being asked,
her merit is immeasurable.”
At that time, the powerful and noble householders of various kingdoms,
the wealthy Sàbó, and others,
heard that the Buddha had eaten horse barley for three months.
They prepared various offerings and diverse fine dishes.
Carriages and horses filled the road
as they came to offer provisions.
When only seven days remained until the Shìzūn's *Pravāraṇā* (formal ending of the retreat),
he instructed Ānán,
“Go into the city
and tell Āqídá
that the retreat is over,
and we will travel to other kingdoms.”
Ānán and one Bhikkhu
both went to the King’s residence
and fully conveyed the Buddha’s words.
The King was still oblivious.
He then asked,
“Where is the Buddha now?”
Ānán said,
“The three months of the King’s invitation have just ended; he is still in the kingdom now.”
The King then asked Ānán,
“Who provided the supply?”
Ānán said,
“The poverty was extreme.
The Buddha and the Saṅgha ate horse barley for three months.”
Only then did the King realize and feel ashamed,
saying, “How could I allow the Buddha and the Saṅgha
to eat horse barley for three months?
This bad reputation and ugly name will spread throughout all kingdoms.”
Anxious, remorseful, and distressed,
he went with his relatives
to visit the Buddha,
repenting deeply.
He further invited the Buddha to stay.
The Buddha accepted to stay for seven days while he prepared various foods.
He offered four pieces of *jiébèi* cloth
and one measure of leather sandals to the Buddha.
Two pieces of *jiébèi* cloth
and one measure of leather sandals were given to the Saṅgha. The King took these offerings
and scattered them all along the road,
wishing for the Buddha to walk over them.
The Buddha said,
“Food should be eaten.
Out of respect, it is not appropriate to step upon it.” The Buddha then accepted the offerings,
and pronounced blessings upon all.
The King’s mind was delighted, his confusion was dispelled,
and he attained the purity of the Dharma Eye.
A long, long time ago in the past,
the Buddha was named Bǐpáyè.
He was in Pántóumóbá chéng.
The King was named Pántóu.
There was a Brahmin
named Yīndíqílì.
He was broadly versed in the Four Vedas
and various calculations
and the Brahmanical precepts.
He taught five hundred youths.
The King held an assembly and invited the Buddha, offering refined and beautiful food.
Among the assembly, there was a Bhikkhu
named Mílè,
who was ill and could not walk. After the meal,
someone requested food for the sick person.
The Brahmin did not give it and cursed, saying,
“A shaven-headed Śramaṇa should only eat horse barley!
He should not eat such sweet and delicious offerings.”
At that time, his disciples said,
“Indeed!”
“Shèlìfú,
that Brahmin at the time is myself now.
The five hundred youths
are the five hundred Arhats now.
That sick Bhikkhu is Mílè now.”
*Shèwèi Chéng* there were twenty men.
They were enemies with another twenty men.
At that time, the forty men all desired to harm each other.
They sought opportunities.
Relying on the powerful majesty of the *Fó*, they immediately went to the *Fó*'s location.
The *Fó* transformed the forty men.
There appeared an iron spear that naturally came and went, penetrating the great toe of the *Fó*'s right foot.
Before the words were finished, the spear was in front of the *Fó*.
*Mùlián* reported to the *Fó*.
"I shall now pull out the iron spear and place it in a different world."
The *Fó* said.
"If you use the power of diligence to try to pull out the iron spear,
the Three Thousand Great Thousand Worlds may greatly shake,
but you cannot move the spear by so much as a hair's breadth."
The *Fó* went to *Fàntiān*.
The spear immediately followed him.
He returned to *Shèwèi Chéng*.
The spear was also in front.
The *Rúlái* took the spear and stepped on it with his foot.
*Mùlián* reported to the *Fó*.
"What offense did the *Rúlái* commit to suffer this spear calamity?"
The *Fó* said.
"In the past, five hundred merchants harbored malicious intent.
I then harmed them.
This is the remainder of that misfortune."
When the forty men heard this,
they said to each other.
"If the *Fǎwáng* is still subject to this,
how much more so for us?
How could we fail to suffer retribution?"
They repented their faults and confessed them,
and entered into Universal Wisdom.
Formerly, there were four *Póluómén*.
All had attained spiritual powers.
Their bodies could fly, and their divine feet (*shénzú*) were unimpeded.
These four *Fànzhì* said to each other.
"Those people who,
give food offerings to *Qútán Shāmén*,
will then be reborn in heaven and not leave the Hall of Blessings.
Those who hear the Dharma enter the Gate of Liberation.
Today, we desire the blessings of heaven.
We do not wish for liberation, nor do we need to hear the Dharma."
At that time, the four men each carried four jars of sweet rock honey.
One person arrived first and presented it to the *Shìzūn*.
The *Fó* informed the *Fànzhì*.
He spoke, saying that all conditioned things are impermanent.
The *Fànzhì* heard this and immediately covered his ears.
Next, the second person came, and the *Fó* spoke again.
He spoke of the rise and decline of the Dharma.
The *Fànzhì* heard this and also covered his ears.
Next, the third person came, and the *Fó* spoke again.
He spoke: "Indeed, birth immediately implies death."
The *Fànzhì* heard this and also covered his ears with his hands.
Next, the fourth person came, and the *Fó* spoke again.
He spoke: "This extinction is bliss."
The *Fànzhì* heard this and also covered his ears.
They each discarded the honey and departed.
They said to each other.
"What teaching did *Qútán Shāmén* give?"
The first replied.
"I heard one phrase: 'All conditioned things are impermanent.'"
The second, third, and fourth in sequence,
repeated what they had been told.
After these verses were spoken,
their minds opened, their thoughts understood, and they attained the *Ānàhán Dào*.
At that time, the four men,
knowing that they had each attained the fruit of the Way,
returned and earnestly reproached themselves.
They went to the *Rúlái*'s location.
They bowed their heads and faces to his feet,
and stood to one side.
They reported to the *Shìzūn*, saying.
"We only wish that the *Rúlái*,
would permit us to join the ranks of the Way and become *Shāmén*."
The *Shìzūn* declared.
"Welcome, *Bǐqiū*!
Diligently practice *Fànxíng*."
At that time, the four men,
their hair and beards automatically fell away,
the clothes they wore transformed into *Jiāshā*,
and they immediately attained the *Luóhàn Dào* in front of the *Fó*.
Formerly, there was a *Póluómén Guó*.
named *Duōwèixiàng*.
Its king served heterodox paths.
One day, the king suddenly initiated a good thought,
wishing to perform a great *Bùshī*.
following the *Póluómén Fǎ*.
He piled the seven treasures high like a mountain.
If there was someone who came to beg,
he allowed them to take for themselves,
taking a heavy handful and departing.
After several days like this,
the heap did not diminish.
The *Fó* knew this king's past merit meant he should be saved.
He manifested as a *Fànzhì* and went to that kingdom.
The king came out to meet him.
He greeted him and inquired about his well-being, saying.
"What is it you seek?
Do not hesitate."
The *Fànzhì* replied.
"I have come from afar.
I wish to beg for treasures to build a house."
The king said, "Excellent!
Take a heavy handful yourself and depart."
The *Fànzhì* took a handful and walked seven steps.
He returned and put it back in the original place.
The king asked, "Why?"
The *Fànzhì* replied.
"This is only enough to build a house.
I will also need to marry a wife.
I fear it won't be enough to use.
Therefore, I did not take it."
The king said.
"Take three more handfuls."
The *Fànzhì* immediately took them.
He walked seven steps and again returned it to the original place.
The king asked, "Why is that?"
He replied.
"This is enough to take a wife,
but I have no fields, land, slaves, maidservants, oxen, or horses.
Therefore, I ceased my intention."
The king said.
"Take seven more handfuls."
The *Fànzhì* immediately took them.
He walked seven steps and again returned it to the original place.
The king said.
"For what other reason?"
The *Fànzhì* replied.
"If I have sons and daughters, they will need to be married off.
The expenses for auspicious and inauspicious events, when calculated, would not be sufficient.
Therefore, I did not take it."
The king said.
"I shall give you all the accumulated treasures."
The *Fànzhì* accepted it, then abandoned it and left.
The king was greatly astonished.
He repeatedly asked the reason for his intention.
The *Fànzhì* replied.
"Originally, I came to beg for sustenance to live.
Reflecting deeply, human life in this world is fleeting.
The myriad things are impermanent, and the morning and evening are hard to secure.
Causal conditions become heavy, and worry and suffering deepen daily.
Piling up treasures like a mountain offers no benefit to oneself.
Schemes motivated by craving and desire are merely wasted effort and pain.
It is better to cease such intentions and seek the Way of Non-Action (*Wúwéi Dào*).
Therefore, I did not take it."
The king's mind opened and understood, and he submitted to the teaching.
Thereupon, the *Fànzhì* revealed the form of the *Fó*'s light.
He leaped and stood in the air,
and spoke the verse, saying.
"Though one may accumulate treasures piled high, reaching up to the heavens,
filling the world in this manner, it is inferior to seeing the traces of the Way.
Evil appears like goodness; attachment seems like non-attachment.
The image of taking suffering as pleasure is rejected by the wise."
When the king saw the *Fó*'s light,
and also heard this verse,
the king and his ministers,
immediately accepted the Five Precepts,
and attained the *Xūtuóhuán Dào*.
In South Tiānzhú there was a great city.
Its name was Shǒubōluó.
In the city there was an elder
whose name was Lú Zhì.
He served as the guide and leader for the populace.
He had already planted various good roots
in the presence of countless Buddhas
However, all the common people
in that great city believed in and submitted to heterodox paths, serving the Nígàn.
At that time, desiring to save that elder,
I traveled from Wángshě Chéng to that city.
When the Nígàn heard I intended to arrive at that city,
he immediately formed this thought:
"If the śramaṇa Qútán arrives here,
these people will abandon me and no longer provide for me."
He informed the people of that city,
"The śramaṇa Qútán now intends to come here.
However, that śramaṇa
abandoned his parents, racing around the east and west.
Wherever he goes, he causes the land to fail to yield the five grains.
The people suffer famine, and deaths are numerous, bringing absolutely no peace or happiness."
When those people heard this, they immediately harbored fear.
They reported,
"Great Master,
what plan should be made?"
The Nígàn replied,
"The śramaṇa Qútán
naturally loves groves, forests, flowing springs, and clear water.
If there are any such places outside the city, they should be destroyed.
You should go out of the city together and fell the trees and forests.
Do not leave any remaining flowing springs, wells, or ponds.
Fill them with filth and stench.
Securely close the city gates.
Each of you should prepare weapons
and guard along the walls,
diligently defending yourselves strongly.
If he comes,
do not let him advance.
We will also employ various magical arts
to make that Qútán return the way he came."
Those people respectfully followed and carried out the instructions.
At that time,
I arrived at that city.
Having seen these events,
I immediately gave rise to compassion.
Directing my kind heart toward them,
all the trees and woods grew back exactly as they were before, beyond calculation.
The water in the rivers, ponds, and wells was pure and clean, filling them completely,
like blue lapis lazuli.
Various mixed flowers grew, covering the surface.
I transformed the city walls into deep blue lapis lazuli.
The people inside the city could clearly see me and the great assembly.
The gates opened themselves, and no one could stop them.
The prepared weapons turned into mixed flowers.
The elder Lú Zhì served as the leader.
He, together with his people,
came accompanying one another
to my location. I immediately preached various essential doctrines to them,
causing all those people to arouse the resolve for Anuttarā Samyak Sambodhi.
Formerly, in the kingdom of Bōluónài,
there was a mountain forty or fifty *lǐ* away from the city.
There were five śramaṇas
residing on the mountain studying the Way.
In the early morning they left the mountain to beg for food among men.
After eating, they returned to the mountain, only arriving late in the evening.
The back-and-forth travel exhausted them, making them unable to practice sitting meditation.
Contemplating the proper samādhi, they spent years doing this,
yet they could not attain the Way.
The Buddha had compassion for them,
seeing their effort yielded nothing.
He transformed himself into a dào rén and went
to their location.
He asked the various dào rén,
"Are you not weary from cultivating the Way in seclusion?"
The śramaṇas replied,
"We are here.
We are far from the city.
The body, composed of the Four Great Elements, requires rice and food.
Traveling back and forth daily,
we are exhausted year after year
and cannot cultivate the Way.
Should we simply continue like this until the end of our lives?"
The dào rén said,
"One who pursues the Way takes precepts as the foundation
and collecting the mind as the practice.
One holds the form as base and the true [nature] as precious, letting the body decay
and abandoning this life.
Food is merely to sustain the form.
Guard the intention and maintain proper samādhi.
Internally study cessation and contemplation.
Extinguish intentions and attain the Way.
If you nurture the body
and follow your emotions, how can you be freed from suffering?
I urge you dào rén,
do not travel tomorrow.
I shall make an offering to you."
The dào rén rested for one day.
At that time, the five śramaṇas were greatly delighted in spirit.
They marveled at this unprecedented event.
They settled their minds and fixed their intentions,
no longer worrying about traveling.
The next day at noon, this transformed dào rén delivered food.
After they finished eating, their minds felt peaceful, harmonious, and tranquil.
Then the transformed dào rén preached gāthas to them and manifested the form of the Buddha's body, features, and light.
The spirits of these five śramaṇas shook with awe.
All contemplated the precepts
and immediately attained the path of Arhatship.
In the kingdom of Shèwèi,
there was a poor family. The husband and wife were greedy and stingy, having no faith in virtue or the Way.
The Buddha pitied their ignorance and appeared as a śramaṇa.
He approached their door to beg for food.
The husband was absent at the time.
The wife cursed him
without reason.
The śramaṇa said,
"I am a man of the Way.
I support myself by begging.
I do not mind the abuse.
I only hope for one meal."
The wife said,
"Even if you died standing right now,
food would still be impossible to get,
let alone now that you are healthy and strong and desire my food.
You are just wasting time; you had better leave soon."
Thereupon, the śramaṇa
stood before her,
widened his eyes, and gasped for breath,
and then appeared to drop dead standing upright.
His body swelled up, and worms emerged from his nose and mouth.
His belly burst, his intestines decayed, and foulness flowed out.
The wife saw this, was terrified, screamed, and ran away.
Thereupon, the dào rén
suddenly departed.
A few *lǐ* away from the house,
he sat under a tree to rest.
Her husband returned home.
On the road, he saw his wife,
and wondered at her terror.
His wife told her husband,
fully recounting the matter.
The husband became greatly enraged
and asked where the śramaṇa was.
The wife said,
"He has already gone,
but I imagine he is not far."
The husband immediately seized his bow, wore his sword, followed the tracks, and chased after him.
He drew his bow, drew his sword, ran straight ahead,
intending to chop the dào rén.
The dào rén immediately transformed a small city of lapis lazuli,
surrounding himself with it. The man circled it several times but could not enter.
He immediately asked the dào rén,
"Why don't you open the gate?"
The dào rén said,
"If you want the gate to open, throw away your bow and sword."
That man thought to himself,
"I should follow his words.
If I can get in, I will twist my hand and attack him anyway."
He immediately threw away his bow and sword.
Yet the gate did not open.
He spoke to the dào rén again,
"I have already thrown away the bow and sword.
Why does the gate not open?"
The dào rén again said,
"I told you to throw away the bow and sword of malicious intent in your heart,
not the bow and sword in your hand."
Thereupon, the man
was startled in his mind and trembled in his body.
"The dào rén is divine and sagely.
He actually knows my heart!"
He immediately kowtowed, repented his faults, and blamed himself.
He addressed the dào rén, saying,
"I have a wretched wife who does not recognize the True Man,
causing me to conceive evil intent.
I ask you to show a little compassion,
and do not forsake me yet.
I now wish to bring her here and persuade her to cultivate the Way."
He immediately rose and returned home.
His wife asked,
"Where is the śramaṇa?"
Her husband fully described the virtue of the divine transformation.
"He is now over there.
You should go yourself
to reform, repent, and extinguish your offenses."
Thereupon, the husband and wife went to the location of the dào rén.
They repented their faults with their five limbs touching the ground
and requested to become his disciples.
They then asked about the city of lapis lazuli:
"It is firm and strong, beyond comparison.
The intent is luminous,
the mind is stable, and there are no worries or calamities forever.
What virtue attains this divine marvel?"
The dào rén replied,
"I study broadly without satiety,
follow the Dharma without slackening,
diligently uphold the precepts,
and my mind is not reckless.
Due to this, I attained the Way
and naturally reached Nirvāṇa."
Formerly there were five hundred Brāhmaṇas (Bóluómén).
They constantly sought an opportunity concerning the Buddha (Fó),
desiring to slander him.
They consulted among themselves, saying:
We should instruct a butcher (tú'ér) who slaughters life
to invite the Buddha and all the monastics (zhòngsēng).
The Buddha will certainly accept the invitation
and praise the butcher.
We can then come forward together and mock him.
The Buddha immediately accepted the invitation
and told the butcher:
When the fruit ripens, it falls naturally.
When merit (fú) ripens, it saves naturally (dù).
The butcher returned home and prepared food and drink offerings.
The Buddha led his disciples (dìzǐ) to the butcher's village.
He arrived at the house of the donor (tán'yuè).
The Brāhmaṇas (Fànzhì), old and young, were all joyful together.
Today we have finally gained an opportunity against the Buddha!
If he praises his merit (fú),
we will use his former and subsequent crimes of slaughtering life
to mock him with.
If he speaks of his accumulated past crimes,
we will use today's merit to challenge him.
Amongst these two scenarios, we now have an advantage.
The Buddha arrived and immediately sat down.
Water was poured and food was served.
Thereupon the World-Honored One (Shìzūn),
observed the minds of the assembly,
[knowing] that there were those who ought to be saved (dù).
He immediately put out his tongue, covering his face and licking his ears.
He emitted a great bright light, illuminating the entire city.
He immediately spoke verses (jì) of blessing (zhùyuàn) in a pure, clear voice (Fànshēng):
Just as a true person (zhēnrén) teaches the Way (dào) to nurture life, the ignorant are jealous of it;
They see it and commit evil, practicing evil, obtaining evil, just like planting bitter seeds;
The evil one receives his own sin, the good one receives his own fortune, each must ripen
and they do not substitute for each other. Practicing goodness obtains goodness, also like planting sweet [seeds].
The five hundred Brāhmaṇas opened their hearts and attained understanding.
They immediately came forward to bow to the Buddha,
prostrating their five limbs (wǔtǐ tóu dì).
They sought to reach the sacred teachings (shèngxùn).
We only wish for your compassionate nurture so that we may become Śramaṇas (Shāmén).
The Buddha immediately consented
and they all became Śramaṇas.
The villagers, old and young,
saw the Buddha's transformations.
None were without joy,
and they all attained the traces of the Way (dàojì).
[The village] was called Xiánlǐ (Village of Worthies).
There was no longer the name of "butcher."
Southeast of Śrāvastī (Shèwèi) there was a great river.
It was both deep and wide.
Over five hundred households lived along the bank.
They had not yet heard the practices of the Way and Virtue (Dàodé) for crossing the world (dù shì).
They habitually focused on being stubborn, coercive, deceitful, and fraudulent.
They indulged in greed for profit, pleasing their minds and satisfying their desires.
The Buddha knew that the merit of these households indicated they should be saved.
He went to the water's edge
and sat beneath a tree.
The villagers saw the Buddha's light (guāngmíng), which was marvelous and extraordinary.
None failed to be astonished and reverent; they all went to pay homage.
Some bowed, some greeted, and they inquired about his well-being (qǐjū).
The Buddha commanded them to sit and preached the sūtra teachings (jīngfǎ) for them.
When the crowd heard this, their minds were still unbelieving.
The Buddha manifested a person (huàrén),
who came from the south bank of the river.
His feet walked upon the water,
only submerging his ankles.
He came before the Buddha, bowed his head to the ground, and paid homage to the Buddha.
When the crowd saw this, none failed to be startled and amazed.
They asked the manifested person:
Our ancestors have lived by this river since old times.
We have never heard of anyone walking on the water.
Who are you, sir?
What kind of magical technique (dàoshù) do you possess that allows you to walk on water without sinking?
The manifested person replied:
I am a simple, honest person from the south of the river.
I heard that the Buddha was here.
I longed for the Way and Virtue (Dàodé).
I arrived at the south bank.
I could not cross immediately.
I asked a person on the opposite bank,
"How deep was the water?"
That person told me,
"The water is only ankle-deep."
I believed his words
and thus crossed over.
I possess no other marvelous technique.
The Buddha praised him, saying, "Excellent!"
Indeed, holding firmly to sincere faith (xìnchéng) allows one to cross the abyss of samsara (shēngsǐ).
A river of a few leagues, why is that remarkable?
When the villagers heard this,
their minds were enlightened and their faith (xìn) became firm.
They all accepted the Five Precepts (Wǔjiè)
and became pure lay believers (qīngxìnshì).
At that time, Shèwèi and Píshèlǐ.
The two kingdoms held grudges
and mutually plundered and attacked each other.
The king of Shèwèi Guó conceived this thought:
"I am the king;
I should repel the enemy and bring peace to the people.
How can I allow thieves to rob and plunder property and persons?"
He immediately ordered his generals and soldiers,
"I rely on you to pursue and capture them.
You must ensure they are seized."
At that time, the Bǐqiū of Shèwèi had completed their summer retreat (Anjū)
and wished to proceed to Píshèlǐ.
The Bǐqiū lost the way
and fell among those thieves.
Then the thieves asked the Bǐqiū,
"Elders, where are you going?"
They replied,
"We are heading toward Píshèlǐ."
The Bǐqiū then said,
"We should travel together as companions."
They immediately replied,
"We are thieves.
We pass through thickets and brambles,
and do not choose our paths when traveling.
You are good people;
why would you follow us?"
The Bǐqiū insisted again,
"Please take me along."
Before the words were finished,
the pursuers immediately arrived.
They seized the Bǐqiū along with the group
and brought them to the king's residence, saying,
"These are the bandits."
The king said,
"First, bring the Bǐqiū forward."
The king said,
"You are renouncers of the home life;
why are you acting as thieves?"
They replied,
"We are not thieves."
"Then why were you accompanying them?"
The Bǐqiū fully informed the king of the preceding events.
The king ordered them to be released.
The king asked the thieves,
"Are these renouncers your companions?"
They replied,
"They are companions."
The king said,
"Take the thieves away and summon the Bǐqiū again."
The king asked,
"Bǐqiū, you are lying and deceiving the officials.
The thieves said you are their companions;
why do you say you are not?"
The Bǐqiū replied as they had initially.
The king then ordered the release of the Bǐqiū and that the thieves be punished according to the law.
They seized five hundred thieves,
placed Jiāpíluó flower garlands on them,
beat drums, and paraded them publicly,
intending to lead them out for execution.
The thieves cried and wailed loudly.
The Buddha (Fó), knowing the situation, deliberately asked,
"What is the sound of many people?"
The Bǐqiū replied,
"World-Honored One (Shìzūn),
these are five hundred thieves
who have been ordered by the king to be executed.
That is their sound."
The Buddha instructed Ānán,
"Go and tell the king:
'You are the king of men.
You ought to treat the people with compassion as if they were your children.
Why are you killing five hundred men at once?'"
Ānán received the instruction
and immediately proceeded to the king’s residence.
He fully recounted the Buddha’s words.
The king said,
"Venerable One,
I understand this matter.
The offense of killing one person is great,
let alone five hundred.
However, they frequently destroy villages
and plunder the people.
If the World-Honored One can ensure they will never act as thieves again,
they may be released and allowed to live."
Ānán returned and fully reported this to the Buddha.
The Buddha told Ānán,
"Tell the king merely to release them.
I will ensure that these men will never act as thieves again from this day forward."
Ānán received the instruction
and first went to the execution grounds.
He told the execution supervisor,
"These criminals
have been saved by the World-Honored One.
You must not kill them immediately."
He then went back to the king's residence
and conveyed the World-Honored One’s message to the king:
He is able to ensure that these men will never act as thieves again.
The king immediately pardoned their lives,
but without yet untying their bonds,
he sent them to the World-Honored One (Shìzūn).
At that time, the World-Honored One,
wishing to save these people,
sat in an open area.
When the thieves saw the Buddha from afar,
their bonds spontaneously loosened.
They bowed their heads to His feet
and stood back to one side.
The Buddha observed their capacity
and spoke the Dharma accordingly:
the retributions of generosity (bùshī), upholding the precepts (chíjiè), and karmic actions;
and the Four Noble Truths (Sì Zhēndì Fǎ)—Suffering, Cause, Cessation, and the Path.
Immediately at that moment,
they attained the Stream-Enterer stage (Xūtuóhuán Dào).
The Buddha asked them,
"Do you wish to leave the home life?"
They replied,
"World-Honored One,
if we had renounced the home life earlier, we would not have encountered this suffering.
We earnestly request that you now guide us to leave the home life."
The Buddha said,
"Welcome, Bǐqiū."
At that moment, the clothes covering the entire bodies of the five hundred thieves transformed into the three monastic robes (Sānyī).
They naturally possessed alms bowls and their demeanor became dignified and composed,
resembling Bǐqiū who had been ordained for a hundred years.
They all achieved Arhatship (Āluóhàn).
In the Kingdom of Jiāosàluó Guó,
there were five hundred thieves.
King Bōsīní Wáng
was troubled by their rampant violence
and sent soldiers to seek them out and capture them.
Having caught them, he gouged out their eyes
and chased them away to live beneath dark, dense thickets.
These bandits
had already planted many roots of virtue under previous Buddhas.
Having lost their eyes, they endured great suffering and distress.
Each of them spoke this phrase:
"Námó Fótuó (Homage to the Buddha)."
At that time, I was residing in the Qíhuán Jīngshè.
Hearing their voices,
I immediately generated a heart of compassion.
Then a cool wind arose,
blowing various fragrant medicinal herbs from the Fragrant Mountain,
filling their eye sockets.
Immediately, they recovered their eyes, exactly as they were originally.
The thieves opened their eyes and immediately saw the Tathāgata (Rúlái)
standing before them, speaking the Dharma for their benefit.
After the thieves heard the Dharma,
they awakened the aspiration for Supreme Perfect Enlightenment (Ānòuduōluó Sānmiǎo Sānpútí Xīn).
In Píshèlǐ Guó,
there was a Brahmin (Póluómén)
who adhered to wrong views.
He had no sons
and worried that if he suddenly died,
his wealth would be confiscated by the government.
He offered sacrifices to all the mountains
and various tree spirits.
He realized his wife was pregnant.
When the months were completed, she gave birth to a son.
The child was handsome and correct in appearance.
The parents loved and cherished him.
When he reached the age of twelve,
he went outside to stroll and view the sights.
On the road, he encountered a drunken elephant,
which immediately trampled him to death.
The parents were heartbroken and distressed,
and their minds became wild and deranged.
They ran about naked.
The Tathāgata thought of them compassionately
and magically manifested as their son.
The parents rushed forward and embraced him,
experiencing boundless joy.
Their madness and derangement immediately ceased.
They recovered their original minds.
The Buddha spoke the Dharma for them,
and they immediately awakened the mind for the Path (Dào Xīn).
The Buddha told Ānán.
In the past, during my summer retreat (vārṣika),
in the kingdom of Bōluónài,
there was a courtesan,
whose name was Miàoyì,
who had a connection (karma) with the Buddha.
The Buddha, along with Nántuó,
went to the courtesan’s residence.
They begged for food daily.
This woman had never shown me respect,
but toward Nántuó, she particularly developed attachment and desire.
Seven days had passed.
The woman thought in her heart, saying:
"If Śamāṇa Qútán
could send away Nántuó and Ānán,
and grant my wish,
I would offer various kinds of offerings."
The Buddha told Ānán and Nántuó,
"From today onward, do not go to that village."
The World-Honored One went alone to the woman's mansion.
From the first day to the third day,
he emitted a golden radiance,
converting all the devas and humans.
This woman did not awaken.
On a later day, the World-Honored One,
again took Ānán and Nántuó
and walked beneath a tree.
Because the courtesan loved and respected the two Bhikṣus,
she scattered various flowers from afar upon the Buddha and the two Bhikṣus.
Ānán addressed her, saying,
"You should pay homage to the Buddha."
The woman loved Ānán,
and immediately paid her respects.
The Buddha magically manifested three youths,
all fifteen years of age,
with handsome faces.
The woman saw them and was delighted.
In order to transform the young man,
she prostrated herself on the ground in reverence.
She spoke to the young man, saying,
"Noble Sir, my residence is now like the palace of Gōngdé Tiān.
It is rich and powerful, entirely unrestricted,
adorned with various treasures.
I now dedicate my body and my servants
to serve you, noble sir.
They can be used for sweeping and cleaning.
If you can look upon me favorably and accept me,
I will follow your every wish.
All provisions will be supplied without reservation."
The manifested person sat on the couch.
Before the time for a meal had passed,
the woman approached him intimately and said,
"I wish you would fulfill my desire."
The manifested person did not refuse.
For one day and one night, her heart felt no exhaustion or disgust.
By the second day, her loving passion gradually subsided.
By the third day,
she said,
"Noble sir, please rise and take food."
The manifested person immediately rose.
They continued their close entanglement without cessation.
The woman developed revulsion and regret.
She said,
"Noble sir, you are truly different from other people!"
The manifested person replied,
"According to the custom of my ancestors,
whenever we consort with a woman,
we only rest after twelve days."
When the woman heard this,
it was like a person choking on food;
she could neither spit it out,
nor swallow it.
Her body ached painfully,
as if she were being pounded by a pestle.
By the fourth day,
it was as if she were being crushed by a carriage.
By the fifth day,
it was as if iron balls had entered her body.
By the sixth day,
all her limbs ached,
as if an arrow had pierced her heart.
The woman thought, saying,
"I heard that the Prince Jìngfàn
constantly rescues and assists suffering people.
Why does he not come to save me today?"
Having formed this thought,
she felt regret and reproached herself:
"From today until the end of my life,
I shall not covet sensual desires.
I would rather be in the same room
with tigers, wolves, lions, and fierce beasts,
than endure this suffering."
Having spoken these words,
she again arose for food and drink.
Whether walking or sitting, they were always together, and she could do nothing about it.
The manifested person also became angry, spat, and said,
"Wicked, vile woman!
You have ruined my affairs!
Now that I am together with you,
our bodies joined in one place,
it would be better to die quickly.
If my parents and relatives
come looking for me,
where shall I hide myself?
I would rather hang myself and die,
unable to bear this shame."
The woman said,
"Vile creature, I do not want you!
If you wish to die, do as you please."
The manifested person took a knife and stabbed his own neck.
Blood stained the woman's body.
He collapsed and fell to the ground.
The woman could not endure it,
nor could she escape death (i.e., being stained by the corpse).
After two days, the body became bruised, blue-black, and foul-smelling.
On the third day, it was swollen and bloated.
On the fourth day, it was putrid and festering.
Excrement and urine,
along with various vile insects,
splashed blood and pus,
smeared and coated the woman's body.
The woman was utterly disgusted and repulsed, yet she could not leave.
By the fifth day,
the skin and flesh gradually decomposed.
By the sixth day,
all the flesh had fallen away completely.
By the seventh day,
only the foul-smelling bones remained.
Like glue or lacquer,
they stuck fast to the woman's body.
The woman uttered a solemn vow,
"If all the heavenly gods,
and the immortals (Ṛṣis),
or the Prince Jìngfàn,
can relieve me of this suffering,
I will take this dwelling
and all its precious treasures
and dedicate them as alms."
While she was thinking this thought,
the Buddha, accompanied by Ānán, Nántuó, and Dìshì walking in front,
holding a jeweled censer,
burning priceless incense.
Fànwáng was following behind,
holding a great jeweled canopy.
Innumerable devas played instrumental music.
The Buddha emitted his constant light, illuminating Heaven and Earth.
All the great assembly saw the Tathāgata
approach this woman's mansion.
At that time, the woman saw the Buddha.
Shame and repentance filled her heart.
Having nowhere to hide the bones,
she took various white cloths and boundless fragrant substances
to wrap the foul-smelling bones.
The intensity of the stench remained the same;
it could not be covered or hidden.
The woman saw the World-Honored One
and immediately paid her respects to him.
Because of her shame and repentance,
her body inclined over the bones.
The foul bones suddenly appeared upon the woman's back.
The woman wept and said,
"The Tathāgata's merits, compassion, and loving-kindness are boundless.
If you can enable me to be free from this suffering,
I vow to become your disciple and never retreat in my resolve."
Due to the Buddha's spiritual power,
the foul bones disappeared.
The woman was greatly delighted.
She paid homage to the Buddha.
She said to the Buddha,
"World-Honored One,
I now dedicate everything I possess as precious offerings to the Buddha."
The Buddha bestowed a blessing and a vow for her, his sacred voice flowing smoothly.
The woman heard it and rejoiced.
At that moment, she immediately attained the path of Sūtuóhuán (Stream-Enterer).
"Good man,
when I entered the great city of Wángshě,
begging for food sequentially,
Típódádūo
instructed King Āshéshì
to immediately release the madly intoxicated elephant Hùcái,
intending it to harm me and all my disciples.
At that moment, I immediately entered the samādhi of loving-kindness (mettā).
I extended my hand and showed it to the elephant.
Immediately, from my five fingers emerged five lions.
When the elephant saw this, its heart was struck with fear.
It lost control of its urine and feces,
and threw its entire body onto the ground,
paying homage to my feet.
Good man,
at that time, there were truly no lions in my fingers.
It was solely due to the power of cultivating the wholesome roots of loving-kindness and compassion
that caused the elephant to be subdued."
Furthermore, good man.
When I desired Nirvāṇa,
and first set out,
heading towards Kūshīchéng,
there were five hundred strongmen (Lìshì)
along the road.
They were leveling, sweeping, and sprinkling (the path).
In the middle, there was a stone.
The multitude wanted to lift and move it,
but though they exerted all their strength, they could not.
I then felt compassion,
and immediately aroused a heart of loving-kindness (Cíxīn).
Those Lìshì immediately saw
that I used my big toe
to lift this great stone,
and toss it into the void.
Then, I received it with my hand,
placed it on my right palm,
and blew upon it, causing it to shatter into fine dust.
Then, I re-formed it back together,
so that the Lìshì ceased their proud and arrogant thoughts (Gōnggāoxīn).
I then briefly explained various essential doctrines (Fǎyào) to them,
causing them all to arouse the mind of Anòuduōluó Sānmiǎo Sānpútí.
After the Buddha entered Nirvāṇa,
at that time, the multitude of Móluó (Malla) from Bōbō Guó, and the multitude of Bálí (Vṛji) from Zhēluōpō Guó,
the multitude of Jūlí (Koliyas) from Luómójiā Guó,
the multitude of Brāhmaṇas (Póluómén) from Pílíutí Guó,
the multitude of Shì (Śākya) residents from Jiāluówèi Guó,
and the multitude of Líshē (Licchavi) from Píshèlǐ Guó,
and King Āshéshì (Ajātaśatru) of Mójiétí Guó, each arrayed their four divisions of troops. The king sent the Brāhmaṇa named Xiāng Xìng to speak to the Kūshī Lìshì, saying:
“The Buddha is my teacher and the one I revere.
He attained extinction (Mièdù) within your country.
Therefore, I have come from afar to request a portion of the relics (Shèlì) to return to my kingdom and erect a stūpa.
If you divide it and give it to me, I will share the treasures and wealth of my entire kingdom with you.”
The Lìshì replied:
“The World-Honored One (Shìzūn) condescended to descend upon this land and attained extinction here.
The officials and citizens of our country naturally must make offerings.
You gentlemen have labored from afar, but this cannot be granted.”
The kings consulted together, saying:
“We requested them with humble words and in harmony, but since they are unwilling to give them,
we shall not spare our bodies and lives, and must take them by force.”
The king of the Lìshì said:
“If you wish to raise arms, our strength is sufficient to counter yours.
They definitely cannot be obtained.”
The Brāhmaṇa Xiāng Xìng loudly proclaimed among the eight groups:
“The Buddha accumulated good deeds and practiced forbearance (Rěn) throughout countless kalpas.
You gentlemen should also listen to and praise forbearance.
How can you raise troops to mutually invade and seize them?
This is not an act of reverence.
Now that the relics are present, they should simply be divided into eight parts,
so that the people in every place may receive them and make offerings.
You gentlemen have all received the Buddha’s precepts and recite his teachings.
Is it right to fight over the relics and consequently harm each other?”
The Lìshì replied:
“We respectfully agree with your proposal.”
At that time, the Brāhmaṇa Yān (Doṇa)
immediately divided them into eight parts.
Then, Shìtíhuányīn (Śakra Devānām Indra) appeared in human form and spoke to the kings, saying:
“We devas (Zhūtiān) should also have a share.
If we fight using our strength, there will be winners and losers.
Please grant us a share; do not make difficulties over this.”
Then, the Dragon King Ānòudá (Anavatapta), the Dragon King Wénlín, and the Dragon King Yīnàbō spoke to the eight kings, saying:
“We also should have a share of the relics.
If you do not grant us a share, our strength is sufficient to subdue you.”
Then, Yōupōjí (Upagupta) spoke, saying:
“Gentlemen, cease this conflict. It is proper that they be divided among all.”
They were immediately divided into three parts:
one part was given to the devas,
one part was given to the Dragon Kings,
and one part belonged to the eight kings.
They smeared the inside of a jar (wèng) with honey and used the jar to measure them.
The devas, having received their share, returned to heaven and erected a stūpa of seven treasures.
The dragons, having received their share, returned to the dragon palace and also erected a precious stūpa.
King Āshéshì calculated his share along with the others, finding that they each received eighty-four thousand relics.
There remained one tooth (chǐ) of the Buddha, which no one dared to take.
Because King Āshéshì was the most sincere in his initial request for the relics, having collapsed to the ground exhausted, they jointly gave it to him.
Āshéshì rejoiced, and the sound of drums and music shook the heavens.
The Dragon King Nántóushì met him halfway and said:
“The Buddha left relics—give me one portion.”
The king said:
“That is impossible.”
The Dragon King said:
“I am Nántóushì.
I can pick up your kingdom, toss it eighty thousand *lǐ* away, and grind it into dust.”
The king was immediately frightened and gave the Buddha’s tooth to him.
The Dragon King erected a stūpa beneath Xūmí Shān (Mount Sumeru),
eighty-four thousand *lǐ* high,
a towering tower of crystal and lapis lazuli (liúlí).
When King Āshéshì died,
Āyù (Aśoka) obtained his kingdom.
At that time, a high official reported to King Āyù, saying:
“The Dragon Nántóushì previously threatened Āshéshì and snatched the Buddha’s tooth.”
When Āyù heard this,
he immediately commanded the kings of the ghosts and spirits to make iron nets and iron cages,
and place them in the water beneath Xūmí Shān, intending to capture and bind the Dragon King.
The Dragon King was greatly frightened and conspired with others, saying:
“Āyù serves the Buddha. Wait until he is soundly asleep, take his palace, and move it to the water beneath Xūmí Shān.
If I emerge from beneath the crystal stūpa and meet him, fully explaining the whole matter, his anger will surely cease.”
He then sent a dragon to hold and carry King Āyù’s palace.
When the king awoke, he did not know where he was.
He saw the crystal stūpa, eighty-four thousand *lǐ* high.
Joy and fear mixed in his heart.
The Dragon Nántóushì emerged and offered his apologies, saying:
“King Āshéshì willingly gave it to me; I did not snatch it.
Śākyarulai (Tathāgata Śākya) formerly made a pact with me, saying:
‘After my Nirvāṇa, when the kalpa is nearing its end, take all the sūtras, the Vinaya, the kāṣāya robes, and the alms bowls, and store them within this stūpa.
When MiLè (Maitreya) descends, they shall be brought out again.’”
The dragon sent the king’s palace back and placed it in its original location.
The Brāhmaṇa Yān said:
“I request the relic jar. I will return to the village of Tóunàluó and erect a Jar Stūpa (Píngtǎ).”
The Lìshì granted it to him.
Using the jar and the relics clinging to it, he jointly erected a precious stūpa.
The Brāhmaṇa lay follower Bōluóyánnà further requested:
“Give me the charcoal from the place where the Buddha was cremated.
I will return to my native land and erect a Charcoal Stūpa (Tàntǎ).”
A heterodox ascetic from Héng Guó requested the ashes from the ground to return to his kingdom and erect a stūpa.
The Lìshì granted both requests.
Furthermore, there were those who erected precious stūpas at the place of cremation (shéwéi).
The ashes, charcoal, and earth amounted to forty-nine *hú* (bushels).
Forty-nine precious stūpas were erected.
All of them were fitted with high signposts, Dhárma wheels (Fǎlún), and silk banners (zēngfān).
King Āyù arrayed his four divisions of troops,
and went to open the seven ancient stūpas and retrieve the relics, leaving only the Dragon’s Stūpa intact.
The dragon led the king into the palace and said:
“This stūpa is the object of my offerings; I pray that you leave it alone.”
The king immediately agreed.
He returned to his kingdom and manufactured eighty-four thousand precious caskets (bǎohán), distributing the relics throughout these caskets.
He also made eighty-four thousand precious vases (bǎopíng) and various banners and canopies (gài).
He entrusted them to various Yakṣas (Yèchā) to erect stūpas everywhere throughout Jambudvīpa (Yánfútí), over all the land and even in the great ocean.
He first consulted the Arhat (Luóhàn) Yéshè, saying:
“I wish to erect eighty-four thousand stūpas simultaneously, completed in a single day and a single thought-moment (yīniàn).”
The Arhat Yéshè greatly praised him.
Later, the king compared his merit (gōngdé) with that of the Dragon King.
They weighed two images.
The Dragon’s image was heavier, and the King’s was lighter.
The King extensively invited the community of monks (Zhòngsēng) and tirelessly cultivated merit.
Later, they weighed them again.
The weights were equal and balanced.
The King then resumed his practice.
Knowing that his merit was increasing daily,
he raised troops to go and subdue the Dragon King.
As soon as he reached the halfway point,
all the dragons, great and small, came forth to respectfully greet him.
They reverently presented the relics of the remaining stūpa to the King.

Afterward, he observed the places where the Buddha attained enlightenment and converted people, and consequently built stūpas. Within the king’s territory, there were one thousand two hundred monasteries (sì).
He also commissioned one thousand two hundred banners woven with gold threads.
He also prepared a thousand-petaled golden flower, intending to hang and scatter them himself.
Just as he finished preparations, he was struck by a severe illness.
Fearing that he would violate his original vow, he wept sorrowfully.
A Śramaṇa (Shāmén) said to the king:
“The merit you have cultivated is countless.
You should simply be open-minded; why weep?
Just keep your mind focused.
I will enable the King to fulfill his wish.”
The Shāmén immediately used his spiritual power (Shénlì) to make all one thousand two hundred monasteries appear before the king.
The suffering from his illness immediately vanished.
When he wished to hang the various banners,
all the finials (chà, stūpa spires) bowed down to meet the king’s hand.
He thus accomplished his original vow.
His lifespan was extended by twenty-five years, and he further cultivated merit for twenty years.
When approaching the end of his life,
he continuously contemplated the Three Jewels (Sānbǎo), his mind never ceasing its focus.
Having nothing to regret or begrudge, he ultimately attained Bodhi (Pútí).
Ānán (Ānanda) said to the Buddha:
“What previous cause did he create
to be able to divide your relics (fēnshēn shèlì) and erect eighty-four thousand precious stūpas?”
The Buddha said:
“In the past, there was a king named Bōsāiqí (Prasenajit), who governed eighty-four thousand kingdoms in Yánfútí.
At that time, there was a Buddha named Fúshā (Puṣya).
The king, along with his ministers and people, made offerings to the Buddha and the Bhikṣu Saṅgha (Bǐqiūsēng).
The king then reflected:
‘The small kingdoms on the remote frontiers are secluded, and the people there have no means to cultivate blessings (xiūfú).’
He immediately summoned painters to draw images of the Buddha,
and distributed them to distant countries so that all might make offerings.
At that time, the painters observed the Buddha’s physical marks (xiànghǎo),
but as soon as they grasped one feature, they forgot the rest and could not complete the image.
Then King Bōsāiqí
mixed the various pigments and painted the image himself, setting the standard (mókǎi).
The masters copied and learned, painting eighty-four thousand images,
and distributing them to eighty-four thousand small kingdoms.
The kings of the various small kingdoms all received them and made offerings.
King Bōsāiqí is now me.
Due to this merit, I possess the thirty-two physical marks (Sānshí’èr Xiàng).
And after Nirvāṇa, I again received eighty-four thousand stūpas.”
King Āyù passed away.
All the ministers wished to enthrone the Crown Prince to succeed to the royal position.
There was one chief minister,
named Ātúluódì,
who said:
“Great King Āyù
vowed to donate a full ten myriad-myriads of gold
to perform various meritorious deeds,
but still lacked four hundred million.
The Crown Prince sealed it away and did not give it.
The King donated the land of Yánfútí
as alms to the Buddha, the Dharma, and the Sangha,
desiring to fulfill [his vow] therewith.
Today, the Great Earth entirely belongs to the Sānbǎo.
How then can we allow the Crown Prince to become king?”
All the ministers immediately prepared the four hundred million gold pieces and sent them to the monastery, and only then did they jointly enthrone him.
This one was known as the king of the fourth generation,
named Fúshāmìduōluó.
He asked all the ministers, saying,
“What deeds should I perform
so that my name and deeds endure for a long time?”
A minister reported, saying, “O King,
the former King Āyù
constructed eighty-four thousand stupas of the Rúlái,
and furthermore promoted various offerings.
His fame and virtue have been handed down without interruption.”
The King said,
“The former king possessed great prestige and virtue
and was able to accomplish this matter.
I cannot do it.
Think of some other matter.”
One minister said,
“There are two types of methods
by which a name is passed down and not extinguished:
First, performing good deeds;
Second, performing evil deeds.
The former king built stupas;
the current king should destroy stupas.
Both will be immortal.”
The King then followed this advice.
He immediately raised the four divisions of the army and went toward the monastery dwellings.
He first arrived before the central gate of the Jīquè Sì.
There was a stone lion,
which immediately made a lion's roar.
The King heard it and was terrified,
and returned into the city.
This happened repeatedly.
He called for all the Bǐqiū and asked them, saying,
“Is it better for me to destroy stupas or destroy dwellings?”
The Bǐqiū replied,
“Neither should be done.
If it absolutely cannot be avoided, it is better to destroy the Sangha dwellings than to destroy the stupas.”
The King immediately murdered the Bǐqiū
and destroyed the stupas and monasteries.
He arrived at Pógāluó Guó,
and further announced loudly,
“If anyone obtains the head of a Shāmén, they shall be rewarded with a thousand gold pieces.”
In this country, there was one Luóhàn,
who miraculously transformed many Bǐqiū heads
and passed them to the common people to take and request the gold.
The gold and treasures in the King’s treasury were exhausted.
Afterward, knowing it was the work of the Luóhàn, his anger increased twofold.
The Luóhàn entered the Mièjìn Dìng.
The King went to kill him but ultimately could not succeed,
because of the power of the Mièjìn Dìng, his body could not be harmed.
Thus, he gradually advanced to the tooth relic stupa by the stupa gate.
The spirit said,
“A Chóngxíng Shén
previously sought my daughter.
I did not give her to him. Now, for the sake of Hù Fǎ, I immediately called my daughter and gave her to him.
They jointly established a vow, saying,
‘You must subdue this king and not let him destroy the Zhèng Fǎ.’”
At that time, the Chóngxíng Shén went into the southern sea, pushed aside a great mountain, and pressed it down upon the king and the four divisions of the army.
None failed to die completely.
The multitude exclaimed,
“Excellent! Excellent!
The descendants of the Kǒngquè (Peacock) are here permanently eliminated.”
Móxǐnduō and the other Bhikṣus,
having received [the hospitality of] the King of Sīzǐ Guó, whose name was Tiān'àidìxū,
and having completed the three months of summer *sìshì* offerings,
took leave of the King, saying:
"Previously, we relied upon the presence of our teacher.
Morning and evening, we served him,
made offerings, and bowed in reverence.
Since we have been separated for a long time,
we now wish to return."
The King said:
"Relying on the Fǎshī,
I have received refuge and precepts.
What is unsatisfactory about the *sìshì gōngyǎng*?
You previously said
the Buddha had already entered Nièpán.
Now you say
you wish to return to inquire after him."
The Bhikṣus said:
