"The Buddha has entered *bōnièpán*,
but the Shèlì are still present."
The King said:
"Venerable Great Virtues,
please designate a good site and measure it out, so that I may raise a Tǎ."
Immediately, he went to the novice *Shāmí* Xiūmónà
and asked:
"How can I obtain the Tathāgata's Shèlì?"
The novice replied:
"Only cleanse and prepare the roads, burn incense, and scatter flowers."
The King, along with his retinue, all received the Eight Precepts.
He departed from the Nuójī Yuánlín.
He always committed himself [to the task].
The King immediately prepared the necessary provisions.
Xiūmónà returned and informed his grandfather, fully relaying the previous events,
that the King desired to erect a Tǎ.
"We request the gift of Shèlì."
Āyù said: "You may go to the Tāolì Heaven Palace and inform Dìshì.
Dìshì possesses two relics.
One is the right tooth, kept by Dìshì for offerings.
The second is the missing right collarbone relic—he will certainly give it to you."
He opened the casket, took the relics, and placed them in a Bō.
The bowl was filled with white light, like pearls, and he handed it to the novice.
The novice then went to Dìshì's palace to request the missing right collarbone relic.
Dìshì said:
"Excellent!"
He opened the casket and gave it to him.
The novice gave the King the Shèlì provided by his grandfather.
The King thought:
"I ought to carry the Tathāgata's Shèlì upon my head."
Before he had finished this thought,
the elephant immediately knelt down.
The white parasol lowered itself.
The casket immediately rose to the King's head.
The King's whole body felt tranquil and joyful, as if he had received sweet dew.
A fine rain fell, and the great earth shook.
The King asked the Great Virtue:
"Where should I place [the relic] now?"
He replied:
"Place it down upon the elephant's head."
The elephant uttered a sound, offering reverence to the Shèlì.
Devas, Dragons, and Guǐshén were all greatly delighted.
Immediately entering the city, the people made offerings.
They exited the Southern Gate and encircled the area intended for the Tǎ.
The relics of the three previous Buddhas were also in this Tǎ garden.
They immediately chopped down the thorns and weeds and first erected the Tǎ's foundation.
[The foundation was] equal in height to the elephant's head.
The King said to the Great Virtue:
"What should the shape of the Tǎ be?"
Móxǐnduō replied:
"Like a heap of rice grain."
The King said:
"Excellent!"
He immediately built a small Tǎ and wished to deposit the Shèlì.
All the people of the entire country gathered.
The Shèlì ascended from the elephant's head into the void.
It rose as high as seven Tāluó trees and displayed various spiritual transformations.
[It shone with] five colors—black (dark) and yellow.
Sometimes it emitted water.
Sometimes it emitted fire.
Then, they took the Shèlì and placed it within the Tǎ.
Heaven and earth shook.
The Great King's queen,
whose name was Ātúluóqiú,
sought to leave home following Móxǐnduō.
Móxǐnduō said:
"I am not permitted to ordain women.
My younger sister is named Sēngjiāmìduō.
She is in the country of Bōzhālìfú Guó.
The King should go and welcome her, along with the Pútí Shù."
The King dispatched his nephew, named Ābiāochā.
Móxǐnduō used his supernatural powers to make him board a boat and arrive [at Bōzhālìfú] in one day.
He reported to King Āyù, saying:
"Móxǐnduō sent me here to fully relate the purpose described above."
The King said:
"My son, Móxǐnduō,
and my grandson, Xiūmónà,
since their departure, I have worried about them and felt unhappy in my heart.
Day and night I have been troubled, as if my hands and feet had been severed.
Now, seeing this Bhikṣuṇī, I gain relief in my heart.
If she leaves again, I will surely die!"
He told the Bhikṣuṇī not to go.
The Bhikṣuṇī reported to the King, saying:
"The intention [to go] is difficult to contravene.
The Kṣatriya noblewomen are waiting to leave home (be ordained)."
The King granted [the request for] the Pútí Shù, but it could not be separated using knives or axes.
Mùjiànliánzǐ Dìxū said:
"When the Tathāgata was alive, he already gave five special instructions.
First, King Āyù shall take the Pútí Shù and give it to Sīzǐ Guó without using knives or axes.
The southern branch shall cut itself off and enter a golden bowl.
Second, it shall ascend into the void, floating above the clouds.
Third, after seven days, it shall descend by itself back into the golden bowl.
Its leaves shall spread abundantly, flourishing, and fruit shall hang in clusters; its leaves will be dark blue/black and yellow.
Fourth, Sīzǐ Guó,
when it first desires to obtain my Shèlì,
it shall exhibit various spiritual transformations.
Fifth, whatever excellent characteristics it possesses,
upon reaching Sīzǐ Guó, it will be as if I were alive in the world."
The King heard this and rejoiced, and thereupon made a vow, saying:
"If [the Buddha] permits the cutting of the branch, let the tree immediately manifest branches on all sides.
If [the Buddha] permits it to go to Sīzǐ Guó, may it fall by itself into the golden bowl, and may the original tree return to its original state."
He immediately filled the golden bowl with fragrant mud.
At dusk on the fifteenth day of the eighth month,
he used a pen to mark the bends of the branches, making ten marks in total.
At the first mark, a root grew.
At the last mark, it immediately severed.
The root was four inches long and grew fine roots.
Branches sprouted crisscrossing, resembling a net.
The main branch was ten cubits long.
Furthermore, there were five branches, each four cubits long.
From the five branches, one seed grew on each.
There were also a thousand small branches.
The King saw the spiritual transformation and rejoiced greatly in his heart.
He shouted loudly toward the tree.
The assembly of monks chanted *Sà*.
Lesser kings and their subordinates, along with the entire multitude, all shouted loudly.
The Earth Spirits were astonished and also shouted loudly, their voices penetrating the void.
Thus, the sound propagated upward, reaching as far as Fàntiān.
Where the branch had been severed from the main trunk, one hundred roots immediately emerged.
Ten roots went straight down to the bottom of the bowl, piercing the bowl and going lower.
Ninety fine roots grew around them.
In this sequence, they grew day and night.
At that time, the earth performed six types of shaking.
The Devas in the sky performed various music and dances.
Mountains and trees appeared as if people were dancing.
Devas and humans clapped their hands.
Yèchā laughed joyfully.
The Āxiūluó Wáng sang and chanted praises.
Fàn Wáng was delighted.
In the void, thunder and lightning flashed.
Four-footed creatures ran about, roaring and calling.
Birds flew about, emitting various sounds.
The Pútí Shù seed emitted six-colored light.
The brightness fully illuminated the Suōpó world, reaching up to Fàntiān.
The Pútí Shù then ascended into the void.
It remained suspended for seven days.
The multitude saw only the light and not the tree in the basin.
The King immediately descended from his seat and made offerings to the Pútí Shù.
After seven days passed, the tree emitted light again.
Illuminating the Suōpó world up to Fàntiān.
When the light was withdrawn, the void became clear again.
Spreading its leaves and bearing fruit, it descended from the void and returned into the golden bowl.
The King saw this and rejoiced, and again used the land of Yánfúlì to make offerings to the small Pútí Shù for seven full days.
For seven days, the King paid homage to the Pútí Shù as the King of the land of Yánfúlì.
On the fifteenth day of the ninth month, the assembly of monks performed the Pùsà.
The Pútí Shù, from its original birthplace,
came to the east of the city of Bōzhālìfú Guó.
It rested beneath a Suōluó Shù, its branches and foliage dense and flourishing.
The King saw this and rejoiced.
He again paid homage to it as the King of the land of Yánfúlì.
He addressed Sēngjiāmìduō, saying:
"The time has come for you to depart."
She replied:
"Excellent,
Great King."
Immediately, [the King appointed] eight types of Guǐshén to protect the Pútí Shù,
eight types of high officials,
eight types of Póluómén,
eight types of Jūshì,
eight Jùbōjiā people,
eight Lùluó Chē people,
and eight Jiālíngqié people.
The King, using eight golden urns and eight silver urns, carried water to irrigate the Pútí Shù.
Having received the King's command, they acted accordingly.
The King and the multitude escorted the Pútí Shù along the road, circling it.
Devas, humans, Yèchā, Qiántápó, and Āxiūluó made offerings day and night.
They reached Duōmóbiāo.
The various kings carried the Pútí Shù themselves.
They entered the water up to their necks.
They immediately placed it onto the ship and handed it to Sēngjiāmìduō.
The King called Biāochā, Ābiāochā:
"The Pútí Shù was in my country.
I paid homage to it three times as the King of Yánfúlì.
I personally carried the Pútí Shù on my head, entering the water up to my neck,
and escorted it onto the ship.
I command Ābiāochā:
When the Pútí Shù travels and arrives in that country,
you must tell your King
to personally go down into the water.
The water should cover him up to his neck.
He must welcome the Pútí Shù, carry it on his head, and bear it ashore.
He must make all sorts of offerings, just as I have done here."
Having issued this command, the ship immediately set sail.
At that time, in the sea where the ship was anchored, for a vertical and horizontal extent of one *yóu xún* (yojana), there were no waves.
The King thought to himself,
“The Buddha’s Bodhi Tree is now leaving my kingdom.”
As he had this thought, he shed tears and choked with sorrow.
After the ship left, the King looked from afar and saw
various flowers emerging from the seawater, following the ship to make offerings to it.
Furthermore, in the sky, various flowers, musicians, and instruments scattered offerings.
The water deities also made offerings of various flowers and incense.
This chain of events continued until it reached the palace of the Dragon King (*Lóng Wáng*).
The Dragon King immediately emerged, wanting to seize the Bodhi Tree.
Thereupon, the Bhikṣuṇī Sēngjiāmìduō (Saṅghamittā)
transformed herself into the King of the Golden-Winged Garuḍas (*Jīnchì Niǎo Wáng*).
The Dragon King bowed his head and said,
“Now I wish to invite the Bodhi Tree and the Great Worthy
to return to my palace for seven days of offerings.”
Thereupon, the Bodhi Tree and the assembly all entered the Dragon Palace.
The Dragon King offered his royal throne, designating the tree as king, and made offerings for seven days.
After the seven days had passed,
the Dragon King personally escorted the Bodhi Tree to the sandbar of Yánfú Jùnàwèi.
King Āyù (Aśoka) looked from afar but no longer saw the Bodhi Tree.
He wept and returned.
At this time, Tiān'ài Wáng Dìxū (Devanampiya Tissa)
leveled the road from the city to the Jùnà sandbar.
The ground was as flat as a palm.
Sēngjiāmìduō, using her supernatural powers,
allowed the King, while inside the palace city, to see the arrival of the Bodhi Tree from afar.
The King went out to the sandbar to welcome the Yánfú
Jùnàwèi, entering the water up to his neck.
The tree emitted six-colored light.
The King saw this and rejoiced.
He immediately carried it on his head and brought it ashore.
In the kingdom, there were sixteen great clans (*shí liù dà xìng*) of elders,
who joined the King in welcoming the Bodhi Tree.
When the tree reached the bank,
for three days, the Bodhi Tree was worshipped using the resources of Shīzǐ Zhōu (Siṃhala Dvīpa).
The sixteen great clans took charge of the king’s affairs.
The three days finished and on the fourth day,
carrying the Bodhi Tree, they proceeded sequentially to the kingdom of Ānóuluótuó (Anurādhapura).
The people of the whole kingdom rejoiced, prostrated, and made offerings.
On the fourteenth day of the tenth month, after noon,
the Bodhi Tree entered the center of the city through the North Gate.
It then exited again through the South Gate.
Five hundred bow-lengths away from the South Gate,
at this place, all past Buddhas also entered *sānmèi* (samādhi).
The Bodhi Tree of Jùnàwèi Fó (Konāgamana Buddha)
was named Móhēshālìpó.
The Bodhi Tree of Jūnàhán Fó (Konāgamana Buddha) was named Yōutánbō.
The Bodhi Tree of Jiāyè Fó (Kāśyapa Buddha) was named Nígùtuó.
In the kingdom of Gāmí,
the Śrāmaṇera Xiūmónà (Sumana) ordered the foundation to be laid.
The overall enclosure was measured, the gates and buildings arranged,
and the place where the Bodhi Tree would rest was made perfectly square, setting the location for the King's Gate building.
At that time, the sixteen great clans all submitted.
They surrounded the ground where the King's Gate building was to be planted.
When the tree was first released (lowered),
it rose into the air, eighty cubits high.
It immediately emitted six-colored light, illuminating Shīzǐ Guó (Lanka).
It covered everything completely,
extending up to the Brahmā Heavens (*Fàntiān*).
When the assembly saw the tree's transformation, their hearts were greatly rejoiced.
Ten thousand people in the assembly simultaneously recited the name of the Buddha.
Sequentially, they left home and attained the path of the Arhat (*Luóhàn*).
Before the sunlight vanished, the tree was still in the void.
After sunset, the stars and comets all descended, and the earth greatly shook.
Then Móxǐntuó (Mahinda),
together with Sēngjiāmìduō, the King, and the people of the kingdom,
gathered beneath the Bodhi Tree.
One fruit on the north branch ripened and fell from the branch, offered to Móxǐntuó.
Móxǐntuó gave the seed to the King, instructing him to plant it.
The King immediately received it in a golden bowl.
He covered it with rich soil.
He also covered it with perfumed ointment.
In a moment, eight shoots immediately sprouted.
Each was four cubits long.
The King saw this and sighed in astonishment.
He covered them with white parasols,
and consecrated the small trees as kings.
The King took one shoot
and planted it on the sandbar of Yánfú Jùluówèi.
He also took one shoot and planted it in the village of Bó Jūluópó Mén.
He also took one shoot and planted it inside the Zhí Mén (Dormitory Gate).
He also took one shoot and planted it in the pagoda garden (*tǎ yuán*).
He also took one shoot and planted it at the Móxīshǒuluó Sì (Maheśvara Temple).
He also took one shoot and planted it in the center of Zhīdìyē Shān (Cetiya Mountain).
He also took one shoot and planted it in Lóuxīnà Cūn (Rohana Village).
He also took one shoot and planted it in Wǎngluó Cūn (Vāḷa Village).
The remaining four fruits were on the tree.
They ripened and fell sequentially, together sprouting thirty-two shoots.
They were all taken and planted in the *yóu xún* garden.
Thus, the stupas circulated, filling Shīzǐ Guó.
Because of the Bodhi Tree, the kingdom was peaceful and secure, without suffering or calamities.
At that time, Lady Ānóuluó (Anulā Devī), together with one thousand maidens,
went to Sēngjiāmìduō to become Bhikṣuṇīs.
After being ordained, they sequentially attained Arhatship.
The King's nephew, Ābiāochā (Abhaya), left home with five hundred people and sequentially attained Arhatship.
Another day, the King and Móxǐntuó went to pay homage to the Bodhi Tree.
They arrived at the location of the Iron Palace (*Tiě Diàn*).
The people presented flowers to the King.
The King offered the flowers to Master Móxǐntuó to make offerings to the Iron Palace; when the flowers fell, the earth shook.
The King saw the earth shake and immediately asked the Great Worthy,
“Why does this ground suddenly shake?”
He replied,
“Great King, in the future, the assembly of monks will recite the precepts in this palace.
Therefore, the ground manifests this auspicious sign.”
They proceeded sequentially and arrived at the mango (*Ānluó*) location.
Someone offered the King a mango fruit, complete in fragrance and flavor.
The King offered it to Móxǐntuó. Móxǐntuó
ate the fruit and told the King,
“You may plant this seed.”
The King immediately planted it.
He sprinkled water on the ground.
The earth all shook.
The King asked,
“Why did the earth shake?”
He replied,
“In future generations, this place will be where the assembly of monks gathers; thus, the auspicious sign is manifested.”
The King immediately scattered flowers, paid homage, and departed.
They arrived at the Zhīdìyē (Cetiya) location.
Someone offered Jāmpaka flowers to the King.
The King offered them to Móxǐntuó.
The earth shook.
The King asked,
“Why did the earth shake?”
He replied,
“In the future, a great Buddha stupa will be erected here; thus, this auspicious sign is manifested.”
The King said,
“I must now erect the stupa.”
Móxǐntuó replied,
“The King does not need to erect it.
The King has many construction projects.
In future generations, there will be a grandson of the King,
named Mùchāgāmání Āpóyē (Duṭṭhagāmaṇī Abhaya),
who will erect the great stupa.”
The King asked, “Is he my grandson? Will I obtain merit from this?”
He replied,
“You will not.”
The King took a stone pillar, twenty feet high,
and inscribed a record upon the stone pillar:
“My grandson, named Mùchāgāmání Āpóyē,
shall in the future erect a great stupa here.”
In the past, in the kingdom of King Āyù, there was a *Jiāluóyuè* (gahapati/householder)
who made offerings to twenty thousand Bhikṣus.
For an entire year, he maintained invitations, and his reputation reached the King.
The King summoned him for an audience.
“I hear your family is immensely wealthy. What exactly do you possess?”
He replied,
“I truly possess nothing.”
The King did not believe him.
He detained the *Jiāluóyuè* and sent someone to observe his home.
They saw seven layers of residences at the gate.
The halls and mansions were all made of the seven treasures.
They surpassed the King's palace.
His women were also superior.
However, there was no grain, silk, money, or ordinary possessions.
The messenger returned and reported to the King.
The King’s doubt gradually cleared.
The *Jiāluóyuè* smiled.
The King asked,
“Why are you smiling?”
He replied,
“Because the King did not believe me.”
The *Jiāluóyuè* pointed his finger toward the eastern sky, and the seven treasures immediately rained down.
He pointed south, and treasures also rained down, limitless in amount.
The King then dismissed him.
Now, the monastery (*jīngshě*) of the assembly of monks was not far from the palace.
The King immediately prepared his carriage and proceeded to the monastery.
He saw the Bhikṣus, bowed respectfully, and asked the Head Seated monk (*Shàngzuò Dàorén*),
“What past merit does this *Jiāluóyuè* possess, such that natural treasures appear merely by thinking of them?”
The Head Seated Bhikṣu entered *sānmèi* and contemplated the sentient beings within four hundred *yóu xún*.
He saw the son of the elder (*zhǎngzhě zǐ*).
Formerly, during the time of Wéiwèi Fó (Vipaśyin Buddha), four people jointly erected a stupa and temple.
One among them was particularly earnest in his intent.
After the stupa and temple were completed, he mixed gold, silver, the seven treasures, and various beautiful flowers together.
He scattered them over the three uppermost tiers of the stupa.
He made them rain down in all four directions.
He vowed that in the future, the merit of food would never be exhausted.
The one who now obtains natural treasures is this person.
The King heard this and greatly cultivated merit.
The Buddha had long toured various kingdoms.
The elder Xūdá (Sudatta) missed Him, longed for Him, and yearned for Him.
He reported to the Buddha, saying,
“I pray you will leave a small object so that I may constantly make offerings.”
The Buddha gave him hair and nails.
He requested permission to erect a stupa.
The Buddha then permitted it.
In Shěwèi Guó (Śrāvastī), he built brackets and beams,
and decorated them with colorful paintings.
The Buddha arrived at the Yuèzhī guó.
He subjugated the female Rākṣasa in the west.
He stayed overnight in a stone grotto at that time.
To this day, the Buddha's shadow remains.
If a person goes inside to look at it,
they cannot see it.
If they leave the aperture, the luminous form is like the Buddha.
Sometimes, he flew to the mountains of the Xianrén Lìbáduó in Jìbīn guó.
He stayed in the void (mid-air).
He subjugated this Xianrén.
The Xianrén said,
“I enjoy dwelling here.
I wish the Buddha would grant me hair and nails so I may erect a stupa and make offerings.”
The stupa is now located at the base of this mountain.
There is the Líyuè sì.
Líyuè should be rendered as Lìbáduó.
The Buddha's right tooth and right collarbone (lit., incomplete bowl bone)
were used to erect a stupa on Shīzǐ Zhōu in Dāolì Tiān.
He was requested and obtained two collarbones and the tooth.
They are now in the Shì Gōng.
When the Buddha was traveling in Bōluónài,
five hundred young boys gathered together as companions.
They went together to play by the river and piled sand to form a stupa.
Each one said,
“My stupa is very good, you should learn from me and make yours like mine.”
Although these five hundred boys had good intentions, their merit from previous lives was slight.
A great storm came, and the river suddenly swelled.
The five hundred young boys all drowned at the same time.
Their parents wailed and sought their remains.
They did not know where they were.
The Buddha said,
“Do not generate resentment based on unfulfilled requests concerning past lives.
These children’s destiny was such due to past lives.
They are now reborn in Dōushuài Tiān.”
The Buddha emitted a bright light,
allowing the parents to see their children from afar.
Immediately, they all came to scatter flowers and make offerings.
The Buddha said,
“Excellent!
Because they built the sand stupa, they immediately attained rebirth in heaven and saw Mílè Fó.”
The five hundred sons of heaven each addressed their parents, saying, “Do not be anxious or sorrowful anymore.
Just strive diligently with vigor.”
They circled the Buddha three times, bowed, and flew away.
The Buddha was in Luóyuèzhī guó.
He sent an Arhat named Xūmàn.
Who carried the Buddha's hair and nails to the southern mountains of Jìbīn to build a monument (fútú).
The monastery permanently housed five hundred Arhats.
Morning and evening, they burned incense, circled the stupa, and paid homage.
Five hundred monkeys saw the practitioners making offerings.
They entered the deep ravine and carried mud and stones on carts to erect a Buddha stupa.
They erected a wooden mast (chà) and attached worn banners to it.
Morning and evening, they paid homage.
Violent flooding swept them away, and they all died.
They were reborn in Dāolì Tiān.
They immediately used their divine eyes to see their previous deeds.
Each carrying flowers, incense, music, and instruments, they stood over their former corpses and circled them seven times.
The humans saw the Devas from afar scattering flowers, playing music, and circling the monkey corpses.
There were five hundred Brahmanas, external students holding heterodox views.
They asked the Devas,
“Why do you condescend to make offerings here?”
They replied,
“These were our former bodies.
When we were in the world, we imitated the Śramaṇas and playfully erected stupas and monasteries.
Based on this, we were reborn in heaven; now we repay this kindness.
You, holding heterodox views, labor arduously for a hundred eons without gaining anything.
It would be better to go together to Qíshéjué Shān to bow and serve, for that merit is limitless.”
The Brahmanas were immediately joyful.
They went together to where the Buddha was, prostrated their five limbs (five-point prostration), scattered flowers, and made offerings.
In the Garden of Illumination east of the city in Dāolì Tiān, there is a stupa of the Buddha’s hair.
In the Garden of Roughness south of the city, there is a stupa of the Buddha’s nails.
In the Garden of Joy west of the city, there is a stupa of the Buddha’s bowl.
In the Garden of Chariots north of the city, there is a stupa of the Buddha’s tooth.
In Jiāwéiluówèi guó, which is considered the center of heaven and earth, the Stupa of Birth was established.
In Mójiětí guó, at the Auspicious Victory Bodhimaṇḍa,
under the Primordial Fortune Tree, the Stupa of Attaining the Way was erected.
In Bōluónài guó, at the dwelling place of the Xianrén, the Deer Park (Lùyě Yuàn), the Stupa of Turning the Dharma Wheel was established.
In Kūshīnà guó, the birthplace of the strongmen, between the beautiful Sāla twin trees, the Stupa of Parinirvāṇa (Bān Nièpán) was erected.
A former prince,
named Móhēsàduǒ,
went out traveling in the forests and wilderness.
He saw a tigress that had recently given birth to seven cubs; having been hungry for many days, her life was about to expire.
He immediately took off his clothes, pricked his neck with a bamboo stick, threw himself down from a height, and lay before the tigress.
The tigress licked his blood and gradually consumed his flesh entirely.
The Great King and the inner palace heard that the son had not returned.
They immediately sent people to search for him.
The envoys returned and reported the full account.
The King commanded that his Śarīra be collected
and a seven-jewel stupa be erected.
There was a seven-jewel stupa
that sprang forth from the ground.
The Buddha rose from his seat
and paid homage to the stupa.
At that time, the spirit of the Bodhi Tree at the Bodhimaṇḍa asked,
“The Tathāgata is the most supreme and most honored, for what reason does he bow to this stupa?”
The Buddha answered,
“In the past, when I practiced the Bodhisattva path, my complete physical Śarīra was in this stupa.
Because of this body, I quickly attained the Buddha Way.”
He commanded Ānán to open the stupa, retrieve the Śarīra, and show it to the assembly.
Ānán opened the stupa and opened the seven-jewel casket.
The Śarīra were white and red.
The Buddha said,
“These are cultivated through the merits of discipline (śīla), concentration (samādhi), and wisdom (prajñā).
They are extremely difficult to obtain and represent the highest field of merit.”
The great assembly rejoiced, paid reverence, and bowed their heads.
In a past age, there was a king named Jìnmèi Wáng.
After Jiāshè Rúlái entered Parinirvāṇa,
this king immediately made a stupa of gold and silver.
It was one thousand yojana in length and width, and one yojana high.
He piled silver and gold to make a moat, which is still underground today.
At that time, the Tathāgata immediately brought forth this stupa to show the four assemblies.
Jiāshè’s complete physical Śarīra were perfectly preserved as they were originally.
After Jiāshè Fó entered Nirvāṇa and was cremated,
a seven-jewel stupa was erected using the Buddha’s Śarīra.
Reverent offerings were made.
After numerous generations passed,
the stupa naturally decayed and broke down,
and there was no one to repair it.
There were ninety-three thousand people in the communal settlement (Yìhé Yì).
At that time, Píngshā Wáng was the leader.
He addressed the assembly, saying,
“You should all encourage and strive yourselves
to cultivate merit and virtue together.
A Buddha's age is hard to meet,
a human body is hard to obtain.
Even if one attains a human form,
one might fall into a border region,
or be born into a family with heterodox views.
Why should we
covet these worldly pleasures?
It is better to open our hearts and restore the decaying stupas and monasteries.”
They immediately repaired them together.
They further jointly made this vow:
“If there is any merit accrued,
may we not fall into the Three Evil Paths or the Eight Difficult Places.
May we be reborn together among humans and gods,
see Shìjiāwén (Śākyamuni)
at his first gathering when he preaches the Dharma,
and all attain liberation.”
With the King as the leader,
when the people of that time passed away,
they were reborn in Dāolì Tiān.
After several generations passed,
when Shìjiāwén appeared,
the ninety-three thousand people
were reborn in Mójié Guó, with Píngshā serving as the king.
In a past age,
there was a Cakravartin (Zhuǎnlún Wáng),
named Dézhǔ.
He once, in a single day,
erected five hundred stupas,
each five hundred yojana high.
At that time, before the Buddha,
there was a seven-jeweled stūpa (precious pagoda).
It was five hundred *yóuxún* high,
and two hundred fifty *yóuxún* in length and width.
It emerged soaring from the ground
and remained suspended in the air.
It was adorned
and embellished with various kinds of precious objects.
It had five thousand railings, balustrades, and ten million niches and chambers.
Countless banners and streamers
served as its solemn decoration.
Precious pearl necklaces hung down,
and ten billion precious bells
were suspended above it.
From its four sides issued the fragrance of *Duōmóluóbá Zhāntán* (Tāmālapattra Candana),
which filled the entire world.
Its various banners and canopies
were composed of the seven treasures: gold, silver, *liúlí* (lapis lazuli/crystal), *chēqú* (tridacna gigas), *mǎnǎo* (agate), pearls, and amber.
They reached high up to the Palace of the Four Heavenly Kings (*Sì Tiānwáng Gōng*).
The inhabitants of the Thirty-three Heavens (*Sānshísān Tiān*)
rained down heavenly *Mantuōluó* flowers
to make offerings to the precious stūpa.
Down below, the Eight Classes (*Bābù*)
used all manner of flowers, incense, necklaces, banners, canopies, and music
to make offerings to the precious stūpa.
At that time, from within the stūpa,
a great voice issued forth, praising,
"Excellent! Śākyamuni Buddha (*Shìjiā Móuní Fó*)!
Using wisdom of equality,
you teach the Dharma of the Bodhisattvas!"
The four assemblies, upon hearing the sound coming from the stūpa,
all attained the joy of the Dharma
and marveled at this unprecedented event.
In this precious stūpa
is the complete body of a Tathāgata (*Rúlái*).
In the eastern direction, in countless tens of millions of *ā-sēng-zhī* worlds of the past,
the country was named Precious Purity (*Bǎojìng*),
and the Buddha's title was Many Treasures (*Duōbǎo*).
When that Buddha was practicing the Bodhisattva path,
he made a great solemn vow:
"If, after I attain Buddhahood and enter *nièdù* (Nirvāṇa),
in the lands of the ten directions,
there is a place where the *Fǎhuā Jīng* (Lotus Sūtra) is preached,
my stūpa or temple shall, for the purpose of hearing the sūtra,
spring forth and appear before them to serve as proof."
"Whenever the *Fǎhuā* is preached,
my complete body *shèlì* (relics) remains within the stūpa,
praising, 'Excellent!'"
The Bodhisattva Mahāpramoditarāja (*Dà Lèshuō Púsà*)
said to the Buddha,
"World-Honored One (*Shìzūn*),
we wish to see this Buddha body."
The Buddha said,
"*Duōbǎo* Buddha has a solemn and profound vow:
'If my precious stūpa
appears before various Buddhas for the purpose of hearing the *Fǎhuā Jīng*,
and if I desire to show my body to the four assemblies,
the emanated Buddhas (*fēnshēn zhū fó*) of that Buddha,
who are present in the ten directions,
must all return to one place,
and only then will my body appear.'"
*Dà Lèshuō* said,
"We also wish to see the World-Honored One's emanated Buddhas."
The Buddha released a ray of light from his white *háo* curl (*báiháo*).
The Buddhas in the east, west, south, north, the four intermediate directions, and above and below (all directions)
each addressed the Bodhisattvas in their assembly, saying,
"Good men,
we should now proceed to the place of Śākyamuni Buddha in the *Suōpó* (Saha) world,
and also make offerings to the precious stūpa of *Duōbǎo Rúlái*."
Thereupon, the *Suōpó* world immediately transformed and became pure.
*Liúlí* served as the ground,
and precious trees provided adornment.
Golden ropes
delimited the eight paths.
There were no villages, encampments, cities, towns, great seas, rivers, mountains, streams, forests, or marshes. Great precious incense was burned.
All heavenly beings and humans were removed and placed in other lands.
At this time, all the Buddhas, each taking a great Bodhisattva as attendant,
arrived at the *Suōpó* world.
They each went beneath a precious tree.
Beneath the trees, there were all *shīzǐ zhī zuò* (lion thrones),
five hundred *yóuxún* high.
The Buddhas from the ten directions all assembled
and sat down in the eight directions.
When the Buddhas desired to jointly open the precious stūpa,
they immediately rose from their seats and stood in the empty sky.
All the four assemblies rose, pressed their palms together, and focused their minds on observing the Buddha.
Thereupon, Śākyamuni Buddha
used his right finger to open the door of the seven-jeweled stūpa.
A great sound issued forth,
like the removal of a bolt and key.
The entire assembly
saw *Duōbǎo Rúlái* seated on the lion throne within the precious stūpa,
his complete body intact, appearing as if in *chándìng* (meditative absorption).
They further heard his words:
"Excellent! Excellent!
Śākyamuni Buddha!
You have quickly preached this *Fǎhuā Jīng*.
I have come here for the purpose of listening to this sūtra."
At that time, the four assemblies, seeing a Buddha who had entered *nièdù* countless tens of millions of billions of eons ago,
speaking such words,
praised the unprecedented event.
They scattered heaps of heavenly precious flowers upon *Duōbǎo Fó* and Śākyamuni Buddha.
Then *Duōbǎo Fó*,
within the precious stūpa,
shared half of his seat, inviting Śākyamuni Buddha to sit.
Then Śākyamuni Buddha took that half seat.
Using his divine powers (*shéntōng lì*), he lifted all the great assemblies,
so they were all in the empty sky.
The Buddha addressed the great assembly,
"Reflecting on the merits I cultivated in ancient times,
casting off bodies and receiving bodies was neither single nor double.
I shall now speak of it.
Regarding the body form of this Dharma: this seed of the great earth is eighty-four myriad billion *lǐ* thick.
Below that, the wind layer is eighty-four myriad billion *lǐ* thick.
Below the wind, the water layer is eighty-four myriad billion *lǐ* thick.
Below the water, the fire layer is eighty-four myriad billion *lǐ* thick.
Below the fire, the sand layer is eighty-four myriad billion *lǐ* thick.
Below the sand, the diamond (vajra) layer is eighty-four myriad billion *lǐ* thick.
The complete-body *shèlì* and fragmented-body *shèlì* of all Buddhas are all within the vajra boundary realm (*jīngāng jì chà*).
This vajra realm is also eighty-four myriad billion *lǐ* thick.
It is named Wondrous Fragrance (*Miàoxiāng*).
The Buddha's title is Non-Abiding (*Bùzhù*).
He possesses the Ten Titles
and is currently preaching the Dharma.
Formerly, there was a *shāmen* (monk) whose family was very wealthy.
He was constructing a stūpa and a temple.
He used sandalwood for the pillars and the seven treasures for the spire (*chà*).
Before it was completed, five hundred *shāmen* came from distant regions.
Now, within his country, there were five hundred virtuous ones (*xiánzhě*).
They each provided the *shāmen* with *jiāshā* (cassocks) and clothing.
The people of the country said to the temple master:
"The distant visitors ought to leave.
We shall dismiss them first.
The *Āshélí* (Acārya) who constantly abides here should naturally act as the temple master."
The *shāmen* thought:
"My accumulated merit is like Mount Sumeru (*Xūmí*), immeasurable.
Yet the people of the country refuse to assist me.
I labor only for everyone—humble and noble, near and far."
Then he burned the temple and stūpa with fire.
Afterwards, he entered hell and the animal realm, remaining in each for ninety eons (*jié*).
Later, he became a great fish.
His body was in the sea,
forty myriad *lǐ* long.
His eyes were like the sun and moon.
His teeth were twenty thousand *lǐ* long,
purely white, resembling snow mountains.
His tongue was forty thousand *lǐ* wide,
purely red, resembling volcanic mountains.
His mouth was fifty thousand *lǐ* wide.
At that time, there were five hundred people
who entered the sea to gather treasures.
These were precisely the people who in a former life had provided clothing to the five hundred *shāmen*.
Due to past karma and reckoning, the fish opened its mouth and drank water.
The boats were carried rapidly by the current.
All were greatly terrified
and unanimously cried out, "*Námó Fó* (Homage to the Buddha)!"
The fish heard the sound, closed its mouth, and listened.
The water ceased flowing.
Hearing the sound of sūtra recitation coming from the boats,
the fish shed tears.
It thought to itself, "It has been a very long time since I heard this sound."
Consequently, it stopped eating and died in the sea after seven days.
Its floating corpse drifted ashore, and its spirit was reborn into a Dharma-abiding family.
It could speak as soon as it fell to the ground
and immediately recognized its past lives.
When it reached the age of eight,
it attained the path of *Luóhàn* (Arhat).
He returned to the seashore and saw his former body.
The accumulated bones were like a mountain; he gazed into the skull for seven days and could not finish contemplating it.
Because he had burned the stūpa and temple, he remained in the evil path for one hundred eighty eons.
The four assemblies were lax in asking about and listening to the Dharma.
Śakra Devānām Indra (*Shì Tí Huán Yīn*) invited the Buddha
to ascend to the Thirty-three Heavens (*Sānshísān Tiān*)
to preach the Dharma for his mother during the three-month summer retreat (*xià ān jū*).
The Tathāgata desired to create yearning among the people.
He departed without taking an attendant and without informing anyone.
At that time, King Prasenajit (*Bōsī Nì Wáng*) of Śrāvastī (*Shèwèi Guó*) and King Udayana (*Yōutián Wáng*) of Kausāmbi (*Jūyì Guó*) came to the residence of Ānanda (*Ānán*).
They asked where the Buddha was.
Ānanda replied,
"I also do not know."
The two kings, yearning to see the Tathāgata, subsequently fell ill.
King *Yōutián* immediately commanded the skilled artisans in his country
to construct an image of the Tathāgata using ox-head sandalwood (*niú tóu zhāntán*).
It measured five *chǐ* high. King *Yōutián* asked the Buddha:
"After the Tathāgata's *nièdù*, what merit
would be gained by making a Buddha image, reverently serving it?"
The Buddha said,
"If one makes an image of the Buddha,
in every life and every place of rebirth, the body and appearance will be excellent, and after death, one will be reborn in the Seventh Brahmā Heaven (*Fàntiān*).
Furthermore, one will surpass all other heavenly beings in having incomparable beauty and uprightness.
One will always be born into wealthy and noble families,
with outstanding vigor and power.
One will be loved and respected by the multitude,
and possess immeasurable wealth.
Or one may be born into the families of emperors, kings, dukes, marquises, or virtuous and good people in *Yánfú Dì* (Jambudvīpa).
Or one may be born as a *Zhuǎnlún Wáng* (Cakravartin, Wheel-Turning King) who flies between heaven and earth.
Or one may be born into a family that follows filial piety and the gate of morality.
After death, one will not enter the Three Evil Paths (*sān tú*)."
Fó ascended to the Dāolì Heaven. King
Yōutián could not overcome his longing. He

cast a golden image. Hearing that the Fó was about to descend, he carried the image on an elephant and looked up to await the Shìzūn (World-Honored One), treating the image as if it were the living Fó.
Then, he saw the Fó’s feet remotely, walking in empty space, treading on double lotus flowers, and emitting great light.
The
Fó spoke to the image, saying: “In future ages, you
shall widely carry out the affairs of the Fó. After my nirvāṇa (Mièdù),
I entrust all my disciples to you. If there are sentient beings who create statues and make various offerings,
these people shall certainly attain
the pure *niànfó* (recollection of the Fó) *sānmèi* (samādhi) in future ages.” The
Fó addressed Ānán (Ānanda): “Take my words
and announce them throughout the disciples. After my nirvāṇa, create images of the Fó.
Let their
distinctive marks and features be complete. Also create
immeasurable manifestation Fós (Huàfó). And paint the footprint
of the Fó with subtle and wonderful colors. Place colored jewels
and *pōlí* (crystal) gems where the white curl (*báiháo*) is located. If people see this, joy will arise in their hearts.
They can extinguish the sins of life and death accumulated over hundreds of millions of nayutas
and Ganges River sands of *kalpas* (jié).” At that time, King Bōsīní (Prasenajit),
hearing that King Yōutián had made and offered a Tathāgata (Rúlái) image, again summoned skilled artisans and cast
a Tathāgata image from purple-colored fine gold. It was
more than five *chǐ* (feet) tall. At that time, there were only
these two images within Jambudvīpa (Yánfútí). When the
Fó ascended to the Dāolì Heaven to preach the
Dharma to his mother, ninety days
passed. King Bōsīní
longed to see the Fó. He carved a Tathāgata image from ox-head sandalwood (*niútóu zhāntán*) and placed it where the Fó usually sat.
Later, when the Fó returned and entered the *jīngshè* (vihara/monastery), the image came out to greet the Fó.
The
Fó said: “Return to your
seat.” (The image)
said: “After my *bōníhuán* (parinirvāṇa), you
may serve as the model for the Four Assemblies.” The image immediately
returned to its seat. This image was truly the origin of all images,
and the one later generations followed.
The
Fó then moved to dwell in a small *jīngshè* on the side, separated from
the image, a distance
of twenty paces. The Jìhuán Jīngshè (Jetavana Vihara) originally had seven stories.
Various kingdoms
competed to offer continuous worship. A rat carried a lamp wick, burning the banners and canopies,
and subsequently, all seven stories of the *jīngshè* were destroyed.
The kings and people of various countries were all deeply grieved and distressed.
They believed that the sandalwood image had been burned.
Four or five days later, they opened the door of the small *jīngshè* on the east side,
and suddenly saw
the original image. The multitude
was greatly delighted. They collectively
repaired the *jīngshè*. They managed to build two stories and moved the image back to its original place.
King Shànróng
entered the mountains to hunt. He saw various Brāhmaṇas (Fànzhì).
They were
naked and exposed, some eating
tree leaves, some inhaling
wind and absorbing vital energy, some lying
among thorns, practicing various self-torments
in pursuit of divine immortality (Shénxiān). Shànróng asked:
“Why have
you not succeeded?” The Brāhmaṇas
replied: “There was a herd of deer nearby
that often mated. When I saw them, my mind was aroused,
and I could not restrain myself.” The
King said: “Even when weakened by extreme fasting, you still have sexual desire.
The Śākya (Shìzǐ)
Śramaṇas (Shāmén), eat sweet
and delicious food, sit on
comfortable seats, their clothes
appropriate for the season, perfuming
themselves with incense and flowers—how can they be without it?”
Āyù (Aśoka) heard this and immediately became worried and distressed.
“He is my
only brother, and has suddenly
produced wrong views. Fearing he will be eternally lost and sunk, I must remove this evil.”
He ordered that dancing girls be given to him
to share joy and pleasure. The
King personally spoke to his brother: “Why have you taken
your brother’s concubines and entertainers? Indulge yourself
in pleasure!” He immediately
intended to kill him. The
ministers remonstrated, saying: “The King has only one brother,
and the successor/heir is young. We beg you to grant
him seven days.” (The King said he would) respectfully
follow the royal command. The
King then remained silent. He spoke
to his various ministers: “Allow my brother to wear my robes and crown, enter my palace,
and amuse himself with music and entertainment.” When the seventh
day arrived, the
King sent an envoy to ask: “Are your intentions unrestrained
and are you happy?” Shànróng
replied: “I neither see nor hear;
what happiness is there?” The
King said: “You deal with matters just like me.
Why do you say you neither hear nor see?” The
brother replied: “A person who is destined to die, though his life is not yet ended,
is no different from the dead. How could I have any feeling
for attachment to the five desires?” The
King said: “Now, this
single body faces myriad worries. When this
single body must perish, dwelling in desire brings no joy.
The *Shāmén* who preach the path worry about the three ages (past, present, future).
When one body dies and decays, another body is received.
Over hundreds of thousands of millions of ages, body after body endures suffering
and measureless affliction and distress.
Although one is born as a human,
one is sent to run errands for others,
lacking clothes
and food. Thinking of this bitterness and hardship, one leaves home to practice the Way,
seeking the essentials of *wúwéi* (non-action)
to cross over the world. If one is not diligent, one must endure the suffering of countless *kalpas* again.”
Shànróng’s mind was then opened and his understanding released.
He reported
to the King, saying: “Having now heard the King's instruction, I have achieved awakening.
Birth, old age, sickness, and death are truly causes for loathing and distress.
Grief, worry, suffering, and distress circulate endlessly.
I only wish that the Great King would permit me to practice the Way.”
The
King said: “You should
know that this is the time (to act).” The brother immediately left home, observed the precepts and prohibitions, was diligent day and night, and attained the path of the Arhat (Luóhàn).
The *Āyù Wáng Zhuàn* says: Āyù Wáng heard that his brother had attained the Way,
was deeply delighted in his heart, bowed his head in respectful veneration, and requested to provide long-term offerings.
The brother vowed to rely on the forests and wilderness to live out the rest of his life.
Āyù then commanded spirits and deities to build a mountain several tens of *zhàng* high inside the city.
All interaction and traffic with outsiders were cut off.
(The brother) then accepted
the King’s command. He gathered and gave up his clothing and possessions to create a stone image.
It was one *zhàng* and six *chǐ* high, and the mountain itself became the niche (kānshì).
There was a Dragon King (Lóngwáng) who requested the Fó to reside there permanently.
“If you do not stay, I will develop evil thoughts, and there will be no means for me to attain the Way.”
The various Brahmā (Fàntiān) Kings also earnestly urged and requested,
“We beg you, for the sake of all sentient beings,
do not dwell here alone.” The Dragon offered the Tathāgata
a palace made of seven treasures. The
Fó said: “I do not need it; just grant me the Ràchà (Rākṣasa) stone cave.”
The Fó withdrew his supernatural powers and entered the stone chamber alone.
He spread his own sitting mat, and sat cross-legged (jiāfū).
At that time, the Rākṣasī woman
and the Dragon, for the Four Great Disciples and Ānán,
constructed five more stone chambers.
The Fó accepted the invitation of the King of Nàxiānhē City and the various kingdoms.
Everywhere, they saw the Fó, with flowery thrones in the empty sky, filled with manifestation Fós (Huàfó).
The Lóngwáng was delighted and issued a great vow:
“May I attain Fóhood like this in future ages.”
The Fó accepted the King’s invitation for seven days.
He withdrew
his supernatural powers, came out
of the stone cave, and traveled to various places with the numerous Bhikṣus (Bǐqiū).
The Dragon followed him.
Afterwards, when the Fó returned to the kingdom, (the Dragon) wept and shed tears,
and pleaded,
saying: “Please do not abandon me.”
The Shìzūn comforted him, saying:
“I will sit in your cave for fifteen hundred years.”
Then the Lóngwáng and others joined their palms and requested the Fó to enter the cave.
The Fó sat in the cave and manifested eighteen transformations.
He sprang
his body into the stone, like a bright mirror.
The image (Yǐng) was inside the stone but appeared outside.
When viewed from afar,
it was visible; when viewed up close,
it was gone. Hundreds of thousands of heavenly beings (Zhū Tiān) made offerings to the Fó’s Yǐng.
The Yǐng also preached the Dharma.
The stone cave was one *zhàng* and eight *chǐ* high,
and twenty-four paces
deep. The stone color was clear and white.
The Buddha said:
Regarding the granting of the Correct Dharma (Zhèngfǎ) to humans and devas (tiān):
My Dharma will be unshakable for a thousand years.
He addressed Dìshì and the Four Heavenly Kings (Sì Wáng):
After my Nirvāṇa (Nièpán), each of you shall protect and uphold the Correct Dharma in your respective kingdoms.
After a thousand years pass,
evil winds, sudden downpours, and many calamities and misfortunes will arise.
The people will suffer famine, and objects, upon being touched, will disintegrate.
Food and drink will lose their flavor, and rare treasures will sink (disappear).
In the West, there will be a king named Bōluóbā.
In the North, there will be a king named Yēpónà.
In the South, there will be a king named Shìjiā.
In the East, there will be a king named Dōushāluó.
These four kings will all have many retainers.
They will kill Bhikṣus (Bǐqiū) and destroy stūpas and monasteries (tǎsì).
The four directions will be utterly chaotic.
At that time, many Bhikṣus will gather and come to the Central Kingdom (Zhōngguó).
The king of the Kuśāmbī (Jūshǎnmí) Kingdom was named Móyīntuóluóxīnà.
He had a son.
His hands seemed smeared with blood.
His body resembled armor (jiǎzhòu).
He possessed great courage and strength.
Five hundred ministers simultaneously had sons on the same day.
All had bloodied hands and armored bodies.
On that day, in the Kuśāmbī (Jūshǎnmí) Kingdom, it rained blood.
The king saw the ominous signs and was greatly terrified, so he inquired of the physiognomist (xiàngshī).
The physiognomist replied:
The son born to Your Majesty today
is destined to rule Jambudvīpa (Yánfútí) and will kill many people.
He should be named Nándāng.
As he gradually grew older,
the four wicked kings
arrived from the four directions.
The king was greatly worried and fearful.
A heavenly deity (tiānshén) announced to him:
Great King, just establish Nándāng as king;
he is fully capable of subduing the four great wicked kings.
He then followed the deity's words, relinquished the throne, and gave it to his son.
Using the bright pearl from his topknot,
he crowned his son.
He assembled the five hundred ministers,
performed the consecration (guàndǐng) with perfumed water,
and commanded him to go forth and conquer.
The sons of the ministers, clad in armor,
followed the king in the campaign.
They fought against the four wicked kings
and killed them entirely.
He reigned over Jambudvīpa (Yánfútí),
governing the Kuśāmbī (Jūshǎnmí) Kingdom (Píguó).
The Buddha addressed the Four Great Heavenly Kings (Sì Dà Tiān Wáng):
In Pāṭaliputra (Bāliánfú) Kingdom,
there will be a Brāhmaṇa (Póluómén)
named Ājīnídáduō.
He will be thoroughly versed in the Vedas (Bǐtuó) sūtras and śāstras.
This Brāhmaṇa will take a wife.
When his wife became pregnant,
she desired to debate with people.
She therefore asked the physiognomist.
The physiognomist replied:
This child in the womb
is destined to be thoroughly conversant with all sūtras and śāstras.
The son born will clearly understand all sūtras, śāstras, and various medical methods.
He will teach five hundred disciples.
He will leave home and study the Dao in my Dharma.
He will be thoroughly versed in the Tripiṭaka (Sānzàng),
skilled at expounding the Dharma,
eloquent and ingenious, gathering many followers.
In this city of Pāṭaliputra (Bāliánfú Yì),
there will be a great merchant leader
named Xūtuónà.
When his wife became pregnant,
she became simple, honest, gentle, and her sense faculties (zhū gēn) became calm.
At that time, the merchant leader immediately asked the physiognomist.
The physiognomist replied:
The child in the womb will be extremely virtuous and good.
When the months are complete, a son will be born named Xiūluótuó.
As he gradually grows older, he will leave home and study the Dao in my Dharma.
He will diligently practice zealous effort and attain the fruition of Arhat (Luóhàn Guǒ).
However, he will have little learning, few desires, and be content.
And he will be known by few former acquaintances.
He resides on Mount Gāndhamāla (Jiàntuó Móluó Shān).
He constantly expounds the Dharma for King Nándāng.
When Nándāng saw that his father, the king, had passed away,
he held his father's corpse with both hands, wailed, wept bitterly, and was heartbroken with grief.
At that time, that Tripiṭaka (Sānzàng) master expounded the Dharma for the king.
The king's sorrow and distress immediately ceased.
He developed great reverence and faith in the Buddha Dharma.
And he proclaimed aloud:
"From now on, I shall offer all Bhikṣus fearlessness, comfort, and happiness."
Then he asked the Bhikṣus:
"How many more years will it be until the four former wicked kings destroy the Buddha Dharma?"
The Bhikṣus replied:
"After twelve years."
The king thought in his heart:
He roared the lion's roar (shīzǐhǒu),
"For these twelve years, I shall
provide abundant supplies of all kinds to the five assemblies (wǔ zhòng)."
On the day of the offerings,
Heaven rained fragrant, moisturizing dew,
causing all crops in the entirety of Jambudvīpa (Yánfútí) to flourish and grow.
People from all directions brought offerings and came to the Kuśāmbī (Jūshǎnmí) Kingdom,
making offerings to the monastic assembly (zhòngsēng).
At that time, the Bhikṣus did not diligently practice the Three Practices (Sān Yè).
They spent their days in frivolous talk.
They were greedy for profit and gain, loved to adorn themselves, wore fine clothes, deviated from the path of leaving home (chūjiā fǎ), and were Bhikṣus only in outward appearance (xínglèi bǐqiū).
They were the great thieves within the Dharma.
They destroyed the banner of the Correct Dharma (Zhèngfǎ chuáng),
erected the evil banner of Māra (Mófān),
extinguished the torch of the Correct Dharma (Zhèngfǎ jù),
ignited the fire of defilements (fánnǎo huǒ),
caused the sea of the Correct Dharma to melt away,
ruined the bridge of the Correct Dharma,
sunk the boat of the Correct Dharma,
and submerged the tree of the Correct Dharma.
At that time, devas (tiān), nāgas (lóng), ghosts (guǐ), and spirits (shén) all developed ill will toward the Bhikṣus.
They scorned them and kept far away,
no longer providing protection.
And they simultaneously proclaimed:
"In seven days, the Buddha Dharma will be entirely extinguished!"
They wailed and wept mournfully,
saying to each other:
"When the day of recitation of the precepts (shuōjiè rì) arrives, the Bhikṣus will quarrel,
and the Tathāgata's (Rúlái) Correct Dharma will perish here."
The Upāsakas (Yōupósāi) heard the words of the devas,
and together they went to the assembly to remonstrate with the quarreling Bhikṣus.
When the fifteenth day arrived for the recitation of the precepts,
at that time, the Arhat (Luóhàn) Xiūluótuó of Mount Gāndhamāla (Jiàntuó Móluó Shān)
surveyed Jambudvīpa (Yánfútí):
"Where today
is there a monastic assembly planning to recite the precepts?"
He immediately went to Kuśāmbī (Jūshǎnmí).
At that time, that monastic assembly numbered a hundred thousand people,
but only this Arhat Xiūluótuó came.
Furthermore, there was one Tripiṭaka master whose name was Dìzǐ (Disciple).
This was the Tathāgata's last great assembly gathering.
At that time, the Karmadāna (Wéinà) distributed the tally sticks (shèluóchóu).
He announced to the Tripiṭaka master:
"The monastic assembly has gathered.
Now we should recite the Prātimokṣa (Bōluótímùchā)."
At that time, that Sthavira (Shàngzuò) replied:
"All the Tathāgata's disciples in Jambudvīpa (Yánfútí) have gathered here, numbering a hundred thousand.
Among such a crowd, I am the chief (shǒushǒu).
I am thoroughly conversant with the Tripiṭaka (Sānzàng), yet I do not study the Vinaya (jièlǜ).
How much less do the others have anything to learn?
For whom should I now recite the Vinaya?"
At that time, the Arhat Xiūluótuó stood before the Sthavira (Shàngzuò).
He pressed his palms together and addressed the Sthavira:
"Just recite the Prātimokṣa (Bōluótímùchā).
Just as when the Buddha was alive,
I have now completely studied the Dharma practiced by the great Bhikṣu assembly, such as Śāriputra (Shèlìfú) and Maudgalyāyana (Mùjiànlián).
Although the Tathāgata has passed into Nirvāṇa (miè) for a thousand years,
I have completely maintained the monastic regulations (lǜyí) established by him."
The Sthavira's disciples heard Bhikṣu Xiūluótuó say that he completely maintained the Vinaya established by the Tathāgata,
and they became enraged.
There was one disciple named Ānjiātuó.
He became extremely angry and resentful.
He rose from his seat and insulted that noble one (shèng):
"You are a junior Bhikṣu, foolish and ignorant, yet you insult my master!"
He immediately took a sharp knife and killed that noble person.
At that time, there was a ghost named Dàtímùfǎ.
He thought:
"In the world, there was only this one Arhat (Luóhàn),
yet he was murdered by the wicked Bhikṣu's disciple."
He held a Vajra (Jīngāng chǔ) and struck the disciple's head, causing him to die.
Then the Arhat's (Luóhàn) disciple,
seeing his master murdered, was unable to bear his fury and resentment.
He immediately killed the Tripiṭaka (Sānzàng) master.
At that time, all the devas and common people grieved and wept bitterly,
crying out, "Alas, how dreadful!"
"The Tathāgata's Correct Dharma is now entirely finished."
Immediately, this great earth shook in six ways.
Countless sentient beings wailed, roared, and wept.
They scattered in all directions.
At that time, the King of Kuśāmbī (Jūshǎnmí)
heard that the Bhikṣus had killed the Arhat (Luóhàn) and the Tripiṭaka (Sānzàng) Dharma Master.
His heart became anguished and regretful.
Those holding heterodox views (xiéjiàn) rushed to destroy stūpas and temples,
and murder Bhikṣus.
Following this, the Buddha Dharma suddenly and completely perished. The Buddha addressed Ānán:
After my Nirvāṇa (Níhuán),
when the Dharma is about to perish,
in the Evil Age of the Five Corruptions (Wǔ Zhuó È Shì), the path of Māra (Módào) will flourish.
Māra's Śramaṇas (Shāmén) will sabotage and confuse my Path.
They will wear common clothes beneath beautifully embroidered kasayas (jiāshā), garments of five colors.
They will drink wine, eat roasted meat, kill living beings, and be greedy for flavor.
They will have no compassion and will hate and envy one another.
At that time, there will be Bodhisattvas (Púsà) who diligently cultivate virtue.
They will be respected and esteemed by all people.
They will teach and transform with impartiality,
pitying the poor and caring for the elderly,
saving and nurturing the distressed and destitute.
They will constantly use sūtras and images
to instruct people in reverence and service,
creating various meritorious blessings (fú dé).
Their will and nature are gentle and good.
They do not harm or violate others.
They abandon their bodies to aid sentient beings,
not sparing themselves.
They practice patience, benevolence, and harmony.
If such a person exists,
All the demonic Bhikṣus mutually envied him.
They slandered, publicized his faults, expelled, and drove him away, not allowing him to stay.
Afterward, they themselves together did not cultivate morality/virtue.
The monasteries and temples became derelict, no longer being repaired.
They turned toward ruin and destruction.
They merely craved wealth and property.
They accumulated and did not distribute it.
They did not perform meritorious deeds.
They bought and sold slaves, farmed the fields, and planted crops.
They burned mountain forests and harmed living beings.
They had no compassion.
Slaves became Bhikṣus.
Maidservants became Bhikṣuṇīs.
They possessed no morality or virtue.
They indulged in lust and impurity and disorder.
Males and females were not segregated.
They caused the Way to become thin and weak.
It was all due to these types of people.
Some avoided government officials.
Relying on My Way (Buddhism).
They sought to become Bhikṣus.
They did not cultivate the precepts.
At the half-month and the end of the month.
Nominally, they preached the precepts.
Being weary, exhausted, and negligent.
They did not wish to listen.
They copied out the front and back (sections) briefly.
They were unwilling to speak completely.
The sūtras were not recited or read.
Even if there were readers.
They did not recognize the characters or sentences.
They forcefully claimed they were right, not consulting the enlightened ones.
They were arrogant, seeking fame, claiming to understand the heavens and predict the movements
of stars. They considered this glorious and noble, hoping people would make offerings.
After these demonic Bhikṣus die.
Their spirits shall fall into Wúzédi Yù (The Hell of No Moisture).
Among the Five Rebellious Sins, hungry ghosts, and animals—none shall they fail to pass through.
After the sins of Ganges-sand kalpas are finished.
They will then be born in remote lands where the Sānbǎo (Three Jewels) do not exist.
When the Dharma is about to perish.
Women will be diligent and constantly perform meritorious deeds.
Men will be negligent and arrogant, paying no heed to the words of the Dharma.
They see Śrāmaṇas as if looking at manure and dirt.
They have no faith.
The Dharma Wheel vanishes, and the devas weep tears.
Floods and droughts are erratic, and the five grains do not ripen.
Disasters and plagues spread, and those who die are numerous.
The common people suffer severely, and government officials seize and oppress them.
They do not cultivate righteousness, and all yearn for disorder.
Wicked people become increasingly numerous, and good people are extremely few.
Days and months hasten rapidly, and human lives become increasingly short.
At forty, their heads turn white; they barely live to sixty.
The lifespan of men is short.
The lifespan of women is long.
Seventy, eighty, ninety, or even up to one hundred years.
Great floods suddenly arise, arriving without warning.
People of the world do not believe, so they claim there is permanence.
Living beings of mixed species, regardless of whether noble or base.
They sink, drown, and float.
They drift; fish and turtles consume them. The Bodhisattva Bhikṣus are driven out by the multitude of demons and are not allowed to participate in the assemblies.
Bodhisattvas enter the mountains, places of merit and virtue, keeping themselves aloof and tranquil, finding joy in this.
Their lifespans are extended, and the devas guard and protect them.
Yuèguāng (Moonlight) will appear in the world, and they will be able to meet him.
Together, they will promote My Way for fifty-two years.
The Shǒuléngyán Jīng.
The Bānzhōu Sānmèi.
They will first perish and pass away.
The twelve divisions of the Sūtra Pitaka will quickly perish and vanish completely, no longer reappearing, and the characters will not be seen.
The robes (kāṣāya) of the Śrāmaṇas will naturally turn white.
After the sage king departs, My Dharma will be completely extinguished.
Just like an oil lamp, when it is about to go out, its light becomes intensely bright again.
Then it goes out.
When My Dharma is extinguished, it is also like the lamp going out.
After this, it will be difficult to govern (or maintain order).
After such a long time, Mílè (Maitreya) shall descend into the world and become a Buddha.
The world will be greatly peaceful, and toxic vapors will be eliminated.
Rain will moisten appropriately, and the five grains will flourish.
Trees will grow tall, and people will be eight zhàng tall.
All will live for eighty-four thousand years.
The number of living beings attaining liberation cannot be
reckoned or calculated.
In the past, there was a king named Yùmó Wáng.
He had four concubine sons.
The first name was Zhàomù.
The second name was Cōngmù.
The third name was Tiáofú Xiàng.
The fourth name was Nílóu. They were all intelligent, divinely martial, and possessed great majesty and virtue.
The First Lady (Queen) had a son named Chángshēng.
He was dull, weak, and ugly, despised by everyone.
The Lady said to the King.
"The four sons are divinely talented, but my son is dull and weak.
If he succeeds you, they will surely compete, oppress, and seize [the throne].
If Your Majesty expels the four sons, my heart will be at ease."
The King said.
"The four sons are benevolent and filial and have committed no fault or error.
Why should I expel them?"
The Lady spoke again.
"My heart suffers toil, truly concerning the state and country.
The four sons are heroic and martial, and the people each yearn to return to them.
If factions are established, once they compete, they will surely annihilate each other.
The great country’s prosperity will instead become another's possession.
I hope Your Majesty will plan for this."
The King said.
"Your words are right."
He immediately summoned the four sons.
And commanded them, saying.
"You have transgressed against Me.
I cannot bear to have you killed.
Each of you must quickly leave the country.
Overcome yourselves and plan for survival.
Do not return (to the capital) and bring future regret upon yourselves."
The four sons received the decree.
And immediately made preparations.
Their mother and their own sisters.
All requested to leave together.
At that time, many warriors and all the common people.
Were happy to follow them.
The King permitted all of them.
They arrived at the foot of the Snow Mountains and lived in the Zhíshù Lín (Straight Tree Forest).
The mothers became their wives/consorts, and they managed their settlement and stay.
Within a few years, those who submitted to their virtue were like a market (crowded).
They consequently became greatly flourishing.
They grew into a powerful state.
After a few years, the father wished to see them.
He sent messengers to report and summon them.
They all declined, citing distance, and did not return.
The King then sighed three times.
"My sons are capable.
They are able to establish themselves."
Due to this, he named their clan Shì; thus, there are the Shìzhǒng (Śākya clan).
Their distant ancestor was Nílóu Wáng.
Who begot Wūtóuluó.
Great-grandfather Wūtóuluó was the King of Jiāwéiluówèi Guó (Kapilavastu).
Who begot Qútóuluó.
Great-great-grandfather Qútóuluó Wáng.
Begot Shīxiūluó; grandfather Shīxiūluó Wáng.
Begot four sons, the eldest being Jìngfàn.
Jìngfàn Wáng encountered sickness.
His limbs and joints seemed to be dissolving.
His breathing was like a swift current.
All the treatments were useless.
His two younger brothers, the various kings, and the court officials said:
"The Great King has fundamentally done no evil,
sowing virtue without weariness.
You have nourished and allowed everyone to attain peace.
Why are you distressed and anxious?"
The King said:
"I regret not seeing Sìdá (Siddhārtha),
along with Nánduó, Ānánduó, Luóhóu, and the others,
to dispel my longing and desires."
Tears fell like rain.
At that time, the Buddha was in Wángshè Chéng.
The distance was fifty *yóuxún*.
The King was now becoming weaker,
fearing they would not arrive in time.
The Buddha knew his father's heart.
He immediately commanded Nánduó and Luóhóu, etc.,
and immediately used spiritual power to leap into the void,
suddenly appearing in Wéiluówèi.
He emitted a great bright light.
The people of the kingdom saw it from afar.
Raising their voices, they cried, saying:
"If the Great King dies,
this Shèyí kingdom, having lost him, will surely be cut off and destroyed!"
The people in the city
wept mournfully toward the Buddha, rolling about and throwing themselves down.
The Buddha said:
"Imperfection and separation have existed throughout antiquity and the present.
Life and death are suffering; only the Way is true."
The Buddha's light shone brilliantly, penetrating inside and out.
It shone upon the King's body.
The King said:
"What kind of light is this?
Since it touched my body, my suffering and illness have ceased.
Is this not the light I first saw from my Sìdá
returning from outside?"
The Buddha, Ānán, Luóyún, and others came riding through the sky.
The King's heart leaped with joy, and he unconsciously sat up.
He said: "I only wish the Rúlái would touch my body with his hand.
My body is in unbearable pain, like being pressed for oil.
If I see the Shìzūn, my suffering will immediately be removed."
The Buddha told Nánduó:
"Observe the King's original form: upright, majestic, his fame spreading far.
Now, seriously ill, emaciated and frail, he is scarcely recognizable.
Where are his appearance, strength, and fame now?"
The King, wholeheartedly putting his palms together,
said: "I only wish you would not worry.
Your virtue is pure and without blemish."
He rubbed the King's forehead and said:
"The King is a person of pure precepts and conduct.
Mental defilements have been cast aside.
You should only rejoice and ought not grieve or worry.
You should reflect deeply.
Meditate on the meaning of the various Sūtras and Dharma.
Regarding what is impermanent,
attain a firm and resolute will,
thereby planting good roots.
The King ought to rejoice."
Dàshèng Wáng wished:
"The Buddha, Nánduó, Ānánduó, and Luóyún—
these four sons having destroyed the net of Māra—the King is indeed joyful."
The Buddha preached the *Liàngmó Bōluó Běnshēng Jīng* for him.
The King attained the path of Ānàhán.
He grasped the Buddha's hand and placed it upon his heart.
The Buddha preached the Dharma again.
[The King] attained the fruit of Āluóhàn.
His life ended, and his breath ceased.
All the Zhū Shì wailed mournfully.
[They used] fragrant liquid to bathe his body.
They wrapped it in *jiébèi* and silk floss and placed it in the coffin.
Seven treasures adorned it, and a pearl net hung down surrounding the sides.
They lifted the coffin, placed the corpse on the Lion Throne, scattered flowers, and burned incense.
The Buddha and Nánduó were positioned at the head.
Ānán and Luóyún were positioned at the feet.
Nánduó and the others informed the Buddha:
"Looking back, we recall the upbringing [given by the King].
We beg to carry the coffin ourselves."
The Buddha, on behalf of future unfilial sentient beings who do not repay their upbringing,
personally desired to carry the coffin himself.
The Great Thousand World trembled.
All the mountains were like boats upon the waves.
Countless retinues from the Six Heavens of the Realm of Desire all came to attend the funeral.
The Sì Tiānwáng, leading hundreds of thousands of millions of ghosts and spirits, all joined in mourning.
The kings informed the Buddha:
"We are disciples of the Buddha.
We heard the Dharma from the Buddha
and achieved the state of Xūtuóhuán.
We ought to carry it."
The Buddha permitted the Sì Tiānwáng to carry it.
They immediately transformed their bodies into human forms.
They lifted the coffin with their hands,
placing it on their shoulders.
The Buddha's majestic light was like ten thousand suns.
Holding an incense burner in his hand,
he walked foremost,
arriving at the burial site.
One thousand Āluóhàn from Língjiù Shān came soaring through the void.
They bowed their heads at the Buddha's feet, requesting instructions on what to do.
The Buddha said:
"Go to the great ocean isles and retrieve Niútóu Zhāntán and various kinds of fragrant wood."
In the space of a finger-snap, they obtained the fragrant firewood.
The assembly worked together to use it to burn the coffin.
When the crowd saw the fire flare up,
their mournful wailing intensified.
The Buddha said:
"Suffering, emptiness, impermanence,
are like magical illusions, the moon in water, or images in a mirror."
When the burning of the body was finished,
they extinguished the fire with milk.
They collected the bones and placed them in a diamond casket.
They immediately worked together to erect a Stūpa.
The assembly consulted [the Buddha], asking where the spirit was reborn.
The Buddha said:
"He was reborn in Jìngjū Tiān."
The Buddha ascended to Dāolì Tiān.
He entered Huānxǐ Yuán.
He stayed beneath the Bōlìzhìduōluó tree.
He observed the three-month *Ānjū*.
He emitted light from his pores, illuminating the Great Thousand Realm.
The sons of heaven did not know the reason.
The Buddha told Wénshū:
"You go to my mother and tell her that I am here.
I hope Mother will briefly condescend to come."
[Wénshū] went to Móyé herself.
Móyé's milk flowed naturally.
[She thought]: "If this is Sìdá,
the milk ought to enter his mouth."
The milk from both breasts flowed out,
and entered the Buddha's mouth from afar.
Móyé was joyful.
The earth universally trembled.
Various exquisite flowers and fruits bloomed and ripened out of season.
She immediately told Wénshū: "The mother and son have come, joyful and peaceful as never before."
Together, they went to the Buddha's place.
The Buddha saw his mother from afar and said:
"The experiences undergone by the body are paired with suffering and joy.
You should cultivate Nièpán in order to seek eternal separation."
Móyé, with undivided concentration, threw her five limbs to the ground, focusing sincerely on right mindfulness, and the bonds of defilement disappeared and were suppressed.
The Buddha preached the Dharma for her, and she immediately recognized her past lives.
She attained the fruit of Xūtuóhuán.
She immediately informed the Buddha:
"I have now been freed from the prison of life and death."
The entire assembly said:
"May all sentient beings attain liberation."
[The Buddha] widely converted humans and devas, resulting in great benefit.
When the three months were about to end,
he instructed Jiūmóluó:
"You may now descend to Yánfútí.
The Rúlái will soon enter Nièpán."
At that time, the assembly was distressed and worried.
"We did not know earlier that [the Buddha] would soon enter Nièpán.
The eye of the world is about to be extinguished.
How bitter this is!"
Dìshì commanded the ghosts and spirits to build three flights of jeweled stairs.
Móyé wept.
They parted there.
[The Buddha] set foot upon the jeweled stairs.
Fàn Wáng held the canopy.
The Sì Tiān stood attending on the left and right.
The four assemblies sang, chanted, and praised him.
Devas performed music filling the void.
Scattering flowers and burning incense, [the Buddha] arrived in Yánfútí.
Móhē Bōshé Bōtí,
of the family name Qú Tánmí, sought permission from the Buddha to leave home and sorrowfully requested this up to three times. The Buddha did not permit it.
She withdrew and stayed outside the gate.
Wearing filthy, ragged clothes,
standing barefoot,
sighing and weeping mournfully.
Ānán asked,
saying: Why do you weep?
She replied:
Women are not allowed to leave home; I am sad about this.
Ānán stopped her and reported to the Buddha:
I heard from the Buddha
that if women are diligent, they can attain the Four Fruits.
Now Dà Àidào,
sincerely desires this joy. The Buddha said:
Do not allow
women to enter my Law and Discipline and become shāmén.
For instance, if a family has many daughters and few sons, the family will surely decline and weaken.
If women leave home, the pure Brahma-practice will not long endure.
Also, like weeds mingling with the grain, the good crops are damaged and destroyed.
Women entering the Dharma is also like this.
Ānán said:
Dà Àidào has much good will.
When the Buddha was first born, she herself raised and nurtured him until he became an adult.
The Buddha said:
She has great faith and good will; she has been gracious to me.
I, towards Àidào, also have great kindness.
Through me, she was able to take refuge in the Sān Bǎo, not doubt the Four Noble Truths, establish the Five Faculties, have faith, and uphold the Five Precepts.
Even if someone offers their body in homage, it does not compare to this.
If women wish to become shāmén,
the Eight Revered Rules must not be violated.
They must study them for their entire lives.
For instance, to prevent water, one must skillfully manage dikes and dams.
Do not allow any leaks or losses.
If they can do this,
they may enter the Law and Discipline.
Ānán fully informed Àidào.
Àidào was joyful and thus left home.
Becoming a Dà Bǐqiūní.
She practiced the Law and Discipline reverently.
Consequently, she attained realization.
Later, along with various elder nuns,
she went to where Ānán was.
(She said:) We have long practiced the Brahma-conduct,
and have already seen the Truth.
How can we be made to bow down to young, small bhikṣus?
Ānán reported to the Buddha.
The Buddha said:
Stop, stop! Do not speak of this.
If I had not allowed women to leave home,
external practitioners, heterodox learners, and all worthy ones
would all offer the four kinds of support.
They would unbind their hair and spread it on the ground, humbly inviting me to walk upon it.
My True Dharma would surely abide for a thousand years.
Because women were admitted, it will now only last five hundred (years).
Àidào heard this, was joyful, and respectfully carried it out. She resided in the Wáng Yuán jīngshě and was about to relinquish her life.
She said:
I cannot bear to see a time when the world lacks a Tathāgata and Arhats extinguished (in Nirvāṇa).
I should first cause my spirit to rest in the original nothingness.
The Buddha perceived this intention,
and informed Ānán.
Ānán’s body drooped; his heart was blocked and he was unconscious (with grief).
The Buddha said:
Do you think that the Fivefold Dharma, the Four Foundations of Mindfulness, and the Eightfold Noble Path will leave with them?
He replied:
No.
But I only consider that seven days after the Buddha was born, the queen mother died.
As a compassionate mother, she had kindness towards the World-Honored One.
The Buddha said:
You say the grace of nursing is profound, and this favor is difficult to repay.
I have already provided the teaching,
(so that she) took refuge in the Three Honored Ones.
Hearing the Truths of Suffering, Accumulation, Cessation, and the Path,
her Eye of Wisdom became clear.
She extinguished all attachments to existence,
and attained non-attachment.
This grace also surpasses Xūmí.
Àidào, together with five hundred novice nuns,
came to the Buddha's place. She fully stated her intention mentioned above.
She rubbed the Buddha's feet with her hands and said:
From now on, I will no longer see the Most Perfectly Enlightened One.
She circumambulated the Buddha three times and returned to the monastery.
She and the five hundred novice nuns performed eighteen transformations.
Shining brightly towards the devas above, they simultaneously entered Nirvāṇa.
The Buddha told Ānán:
You enter the city, go to the house of Yēyóu Lǐ Jiā, and announce that the Buddha's foster mother and the five hundred elders have passed into Nirvāṇa.
Ānán entered the city at dawn and reached Lǐ Jiā’s gate.
He fully stated the matter.
Those who heard lifted up their voices in sorrow, collapsed onto the ground, and held back tears,
and said: From now on, we will no longer look up and behold the spiritual powers! How profound is this grief!
Ānán said:
The Buddha said: Although Heaven and Earth endure long, what begins must eventually end.
The Three Realms are impermanent,
just like an illusion or a dream.
The living seek immortality.
When gathered, they hope not to be separated,
but ultimately, this cannot be attained.
Lǐ Jiā’s heart understood, and he then went to the houses of the various Brahman Lǐ Jiā.
He informed them, saying:
The Buddha encourages all worthy ones to prepare five hundred burial furnishings,
to be offered to the five hundred novice nuns.
The Brahman Lǐ Jiā prepared them and sent them into the monastery.
The central door of the monastery was closed; when they entered, they opened it.
They wished to proceed to the Lecture Hall.
There was a female novice nun
who announced, saying:
My teacher has entered samādhi.
Be cautious and do not disturb her.
They replied:
She is dead, not in samādhi.
The novice nun collapsed her body and fell silent.
After a long time, she revived.
Lamenting grievously, she wailed, saying:
Who will now teach and transform us?
The sacred instruction is severed!
Lǐ Jiā spoke to the novice nun, saying:
Although kindness and affection meet,
