they must eventually separate.
You must establish your resolve and strive to attain Arhatship.
After the cremation was completed, they carried the śarīra to the Buddha's place.
The Buddha told Ānán:
Face east, clasp your hands, kneel down on your right knee, and say:
Those who possess straight faith, straight karma, the Three Spirits, the Six Wisdoms, and have fully accumulated the spiritual power of the Path, all come!
The five hundred novice nuns have all now passed away happily.
It is proper that a Dharma assembly be held.
The four directions responded immediately.
From each of the four directions, two hundred and fifty Arhats flew there.
The Buddha told Ānán:
Place the śarīra in the bowl and set it in my hands.
Ānán presented it, and the Buddha received it with both hands.
He announced to all the bhikṣus and the Lǐ Jiā:
This (body) was originally filthy,
stupid, fierce, and violently temperamental,
full of jealousy, envy, and secret schemes.
It ruined the Path and corrupted virtue.
Yet, they were able to eliminate the fierce and foolish, and perform the conduct of a great person,
attaining the Path of the Arhat.
Their spirits ascended to the original nothingness.
How mighty they were!
It is proper for all of you to erect temples and appropriately perform offerings.
All said:
Yes, truly. Thereupon, the Four Assemblies, devas, humans, dragons, and ghosts,
each established stupas and temples and offered various forms of homage.
Xīdá Tàizǐ (Crown Prince Siddhārtha) had two wives.
One name was Qú pí yē.
The second name was Yé shū tuó luó.
Qú pí yē was a precious daughter, and thus had never been pregnant.
Yé shū tuó luó, on the night the Púsà (Bodhisattva) left home,
realized she was pregnant.
The Púsà practiced suffering (asceticism) for six years.
Yé shū tuó luó did not give birth for six years.
The Śakyas (Zhū Shì) criticized her.
How could this have happened when the Púsà had left home?
Yé shū tuó luó said:
"I have no other sin.
The child I carry truly is the Tàizǐ's residual body (heir)."
The Śakyas said:
"Why has it been so long without birth?"
She replied:
"This is not known to me."
The Śakyas assembled to deliberate.
They heard the King wished to punish her according to the law.
Qú pí yē petitioned the King:
"I have always lived together with Yé shū tuó luó.
I serve as her witness, knowing she is innocent.
Wait until her son is born.
See if he resembles his father or not.
What is the delay in punishing her?"
The King then leniently postponed the matter.
When the Púsà's ascetic practices were completed, on the night of his first becoming a Fó (Buddha),
she gave birth to Luó hóu luó (Rāhula).
The King saw that he resembled his father.
His love and affection made him forget his worries.
He spoke to his officials, saying:
"Although my son left, now having his child is no different from having my son."
Yé shū tuó luó's bad reputation was already established, and she wished to eliminate the bad name.
The Fó returned to Jiā pí luó (Kapilavastu).
He converted the Śakya youths.
At that time, Jìngfàn Wáng (King Śuddhodana) and Yé shū tuó luó
often invited the Fó to enter the palace for a meal.
At this time, Yé shū tuó luó gave Luó hóu luó a hundred-flavored Huānxǐ Wán (Joy Pills), which he respectfully offered up.
The Fó used his divine power to transform five hundred Ā luó hàn (Arhats).
All were exactly the same as the Fó's appearance, without distinction.
Luó hóu luó was seven years old.
He carried the Huānxǐ Wán directly before the Fó and respectfully presented them to the Shìzūn (World-Honored One).
At this time, the Fó retracted his divine power, and the Bhikkhu forms reappeared.
Inside their bowls, all were empty.
Only the Fó's bowl was full of Huānxǐ Wán.
Yé shū tuó luó asked:
"In the past, what was the cause for me to be pregnant for six years?"
The Fó replied:
"When Luó hóu luó was in a past life,
he was once a Guó Wáng (King).
At that time, a Xiānrén (Immortal) possessing the five divine powers came to the kingdom.
He spoke to the King, saying:
'O King, you govern thieves according to the law.
Please punish my crime.
I presumptuously stole the King's water.
I used the King's willow stick (for cleaning teeth).
This was taking what was not given.'
The King said:
'When I first ascended the throne, I issued an order that water and willow sticks
should be bestowed upon everyone.'
The Xiānrén said:
'Although the King has already bestowed them, my mind was still confused.
I pray that I may be punished now, so as not to incur future sin.'
The King said:
'If you must truly wish this, wait briefly while I enter the palace.'
He entered the palace and only came out after six days.
The Xiānrén was hungry and thirsty.
The Xiānrén said:
'I fear the King is deliberately punishing me with this (delay).'
The King came out, apologized, and left the place.
Because of this, in five hundred successive lives, he was constantly six years in the womb."
Go to Jiāpílúo Chéng (Kapilavastu).
Inquire about my father, my mother, my uncle, and my Yímǔ (aunt).
Console Rólóuluó's (Rāhula’s) mother.
Make her sever her affectionate attachment.
Allow Rólóuluó to be released to become a Shāmí (novice monk).
The affectionate joy between mother and son lasts but a moment.
Dying, they fall into Diyù (hell) and are mutually unaware.
When Rólóu attains the Dao, he will return and save his mother.
Forever cutting off Saṇsāra (birth and death), just as I have now.
Mùlián arrived at the kingdom.
He fully conveyed the Buddha's intent.
Yéshūtuóluó (Yaśodharā) heard that the Buddha had sent an envoy.
She took Rólóu and ascended a tall tower.
She commanded the supervising officials to tightly seal the doors and gates, ensuring they were all secured.
Mùlián flew up.
Yéshūtuóluó, having no alternative, paid obeisance.
She asked:
Is the Shìzūn (World-Honored One) well?
What purpose does sending this high-ranking person (Mùlián) serve?
Mùlián said: Prince Rólóu is already nine years old.
He should be allowed to leave home and study the Holy Dao.
He fully relayed the Buddha's intent.
She replied:
When Shìjiā Rúlái (Tathāgata Śākya) was the Crown Prince, he took me as his wife.
I served the Crown Prince as one serves a Tiānshén (heavenly deity).
Before three full years had passed, he abandoned the joys of the five desires.
He vaulted over the palace walls.
He fled to the royal fields.
He vowed that upon attaining the Dao,
he promised to return.
Having attained the Dao and returned to the kingdom,
he did not see any relatives.
He forgot his kindness and former connections.
He treated us worse than strangers on the road.
He left me to guard my loneliness and endure poverty.
Now he takes my son to be his dependent (follower).
What cruelty is like this?
The Crown Prince, having attained the Dao, speaks of Cíbēi (compassion).
If he separates mother and son now, what compassion is there?
Return to the Shìzūn and tell him what I have stated.
Mùlián took his leave and withdrew.
He returned to Jìngfàn Wáng (King Śuddhodana) and fully related the preceding matters.
The King heard these words and immediately informed the Fūrén (Madam) Bōshépōtí (Prajāpatī):
My son, Xīdá (Siddhārtha),
has sent to welcome Luóyún (Rāhula) to cultivate and study the sacred Dharma.
His mother is a woman entangled in foolish attachment, unable to let go of her love.
You should go and admonish her so that her heart may awaken.
The Fūrén went back and forth repeatedly.
Yéshūtuóluó still refused to listen.
She said to the Fūrén:
When I was at home,
kings from eight kingdoms
competed to seek my hand.
My parents did not consent.
Because the Crown Prince's talent and skill surpassed others,
therefore, my parents gave me to him.
If the Crown Prince did not intend to remain in the world,
why did he earnestly and desperately seek me?
When a man takes a wife,
it is precisely for affection and harmony,
and for the continuation of descendants.
This is the correct ritual of the world.
Since the Crown Prince has already departed,
now he demands Luóhóu as well,
permanently severing the royal line.
What meaning is there in this?
The Fūrén heard this
and fell silent, unable to speak.
The Buddha sent a manifested being (phantom).
The voice from the sky said:
Do you remember your vow from ages past?
When I was a Púsà (Bodhisattva),
I used five hundred silver coins to buy five lotus stalks from you to offer to Dìngguāng Fó (Dīpaṅkara Buddha).
You requested to entrust two flowers, begging that in every life you might always be my wife.
I told you:
As a Púsà, I practice universal charity (Bùshī).
You immediately made a vow:
In every life, the kingdom, cities, wife, children, and even my own body,
I would grant them all to you to dispense.
Why today do you begrudge Luóhóu?
Yéshūtuóluó instantly awakened, recalling it as if it had happened yesterday.
Her love for her son slightly abated.
She sent for Mùlián, calling him back to apologize.
She grasped Luóhóu's hand and earnestly instructed him.
They separated with tears and weeping.
Luóhóu reported to his mother:
I will see the Shìzūn and attend upon him.
I hope mother does not worry.
I will soon return to pay respects.
Jìngfàn Wáng instructed the noble clans:
You must each send one son
to accompany my grandson.
Immediately fifty people (sons)
followed and went to the place of the Buddha.
They bowed their heads and faces in obeisance.
The Buddha instructed Ānán (Ānanda) to shave the heads of Luóhóu and the fifty young noblemen.
All were ordered to leave home.
He commanded Shèlìfú (Śāriputra) to be their Héshàng (Upādhyāya).
Dà Mùlián (Mahāmaudgalyāyana) acted as the Shé lì (Ācārya) and administered the ten precepts.
The Buddha, for the fifty Shāmí,
spoke about the karmic retribution for the past sins of Shàntíluó and others, causing them great distress.
They all said to the Buddha:
The Héshàng possesses great wisdom and virtue and receives the highest offerings.
We young ones are foolish and lack virtue.
If we consume the excellent charity of others,
in future lives, we will suffer like Shàntíluó.
Therefore, we are truly anxious.
We wish the Buddha would graciously permit us to abandon the path (Dào),
hoping to avoid sin and fault.
The Buddha said:
Suppose two people were starving.
They suddenly encountered a royal messenger who offered fine food and drink.
They ate greedily and became overly full.
One person had wisdom.
He consulted a doctor, took emetic medicine,
observed strict moderation and rest,
and managed to escape disaster and ultimately preserve his lifespan.
The other person lacked wisdom.
He killed living creatures for sacrifice in order to seek salvation for his life.
The undigested food caused severe cramping.
Dying of a heart ailment,
he was reborn in Diyù.
Fearing sin and wanting to return home,
this is the unwise person.
You possess good roots (causes).
You have encountered and met me.
Taking the medicine saves you from suffering.
You will certainly attain the Undying (Nirvāṇa).
Luóhóu heard this,
and his mind opened and his intentions became clear.
Later, when the Buddha returned to the palace,
people doubted Jūyí (Yaśodharā):
The Prince abandoned the kingdom for twelve years.
How could she have given birth to a child?
The Buddha enlightened his father, the King, saying:
Jūyí guarded her chastity, was pure and faithful, without blemish.
She transformed many Bhīkṣu (monks), making them all like the Buddha.
When Luóyún was seven, he was asked, "Who is your father?"
Luóyún immediately went straight forward to the Buddha and paid obeisance.
He took the ring given to him by his mother as a token of trust
and handed it to the Shìzūn.
In the past, Luóyún.
When he had not yet attained the Dào,
his nature was coarse and fierce, and his words lacked sincerity and credibility.
The Buddha instructed Luóyún,
“You go and stay in the Xiántí [Xián Tí] monastery.
Guard your mouth, restrain your mind, and diligently cultivate the Sūtras and precepts.”
Luóyún accepted the instruction, paid homage, and left.
He stayed for ninety days,
feeling shame and repenting inwardly.
Day and night he did not cease (his efforts).
The Buddha went to see him.
Luóyún was joyful.
He went forward, paid homage at the Buddha’s feet, set up a rope bed (chair), and received the Buddha’s bowl and staff.
The Buddha sat upon the rope bed.
He spoke to Luóyún, saying,
“Fetch a wash basin and water to wash My feet.”
After the feet were washed,
the Buddha said to Luóyún,
“Is this water usable for food, drink, washing, or rinsing now?”
Luóyún replied,
“This water was originally truly clean.
Now that it has washed the feet, it has received dirt and grime,
and it cannot be used again.”
The Buddha said to Luóyún,
“You are also like this.
Although you are My son and a king’s grandson,
you abandoned worldly glory and wealth and became a Shāmen (monk).
Yet you do not practice diligence, restrain your mind, or guard your mouth.
The filth and impurity of the Three Poisons [Sāndú] fill your heart,
and it is also like this
water which cannot be used again.”
The Buddha further said to Luóyún,
“Although the wash basin is empty, can it be used to hold food and drink?”
Luóyún replied, “It cannot.”
“Why is that? Because it bears the name ‘wash basin’
and has previously received impurity.”
The Buddha said to Luóyún,
“You are also like this.
Although you are a Shāmen,
your mouth lacks sincerity and trustworthiness.
Your nature is stubborn and harsh.
You do not strive for diligence.
You have previously earned a bad name,
just like the wash basin,
which is unfit to hold food.”
The Buddha used His toe
to push the wash basin away.
It immediately tumbled, jumped, and fell several times before finally stopping.
The Buddha said to Luóyún,
“Do you regret or fear this wash basin being broken?”
Luóyún replied to the Buddha,
“A foot-washing vessel is a thing of low value.
Although I feel some regret in my heart, I am not overly concerned.”
The Buddha said to Luóyún,
“You are also like this.
Although you are a Shāmen,
if you do not restrain your body and mouth, speak coarsely and slander others greatly,
you will not be accepted by the assembly, nor cherished by the wise.
When the body dies and the spirit departs, you will circulate through the Three Evil Paths [Sāntú].
Self-born and self-dying, suffering and vexation will be immeasurable.
You will not be loved or cherished by the Buddhas and the wise Sages,
just as you said you do not cherish the wash basin.”
When Luóyún heard this,
he felt shame, fear, and apprehension.
The Buddha addressed Luóyún,
“Listen to Me tell a simile.
In the past, a king possessed a great elephant,
fierce, strong, and capable in battle.
The king raised an army, wishing to attack a rebellious country.
The elephant was fitted out, and the troops were deployed to march in formation.
The elephant, however, concealed its trunk, fearing combat and refusing to fight.
The mahout rejoiced, knowing the elephant was protecting its body.
Why was that?
Because the elephant’s trunk is soft and brittle; if struck by an arrow, it dies instantly.
It must protect its mouth just like this.”
“The great elephant protected its trunk and did not fight.”
Luóyún heard the Buddha’s earnest and sincere instruction,
was moved and roused himself to effort.
He attained the path of Arhat [Luóhàn Dào].
The Buddha’s younger half-brother, Sūntuóluó Nántuó,
was one *zhàng*, five *chǐ*, and four *cùn* tall.
The Buddha and Ānán were entering the city in Jiāwéiluōjié Guó to beg for food.
Nántuó saw them from a high tower.
He descended and performed a prostration, saying,
“The Rúlái ought to be the Wheel-Turning Sage King [Zhuǎnlún Shèngwáng].
Why do you humiliate Yourself by carrying a bowl and begging for food?”
He took the bowl and filled it with delicious food.
The Buddha immediately returned to Nígūlèi Yuán and told His attendants,
“If Nántuó comes out, do not accept the bowl, but let him bring it himself.”
Nántuó carried the bowl to the Buddha’s location.
His wife came out and instructed him, saying, “Wait until you return before you eat.”
He offered the bowl, urging the Buddha to receive it quickly.
The Buddha said,
“Since you have arrived here,
it is now proper that you leave home (become a monk).”
He then applied His divine power and confined him in a quiet room.
After a long time, the others would take turns on duty sequentially.
Nántuó rejoiced, saying,
“I have an opportunity now that they are busy; I will escape and return home.”
At that time, Nántuó performed everything he was supposed to do without omission.
But the nature spirits followed him.
When he drew water and the bucket was full, it spontaneously spilled out.
On the ground that he cleaned, grass and soil immediately grew again.
When he closed the doors and windows,
the doors immediately opened again.
Nántuó thought,
“If there is anything lost, the family can certainly afford to compensate for it.”
He took off the three monastic robes,
changed into other clothes,
secretly followed a small path,
and avoided the Buddha to return home.
He had not gone far
when he encountered the Rúlái directly.
He ran toward a large tree
to hide himself.
The tree instantly appeared behind him.
The Buddha used His divine power,
pulling the tree up and suspending it in midair.
Nántuó entered the base of the tree (to hide).
The Buddha said,
“Why have you come here?”
He remained silent and ashamed.
The Buddha asked him repeatedly,
“Where do you intend to go?”
He replied,
“To return home and see my wife.”
The Buddha said,
“O seeker of the Dào,
you cling to lustful craving and disregard the future calamity of being burned.”
“I will now take you up to heaven for observation.
You must focus your mind and harbor no fear.”
The Buddha took him up to heaven.
They saw a palace,
adorned with the Seven Treasures, attended by countless celestial maidens.
But it had no husband.
Nántuó asked the Buddha,
“What celestial palace is this,
that alone has no husband?”
The Buddha said,
“You may ask them yourself.”
Nántuó asked them.
The celestial maidens replied,
“The Buddha’s brother, Nántuó,
if he upholds the precepts, is destined to be born here.”
He returned and fully reported this to the Buddha.
The Buddha said,
“Diligently cultivate the Pure Practice; you will certainly be born here shortly.”
Then, again using divine power,
He led him to the hells [Dìyù].
They passed along the exterior of the Mountain of Iron Rings [Tiěwéi Shān].
They saw a blind monkey.
The Buddha asked Nántuó,
“How does your wife, Sūntuólì, compare to this monkey?”
He replied,
“Sūntuólì
is the absolute finest among women.
How can she be compared to this?”
The Buddha said,
“Compared to the celestial maidens, she is also hundreds of millions of times worse.”
They traveled throughout the hells,
seeing various kinds of suffering and pain.
There was one cauldron of fire,
surrounded by prison guards.
The liquid was boiling and the fire was raging,
but no sinner could be seen.
Nántuó reported to the Buddha,
“Why is there no sinner here alone?”
The Buddha said,
“You ask the guards yourself.”
The prison guards replied,
“The prince of sweet dew [Gānlù Wángzǐ], Nántuó,
whose feelings of lust and craving are heavy,
and who relies on his nobility to slight others,
will be born here after death.”
Nántuó turned pale,
and urgently asked the World-Honored One [Shìzūn],
seeking release from the hells.
The Buddha preached the subtle and profound Dharma,
causing him to attain the path of enlightenment [Dàochǎng].
The first name was Ānán.
His height was one *zhàng*, five *chǐ*, and three *cùn*.
The second name was Tiáodá.
His height was one *zhàng*, five *chǐ*, and four *cùn*. Bái Jìng Wáng went to the place of the Buddha.
He saw that Jiāshè’s followers were ugly in appearance.
He immediately gathered the royal clan members and said:
“Āyí said,
‘If the Buddha had not left home, he would have become a Sagely King ruling the Four Continents.’
His attendants should have been extremely handsome.
Now, look at these disciples—they are greatly lacking in appearance.
If anyone wishes to pursue the Way and whose demeanor is adequate,
I permit them to join the monastic ranks and bring glory to the World-Honored One (Shìzūn).”
They all said,
“Excellent.”

Tiáodá said, “We, being the sons of the prince, now abandon worldly glory and leave home to pursue the Way. We should certainly be equipped with clothing and decorations of the utmost worldly refinement.”
Their elephants, horses, and chariots were worth ten thousand pieces of gold.
On that day, they set out splendidly.
Onlookers filled the road, and their caps and headcloths fell to the ground.
The horse ridden by Qúhélí planted all four feet on the ground and made a bird cry.
The physiognomists observed them and predicted:
“The others will all attain the Way,
but these two men are not auspicious.”
They all went together to the place of the Buddha
requesting to become *shāméng* (monks).
Their stubborn natures were subdued, and there was none who did not gladly accept (the teaching).
Húfàn Wáng had two sons.
The first name was Móhēnán.
The second name was Ānàlǜ.
Ānàlǜ was cherished and beloved by his mother.
Móhēnán said,
“Many members of the Śākya clan are pursuing the Way.
Why is our family the only one not doing so?
Let one manage worldly affairs,
and let the other seek to leave home.”
Ānàlǜ found household duties bothersome and tedious.
He petitioned his mother to leave home.
His mother said,
“If Bátí goes, then I will allow you.”
His repeated requests did not cease, and eventually, both were permitted.
Bátí requested to wait seven years to enjoy the pleasure of the five desires.
Ānàlǜ said,
“Human life is impermanent; it is difficult to guarantee.”
(Bátí) then requested one year, and finally even seven days.
After seven days, eight Śākya princes,
and Yōubōlí as the ninth,
each adorned a precious elephant.
They rode them out of the city.
They removed their clothes, as well as the elephants and horses,
and handed them to Yōubōlí, saying:
“You should live by depending on us.
We are now leaving home. We give you these clothes and elephants as means of livelihood.”
Yōubōlí then hung the clothes on a tree.
He thought:
“If someone takes them, I will give them away.”
He went with them to the place of the Buddha and also requested to leave home.
(The princes) begged that Yōubōlí be ordained first,
to eliminate their own arrogance.
Ānàlǜ was next.
Gānlùfàn Wáng had two sons.
The first name was Típó.
The second name was Bátí.
Bátí was beloved by his mother.
He asked his mother to allow him to leave home.
His mother said,
“If Ānàlǜ leaves home, I will also allow you.”
Later, they both did so.
They went to the place of the Buddha, requesting to leave home.
“Our parents have already given permission; we wish you would kindly grant us salvation (ordination).”
At that time, Bátí was meditating alone beneath a tree in a burial ground.
As the night passed, he shouted loudly, proclaiming, "Great bliss! Great bliss!"
The nearby *bǐqiū* reported this to the Buddha.
The Buddha summoned Bátí and asked why he was happy.
Bátí said,
“When I was originally
at home, both inside and out, I constantly used swords and staffs to protect myself, yet I still felt fear.
Now I dwell alone among the graves, my body hair does not stand up, and the release (from home life) is great bliss.”
The Buddha said, “Excellent.”
newly inherited the throne.
Immediately, he formed this thought:
"I should first marry a Shì (Śākya) woman."
He immediately informed a minister,
"Take my name and go to Jiāpíluówèi (Kapilavastu),
and request a marriage with a daughter there."
Five hundred members of the Shì clan gathered in one place, all greatly enraged.
"Our family is a great lineage.
On what grounds should we form a marriage alliance with the son of a maidservant?"
Some said they should give her,
others said they should not.
At that time, Móhē Nán (Mahānāma) spoke to the Shì clan members, saying,
"Bōsīnì Wáng is a violent and wicked man.
He might destroy our kingdom."
At that time, Móhē Nán had a daughter born to a maidservant.
Her appearance was beautiful and proper.
After bathing and dressing her,
he used a feathered jeweled carriage
and personally escorted her
to Bōsīnì Wáng.
He then reported to the King, saying,
"This is my daughter;
she can form the marriage bond."
The King was delighted
and immediately appointed this woman as the First Fū Rén (Lady).
After a few days, she conceived
and gave birth to a son.
He was uniquely handsome, extraordinary in the world.
The King assembled diviners to give the son a name.
The diviners said:
"When requesting the Fū Rén, the Shì clan members debated
whether to give her, resulting in reciprocal Lúlí (Glass/Deceit)."
Thus, the Crown Prince was named Lúlí (Virūḍhaka). He was approaching eight years old.
The King instructed him, saying,
"You may go to Jiāpíluówèi to learn the various archery techniques."
He drove a large elephant, accompanied by many attendants,
and went to Móhē Nán’s house.
Móhē Nán gathered five hundred boys to study together.
A new lecture hall was erected,
resembling a celestial palace.
(The Śākyas said:) "We should first invite the Buddha and the Sangha to make offerings within it, thereby receiving measureless blessings."
They spread out cushions,
hung up banners and canopies,
sprinkled the ground with fragrant water,
and burned various famous incenses.
Prince Lúlí arrived at the lecture hall
and ascended the Lion Throne.
When the Shì clan members saw him, they cried out, "The son of a maidservant!"
They dragged him outside the gate
and threw him onto the ground.
"These members of the Shì lineage have greatly humiliated me.
When I later inherit the throne, you must remind me of this matter."
His father, the King, passed away.
The Crown Prince succeeded to the throne.
The ascetic reminded the King.
The King commanded his ministers
to assemble the four divisions of the army
and go to conquer the Shì lineage.
When they arrived at Jiāpíluóyuè,
the World-Honored One (Shìzūn) went to meet them and sat beneath a withered tree,
seated in the lotus position.
The Prince saw him from afar, descended from his carriage, and performed a reverence.
He asked,
"There are other good trees; why are you sitting here?"
The Buddha said,
"The shade of one’s own kin
is superior to that of outsiders."
"Today, the World-Honored One is here for his kin; I should not attack."
The Brahmin insisted on the plan,
and the King again raised the army.
Mùlián (Maudgalyāyana) addressed the Buddha,
"King Lúlí is going to attack the Shì lineage.
I wish to move his four divisions of the army and throw them to another region.
Or I wish to lift them out into the void.
Or I wish to move and place them into the sea.
Or I wish to move and place them between the Tiěwéi Mountains.
Or I wish to move the people and place them in a great kingdom in another region.
Or I wish to cover the city with an iron cage."
The Buddha said,
"You have wisdom and virtue,
but ultimately you cannot securely settle
the people of Shèyí Guó (Śākya kingdom).
There are seven things for sentient beings
that cannot be avoided:
one is birth, two is aging, three is sickness, four is death, five is offense, six is blessing, and seven is cause and condition.
Though the mind wishes to avoid them, one cannot ultimately escape.
How can one overturn their past karma?"
Mùlián’s intention was ultimately unwavering.
He accordingly took four or five thousand acquaintances
and put them all inside his bowl.
He lifted the bowl and placed it in the void near the stellar constellations.
The Shì clan members also assembled their four divisions of troops
and went out one yóuxún (yojana)
to meet King Lúlí.
Within one yóuxún, the Shì clan members
saw King Lúlí from afar.
Their arrows either pierced the ears or the topknots;
their bowstrings, weapons, banners, and standards were all destroyed,
but ultimately, they did not injure any person.
At that time, King Lúlí felt great terror.
He told his ministers,
"Look at these arrows—where do they come from?
If they had intended to harm us, we would certainly have all perished."
He ordered the return to Shèwèi (Śrāvastī).
The ascetic Brahmin said,
"Great King, do not fear.
The Shì clan members uphold the precepts; they do not even harm insects,
much less people.
It is proper to advance now."
The King then followed this advice.
The Shì clan members indeed retreated and returned inside the city.
King Lúlí said,
"You must quickly open the city gates!
If you do not, I will kill you all."
A boy in the city,
only fifteen years old,
named Shēmó (Kṣema),
ascended the wall and fought alone.
He injured many,
scattering the enemy army
who hid in holes in the earth.
told the boy,
"You have disgraced our family name!
Who among us does not know how to fight?
The Shì clan members cultivate goodness
and do not kill insects or ants,
much less human lives!
One of us could oppose ten thousand;
we could easily destroy the army.
But killing human lives
leads to rebirth in hell after death.
If reborn among humans, the lifespan will be short.
You should leave quickly now; there is no need to stay."
Shēmó immediately left the country.
King Lúlí’s army returned and arrived at the gate.
The wicked Māra Bōxún (Pāpīyas) transformed into the shape of a Shì clan member
and shouted for them to quickly open the gate.
The Shì clan members opened the gate.
King Lúlí said,
"Since the Shì multitudes are numerous,
bury all their legs
and have fierce elephants trample them to death."
He selected five hundred Shì women
and brought them to the King's location.
At that time, Móhē Nán requested a wish from the King.
The King immediately granted it.
Móhē Nán said,
"I will now immerse myself in the water. According to how fast or slow I am, allow
the Shì clan members to flee as they wish.
If I emerge from the water, kill anyone who remains."
The King said, "Excellent."
He immediately entered the water,
tied his hair to a tree root, and ended his own life.
The Shì clan members in the city
scrambled to flee through the four gates.
The King told his ministers,
"Móhē Nán has not emerged yet."
He immediately entered the water
and pulled him out; he was already dead.
Regret arose in the King's heart.
"My maternal grandfather
has now ended his life, all because of his love for his kin.
If I had known this earlier,
I would never have attacked."
Lúlí killed ninety-nine million nine hundred thousand people.
The flowing blood formed a river
surrounding the city of Jiāpíluóyuè.
After the soldiers departed,
Mùlián addressed the Buddha:
"Relying on the Buddha's spiritual power,
I protected four or five thousand people."
The Buddha said,
"Go and look at them."
Mùlián lowered his bowl,
but the people were all dead.
(King Lúlí) went to Nígūliú Yuán (Nigrodha Park)
and spoke to the five hundred Shì women, saying,
"Do not worry or grieve.
I am your husband."
He took hold of one Shì woman, who said,
"Why should I have relations with the son of a maidservant?"
The King immediately cut off her hands and feet
and placed her in a deep pit.
The five hundred Shì women all cursed the King, saying,
"Who gave my body to consort with the son of a maidservant?"
The King ordered the five hundred Shì women to be punished according to the former method.
Returning to Shèwèi Guó,
Prince Qítuó (Jeta) was in the deep palace performing various songs and dances.
The King heard his voice and turned his carriage to approach him.
Qítuó came out of the gate to meet him and said,
"Welcome, Great King!
You may stop your carriage for a moment."
King Lúlí said,
"Did you not hear that I was fighting the Shì clan members,
yet you played with courtesans and did not come to assist me?"
Qítuó replied,
"I heard about it,
but I cannot bear to kill sentient beings."
King Lúlí personally chopped down Qítuó.
At that time, the five hundred Shì women took refuge (in the Buddha) and called upon the name of the Rúlái (Tathāgata).
Were born together into the Śākyá (Shì) clan.
Left home and achieved Buddhahood.
Suffering this pain and poison, yet not remembering.
The Buddha and the various Bhikkhus (bǐqiū).
Went to Jiāpíluó.
When the women saw them from afar, they all felt shame and remorse.
The Shìzūn looked back and spoke to Shìtí Huányīn, saying:
“The women feel shame.”
Dìshì immediately covered the women with divine clothing.
The Buddha told Píshāmén:
“The women have been hungry and thirsty for a long time.” He immediately prepared heavenly food, and they were all satisfied.
The Buddha preached to them about suffering (kǔ), accumulation (jí), cessation (jìn), and the way (dào).
All the defilements and impurities (chén gòu) of the women ceased, and they attained the purity of the Dharma eye (fǎ yǎn).
Each died in their respective place.
They were all reborn in Heaven.
The Buddha went to the East Gate and saw within the city.
Smoke and fire were raging fiercely.
He looked back and spoke to the various Bǐqiū:
“In the past, I preached the Dharma here with you Bǐqiū.
Now it is like an empty ruin, without people.
From now on, I will not come here again.”
He returned to Shěwèi Guó, to the Jíshùyuán.
He informed the various Bǐqiū:
“Liúlí Wáng and all his soldiers.
Seven days hence, they shall all be utterly annihilated.”
The King heard this and was terrified.
The Fànzhì who delighted in ascetic practices reported that there was no dust (danger) internally or externally, and the King merely amused himself.
The King ordered people to count the days until the morning of the seventh day.
The King was greatly rejoiced.
He led his soldiers, army, and concubines.
They went to the banks of the Āyíluó Hé.
And held a banquet together.
A great clap of thunder suddenly struck.
Clouds gathered out of season.
Violent winds and swift rain [followed].
They were injured, damaged, swept away, and drowned.
In an instant, they were all finished.
The King was reborn directly into Ābí Dìyù.
Furthermore, heavenly fire burned and washed away the palace city.
A Bǐqiū asked the Buddha:
“For what cause do the various Śākyas (Shì) now encounter this suffering?”
The Buddha said:
“In the past, in Luóyuè Chéng, there was a fishing village.
At that time, there was a famine, and people ate grass roots.
One measure (dǒu) of gold was exchanged for one liter (shēng) of rice.
The village had a large pond.
It was extremely abundant with fish.
The people caught them and ate them.
There were two kinds of fish.
One was named Jūsuǒ, the second was named Duōshé.
They spoke to each other, saying:
‘We are water creatures.
We do not live on dry land.
Yet these people have all come to eat us.’
There was a boy in the village.
His age was still eight years.
Although he did not catch fish.
When he saw them, he rejoiced.
The villagers of Luóyuè are the present-day Śākyas (Shìzòng).
The Jūsuǒ fish is Liúlí Wáng.
The two-tongued (Duōshé) fish is the Fànzhì who delighted in ascetic practices.
The small child who saw the fish and laughed, that is I today.
The sin of catching the fish resulted in suffering the pains of hell for countless kalpas (jié).
Now, this consequence remains.
Seeing it and laughing happily.
Now results in suffering a headache, as if pressed by a stone.
Furthermore, like wearing Xūmí Shān [as a hat]. Many people sitting there heard the Buddha preach the Dharma of impermanence (wúcháng).
And attained the Xūtuóhuán Guǒ.”
A Śākya woman (Shì Nǚ) spoke to five hundred women, saying:
"I once heard from the Buddha
that if a person, amidst great distress and urgency,
single-mindedly contemplates the Buddha,
reaching the point of taking refuge (guīmìng),
they will immediately attain peace and safety (ānyǐn)."
At that time, the five hundred women, with different mouths but the same voice, sincerely contemplated the Buddha,
crying out, "Námó Shìjiā Móuní! How bitter! Alas, how painful!"
At that moment, in the sky, by the root power (gēnlì) of the Tathāgata's (Rúlái) compassion and goodness,
a great cloud of compassion arose,
and rained down the rain of great compassion.
The hands and feet of all the women were restored.
The women then thought:
"How can we repay the Buddha's merciful kindness?"
They immediately took their robes and bowls (yī bō)
and went to the monastery (jīngshè) in the Royal Park (Wáng Yuán),
seeking permission to leave home (chūjiā).
At that time, there were Nuns of the Six Groups (Liù Qún Bǐqiūní).
Seeing that these Śākya women were young, beautiful, and graceful,
they should speak to them about the pleasures of worldly desires (shìjiān zhī yù).
"Wouldn't it be delightful if they waited until the period of their youth passed before leaving home?
If they all return to lay life (huánsú), they will surely donate their robes and bowls to us."
When the women heard this, they were distressed and said,
"This is like mixing poison with savory food and drink.
The Five Desires (wǔ yù) of the world have many faults and dangers.
We already fully understand this.
Why praise their beauty
to persuade us?"
They raised their voices and wept loudly.
Huāsè Bǐqiūní (Bhikkhuṇī Huāsè) asked the reason.
They replied, "We wish to leave home,
but have not been granted permission."
Huāsè immediately ordained them as disciples.
At that time, the Śākya women felt mixed sorrow and joy.
They fully explained the loss of their clan and their bodily mutilation,
presenting it respectfully to their Master (Héshàng).
[Huāsè] replied, "Your suffering and hardship is insignificant!
When I was a layperson in the past,
I was a native of the Kingdom of Shèwèi (Śrāvastī).
My parents married me
to a man from the north.
According to the customs of that country,
when a wife was about to give birth,
she returned to her parents' home.
Later, when the day approached for her to give birth,
my husband and I traveled together by chariot and horseback.
Midway, there was a river whose waters were violently swollen.
The road was vast and deserted, full of bandits and danger.
We reached the river but could not cross.
We lodged on the riverbank.
Early in the night, I gave birth to a son.
A large poisonous snake, smelling the scent of fresh blood,
immediately approached me.
First, it bit and killed the servant.
I called my husband, but he did not respond.
Soon after, it killed my husband.
Next, it killed the oxen and horses.
By the time the sun rose,
my husband's body was swollen and decaying.
Distressed and terrified,
I raised my voice and wept loudly.
I stayed there for several days,
alone on the riverbank.
The water gradually subsided.
I carried the older child on my back,
led him by the hand,
put the newborn child in my skirt,
and held the skirt hem in my mouth.
I then stepped forward into the water.
When I was about halfway across the river,
I looked back at the older child
and saw he was being chased by a tiger.
I screamed and lost hold of the skirt.
The infant sank and drowned.
I used my hands to search and grasp,
but ultimately failed to retrieve him.
The one on my back
slipped from my grasp and fell.
The one on the bank
was eaten by the tiger.
My heart and liver felt torn apart.
I vomited hot blood from my mouth.
When I reached the shore, I fainted.
A large group of travelers arrived.
Among them was an elder (zhǎngzhě)
who knew my parents.
I asked him for news.
The elder replied, saying:
"Last night, a fire broke out, and your family home was completely destroyed.
Your parents both perished."
Hearing this, I collapsed in a faint.
After a long time, I revived.
There were five hundred bandits (zéi).
They immediately dispersed the company of travelers
and took me away,
making me a bandit's wife.
I was regularly made to guard the gate.
If there was an emergency,
and we were being pursued by others,
I had to open the gate during the daytime.
Later, the group of bandits went out together to plunder.
The owner of the property reported it to the King (wáng) and the village.
[The bandits] returned to their home.
I had given birth to a child inside the house.
[The bandit] called out three times, but no one opened the door.
He immediately climbed the wall to enter and asked,
[I] replied that I had given birth to a son.
The bandit said,
"Because of this son, you endangered me! What use is this child?"
He drew his knife, chopped off the child's hands and feet, and ordered the wife to eat them.
The wife, overcome by terror, ate them.
His rage then subsided.
My husband continued to commit robbery.
He was caught by the king's officers.
They cut him in half at the waist, ending his life.
He was buried alive along with his wife.
Someone coveted the wonderful necklace (yīngluò) I wore.
They opened the grave to take it,
and took me away as well.
After a short time again,
the King's agents watched for and captured him.
They executed the bandit and his companions,
and buried us all together again.
The burial was not secure.
At night, a tiger dug us up to eat.
As a result, I was able to escape again.
I was lost and disoriented, not knowing east from west.
I ran quickly along the road,
and saw many people.
I asked them:
"Sirs, where is there someone who can remove this suffering and distress?"
At that time, there was an elder and a Brāhmaṇa (Pólúomén)
who, out of compassion, asked me:
"Have you heard of the Dharma of Shìjiā Móuní Fó?
It brings much peace and safety and is free from all decline and affliction."
Hearing this, my heart rejoiced.
I went to the Bhikkhuṇī Dà Àidào Jiāotánmí (Mahāprajāpatī Gautamī).
Step by step, I cultivated the practice and eventually attained the fruit of the Way (Dàoguǒ).
When the Śākya women heard this,
their hearts were greatly joyful
and they attained the purity of the Dharma Eye (Fǎ Yǎn Jìng).
Then Jiāotánmí said:
"In the Tathāgata's Ocean of Dharma,
all sentient beings
surely have a share.
But for women like us,
the Tathāgata did not initially permit [ordination],
because we have many doubts, attachments that are difficult to relinquish,
minds covered by ignorance and love, submerged in the water of desire (ài shuǐ).
We cannot extract ourselves.
We are lazy and indolent,
unable in this current life to adorn Bodhi (Pútí) or attain the Three Vehicles (Sān Chéng)."
Ānán requested [permission for her], saying,
"Jiāotánmí nursed and nurtured the Tathāgata's physical body until he achieved Buddhahood (Chéng Fó)."
The Buddha said, "If women are permitted [to join the Dharma], the Dharma will gradually decline and perish."
Ānán requested again:
"All past Buddhas possessed the Four Assemblies (Sì Bù Zhòng).
Why are you alone incomplete now?"
The Buddha instructed Ānán:
"Jiāotánmí,
because she loves and delights in the Buddha Dharma and has aroused great diligence (dà jīngjìn),
and purely practices the Eight Statutes of Respect (Bā Jìng zhī Fǎ),
she is permitted to enter the Buddha Dharma."
"After I was able to leave home,
having cultivated myself through great compassion (dà bēi),
and universally for all women in the future,
I made a renewed request to the Buddha, saying:
'For virtuous women in the future,
who believe, delight in, love, and respect the Tathāgata's Dharma,
may you kindly grant permission.'
The Buddha said,
'If there are women
who guard and uphold the Buddha Dharma and gradually cultivate their learning—
precepts (jiè), giving (shī), great learning (duō wén), the Three Refuges (Sān Guī), the Five Precepts (Wǔ Jiè),
and even the full precepts (jù jiè),
and various Dharma supporting the Way (zhù dào fǎ) —
all shall be permitted.'
'You should constantly and sincerely remember the kindness of Ānán,
make offerings to him, and revere him,
six times, day and night,
so that your mind does not forget him."
“What merit did Chē’nì possess in a former life, that he was able to guide the Bodhisattva into the mountains, allowing him to attain Buddhahood?”
The Buddha said:
“Chē’nì did not only possess this merit in the present life.
In the past, when I was a Bodhisattva,
I was in the kingdom of Shīhē Biànléi.
King Xūdán Móshí heard that people in the world might ascend to heaven through cultivating the Way, or through offering sacrifices.
The King constantly desired to ascend to heaven but did not know the proper method.
In the kingdom, there were followers of the Brāhmaṇa Way,
totaling more than forty thousand people.
Among them was a great, respected Brāhmaṇa.
The King consulted him.
He replied:
‘Do you wish to ascend to heaven while alive, or after death?’
The King said:
‘While alive, flying up to heaven.’
He replied again:
‘Great King, you must perform sacrifices.’
The King was pleased and brought out treasures from his stores and gave them to the Brāhmaṇa.
He requested one hundred handsome men and one hundred beautiful women from the kingdom.
And one hundred heads each of elephants, horses, and other animals.
First, he fed the four Brāhmaṇas.
Then he killed the people and animals,
using them for the sacrifices to heaven.
He collected the blood to make a staircase,
to allow the Brāhmaṇa to ascend.
He further sought a divine maiden in Xiāngshān, named Zhēnduóluó.
He wanted to obtain her blood to combine with the rest to make the staircase.
The King heard this and said happily, ‘Why were you so late in telling me?’
The King immediately ordered throughout the kingdom, asking who could capture Zhēnduóluó.
One man reported to the King:
‘In the seventh mountain, there are two men.
One is named Shélí, and the other is named Yōulí.
They know the location of Zhēnduóluó.’
The King said:
‘Quickly summon these men.’
They were brought forward.
The King was extremely joyful, immediately offering wine and food, and indulging them in entertainment for seven days and seven nights, rewarding them lavishly to their utmost satisfaction.
The King said to Shélí and the other man:
‘If you can capture the maiden Zhēnduóluó and bring her here so that I may ascend to heaven,
I shall entrust this kingdom entirely to the two of you.’
The men accepted the command and immediately exerted all their strength to search for Zhēnduóluó.
After more than two months, traversing eight ranges of mountains,
they arrived deep within Xiāngshān and found a large pool of water.
They saw Śakradevendra
with countless multitudes of celestial maidens and musicians.
They had come out of the city to play, bathed in the pool, and then all flew up to heaven.
At that time, by the side of the pool, there was a Brāhmaṇa.
He had attained the Four Dhyānas and the path of Bānzhē Xún.
Then Shélí and the others stepped forward, bowed to him, and asked:
‘What kind of sound is this place, and why is the pleasure so great?’
He replied:
‘King Tóumó and over a thousand people are in this city.
After playing and bathing, they will come to my place to bow.
You should depart.’
Shélí and the others then left.
They discussed in private, saying:
‘This is a great deity (or sage). How can we capture that divine maiden?’
The man thought to himself, took grass, tied a knot, and threw it into the water to suppress the sage.
Making the Brāhmaṇa unable to move.
He also cast a spell on the celestial maidens, making them unable to fly.
After finishing the binding divine incantation,
Śakradevendra and all the celestial maidens flew up to heaven.
Only the King, the maiden, and the King's attendant Mónà Hēluó remained stuck in the water and could not fly.
They immediately went forward, bound the maiden, and brought her to their former country.
The King invited them into the palace, offered food, and rewarded them for their efforts.
Prince Nánluó Shī was a king in a neighboring country.
The King had a crown prince named Xūluó.
He was previously the King's grandson.
He possessed great compassion and practiced the Bodhisattva Way.
He sent someone to call for him to come and see this maiden, wishing to take her as his wife.
The King said:
‘I will take another wife for you.
The blood of this celestial maiden is needed for the sacrifice so that I may ascend to heaven.’
The Bodhisattva replied:
‘If you do not give her to me, I will die of despair.’
The King feared his death and gave the maiden to him.
After more than four months, the Brāhmaṇa came and reported to the King:
‘We have obtained the maiden Zhēnduóluó previously; now we must kill her.
For the people and animals, we dug a pit, eight cubits square/round.
We should take her blood and choose a day to perform the sacrifice.’
The King said:
‘Excellent!’ The Bodhisattva heard this and asked what they were doing.
The Brāhmaṇa replied:
‘By performing the sacrifice, we shall ascend to heaven.’
The Bodhisattva said:
‘Killing people and animals leads to entering Avīci Hell.
How could one possibly ascend to heaven?’
The Brāhmaṇa said:
‘You are still young; this is not your concern.’
The Bodhisattva said:
‘I know all your underlying causes and conditions.’
The Brāhmaṇa said, ‘If you know, please try to tell us.’
The Bodhisattva then recounted his conduct.
The Brāhmaṇa felt shame, paid his respects, and departed.
The Bodhisattva immediately preached the Dharma to the King, saying:
‘If one desires to ascend to heaven, one must observe the Five Precepts and practice the Ten Good Deeds.
Share in charity and practice giving, be filial to parents, and serve śramaṇas.
Have a compassionate heart toward the ten thousand people and all crawling creatures. Supply them sufficiently with whatever they need for food; only then can one ascend to heaven.’
The King heard this and immediately followed the Bodhisattva's words.
He brought forth the gold, silver, and precious jewels from his treasury.
He allowed the Prince to dispense charity freely for seven days.
Then the Prince paid his respects and departed with his wife, returning to his former country.
Day and night, gold, silver, and precious jewels rained down.
The Bodhisattva lived with the maiden for one year, neglecting the affairs of the state.
The ministers reported to the King, saying:
‘You must kill Zhēnduóluó;
only then will the Prince attend to the kingdom.’
The King heard this, reluctantly ordered the capture and binding of the Prince.
The maiden immediately flew away.
She passed by the place where the two men, Shélí and the other, were.
She immediately spoke to them, saying:
‘The Prince is coming after me.
I trouble you to guide him.’
She left her ring as a token of trust
and gave it to the practitioners of the Way.
The King released the Prince.
He could not see Zhēnduóluó.
He fell to the ground and said:
‘How am I to find the maiden?’
A deity spoke to him:
‘You do not need to weep.
I will tell you where she is.
Go up the seventh mountain, and quickly pursue her.’
He then put on his jeweled robe, belted his sword, and carried his bow.
The light of the jeweled robe illuminated forty *lǐ*.
The Prince left the kingdom, and the next morning arrived at the seventh mountain, where he saw the two men mentioned earlier.
He immediately said:
‘Have you seen the maiden Zhēnduóluó?’
They replied that they had seen her.
They gave the ring to the Prince.
They immediately proceeded together.
They ascended the eighth mountain, Xiāngshān.
They saw the Brāhmaṇa who had attained the Four Dhyānas and approached him to pay respects.
At that time, the Heavenly King Śakra transformed into a terrifying monkey that shook the mountain.
The Bodhisattva was greatly frightened.
The Brāhmaṇa said:
‘This monkey often serves me. When it sees people, it is unwilling to come down.’
The Brāhmaṇa said:
‘Come down, monkey!’ It immediately came, bringing fruit and offering it.
The Brāhmaṇa accepted it, and the three men shared and ate it.
He said to the monkey:
‘Guide these three men to the residence of the celestial maiden.’
The monkey said:
‘What kind of people are these, that you ask me to guide them up to heaven?’
The Brāhmaṇa said:
‘This is the Crown Prince of the kingdom.
They are all Bodhisattvas who will uphold the Buddha Way and save all celestial beings, humans, and crawling creatures.’
The monkey said, ‘Excellent!’
And guided them up to heaven.
On the way, they passed by the residence of five hundred Pìzhīfó.
The three men sent the monkey back to fetch flowers to scatter over the Buddhas and Bodhisattvas.
They made a vow, saying:
‘May I swiftly attain Buddhahood.’
The monkey further said:
‘May I be a horse for the Buddha.’
Shélí further said:
‘May I be a servant for the Buddha.’
The other man said, ‘I vow to attain Āluóhàn.’
When they arrived at Zhēnduóluó’s residence,
the monkey bowed and departed.
The Bodhisattva and the two men sat outside the gate.
A servant in green clothes fetched water.
The Bodhisattva asked, ‘What is this water for?’
She replied:
‘It is for bathing Zhēnduóluó.’
The Bodhisattva removed his ring and secretly dropped it into the water.
When the maiden bathed and saw the ring, she stopped immediately.
She went inside and reported to her parents:
‘My husband is outside.’
Her parents were delighted.
Her father's name was King Tóulóu.
He immediately came out to meet them.
He paid respects to the Bodhisattva.
Shélí and the other man paid their respects again and departed.
The King invited him into the city and greeted him warmly.
He washed the Bodhisattva's hands with water.
He handed over the maiden and more than a thousand serving girls entirely to the Bodhisattva.
The Bodhisattva stayed there for seven years.
The Bodhisattva reported to the King, saying:
‘I wish to return home to see my parents.’
The King said, ‘Wait a moment.’
Seven days later, a ghost arrived at the King's residence and said:
‘I heard that the Great King's daughter, who was lost earlier, has happily returned, and you have also gained a noble son-in-law. Congratulations.’
The King said:
‘My daughter is fine, but my son-in-law is extremely noble.
He is a prince from a certain kingdom and has long wished to return home. I trouble you, sir, to escort him.’
The Ghost King replied, ‘Yes.’
He immediately took seven treasures of the kingdom and built a seven-story pagoda.
The Ghost placed the Prince in his palm, escorted him back to his former country, paid his respects, and departed.
The Bodhisattva went forward, paid respects to his parents, and inquired about their daily health.
The King received the Crown Prince.
He immediately handed over the national treasury, gold, and silver.
The King commanded his nearby ministers and attendants:
‘Anyone, far or near, who desires gold, silver, rice, or grain,
should come to the palace gate and be granted whatever their heart desires.’
Later, when the King's lifespan ended, he was immediately reborn in heaven.
That Crown Prince then is now my present body.
That Brāhmaṇa who attained the Four Dhyānas then is Shèlìfú now.
That Shélí then is Chē’nì now.”
The one person who wished to become an Arhat at that time is now Mùjiànlián.
Śakra, the King of Heaven, who transformed into a monkey and wished to become a horse at that time, is now Jiānzhì.
The king who was the father at that time is now my father, Yuètóután.
The mother at that time is now my mother, Móyē.
Zhēntuóluó is now Qiúyí.
Bodhisattva Sàtuópōlún practiced the Bodhisattva Path at the place of the Buddha Dàléiyīn.
When originally seeking the Bōrě Bōluómì,
he did not begrudge his body or life, nor did he seek fame or profit.
There was a voice in the air which admonished and instructed him.
“I ought to seek the Bōrě Bōluómì everywhere.”
He was immediately distressed and wept for seven days.
His body was extremely weary, suffering even from hunger, thirst, cold, and heat.
There was a Buddha in the air who spoke to him, saying.
“Good man, the Buddhas of the past, practicing the Bodhisattva Path, sought to hear the Bōrě Bōluómì.
Just as you today, because of this diligent vigor and love for the Dharma,
make offerings to the Bōrě Bōluómì.
Bodhisattva Tánwújié is preaching the Bōrě Bōluómì on this seat.
If there are those who receive, uphold, read, recite, and practice as taught,
from now on, you do not distinguish between day and night, and soon you shall be able to hear the Bōrě Bōluómì.”
“I am now poor and have no objects which I can use to make offerings to the Bōrě Bōluómì and the Dharma Master.
I should not go empty-handed.
I ought to sell my body to gain wealth for the sake of the Bōrě Bōluómì and to make offerings to the Dharma Master.
In life after life, I have lost my body countless times.
Throughout beginningless cycles of birth and death, I have sometimes died or sometimes been sold.
Sometimes, due to greed and desire, I have endured measureless suffering, life after life in hell.
I have never yet sacrificed my body and life for the sake of the pure Dharma or making offerings to the Dharma Master.”
He immediately entered a great city and went to the marketplace.
He loudly proclaimed.
“Who needs a person? Who needs a person?”
At that time, the Evil Māra held this thought.
“Is Sàtuópōlún seeking the Dharma, intending to sell his body?
I must now ruin this endeavor.”
Māra obscured all the people, causing them not to hear his voice.
He tried to sell himself but failed, and became extremely distressed.
Shìtíhuányīn transformed into a Brāhmaṇa and said.
“I now wish to make offerings to Heaven; I need a person’s heart, a person’s blood, and a person’s marrow.
Can you give them?”
He replied.
“I have now attained great good fortune.”
He immediately took a knife and pierced his left arm to draw blood, cut the flesh of his right thigh, and intended to break the bone to extract the marrow.
At that time, the daughter of an elder was on the tower, saw him from afar, and immediately descended and asked the Bodhisattva.
“Why do you inflict suffering upon yourself? What do you intend to do with your heart, blood, and marrow?”
He replied.
“I am selling them to the Brāhmaṇa for the sake of the Bōrě Bōluómì and to make offerings to Bodhisattva Tánwújié.”
The girl asked, “What merits will you gain?”
He replied.
“That person has well studied the power of the skillful means of Bōrě.
If I learn this Dharma, I will be able to attain the unsurpassed Way.
I will become a refuge for sentient beings.
I will obtain a body of golden color and possess all merits.
I will distribute these benefits to all sentient beings, equally sharing the benefits of merit.”
The girl said, “This is subtle and wonderful, difficult to encounter. For the sake of these merits,
one should abandon bodies as numerous as the sands of the Ganges.
What do you need? I shall give you everything.
I also wish to go to Tánwújié’s place and together plant good roots.”
Shìtíhuányīn immediately resumed his original form.
and praised him, saying.
“Excellent, good man!
All past Buddhas, practicing the Bodhisattva Path, also sought thus.
I truly do not need a person’s heart, blood, or marrow.
I only came to test you.
What do you wish for?
I shall give it to you.”
“I pray that this body of mine be restored to its former state.”
He arrived at the elder’s daughter’s house.
The girl’s parents gave all kinds of wonderful flowers and incense, as well as necklaces, perfumes, burnt incense, banners, canopies, clothing, seven treasures, and musical instruments.
The girl and her attendants went together to make offerings to the Sūtra and to Tánwújié.
Tánwújié preached the Bōrě Bōluómì and the power of skillful means.
Sàtuópōlún sought water to sprinkle the ground but could not obtain it.
He immediately pierced his own body and sprinkled the ground with his blood, so that no dust would come to settle on the Great Master.
Bodhisattva Sùwánghuá said to the Buddha.
“World-Honored One, how did Yàowáng wander in this Suōpó Shìjiè?
He possessed hundreds of billions of nayutas of difficult and ascetic practices.
I pray you explain a little.”
The Buddha said.
“In the past, kalpas numerous as the sands of the Ganges, there was a Buddha named Rìyuè Jìngmíngdé.
In that land there were no women.
Bodhisattva Xǐjiàn, in the Dharma of this Buddha, diligently practiced walking meditation, single-mindedly seeking Buddhahood.
After a full twenty thousand years, he attained the Samādhi of Manifesting All Forms of Body.
All this was due to the power of hearing the Fǎhuá Jīng.
In the empty sky, he rained down Màntuóluó flowers and the fragrance of sandlewood from this shore of the ocean.
He wrapped his body in heavenly robes, poured fragrant oil over it, and burned his own body.
The brightness illuminated everywhere eighty billion worlds numerous as the sands of the Ganges.
This is true vigor, a true Dharma offering.
His body burned in the fire for twelve hundred years; after that had passed, his body was finally consumed.
All sentient beings, having seen Bodhisattva Xǐjiàn’s Dharma offering.
were magically born in this land into the household of King Jìngdé.
and spoke verses to his father.
“At the place where I formerly practiced walking meditation, I attained the Samādhi of Manifesting the Body.
Diligently performing great vigor, I abandoned my beloved body.
The Buddha Rìyuè Jìngmíngdé is still presently residing (in the world).
I shall immediately return there to make offerings to this Buddha.”
Sitting on a seven-jeweled platform, he ascended into the empty sky.
He went to the Buddha’s place, joined his palms, and praised the Buddha.
“Your countenance is exceedingly marvelous, Your light illuminates the ten directions.
I have previously made offerings, and now I have returned again to behold you closely.”
The Buddha told Xǐjiàn.
“The time for my parinirvāṇa has come.
Tonight I shall enter Nirvāṇa.
I entrust my Dharma to you, and entrust the Śarīra to you; you must ensure they are spread widely and extensively make offerings.”
Xǐjiàn immediately used sandalwood logs from this shore of the ocean and burned the body.
He collected the Śarīra and made eighty-four thousand jeweled vases.
He erected eighty-four thousand stūpas.
Although this was an offering, his heart was still not satisfied.
He then, in front of the eighty-four thousand stūpas.
burned his arms, adorned with the hundred marks of merit, for seventy-two thousand years.
thereby making an offering.
Countless multitudes seeking Śrāvaka status and innumerable people generated the Pútí Mind.
All attained dwelling in the Samādhi of Manifesting All Forms of Body.
The Bodhisattvas, devas, and humans, etc., seeing that he had no arms, were distressed, sorrowful, and grieving, and spoke these words.
“Bodhisattva Xǐjiàn, the great master who teaches and transforms us sentient beings, is now incomplete (lacking limbs).”
Bodhisattva Xǐjiàn, in the midst of the great assembly, took this vow.
“Because I abandoned my two arms, I shall certainly attain Buddhahood.
If this is truly not false, may my arms be restored.”
At that time, the triple thousand great thousand world underwent six types of shaking, and the heavens rained jeweled flowers.
Then his two arms were restored to their former state.
The Buddha told Bodhisattva Sùwánghuá.
“The one who was Xǐjiàn at that time is now Yàowáng.
If there is anyone who generates the mind wishing to attain the unsurpassed Pútí Way.
and is able to burn a finger, or even one toe, to make offering to a Buddha stūpa.

This surpasses using one's country, cities, wife, and children, and the triple thousand great thousand world with its mountains, forests, rivers, ponds, and all precious treasures, to make offerings to the Buddha, Bodhisattvas, Pìzhī, and Āluóhàn, etc.
Going back to the past, there was a Buddha.
named Yúnléiyīn Sùwánghuázhì.
There was a king named Miàozhuāngyán.
The king’s consort was named Jìngdé.
They had two sons.
One was named Jìngzàng.
The second was named Jìngyǎn.
These two sons possessed great spiritual power.
meritoriousness and wisdom, practicing the Bodhisattva Path.
The Buddha, wishing to guide King Miàozhuāngyán and pitying sentient beings, preached this Fǎhuá Jīng.
Then Jìngzàng and Jìngyǎn told their mother.
“We wish Mother to go and visit the Buddha Yúnléiyīn Sùwánghuázhì.
We also should follow, make offerings, and bow in reverence.”
The mother told her sons.
“Your father believes in and accepts external paths and is deeply attached to the Brāhmaṇa Dharma.
You should go and inform your father and go together with him.”
The mother further instructed.
“You should keep in mind that your father should see your spiritual transformations.”
Thereupon, the two sons leaped into the empty sky, seven tāla trees high, and manifested eighteen types of transformation.
The father saw their spiritual power, his heart greatly rejoiced, joined his palms toward his sons, and said.
“Who is your teacher?”
The two sons told him.
“The Buddha Yúnléiyīn Sùwánghuázhì is now sitting under the seven-jeweled Pútí tree, seated on the Dharma seat, preaching the Fǎhuá Jīng.
He is our teacher.”
The father spoke to his sons, saying.
“I now wish to see him.”
The two sons descended from the air and told their mother, “Father the King has now believed, understood, and generated the Pútí Mind.
We have already performed Buddha-work for Father.
We pray Mother grants us permission.
to leave home at the place of that Buddha and cultivate the Way.”
The mother said, “I permit you.
because the Buddha is difficult to encounter.”
Thereupon the two sons told their parents.
“We wish that now you may go and visit the Buddha’s place, to see him closely and make offerings.”
Thereupon, King Miàozhuāngyán, with his officials and dependents.
Consort Jìngdé, with the palace maids, and their two sons, a total of forty-two thousand people.
all together went to the Buddha.
The Buddha preached the Dharma for them, showing them the teachings, benefiting them, and causing joy.
The King was greatly joyful.
Then the King and the Consort.
immediately removed the pearl necklaces from their necks and scattered them above the Buddha.
In the empty sky, they transformed into a four-pillared jeweled platform.
In the middle was a great jeweled couch, spread with hundreds of thousands of millions of heavenly robes.
On top of it was a Buddha, sitting cross-legged, radiating great light.
At that time, the Buddha Yúnléiyīn Sùwánghuázhì told the four assemblies.
“Do you see this King Miàozhuāngyán standing before me with palms joined?”
“This King, in my Dharma, shall become a Bhikṣu, diligently cultivating and practicing the methods that aid the Buddha Way, and shall attain Buddhahood, named Suōluóshùwáng.
His land shall be named Dàguāng, and his kalpa shall be named Dàgāowáng.”
The King immediately entrusted the country to his younger brother.
The King, the Consort, and the two sons, along with all their dependents, left home in the Buddha’s Dharma to cultivate the Way.
After the King left home, for eighty-four thousand years, he constantly practiced diligence, cultivating the Miàofǎhuá Jīng.
After that had passed, he attained the Samādhi of Adornment with All Pure Merits.
He immediately ascended into the empty sky, seven tāla trees high.
King Miàozhuāngyán is now Bodhisattva Huádé.
Consort Jìngdé is Bodhisattva Guāngzhào Zhuāngyánxiāng.
Their two sons are now Bodhisattvas Yàowáng and Yàoshàng.
Formerly, when the Bodhisattva was a Brahman, his name was Shàntíhéshān

He dwelt beneath a tree, eating fruits and drinking spring water. Internal defilements were entirely eliminated, his vast enlightenment and Six Supernatural Powers (liù tōng) were attained, and he acquired the wisdom that knows all things
His renowned fragrance universally pervaded, heard in the eight directions, above and below
Sages and ordinary people lamented and protected his kingdom.
The winds and rains came at the proper times, the five grains ripened abundantly, and disasters and poisons vanished
The king was named Jiālí
He entered the mountains to hunt, chasing elk and deer.
Following their tracks, he passed directly in front of the Bodhisattva
The King questioned him.
The Bodhisattva remained silent
The King said
“You are a wretch who ought to die! I am the sovereign of a whole kingdom
When questioned, you do not reply instantly, yet animal tracks passed this way.
And you falsely lower your head. My authority allows me to execute you
The Bodhisattva said
“I listen to the King
He said, “Who are you?”
He said, “I am a person who endures insult (rěnrǔ rén)
The King, enraged, drew his sword and severed his right arm
The Bodhisattva said
“My aspiration is the Supreme Way (wú shàng dào), and I contend with nothing in this world
Since this King still subjects me to endurance, how much more so the common people?
I vow that when I attain Buddhahood, I will surely deliver him first
And not allow sentient beings to imitate his evil acts.”
The King said
“Who are you, Sir?”
He replied
“I am a person who endures insult
He again severed his left hand, and then his two feet, ears, and nose
Blood flowed like a running spring; the pain was immeasurable
Heaven and Earth trembled, and the sun and moon lost their brightness
The Four Great Heavenly Kings (sì tiān dà wáng) all arrived together and angrily spoke in unison
“This King is cruel and violent
They said to the Taoist (Bodhisattva)
“We should execute him and his wife and children
And destroy the entire kingdom to manifest his wickedness
The Taoist replied
“What are these words
This is because in my former life, I did not honor the teachings of the Buddha and inflicted malice upon others
Evil deeds cause misfortune to follow, just as a shadow clings to the form
The common people, seeing the transformation, rushed forward to confess their faults, saying in unison
“The Taoist dwells here to dispel calamities and achieve Nirvāṇa (miè dù)
The foolish ruler does not recognize good or bad, nor does he know what to abandon or what to pursue.
He inflicted evil upon the Original Sage
We only pray that the Holy One (shèngrén) does not hold us responsible before the Supreme Deity (Shàngdì)
The Bodhisattva replied
“Though the King subjected me to fierce cruelty, my heart pities him as a mother cherishes her newborn child
What fault do the common people have? Do not allow doubt to arise
The Bodhisattva had a younger brother residing on a different mountain
He viewed the situation with his Divine Eye (tiānyǎn)
At that time, the heavenly spirits and dragons discussed the King's evil, and none failed to harbor indignation
Fearing his elder brother might harbor a mind that diminishes virtue
He came to his brother's location using his Spiritual Power (shénzú lì)
He took the severed hands, feet, ears, and nose and placed them back in their original positions
The brother reattached them, and they instantly returned to normal
The elder brother said
“My conviction in universal compassion (pǔ cí) is now manifest
There were no heavenly spirits or earthly deities who were not moved by sorrow and joy
They bowed their heads, praised him, mutually encouraged and instructed each other, received the injunctions, and withdrew
Shàntíhé (羼提惒) is my current body
The younger brother is Mílè
The King is Jūlín
At that time, in Rájagriha (Wángshěchéng), the family of General Shīzǐ (Lion) gave birth to a son
When he was born, the various devas in the heavens spoke thus
“This child shall constantly contemplate the Dharma (fǎ), meditate on the Dharma. Whatever he says, he must not speak of worldly matters
He must constantly proclaim and spread the Dharma that transcends the world (chūshì zhī fǎ)
He must constantly guard his mouth, be cautious in speech, and speak little
He must not give rise to various thoughts or observations regarding worldly affairs
He must rely upon meaning (yì), not upon written words (wénzì)
At that time, the child, hearing this, ceased to weep and had no characteristics of an infant
Even after seven days, his appearance was pleasant and gentle; he was joyful upon seeing people, and his eyes never blinked
At that time, some people spoke to his parents
“This child is inauspicious and should not be raised
The parents replied
“Although this child is silent
Nevertheless, his physical faculties (shēn gēn) are complete
We must recognize that this child definitely possesses merit and virtue (fú dé); he is not a cause of misfortune
They named him Wúyán (No Speech)
The child Wúyán gradually grew up, like an eight-year-old boy
People enjoyed seeing him
Wherever the Dharma was taught and the Dharma Wheel (fǎ lún) was turned
He delighted in the Dharma, listened and received it, but proclaimed nothing with his mouth
At that time, Wúyán, along with his parents, dependents, and relatives
Journeyed between the Form Realm (sè jiè) and the Desire Realm (yù jiè) to the jeweled monasteries (bǎo fāng)
Seeing the Buddha and the Bodhisattvas arriving from the ten directions, they gave rise to great joy
Shèlìfú addressed the Buddha, saying
“World-Honored One (Shìzūn)
The son born to General Shīzǐ
His physical faculties are complete, yet he cannot speak. What karma (yè) caused this
The Buddha said
“You should not slight this child
Why is this
This person is truly a Great Bodhisattva (Dà Púsà)
He has already planted various wholesome roots (shàn gēn) under countless Buddhas
And will not turn back from the Way of Bodhi (pútí zhī dào)
When this child was born, many devas came to admonish and command him, just as mentioned before
Following the heavenly instructions, he meditated silently and attained the Four Dhyānas (sì chán)
Manifesting such a body, he is able to tame and subdue immeasurable sentient beings
By his own power of vow (yuàn lì) and spiritual power (shéntōng lì)
He caused the Eight Classes of Beings (bā bù) and the Four Assemblies (sì zhòng) to each see a great lotus flower in his right hand, resembling a chariot wheel
The color and fragrance were complete, sublime, and foremost
A sight that people rejoiced to see
On every flower pedestal sat a Bodhisattva in the full lotus position (jié jiā fū zuò), adorned with the Thirty-Two Marks (sānshí'èr xiàng) and the Eighty Minor Characteristics (bāshí zhǒng hǎo)
Wúyán saw this great spiritual power
He lowered his head, joined his palms, and exclaimed, “Namo Buddhāya” (Námó Fótuó)
All the Bodhisattvas on the flower pedestals spoke the same words
The worlds equal to the sands of the Ganges (Hénghé shā) in the ten directions trembled in six ways
The devas in the heavens offered exquisitely fragrant flowers and various kinds of musical instruments to the Buddha
At that time, Wúyán, along with the various Bodhisattvas, leaped into the void
Rising seven Tāla trees high
They spoke verses in praise of the Buddha
“The Benefactor of All Beings (zhòng yòu) was formerly a Bodhisattva
Named Chángbēi (Constant Compassion)
He saw the Buddha, the Dharma, and the Sangha (sēng) in the world
If the world is filthy and turbid
Turning away from righteousness and toward evil, blooming falsely in pursuit of profit
Like moths delighted by fire
They take the Four Immeasurables (sì děng) and the Six Pāramitās (liù dù) as the dwelling of eternal peace
Yet the world abandons the Buddha and proceeds toward danger and calamity, thereby shattering itself
The Bodhisattva was constantly distraught with worry and grief
Long ago, there was a Buddha named Jǐngfǎ Wúhuì
He had not long entered Nirvāṇa (miè dù)
And the sūtras and Dharma were entirely exhausted
Chángbēi dreamed that he saw that Buddha preaching the Dharma for him
Upon hearing this, the Bodhisattva eliminated the defilements of his mind and entered Pure Concentration (qīngjìng dìng)
He immediately abandoned his wife and children and entered the mountains for quiet solitude
Fruits and water provided his sustenance
He beat his chest and cried out sorrowfully
‘I did not encounter the Buddha, nor did I see the Dharma and the Sangha
The Ultimate Destination of the Great Way!’ Just as his sorrowful cry ended
A heavenly spirit descended and said, ‘Enlightened Gentleman (Míng Shì)
It is so! Do not cry out sorrowfully anymore
The Buddha has a Great Dharma (dà fǎ) called the Light of Ultimate Illumination (Míng Dù Wújí zhī Míng)
All Buddhas of the three periods of time are perfected by means of this
You must seek it out, recite and practice its text, and remember and know its meaning
Revere it and practice it
You will certainly attain Buddhahood
Chángbēi looked up and said
‘From whom should I hear this noble Dharma
By what means (fāngbiàn), to what land, and what is the name of that teacher's clan
The heavenly being replied
‘You must travel directly east
Do not contemplate form (sè), feeling (tòng/shòu), perception (xiǎng), volition (xíng), or consciousness (shí)
Let your intention cease all desires, and hold your mind without opposition
I will instruct you to perceive the Sacred Canon (shèng diǎn) of the Light of Ultimate Illumination
Chángbēi said, ‘Yes’
‘I will guard it from beginning to end
The heavenly being reiterated
‘Maintain diligence (jīngjìn) in keeping it
Suddenly, he disappeared
The Bodhisattva accepted the instruction and traveled east to seek it
After several days, he stopped
He reflected deeply, saying
‘My past merits (sù báo yòu) are shallow
The ruler and ministers are confused
There is no one who knows the Buddha
The Venerable Master (zūn shī) who removes darkness
How many miles away is he from here
His sincerity (jīng chéng) was utmost
This sincerity moved a Buddha from the Upper Realms (shàng fāng) to come before him, attended by various devas
The Buddha praised the Bodhisattva, saying, ‘Excellent! Excellent! You are rare in the world
The Bodhisattva, seeing the Buddha, was both joyful and sorrowful
He bowed his head and spoke
‘May the Buddha pity me and preach the Sūtra (jīng) for me
The Buddha told him
‘The Three Realms (sān jiè) are all empty
That which exists must inevitably perish. All things are like illusions, arising and ceasing like water waves. Observe that the world is entirely so, and be careful not to forget this
From here, travel east twenty thousand leagues (lǐ)
There is a kingdom named Jiàntuóyuè
It is the city of all Bodhisattvas
Within that kingdom, all are superior persons; there are no common or mediocre people
I wish to speak to you of the Bodhisattva's virtue
Though the duration of the kalpa (jié shù) is exhausted, their virtue remains in surplus
The Bodhisattva is named Fǎlái
Among those various sages, he is like the moon among the stars
He holds various classical scriptures (jīng diǎn) and repeatedly teaches people
The various Bodhisattvas receive, chant, copy, and read
The originator of this Sūtra (jīng yuán) will certainly be your teacher. I urge you to go to him, and he will preach it for you
Chángbēi awoke from his concentration, looked left and right
He no longer perceived the Buddha
His heart was sorrowful, and tears flowed
And he said, ‘From where did the spiritual splendor (líng yào) of all the Buddhas come, and where has it now departed
Shànxìn Púsà, in an age without the Dharma, sought the True Dharma. A voice in the air said:
To the east, at a distance of ten thousand *yóujūn*, there is a king named Shànzhù.
Long ago, a Tathāgata appeared in the world but has long since entered Nirvāṇa.
As the Semblance Dharma declined, there was a woman.
Born of low status, her appearance was ugly, unmatched in the world.
Yet, she vaguely understood half a sentence and one verse.
She indicated that she had received a teaching, and you can go and ask her your doubts.
There is an expanse of mud, ten thousand *lǐ* wide and long. Anyone who treads upon it sinks.
Not even birds flying over it can surpass it; not a hair can overcome it.
You are now distressed and emaciated, your hands and feet are cracked and broken.
How can you proceed further?
Hearing this, I rejoiced, sped eastward, and reached the mud.
I resolved to abandon my life, threw my body into it, intending to sink and be lost.
When I cast my body,
where my body touched,
a small path emerged,
clean, white, long, and straight.
I trod upon it without further difficulties.
I went directly to that kingdom and entered Shànzhù chéng.
I lamented and blamed myself for not seeing the Bhagavān (World Honored One).
I saw this woman dwelling in squalor.
Her dwelling was full of holes.
Her human form was common and vulgar.
Yet, I respectfully viewed her as if she were the Buddha.
I looked upon her, paid homage, circumambulated her, and praised her.
I looked up and requested the woman to be my Great Master.
