May you condescend to teach and guide me so that I may achieve profound faith.
The woman replied:
The subtle Dharma of the Buddhas is measureless and boundless. What I have heard is only half a verse.
If you wish to hear it, I shall now speak it.
Commit no evil; perform all good.
Hearing these words, my body and mind became cool and pure, my faculties became tranquil, and I was spontaneously subdued.
I recited and practiced it, pondered its meaning, and thoroughly grasped its purport.
Immediately, I attained supernatural powers, flew back to my native land, and everywhere proclaimed this verse.
Through this merit, I achieved firm and unshakable faith in the Buddha Dharma.
All the *māras* were subdued and everyone submitted to transformation.
Before I had this faith, I constantly cycled through Saṃsāra.
For the sake of sentient beings, I revealed this faith, enabling them to practice it.
Not far north of Shèwèi chéng, in a village named Sànà, there was a poor Brāhmaṇa woman.
Named Bá tuóluó.
She bore a son.
Named Yīqiè Shìjiān Xiàn.
He lost his father while young.
When he was twelve years old,
his complexion, strength, and physical marks were unsurpassed.
He was intelligent, eloquent, wise, spoke subtly, and spoke well.
Furthermore, there was another village named Pō luóhēsī.
There resided an old Brāhmaṇa master.
Named Móní Bátuóluó.
He was skilled and proficient in the four Vedas (Pītuó jīng).
Yīqiè Shìjiān Xiàn studied under him.
Humble and reverent, he served him wholeheartedly, possessing pure faculties, retaining everything he was taught.
The master received an invitation from the king,
leaving Yīqiè Shìjiān Xiàn to guard the house before departing.
The Brāhmaṇa's wife was young and attractive.
She developed deep lustful feelings toward Shìjiān Xiàn.
Suddenly forgetting propriety and shame, she advanced and grasped his garment.
At that moment, Shìjiān Xiàn said:
Honorable one, you are now just like my mother.
How can you commit unlawful acts?
Harboring internal shame and fear, he dropped his garment and fled far away.
The master's wife, filled with intense desire, wept and spoke thus:
If I am suddenly rejected and you do not comply with my wishes,
and if you definitely do not follow me, I will take your life.
She immediately clawed her own body with her fingernails.
She acted with feminine deceit to adorn her body (or staged the scene).
She tied herself with rope, securing her feet so they would not leave the ground.
When her husband returned, he saw his wife and cut the rope with a knife.
He cried out loudly and asked why this was done.
The wife replied:
It was Shìjiān Xiàn who forcefully humiliated and oppressed me, causing this to happen.
Her husband pondered and said:
On the day Shìjiān Xiàn was first born, all the swords held by the *Kshatriyas* spontaneously slipped out (of their scabbards).
Their sharp edges curled up, and they fell to the ground.
At that time, all the *Kshatriyas* were greatly terrified.
Since there was such an omen on the day he was born,
one should know that this person possesses great virtue and power.
He said to Shìjiān Xiàn:
You are an evil person who has insulted your superior.
You are no longer a true Brāhmaṇa.
You must kill one thousand people to eliminate your sin.
Shìjiān Xiàn, by nature obedient and respectful of his master's teachings,
immediately reported to the master:
Alas, Venerable Sir, killing one thousand people is not what I should do.
The master then said to him:
Are you an evil person who does not desire to be born in heaven and serve as a Brāhmaṇa?
He replied:
Venerable Sir, very well. I obey your command. He killed a thousand people and returned to pay homage at his master's feet.
The master, having heard and seen this, conceived an extraordinary thought.
Are you a great evil person who therefore does not die?
He further considered: Now I shall make him die.
And he told him:
For every person you kill, take one finger.
When you have killed a thousand people, take the fingers, make a wreath, crown your head with it, and return.
Only then can you become a Brāhmaṇa.
Because of this cause and condition, he was named Yāngjuémóluó (Aṅgulimāla).
He immediately reported to the master:
Excellent, Venerable Sir. I accept the instruction.
He immediately killed a thousand people, but was still short one person.
At that time, Yāngjuémóluó’s mother thought her son must be hungry.
She personally carried four kinds of delicious food and brought it to him.
When the son saw his mother, he thought thus:
I should enable my mother to be born in heaven.
He immediately grasped his sword and advanced, intending to take her life.
At a distance of ten *yóujūn* less one *zhàng* from Shèwèi guó,
there was a tree named Āshūjiā (Ashoka).
At that time, the Buddha, possessing omniscient wisdom, arrived like the King of Elephants.
Yāngjuémóluó, upon seeing the Bhagavān, grasped his sword and rushed forward swiftly.
He thought thus:
I shall now kill this *śramaṇa* as well.
The Bhagavān manifested (a power) to evade him.
Yāngjuémóluó spoke this verse:
Stop, stop, Great *Śramaṇa*, son of the King of Śuddhodana!
I am Yāngjuémó, and now I must collect a finger.
The Bhagavān spoke this verse:
Stop, stop, Yāngjuémó! You should dwell in pure precepts!
I am the Samyaksaṃbuddha; I grant you the tribute of the sword of wisdom.
At that time, the mother saw the Buddha and Yāngjuémóluó engage in painful verbal dispute.
The son’s heart was subdued, and he let his body droop in mindfulness, thus speaking this verse:
The long-lost treasure is now recovered; eyes spoiled by dirt are now clean.
Alas! My son’s mind was deluded and confused, constantly covering his body with human blood.
The sharpest sword was always in his hand, killing many people until corpses piled up.
I should make this son follow me, and from now on, respectfully bow to the Samyaksaṃbuddha.
Many people saw him and cursed him, the words were hard to bear—your son bitterly criticized me thus.
In countless past *kalpas*, there was an aspiring practitioner.
Named Zhàn guāng.
He dwelled in the thickets of the forest, practicing auspicious vows.
For four million two hundred thousand years, he practiced unhindered.
He entered Shājié guó, where there was a potter’s daughter.
She saw this practitioner, whose appearance was beautiful and excellent.
Her lustful desire greatly increased, and she immediately threw herself at him.
The practitioner replied:
I do not desire this.
The woman said:
If it is not so, I shall kill myself.
Zhàn guāng thought to himself, "I protect the precepts."
If I violate them now, it would be inauspicious.
He stepped seven paces away, then felt compassion.
Violating the precepts brings the sin of falling into hell.
If I do not comply, the woman will harm herself.
I would rather allow this woman to attain peace and safety.
I shall patiently endure the pain of hell.
Zhàn guāng immediately returned and complied with the woman's desire.
He abandoned his practice and engaged in domestic life for twelve years.
After his life ended, he was born in the Brahmā heaven.
The Buddha said:
Do you wish to know who Zhàn guāng, the aspiring practitioner of that time, was?
He was none other than myself.
And the potter's daughter was Qúyī.
In the past, there were two Bodhisattvas whose aspirations were pure and conduct was clean.
They were inwardly tranquil and desireless, their appearance was like divine gold.
They carved rock to make their chamber, dwelling peacefully and settling their minds.
They wore rush garments, used grass mats, and drank spring water for sustenance.
They were pure and non-active (Wúwéi), their aspiration was like empty space.
They fully possessed the Four Jhānas (Sì Chán) and attained the wisdom of the Five Supernatural Powers (Wǔ Tōng Zhì).
All ordinary people, Śramaṇas, immortals, sages, various celestial beings (Tiān), dragons, ghosts, and spirits bowed down to them.
They resided in the mountains and marshes for over sixty years.
They compassionately pitied sentient beings and reverently served the Three Treasures (Sān Zūn).
The first name was Tíqíluó.
The second name was Nàlài.
Tíqíluó rose late at night, recited sūtras until extremely weary, and lay down outside.
Nàlài was also reciting sūtras at that time and accidentally stepped on Tíqíluó’s head.
Tíqíluó immediately arose and said:
"Who stepped on my head?"
"When the sun rises tomorrow morning, it will split your head into seven parts."
Nàlài said: "I stepped on your head by mistake. Why is your curse so severe?
Even inanimate objects sometimes touch each other.
How much more so people who live together year-round, how could they not make a mistake?
If your words are true, then when the sun rises tomorrow morning, my head will surely break.
I will control the sun and prevent it from coming out."
Consequently, the sun did not emerge, and for five days the entire country was pitch black.
Torches and candles were needed to search, officials neglected their duties, and the ruler and the people were terrified and confused.
The King gathered all his subordinates and invited the various Daoist masters (Dàoshì).
The King said:
"Where does the fault lie for the sun not emerging?"
Among the Daoist masters, one who possessed the Five Supernatural Powers said:
"Two Daoist masters in the mountains had a minor dispute, and one is restraining the sun, preventing it from rising."
The King said: "What should be done?"
He replied:
"If the King leads all his officials and people, regardless of rank, and rushes to them, bowing their heads in reconciliation, they will surely be merciful and harmonious."
The King immediately issued an edict, went to the mountains and marshes, knelt and bowed, saying:
"The prosperity of the nation and the tranquility of the people are due to the grace of the two venerables.
But now there is disharmony, and the entire kingdom is in distress.
The fault lies with me; the common people are blameless.
I beg you to have compassion and forgive us."
Nàlài said:
"O King, please admonish and enlighten his mind.
If his intention is resolved, I will let the sun rise."
The King went to Tíqíluó and announced Nàlài's instruction.
Tíqíluó immediately considered the other's welfare, smeared mud upon his head, and allowed the sun to rise.
The mud-covered head immediately broke into seven pieces.
Nàlài was non-active (Wúwéi), and the King, ministers, and common people were all joyful.
The two Daoist masters extensively expounded upon governing the country for the King.
They advised that he should encourage the people using the Four Immeasurables (Sì Děng) and unending compassion.
They should uphold the Five Precepts (Wǔ Jiè) and observe the Ten Virtuous Deeds (Shí Shàn Xíng).
The King and his officials and people all accepted the precepts.
When the King returned to his country, he issued an edict saying:
"Regardless of whether people are noble or humble, they shall observe the teachings of the Five Precepts and the Ten Virtuous Deeds,
and this shall be the standard for the nation."
From then on, the King's beneficence reached even the grass and trees.
The ministers were loyal and pure.
The Buddha told the Bhikṣus:
"Nàlài was myself.
Tíqíluó was Mílè.
In a past age, there was a Bodhisattva,
named Yuèfǎ.
He was born and raised in a royal family, and he transcribed, read, and recited all the virtuous teachings he heard.
In order to seek the Dharma (Fǎ), he traveled through various kingdoms and cities.
At that time, there was a person standing by the side of a deep pit who spoke to Yuèfǎ, saying:
"Come, come! I will give you a verse (jì) spoken by the Buddha."
The Bodhisattva replied:
"Give it to me."
That person then said:
"Give me your jeweled robes and Māṇi (Móní) pearl necklace,
and then I will give it to you."
The Bodhisattva agreed to this.
That person’s greed grew.
He also said: "If you can give me the chance to hear the Buddha's verse and then throw yourself into this deep pit,
if you can do this, you must first make a vow, and only then will I speak the verse for you."
The Prince replied:
"Alas, benevolent one!
If you wish me to throw myself into this deep pit, what benefit do you gain?"
That person replied:
"I gain nothing.
But I fear that the King (Prince) now gives up these treasures,
and once he hears the verse, he will generate regret.
Relying on his prestige and power, he will take them back from me."
The Prince replied:
"You just speak the verse.
I will never regret giving you the treasures, nor will I regret throwing myself into the deep pit."
That person heard his vow and spoke the Buddha’s verse to him.
The Bodhisattva immediately gave him the jeweled robes and the Māṇi (Móní) pearl necklace.
He then made another vow, saying:
"If I sincerely relinquished this without regret,
by the power of this truthful statement, let me, when I fall from this height, settle safely and unharmed upon the ground."
Having made this vow, he then threw himself down.
Before he reached the ground, the Four Heavenly Kings (Sì Tiānwáng) came, gently caught him, and placed him on the ground, saying:
"The verse spoken by the Buddha is profoundly subtle and has great benefit."
That person also descended from the height and came to the Bodhisattva.
He spoke thus:
"O Prince, this is rare! You were able to perform such a difficult act. What Dharma are you seeking?"
The Bodhisattva replied:
"Through this deed, I shall attain Buddhahood (Fó Dào).
I have made the Four Great Vows (Sì Hóng Shì)."
When that person heard this, he immediately generated faith.
He said to the Bodhisattva:
"Return, O Prince, your jeweled robes and pearl necklace.
It is right for the King (Prince) to have them." [The Prince] replied:
"It is like something that has been cast out or spit up; how can one eat it again?"
That person pleaded, saying:
"If you will not take them back, please accept my repentance.
When you attain Buddhahood later, please save and deliver me."
The Prince Yuèfǎ was Śèlìfú.
The person who spoke the verse at that time was Lǐqiélì.
Good men, long ago in the past, before the Buddha Sun had yet arisen,
I was a Brahmin (Póluómén) at that time.
I practiced the conduct of a Bodhisattva.
I was able to thoroughly understand the sūtras and treatises of the heterodox ways (Wàidào).
I practiced tranquil extinction (jìmie) and was fully endowed with dignity.
My mind was pure and could not be corrupted by external desires.
I extinguished the fire of anger and hatred (chēnhuì).
I accepted and upheld the Dharma of permanence, bliss, self, and purity.
I traveled everywhere seeking the Mahāyāna (Dàchéng) scriptures.
I had not even heard the name of the Vaipulya (Fāngděng) teachings.
I resided on Snowy Mountain (Xuě Shān), concentrating my mind in meditation for immeasurable years.
I practiced difficult asceticism (kǔ xíng).
At that time, Śakra Devānām Indra (Shì Tí Huán Yīn) transformed himself into the appearance of a Rākṣasa (Luóchà).
His form was extremely terrifying.
He descended to Snowy Mountain, stood nearby, and remained there.
This Rākṣasa was fearless in heart, valiant, and difficult to oppose.
His eloquence was ordered, and his voice was clear and refined.
He proclaimed half a verse (bàn jì) spoken by a past Buddha:
"All conditioned phenomena (zhū xíng) are impermanent, they are the dharma of arising and cessation."
Having finished speaking, [he/it] then stopped.
The appearance manifested was extremely frightening.
Flipping its eyes, it looked around everywhere, observing the four directions.
This ascetic, hearing this half *gāthā* (verse), felt joy in his heart.
He immediately sat up, raised his hair with his hands, and looked around in the four directions.
And spoke these words:
“The verse I just heard, who spoke it?”
At that time, looking in the four directions, he saw no other person.
He only saw the *Róuoshā*.
He immediately spoke these words:
“Who opened such a gate of liberation?
Who can thunder forth the sounds of all Buddhas?
Who, amidst the sleep of birth and death (*shēngsǐ*), is solely awakened?”
Crying out such words:
“Who here can show and guide living beings starved in the realm of birth and death to the unsurpassed taste of the Path?
Innumerable living beings are sinking in the ocean of birth and death (*shēngsǐ*).
Who can be a great shipmaster among them?
These living beings are constantly entangled by the severe illness of afflictions (*fánnǎo*).
Who can act as a good doctor among them?
The speaking of this half *gāthā* enlightened my mind,
just like the crescent moon gradually opening the lotus flower.”
At that time, I again had this thought:
“Could it be this *Róuoshā* who spoke this verse?”
I immediately gave rise to doubt that it was spoken by him.
Why?
“This person's appearance is extremely frightening.
If there is one who can hear these verses and phrases,
all fear and ugliness would immediately be removed.
How can an appearance like this be capable of speaking this verse?”
Good man,
at that time, I again had this thought:
“However, this *Róuoshā* might have been able to meet past Buddhas,
and heard this half verse spoken by the Buddhas.”
I immediately went to the *Róuoshā* and said:
“Excellent, great being (*dàshì*).
Where did you obtain this half verse spoken by those in the past who have transcended fear?”
He immediately replied to me:
“Great *Bólúomén* (Brahmin),
you should not ask me this meaning now.
Why?
I have not eaten for many days already.
I have searched everywhere but could not find anything.
My mind is disturbed by the suffering of hunger and thirst, and I speak confusedly.
This is not known by my original mind.”
At that time, I again spoke to the *Róuoshā*, saying:
“Great being, if you can complete the speaking of this verse for me,
I shall become your disciple for life.
That which you speak—the name does not end, nor does the meaning run out.
For what reason do you not wish to speak it?
Indeed, the giving of material wealth will be exhausted.
The cause/condition of the giving of the Dharma (*fǎshī*) cannot be exhausted.
The inexhaustible giving of the Dharma provides much benefit.”
The *Róuoshā* replied:
“Your wisdom is excessive.
You only worry about your own body and do not think of me, who is oppressed by the suffering of hunger; truly, I cannot speak.”
I immediately asked:
“What is the object that you consume?”
The *Róuoshā* replied:
“You do not need to ask.
If I speak of it, it will cause many people fear.”
I spoke to him again:
“This place is secluded, and there is no one else here.
I do not fear you.
Why do you not speak?”
The *Róuoshā* replied:
“That which I consume is only the warm flesh of humans.
That which I drink is only the hot blood of humans.
Although there are many people in the world, they all possess meritorious virtue (*fúdé*) and are moreover protected by the various heavenly beings.
But I am without power and cannot kill them.”
I spoke to him again:
“You only need to complete the speaking of the whole verse.
I will offer my body as a gift and offering to you.
Even if I die, a body like this will be of no further use.
It will be devoured by tigers, wolves, owls, eagles, and vultures.
And yet I will not obtain even a hair's breadth of merit (*fú*).
In order to seek the Buddha, I will renounce this non-enduring body to exchange for an enduring body.”
The *Róuoshā* replied:
“Who would believe that you would abandon your beloved body just for eight characters?”
I immediately replied:
“It is like someone giving a clay vessel to another and receiving a vessel of seven treasures.
I renounce this non-enduring body to obtain the Vajra body (*Jīngāng shēn*).
The Great *Fàntiānwáng* (Brahma King) and *Shìtíhuányīn* (Śakra Devānām Indra),
as well as the *Sìtiānwáng* (Four Heavenly Kings), can attest to this matter.
Furthermore, the various *Púsà* (Bodhisattvas) possessing the heavenly eye, who wish to benefit countless sentient beings,
those who practice the Mahāyāna and possess the Six Pāramitās can also attest to it, up to and including the Buddhas of the ten directions.”
The *Róuoshā* immediately spoke:
“That which is produced and destroyed—when the destruction is extinguished, Nirvāṇa (*jìmìe*) is bliss.”
The *Róuoshā* said:
“*Púsà Móhēsà*, you have now heard the complete meaning of the verse.
Your vow is entirely fulfilled.
If you truly wish to benefit all sentient beings, then offer me your body now.”
At that time, I deeply pondered this meaning.
Then, in various places—on rocks, walls, trees, and paths—
I wrote down this verse.
I immediately retied the clothes I was wearing,
fearing that after death my body might be exposed.
I immediately climbed a high tree and threw myself down from it.
Before I reached the ground, various sounds arose in the empty sky.
The sounds reached up to the *Ājiānìzhà* (Akaniṣṭha Heaven).
At that time, the *Róuoshā* reverted to the form of *Shì* (Śakra/Indra).
He immediately caught my body in mid-air and placed it on the flat ground.
Due to this cause and condition, I was then able to transcend
a full twelve *kalpas* (eons).
I will achieve *Ānòuduōluó Sānmiǎo Sānpútí* (Anuttara Samyak Sambodhi) before *Mílè* (Maitreya).
Question:
The body of a *Púsà* is not wood or stone.
How is it that when sentient beings come and cut and sever him, he does not give rise to any different thought (of anger)?
Answer:
Some people say:
A *Púsà* has cultivated *Chàntíbōluómì* (Kṣānti-pāramitā, the perfection of patience) for a long time, and thus he can remain without sorrow or distress.
Just like the Immortal *Chàntí Xiānrén*, when his hands and feet were severed, his blood turned into milk.
Some people say:
A *Púsà*, having deeply cultivated great compassion for countless generations, does not grieve or worry even when cut and severed.
This is comparable to plants and trees which possess no thought of anger.
Some people say:
A *Púsà* deeply cultivates *Bōrěbōluómì* (Prajñā-pāramitā, the perfection of wisdom).
In transforming his body, he obtains the fruit and retribution of *Bōrěbōluómì*.
Because his mind is empty, he clearly knows emptiness.
When his body is cut and severed, his mind remains unmoved.
Just as outer objects are unmoved, so is his inner being.
Due to the fruit of *Bōrě* (wisdom), he makes no distinctions among all phenomena (*fǎ*).
Some people say:
This *Púsà* does not possess a body subject to birth and death (*shēngsǐ shēn*).
It is a body born of the Dharma nature (*fǎxìng*), having transcended the Three Realms.
Because he dwells within the resulting fruit of the undefiled sage mind,
his body is like wood or stone, yet he can compassionately remember those who cut and sever him.
Because this *Púsà* can give rise to such a mind,
when cut, severed, seized, or stolen, both internal and external possessions (*fǎ*),
his mind is unmoved.
This is the rare quality (*fǎ*) of the *Púsà*.
With the Buddha Eye, I see that in worlds throughout the ten directions, numerous as the sands of the Ganges,
when a *Púsà* enters the hell realms,
he causes the fires to extinguish and the boiling cauldrons to cool.
He converts sentient beings using three matters.
Throughout immeasurable *Āsēngqí jié* (asaṃkhyeya kalpas),
he deeply practices compassion, distributing external possessions.
Yet his intent is still not satisfied.
Only by giving his body in *bùshī* (dāna/giving) is his satisfaction complete.
For example, *Yàowáng Púsà* (Medicine King Bodhisattva) offered external rare treasures to the Buddha.
His intent was still not satisfied; only by making his body into a lamp was his satisfaction complete.
Though external objects are many, they are not considered a great kindness.
Why is that?
Because they are not held in high regard.
Only when the body is obtained can there be astonishing resonance.
Therefore, the body is given.
I recall in the past, during immeasurable *kalpas* (eons),
at that time, the world was named *Suōpó* (Sāha).
A Buddha appeared in the world,
titled *Shìjiāwén* (Śākyamuni).
He preached the *Dà Nièpán Jīng* (Mahāparinirvāṇa Sūtra) for the great assembly.
At that time,
from a good friend,
I heard that the Dharma should be expounded.
When I heard this, my heart was full of joy.
I wished to prepare an offering.
Being poor and having no possessions, I went around selling my body, hoping for a small gain.
Then, on the road, I saw a person who said:
“I wish to buy a servant.
But for household work, no one is suitable.
I have a terrible illness, and the good doctor prescribed medicine.
I should take three *liǎng* (ounces) of human flesh daily.
If you can provide me three *liǎng* of your body's flesh daily,
then I will give you five pieces of gold coinage.”
When I heard this, my heart was greatly delighted.
I immediately replied: “Give me the money and grant me seven days.
Wait until my affairs are completed.
Then I will return to you.”
That person replied:
“Seven days is not possible.
If you can truly do this,
I will allow you one day.”
At that time,
I took the money.
I returned to where the Buddha was.
I bowed my head to the ground, performed the full prostration, and offered everything to the Buddha.
Afterwards, with a sincere mind, I listened to and received the Sūtra.
At that time, I was dull and slow, and although I had heard the Sūtra,
I was only able to receive and retain one verse.
I immediately returned to the home of that sick person.
Although I provided the flesh daily at that time,
because I remembered the verse, I did not feel it as pain.
A full month passed.
Due to this cause and condition, his illness was cured.
My body was restored and had no wounds or scars.
When I saw my body was complete and whole,
I immediately developed the mind of unsurpassed *Pútí* (Bodhi).
The power of one verse is already capable of this.
How much more so if one completely receives, retains, reads, and recites! I saw that this Sūtra had such great benefit.
I again redoubled my resolve.
I vowed that afterward, upon achieving Buddhahood, my title would be *Shìjiāwén*.
At that time, the *Rúlái* (Tathāgata) preached the *Fǎhuá Jīng* (Lotus Sūtra).
The other *Púsà* requested to protect and uphold it.
The Buddha immediately stopped them, saying:
“There are countless and immeasurable *Púsà* from the realms below.”
Due to the earth cracking and splitting, they simultaneously leaped forth and manifested, dwelling in the empty sky.
They went to the Stūpa of Seven Treasures, to the *Duōbǎo Rúlái* (Prabhūtaratna Tathāgata) and the *Shìjiāwén Fó* (Śākyamuni Buddha).
They bowed their heads to the ground in reverence toward the two World Honored Ones.
In the past, when the Shìzūn traveled in Rōuyuèqí (Rājagṛha).
The King commanded dozens of men constantly to gather beautiful flowers.
After one day, the great and small nobles and the flower-gathering women all went out of the city to gather flowers.
Wishing to return and enter the city,
they saw from afar the Shìzūn, whose excellent marks and majestic light were towering and immeasurable.
He was like the moon among the stars, or like the sun when it first rises, illuminating the world.
He was surrounded by disciples and Púsàs (Bodhisattvas) in front and behind.
They immediately went to the place of the Fó (Buddha), bowed their heads, and paid homage.
They thought to themselves,
"Human life is difficult to protect, a Buddha's era is difficult to encounter, and the teachings of the Sūtra are difficult to meet.
To encounter the Great Sage now is like the sick receiving a physician.
Since we are poor and lowly, moreover belonging to the county officials and suffering the hardship of forced labor,
we are constantly not masters of our own actions.
The King is strict and urgent.
We are responsible for providing gathered flowers, always submitting them early.
If we miss the time, we might be executed.
The assembly of Sages is difficult to encounter;
it happens only once in a hundred million ages.
We would rather abandon our bodies and lives
to offer the flowers to the Fó and scatter them among the assembly of Sages.
Thereby we may receive the precepts of the Sūtra, listen to and observe the profound Dharma, and attain endless wisdom.
Since countless eons, we have been harmed by others, in numbers too great to count.
Never before have we sacrificed our lives for the Dharma.
Now we make offerings to the Shìzūn in the karma of the Sānbǎo (Three Jewels).
Even if we are killed, we will not fall into suffering but will surely be born in a peaceful place."
They stepped back, took refuge, concentrated their minds, and paid homage again.
The Fó knew their thoughts.
He manifested the intent of the Great Dào (Way) and had deep compassion for them.
He fully expounded the Dharma of Great Joy,
the boundless Six Pāramitās, the Four Immeasurable Minds (Sìděng), the Four Favors (Sì'ēn), and the Three Emancipations of the Púsà.
All the flower gatherers generated the intent for the Way.
Their minds understood the Fó’s wisdom, reaching the state of non-retrogression and no-origination.
The Fó immediately granted them assurance (Vyākaraṇa).
In the future, they would attain Buddhahood.
Their title would be Miàohuá (Wonderful Flower).
Possessing the complete Ten Titles.
When the people nearby heard this, none were not delighted.
They requested and received the Great Dharma and made offerings to the Sānbǎo.
At that time, the flower gatherers returned to their homes.
They bid farewell to their two parents and wives and children.
"Our lives end today, we will be killed by the King."
The parents were astonished and asked, "What crime or fault have you committed?"
The sons fully answered,
"The King is extremely strict and urgent.
Since we have violated and missed the proper time,
and furthermore have no flowers,
we will surely meet mortal danger, therefore we say farewell."
The two parents, hearing this, grew even more distressed.
"What should be done?"
They opened the baskets and looked, and they were full of beautiful flowers.
The fragrance of various Mandārava (Sūmàn) blossoms wafted far in the four directions.
The parents said,
"You can present these to the King."
The sons each replied,
"If others see this, they will surely report it to the King.
Furthermore, having violated the time, we fear we will not be safe."
At that time, the King was greatly enraged.
Seeing them arrive late and having scattered all the flowers,
he dispatched soldiers to apprehend them.
They accepted the King's order and were bound with their hands behind their backs and taken into the palace.
Their crime was punishable by execution in the marketplace.
The men were not afraid, and their facial expressions did not change.
The King was puzzled and asked them,
"You all have committed a crime, your lives are uncertain, you have been bound and are about to be executed.
Why are you not fearful, and why has your facial expression not changed?"
They immediately reported to the King, saying,
"In life there is death; when things are formed, they decline.
Since countless eons, we have constantly practiced non-Dharma, not cherishing our bodies or lives.
This morning, while gathering flowers, we happened to encounter the Shìzūn.
We offered the flowers as tribute, bowed our heads, and took refuge.
We knew that violating the command meant death.
We would rather die with virtue
than live without virtue.
Returning home, we looked at the flower baskets, and they were full again as before.
This is all due to the grace and compassion of the Rúlái (Tathāgata)."
The King inquired about this to the Fó.
The Fó indicated that it was so.
The King said,
"These people sincerely desire to save the ten directions and did not begrudge their bodies or lives.
Therefore, they took the collective flowers and scattered them upon the Fó.
Having no thought of retribution (reward) in mind, they have already received assurance (Vyākaraṇa).
In the future, they will attain Buddhahood, titled Miàohuā."
The King was greatly joyful.
He quickly unbound them all, repented of his error, and blamed himself.
"My foolish intention failed to realize that I was binding Púsàs."
The Fó said,
"Excellent, excellent!
One who can correct oneself is the same as one who has no fault.
Virtuous man, a Púsà who receives and upholds the moral precepts (Jìnjiè)
makes this vow:
'I would rather throw this body into a fiery pit
than violate the prohibitions set by the Buddhas of the three ages by engaging in impure conduct with women.
I would rather wrap my body with hot iron
than dare to receive the clothing of faithful Dànyuè (Dānapati/donors) with a precept-breaking body.
I would rather swallow hot iron pellets with this mouth
than dare to eat the food and drink of faithful Dànyuè with a precept-destroying mouth.
I would rather sleep upon a great hot iron
than dare to receive the bedding and sleeping mats of faithful Dànyuè with a precept-breaking body.
I would rather receive three hundred spears through this body
than dare to receive the medicine of faithful Dànyuè with a precept-destroying body.
I would rather throw this body into a cauldron of hot iron
than dare to receive the houses and residences of faithful Dànyuè with a precept-breaking body.
I would rather have this body shattered by an iron hammer, from head to foot, until it is like fine dust,
than receive the reverence and prostration of all Kèlì (Kṣatriya), Póluómén (Brāhmaṇa), and householders with a precept-breaking body.
I would rather have my two eyes gouged out with hot iron
than look at the attractive forms of others with a contaminated mind.
I would rather have my body pierced all over with an iron awl
than listen to attractive sounds with a contaminated mind.
I would rather have my nose cut off with a sharp knife
than greedily smell fragrances with a contaminated mind.
I would rather have my tongue cut open with a sharp knife
than greedily cling to delicious tastes with a contaminated mind.
I would rather have my body hewn and chopped by a sharp axe
than greedily cling to various sensations of touch with a contaminated mind.
Why is this?
Because these causes and conditions can lead the practitioner
to fall into the hells, the realm of animals (Chùshēng), or the realm of hungry ghosts (Èguǐ).
Jiāshè (Kāśyapa), this is called the Púsà Móhēsà (Mahāsattva) protecting and upholding the moral precepts.
He universally bestows them upon all sentient beings.
By these causes and conditions, he vows to enable sentient beings to guard all prohibitions and attain pure precepts.
Virtuous man, when the Púsà cultivates these precepts,
he immediately attains abiding in the First Immovable Stage (Bhumī).
Like Xūmí Shān (Mount Sumeru),
it cannot be moved by violent winds arising from the oceans.
The Púsà, abiding in this stage,
is not moved by form, sound, smell, taste, or touch.
He does not fall into the hells, the realm of animals, or the realm of hungry ghosts.
He does not regress to the stage of Shēngwén (Śrāvaka) or Pìzhīfó (Pratyekabuddha).
He is not scattered by the evil winds of aberrant views.
There are two types of Púsàs who generate the initial thought (Fāxīn):
The first performs all the Bōluómìs (Pāramitās).
The second merely generates the initial thought in emptiness.
Those who practice the Púsà Way,
although their deeds are not yet complete, can surpass all others.
Like the Jiāluópínjiā (Kalaviṅka) bird,
although still in the egg, it can already utter a sound that surpasses all other birds.
For example, a Luóhàn (Arhat) who possesses the Six Supernatural Powers (Liùtōng)
led a Shāmí (Śrāmaṇera/novice monk) and ordered him to carry the robes and bowl.
The Shāmí thought,
'I should enter Nièpán (Nirvāṇa) through the Fó Vehicle.'
The master knew his thought and immediately took the robes and bowl to carry them himself.
He pushed the Shāmí to walk ahead.
The Shāmí again reconsidered,
'The Fó Way is extremely difficult.
I would dwell long in Saṃsāra and endure immeasurable suffering.
Let me quickly enter Nièpán using the Lesser Vehicle (Xiǎochéng).'
The master again returned the robes and bowl pouch to the Shāmí, telling him to carry them and walk behind.
This happened up to three times.
The Shāmí reported to the master,
'Master, you are old and frail, acting like a child.'
The master immediately replied,
'When you first generated the thought to become a Fó, that esteemed mental stage was my teacher.
Even all Pìzhīfós should still make offerings to it.
How much more so an Luóhàn?
Therefore, I pushed you to walk ahead.
Now your mind regrets and you wish to take the Lesser Vehicle,
but you have not yet attained it easily.
You are far removed from me.
Therefore, I ordered you to stay behind.'
The Shāmí was startled and enlightened, and immediately abided in the Great Vehicle (Dàchéng).
In the countless eons of the past, there was a Fó
named Yīqièdù (All-Crossing).
He traveled with his retinue to collect alms (fēnwèi).
There were three sons of respected elders, dressed elaborately and playing together.
They saw the Fó and the various Púsàs, whose light was towering and majestic.
Pointing at each other with their hands, they said,
"We should all make offerings together."
Two children replied,
"Since we have no flowers or incense, what should we use?"
One child removed the white pearl from his head and placed it in his hand.
He then told the two children, "We can use this to make offerings to the Fó."
The two children imitated him, removing the white pearls from their heads and placing them in their hands.
They immediately went to the place of the Fó.
One child then asked the other two children,
"For what should we seek (vow) by possessing this merit?"
One child said,
"I vow to be like the respected Bhikṣu (Bǐqiū) on the Fó's right side."
The other child said,
"I vow to be like the Bhikṣu with divine powers (Shénzú) on the left side."
Together they asked the remaining child.
He replied,
"I want to be like the Fó."
Eight thousand heavenly beings (Tiānzǐ) all exclaimed, "Excellent!"
"If you achieve what you have vowed, all beings above and below will receive grace."
When the three young children had arrived before the Fó,
they each scattered their white pearls upon the Fó.
The pearls of the two children who generated the Shēngwén intention
rested upon the Fó's shoulders.
The pearl of the one child who generated the intent for Pútí (Bodhi)
rested upon the Fó's head.
It transformed into a canopy woven with pearls and flowers, within which was the Fó.
The Fó told Shèlìfú (Śāriputra), "The central child is precisely my present body.
The child on the right side is Shèlìfú.
The child on the left side is Mùlián (Maudgalyāyana).
Shèlìfú, because you originally feared Saṃsāra,
you did not generate the Púsà mind and wished quickly to enter Níhuán (Nirvāṇa).
Observe this one child who generated the mind for Anòuduōluó Sānmiǎo Sānpútí (Anuttarā Samyak Sambodhi)."
In the past, the Púsà,
was, at that time, an ordinary man.
His age was sixteen.
He dedicated himself to profound study, mastering various Sūtras.
Sighing deeply, he said:
“Only the Buddhist Sūtras are the most true and the most marvelous.
I ought to embrace their true essence and thereby find self-peace.”
His parents wanted to arrange a marriage for him.
He replied sorrowfully:
“No greater calamity or evil exists than lust (form, *sè*).
If this seductive calamity arrives, moral virtue will be utterly lost.
If I do not escape and retreat, will I not be swallowed by the wolf?”
Thereupon, he fled to a foreign country.
He labored for wages to sustain himself.
At that time, there was an old farmer (*wēng*) who had no heir.
Walking through the reeds, he found a girl.
Her beauty surpassed all others in the land, and he happily raised her as his heir.
He sought a husband for her, but there was no suitable old man in the entire country.
He said:
“Young man, I have enough resources at my dwelling to give you my daughter as your wife and for you to become my heir.”
The girl possessed a mystical virtue that confused the Púsà’s heart.
Not long after taking her [as wife],
he immediately realized:
“I have seen the clear teachings of all Buddhas,
which take lust (form) as fire,
and humans as flying moths.
The moth covets the fire’s color,
and its body is burned and cooked.
This old man used the fire of lust,
to burn my person.
The bait of wealth hooks my mouth,
and the domestic afflictions destroy my virtue.”
That night, silently and swiftly, he traveled over a hundred *lǐ*.
He sought refuge in an empty pavilion for the night.
The attendant of the pavilion said:
“Who are you, sir?”
He replied: “I just wish to spend the night here.”
Upon entering and seeing the bedding,
there was already a woman there.
Her face resembled his wife’s.
She confused the Púsà’s heart, and he lived with her.
Five years accumulated again.
His bright mind awoke, and he said:
“Lasciviousness is like an oyster worm, destroying and endangering life.”
He silently and swiftly departed.
Again, he saw a woman and lived with her for ten years.
Again, his bright mind awoke, and he said:
“My calamity is serious!
I run but cannot escape.”
He swore a deep oath to himself, saying:
“I will never seek lodging again.”
He fled once more.
He saw a large house from afar and avoided it, traveling through the grass.
The gatekeeper said:
“Who travels at night?”
He answered:
“I am heading for the village ahead.”
The gatekeeper also said:
“There is an inner forbidden person calling out what you saw before.”
The woman, similar to the previous ones, said:
“Since countless *kalpas*, we have sworn to be husband and wife. Where are you running to?”
The Púsà reflected:
“The root of desire is difficult to extract! Is it truly like this?”
Immediately, he generated the thought of the Four Impermanences.
He extinguished all afflictions of the Three Realms.
How could the remaining impurities not be completely destroyed?
The ghost-wife immediately vanished.
He then saw the various Buddhas standing before him,
preaching the concentration of non-thought, granting him the monastic precepts, making him the master Wúshèng Shī, and the Púsà saved all beings universally and boundlessly.
Shàng Jīnguāngshǒu, along with the elder’s son, Wèiwén,
were together in the pleasure garden, scattering flowers, burning incense, and playing musical instruments for adornment.
At that time, that woman, observing the elder’s son, felt satisfied in her mind.
Wénshū Shīlì transformed this woman’s body, and she immediately died.
Her color changed for the worse.
Pus and blood flowed from her eyes, ears, nose, and mouth.
Her body was rotten and decomposed, unbearable to look upon.
Green flies flew over and around, sharing in the meal [of her corpse].
When the elder’s son saw the woman’s body transformed and ruined in this way,
he was terrified and distressed, seeking refuge to escape and be delivered from this calamity.
Where should I go to be free from this suffering?
At that time, Wénshū Shīlì, by his pure spiritual power,
caused the trees in the garden naturally to utter praises.
When the elder’s son heard the trees’ praises and hymns,
he was joyful and leaped up, and good intentions immediately arose.
He wrapped the woman’s corpse in a cloth, abandoned it among the thicket of trees, and left.
Thereupon, the World-Honored One, wishing to enlighten and transform that elder’s son,
emitted light from his body, and its brightness universally illuminated the borders of the Mójié country.
The elder’s son saw the majestic divine power of the Tathāgata,
and joy arose in his heart.
Tiāndì Shì (Indra) then stood before him.
He saw the elder’s son and praised him, saying:
“Young man, you have good karma.
You have obtained blessings and benefits,
since you are able to see the Buddha.”
When the young man heard this encouragement and praise,
he immediately went with the Heavenly Emperor to the place of the Buddha.
Tiāndì Shì, understanding the young man’s mind,
used flowers and spoke to the young man:
“You should take these flowers and scatter them upon the Tathāgata.”
After scattering them, he bowed at the Buddha’s feet, stood before him, and reported:
“I now take refuge in the Buddha, the Dharma, and the Holy Assembly.
There was a reckless woman, Shàng Jīnguāngshǒu,
with whom I truly went to the pleasure garden for amusement and delight.
But today, her appearance turned vile, and she died instantly.
She abandoned all her clan relatives and dependents.
I am struck by great fear.
Will the King not investigate and question this matter?”
The Buddha said: “Wait a moment.”
At that time, Shàng Jīnguāngshǒu,
seeing that the elder’s son had received enlightenment and transformation,
and was following the Vinaya teachings,
immediately went to the Buddha’s place with musical instruments.
She bowed at the Buddha’s feet and withdrew to stand aside.
Then Wénshū Shīlì said to the elder’s son:
“Do you recognize this older sister?”
He replied:
“I know her already.”
He further asked:
“How do you know?”
Thereupon, the elder’s son responded to Wénshū Shīlì,
and spoke in verse:
“Form (*sè*) is like a mass of foam,
feeling and sensation are like bubbles arising briefly.
Imagination is like a mirage.
I understand it thus.”
The Buddha told Ānán:
“It was Wénshū Shīlì who, in a past ancient age, converted this woman and caused her to initiate the Bodhi-mind.
It was I, in a former life, who converted him and caused him to initiate the Bodhi-mind.
Shàng Jīnguāngshǒu, after ninety-two hundred thousand *kalpas*,
will attain Buddhahood.
Her title will be Bǎo Guāngmíng.
The elder’s son will become a Púsà,
named Dé Guāngyào.
When he again achieves Buddhahood,
before he enters Nirvāṇa,
he will confer the prediction upon the Púsà Dé Guāngyào.
Then, upon entering Nirvāṇa, his title will be Chízhú.”
There were two hundred *Tiānzǐ* (sons of heaven) who aroused the *Púsà* (Bodhisattva) mind,
but their resolve was not yet firm, and they all desired to fall away.
They each thought, "The Dharma of the Buddha is difficult to obtain.
We are now determined not to study the *Púsà* path.
It is better to achieve *Luóhàn* (Arhat) or *Pìzhīfó* (Pratyekabuddha) status and enter *Bānnihuán* (Parinirvāṇa)."
The Buddha knew that these people could become *Púsà*,
but their intent was retreating.
The Buddha then miraculously transformed into a *Jiāluóyuè* (Householder).
He held a bowl full of hundred-flavored rice and arrived before the Buddha.
He bowed immediately and offered the bowl to the Buddha.
The Buddha accepted the bowl instantly.
Wénshū Shīlì said to the Buddha,
"Shìzūn,
you should duly repay this kindness."
Shèlìfú was puzzled and immediately questioned the Buddha.
The Buddha immediately placed the bowl down on the ground.
The bowl then descended, submerging and passing through various *Chà* (Buddha-fields).
It went straight past seventy-two *Héngshā* (Ganges sands) equivalent *Chàtǔ* (Buddha-lands),
the name of which was Ōuhēshā.
The Buddha there was named Guāngmíng Wáng.
He is now present in the world.
The bowl stopped in the air above that Buddha-land; there was no one holding it.
In all the Buddha-fields the bowl passed through,
the attendants of those Buddhas all questioned their respective Buddhas.
The Buddhas answered, "Above, there is a Buddha named Shìjiāwén.
The bowl came from there,
to save and protect the minds of the retreating *Púsà*."
The Buddha said to Shèlìfú,
"Go and seek the bowl and bring it back."
Shèlìfú immediately relied on the majestic spiritual power of the Buddha,
and using his own wisdom power and ten thousand *Sānmèi* (Samādhi), he passed ten thousand Buddha-fields, yet did not see the bowl at all.
Rising from his *Sānmèi*, he reported back to the Buddha, saying,
"I sought it but did not find it."
The Buddha then sent Mùlián, and he also failed to see it.
Xūpútí and five hundred other *Zūnzhě* (Venerables) were all unable to see it.
Mílè Púsà was also unable to see it.
The Buddha commanded Wénshū Shīlì to seek the bowl.
Wénshū Shīlì did not rise from his seat but immediately entered *Sānmèi*.
He pointed his right finger toward the ground.
He traveled through all the Buddha-fields, and there was none that did not hear and know of it.
All the Buddha-lands he passed through were shaken.
In all these Buddha-lands, everyone saw Wénshū.
He passed seventy-two *Hénghéshā* (Ganges sands).
Between every single hair on his arm, there were hundreds of thousands of millions of rays of light, and hundreds of thousands of millions of lotus flowers.
Upon each lotus flower sat a *Púsà*.
They all praised the merits and virtues of Shìjiāwén Fó, the *Shēngwén* (Hearers), the *Púsà*, and the Buddha-land.
Then Shìjiāwén emitted light from under his foot,
illuminating the lands below, past seventy-two *Hénghéshā* equivalent Buddha-fields.
Seeing this light, they all attained the *Móbǐdī Sānmèi*.
Wénshū Shīlì used his right hand to take the bowl.
He returned, accompanied by countless *Púsà*.
Holding the bowl in his hand, he bowed and offered the bowl.
The Buddha said to Shèlìfú,
"I will now speak to you of events from past *Jié* (Kalpas).
Long ago, there was a Buddha
named Yǒng Mònéngshèng.
There was a *Bǐqiū Sēng* (Monk),
named Huìwáng,
who carried his bowl and entered the kingdom of Wéizhì Guó for alms-gathering.
He obtained hundred-flavored rice.
At that time, there was the son of a *Zūnzhě*, named Lígòu Wáng,
who was being held by his wet nurse
above the city gate.
The child saw the *Bǐqiū* from afar,
got down from the embrace, and went toward him,
asking for food and drink.
The *Bǐqiū* immediately gave him a honey cake.
The child ate it and knew the taste was sweet and delicious.
He followed the *Bǐqiū*, ignoring his wet nurse.
He then followed him to the place where Yǒng Mònéngshèng Fó was.
He bowed to the Buddha and sat to one side.
The *Bǐqiū* gave the food held in the bowl to the small child, asking him to offer it to the Buddha.
The child then presented it to the Buddha.
The Buddha ate until satisfied.
By this means, the food reached eighty-four thousand *Bǐqiū* and twelve thousand *Púsà*s.
Each and every one was full.
The food held by the child showed no reduction or loss.
The Buddha, using his majestic spiritual power, made the child joyful.
Consequently, the child received the Five Precepts from the *Bǐqiū* and aroused the *Pútí Xīn* (Bodhicitta).
The child's parents sought their son and bowed to the Buddha.
The son said to his father,
"I have now entered the *Púsà* Dharma.
I request to become a *Shāmén* (monk)."
The parents immediately consented.
"We, too, will arouse the mind and follow you."
The Buddha said,
"The *Bǐqiū* Huìwáng is Wénshū Shīlì.
The child at that time was my current body.
Those like my body, uncountable [Buddhas]
in *Asēngqí Chàtǔ* (uncountable Buddha-lands),
were all inspired and set in motion by Wénshū Shīlì.
We all benefit from the grace of Wénshū Shīlì."
The two hundred *Tiānzǐ* immediately thought to themselves,
"Shìjiāwén Fó was inspired and motivated by Wénshū Shīlì, resulting in his attainment of Buddhahood.
Why should we be negligent?"
Because of this thought, their minds became firm.
Pǔxián Púsà,
with renown earned through his mastery of supernatural powers and majestic virtue,
came from the East with an uncountable number of great *Púsà*.
All the kingdoms they passed through shook universally.
They rained down precious lotus flowers and created various kinds of music.
He was also surrounded by an assembly of innumerable *Bābù Guǐshén* (Eight Classes of Deities and Spirits) and other multitudes.
They paid homage to Shìjiāmóuní Fó.
They said to the Buddha,
"In the Buddha-land of Bǎowēidé Shàngwáng Fóguó,
we remotely heard that the *Fǎhuá Jīng* (Lotus Sūtra) was being preached in this *Suōpó Shìjiè* (Sahā World), and we have come together to listen and receive it.
We only request, Shìzūn, that you preach it."
The Buddha instructed Pǔxián,
"If there are good men or women
who achieve four Dharmas,
they shall attain this *Fǎhuá Jīng* after the Tathāgata's extinction."
Pǔxián Púsà said,
"If there is someone who diligently recites this Sūtra, whether walking or standing, and contemplates this Sūtra,
if that person should forget a single phrase or verse of this Sūtra,
the great *Púsà* assembly shall collectively go to that place,
manifesting themselves to make offerings, guard, protect, and comfort that person's mind.
Also, as an offering to the *Fǎhuá Jīng*, they shall enable that person to understand and master it again.
Those who see this will rejoice and become even more diligent.
By seeing me, they shall immediately attain *Sānmèi* and *Tuóluóní* (Dhāraṇī).
If in the later evil age, the four assemblies come seeking [the Dharma],
those who uphold it,
those who read and recite it,
those who copy it,
and those who wish to cultivate and practice this *Fǎhuá Jīng*—
they should strive diligently with a single mind for twenty-one days (three sets of seven days).
When the twenty-one days are complete, I shall also appear before that person and preach the Dharma for them."
In a past *Jié*, the son of the king of the Buddha named Guǎng Guāngmíng, whose name was Cái Gōngdé, was sixteen years old.
He was proud and arrogant, relying on his dignified appearance.
He never showed reverence or paid homage to the Buddha.
The Buddha immediately distributed tallies, asking who could teach and transform him.
Eighty-four thousand *Púsà* refused to accept the tally.
There was one *Púsà* named Jìng Jīngjìn
who said,
"I can."
Immediately, the great thousandfold world shook six times.
He then went and stood at the king's gate.
When the prince saw him, he reviled and slandered him with abusive words.
He threw dirt in his face.
He inflicted knives, staffs, tiles, and stones upon his body.
The *Púsà* at that time neither became angry nor left, and his mind was not weary or disgusted.
He endured such suffering for a thousand years.
After twenty thousand years, he finally reached the second gate entrance.
He did not reach the seventh gate entrance until eighty-four thousand years and seven days had passed.
At that time, the prince saw this *Púsà* and said,
"Ascetic, what are you seeking now that you have come?"
He immediately developed an inconceivable thought toward the *Púsà*.
"How is this person
able to constantly endure such suffering over this long period,
yet his mind is not weary?"
At that time, the *Púsà* knew that the prince's mind had already disciplined itself.
He immediately spoke a *Gè* (Gātha/verse), instructing him to go to the Buddha.
At that time, the prince immediately renounced his royal position.
He left home under the Buddha's Dharma, listened to the Dharma, dwelt in accordance with the Dharma, and attained the *Wúshēng Rěn* (Patience in the Unborn Dharmas).
The Jìng Jīngjìn of that time is my current body.
Cái Gōngdé is Mílè.
Shùtí Mónà
was before Bǎozàng Fó.
He placed his right knee on the ground, knelt respectfully, and clasped his hands.
He said to the Buddha,
"Shìzūn,
I have now aroused the unsurpassed *Pútí Xīn* and completed the roots of goodness.
Regarding the Dharma of the Three Vehicles, if I only seek my own benefit,
may white dragon-elephants naturally emerge from my two hands."
Due to the spiritual power of the Buddha, dragon-elephants immediately emerged from his two hands.
Their color was pure white, and seven parts of their bodies touched the ground.
When he saw this, he instructed them,
"Dragon-elephants, you all,
now ascend into the void and go from here.
Not far from here, universally rain down the eight virtuous fragrant waters over this world,
to awaken all sentient beings in this world.
If any sentient being encounters a single drop,
and smells its fragrant aroma, they shall entirely cut off the Five Coverings (obstacles to cultivation):
namely, lust, hatred, drowsiness, excitement/restlessness, and doubt."
At that time, the dragon-elephants were in the void,
traveling around swiftly and rapidly, just like a strong archer shooting arrows.
When all the tasks performed by these two dragon-elephants were accomplished,
they returned and stopped before the *Mónà*.
At that time, Shùtí was greatly delighted in his heart upon seeing them.
In the past, the Bodhisattva was born into the four castes.
Upon falling to the ground, he immediately said,
"I shall save sentient beings from ten thousand calamities.
I shall remove the blindness and deafness caused by ignorance and lack of Dharma, allowing them to hear and see the clear examples of the various Sages."
His nine generations of relatives exclaimed in surprise,
"We have never heard of a newborn child being able to speak.
Is this perhaps not the spiritual essence of the *Tiānlóng Guǐshén*?
We should consult the oracle about this."
He replied,
"I am transformed by the Supreme Sage.
I possess the wisdom of Universal Illumination (*Pǔmíng*).
I am not one of those minor spirits; do not harbor doubts."
Having finished speaking, he immediately fell silent.
His parents/relatives said,
"This child has the aspiration to nourish and broaden the cosmos (*Qiánkūn*).
He must not be an ordinary person."
They named him Pǔshī.
When he reached the age of ten,
he had thoroughly mastered all the Buddhist canons, scriptures, and various popular arts.
He took leave of his parents to help sentient beings and give charity to the poor.
His parents said,
"We have the highest fame of extreme wealth.
You may do as you please."
He replied,
"It is not enough; I beg to become a Śramaṇa (monk).
Please bestow upon me the Dharma robe, the alms bowl, and the tin staff, so that I may use these to save sentient
beings." His parents permitted it.
He traveled widely, teaching and transforming, passing through a great kingdom.
In that kingdom, there was a wealthy clan who also understood many scriptures.
Observing the demeanor of Pǔshī, they saw that his mind and nature were placid, fearful (of faults), and pure like heavenly gold.
He had the appearance of a Supreme Sage.
He would become a Hero of the World.
They said to Pǔshī,
"We have a humble daughter whom we wish to give to serve you (as a wife)."
He replied,
"Excellent.
Wait until I return."
Immediately, he boarded a vessel, crossed the sea, landed on the shore, and entered the mountains.
When he reached an uninhabited place, he saw a Silver City (*Yínchéng*) in the distance.
A venomous serpent guarded the palace, encircling the city seven times.
Its body was a hundred spans thick, and it raised its head to look at him.
Pǔshī thought,
"This creature has a harmful intent; I must generate compassion."
The serpent's venom immediately subsided, and it lowered its head and slept.
Pǔshī climbed over its head and entered the city.
The Deva-spirit (*Tiānshén*) inside the city saw him.
Happily, he said,
"We have long revered your sacred virtue; now you have come to dwell here.
This is truly my heartfelt wish."
Pǔshī stayed for thirty days.
Pǔshī entrusted the affairs to the minister who served nearby.
He personally received the offerings and food.
When the period of offerings was complete, the *Tiānshén* gave him a Bright Moon Pearl (*Míngyuè Zhēnzhū*).
The pearl illuminated forty thousand *lǐ*.
If an aspiration was made, all treasures would be supplied.
The *Tiānshén* said: "If you later attain Buddhahood, I vow to be your disciple."
Pǔshī replied, "It shall be so."
He then proceeded forward again.
He saw the Golden City (*Huángjīn Chéng*). A venomous serpent encircled the city fourteen times.
Its massive body was double the size of the previous one, and it raised its head several *zhàng* high.
Pǔshī again entered the concentration of compassion, and the serpent immediately lowered its head.
He climbed over it and entered the city.
The Celestial Being (*Tiānrén*) inside met him and joyfully said,
"We have long revered your spiritual radiance; it is extremely good that you dwell here.
I request that you remain for a hundred and eighty days.
I shall provide offerings."
After this period, Pǔshī took his leave.
The Celestial Being again presented him with a divine pearl.
It shone with a radiance extending two hundred thousand *lǐ*.
Whatever was wished for would be filled with all treasures.
"If you attain the Way, I vow to be your disciple, possessing unsurpassed spiritual powers (*shénzú*)."
He immediately went forward again and saw the Lapis Lazuli City (*Liúlí Chéng*).
Again, there was a venomous serpent whose body encircled the city twenty-one times.
It raised its head, glared angrily, and blocked the city gate.
Pǔshī again generated the concentration of compassion and vowed to save all sentient beings.
The venom ceased, it lowered its head, and Pǔshī climbed over it and entered the city.
The Celestial Being rejoiced as before.
He invited Pǔshī to stay for three seasons.
"I vow to provide offerings for your aspiration." When the period was completed, Pǔshī departed.
The *Tiānrén* also gave him a divine pearl whose light shone for one million six hundred thousand *lǐ*.
Wherever the pearl was located, all treasures would follow it.
Filling the space illuminated by its light, whatever the mind desired, if sought, would be obtained.
"If you attain Perfect Enlightenment, I vow to be your disciple, possessing the most luminous wisdom."
Pǔshī said, "You shall certainly attain your wish."
Pǔshī, having obtained the pearls, returned to his former location.
The various spirits of the sea held a joint conference and said,
"These three pearls are the only glory and splendor of our great ocean.
The ascetic has taken them all.
We would rather lose all other treasures than lose these pearls."
A Sea Spirit (*Hǎishén*) transformed into an ordinary man.
He stood before Pǔshī and said,
"I hear that the virtuous one has obtained the world's most excellent treasures.
May I see them?"
Pǔshī immediately showed them to him.
The spirit snatched them away.
Pǔshī said,
"I endured dangers and crossed the sea to obtain these treasures, wishing to relieve the destitute.
Instead, they have been taken by this spirit!
Return my pearls! If not, I shall drain your sea!"
The spirit replied,
"The great sea is deep and vast; who can empty it?"
Heaven encouraged him to create a wind.
Pǔshī said,
"Before Dìngguāng Fó (Dīpaṁkara Buddha),
I vowed to gain the power of the Way to overturn all the oceans.
I vowed to point and lift Mount Xūmí, shake Heaven and Earth, and move all the *kṣetra* (Buddha-fields).
The Buddha consented to my aspiration.
Now I have obtained that power!
You ghostly creature, with the strength of a thread of silk,
how can you restrain the momentum of my true righteousness?"
He immediately put both feet together and scooped up the seawater, throwing it beyond the Iron Ring Mountains (*Tiěwéi*).
The Pervading Pure Heaven (*Biànjìng Tiān*) said,
"I heard his aspiration before Dìngguāng Fó in the past.
He is certainly destined to become the World-Honored One (*Shìzūn*) and save beings like us."
The *Biànjìng Tiān* immediately descended and helped him scoop the water, removing eight parts out of ten.
The Sea Spirit (*Hǎishén*) cried out in fear,
"The water will be completely gone!
My dwelling is ruined!"
He immediately returned the pearls.
Pǔshī distributed charity along the way.
In the kingdoms he passed through, there were no longer any poor citizens.
The various kings everywhere reformed their conduct.
They adopted the Five Precepts (*Wǔjiè*) and Ten Good Deeds (*Shíshàn*) as the governing law of the nation.
They opened the prisons and granted great amnesties.
He benefited sentient beings, and eventually attained Buddhahood.
Pǔshī was I myself.
The father was Báijìng Wáng.
The mother was my mother, Shěmiào.
The ascetic's daughter at that time is now Qiúyí.
The Deva in the Silver City (*Yínchéng*) at that time is now Ānán.
The Deva in the Golden City (*Jīn Chéng*) is Mùlián.
The Deva in the Lapis Lazuli City (*Liúlí Chéng*) is Shèlìfú.
Ānán addressed the Buddha:
"I recall that when I previously entered Shèwèi Chéng (Śrāvastī),
I saw the Bodhisattva Chóngshèng Wáng sharing a bed with a woman.
I thought he had violated the purity of conduct, and I pondered in my heart whether there was any other person [who was not fully enlightened].
Should a practitioner of pure conduct (*fànháng*) in the teachings of the Tathāgata (*Rúlái*) generate improper sight, hearing, thought, or recollection?"
When he uttered these words, the Three Thousand Great Thousand Worlds (*Sānqiān Dàqiān Shìjiè*) shook six times.
At that moment, the Bodhisattva Chóngshèng Wáng immediately leaped up and remained suspended in the air.
He was forty-nine *chǐ* (cubits/feet) above the ground.
He replied to Ānán,
"Could one who has violated purity and prohibitions leap up and stand in empty space?
Before the Tathāgata,"
Ānán prostrated himself and immediately confessed his faults.
"How could I harbor prejudiced views and seek out the shortcomings of the Great Dragon?"
The Buddha informed Ānán,
"As for that woman,
in ages past, she was the consort of Chóngshèng Wáng for a hundred lifetimes.
Her karmic attachment from previous lives had not been removed, and she coveted Chóngshèng's appearance.
She spoke an oath:
'If Chóngshèng Wáng grants my wish and allows me to satisfy my pleasure, then I will follow his teachings.'
At that time, Chóngshèng Wáng knew her thoughts in his heart.
Early in the morning, dressed formally, he entered her chamber.
He then spoke a verse:
'I am foolishly opposed to desire, which the Buddhas do not praise.
One who can discard kindness and attachment attains Buddhahood, the highest among humans.'
At that, the woman leaped for joy.
She immediately rose from her seat and prostrated herself on the ground.
She sought refuge, condemned herself, submitted to her faults, and repented.
And she praised Chóngshèng Wáng with a verse:
'I have now departed from all desires, which the World-Honored One praises.
I shall restrain and cease attachment to kindness and love, seeking the unsurpassed Way of the Buddha.'
'The thoughts my former mind entertained, I now confess and repent of them.
Pitying and grieving for all living beings, I ultimately generate the Aspiration for the Way (*Dàoyì*).'
At that time, Chóngshèng Wáng bestowed a prediction upon that woman.
After passing beyond this female body, in ninety-nine *kalpas*, she would attain Buddhahood.
Her title would be Lí Wúshù Bǎiqiān Suǒshòu Rúlái (The Tathāgata Who Has Left Innumerable Hundreds of Thousands of Afflictions).
When Shìjiā Móuní Fó (Śākyamuni Buddha) was a Bodhisattva,
his name was Dàsàtuópó (Mahāsattva).
As he was crossing the great sea, a fierce wind wrecked the ship.
He told the merchants, 'Grasp my hair, hands, and feet, and I shall carry you across.'
After everyone had grasped him, he killed himself with a knife.
By the law of the great seawater, dead bodies do not sink.
Immediately, the swift wind blew them to the shore.
The Bodhisattva was in the mountains.
Sitting upright with a compassionate heart, contemplating without moving.
A bird nursed its young on his head. Realizing the bird was on his head,
fearing the eggs would fall, he did not move or shake his body.
He maintained the concentration of abandoning the body, remaining motionless in that place until the birds grew wings.
As long as they could not fly, he ultimately refused to leave.
Knowing this himself, he then spoke this verse:
'If one can accomplish this deed, one is a Heaven among humans and Devas (*Tiānrén*).
Being able not to disturb either party, this virtue is unsurpassed.'
'Therefore, that World-Honored One (*Shìzūn*) is the foremost spirit.
Thus, in the place of the Bodhimaṇḍa (*Dàocháng*), his merit and virtue are all fully perfected.'
I have diligently sought the Way (Dào) since innumerable Kalpas (jié) ago.
Initially, I never slacked off, thereby attaining Buddhahood (Fó).
I surpassed nine Kalpas (jié), appearing before Mí Lè.
I recalled a past time when the people of the country were poor, and I felt compassion for them.
Therefore, I wished to enter the sea to seek the Wish-Fulfilling Pearl (Rú Yì Zhū).
The multitude gathered, watching the wind, and hoisted the sails.
We proceeded to the Sea Dragon King (Hǎi Lóng Wáng) and requested the Wish-Fulfilling Pearl (Rú Yì Zhū) from his head.
The Dragon King (Lóng Wáng), hearing that I wished to save the poor scholars, immediately gave the pearl.
At that time, the various merchants each gathered treasures; all were fully satisfied and returned by boat.
The various dragons (lóng) and divine spirits (shén guǐ) in the sea all conferred, saying:
“This Wish-Fulfilling Pearl (Rú Yì Zhū) is the highest treasure in the sea.
It should not be obtained by common mortal people.
How can we diminish the sea to benefit Jambudvīpa (Yán Fú Lì)?
Truly, it is a great pity.
We must devise a plan to take the pearl back; it must not be lost.”
At that time, the various dragons (lóng) and spirits (guǐ) surrounded them day and night, intending to seize the pearl.
Because the Guide (Dǎo Shī) possessed honored virtue (dé zūn) and the power of the Wish-Fulfilling Pearl (Rú Yì Zhū), they could not take it.
When the sea crossing was finished,
the Bodhisattva (Pú Sà) leaped for joy and stood by the seaside.
He bowed his head, lowered his hands, and offered incantations and wishes to the sea spirits (hǎi shén).
He tied the pearl around his neck.
At that moment, the sea dragons (hǎi lóng) and spirits (shén) seized the opportunity and caused the pearl to fall into the sea.
The Guide (Dǎo Shī) was moved to anger, thinking: “I traveled and entered the sea,
traversed difficulties by boat, and endured immeasurable hardship to obtain this treasure.
It was meant to save the many who are in need.
But now, the sea spirits (hǎi shén) have instead caused it to fall back into the sea.”
He commanded his attendant nearby: “Bring containers here.
I will scoop up the seawater until it reaches the bottom mud.
If I do not retrieve the pearl, I will never cease or rest.”
He immediately began scooping the water, heedless of his life span.
The water naturally flowed and completely entered the containers.
The various sea dragons (hǎi lóng) and spirits (shén), seeing this, were struck with fear.
“This person’s mighty power and strength of diligence (jīng jìn zhī lì)
truly are not found in the world.
The water will soon be exhausted.”
They immediately brought the pearl, apologized, and returned it to him.
“We merely sought to test you, not realizing that the power and might of your diligence (jīng jìn lì shì) were thus.
There is none in heaven or on earth who can overcome you.”
The Guide (Dǎo Shī) obtained the treasure and brought it back to his country.
He caused the Seven Treasures (Qī Bǎo) to rain down to supply the whole world, so that none remained unsettled.
That Guide (Dǎo Shī) at that time was I myself.
In the past, the Bodhisattva (Pú Sà), along with five hundred merchants, entered the sea to gather treasures.
After several months in the sea, they obtained a heavy load of treasures.
As they were about to return to their homeland, they encountered a gale wind on the way.
Thunder and lightning shook the earth; the water spirits (shuǐ shén) gathered like clouds.
The surroundings resembled a wall, fire shot from their eyes, and the waves surged and flooded the mountains.
The crowd wept, saying:
“We are dead!”
Terrified, their faces changed, and they looked up to heaven, begging for mercy.
The Bodhisattva (Pú Sà) was sorrowful and resolved in his mind, saying:
“My seeking of Buddhahood (Fó) is only for the sake of sentient beings.
The sea spirits (hǎi shén) detest corpses.
To endanger one's life to save the multitude—
this is the supreme practice of an enlightened being (kāi shì).”
“If I do not use my body and blood to appease the sea,
which is to counter the intent of the malevolent sea spirits (hǎi shén), the boat people will ultimately not reach the shore.”
He addressed the crowd, saying:
“You should link hands, hold together, and also support my body.”
The multitude obeyed the command.
The Bodhisattva (Pú Sà) immediately took out a knife and killed himself.
The sea spirits (hǎi shén) were pacified by this virtue (dé), and the boat drifted ashore.
The multitude was universally saved.
The boat people embraced the corpse, wailing and crying, saying:
“This must be a Bodhisattva (Pú Sà), not a common person!”
They stomped their feet, leaped, and cried out to Heaven.
“It would be better had our lives perished here,
than to lose this supreme virtuous man (shàng dé zhī shì)!”
Their sincere words moved all the Heavens (zhū tiān).
Indra, the King of Heaven (Tiān Dì Shì), beheld the vast compassion of the Bodhisattva (Pú Sà).
Dì Shì descended and said:
“This supremely virtuous Bodhisattva (Pú Sà) is destined to become a Sage Hero (shèng xióng).
I shall now bring him back to life.”
He poured the heavenly divine medicine (tiān shén yào) into the mouth of the corpse.
and thoroughly anointed the body.
The Bodhisattva (Pú Sà) immediately revived, suddenly sat up, and greeted the multitude.
Dì Shì filled the boat with famous treasures.
It was a thousand times more than before.
They immediately returned to their homeland, and when their family and relatives met them, none were unhappy.
They relieved the poor, aided the destitute, and extended kindness to all sentient beings.
They clearly proclaimed the Buddhist scriptures (Fó Jīng) and enlightened the ignorant and deluded.
The king of that country admired the Bodhisattva’s (Pú Sà) virtue and went to receive his pure teachings.
The ruler was benevolent, the ministers were loyal, the entire realm observed the precepts (chí jiè), and every family had filial children.
The country was prosperous, calamities ceased, and the common people rejoiced.
Eventually, they were reborn in Heaven (Tiān Shàng) and forever departed from all suffering.
The Bodhisattva (Pú Sà) practiced continuous diligence (jīng jìn) throughout accumulated Kalpas (jié), thereby attaining Buddhahood (Fó).
He who killed himself to save the multitude—that was I myself.
Indra, the King of Heaven (Tiān Dì Shì), was Mí Lè.
The five hundred merchants are the five hundred Arhats (Yīng Zhēn) who are sitting here today.
At that time, Bodhisattvas Mahāsattvas (Pú Sà Mó Hē Sà) equal to the dust motes of a thousand worlds,
leapt forth from the earth, united in heart, pressed their palms together, and looked up at the Honored Face.
And they addressed the Buddha (Fó), saying:
“After the Buddha’s (Fó) Parinirvāṇa (miè hòu),
wherever the World Honored One’s (Shì Zūn) emanated bodies reside, and in the places where they attain Parinirvāṇa (miè dù zhī chù), we shall widely preach this sūtra.
We also personally wish to receive and uphold, read and recite, explain and transcribe this truly pure Great Dharma (Dà Fǎ), and make offerings to it.”

Thereupon, the World Honored One (Shì Zūn), before the great assembly, which included Wén Shū Shī Lì and measureless hundreds of thousands of millions of Bodhisattvas (Pú Sà) who formerly resided in the Sahā World (Suō Pó Shì Jiè), along with various Śrāvakas (Shēng Wén), humans, non-humans, and others,
extended his broad and long tongue upward, reaching the Brahma Heavens (Fàn Shì).
From every pore, he emitted light of measureless colors,
completely illuminating the worlds of the ten directions.
The various Buddhas (Zhū Fó) beneath the jeweled trees, seated upon lion thrones, were also thus.
In the past, there was a Bhikṣu (Bǐ Qiū) who was diligent (jīng jìn) in upholding the precepts (chí jiè) and never transgressed them.
He resided in a monastery (jīng shě).
What he recited was the Prajñāpāramitā (Bān Ruò Bō Luó Mì).
Whoever heard the voice of this Bhikṣu (Bǐ Qiū) could not but rejoice.
There was a small child, just seven years old, who grazed cattle outside the city.
He heard the sound of the Bhikṣu (Bǐ Qiū) reciting the sūtra from afar.
Following the sound, he went to the temple, listened, and immediately understood.
His expression showed great joy, and he immediately questioned the Bhikṣu (Bǐ Qiū).
The answer was not to his satisfaction.
The child instead explained the meaning, which was extremely subtle and rarely heard before.
The Bhikṣu (Bǐ Qiū) heard this and praised the child, saying:
“He truly possesses wisdom; he is not an ordinary person.”
The child then left and returned to where the cattle were.
The calves he was grazing scattered and ran into the mountains.
The child followed their tracks, encountered a tiger, and was killed.
He was reborn as the son of the primary wife (fū rén) in the house of a great elder (zhǎng zhě).
When the wife (fū rén) became pregnant, her mouth was already able to speak the Prajñāpāramitā (Bān Ruò Bō Luó Mì).
From morning till evening, she was unable to stop.
The household of the elder (zhǎng zhě) had never previously revered the Dharma (Fǎ).
They found this wife (fū rén) strange, thought she was speaking nonsense, and suspected she had been afflicted by a spirit disease (guǐ bìng).
They consulted oracles and exorcists, but none could determine the cause.
Everyone inside and outside the household was anxious and fearful.
At that time, the Bhikṣu (Bǐ Qiū) entered the city to seek alms (fèn wèi) and arrived at the elder’s (zhǎng zhě) gate.
He heard the sound of the sūtra from afar and was greatly delighted in his heart.
He immediately asked the elder (zhǎng zhě): “Who inside is speaking this profound sūtra? The sound is subtle and marvelous.”
The elder (zhǎng zhě) replied:
“My wife (fù) has contracted a spirit disease (guǐ bìng).
She speaks nonsense day and night, and her mouth never stops.”
The Bhikṣu (Bǐ Qiū) replied:
“This is not a spirit disease (guǐ bìng).
She is only speaking a profound sūtra which has deep meaning.
I suspect that the child this wife (fū rén) is carrying is a disciple of the Buddha (Fó dì zǐ).”
The elder (zhǎng zhě) was relieved.
He immediately invited the Bhikṣu (Bǐ Qiū) to stay and offered him food and drink.
When the days and months were fulfilled, she gave birth to a son.
Moreover, there was no post-natal discharge.
Immediately upon birth, the child folded his hands, knelt upright, and spoke the Prajñāpāramitā (Bān Ruò Bō Luó Mì).
After the wife (fū rén) had given birth, she returned to her original state.
It was as if she had woken from a dream, entirely unaware of what had happened.
The elder (zhǎng zhě) gathered the Saṅgha (sēng), who watched the child speak the sūtra without any hindrance.
At that time, the multitude of monastics (zhòng sēng) watched the child with undivided attention.
The elder (zhǎng zhě) asked:
“What manner of being is this?”
The Bhikṣu (Bǐ Qiū) replied:
“He is a true disciple of the Buddha (Fó dì zǐ).
Be careful not to be alarmed or suspicious.
You must raise him well.
When this child grows up, he will become a teacher to all people.
We must all receive instructions from him.”
By the age of seven, he knew all subtle doctrines.
He surpassed the multitude; his wisdom and deliverance (zhì dù) were boundless.
All the Bhikṣus (Bǐ Qiū) and others received teachings from him.
Where the sūtra contained errors, omissions, or deficiencies,
he edited and corrected it, supplying what was lacking.
Whenever the child went out or arrived somewhere,
he instantly enlightened people, causing them to conceive the Great Vehicle (Dà Chéng).
The five hundred people, young and old, inside and outside the elder’s (zhǎng zhě) household,
all learned from the child, conceived the intent for the Great Vehicle (Dà Chéng yì), and entirely practiced the Buddha’s (Fó) work.
In the cities, outer walls, marketplaces, and villages where the child taught,
all those who conceived the Supreme Way Intent (Wú Shàng Dào Yì) numbered eighty-four thousand.
Those who accepted discipleship numbered five hundred.
The various Bhikṣus (Bǐ Qiū), hearing this, were mentally relieved and resolved to seek the Great Vehicle (Dà Chéng); they all attained the pure Dharma Eye (Fǎ Yǎn Jìng).
The Buddha (Fó) informed Ā Nán:
“The child at that time was I myself.
The Bhikṣu (Bǐ Qiū) at that time was Kāśyapa Buddha (Jiā Shè Fó).”
The Bodhisattva was Śakra Devānām Indrá (Tiān Dì Shì).
