His resolve maintained the nature of suffering (kǔ), emptiness (kōng), and the non-existence of a self (fēi shēn).
When seated, he contemplated.
When traveling, he taught and transformed others.
He pitied the ignorant, loved the wise, and advanced tirelessly.
He saw that his former friend had received the body of a woman.
She was the wife of a wealthy man, captivated by wealth and sex.
Unaware of impermanence (wú cháng), she lived in the city, seated in a marketplace stall.
Dì Shì transformed himself into
a merchant and invited the woman to sit.
The merchant gazed intensely and laughed.
The woman found this strange.
Next to them, a child was throwing tiles and leaping in play.
The merchant laughed again.
Someone whose father was ill sacrificed an ox.
The merchant also laughed.
There was a woman holding a child.
The child scratched the mother’s cheek, and blood flowed down her neck.
The merchant laughed again.
The wife of the wealthy man asked,
“Sir, you sit before me, smiling continuously.
Regarding the matter of the tile-throwing child, why did you laugh?”
The merchant replied,
“You are my good friend, have you forgotten me now?”
The woman was disappointed and even more displeased,
finding the merchant’s words strange.
The merchant further said,
“The reason I laughed at the tile-throwing child is this:
This child is your former father.
His spirit (hún shén) is now reborn as your son.
In the span of one lifetime, the father is not recognized; how much less over a long period?
The child throwing tiles was originally born as an ox.
The ox died and was reborn as the master’s son.
The family used the ox hide to make the tiles which he throws.
The child is now throwing and striking, unaware of his former body.
Regarding the man who used the ox for sacrifice, his father asked for healing from his illness.
This is like consuming zhèn poison to cure a disease.
The father died and became an ox, slaughtered repeatedly over generations.
Now, this sacrificial ox has regained a human body.
The child scratching the mother,
that child was originally the concubine (xiǎo qī).
The mother was the official wife (dí qī).
The woman, due to jealousy (dù jí), often inflicted cruel abuses.
The concubine harbored resentment.
The concubine died and became the child of the official wife (dí qī).
Scratching her face and harming her body, she thus dared to complain (or seek revenge).
The husband’s heart lacks constancy.
He who was once hated is now loved—what constancy is there?
One generation does not know, let alone countless kalpas (jié).
The sutra says,
‘By obstructing oneself with sensuality (sè), one is blinded to the Great Way (Dà Dào).’
Those devoted to evil sounds do not hear the sound of the Buddha.
That is why I laughed.”
Worldly glory is like lightning; it flashes and immediately vanishes.
You should realize impermanence; do not associate with the foolish.
Venerate virtue and the Six Pāramitās (liù dù).
I must now return, but later I will certainly visit your house (zǐ mén).
Having finished speaking, he vanished.
The woman returned, disappointed.
She purified her heart and awaited him reverently.
Afterward, he indeed appeared at her door.
His appearance was ugly and his clothes were tattered.
He said, “My friend is inside.
Call her to come out.”
The doorman went in and reported the situation fully.
The woman came out and said,
“You are not my friend.”
Shì (Dì Shì) laughed and said,
“If you do not recognize me when I merely change my form and clothing,
how much less so after different lifetimes (yì shì)?”
He further said,
“You should diligently serve the Buddha.
The time of a Buddha is hard to encounter.
Monks (bǐ qiū) of high conduct are difficult to provide offerings (gōng yǎng) for.
Life is in the breath; do not fall into worldly delusion.
When he finished speaking, he vanished.
The entire country rejoiced and marveled.
They each upheld the lofty and marvelous practices of the Six Pāramitās (liù dù).
The Buddha told Qiū Lùzǐ,
“The woman was Mílè (Maitreya).
Śakra Devānām Indrá (Tiān Dì Shì) was I myself.”
In a past lifetime, in the kingdom of Yōubōluó Yuè Guó,
the five grains were abundantly ripe and the population was numerous.
In the kingdom, there was a king named Bōluó.
Previously, there was a prostitute (yín nǚ) of beautiful appearance.
She happened to go to another dwelling and found a woman who had just given birth to a boy, intending to eat her child.
The prostitute asked her (the mother).
She replied, “I am hungry.”
The prostitute said,
“Wait a moment while I search for food for you.”
She replied,
“The hunger is urgent.
Before you leave the door, I will starve to death.
How can I wait for you?”
The prostitute reflected,
“If I take the child away, the mother will starve to death.
If I leave it here, she will eat it. I must save both of them.”
The prostitute cut off both of her breasts and gave them to her to eat.
The mother then ate them.
The prostitute asked,
“Are you satisfied yet?”
She replied, “I am satisfied.”
The prostitute returned home.
There was a man who came to the prostitute’s dwelling.
Seeing her, he immediately said,
“Who cut your breasts?”
He immediately felt compassion and no longer arose lust.
The man asked,
“Sister, you should demonstrate this sincerity for me.”
The prostitute said,
“If I have genuine sincerity, may my breasts be restored to normal.”
Immediately, both breasts were restored to their former state.
Śakra Devānām Indrá (Shì Tí Huán Yīn) saw the merit (fú) of this prostitute’s act of giving (bù shī).
Fearing she would usurp his throne,
he transformed into a Brāhmaṇa (Póluómén) and went to her house.
The prostitute then filled a golden bowl with rice and offered it to the Brāhmaṇa.
At that time, the Brāhmaṇa refused to accept it.
The woman asked the religious practitioner (Dào Rén), “Why do you not accept it?”
He replied,
“I do not need food.
I heard that you donated your breasts—is that truly so?”
She replied, “It is true.”
The Brāhmaṇa said,
“When you donated your breasts, did your intention contain any regret?”
The woman said,
“If I sincerely donated my breasts and my intention was unwavering,
may I, upon rebirth, attain the body of a man.”
As soon as she finished speaking, she transformed.
At that time, the King of Yōubōluó Yuè,
had ruled the country for fifty years.
His life span was exhausted and he passed away.
The attending ministers and courtiers heard that the prostitute (yín nǚ) had transformed her body into that of a man.
They thought,
“We ought to enthrone him as king.”
They then jointly requested him to take the throne.
After being enthroned, he delighted in giving (bù shī).
Whatever anyone needed, he provided it.
He instructed the entire realm to observe the Eight Precepts Fast (Bā Guān Zhāi).
Thus, the country was governed well, the people were joyful, and their life spans were extended.
The King then reflected,
“Although I practice giving, I have not yet given my body.
To give one’s body—that is truly difficult.”
The King immediately smeared his body with aromatic oil (sū xiāng).
He then entered a remote mountain and lay upon a rock.
All the various birds came and ate his flesh.
After he passed away, he was born into a Brāhmaṇa (Póluómén) family.
He was handsome and beautiful.
When he grew older, he secretly left for the marketplace.
He observed the poor and beggars selling goods, and was heartbroken, saying,
“If these people were rich and happy, they would not be selling goods.”
He rushed back and pleaded with his parents to allow him to become a Śramaṇa (Shāmén).
His parents would not consent.
He then refused to eat for five days.
His relatives and friends came and jointly advised and admonished him.
The young man did not respond.
The relatives then persuaded his parents to agree to let him study the Way (Xuédào).
The parents looked at each other, wept mournfully, and agreed.
The son served and honored his parents for six or seven days.
He then circumambulated them three times, performed a prostration, and left.
He went to a grove of trees and saw two practitioners (dào rén).
They had attained the Five Supernatural Powers (Wǔ Shén Tōng) and were sitting in the open air contemplating the Way.
For the sake of the common people, they performed diligent ascetic practices (kǔ xíng).
The young man immediately sat beneath the grove of trees.
Through meditation (chán sī) and severe ascetic practice, he immediately attained the Five Supernatural Powers.
His diligence and courage surpassed the two practitioners.
It was the custom of these practitioners to only eat fruit that had fallen naturally from the trees, not picking it directly.
The practitioners traveled together searching for fallen fruits.
They saw a pregnant tigress.
The young practitioner said to the two practitioners,
“The tigress will give birth soon.
Having been hungry for many days, she might eat her own cubs.
Who is able to give his body for her to eat?”
Mílè (Maitreya) said,
“I will give my body for her to eat.”
When they returned after gathering fruit, they saw that the tigress had already given birth.
She was extremely hungry and about to eat her cubs.
The young practitioner said to the two practitioners,
“The tigress has given birth and is hungry and wishes to eat her cubs.
Who can give his body to save her from this suffering of hunger? Let us go together to the tigress.”
The tigress opened her eyes and mouth toward the two practitioners.
The practitioners, fearing her, flew into the void (xū kōng).
One of them said,
“Is your supreme sincerity like this?
You pledged your body to feed the tigress, so why are you flying away now?”
The other practitioner wept with sorrow for her (the tigress).
He looked around but found nothing (to feed her).
The young practitioner immediately took a sharp knife and cut his arm, causing blood to flow.
He did this in seven places. The blood entered the tigress’s mouth and she drank it; he then threw himself before the tigress, giving his body for her to eat.
The Buddha spoke to Ānán (Ānanda),
“If you wish to know, the prostitute (yín nǚ) at that time, and the one established as king, and the Brāhmaṇa (Póluómén) son who threw himself to feed the tigress—all were I myself.
The practitioners (dào rén) at that time were the two Bodhisattvas (Púsà), Jiāyè (Kāśyapa) and Mílè (Maitreya).
I diligently advanced and practiced the giving of my body for sixty kalpas (jié).
I surpassed Mílè by nine kalpas and attained Buddhahood.”
In the past, Shìjiā Púsà (Shakyamuni Bodhisattva) was a great king.
Named Sàpó Dá.
He universally bestowed gifts upon sentient beings, letting them take whatever they sought, compassionately aiding those in distress and calamity.
The celestial spirits, ghosts, and dragons all said:
"The position of the Heavenly Emperor (Tiāndì) is honored, but originally, there is no eternal holder.
Recognizing his high conduct, vast compassion, wisdom, and profound blessings,
when he dies, he will become (the Emperor)."
Fearing the king would seize his celestial position, [Dìshì] went to test him in order to verify his sincerity.
Dìshì (Indra) appeared and commanded a nearby king, saying:
"Now that human king's compassionate generosity is vast and abundant, and his blessings and virtue are towering.
I fear he intends to seek and seize my imperial position."
[Dìshì] immediately transformed into a hawk.
The nearby king transformed into a dove.
The dove rushed beneath the king's feet and cried out in terror:
"Great King, alas! My life is finished!"
The King said:
"Do not fear, I will now save you."
The hawk immediately arrived afterward and said:
"My dove just came here.
The dove is my food. I ask the King to return it."
The King said:
"The dove came seeking to save its life; I cannot violate my initial promise.
If you must have meat, I will make the weight a hundred times greater."
The hawk said:
"I only wish to obtain the dove; I do not need other meat."
The King said:
"What must I use to make you abandon the dove and happily depart?"
The hawk said:
"If the King is truly compassionate and merciful to sentient beings, then cut off your own flesh and trade it for the dove. I would gladly accept this."
The King was greatly pleased.
He personally cut flesh from his thigh and weighed it against the dove, making sure it was equal to the dove's weight.
However, the dove constantly became heavier [on the scale], and he cut off all the flesh from his body.
Even so, he still could not match it. The pain from the wounds was immeasurable.
The King, with compassionate forbearance, commanded his close minister, saying:
"You shall kill me, and weigh my marrow until it is equal to the dove's weight.
I observe the severe precepts of the Buddha to save beings from peril and distress.
Although there are many afflictions, they are like a slight breeze—how can they move Tàishān (Mount Tai)?"
The hawk, realizing the King's intent, and the dove each resumed their original form.
They bowed their heads to the ground and said:
"Great King, what aspiration do you pursue that you would endure such suffering and distress?"
He replied: "I do not aspire to Dìshì, the Heavenly Emperor, nor to the Flying Emperor.
I see that sentient beings are submerged in blind darkness and do not perceive the Three Jewels (Sān Zūn).
They freely commit malevolent misdeeds and cast themselves into the prison of endless suffering (Wú Zé zhī Yù).
Because of this, I feel sorrow and pity.
I swear an oath to seek Buddhahood,
to rescue and save all sentient beings, enabling them to attain Nirvāṇa (Níhuán)."
The Heavenly Emperor was startled and said:
"I foolishly thought the Great King wished to seize my position,
and therefore disturbed you. How can this be remedied?"
The King said:
"May the wounds on my body heal and restore me to my former state, so that I may constantly practice giving (bùshī)."
Dìshì commanded a celestial physician to apply divine medicine to the wounds.
The sores and injuries immediately healed, and his complexion and strength surpassed their former state.
Dìshì bowed his head, circled the King three times, and departed joyfully.
The Buddha traveled to Wángshě Chéng (Rājagṛha).
There was a loose woman (a courtesan),
named Shàngjīnguāng Shǒu.
She was exceptionally beautiful, possessing a purplish golden complexion.
Kings, crown princes, ministers, elders (zhǎngzhě), and others developed lustful desire for her, following wherever she went and seeking her company.
Men and women, young and old, all followed after her.
At that time, Shàngjīnguāng Shǒu, on a certain day,
went to the market with the son of the elder Wèiwén to buy goods.
They presented gifts to each other, prepared fine delicacies, and together went to the viewing gardens (guānyuán).
Wénshū Shīlì (Mañjuśrī) emerged from his private chamber at that time.
He manifested great compassion and pitied all living beings.
[He thought:] "Who among these people can be persuaded and transformed to generate the Mahāyāna (Dàchéng) aspiration?"
He saw Shàngjīnguāng Shǒu.
Riding in one carriage with the son of elder Wèiwén, heading toward the viewing gardens, she was fit to be converted.
Wénshū Shīlì immediately transformed his body into a young man.
He was exquisitely handsome; his appearance surpassed that of the gods, and those who saw him were filled with joy.
The clothes he wore illuminated forty *lǐ*.
He observed the path the loose woman was traveling and stood before her.
The carriage, horses, and clothing of the elder's son and Shàngjīnguāng Shǒu,
when compared to Wénshū Shīlì,
were like a pile of ink next to a shining pearl.
Shàngjīnguāng Shǒu saw Wénshū Shīlì's appearance, which was glorious and refined, like a Son of Heaven (Tiānzǐ).
The radiance of his body was dazzling and unreachable.
Coveting the brightness of his clothes,
she thought to herself:
"Now I want to abandon this son of the elder,
get out of the carriage, leave him, and amuse myself with this man,
and obtain these clothes."
Having had this thought,
Wénshū Shīlì manifested his divine power to make her quiet her intention.
A Heavenly King (Tiānwáng) transformed himself into a man.
He said to the woman:
"Stop! Stop!
Why do you generate this loose and wanton mind?
Why is this?
Such a person does not aspire to carnal desires."
The woman asked: "Why not?"
The Heavenly King replied:
"This person is named Wénshū Shīlì Púsà.
He is able to completely fulfill the wishes of all people.
Seeing what sentient beings seek in their hearts, he does not go against their intentions."
The woman thought in her heart:
"As I have heard, he will certainly bestow his wonderfully fine clothing upon me."
She got out of the carriage and respectfully said:
"Noble one,
I wish that you would graciously bestow this robe upon me."
Wénshū Shīlì replied:
"Elder Sister,
If you are able to generate the aspiration for the unsurpassed, correct, and true Way (Dào Yì),
then I will bestow the robe upon you."
The woman said: "Yes, indeed."
She immediately generated the mind set on the unsurpassed Way and received and upheld the Five Precepts (Wǔ Jiè).
In a past world age.
In the country of Jiāyí Guó, there was an elder.
He had no son.
The husband and wife had lost their sight.
They wished in their hearts to enter the mountains to seek the unsurpassed determination (resolution).
They cultivated purity of aspiration and delighted in solitude.
At that time, there was a Bodhisattva named Yīqiè Miàojiàn.
He thought in his heart,
“Although this person has made a subtle resolution, his eyes see nothing.
If he enters the mountains, he will certainly meet with misfortune and harm.”
When the Bodhisattva’s life ended, he vowed to be born into the elder’s family and was named Shǎn.
He was extremely filial, benevolent, and kind, practicing the Ten Good Deeds.
Day and night he diligently served his parents,
just as people serve Heaven.
When he passed ten years of age,
Shǎn knelt down and addressed his parents,
“You originally made a great resolution to enter the deep mountains,
seeking the aspiration for emptiness, stillness, and the unsurpassed true Dharma.
Should you abandon your original vow just because of your son?
People in the world are impermanent and subject to a hundred changes.
Life is not like metal or stone; when its end arrives, there is no fixed date.
Please follow your original intent and take advantage of this good time to enter the mountains for purity.
I myself will provide for you without missing any season.”
The parents then entered the mountains.
Shǎn gave all the family's possessions to the poor people in the country.
He then entered the mountains together with his parents.
When Shǎn arrived in the mountains, he used reeds to build a hut and constructed beds and mats, which were always perfectly suited, neither too cold nor too hot.
A year after entering the mountains, various fruits were plentiful, tasting fragrant and sweet.
Spring water surged forth, clear and cool.
Lotus flowers in the pond shone brightly with five colors.
Sandalwood and various other trees emitted a fragrance double the usual.
Various species of birds made musical sounds.
Lions, bears, tigers, wolves, and venomous beasts
faced each other with compassion and no longer had the intention to harm.
They ate grass and consumed fruits without fear.
Shǎn was so supremely filial and kind that he feared causing pain when stepping on the ground.
Heavenly spirits and mountain spirits often appeared in human form, offering comfort day and night.
Shǎn wore deerskin clothes and carried a bottle to fetch water.
Elk, deer, and various birds also went there to drink, unafraid of difficulty or each other.
At that time, the King of Jiāyí Guó entered the mountains to hunt.
The King saw a flock of birds and deer by the water's edge and drew his bow to shoot them.
The arrow mistakenly struck Shǎn's chest.
Shǎn was hit by the poisoned arrow.
He immediately raised his voice and cried out loudly,
“Who has used one arrow to shoot and kill three practitioners of the Way (dào rén)?”
The King heard the human voice and immediately dismounted, going toward Shǎn.
Shǎn spoke to the King, saying,
“Elephants die because of their tusks.
Rhinoceroses perish because of their horns.
Kingfishers die because of their feathers.
Elk and deer die because of their skin and meat.
For what reason am I dying right now?”
The King asked Shǎn,
“What kind of person are you,
wearing deerskin clothes, indistinguishable from the beasts?”
Shǎn said,
“I am a person of your country.
I came here with my blind parents to study the Way for over twenty years.
I have never been wrongfully harmed by tigers, wolves, or venomous creatures.
Yet now I have been shot and killed by the King.”
At that moment, a fierce gale suddenly arose in the mountains, breaking and snapping the trees.
A hundred birds cried mournfully, and the lions, bears, and running beasts all howled loudly.
The sun lost its brilliant light, and the flowing springs dried up.
All the flowers withered and died, and thunder and lightning shook the earth.
At that time, the blind parents rose up in alarm and spoke to each other,
“Shǎn went to fetch water and has not returned for a long time.
Could he have been harmed by a venomous creature?
The sounds of the wild beasts and flying birds howling are not as usual.
Wind rises from the four directions, and trees are broken and snapped.
There must be a calamity.”
The King was then terrified and greatly reproached himself.
“What I have done is outrageous.
I originally shot at a deer.
The arrow mistakenly struck and killed a practitioner of the Way; this sin is extremely grave.
By being greedy for a small amount of meat, I have incurred heavy disaster.”
“I would now give the treasures and stored wealth of my entire country,
my palaces, singing girls, districts, cities, and towns, to save the life of this son.”
The King then stepped forward and tried to pull out the arrow from Shǎn’s chest with his hand.
It was too deep to be removed.
Flying birds and running beasts gathered like clouds from all four directions, howling and shaking the mountain.
The King became even more fearful.
His three hundred and sixty joints all trembled.
Shǎn spoke to the King,
“This is not the King’s fault; it is caused by my own past karma (sù zuì).
I do not regret my body or life.
I only pity
my blind parents, who are both old and infirm and whose eyes are sightless.
If I suddenly disappear, they will surely die, having no one to look after them.
It is for this reason that I am afflicted with distress,
not because of the pain of the poison.”
The King repeated earnestly,
“I would rather enter Nirí (hell) and suffer punishment for a hundred kalpas so that Shǎn may live.”
He knelt down and repented his wrongdoings to Shǎn.
“If the son dies, I shall not return to my country but will remain in the mountains and provide for your parents just as you did; do not worry about this.
All the devas (tiān), nāgas (lóng), and spirits (shén) shall bear witness that I will not violate this vow.”
Shǎn heard the King’s vow
and, though struck by the poisoned arrow, his heart was joyful and pleased; even dying, he had no regret.
“My parents must now rely upon the Great King.
By providing for practitioners of the Way (dào rén), present world sins are extinguished, and limitless blessings are obtained.”
The King said,
“Tell me where your parents are and speak to them before you die, so they may know.”
Shǎn immediately pointed it out:
“Walk this way; it is not far from here.
You will certainly see a grass hut.
My parents reside inside.
May the King proceed slowly and not cause my parents fright or alarm.
Use skillful means (shàn quán fāng biàn) to explain the situation.
Please present my apology to my parents:
Imperfection has now arrived, and I must proceed to the next existence.
I do not regret my life, but I think of my parents, who are elderly and blind.
If I suddenly disappear, they will have nothing to depend upon.
It is this anxiety and distress that is so painful to me.
Death is a common fate, caused by past karma (sù zuì); no one can escape it.
I now confess my faults to my parents,
all the evils I have committed since countless kalpas.
May my sin be extinguished and blessings arise from this.
I pray that my parents and I may meet in lifetime after lifetime and never be separated.
May my parents live out their full years without sorrow or worry.
May the devas (tiān), nāgas (lóng), spirits (guǐ shén) constantly follow and protect them,
and may calamities and harm be eliminated.”
The King then took several men and went toward the parents’ dwelling.
After the King left,
Shǎn immediately succumbed (died).
Birds and beasts cried out, circling above Shǎn’s corpse,
licking the blood on Shǎn’s chest with their mouths.
The blind parents heard these sounds, which increased their terror.
Since the King was traveling quickly, stirring the grass and trees, a human voice sounded sternly.
The parents exclaimed in alarm,
“Who is this person? This is not the sound of our son walking.”
The King said, “I am the King of Jiāyí Guó.
Hearing that practitioners of the Way (dào rén) are studying in the mountains, I have come to make offerings.”
The parents said,
“It is good that the Great King has come.
You trouble your dignified presence to visit this remote wilderness.
Is the King’s body well and peaceful?
Are your palaces, ladies, crown prince, officials, and citizens all safe and well?
Are the winds and rains harmonious, are the five grains abundant, and are neighboring countries not invading each other?”
The King replied to the practitioners of the Way,
“By the grace of the practitioners of the Way, all is peaceful and safe.”
The King inquired of the blind parents,
“You have come to the mountains, laboring in heart and body.
Among the trees, have the flying birds and running beasts refrained from harming the practitioners of the Way?
Are you currently safe and peaceful here in the mountains, with the seasonal cold and heat being tolerable?”
The blind parents said,
“By the great kindness of the King, we are always safe and peaceful.
We have a filial son named Shǎn.
He constantly fetches fruits, berries, and spring water for us, which are always abundant.
The winds and rains in the mountains are harmonious, and we lack nothing.
We have grass mats to sit on and fruits and berries to eat.
Shǎn went to fetch water and is about to return.”
The King heard this, his heart aching, and tears flowed.
He then said,
“My sin is outrageous. I entered the mountains to hunt.
I saw a group of deer by the water and drew my bow to shoot them.
The arrow mistakenly struck Shǎn, and therefore I have come to tell you.”
When the parents heard this, they threw themselves down completely, like a great mountain collapsing, and the earth trembled because of it.
The King then stepped forward and helped lift and support them.
The parents wept and cried out, speaking to Heaven,
“Our son was so filial and kind that he feared causing pain when stepping on the ground.
What sin did he have that he should be shot and killed?”
“Just now the wind rose, the trees broke, and a hundred birds cried mournfully.
We suspected our son had died.”
The parents wept and wailed.
The father said,
“Stop for a moment.
Life inevitably ends in death; it cannot be avoided.
Now let us ask the King:
Where was Shǎn shot? Is he dead or alive now?”
The King spoke about Shǎn, and the parents were overcome with emotion and fainted.
“If we suddenly lose our son, we too will surely die.
We beg the King to lead the two of us to stand over his corpse.”
The King then led the blind parents to the corpse.
The father embraced his feet, and the mother embraced his head, crying out loudly to Heaven.
The mother then licked the wound on Shǎn’s chest with her tongue.
“I pray that the poison may enter my mouth.
I am already old.
My eyes see nothing.
I wish to take my son’s place with my body.
If Shǎn lives and I die,
I shall have no regrets in death.”
“If Shǎn is truly so filial that Heaven and Earth know it,
then the arrow must pull itself out, the poison must be removed, and Shǎn must live again.”
Thereupon, the seat of the King of the second Daolì Tiān (Trāyastriṃśa Heaven) trembled.
Using his divine eye (tiān yǎn), he saw the two practitioners of the Way (dào rén) embracing their son and crying out.
The sound reached even the fourth Dōushù Tiān (Tuṣita Heaven).
The palaces of all the devas (tiān) trembled.
Shì Fàn (Śakra and Brahmā) and the Four Heavenly Kings (Sì Tiān Wáng) immediately descended from the fourth Heaven,
arriving before Shǎn in the time it takes a person to flex and extend an arm.
They poured divine medicine into Shǎn’s mouth.
When the medicine entered Shǎn’s mouth, the arrow pulled itself out, and he came back to life, just as before.
His parents were greatly astonished and delighted.
Seeing Shǎn, who had been dead, revive, their two eyes both opened.
The flying birds and running beasts were all overjoyed.
The wind ceased, the clouds dispersed, and the sun regained its brightness.
Spring water surged forth, the flowers shone with five colors, and the trees flourished and blossomed twice as much as usual.
The King was exceedingly delighted, unable to control himself.
He bowed to the Heavenly Emperor Shì (Śakra), then bowed again to the parents and their son Shǎn.
He offered the wealth of his country to the superior practitioners of the Way (dào rén).
Shǎn said,
“If the King wishes to repay this kindness...”
The king should return, comfort the people, and ensure all uphold the precepts.
The king must no longer hunt, shoot, or prematurely harm insects and animals.
In this present life, your body will be neither peaceful nor secure, and when your lifespan ends, you will enter Nirí [Hell].
People dwelling in the world possess affection and love only temporarily.
Separation is perpetual; it cannot be constantly maintained.
Because the king previously accumulated merit and virtue, he is now able to be king.
Do not indulge yourself merely because you have obtained freedom (sovereignty).
The king must repent and reproach himself.
From this point forward, you must follow the teachings of Shǎn.
The hundreds of followers were all greatly overjoyed and upheld the Five Precepts.
The king returned and commanded that all those within the country who had blind parents, similar to Shǎn,
must provide for them and must not abandon them.
Those who violate this decree shall now be punished with severe crime.
Thereupon, the people of the country, because Shǎn was alive,
taught each other to observe and cultivate the Five Precepts and the Ten Virtuous Deeds.
When they died, they were born in heaven, and none entered the Three Evil Paths.
The Fó told Ānán:
In a past life, Shǎn was my own body.
The blind father is now the royal father, Yuètóután Wáng.
The blind mother is the queen, Móyē.
The king of the Jiāyī kingdom is Ānán.
At that time, the Heavenly King Shì is Mílè.
What enabled me swiftly to achieve the decisive, supreme, and true path [Enlightenment],
was all the grace of my parents’ offerings, compassion, and kindness.
Being revived from death moved the heavenly dragons, ghosts, and spirits.
The gravity of parents' grace is achieved by the filial child.
That I am now able to be the Fó and save the people of the kingdom,
is all due to filiality derived from virtue.
At that time, Kuàngyě Púsà manifested as a ghost body.
Sǎnzhī Púsà manifested as a deer body.
Huìjù Púsà manifested as a macaque body.
Lí'ài Púsà manifested as a goat body.
Jìn Lòu Púsà manifested as a gander king body.
Thus, these five hundred Púsàs,
each manifested and received various kinds of bodies.
Their bodies entirely emitted great fragrant light.
Each Púsà held a bright lamp in hand,
intending to make offerings to the Fós of the ten directions.
At that time, Yíxīn Púsà observed the five hundred people,
and immediately knew they were all Púsàs.
He spoke to Kuàngyě Guǐ:
Good sons,
why do you manifest such bodies to make offerings to the Fós?
Kuàngyě Guǐ said:
Good sons,
ninety-one kalpas ago in the distant past, there was a Fó, the World Honored One,
named Pípóshī.
At that time, I
and these others were born of the same parents, were brothers, upheld the Five Precepts, and initiated the Bodhi-mind.
For the purpose of subduing all sentient beings,
Shīqì, Píshèfú, and Jiūliúsūn Fó were also all offered to.
Sǎnzhī Dàshì, before those Fós, established a great vow:
“May I, in future lives, use the body of a ghost or spirit to teach and transform sentient beings.”
If there are depraved and evil ghosts,
I shall preach the Three Vehicles to them and subdue them.
Only then shall I achieve the Bodhi path.
There are also twelve thousand great ghosts
who in this world have established great vows to subdue sentient beings.
They further established a great vow:
"If there are evil ghosts attempting to destroy the True Dharma,
I shall govern them."
Therefore, I receive such a ghost body to subdue and transform them, compelling them to dwell in the Three Vehicles.
If there are sentient beings who distance themselves from virtuous dharmas,
and commit non-virtuous deeds by body, mouth, and mind,
these bodies are already born in the Three Evil Paths.
Or perhaps due to mixed good and evil karma, they receive a ghost body;
the evil ghosts multiply while the benevolent ghosts are few.
I manifest and receive this body because I wish to subdue them.
I also cause the Kèlì, Bóluómén, Píshě, and Shǒutuó to distance themselves from evil thoughts.
Good sons,
there is the Jīngāngchuí mantra that ensures all evil ghosts cannot commit evil against these four castes.
Even birds and beasts all give rise to benevolent minds,
and distance themselves from all evil fears.
I have established a great vow to speak this mantra.
When the Fó was previously in the Dōushuài Heaven,
the immortal Pósù Xiān was in Yánfútí.
He regularly served as the chief merchant for six hundred and twenty thousand traders who entered the sea to gather treasures.
They embarked on a large ship, intending to return to their home country.
Midway, they encountered difficulties from Makara fish, great winds and waves, and Yèchā.
The six hundred and twenty thousand people,
immediately each made a promise to Móxīshǒuluó Tiān:
one sacrificial animal per person.
They then escaped the four difficulties,
and returned, reaching their home country.
Each prepared a sheep
intending to go to the Heavenly Temple.
At that time, Pósù silently thought:
"How can I now teach these merchants to perform unwholesome deeds?
I must devise a skillful means."
He immediately transformed himself into two people:
one, a tonsured Shāmén;
two, a layman Bóluómén. The Bóluómén then announced among the crowd:
"The Heavenly Lord and the six hundred and twenty thousand people wish to go to the Heavenly Temple."
At that time, the Shāmén, seeing this Bóluómén far off along the road,
asked:
"You and this great assembly, where do you intend to stop?"
The layman replied:
"We are going to the Heavenly Temple to seek great benefit."
The Shāmén answered:
"I observe that you are seeking great misfortune.
How can this be great benefit?"
The argument did not cease.
At that time, the crowd asked the Bóluómén:
"Who is this person?
His appearance is thus."
The Bóluómén said:
"This is called a Shāmén."
The people asked:
"What does the Shāmén say?"
He replied:
"Killing creatures and sacrificing to Heaven will incur great sin."
The crowd said:
"Why should we use the words of this foolish Shāmén?
Quickly go to the Heavenly Temple and obtain great benefit."
Then the Bóluómén said:
"Our great master is now at the Heavenly Temple. There is nothing he does not understand. We can jointly ask him."
Everyone said, "Excellent!"
The Shāmén, the Bóluómén, and the others proceeded to the place of the Great Immortal.
At that time, the Shāmén asked the Great Immortal:
"By killing creatures and sacrificing to Heaven, should one gain rebirth in Heaven or enter Nirí [Hell]?"
The Great Immortal answered:
"What foolish Shāmén! Killing creatures and sacrificing to Heaven certainly leads to falling into Nirí [Hell]."
Pósù said:
"No."
The Shāmén said:
"If he does not fall, you should bear witness."
At that time, Pósù immediately sank his body into the Ābí Yù [Avīci Hell].
When the people saw this, they cried, "Alas, what a disaster! Such a thing has happened!"
"The Great Immortal's intelligence and wisdom are now extinguished.
How much less can we avoid entering Nirí [Hell]?"
At that time, the crowd released all the sheep and scattered, running in four directions.
They went into the various mountains to seek and find the immortals.
Having found the immortals, they received the immortal doctrines.
After twenty-one years, they each died and were born in Yánfútí.
At that time, I descended from the Dōushuài Heaven and was born into the family of Báijìng Wáng in Yánfútí.
At that time, the six hundred and twenty thousand people were born in Shèwèi Guó and received human bodies.
When I first arrived in Shèwèi in the past, I subdued the six hundred and twenty thousand people and caused them to leave home and initiate the Bodhi-mind.
These are precisely those former traders.
Good sons,
Pósù Xiānrén possessed such great spiritual power
that he transformed these people and led them to me.
In the past, in the east, there was a Púsà in Yánfútí named Lú Póluó.
Due to the power of his vows, he was born here,
becoming a Cakravartin Sèngwáng [Holy Wheel-Turning King], ruling the four continents.
He was titled Xūkōngjìng.
He addressed all sentient beings,
urging them to abide in the Ten Virtuous Deeds and the Three Kinds of Vehicles.
During that time, he gave charity to all without distinction.
The treasures he had were insufficient for the countless beggars.
He immediately asked his ministers:
"Where do such treasures originate?"
The ministers replied:
"Although the Dragon King possesses them, they are only for the Holy King's provision."
In the age of the Five Turbidities, when afflictions are heavy,
and human lifespan is one hundred years, he will certainly achieve Ānàduōluō Sānmiǎo Sānpútí [Anuttara Samyak Sambodhi].
He became a Great Dragon King, manifesting various kinds of treasure stores.
He chose various evil worlds,
and in various places throughout the four continents,
in each continent, he received a body seven times.
In each body, he displayed measureless hundreds of thousands of millions of nayutas of treasured stores.
Following this sequence, he traversed the ten directions.

In the evil age of the Five Turbidities, hundreds of thousands of millions of devas and humans in the void rained down flowers, praised his virtues, and proclaimed that his wishes were fulfilled, which the great assembly heard.
The Xūkōngjìng Wáng was named "All-Giver" by the various devas.
At this time, all people individually begged the king for his consorts, maidens, and children.
The king gave them all away.
There was one beggar named Qīng Guāngmíng.
Upholding the Dog Precept, he begged the king for Yánfútí.
The king happily gave it, consecrating him with perfumed water and installing him in the Holy King position.
The people also came to serve and revere this king.
The king's lifespan was unchanged.
When I achieve the Fó path, I shall give him a prediction [of enlightenment], that he shall unify and be the next Bodhisattva in Tusita Heaven.
Lú Zhì Bóluómén begged him for both his feet.
Yá Bóluómén demanded his two eyes.
Jìng Jiānláo Bóluómén begged him for both his ears.
Xiǎng Nígānzi begged him for his male organ.
Mìwèi Bóluómén begged him for both his hands.
He immediately cut, plucked, and gave them away at the appropriate time.
Then the various minor kings and ministers all said:
"Alas, foolish man!
Why did you cut yourself? What good is the remaining flesh?"
"Send it to the wilderness where insects, beasts, vultures, and eagles will all come and devour it."
"If my vows are to be fulfilled,
may this body become a great mountain of flesh."
May all sentient beings that drink blood and eat flesh come here and drink and eat as they wish, and may this body continue to grow.
The tongue root he gave away was due to the power of a vow:
"May I, in a future life, obtain a broad and long tongue."
When my life ended at that time in Yánfútí,
by the power of my original vow, I was born as a Dragon King.
named Shìxiàn Bǎozàng [Manifested Treasure Store].
Immediately on the night of my birth, I displayed hundreds of thousands of millions of nayutas of kinds of
treasure stores.
I proclaimed that they contained all rare treasures, even Mani pearls.
Use them as you wish.
Fully practice the Ten Virtuous Deeds,
and initiate the supreme Bodhi-mind.
Thus, he received a body seven times.
His lifespan was always seventy-seven thousand billion nayutas of hundreds and thousands of years.
The measureless treasure stores were also thus.
The Buddha spoke to the virtuous **Ānán**.
Now, in past ages, there was a king.
Named **Rìyuè Míng**.
He was handsome, attractive, and his divine might was majestic.
He emerged from the palace and on the road saw a blind man.
impoverished and starving, begging for sustenance along the path.
He went toward the king.
and addressed the king, saying:
"The King alone is honored, noble, secure, and joyful.
I alone am poor, moreover, I am blind."
The King, seeing his plight, took pity on him and asked the blind man, "What kind of medicine can cure your illness?"
The blind man replied:
"Only obtaining the King's eyes can heal mine."
At that moment, the King personally took out his two eyes and gave them to the blind man.
His mind was pure and bright, without a single thought of regret.
The King **Yuèmíng** is none other than my present self.
The Buddha said, "Even Mount **Xūmí** can still be measured in weight.
But the gift of my eyes cannot be weighed or calculated."
Formerly, the Bodhisattva was a great king.
He took refuge in the Three Jewels and fully observed the Ten Virtues.
Weapons were not used, and there were no prisons.
Wind and rain arrived in season, grain was plentiful, and the people were rich.
Even small offenses were recorded in the penal code, yet throughout the entire kingdom, no one spoke of them.
The true transformation of the Six Pāramitās was recited by everyone.
At that time, there was a **Fànzhì** (Brahman) who maintained a pure and tranquil conduct, residing quietly in the mountain forests, not participating in worldly customs.
One night, being thirsty, he went to drink.
He mistakenly drank the water from a lotus pond planted by the people of the state.
After drinking, he awoke to the realization.
He went to the authorities and reported himself, saying he had committed theft.
"I only wish the Great King would punish this crime according to the law."
The King said:
"This is natural water, not a tangible object. What crime is there?"
He replied:
"I drank without informing anyone.
Is this not theft?
I request the King deal with it."
The King said, "State affairs are numerous. For now, sit in the royal park."
The Crown Prince ordered him to a deep secluded spot within the park.
The King, overwhelmed by various state matters, forgot about him for six days.
Suddenly, he realized and said:
"Where is the **Fànzhì**?
Quickly summon him here!"
The **Fànzhì**, upholding his precepts, had gone hungry and thirsty for six days.
His body was emaciated and scarred. When he stood up, he stumbled to the ground.
The King saw this and, weeping, said:
"My transgression is grave!"
The Queen laughed at this.
The King sent someone to bathe him, prepared a feast, and personally offered provisions, bowing his head and repenting his fault.
Because of this, throughout countless cycles of rebirth and death, until he was about to attain Buddhahood, he did not eat for six years.
The Buddha told the various Bhikṣus:
"The king at that time was my current self.
The Queen was **Jūyī**.
The Crown Prince was **Luóyún**.
The King forgot the Daoist, causing him to starve for six days; this sin resulted in six years of near-starvation being relieved.
After the six days (of neglect), the King personally offered sustenance.
Thus, now the six years of misfortune finished, and the Way was accomplished.
**Jūyī** laughed at him.
Now, she carried **Luóyún** for six years with a severe illness, because the Crown Prince deeply secluded the **Fànzhì** within the park.
Therefore, he spent six years in darkness.
Formerly, the Bodhisattva was a great king.
He governed the people with compassion and conducted inspection tours monthly.
He provided gruel, medicine, and medical treatment for the poor, widowed, and sick.
Whenever he went out on an inspection tour or hunt, he commanded servants to load the carriage behind him fully with necessary clothing, medicine, and drugs.
The deceased he buried.
The name of the ruler spread throughout the ten directions.
**Dìshì** (Indra), seeing his virtuous conduct, feared losing his position and sought to ruin him.
He transformed into an old **Fànzhì** and begged the king for one thousand silver coins.
The King immediately gave them to him.
The **Fànzhì** said, "I live in hardship, and I fear others might steal it. I wish to entrust it to the King."
The King said:
"My country has no thieves. I accept this heavy deposit."
**Dìshì** again transformed into a **Fànzhì**.
He approached the palace gate again.
The King immediately appeared before him.
The **Fànzhì** sighed and said:
"The Great King's name spreads throughout the eight extremities, and his virtuous conduct is rare.
I was born among common folk, but I admire nobility and honor. I wish to beg for this country."
The King said, "Excellent."
He immediately took his wife and children and lightly rode away.
The Heavenly Emperor then transformed again into another **Fànzhì**.
He begged the King for his carriage.
The King bestowed the carriage and horses upon him.
He proceeded on foot with his wife and children and stopped to camp near a mountain.
There was a Daoist possessing the Five Supernatural Powers who was friends with the King.
Suddenly remembering the King's virtue, he saw that the King had lost his country, so he calmed his mind and entered meditative rest.
He observed that the Heavenly Emperor **Dìshì**, due to greed and envy, had usurped the kingdom, causing the King great distress and emaciation.
The Daoist used his spiritual power to instantly appear before the King and said, "What do you seek that you labor your will so greatly?" The King replied:
"What my will holds, you already fully know."
The Daoist immediately transformed a one-shafted carriage to send the King on his way.
The **Fànzhì** transformed by Heaven again begged for the carriage.
They were still several thousand *lǐ* away from that country.
Heaven again transformed into the former **Fànzhì** and came requesting the silver money.
The King said:
"I have bestowed the country upon someone else, and I fear I forgot your money."
The King immediately pawned his wife and children to obtain one thousand coins to return to the **Fànzhì**.
The wife initially served the pawn-broker's family.
The daughter, when undressing for a bath, removed her pearls and various treasures.
Heaven transformed into a hawk and snatched the clothes and treasures away.
The daughter cried out, "Why did this woman steal them?" They recorded the event and imprisoned her.
Her son slept alongside the pawn-broker's son.
Heaven killed the pawn-broker's son during the night.
The family took the son and handed him over to the prison.
Mother and son were detained.
Starving, their bodies ruined, they wailed in distress with no one to save them.
Holding back tears all day, they were convicted of the crime and condemned to be executed in the market place.
The King obtained one thousand silver coins through hired labor.
He went to redeem his wife and children.
He passed through the market place and saw them.
He immediately contemplated the Buddhas and repented, saying:
"Must my past karmic debt result in this?"
Calming his mind, he entered into clarity and saw what Heaven had done.
A voice in the air said:
"Why don't you hurry up and kill them?"
The King said:

"I heard that **Dìshì** universally saves sentient beings with a sincere and compassionate heart, nurturing them more than a kind mother, and that no creature with blood fails to receive his protection.
You obtained the position of Emperor due to performing good deeds without evil causes.
Now, **Shì** harbors grave malice; when the evil ripens, the crime will be completed.
He shall be born and enter Mount **Tàishān**.
Heaven, humans, dragons, and ghosts all proclaimed their approval.
The King who governed that land immediately absolved his wife and children of their crimes.
The two kings met and immediately inquired into the origin of the events.
Throughout the country, regardless of rank, no one failed to shed tears.
The King who governed that land divided the kingdom and ruled jointly.
The ministers and people of the former country searched for the King's location, and the entire land greeted and welcomed him.
The residents of the two countries were simultaneously sad and joyful.
The King at that time was my present self.
The wife was **Qiúyí**.
The Prince was **Luóyún**.
The Heavenly Emperor was **Tiáodá**.
The **Fànzhì** in the mountains was **Shèlìfú**.
The King of that land was **Mílè**.
The Buddha was in the Shèwèi Kingdom and instructed the various Bhikkhus.
In the past, the Bodhisattva was a great king,
named Pǔmíng.
His kindness and benevolence illuminated the ten directions, and songs praised his excellence.
The people desired his peace, like a filial son wishing comfort for his parents.
A neighboring country had a king,
named Ēqún.
He governed using severe laws.
His power was like a lion’s; when running, he seized like a flying hawk.
His cook sought meat, rushing to the market early to search for it.
On the road, he saw a fresh corpse and took it, mixing it with animal meat to make a delicacy.
The next day, when preparing food, the taste was not as sweet.
The King reprimanded the chief cook.
The cook confessed honestly, bowing his head in submission.
The King, feeling secretly ashamed, said,
“Is human flesh sweet?”
Then he commanded the cook to make this standard practice.
Therefore, it is said:
He who is devoted to thick flavors has thin humanity (Rén Dào).
He whose humanity is thin develops the heart of a jackal or wolf.
Now, wolves and dogs crave the taste of meat
and destroy the lives of beings.
Therefore, the world becomes their enemy.
The cook received the command and secretly went out killing people to supply the King's meal.
The subjects and common people cried out loudly, unified in purpose and voice, and chased him away.
The King fled into the mountains and waited for other kings to come out,
capturing them using his fierce followers.
It was like a hawk or falcon seizing swallows and sparrows.
He captured ninety-nine kings.
At that time, King Pǔmíng went out to observe the suffering and joy of the people.
On the road, he met a Fànzhì (Brāhmaṇa).
The Fànzhì said, “Your Majesty, do not go out.”
The King replied,
“Having made a promise to go out, truthful words are hard to violate.”
Thereupon, he went out.
He was captured by Ēqún.
King Pǔmíng said,
“I do not fear losing my life, but I regret breaking my word.”
Ēqún asked,
“What do you mean?”
The King explained everything fully:
“The Daoist I met, having come out, gave me an instruction.
I wished to see him once and receive his important instruction
and genuinely carry it out.
If I then die, I will have no regrets.”
Ēqún released him, allowing him to return temporarily.
After seeing the Daoist, giving him money, and receiving the teaching, he came to Ēqún smiling.
Ēqún asked,
“Your life is in danger right now, why are you so delighted and laughing?”
Pǔmíng answered,
“The words of the Shìzūn (World-Honored One) are rarely heard in the Three Realms.
Now that I hold them in my heart, how can the life of a king be regrettable?”
Ēqún further said,
“I wish to hear this esteemed teaching.”
The King took it out and gave it to him.
Ēqún was startled and delighted, saying,
“The mighty Shìzūn has expounded the Four Impermanences (Sì Fēicháng)!
Indeed, not hearing or seeing this is called perverse madness.”
He immediately released the hundred kings, allowing each to return to his country.
Ēqún repented his errors, reformed himself, lived beneath a tree, and memorized the four verses daily.
When his life ended, his spirit moved and he became the Crown Prince of a king.
He took a wife but could not sire a male heir, which caused the King great worry.
Consequently, the King sought women of the realm who could transform and give birth to a male child.
Later, however, he became dissolute and did not follow the path of chastity.
The King had him impaled and placed at the four crossroads.
He commanded passersby, saying,
“Use your finger to strike his head and truly disgrace him.”
Just as the ninety-ninth person passed, the Crown Prince died.
His soul and spirit transformed and continuously underwent transmigration without end.
Meeting the time when the Buddha was in the world, he was born in the Shèwèi Kingdom.
He lost his father early, lived alone with his mother, and practiced the path of the Fànzhì.
His nature was earnest, his words trustworthy, and his courage and strength could topple an elephant.
His teacher loved him, his friends respected him, and distant people praised his virtue.
Whenever the teacher traveled on his weekly rounds, he entrusted the residence to him.
The teacher's wife, harboring malicious intent, went forward, grabbed his hand, and tried to seduce him with lustful words.
Ēqún refused, saying,
“Any elderly person in the common world—
if male, is my father;
if female, is my mother.
How much more so the teacher's wife!
I would rather burn my body than dare to violate this command (of chastity).”
The teacher's wife was displeased, but pretended to assent, and went away to devise a scheme.
She falsely spoke to her husband, saying,
“You praise that disciple's virtue; is it enough to enlighten you or not?” She detailed his supposed faults and womanly seductions that seemed real, and the Fànzhì believed it.
The teacher told Ēqún, “Do you wish to become an immortal?”
He replied, “Yes.”
The teacher instructed him to kill a hundred people and cut off their fingers,
which would enable him to attain immortal status.
Receiving the command, he wielded a sword and killed everyone he met.
He obtained the fingers of ninety-nine people.
The populace fled, and the country shook with fear.
He saw his mother and was delighted, saying,
“Mother, when you arrive, the number will be complete, and I shall now become an immortal.”
The Buddha reflected that this evil path was confusing the masses, and this prayer was spreading throughout the world.
He transformed into a Śrāmaṇa and walked in front of him.
Ēqún said, “The number of people is complete.
If I pursue you, I will not catch up.”
He said, “Śrāmaṇa, stop!”
The Buddha replied, “I have stopped.
You have not stopped.”
Ēqún's mind opened instantly, like the clearing of clouds.
He cast his five limbs to the ground, bowed, and repented his errors.
He clasped his hands, immediately followed the Buddha, and was led back to the Vihāra, where he became a Śrāmaṇa.
The Buddha spoke to him about his past deeds and revealed the Four Impermanences, enabling him to attain the path of the stream-entry.
The King wished to punish him, but hearing of this, he sighed and requested the Buddha to allow him to see Ēqún once. The Buddha said,
“A person of supreme virtue and worthiness may open one eye to look upon him.”
This was repeated three times.
Ēqún answered,
“The radiant splendor of my eye is difficult to withstand.”
The King bowed his head and said,
“Tomorrow I will set out a humble meal. I wish you would glance upon it once.”
Ēqún replied,
“To the privy, I will go.
To the palace hall, I will not.”
The King said,
“As you command.”
Returning, he tore down the privy and dug up the ground.
Then he used new camphor wood and catalpa wood for the pillars and beams.
He washed the ground with fragrant water, mixing sandalwood, liquid storax (Sūhé), turmeric (Yùjīn), and various other spices into a paste for the mud.
He used fine wool, blankets, and mixed silk to make the seating mats.
The carved patterns and engravings were beautified with various jewels.
It shone brightly, surpassing the palace hall.
The next day, the King personally carried an incense burner to welcome him.
Ēqún took his seat.
The King tucked up his robes and advanced on his knees until the offering was completed.
Ēqún then spoke a scripture, saying,
“The privy was filthy in the past.
Could one eat upon it?” The King replied, “No.”
“Is it acceptable now?”
The King answered, “It is acceptable.”
Ēqún said,
“Before I saw the Buddha, I was like that filthy privy.
Thanks to blessings from past lives, I was born when the Buddha was in the world.
I bathed in his pure transformation, eliminating the stench and holding fragrance.
My inside and outside are now pure, like a genuine heavenly pearl.”
While drinking, he intended to pass through the market when he heard that a woman
was experiencing a difficult delivery and her life hung in the balance.
He returned and reported the matter to the Buddha.
The Buddha said,
“You go and help her give birth.”
Ēqún received the instruction and went to proclaim the Buddha’s grace.
Both mother and son survived.
The Buddha told Ēqún,
“The day you received the Dao (Path) can truly be called the day you were first born.
Not having seen the Three Honored Ones or received the important precepts,
is like a child in the womb: although it has ears and eyes, how can it hear or see?
It is called ‘not yet born.’”
Ēqún’s mind opened and he immediately attained the path of the Arhat.
The Buddha told the Bhikkhus,
“The King Pǔmíng of that time was myself.
In my previous life, I gave him the four verses.
I saved the lives of a hundred kings and now caused him to attain the Path.
He did not incur the accumulation of evils.”
In Ēqún’s former lives, he was once a Bhikkhu.
He carried one measure of rice and delivered it to the monastery.
He offered one knife to the Buddha.
Joyfully praising the Honored One, he bowed his head and departed.
Carrying the rice enabled him to gain great strength.
Offering the knife enabled him to gain many treasures.
Being joyful enabled him to gain good looks.
Praising the Honored One enabled him to become a king.
Performing the ritual bow enabled him to gain a kingdom and be revered by the multitude.
Ninety-nine people struck his head, which led to the loss of his body [as the Crown Prince].
Therefore, he killed his former enemies and severed their fingers.
The last person who intended to strike him saw that he was already deceased.
Moreover, seeing the Śrāmaṇa, he developed a compassionate heart.
The last person [he planned to kill] was his mother.
Because he initially had evil intentions, Ēqún's subsequent intentions were also evil.
Seeing the Śrāmaṇa, he turned compassionate, and upon seeing the Buddha, he became filial.
If the seed is pure, the fruit is pure.
If the seed is mixed, the fruit is mixed.
Having dispensed good deeds or hatred, misfortune or fortune follows immediately.
The shadow pursuing and the echo responding all have their origins.
They do not arise from spontaneity.”
“Ānán,
in a past lifetime,
there was a Crown Prince of a king.
His title was Liánhuá Wáng (King Lotus Flower).
He was proper, handsome, and majestic in divine power.
While traveling abroad, he saw a person on the road.
His body was afflicted with leprosy.
Seeing this, the Prince felt compassion.
He asked the sick person what medicine could heal him.
The person replied,
“If I obtain the marrow from the King’s body and smear it on my own, then my illness will be cured.”
At that time, the Crown Prince immediately broke his body and bone to give the marrow to the sick person. He performed the benevolent giving joyfully, with no regrets in his heart.
The Crown Prince of that time was precisely my present self.
The waters of the great ocean can still be measured by the peck (dǒu),
but the giving of my body and marrow cannot be counted or weighed.”
Ānán.
When I originally sought the Way, the diligent suffering was innumerable.
In a past life, I was a Crown Prince.
His name was Xiànzhòng.
His appearance was proper, upright, and beautiful.
He exited the park grounds.
On the road, he saw a person
who had contracted a severe illness.
Seeing him, he asked the patient:
"By what medicine can your illness be cured?"
The sick person replied, saying:
"Only the blood from a royal body can cure my illness."
The Crown Prince immediately used a sharp knife to pierce his body, drawing blood, and gave it to the patient.
He gave it with utmost sincerity, his mind having no regret or remorse.
That Crown Prince is precisely myself.
Ānán.
The water of the four great oceans can still be measured by the bushel.
But the donations of blood from my body cannot be weighed or limited.
This was for the sake of seeking Perfect Enlightenment.
A time of kalpas (aeons) long past and countless.
There were five *xiānrén*.
Dwelling in the mountains and wilds.
Four men were the masters.
One man provided supplies and served them, never failing to please them by gathering fruits, drawing water, and offering things punctually according to the season.
One day, he went far to gather fruits and juice, became weary and fell asleep.
He did not return at the appointed time.
The sun had already passed noon.
The four men missed their meal.
Harboring resentment, they decided to utter a malevolent curse.
The attendant heard this and retreated under a tree.
He contemplated and blamed himself, thinking he had labored for many years.
Now, he had failed to provide the four *xiān* with their meal.
Having violated the spiritual teachings and disobeyed the four masters.
He became distressed and died.
His feet usually wore *qībǎo zhī jī* (seven-jeweled clogs).
He was sitting with his foot raised.
One of the jeweled clogs fell into the water and sank.
After his death, he was immediately reborn among the *wàidào* (heretics).
He became the son of a curse-master, *Xiōngzhòuzǐ*.
He was over ten years old.
He was playing by the roadside with his peers.
At that time, there was a *Fànzhì*.
He happened to see the playing children.
Although the crowd of people was large, he observed them all carefully.
He saw that *Xiōngzhòuzǐ* uniquely possessed a noble appearance.
He was destined to become a king.
His countenance was distinct and superior among men.
The *Fànzhì* said:
“You possess the characteristics of a king; it is unsuitable for you to mingle with the common crowd.”
The boy replied:
“I am the son of a curse-master, *Xiōngzhòuzǐ*; how can I have the characteristics of a king?”
The *Fànzhì* further said:
“According to my classics,
your bearing and physique match the prophecies (in the *chènshū*).
You are the one who fulfills them.
When the king of this country dies, he will certainly yield his position to you.”
The boy said:
“If what you, benevolent one, say is true, I shall always bear your great kindness in mind.”
The *Fànzhì*, having finished speaking,
immediately hid himself and ran away.
He traveled forth to another country.
Not many days later,
the king died without an heir.
They sought and recruited a worthy man to become the heir of the kingdom.
Messengers were dispatched everywhere.
They spotted the boy from afar, noting his exceptional demeanor.
They immediately sent someone back to inform the assembled officials.
They requested that the *fǎjià* (royal chariot) be prepared immediately to come and welcome him.
All the officials and *bǎiliáo* (civil servants) were overjoyed.
He was bathed in fragrant water and dressed in court robes for the five periods (of the day).
With a jeweled crown and sword belt, he ascended the throne in the palace.
Facing south, he proclaimed his rule.
The territory was peaceful and the common people were delighted.
At that time, the *Fànzhì*,
looked up at the heavenly phenomena and examined the earthly signs below.
He knew that the boy had succeeded to the throne.
He immediately went to the palace gate and requested an audience with the king.
The *Fànzhì* performed divination, offered thanks,
and uttered a blessing, saying:
“The prediction was truly accurate!”
The king said:
“It is indeed true.
You shall have whatever you desire.”
The *Fànzhì* replied:
“I ask only for two things.
First,
that my food, movement, clothing, rest, and arising be exactly the same as the king’s.
Second,
that I may participate in deliberating state affairs, and that no decision shall be made without my agreement.”
The king said:
“Excellent.”
The king ruled according to the righteous Dharma and did not wrong the populace.
The *Fànzhì*, however, became arrogant, reckless, and disrespectful toward the senior ministers.
The officials became resentful and angry,
and together they presented a remonstrance, saying:
“Your Majesty occupies an honored and high position.
It is proper to deliberate with the elders and ministers of the state.
Yet, you trust a mere *qǐshì* (beggar) exclusively.
This allows him to be reckless, arrogant, and insulting to all the court officials.
Neighboring countries will hear of this, ridicule us, and bring about invasion and difficulty.”
The king said: “I have made a promise to him; how can I break it?”
The ministers insisted on their advice:
“When the king eats,
do not eat with him.
Then he will surely change.”
The king agreed to this.
He waited until the *Fànzhì* went out, and then ate first.
The *Fànzhì* was enraged and said:
“What about the original pact? Why do you eat alone first?”
He cursed, saying:
“Hmph, you son of a curse-master, *Xiōngzhòuzǐ*!”
The king simply supplied him with provisions and drove him out of the country.
He traveled a long road alone, enduring the cold and heat.
Exhausted and withered, he arrived in another country.
He went to the house of another *Fànzhì* with whom he had an old friendship.
The friend asked him:
“Where have you come from, and what have you mastered?
Which classics do you professionally practice, and can you recite them entirely?”
He replied:
“I have come from far away, pressed by hunger and cold.
I have forgotten what I learned and recited.”
The friend *Fànzhì* thought to himself:
“This man is incapable of doing anything.
I must make him work the fields.”
He immediately provided him with a slave, an ox, and farming tools.
The *Fànzhì* worked the fields and bitterly exploited the slave.
He cruelly forced him to run back and forth across the flat ground to perform errands.
The slave, having no comfort,
decided to throw himself into the water, and went to the riverbank.
There, he found one of the seven-jeweled clogs.
He thought to himself:
“The *Fànzhì* oppresses and exploits me mercilessly.
I should present this to him.
By giving him the clog, I might gain leniency.”
He immediately took the clog back and presented it to him.
The *Fànzhì* was delighted and thought to himself:
“The price of this seven-jeweled clog is immeasurable.
If I present this clog to the king, though I disobeyed his wishes,
my transgression and fault might be resolved.”
He immediately returned to the kingdom
and presented the clog to the king.
He deeply expressed his remorse for his previous offenses and faults,
begging for pardon and amnesty.
The king said:
“Excellent.”
He immediately brought the clog inside the curtain
and invited the *Fànzhì* to be seated.
He assembled all the officials
and issued an edict, saying:
“Have you gentlemen seen the former *Fànzhì*?”
They replied:
“We have not.”
The king asked:
“If you were to see him, what should be done with him?”
They all said:
“He should be punished by the *wǔdú* (Five Poisons).”
The king brought out the jeweled clog and showed it to the officials,
and then commanded the *Fànzhì* to come out and meet the ministers.
“Since he has presented this rare treasure, we should jointly pardon him.”
The officials petitioned, saying:
“The crimes of this *Fànzhì* are like mountains and seas.
What relief can the offering of a single clog provide?
If he could obtain a pair (*yī liǎng*), then his crime might be removed.”
The king agreed to this,
and once again banished the *Fànzhì*.
He ordered him to find the other clog.
The *Fànzhì*, distressed and vexed, returned to his former host,
and asked the slave:
“Where did you originally obtain the jeweled clog?”
The slave went with him and showed him the place where he had found the clog.
Arriving at the riverside, they searched everywhere but could not find its mate.
The slave departed.
The *Fànzhì* thought:
“This clog must have drifted down from upstream.”
He immediately walked upstream against the current,
and saw a large lotus flower.
It was caught in a whirlpool, and a fish held it in its mouth.
The flower had over a thousand petals.
The *Fànzhì* thought:
“Although I couldn't find the clog, I will present this flower.
Perhaps this will resolve my error and allow me to regain my former favor.”
So he took the flower,
and then saw the four *xiānrén* sitting beneath a tree.
The *xiānrén* said:
“Where have you come from?”
He replied:
“I have lost the king’s favor.
Although I presented one clog, it was not enough to resolve my fault.
Therefore, I came upstream searching for it, but have not yet found it.”
The *xiānrén* informed him:
“As a scholar/practitioner, you should know when to advance and when to retreat.
The king of that country is our disciple.
He lived and served us with love and respect, and shared meals and discussions with us.
How could you suddenly curse him, calling him the son of a curse-master, *Xiōngzhòuzǐ*?
Your crime warrants execution and murder.
Now, we will not question you further, but look beneath the tree.”
The king’s former body was our attendant.
He died while sitting with his foot raised.
One jeweled clog fell into the water; the other remained on his foot.
The *Fànzhì* took the clog, bowed his head to apologize for his error,
returned to his home country, and presented the second clog.
The king was immediately pleased, and the ministers’ anger was assuaged.
He restored his position of favor.
The Buddha said:
The king was Myself (in a former life).
The four *xiānrén* were
*Jūliúqín Fó* (Krakucchanda Buddha),
*Jūnàhán Móuní Fó* (Kanakamuni Buddha),
*Jiāyè Fó* (Kāśyapa Buddha),
and *Mílè Fó* (Maitreya Buddha).
That *Fànzhì* was *Tiáodá* (Devadatta).
In the past, there was a Bodhisattva and his paternal uncle, two people.
Each carried national goods and went together to the country of the naked people (Luǒxiāng).
The uncle said,
“Upon entering the country, follow the local customs; advance and retreat according to etiquette.”
“Maintain a scholarly heart, be humble in speech, and conceal brilliance when accompanying the ignorant.”
The cousin said,
“Ritual cannot be diminished, and virtue cannot be withdrawn.
How can we strip naked and destroy our former decorum?”
The uncle said,
“The precedent set by the former Sages is to sacrifice the body, but not to sacrifice conduct.”
“To comply with the times and endure initial criticism is also to laud the greatness of expedient methods (quán dào).”
So they both went there.
The cousin said,
“You go in first to observe the gains and losses, and then send a messenger to tell me the truth.”
The uncle said,
“I respectfully accept.”
Within ten days, the messenger returned and reported.
The cousin said,
“It is imperative to follow the local customs.”
The cousin flared up and said,
“To abandon benevolence and follow the beastly is that the conduct of a noble person (jūnzǐ)?”
“Uncle, you do not side with me!”
The custom of that country was on the night of the last day and the fifteenth day of the month,
to hold a complete circle of festivities.
They anointed their heads with sesame oil, painted their bodies with white clay,
strung miscellaneous bones around their necks,
and men and women held hands, clanking two stones together.
They strolled, sang, and danced freely.
The Bodhisattva followed them.
The people of the country admired and praised him.
The King loved him and the people respected him.
The King treated him as an honored guest and took all his goods, hiring him at ten times the price.
The cousin entered the country by carriage.
His speech employed strict laws, immediately contravening the hearts of the people.
The King was angry, the people were slow to respond, and he had his property seized and was whipped.
The uncle petitioned, and only then was he released.
They returned together to their home country.
Those who saw off the uncle cursed the cousin along the road; those who saw the cousin pulled their ears (in disgust).
The cousin felt shame and anger, saying,
“What closeness does he have with you?
What enmity do you have with me?
You favor him and reject me—is this not slanderous talk?”
He made a vow with the uncle, saying,
“From now on, through successive generations, I will constantly afflict you, and I will never forgive you.”
The Bodhisattva was mournful and wept, and swore this vow:
“May I, through successive generations, encounter the Buddhas, see the Dharma, and personally serve the Śramaṇas.”
“May the Four Graces universally cover and moisten all sentient beings.”
“I will serve my cousin as before and will not violate this vow.”
From this time onward,
the cousin constantly oppressed the uncle, and the uncle constantly aided him.
The Buddha told the Bhikṣus,
“The uncle at that time was my present self.”
“The cousin was Devadatta (Diàodá).”
“In the immeasurable Asaṃkhyeya Kalpas of the past,”
“at that time, this world was named Wúgòu Xūmí.”
“Human life span was a hundred years.”
“A Buddha appeared in the world,”
“named Xiāngliánhuā.”
“In the age of Semblance Dharma (Xiàngfǎ) after his Parinirvāṇa,”
“I, at that time,”
“was a greatly powerful Cakravartin (Zhuǎnlún Shèngwáng),”
“named Nánjǔhuài.”
“I reigned over Jambudvīpa (Yánfútí).”
“I had a thousand fully endowed sons.”
“I persuaded and transformed them all,”
“causing them to generate the resolve for Anuttarā Samyak Sambodhi (Ānòu duōluó Sānmiǎo Sānpútí).”
“They desired to leave home and cultivate the Way during the age of Semblance Dharma,”
“ardently increasing the residual Dharma of the Buddha.”
“Only six sons were excluded;”
“they refused to leave home and generate the Bodhi resolve.”
“I spoke to them using kind words,”
“but they ultimately would not leave home.”
“I asked them again heavily,”
“to generate the resolve for the Supreme Way.”
“The six sons replied,
‘If you can give us Jambudvīpa,’
‘then we shall generate the resolve for Anuttarā Samyak Sambodhi.’”
“When I heard this, my heart generated joy.”
“I thought thus:
‘I have already transformed the people of Jambudvīpa.’”
“‘I shall now divide this Jambudvīpa
into six parts
and give them to these six sons,’
‘causing them to attain the generation of the resolve for the Supreme Way.’”
“‘Only then shall I leave home and cultivate the Way.’”
“I immediately divided Jambudvīpa into six parts and bestowed them upon the six sons.”
“And then I left home.”
“At that time, the six sons
were at odds with each other, engaging in plunder, attack, and conquest.”
“At that time, throughout all of Jambudvīpa,”
“the crops failed, and the people starved.”
“Rain and water were untimely, and the various trees withered,”
“producing neither flowers nor fruits.”
“Birds and beasts were all hungry,”
“their bodies burning with fever.”
“I, at that time, sacrificed my body, my skin, flesh, and blood,”
“to give alms to the sentient beings, causing them to be full.”
“I, at that time,
cast my body down.”
“Due to the power of my vow, it immediately became a mountain of flesh,”
“one Yojana (Yóuxún) high,”
“equal in length and breadth.”
“At that time, the people,”
“flying birds, and animals,”
“began at this time
to eat the flesh and drink the blood.”
“Due to the original vow,
the body within it multiplied and vastly expanded,”
“reaching a height of a thousand Yojanas,”
“and equally a thousand Yojanas in length and breadth.”
“Along its edges, human heads naturally grew,”
“fully endowed with hair, pupils, ears, noses, mouths, and lips.”
“Within those heads, there were individual voices,”
“proclaiming these words:
‘O all sentient beings,’
‘each of you may indulge and take as you please.’
‘Drink the blood and eat the flesh.’
‘Take the eyes, ears, nose, tongue, teeth, etc., until you are fully satisfied.’
‘Afterward, resolve all of you to generate the resolve for Anuttarā Samyak Sambodhi,’
‘or generate the resolve for Śrāvakayāna (Shēngwén) and Pratyekabuddha (Pìzhīfó),’
‘or seek the wealth and happiness in the heavens or among humans.’”
“Due to the original vow, the body was not damaged,”
“for as long as ten thousand years.”
“Within Jambudvīpa,”
“humans and various ghosts and spirits,”
“flying birds and animals,”
“were all fully satisfied.”
“You should now know
that I, in the past, during ten thousand years,”
“sacrificed an immeasurable, boundless Asaṃkhyeya of bodies,”
“giving blood and flesh to immeasurable and boundless beings, causing them all to be satisfied.”
“I did not generate a single thought of regret, even for an instant.”
“In this sequence, I filled the ten directions, extending through worlds of Buddhas numerous as the sands of the Ganges.”
“I sacrificed my body, blood, and flesh, giving alms to sentient beings, causing them all to be satisfied.”
“This was the Pāramitā (Bōluómì) of Dāna (Tán).”
In the past, a Púsa
was a great wealthy man.
He accumulated immense wealth.
He constantly served the Sānzūn.
He showed compassion toward all living beings.
He went to the market to watch the performances.
He immediately saw a turtle and his heart was deeply moved by pity for it.
He asked the price.
The turtle owner knew that the Púsa possessed the virtue of universal compassion, always helped living beings, had uncountable wealth, and never haggled over price.
He replied:
"A million [coins].
If you can take it, good.
If not, I will eat it."
The Púsa replied,
"Excellent."
He took the turtle home, washed it carefully, ensuring it was not harmed.
When he went to the water to release it, he watched it swim away.
With sadness and joy, he made a vow, saying:
"May the hungry ghosts of Mount Tàishān and all living beings of that kind,
and all those in the prisons of the worldly lords, quickly gain freedom from suffering,
their bodies safe and lives whole, just as you are now."
He bowed his head to the ten directions, clasped his hands, and vowed:
"Living beings are distressed, their suffering is immeasurable.
I shall become the earth [for them].
I will be the moisture for the drought.
I will be the raft for the wet.
I will be food for the hungry and drink for the thirsty.
I will be clothes for the cold and coolness for the hot.
I will be the doctor for the sick and the light for the darkness.
If there arises a time of defiled age and perversion,
I shall become a Buddha within it to save those living beings."
The Buddhas of the ten directions all approved of his vow.
They praised him, saying,
"Excellent!
You will surely attain your goal."
Later that night, the turtle came and gnawed at his gate.
He was surprised that the gate made a sound.
He sent someone out to see the turtle.
The servant returned and reported the matter.
The Púsa looked at the turtle, and it immediately spoke in a human voice, saying:
"I received great kindness and my life was spared.
I have no means to repay your gratitude.
Creatures that dwell in the water know when the water level rises and falls.
A great flood is coming and will surely cause immense harm.
Please quickly prepare a boat, and come to receive [the people] when the time comes."
[The Púsa] replied,
"Excellent."
The next morning, he went to the palace gate and reported the matter to the King.
The King said,
