"The Púsa has long had a good reputation.
We trust his words. Move from the low ground to the high ground."
At that time, the turtle came and said,
"The great flood has arrived.
You should quickly board the vessel.
Follow where I go.
You will surely avoid disaster."
The boat followed behind it.
A snake headed toward the boat.
The Púsa said,
"Take it aboard."
The turtle said,
"Excellent."
Next, they saw a floating fox.
He said, "Take it aboard."
The turtle also said, "Good."
Then, they saw a floating person,
beating his cheeks and calling upon Heaven to pity and save his life.
Again, he said,
"Take him aboard."
The turtle said,
"Be careful not to take him."
"The human heart is deceitful and false.
Few maintain faith until the end.
They turn against kindness to pursue power,
and they delight in evil and wickedness."
The Púsa said,
"If all the insect and animal species have been saved,
yet we reject a distressed person,
how can that be benevolence?
I cannot bear to do it."
Thereupon, he took him aboard.
The turtle said,
"Regret it you will!" Eventually, they reached fertile land.
The turtle took his leave, saying,
"My debt of gratitude is repaid; I ask to withdraw."
[The Púsa] replied,
"When I attain the state of Tathāgata, the Unattached, the Ultimate True, the Perfectly Enlightened One,
I will surely save you."
The turtle said,
"Excellent."
The turtle withdrew.
The snake and the fox each departed.
The fox lived in a den.
He discovered an ancient hidden cache containing one hundred *jīn* (catties) of purple-tinged refined gold.
Joyfully, he said,
"I must use this to repay his kindness!"
He quickly returned and reported, saying:
"This small creature received great kindness and had its humble life saved.
A den-dwelling creature seeking comfort in its den discovered one hundred *jīn* of gold.
This gold was neither obtained by clearing ground nor inherited.
It was neither seized nor stolen.
It was obtained through my sincere efforts.
I wish to present it to the virtuous one."
The Púsa deeply considered it, [deciding] not to take it.
[He thought:] "To lose it needlessly is not beneficial to the poor people.
If I take it and practice generosity, all living beings will be saved.
Wouldn't that be good?"
Immediately, he took it.
The floating person saw this and said,
"Divide half of it with me!"
The Púsa immediately gave him ten *jīn*.
The floating person said,
"You excavated, cleared, and stole this gold.
What should your crime be?
If you do not divide half of it,
I will certainly report you to the authorities."
[The Púsa] replied,
"I wish to equally distribute [this wealth] to those poor and distressed people.
You wish to monopolize it.
Is that not biased?"
The floating person then reported him to the authorities.
The Púsa was arrested and had no means to appeal.
He only took refuge in the Sānzūn, repenting his faults and blaming himself.
He compassionately wished that living beings would soon leave the Eight Difficulties,
and that none would harbor resentment and strife like he faced now.
The snake and the fox met and said,
"What shall we do about this situation?"
The snake said,
"I will save him."
Thereupon, it held a potent medicine in its mouth, opened the lock, and entered the prison.
Seeing the Púsa's appearance, his complexion harmed, its heart was sorrowful and grieved.
It said to the Púsa:
"Keep this medicine with you.
I will go bite the Crown Prince.
The poison will be exceedingly potent, and no one will be able to save him.
When the wise man applies the medicine himself, he will be instantly cured."
The Púsa remained silent.
The snake did as it had said.
The Crown Prince was about to die.
The King issued a command, saying,
"Whoever can save him
shall be enfeoffed as Prime Minister."
They announced the opportunity to participate in the cure.
The Púsa heard the announcement, applied the medicine, and the Prince was immediately cured.
The King was delighted and asked the cause.
[The Púsa] then recounted the whole story from beginning to end.
The King was mournful and blamed himself.
He immediately executed the floating person.
He granted a general amnesty to his kingdom.
He enfeoffed [the Púsa] as Xiàngguó.
Holding his hand, they entered the palace.
Sitting side by side, the King said,
"What scriptures does the wise man explain?
What Way does he hold in his heart,
that he practices such benevolence and grace reaching to the Two Powers,
and extends to all living beings?"
[The Púsa] replied,
"I explain the Fó scriptures and hold the Fó Way in my heart."
The King asked,
"Does the Fó have essential teachings?"
He replied,
"He does.
The Fó speaks of the four impermanences.
Those who preserve them will have great fortune and prosperity."
The King said,
"Excellent!
I wish to attain the truth of it."
The Púsa explained it.
The King said,
"Excellent!
I believe in my heart the Fó's teaching that the body is not the Self.
If the body itself cannot be preserved,
how much less the kingdom?
Alas for the former kings,
who did not hear the teaching of the Supreme, Perfectly True, and Ultimate Enlightenment, concerning Impermanence, Suffering, Emptiness, and Non-Self!"
The King immediately emptied his treasury to give alms to the poor.
He treated widowers, widows, and orphans with compassion, as if they were his own children.
The whole kingdom was joyful, smiling, and content in their actions.
Looking up to Heaven, they sighed, saying,
"The Púsa's divine transformation reaches even to this degree!"
People in the four directions praised his virtue, and consequently, a state of Great Peace was achieved.
The Fó told the Shāmén:
"The Púsa was I myself.
The King was Mílè.
The turtle was Anán.
The fox was Qiūlùzǐ.
The snake was Mùlián.
The floating person was Diàodá."
Formerly, the Bodhisattva.
was once a lion.
He lived in the forest
and shared a close friendship with a monkey.
The monkey entrusted its two children to the lion.
At that time, there was a vulture, flying hungry, seeking food.
It happened upon the sleeping lion.
It took the monkey's child away and settled in a tree.
When the lion awoke,
he searched for the monkey's child but did not find it.
He saw the vulture holding it up in the tree.
He then spoke to the vulture, saying:
"I accepted the monkey's entrustment of two children.
I guarded them carelessly,
allowing you to take one.
I have violated my word and trust.
I beg to request it back from you.
I am the king among beasts,
and you are the sovereign among birds.
Our noble power is equal.
It is fitting that you return it to me."
The vulture said:
"You do not understand the circumstances.
I am now weak from hunger; why discuss equality or difference?"
The lion knew it would be difficult to recover.
He used his own sharp claws,
tore the flesh from his ribs,
and exchanged it for the monkey's child.
Furthermore, in a past life,
when people suffered from many illnesses,
yellowing, wasting away, and suppurating.
The Bodhisattva at that time was embodied as a red fish.
He offered his own flesh to all the sick people,
thereby saving them from their ailments.
Also, formerly the Bodhisattva,
embodied as a bird, lived in the forest.
He saw a person enter deep water,
a place where humans do not tread, and was ensnared by the water spirit (Shuǐshén).
The Shuǐshén's
method of snaring was fast and could not be undone.
If one can go into the Xiāngshān (Fragrant Mountain)
and take a medicinal herb and place it upon the snare,
the cord will immediately rot and break, and the person will escape.
Such countless previous births (Běnshēng)
where he saved many are called the Běnshēng Jīng (Jātaka Sutras).
Sūbōtí (Subhūti) asked:
"If the Bodhisattva has perfected good roots (shàn'gēn),
why is he born as an elephant or a horse?"
The Fó (Buddha) said:
"The Bodhisattva truly possesses merit and virtue (fúdè),
having perfected good roots.
In order to benefit sentient beings, he accepts the form of a beast,
but he is free of the guilt of a beast.
When the Bodhisattva is among the beasts,
his compassionate pity extends even to enemies and thieves,
something the Āluóhàn (Arhats) and Pìzhīfó (Pratyekabuddhas) do not possess.
When an Āluóhàn or Pìzhīfó
is approached by an enemy or thief intending harm,
though they do not retaliate,
they cannot feel affection for them, nor offer them reverence or sustenance.
Consider the Bodhisattva in a past embodiment,
when he was the Six-Tusked White Elephant (Liùyá Báixiàng).
A hunter shot him in the chest with a poisoned arrow.
At that time, the Bodhisattva elephant embraced the hunter with his trunk,
preventing other elephants from harming him.
He spoke to the female elephant, saying:
'You are the Bodhisattva's consort (fù).
Why do you give rise to evil thoughts?
The hunter is controlled by the sin of affliction (fánnǎo zuì),
it is not the fault of the person himself.
When I attain Ānòu duōluō Sānmiǎo Sānpútí (Anuttara Samyak Sambodhi),
I shall destroy his afflictions.'
It is like a spirit possessing a person: the exorcist treats the spirit and ignores the person.
He gently asked the hunter:
'Why did you shoot me?'
He replied:
'I need your tusks.'
The elephant immediately pressed his tusks against a rock, pulled them out, and gave them to him.
Blood and flesh came out together, yet he felt no pain.
He provided him with provisions and food, and pointed out the path to him.
Such compassion and mercy
are not possessed by Āluóhàn or Pìzhīfó.
[The disciples] asked:
"Why does he not take a human form to preach the Dharma,
but instead assumes this beast form?"
[The Fó] answered:
"Sometimes sentient beings, upon seeing a human body, do not accept the teachings with faith.
But seeing a beast body preach the Dharma,
they immediately give rise to faith and joy,
and accept his spiritual transformation (jiàohuà).
The Bodhisattva,
desiring to complete the Great Compassionate Heart,
and desiring to perform actual deeds,
causes sentient beings who see him to be amazed and delighted, and all attain entrance to the Way.
Formerly, the Bodhisattva,
together with Ānán (Ānanda),
finished their karmic punishment.
Each became a dragon body.
One dragon said:
'Only you and I share life in the sea.
There is nothing we have not seen.
How about we both go up onto the land to roam and play?'
[The other] replied:
'The people on land are malicious; should we encounter disaster, we cannot escape.'
The first dragon replied again:
'We can transform into small snakes.
If the road is empty, we will follow the main path to play.
If we meet people, we will hide. What is there to worry about?'
Thereupon, they agreed,
and together ascended to roam and observe.
They had not been out of the water long
when they encountered a poisonous snake (huǐ) on the road.
The huǐ saw the two snakes, had murderous thoughts, and desired to harm them.
It immediately spewed poisonous foam.
One snake wanted to kill the poisonous huǐ.
The other snake, being compassionate and patient, advised him to stop.
He said:
'Indeed, one who is a noble scholar (gāoshì) ought to pardon the multitude of fools.
To endure the unendurable
is the solemn instruction of the sages.'
He immediately spoke a verse (gè) saying:
'Greed and desire make a crazy man, having no humane or righteous heart.
Against jealousy desiring harm, the precept is only silent patience for peace.'
The snake extolled patience.
The other snake respectfully accepted, and thus did not harm the huǐ.
One snake said:
'Let us return to the sea.'
They agreed and went together.
They then displayed their awe-inspiring divine power,
shaking heaven and moving earth.
They raised clouds and brought down rain.
Humans and spirits alike were alarmed.
The huǐ, terrified,
stared like a corpse, unconscious.
For seven days, it refused food and desired death.
The frightened dragon (huánlóng) was Ānán.
The dragon who spoke of patience was myself.
The poisonous huǐ was Tiáodá (Devadatta)."
There was a person.
He entered the forest to fell trees.
He became confused and lost his way.
At that time, a heavy rain began.
Dusk fell, and he was hungry and cold.
Vicious insects and poisonous beasts wanted to harm him.
This person entered a stone cave.
There was a large bear.
Seeing it, he fled in terror.
The bear spoke to him, saying:
"Do not be afraid.
This dwelling is warm, you may stay here overnight."
At that time, it rained continuously for seven days.
[The bear] constantly provided this person with sweet fruits and fine water.
After seven days, the rain stopped.
The bear led this person out and showed him the path.
The bear said to the person:
"I have a sinful body; humans are my enemies.
If anyone asks,
do not say that you saw me."
The person replied, "I will."
This person walked forward.
He saw several hunters (lièzhě).
The hunters asked:
"Where have you come from?
Have you seen any wild animals?"
[He] replied:
"I saw a large bear.
It showed me kindness.
I cannot point it out to you."
The hunters said:
"You are a human being (rén dǎng).
Considering the human species (rénlèi xiāng guān),
why protect a bear?
Now that we have lost the track,
when will it return?
If you show us,
we will give you a large share."
This person’s mind changed.
He immediately led the hunters and showed them the bear's location.
The hunters killed the bear.
They immediately gave him a large share.
When this person stretched out his hand to take the meat,
both his elbows fell off.
The hunters said:
"What crime did you commit?"
[He] replied:
"This bear regarded me
like a father regards his son.
I have now betrayed his kindness.
This must be the retribution for that crime."
The hunters were terrified,
and dared not eat the meat.
They took it and offered it to the assembled monks (zhòng sēng).
The senior monk (Shàngzuò) was an Arhat (Āluóhàn) who possessed the Six Supernatural Powers (Liùtōng).
He said to the junior monks (Xiàzuò):
"This is a Bodhisattva (Púsà).
In a future life, he will become a Buddha (Fó).
Do not eat this meat."
Immediately, they erected a stūpa (tǎ) and made offerings.
The King (Wáng) heard of this matter.
He issued a decree throughout the country (guónèi):
"Let no person who betrays kindness dwell here."
People, using various analogies (yīnyuán),
praised those who recognized kindness.
Formerly, when the Buddha (Fó) was in the country of Bōluónài, at the park of the immortals, Lùyěyuàn (Deer Park).
All the divine immortals (shénxiān) who possessed the Five Supernatural Powers (Wǔtōng)
often traveled and studied in this country.
It was not a place where ordinary mortals (fánfū) dwelled.
The King (Wáng) went out hunting.
He encountered a herd of a thousand deer, all trapped inside nets.
The King (Wáng) deployed infantry soldiers (bùbīng) to surround them in a circle.
The herd of deer was terrified.
Some made panicked noises and rushed about frantically, while others lay prostrate on the ground, hiding themselves.
Śākyamuni Buddha (Shìjiāmóuní Fó),
when he was formerly a Bodhisattva (Púsà),
was the King of the Herd of Deer (Qúnlù Wáng).
The Buddha (Fó) told the herd of deer:
"Rest easy, and fear no more.
I will devise a skillful means (fāngbiàn).
I will surely plead for mercy with the King (Wáng) and secure your lives."
Each one had no other choice.
The Deer King (Lùwáng) came before the Human King (Rénwáng), knelt down, and begged for mercy.
The Human King (Rénwáng) saw him from afar,
and commanded his attendants not to harm the deer.
The deer said:
"Now observing the King's (Wáng) intention,
you wish to kill a thousand deer to supply the kitchen for one day.
It is currently very hot,
the meat cannot be stored long.
We beg the King (Wáng) to have pity.
Kill one deer daily to supply the kitchen butchery."
"It will not trouble the King's (Wáng) messengers.
The deer will go to the kitchen themselves,
accept death.
The supply of meat will not cease,
and the deer population will be able to increase."
The King (Wáng) asked the deer:
"Are you the elder among this herd of deer (Qúnlù)?"
[The deer] replied:
"It is so."
The King (Wáng) further asked the deer:
"Is this truly the case?"
[The deer] replied:
"It is truly the case."
The King (Wáng) then released the deer, gathered his forces, and returned to the city.
At that time, the Bodhisattva (Púsà) led five hundred deer,
and Devadatta (Diàodá) also led five hundred deer.
Every day, one deer was selected
to go to the King (Wáng) to supply the kitchen.
When it was Devadatta's (Diàodá) turn to send a deer to the King (Wáng),
it happened to be a doe who had been pregnant for several months.
It was her turn to supply the kitchen.
The doe (Lùmǔ) said to the King (Wáng):
"I am about to give birth.
It is currently my turn,
but my child's turn has not yet arrived.
I beg that my turn be changed and allow me to wait a little later."
Devadatta (Diàodá) angrily said:
"Why do you not go quickly?
Who can die first in your place?"
The doe (Lùmǔ) wept mournfully, crying out.
She immediately approached the Bodhisattva (Púsà) and presented her case thus:
"I beg the King (Wáng, referring to the Deer King) to grant me pardon
and allow me to wait for a later turn."
The Bodhisattva (Púsà) asked the deer:
"Did your master allow you to present your case?"
[She] replied:
"My master did not permit it."
The Bodhisattva (Púsà) comforted that deer:
"Do not be afraid for now.
I will now take your place
to supply the kitchen butchery."
The Bodhisattva Deer King (Púsà Lùwáng)
immediately summoned the thousand deer
and earnestly warned and commanded them:
"Do not harbor any laziness or negligence.
Also, do not trespass upon the King's (Wáng) autumn sprouts and grain fields."
Devadatta (Diàodá) angrily scolded the doe (Lùmǔ), saying:
"Since it is your turn, why do you make excuses?"
The Bodhisattva (Púsà) said to Devadatta (Diàodá):
"Stop! Stop speaking these words.
The doe (Lùmǔ) truly should die next,
but out of pity for her fetus, she should not yet die.
I will take her place to save the life of the fetus."
The herd of deer stated:
"We willingly desire to take death in the King's (Wáng) place.
If the King (Wáng) survives with us,
we can eat water and grass,
and roam freely as we wish,
without fear or reservation."
The [Deer] King (Wáng) then went to the kitchen.
The herd of deer followed closely behind him all the way to the royal palace (Wánggōng).
The Deer King (Lùwáng) approached the kitchen and voluntarily asked to be supplied and butchered.
The chef (chúshì) saw the Deer King (Lùwáng).
He immediately went to report to the King (Wáng):
"The Deer King (Lùwáng) has entered the kitchen,
and it is his turn to be supplied and butchered.
We humbly ask the Great King (Dàwáng),
should he be killed or not?"
The King (Wáng) commanded his officials:
"Quickly bring the Deer King (Lùwáng) here."
The King (Wáng) asked the deer:
"Are the thousand deer all gone?
Why have you come?"
The deer reported to the King (Wáng):
"The thousand heads are nursing their young and have formed a large herd.
They increase daily
and do not decrease."
[The deer] fully explained the previous incident.
The King (Wáng) earnestly reproached himself,
grieving that he was unworthy.
"I, behaving like a beast (chùshòu), failed to distinguish virtue from deceit,
and unjustly killed living creatures,
reaching such a point."
The King (Wáng) instructed his ministers:
"Let it be widely commanded throughout the country (guójiè) that anyone who hunts and kills deer
shall be punished and executed."
He immediately sent the Deer King (Lùwáng) back,
commanding that deer meat must not be eaten within the country (guónèi).
If there was anyone who ate the meat,
their head should be exposed.
Because of this, the name Lùyěyuàn (Deer Park) was established.
The Buddha (Fó) said:
In a past age, near the foot of Snow Mountain (Xuěshān),
there was a Deer King (Lùwáng)
named Wēidé.
He was the leader of five hundred deer.
At that time, there was a hunter (lièshī).
He laid grain and set snares.
The Deer Leader (Lùzhǔ) walked forward,
and his right foot fell into a hair snare.
The Deer King (Lùwáng) thought:
"If I reveal my situation,
then the other deer will not dare to eat the grain.
I must wait until the grain is completely eaten,
and only then reveal the condition of my foot."
At that time, all the deer departed.
One female deer (nǚlù) remained,
and spoke a verse (jì), saying:
Dàwáng ought to know that the hunter is coming. I wish for diligent effort and skillful means
to get out of this snare.
At that time, the Deer King (Lùwáng) replied with a verse.
"My diligent effort and skillful means, strength and potential, are already exhausted. The hair snare is getting tighter
and I cannot get out."
The female deer (nǚlù)
saw the hunter (lièshī) had arrived.
She spoke to him with a verse, saying:
"I wish that you would first use your sharp knife to kill my body, and then release
the Deer King and let him go."
The hunter heard this,
and gave rise to a heart of pity.
He replied with a verse, saying:
"I will never kill you, nor will I kill the Deer King.
I release you and the Deer King; go wherever you wish."
The hunter immediately released the Deer King.
The Buddha (Fó) said:
"The Deer King of the past is now my present body.
The five hundred deer are the five hundred Bhikṣus (Bǐqiū)."
In the past, the Bodhisattva (Púsà),
took the form of the Nine-Colored Deer (Jiǔsèlù).
His fur was nine kinds of color,
and his antlers were white as snow.
He lived by the side of the Héngshǔi (Ganges River), eating water plants.
He always kept company with a crow (wū).
At that time, there was a drowning man (nìrén) in the water.
He drifted downstream,
sometimes emerging, sometimes submerged.
He lifted his head and called out to Heaven:
"Mountain spirits, tree spirits, all Devas (Tiān), and Dragon Spirits (Lóngshén)!
Why do you not pity me?"
The deer heard him in the water and said:
"You may ride on my back and grasp my antlers.
I will carry you out onto the bank."
The drowning man stepped onto the land.
He circled the deer three times,
bowed his head to the deer,
and begged to be allowed to become a slave to the great lord (dàfū),
serving him by fetching water and plants.
The deer said, "That is unnecessary.
Just go your own way.
If you wish to repay my kindness,
do not speak of my presence here.
People are greedy for my skin and antlers,
and they will certainly come and kill me."
At that time, the King's wife (Guówáng Fūrén)
dreamt in the night that she saw the Nine-Colored Deer.
She immediately feigned illness and refused to rise.
The King (Wáng) asked why.
She replied:
"Last night I dreamt of an extraordinary deer.
Its fur was nine kinds of color,
and its antlers were white as snow.
I am thinking that I wish to obtain its skin to make a cushion,
and its antlers to make a fly-whisk handle.
The King must obtain it for me.
If the King cannot obtain it, I shall surely die."
The King offered a reward throughout the country:
"If anyone can obtain it, they shall divide the kingdom and rule it [with me]."
He would bestow a gold bowl (jīnbō) filled with silver grains
and a silver bowl (yínbō) filled with gold grains.
The drowning man heard this and desired wealth and honor.
He thought:
"The deer is a beast.
What does its life or death matter?"
He went to the King's residence and reported the location of the deer.
The King was greatly pleased and said:
"If you can bring its skin and antlers,
I shall reward you with half the kingdom."
Immediately, leprosy sores (làichuāng) broke out on the drowning man's face.
The drowning man said:
"Dàwáng, although this deer is a beast,
it possesses great majestic power (wēishén). The King should properly dispatch many men and soldiers before it can be captured."
The King immediately sent out a great crowd of men.
They journeyed until they reached the side of the Héngshǔi. The crow was perched on a treetop.
Seeing the soldiers approaching, it immediately cried out to the deer:
"Friend, get up quickly! The King has arrived!"
The deer was still soundly asleep and did not wake up.
The crow flew down and pecked its ear.
The deer was then startled awake, looked around in the four directions, and had no means left to run away.
It then went straight toward the King's chariot.
The attending officials wished to shoot it.
The King said:
"Do not shoot!
This deer is extraordinary.
It must be a Celestial Spirit (Tiānshén)."
The deer spoke:
"Dàwáng,
please do not shoot me.
I previously saved a person from the King's country."
The deer then knelt and asked the King, saying:
"Who reported my location here?"
The King immediately pointed
and said, "It is the man with the leprous face next to the chariot."
The deer immediately lifted its head
and looked at the man's face.
Tears flowed from its eyes,
unable to control itself.
"This man was previously drowning in the water.
I did not begrudge my body or life;
I threw myself into the water
and carried this man out.
We promised not to reveal my whereabouts.
Having no gratitude or reciprocity, he is worse than floating wood in the water."
The King showed shame.
He repeatedly rebuked his subject:
"You received his kindness,
how can you turn around and wish to kill him?"
He immediately issued a decree throughout the country:
"If there is anyone who pursues this deer,
they shall be punished by the execution of their five immediate kindreds (wǔzú)."
Several thousand deer all came to rely upon him.
They ate water plants and grass and did not trespass on the crops.
The wind and rain came in their proper seasons, and the five grains ripened abundantly.
People were without illness.
That era was Great Peace (Tàipíng).
The Nine-Colored Deer of that time is my present body.
The crow is Ānán.
The King (Guówáng) is now my father, King Yuètóután.
The King's wife of that time is now Sūntuólì.
The drowning man of that time is now Tiáodá (Devadatta).
Although I showed kindness toward him,
he still wished to harm me.
Ānán possessed ultimate sincerity."
In a past age,
there was the city of Bōluónài (Vārāṇasī).
By the side of the city was a pond.
The pond was named Yǔchéng.
In this pond were many fish, turtles, geese, wild geese, ducks, and so forth.
Among them was a Wild Goose King (Yànwáng),
named Zhìguó,
who was the leader of five hundred wild geese.
At that time, there was a hunter.
He had previously set a hair snare.
The Wild Goose King walked ahead,
and his right foot was caught in the snare.
He made this thought:
"If I were to pull my foot out of this snare,
the other geese would not dare to eat grain
until it was finished. So I will display my foot (as if eating)."
The flock of geese flew away.
Only one wild goose,
named Sūmó,
did not abandon the King and depart.
The King said to his minister:
"I grant you the position to be King.
Walk ahead of all the geese."
[Sūmó] replied:
"I cannot."
[The King] asked:
"Why is that?"
At that time, the minister (dàchén)
replied with a verse, saying:
"I vow to follow the King, whether in life or death, without change. I would rather die together with the King
than live separated from you. Dàwáng, you ought to know that the snare setter is coming.
Just diligently employ skillful means to seek release from this snare."
At that time, the Wild Goose King
replied with a verse, saying:
"My diligent effort and skillful means, strength and potential, are already exhausted. The hair snare is getting tighter
and I cannot gain release."
Minister Sūmó,
seeing the snare setter arrive,
spoke to him with a verse, saying:
"Dàwáng's feathers, fat, and flesh are no different from mine.
If you kill me with your knife and release the King, it will not harm you."
At that time, the snare master
said to the minister:
"I will not kill you.
I release you and the King.
Go wherever you please."
The hunter immediately untied the Goose King.
The two geese both departed.
They spoke to each other, saying:
"This hunter has performed a rare deed,
granting us life.
We must greatly repay his means of livelihood."
The hunter asked them, saying:
"You are animals.
What provisions do you possess to repay me?"
The two geese replied:
"The King of Bōluónài is named Fàndé.
You carry us, (which is what we offer) to the hunter."
(The hunter) carried the geese placed upon his two shoulders.
He arrived in the city streets.
These geese were handsome and proper.
All the people enjoyed seeing them.
There were those who offered five coins, ten coins, or twenty coins,
all saying, "Do not kill them."
This man, arriving near the royal palace,
obtained great wealth.
The hunter arrived at the royal palace gate.
He placed the geese upon the ground.
The Goose King spoke to the gatekeeper, saying:
"Report to King Fàndé:
‘The ruler of the geese (Zhìguó Yànwáng) is now outside the gate.’"
(The gatekeeper) immediately went and reported to the King.
The King immediately permitted entry.
He set up a golden couch for them.
The minister Sūmó proceeded to exchange greetings as appropriate.
Thereafter, he took his seat.
He greeted King Fàndé with a verse, saying:
"Is Your Majesty well? Is the kingdom abundant?
Do you transform the people according to the Dharma? Do you rule the state with equal impartiality?"
At that time, King Fàndé
replied with a verse, saying:
"I am always peaceful and well, transforming the citizens with the Dharma.
The kingdom is consistently prosperous and peaceful; my impartial heart has no favoritism."
They responded to each other in this manner,
speaking five hundred verses.
Minister Sūmó remained silent at that time.
King Fàndé said:
"Why are you silent?"
The Minister replied:
"You are the human king and ruler of the state.
This Goose King is the ruler of the marshlands state.
How dare I interrupt when the two kings speak together?"
The King said:
"I have a good park.
Will you be able to reside there?"
(The Goose King) replied:
"No."
The King asked:
"Why?"
The Goose replied:
"Perhaps when Your Majesty wakes up,
forgetting to spare me,
you might order my flesh to be cooked and eaten.
If the butcher cannot obtain other geese,
he might kill us to fill the royal kitchen."
When the Zhìguó Yànwáng entered the royal palace,
the other geese, rising from a pond formed by rain, gathered above the royal palace,
circling and sadly calling.
Their wet wings shed water, defiling the palace hall.
The King asked:
"What is this?"
The Goose King replied:
"These are my dependents."
The King said:
"Do you wish to leave?"
(The Goose King) replied:
"We wish to leave."
The King said:
"What do you require?"
(The Goose King) replied:
"We were caught by the hunter.
He performed a rare deed for us,
granting us life.
If he had first killed one and then killed the other, who could have stopped him?"
The King said:
"How should he be rewarded?"
The two geese answered:
"Give him gold, silver, giant clams (chēqú), agate (mǎnnǎo), clothing, and food."
Having said this, they flew up into the void.
The Buddha said:
"The Goose King was myself.
The five hundred geese
were the five hundred Bhikṣus.
The hunter was Shǒucái Xiàng (the elephant Shǒucái).
King Fàndé was Jìngfàn Wáng.
Minister Sūmó was Ānán."
In the past, the Bodhisattva
manifested as a parrot, constantly dwelling in a tree.
The wind blew, causing the trees to rub and grind against each other.
Then fire broke out.
The fire gradually grew fierce,
and consequently burned down a mountain.
The parrot reflected:
"Even flying creatures whose bodies rest on a tree
ought to return repeatedly to harbor a heart of gratitude and recompense.
How much more so should I, who have dwelled here for a long night (long time),
not fail to extinguish this fire?"
It immediately went to the sea.
Using its two wings, it gathered sea water.
It flew above the fire and sprinkled it onto the flames.
Sometimes using its mouth to sprinkle water, it rushed back and forth, east and west.
At that time, there was a good deity.
Moved by its diligent suffering,
(the deity) promptly extinguished the fire.
In the past, the Bodhisattva embodied the Sparrow King.
With a heart of compassion, he aided the multitude by protecting a sore on his body.
A tiger, having eaten an animal, had a bone stuck between its teeth.
It was sick, distressed, and about to die.
The sparrow entered its mouth and pecked at the bone, day after day, thus.
The sparrow’s mouth developed sores, and its body became thin and scarred.
The bone came out of the tiger’s mouth.
The sparrow flew up and perched on a tree.
It preached the Buddhist scripture, saying:
"Killing is a harbinger of plague; there is no evil greater than it."
The tiger heard the sparrow's admonition.
It suddenly became angry and said:
"You have only just escaped my mouth,
yet you dare to speak so much."
The sparrow, seeing that it could not be converted,
immediately flew away quickly.
The Buddha said:
"The sparrow was myself.
The tiger was Diàodá."
In the past, the Bodhisattva was poor.
He went with various merchants to another country.
The Bodhisattva saw fish in the sea, both large and small, swallowing each other.
He sacrificed his body for the small ones, allowing them to gain temporary life.
He immediately threw himself into the sea; the large fish were sated, and the small ones survived.
His spirit transformed into the King of Whales.
Its body was several *lǐ* long.
A coastal kingdom suffered from drought, and the people starved.
They began eating each other.
The whale immediately washed its body ashore in the kingdom.
Those who consumed its flesh survived.
They hauled away the flesh for several months, yet the whale remained alive.
A Heavenly deity descended and said:
"Can you endure this suffering for the sake of kindness and compassion?
Why do you not retrieve your lifespan and leave this pain?"
The whale replied:
"If my spirit departs and my body rots,
the people will later starve.
They will again eat each other.
I cannot bear to witness that."
The deity said:
"You will certainly achieve Buddhahood and deliver sentient beings from suffering."
Someone took its head; at that point, the whale died.
His spirit became a prince.
He possessed supreme sagely wisdom.
His four kinds of loving-kindness were vast and nurtured (the people), matching the two cosmic forces (Heaven and Earth).
He pitied the people in their distress and poverty.
When he spoke of it, he choked up.
However, the state was still suffering from drought.
He calmed his mind and purified himself with solemnity.
He rejected food and ceased offerings.
He prostrated himself in repentance, saying:
"The misfortune of the people
is due to the fault in my own person.
I pray that I may lose my life to bestow rain and moisture upon the people."
He mourned month after month,
like a most filial son grieving the loss of his sage father.
His sincerity spread far and wide, gaining fame.
The Buddha, with five hundred followers, came to his kingdom.
The King heard this and his heart rejoiced.
He welcomed them reverently, bowed low, kowtowed, and wept.
"My heart is polluted and my conduct turbid,
not conforming to the teachings of the Three Venerables and the Four Kinds of Gratitude.
I have tyrannized the people.
Drought has persisted for years.
The common people are starving.
Grievance and pain wound their feelings.
I pray that the calamities of the people be removed, and the misfortune and guilt placed upon me."
The Buddhas replied:
"As a ruler,
your compassion, sympathy, benevolence, and virtue equal Dìshì.
All Buddhas universally know this.
May the King receive blessings, be cautious, and have no sorrow."
He ordered the people to sow grain.
There was no family that did not cultivate.
The rice transformed into plumpness.
The King said:
"Wait for it to ripen."
The grain covered the state.
All the grains of rice were large.
Each contained several *hú*.
The rice was fragrant, and the whole state was joyful and delighted.
They praised and recited the King's virtue.
The entire land observed the precepts.
They took refuge in the Three Jewels.
The King, ministers, and common people were reborn in heaven at the end of their lives.
The poor man (at that time) was myself.
In the past, the Bodhisattva,
once became the Turtle King (Biēwáng),
growing up in the great ocean and transforming all his kin.
His subjects and the masses all cultivated benevolence and virtue (réndé).
The King himself practiced loving-kindness, compassion, joy, and equanimity (cíbēixǐhù).
He pitied sentient beings as a mother loves her child.
That sea was deep and vast, its boundaries hard to measure,
yet he fully traversed it, leaving nothing unexperienced.
At that time, the Turtle King (Biēwáng) came out to the foreign shores,
and rested on the edge for days and months.
His back was hard and dry, just like land.
Merchants (gǔrén) traveling far came and stopped upon him.
They broke firewood, lit fires, and cooked meals.
They tethered their oxen and horses, and placed their wagons loaded with stones all upon him.
The Turtle King (Biēwáng) wanted to rush into the water,
but feared drowning the merchants (shāngrén).
Though he tried to endure the unbearable pain,
he then devised a skillful plan (quánjì) and entered shallow water.
He extinguished the fire's harmful heat without endangering the multitude of merchants (zhònggǔ).
The multitude of merchants (zhònggǔ) were terrified, thinking the tide had suddenly risen.
Sorrowfully sighing, they pledged their lives to all the deities (zhūtiān):
Śakra (Shì), Brahmā (Fàn), the Four Heavenly Kings (Sì Wáng), and the gods of the sun and moon (rìyuè shénmíng).
They prayed that, by their awesome power and virtue (wēidé), they would receive deliverance and aid.
The Turtle King's (Biēwáng) heart was increasingly moved with pity for them.
Thereupon, he addressed the merchants (gǔrén):
"Be sure not to panic!
I was being burned by the fire, so I moved into the water
hoping the pain would cease.
I shall now keep you safe and will absolutely not endanger you."
When the multitude of merchants (zhònggǔ) heard this, they knew they had hope of survival.
All together they raised their voices and said:
"Námó Fó!"
The turtle (biē) summoned great compassion,
and carried the multitude of merchants (zhònggǔ) back, moving them to the riverbank.
The people, having escaped, were universally joyful.
They bowed from afar to the Turtle King (Biēwáng) and praised his virtue.
"You have been a noble bridge, carrying many across.
Your actions are like a great vessel, transporting us beyond the Three Realms (Sānjiè).
Should you attain the path of Buddhahood (Fódào), you will surely rescue and deliver us from the calamity of birth and death (shēngsǐ zhī è)."
The Turtle King (Biēwáng) replied:
"Excellent! Excellent!
It shall be as you say."
They each departed separately.
The Buddha (Fó) said:
"The Turtle King (Biēwáng) at that time was I myself.
The five hundred merchants (gǔrén)
were the five hundred disciples, Shèlìfú (Śāriputra) and the rest."
Formerly, during the time of the Buddha Kūlóuqín (Krakucchanda),
there was a Bhikṣu (bǐqiū)
named Wúgòu,
dwelling in solitary retreat
in a mountain cave near the border of a state.
Not far from there,
there were five divine immortals (shénxiān).
A woman encountered heavy rain on the road,
entered the Bhikṣu’s (bǐqiū) cave, and left when the rain stopped.
At that time, the five immortals (xiānrén) saw her.
Each of them said:
"The Bhikṣu (bǐqiū) is depraved and impure."
Wúgòu heard this,
and immediately leaped into the void,
forty-nine feet above the ground.
The immortals (zhūxiān) saw him flying in the void,
and each said:
"As recorded in our scriptures:
those contaminated by the dust of desire cannot fly."
They immediately prostrated themselves, touching the ground with five parts of their bodies (wǔtǐ tóudì), and confessed to their slander.
If the Bhikṣu (bǐqiū) had not displayed his spiritual power (shénbiàn),
those five immortal kings (xiān wáng) would have fallen into the great hell (dà dìyù).
The Bhikṣu Wúgòu (Wúgòu bǐqiū) at that time
is now the Bodhisattva Císhì (Maitreya).
In the past, there was a Buddha (Fó)
named Mònéngshèng (Anabhibhūta, "None Can Conquer").
There was a Bhikṣu (bǐqiū)
named Huìwáng ("Wisdom King").
At dawn, performing his alms round (fēnwèi), he obtained hundred-flavored rice and various kinds of food.
On the road was the son of a venerable one,
named Lí'gòubì ("Stainless Arm").
He was being carried by his wet nurse.
He saw the Bhikṣu (bǐqiū) from afar.
He descended from the wet nurse's embrace
and immediately followed the Bhikṣu (bǐqiū), asking him for food.
At that time, the Bhikṣu (bǐqiū) gave him a honey cake (mìchuǎi).
The young boy immediately ate it and knew its sweetness.
He continued following the Bhikṣu (bǐqiū) until the honey cake (mìchuǎi) was nearly finished.
The Bhikṣu (bǐqiū) gave him more.
They proceeded to the place of the Buddha (Fó).
They bowed their heads at the Buddha’s (Fó) feet.
Huìwáng took the food he had obtained
and gave it to the young boy, urging him to offer it to the Buddha (Fó),
causing him to generate the aspiration for the Way (dàoyì).
The Buddha (Fó) immediately received it, filling the Buddha's bowl (Fóbō).
The food was not diminished or lessened.
Next, he gave it to the eighty-four thousand Śrāvakas (shēngwén),
and the twelve hundred million Bodhisattvas (púsà).
The Buddha (Fó) and the holy assembly
were all completely full.
This kind of offering lasted for seven days,
and the rice remained as it was, neither lessened nor diminished.
The young boy, joyful, spoke verses praising the Buddha (Fó).
He immediately generated the aspiration for the Unsurpassed, True and Right Dharma (wúshàng zhèngzhēn fǎ yì).
At that time, his parents searched for their son
and went to the Buddha's (Fó) place.
The young boy greeted them and praised his parents in verse.
At that time, the young boy
converted his parents and five hundred people,
making them all aspire to the Unsurpassed, True and Right Dharma (wúshàng zhèngzhēn fǎ).
They all immediately abandoned home and became Śramaṇas (shāmén).
They practiced the Bodhisattva Path (Púsà Dào) and consequently attained Buddhahood (Fó).
The King Huìwáng (Huìwáng) at that time is now Pǔshǒu Tóngzhēn.
As for Lí'gòubì, that is I myself.
At that time, there was a Bodhisattva (púsà)
named Shàngshǒu ("Foremost Head").
He acted as a mendicant (qǐshì),
entering the city to beg for food.
There was a Bhikṣu (bǐqiū)
named Héngjiā (Gaṅgā).
He said to the mendicant:
"Where do you come from?"
He answered:
"I come from within Reality (zhēnshí)."
Héngjiā asked:
"What is meant by Reality (zhēnshí)?"
He replied:
"It is called Reality (zhēnshí) because it is the characteristic of tranquility and extinction (jìmie xiàng)."
Héngjiā said:
"Where should one seek the true Dharma (shífǎ)?"
He replied:
"You should seek it within the Six Pāramitās (liù bōluómì)."
Héngjiā was joyful.
He bowed at the feet of Shàngshǒu
and then asked:
"With what food should I make offerings to this person?"
Shàngshǒu replied:
"You should offer Sūtuówèi (Sudhā) taste."
Héngjiā immediately went to the metropolis
and announced himself, saying:
"I wish to sell my body!
Who wants it?"
There was a householder (jūshì)
named Pínúlǜ (Vinulūta).
He immediately asked me:
"I wish to buy it.
What price do you ask?"
Héngjiā replied that he asked for
Sūtuónàluó (Sudhanāra).
He asked:
"How many pieces do you require?"
Héngjiā replied:
"I require five pieces."
The householder (jūshì) bought this practitioner of the Way (dàorén) for five coins to serve as a retainer.
Héngjiā addressed the great family, saying:
"My body belongs to you.
Grant me seven days,
for I wish to make offerings to the Bhikṣu (bǐqiū) Shàngshǒu."
The householder (jūshì) told Héngjiā:
"I shall take you to see the residence
and then let you return."
At that time, Héngjiā, having seen the residence, proceeded along the road back.
He saw Shàngshǒu,
who had not yet obtained the alms food.
He immediately brought Shàngshǒu
into the metropolis,
bought hundred-flavored food and drink,
and led him to a monastery.
The monastery was named Sì Wáng ("Four Kings").
He set up beds and seats, burned incense, scattered flowers,
and presented various kinds of food and drink.
Xūmótí addressed the Buddha, saying:
World-Honored One,
the forty matters of the Púsà (Bodhisattva) that you preach,
I shall respectfully practice them,
ensuring nothing is lacking or diminished.
At that time, the Elder Mùlián asked:
These forty matters are practices performed by Great Beings.
How can you, a young woman, accomplish them?
She replied:
I am truly able to practice them.
If you do not believe me, then the three thousand great-thousandfold world systems shall all tremble for me six times.
Heavenly flowers shall rain down.
All musical instruments shall sound without being struck.
Immediately, it happened as she said.
The girl said:
To prove my utmost sincerity,
if my future attainment of Buddhahood is not false,
then all those in this assembly shall turn golden in color.
Forthwith, according to her words, their color became like gold.
Mùlián addressed the Buddha, saying:
I pay reverence to those who first generate the great resolve to become a Púsà.
I worship them.
Why is this?
An eight-year-old girl can manifest such responsiveness.
How much more so should the noble ones, the Móhēsà (Mahāsattvas), be revered?
Wénshūshīlì asked her, saying:
Why do you not transform your female body?
Xūmótí replied, saying:
There is nothing to be attained in this matter.
Why is this?
The Dharma fundamentally lacks male or female characteristics.
Now, I shall resolve the doubt held by you, kind sir.
Xūmótí declared:
Since I will soon attain Perfect Enlightenment,
I shall now immediately transform into a male.
Immediately upon saying this,
she achieved a male body.
Her hair fell off naturally, and a kāṣāya robe appeared on her body.
She became a śrāmaṇera (novice monk).
She further said:
When I attain Buddhahood,
let there be no three things in my land:
First, the affairs of Māra (demons);
Second, the Nílī (hells);
Third, the female form.
If I am utterly sincere,
my body shall now resemble a monk of thirty years.
Immediately upon saying this,
her form and complexion became like that of a thirty-year-old.
She further addressed Wénshūshīlì, saying:
When I attain Buddhahood,
let the people of my land all have a golden complexion.
Let the ground and the city walls have seven-jeweled trees.
Let the jeweled ponds and jeweled flowers be neither too numerous nor too few,
but all perfectly balanced.
She further declared that everyone present in the assembly should become golden in color.
At that moment, the entire assembly simultaneously gained golden countenances.
Then the earth-holding deity immediately emerged from the ground,
manifesting a heavenly body.
Raising her voice to praise,
she extolled Xūmótí
for the merit of her three declarations,
stating that she would soon become a Buddha.
The Bhikṣu Móhēlú.
The king considered him a great reader of the Móhēchéng (Mahāyāna).
He often unbound his hair and let the Bhikṣu step over it.
There was another Bhikṣu
who said to the king:
This Móhēlú does not read many scriptures.
Why do you offer him such great reverence?
The king replied:
Day and night I wished to see this Bhikṣu.
He then went to see him, and found him reading the Fǎhuājīng (Lotus Sutra) inside a cave.
He saw a golden radiance,
and a person riding a white elephant, joining hands in reverence.
As the king pressed closer, the vision vanished and did not reappear.
He immediately asked,
"Great Virtuous One,
why did the golden, radiant person vanish when I arrived?"
The Bhikṣu said:
That was Biànjí Púsà (Samantabhadra Bodhisattva) who came to instruct me in reciting this scripture.
The Bhikṣu Shànhuì
addressed Pǔguāng Rúlái (Tathāgata) saying:
When I was previously dwelling deep in the mountains,
I had five types of dreams.
First, I dreamt I was lying upon the Great Ocean.
Second, I dreamt my head was resting on Xūmí (Mount Sumeru).
Third, I dreamt that all sentient beings in the ocean entered my body.
Fourth, I dreamt I held the sun in my hand.
Fifth, I dreamt I held the moon in my hand.
I only pray, World-Honored One, that you explain them for me.
The Buddha then answered:
The dream of lying upon the Great Ocean means
that your body is currently situated in the great ocean of life and death (saṃsāra).
The dream of resting your head on Xūmí (Sumeru) means
you shall emerge from life and death and attain the characteristics of Nièpán (Nirvāṇa).
The dream that all sentient beings in the ocean enter your body means
you shall reside in the great ocean of life and death
and become a place of refuge for all sentient beings.
The dream of holding the sun in your hand means
that the light of your wisdom will universally illuminate the Dharma realm.
The dream of holding the moon in your hand means
you will enter life and death using skillful means and wisdom,
and guide sentient beings using the cooling Dharma.
Elder Xūfú had a daughter,
named Lóngshī.
She was fourteen years old.
At that time, she was in the bathroom, having finished bathing, applying perfume, and donning fine clothes.
The Buddha, with his retinue, emitted the light of the white curl between his eyebrows,
illuminating the inside of the sevenfold gate,
making the halls and residences bright.
The girl saw the radiance surpassed the sun and moon.
She knew in her heart that this was extraordinary.
She immediately ran up to the top of the seven-story tower.
Facing east, she saw the Buddha standing outside the gate.
The girl was greatly delighted.
She then thought to herself:
If I can now give offerings to the Buddha and his many disciples,
and generate the resolve to practice the Púsà Vow,
may I later attain enlightenment like the Buddha.
Māra saw the girl generating the great resolve and was displeased.
He immediately descended, transforming himself into the girl's father.
He said to Lóngshī:
Your aspiration is too ambitious.
The Buddha path is difficult to attain.
Since there is fortunately a Buddha in this world,
it is better to seek the path of the Luóhàn (Arhat).
Both paths lead to deliverance from the world and Níhuán (Nirvāṇa) without difference.
Lóngshī countered:
What you say is incorrect, Father.
The Buddha's wisdom is vast and boundless in saving beings.
The wisdom of an Arhat is tiny, like a single speck of dust.
What noble person would prefer the lesser path?
Māra spoke again:
I have never heard of a woman becoming a Cakravartin King,
much less attaining Buddhahood.
It is better to seek the Arhat path and quickly attain Níhuán (Nirvāṇa).
Lóngshī replied:
I have also heard
that women cannot become Cakravartin Kings
or become Buddhas.
I shall diligently strive to transform this female body into a male body.
Furthermore, I have heard
that those who practice the Púsà Dharma throughout the world
and persevere without slackening for hundreds of millions of eons (kalpas),
will later attain Buddhahood.
Māra saw that the girl's intention did not change,
and became increasingly worried and hateful.
He delivered a more urgent instruction, saying:
If one practices the Púsà path,
one must not covet the world,
nor begrudge one's lifespan.
If you are diligent now,
and are able to throw yourself from the top of this tower to the ground,
then you may later attain Buddhahood.
Lóngshī thought in her heart:
I have now seen the Buddha,
and I yearn for the Púsà Path.
My father also teaches diligence,
and that my body can attain Buddhahood.
Why should I begrudge this perilous and fragile life?
She immediately stood by the railing,
faced the Buddha, joined her hands, and said:
I take refuge in the Heaven among Heavens.
With your omniscience,
you know what I seek.
I request to cast aside my body and life, never abandoning the Púsà Path.
I offer my body as a gift to the Buddha.
May it be like scattering flowers.
Thereupon, she flung herself down from the tower.
Before she reached the ground,
she transformed into a male.
The Buddha smiled.
Five-colored light issued from his mouth, illuminating one Buddha-field.
It returned, encircled the Buddha’s body three times, and entered through the crown of his head.
(The Buddha/A voice asked:) Did you see this girl throw herself into the air and transform into a male?
This girl, in her previous lives,
had already served ten thousand Buddhas.
Afterwards, she will serve future Buddhas numerous as the sands of the Ganges.
In seven hundred and sixty million kalpas, she shall attain Buddhahood.
Her title shall be Míngshàng.
Her lifespan shall be one kalpa.
After her Bānnítuán (Parinirvāṇa),
her Dharma teachings will flourish,
and will disappear only after half a kalpa.
Thereupon, Lóngshī, standing before the Buddha, addressed her parents:
I ask that you release me so I may become a Shāmén (monk).
Her parents immediately consented.
All her inner and outer relatives also generated the aspiration for the unsurpassed path.
. The Bodhisattvas and the assembly of the four groups
. The Buddha preached the Dharma
. A Kālā woman, pregnant, was in the seat
. The child carried within her belly
listened to the Sūtra with clasped hands
. The Buddha wished the assembly to see this
, and immediately great light shone upon the seat of the Kālā woman
. Everyone saw the girl inside the belly listening to the Sūtra with clasped hands
, just like viewing an illuminated mirror
. The Buddha, using eight kinds of voices
, asked the girl in the belly, saying, "For what reason do you listen to the Sūtra with clasped hands?"
Using the Buddha’s divine power, she immediately answered the Buddha, saying
: "Because people in the world all practice the Ten Evils
, I wish to make them practice the Ten Goods
. Also, because the cycle of birth and death for worldly beings is unceasing
. Furthermore, worldly people are unfilial to their parents
and do not make offerings to Śrāmaṇas, Brāhmaṇas, or practitioners of the Way
. For this reason, I listen to the Sūtra with clasped hands."
When the girl finished speaking these words, she was born
, just like the Crown Prince being born from the right flank
. The earth shook six times
. In the void, there was spontaneous heavenly music
, and a shower of heavenly flowers
. A thousand-petaled lotus flower, as large as a carriage wheel
, had a stem made of jewels
, appearing like blue lapis lazuli (liúlí)
. The girl immediately sat upon the lotus flower
. Dìshì [Śakra] carried a celestial robe
and gave it to the girl to wear
. The girl replied, saying
: "You are an Arhat
, and I am a Bodhisattva
. You are not of my rank
and not of my kind
. I have my own clothes."
Shèlìfó [Śāriputra] addressed the Buddha
: "From which land did this girl come
? And why is she sending away the clothing?"
The Buddha said
: "This girl comes from the southeastern Buddha-land, the Pure Land (Qīngjìng Guó)
, which is one hundred thousand Buddha-lands distant from here."
Her native country's clothing spontaneously appeared in the void, rustling with sound
. When the girl saw the clothing arrive, she put it on
. She immediately attained the Five Supernormal Powers
. Moreover, all the people in her native country attained the Five Supernormal Powers
. After the girl had received and put on the clothing
, she descended from the lotus flower and walked to the front of the Buddha
. As soon as the girl raised one foot
, the earth shook six times
. She bowed her head and face to the ground, performing obeisance to the Buddha
. She said "Námó Fó" (Homage to the Buddha) three times
, and then knelt with elongated knees, addressing the Buddha
: "Among the assembly now, there are many Kālā women
. I wish the Buddha would preach the Sūtra for them
so that they may attain a male body."
The Buddha said
: "I neither cause you to become a man
, nor do I cause you to become a woman
. Everything is attained through one's own bodily actions."
The Buddha said
: "There is one condition by which one can quickly attain a male body
. What is that one condition?
To awaken the thought (fā xīn) for the Bodhisattva Way."
"Furthermore, a woman's body must be internally observed
. It is like a mechanism
, with bones and joints supporting each other
, merely covered by sinews and skin
. Women are constantly afraid of people
, like salamanders, snakes, or frogs
, daring not to go out during the daytime."
At that time, seventy-five Kālā women in the assembly
, hearing the Buddha preach the Sūtra, were joyful and leaped with excitement
. They went forward, placing their heads and faces on the ground
, performed obeisance to the Buddha, and addressed the Buddha, saying
: "We vow to awaken the Bodhisattva mind and become men
. If we do not attain a male body
, we shall not rise."
At that time, seventy-five Kālāyuè (householders)
, who had come from Shèwèiguó [Śrāvastī] to the Buddha’s location
, saw all their wives before the Buddha
. They immediately thought in their hearts
: "We have already lost our wives."
Then they asked Shèlìfó
: "These women are our wives
. Why are they here?"
Shèlìfó answered, saying
: "They wish to become Bhikṣuṇīs
. Will you permit it?"
The Kālāyuè answered, saying
: "First, let us become Bhikṣus."
Shèlìfó addressed the Buddha, saying
: "These seventy-five Kālāyuè
all wish to become Bhikṣus."
The Buddha called out
: "Come, good men!"
They all became Bhikṣus
. Their hair naturally fell away
, and the kāṣāya robe came and covered their bodies
. Holding the begging bowl in their hands
, they all advanced and paid obeisance to the Buddha
. Then the seventy-five wives
each removed their pearl bracelets and scattered them over the Buddha
. They spontaneously transformed in the void
, creating seventy-five strings of interwoven, dewy pearl necklaces (yīngluò)
. Within the canopy were seven jeweled couches
, and seats were placed upon them
. Beside the Buddha were countless Bodhisattvas listening to the Sūtra
. The seventy-five women
, seeing this transformation
, were all greatly joyful and immediately used the Buddha’s divine power to fly and remain suspended in the void
. A spontaneous rain of flowers scattered upon the Buddha
. They came down from the void
and immediately attained male bodies
. They came forward and addressed the Buddha, saying
: "We vow to become Bhikṣus."
The Buddha spoke to Mílè Púsà [Maitreya Bodhisattva]
: "Take them and administer the precepts."
Mílè Púsà immediately administered the precepts
, and they became the Bhikṣu Saṅgha
. The girl spontaneously possessed a magical flower canopy, seven layers high, with a stem like a lotus flower
. She immediately held it out and said to her mother
: "The Buddha is the teacher who guides people in heaven and earth."
The mother presented the flower canopy to the Buddha
, saying, "This cover is for the Teacher of heaven and earth
, and later, Mother shall also become a cover for the world."
The girl spoke to her mother
: "You should now awaken the Bodhisattva mind."
The mother answered the girl, saying
: "When I first carried you
, I constantly saw the Buddha, the Dharma, and the Bhikṣu Saṅgha in my dreams
. I had no mind of the Three Poisons
, and my body was peaceful and comfortable
. I knew that the child in my belly was a Bodhisattva Mahāsattva
. Because of this peace and comfort
, I awakened the Bodhisattva mind at that time."
When the mother attained the flower canopy
, she took it and presented it to the Buddha
. The earth shook six times
. The Buddha said to Shèlìfó
: "The stars in the four continents
can still be counted
, but the parents whom this girl has guided and saved, both past and future
, are uncountable."
Formerly there was a country.
Grain and rice rose sharply in price.
The people were starving.
At that time, there was a Shāmén (Buddhist ascetic).
[He] entered the city for alms (fēnwèi).
[He] did not obtain a single thing.
Next, [he] arrived at the gate of a great, wealthy Zhǎngzhě (Elder).
[He] obtained coarse, poor food.
Just as [he] was about to leave the city,
inside the gate, [he] met a butcher, a slayer of living beings, who hunted with a bow.
[He] was carrying a puppy (gǒuzǐ), bringing it home intending to kill it.
Seeing the Shāmén, [he] happily stepped forward and paid homage (lǐ).
The Shāmén blessed him (zhùyuàn), wishing him old age and long life.
The Shāmén knew there was a puppy that [the butcher] intended to kill and eat.
[He] asked what [the man] was carrying (jī).
[He] replied:
"Walking empty-handed."
The Shāmén asked further:
"I have seen the sin of taking life,
which is extremely unwholesome.
I wish to exchange my food for this puppy.
If [you] allow it to save its life, your merit (fú) will be immeasurable."
The man would not give it.
The Shāmén earnestly persuaded and pleaded, but [the man] refused to comply with his words.
The Shāmén spoke again:
"If you are unwilling,
you can show it to me."
The man immediately produced it,
showing it to the Shāmén.
The Shāmén held up the food and fed it to the puppy.
[He] stroked it with his hand, offered a blessing (zhùyuàn), and tears flowed out.
"Due to the karma caused by your sins, you obtained this dog body (quǎnshēn).
[You] cannot be self-possessed, seeing [yourself] killed, eaten, and consumed.
May your sins be extinguished and merit arise life after life,
leaving the body of a puppy to be born as a human.
Wherever [you] are, may [you] encounter the Dharma (Fǎ)."
The puppy, having received the food, developed a wholesome mind (shànxīn).
[The man], having finished the affair, joyfully took [the puppy] away.
[He] returned home, killed, and ate it.
The puppy died.
[It] was born into the house of a great, wealthy Zhǎngzhě.
Immediately upon birth, falling to the ground,
[it] already possessed a mind of loving-kindness (cīxīn).
At that time, that Shāmén,
on his alms rounds (fēnwèi), arrived inside the gate of the Zhǎngzhě.
Then the Zhǎngzhě's son saw that Shāmén.
[He] recalled and recognized the former karmic connection (běnyuán).
[He] immediately stepped forward, bowed his head to the ground (qǐshǒu), and paid homage to the Shāmén's feet.
[He] invited [the Shāmén] forward and offered food of a hundred flavors (bǎiwèi yǐnshí).
[He] stepped forward and informed his parents:
"Now I wish to follow this great Héshàng (master/reverend),
reverently receive the sūtras and precepts, and become his disciple."
His parents loved and valued him and were unwilling to permit it.
"Now, in our family, we have only you as a son.
You should continue our lineage.
You are the master of our family gate—why do you immediately wish to abandon us and leave?"
The young boy cried and refused to eat or drink.
"[If] you are unwilling to permit me, I will simply go and die."
When the parents saw this, they permitted him to go.
[He] followed his master to study the Way (Dào).
[He] shaved off his beard and hair and wore the three Dharma robes (sānfǎyī).
[He] recited the Buddhist Sūtras (Fójīng).
[He] deeply understood their meanings.
[He] then attained Samādhi (Sānmèi).
[He] established himself in the stage of Non-retrogression (Bútuìzhuǎn).
[He] opened and transformed all beings.
[He] aroused the intent for the Great Way (Dàdào Yì).
The Shāmén immediately recognized the past life (sùmìng).
[He] aroused the Bodhisattva (Púsà) Mind.
[He] established himself in Non-retrogression (Bútuìzhuǎn).
How much more so for a person
who makes offerings to the Three Jewels (Sānbǎo)
and recites the Mahāyāna (Dàshèng) [scriptures]?
Jiāshè's father
was named Níjùlǜtuó.
He was a man of the Mójié Guó.
He came from the Brahmin (Póluómén) lineage.
Due to merit from past lives, he was extremely wealthy in this lifetime.
His rare treasures were unrivaled in the nation.
His wealth compared to the king's,
lacking only one part in a thousand.
The couple was solitary, lacking children.
Near their dwelling, there was a great tree spirit (Shùshén).
At that time, the couple, wishing for a son,
offered sacrifices of three animals for several years, but their wish was not granted.
The man became greatly angry and set a period of seven days.
If there was still no sign, "I will cut you down and punish you.
I will cast you at the head of the main road and burn you with fire."
The spirit heard this and was terrified.
It ascended and reported this to Xīyì Tiānwáng.
The Tiānwáng immediately took the spirit
and informed Tiāndìshì (Sakra/Indra).
Dìshì immediately used his divine eye to observe the desire realm (Yùjiè).
There was no one suitable yet to be his son.
So, he informed Fànwáng (Brahma).
Fànwáng observed everywhere
and saw one Brahmā being who was about to finish his lifespan.
He then told him:
You should descend and be born in Yánfútí (Jambudvīpa),
to become the son of Níjùlǜtuó.
The Brahmā replied:
The Brahmins (Póluómén) hold many wrong views (Xiéjiàn).
If I descend and am born, I will not be able to be his son.
Fànwáng answered:
That Brahmin had great virtue in past lives.
No sentient being in the desire realm is suitable to be his son.
If you go and are born,
I shall command Tiāndìshì to protect you,
preventing you from falling into wrong views midway.
The Brahmā said, "Yes."
Dìshì immediately informed the tree spirit.
The tree spirit then told the elder (Zhǎngzhě):
Do not harbor anger.
In seven days from now, you will certainly have a son.
After the seven days were completed, the wife became pregnant.
After ten months, she gave birth.
His body was golden-yellow and emitted light.
The physiognomist prophesied:
This child has past merit and great power (Wēidé).
His will and strength are pure and detached; he does not cling to worldly affairs.
If he later leaves home (Chūjiā), he will certainly ascend to the holy path (Shèngdào).
The parents heard this and became greatly worried again.
Worried and fearing the child would leave home, when he reached the age of fifteen,
they wished to find him a wife.
Jiāshè heard this and repeatedly petitioned his parents:
My will delights in purity; I do not need a wife.
His parents did not listen. Jiāshè said again:
If so, I will not accept an ordinary woman.
I must obtain a woman of purple-gold complexion, peerlessly beautiful,
only then will I take her.
He intended to make this matter impossible to achieve.
His parents ordered searches throughout the entire nation.
The Brahmins (Póluómén) immediately devised a plan for them.
They cast a divine woman out of gold (Jīnshénnǚ).
Her face was beautiful, and her radiant color was subtle and exquisite,
like the image of various heavenly beings.
They went from nation to nation, loudly proclaiming:
Any woman who sees the gold deity (Jīnshén),
and pays respect and makes offerings, when she later marries,
will surely obtain a good husband.
He will have a golden-yellow body and a beautiful face,
and incomparable wisdom.
In villages, nations, and cities, all women
who heard this proclamation were wholeheartedly moved.
They all came out to welcome, pay respect, and make offerings.
There was only one girl whose body was golden-colored.
She was beautiful and excellent, dwelling alone in a quiet room, refusing to come out to welcome them.
The other women advised her, saying:
Those who see the gold deity
all have their wishes fulfilled.
Why are you the only one who does not come out to welcome it?
She replied:
My will is tranquil; I do not desire other wishes.
The women said again:
Even if you have no wish, just look at it together for a moment.
What harm could there be?
The women led her out together to look.
The golden color and radiance of the girl actually overshadowed the gold deity.
The Brahmins returned and fully reported to the elder (Zhǎngzhě).
He immediately sent a matchmaker to the girl's house,
to express the elder's intentions.
The girl’s parents had also previously heard the name of Jiāshè.
They respectfully accepted the proposal and agreed. When the girl heard this, she was extremely distraught and worried.
Compelled by her parents, the matter was unavoidable.
Thus, she married Jiāshè.
When the two faced each other, their wills were mutually reserved.
Although they were husband and wife, there was absolutely no affection between them.
They then made a mutual oath:
You and I shall occupy separate beds.
We vow not to touch each other.
At that time, the couple occupied separate beds.
When his parents heard that Jiāshè, although in the same room,
was using separate beds,
his father immediately sent someone to take the extra bed away.
Thereupon, the couple shared only one bed.
The wife made another vow with her husband:
When I sleep,
you must practice walking meditation (jīngxíng).
At that time, the wife lay down.
One arm hung down to the ground.
A large poisonous snake was about to bite her.
Jiāshè saw it and, having a compassionate heart,
wrapped his hand with clothing and lifted her arm onto the bed.
She immediately woke up in surprise and became greatly enraged.
She spoke to Jiāshè, saying:
We previously had an agreement.
How dare you violate it?
Jiāshè replied:
Your arm was hanging down, and a poisonous snake was about to bite you.
Therefore, I saved you; I did not touch you intentionally.
He pointed to the snake to show her.
Only then did his wife understand.
Thereupon, the couple consulted with each other:
Why don't we leave home and cultivate the Way (Xiūdào)?
They then took leave of their parents.
Both left home.
They entered the mountain to practice the Way.
At that time, there was a Brahmin (Póluómén)
who led five hundred disciples,
also dwelling on this mountain.
Seeing Jiāshè and his wife accompanying each other,
Jiāshè immediately left his wife.
Using five hundred ounces of gold,
he purchased fine ragged robes and dwelled separately in a different forest.
His wife then sought refuge with the Brahmin,
requesting to become a disciple.
The five hundred disciples of the Brahmin,
seeing that this woman was beautiful in form and complexion,
daily engaged in lustful conduct.
The woman lacked freedom.
Eventually, she could not endure it.
She then informed her teacher.
The teacher then,
admonished and restrained his disciples,
ordering them to moderate their desires.
Later, Jiāshè encountered the Buddha when He appeared in the world,
heard the Dharma and received transformation,
and immediately attained Arhatship (Luóhàn).
Hearing that his former wife was with the Brahmin (Fànzhì) group,
he led her to the Buddha.
The Buddha taught the Dharma for her.
She attained Arhatship (Āluóhàn).
Her hair naturally fell out, and the Dharma robes appeared on her body.
She became a Bhikṣuṇī (Bǐqiūní).
She traveled and taught the Dharma.
She happened to be present during a great assembly held by King Bōsīnì Wáng.
The Bhikṣuṇīs were then allowed to enter the King’s palace.
She taught and transformed the various royal ladies.
She persuaded them all to observe the one-day fast (Zhāi).
When the King returned to the palace in the evening,
he summoned his ladies.
They all said they were observing the fast.
None of them were willing to come.
The King became greatly enraged.
He spoke to his attendant, saying:
Who taught these ladies to fast?
The attendant replied:
A certain Bhikṣuṇī.
The King then summoned her.
He commanded her to endure lustful acts for ninety days on behalf of the ladies.
This was all due to the karma (Yīnyuán) of former days,
created by vows and wishes.
Therefore, although she attained Arhatship (Luóhàn),
she could not escape it.
abandoned wealth and followed poverty (begging). Entering Wángshěchéng,
he saw a solitary mother. She was extremely
poor. On a large pile of excrement
in the alleyways, she had dug nearby into the pile of excrement
to form a cave (dwelling). Weak, ill,
she constantly lay within it. She had neither
clothes nor food. (She had) set up a small fence
to shield her five parts (body/form). Her lifespan
was nearing its end. An elder’s servant/attendant
was walking, discarding rice gruel/water that was foul-smelling
beyond description. The mother begged
for it. (The servant) immediately poured it into broken tiles
placed on the left and right (of the mother). Kāshè, pitying her, went
to beg for some (of the food). The old mother recited a gāthā
(verse), speaking of its foul
smell. Kāshè, still moved by
compassion, endured it and begged
for it. The old mother was delighted
and immediately gave it. Kāshè feared the mother would not believe
he could eat it. He immediately drank it in front of
the mother, then cleaned his bowl. (He) displayed
supernatural power. The mother greatly
rejoiced. She gazed
at him wholeheartedly from afar. Kāshè said
to her, "Mother, what
is your current wish?" At that time, the mother, weary
of worldly suffering, having heard of heavenly joy, wished
to be born in heaven. A few days later,
she died. She was immediately born into the second
Dāolì Tiāngōng (Trāyastriṃśa Heaven Palace). She immediately remembered his past kindness
and sought to make offerings. Shìdì Huán Yīn (Śakra Devānām Indra), having
heard this matter, immediately took the Queen of Heaven (Tiān Hòu) and held food of a hundred flavors
, placing it inside a small flask. They descended to the humble (leaking)
dwelling. They transformed
their appearance, resembling
old people, poor and weaving
mats. Kāshè, while begging for alms,
saw them and went to beg. The couple said
to him, "We are now poor
and distressed, yet we willingly sacrifice ourselves, to give
this offering to the worthy one. May we thereby gain
merit." Kāshè lowered
his bowl. (They) then opened
the small flask. The fragrance permeated
the great city. Kāshè immediately
suspected (it was heavenly food). He then entered
Samādhi. He flew away,
hiding his body. (Shìdì Huán Yīn) snapped his fingers
in delight. All the devas bowed
at Kāshè’s feet. They spoke verses
in praise. "Great Virtuous One (Dà Dé), do
you not know? The Dharma Boat
is about to break. The Dharma City
is about to collapse. The Dharma Ocean
is about to dry up. The Dharma Banner
is about to fall. The Dharma Lamp
is about to be extinguished. The one who preaches the Dharma
is about to leave. Those who practice the Way
are gradually decreasing. Evil people
are becoming increasingly prevalent. You ought to use great compassion
to establish the Buddha Dharma." Kāshè's heart was
like the great ocean, clear and
unmoving. After a long time,
he replied, "The world
will not last long. (It is filled with) ignorance and
darkness (blindness)." Kāshè pondered,
"How should
I now proceed? How can I make the Buddha Dharma, which was difficult
to obtain over three Saṃkhyeya Kalpas (Sēngqí jié), endure for a long time? Only by compiling
the Sānzàng (Triple Canon) can it endure
for a long time. Future generations
can then receive and practice it. The Buddha exerted himself
through world after world, compassionate towards all sentient beings,
learning and obtaining this Dharma. He revealed and preached
it for people. We, too, should receive
and use it to enlighten others." He ascended to the summit
of Xūmí Shān (Mount Sumeru). (He) rang the bell and struck
the *ghanta*. And spoke
a verse: "Disciples of all Buddhas, if you remember the Buddha, you must repay the Buddha’s grace,
Do not enter
Nirvāṇa."
This is the sound of striking the wooden fish drum,
and the speech of Kāshyè (迦葉).
The sound reached throughout the Three-Thousand Great-Thousand Worlds (sān qiān dà qiān shìjiè);
all heard and understood it completely.
All disciples who had attained spiritual powers (shén lì)
gathered where Kāshyè was.
Kāshyè used the heavenly voice (tiān yǔ) to announce,
"The Buddha (Fó) has entered Parinirvāṇa (bān nièpán), and the disciples who understood the Dharma
have all followed him into extinction (miè dù).
The Buddhadharma (Fó Fǎ) is about to perish.
Future sentient beings are deeply pitiable;
they will lose the eye of wisdom (zhì huì yǎn),
becoming foolish, blind, and ignorant (yú chī máng míng).
We ought to carry out the Buddha's teachings.
After the compilation of the Dharma Treasury (fǎ zàng) is complete,
we may enter extinction as we please."
Kāshyè selected a thousand people.
Except for Ānán (阿難), all had attained Arhatship (luóhàn).
King Bīnbósuōluó (Pīnbósuōluó Wáng)
attained the Way and constantly commanded his palace to provide food for a thousand people.
King Āshéshì (Āshéshì Wáng) did not discontinue this practice.
Kāshyè reflected,
"If we constantly beg for food,
outsiders (wàidào) will surely come strongly questioning and challenging us,
disrupting the Dharma work."
He went to Wángshě Chéng (王舍城) and informed the king of the matter.
"The king should provide food,
sending it daily."
They observed the Summer Retreat (ān jū) for three months.
Kāshyè observed who still had afflictions (fánnǎo).
There was only Ānán.
Great Kāshyè (Dà Kāshyè) immediately counted them, saying,
"You have committed six Dújíluó (Tujikira) offenses.
You must repent them all within the Saṅgha (sēng zhōng)."
Ānán immediately followed the instruction.
He knelt, put his palms together,
bared his right shoulder, took off his leather sandals, and repented.
Kāshyè rose from the Saṅgha,
led him out by the hand,
and said,
"You must exhaust your outflows (jìn lòu).
If remaining bonds (cán jié) have not been eliminated,
you must not come back."
Then he closed the door
and discussed with the various Arhats,
"Who can compile and collect the Vinaya Dharma Treasury (Píní Fǎ Zàng)?"
The Elder Ānílúdòu (Ānílúdòu) said,
"Shèlìfú (Shèlìfú) is the Second Buddha.
Jiàofànpōtí (Jiàofànpōtí) is gentle and refined,
skilled in solitary dwelling and stillness, and fully understands the Vinaya Treasury (Píní Zàng).
He is currently in the heaven in the Shīlìshā (Śirīṣa) tree garden.
Send a junior Bhikṣu to convey the message."
Kāshyè's meaning was,
"All Arhats who have exhausted their outflows should gather in Yánfú Tí (Jambudvīpa).
The Saṅgha has great Dharma work.
You must come quickly now."
Jiàofànpōtí was suspicious in his heart.
He asked,
"Is the Saṅgha being divided by conflict and strife?
Or has the Buddha (Fó) entered extinction?"
The reply was,
"The Great Master (Dà Shī) has entered extinction."
"Where is my Upādhyāya (héshàng), Shèlìfú, now?"
The reply was,
"He entered Nirvāṇa (Nièpán) earlier."
Jiàofànpōtí asked,
"What are Mùlián (Mùlián), Ānán, and Luóhóu (Luóhóu) doing now?"
The reply was,
"Mùlián has already entered extinction.
Ānán still has lingering grief and bonds;
he is sorrowful, suffering, weeping, and unable to compose himself.
Luóhóu has already attained Arhatship and is free from sorrow and suffering."
Jiàofànpōtí said,
"My Upādhyāya and the Great Master have both entered extinction.
I cannot descend again now."
He immediately entered Nirvāṇa.
Ānán contemplated the various Dharmas, seeking to exhaust his remaining outflows.
While sitting in meditation and walking meditation, his concentration power was slightly insufficient, and he did not attain the Way right away.
In the deep night, exhausted, he wished to rest and lie down.
Before his head touched the pillow, he suddenly gained Enlightenment (dé wù).
He became a Great Power Arhat (dà lì luóhàn).
That night he reached the monastic hall (sēng táng) and knocked on the door,
calling out to Dà Kāshyè.
Dà Kāshyè said,
"Why have you come?"
He replied,
"I have exhausted my outflows this very night."
Kāshyè said,
"I will not open the door for you.
You must come through the keyhole."
Ānán immediately entered through the keyhole and repented,
"Dà Kāshyè, please do not criticize me again."
Kāshyè rubbed his head with his hand,
"I merely intended for you to attain the Way.
You should hold no resentment.
I am the same way."
Dà Kāshyè said to Ānán,
"From the Dhammacakkappavattana Sūtra (zhuǎn fǎ lún jīng)
until the Mahāparinirvāṇa (Dà Bān Nièpán),
gather them into the Four Āgamas (Sì Āhán):
Ekottara (Zēngyī), Madhyama (Zhōng), Dīrgha (Cháng), and Saṃyukta (Xiāngyìng).
This is called the Sūtra Dharma Treasury (Xiū Dù Luò Fǎ Zàng)."
The Arhats then asked,
"Who can clearly compile the Vinaya Dharma Treasury (Píní Fǎ Zàng)?" They all said,
"The Elder Yōupōlí (Yōupōlí).
Among the five hundred Arhats,
he is foremost in upholding the Vinaya (chí lǜ).
We now request him."
Yōupōlí accepted the instruction.
Sitting upon the Lion Throne (shīzǐ zuò), he asked,
"Where was the Buddha
