when he spoke the Vinaya and established the precepts?"
"It was when Sudatta Kālandaka (Xū Tídúo Jiālántuó), the Elder's son,
first violated the rule concerning lust,
initiating the establishment of the major offense."
The Arhats reflected,
"Who can clearly
learn and explain the Abhidharma Treasury (Āpítán Zàng)?"
They thought,
"The Elder Ānán, among the five hundred Arhats,
is foremost in understanding the meaning of the Sūtras (Xiū Duō Luó).
We now request him."
Ānán accepted the request.
"The Buddha was in the city of Shèpótí (Shèpótí Chéng)
when he spoke of the five fears, the five offenses, the five removals, and the five extinctions (wǔ bù wǔ zuì wǔ chú wǔ miè).
Because of these causes and conditions,
the body and mind in this life receive immeasurable joy.
Alternatively, they fall into the evil paths.
Teachings such as these are called the Abhidharma Treasury (Āpítán Zàng)."
After Kāshyè finished compiling the Dharma Treasury,
he entered Jīzú Shān (鷄足山, Cock's Foot Mountain).
He split the mountain into three sections.
Inside, he spread grass upon the ground.
He then reflected
and spoke to his own body,
"The Tathāgata (Rúlái) once used a rag robe (fènsǎo yī)
to cover you.
You must remain here until the time of the Dharma Treasury of MiLè (Mílè)."
He then spoke a Gāthā (gè) (verse), saying:
"By my divine power (shéntōng lì) I shall preserve this body,
covered by a rag robe, until MiLè appears in the world.
At that time, I will teach and transform the various disciples on behalf of MiLè."
He then established the three Samādhis (sān sānmèi).
As he entered Nirvāṇa, the three mountains covered his body,
like a child entering the mother's womb,
remaining intact and undestroyed.
Second: If King Āshéshì comes,
having previously made an agreement to meet,
the mountains should open upon his arrival.
If Āshéshì does not see me,
he will vomit hot blood and die.
Third: When Ānán comes, the mountains will open.
MiLè, along with ninety-six thousand myriads of disciples, will come here.
He will take Kāshyè's body and display it to his followers,
instructing them all to learn the merits of my adherence to the precepts (chí jiè gōng dé).
Mílè Fó (彌勒佛)
will also use the Dharma of the Three Vehicles (sān chéng fǎ)
to teach my disciples.
Dà Kāshyè
will assist Mílè in his persuasive transformation.
Moreover, Bhikṣu Jūntúpōtàn (Jūntúpōtàn),
Bhikṣu Bīntóulú (Bīntóulú),
Bhikṣu Luóyún (Luóyún)
and the Four Śrāvakas (sì dà shēngwén)
vowed not to enter Parinirvāṇa.
They must wait until the Buddhadharma has completely vanished;
only then will they enter Parinirvāṇa.
Dà Kāshyè resides in the mountains of Pítí Cūn (Pítí Village) within the kingdom of Mójié (Mójié Guó).
Mílè will go there with several thousand people.
The various ghosts and spirits
will open the stone door for them to see his meditation cave (chán kū).
At that time, Mílè Fó
will extend his right hand
to point out Kāshyè
and inform all the people,
"In the distant past, there was a disciple of Shìjiā Fó (釋迦佛)
named Kāshyè,
foremost in Dhūta (tóutuó) practices.
He is still present now."
Mílè Fó
will take Kāshyè's Saṃghāṭi (sēngqiélí) robe and put it on.
Kāshyè's body will suddenly disperse like scattered stars.
Mílè will take various flowers
and offer them to Kāshyè,
due to his feeling of reverence.
In the city of Rájaghé, there was a householder named Shùtí.
Guests who had returned from the sea voyage
presented him with a sandalwood bowl.
He placed it in a netted bag
and hung it high on a pole, saying,
"If any Shàmén or Bràmén
can obtain it without using a ladder or staff,
they may take it."
Phúlóunà and others all said,
"We want to see the spiritual power," and shook their heads and departed.
Bīndóulú,
whose clan name was Pǒluódò, went to Shùtí.
Shùtí said,
"Welcome, Pǒluódò.
I will give the bowl to anyone who can retrieve it without using a ladder or staff."
Bīndóulú entered samádhi
and extended his arm to take the bowl.
The householder filled it with rice and offered it to him.
After eating, Bīndóulú took it and left.
There was a Bhikṣu
who had few desires and was content.
He asked where Bīndóulú had obtained it.
Bīndóulú fully recounted the matter above.
The Bhikṣu of few desires reproached him, saying,
"You accepted an object from naked externalists.
How can you be called a Bhikṣu?
Before people who have not yet received the great precepts,
you manifested extraordinary sagely dharma."
Having rebuked him, he reported it to the Buddha.
The Buddha assembled the Sangha
and asked Bīndóulú,
"Did you truly perform this act?"
He replied,
"It is true."
The Buddha said to Pǒluódò,
"You are expelled for the rest of your life.
You should not be allowed to stay in Yánfútí."
Bīndóulú
followed the instruction and returned to his dwelling,
returned his bedding and couch to the Sangha,
took his robes and bowl,
disappeared from Yánfútí,
and appeared in Qúyení,
where he taught the four assemblies and widely promoted the affairs of the Buddha.
The Buddha was in the country of Jiāpíluówèi,
in the Nígūluódà Sēngjiālán.
The Shì clan members asked the Buddha,
"What past causes did Jiàochénrú and the others have,
that when
the Tathágata appeared in the world and the Dharma drum first sounded,
they were the first to hear it? The sweet dew initially descended, and they received its moisture
and praised him infinitely with one voice."
The Bhikṣus heard this
and reported the matter to the Buddha.
The Buddha said,
"It is not only today that I first saved these five people.
In the distant past, I also rescued these same ones.
I used my body as a boat
to save them from drowning and preserved their lives.
Now that I have attained Buddhahood, I first deliver and rescue them."
The Bhikṣus asked the Buddha,
"What was this matter?"
The Buddha said,
"In the past in Yánfútí,
the king of the country Bōluónài
was named Fànmódá.
At that time, there was a Sàbó
named Lènàshéyé.
While wandering in the outer woods, he saw a person
weeping and grieving bitterly.
He had tied a rope to a tree
and put his head into a loop,
trying to kill himself.
The Sàbó went forward and asked him,
'Why are you doing this?'
He persuaded him to put down the rope.
The man replied,
'I am poor and in debt.
The creditor exploits and strips me.
They press me day and night.
Although heaven and earth are vast, I have nowhere to hide my body.
Therefore, I want to escape this suffering.'
At that time, the Sàbó
immediately said to him,
'You just free yourself.
Whatever amount you owe, I will repay it all on your behalf.'
After he said this,
the person ceased the act.
He was joyful and leaped up,
and followed the Sàbó to the marketplace.
The Sàbó announced to everyone, saying,
'I wish to repay the debt.'
At that time, the creditors
gathered rapidly, like clouds; there was an endless stream of them coming.
He exhausted his wealth, but still could not settle the price.
His wife and children were impoverished and freezing, having to beg for a living.
At that time, a group of merchants
encouraged the Sàbó,
wishing to go to sea together.
He immediately replied,
'I am now poor and have nothing left.
How can I join you?'
The people replied,
'There are five hundred of us in total.
We will contribute money and divide the shares, and together prepare the ship equipment.'
The group raised three thousand ounces of gold.
The Sàbó used a thousand ounces of gold to prepare the ship,
a thousand ounces to prepare provisions,
and a thousand ounces to cover necessary expenses on the ship, with the rest given to his wife and children.
Then, by the seaside,
he built a large ship, and when the ship was ready, they set sail quickly.
While on their way,
they suddenly encountered a black wind,
which smashed the ship.
The people had nowhere to rely on.
Among them were five individuals
who together said to the Sàbó,
'We came here relying on you.
Now we are about to drown and die.
Danger is imminent.
We beg you to rescue and deliver us.'
The Sàbó replied,
'I have heard that the great sea does not keep corpses overnight.
Now you all seize hold of me.
I shall kill myself to save you from this peril.
I vow to seek to become a Buddha.
When I achieve Buddhahood later,
I shall use the supreme Dharma ship to ferry you across life and death.'
Having said this,
he slit his own throat with a knife.
After his life ended,
the sea spirit raised a wind and blew the five to the other shore.
They were able to cross the great sea and all obtained safety and peace.
If you wish to know who Lènàshéyé was at that time,
it is my current body.
The five people at that time
are Jūlín and the others."
The Buddha was in the Bamboo Grove in Luóyùejí.
Ānán also asked the Buddha,
"What past causes did Ārǔn Jiàochénrú and his party of five have,
that
when the Dharma drum first sounded, they alone were the first to hear it?"
The Buddha said,
"In a former life, they ate my flesh and thereby obtained safety and peace.
Therefore, today they are first to obtain the Dharma food and achieve liberation.
In a past Kalpa, in this Yánfútí,
there was a great king
named Shètóuluójiànníng.
He governed eighty-four thousand countries in Yánfútí.
A fiery star appeared.
The physiognomers reported to the King,
'There will be a drought.'
Heaven subsequently did not rain for twelve years.
The King was greatly sorrowful.
He calculated the current population.
Calculating the storehouses, every person could only get one shēng per day,
yet it was still insufficient, and many were dying.
The King thought to himself,
'What plan shall I devise to save the lives of the people?'
He immediately made a vow, saying,
'The people of this country are starving and weak without food.
I shall abandon this body and wish to become a great fish,
using my body's flesh to sustain and help everyone.'
He immediately climbed to the top of a tree and threw himself onto the ground.
He died instantly.
In a great river, he was reborn by transformation as a fish.
Its body was five hundred Yóuxún long.
At that time, there were five carpenters
who each carried an axe and went to the riverbank,
planning to cut down trees in the forest.
The fish said,
'If you need food,
come and take my flesh, eat your fill, and return.
When I achieve Buddhahood later, I shall save and liberate you with the Dharma food.
Tell the people of the country that those who need food should come.'
The five people were joyful and did exactly as he had said.
They told the people of the country, who reported it to others, spreading the news throughout Yánfútí, and all came and gathered.
They consumed its flesh until one flank was used up.
The fish immediately turned its body and they took the other flank.
When the flesh was consumed, it grew back again.
In this manner, repeatedly turning over,
he constantly used his body's flesh to sustain and help everyone.
This lasted for twelve years.
All those sentient beings who ate the flesh developed a heart of compassion
and were reborn in heaven upon death.
The King Shètóuluójiànníng at that time
is my current body.
The five woodcutters at that time
are Jiàochénrú and the others.
The people who later ate the flesh
are the eighty thousand Devas today,
and the disciples who obtained deliverance."
there was a Brahmin.
Named Uruvelā Kāśyapa (Píluó Jiāyè).
Leading five hundred Brahmins with coiled locks.
He was already considered a venerable person.
In the kingdoms of Anga (Āngjiā) and Magadha (Mójié), he was universally called an Arhat (Luóhàn).
The Buddha arrived at Kāśyapa's place and spoke.
"I wish to stay for one night."
He replied,
"I do not begrudge it,
but this chamber contains a poisonous dragon, and I fear it might harm you."
The Buddha said,
"No trouble."
Kāśyapa said,
"As you wish."
The Buddha immediately entered the stone chamber,
sat in the lotus position (jiājūzuò), straightened his body, and calmed his mind.
The dragon saw him and emitted smoke; the Buddha also emitted smoke.
The dragon again emitted fire; the Buddha also emitted fire.
At that time, smoke and fire both arose inside the stone chamber.
Kāśyapa saw from afar,
"How regrettable! Gautama (Qútán) has been harmed by the poisonous dragon."
The Buddha immediately subdued the dragon and placed it in his alms bowl.
The next morning, he took it and went to Kāśyapa's place.
He announced,
"The poisonous dragon is now inside the bowl."
Kāśyapa thought,
"Although Gautama (Qútán) has attained the Arhat (Luóhàn) stage and possesses great magical power,
he is still not as good as I am."
He said to the Buddha,
"You may stay; I shall provide food."
The Buddha said,
"If you can come yourself and arrive at the appointed time, I shall accept the invitation." Kāśyapa said,
"I shall come myself." The Buddha stayed and ate.
After eating, he returned to the stone chamber for the night.
That night, he entered the Fire-Light Samādhi (huǒguāng sānmèi), illuminating that stone chamber.
Kāśyapa immediately gathered his disciples and surrounded the chamber.
He reported to the Buddha,
"The time is now come.
You may return to eat.
Disciple (Shāmé)n, why was there such a great fire last night?"
The Buddha told Kāśyapa,
"Last night I entered the Fire-Light Samādhi (huǒguāng sānmèi).
Causing this stone chamber to be brilliantly illuminated."
Kāśyapa praised his great majesty and virtue,
yet still said, "He is not as good as I, who have attained Arhatship (Luóhàn)."
After the Buddha finished eating, he stayed overnight in another forest.
The next day, Kāśyapa again welcomed him back to eat.
The Buddha said,
"You all go ahead; I will follow shortly."
He first went to a Jambu (Yánfútí) tree,
took fruit from this tree, and sat in Kāśyapa's seat.
When Kāśyapa arrived later, he said,
"How is it that you have already arrived first?"
The Buddha said,
"This fruit is beautiful in color and fragrant and delicious. You should eat it."
Kāśyapa thought,
"This disciple (Shāmé)n possesses great spiritual power (shénzú),
but he is still not as good as I, who have attained Arhatship (Āluóhàn)."
After the Buddha finished eating, he returned to the original forest and sat.
He then displayed various kinds of magical power,
intending to subdue Kāśyapa.
The Four Heavenly Kings (Sì Tiānwáng Tiān), Śakra Devānām Indra (Shìtí Huányīn), and others,
all brought offerings to make tribute to the Buddha.
Kāśyapa, along with his five hundred disciples,
abandoned their fire-worship implements, clean robes, and water pitchers.
They tossed them into the Nirañjanā (Níliánchán) River.
And went to the place where the Buddha was.
The Buddha subsequently taught the Dharma (Fǎ) to the five hundred people.
Immediately, while still seated, they cleansed all defilements and attained the pure Dharma Eye (Fǎyǎnjìng).
They all said to the Buddha,
"We wish to renounce our homes."
The Buddha said,
"Welcome, Bhikṣus (Bǐqiū)!
Cultivate the Brahma-practice (fànxíng) diligently,
to attain the cessation of suffering."
And immediately conferred upon them the full ordination precepts.
Kāśyapa's middle brother was named Nadī (Nàtí).
He resided downstream on the Nirañjanā (Níliánchán) River.
He had three hundred disciples.
Kāśyapa's youngest brother was named Gayā (Jiāyé).
He resided on Elephant Head Mountain (Xiàngtóushān).
He had two hundred disciples.
When the two brothers saw that their elder brother had adopted the Way,
they both went and asked him,
"Following this Great Disciple (Dà Shāmé)n,
is practicing and learning the Brahma-practice (fànxíng) superior?"
He replied,
"It is exceedingly superior and wonderful."
Each, with his followers, went together to the World-Honored One (Shìzūn).
The Buddha taught the Dharma (Fǎ) to them.
While seated, they attained enlightenment and the pure Dharma Eye (Fǎyǎnjìng).
They said to the Buddha,
"We wish to cultivate the Brahma-practice (fànxíng) within the Buddha's Dharma (Fǎ)."
The Buddha said,
"Welcome, Bhikṣus (Bǐqiū)! Cultivate the Brahma-practice (fànxíng) diligently to attain the cessation of suffering."
In the kingdom of Śrāvastī (Shèwèi Guó) there was a householder.
Named Kurū (Jūliú).
He had no son.
He prayed to the spirits, seeking one.
A Deva (Tiān) spoke to him from the air, saying,
"Householder, your blessings are numerous, and there is no ordinary being capable of being born to you.
Therefore, you have no son.
A Deva King (Tiānwáng), whose life span is ending, should be born into your family."
Later, a son was born named Subhūti (Xūpútí).
He was handsome, articulate, compassionate, benevolent, and widely loving.
He informed his parents,
"I now wish to invite the Buddha."
His parents agreed.
He immediately invited the Buddha and provided extensive offerings.
He then requested his parents to allow him to become a disciple (Shāmé)n.
His parents permitted it.
He immediately followed the Tathāgata (Rúlái) back to Jetavana (Qíhuán) and became a disciple (Shāmé)n.
He immediately attained Avaivartika (Āwéiyán).
Complete in spiritual powers, he taught and transformed people according to local customs.
Among the disciples, he appeared as an Arhat (Luóhàn).
Ānanda (Ānán) said to the Buddha,
"What meritorious deeds did this Subhūti (Xūpútí) cultivate in the past?"
The Buddha said,
"Countless lifetimes ago, this person was the son of a poor family.
He met a Bhikṣu (Bǐqiū) who entered the city for alms, but obtained nothing anywhere.
At that time, the youth saw that the bowl was empty.
He paid homage and said,
'Please come home with me, and I shall make an offering to you.'
The Bhikṣu (Dàorén) followed him home, and the youth took his own portion of food and offered it to him.
He himself did not eat.
After the Bhikṣu (Dàorén) finished eating, he displayed flight and departed.
The youth rejoiced and immediately resolved to seek the Way (Dàoyì).
Because of this meritorious deed,
he was later born in the heavens for ninety-one kalpas (jié).
Now he has again come to be born in the householder's family.
The youth of that time is now Subhūti (Xūpútí).
The blessing of a single gift is already like this—
how much more so for many?"
Formerly, in the kingdom of Śrāvastī (Shèwèi Guó), there was a great householder.
Named Kurū (Jiūliú).
His wealth was immense, but he had no sons or heirs.
He prayed to all the spirits but could not obtain one.
A Deva (Tiān) in the air said,
"You are destined to receive a son of great merit (fúzǐ).
A Deva King (Tiānwáng), whose life span is about to end, should be born into the householder's family."
The householder was greatly delighted.
Seven days later, his principal wife felt that she had conceived.
When the month was full, she gave birth to a boy named Subhūti (Xūpútí).
He was foremost in appearance, clever, and eloquent.
Broadly loving and knowledgeable, he was respected by nobles and commoners alike.
Those who saw or heard him were influenced by his actions.
He in turn encouraged and benefited everyone with the joy of the Dharma (Fǎ).
His uncles and older male cousins all became jealous and resentful of him.
They said to his mother,
"This child is heedless.
He manages the household extravagantly and roams without restraint."
His mother said,
"This child's blessings and virtues are not ordinary."
Afterwards, when Subhūti (Xūpútí) asked for food, his mother ordered a maidservant to wash an empty vessel beforehand.
The maid replied that there was none.
Subhūti (Xūpútí) opened the vessel and looked.
Naturally, there appeared food (fàn) of a hundred delicious flavors, fragrant and tasty.
Everyone who shared the meal attained peace and comfort.
Only then did his uncles and older male cousins know that he was not ordinary.
They invited the Buddha and the great assembly of Bodhisattvas (Púsà) and prepared a meal.
After the meal was finished, the son requested his parents' permission to become a disciple (Shāmé)n.
The father immediately permitted it.
He followed the Buddha back to Jetavana (Qíhuán).
And immediately became a disciple (Shāmé)n.
He immediately attained Avaivartika (Āwéiyán).
Among the disciples, he appeared as an Arhat (Luóhàn).
Aniruddha (Ānàlǜ) had attained Arhatship (Luóhàn).
He had a beautiful face and appearance, resembling a woman.
He was walking alone in the grass.
At that time, a youth saw him.
Thinking he was a woman,
his wicked desires arose, and he intended to violate him.
When he realized it was a man,
he looked at his own form, and it had transformed into a woman.
Ashamed and distressed,
he abandoned himself in the deep mountains and dared not return home.
Several years passed.
His family, wife, and children did not know where he was.
They believed he had died.
Aniruddha (Ānàlǜ), traveling for alms, arrived at his home.
The man's wife wept and recounted that her husband had not returned.
She begged him to use his merit (fúlì) to help her husband survive.
Aniruddha (Ānàlǜ) remained silent, offering no reply.
Out of compassion and concern, he went into the mountains seeking to meet him.
This person then repented and blamed himself.
His body reverted to that of a man.
And thus, he was able to return home and be reunited with his family.
The Fó was at Qíshùyuán.
At that time, Ānālydà
went to the kingdom of Kūsàluóguó.
On the road, there was no dwelling place for Bhikṣus.
There was a young prostitute (yínnǚ) who housed guests.
Ānālydà immediately went and spoke to her.
“Elder Sister, I wish to stay for one night.”
The woman replied.
At that time, there was an elder (zhǎngzhě) and a layman (jūshì)
who had also sought lodging there.
Since the dwelling was cramped,
the woman invited Ānālydà to enter her inner chamber.
At that time, the Venerable One (zūnzhě) was in his sitting place,
sitting in the full lotus position (jiāfūzuò), fixing his mindfulness forward.
Then the woman of impure conduct lit the lamp and finished her duties.
Towards the end of the first watch of the night, she went to Ānālydà and spoke.
“Recently, there have been elders and men of the Brahmin (Póluómén) caste,
who possess much wealth and treasure,
all coming to speak to me, saying,
‘Will you be my wife?’
I immediately told them,
‘You are all ugly,
I cannot be your wife.’
I observe that the Venerable One’s appearance is upright and proper; you could be my husband.”
Ānālydà remained silent and did not reply.
The woman came again in the last watch of the night and repeated the same words.
He still remained silent.
Then this prostitute, having taken off her clothes, came intending to embrace him.
At that moment, Ānālydà, using his spiritual power (shénzúlì),
leapt into the air.
The prostitute saw this and felt shame and remorse (cánkuì).
She quickly put on her clothes, crossed her hands, and pressed her palms together (hézhǎng).
She looked up and confessed her errors (chànhuǐ), repeating this three times.
“I pray that the Venerable One returns to his original seat.”
Then Ānālydà descended to his original seat.
The woman paid homage to his feet and sat back down on one side.
Ānālydà preached various wonderful Dharmas (Miàofǎ) for her, condemning desire as impure and praising the abandonment of desire (líyù).
As the woman sat, all the dust and defilements vanished, and she attained the purity of the Dharma Eye (fǎyǎnjìng).
When the woman perceived the Dharma and had attained the Dharma,
she requested, “I only ask for permission to become an Upāsikā.”
She immediately accepted the Five Precepts (wǔjiè) and became a disciple of the Fó.
She looked up and prayed, “May the Venerable One accept my offering (gōngyǎng).”
He silently accepted it.
After she had set out and finished serving various sweet and excellent foods,
he preached the Dharma, causing her heart to rejoice.
Ānán addressed the Fó,
“What Ānālydà sees with his divine eye (tiānyǎn),
how is it different from what the Fó sees?”
The Fó said to Ānán,
“What the Rúlái sees
is not known by Arhats (Luóhàn) or Pratyekabuddhas (Pìzhīfó),
much less by you, a Bhikṣu still bound by birth and death (shēngsǐ).
How could you know how far the Rúlái penetrates with his vision? Starting from here and going east, through Kṣetras (chà) equal to the sands of the Gaṅgā (Héngshā).
‘Gaṅgā’ refers to the river, streams, pools, and extending to the great sea.
It is forty *lǐ* wide.
If you were to take a square measure of the sand inside, down to the bottom,
it would measure 120 *hú*.
Taking one grain of sand (shā) and placing it in each Kṣetra until all those sands are exhausted.
All the beings and things in the Fó-lands,
things in deep and secluded places, obscure objects,
and the minute forms of sentient beings (zhòngshēng)—all are completely seen.
The surrounding ten directions are also like this.
What Ānālydà sees,
how can it be spoken of or compared to the Fó?
Ānán addressed him, saying,
“What prior condition (sùyuán) did Ānālydà have that allowed him to see so clearly?”
The Fó said,
“Long ago, after the Nirvāṇa (Níhuán) of Vipaśyin Buddha (Wéiwèi Fó),
there was a robber (jiézéi) who, having committed a robbery, passed through a Fótú (Stupa area).
He wished to steal objects inside the sacred temple (shén sì).
At that time, the lamp wick before the Fó was about to go out, and it was dark, so he could see nothing.
The robber used an arrow to straighten the lamp wick,
causing the lamp light to brighten.
Seeing the shining majestic light, his eyes were dazzled, and his hair stood on end.
He thought to himself,
‘Other people still use precious objects to seek blessings (fú).
How can I steal things?’
He immediately abandoned the idea and left.
For ninety-one Kalpas (jié), all his evil karma gradually disappeared,
and his good fortune (fúyòu) increased daily.
The robber at that time was Ānālydà.
Because of the merit (fú) from straightening the lamp, he was always born in good realms.
He met the Fó, left home (chūjiā), attained the Dao (Dào), and became foremost in penetrating vision (chèshì dìyī).
How much more immeasurable is the merit of sacrificing what one holds dear with a sincere heart,
and lighting a lamp before the Fó!
The Fó was in Lùyěyuàn (Deer Park).
Ānālydà spoke to the Bhikṣus.
“I recall the past.
I was here in Bōluónài (Vārāṇasī), a poor person,
living by working as a laborer and carrying burdens.
At that time, grain was expensive, and many died from starvation.
It was hard to obtain food through begging.
There was a Pratyekabuddha (Pìzhīfó),
named Pīlìzhà,
who also lived relying on this area.
The Pìzhīfó rose early to beg for food.
I also rose early, intending to go out and carry burdens.
I saw the Pìzhīfó.
When I returned from carrying burdens, I saw him again.
I immediately thought this:
‘I saw this person when I rose early,
and now I see him coming out again; he must not have obtained food yet.’
He then followed behind me until he reached my home.
I immediately had this thought:
I wished to invite him.
I immediately divided my food and brought it to where he was.
Having arrived, I said, “Immortal (xiānrén),
this is my portion.
Out of compassion for me, please accept this food.”
The Pìzhīfó then received half (of the food) in his bowl.
“If you eat the other half yourself, it will be complete for both of us.”
I replied,
“Immortal,
I have a home and can obtain food when needed.
O Immortal, seeing my compassion, please accept this entire donation (shī).”
This Pìzhīfó, out of compassion,
accepted all of it.
Because of this donation, I was born in the heavens seven times,
and attained the status of Heavenly King (Tiānwáng).
I was born among humans seven times and was also a Human King (Rénwáng).
In this present life, I was born into the Śākya (Shì) clan with immeasurable wealth.
I abandoned this, left home to study the Dao, and attained realization.”
Ānàlǜ,
Dàjiāyè,
Mùlián, and
Bīntóulú discussed together, saying:
“Currently in Wángshèchéng,
there are those who do not believe in or delight in the Buddha, the Dharma, and the Saṅgha.
We should work together to make them believe and delight.”
Having made this discussion,
they observed everywhere, far and near.
They only saw the elder Bátí zhǎngzhě and his sister who did not believe in the Three Jewels.
The three previously mentioned Śrāvakas said:
“We can convert Bátí.”
At that time, the elder had seven layered gates constructed.
He had three groups of entertainers.
Whenever it was time to eat, all seven gates were closed.
One group of entertainers performed during one meal.
Ānàlǜ went before him to beg for food during his mealtime.
The elder asked,
“From where did you enter?”
He replied, “I entered through the gate.”
The elder immediately questioned the gatekeeper,
but the gates were closed as before,
and no one had been seen entering.
The elder then placed one slice of sesame cake into his bowl.
Having received it, he immediately departed.
During a subsequent mealtime,
Jiāyè came to beg again, and the situation was likewise.
He received one slice of fish placed in his bowl.
His sister asked,
“Do you mean that the Bhikṣus cannot obtain food and thus come begging?” He replied, “That is correct.”
The sister said:
“The Bhikṣu who came before is named Ānàlǜ,
a son of the Shìzhǒng clan.
He abandoned the pleasures of the five desires in the three-season palace
to leave home and study the Dao.
The Bhikṣu who came later is Bìpōluóyán,
the son of a great Mónà family.
He abandoned nine hundred and ninety fields, dwellings, and plowing oxen
to leave home and study the Dao.
It is out of pity for you that they come to beg for food.”
When the elder heard this, he felt reverence and submission internally.
Thereupon, Mùlián
flew through the air and taught the Dharma, demonstrating instruction, benefit, and joy.
Immediately, while still seated, the elder removed the dust, separated from the defilements, obtained the purity of the Dharma Eye, saw the Dharma, and attained the Fruit.
He immediately accepted the refuges and precepts.
The three previously mentioned Śrāvakas said to Bīntóulú:
“We
have now converted Bátí and caused him to believe in the Dharma.
It is now appropriate for you to go and convert his sister in turn.”
Then Bīntóulú, carrying his bowl in the early morning, went to her dwelling.
At that time, the elder’s sister was making cakes herself by hand.
Suddenly seeing him come to beg,
she said to him,
“I will not give you anything.”
She stared intently at his bowl, asking, “What do you intend to do with it?”
Bīntóulú then caused smoke to emerge from his body.
She spoke to him again,
“Even if your entire body emits smoke, I will not give you anything.”
Bīntóulú then caused his entire body to burst into flame.
She spoke to him again,
“Even if your entire body burns with fire, I will not give you anything.”
Bīntóulú then flew high into the sky.
She spoke to him again,
“Even if you fly high into the sky, I will not give you anything.”
Bīntóulú then hung upside down in the air.
She spoke to him again,
“Even if you hang upside down in the air, I will not give you anything.”
Bīntóulú formed this thought:
“The World-Honored One does not permit us to forcefully beg from people.”
He then left on his own.
Not far from Wángshèchéng, there was a large stone.
Bīntóulú sat upon it,
caused the entire stone to fly into Wángshèchéng.
When the people in the city saw it, they were all greatly terrified,
fearing the stone would fall to the ground, and everyone fled.
The stone stopped right above the elder’s sister and did not move away.
When she saw this, she became extremely terrified
and said respectfully,
“I beg you to spare my life, put the stone back where it was before,
and I will give you food.”
Bīntóulú then took the stone back and placed it in its original location, and stood before her.
The elder’s sister formed this thought:
“I cannot give him a large cake.
I must make a smaller one to give him.”
She then made a small round cake, but it immediately turned into a large one.
This happened three times, each time becoming larger than the last.
Finally, she thought:
“I wanted to make small ones, but they all turned out large.
Now I might as well just give him one cake.”
She immediately took one cake and handed it to him.
All the cakes stuck together and adhered to the cake container.
When she touched the container with her hand, her hand also stuck to it.
She then spoke to Bīntóulú, saying,
“If you need the cakes, I will give them all to you.
Take them all; I will not begrudge them.
Why must you cause me
to have my hand stuck?”
He replied,
“I do not need the cakes,
nor do I need the container,
nor do I need you.
We four people discussed together
how to save you and the other person.
I have already converted your brother;
I ought to convert you.
That is the reason.”
She asked,
“What do you want me to do now?”
He replied,
“Sister, carry this cake
and follow me to offer it to the Buddha and the twelve hundred and fifty Bhikṣus.
They will all be fully satiated, yet the cake will still not be exhausted.”
She carried it and went to inform the Buddha:
“My small cake,
when offered to the Buddha and the Saṅgha,
all are fully satiated,
yet it is still not exhausted.
Where should I now place this?”
The Buddha said:
“You may place it on ground where no grass grows,
or in water where there are no insects.”
That woman then placed it in water where there were no insects.
The water boiled, making a sound like hot iron dropped into a small body of water.
She became frightened
and returned to the Buddha’s presence.
The Buddha spoke the Dharma for her, and she attained the purity of the Dharma Eye.
She immediately accepted the refuges and precepts, differing in no way from a disciple.
The elders then reported this to the Buddha.
The Buddha immediately admonished the Bhikṣus:
“From now on, you are not permitted to demonstrate spiritual powers again.”
Shèlìfú, while practicing the Bodhisattva Path through sixty kalpas,
wished to cross the river of generosity. At that time, a man came to beg for his eye.
Shèlìfú said,
“An eye is useless; why do you request it?
If you need my body or property, I will give it to you.”
The man replied,
“I only want the eye.”
Shèlìfú removed one eye and gave it to him.
The beggar received the eye, spat on it, and trod upon it with his foot.
Shèlìfú said,
“It is difficult to convert people such as this.
It is better to regulate myself and quickly subdue transmigration (saṃsāra).”
Thereupon, he turned his aspiration toward the xiǎochéng.
In Nántiānzhú, there was a Póluómén.
Named Tíshě.
He was a great debate master.
His wife became pregnant.
She dreamt she saw a person clad in armor, holding a vajra in hand,
destroying all mountains and standing by the mountain edge.
Tíshě heard this and said:
“You will give birth to a son who will subdue all debate masters.
However, he will be inferior to one person, becoming his disciple.”
After the pregnancy,
the mother became extremely intelligent and highly skilled in debate.
Her younger brother, Jūxīluó, talked with his elder sister.
In every matter, he was defeated and stuck.
Knowing that the child she carried must possess great wisdom,
he left home to study, neglecting to trim his nails.
People at the time called him Chángzhǎo Fànzhì (The Long-Nail Brahman).
Seven days after the elder sister gave birth to the child,
his courtesy name was Yōupōtíshě. People, based on the mother's family name,
collectively gave him the appellation Shèlìfú.
When he was eight years old, he had recited the eighteen collections of scriptures.
He thoroughly understood all books.
At that time, in the kingdom of Mójiātuó, there were Dragon King brothers.
The first was named Jílì.
The second was named Ājiāluó.
They brought rain in due season, and the country had no years of famine.
The people were grateful for this.
They always gathered the entire population
during the middle month of spring,
going to the dragons' dwelling place to hold a grand assembly.
They performed music and discussed righteousness until the end of that morning.
From ancient times until the present, this assembly had never been discontinued.
Four high seats were set up:
one for the king,
two for the crown prince,
three for the high ministers,
and four for the debaters.
Shèlìfú, though only eight years old,
observed the demeanor and direction of the people present.
Finding none superior to himself,
he immediately ascended the debate seat and sat cross-legged.
The crowd was suspicious and perplexed.
Some called him foolish, young, and unwise.
Others believed his measure of wisdom surpassed others.
Although they praised his spiritual uniqueness,
they still felt a sense of pride and shame.
Because he was young, they did not speak to him directly.
They all sent their younger disciples to relay questions to him.
His replies flowed fluently, and his logic and reasoning were exceptionally brilliant.
The debate masters of the time exclaimed that this had never happened before.
The foolish and the wise, the young and the old, were all subdued.
The King was extremely delighted.
He immediately ordered the officials to grant him a fief of one village for his constant sustenance.
Everyone in the country, great and small, rejoiced.
At that time, an auspicious diviner, named Jūlǜtuó,
whose family name was Dàmùjiànlián.
He and Shèlìfú were close friends.
Shèlìfú was honored for his talent and brilliance.
Mùjiàn was generous and straightforward, leading to their mutual acquaintance.
Their talents and wisdom were comparable, and they always went and stayed together.
They made a covenant that would last their whole lives.
Later, both were weary of the world and left home to study the Way.
They became disciples of the Brahman Sānshéyé.
They asked their master:
“Have you attained the Way you sought?”
The master replied:
“Since I started seeking the Way, many years have passed.
I do not know if the fruit of the Way exists,
or if I am not the right person,
but I have not attained it.”
One day, their master fell ill.
Shèlìfú stood by his head.
Dàmùlián stood by his feet.
As he gasped and was about to die,
he suddenly showed pity and smiled faintly.
The two disciples asked the meaning of the smile.
The master answered:
“Worldly people are blind, afflicted by attachment and affection.
I see the King of Jīndì Country dying.
His queen threw herself into the pyre, seeking to be in the same place as him.
Yet these two people,
due to their differing actions and retributions, will be born in completely separate places.”
At that time, the two disciples wrote down the master's words
to verify their truth or falsity later.
Later, there was a merchant from Jīndì
who traveled far to the Mójiātuó Kingdom.
The two disciples used their notes to verify the facts.
It turned out exactly as their master had said.
They sighed dejectedly and exclaimed:
“Are we not the right people,
or did our master conceal the truth from us?”
The two swore to each other:
“If one of us first attains the Sweet Dew, we must share the flavor with the other.”
The Buddha converted Jiāyè and his thousand brothers.
He then traveled to Wángshěchéng.
At that time, a Bhikkhu named Āshuōshì, wearing his robes and holding his begging bowl, entered the city to seek alms.
Shèlìfú saw that his demeanor was exceptionally distinct and his faculties were calm and silent.
He asked:
“Who is your master?”
He replied:
“The Prince of the Śākya clan,
who, weary of the suffering of aging, sickness, and death, left home to study the Way and attained the highest Bodhi,
he is my master.”
Shèlìfú said:
“Please tell me the teaching method of your master.”
He replied:
“I am still young,
and the days of my learning are new and shallow.
How could I fully proclaim the ultimate truth
or the vast and great meaning of the Tathāgata?”
He (Shèlìfú) further said:
“Just briefly state the essential point.”
He replied:
“All phenomena arise from causes and conditions;
these phenomena are extinguished by causes and conditions.”
Shèlìfú immediately attained the first stage of the Way.
Returning, he told Mùlián, who also attained the first stage of the Way.
The two masters, each with two hundred and fifty disciples, went together to the Buddha's location.
The Buddha saw them from afar.
Pointing to Shèlìfú, he said:
“He is foremost in wisdom among my disciples.”
He then pointed to Mùlián and said:
“He is foremost in supernatural powers.”
“Now they are coming, together with their assembly of disciples.”
They reported to the Buddha:
“We wish to leave home and join the Buddha's Dharma.”
The Buddha said:
“Welcome, Bhikkhus.”
Instantly, their hair and beards fell off by themselves.
The Dharma robes appeared on their bodies.
Their robes and bowls were complete.
They received the full ordination.
More than half a month later,
hearing the Buddha preach the Dharma for Chángzhǎo Fànzhì,
he immediately attained the stage of Arhat.
The Buddha was staying in Shèwèichéng.
Shèlìfú requested the Buddha to establish disciplinary rules.
The various Bhikkhus said:
“How can he request the establishment of rules when no fault has yet occurred?”
The Buddha said:
“It is not only today that Shèlìfú, when no fault has occurred, requests the establishment of rules.
In the distant past,
when he was in a certain village,
and the people and laymen had not yet committed any transgressions,
he also once requested me to establish various penalties and punishments.
The country at that time was named Jiāshī.
The city was named Bōluónài.
The king was named Jìngchēng.
Jìngchēng governed and civilized the people through Dharma.
He practiced generosity, maintained precepts, and broadly loved (the people) through the Way.
The people achieved prosperity, happiness, wealth, and abundance.
Villages, hamlets, and houses were so close that cocks flying between them touched wings.
The whole country respected each other and constantly performed various arts for mutual enjoyment.
At that time, there was a high minister
named Táolì.
He possessed many strategies and plans.
He addressed the King, saying:
“Currently, within our borders, there is natural wealth and joy.
The people respect each other.
I ask that Your Majesty establish penalties and punishments,
lest extreme pleasure give rise to faults.”
The King said:
“The various ministers are intelligent and wise.
Many have factions, and they cannot be suddenly controlled.
If I suddenly reprimand them, it might cause resentment or trouble.”
The King wished to gently instruct them.
Thus, he spoke a verse, saying:
“Though power grants joy and anger, compassion must surely govern and regulate.
Transform the people with righteous decrees and laws, so that their hearts bear no resentment or malice.”
All the ministers rejoiced.
They also spoke a verse, saying:
“The Most Victorious, the Honored One among men, who tames and resides long in the world,
Governs the masses through the Way, with boundless shade of compassion.”
The Buddha said:
“Jìngchēng was precisely my current body.
The high minister was Shèlìfú.”
Shèlìfú.
When summer heat was intense,
he traveled in the Ānluó Yuán.
A temporary worker drew well water to irrigate the trees.
He did not have great faith in the Buddha,
but upon seeing Shèlìfú, he developed a small measure of faith.
He called to Shèlìfú, saying,
"Venerable one, come!
Take off your robes and sit under the tree.
I will pour water over you without delaying my irrigation work,
and we can benefit each other."
Shèlìfú took off his robes and accepted the washing.
His body enjoyed coolness and comfort, and he traveled wherever he wished.
That temporary worker died that very night.
He was immediately born in the Dāolì Heaven,
possessing great divine power,
second only to Shìtí Huányīn.
He then thought to himself,
"For what reason was I born here?"
He examined his previous life.
"My faith was weak and thin.
Because I was irrigating as a temporary worker,
drawing water to wash the body of Shèlìfú.
Had my faith been pure and profound,
knowing there must be reward, I would have set up bathing tools for offerings.
I realized that although my meritorious deed was small,
because I encountered a good field (of merit), I obtained a great reward."
He immediately went to the dwelling place of Shèlìfú.
He scattered flowers as an offering.
Shèlìfú, because of his pure heart of faith,
preached the essentials of the Dharma for him, and he attained the fruit of Su-tuóhuán.
In the past, in the country of Shèwèi Guó, blood suddenly rained down one day,
covering an area forty *lǐ* wide.
The king and his officials were all greatly shocked and alarmed.
They immediately summoned various practitioners of Taoist arts and those who understood prognostication to determine whether it was auspicious or ill-omened.
The diviners replied,
"The old records say,
'The disaster of raining blood
is correlated with the birth of a venomous creature, a 'Man-Python' (Rénmǎng), bringing calamity.'
It is advisable to investigate within the country to clearly distinguish the disaster."
The king asked,
"How can we distinguish it?"
The diviner answered,
"This Rénmǎng is difficult to identify specifically.
We should command everyone in the country
to bring all newborn infants here.
Use an empty jar and have all the infants spit into it.
If one child's spit immediately turns into flames,
you should know that this child is truly the Rénmǎng."
They debated, saying,
"This one cannot remain among humans."
They immediately moved and placed him in an isolated, hidden, and uninhabited place.
Any person in the country who was supposed to die could be sent to him.
The Rénmǎng killed people by spitting venom in this manner.
Seventy-two thousand people were killed by his poison over time.
Later, a *shīzi* (lion) appeared, emitting a roaring sound.
People and creatures within four thousand *lǐ* were terrified and subdued.
It roamed about violently, causing harm, and no one could control it.
Thereupon, the King immediately recruited people within the country who could repel the *shīzi*.
He offered them one thousand *jīn* of gold and a large district to govern.
No one stepped forward to answer the call.
The officials reported to the King,
"Only the Rénmǎng will be able to repel it."
An edict was sent to summon the Rénmǎng.
The Rénmǎng met the approaching *shīzi*.
He went and stood before it and blew his poisonous breath.
The *shīzi* immediately died, and the country attained peace and tranquility.
Later, when the Rénmǎng was old and fell ill, and his life was about to end,
the Buddha, pitying his heavy karma which would doom him to the evil paths with no prospect of release,
told Shèlìfú,
"Go and instruct him,
so that he may escape heavy calamity."
Shèlìfú suddenly appeared before him.
The Python was greatly enraged.
He thought,
"I am not dead yet,
yet someone treats me lightly and doesn't even introduce himself.
He comes directly before me."
He immediately released his poisonous breath, thinking he could harm him.
Shèlìfú,
with compassionate wisdom, repelled it.
His luminous countenance was serene and pleasant, and not a single hair moved.
He released poisonous breath three times, yet failed to harm him.
He instantly recognized the Venerable One's superiority.
His mind softened, and goodness arose.
He looked at Shèlìfú with compassion, gazing up and down seven times.
Shèlìfú then returned to the *jīngshè*.
The Rénmǎng drew his last breath and died that same day.
Immediately, the heavens and earth shook greatly.
Extreme goodness can cause shaking.
Extreme wickedness (heaven and earth)
can also cause shaking.
At that time, the King of Mójié
immediately went to the Buddha's place, prostrated himself upon the ground,
and asked the World-Honored One,
"What path will the Rénmǎng take after his death?"
The Buddha said, "He has now been born into the First Heaven."
The King heard the Buddha's words,
was astonished, and asked again,
The Buddha said,
"How can a person of great sin be born into heaven?"
The Buddha said,
"Because he saw Shèlìfú and looked at him with a compassionate heart, gazing up and down seven times.
Due to the merit of this action, he was born into the First Heaven.
When that merit is exhausted, he will be born into the Second Heaven.
After seven rebirths, he will attain Pìzhīfó and enter Bān Nièpán."
The King addressed the Buddha, saying,
"Will the karma for the seventy-two thousand people he killed not be repaid?"
The Buddha said,
"When he finally becomes a Pìzhīfó, his body will be like refined purple-gold.
At that time, he will be meditating beneath a roadside tree.
At that time, there will be a great army of over seventy thousand people.
They will encounter the Pìzhīfó and assume he is a golden statue.
They will immediately take him, chop him up, and divide the pieces among themselves.
When the pieces surely fall into their hands, they will look and see that it is flesh.
They will all gather the pieces back together and leave.
Because of this, he will enter Bān Níhuán.
The sins of this lifetime will be repaid with such a light retribution, and then they will be finished."
The Buddha informed the King,
"For those who encounter a worthy mentor,
sins piled up like mountains can be extinguished,
and they can also attain the Way."
The Fó was in Luóyuèchéng, in the Kālánntuó Bamboo Garden.
At that time, the Venerable Shèlìfú was on Jíshéjué Mountain.
He entered the Jīngāng sānmèi (Vajra Samādhi). At this time, there were two spirits (guǐ).
The first was named Jiāluó.
The second was named Yōupó Jiāluó.
They were sent by the heavenly king Píshāmén.
They were going to the residence of King Píliúlèchā.
They intended to discuss matters concerning humans and devas.
At this time, the two spirits,
were passing through the void (sky).
They saw Shèlìfú from afar, seated cross-legged, maintaining mindfulness before him, his mind still and settled in meditation (dìng).
The spirit Jiāluó spoke to the other spirit, saying,
"I am capable right now of punching this shāmén's head."
The spirit Yōupó Jiāluó addressed the first spirit, saying,
"You must not harbor this intention of hitting the shāmén's head."
"The reason for this is,
this shāmén possesses immense spiritual virtue and great power.
Among the disciples of the Shìzūn, he is foremost in cleverness and wisdom.
He has endured immeasurable suffering throughout the long night (of saṃsāra)."
At that time, that spirit repeated three times,
"I am capable of hitting this shāmén's head."
The spirit Yōupó Jiāluó replied,
"If you do not follow my words now,
then you stay here.
I shall leave you and depart."
The wicked spirit said,
"Are you afraid of the shāmén?"
Yōupó Jiāluó said,
"I am truly afraid of him. If you strike this shāmén with your hand,
the earth will split into two halves.
There will be violent winds and swift rains, and the earth will also shake.
All the devas will be terrified, and the Four Heavenly Kings will become aware of it.
We will not be safe in our places."
At that time, the wicked spirit said,
"I am still capable of insulting this shāmén."
When the good spirit heard this, he abandoned him and left.
Then that wicked spirit immediately struck Shèlìfú's head.
At that moment, heaven and earth greatly shook, and violent winds and swift rains immediately arrived from the four directions.
The earth split into two halves,
and the wicked spirit, whole body and all, fell into the Dìyù (hell).
Shèlìfú rose from his meditation.
He straightened his robes and went to the Bamboo Garden.
He arrived at the Shìzūn's place, bowed his head and face to the Fó's feet, and sat down on one side.
Then the Fó addressed Shèlìfú:
"Is your body free from illness now?"
Shèlìfú replied,
"My body is normally fine, but I suffer from a headache."
The Shìzūn said,
"There was the spirit Jiāluó who struck your head with his hand.
If that spirit
had struck Mount Xūmí with his hand,
the mountain would have split into two halves.
The reason for this is,
that spirit possessed great strength.
Now this spirit has received the retribution for his sin, so his entire body has entered Ābí Hell."
At that time, the Shìzūn addressed all the Bhīkṣus:
"How wondrous and extraordinary is the power of the Jīngāng sānmèi!
Even up to this point, by means of this samādhi, one cannot be harmed by anything.
Even if Mount Xūmí were to strike his head, it ultimately could not move a single hair.
The reason for this is,
Bhīkṣus, listen.
In this Bhadrakalpa, there was a Fó
named Jūlóusūn.
That Fó had two great Śrāvakas.
The first was named Děngshòu.
The second was named Dàzhì.
Děngshòu was foremost in spiritual powers.
Dàzhì was foremost in wisdom.
Just as today, my Shèlìfú is foremost in wisdom,
and Mùjiànlián is foremost in spiritual powers.
At that time, the two Bhīkṣus, Děngshòu and Dàzhì,
had both attained the Jīngāng sānmèi.
Once, Děngshòu was in a secluded, quiet place, entered into tranquil meditation.
At that time, cowherds, shepherds, and wood and grass gatherers
saw him and said to each other,
"This shāmén has now met with impermanence."
They immediately gathered grass and wood and piled it upon his body,
burned him with fire, and then left.
At that time, Děngshòu soon arose from his meditation.
He straightened his robes and entered the village to beg for food.
The wood gatherers saw the Bhīkṣu again.
They said to each other,
"This Bhīkṣu died yesterday.
We burned him with fire.
Today he is alive again.
Now we should give him the nickname 'Returned to Life.'"
If a Bhīkṣu attains the Jīngāng sānmèi,
entering water, fire, or being struck by swords and blades cannot harm him.
The majestic virtue of the Jīngāng sānmèi is like this."
"Now Shèlìfú has attained this samādhi.
He often dwells in two places: Kōngkōng Sānmèi and Jīngāng Sānmèi."
Shèlìfú and others received an invitation from the Six Classes of Bhīkṣuṇīs.
They prepared many delicious foods and drinks.
The lower-seated monks and the Śrāmaṇeras
were served sixty-day old rice, sesame dregs, and boiled mixed vegetables.
The Fó asked Luóhóuluó,
"Did the Sangha eat their fill?"
(Luóhóuluó) fully replied.
(The Fó) further asked, "Who was the most senior monk?"
(Luóhóuluó) replied again, "The Upādhyāya Shèlìfú."
The Fó said,
"Shèlìfú ate impure food."
Shèlìfú spat out what he had eaten.
He swore that for the rest of his life he would cease accepting outside invitations and would constantly go on alms rounds.
Afterwards, many great noblemen wished to offer meals to the Sangha.
They wished to have Shèlìfú present.
They requested an order from the Fó.
(Allowing) Shèlìfú to accept outside invitations again.
The Fó said, "Do not request this.
His nature is wicked and narrow-minded."
In his past life, there was a certain king.
(The king) was bitten by a poisonous snake.
A poison-curing master performed the Shèjiāluó incantation and summoned the poisonous snake to come.
He first built a pile of fire and spoke to the snake, saying,
"Would you rather enter the fire or suck the poison back?"
The snake reflected,
"I have already spat it out completely."
So it threw its body into the fire.
That poisonous snake was precisely Shèlìfú.
The Buddha told Ānán.
He who has attained the four bases of spiritual power (sì shén zú)
is able to remain alive for one *kalpa* (jié).
How long will the Tathāgata's (Rúlái) lifespan be now?
He asked this up to three times.
Ānán, having been confused by Māra (Mó), remained silent and did not reply.
He again told Ānán,
"You may arise, go to a quiet place, and contemplate."
He immediately arose and went into the forest.
At that time, Māra Pāxún came to where the Buddha was.
He addressed him, saying,
"Honored of the World (Shìzūn),
your teaching and conversion of beings in the world is complete.
The number of those who have attained liberation from birth and death is like the sands of the Ganges (Héngshā).
Your age is now advanced, and you may enter Nirvāṇa (Nièpán)."
The Buddha immediately told Māra,
"In three months hence, I shall enter complete Nirvāṇa (bō nièpán)."
Pāxún heard this pronouncement, rejoiced, and departed.
Ānán, while sleeping, dreamed he saw a great tree universally covering the sky.
All living things relied upon it without exception.
A sudden whirlwind arose and struck the tree,
and it vanished from the place where the Mighty One resided.
All sentient beings mourned grievingly.
Ānán awoke in terror, unable to calm himself.
Contemplating his dream,
he thought, "Is it possible that the Honored of the World intends to enter complete Nirvāṇa?"
He came to where the Buddha was and addressed the Buddha, saying,
"The things I just dreamed were like this.
Is it possible that the Honored of the World intends to enter complete Nirvāṇa?"
The Buddha told Ānán,
"It is as you say.
I shall enter complete Nirvāṇa three months from now.
I just asked you,
'If there is one who has attained the four bases of spiritual power,
he is able to remain alive for one *kalpa*.'
My four bases of spiritual power have been extremely well cultivated.
I asked this fully three times, yet you did not reply.
Māra came and urged me to attain Nirvāṇa.
I have already consented to him."
Ānán was heartbroken with grief and could not control himself.
His various disciples relayed the news amongst themselves.
Each harboring sorrow and reverence, they came to where the Buddha was.
"Who can live forever?"
"For your sake,
what ought to be done has been done.
What ought to be taught has been taught.
You should simply exert yourselves diligently in cultivation; why are you grieving?"
Shèlìfú heard that the Buddha would enter Nirvāṇa and felt profound admiration and emotion.
He could not bear to see the Honored of the World attain extinction (mièdù).
Now he desired to precede him and enter Nirvāṇa first.
"I only pray, Honored of the World, that you grant me permission."
He asked this up to three times.
The Honored of the World said,
"It is fitting to know that the time has come.
All worthy sages must achieve quiet extinction (jímiè)."
Shèlìfú immediately straightened his robes, made offerings with his three karmas (sān yè), walked backwards, and departed.
He took the *śrāmaṇera* (novice monk) Jūntíluó
and proceeded to Luóyuèqí (Rājagṛha), reaching his birthplace (Nāla).
He immediately instructed Jūntí,
"You go into the city and the villages,
and inform the king, the high officials, the old acquaintances, and all the *dānapati* (tányuè) to come and bid farewell together."
Jūntí proclaimed the message:
"The Upādhyāya (héshang) Shèlìfú is about to enter complete Nirvāṇa.
Those who wish to see him should go immediately."
King Āshéshì (Ajātaśatru) and the people of the four classes (sì bèi) all rushed there.
Shèlìfú variously and extensively taught these people, administering medicine according to their ailment.
Among the assembly, some attained the first fruition up to the third fruition.
Some others attained Arhatship (Āluóhàn) upon leaving home.
Furthermore, there were those who vowed to seek the Buddha Path (fó dào).
Having heard the teaching, they made obeisance and departed.
During the latter part of the night,
he straightened his body and mind, focused his intention forward, and entered the first *dhyāna* (chū chán).
Rising from the first *dhyāna*, he entered the second *dhyāna*.
In this sequence, he entered the trance of total extinction (mièjìn dìng).
Rising from the trance of extinction, he entered complete Nirvāṇa.
At that time, Tiān Dìshì (Sakra, Ruler of Devas) and many heavenly beings came to his place, praising and making offerings.
Dìshì further commanded Píshǒujiémó (Viśvakarman),
"Gather all the jewels, adorn a high chariot, and send it to level the ground."
He commanded the various *yakṣas* (Yèchā),
"Go to the seashore, fetch ox-head sandalwood (niútóu zhāntán), and pile it up into a large pyre (dà jù)."
They placed the body upon it, poured butter oil (sūyóu) over it, set it on fire, and performed the cremation (*jhāpenā*, shéwéi).
After the fire was extinguished,
Jūntí
collected the relics (shèlì), placed them in a bowl, took the three robes (sān yī), and carried them to the Buddha's location.
Ānán grieved mournfully, saying,
"The great general of the Dharma Wheel (Fǎlún dà jiàngjūn) has already attained Nirvāṇa; upon whom shall I now rely?"
The Buddha said,
"Although he has achieved extinction (mièdù), the five-part Dharma body (wǔ fēn fǎshēn) is not extinguished."
When Shèlìfú was in a past life,
he also could not bear to see me die, and so he died before me.
Ānán addressed the Buddha,
"We are unclear about the ancient past: how did the matter of him dying first come about?"
The Buddha told Ānán,
In the far distant past, during an inconceivable *kalpa* (jié),
there was a king in this Jambudvīpa (Yánfú tí).
His name was Zhāntuó Póluópí.
The King had twenty thousand court ladies and palace women.
His primary consort was named Xūmótán. There were ten thousand ministers.
The primary minister was named Mózhāntuó.
The King had five hundred princes.
The eldest prince
was named Shīluóbáhé.
The city where the King resided was named Bánhéqíbō.
The city measured four hundred *yojanas* (yóuxún) in length and breadth.
In total, it had one hundred and twenty gates surrounding it.
The King proclaimed the great gift of charity (dà tán shī), providing everything the multitude needed.
Moreover, he issued a decree to eighty-four thousand small kingdoms,
ordering them all to open their treasuries and give charity.
All the ministers obeyed the command.
They immediately erected a golden banner, beat a golden drum, broadly proclaimed the decree, and promulgated the King’s benevolent edict.
They ensured that everyone near and far, inside and outside, heard and knew it.
At that time, *śramaṇas* (shāmén) and *brāhmaṇas* (póluómén) within the kingdom,
the poor, the solitary elderly, and those in need,
the strong helping the weak, gathered like clouds and rain, and were given everything according to their desires.
The people of Jambudvīpa received the King's favor and grace.
There was a small kingdom.
Its king was named Pímósīnà.
He heard that King Yuèguāng's (Moonlight King) excellent reputation was grand and lofty.
He harbored jealousy in his heart and could not rest in his bed.
He immediately pondered to himself,
"If Yuèguāng is not eliminated, my name will not emerge.
I must devise a means."
He invited various *dào shì* (practitioners) and solicited people.
The *brāhmaṇas* said,
"What worry does the King have that he should tell us?"
The King said,
"That King Yuèguāng's fame and virtue are widely renowned, and everyone follows his example.
I alone am humble and ugly and lack this wonderful reputation.
I wish to eliminate him; what means should I use?"
The *brāhmaṇas* said,
"Yuèguāng's compassion and kindness benefit the poor and afflicted, like parents to the common people.
How can we possibly agree to this evil plot?
We would rather kill ourselves than do this."
They immediately dispersed, disregarding the offerings.
At that time, Pímósīnà grew even more anxious and distressed.
He immediately put out a wide appeal, announcing everywhere,
"Who can obtain Yuèguāng's head for me?
I will divide the kingdom and rule half, and give him my daughter as his wife."
At that time, there was a *brāhmaṇa* residing beside a mountain,
named Láodùchà.
He came in response to the King's appeal.
The King was extremely happy and spoke to him again, saying,
"If you are indeed able to accomplish this, I will not violate my oath of trust.
If you are able to depart, on what day will that be?"
The *brāhmaṇa* replied,
"Prepare the provisions and food required for my journey,
and seven days hence I shall set out."
At that time, the *brāhmaṇa* cast incantations to protect himself.
When the seven days were completed,
he came to take leave of the King.
The King provided what was necessary, and the *brāhmaṇa* continued on his way.
At that time, strange portents occurred beforehand in King Yuèguāng's kingdom.
The kings of the eighty-four thousand small kingdoms
all dreamed that the Great King's golden banner suddenly broke and the golden drum suddenly split.
The chief minister Dàyuè dreamed that a ghost snatched the King's golden crown.
Each harbored sorrow and worry, unable to calm themselves.
At that time, the city gate spirit knew that the *brāhmaṇa* intended to beg for the King's head, and blocked him, refusing entrance.
The *brāhmaṇa* circled the city several times but could not proceed.
A Śuddhavāsa (Shǒutuóhuì) heaven dweller knew that King Yuèguāng, by giving this head in charity (tán, *dāna*), would achieve fulfillment.
So, in a dream, he enlightened the King, saying,
"You vowed to give charity and not oppose the wishes of the multitude.
The beggar is at the gate, but has no means to proceed.
To desire to be a benefactor (shī zhǔ) while this happens is inappropriate."
The King awoke in astonishment.
He immediately commanded Dàyuè,
"You go to the gate and instruct them not to block anyone."
The minister Dàyuè went to the city gate.
At that time, the city gate spirit immediately manifested its form.
It told Dàyuè,
"There is a *brāhmaṇa* who came from another country.
He harbors malicious intent, wishing to beg for the King's head, which is why I did not allow him passage."
The minister replied,
"This is a great disaster!
However, the King has issued a command, which must not be violated.
What shall we do about this?
We should create five hundred jeweled heads, each made of the seven treasures (qī bǎo), and use them for exchange."
He immediately commanded that they be made.
At that time, the *brāhmaṇa* went directly to the front of the palace hall and called out loudly, saying,
"I am from a distant land, having heard of the King's meritorious virtue.
He gives all things in charity and does not go against people's wishes.
Therefore, I have traveled far, desiring to obtain something."
The King heard this, rejoiced, welcomed him, and performed obeisance.
He inquired, "Are you not extremely tired from your journey?"
"Whatever you wish will be granted."
The *brāhmaṇa* said,
"Although all external things can be given in charity, they are not what I require.
I traveled far specifically only to beg for the King's head.
If you do not disappoint or oppose me, you should grant it to me."
When the King heard these words, he rejoiced immeasurably.
The *brāhmaṇa* said,
"If you grant me your head, when will you give it to me?"
The King said,
"Seven days from now, I will give you my head."
At that time, the great minister held a head made of seven treasures and came.
He advanced and spoke to the Brāhmaṇa, saying:
"This king's head is merely an impure thing composed of bone, flesh, and blood. Why do you seek this?
Now I hold a head made of seven treasures for you to use in trade.
You may take it.
This trade is sufficient to secure wealth for your entire life."
The Brāhmaṇa said:
"I do not want this.
I wish to obtain the king's head to fulfill my intention."

At that time, the great minister Dà Yuè Chén attempted various means of persuasion, but when the Brāhmaṇa never relented, Dà Yuè Chén's heart, overcome by anger and grief, split into seven parts, and he died.
The king previously issued an edict, saying:
His subordinates, riding elephants capable of traveling eight thousand *lǐ*, traversed all the kingdoms announcing:
"Seven days from now, King Yuèguāng Dàwáng will offer his head as a gift to the Brāhmaṇa.
Those who wish to come should rush here immediately."
At that time, eighty-four thousand kings sped along the relay roads and arrived.
They all saw the great king and prostrated themselves before him.
"The people of Yánfútí rely on the king’s grace and beneficence.
Why, in one day, for the sake of one person, do you abandon the masses forever and cease to pity them?
We only beg you to show compassion and not bestow your head as a gift."
Ten thousand ministers all threw themselves onto the ground, prostrating themselves before the king, only begging for pity and compassion upon them.
"Do not bestow your head as a gift."
Twenty thousand royal ladies also threw themselves onto the ground, looking up and saying to the king:
"Do not forget or abandon us. Only extend your protection and shelter.
If you bestow your head, upon whom shall we rely?"
Five hundred crown princes cried before the king.
"We are mere children. Where shall we go?
We beg you to pity and cherish us, and not bestow your head as a gift.
Nurture and raise us so that we may achieve human propriety."
Thereupon, the great king addressed the ministers, the populace, the royal ladies, and the crown princes:
"Calculating since the time I first received a body,
I have traversed birth and death for a long time now.
If I were in the Three Lower Realms (Three Paths), my head would be cut off, I would die, and be reborn again.
Doing this countless times would yield no meritorious reward.
If I were born among humans, striving over wealth and beauty,
due to greed, hatred, and delusion, I would constantly destroy many bodies.
Never yet have I cast off this life for the sake of merit.
My current body, being impure in various ways, must eventually be discarded and cannot last long.
By discarding this foul head in exchange for great benefit, how could I not give it?
I offer this head as a gift to the Brāhmaṇa.
By means of this merit, I vow to seek the path of the Buddha and save you all from suffering.
Now my heart of giving is about to be perfectly fulfilled.
Be careful not to obstruct my aspiration for the unsurpassed path."
When all the kings, ministers, populace, royal ladies, and crown princes heard the king's words, they fell silent and spoke no more.
At that time, the great king spoke to the Brāhmaṇa:
"If you wish to take the head, now is exactly the time."
The Brāhmaṇa said:
"Currently, the king’s ministers, the populace, and the great assembly surround us.
I am alone, my strength and power are weak, and I cannot chop off the king's head here.
If you wish to give it to me, you must go to the rear garden."
At that time, the great king instructed the lesser kings, crown princes, ministers, and populace:
"If you truly love and revere me,
be careful not to harm this Brāhmaṇa."
After speaking these words,
he entered the rear garden together with the Brāhmaṇa.
At that time, the Brāhmaṇa spoke to the king again:
"Your body is strong, possessing the strength of a warrior.
If you experience the pain of the chopping, you might regret it.
Tie your hair tightly to a tree, and then I will be able to chop it."
The king used words to speak to the Brāhmaṇa:
"When you chop off my head, let it fall into my hand, and then you may take it away.
I am now giving this head as a gift to seek the unsurpassed, correct, and true path, vowing to save all sentient beings."
At that time, the Brāhmaṇa raised the knife, intending to chop.
The tree spirit saw this and was greatly distressed.
"How can one seek to kill such a person?"
Immediately, the tree spirit struck the Brāhmaṇa’s ear with its hand.
His head twisted backwards, and his arms and legs became contorted.
He dropped the knife to the ground and could not move.
At that time, the great king looked up and spoke to the tree spirit:
"Since my past lives, I have been beneath this tree.
I have previously bestowed nine hundred and ninety-nine heads as gifts.
By giving up this head, the total will reach one thousand.
After giving up this head, the Perfection of Giving (Dàna Bōluómì) will be complete.
Do not obstruct my aspiration for the unsurpassed path."
At that time, the tree spirit heard the king's words.
It allowed the Brāhmaṇa to return to his former normal state.
The Brāhmaṇa then rose from the ground.
He picked up the knife again and chopped off the king's head. The head fell into the king's hand.
At that time, heaven and earth shook six times, and the palaces of the various devas (heavenly beings) moved and were unsettled.
Each felt dread and wondered about the cause.
They soon saw that the Bodhisattva had sacrificed his head as a gift for the sake of all beings.
They all descended, moved by this extraordinary act, and wept tears of sorrow like rain.
They then praised him together, saying:
"King Yuèguāng Dàwáng has offered his head as a gift.
The Dàna Bōluómì is now fulfilled."
The sound spread everywhere.
When King Pímóxiàn Wáng heard these words,
his heart, overwhelmed by joy, excitement, and shock, split open, and he died.
At that time, the Brāhmaṇa carried the king's head away.
The various kings, ministers, populace, royal ladies, and crown princes,
having seen the king's head, threw themselves onto the ground.
They cried out in unison in great sorrow, fainted, and then revived.
At that time, the Brāhmaṇa found the king's head foul-smelling, so he immediately threw it on the ground, kicked it with his foot, and left.
Some people then spoke to the Brāhmaṇa:
"Your cruelty and malice are severe indeed!
Since it was not useful to you, why did you demand it?"
At that time, the Brāhmaṇa continued on his way.
People who saw him criticized him, and no one gave him food.
He became extremely worn out and tormented by hunger and exhaustion.
Along the way, someone asked him for news.
Learning that King Pímóxiàn Wáng had died again,
he lost what he had hoped for, and due to fatigue, illness, and death,
they all fell into Ābí Nílí (Avīci Hell).
The rest of the ministers and populace who died from sorrow while remembering the king's grace were all reborn in heaven.
"Thus, Ānán,"
"if you wish to know who the King Yuèguāng Wáng was at that time,
it is I, myself, now.
King Pímóxiàn Wáng is Bōxún now.
The great minister Dà Yuè Dàchén is Shèlìfú now.
At that time, he could not bear to see me die and died before me.
Even today, he cannot bear to see me enter Nièpán (Nirvāṇa).
And thus, he attains extinction (Nirvāṇa) first."
The Buddha was in the Jíshù Jǐgūdú Yuán (Jetavana Monastery) in Shèwèi Chéng (Śrāvastī).
At that time, the Bhagavān (World-Honored One) spoke the precepts on the fifteenth day.
The assembly of Bhikṣus and five hundred Bhikṣus vanished from Jíhuán (Jetavana) and went to Ānòudá Chí (Anavatapta Lake).
At that time, the Dragon King Ānòudá Lóngwáng came to the Bhagavān, bowed his head to the feet, and sat to one side.
He observed the Tathāgata’s appearance and the various Bhikṣus.
He immediately addressed the Buddha, saying:
"Observing this assembly, it is empty and lacks someone.
The Bhikṣu Shèlìfú is not in this seat now."
The Buddha spoke to Mùlián (Maudgalyāyana), saying:
"Hurry to Shèlìfú and convey my message to him."
Mùlián accepted the command.
He went to Shèwèi Chéng and said to Shèlìfú:
"The Buddha calls you to come. The Dragon King Ānòudá Lóngwáng wishes to meet you."
Shèlìfú untied his *jīzhǐ* and placed it before Mùlián.
He said to Mùlián:
"You possess spiritual powers. Lift this belt and tie it to a tree in Yánfútí (Jambudvīpa)."
Mùlián grabbed the belt but could not move it.
When he exerted all his strength to lift it, the ground shook greatly.
Shèlìfú then feared that Mùlián would become attached to Fúyúdài (Pūrvavideha).
He then wrapped it around Xūmí Shān (Mount Sumeru).
Mùlián then lifted and moved Xūmí Shān.
Shèlìfú then wrapped the belt around the Tathāgata's seat.
Mùlián ultimately could not move it, so he discarded the belt and returned to the Dragon King's location.
From afar, he saw that Shèlìfú had already arrived beforehand.
Shèlìfú was seated in the lotus posture, upright in body, correct in mind, fixing his thoughts ahead.
Mùlián went to the Bhagavān, bowed his head to the feet, and said:
"Did I not lose my spiritual powers?
Why?
I vanished first from Jíhuán, reappeared here, and arrived at this lake later.
Shèlìfú vanished later, reappeared, and arrived at the seat first.
The Bhagavān always says that I am foremost. Why did I arrive later?"
The Buddha said: "You have not regressed.
The Bhikṣu Shèlìfú possesses great wisdom."
Returning to Shèwèi Chéng, the assembly also generated doubt.
The Buddha addressed Mùlián:
"Many Bhikṣus have no respect for you, saying that Shèlìfú's spiritual powers surpass yours.
You should display your awesome power before this assembly."
He replied: "I accept the instruction."
Immediately, he rose from his seat and went to the summit of Xūmí Shān.
He stepped on the summit of Xūmí Shān with one foot.
He raised his other foot and placed it in the Brahma Heaven.
He kicked Xūmí Shān, causing the earth to shake six times.
At that time, he spoke this verse in a Brahmic voice:
"You should quickly seek skillful means within this assembly of the Buddha's Dharma,
You should eliminate the afflictions of birth and death, like an elephant eating bamboo leaves.
If, within this Buddha's Dharma, you practice all actions free of desire,
you will have eliminated all dust and defilement, extinguishing them at their source."
At that time, all the Bhikṣus praised this as an unprecedented occurrence.
When Dà Mùjiànlián spoke this verse,
sixty Bhikṣus achieved the exhaustion of defilements (*āśrava kṣaya*) and released their minds.
The people of Shèwèi Chéng organized a great assembly for charity.
They offered food to ninety-six types of renunciants.
They also invited King Bōsīní Wáng, the crown princes, officials, and heads of various villages.
The long-established elders and the Sàbó (caravan leaders), and others.
One day earlier, they gathered on the banks of the Āqí Hé (Ajiravatī River).
They wanted to arrive first, ahead of the senior Bhikṣu Mùlián.
The river water suddenly surged, and foam covered the banks.
The various heterodox practitioners competed to tie up rafts.
They intended to cross first and claim the foremost seat.
However, the water was violently swift, and the rafts overturned and drifted back.
Through the night, they suffered fatigue. Their rafts broke apart, and they were submerged, drowned, and cold.
They climbed back onto the riverbank and squatted facing the sun.
At that time, someone invited the Sangha from the Jíhuán Jīngshè (Jetavana Monastery).
The Buddha remained, waiting for the proper time.
A young Bhikṣu said:
"The Bhagavān is leaving late; I fear the heterodox practitioners might claim the senior seat."
The Buddha knew the time had arrived.
Accompanied by the great assembly, maintaining dignity and decorum, they all proceeded to the riverbank.
The heterodox practitioners said:
"We are unable to cross.
What plan will these Śramaṇas (Buddhist monks) make?"
Mùlián miraculously created a bridge of jewels, adorned with various decorations, flowers, incense, and musical instruments.
When the heterodox practitioners saw it, they each said:
"The Śramaṇas are late. We will cross first."
They stepped on the bridge, fell into the water, and their bodies and clothes became soaked. They submitted and drifted with the current.
The Buddha used his spiritual power so that none died.
The Buddha and the Bhikṣus advanced solemnly.
Following in order and with decorum, wherever they stepped, the jewel bridge immediately vanished.
Mùlián retracted his spiritual power.
The ground returned to its former state.
This allowed all the heterodox practitioners to advance.
The Buddha spoke a verse, saying:
"Those who have first reached this shore, having already crossed the sea of birth and death,
cannot be swept away by swift currents. Such are called those with right wisdom."
Mùlián first achieved the Way (attainment).
He wished to save his father and mother to repay the kindness of nursing and feeding.
He saw his deceased mother reborn among the hungry ghosts.
She could not find food or drink; skin and bone were connected.
Mùlián was mournful and sorrowful.
He immediately filled a bowl with rice and went to offer it to his mother.
When the mother received the bowl of rice, before the food reached her mouth, it transformed into fiery charcoal.
Mùlián rushed back and fully reported this matter.
The Buddha said:
“The roots of your mother's sin are deeply entrenched.
It is not something your strength alone can handle.
It requires the majestic, spiritual power of the assembly of monks (sēng) for her to achieve liberation.
On the fifteenth day of the seventh month,
for the ancestors of seven generations who are suffering calamity,
prepare rice, five kinds of fruit, vessels for drawing water, censers, oil lamps and candles, bedding, and all the sweetest delicacies of the world, and offer them to the assembly of monks (sēng).
