On that day, all the Sages, those with the Six Supernatural Powers (liù tōng), the Shēngwén (Hearers), Yuánjué (Pratyekabuddhas), and Púsà (Bodhisattvas), manifest as Bǐqiū (monks) within the great assembly.
All with one mind receive the bowl (bō) and the robe (héluó), possessing pure precepts.
For those who make offerings to these monks,
their ancestors of seven generations and five types of relatives,
will emerge from the Three Evil Paths (sāntú), achieve timely liberation, and have clothing and food naturally supplied.”
The Buddha commanded the assembly of monks:
“All of you, for the seven-generation ancestors of the donor’s household,
engage in meditation (chán dìng) and concentration before consuming the offerings.”
Mùlián traveled at night.
Bì Mó (The Evil Demon) transformed into a shadow and entered Mùlián’s belly.
Mùlián thought to himself:
“Why does my belly thunder as if I were hungry and carrying a burden?”
He entered concentration and perceived it.
He immediately said to it:
“Bì Mó, get out quickly!
Do not disturb the Tathāgata (Rúlái) or his disciples.”
The Demon immediately became frightened, and the transformed shadow emerged and stood before his body.
Mùlián had a full brother.
He was wealthy, possessing many treasures, and his storehouses were overflowing.
His attendants, male and female slaves were beyond counting.
Mùlián told his brother:
“I hear you are stingy and jealous, and do not like to practice generosity (huì shī).
The Buddha constantly clearly explains that people who practice huì shī gain immeasurable rewards.”
His brother heard his elder brother’s instruction and opened his storehouses to practice huì shī.
He newly established storehouses, intending to receive the reward there.
Before ten days had passed,
his wealth was exhausted, the old storehouses were all empty, and the new storehouses received no reward.
His heart was vexed and distressed, and he said to his brother:
“Previously you instructed me that generosity yields great rewards.
I dared not disobey your teaching and exhausted my storehouses practicing huì shī.
All the poor people, both present and past, were fully provided for.
My treasures are exhausted, yet the new storehouse has no reward.
Could it be that I was misled by my elder brother?”
Mùlián said:
“Stop! Stop! Do not state these words.
Do not let followers of other doctrines or men of heterodox views hear this rough speech.
If merit (fú dé) were to have a physical form,
it could not be contained even by the realm of empty space.
I shall now temporarily show you a small part of your reward.
If you wish to see it, follow me.”
Mùlián, using his spiritual power (shén zú lì),
took his brother by the hand and ascended to the Sixth Heaven.
There was a palace made of the seven treasures.
Bathing pools lay before and behind it, and fragrant breezes spread far and wide.
The storehouses were overflowing, beyond counting.
Jade maidens surrounded him, tens of millions in number.
They were purely female, with no men and no husbands.
The brother asked Mùlián:
“What palace is this, so majestic and grand?
I see no men, only women.”
Mùlián told his brother:
“You should go and ask yourself.”
He asked: “Whose palace is this?”
The heavenly maidens replied:
“In the country of Jiāpí Guó (Kapilavastu), within Yánfú Tí (Jambudvīpa),
there is a disciple of Shìjiāwén Fó (Śākyamuni Buddha) who possesses spiritual power,
named Mùlián.
He has a younger brother who is very rich, who enjoys practicing huì shī (generosity) and helping the poor and needy.
After his life ends, he is destined to be born here and become our husband.”
When the man heard this, joy arose, and a good mind was generated.
He returned to his elder brother, filled with great shame and remorse.
He confessed his faults with bowing and returned to the human world, where he practiced vast generosity without weariness.
Mùlián, having received the Buddha’s sacred intent,
there is a world in the West.
Its name is Guāngmíng Fān (Banner of Light).
The Buddha’s name is Guāngmíng Wáng (King of Light).
He is currently expounding the Dharma.
Mùlián arrived there to hear the Buddha’s teachings and words.
The Buddha’s body was four thousand *lǐ* long.
The bodies of the various Púsà were two thousand *lǐ* long.
The bowls (bō qì) from which the Púsà ate,
were one *lǐ* high.
Mùlián walked along the rim of the bowl.
At that time, the various Púsà said to the World-Honored One (Shìzūn):
“Indeed, O Great Sage,
where did this insect come from?
It is wearing the robes of a śramaṇa (shā mén),
and walks along the rim of the bowl.”
At that moment, that Buddha said:
“O noble sons, beware! Do not harbor contempt for this virtuous one.
Why is this so?
This young man is named Dà Mùlián (Mahāmaudgalyāyana).
He is the foremost in spiritual power (shén zú) among the Shēngwén disciples of Shìjiāwén Fó (Śākyamuni Buddha).”
Then Guāngmíng Wáng Fó (King of Light Buddha) informed Dà Mùlián:
“The Púsà and Shēngwén of my land,
seeing your small body, are all generating contempt.
You should manifest your spiritual power (shén zú lì) to uphold the majesty and virtue of Shìjiāwén.”
Mùlián bowed down, touching his head to the Buddha’s feet, circumambulated him seven times clockwise, and then withdrew to stand before the Buddha.
He addressed him, saying:
“I now wish to sit cross-legged (jiā fū). Will this ground accommodate me?”
The Buddha replied:
“Do as you wish.”
Then Dà Mùlián leaped into the air, hundreds of millions of *rèn* high (an ancient measure).
In that jeweled space, he immediately created a seat.
He sat down cross-legged (jiā fū).
From his seat hung multitudes of jeweled strings, hundreds of thousands of millions of *gāi* (a large number).
Each pearl emitted hundreds of thousands of rays of light.
In each ray of light, there was a lotus flower.
All the lotus flowers manifested the body of Shìjiāwén (Śākyamuni), sitting upon the lotus flower.
The words he spoke were exactly like Shìjiāwén.
The sound was pure and clean, proclaiming the scriptures without any difference.
After Mùlián had manifested his spiritual power (shén zú),
he again stood before the Buddha.
At that time, the Púsà sighed, saying it was something never before seen.
They addressed the Buddha, saying:
“For what reason did this Mùlián come to this world?”
The World-Honored One (Shìzūn) replied:
“He came to this land because he wanted to test how far the sound of Shìjiāwén Fó’s voice penetrates.”
Then Guāngmíng Wáng Fó informed Dà Mùlián:
“O worthy one, it is inappropriate to test the sound of the Tathāgata (Rúlái).
The sound of the Tathāgata is neither far nor near; its vast extent is immeasurable and beyond comparison.”
Then Dà Mùlián threw himself at the Buddha’s feet and repented of his fault, saying:
“Indeed, O World-Honored One (Shìzūn),
I was imprudent.
The Buddha’s voice is immeasurable, yet I rashly generated the thought to know its limit.”
Guāngmíng Wáng told Dà Mùlián:
“Although you came far to reach this Buddha land,
he again said to the Buddha:
The distance is extremely far, O God among Gods (tiān zhōng tiān).
My body is extremely weary, and I cannot return to my own land.”
The World-Honored One (Shìzūn) replied:
“How could you have reached this world using your own spiritual power?
It was fundamentally established by the majestic virtue of the World-Honored One Shìjiāwén Fó.
You should make obeisance and perform the ritual of bowing to Shìjiāwén Fó from afar.
Then you will naturally be able to reach your destination.
Even if you used your own spiritual power (shén zú) to return to your original country, you would not arrive in one *kalpa* (jié).”
Mùlián placed his right knee on the ground, faced the East towards Shìjiāwén Fó, clasped his hands, and took refuge.
In the time it takes to flex and extend an arm, he immediately arrived.
The Buddha informed Mùlián:
“There is a great country,
eight thousand *lǐ* away from here, situated on the borderlands.
They do not see the Three Jewels (sān zūn) and practice perverted views.
The king, officials, and citizens serve the Brahmins (Fànzhì).
There are five hundred men who have all attained the Five Supernatural Powers (wǔ tōng).
They can move mountains, stop running water, and transform by multiplying their bodies.
In that country, there is a great mountain blocking the people’s pathway, and the whole country suffers because of it.
The King spoke to the Fànzhì.
The Fànzhì immediately sat down surrounding the mountain.
Each concentrated his mind, using the power of their meditation (dào dìng lì); the mountain rose, preparing to move.
The Buddha commanded Mùlián:
“You go to that country, manifest spiritual transformation through the Way, and widely save the Fànzhì, the king, and the citizens.
Let them avoid the Three Evil Paths (sāntú) and dwell forever in the Hall of Merit (fú táng).”
Mùlián emitted light, eclipsing the sun and moon, and hung suspended in the empty sky.
When he stood directly above the mountain peak, the mountain became immovable.
The Fànzhì were astonished and exclaimed:
“This mountain has already risen! Who is suppressing it?
The sun lacks brightness—surely there is a reason for this.”
One among them who was perceptive observed his disciples, [thinking]:
“Who among the defiled ones is causing the mountain not to move?”
He raised his head to look and saw a śramaṇa (shā mén) directly above the mountain.
The Fànzhì all said:
“This must be the work of a disciple of Qú tán (Gótama).”
The Fànzhì shouted:
“The King ordered us to remove this calamity for the people.
Are you suppressing it?”
Mùlián replied:
“I am merely suspended in the void. Who is suppressing your mountain?”
The Fànzhì exhausted their power of the Way three times, wanting the mountain to move.
The mountain sank three times and eventually became flat ground.
The Fànzhì looked at each other and said:
“Truly, he who is enlightened and whose morality (dào dé) is profound must be our teacher.”
They all rose, donned their proper attire, bowed their heads respectfully, and addressed him:
“We beg to become your disciples.
Show us the utmost of your spiritual effectiveness.”
Mùlián said:
“It is good that you wish to leave the darkness and approach the light.
I have an honored Teacher.
His title is the Unsurpassed, the Right and True, the God among Gods (tiān zhōng zhī tiān).
He possesses All-Knowledge (yī qiè zhì).
You should all go to the Buddha’s place.”
The Fànzhì said:
“Can the transformative Way of the Buddha truly surpass that of our current teacher?”
Mùlián replied:
“The Buddha’s virtue is like Xūmí (Mount Sumeru).
We are merely like mustard seeds.
Follow me immediately.”
They immediately arrived before the Buddha and fully explained their situation.
Internally and externally purified,
they pleaded: “Only may the World-Honored One (Shìzūn)
wash away their subtle defilements and enable them to achieve true purity.”
The Fànzhì saw the Buddha.
Their hearts opened and their understanding was resolved, and they all became śramaṇas (shā mén).
Formerly, Mùlián went to the Xuě Shān (Snowy Mountain) range.
He converted various ghosts, spirits, and dragons,
including Yèchā, Āxūlún, and Jiàntuóluó.
At that time, there was a Jiàntuóluó spirit
who resided in a palace of seven treasures.
He surpassed the assembly, being handsome in form, highly intelligent, and uniquely outstanding,
but he had a human body and a dog's head.
Mùlián asked in surprise,
“Why is this so?”
He replied:
“I was a greatly wealthy elder during the time of Wéiwèi Fó (Vipaśyin Buddha).
I loved to feed Bhikṣus and Brahmins, and supplied the poor.
However, I was impatient, irritable, and mean in character.
My coarse words and curses came out directly, sparing neither old nor young.
If guests eating my food were slightly unsatisfactory, I would immediately say,
‘They are better off feeding dogs.’
Because of these words, I have a dog’s head and a human body.
Since I loved giving and making offerings, I received this blessed mansion.”
The Buddha commanded the elder Ānàpínzhǐ
to practice giving (Dāna).
He immediately rose, knelt, clasped his hands, and addressed the Buddha,
“I wish for the Buddha and the Saṅgha
to grace my dwelling tomorrow
so I may offer a simple meal.”
The Buddha silently accepted.
The Buddha told the Bhikṣus,
“Tomorrow morning, we will ascend to the heavens and descend at noon to attend the meal at Bīnzhǐ’s dwelling.”
The next morning, the Buddha and the Bhikṣus
ascended into the void in the time it takes to snap one's fingers.
At that time, there was an Arhat
named Hóngtán.
He straightened his robes in the void and addressed the Buddha,
“I have ascended to heaven many times, but never has it been as dark as it is now.”
The Buddha said,
“Two Dragon Kings are extremely angry and are spewing mist.
Therefore, it is dark.”
There was another Arhat named Shòubǐ.
He immediately addressed the Buddha,
“I wish to stop them.”
The Buddha said,
“Dragons possess great spiritual power.
If you go, they will certainly become vicious and spew water.
They might even kill people and living creatures.”
Mùlián addressed the Buddha,
“I wish to go and admonish them.” The Buddha said, “Excellent.”
Mùlián immediately went to where the Dragons were.
When the Dragons saw Mùlián, they immediately emitted smoke from their mouths, and shortly thereafter, fire.
It surrounded Mùlián once.
Mùlián, using his spiritual power, also transformed and emitted fire, surrounding the Dragons three times.
He then changed his body and entered the Dragons’ eyes.
He entered the left eye and exited the right, and entered the right and exited the left.
In this sequence, he entered and exited through their ears and noses, or flew into their mouths.
The Dragons assumed Mùlián was inside their bellies.
Mùlián then transformed his body again, surrounding the Dragons fourteen times, using his body to command the two Dragons.
The Dragons were greatly terrified; their tails fanned the sea water, shaking Xūmí Shān (Mount Sumeru).
The Buddha remotely instructed Mùlián,
“These Dragons are still capable of spewing water and submerging and killing all under heaven.
You must be cautious.”
Mùlián addressed the Buddha,
“I possess the spiritual powers of the Four Dhyānas, which I constantly rely on and practice.
I can take this Xūmí Shān and the two Dragons,
place them in my palm, and throw them to another realm.
I can also crush Xūmí Shān with my hand, reducing it to dust,
without any Devas or humans perceiving it.”
When the two Dragons heard this, they immediately surrendered.
Mùlián reverted to his form as a Śramaṇa.
The Dragons transformed into human form, bowed, paid homage, and repented to Mùlián, saying:
“We were foolish, deluded, and madly confused, failing to recognize the Noble Deity.
We offended you by spewing cloud and mist; we beg for mercy and forgiveness for our sins.”
The two Dragons confessed and then received the Five Precepts.
They paid homage to the Buddha’s feet, saluted, and departed.
At that time, Ānòudá and his family members
invited the Buddha for three months.
They invited him to enter the Great Imperturbable Lake (Wú Rè Dà Chí) to receive offerings.
They also asked for the Bodhisattvas who had attained spiritual fruition and the assembly of disciples, promising to host them for half a month.
The Dragon, delighted, raised clouds, caused thunder and lightning, and sent rain universally across the world.
Suddenly, he ascended back to his palace and summoned his five hundred eldest sons,
whose names included Shànyá and Shànshī.
He addressed the five hundred eldest sons:
“I have now invited the Perfectly Enlightened One (Píngděng Zhèngjué) and the assembly of Bodhisattvas and disciples.
They will all remain here for half a month.
You must be of one mind, extensively encourage each other, and increase your reverence for the World-Honored One (Shìzūn).
Diligently contemplate impermanence, and each of you must remain still and quiet.
Serve the Tathāgata (Rúlái) with humility, respect, and solemnity.
Discard all desire and the pleasures of dragon play.
Eliminate greed, anger, and malice.
Stay away from sight, sound, smell, taste, and subtle touch.
Why is this?
The World-Honored One is without desire, peaceful, gentle, and refined.
You must sincerely and carefully comply with the Buddha’s essential commandments.
For this half month, you must not enter the palace, and must eliminate lust, hatred, and ignorance.
Because the Tathāgata is proclaiming the Dharma, there will surely be Bodhisattvas with spiritual powers from other realms,
and Shì (Indra), Fàn (Brahmā), Chíshì (World-Holding), and pure heavenly sons (Tiānzǐ) from previous existences will universally come to the assembly.
You must diligently practice mindfulness and extensively give offerings, taking care not to slacken midway,
so that the assembled multitude may observe the transformations and rejoice.
In the Imperturbable Lake at the base of Xuě Shān,
he transformed an impeccable lapis lazuli seat,
seven hundred Yóuxún (Yojanas) in length and breadth.
Surrounding it were eight thousand four hundred trees made of various treasures and coral.
In the halls above, there were eighty-four thousand Lion Thrones (Shīzǐ Zuò), all extremely high and wide.
There were two thousand Dragon maids,
whose beauty and charm were immeasurable.
Their mouths emitted perfume, and they carried various flowers, powdered incense, and unguents.
They organized various entertainments to sing the Buddha's virtues and gladden the assembly.
In the void, banners and silks hung between them, and precious bells chimed in harmony, their sound surpassing all other sounds.
Ānòudá offered a hundred flavors of food with his family.
He remotely addressed the World-Honored One:
“The Buddha, along with eighty-four thousand Bodhisattvas who all possess great spiritual power,
and two thousand disciples who also have supreme spiritual powers,
have arrived at the Imperturbable King’s Palace.”
Mùlián, having received the Buddha’s divine command,
moved the Imperturbable Lake so that it appeared in the void, seven *zhàng* (rods) above the ground.
He transformed his body to look like the Jīnchì Niǎo Wáng (Garuḍa King), dwelling above the Dragon Palace.
He then informed the King,
“The Tathāgata has arrived.”
The Dragon multitude were frightened, their hair stood on end, and they scattered in all directions, hiding themselves.
The Dragon King comforted them, saying,
“Calm your minds and do not fear.
This is merely the wise Great Mùlián acting.”
With music and dance accompanying them, they advanced to welcome the Perfectly Enlightened One and his disciples to the Imperturbable Lake.
They established a vast area and the Lion Throne.
The Dragon, together with his multitude, personally served the prepared food.
The food was sweeter and richer than anything in the world,
extended with heavenly flavors for the offering.
After the meal was finished and the vessels washed,
the Buddha preached the Dharma for them.
All those assembled were filled with joy.
The Buddha was staying in Shěwèi Chéng (Śrāvastī City).
At that time, the Bhikṣus gathered in one place
and discussed this:
“Does the Shànfǎ Jiǎngtáng (Dharma Hall of Good Law) have pillars or beams?”
Mùlián said,
“It has pillars and beams.”
Another inexperienced Bhikṣu said,
“It does not have pillars.”
They immediately sent a Bhikṣu with spiritual powers to investigate.
He returned and said, “It has no pillars.”
The Bhikṣus said to Mùlián,
“You did not know,
so why did you say it had pillars?
This is false speech and untrue; you should be expelled and driven out.”
They immediately gathered the Saṅgha.
The Buddha, riding on spiritual power, came down from the void.
Though he knew, he intentionally asked,
“Bhikṣus,
what are you doing?”
They replied,
“Mùlián answered ‘pillars’ when there were none.
He spoke untruthfully and falsely, and we wish to carry out a Karmavācana (formal action).”
The Buddha asked the inexperienced Bhikṣu,
“How did you know there were no pillars?”
He replied, “World-Honored One,
I was once
sitting in meditation in the Shànfǎ Jiǎngtáng.”
The Buddha said to Mùlián,
“Why did you not investigate yourself?
You should be strictly truthful.”
However, Mùlián's heart was sincere and he had not violated the precept.
People asked Mùlián,
“Where does the water in this Duōfú Chí (lake) come from?”
Mùlián replied,
“This water comes from the Ānòudá Lake.”
The Bhikṣus said,
“The water of Ānòudá Lake is sweet and possesses eight merits.
This water is boiling hot and bitter and salty.
How can this be?
Mùlián,
you are making a vain assertion surpassing human bounds,
and speaking falsely; you should be destroyed, expelled, and driven out.”
They reported the matter to the Buddha.
The Buddha said to the Bhikṣus,
“Do not speak of Mùlián’s faults and transgressions.
Why?
The residence of the Ānòudá Dragon is extremely far from here.
This water originally had eight merits and was sweet.
It has passed through five hundred small Hells,
which is why it is salty and hot.”
“If you had asked Mùlián why the water was salty and hot,
Mùlián would have been able to answer according to the phenomena.”
Another time, there was a great drought with no rain.
Mùlián entered meditation and saw
that in seven days, the heavens would have heavy rain,
filling all the ditches and pits.
The cities, towns, and villages all heard this pronouncement and were greatly pleased.
The people of the country abandoned all their tasks, covering and concealing their goods.
Seven days passed.
The Bhikṣus said to Mùlián,
“You said that in seven days the heavens would have heavy rain, filling all the ditches and pits.
Now there is not even wind, much less rain!
You are making a vain assertion surpassing human bounds and speaking falsely; we wish to destroy, expel, and drive you out.”
The Buddha heard of this matter
and said to the Bhikṣus,
“Mùlián sees what is ahead but does not see what comes after.
The Tathāgata sees both what is ahead and what comes after.
On the seventh day, heavy rain did fall,
but Luóhóu Āxiūluó Wáng (Rāhu Asura King)
caught it with his hand and placed it in the great ocean.
Mùlián spoke according to his perception in meditation.
Therefore, he is without fault.”
There was only one young boy,
named Upāli (Yōubōlí),
who shaved the Buddha’s (Fó) head.
The child's parents stood before the Buddha (Fó), joined their palms, and addressed the Buddha (Fó), saying:
"He is very skilled at shaving, but his body is too bent."
The parents instructed their son to straighten up slightly.
Then [they said], "But do not be too straight, lest your outgoing breath become rough and loud."
Again they said,
"You are good at shaving, but your body is too straight."
The parents spoke to him:
"Do not be too straight."
The Buddha (Fó) said,
"He is good at shaving,
but his incoming breath is too rough."
His parents told him,
"Do not let your incoming breath be rough, causing the Buddha (Fó) discomfort."
Again [the Buddha] said,
"He is good at shaving,
but his outgoing breath is too rough."
His parents told him,
"Do not let your outgoing breath be rough, causing the Buddha (Fó) discomfort."
At that time, Upāli (Yōubōlí),
having completely suppressed his incoming and outgoing breath, entered the Fourth Dhyāna (dìsì chán).
The Buddha (Fó) told Ānán (Ānán),
"Upāli (Yōubōlí) has already entered the Fourth Dhyāna.
You take his razor."
Ānán (Ānán) obeyed the instruction.
Ānán (Ānán) used an old container to collect the hairs of the World-Honored One (Shìzūn).
The Buddha (Fó) said,
"It should not be contained in an old vessel."
At that time, there was a crown prince Gūbōlí (Qúbōlí).
His general was setting out on a military expedition and came to ask for the Buddha's (Fó) whiskers and hair.
The Buddha (Fó) gave them.
When the prince received them, he did not know where to place them.
The Buddha (Fó) said,
"Place them in a gold stupa (tǎ), silver stupa, jewel stupa, or stupa made of various treasures.
Wrap them in silk, colored cloth, linen (bō sì), canvas (dān lánhé yī), or cotton cloth (tóu luó yī).
Again he asked,
"How should they be carried?"
The Buddha (Fó) said,
"By elephant, horse, chariot, palanquin (niǎn), or sedan chair (yú).
Or carried upon the head or shoulders."
Then the crown prince carried the World-Honored One's (Shìzūn) hair and departed.
Wherever he went on his military expedition, he achieved victory.
When that crown prince returned to his country, he erected a stupa for the Buddha's (Fó) hair.
This was a stupa (tǎ) built while the World-Honored One (Shìzūn) was still alive.
Afterwards, when the monks (bǐqiū) traveled, they also used the aforementioned materials for containment and carrying.
The Buddha (Fó) said,
"They should not be worn upon the head.
Nor should the stupa (tǎ) be carried to places for excretion."
Out of reverence, the monks (bǐqiū) did not dare to sleep in the same place as the stupa (tǎ).
They placed it in a separate room.
The Buddha (Fó) said,
"Place it on a high stake or set it beside your head."
In the country of Avanti (Āpántí guó), there was a wealthy householder (zhǎngzhě).
He possessed great wealth, but was greedy, miserly, cruel, evil, and lacked compassion.
At that time, he had a maidservant.
She was kept running errands day and night and found no respite.
If she made even a small mistake, she was subjected to whips and beatings.
Her clothes did not cover her body, her food did not satisfy her hunger, she was old and exhausted, yet she sought death and could not obtain it.
At that moment, she happened to be holding a jar to go to the river to fetch water.
Reflecting on this suffering, she raised her voice and wept loudly.
Then Kātyāyana (Jiāzhānyán) arrived where she was.
He asked,
"Old woman, why?"
She replied,
"Venerable One,
I am old and constantly perform hard labor.
Furthermore, I am poor and destitute; my clothes and food are insufficient, and though I wish for death, I cannot obtain it."
Kātyāyana (Jiāzhānyán) said,
"If you are poor, why don't you sell your poverty?"
The woman said,
"How can poverty be sold? Who would buy poverty?"
Kātyāyana (Jiāzhānyán) said,
"Poverty can indeed be sold." He repeated this three times.
The woman said, "I will sell it."
Kātyāyana (Jiāzhānyán) said,
"If you truly wish to sell it, follow my instructions completely."
She replied,
"Yes, I consent."
He told her,
"First, you must bathe."
After she had finished bathing,
he told her,
"You must practice giving (bùshī)."
She addressed him, saying,
"Venerable One,
I am extremely poor and destitute; now my body does not possess even a hair's breadth of unbroken wealth.
Only this jar belongs to my master. What shall I use for giving?"
He immediately handed her his begging bowl (bō), saying,
"Take this bowl and fetch a little clean water."
As instructed, she fetched it and offered it to Kātyāyana (Jiāzhānyán).
Kātyāyana (Jiāzhānyán) accepted it and immediately offered blessings (zhùyuàn).
Next, he instructed her to receive the precepts of fasting (shòu zhāi).
Afterwards, he instructed her to contemplate the various merits and virtues of the Buddha (Fó).
Then he asked,
"Do you have a place to stay?"
She replied, "No."
"If it is time for grinding, I sleep under the grinding mill.
When pounding, cooking, or performing other tasks, I sleep there.
Sometimes when there is no work, I take shelter and sleep on the dung heap."
Kātyāyana (Jiāzhānyán) said,
"You must maintain a good heart and respectfully run your errands.
Do not generate resentment or hatred.
Watch for when your master and everyone else has gone to sleep.
Secretly open the door.
Inside the curve of the doorway, spread clean grass and sit.
Meditate on the Buddha (Fó) and do not generate evil thoughts."
At that time, the old woman honored and took refuge, and performed the instructions as commanded.
In the latter part of the night, she immediately passed away and was reborn in the Trāyastriṃśa Heaven (Dāolì Tiān).
Her master ordered someone to tie her feet with a straw rope and drag her body to the Cold Forest (Hánlín).
There had been a Heavenly Son (Tiānzǐ) who had five hundred heavenly beings (tiānrén) as his retinue.
When his merit was exhausted, he passed away.
This old woman immediately took his place.
According to the dharma of birth in heaven:
Those with sharp faculties know the cause of their coming.
Those born with dull faculties only know how to receive pleasure.
At that time, since this woman had been born in heaven,
with five hundred heavenly maidens,
she indulged in amusement and received pleasure, not knowing the cause of her birth.
At that time, Śāriputra (Shělìfú) was in the Trāyastriṃśa Heaven (Dāolì Tiān).
He knew the cause and condition for this Heavenly Son's (Tiānzǐ) birth in heaven.
He asked,
"Heavenly Son (Tiānzǐ),
by what merit were you born in heaven?"
She replied, "I do not know."
Then Śāriputra (Shělìfú) used his Dharma Eye (dàoyǎn) and observed her former body.
[He saw that] through Kātyāyana (Jiāzhānyán), she had attained birth in heaven.
Immediately, she led her five hundred heavenly beings (tiānzǐ) to the Cold Forest (Hánlín).
They scattered flowers, burned incense, and made offerings to the corpse, illuminating it with radiance.
The master saw this and was astonished at the cause.
He announced it, ordering people far and near to go to the forest and observe.
They saw all the heavenly beings (tiānzǐ) making offerings to this corpse.
He immediately asked the heavenly beings,
"This maidservant was ugly and filthy.
While she was alive, people still hated to look at her.
Why do you heavenly beings now bestow offerings upon her?"
At that time, the Heavenly Son (Tiānzǐ) recounted the full story.
The Buddha (Fó) was in Vaiśālī (Píshèlǐ).
At that time, the Mango Girl (Nàinǚ) prepared and mounted an ornate feather-jeweled chariot and proceeded to where the Tathāgata (Rúlái) was.
She personally approached him to inquire after his health, got out of her chariot, and went to the Buddha (Fó).
At that moment, Nánduó (Nánduó) was walking meditation (jīngxíng) not far from the Buddha (Fó).
The Mango Girl (Nàinǚ) then went up to Nánduó’s (Nánduó) walking place.
She used her hand to touch Nánduó's (Nánduó) foot.
She then spoke these words:
"Nánduó,
I am the Mango Girl (Nàinǚ)."
At that moment, Nánduó (Nánduó) immediately lost semen, and the semen soiled her hand.
The Mango Girl (Nàinǚ) immediately placed it on her head [in reverence].
She went to the World-Honored One (Shìzūn) and addressed him, saying,
"World-Honored One (Shìzūn), should a person like this be allowed to remain among the assembly?"
The Buddha (Fó) told the Mango Girl (Nàinǚ),
"A person like this should remain in the assembly.
The reason is this:
Nánduó (Nánduó) will shortly achieve the absence of defilements (wúlòu)."
The Mango Girl (Nàinǚ) remained silent, gave no reply, and departed.
When the Mango Girl (Nàinǚ) was not far away,
the Buddha (Fó) told Ānán (Ānán),
"Gather all the monks (bǐqiū) in the lecture hall."
After they had assembled,
the Buddha (Fó) addressed the monks (bǐqiū),
"I have fully observed among the monks (bǐqiū).
All must fully wear the *saṅghāṭi* (shèlè) to cover their inner form.
All you monks (bǐqiū) should practice this way."
The Buddha (Fó) told Nánduó (Nánduó),
"How is it, Nánduó (Nánduó)?
You behaved in such a manner."
Nánduó (Nánduó) felt internal shame.
He addressed him, saying,
"Excellent, World-Honored One (Shìzūn)!
I pray that you quickly speak the Dharma (fǎ) for me,
so that having heard the Dharma,
I may dwell in a quiet place, observe reality as it is, and find joy in myself."
The Buddha (Fó) told Nánduó (Nánduó),
"Observe this body.
Follow its actions.
From head to foot—hair, body hair, nails, and teeth—
various impurities fill the body.
Observe them as they truly are.
Is this clean, or is it unclean?
You must observe those defilements (lòu).
Where do they reside, and from where do they arise?"
At that time, Nánduó (Nánduó) received the teaching from the Buddha (Fó), bowed at his feet, and departed.
Observing the various impurities within this body, from head to foot,
in all places, he fully understood that they arose from combination and assembly.
"I must now depart from them."
Thus, he had no lustful intentions.
He then spoke a verse (jì), saying:
"Lust (Yín), I know you: your origin arises from thought.
If I do not think of you, then you will not exist."
At that time, Nánduó (Nánduó),
residing in a quiet place,
achieved Arhatship (Āluóhàn).
The Fó first attained the Way (Dào).
The light from his body and form mutually illuminated the great chiliocosm (dàqiān).
Humans, devas (tiānlóng), and Bodhisattvas (Púsà) from the ten directions
all listened to the preaching of the Dharma (shuōfǎ) and were profoundly joyful.
According to their original practices, they each attained the Way.
Only Nántuó, the Fó’s younger brother, did not follow and accept (it).
He rebelled against the Fó’s teachings (Fójiào) and wished to make his own way (dào).
He had thirty marks (of distinction).
He led a number of disciples.
He wore the *bō* (alms bowl) and the *zhēn yuè yī* (robe) and his countenance resembled the Fó.
There were Bhikṣus (bǐqiū) who had not yet attained the Eye of the Way.
When they saw Nántuó from afar, they performed a ritual bow (zuòlǐ) to him.
The Fó instructed Nántuó:
"From now on, you must not wear the *zhēn yuè yī* again; wear a black *jiāshā* (kasaya) instead.
Why is this?
You have violated my precepts (jiè) and accepted the bǐqiū’s bows.
You shall fall into *nílí* (hell)."
Bìlíngjiā Pócuō (Piligindavatsa) was in Wángshě Chéng (Rājagṛha).
As the time approached, he intended to go begging for food (qǐshí).
He arrived at the home of a herdsman to eat.
The woman of that household was weeping.
He immediately asked the woman:
"Why are you weeping?"
She replied:
"Ācārya (Shélí),
today is a festival day, and everyone has gathered for amusement.
I have no clothes, so I alone cannot go."
At that time, the Venerable One immediately manifested various clothes, pearls, jewels, necklaces (yīngluò), and ornaments decorated with gold and silver.
Having given them to her, he departed.
When the people saw her, they asked how she obtained them.
She fully recounted the circumstances (yīnyuán).
The news reached the King.
The King immediately summoned the cowherd woman and the bǐqiū to come.
He asked the Venerable One:
"Where did you get this fine gold? It is not of this world."
The bǐqiū immediately took his staff and struck the wall and tapped the bed; everything transformed into yellow gold.
He spoke thus:
"Śūdra (Shǒutuóluó), where did you get the gold? This is it."
The King said, "Ācārya (Shélí),
you possess great divine power (shénzú). You may both return now."
The Fó was in the state of Jiàosàluó Guó (Kauśala).
He held the summer retreat (ānjū) with many bǐqiū.
The lay householders (jūshì) in white robes saw the large assembly of Saṅgha (zhòng sēng).
They made dwellings and offered robes for them.
The following year, the Fó returned to Qíhuán (Jetavana) for the ānjū.
In that previous location, there were still two Elder Bhikṣus (zhǎnglǎo bǐqiū).
The householders thought in their hearts:
"The donations (bùshī) we make this year should be like last year,
so that the bǐqiū receive robes and our merit (fú) is not interrupted."
They brought many robes and objects and donated them to the two Elders.
(The two Elders) had this thought:
"These robes and objects are numerous.
If we divide them, we do not know what offense (zuì) we might incur, so we dare not divide them."
Bánántuó (Bhadra) traveled around various places, inspecting the quantity of donations everywhere.
The two Elders saw him from afar.
They rose from their seats, welcomed him, offered him a seat, and inquired after him.
Bánántuó asked:
"Did the assembly of Saṅgha receive any donations during the ānjū?"
They replied, "Yes, we did."
He asked, "Have you divided them yet?"
They replied, "Not yet divided."
"Why?"
The Elders replied:
"These robes and objects are numerous, but there are few of us.
If we divide them, we do not know what offense we might incur."
Bánántuó said:
"It is good that you have not divided them yet."
The two Elders spoke to Bánántuó:
"Can you divide them?"
He replied, "I can." Bánántuó said:
"In this case, a *jiémó* (karma/formal motion) must be performed; they cannot be simply divided."
Then the two Elders brought out all the robes and placed them before Bánántuó.
Bánántuó divided these robes into three piles.
He said to them:
"You two sit beside one pile.
I will sit myself between the two piles."
He said to them:
"You Elders, listen attentively to the words of the *jiémó*:
The one pile of robes for the two of you is called 'three.'
The two piles of robes for me alone are called 'three.'
Is this *jiémó* acceptable?"
They replied, "It is acceptable."
He gathered the robes, tied them up, and intended to carry them away.
The two Elders said:
"This pile of robes—we have not divided it yet.
How can you just leave?"
Bánántuó said:
"If I were to divide it for you,
the finest robe among them should be given to the one who knows the Dharma (zhī fǎ rén).
Then it should be divided."
They replied, "Give it." He immediately took out the most valuable robe and placed it to one side.
He divided the remaining robes into two portions and gave them to the two Elders.
Bánántuó immediately tied up the larger collection of robes and objects.
He loaded them onto his back and arrived at Qíhuán (Jetavana).
The bǐqiū were engaged in walking meditation (jīngxíng).
Seeing Bánántuó approaching from afar,
they said amongst themselves:
"Here comes the shameless and unblushing one (wú cán wú kuì),
who commits offenses suspected by sight, hearing, and doubt,
the person of great desire and insatiable greed."
After he gradually approached,
they asked:
"Bánántuó,
where did you get this great quantity of robes and objects?"
Bánántuó fully recounted the preceding events.
Among them were bǐqiū who had few desires, were content (zhīzú), and practiced ascetic disciplines (tóutuó).
Hearing these events, their hearts were offended and resentful, and they rebuked him in various ways.
"How can he be called a bǐqiū?
He intentionally took the possessions of the two Elders!"
They reported the matter to the Fó.
The Fó also rebuked him in various ways.
He said to the bǐqiū:
"This Bánántuó,
did not only steal the possessions of these two Elder Bǐqiū in this present life.
In a past life, by a bend in the river,
there were two otters living in the river.
They found a carp by the riverbank.
Since neither could divide it, the two otters guarded it.
A jackal (yěgān) came to drink water.
Seeing them, it asked:
'Uncles (ājiù), what are you doing?'
The otters replied:
'Nephew (wàishēng),
we have obtained this large fish but cannot divide it.
Can you divide it for us?'
It replied, 'I can.'
'This should be divided according to the scriptures; it cannot be simply divided like that.'
The jackal then divided the fish into three portions: the head as one portion, the tail as one portion,
and the fatty middle section as one portion.
It asked:
'Who likes to travel close to the bank?'
They replied:
'This one is.'
'Who likes to travel in deep water?'
They replied:
'This one is.'
Then the jackal said:
'Listen attentively to what I say.
The scriptures say:
The one who travels close to the bank is given the tail.
The one who travels in deep water is given the head.
The middle portion of the body is given to the one who knows the Dharma (zhī fǎ zhě).'
At that time, the jackal took the body of the large fish in its mouth and returned home.
His wife saw it and asked:
'Where did you get that?'
He replied:
'I obtained it from those who are ignorant and do not know how to resolve disputes (duàn shì).'
O bǐqiū,
these two otters
are precisely the two Elder Bǐqiū of today.
The jackal (yěgān) of that time
is Bánántuó today."
The Fó was in Shèwèi Guó.
At that time, the elder Jiālìu tuóyí attained the path of Āluóhàn.
He thought:
Previously, I was among the six groups of Bhikṣus,
and in Shèwèi Guó, I disgraced various families.
I thought I should return and help them achieve purity.
He immediately entered the country and converted 999 families.
If the husband attained the Way but the wife did not,
or if the wife attained the Way but the husband did not attain the Way,
they were not counted.
At that time, there was a Brahman family in Shèwèi Chéng.
They were destined to be converted through the Shēngwén.
Jiālìu tuóyí thought:
If I convert this family too,
it will complete 1,000 households in Shèwèi Chéng.
Early in the morning, holding his bowl, he entered the city to beg for food.
He reached the Brahman’s house, but the master was absent.
His wife had closed the door and was frying cakes.
Jiālìu tuóyí immediately entered meditative concentration. When he emerged, he snapped his fingers.
The wife immediately looked back and saw the door was still closed.
She thought:
Where did this Shāmén enter from?
He must have come because he is greedy for the cakes.
I will definitely not give them.
Even if his eyes fall out, I will not give them.
Using his spiritual power, both his eyes fell out.
She thought again:
Even if the eyes come out like bowls, I will not give them.
He immediately used his spiritual power to transform his eyes into bowls.
She thought again:
If he stands upside down in front of me, I will not give them.
He immediately used his spiritual power to stand upside down in front of her.
She thought again:
Even if he dies, I will not give them.
He again used his spiritual power to enter the concentration of cessation.
All mental activity ceased, and he was unaware of anything.
The Brahman woman pulled and tugged, but he did not move.
She was immediately greatly frightened.
She remembered that this Shāmén frequently visited the palace of King Bōsī nì.
He was the master of Mòlì Fūrén.
If it is heard that he died in my house,
we will be greatly ruined.
If he lives, I will give him one cake.
Jiālìu tuóyí then emerged from concentration.
The wife then looked at the cakes.
She cherished the ones fried previously and begrudged giving them.
She scraped the edge of the pan again, made another small cake, and fried it; it turned out even better.
She gave him the former ones.
As soon as she lifted one cake, the rest stuck together.
Jiālìu tuóyí said:
Sister, give me as many as your heart desires.
She managed to lift four cakes and intended to give them to him.
Jiālìu tuóyí refused them, saying:
I do not need these cakes. If you wish to donate,
you can give them to the Saṅgha in Jīhuán.
This woman had already planted good roots in former lives.
She immediately thought to herself:
This Bhikṣu Saṅgha truly is not greedy for cakes.
He only came to beg out of pity for me.
She immediately took the basket of cakes and went to Jīhuán.
She offered them to all the members of the Saṅgha.
After giving the cakes to the Saṅgha,
she sat down in front of Jiālìu tuóyí.
Then Jiālìu tuóyí,
observing her causes and conditions, preached the sublime Dharma for her, and immediately while sitting, she removed the dust and left the defilement, attaining the purification of the Dharma eye.
She took refuge in the Sānbǎo and became a Yōupóyí.
Then she returned home.
When her husband later returned home, she fully informed him.
"I have now attained the path of Sūtuóhuán.
You should go now."
The Brahman immediately went there.
Jiālìu tuóyí preached the sublime Dharma for him.
He attained the purification of the Dharma eye and became a Yōupósāi.
He constantly used all his wealth to make offerings to the Shélí.
Even when he died, he commanded his son to make offerings as if he were still alive.
His son obeyed the command and made offerings according to the Dharma.
Later, the son's wife was weaving at the loom.
She happened to see the chief thief, who was young and handsome.
The wife called out to him; she spoke to him and made him come so they could amuse themselves together.
At that time, Jiālìu tuóyí went to their house to eat.
He spoke to the Brahman’s wife about the faults of lust and condemned the sin of breaking precepts.
The wife immediately became suspicious and feared that he knew about the affair and might tell her husband.
She immediately devised a scheme, feigning illness and inviting him to stay.
Jiālìu tuóyí stayed and preached the Dharma for her.
She desperately detained him until sunset.
When Jiālìu tuóyí arose, he went to the midden.
The chief thief used a sharp knife to cut off his head and buried it in the dung.
When the day for reciting precepts arrived, the number of tokens was short by one.
They consulted one another again.
The Fó said:
Jiālìu tuóyí has already entered Nièpán.
When the night had passed and it was morning,
the Fó and the assembly of monks entered Shèwèi Chéng and arrived at the midden.
Due to the Fó's spiritual power, the corpse sprang up into the empty sky.
The Bhikṣus took it and placed it on a bed.
They carried it out of the city, cremated the body with fire, built a stūpa, and made offerings.
King Bōsī nì heard that Jiālìu tuóyí had died at a certain Brahman's house.
He immediately ruined seven generations (of that family) and ten neighboring families, confiscating all their property.
He arrested 500 thieves.
He cut off all their hands and feet and put them in the ditch at Jīhuán.
While begging for food, the Bhikṣus heard about these events.
They fully reported them to the Fó.
The Fó said:
The fault and crime all resulted from entering the village at the wrong time.
The Fó traveled to Bōluónài Guó.
He sat beneath a tree and smiled joyfully.
Five-colored light emanated.
Ānán knelt and asked.
The Fó said:
Formerly, in the time of Jiāshè Fó,
there was a Vihāra here.
There were 20,000 Shāmén in the Vihāra.
Jiāshè Fó constantly preached the upright Dharma.
Ānán immediately set up a rope bed, knelt, and urged him, saying:
"May you take this honored seat.
This ground is blessed, having hosted two Fó."
When the Fó finished seating himself,
he raised his finger and said:
"There is a great district called Wéilíng."
At that time, there was a potter's household.
The head was named Huānyù.
Out of filial love for his parents, he frequently went to the Fó's place to receive the Fó's purifying influence.
Although he was a potter, he never dug the ground.
Fearing harm to insects and creeping things,
he only took soil from collapsed river banks or that piled up by mice.
He mixed it to make vessels.
He traded these for grain.
Regardless of the amount, he never disputed the price with others.
He used this to support his aged parents.
His parents were old, weak, exhausted, and blind.
The compassionate filial piety of Huānyù was unmatched.
Jiāshè Fó rose early, tidied his robes, held his bowl, and entered the city, arriving at Huānyù's house.
He asked the parents:
"Where is the filial son?"
They replied:
"The Fó's disciple just stepped out briefly."
The family had good rice and bean soup.
The Fó received it in his bowl, sat down, ate the meal, and immediately left.
When the son returned, he saw that the soup and rice were diminished.
He asked:
"Who took this food?"
The parents said:
"The Tiānzhōngtiān came to look upon you."
"He took the soup and rice himself, finished eating, and immediately left." Huānyù was overwhelmed by mixed feelings of sadness and joy.
He said:
"The Fó is the Rúlái, the Wúsuǒzhù, the Zhìzhēn Děngzhèngjué, the leader of the Dharma, the teacher of gods and humans.
Devas and kings respectfully offer splendid food, always fearing they cannot reach the Shìzūn.
I live in this humble state, and my food is not plentiful.
He only took it himself out of pity for my lowliness!
Overwhelmed by sadness and joy, he prostrated himself on the ground.
Reflecting on the Fó’s grace, which was so vast and universal,
his joy made him forget hunger for fifteen days.
His parents shared his joy and forgot hunger for seven days.
More than a month later, the Fó again arrived at his house.
The son was again absent.
The Fó again took the soup and rice, finished eating, and immediately left.
The son soon returned home, and his parents recounted the event exactly as it happened.
Huānyù and his parents
were again joyful and forgot hunger for the same number of days as before.
At that time, the dragon rain did not stop day and night, and the Vihāra was damaged and leaking.
The Fó told the Shāmén:
"Huānyù has newly built a residence.
You should go, remove his tiles, and bring them back to protect the Vihāra."
The Shāmén went.
The son was again absent.
The parents said:
"Who is removing our roof?"
The Shāmén replied:
"The Fó's Vihāra is leaking.
We were sent to remove this roof to repair the Vihāra."
The parents said:
"Excellent!
Has the great virtue of our son brought about this request?"
Joyfully, they prostrated themselves and said:
"Please take more!
My blessing is immeasurable."
As soon as the Shāmén left,
the son returned and saw it, saying:
"Who removed the roof?"
The parents said:
"The Fó's Vihāra was leaking, and he sent Shāmén to take the tiles to repair it."
Where Huānyù stood, he prostrated himself to the ground toward the Fó.
"Your wisdom is immeasurable!
Emperors and nobles raise palaces of seven treasures and make contributions to supply needs,
yet the Fó does not reside in them.
Taking these coarse tiles is only to bless me!"
Happily, he did not eat and forgot hunger as before.
The Fó led five hundred Shāmén forward and entered the Royal Kingdom.
The King's name was Zhīwéi.
He personally went to meet the Fó.
The King descended from his chariot, discarding the five regal insignia.
He performed a ritual greeting, sat down, and finished listening to the sūtra, then said:
"May the Tiānzhōngtiān,
together with the Shāmén, condescend to accept a humble meal."
The Fó silently assented to this.
When all the food preparations were complete, he sent an envoy to respectfully welcome them.
The King personally poured water from the ewer, offered the meal, made offerings, completed the rites, and sat down in front of the Fó.
Fó informed the Wáng, saying:
The Wáng previously served the Three Jewels (Sānzūn); now you receive your past blessings (sùfú).
You have attained birth in the human realm, left the form of a woman to become a man, and obtained the highest position in the world.
The proper law for one who is a Wáng is to use the sacred teachings and commandments to control his mind.
Forgive yourself and nurture the people.
Slanderous speech is the fire that burns the nation.
The Wáng should be careful of it.
The Wáng bowed his head (jīshǒu) and received the teaching. The Wáng then detained Fó.
At that time, for three months, the offerings of the seven-jeweled couch (qībǎo chuángjī), curtains, mattresses (yīnrù), medicines for illness, and provisions exhausted the nation's treasures.
Fó did not yet consent to this.
The Wáng thought in his heart, saying:
Among those who make offerings, who surpasses me?
Fó knew that the Wáng’s heart held an intention of arrogance (gònggāo yì).
He immediately addressed the Wáng, saying:
There is one who surpasses the Wáng; his kindness (huì) is immeasurable.
The Wáng said:
I wish to hear his name.
Fó said:
In Wéilíng Xiàn, there is a son of ultimate filial piety (zhìxiào).
His name is Huānyù.
He serves Fó and the Three Jewels (Sānbǎo), and receives my bright Dharma (míngfǎ).
He forgives himself and views others equally, nurturing all sentient beings (qúnshēng).
Pure, chaste, and adhering to truth (shǒuzhēn), his hand does not hold treasures.
He sells cutlery and sharp implements (lìrèn mài qì) to support his parents.
He does not dispute the price, practicing forbearance (rěnrǔ) and compassion (cíhuì).
He takes the Right Path (zhèngdào) as his heart.
He takes the sacred canon (shèngdiǎn) as his joy.
He dares not marry a wife.
He fears being haughty toward his parents, thereby deeming himself unfilial.
Every time he goes to Fó's location, he earnestly listens to the Dharma.
He describes the suffering of his parents losing their sight, unable clearly to see Fó.
When speaking of this, tears stream down.
Fó takes his food, removes his roof tiles, and lifts his door, without complaint.
He is so joyful that he forgets his hunger for fifteen days.
His utmost benevolence (zhìrén) and ultimate filial piety (zhìxiào) are virtues difficult to fully enumerate.
I must travel widely to teach and transform the world, and I cannot accept the Wáng’s invitation.
The Wáng had a feeling of resentment (yùnxīn) toward him.
Fó said:
Discussing merit and comparing virtue—
His benevolence, purity, chastity, faith, and filial conduct (xiàoxíng) are hard to match.
In rising, resting, and moving about, he has never failed to be filial.
His benevolent virtue (réndé) and remembrance of his parents—these deeds are hard to equal.
You (Wáng) are not able to attain this.
The Wáng said, "Excellent indeed!"
Huānyù’s ultimate filial piety is praised by Fó.
The beauty of his virtuous reputation reaches such a point.
I ought to give contributions to assist his support (of his parents).
Jiāshè Fó finished preaching the Sūtra.
He traveled about, teaching and transforming.
The Wáng dispatched messengers.
They were heavily loaded with five hundred carts [of goods]:
polished rice (jīngmǐ), sesame oil (máyóu), clarified butter (tíhú), rock candy (shímì), various materials, and treasures.
With humble words, they conveyed respect.
When the messengers arrived, they said:
“O Heaven of Heavens! (Tiānzhōngtiān)”
“[The Wáng] deeply praises the ultimate filial piety and universal compassion (pǔcí) of the worthy one (xiánzhě).
The Great Wáng is delighted and happy, and has sent us to offer reverence.
May you accept this contribution,
to support your parents and simultaneously make offerings to Fó.”
Huānyù replied, saying:
“The Great Wáng’s compassion and kindness assist me.
When you return to the palace, fully convey this sentiment.”
In the same county, there was a son of a Brahmin (Fànzhìzǐ) named Huājié.
He and Huānyù were close and excellent friends (shànyǒu).
For accumulated kalpas (lěi jié), they had formed closeness, completing each other in the Dharma-teaching (dàohuà).
Over time, their relationship became thicker.
Together they bathed in deep water.
They remotely sighted a great tree.
Huānyù pointed and said:
“Jiāshè Rúlái (Tathāgata), the Sagely One (shèngrén), is here.”
“We must first seek an audience and bow down.”
Huājié said: “The Buddha-way (Fódào) is difficult to forget, but how dare I hope for it?”
Huānyù sorrowfully said:
“A Buddha-age (Fóshì) is difficult to encounter, like the Udumbara flower (Yōután Huā).
Perhaps after accumulated kalpas (lěi jié) does one appear.
How can we miss this time?”
He pulled his clothes and forcibly dragged him to Fó's location. Huānyù bowed his head (jīshǒu), but Huājié did not bow.
He clasped his hands (yīràng) and sat down.
Huānyù addressed Fó, saying:
“Huājié is my excellent friend,
but he is still deluded by error (xiémí) and has not yet awakened.
I pray that you eliminate his ignorance.”
Jiāshè Rúlái preached the Dharma according to his affliction.
His mind immediately opened and understood, and he respectfully believed in the Three Jewels (Sānbǎo).
The two men, joyful, bowed their heads and retreated together.
Huājié, following the path, said:
“The world is fortunate to have Fó; my home is a mire of defilement (huìsǒu).
Why don’t you become a Shāmén (monk)?”
Huānyù replied:
“My parents are advanced in age, nearing the end [of life].
Furthermore, they are both blind and rely on me for their survival, so I cannot leave home.”
Huājié said:
“Then I shall become a Shāmén.”
Huānyù immediately informed Fó about the matter, and Fó immediately conferred the precepts upon him.
After a hundred million years (yì suì),
he was born in the Fourth Tuṣita Heaven (Dōushuài Tiānshàng).
Descending from Heaven, he himself attained Buddhahood (chéng Fó).
Fó informed the various Bhikṣus:
“The Huājié of that time is my present body.
Huānyù is Ānán.”
“Ānán was my good friend (liángyǒu).
He forcibly dragged me to Fó’s location to hear the Sūtra, enabling me to attain Buddhahood.
Indeed, the metaphor of a worthy friend (xiányǒu) is the foundation of ten thousand blessings (wàn fú).
In the present world, one avoids the Wáng’s prison (láoyù).
Upon death, one blocks the doors of the three evil paths (sāntú).
Ascending to Heaven and attaining the Way (dédào) are all due to the assistance of a worthy friend.”
Fó informed Wénshū:
“Since I attained Buddhahood,
more than thirty years have passed.
In this assembly today,
who can receive and uphold the twelve divisions of the scriptures (shí’èr bù jīng) for me,
and supply everything needed by my side,
so that I do not lose my own benefits?”
The five hundred Luóhàn (Arhats) all said:
“I can.”
Fó said they were mistaken (bù liǎo).
Mùlián observed and perceived that Rúlái’s
mind was set on Ānán.
Mùlián repeatedly urged Ānán.
Ānán said:
“I am impure and weak, unfit to serve.
If Fó grants me three wishes,
I shall obey the Saṅgha’s command.
First, if Rúlái bestows old robes (gù yī),
allow me not to accept them.
Second, if I receive separate invitations from patrons (Tányuè),
allow me not to follow them.
Third, allow me to enter and exit without limitation of time.”
Wénshū said, “Excellent indeed!
He foresaw criticism and suspicion.”
“Ānán has served me
for more than twenty years,
possessing eight types of incomprehensible qualities (bùkě sīyì).
First: He does not accept separate meal invitations.
Second: He does not accept worn-out clothing.
Third: His arrival is never at an inappropriate time.
Fourth: Although he initially possessed afflictions (fánnǎo),
following me, he entered and exited the homes of various kings and powerful nobles.
Seeing women, he did not give rise to desires (yù xīn).
Fifth: When I preach the twelve divisions of the scriptures,
once it passes through his ear, he never needs to ask again.
It is like pouring from one bottle into another bottle.
Sixth: He knows the wisdom of others’ minds, like Fó entering meditative absorption (rùdìng).
Seventh: Although he has not attained Vows Wisdom (yuàn zhì), he is able to perfectly understand
those who presently attain the Four Fruits (sì guǒ) or those who will attain them later.
Eighth: All secret words, he is able to perfectly comprehend.
Therefore, I constantly call him ‘The Much-Hearing’ (Duōwén).
Ānán possesses these eight Dharmas (fǎ),
and is capable of receiving and upholding the twelve divisions of the scriptures.
First: The root of faith (xìngēn) is firm and solid.
Second: His mind advances bravely (yǒngjìn).
Third: His body is without suffering from illness.
Fourth: He is always diligently vigorous (jīngjìn).
Fifth: He fully possesses mindfulness (niàn xīn).
Sixth: His mind is without arrogance (jiāomàn).
Seventh: He accomplishes concentration (dìng yì).
Eighth: He fully possesses wisdom born from hearing.”
. Ānán
in a separate place dreamed seven things. Immediately startled, his hair stood on end
. "Last night I dreamed and generally saw seven things
: The first was that streams, rivers, and seas were all ablaze
. The second was that the sun was about to set, and Yánfú Tí was dark
. I saw my own body carrying Xūmí on its head
. The third was Bhikṣus rolling around in a cesspit
. I also saw a person stepping on the heads of the Bhikṣus and crossing out onto clean ground
. The fourth was seeing Bhikṣus whose Dharma robes were incomplete, only tying the *jiāshā* (kasaya)
. Holding torches in their hands, they enjoyed entering wicked paths
. In the midst of thorns, their robes were torn and ripped
. The fifth was seeing a very large, lush, and beautiful Zhāntán tree
. Pigs came out of filth and rubbed against the Zhāntán tree
. The sixth was seeing three classes of young elephants
, who bit, touched, grabbed, gnawed, struck, and rammed the great elephant
. They trampled the good grass and stirred up the clear water
. The great elephant worried about this, avoided them, and fled
, going to a place with great clear water and good grass
. The young elephants played and frolicked, completely unaware
. Therefore, the water and grass where they remained became exhausted
. Suffering intensely from hunger and thirst, they bit and chewed trees, and consequently, all starved to death
. The seventh was seeing a dead Lion King
, whose name was Qǐsà
. White hair grew on his head, like attached adornments
. Flying birds and all beasts dared not approach him
. From within the lion's own body, worms emerged and consumed his flesh
." Because of these dreams, he proceeded to the Buddha in the morning
. The Buddha said
: "The dream of fire burning in the water
means that in the future, Bhikṣus will violate the Buddha's teachings
. They will commit wrongful and illicit acts for the sake of obtaining offerings
, and moreover, they will raise disputes and quarrels
. The dream of the sun about to set and carrying Xūmí on your head
means that the World-Honored One will, after ninety days
, enter *Pānnihuán* (Parinirvāṇa)
. Afterward, the assembly of Bhikṣus, the various devas, nāgas, and humans
must request and receive the sūtra teachings from Ānán
. The dream of seeing Bhikṣus wearing Dharma robes that do not conform to the usual regulations
, only tying the *jiāshā* and rolling around in a cesspit
, and a person stepping on their heads and exiting onto clean ground
, means that after the Buddha's Nirvāṇa, the Dharma is heading toward exhaustion
. There will be Bhikṣus gathering in great assemblies to preach sūtras
, but they will not uphold and practice the profound Dharma of the Buddha
. They will associate closely with laypersons, seeking after wealth and sensual pleasure
. When the *Jūshì* (lay devotees) advise and reprimand them, they will not believe or follow
. The Bhikṣus will receive misfortune, but the *Jūshì* will obtain blessings
. The dream of seeing Bhikṣus wearing the *jiāshā* tied up
, holding torches in their hands, and enjoying entry into wicked paths
, and being in the midst of thorns, tearing their robes
, means that after the Buddha's Nirvāṇa, there will be Bhikṣus
who have no Dharma robes and wear secular clothing
. They will only have one *jiāshā*, tied around their shoulder
. Abandoning the precepts, they will enjoy secular life, raising children and wives
. If there are *fēnwèi* (alms/support) and supplies, they are joyful; if there are none, they are sorrowful and bitter
. The dream of the very large, lush, and beautiful Zhāntán tree
, and pigs coming out of filth and rubbing against the tree
, means that after the Buddha's Nirvāṇa, there will be Bhikṣus
. They will not inherit the Dharma practices, they will drink alcohol and be confused and disorderly, eating without proper timing or measure
. When enlightened scholars explain things to them with good intentions
, they will further engage in slander and abuse the Arhats
. The dream of the three classes of young elephants biting and ramming the great elephant
, trampling the good grass and stirring up the clear water
, and the great elephant worrying about it, avoiding them, and fleeing
, and going to a place between clear water and beautiful grass
, while the young elephants played and frolicked, completely unaware
, until the water and grass became exhausted, and they starved to death
, means that after the Buddha's Nirvāṇa, there will be elder Bhikṣus who understand the scriptures
. They will teach and admonish the young, showing them their faults and blessings
. But the young ones will refuse to follow and accept, and upon death, will fall into the hells
. The dream of seeing the dead Lion King
, whose name was Qǐsà
, white hair growing on his head like attached adornments
, flying insects, birds, and beasts daring not violate or consume him
, but worms emerging from within his own body and consuming his flesh
, means that while the Buddha was in the world, he extensively preached the sūtras and Dharma
. After the Buddha's Nirvāṇa, no external paths (non-Buddhist doctrines) will be able to destroy this Dharma
, but rather, it will be by disciples that my Dharma will be destroyed
." Ānán, traveling the road, became parched and thirsty halfway through
. There was a Caṇḍāla woman named Bōjí Tí, drawing water
. Ānán approached her to beg for water
. The woman replied to Ānán
: "I am of the Módèngqié clan
." Ānán said
: "I am not asking about that matter, just give me water
." The woman said
: "Your mother's lineage is perfected
. You are the foremost disciple of Śāmaná Qútán (Gautama the renunciant)
, respected by Pōsīní Wáng (King Prasenajit)
, and the Āshélí (Acarya/teacher) of Mòlì Fūrén (Queen Mallikā)
. I am low and base
, I dare not give you water
." Ānán said again
: "I am not asking about that
. Just give me the water
." The woman consented
. At that time, the woman first scooped water and poured it over Ānán's feet
. She then scooped water and poured it over Ānán's hands
. She immediately conceived lustful thoughts
. After Ānán drank, he left
. Bōjí Tí returned and told her parents
: "Mother, I wish to take the Śāmaná Ānán as my husband
." The mother said
: "He is the son of a Cakravartin King
, a Kṣatriya of the Śākya clan, a holy teacher, and the master of a noble family
. He is revered by devas and humans
. We are of a lowly clan; how can he become your husband
?" The woman said
: "If I cannot obtain him, I will surely drink poison and stab myself with a knife
, or hang myself to death
." The mother said
: "I possess the spiritual formula and spells transmitted by the Módèngqié gods
. They can move the sun and moon and make them fall to the ground
. They can also command Indras and Brahmā Devas to descend
. How much less, then, is obtaining a Śāmaná
? If Ānán comes here, whether dead or alive, he will not be able to abstain from lust
. However, if he is protected by Qútán
, I will be unable to obtain him
. Apart from this, all others are obtainable
." The woman then arose, bathed, and adorned her body
. She wore white clothing and laid out all the bedding
. She looked out longingly
. The mother smeared the ground with cow dung
. She tied threads of five colors
, filled four pitchers with water
, and filled four bowls with fragrant liquid
. She stuck four large knives upright into the cow dung
, placed four arrows at the four corners
, lit eight bright lamps
, and took four deceased human skulls
. She smeared the skulls with various kinds of incense
. She spread flowers on the ground
, held an iron and burned incense
. She circled three times, knelt facing the east
, and recited the Módèngqié spells and incantations
. At that time, Ānán was in the Qíhuán Forest
. His mind became confused, bound by the spell
, like a fish or elephant caught by a hook
. Following the magic spell, he arrived at the Caṇḍāla household
. The mother immediately told the daughter
: "Ānán has arrived
." At that moment, the woman went forward and embraced Ānán
, seating him on the bed
. She pulled and restrained his robes
, and kneaded and pressed Ānán
, just like a strong person holding a long-haired
small sheep in their hand
. Ānán saw the ten directions become completely dark
, like the sun and moon being oppressed by Rāhula
. Ānán possessed great strength
, equal to the strength of ten strong warriors
, yet he was unable to move
. Ānán used the power of the Noble Truth of the Way and, focusing his thought, regained consciousness
. "I am now in distress and suffering! Surely the World-Honored One, in his great compassion, will not fail to pity me
?" The Buddha immediately knew this
, and recited the Buddha's verses, saying
: The Buddha is the utmost honored truth in the world; there is none who can surpass the Buddha's presence
. The Buddha is the utmost honored truth among humans and devas; the King of all Dharmas, the supreme field
. The Dharma is the utmost honored truth in the world; there is none who can surpass the Dharma's presence
. The Dharma is the utmost honored truth among humans and devas; severing all bonds and knots, the field of eternal rest
. The Saṅgha is the utmost honored truth in the world; there is none who can surpass the presence of the Saṅgha
. The Saṅgha is the utmost honored truth among humans and devas; the foremost beautiful blessing, the supreme field
Ānán
He gained release from the Zhāntuóluó (Caṇḍāla) house.
As soon as the verses had been chanted,
inside the Zhāntuóluó’s house,
the ritual objects set up—knives and arrows—broke and shattered.
Jars and pots were destroyed.
The lamps went out, and the skulls burst apart.
A black wind arose, and they turned about, unable to see each other.
The Zhāntuóluó’s magic spells were rendered ineffective.
The mother then told her daughter:
"This must be the supernatural power of the Shāmén (Śramaṇa) Qútán (Gautama).
All the objects are shattered, and the magic spells are ineffective."
Ānán
"This is the gracious power of the Shìzūn (World-Honored One)."
Ānán gained release,
like a great King Elephant, sixty years old in his prime, intoxicated, violent, and fierce,
large in body and long in tusk,
gaining release from iron fetters.
It walks away from the city towards an open, unoccupied area.
Ānán was also like this.
Reciting the Buddha’s words of the Shìzūn,
he gained release from the Zhāntuóluó house
and returned toward Jíhuán (Jetavana).
At that time, this woman
pursued Ānán to the gates of Jíhuán.
She also spoke these words:
"Ānán is my husband! Ānán is my husband!"
She followed Ānán, not leaving him for an instant.
Ānán fully reported this to the Fó (Buddha).
The Fó said,
"Among all Dharmas, I have never seen an illusion or delusion like this.
The woman’s mind is bound by lust."
Ānán, early in the morning, donned his robes and took his bowl,
entering Shèwèi Chéng (Śrāvastī City) for alms.
This woman also followed behind him,
telling all the elders,
"Ānán is my husband! Ānán is my husband!"
Ānán returned to the Fó’s residence
and again stepped forward to report to the Fó.
The Fó said,
"Go and speak with her,
treating each other like sisters.
Why?
This woman ought to become a Bǐqiūní (Bhikkhunī)."
The woman reported to the Fó, saying,
"We only ask, Shìzūn,
that you return my husband to me."
The Fó said,
"If you desire Ānán,
then become a Bǐqiūní in my Dharma.
I shall then give him to you."
The woman was delighted. She returned to pay respects and say farewell.
Her parents were delighted that she had fundamentally planted good roots.
Each of them ought to attain the Way (Dào).
The parents and the daughter went together to visit the Fó.
The Shìzūn extensively preached the Dharma for them,
using countless skillful means to manifest the meaning of the various Dharmas.
He spoke of the meaning of gentleness (róuruǎn yì), the meaning of giving (dán yì), and the meaning of morality (shī yì).
He spoke of the meaning of lust as impurity (yín bùjìng yì),
the meaning of the root causes that generate and increase all afflictions (jié gēn yì),
the meaning of leaving home (chūjiā yì), and the meaning of the various stages of the Way (dào pǐn yì).
He also spoke of the Four Noble Truths (Sì Shèngdì).
At that time, this woman, right where she was seated, understood the Four Noble Truths.
Her parents attained the Way of the Ānàhán (Anāgāmi).
The daughter attained the Way of the Xūtuóhuán (Sotāpanna).
This was like pure white cloth, easy to dye.
Then the parents took refuge in the Fó, took refuge in the Dharma, and took refuge in the Sēng (Sangha).
They requested to become Yōupósāi (Upāsakas) before the Fó.
Ānán regretted her foolish transgression
and requested to become a Bǐqiūní.
She was permitted to practice the pure conduct (Fànxíng) under the guidance of the Shìzūn.
The Fó instructed Ānán:
"Take two Bǐqiūnīs and this woman
to Bōtuòbōtí Qútánmí’s (Prajāpatī Gautamī’s) residence,
and grant this woman the full ordination (jùzújiè) for the Way (Dào)."
Dà Àidào (Mahāprajāpatī) asked Ānán,
"How is this, Ānán?
Has the Shìzūn
permitted the Zhāntuóluó woman to attain the Way?"
Ānán replied to Qútánmí,
"Yes," and immediately shaved her head and administered the precepts.
She attained Āluóhàn (Arhatship).
When the Fó was in the state of Shèwèi Guó,
he suffered from a stroke (zhōngfēng).
He called Ānán,
telling him to go to a Póluómén’s (Brāhmaṇa’s) house and beg for cow’s milk.
Ānán immediately sought it as instructed.
The Póluómén said,
"The cow is over there. Go and milk it yourself."
Ānán immediately went to where the cow was.
The cow usually enjoyed butting and kicking people, making it impossible to approach.
Ānán thought to himself,
"According to the Dharma of the teacher I serve,
I cannot milk the cow myself."
Diāolì Tiānwáng Shì (Śakra, King of the Trāyastriṃśa Heaven) immediately descended.
He transformed into a Póluómén, dressed in the garments, and stood beside the cow.
Ānán requested him to milk the cow.
The Póluómén agreed, saying "Yes."
He immediately stroked the cow's udder with his right hand and said,
"The Fó is suffering a little from a stroke.
Give me your milk
so the Fó may drink it.
If the Fó recovers, the merit you gain will be incalculable."
The cow said,
"How enjoyable is it for this hand to stroke my udder?
Take two udders (of milk) from me,
and leave the other two udders
for my calf.
My calf has not eaten or drunk since morning."
The calf was standing beside its mother.
Hearing the voice speaking of the Fó, it immediately spoke, saying,
"Take my share completely and give it to the Fó.
The Fó is the great teacher of humans in heaven and on earth.
He is extremely difficult to encounter.
I will feed myself on grass and drink water.
When I was human, I was caused to follow evil friends (è zhīshi),
and I did not believe the Buddhist Sūtras (Fójīng).
This caused me to become an ox or a horse for sixteen kalpas (jié).
Only now have I been able to hear the Fó's voice.
Take the milk that I would drink
and give it all to the Fó.
Fill the vessel and go.
May this cause me, in future lives, to gain wisdom and attain the Way of the Fó (Fódào)."
Ānán took the milk and returned.
The Fó asked,
"What did the cow mother and calf say?"
Ānán answered according to the events.
The Fó said,
"The cow mother, in the time of future Mièlè Fó (Maitreya Buddha),
shall become a Shāmén and attain the Way of the Āluóhàn.
The calf, after death, will be reborn as a human,
and shall hang silks, scatter flowers, and burn incense for me.
After upholding the Sūtras and precepts (jīngjiè) for twenty kalpas,
he shall become an Āluóhàn."
The Fó delivered and saved all the people under heaven.
In Shèwèi Guó, there was a famine that year.
The various Bǐqiūs (Bhikkhus) all wanted to scatter
to observe the annual retreat (suìjié).
Ānán said,
"If the various Bǐqiūs go to other countries to observe the annual retreat,
then these countless people will lose their root of virtue (déběn).
If the Rúlái (Tathāgata) stays here,
Shèwèi will have much peace and security."
Bōsīnì (King Prasenajit) heard this
and invited the Fó and the Sēng (Sangha) for a three-month offering.
The Fó said,
"In a past age,
the King of Bōluónài Guó (Vārāṇasī),
named Fàndá, possessed great majesty and virtue,
and his reputation spread far and wide.
At that time, the country suffered famine, and there were many beggars.
The King gladly gave offerings,
and they gathered like clouds from the four directions.
Heaven had long failed to give rain.
Grain and rice became increasingly expensive, and the people were famished and distressed.
The number of beggars increased daily, and the granaries were exhausted.
The ministers requested the King to stop [the giving].
The King said,
"If so, it would violate my original intention.
How can I bear to oppose them?"
At that time, the officials skilled in Dharma announced throughout the four directions,
"Anyone who dares to beg must leave the city."
The beggars were distressed. The King asked.
The ministers replied,
"There is one who has come from afar."
A Fànzhì (Brāhmaṇa) then entered.
The King asked,
"Who sent you here?" The Fànzhì replied,
"My belly sent me here."
At that time, the King, out of compassion, replied with a verse (jì):
"I grant a thousand red calves and all their offspring."
That Fànzhì was Ānán.
Ānán and two Bhikṣus.
arrived at the kingdom of Āyù Wáng.
In a mountain ravine.
above the pine tree of the Bhikṣu.
Fragrant flowers spontaneously appeared.
Bells chimed as if speaking.
The Bhikṣu of Shānxiàng.
did not know why.
He went out and bowed in the four directions.
He then returned to the refectory and recited scriptures.
Ānán and the two Bhikṣus.
transformed themselves into beggars.
They then led three hundred other beggars to beg for food.
The Bhikṣu of Shānxiàng prepared the food, and when finished.
they asked for robes, and he immediately provided them.
The three hundred beggars refused to leave.
So he provided offerings morning and evening, until all the beggars fell ill.
The Bhikṣu of Shānxiàng then burned incense morning and evening, praying for blessings and compounding medicine.
All three hundred beggars died.
The Bhikṣu of Shānxiàng then went begging for help, bathed the bodies, and placed them in coffins for funeral rites.
Āyù Guówáng commanded his men to bury them.
A few days later.
Ānán.
again transformed himself and the two Bhikṣus into three scholars (shūshēng).
Their clothing was clean.
They went to the pine tree area.
The Bhikṣu of Shānxiàng descended from the lecture hall to welcome them.
He arranged seats and invited them to sit.
The three scholars said to the Bhikṣu of Shānxiàng.
What do you seek by serving the Buddha?
The Bhikṣu of Shānxiàng replied.
The Way of the Buddha (Fódào) is the Divine Way.
Between Heaven and Earth, only the Fódào is divine.
I serve the Buddha.
wishing that the Fódào may save both human and non-human beings.
I have no other demands.
The three scholars said.
The Fódào is not divine.
It is merely empty and void.
Few people serve it.
Why are you so foolish.
to follow men and serve the Buddha?
The Bhikṣu of Shānxiàng said.
What you gentlemen say is contrary to the Dharma.
The Fódào is the most divine, not to be seen by ordinary men.
Its transformations are impermanent, not to be known by ordinary men.
Common people are ignorant and do not know this themselves.
Vainly speaking these words only increases your sins.
The three scholars immediately became angry.
You serve the Buddha, yet you do not oppose the will of others.
Are you capable of following us and becoming our slave?
The Bhikṣu of Shānxiàng said.
Yes.
The three scholars said.
You are not fit to be a good slave.
We must order you to carry night soil.
You must collect one hundred *shí* of manure.
If you fail to get one hundred *shí* of manure.
your head will be cut off.
The Bhikṣu of Shānxiàng immediately went and carried night soil.
He could not collect much, so he returned and apologized to the scholars, saying his strength was exhausted and he could not collect much.
He begged forgiveness for his failure.
The three scholars were greatly enraged.
They immediately seized and bound him.
and brutally whipped him three hundred times.
Then they suddenly departed.
Ānán then transformed himself into an Upāsaka.
and went to speak to the Bhikṣu of Shānxiàng.
What the three scholars did was wicked.
Should you not tell the King to punish them?
The Bhikṣu of Shānxiàng said.
This came about because of my own past transgression.
Those who serve the Buddha spare nothing.
If a head is sought, the head is given; if a body is sought, the body is given.
I only carried night soil and was whipped; what suffering is there in this?
Ānán and the two Bhikṣus.
again transformed into Āyù Wáng.
and went to tell the Bhikṣu of Shānxiàng.
Serving the Buddha is certainly useless.
You toil in vain.
A person is born into the world and will soon die.
Why do you alone toil and suffer serving these scriptures?
I now wish to discuss a matter with you.
It is best if you follow my proposal.
If you do not follow me.
the Daoist will surely die.
The Bhikṣu of Shānxiàng said.
