Great King, what matter do you wish to discuss?
The King said, I have a noble daughter.
whose talent and conduct surpass others.
Her face and eyes are beautiful.
Her hands are like bee larvae.
I admire the Daoist for being gentle and good natured.
I wish to give her to you, and thus I have come to report my intention.
The Daoist must certainly consent.
The Bhikṣu of Shānxiàng said.
I know the King's generous intention.
I have served the Buddhist Dharma for many years.
My merits are yet incomplete, and yet I should covet the King's daughter?
Bringing shame upon the Fódào—this sin is not small.
If the King wishes to kill me, I shall certainly accept it.
The King then ordered men to take the Bhikṣu of Shānxiàng to the marketplace and behead him.
The Bhikṣu of Shānxiàng bowed to the Buddha and departed.
He looked back and thanked the King.
It turned out to be Ānán.
The Bhikṣu of Shānxiàng immediately advanced and bowed, touching his head and face to the ground.
Ānán stood up and helped him.
He bade him return to his seat, and they all recognized each other.
Ānán said to the Bhikṣu of Shānxiàng.
Your merit is complete.
You shall attain the Way.
I deliberately tested you.
merely to observe your resolve.
The Bhikṣu of Shānxiàng knelt down and said.
I, ignorant one, have received the Buddha’s grace.
Though I am within the Dharma, I fail to perform good deeds.
troubling and distressing the Divine Person to come and worry about me.
Ānán imparted the Way to the Bhikṣu of Shānxiàng.
Together they ascended the upper story to recite scriptures and discuss the meaning.
They shared joy and happiness.
Āyù Wáng performed a ritual bow and knelt for a long time.
Ānán asked the King.
How many volumes of Buddhist scriptures are there?
The King replied.
The Buddhist scriptures are extremely numerous, impossible to calculate.
The scriptures currently existing are in twelve categories.
numbering eighty-four thousand volumes.
Ānán asked the King.
How many volumes has the King retained?
The King replied.
I have already recited the Sānmèi Jīng, twelve thousand volumes.
and the Bānruò Bōluómì Jīng, twelve thousand volumes.
Ānán asked the King.
The King has seen so many scriptures.
Do you know how many *lǐ* separate Heaven and Earth?
The King replied.
The Dàpǐn Sānmèi Jīng says.
Heaven and Earth are separated by eight hundred and ten thousand *lǐ*.
Ānán asked the King.
How many categories of land are there on Earth?
The King replied.
The Bānruò Bōluómì Jīng says.
The Earth has eighty-one cities.
Each city has its own people.
The people in the northern city are ten *zhàng* tall.
The people in the middle city are eight *chǐ* tall.
The people in the southern city are three *chǐ* tall.
Ānán asked the King.
Does the King know who he originally was?
The King replied.
I cannot know my distant past, but I can know my recent past.
I have previously entered Nílǐ.
I have previously ascended to heaven.
I have previously endured toil and suffering.
I have previously been a slave or servant.
I have previously been one of the six domestic animals.
I have previously entered fire.
I have previously been a good person.
Having been a good person.
I was able to become King.
Having seen the affairs of toil and suffering.
I dare not commit evil again.
Ānán said.
The King was originally a Bhikṣu of Dīpaṃkara Buddha (Tíhégé Fó).
named Títóuluó.
The Bhikṣu of Shānxiàng was a Bhikṣu of Shìjiāwén Fó.
named Xūbá.
Since the Buddha passed away.
we have been isolated and impoverished, not holding firmly to the Dharma.
thereby incurring transgression.
After many years passed.
we no longer recognized each other.
In the past, the Bhikṣu of Shānxiàng and I.
were both born into a humble family; I was the elder brother, and the Bhikṣu of Shānxiàng was the younger brother.
We constantly cared for each other and followed each other when coming and going.
(Even then) we initially did not recognize each other.
I was later destined to become a King.
When the Bhikṣu of Shānxiàng was reborn, I did not recognize him either.
The world overturns, and beings are reborn into different forms repeatedly.
impossible to count.
Now that the King knows he can escape transmigration.
[Ānán] then imparted the Way of the Luóhàn to Āyù Wáng.
The Luóhàn Mòtiándì.
received the transmission of the Dharma treasury entrusted by Ānán.
and was instructed to go to the kingdom of Jìbīn Guó.
and first subdue the dragon there.
He immediately entered *sānmèi*.
causing that land to shake in six different ways.
The dragon was disturbed.
and went to Mòtiándì.
Mòtiándì entered the Samādhi of Loving-kindness (*cí sānmèi*).
The Dragon King raised winds and blew at him.
but the corner of his *jiāshā* did not move.
He then raised thunder, lightning, and weapons.
and even held up a volcano, wishing to cover and crush him.
[Mòtiándì] immediately used divine power to transform them into heavenly flowers.
Then a *jì* was heard in the air, saying.
Just as the snow mountain, struck by the intense sun, melts away without residue.
so entering the Samādhi of Loving-kindness transforms peak-fire into heavenly flowers.
Shènàpósi, having received the injunction from Ānán,
went to the country of Móutóuluó.
On the path there was a monastery
named Píntuó pó nà.
Shènàpósi stayed in the monastery for one night.
There were two elderly Bhikṣus in the monastery
who debated and recited a gāthā:
“The foremost in avoiding offense is choosing the Dharma, the foremost in hearing.”
These Bhikṣus said to Shènàpósi:
Shènàpósi said to them:
“The meaning you spoke is not what I spoke.
Elders,
in a past age, there was a merchant chief in Bōluónài
who intended to enter the great ocean with five hundred merchants.
He saw a Pratyekabuddha who was ill.
The merchant chief personally provided medical treatment.
The illness gradually improved.
The merchant chief took a rough cloth, washed and treated it to make it soft, and gave it to the Pratyekabuddha.
The Pratyekabuddha accepted the cloth, manifested eighteen transformations, and immediately entered Nirvāṇa.
That merchant chief at that time is my present self.
Therefore, I have now met the most excellent Master,
who allowed me to attain the Way.”
Shènàpósi gradually traveled to the mountain of Yōuliúmàn tuó in the country of Móutóuluó.
There were two Nāga Kings, brothers, with five hundred lesser Nāgas.
Shènàpósi reflected:
“If I do not subdue them, I cannot teach and transform them.”
He immediately used spiritual power to shake the mountain.
The two Nāga Kings became angry.
They raised fierce winds and rains,
and also produced fire.
Shènàpósi entered the Samādhi of Loving-Kindness (Cí Sānmèi).
The wind, rain, and fire could not come near his body.
They all transformed into flowers,
specifically Utpala flowers and others.
They all fell to the ground.
Then, thunder, lightning, and various weapons arose.
He also used spiritual power to transform them into celestial flowers.
At that moment, a gāthā was spoken in the air:
“Fierce wind and swift rain cannot cause harm; thunder, lightning, and weapons
transform into celestial flowers. Just like a snow mountain illuminated by sunlight,
they all melt and dissolve without any residue. Entering the Samādhi of Loving-Kindness,
fire cannot burn, and weapons and poisonous harm do not approach the body.”
Thereupon, the two Nāga Kings
went to the presence of Shènàpósi and said:
“Holy one, what do you intend to do?”
He replied:
“I intend to build a monastery here.
You should permit me.”
The Nāgas replied:
“It cannot be done.”
The Elder said:
“The World-Honored One has already said:
‘A hundred years after my Nirvāṇa,
a monastery shall be built at the most excellent place on the great mountain of Dáigū,
named Nàduō póduō.’”
The Nāga Kings repeated:
“Did the World-Honored One say so?”
The Elder replied:
“It is so.”
The Nāga Kings said:
“If the World-Honored One has said it, we shall follow your wishes.”
Shènàpósī.
He established a monastery on Dàtíhú Shān.
The master of the incense merchants
was named Jípduō.
Shènàpósī, through the power of expedient means,
converted the master of the incense merchants,
making him diligently advance [in the Dharma].
At that time, Shènàpósī entered his house alone.
Jípduō asked,
“Why does the holy man alone have no disciples?
I enjoy staying at home and indulging in the five desires;
I cannot renounce the householder life.
If I have a son, he shall follow the Elder.”
Eventually, Jípduō had a son
named Ābōjípduō. When the son grew up,
Shènàpósī went to Jípduō
and said,
“You previously made a vow
that if you had a son, you would give him to the Elder.
Now that a son has been born, you should allow him to follow me and renounce the householder life.”
Jípduō said,
“I now have only one son.
If a second son is born,
I will give him to the Elder.”
Eventually, the second son was born,
named Tuónàjípduō. Again, [Shènàpósī] sought him, but he was not given.
The third son, Yōupōjípduō, was also sought by him.
Jípduō replied,
“I shall make a solemn vow: I will have Yōupōjípduō manage the business.
If he profits or if he loses, he may not renounce the householder life.
If he neither profits nor loses, then I will allow him to renounce the householder life.”
At that time, the Demon King
caused all the inhabitants of Mótóuluó Guó
to buy his goods, causing him to profit.
At that time, Yōupōjípduō was selling incense.
The Elder Shènàpósī said to him,
“Concerning your mind and mental functions,
how do you distinguish what is good and what is evil?”
He replied, “I do not know.”
The Elder then said,
“If the mind and mental functions
are associated with greed, hatred, and delusion,
this is called evil.
If they are associated with non-greed, non-hatred, and non-delusion,
this is called good.”
At that time, the Elder made pellets, some of black earth and some of white earth,
and said to him,
“If a black thought arises in your mind, take a black pellet.
If a white thought arises, take a white pellet.”
Yōupōjípduō
immediately followed his instructions.
When his mind failed to generate goodness,
he had only received one white pellet so far.
Gradually advancing in this way,
he took two parts black pellets and one part white pellets.
He reflected further,
reaching half black pellets and half white pellets.
Next, he consecutively focused on goodness, and thus, evil did not arise, and he took only white pellets.
At that time, in Mótóuluó Guó,
there was a courtesan, Pósuōdá, who had a maid.
The maid went to Yōupōjípduō’s place and bought a large quantity of incense.
Her mistress asked,
“Where did you get so much incense?
Did you perhaps steal it?”
The maid replied,
“There is a merchant named Yōupōjípduō.
He is perfect in form and his speech is subtle and refined.
He sells his goods according to the Dharma.”
When her mistress heard this, she aroused lustful desire.
She again sent her maid to Yōupōjípduō’s place,
saying, “You must tell him,
‘I wish to enjoy pleasures together with you.’”
Yōupōjípduō replied,
“The time for meeting is not yet right.”
The situation remained thus for a time,
but she still would not accept [the refusal].
Then, a merchant’s son was summoned to go to her place.
The merchant master came from Northern India,
bringing five hundred horses and various kinds of goods,
and arrived in Mótóuluó Guó.
Upon arrival, he asked the people of Mótóuluó Guó,
“Where in this country is the most beautiful woman?”
The people of the country replied,
“There is a woman,
the most beautiful of all,
named Pósuōpó Dádduō.”
The merchant master said,
“I now wish to go to her place with five hundred silver coins and various kinds of goods.”
At that time, the courtesan,
due to her greed for the goods, killed the merchant’s son,
and placed his corpse in an unclean place
after enjoying pleasures with the son.
The close friends of that merchant’s son
searched and found the corpse in the unclean place.
They went and reported it to the King.
The King said,
“You may seize that Pósuōpó Dádduō.
Cut off her hands and feet, as well as her ears and nose, and scatter them in the wilds.”
They immediately followed the King’s command.
At that time, Yōupōjípduō reflected,
“Previously, I was unwilling to see her or share in the five desires.
Now, I wish to see her and observe her hands, feet, ears, and nose.”
He then went to observe her
and spoke a verse to her.
Pósuōpó Dádduō,
having heard his words, felt deep fear of saṃsāra (the cycle of birth and death).
Hearing the merits of the Buddha, her mind changed, and she desired Nirvāṇa.
She then spoke a verse in reply to Yōupōjípduō.
Yōupōjípduō explained the Four Noble Truths to her.
Observing her body further, he developed detachment from the Desire Realm
and attained the stage of Anāgāmin (Non-Returner).
Pósuōpó Dádduō attained the stage of Srotāpanna (Stream-Enterer).
Not long after Yōupōjípduō departed,
Pósuōpó Dádduō passed away and was born in the heavens.
At that time, the Elder Shènàpósī
went to Jípduō’s place and said,
“You should allow Yōupōjípduō to follow me and renounce the householder life.”
Jípduō replied,
“I previously made a vow that he must manage the business;
only if he neither profits nor loses will I allow him to renounce the householder life.”
Shènàpósī then used his spiritual power
to cause the business to be managed neither profitably nor lossfully.
At that time, Yōupōjípduō reflected for himself,
weighing and calculating that he was neither profiting nor losing.
Shènàpósī
went again to Jípduō’s place
and said to him,
“This son of yours was prophesied by the Buddha.
One hundred years after my entry into Nirvāṇa, he shall perform the Buddha’s work.
You should allow him to follow me and renounce the householder life.”
Jípduō immediately consented.
Shènàpósī took Yōupōjípduō to Nàjí Sì and ordained him.
After receiving the full precepts up to the fourth karma (procedure),
he eliminated all attachments and attained the fruit of Arhat.
At that time, Shènàpósī said to Yōupōjípduō,
“Good man,
as prophesied by the Buddha,
one hundred years after my entry into Nirvāṇa,
a monk named Yōupōjípduō
shall perform the Buddha’s work.
Later, he shall become a Buddha
named Wúxiàng (Formless).”
He spoke the Dharma in this manner.
At that time, the Demon King
rained down pearls upon the great assembly
to confuse the minds of the people.
Because the crowd was confused, there was not a single person who could realize the Truth.
The Elder immediately thought and knew it was the Demon King.
On the second day, twice as many people came.
The Demon King rained gold and again confused the minds of the crowd.
On the third day, twice as many people came.
The Demon rained pearls and gold and produced celestial music.
At that time, the people had not yet departed from desire.
Seeing the sights and hearing the sounds, their minds were stirred, and they no longer listened to the Dharma.
At that time, the Demon King
tied a garland of flowers onto the head of Yōupōjípduō.
When Yōupōjípduō thought,
“Who performed this deed?”
he immediately knew it was the Demon.
Yōupōjípduō then had this thought:
“Why did the World-Honored One not convert him?”
He immediately reflected that it was his responsibility to convert him.
“The Buddha prophesied that I
would become the Wúxiàng Buddha
to convert sentient beings.”
Yōupōjípduō caused three corpses to be taken:
first, a dead snake;
second, a dead dog;
third, a dead human.
He transformed the three corpses with his spiritual power
into a garland of flowers.
He went to the Demon King’s place and tied it around his neck.
Thereupon, the Demon King went to Móxīshǒu Luó
and Dìshì and the Thirty-three Heavens, as well as the Four Heavenly Kings,
to have the corpses removed,
but they could not be removed.
He went again to the abode of Dàfàn Tiān.
Dàfàn said,
“Good man,
what has been done by the spiritual power of the disciple of the Ten Powers (Buddha)
cannot be removed by anyone.
It is like the shore of the great ocean which cannot be broken by water.”
The Demon King said,
“How do you instruct me?
Upon whom, right now,
should I take refuge?”
Dàfàn spoke, saying,
“You should quickly go and take refuge in Yōupōjípduō.
Just as a person who falls upon the ground
must rise from that same ground.”
At that moment, the Demon King finally knew that the spiritual power of the Buddha’s son was great.
He then spoke a verse, praising the Buddha and reproaching himself.
The Demon King of the Desire Realm immediately abandoned his arrogant mind
and spoke of his former transgressions.
In the country of Nántiānzhú (Southern India) there was a man.
He lusted after another man's wife and constantly went to that man's house.
His mother forbade it.
So he killed his mother.
He went to another country but could not fulfill the five desires.
He was deeply worried and distressed.
He then left home and became a monk in the Buddhist tradition.
He mastered the Sānzàng (Three Treasuries) and achieved great learning.
Surrounded by his disciples, they went together to the Nàduōpóduō Monastery in the country of Móuóluó, to the presence of Yōupōjíduō.
Yōupōjíduō saw that he had killed his mother.
(Knowing) he had not attained the fruit of the Way, he did not greet or comfort him.
At that time, that Bhikṣu felt shame and remorse
and departed far away.
Those among Jíduō’s disciples who had not yet attained the Way,
thought thus:
"Our Upādhyāya (Wèishàng) has little wisdom.
He sees an old Bhikṣu whose mind is dull and ignorant, and preaches the Dharma for him.
But this Bhikṣu is bright, clever, and wise.
He is well-versed in the Sānzàng and is followed by his retinue,
yet he does not preach the Dharma for him."
Then Yōupōjíduō saw the intentions of his disciples, who were generating anger toward the matter.
Furthermore, he saw that the opportunity was ripe (for conversion).
(He thought:) "My Upādhyāya, Shènàpósī, shall convert and subdue them."
At that time, Shènàpósī resided in the country of Jìbīn.
He observed what kind of Buddhist activities Yōupōjíduō was undertaking.
(He saw that) his disciples’ minds were generating anger and surprise.
He also observed that these people should receive his teaching.
He immediately used his divine power to come and enter this monastery.
His beard and hair were long, and his clothes were coarse and worn.
The five hundred disciples all spoke thus:
"Where did this ignorant old man come from?
He sits in Yōupōjíduō's sleeping place."
The disciples pulled him out by hand,
but could not move him; he was like Mount Xūmí.
They immediately tried to curse him but no sound came out.
Finally, they reported the matter to Yōupōjíduō, saying,
(Yōupōjíduō) replied:
"No one except my Upādhyāya is able to sit on my bed."
Yōupōjíduō returned to the monastery.
He served his Upādhyāya with the utmost reverence.
He personally took a small seat and sat beside the Master.
The disciples thought:
"If this Bhikṣu
is the master of our Upādhyāya,
still, his wisdom is surely inferior to our Upādhyāya."
Then Shènàpósī saw their thoughts.
He raised his right arm and milk flowed from his hand.
He addressed Yōupōjíduō, saying:
"What is this Samādhi called?"
(Yōupōjíduō) replied: "I do not recognize it.
I wish to hear its name."
The Upādhyāya said:
"It is called the Lóngpínshēn Samādhi."
Subsequently, he entered various other Samādhis.
Jíduō consistently said,
"I do not recognize (them)."
(Shènàpósī) also said:
"When I enter Nièpán (Nirvāṇa), all these Samādhi methods will be lost."
When Yōupōjíduō's disciples heard these words,
they immediately thought:
"The wisdom of this Bhikṣu surpasses our Upādhyāya."
They immediately extinguished their arrogance.
Shènàpósī taught and preached the Dharma.
All those disciples attained the fruit of Āluóhàn.
When Yōupōjíduō was about to enter Nièpán,
he entrusted the Dharma Treasury (Fǎzàng) to the last disciple he converted, Xīwēikē.
He said:
"Good man,
the World-Honored One entrusted the Dharma Treasury to Móhējiāshè.
Jiāshè entrusted it to Ānán.
Ānán entrusted it to Mòtiándì.
Mòtiándì entrusted it to the Upādhyāya Shènàpósī.
Shènàpósī entrusted it to me.
Now that I am entering Nièpán, I entrust it to you."
He proclaimed it throughout Yánfú Tí.
One hundred thousand Luóhàn assembled at the same time.
The number of ordinary Bhikṣus was countless.
He immediately displayed divine powers, exhibiting the eighteen transformations.
Having completed the matter, he immediately entered Nièpán.
The disciples he converted who had attained the four fruits of the Way,
all took tally sticks and placed them inside a stone chamber.
They then cremated his body using the tally sticks.
Following this, they erected a stūpa.
At that time, there was also one thousand Luóhàn
who entered Nièpán together.
Xīwēikē guarded the Dharma Treasury.
There were twenty-eight people who attained the four fruits from Yōupōjí's lineage.
At that time, there was a Luóhàn,
named Yōupōjíduō.
He resided at the Nàduōpóduō Monastery on Dàtíhú Mountain in the country of Móuóluó.
Not far from the monastery,
a tigress gave birth to cubs.
(The tigress) could not find food and died of starvation.
Yōupōjíduō,
through the power of compassion, gave the tiger cubs food.
He had five hundred disciples,
who had not yet attained the Way, and they said:
"Why do you feed such difficult beings?"
He replied:
"It is for the sake of the cause of liberation."
At that time, the lives of the tiger cubs were short.
They were nearing death.
Jíduō spoke to the tiger cubs, saying:
"All conditioned things are impermanent.
All phenomena are without self.
Nièpán is quiescent.
You should generate faith toward me.
You should generate disgust and detachment from the animal realm."
At that time, the tiger cubs toward Jíduō
generated faith and respect in their hearts.
They immediately died.
They were reborn among the people in the country of Móuóluó.
When they reached the age of seven,
Jíduō converted and guided them to leave home (become monks).
Within seven years, they attained the fruit of Luóhàn.
Using their divine power, they gathered various flowers,
offered them to Jíduō, and encircled his side.
The five hundred disciples who had not yet attained the Way reported:
"These fellow students are still young in age,
how have they already achieved the merit of divine powers?"
Jíduō replied:
"They were all the former tiger cubs."
Jíduō preached the Dharma.
The five hundred disciples felt deep shame and remorse.
They cut off their afflictions and attained the fruit of Āluóhàn.
At that time, a Brāhmaṇa (Pólúomén) had a son.
He ordered a physiognomist to examine him.
The master said:
"This child has no auspicious marks (xiàng). He should be named Ābǎo."
When his parents heard this,
although he was raised despite having no auspicious marks, they did not pity or cherish him initially.
When he reached the age of twelve, he was able to sustain himself.
His parents then drove him away, ordering him not to return again.
The son dared not stay and immediately went forth begging for food.
He arrived at the Jetavana Grove (Qíhuán).
Fó, thinking of his diligence and suffering with great compassion,
immediately ordered Ānán to call and ask him:
"Can you leave home (become a monk)?"
The boy was immediately joyful and wished to become a Śramaṇa (Shāmén).
Fó then touched his head with his hand.
His hair immediately fell off, and the kasaya robe adhered to his body.
Fó established a name for him, naming him Luóxún Yú.
At that time, whenever the Saṅgha of the Five Sections (Wǔ Bù Sēng) went out to beg for food (fēnwèi),
the section where Luóxún Yú was located would always return with empty bowls.
Fó commanded the Bhikṣus to divide their food and give it to him.
This happened more than once.
Mùlián thought:
"These Bhikṣus themselves cannot obtain food.
Why do the others also return completely empty-handed?
If I go along with them, they might still obtain something."
Fó knew his thoughts and went together with Shèlì Fú.
He arranged for Mùlián to go together with Luóxún Yú.
Each was divided into one section (group).
Fó told Mùlián:
"Wherever I am, you must not go."
Mùlián immediately traveled together with Luóxún Yú.
Wherever they intended to go, they immediately saw Fó,
along with Shèlì Fú, standing at the gate.
Having experienced this, crossing over hundreds of millions of kingdoms,
they eventually obtained no food.
Mùlián thought:
"I am certainly not going to obtain food today."
(He spoke to) Luóxún Yú.
At that time, being extremely hungry, they stopped by the side of the Gaṅgā River (Héngshǔi).
Mù Jiánlián
immediately returned to where Fó was.
Fó still had leftover food in his bowl at that time.
He immediately gave it to Mùlián.
(Mùlián) thought:
"I am so extremely hungry now.
Even if I were to swallow Mount Sumeru (Xūmí), I would still not be full.
How could this small amount of rice be enough to eat?"
Fó told Mùlián:
"Just eat this rice and do not worry that it will be insufficient."
Mùlián immediately ate the rice.
After he was full, the bowl was not empty.
Only Shèlì Fú immediately thought:
"Luóxún Yú
has not yet obtained food today
and must be suffering greatly from hunger."
He then addressed Fó, saying:
"I beg for the leftover rice to give to Luóxún Yú."
Fó immediately told him:
"I do not begrudge the rice,
but Luóxún Yú's karmic retribution from previous deeds dictates that he should not obtain it.
If you think this is not true,
then you may give it to him."
Shèlì Fú then gave the rice to him.
When Luóxún Yú received it and was about to accept the rice,
the bowl immediately sank a hundred zhàng into the earth.
Shèlì Fú, using his spiritual power (dàolì),
followed the bowl with his hand and immediately retrieved it and returned it to Luóxún Yú.
Just as he was about to eat it,
he accidentally overturned the bowl, spilling its contents.
All the food scattered into the water.
Luóxún Yú returned to his seat and settled his mind (entered samadhi).
He thought to himself, saying:
"Whenever I travel together with the Bhikṣus,
I always return having obtained nothing, with an empty bowl.
Now Shèlì Fú gave me Fó’s leftover rice,
and yet it was spilled again.
This is all the karmic retribution that I deserve to receive due to my sins."
He then contemplated by himself,
unbound his attachments, cleansed his defilements, and attained the path of the Arhat (Luóhàn).
He then ate earth and entered Parinirvāṇa (Bānníhuán).
If you wish to know about Luóxún Yú:
In the time of Fó Vipaśyin (Wéiwèi Fó),
he was an ordinary person.
He constantly harbored avarice and greed and was unwilling to practice charity (bùshī).
When he was about to eat, he would remove his clothes and spread them on the ground, fearing rice grains would drop.
A Śramaṇa (Shāmén) passed by and sought food from him (fēnwèi).
Luóxún Yú saw him and said to him:
"What should I give you?"
He then scooped up earth with his hand and gave it to the Śramaṇa.
The Śramaṇa immediately blessed him and wished, saying:
"This is merely due to your foolishness.
May you quickly attain liberation and deliverance."
Since that distant past, repeatedly cycling through birth and death,
until the present time, wherever he went, he never obtained food.
Now, he has attained the Way (Dào), eating earth and entering Nirvāṇa (Níhuán).
At that time, Luóxún Yú was the one who gave the earth, and the Śramaṇa was Shèlì Fú.
Due to the retribution of sins and merits, even though he attained the Way now, he still suffered the disaster caused by his past actions.
Worldly people are ignorant
and believe that committing evil bears no sin.
Luóxún Yú is proof of this.
When Fó was alive, the community of monks (Zhòng Sēng) wore clothing
made only of pure, genuine silk and rags pieced together from dead people's clothes.
Later, the Bhikṣu Luóxún Yú arose.
Every time he went out begging for food (fēnwèi), he returned hungry and empty-handed.
Fó, knowing his past deeds,
ordered the community of monks to divide the Vinaya (Lǜ) into five sections (Wǔ Bù).
The color of the robes was also of five types.
He commanded that Luóxún Yú should travel daily with one of the sections.
Consequently, regulations and norms were established.
Each section listed its particular strengths and was named after the color of its robe.
The Sarvāstivāda Section (Sàhédūo Bù)
broadly understood and expertly attained the Way, leading beings through the Dharma.
They should wear dark gray (zào) kāṣāya robes.
The Kāśyapīya Section (Jiāshèwéi Bù)
was diligent, courageous, and quick, gathering and protecting sentient beings.
They should wear mu lan (magnolia/dark red) kāṣāya robes.
The Mahīśāsaka Section (Míshāsāi Bù)
entered subtle depths through contemplation (Chán Sī), thoroughly investigating profound mysteries.
They should wear blue kāṣāya robes.
The Mahāsaṅghika Section (Móhē Sēngqí Bù)
diligently studied all sūtras and expounded on their principles.
They should wear yellow kāṣāya robes.
After that time, (Luóxún Yú) greatly obtained food.
Why was this?
It was caused by the lack of virtue
of Luóxún Yú
in a previous life. Ānán asked Fó, saying:
"If Luóxún Yú lacked virtue in a previous life,
how did he manage to become a Śramaṇa?"
Fó said:
"This Luóxún Yú, in a past life, was the son of a worthy man.
He was a jealous person.
When he saw a Śramaṇa coming to beg for food (fēnwèi),
he would immediately close the gates and doors and say:
'The master is not home.'
When the Śramaṇa went to another house,
he would again go to that house and close the gates and doors,
and also say:
'The master is not home.'
Therefore, today he cannot obtain food when begging.
However, when he saw others practicing charity by giving food and drink and joyfully participating in gatherings,
he also thought, 'I also wish to become a Śramaṇa.'
Therefore, he is now destitute and distressed like this."
Fó was residing in Śrāvastī City (Shèwèi Chéng).
At that time, there were two sisters in this city
who left home to follow the Way while they were pregnant but had not yet given birth.
The Bhikṣuṇīs (Bǐqiūní) saw the state of their bellies
and immediately expelled them.
Because of this incident,
they went to report it to the World-Honored One (Shìzūn).
The Shìzūn replied, saying:
"If they became pregnant while still at home, they can be considered blameless."
These Bǐqiūnís later gave birth to male children.
One was named Tóngzǐ Jiāshè (Kāśyapa the Boy).
When he reached the age of eight,
he left home to follow the Way and became an Arhat (Āluóhàn).
Together with sixteen Bhikṣus,
each carrying their washing pot, they went to the edge of the Aciravati River (Āqíluó Hé).
They washed and entered the water, swimming and playing, sometimes floating on their back, sometimes face down.
They crossed the river, splashing the water, and bathed.
At that time, King Prasenajit (Bōsīnì Wáng),
was watching from the top floor of his tall building.
The King had not yet truly believed in the Buddha Dharma (Fó Fǎ).
After seeing this incident, his disbelief doubled.
He immediately said to Queen Mallikā (Mòlì Fūrén):
"The Great Being (Dàshì), the field of merit whom your family serves
and deeply believes in without doubt—why do you not look at this?"
She immediately replied to the King, saying:
"Perhaps they are young Bhikṣus who have just left home,
who have just received the full precepts (Jùzú Jièlǜ) and do not yet know the regulations,
or perhaps the Shìzūn has not yet established this specific precept, and that is why they are acting like that."
Tóngzǐ Jiāshè,
using his celestial ears (Tiān Ěr), heard the sound of the King's words.
He immediately told his companions:
"The King's disbelief has doubled, and Mòlì Fūrén is unhappy.
We must now cause them to feel joy."
They all replied, "Excellent!"
Each took their washing pot, filled it with water, and placed it in front of them.
They sat in the full lotus position (jiāfū zuò) in ordered ranks,
traversing the void and passing through the air above the King's palace.
Mòlì Fūrén was sitting in the open area.
When she saw the shadow of the sitting figures, she immediately looked up.
She saw the ordered ranks sitting in the full lotus position, with washing pots in front, traveling through the void, resembling a flock of geese led by their king.
Seeing this, her heart was greatly delighted.
She immediately addressed the King, saying:
"Look! The spiritual virtue of my family's field of merit is like this!"
When the King saw this, his heart was greatly delighted.
He spoke these words:
"Excellent! Excellent!
I have obtained great benefit.
I pray that Fó Shìzūn and the community of Bhikṣus
may remain in this kingdom for the rest of their lives as a superb field of merit."
Fó heard of this incident,
and immediately established a precept so that they would not act like that again.
In Jìbīn Guó, the rice crops first began to head.
The Dragon King Āluópólóu
poured down great torrential rain, causing the grain and rice to be submerged and die.
At that time, the Virtuous Bhikṣu Mòchǎntí and four others,
came from Bōzhàlìfú Guó,
flying through the air until they reached the edge of the snowy mountains,
in the middle of the Āluópólóu pool.
They immediately walked, stood, sat, and lay down upon the water.
The Dragon King's retinue entered and reported to the Dragon King.
The Dragon King, enraged, exerted various divine powers.
Violent winds, swift rain, thunder, and lightning bolts;
mountain cliffs collapsed, and trees were shattered.
His body emitted smoke and fire, and he rained down great gravel and stones.
He wished to make the Virtuous Mòchǎntí afraid.
He then summoned his troops, but still could not subdue them.
Mòchǎntí said,
“Even if you commanded all the devas and all people of the world to come and frighten me, not one hair on my body would move.
If you were to seize Mount Sumeru and all the small mountains
and heap them upon me, I still would not move.”
Thereupon, he gradually taught and transformed him with the flavor of the Dharma, demonstrating it until the Dragon King was delighted and subdued.
The Dragon King, hearing the Dharma, immediately accepted the Refuges and Precepts.
He and his retinue all became disciples.
The ghosts, yakṣas, gandharvas, and kūbhāṇḍa demons of the snowy mountains, hearing this, all believed and submitted, and also became disciples.
They all achieved the Path.
Mòchǎntí told the dragons and demons,
“From now on, do not give rise to anger or rage, do not harm the people, and do not destroy the grain and rice crops.
You should give rise to kindness and allow them to achieve peace and happiness.”
They all bowed their heads and respectfully received the teachings and precepts.
They offered a jeweled bed for Mòchǎntí to sit upon.
The Dragon King stood attending him, fanning him with a fan.
The citizens of Jìbīn Qiántuólèchā,
having seen this event, gave rise to great reverence.
They all came to listen to the Dharma, and many achieved the fruits of the Path.
During the time of King Āyù,
the Buddha had already entered Nirvāṇa
for more than two hundred years.
At that time, Bhikṣu Móxǐntuó
arrived in Shīzǐ Zhōu (Lion Island).
At that time, the king wished to go hunting.
There was a tree deity
who wished to enable the king to see Móxǐntuó.
The tree deity transformed into a deer.
Not far from the king, it appeared eating grass, and then slowly walked away.
The king, seeing the transformed deer, immediately drew his bow, took an arrow, pulled the string, and intended to shoot.
The king then thought,
“I must shoot this deer carefully.”
The deer then turned toward the Shéluótuóluó road and fled.
The king immediately pursued it.
When they reached Shéluótuóluó,
the deer vanished not far from Móxǐntuó.
At that time, Móxǐntuó saw the king approaching
and thought thus:
“Now I shall use my divine power to make the king clearly see me alone, and not see anyone else.”
The Virtuous Móxǐntuó immediately called the king by his name:
“Dìxū, you come here.”
The king, hearing the call,
then thought,
“In this country, who dares to call me by my name?
What kind of person is this?
Dressed in red, cut and stitched together,
calling my name?”
He gave rise to intense suspicion.
“What is this?
Is it a human?
Or is it a ghost or spirit?”
Móxǐntuó answered,
“I am a Śramaṇa, a son of the Dharma of the Śākya clan.
Out of compassion for the King,
I have come here specifically
from Jambudvīpa.”
At that time, King Tiān'ài Dìxū
had exchanged letters with King Āyù.
They had become distant acquaintances, offering rare treasures as tribute.
They corresponded with one another.
The Dharma Master then said,
“I have the Three Jewels to offer to the King.
They are not comparable to those earthly treasures offered by Tiān'ài.”
He immediately preached the Three Refuges and the Dharma to the King.
The King received the Three Refuges and became a Upāsaka (lay disciple).
He then reported on the Buddha's Dharma (Śākya Dharma),
and showed it to King Tiān'ài Dìxū.
While still in the hunting grounds,
the King remembered
that King Āyù’s letter mentioned a son of the Śākya clan.
He immediately threw down his bow and arrows and cordially inquired after him.
The Dharma Master preached a sutra for him and administered the Three Refuges.
Then Móxǐntuó sent for
the Śrāmaṇera Xiūmónà, saying,
“You should now preach the Dharma.
You must proclaim the turning of the Dharma Wheel.”
Xiūmónà said,
“When I proclaim it now, how far should the sound reach?”
He replied,
“Let the sound fill Shīzǐ Guó (Lion Country).”
Then Xiūmónà immediately entered the Fourth Dhyāna (meditative absorption).
Rising from the absorption, he proclaimed the turning of the Dharma Wheel.
The citizens of Shīzǐ Guó all heard it.
All the spirits and devas in the sky assembled.
After the three proclamations were finished,
Móxǐntuó then preached the Dharma for them.
Countless devas and humans all attained the path.
There was Nàlì Guó, near the southern sea.
The people there took the collection of pearls and sandalwood
as their constant livelihood.
In the country, there was one family with two brothers.
Their parents died, and they wished to divide the property and separate.
The family had a slave named Fēnnà.
He was young, intelligent, and excelled at trade and commerce.
He went to sea to make a living and was knowledgeable about everything.
The household wealth and possessions were divided into one portion.
The slave Fēnnà was taken as another portion.
The brothers drew lots, and the younger brother obtained Fēnnà.
Taking his wife and children, he left the house empty-handed.
At that time, the world suffered famine, and although he obtained Fēnnà, he feared they could not survive together, causing him anxiety and worry.
The slave Fēnnà reported to his master,
“Please do not worry. Fēnnà will make a plan.
Within a month, I shall make you wealthier than your elder brother.”
The master said,
“If you can truly do this, I will release you to be a free man.”
The master's wife had some private pearls and goods.
She gave them to Fēnnà as capital.
At that time, the sea tide came in.
The people in the city went to the waterside to collect firewood.
Fēnnà took the pearls and goods outside the city.
He saw a beggar carrying firewood.
In the firewood was ox-head sandalwood incense.
It could cure serious illnesses.
One ounce was worth a thousand ounces of gold.
In that era, it was rare and difficult to obtain.
Fēnnà recognized it.
He used two gold coins to buy it and took it home.
He broke it into several dozen pieces.
At that time, a certain Elder was suffering from a serious illness.
He needed two ounces of this ox-head sandalwood to mix into medicine.
He searched but could not find it.
Fēnnà took it to him and immediately received two thousand ounces of gold.
Having sold it all in this manner, the profit was incalculable, making him ten times wealthier than the elder brother. The master was deeply grateful, remembering
that Fēnnà had not violated his vow.
He released him to be a free man, allowing him to follow his inclinations.
Fēnnà took his leave to pursue the Path.
He arrived in Shèwèi Guó and paid homage to the Buddha.
Kneeling long, he reported to the Buddha,
“Although my origin is humble, my heart delights in the Way and Virtue.
I only pray that the World-Honored One extends his compassion and saves me.”
The Buddha said, “Ehi Bhikṣu (Well come).”
Fēnnà’s hair immediately fell out, and the Dharma robe clothed his body.
He instantly became a Śramaṇa.
The Buddha preached the Dharma for him, and soon he attained the path of Arhat.
Sitting, he reflected:
“Now that I have attained the Six Superknowledges and am free over life and death,
this is all due to the kindness of my former master.
Now I should go and save him, and also convert the people of his country.”
Thereupon, the Venerable Fēnnà traveled to his former country and went to his master’s house.
The master was delighted and invited him to sit and prepared a meal.
After the meal, and having washed his hands,
he ascended into the sky,
multiplied his body, and scattered his limbs.
Water and fire emanated from his body.
Shining with brilliant light, he descended from above.
He informed his master, saying,
“These divine virtues are all the fruit of the merit accrued when the master released me.
This is what I learned after going to the place of the Buddha.”
The master replied,
“Your divine transformations are subtle and wonderful.
I wish to see the World-Honored One and receive his teachings.”
Fēnnà replied,
“You only need to wholeheartedly prepare the offerings and provisions.
With the Buddha’s wisdom of the Three Clairvoyances, he will surely come himself.”
The preparations for the offering were completed overnight.
Facing Shèwèi Guó, he bowed his head, knelt long, burned incense, and invited the Buddha, saying,
“I only pray that you condescend to come and broadly save all beings.”
The Buddha knew his intention.
He immediately took five hundred Arhats
and each used divine power to travel to his house.
The king and the people were all astonished and awestruck.
They came to the Buddha and prostrated with five limbs touching the ground.
The king then sat back in his seat.
When the meal was finished and the washing rites completed,
the Buddha, for the benefit of the host and the king's officials and retinue,
widely expounded the Bright Dharma.
They all received the Five Precepts and became disciples of the Buddha.
The host arose and stood before the Buddha,
praising Fēnnà, saying,
“He was diligent at home, and after leaving home, he attained the Path.
His divine virtue is lofty and profound, and his family and country have been delivered through him.
How should I repay his kindness?”
Thereupon, the World-Honored One praised Fēnnà
and spoke a verse, saying:
“When the mind has rested and words and deeds have also ceased, from that cessation comes liberation,
calmly returning to Nirvāṇa, having abandoned desire and attachment, piercing the barrier of the Three Realms.
One whose hope and intention are cut off is called the Supreme Man, whether in the marsh or the wilderness.
Whether on flat ground or high cliffs, wherever the one who accords with Reality passes, all receive protection.
He delights in empty tranquility, which ordinary people cannot attain; how joyful he is, without lust,
and without desires or cravings.”
The host and the king were increasingly joyful.
They made offerings for seven days.
They attained the path of Srotāpanna (stream-entry).
The Fó dwelled in the village of Ānluó, in the Ānluó Grove.
He was accompanied by the assembly of Bhīqīu.
At that time, there was an elder named Zhìduōluó.
He addressed the senior Bhīqīu, saying:
“We only wish, O Venerable Ones,
that you accept my invitation for food in this grove.”
At that time, the senior Bhīqīu remained silent.
The senior Bhīqīu donned their robes and took their bowls.
They went to the elder’s house, took their seats, and sat down.
The elder personally served various foods and drinks.
After washing (hands and mouth), they listened to the teaching of the Dharma.
The senior Bhīqīu taught the Dharma to the elder.
They demonstrated, taught, benefited, and delighted him.
The senior Bhīqīu ate ghee, curds, and honey until satisfied.
In the late spring afternoon, the heat was extremely intense.
There was a junior Bhīqīu,
named Móhējiā.
He said to the senior Bhīqīu:
“Today is very hot. I wish to raise clouds, cause rain, and fan a cool breeze.”
The senior Bhīqīu replied:
“If you are able to do so, it is excellent.”
Then Móhējiā immediately entered samādhi.
As he attained perfect absorption,
clouds rose instantly and a fine rain gently fell.
A gentle, cool breeze wafted from the four directions and arrived at the Vihāra gate.
He immediately ceased his psychic power and returned to his own room.
At that time, the elder thought:
“The most junior Bhīqīu is able to possess such great supernatural power.
How much more so the middle and senior ones?”
He paid homage to the Bhīqīu.
He followed Móhējiā to his residence.
He bowed at his feet and said:
“Venerable Sir, I wish to see the manifestation of your divine power.”
Móhējiā said:
“Elder, you need not see this.”
He refused him after three requests.
The elder still requested repeatedly.
Móhējiā spoke to the elder, saying:
“You should go outside and gather dry grass,
and cover it with white cloth.”
The elder followed the instruction, gathering firewood into a pile.
He came back and informed the Venerable Sir.
Móhējiā immediately entered the Fire Luminosity Samādhi.
He caused flames to emerge from the hole where the door latch connected.
The light burned up the accumulated firewood completely.
Only the white cloth did not burn.
He spoke to the elder, saying:
“Have you seen it now?”
He replied:
“I have seen it.
It is truly marvelous and extraordinary.”
Móhējiā spoke to the elder, saying:
“You should know that all this has non-negligence as its foundation.
Because of non-negligence, one attains Ānòuduōluó Sānmiǎo Sānpútí,
and the other Dharma of the elements of the path.”
The elder said:
“Venerable Sir,
Móhējiā,
I wish you would permanently reside in this grove.
I shall provide the four necessities as long as I live.”
Móhējiā had reasons for traveling and did not accept his invitation.
The elder, having heard the teaching, paid his respects and departed.
Yuànzú Āluóhàn
constantly guided and transformed hungry ghosts.
He saw a hungry ghost whose form was hideous.
Anyone who saw it felt their hair stand on end, filled with terror.
Flames erupted from its body like a great pile of fire.
Maggots and insects came out of its mouth, and pus and blood overflowed.
The stench carried far and it was impossible to approach.
Sometimes its mouth spat flaming fire several tens of measures long.
Sometimes its ears, nose, eyes, body, and limbs
released flames several tens of measures long.
Its lips and mouth hung down like a wild boar.
Its body was one yóuxún in size and breadth.
It scratched and clawed itself with its hands, crying out loudly, running east and west.
At that time, Yuànzú asked the hungry ghost:
“What sin did you commit in a former life to suffer this torment now?”
The hungry ghost replied:
“In the past, I acted as a Shāmen.
I was attached to dwellings, grasping, and unwilling to give them up.
Although my body maintained the proper deportment, my speech was foul and wicked.
Whenever I saw Bhīqīu who upheld the precepts and were diligent,
I would immediately curse and insult them, regarding them with malicious side-glances.
Relying on my noble family, I considered myself immortal.
I created countless roots of unwholesomeness.
I would rather use a sharp knife to cut off my own tongue,
and willingly endure suffering for countless kalpas,
than spend a single day slandering diligent Bhīqīu.
If I were able to return to Yánfúlí Dì,
I would use my appearance to instruct and caution all Bhīqīu
to carefully guard the faults of the mouth and not speak carelessly.
If they see Bhīqīu who practice pure conduct and uphold the precepts,
they should remember to proclaim their virtues.
Since I took on the form of a hungry ghost,
hundreds of thousands of years have passed,
suffering this torment.
When my life here ends, I will enter the hells.”
When the hungry ghost finished saying this,
it cried out loudly and threw itself onto the ground,
like Mount Tàishān collapsing, heaven turning over, and earth overturning.
This outcome was caused solely by the faults of the mouth.
Those who are able to guard the faults of the mouth receive boundless fortune.
Furthermore, when Jiāshè Rúlái appeared in the world,
He expounded the Dharma teachings and his transformation was complete.
He attained Pānnihuán in the state of Nirvāṇa without remainder.
After his Nirvāṇa, there was a Sānzàng Bhīqīu,
named Huángyán.
The Saṅgha instructed him:
“We will not allow you to be involved in miscellaneous duties.
Just teach the wondrous Dharma to those who are later learners.”
At that time, the Sānzàng Bhīqīu felt contempt in his heart but did not refuse the Saṅgha’s order.
He then expounded the meaning of the Sūtras to the later learners.
He called those receiving the meaning, saying:
“Hurry forward, Elephant Head!”
Next, he called the second person.
And again said, “Horse Head!”
Next, “Camel Head!”
Next, “Donkey Head!”
Next, “Pig Head!”
Next, he called, “Sheep Head!”
“Ram Head!”
Next, he called, “Lion Head!”
Next, he called, “Tiger Head!”
Next, he called, “Bird Head!”
Next, he called, “Brown Bear Head!”
In this way, he called them all sorts of beasts, all sorts of animal categories,
which were countless.
Sānzàng Huángyán,
uttered such immeasurable wicked words from his mouth.
Although he taught the meaning of the Sūtras, he could not escape his offense.
After his body perished and his life ended, he entered the hells.
He passed through tens of millions of kalpas, suffering immeasurable torment.
His remaining sins not yet fully exhausted, he emerged from the hells.
Born in the great sea, he took the form of an aquatic creature.
He had one body and a hundred heads, and his form was extremely vast.
When other creatures saw him, they all ran away.
The Buddha was in the country of Shèwèi.
At that time, in the country of Xūyé, there was a poor person.
He hired himself out to shave children's heads, agreeing to take one hú of grain as payment whenever the wheat ripened.
On the road, he encountered an old friend and wished to drink wine together.
Returning, he sought the wheat payment, but searched everywhere and could not obtain it.
He immediately conceived malicious intent.
"I vow that when my life ends, I will become a great divine nāga (dragon)."
"I shall submerge this country."
When his life ended, he consequently became a great nāga.
For several years, his country suffered from unseasonable wind and rain.
The Buddha, thinking of the famine, sent the bhikṣu Shāhé to go and convert that nāga.
The nāga saw the bhikṣu and immediately generated malicious intent.
He wished to kill the people of the country and the body of Shāhé.
Shāhé transformed his alms bowl to cover the entire country.
The nāga immediately sent down rain, believing the country was already submerged.
The bhikṣu, by the majestic power of the Buddha, caused the nāga to see the people safe and peaceful as before.
The nāga again grew enraged.
He further sent down great snow.
The bhikṣu's bowl received it, and he swept it with his hand, piling it in one spot.
Then he entered the nāga's dwelling.
The nāga immediately came out.
The bhikṣu came out again.
The nāga entered, and the bhikṣu entered again.
When this continued without stopping, the nāga was exhausted and finally ceased.
He knelt reverently and asked:
"What kind of deity are you?"
"You annoy me thus."
The bhikṣu replied:
"I am a disciple of the Buddha."
The nāga said:
"I wish to take refuge."
He then followed the bhikṣu away.
The bhikṣu Shāhé,
immediately placed this nāga inside a basket.
When the people saw the bhikṣu capture the nāga in this manner, they were all greatly joyful.
They asked:
"Master, what kind of deity are you, who has subdued the nation's calamity?"
He informed them:
"I am a disciple of the Buddha."
The people asked:
"Can the Buddha be seen?"
He replied: "He can be seen."
"Wait until I return when the sun is approaching noon."
On the way, he passed by places giving alms.
Some people gave him rice, and others gave him wine.
The bhikṣu received it under a tree.
He became drunk and lay down.
The nāga, the bowl, and the kaṣāya robe were each in a different location.
At that time, the Buddha smiled, and five-colored light shone forth.
Ānán respectfully requested an explanation.
The Buddha responded regarding what had occurred.
Furthermore, He spoke of four matters.
First, an Āluóhàn cannot know something unless he enters samādhi.
Second, they cannot immediately manifest divine powers.
Third, they aggressively urge people to give alms.
Fourth, there are still insects in their body.
Due to these four matters, the Āluóhàn is inferior to the Buddha.
At that time, there was one Púsà who intended to become a Shēngwén.
Having seen this matter, his resolve immediately became firm.
The Buddha sent Mùjiànlián to the place where the bhikṣu Shāhé was.
He commanded him to bring the nāga.
The Buddha then spoke to him about his past lives.
The nāga's heart was immediately opened.
He then received the Five Precepts.
And upheld and practiced the Ten Virtues.
He attained Xu-tuó-huán.
Ānán asked the Buddha about the cause and condition of this event.
The Buddha instructed Ānán:
"An Āluóhàn no longer experiences hunger or thirst.
He was seen drunk and lying down because of three specific reasons.
First, the Buddha wished to enlighten and convert the Púsà's mind.
Second, He did not wish to violate the intent of the donor families.
Third, He feared that those disciples who had not yet attained the Way would commit many transgressions by drinking alcohol.
Therefore, this incident was manifested to inspect the precepts.
Although the bhikṣu Shāhé drank the wine,
he was not affected by intoxication."
An Āluóhàn traveled to the country of Móutóuluó, going to Mount Yōulóumàntuó.
He sat upon a cord bed.
There were two nāga kings, who were brothers.
They were accompanied by five hundred dependents.
Shènàpósī considered.
He wished to subdue them.
Immediately, using divine power,
he shook the mountains and valleys.
The two nāga kings became angry.
They went to Pósī's location and conjured fierce wind, rain, thunder, lightning, weapons, raging fire, and other dangers.
At that time, Pósī entered the Samādhi of Loving-Kindness.
He was able to prevent the wind, rain, fire, and other dangers from approaching his body.
He transformed his precepts into Yōubōluó, Jūmóutóu, and Féntuólì lotuses.
Shèwèi guó
was named Lì. His family was extremely wealthy.
He was already old and without any heir.
He worshipped and offered sacrifices to the sun, moon, and heavenly spirits, omitting nothing
but still could not obtain a son.
He thought to himself that prayer and supplication were useless.
His treasured wealth was scattered and his enterprises neglected.
Illnesses followed one after another, and calamities afflicted him from beginning to end.
His servants and maids died, and his livestock failed to reproduce.
He was misled by practitioners of witchcraft and spirit masters.
They said he would obtain fortune, but instead, great misfortune arrived.
It was like a blind person swallowing poison, believing it to be a good medicine.
Hoping for recovery or lessening of the illness, he instead lost his life.
Since I have killed living beings for offerings and sacrifices, I am bound to enter the hells.
How deluded is it to hope for heavenly blessings?
In the world, there exists the path of the Buddha and sages of lofty conduct.
Those who study and attain the immortal way are called
Yìngzhēn. They are pure as lapis lazuli; only by diligently concentrating thought may one behold them.
Those who follow this path only maintain tranquility and solitude.
Without desire and without craving, they find happiness in this.
In the present life, they obtain peace, and upon death, they are born in heaven.
Lì then established permanent offerings to the Three Venerables of the Buddha.
After the span of one year, his wife bore a son.
He was named Fódà.
Later, she bore another son.
He was named Sēngdà.
Lì instructed his two sons,
showing them the sacred path.
Sēngdà was naturally compassionate and filial, loving all creatures.
He observed the Dharma precepts of the Buddha and stayed close to the śramaṇas (monks).
Pure and contented, his parents loved him.
Lì became gravely ill and bedridden.
He immediately called his eldest son and, weeping, gave him this warning:
"Life must end in death. Those who hold the precepts are safe; those who violate them are in danger.
Sēngdà is still young, but he is virtuous, filial, and innocent.
I entrust him to you." After Lì finished speaking, he died.
Afterward, Sēngdà frequently told and implored his elder brother that he wished to become a śramaṇa.
According to the laws of that country, one must take a wife.
His brother ignored Sēngdà's words about becoming a śramaṇa.
Fódà immediately arranged a marriage for him,
seeking a girl from a virtuous family named Kuàijiàn.
Her brilliance shone brightly; she was peerless in her beauty.
When the wife returned home and ascended the hall, the elder brother hosted guests, and the nine generations of relatives were delighted.
In front of the crowd, the elder brother said to his younger brother:
"On this very day, do you still wish to become a śramaṇa?"
Sēngdà replied:
"Indeed, it is my long-cherished aspiration."
The elder brother mocked him, saying:
"You may follow your ambition."
The younger brother rejoiced in his heart, performed a respectful salutation to his brother, and immediately went into the mountains.
He saw a śramaṇa,
young and handsome, sitting alone beneath a tree.
Sēngdà asked:
"Venerable one, for what reason did you decide to become a śramaṇa?"
That person had already attained the path of the
Yìngzhēn and knew in advance of countless kalpas of past and future affairs.
He said to Sēngdà:
"The Buddha said that those who love lust and debauchery
are like a person carrying a blazing torch and walking against the wind.
The flame gradually turns back, and if he does not drop the torch, the fire will burn his hands.
It is also like a crow holding meat in its beak.
Eagles and falcons pursue it to snatch the meat away.
If the crow does not relinquish the meat, calamity will reach its body and life.
It is because of this that I decided to become a śramaṇa.
Furthermore, it is like honey spread on a sharp knife.
A young child, greedy for sweetness, licks it with his tongue,
suffering the danger of having his tongue cut off.
The person of lust and debauchery merely pleases his foolish heart,
not considering the consequences thereafter.
He incurs the harm of burning his own body.
It is like the moth, greedy for the color of the flame, throwing itself into the lamp.
Its body is burned and boiled; what gain will it achieve?
Those bewildered by lust do not distinguish between good and evil.
They distance themselves from the wise and cling to the foolish, daily sinking into darkness.
They destroy their nation, exterminate the populace, and die, entering the hells.
When evil attachments lead to accomplished crimes, what use will repentance be then? These are the analogies."
Sēngdà bowed his head to the Venerable One's feet,
saying, "I wish to leave this defiled world and tread the path of purity.
I shall observe the precepts of the śramaṇa and hold them as my honor and fortune."
The Master said, "Wait a little."
Sēngdà said,
"I intend to enter the mountains for meditation and solitude."
The Master said,
"One who dwells in the mountains and marshes must study the constellations
to clearly know the time of day, and must always prepare and store water, fire, ghee, and honey.
The reason for this is
that thieves may come seeking water, fire, ghee, or honey.
If they arrive between midnight and dawn,
you must explain and give
the thieves what they desire. If you go against their wishes,
the thieves will immediately kill you."
Sēngdà replied, "Understood.
I shall reverently observe your kind instructions."
Then he retreated and entered the mountains.
His elder brother thought:
"My brother has become a śramaṇa and will never keep his wife.
Kuàijiàn is beautiful, and my heart is extremely pleased with her."
He arose, went to Kuàijiàn, and took a lute to play.
He sang a song of lust and debauchery, saying:
"The glorious turmeric
grows in the wilderness. If it passes its season unpicked, the flower is abandoned and rejected.
You are so abundantly lush and radiant, your beauty ever new.
Come and share joy with me."
Kuàijiàn realized his desire was for wicked deeds.
She answered him with a song:
"Mighty is my Master, the World Honored One, venerable to heaven and humans.
His disciples are pure and called śramaṇas.
To contemplate the truth is sagely; lust is the conduct of beasts.
I have received strict precepts and serve no two masters.
I will never give birth in lust; I would rather be cut into inches."
Fódà played a song of profound emotion and used languid words:
"My heart has long been attached to you. Therefore, I used a good matchmaker to ask for your name,
and went to a diviner to select an auspicious time.
I felt apprehensive and worried,
fearing you would not come.
Now that I behold your face, my heart is content.
If we do not unite in joy now, would that not be a waste?
This oath is firm. Good lady, why do you doubt?"
Kuàijiàn was anxious and fearful.
She replied with a song:
"The Buddha established rites and propriety, setting the order of seniority and status.
A brother's wife is as a daughter.
The husband's elder brother is as a father.
I personally observe the precepts and daily strive for perfection.
The truth is aligned with the sage; lust is merely
the behavior of insects and rodents.
Alas, elder brother, why
do you speak such words?"
The elder brother's heart was blinded by greed.
Kuàijiàn knew that his intent was firmly set and could not be shifted.
Kuàijiàn sang again:
"When a person lives in the world, they must keep far away from two things: unfilial conduct and licentious disorder, which violate the Buddha's precepts.
Heaven and the wise
all note such deviation."
Fódà sang:
"Your countenance shines brightly and radiantly.
Among the beauties of the whole world, is there any face like yours?
My heart delights in you, hence I crossed great mountains."
Kuàijiàn thought to herself:
"This man desires me for perverse and insane debauchery.
This will lead to great disaster.
I must speak of the repulsive discharge and impurity within the body,
and only then will he retreat."
Kuàijiàn spoke emphatically again:
"Sir, you desire my body, but what good is there in this body?
The head consists of nine bones joined together into a skull."
In this way, she fully described all impurities.
Fódà thought to himself:
"You remember your husband; why would you listen to me?
Only if I kill my younger brother will you then follow me."
He immediately went out to recruit men who were professional bandits.
He spoke to them, saying:
"Do you know that the slave boy kept by my family, who was registered in the six archives, has escaped and become a śramaṇa, and is now in the mountains?"
The thieves said, "We know him."
Fódà immediately gave them gold and silver.
"You kill the slave boy and quickly bring his head,
along with the clothes on his body, the Dharma robe he wears,
and the sandals on his feet, bring them all back.
I will reward you all with more gold and silver."
The thieves were delighted and said,
"Take as much as you need from us," and immediately went into the mountains.
They arrived at the dwelling of the younger brother and shouted:
"Śramaṇa! Come out quickly!"
His brother came out and said:
"Gentlemen, what do you seek?
I have water, fire, ghee, and honey available for food.
It is already past midnight."
The thieves said:
"We do not seek water or fire.
We do not ask for ghee
or honey. We only want your head now, to take it away."
When his brother heard this,
he became greatly frightened and, weeping, said:
"I am not the son of any elder or lord.
I abandoned the world for the Way and have no contention with the world.
I have only recently begun studying the Way and have not yet attained the smallest understanding. What good does killing me do?"
The thieves said:
"Come here for your head."
His brother said to the thieves:
"If you wish for treasure, I will write a letter to my brother, asking him to give you treasure."
The thieves said:
"Your brother ordered us to come and kill you now."
The brother said, "I am going to die now,
and it is because of that woman.
My Master previously warned me:
A person who dwells in lust
is like holding a blazing torch and walking against the wind.
If he does not let go of it, the fire will burn his hands."
As the day darkened, he recalled the Master's warning and wept.
He begged the thieves for one year of life.
The thieves said:
"We must take your head quickly."
His brother pleaded again:
"I beg you, do not kill me immediately.
First, cut off one of my thighs and place it before me."
The thieves cut off one thigh and placed it before him.
As the brother endured this pain,
a deity came to his side and said:
"Be absolutely fearless.
Hold fast to your mind."
you entered the realm of animals. People have slaughtered, cut, and sold
your flesh for more than one lifetime. You have experienced the Hells (Dìyù) and the hungry ghosts (Èguǐ)
all alike. This suffering and pain have not just begun today. The monastic Sēngdà appealed to
the deity of the sky (Tiān). "Please inform my Master." The deity (Tiān) immediately told the Master, saying:
"The bandits intend to kill him. Your disciple, being a man, is weeping sorrowfully, pleading for mercy, and wishes to see you." The Master immediately flew there and taught the Dharma (Fǎ), saying:
"Even the heavens, the earth, and Mount Xūmí will perish.
The seas will dry up and exhaust themselves, and seven suns will cause destruction. There is a wind under heaven, its name is Wéilán.
As soon as Wéilán rises, the mountains collide with each other, and even this wind eventually ceases. How much less is your small body worth counting?
You should only contemplate the Buddha (Fó).
The Buddha (Fó) constantly speaks of himself, saying: 'Prosperity must lead to decline, gathering must lead to separation, and glorious positions are hard to maintain.' The body is also like this."
Sēngdà then attained the Gōugǎng Dào (Path of Stream-Entry).
Again, one of his thighs was severed. He repeatedly contemplated the Master's precepts.
He again attained the Pínlái Dào (Path of Once-Returner). The bandit severed his left hand; he again contemplated the Master's precepts.
He attained the Bùhuán Dào (Path of Non-Returner). The bandit severed his right hand.
He again contemplated the Master's precepts and attained the Yìngzhēn Dào (Path of the Worthy). Immediately, he no longer feared the three evil paths (Sān È Dào).
He achieved mastery over life and death and had nothing left to fear. Sēngdà said:
"Bring me tree bark." They immediately stripped off bark and gave it to him.
Sēngdà took a twig to use as a brush. He pricked himself and used his own blood to write on the tree bark, saying:
"Elder Brother, I trust your daily life is peaceful and well at all times. When our two parents were alive, they entrusted me to you, Elder Brother.
You failed to accept this responsibility, violating and abandoning our parents' teachings. Because of a woman's beauty, blood relatives have mutilated each other.
Violating the kind teachings of our parents is unfilial (bù xiào). Mutilating and killing a person is inhumane (bù rén). Killing a single animal results in considerable sin.
How much more so for killing an Yìngzhēn (Arhat), committing five unstoppable (crimes)? Now I joyfully travel toward tranquility; from this moment, we are separated forever.
Strive! Strive! May you honor the True Path (Zhēndào)." He stretched his neck out two *chǐ* (feet) long. He spoke to the bandits, saying:
"Sirs, sever my head. It is just like cutting off a muddy clod."
"I fear you all will fall into the Hells (Dìyù)." The bandit stepped forward and severed his head. They took the clothes, staff, *xǐ* (sitting mat), and bowl (bō) from his body.
They brought them to the Elder Brother, who heavily rewarded the bandits with gold and silver. The Elder Brother took his younger brother's head and created a false body for it.
He placed the head upon it and clothed it with the robes. The staff, bowl, and sitting mat were all placed beside it.
He said to Kuàijiàn: "Your husband has returned. You may go greet him." Kuàijiàn was overjoyed and rushed to his location.
She saw him sitting with his eyes lowered, believing he was contemplating the Path (Dào). The wife (Qī) dared not call out, but prepared delicious food.
She waited for him to wake from his contemplation of the Path (Dào) before feeding him. Noon arrived, and he did not stir.
The wife (Qī) approached and said, "It is now noon, I fear it will be too late to eat." Surprised that he did not respond,
when she pulled his robe, the head detached, and the body scattered. The wife (Qī) stamped her feet and cried out:
"You were ultimately sitting because of me, leading to this cruel tragedy!" Grieving and enraged, she cried out to Heaven (Tiān); her liver and heart burst open.
Blood flowed from her mouth, and she instantly passed away. His adherence to the precepts was pure and white, impossible to defile, like the sky.
His saintly example was firm, impossible to move, like the earth. His true purity and high practice were impossible to reach, like the heavens (Tiān).
Before his life ended, all the deities (Zhū Tiān) sighed in admiration. They welcomed his soul and spirit to reside in Dāolì Tiān.
Enduring for a short moment, he gained heavenly glory that is difficult to exhaust.
The Elder Brother entered the meditation chamber (Chánshì). He saw his younger brother's head and body scattered.
His wife (Fù) had vomited blood and died. He cried out, saying:
"Alas! Alas! My heinous acts, perpetrated in defiance of Heaven (Tiān), have led to this result."
He immediately went to the location of the bandits and asked: "Did my younger brother have any last words before he died?"
The bandits showed him the written message. The language and analogies were mournful; having finished reading, his inner organs were choked with grief, and tears flowed freely.
"I violated the compassionate teachings given by our respected parents upon their death. Blood relatives have mutilated each other.
Moreover, I killed an Yìngzhēn (Arhat). (My wife) was so moved and separated (from him) that she died.
If I die, I will enter the Hells (Dìyù)." The King (Wáng) and the ministers and citizens (Chénmín) all wept. They praised and described his pure virtue, and interred his younger brother.
They established a pagoda (Tǎ) on the four corners of his chariot. Deities (Tiān), dragons (Lóng), ghosts (Guǐ), and spirits (Shén) crowded the sky.
Scattering flowers and burning incense, there was no one who was not choked with sobs. When they bade farewell to Dàkuàijiàn,
the people of the kingdom were deeply grieved. They sang praises of his virtue.
In Shèwèi Guó (the Kingdom of Śrāvastī), there was a certain elder (Zhǎngzhě).
His family was extremely wealthy. They gave birth to a baby boy.
His body was the color of gold. The physiognomist observed and examined him, seeing his extraordinary characteristics.
He immediately established a name for him. His name was Xiūyuènàtípó (Suvarṇadeva). On the day he was born,
a well of water naturally appeared in the household. It was eight *chǐ* (feet) square.
Drawing and using its water satisfied people's desires. Everything needed appeared immediately according to one's thoughts.
As the child grew older, his talent and skill became extensive. The elder (Zhǎngzhě) loved him. He did not dare to oppose his wishes.
And he thought this: "My son is handsome, his appearance is without peer. I must search and select a renowned maiden.
One whose golden countenance and subtle body resembles my son, to her I shall go and propose." He immediately hired various merchants and had them search everywhere for her.
At that time, in Yánpó Guó, there was a great elder (Zhǎngzhě).
He was just then having a daughter. Her name was Xiūbánà Bōpósu (Suvarṇabhāsā). She was extremely handsome; her body was the color of gold.
On the day she was first born,
there was also a well of water, eight *chǐ* square, that naturally appeared. What the well produced perfectly satisfied people's desires.
At that time, that elder (Zhǎngzhě), also thought to himself:
"My daughter is handsome. She must obtain a worthy gentleman,
like my daughter, only then shall I give her in marriage." At that time, the girl's fame spread far and wide to Shèwèi.
Jīntiān's reputation was also heard by the girl's family. Then the two elders (Zhǎngzhě) each harbored great joy.
They sought to form a marriage. After the marriage ceremony was completed,
they returned to Shèwèi. Then Jīntiān's family prepared a supreme offering.
They invited the Buddha (Fó) and the Saṅgha (Sēng) for offerings. On one day, the Buddha (Fó) accepted their invitation.
For the elder (Zhǎngzhě) and Jīntiān's couple, he extensively proclaimed the marvelous Dharma (Miàofǎ). They all attained the fruit of Xūtuóhuán (Stream-Entry).
The Buddha (Fó) returned to the Vihāra (Jīngshè). Jīntiān and his wife (Fù),
reported to their parents, seeking permission to leave home (Chūjiā) and become monastics. Their parents gave permission.
They both went to the place of the Buddha (Fó). The Buddha (Fó) said:
"Welcome, Bǐqiū (monk). Their hair and beard fell away naturally, and the Dharma robes appeared upon their bodies, and they instantly became Śhāmén (ascetics)."
Gradually, through his teaching and transformation, they both fully achieved Luóhàn (Arhatship). The Buddha (Fó) said:
"In the past, after the Pípóshī Fó (Vipaśyin Buddha) entered parinirvāṇa (miè),
his residual Dharma (Fǎ) remained in the world. There were Bǐqiū (monks) traveling and teaching, who arrived at a village.
There were various people, heroes, wise men, and elders (Zhǎngzhě). Seeing the Saṅgha (Sēng) arrive, they all eagerly offered supplies.
At that time, there was a certain couple. They were poor, hungry, and exhausted.
They constantly thought to themselves: 'When my father was alive, treasures were accumulated fully.

Now, my life is extremely poor and distressed. How bitter this is! Although we were wealthy then, we did not encounter this holy Saṅgha (Sēng). Now that we have encountered them, we have no money to make offerings.'
They wept sorrowfully. The wife (Fù) saw her husband weeping and spoke to him, saying:
'You may now go to our old house. Search and seek out money or treasure in the old storeroom, which we should use for offerings.'
The husband followed his wife's instructions. Going inside the old storeroom, he found one gold coin.
At that time, his wife (Fù) possessed a bright mirror. They immediately agreed wholeheartedly to use both for giving (bùshī).
They bought a new jar and filled it completely with clean water. They placed the gold coin into the water inside the jar,
placing the money on top. They carried it to the location of the Saṅgha (Sēng). They gave the offering (bùshī) with utmost sincerity.
At that time, the assembly of monks immediately accepted it. Each one took the water and used it to wash their bowls (bō). Others again took the water and drank it.
At that time, that couple, with joyous and cheerful hearts, died upon encountering sickness. They were born in Dāolì Tiān.
That poor person (couple) is this Jīntiān couple."
There was a merchant leader named Tiānhù.
He journeyed to the country of Lùqiúnà guó.
He constantly delighted in charity and giving.
He developed faith in the Buddha.
He intended to first enter the sea (for trade).
If he returned safely,
he vowed to hold a Five-Year Great Assembly in the Buddha's Dharma.
No one in the country, heavenly or human, failed to hear of this.
At that time, there was an Arhat Bhikṣuṇī.
She journeyed to that country with him.
She contemplated and observed,
and knew that Tiānhù would return safely and hold the Five-Year Great Assembly.
He would invite eighteen thousand Bhikṣus,
all of whom were Arhats.
The trainees were twice that number,
and the ordinary persons were countless.
She immediately saw the elder monk named Āsuōtuó,
who was merely an ordinary person but was extremely diligent.
She entered the Saṅghārāma and paid respects in sequence.
She addressed the elder, saying,
"Venerable Sir, you are truly not dignified."
The elder reflected in his heart,
"How is it that I am considered undignified?"
He immediately examined his body and saw that his hair and beard were long.
He immediately called a young monk to shave off his hair and beard.
The Bhikṣuṇī still said he was undignified.
The elder further called a young monk to wash and dye his robes.
The Nun returned to the Saṅghārāma
and deliberately said he was undignified.
The elder became angry and said,
"I have already shaved my hair and beard, and washed and dyed my robes.
Why do you call me undignified?"
The Bhikṣuṇī said,
"In the Buddha’s Dharma, achieving the Four Fruits is true ornamentation (dignity).
Venerable Sir, have you heard about the merchant leader Tiānhù making the lion's roar regarding the Five-Year Great Assembly?"
He answered, "I have heard."
"Venerable Sir, you are an ordinary person serving as the highest elder,
receiving offerings first among the assembly of Arhats.
Is this dignity?"
The elder then became enlightened and wept bitterly in distress.
The Bhikṣuṇī said,
"Why are you weeping?"
He replied,
"Sister,
I am now old and incapable of achieving anything."
The Bhikṣuṇī said,
"The Tathāgata's Dharma is visible and does not depend on time (age).
Venerable Sir, you may go to Nàduōpóduō sì
to meet with the Bhikṣu Yōupōjíduō.
This Bhikṣu was prophesied by the Buddha:
‘He is the foremost among my disciples in teaching and transforming beings.’"
At that time, the elder Bhikṣu arrived.
Yōupōjíduō came out to welcome him and said,
"Venerable Sir,
please wash your feet and rest."
He replied,
"I have not washed my feet yet.
I wish to see Yōupōjíduō."
At that time, Yōupōjíduō’s disciple said,
"Venerable Sir,
this person who came out to welcome you
is Yōupōjíduō."
Immediately, he was greatly pleased and washed his feet.
Yōupōjíduō then instructed and transformed him.
He sought out donors for him,
providing bathing, food, and various offerings.
He instructed the Vaināyaka, saying,
"Now, there is a Bhikṣu who has attained the two kinds of liberation entering the meditation chamber."
Even up to the eighteen thousand Arhats, all entered the meditation chambers.
At that time, the Bhikṣu entered and sat in the dwelling place of the First Dhyāna.
Then Yōupōjíduō entered the Samādhi of Light of Fire.
Likewise, the eighteen thousand Arhats
all entered the Samādhi of Light of Fire.
The Bhikṣu saw this and his heart was filled with joy.
Yōupōjíduō taught and preached the Dharma.
The Bhikṣu diligently reflected and attained the fruit of Arhatship.
He returned to his original country.
The Arhat Bhikṣuṇī
went to the Saṅghārāma, bowed, and said,
"Today, Venerable Sir, you are dignified!"
He replied,
"It is due to your power, Sister."
When the Five-Year Great Assembly was held,
Tiānhù asked the elder,
"The World-Honored One spoke various Dharmas.
What the elder speaks is no different from them."
The elder replied,
"In the past, ninety-one *kalpas* ago,
we were merchant leaders who entered the sea to gather treasures.
We vowed to fill the ship,
and return to Yánfútí.
At that time, we encountered a great wind that blew the ship onto a sea of sand.
We created a sand stupa for Pípóshī Fó
