and made offerings to it with jewels.
At that time, certain *devas* showed me the way, saying,
‘Exactly seven days from now, a great flood will come,
and it will float your ship into Yánfútí.’
When seven days had passed,
it happened exactly as the *devas* said.
Because of the condition of that sand stupa,
for ninety-one *kalpas* we have not fallen into evil destinies.
Now I have attained the fruit of Arhatship.
Since you are able to make offerings
to so many people in the domain of the Three Jewels,
I predict that the suffering of birth and death is boundless (for those who do not follow this path).
You should now renounce home life."
Tiānhù obeyed the command and immediately became a Śramaṇa.
He attained the path of Arhatship.
In the country of Bāliánfú guó there was a merchant leader
named Xūtuónà.
When the being in the intermediate state came and entered his mother's womb,
it immediately caused his mother to be upright, gentle, and mild,
without any false thoughts.
The husband inquired of his master.
The master replied,
"You are carrying an excellent and virtuous child."
Later, a son was born,
named Xiūluótuó.
As he gradually grew older,
he sought to renounce home life.
His parents immediately granted permission.
He diligently practiced vigor
and attained the fruit of Arhatship.
The Bhikṣu Chàmó became gravely ill in body
and suffered great pain.
The Bhikṣu Tuósuō was the caregiver for the sick monk.
At that time, all the elders commanded the Bhikṣu Tuósuō
to preach the Dharma of the Five Aggregates of Grasping to the sick monk.
He went back and forth twice.
Bhikṣu Chàmó said to Bhikṣu Tuósuō,
"Why bother you to rush back and forth?
Bring a staff; I will lean on it myself
and go to those elders."
The elders saw Chàmó leaning on a staff and approaching from afar.
They personally spread a seat for him and asked him to sit down.
They proceeded to fully discuss past discourses.
Bhikṣu Chàmó then preached the Dharma.
At that time, the elders
removed dust and separated from defilement, attaining the purity of the Dharma Eye.
Bhikṣu Chàmó, without arising any mental outflows,
attained liberation of mind.
Formerly, the Buddha was in Shèwèi guó.
A disciple named Jūtí,
retreated from the fruit of Arhatship six times.
When he reached the seventh instance,
he personally realized and verified (the state).
Yet, fearing he would retreat again,
he immediately sought a sharp sword and ended his own life.
At this time, Mó Bōxún
sought to find out where the Bhikṣu's consciousness was reborn,
but he could not know.
He then went to ask the Buddha.
The World-Honored One proclaimed,
"Bhikṣu Jūtí has already attained *Nirvāṇa*.
His spiritual consciousness resides in emptiness and is united with emptiness."
When the wicked Māra heard this, his heart was filled with intense grief.
He threw his entire body into a pool of blue lotuses to bathe.
The pool water boiled up, and the nature of the water completely perished.
Because of this event, all the Bhikṣus
diligently practiced vigor, fearing they might retreat again.
In the past, there was a kingdom.
Its name was Duōmóluó.
Seven *lǐ* away from the city was a *jīngshè* (monastery).
Five hundred *shāmén* (monks) constantly resided there.
They praised the scriptures and practiced the Way.
There was an elder *bǐqiū* (monk).
Named Móhēlú.
He was ignorant and dull.
The five hundred practitioners collectively tried to teach him.
Over several years, he could not learn a single *jì* (verse).
The community collectively slighted him.
They did not bring him to gatherings but kept him always guarding the *jīngshè*.
They instructed him to sweep and clean.
Later, the king invited all the practitioners.
To enter the palace and receive offerings.
The *bǐqiū* Móhēlú thought to himself,
"I have been born into the world so ignorant and dull.
I do not know even one verse, and people treat me with contempt.
What is the point of living like this?"
He immediately took a rope and went to a large tree in the back garden.
Intending to hang himself.
The Fó (Buddha) saw this from afar with his spiritual eye.
He transformed himself into a tree spirit, appearing as a half-bodied human.
And rebuked him, saying,
"Halt, *bǐqiū*!
Why are you doing this?"
Móhēlú immediately recounted his suffering in detail.
The transformed spirit admonished him, saying,
"You must not do this.
First, listen to my words.
In the time of Jiāshè Fó,
you were a *Sānzàng shāmén*.
You had five hundred disciples.
You relied on your great wisdom to slight and disdain others.
You were stingy with the meaning of the scriptures and never instructed them.
Therefore, in every life you have been born, your faculties have been dull and obscured.
You should only blame yourself; why treat yourself as contemptible?"
Thereupon, the Shìzūn (World-Honored One) immediately revealed his radiant form and spoke a wondrous verse for him.
At that time, Móhēlú bowed his head at the Fó's feet.
Pondering the meaning of the verse, he immediately entered samādhi.
Swiftly, in the presence of the Fó, he attained the path of an Luóhàn.
He spontaneously recalled the countless deeds of his past lives.
The multitude of scriptures of the *Sānzàng* immediately became clear in his mind.
The Fó said to Móhēlú,
"Put on your robes and take your alms bowl to eat in the royal palace.
Sit in the highest seat above the five hundred practitioners.
These practitioners are your five hundred disciples from a previous life.
You must speak the Dharma for them again so they can attain the stages of the Way.
Also, ensure the king clearly believes in retribution and merit."
He immediately accepted the instruction.
He entered the royal palace.
And sat in the highest seat.
The hearts of the assembly were angered and wondered why this was so.
Protecting the king's feelings, none dared to call him out or dismiss him.
They thought of his foolish ignorance, unable to recite the blessings (*dáchèn*).
Their hearts were wearied by him.
The king then served the food, pouring and arranging it himself.
Móhēlú immediately recited the *dáchèn* for him.
His voice was like thunder, and the pure verses descended in torrents.
The practitioners seated there were astonished, frightened, and repented.
All attained Luóhànship.
When he spoke the Dharma for the king, there was no one who did not understand and become enlightened.
The ministers and all the officials,
all attained Xūtuóhuán.
Zhū Lípántè's elder brother said,
"If you cannot uphold the precepts, return and be a layman (*báiyī*)."
Pántè went to the gates of Qíhuán, weeping tears.
The Fó said to him,
"Why are you grieving?"
He answered with his brother's words.
The Fó said,
"Do not fear.
I attained the unsurpassed Right Enlightenment (zhèngjué) of the Lord.
It was not through your brother."
He led Pántè by the hand.
He went to a quiet room and taught him to hold a broom and recite the word.
Pántè would recite "sweeping" and forget "broom," or recite "broom" and forget "sweeping."
After several days, "sweeping" and "broom" were combined and renamed "removing defilement."
Pántè contemplated,
"If ash, dirt, tile, and stone are removed, then it is pure.
Karmic bonds (*jiéfù*) are defilement.
Wisdom is capable of removing them.
Now I use the broom of wisdom to sweep,
removing all karmic bonds (*jiéfù*)."
The Fó was in the state of Shèwèi.
There was a *bǐqiū* named Pántè.
He had recently entered the monastic life and was inherently dull and ignorant.
The Fó ordered five hundred Luóhàn to teach him daily.
Within three years, he could not learn a single verse.
The four classes (monks, nuns, laymen, laywomen) in the kingdom knew of his foolish ignorance.
The Fó pitied him.
He immediately summoned him forward.
And imparted a verse to him:
"Guard the mouth, control the intention, let the body not transgress.
One who practices thus attains deliverance from the world."
Pántè was moved by the Fó’s compassionate grace.
With a joyful and awakened heart, he recited the verse readily.
The Fó told him,
"You are now old, and only now have you mastered one verse.
Everyone knows this.
It is not enough to be remarkable.
Now I shall explain its meaning for you.
The one heart, the three actions of the body, the four of the mouth, the three of the mind—these are the causes.
Observe their arising and examine their cessation.
The Three Realms and the Five Paths revolve endlessly.
Through them one ascends to heaven.
Through them one falls into the abyss, and through them one attains the Way.
Níhuán (Nirvana) comes naturally."
He then explained the measureless subtle Dharma in detail for him.
Suddenly, his mind opened, and he attained the path of a Luóhàn.
At that time, there were five hundred *bǐqiūní* (nuns).
Who had a separate *jīngshè*.
The Fó ordered them to send a *bǐqiū* to speak the scriptural Dharma for them.
The next day, it was Pántè's turn to go.
When the nuns heard this,
they all smiled in anticipation.
"When he comes tomorrow, we will recite his verse back to him.
To make him ashamed and speechless."
The next day, Pántè went there.
All the nuns, young and old, came out to bow and exchanged glances, laughing.
After sitting down, food was served.
After eating, they washed their mouths.
And requested that he speak the Dharma.
Pántè immediately ascended the high seat.
He expressed shame and humility, saying,
"I have meager virtue and inferior talent.
I was not yet a *shāmén*.
I was inherently stubborn and dull.
What I have learned is not much.
I know only one verse.
I roughly understand its meaning.
I shall now explain it.
I wish you would all listen quietly."
The young *bǐqiūní* wanted to recite the verse back to him,
but their mouths could not open.
They were shocked and fearful, blaming themselves, bowing their heads, and repenting their faults.
Pántè then, just as the Fó had explained,
separated and detailed everything:
the causes of body and mind,
merit and retribution, inner and outer, ascension to heaven and attainment of the Way,
the method of focusing the spirit and cutting off thought to enter concentration (*dìng*).
Immediately, the nuns who heard his talk
were greatly surprised by his difference and rejoiced wholeheartedly.
All attained the path of a Luóhàn.
Later, King Bōsīnì
invited the Fó and the Saṅgha to an assembly in the main palace hall.
The Fó wished to display Pántè's divine power.
He gave him his alms bowl and instructed him to hold it and follow behind him.
The gatekeeper recognized him and held him back, refusing him entry.
"You, as a *shāmén*, do not understand a single verse.
Why are you accepting this invitation?
I, being a layman,
still know verses.
How much more so should a *shāmén*?
Since you possess no wisdom,
making an offering to you is useless.
You do not need to enter the gate."
Pántè immediately stopped outside the gate.
The Fó was seated on the platform.
After the water libation was finished,
Pántè held up the bowl, extended his arm, and offered it to the Fó from afar.
The king, the ministers, the royal consorts, and the crown prince,
the four classes of the assembly,
saw the arm come in but did not see his form, and were astonished, asking the Fó,
"Whose arm is this?"
The Fó said,
"It is the arm of the virtuous *bǐqiū* Pántè."
The King said, "He has attained the Way.
I instructed him to hold the bowl a moment ago,
but the gatekeeper did not allow him to enter.
That is why he extended his arm to offer me the bowl."
He was then invited in, his divine majesty far surpassing the ordinary.
The king addressed the Fó, saying,
"I heard that the Venerable Pántè was inherently dull and ignorant.
He only knows one verse.
By what means did he attain the Way?"
The Fó told the king,
"Learning need not be much; practice is supreme.
The virtuous Pántè understood the meaning of one verse.
His refined principle penetrated the spirit.
His body, mouth, and mind are still and pure like heavenly gold.
If a person learns much but does not practice, they merely waste their consciousness and thought.
What benefit is there in that?"
Thereupon, the Shìzūn
immediately spoke a verse, saying:
"Though one recites a thousand chapters, if the meaning is not right, it is not equal to one essential point
which, when heard, can extinguish wrong thoughts. Though one recites a thousand words, if they are meaningless, what benefit is there?
It is not equal to one meaningful saying which, when heard and practiced, leads to deliverance. Though one recites many scriptures
without understanding, what benefit is there? Understanding one Dharma phrase and practicing it leads to the attainment of the Way."
Having heard this same verse,
two hundred *bǐqiū* attained the path of a Luóhàn.
The king, the ministers, the royal consorts, and the crown prince,
none were without joy.
Pógāpó.
Resided in Shèwèichéng,
at Qíshù Jǐgūdú Yuán.
At that time, many Bǐqiū,
when the time came, donned their robes and took their bowls,
entering Shèwèichéng to seek alms.
They heard that outside the palace gate of King Bōsīnì, there were many common people,
holding hands, weeping and shouting,
and they were saying this:
“In this kingdom, there is a great evil bandit,
named Yāngjúmàn.
He kills people, is tyrannical, and without compassion.
Villages and settlements cannot find peace.
He kills people and takes one finger from each to make a garland.
For this reason, he is named Yāngjúmàn.
We wish the King would subdue this man.”
After the Bǐqiū had eaten,
they went to the Buddha Shìzūn and fully reported the above matters.
The Buddha then went toward that area.
At that time, there were many people,
carrying firewood and grass,
as well as farmers,
and travelers,
who encountered the Shìzūn.
They spoke to the Shìzūn, saying:
“Shāmén, do not travel this road.
The reason is this:
On this road there is Yāngjúmàn.
He kills people without compassion.
All cities, towns, and villages of living beings are harmed by that person.
Since he kills people,
he uses their fingers to make a garland.
We fear he will trouble the Shìzūn.”
At that time, the Buddha Shìzūn continued to advance.
At that time, Yāngjúmàn saw the Shìzūn approaching from afar.
Having seen him, he immediately thought:
“This Shāmén has come alone, without companions.
I should kill him.”
At that time, Yāngjúmàn
immediately drew the sword at his waist and went toward the Buddha.
The Shìzūn, seeing him from afar, turned and retraced his path.
Then Yāngjúmàn ran, pursuing the Shìzūn.
He exerted all his strength, intending to reach the Shìzūn,
but he could not reach him.
Then Yāngjúmàn thought:
“When I run, I can overtake elephants,
I can also catch horses,
I can also catch chariots, and I can catch fierce, evil oxen.
I can also catch people.
However, this Shāmén does not walk quickly,
yet even exerting all my strength, I cannot reach him.”
Then Yāngjúmàn called out to the Shìzūn from afar, saying:
“Stop! Stop, Shāmén!”
The Shìzūn replied:
“I have long since stopped,
but you have not stopped.”
Then Yāngjúmàn thought:
“I am committing evil deeds.”
He immediately cast away the sword at his waist,
bowed down with his five limbs (prostrated),
and sought to become a Shāmén and receive the full precepts.
The Buddha said:
“Welcome, Bǐqiū.”
His hair and beard spontaneously fell off, just as if shaved.
The clothing he wore transformed into a *jiāshā*.
The Buddha preached the Dharma for him, and he attained the status of an Āluóhàn.
At that time, King Bōsīnì assembled the four divisions of the army.
He left Shèwèichéng,
intending to go and kill that bandit Yāngjúmàn.
He first passed by the Shìzūn and fully reported the situation to the Buddha.
The Shìzūn said:
“If the King were to now see Yāngjúmàn,
having shaved his hair and beard and wearing the three Dharma robes,
having left home to study the Way with firm faith,
how would the King treat him?”
The King replied:
“If I were to treat him, I would greet him, salute him, and have no intention to harm him.
But that man is fierce and evil, without compassion.
How could he possibly practice the conduct of a Shāmén?”
At that time, Yāngjúmàn was not far from the Buddha.
He was sitting cross-legged, his body straight, his mind focused, concentrating his mindfulness forward.
Then the Buddha raised his hand and pointed out the location of Yāngjúmàn.
When Bōsīnì saw Yāngjúmàn,
he was instantly filled with terror, and the hairs on his robes stood up.
The Buddha said: “Do not fear.
Go to him yourself, and you should speak with the King.”
Then King Bōsīnì
went to the place where Yāngjúmàn was.
Having arrived, he bowed his head and face to his feet and stood to one side.
Then King Bōsīnì asked Yāngjúmàn:
“Venerable Yāngjúmàn,
what is your name now?”
Yāngjúmàn replied:
“Great King, my name is Gāqú.
My mother’s name is Mànduōyēní.”
The King replied:
“You exert yourself well and progress.
I shall now, for the remainder of my life,
make offerings to the Venerable Gāqú.
I will spare nothing in providing robes, food, medicine for illness, and bedding and sleeping gear.
I shall always protect you by the Dharma.”
Then King Bōsīnì
bowed his head and face to the feet (of Yāngjúmàn) and circumambulated him three times.
He then went to the Shìzūn and said:
“Shìzūn, what could not be subdued,
you were able to subdue.”
“Though some people have severed all afflictions,
they still exhibit traces of affliction in their body and speech.
When ordinary people see or hear this, they develop impure thoughts.
For example, Mìpóhézhà Āluóhàn,
for five hundred lifetimes, was among monkeys.
Now, although he has attained the Way, he still leaps and jumps among trees.
When foolish people see this, they immediately give rise to disdain.
Furthermore, Bìlínggāpócuō Āluóhàn,
for five hundred lifetimes, was born among the Brahmins.
He developed a habit of contemptuous speech.
Now, although he has attained the Way,
he still speaks to the Héng Shuǐshén, saying:
‘Stop flowing, little slave girl!’
The Héng Shuǐshén became angry,
and went to the Buddha to complain.
The Buddha instructed him to repent.
Yet, he still called her a ‘little slave girl.’
The Buddha does not have such habits.
For instance, a Brahmin with an evil mouth,
at one time, cursed the Buddha with five hundred insults, but the Buddha showed no sign of anger.
The Brahmin's heart was then pleased.
Immediately thereafter, at another time, he praised the Buddha with five hundred good things.
The Buddha also showed no sign of joy.
It should be known that the Buddha’s habitual traces of affliction are exhausted,
and therefore, good and evil are treated without distinction.”
The Buddha was in the Bamboo Grove (Zhúyuán) in Luóyuèqí.
At that time, there were four brothers, sons of a great clan.
Their parents had died young, and they were disputing over the family property.
They saw Shèlìfú (舍利弗) and happily asked him,
"We wish you would speak about this so that we will no longer dispute."
Shèlìfú said,
"Excellent.
My great teacher, the Buddha, is the most honored in the Three Realms (Sānjiè).
You all follow me.
When we return to the Buddha's residence,
you will surely gain understanding."
They followed Shèlìfú back.
The Buddha saw the four men from afar and smiled, emitting a five-colored light.
The four men paid reverence to the Buddha and said,
"We are ignorant and foolish.
We pray that the Buddha will explain this
so that we may no longer dispute."
In the past, there was a king,
whose title was Wéilóu (惟婁).
His body was afflicted with sickness.
He welcomed a doctor to examine him.
The prescribed medicine required lion's milk (shīzi rǔ).
The king immediately put out a reward.
Whoever obtained it would have land divided and enfeoffed to them,
and the king would give his younger daughter in marriage.
At that time, a poor man petitioned, saying
he could obtain it. The king immediately consented.
This person, being skillful, first tracked the location of the lion.
He slaughtered a sheep and brought several *hú* of grape wine.
He traveled to that mountain.
Waiting until the lion went out,
he slaughtered the sheep
and placed it, along with the grape wine, where the lion lived.
When the lion saw the wine and meat, it immediately ate and drank, became heavily drunk, and lay down.
The man went forward, seized the milk, and returned joyfully.
Before reaching his own kingdom,
he stayed overnight in a village when evening fell.
There was an Arhat (Luóhàn) also staying there.
This man, in his pursuit of the lion,
had traversed dangerous paths.
His body was utterly exhausted, and he slept,
completely unaware of anything.
The holy man observed the six consciousnesses (liù shí) within the sleeping man's body,
each arguing for its own merit.
The foot spirit said,
"It is due to me walking here that the milk was obtained."
The hand spirit replied,
"It is due to my hand seizing and taking it."
The eye spirit replied,
“It is due to me seeing it.”
The ear spirit replied,
“It is due to me hearing the king request the milk that I brought you all here.”
The tongue spirit (shé shén) immediately said,
“You all compete and dispute in vain.
This merit belongs to me.
Life and death now rest with me.”
This man brought the milk to the king's residence,
and reported,
"I have already obtained the lion's milk; it is outside."
The king said,
"Regardless of whether it is true or false, bring it in."
When the king saw the milk,
the tongue immediately said,
"This is not lion's milk.
It is merely donkey's milk."
When the king heard this, he became extremely angry and said,
"I sent you to retrieve lion's milk,
but you brought donkey's milk!"
He immediately intended to kill the man.
The holy man (Dàorén) who had lodged with him at that time
immediately used his divine power (shénzú)
and arrived before the king, reporting,
"This is truly lion's milk.
I stayed overnight with this person in the village,
and I saw that within his body,
the six faculties were arguing over the merit of the effort.
The tongue said,
'I will betray you all.'
Now, the result is exactly this.
Your Majesty, simply use the milk to compound the medicine,
and your illness will certainly be cured."
The king immediately believed the Arhat's (Āluóhàn) words,
used the milk to compound the medicine, and gave his daughter in marriage to the man,
and enfeoffed and appointed him according to the original promise.
The holy man told the king,
"If the consciousnesses within one person's own body contradict each other,
how much more so among other people?"
The man who had obtained the milk at that time,
having benefited from the grace of the holy man,
requested to become a Śramaṇa (Shāmé),
gained understanding, and achieved the path of the Arhat (Luóhàn Dào).
The king was also delighted, accepted the Five Precepts (Wǔjiè),
and attained the path of the Srota-āpanna (Xūtuóhuán Dào).
The four men heard this and gained understanding.
They then followed the Buddha and begged to become Bhikṣus (Bǐqiū).
The Buddha silently placed his hand on their heads.
Their hair fell away, the *jiāshā* appeared on their bodies,
their fetters were untied, and defilements were removed.
Ānán (阿難) said,
"What former merit did these four men have
that upon hearing the scripture they immediately gained understanding
and quickly attained Arhatship?"
The Buddha said,
"In the past, during the time of Mófù Fó (摩父佛),
Shèlìfú was a Bhikṣu.
These four men were traveling merchants.
Together, they presented a *jiāshā* to Shèlìfú.
Shèlìfú made a vow and prayed,
that you gentlemen, in future lives, would quickly attain salvation (dùtuō).
Today, they have attained liberation (jiětuō) through Shèlìfú."
There was a man
who left home under the True Dharma (Zhèngfǎ).
He was capable of attending to needs.
In all the monasteries he visited, the various Bhikṣus
made him serve them.
Later, he became increasingly exhausted.
He thought to himself,
"Who can preach the Dharma and teach and transform me?"
He heard that in the kingdom of Móntóuluó (摩偷羅),
there was Yōupō Jítuō (優波笈多),
who had been prophesied by the Buddha
to be the foremost among the later disciples.
He went and paid reverence to him, joining his palms and saying,
"Great Virtuous One (Dàdé),
please perform the great work of the Buddha (Fóshì) and teach the Dharma for me."
Yōupō Jítuō said,
"If you can follow my instruction, then I will teach the Dharma for you."
He replied, "I can."
Yōupō Jítuō asked,
"In the Nàduōpóduō (那多婆哆) Monastery,
how many members of the Saṅgha (Zòngsēng) are there?
You must first serve the Saṅgha."
He replied,
"There are eighteen thousand Arhats,
the trainees are double that number,
and the diligently striving commoners (fánfū) are innumerable."
At that time, that Bhikṣu
immediately attended to
all the members of the Saṅgha,
enabling the entire Saṅgha to focus purely on cultivating the path.
The attending Bhikṣu rose early at that time,
put on his robes, took his bowl, and entered the kingdom of Móntóuluó.
A respected elder (zhǎngzhě) came out in the morning and met him.
The elder thought,
"I have never seen this before,"
and upon seeing him, paid reverence to his head and feet.
He asked,
"Great Virtuous One,
where have you come from, whether far or near, and for what purpose?"
He replied,
"I came from the Eastern Kingdom
to Yōupō Jítuō's residence,
wishing to hear the Dharma.
However, Yōupō Jítuō instructed me to attend to the Saṅgha.
I currently do not know who among the people of Móntóuluó are diligently striving and who are not."
The elder said,
"You do not need to concern yourself with this matter now.
I will attend to the Saṅgha on your behalf, providing all food, clothing, and medicine."
The Bhikṣu and the elder
together procured the food and drink, etc.,
and made offerings to the Saṅgha.
During the three months of the retreat (Ānjū), the Bhikṣu cultivated the path and attained the fruition of the path (dàoguǒ) due to these offerings.
In the kingdom of Móntóuluó,
there was a man
who petitioned his parents, seeking to leave home.
He went to Yōupō Jítuō's residence,
reverently bowed and reported,
"Great Virtuous One,
may I become a Bhikṣu?"
Yōupō Jítuō saw that he was
bound by attachment to his body.
He said to him, "Welcome!
I will let you leave home."
Happily, the man paid reverence to his feet
and asked permission to return home briefly first.
While on the road, he pondered:
"If I reach home,
I might encounter hindrance."
That evening, he stayed overnight in a shrine along the way. Yōupō Jítuō transformed himself into two Rākṣasas (Luóchà).
One carried a corpse,
and the other was empty-handed.
They both entered the shrine.
They mutually claimed, "I caught it,"
and disputed the matter without resolution.
They then asked this man,
"Who brought the corpse?"
This man thought,
"I must not speak falsely,"
and told them the truth.
The empty-handed demon immediately grabbed his arm and brought it toward its mouth, intending to eat it.
The demon carrying the corpse helped him escape.
He barely managed to get away.
This lasted for quite a while until sunrise.
Two days later, he returned to Jítuō's residence,
left home to practice the path,
diligently and assiduously cultivated,
and attained the fruition of Arhatship (Āluóhàn Guǒ).
In the past, there was a multitude of people.
They were on the side of the great river (Jiāngshuǐ).
They were harmed by the water.
The common people had no limit to their misfortune.
Among them, only one in ten thousand achieved deliverance.
The person who achieved deliverance from the deep water
went to the place of the Fó (Buddha)
and requested to become a Shāmén.
The Fó then permitted this, allowing him to be on the path.
Internally, he did not contemplate, thinking he had left misfortune behind.
The Fó preached the Dharma for him and urged him to practice the Way.
At that time, that Bǐqiū felt internal shame.
He understood and realized that all ten thousand things are impermanent (wúcháng).
His heart opened, his mind understood, and he became detached and free of thought (wúxiǎng).
Right there, before the Fó,
he attained Āluóhàn.
In the time of Kéyè Fó,
there were two brothers.
Both became Shāmén.
The elder brother upheld the precepts, practiced meditation (zuòchán), and wholeheartedly sought the Way,
but he did not practice dāna (bùshī).
The younger brother practiced dāna and cultivated merit,
but was fond of violating the precepts.
The elder brother left home under Shìjiā and attained the path of the Arhat (Luóhàn Dào).
However, his clothing was inadequate, and he was constantly hungry.
The younger brother was born into the form of an elephant.
This elephant possessed great strength
and was able to repel enemies.
He was beloved by the Wáng (King).
Gold, silver, treasures, and jewels adorned his body (yīngluò).
Several hundred households were enfeoffed
to supply this elephant,
providing whatever he required.
At that time, the elder brother Bǐqiū encountered a great famine in the world.
He traveled around begging for food for seven days but received nothing.
Finally, he obtained a little coarse food,
barely enough to sustain his life.
He already knew that this elephant was his brother from a previous life.
He then went to the elephant
and grabbed the elephant's ear with his hand,
and spoke to it, saying:
"In the past, both you and I were culpable."
The elephant reflected on the Bǐqiū’s words,
and immediately recognized its past lives (sùmìng).
Seeing the karmic conditions of its previous existence,
it became distressed and sorrowful and refused to eat.
The elephant keepers were afraid
and went to inform the Wáng:
“The elephant is not eating or drinking.
We do not know the reason.”
The Wáng asked the elephant keepers:
“Has anyone previously offended this elephant?”
The elephant keepers replied:
“There was no other unusual person,
only one Shāmén who came close to the elephant,
and left after a moment.”
The Wáng immediately dispatched men to search for and find the Shāmén.
He questioned him, saying:
“What did you say when you went to my elephant?”
The Shāmén replied:
“I told the elephant,
‘Both you and I were culpable.’”
The Shāmén then fully explained the matter to the Wáng as detailed above.
The Wáng’s mind was enlightened.
He immediately released the Shāmén
and ordered him to return to his dwelling.
In the kingdom of Píshèlǐ,
there were five hundred blind men.
They lived by begging.
At that time, they heard that the Fó had appeared in the world.
Those who merely saw him,
the crippled, the disabled, and those suffering from a hundred ailments, all received healing and relief.
He gave clothing and food to the poor,
and those burdened by anxiety, sorrow, and suffering
were all able to find release and freedom.
The blind men consulted together, saying:
“Our accumulated sins and bitter suffering are especially heavy.
If we can meet the Fó, we will certainly be saved and assisted.”
They then went together to beg,
each managing to obtain one gold coin (jīnqián).
They used this to hire someone, enough money to reach that place.
After begging for some time, each person acquired one coin.
They called out to those around them: “Who will lead us to Shèwèi?”
They offered five hundred gold coins to pay for the effort.
At that time, a man came forward.
Together, they discussed the payment and gave him the money.
He spoke to the blind men:
“Go on, pulling one another along.”
He led them easily at the front.
He brought them to Mójí
and abandoned the blind men,
leaving them in an empty marshland.
The blind men did not know in which country they were.
Holding hands, they trampled on someone else’s field,
damaging the seedlings and grain.
The field owner saw this and became fiercely angry.
He spoke harshly and beat them.
The beggars pleaded for mercy and fully explained the events described above.
The Elder (Zhàngzhě) took pity on them.
He ordered a messenger to lead them to Shèwèi.
Just as they arrived in that country,
they heard that the Shìzūn (World-Honored One) had already gone toward the country of Mójíti.
The messenger led them toward the country of Mójí.
The blind men respected the Fó and were intent on seeing him.
Although their physical eyes were closed, their mind’s eye already perceived him.
Their joyful resolve prevented them from feeling fatigue.
Having reached Mójí,
they again heard that the Shìzūn had already returned to Shèwèi.
They chased him like this, passing through seven round trips in total.
At that time, the Rúlái (Tathāgata) observed that the good roots of the blind men had matured.
He then stopped and waited for them.
The Fó’s light touched their bodies,
and instantly, both their eyes became clear and bright.
They were finally able to see the Rúlái, surrounded by the four assemblies.
His body shone brilliantly like a mountain of purple gold.
They went forward to the place of the Fó and threw their five limbs to the ground.
They performed the ritual of worship to the Fó.
With different mouths but the same voice,
they addressed the Fó, saying:
“We humbly pray that you show us mercy,
and permit us to join the ranks of the Way.”
The Fó said:
“Welcome, Bǐqiū.”
Their beards and hair spontaneously fell away, and the Dharma robes appeared upon their bodies.
He then preached the Dharma again for them,
and they attained Āluóhàn.
Inside Śàwèichéng.
There was a Cūndáluó child who lived by removing excrement.
At that time, the Shìzūn entered the city for alms.
He then came to that man's house.
The laborer who removed the excrement immediately avoided him by fleeing to another alley.
The Rúlái followed him.
That man thought to himself:
“I am carrying impure excrement.
How can I manage to meet the Shìzūn today?”
He then went to a marsh.
The Fó called out from afar, saying:
“I have come for you.”
The man replied, saying:
“I dare not approach you.
I wonder what teachings or admonitions the Shìzūn has for me,
that you could compassionately speak with a sinner.”
The Shìzūn announced, saying:
“I wish to save you and make you a Shāmén.”
That man reported to the Fó:
“Can beings from the hells or animals also attain the Dào?”
The Fó said:
“My emergence in the world now
is precisely for the sake of those suffering from sin.”
He took hold of the man's hand,
and ascended into the void.
They reached the side of the Héng River.
He bathed the man’s body.
Then they returned to Qíhuán.
He commanded the Bǐqiū:
“Ordain him as a Shāmén.”
That man encouraged himself, diligently progressing daily.
In less than ten days, he attained the fruition of Sūtuóhuán,
and eventually reached the fruition of Luóhàn.
His Six Supernatural Powers were perfectly clear, and he could emerge and vanish freely.
He went to a large square stone, sat in the center of it, mending his old robe.
The King heard that the Fó had ordained the Cūndáluó child.
He recalled that the Fó came from the distinguished noble clan of the Shì lineage,
and that His attendant disciples all came from the Four Great Castes.
They entered the palace,
received offerings and donations from the faithful,
performed the full prostration,
and bowed by touching the feet.
“Now I hear the Rúlái has ordained a Cūndáluó.
How can I reverence him?
I must now go and admonish the Rúlái.”
Before he arrived,
he saw the Bhīkṣu seated before him on the large square stone.
Five hundred Pure Abode Devas surrounded him, bowing and paying homage.
The King stepped forward and spoke, saying:
“Please trouble yourself to report to the Shìzūn
that King Bōsīnì wishes to meet the Shìzūn.”
The Bhīkṣu, having heard this, immediately vanished into the stone.
He emerged from the monastery and reported everything fully to the Fó.
The Fó said, “He knows the right time.”
The Bhīkṣu returned, emerging from the stone,
and said to the King:
“The Rúlái has an instruction.
First, ask this Bhīkṣu how he was able to enter this hard, solid stone
and emerge and vanish freely.”
The King proceeded to the Fó’s residence and bowed at his feet with his head.
He sat down on one side.
He then reported to the Fó, saying:
“The Bhīkṣu earlier,
what is his name?
He possesses such divine power.”
The Fó informed the King, saying:
“This is the laborer who removes excrement.”
At that time, the Shìzūn, using this circumstance, spoke two verses.
Just like filth and pollution,
in fields, drains, or deep pits,
a fragrant and pure lotus flower grows.
What do you say, Great King? A person with eyes,
should he pick this flower or not?”
The King said:
“Shìzūn,
the flower is extremely fragrant and pure.
We ought to pick it and use it for decoration, disregarding the filth.
Observe the mother's womb—from that womb grows the flower of merit and virtue.”
At that time, the King reported to the Fó:
“That person has surely gained good benefit,
it is inconceivable.
Beginning from this day forward,
I request this Bhīkṣu
to be given the Four Offerings.”
In the past, when the Fó was in the country of Mójié,
in the Gānlí Garden,
in the stone cave dwelling north of the city.
There were many hunters.
They entered the mountains to roam and hunt.
They widely deployed nets and snares,
killing countless deer.
They then returned up the mountain.
At that time, there was one deer
that fell into their pit trap.
It cried out with a loud voice.
The hunters, having heard this,
each rushed and ran forward,
but they themselves fell back into the pit trap.
The injured people
were countless.
Even if they did not die, they sustained extremely severe wounds.
The pain was indescribable.
They supported each other,
barely making it back to their homes.
They sought various ointments and medicines
to apply to their wounds.
Their family members and five degrees of relatives each received the corpses and mourned.
They returned and cremated the bodies.
Among those sentient beings who were wounded,
they realized their wounds were healing,
and they grew weary of hunting.
Their past karma dictated that they should be saved.
They planted all kinds of good roots.
They then abandoned their homes, studied the Dào, and became Shāmén.
At that time, the Shìzūn,
along with immeasurable hundreds and thousands of sentient beings,
was encircled by them, front and back,
and was teaching the Dharma to them.
At that time, the Shìzūn,
for the sake of those sentient beings,
wishing to uproot their basic defilements and establish their merit and virtue,
demonstrated and taught the precepts,
so they could eternally depart from saṃsāra and perpetually dwell in the Hall of Blessings.
In the great assembly,
he spoke this verse:
Just as the arrow made by oneself turns back and wounds one's own body,
the internal arrow is likewise—the arrow of craving wounds sentient beings.
Although those hunters were now Shāmén,
they did not realize (this deeper truth) themselves.
The Rúlái today
testifies for us,
that they certainly were hunters.
Internally, they felt shame and remorse.
They reflected upon their original faults.
They stayed in quiet, secluded places,
meditating on calming and insight.
They bound their minds so they were not distracted.
Thus, the sons of noble clans shaved off their beards and hair and wore the three Dharma robes,
left home to study the Dào, cultivating the unsurpassed pure conduct (Fànhéng).
They realized the truth themselves and found enjoyment in it.
Saṃsāra was exhausted, and pure conduct was established.
What needed to be done had been done; they would no longer undergo saṃsāra.
They knew this truthfully.
At that time, those Bǐqiū
all attained Āluóhàn.
Their Six Supernatural Powers were perfectly clear,
without obstruction.
Therefore, this verse was spoken:
He who can awaken to this—that craving and suffering are co-existent in existence—
having no desire and no ideation, the Bhīkṣu focuses his attention on crossing over (salvation).
In the country of Shèwèi Guó there was a powerful elder.
His wealth was immeasurable.
Only, he had no descendants, and he always felt distressed.
He prayed and sought [a child] with sincere and devoted piety.
His wife gave birth to a son who was handsome and rare.
The parents and relatives,
when the time came for a feast, gathered together.
They went to the side of a great river to eat and entertain themselves.
The parents took the child to the gathering place.
Cherishing this child, they took him from the seat and danced, carrying him.
When the father had finished dancing,
the mother then carried him again.
Rejoicing and enjoying themselves,
just as they reached the riverside, her mind suddenly became confused.
She held him insecurely and lost the child, who fell into the water.
Although they immediately tried to grab him, they ultimately could not retrieve him.
The parents, remembering their cherished love, were heartbroken.
Due to the child’s merit and virtue, he subsequently did not die.
Floating and sinking with the water, he was swallowed by a fish.
Although he was in the fish’s belly, he still did not die.
In a village downstream, there was a rich family.
They also had no son.
Though they sought in various ways, they struggled and could not obtain one.
That rich family habitually ordered a slave to fish for a living.
[The slave] happened to catch the fish that had swallowed the little child.
He cut open its belly and found the child.
He presented him to the rich master.
The rich master examined him,
and congratulated himself, saying:
“Our family has long prayed and sacrificed to the deities,
seeking offspring; the sincere piety has been answered.
Therefore, Heaven has given him to me.”
He immediately washed him, nursed him, and raised him.
The parents from the upstream village heard that the elder in the downstream village had obtained a child from a fish belly.
They immediately went to his place,
seeking and requesting him, saying:
“This is our son.
We lost this child in that river.
Now you have found him.
We ask that you return him to us.”
At that time, that elder replied, saying:
“My family has long prayed and sacrificed seeking a son.
Now the spirits have answered and bestowed this child upon me.
As for your lost child, where exactly is he?”
The dispute could not be resolved, so they went to the King to seek a judgment.
Thereupon, the two families each presented their reasoning.
The child’s birth parents argued, “This is our son.
We lost him in the river at a certain time.”
And that elder, in turn, stated:
“I obtained him from the belly of a fish in the river.
This is truly my son, not one born to you.”
The King heard their statements but did not know what to do.
He then provided a measured assessment of the situation for the two families:
“You two elders both claim this child.
Now, if I give him to one [side], it is unreasonable based on the principle of the case.
You should instead raise him together.
When the child grows up,
each of you shall find him a wife,
and establish him in a household.
They shall live separately in two places.
If this wife gives birth to a son, he belongs to this family.
If that wife gives birth to a son,
he belongs to that family.”
The two elders then each followed the King’s instruction.
When the child was older, they both arranged marriages for him.
They constantly supplied his needs, and there was no lack.
The son spoke to his two sets of parents:
“Since my birth, I have encountered great hardship.
I fell into the water, was swallowed by a fish, and was saved when near death.
Now my intention is to leave home (become a monk).
I only ask that my parents grant me permission.”
The two sets of parents loved this child dearly
and could not refuse him.
They immediately granted permission.
He went to the place of the Buddha,
seeking to enter the path.
The Buddha said,
“Welcome.”
His hair spontaneously fell off, and he immediately became a śrāmaṇa.
His name was Zhòngxìng.
The Buddha preached the Dharma for him,
and he ended all suffering and achieved Arhatship (Āluóhàn).
The Buddha said:
“In the distant past, there was a Buddha, the World-Honored One,
named Pípóshī (Vipaśyin).
He gathered the great assembly and preached the sublime Dharma.
At that time, an elder came to the assembly.
He heard the benefits of the great Dharma of charity and precepts.
He developed faith and reverence,
and accepted the Three Refuges and the precept against killing.
He further offered one coin in charity to that Buddha.
Throughout lifetime after lifetime, he received blessings, and his wealth was never lacking.
That elder’s son is now the bhikṣu Zhòngxìng.
Because he offered one coin to the Buddha,
for ninety-one kalpas (jié), he was constantly rich in money and possessions.
Up to this present lifetime, the parents of the two families supplied his needs.
Due to his acceptance of the precept against killing, when he fell into the water and was swallowed by a fish, it could not cause him death.
Due to his acceptance of the Three Refuges, he achieved Arhatship (Āluóhàn).”
The Buddha was in the country of Zhàntánpō, beside the Thunder Sound Pond (Léishēng Chí).
The Venerable Èrshí'ěryì (Twenty-Ear Billion) was in a quiet place,
practicing the fundamentals of the Dharma and not abandoning the dhūta practice.
He walked continuously day and night.
The footprints where he walked looked like blood overflowing.
He constantly restrained and encouraged himself.
Yet, because of the outflows of desire in his mind, he did not achieve liberation.
At this time, Èrshí'ěryì then thought this:
“In ascetic practice and diligence, I am foremost.
Now, due to the outflows in my mind, I have not attained liberation.
Moreover, my family business held much wealth and many treasures.
It would be better to abandon my robes and return to being a layperson.
I could take the wealth and give extensive charity.”
The Buddha knew this in his heart and immediately went to that place.
The Buddha spoke to Èrshí'ěryì:
“When you were originally at home, you were skilled at playing the lute (qín).
If the lute string is extremely tight and the sound is uneven, is it pleasing to hear?”
“No, World-Honored One.”
The Buddha said, “If the lute string is extremely loose, is it pleasing to hear?”
“No, World-Honored One.”
The Buddha said,
“If it is neither tight nor loose, is the sound pleasing to hear?”
“It is so, World-Honored One.”
The Buddha said,
“Excessive diligence is like being troubled.
If one is lazy, this falls into erroneous views.
If one can maintain the middle way,
this is the superior practice.
Thus, before long,
you will attain freedom from outflows (achieve Arhatship).”
Èrshí'ěryì heard these words,
and returned to the side of the Thunder Sound Pond.
He contemplated the Buddha's teaching
and achieved Arhatship (Āluóhàn).
The Brahmin Ràizhà sought to leave home (become a monk) under the Buddha.
The Buddha said,
“First, bid farewell to your parents.”
His parents did not allow it.
Ràizhà lay on the ground for many days without eating.
His parents tried to comfort and persuade him,
but he remained silent throughout.
Since they pitied his resolve,
they immediately granted permission.
He left home, received the full precepts, and achieved Arhatship (Āluóhàn).
Ten years later, he returned to the village.
He begged for food in sequence [from door to door].
His father saw him but did not recognize him, and scolded him, giving him nothing.
A maidservant took his bowl, filled it with spoiled, rotten food, and gave it to him.
She returned and informed the master:
“Ràizhà has returned.”
The father immediately went out to look.
He asked,
“When you returned, why did you not come to my door?”
[Ràizhà] replied,
“I already arrived and received scolding.”
The father led him into the room,
and prepared all kinds of delicacies.
Elephants carried gold and silver, placing it in the central courtyard.
It was taller than a person.
The wealth was countless.
“You can return to lay life.”
His mother ordered his former wife to dress elegantly and go to Ràizhà’s place.
Relatives collectively exhorted and urged him repeatedly.
Ràizhà responded, “I seek to be given food (by you),
why bother me like this?”
Shèwèichéng (Jetavana City), there was a great elder.
His wife gave birth to a son,
named Jīncái (Golden Wealth).
He was handsome and extraordinary.
This child's hands were clenched.
His parents were terrified.
They immediately opened his hands.
They saw two gold coins
within the child's hands.
Happily, they took them, but immediately others reappeared.
In this way, they diligently collected them until the storehouse was full, yet the coins were inexhaustible.
As the child grew older,
he requested permission from his parents to leave home (become a monk).
They immediately allowed him.
He went to the place of the Buddha, shaved his hair and beard, and donned the *jiāshā* (saffron robe).
When he reached the appropriate age, he received the precepts.
He approached the assembly of monks at the ordination platform
and bowed to them one by one.
Wherever he paid his respects,
when his two hands pressed against the ground,
in every spot there were two gold coins.
After the ordination was complete,
he diligently cultivated practice and attained the Way of the Arhat.
Ānán (Ānanda) asked the Buddha,
"What merit did this Bhikṣu Jīncái
create previously that allowed him to hold gold coins in his hands?"
The Buddha said,
"Ninety-one *kalpas* (eons) ago,
there was a Buddha named Pípóshī
who appeared in the world.
He traveled throughout the realm with the assembly of monks.
At that time, various elders
established offerings to the Buddha and his disciples.
There was one poor man who collected firewood and sold it.
He obtained two coins at that time.
Seeing the Buddha, he rejoiced,
and immediately gave those two coins as a donation to the Buddha and the Saṅgha.
Because the poor man
donated the two coins to the Buddha and the Saṅgha,
for ninety-one *kalpas* he constantly held gold coins.
Wealth and treasures appeared naturally.
That poor man of that time
is now Bhikṣu Jīncái."
In the kingdom of Shèwèi, there was a wealthy elder
who had a son born.
His face and head were handsome.
Heaven rained various flowers, accumulating and filling the house.
Therefore, the child was named
Fúbătí. As the child grew older,
he went to the place of the Buddha.
He contemplated in his heart:
"I have appeared in the world and met the Holy Venerable One."
He immediately stepped forward and addressed the Buddha, saying,
"We only wish that the World-Honored One and the Saṅgha
would condescend tomorrow to visit my humble home
and accept some simple food."
The Buddha immediately accepted the invitation.
Huātiān (Flower Heaven) then returned [to his home].
Jewel beds materialized, filling the interior of his house.
Everything was arranged and solemnly adorned.
The Buddha and the assembly of monks then sat upon the seats.
Due to Huātiān's merit, the food and drink prepared themselves.
After the Buddha and the Saṅgha had eaten,
he extensively preached the essentials of the Dharma for Huātiān.
The entire household of Huātiān attained the stage of Sūtuóhuán (Sotāpanna).
Huātiān immediately bade farewell to his parents
and requested to leave the secular life.
His parents allowed it.
The Buddha said, "Welcome!"
His hair and beard spontaneously fell away, and the *jiāshā* clothed his body.
Following the cultivation taught by the Buddha, he attained Arhatship.
Ānán asked the Buddha,
"What merit did Huātiān possess
to obtain such a result?"
The Buddha said,
"In the past there was a Buddha
named Pípóshī,
who appeared in the world to deliver sentient beings.
At that time, all the noble families offered support.
There was a poor man.
Seeing the Saṅgha, he rejoiced,
and immediately went to the wilderness marsh
and gathered various grasses and flowers, which he used to scatter over the great assembly.
The Buddha told Ānán,
"The poor man of that time
is now Bhikṣu Huātiān.
Due to the merit of scattering flowers,
for ninety-one *kalpas* his body has been handsome.
Whatever he desires,
arrives as soon as he thinks of it."
In the kingdom of Shèwèi there was an elder
who had a son born.
At that time,
heaven rained seven treasures,
filling the interior of his house.
The physiognomist observed this
and told the elder,
"The child’s appearance is extraordinary.
At birth there was a felicitous omen,
so he shall be named Lè'nàtípó." As the child grew older,
he was skilled and widely knowledgeable.
Hearing of the Buddha's divinity and holiness,
his heart was filled with devotion and admiration.
He bade farewell to his parents and went to the Buddha’s place,
and addressed the Buddha, saying,
"I request to leave home (become a monk)."
The Buddha said, "Welcome!"
His hair and beard spontaneously fell away, and the Dharma robe clothed his body.
The Buddha preached the Dharma for him,
and he immediately attained Arhatship.
When Pípóshī Fó appeared in the world,
there were various lay devotees
who together invited the assembly of monks
and made various offerings.
At that time, there was a poor person
who, although joyful in heart, lacked the means for offering.
He took a handful of white stones, simulating jewels,
and scattered them over the assembly of monks.
He made a great vow.
That poor man is now this Bhikṣu Bǎotiān (Jewel Heaven).
For ninety-one *kalpas* he received measureless blessings,
having abundant wealth and treasures, and his clothing and food appeared naturally.
Now, meeting my era,
he has realized the fruition of the Way."
At that time, in Southern Tiānzhú (India), there was a young man
who left home in the Right Dharma.
He had few desires, was content, and did not seek glory or prominence.
He did not anoint his body with butter oil (ghee).
He did not wash himself with hot water for bathing.
He did not eat butter oil.
He constantly feared transmigration (saṃsāra), and his four great elements (body) lacked strength,
preventing him from attaining the Holy Way.
He immediately formed a thought:
"Only Yōubōjíduō
can preach the Dharma for me."
He immediately traveled to the country of Móutōuluó (Mathura),
joined his palms, and paid respect to
Yōubōjíduō (Upagupta).
Yōubōjíduō perceived his future body,
fearing saṃsāra,
constantly disliking coarseness and evil,
and not desiring glory or splendor.
Yōubōjíduō spoke to him:
"Just follow my instruction,
and I shall preach for you."
He replied, "Yes."
Yōubōjíduō
then instructed the *dānayuè* (donors) to prepare various foods and drinks and bathing facilities for the Saṅgha.
He further told the young *shāmen* (śrāmaṇera),
"You must wash this Bhikṣu with hot water for bathing,
anoint his body with butter oil,
and give him various delicacies."
This Bhikṣu, after eating for several days, regained strength in his body.
Upon hearing the subtle Dharma preached by Jíduō (Gǐptā),
he diligently reflected and attained the fruit of Arhatship.
There was a man.
who left home to become a monastic (in the Buddhadharma).
He was skilled in craftsmanship.
Wherever he went,
all the community of monks
ordered him to build monastery dwellings without rest, day after day.
He became greatly weary and exhausted.
He immediately thought to himself,
I should sit in meditation and contemplation.
When the Buddha was formerly in the world,
he taught that all *Bhikkhus* (monks) should sit in meditation to cultivate the Way.
They should not indulge in laxity.
He immediately went to the place of Yōupōjíduō.
He bowed, joined his palms, and said,
The Buddha has already entered *Nirvāṇa*.
Great Virtuous One, you are now performing the Buddha's work.
I request you to preach the Dharma for me.
At that time, Yōupōjíduō saw that this man, in his future lives, would fear the suffering of transmigration (samsara) due to incomplete causes and conditions.
He continued (to see him) engaging in craftsmanship,
and again saw his exhaustion.
He could not continue the work.
Yōupōjíduō spoke to him, saying,
If you follow my instruction,
I will preach the Dharma for you.
He replied, "It shall be so."
Yōupōjíduō said,
If there is a piece of land where a monastery has not yet been built,
you should build a monastery there.
The Buddha formerly said that doing this attains the merit of *Brahma*.
He replied,
Great Virtuous One,
in Móutóuluó Guó,
I do not know who is diligent and who is not diligent.
Jíduō said,
Can you rise early, put on your robes, take your bowl, and enter the country?
He replied,
I can rise early and enter the country.
He met an Elder (layman) coming out,
whom he had never seen before.
This *Bhikkhu* now saw him.
He immediately bowed to him and asked, saying,
Great Virtuous One,
are you coming from far or near?
The *Bhikkhu* replied,
I have come from the Eastern Country.
He also asked, "For what purpose?"
He replied, "As stated."
The Elder said,
Great Virtuous One,
you do not need to contemplate now.
It is I who shall provide for the *Bhikkhu*
with all kinds of provisions.
Then the *Bhikkhu* and the Elder,
holding string, ink, and a measuring rule, looked for a location.
Before the string even reached the ground,
he immediately contemplated upon
the merits he had created.
He eliminated all vexations (*kleśas*),
and attained the fruit of Āluóhànguǒ.
The Buddha was in Shèwèiguó.
At that time, in Jūsàluó Guó,
King Bōsīnì Wáng commanded the prison warden,
that all thieves and bandits whose crimes warranted punishment by the law should be taken to the marketplace and executed.
At that time, there was a thief among the multitude.
He escaped secretly and gained freedom.
Outwardly, he pretended to wear the Dharma robes,
privately acting as a *Śrámen*.
However, inwardly he did not contemplate,
believing that he was forever removed from the danger of distress and hardship.
He no longer feared harm.
Staying in a tranquil place,
he did not contemplate morality or virtue,
nor did he study the *Sūtras* or the Precepts.
He neglected the path of monastic discipline and meditation chanting.
Although he had not attained realization of the fruit,
he did not diligently seek to realize the fruit.
The Buddha informed that person,
Although you have escaped the immediate danger of robbers (the thief of birth and death),
there is still remaining fear.
The body of the Five Aggregates (Skandhas) revolves through the Five Paths (destinies).
If liberation has not been achieved,
you will be ruined and afflicted by various afflictions (fetters and bonds).
You will then surely fall into the path of hungry ghosts and animals.
At that time, that *Bhikkhu*,
being in a tranquil place,
contemplated and reflected;
he inwardly admonished himself sincerely.
He understood that all things are impermanent,
and that existence does not last long.
All things return to extinction.
The changes of prosperity and decline
have been coming for a long time.
He immediately went before the Buddha,
repented his errors, and blamed himself.
He attained the path of Luóhàndào.
At that time, there was a man in Móutóuluó Guó.
Under Yōupōjíduō,
he left secular life and became a monastic.
Because of his greed for food, he could not attain the Way.
Jíduō said to him,
Tomorrow I will give you food.
When the time came, he filled a bowl with rice gruel in one container,
and placed an empty container beside it in front of him.
Then he spoke to him, saying,
You may take the food and make this container empty.
He also said,
Wait until it is cool, and eat it gradually.
But this *Bhikkhu*'s greed was heavy and intense.
He immediately blew on it to cool it.
He reported to the Héshàng (Upādhyāya/Master), saying,
It is already cool, so I will eat it all at once.
Jíduō said,
Although the milk gruel is cool,
your mind is still hot.
It must be cooled again.
You should use the contemplation of impurity as water,
to remove the heat of this mind.
You should view food and drink as if you were taking medicine.
When the *Bhikkhu* finished eating,
he immediately vomited it out.
It filled the empty container.
Jíduō said,
You may eat it again.
The *Bhikkhu* said,
How can this impurity be eaten again?
Jíduō further said,
You should view all *Dharmas* as being like snot or vomit.
Because of this, he preached the Dharma for him.
The *Bhikkhu* diligently contemplated and observed,
and attained the fruit of Āluóhànguǒ.
Prince Jítuó Tàizǐ sent a messenger,
inviting the Buddha and the *Saṅgha* for a meal the following day.
Only the begging *Bhikkhus* were not invited.
The begging *Bhikkhus* came well-prepared and all followed the Buddha and the *Saṅgha* into the palace to eat.
The begging *Bhikkhus*,
by means of their supernatural powers, traveled to Běiyùdānyuè,
and fetched naturally growing *jīngfàn* (rice).
Each maintaining their dignified bearing, they descended through the air.
They entered the prince’s palace and sat down in order.
The Prince saw them and exclaimed that this was unprecedented.
He asked the Buddha,
Where have these Noble Sages come from?
The Buddha replied,
They are the five hundred beggars who are now *Śrámens*.
The Prince was deeply ashamed.
The Buddha was at the Jīngshè (Vihāra) in Shèwèi.
There were four Bhīkṣus sitting beneath a tree.
They mutually questioned each other, saying,
"Among everything in the world, what is the most suffering?"
One person said,
"The suffering under heaven is none greater than sensual desire (yínyù)."
Another person said,
"The suffering in the world is none greater than hunger and thirst."
Another person said,
"The suffering in the world is none greater than anger and hatred (chēnhuì)."
Another person said,
"The suffering under heaven is none greater than shock and terror (jīngbù)."
They debated the meaning of suffering, but could not settle the issue.
The Buddha knew what they were saying.
He went to their location.
He asked them what they had discussed.
They immediately reported the matter, saying,
"What you have discussed does not fully examine the meaning of suffering."
"The suffering under heaven is none greater than possessing a body."
Hunger, thirst, cold, heat, anger, terror, sensual desire, enmity, and calamity—all originate from the body.
Truly, the body is the root of all suffering and the instrument of affliction and calamity.
Exhausting the mind, intensely worrying, fear and anxiety have myriad forms.
All creatures wriggling in the Sānjiè (Three Realms) mutually harm and destroy one another.
Attachment to the self binds them, and life and death never cease.
All arise due to the body.
If you wish to leave worldly suffering, you must seek ultimate tranquility (jìmǐe).
Control your mind, maintain correctness, and become utterly devoid of thought.
Then you can attain Níhuán (Nirvāṇa).
This is the highest bliss."
The Buddha spoke a Gāthā (verse) to instruct the Bhīkṣus, saying:
In times long past, countless lifetimes ago,
there was a Bhīkṣu possessing the Five Supernatural Powers (Wǔtōng),
named Jīngjìnlì.
He sought the Way (Dào) in secluded tranquility beneath a mountain tree.
At that time, four animals relied on him, remaining nearby, and always obtained peace and safety.
The first was a dove.
The second was a crow.
The third was a poisonous snake.
The fourth was a deer.
These four animals,
during the day, went out seeking food,
and at dusk, they returned to roost.
One night, the four animals
mutually questioned each other, saying,
"What is the gravest suffering in the world?"
The crow said,
"When hunger and thirst strike, the body is weak, the eyes dim, and the spirit and consciousness are restless.
We throw ourselves into nets and traps, disregarding sharp blades.
If we lose our lives, it is invariably due to this.
Judging by this,
hunger and thirst are suffering."
The dove said,
"When sensual desire (sèyù) flares intensely, there is no consideration for anything else.
Endangering the body and destroying life is invariably due to this."
The poisonous snake said,
"Once the intention of hatred (huìyì) arises, we spare neither relatives nor strangers.
It can kill others and can also cause self-destruction."
The deer said,
"When I am in the forest wilderness, my mind is constantly vigilant and anxious.
I fear hunters and all the tigers and wolves.
If I faintly hear a sound, I run and throw myself down embankments or into pits.
Mothers abandon their young, and our gallbladders mourn and palpitate.
Judging by this,
shock and terror (jīngbù) are suffering."
Then Jīngjìnlì replied,
"What you have discussed is superficial.
You have not thoroughly investigated the root of suffering.
The great suffering under heaven is none greater than conditionality (yǒuwéi).
This is the vessel of suffering, and anxiety and fear are boundless.
It is for this reason that I abandoned the secular world to study the Way.
I extinguish intention and sever thoughts.
I do not cling to the Four Great Elements (Sìdà).
Wishing to sever the source of suffering, my will rests upon Níhuán.
The Way of Níhuán is tranquil extinction, without form.
Worries and afflictions are ended forever.
Only then is there great peace."
When the four animals heard this,
their minds immediately became enlightened.
The Buddha informed the Bhīkṣus,
"At that time, that Bhīkṣu possessing the Five Supernatural Powers was myself.
The four animals then are these four people now.
In previous lives, you already heard the meaning of the root of suffering.
How is it that today you are debating this again?"
The Bhīkṣus, hearing this, felt shame and reproached themselves.
Immediately, in the presence of the Buddha, they attained the Way of the Luóhàn (Arhat).
The Buddha was at the Jīngshè in Shèwèi.
At that time, there were four newly trained Bhīkṣus.
They went beneath a nài (apple) tree to sit in meditation and cultivate the Way.
The nài flowers were luxuriant, beautiful in color, and fragrant.
They consequently discussed among themselves, saying,
"Among the myriad things of the world, what is the most enjoyable?"
One person said,
"In the middle month of spring, when all vegetation is flourishing and glorious,
roaming and playing in the wilderness is the greatest bliss."
Another person said,
"When relatives gather for a fortunate assembly, cups and goblets cross back and forth,
with music, singing, and dancing—this is the greatest bliss."
Another person said,
"To accumulate many treasures and instantly obtain whatever one desires;
carriages, horses, clothing, and adornments are different from the ordinary crowd.
Going in and out with splendor and prominence, drawing the attention of passersby.
This is the greatest bliss."
Another person said,
"Wives and concubines are beautiful, dressed in bright, colorful clothes.
Fragrant incense fills the air, and one indulges the senses freely.
This is the greatest bliss."
The Buddha knew they could be converted.
He went and spoke to them.
"This is the greatest suffering."
He spoke of a former King,
named Pǔ'ān.
He and four Kings from neighboring countries were close friends.
He invited these four Kings for a banquet lasting one month,
filled with food, drink, and entertainment.
On the day they were about to part,
King Pǔ'ān asked,
"When people live in the world,
what do they take as bliss?"
The answers given by the four Kings
were not different from yours.
At that time, King Pǔ'ān provided the essence [of the matter].
The four Kings heard this, rejoiced, believed, and understood.
King Pǔ'ān then was myself.
The four Kings then are you four people now.
You discussed this before, yet now you still do not understand.
If life and death are prolonged, how can they ever cease?"
The four Bhīkṣus then,
upon hearing this meaning again, felt shame and repented their faults.
Their minds were opened and enlightened, and they attained the Way of the Luóhàn.
Formerly, there was a man
who left his parents to study the Way (Dào) and succeeded in becoming an Yìngzhēn (Arhat).
He sought out all those to whom he was indebted (in gratitude) and offered salvation.
He observed that his mother was in Nílí (Naraka/Hell).
He extensively sought means (fāngbiàn) to relieve his mother's suffering.
He saw that in a border region there was a King who had murdered his father and usurped the country.
This King had only seven days remaining in his life.
The place where he was destined to suffer punishment was the same as that of his mother.
At night, [the Arhat] went to the King's residence.
He manifested half of his body on the wall.
The King saw this and was terrified.
He drew his sword and chopped at the neck [of the apparition].
The neck immediately fell to the ground.
The Bhīkṣu did not move.
Only then did the King's intention relax.
He kowtowed and apologized for his offense.
The Bhīkṣu spoke to the King,
"Did you or did you not murder your father and usurp the country?"
[The King] replied,
"It is true."
[The Bhīkṣu] said, "You have only seven days remaining in your life.
You are destined to enter the prison of Nílí.
Therefore, I came to inform you."
The King immediately begged for mercy.
The Bhīkṣu said,
"If you perform great meritorious deeds (gōngdé), I fear it may not be enough to reach [salvation].
The King must only chant 'Námó Fó' (Homage to the Buddha).
If you do not cease for seven days, you will be able to escape punishment."
The King then wholeheartedly chanted 'Námó Fó.'
For seven days, he was unremitting.
When his life ended, his spirit, still remembering, entered the Nílí gate.
He therefore chanted 'Námó Fó.'
The Nílí immediately cooled down.
All the people within that city [of Nílí] were able to escape.
The Bhīkṣu then preached the Dharma to them.
The Bhīkṣu's mother and the King,
along with the people in Nílí, all attained salvation (dùtuō).
In the kingdom of Nántiānzhú
He left home in the Buddhadharma.
His body was bound by attachment (desire).
He massaged his body with clarified butter and oil.
Furthermore, he bathed using hot water.
He was provided with various kinds of food and drink.
His body, bound by attachment, could not attain the sacred path.
He went to the place of Yōubōjíduō in the kingdom of Mótóuluó Guó.
He paid reverence to his feet and said,
"I wish to hear the essentials of the Dharma, Yōubōjíduō."
Seeing that his future body would be bound by attachment,
he spoke, saying,
"Man,
if you can accept my instruction, I shall speak for you."
He replied, "I can."
Yōubōjíduō led him into the mountains.
Using supernatural power, he manifested a great tree.
He spoke, saying,
"You must climb up this great tree."
At that time, the Bhikkhu immediately climbed the tree.
Then, beneath the tree, he manifested a great pit (chasm).
It was a thousand cubits deep and wide.
He spoke again,
"Let go of both your feet."
He immediately let go of his feet.
Then he ordered him to release one hand.
He immediately released one hand.
He commanded him to release the other hand.
The Bhikkhu replied,
"If I release this hand too, I will fall into the pit and die."
Yōubōjíduō said,
"I previously made an agreement with you that you would accept all instructions.
Why do you not accept this?"
At that moment, his attachment to the body immediately vanished.
He let go of his hand and fell.
He did not see the tree or the pit.
Jíduō preached the Dharma.
By diligent contemplation, he attained the fruition of Āluóhàn.
In the kingdom of Mótóuluó Guó, there was a man.
He left home following Yōubōjíduō.
Hearing the exposition on the contemplation of impurity and so forth,
he subdued his afflictions using the contemplation of impurity.
He believed that what needed to be done had been done.
Jíduō said,
"You must be diligent; do not entertain thoughts of slackness."
He replied,
"I have already attained Āluóhàn."
Jíduō said to him,
"Have you seen the wine-selling woman in the kingdom of Gāntuóluó Guó?
This woman
claims to have attained the Way.
It is no different from you.
Afflictions are not yet severed, yet one claims they are severed.
This is arrogance born of superior attainment (zēngshàngmàn).
Now, you must observe whether this woman has attained the Way or not."
He replied,
"I have not yet been able to see her.
I wish to go to that kingdom."
The Master immediately allowed him.
At that time, the Bhikkhu
arrived in the kingdom of Gāntuóluó Guó.
He cleaned the earthen ground of the monastery, inquired about the news,
rose early, donned his robes, held his bowl, and entered the village to beg for food.
At that time, the wine-selling woman took food, intending to give it to him.
The Bhikkhu saw the woman.
The heart of lustful desire and attachment immediately arose, and he took the curds/yogurt from his bowl
and gave them to this woman.
When the woman saw this,
her heart, too, was changed by lustful desire, and she revealed her teeth and smiled.
The Bhikkhu immediately entered the contemplation of impurity.
He continued until he contemplated the body as a skeleton (white bones).
Through this contemplation, he attained the fruition of Āluóhàn.
The Fó was in the kingdom of Shèwèi Guó.
He stayed during the three months of summer.
When the new year arrived,
he addressed Ānán, saying,
"You should strike the wooden sounding board (jiānchuí)."
The sound of the jiānchuí spread throughout one Buddha-land.
The hells, hungry ghosts, animals, and all suffering from illness,
hearing the sound, were all cured and found peace and comfort.
At that time, the Fó said,
"Bhikkhus, you should rise and carry out the distribution of tallies (shèluóchóu).
Face one another, repent of your faults, and blame yourselves.
Apologize to one another for all the offenses committed that violate the Dharma.
Each should endure, maintain harmony, and purify body, mouth, and mind,
so that no defilement remains."
At that time, the Bhikkhus immediately received the Buddha's instruction.
When the task was finished, they returned to their seats.
Then the Fó, out of compassion,
rose from his seat.
Facing the Bhikkhus,
he clasped his hands and said,
"Although the Supreme Honored One, the Utmost Reality, has no error,
he ought to practice this as an instruction (for you)."
At that time, the Fó took his time, confessed, and apologized to the sacred assembly.
Having compassion for all, he returned to his grass mat.
As soon as the Fó was seated again, the sacred assembly did likewise,
each returning to his former place.
At that time, ten thousand Bhikkhus attained the path of the Way.
Eight thousand Bhikkhus attained Āluóhàn.
The Fó was in the Qíshù Jīngshě.
The various Bhikkhus
diligently cultivated the work of the Way, casting aside the five hindrances.
There was one Bhikkhu.
Having eaten his fill, he entered his room, closed the door, and slept quietly.
He indulged in the pleasure of the body and did not contemplate impermanence.
He no longer distinguished between day and night.
After seven days, his life was about to end.
The Fó took pity on him
and immediately entered his room, snapping his fingers to wake him.
He spoke a marvelous verse for him.
Startled and awakened, he bowed his head and made obeisance.
The Fó told the Bhikkhu, "In your former life,
during the time of Wéiwèi Fó, you once left home.
You were greedy for bodily comfort and sustenance and did not recall the Sūtras and precepts.
You ate your fill, went to sleep, and did not contemplate impermanence.
When your life ended, your spirit was born among the Wēng insects.
This lasted for fifty thousand years.
When that life ended, you were reborn as a snail/clam insect and a wood-boring insect within trees.
Each lasted for fifty thousand years.
These four classes of insects
lived and grew in the dark, greedy for their bodies and attached to life.
They enjoyed dark, secluded places as their homes and disliked the light.
When they slept once, they only awoke after a hundred years.
Entangled and bound by the net (of existence), they did not seek the means to escape.
Now your karmic obstacles have just been finished.
You have gained the opportunity to be a Shāméng.
How can you sleep without knowing satiety or enough?"
When the Bhikkhu heard this, he was ashamed and fearful and blamed himself.
The five hindrances were immediately removed.
He achieved Āluóhàn.
In the kingdom of Mótóuluó Guó,
there was a man.
He left home following Yōubōjíduō.
He constantly loved to slumber and sleep.
Sometimes, when the Dharma was being preached, he was asleep and did not hear it.
When taught to meditate beneath a tree, he also slept.
Jíduō, using supernatural power,
manifested deep pits one thousand cubits deep on all four sides of him.
When the Bhikkhu awoke,
he was immediately startled and fearful.
Then Yōubōjíduō again manifested a path
so that he could walk out.
At that time, this Bhikkhu
followed the path out
and went to Yōubōjíduō.
Yōubōjíduō commanded him to go back again.
The Bhikkhu replied,
"There are deep pits there."
Yōubōjíduō said,
"This deep pit is small, referring to life and death.
The great deep pit is what is called birth, old age, sickness, death, sorrow, grief, suffering, and distress.
If a person does not know the Four Noble Truths,
then he falls into it."
When the Bhikkhu heard this,
he returned beneath the tree and sat cross-legged.
His mind was constantly contemplating, fearing that he would fall into the deep pit.
He did not sleep again.
Because of this fear, he contemplated diligently.
He eliminated all afflictions
and attained the fruition of Āluóhàn.
There was a female elephant,
named Mótuó.
She carried the Fó's relics to the kingdom of Jìbīn Guó.
Due to this root of virtue, she died and was reborn among humans.
She left home and attained the fruition of Āluóhàn.
Because she ate one *hú* of rice, she entered Bānnièpán.
She addressed the Bhikkhuṇīs, "You should gather together.
I shall personally describe the superior Dharma I attained."
The Bhikkhuṇīs did not believe her words.
She spoke to the Bhikkhuṇīs again, saying,
"Do not harbor disbelief.
In a previous life, I was a female elephant.
Having discarded that elephant body, I immediately obtained this body.
I could eat one *hú* and five *dǒu* of rice,
but I only eat one *hú*.
And so forth, speaking widely...
Although she ate a large amount like this,
she was easy to satisfy.
I have heard that Bōsīní Wáng
ate two *hú* of rice.
This was due to his merits and causes,
stemming from a single stalk of Gēng rice
and a single stalk of sugarcane
that grew daily.
Because of such a quantity of food, his body was extremely large and corpulent.
With this great body, he went to the place of the Fó.
The Fó asked,
"Great King,
are you not exhausted by your great and corpulent body?"
At that time, Bōsīní felt shame and remorse in his heart.
He fully recounted the matter to the Fó (Shìzūn), who then spoke a verse:
"A person should possess right mindfulness, knowing contentment regarding food;
Then he will not encounter painful feelings, digestion will be easy, and life will increase."
At that time, Bōsīní Wáng,
hearing what the Fó had said,
gradually reduced his food
until, in later times, he only ate one *dǒu*.
The Fó was in Shèwèi-guó.
There was a chief elder (zhǎngzhě).
He invited the Fó and the Saṅgha.
At that time, the Bǐqiū went.
The Rúlái did not go.
He sent a messenger to fetch the food.
There were two reasons (yīnyuán).
First, he wished to preach the Dharma to the various heavenly beings (tiān).
Second, he needed to attend to a sick person.
At that time, the Shìzūn surveyed all the Bǐqiū.
They had all accepted the invitation.
He then took a key and opened a room door.
He saw one Bǐqiū.
Stricken by a serious illness, he lay in his own excrement and urine, unable to turn himself over.
The Shìzūn asked,
"What is your illness?"
The Bǐqiū replied,
"I received a nature that is dull and slow, and I constantly harbored laziness and arrogance (xièmàn).
I never encouraged others to look after remaining people.
Therefore, today there is no one who looks after me.
Now I am truly isolated and poor, having no place of reliance."
At that time, the Shìzūn,
out of compassionate pity, personally embraced him,
removed the filth,
washed the sitting mat,
bathed his body with water,
changed his clothes,
spread a new sitting mat,
and put him back in the room.
He personally massaged him.
He instructed the Bǐqiū, saying,
"If you do not diligently seek the superior Dharma (zēngshàng fǎ),
after death you will suffer extreme hardship again."
Gradually, he preached the Dharma to him, encouraging him to be resolute and fierce.
Then he addressed the Saṅgha,
"You Bǐqiū,
