you have no father, mother, brothers,
nor sisters or clansmen (zōngzú).
It is improper not to attend to one another.
My Dharma is complete and correct; those above and below must be harmonious and compliant.
Starting from today,
a disciple shall serve his master as he would serve his parents,
and shall not abandon him until death.
The master shall look after the disciple as if he were his own son (jǐxī).
He shall nurse him according to the time, and shall not abandon him until death.
Master and disciple must be compassionate toward one another, flowing down through endless kalpas.
All possessions (shíwù) should be distributed equally.
If there are no possessions, alms (fēnwèi) should be widely sought.
He who attends to the sick attends to my own body.
The merits (gōngdé) obtained will be no different or diminished."
At that time, the sick Bǐqiū reflected deeply.
He immediately relinquished his form and lifespan (xíngshòu).
Then he attained Nirvāṇa (wúyú).
At that time, in Móntóuluó-guó,
there was a man
who had left home (chūjiā) under Yōupō Jípduō.
He was very fond of sleeping.
Jípduō transformed himself into a ghost (guǐ).
It had seven heads.
Holding a branch in its hand, its body was suspended in the air.
When the Bǐqiū saw it, he was immediately startled awake.
He gave rise to great fear.
He returned to his original place.
Jípduō said,
"Return to your meditation seat (zuòchán chù)."
The Bǐqiū reported,
"Venerable Master (Héshàng), in that forest there is a ghost.
It has seven heads in front of me.
It holds a branch in its hand and is suspended in the air.
It is extremely terrifying."
Jípduō said,
"This ghost is not worth fearing.
Sleep is the most terrifying thing.
If a Bǐqiū were killed by this ghost,
he would certainly not enter saṃsāra (shēngsǐ).
But if he is killed by sleep,
then saṃsāra is endless."
The Bǐqiū immediately returned to his meditation seat.
He saw the ghost again.
Fearing this ghost, he dared not sleep.
At that time, the Bǐqiū diligently reflected.
He attained the fruition of Arhatship (Āluóhàn guǒ).
The Fó resided in Shèwèi-guó.
There was another Bǐqiū
in Kūsàluó territory
who resided in a forest.
The Bǐqiū flirted (xīxì) with a chief elder's wife.
This gave rise to a bad reputation.
The Bǐqiū thought to himself,
"I shall now kill myself."
In the forest there was a sky spirit (tiānshén).
It transformed itself into the body of the chief elder's daughter
and spoke to the Bǐqiū:
"All the people in the world, because of me and you,
falsely speak with bad reputations.
I and you habitually draw near one another,
doing improper things.
Since we already have a bad name,
we might as well return to secular life (huánsú) and enjoy ourselves together."
The Bǐqiū replied,
"Because of this reputation,
I shall now kill myself."
The spirit reverted to its heavenly body
and spoke a verse (jì), saying:
Though there are many bad reputations, the practitioner (xíngzhě) endures them; he should not harm himself.
He should not give rise to affliction. The Bǐqiū was awakened and focused his keen reflection.
He cut off and eliminated defilements (fánnǎo) and attained Āluóhànship.
On the road was a person.
Who had harmed his own mother.
He stopped and stayed beneath a tree,
weeping, crying, and agonizing.
He cried out, "Alas, what shall I do?"
He blamed himself for his lack of character and for committing a great rebellion (unfilial crime).
"By harming my mother, I am bound to fall into hell."
Although that person was such, he was still due to practice the monastic rules.
Pǔshǒu Púsà (Pǔshǒu Bodhisattva),
seeing his present state, knew he ought to be saved.
(Pǔshǒu Púsà) transformed into a different person,
taking along his own parents, and went toward the location of the matricide.
Not far away, he stopped in the middle of the road.
The parents said to the son, "This is the correct path."
The son said, "It is not correct."
Thus, they argued and disagreed.
The son, showing great anger, killed the manifested parents.
After doing so, he wept bitterly and sorrowfully, unable to control himself.
He went to the location of the matricide
and spoke, saying:
"I killed my parents and am bound to fall into hell!"
He wept, saying, "Alas, what shall I do?"
"What plan should be established?"
The person who had harmed his mother then thought to himself:
"This person who has just arrived actually harmed both parents.
I merely endangered my mother.
That person's stupidity and darkness mean his crime is the greatest there is.
My act of rebellion is still less severe than his.
Knowing that he must suffer, I feel my own offense is lighter."
That person (the original killer) was sad, heartbroken, and cruelly pained, and he declared aloud:
"I must go and seek the Venerable Buddha.
For those who are unsaved, the Buddha provides salvation.
For those who are fearful, the Buddha can offer comfort and relief.
I shall follow the teaching that the Buddha provides."
At that time, the transformed person wept and proceeded along the road, walking ahead of him.
This matricide immediately followed behind him.
[He thought:] "If he repents, I must do the same.
My sin is minor compared to that person's heavy offense."
The transformed person approached the Buddha and bowed his head to the ground,
and addressed the Buddha, saying:
"Indeed, O Shìzūn (World-Honored One)!
I have committed a great rebellion and harmed both parents,
committing this grave crime."
The Buddha addressed the transformed person:
"Excellent, excellent!
You are perfectly sincere and have not practiced deceit. Your words and actions match as you come before the Rúlái (Tathāgata).
Your words are perfectly sincere.
Your mouth speaks no duplicity.
Nor do you condemn yourself.
You should examine and observe the nature of the mind.
With what kind of mind
did you endanger both parents?
Did you use the past mind, the future mind,
or the present mind?
The past mind has already perished.
The present mind is immediately separated and gone.
It has no location,
nor does it have any direction.
It is unknown where it resides.
As for the future mind,
this has not yet arrived.
It has no place of assembly.
It has not been seen returning.
Nor does it come and go.
You should understand this:
the mind is not established within the body,
nor does it come from outside, nor does it have any boundary.
It does not dwell in the space between (in the two intervals) and cannot be stopped." The transformed person exclaimed:
"This is unprecedented!
The Rúlái has attained the Most Correct Enlightenment!
He clearly knows the nature of reality (Dhārmadhātu): there is no agent (doer),
nor is there any recipient; there is no one born,
and no one entering Nirvāṇa.
There is nothing to rely upon."
"I pray that I may leave home."
Through the power of the Buddha, Shìzūn, he was able to become a Shāmén (śramaṇa).
He received the full monastic precepts.
The Buddha said:
"Welcome, Bǐqiū (Bhīkṣu)."
At that time, the transformed person came forward and became a Shāmén.
He immediately addressed the Buddha, saying:
"Indeed, O Shìzūn!
I have gained supernatural powers and now wish to enter Nirvāṇa."
The majestic power of the Buddha caused that transformed person to rise forty-nine *zhàng* (units of length) from the ground.
In the empty sky, he entered Nirvāṇa.
Fire issued from his body
and burned his own form.
The rebellious son saw this
and thought to himself:
"He became a Shāmén and immediately attained Nirvāṇa.
I shall imitate this person."
He went to the location of the Buddha
and bowed his head at the sacred feet.
"I also committed an act of rebellion,
endangering the life of my mother."
The Buddha said:
"Excellent!
Be perfectly sincere and practice no deceit.
Your words and actions match."
At that moment, the fires of hell issued from the pores of this rebellious person.
The pain was extremely severe,
and there was no relief or protection.
He addressed the Buddha, saying:
"I am now being burned!
Only the God of Gods (Tiān zhōng Tiān) can grant salvation!"
The Shìzūn extended his golden arm
and placed it upon the person's head.
The fire immediately ceased.
He saw the body of the Rúlái,
with its various major and minor distinguishing marks.
His bodily pain rested
and he attained tranquility.
He then came forward and addressed the Buddha,
wishing to become a Shāmén.
The Buddha immediately permitted it.
He then left home
and (the Buddha) taught the doctrine of the Four Noble Truths (Sì Dì Fǎ).
When that person heard it,
he removed dust and left defilement, attaining purity of the Dharma Eye (Fǎ Yǎn Jìng).
He practiced the Dharma teachings
and attained progress in the way.
He attained certification as an Arhat (Luóhàn).
He again addressed the Buddha, saying:
"I wish to enter Parinirvāṇa (Bān Níhuán)."
The Buddha said, "As you wish."
At that time, the Bǐqiū leaped into the empty sky,
forty-nine *zhàng* from the ground.
Fire issued from his body,
burning his own form.
Hundreds of thousands of heavenly beings and humans, in the empty sky,
came to make offerings.
Then Shèlìfú (Śāriputra) addressed the Buddha, saying:
"The teaching of discipline (Lǜ) granted by the Rúlái's compassion
has allowed even this rebellious person to attain salvation.
Only the Rúlái
and the Great Bodhisattvas (Dà Púsà) can observe the roots and origins of all sentient beings
and save them accordingly.
This is not the scope (realm) of the Śrāvakas (Shēngwén) or Pratyekabuddhas (Yuánjué)."
The Buddha said, "It is so."
In the kingdom of Shèwèi.
There was an old, impoverished man.
He exceeded two hundred years of age.
His eyebrows grew long, elegant hairs, and his ears protruded from his head.
His teeth were like uniform cowries.
His arms extended past his knees.
Observing his appearance, it seemed as if he possessed auspicious characteristics.
Yet he was poverty-stricken and miserable.
His clothes did not cover his body; his five limbs were exposed.
His stomach was constantly empty from hunger while walking.
He barely moved, showing only a flicker of breath.
He desired to go and see the Fó.
Shì Fàn, guarding the gate, commanded that he not be allowed entry.
The old man cried out loudly,
saying:
“Although I am poor,
the lowest of people,
I have been fortunate for a thousand years.
Now I am able to meet the Fó.
I wish to ask about sins and blessings,
and seek separation from all suffering.
I heard that the Shìzūn compassionately reaches everyone;
none fail to receive his grace.
To refuse me alone would slander the Sage's intent.”
The Fó called for him to come forward.
Crawling inch by inch,
he paid reverence to the Fó.
Sorrow and joy mingled.
He spoke of his destitution and suffering,
stating that the fulfillment of his single wish to attend and behold the Fó had taken ten years.
Since his physical strength was failing,
he had no means of advancing or retreating.
He only feared that his life would cease and he would defile the sacred gate.
Thus increasing his sins.
“Tīanzūn, pity me and do not deny my original vow.
If I die thus, I will have no further regrets.
I only wish for my end to come quickly, and may you bestow your grace.”
The Fó said:
“The birth a person receives is mostly caused by karma.
I will explain it for you.
In your previous life,
you were born into the family of Mínghuì Wáng in a powerful and great kingdom.
You were the crown prince at that time.
You were arrogant and noble, not ordinary.
Above, you were cherished by your parents;
below, you were served by officials and common people.
Because of this, you acted willfully and lightly oppressed others.
You looked down upon everyone with great haughtiness and indifference.
The countless treasures and valuables all belonged to the common people.
The populace became poor and distressed due to the levies and taxes imposed.
You only knew how to accumulate wealth and never practiced giving.
At that time, there was a poor and simple Shāmén,
named Jìngzhì.
He came from a distant country.
He specifically went to your place seeking only a small thing,
which was merely a dharma robe.
But you utterly failed to receive him properly.
You treated him very poorly.
Not only did you refuse to give the robe,
you also did not give him food.
He sat empty-handed before you, and you would not allow him to leave.
For seven days and nights,
he was deprived of water and fluids.
He showed only a flicker of breath.
Only then were you greatly pleased.
You gathered a crowd to look at him,
considering it the greatest pleasure.
Your attending ministers remonstrated, saying:
‘This Shāmén is compassionate and respectful.
His virtue is internally complete.
Freezing him does not make him cold,
starving him does not make him hungry.
The reason he came begging was merely to give you an opportunity for merit.
Since you did not give to him,
how can you harass and oppress him?
Please, dispatch him quickly.
Do not invite this sin.’
The Crown Prince then said:
‘Who is this person falsely claiming virtue?
I am testing him slightly.
I will just ensure he does not die.
I will release him right away.
There is nothing to worry about.’
He immediately sent him away.
He was driven out of the kingdom.
After exiting the border by more than ten *lǐ*,
he encountered starving bandits.
They wanted to kill and eat him.
The Shāmén said:
‘I am a poor and chilled Shāmén.
I am so emaciated that only bone remains, my flesh is withered, smelly, and rancid—unfit to eat.
You would needlessly kill me, and gain nothing.’
The starving bandits replied:
‘We have been starving for days, eating only dirt.
Although you are a little thin, you are still meat.
We will definitely not let you go; you must face death.’
This back-and-forth continued for a long time.
When the Crown Prince learned of this, he galloped there quickly, saying:
‘I have already failed to grant him clothing and food.
How can I now let bandits kill him?’
When the bandits saw the Crown Prince, they all kowtowed and begged forgiveness.
They released the Shāmén.
That Shāmén at the time was Mílè.
Therefore, you today are receiving the retribution for this sin of poverty.
This is because of your stinginess.
The reason for your longevity is that you saved the Shāmén’s life. Sin and blessing each meet their corresponding effect, like a shadow follows a form.”
The old man said:
“The past events are so.
May my karmic debt be concluded today.
I beg that, even in my fading life,
I may become a Shāmén.
And in future lives, eternally attend by the Fó’s side.”
The Fó said, “Excellent!”
Immediately, the old man’s
beard and hair fell to the ground.
A dharma robe appeared on his body.
His physical strength became vigorous again.
His hearing and sight became clear.
He immediately attained the superior realization,
and entered the gate of Sānmèi.
He used a verse to praise the Fó,
made obeisance, and withdrew.
In the past, I was a favored son, unaware of the path of benevolence and righteousness;
Arrogant and noble, I indulged myself while my father was the great king.
I believed there was neither sin nor blessing, and thus could maintain permanence.
Vainly realizing life and death, I now receive their disaster.
From sin, I am again shielded by grace, able to behold the Heavenly among the Heavens.
Freed from past offenses, in my fading life I enter the Dharma Gate.
Eternally abandoning the mind of stinginess, I long receive the root of wisdom.
Life after life, I shall not be far from the Fó, enduring for myriad *jié*.
In Mótóuluó Guó, there was a man.
He left home under Yōubōjíduō.
Jíduō preached the Dharma.
The Bǐqiū diligently contemplated,
and attained the fruit of Sūtuóhuán.
Because he was not negligent, he escaped the fear of the evil paths.
He was reborn seven times in the heavens,
and seven times among humans,
enjoying the bliss of humans and devas.
He was destined to enter Nièpán.
Jíduō, seeing his intention,
entered Mótóuluó Guó together with him.
Begging for food sequentially, they reached a Zhāntuóluó dwelling.
There was a son of a Zhāntuóluó,
who had attained the fruit of Sūtuóhuán.
His body suffered from a severe illness.
His entire body was being eaten by insects.
His breath was fetid and foul.
Yōubōjíduō spoke to his disciple, saying:
‘Look at this child.
He has attained Sūtuóhuán,
yet undergoes such suffering.’
Born into the Zhāntuóluó lineage, delighting in attachment for three months;
Evil insects eat his body, because of the mastery of craving.
Life and death have no reality, like a plantain grove.
The Bǐqiū asked what cause led to this:
‘Why did he attain Sūtuóhuán,
yet suffer this torment?’
Jíduō replied:
‘In a former life, he left home.
When the assembly of monks was practicing seated meditation, he acted as the Wéinà.
There was an Luóhàn
who suffered from this same severe illness.
He was scratching, making noise.
The Wéinà spoke to him, saying:
“Evil insects are eating you,
yet you make this noise.”
He then grabbed the Luóhàn by the arm, dragged him out, and said:
“Go and enter a Zhāntuóluó house!”
The Āluóhàn said to the Wéinà:
“You must be diligent.
Do not go into Saṃsāra and suffer torment.”
This Wéinà immediately repented of his action.
After repenting, he attained the fruit of Sūtuóhuán.
He did not proceed diligently further.
The child now is that person.
For dragging the Luóhàn out,
he is now born in the place of the Zhāntuóluó
and receives this retribution.’
The Bǐqiū, fearful, applied diligent effort,
and immediately attained the fruit of Āluóhàn.
In the past, there were two Bhikṣus.
They upheld the precepts, and their wisdom was perfectly equal.
Both attained the path of Sūtuóyuán (Stream-Enterer).
One Bhikṣu only went out begging for alms,
using them for Dàna (charity),
feeding the Bhikṣu Saṅgha and the poor.
The other Bhikṣu only practiced seated meditation and self-discipline.
He said to the one who begged for alms and practiced Dàna:
"Why do you not sit in meditation?
Practicing self-discipline avoids needless exertion."
The first Bhikṣu replied:
"Worthy one,
the Buddha said,
'Even as a Bhikṣu, one must practice Dàna.'
Otherwise, in future lives, one will be poor."
Afterward, both Bhikṣus attained Āluóhàn (Arhatship).
The son of the Jiāluóyuè (Householder) became a Shāmén.
(The one who) begged for alms in his previous life
now obtained many self-disciplined followers,
who brought clothes and food to give him daily.
The other Bhikṣu, who in his previous life had only practiced self-discipline,
was now the son of a maidservant,
and begged for alms as a Shāmén.
No one gave him anything,
and he was constantly greatly hungry and thirsty. Therefore, one ought to uphold the precepts and practice Dàna,
and not merely practice self-discipline.
When the Buddha was in the world,
there was a Daòrén (cultivator)
who studied the Way beneath a tree by the riverbank.
His greedy thoughts were not eliminated;
his mind raced and scattered, dwelling only on the six desires.
Though his body was still, his mind wandered, never achieving peace.
For twelve years he could not attain the Way.
The Buddha knew he could be saved.
He transformed himself into a Shāmén
and went to where the cultivator was.
They lodged together beneath the tree.
In a moment, the moon became bright.
A turtle came out of the river
and arrived beneath the tree.
Then a water dog, hungry, came seeking food,
and encountered the turtle.
It immediately wanted to devour the turtle.
The turtle retracted its head, tail, and four legs,
hiding them within its shell so the dog could not eat it.
When the water dog moved slightly away,
the turtle again extended its head and feet, walking as before,
and thus was able to escape.
The transformed Shāmén then said to the Bhikṣu:
"I consider that people in the world are not like this turtle.
It has armor protecting its life
that prevents the water dog from gaining an advantage.
People in the world are unwise, indulging their six senses (passions).
Tiānmó (Heavenly Māra/Demons) gain advantage, destroying their physical bodies and corrupting their spirit,
leading to endless cycles of birth and death, revolving through the Five Paths,
suffering thousands of agonies."
He immediately spoke a Gà (verse) to encourage him.
The Bhikṣu heard the Gà, severed his greed, and stopped his wandering thoughts.
He attained the path of Āluóhàn.
Knowing that the transformed Shāmén was Fó Shìzūn (the Buddha, the World-Honored One),
he respectfully straightened his clothes and bowed his head at the Buddha's feet.
There was a Shāmén
who practiced Móbōlì (charity).
He fed the Bhikṣus.
He divided the curds and cream, putting some on his hand.
He smeared his hand on a pillar.
The pillar immediately cracked open.
There was a Shāmén
who, without snapping his fingers (to notify spirits), came to urinate.
The urine splashed a ghost's face in the clean water.
The fierce ghost became greatly angry
and wanted to kill the Shāmén.
The Shāmén upheld the precepts.
The fierce ghost followed him,
searching for his fault,
but could not gain an advantage.
Afterward, the Shāmén practiced Móbōlì.
Those who gave offerings of Saṅgha property to him
immediately, while sitting,
attained the path of Āluóhàn.
There were Shāméns who previously studied the Way together,
living in the same hall.
One Shāmén said,
"This Shāmén is ill-tempered; we cannot stay together."
He abandoned him and went to another country.
Later, he returned and passed by to see
if the other had attained the Way yet.
He arrived at his dwelling during the night.
The Shāmén opened the door, beckoned him, and asked him to sit forward.
He raised his five fingertips, and fire issued forth, illuminating the outside.
The visiting Shāmén was greatly astonished
and praised him for attaining the Way.
In the past, there was a man of the Four Castes,
named Yīlìshā,
whose wealth was countless.
He was stingy and begrudged clothing and food.
There was a poor old man
who lived near him.
Daily, he indulged freely
in eating and drinking fish and meat.
His guests were constant.
The man of the Four Castes thought to himself,
"My wealth is countless, yet I cannot compare to this old man."
He then killed a chicken
and cooked one pint of white rice.
He placed it on a carriage and went to an isolated spot.
He got down from the carriage, just about to eat.
Tiāndì (the Celestial Emperor) transformed himself into a dog and approached,
looking him up and down.
He said to the dog,
"If you hang upside down in the air,
will I give you some or not?"
The dog immediately hung upside down in the air.
The man of the Four Castes was greatly terrified and said,
"If your eyes stick to the ground, will I give you some or not?"
The dog's two eyes dropped onto the ground.
The man of the Four Castes then moved away.
Tiāndì transformed himself into the body of the man of the Four Castes,
rode the carriage back home, and gave an order:
"If any outsider falsely claims to be the man of the Four Castes,
drive him away and beat him."
The man of the Four Castes returned late.
The gatekeepers cursed him and ordered him to leave.
Tiāndì took all the wealth and practiced great Dàna.
The man of the Four Castes could not return home either.
Once his wealth was exhausted, he became deranged because of it.
Tiāndì transformed himself into a person and asked,
"Why are you grieving?" He replied,
"My wealth is completely gone."
Tiāndì said,
"Indeed, possessing treasures causes people much anxiety.
If wealth is accumulated but not shared (Dàna), it eventually belongs to the Five Households.
Upon death, one becomes a hungry ghost,
constantly lacking clothing and food.
If by chance one is reborn as a human,
one always falls into a low and base state.
Do you not perceive impermanence (Anitya)?
You were rich yet stingy,
clinging to your wealth and not eating.
What did you hope for?"
Tiāndì explained the Four Noble Truths to him.
The man of the Four Castes understood the meaning.
Tiāndì transformed away.
The man of the Four Castes returned
and regretted his former intentions.
He devotedly gave Dàna until his wealth was gone and attained the Way.
Formerly, near Jīhúán (Jetavana Vihāra),
there was a poor family.
They wished to make offerings to the Shìzūn and all the disciples,
but being destitute and poor, they had no means to do so.
So they went and swept the Buddha's Vihāra,
wholeheartedly and tirelessly.
Near the dwelling of the poor worthy one was a Zhǎngzhě (elder).
As he traveled around, he observed
several dozen seven-jeweled mansions in a great marsh.
Seeing them from afar, he went to ask a person,
"Who built these palace dwellings?
They are so beautiful and wonderful."
That person replied,
"There is a poor worthy one
who sweeps the Buddha's Vihāra.
His merit should produce (a reward) here,
and these palace dwellings were built to await him."
The Zhǎngzhě was pleased and said,
"I will scheme for this."
He immediately went to the poor man's house and said, "Sir,
give me your fine possession,
and I will give you five hundred ounces of gold."
He replied, "I have always been poor and destitute.
How could I have a fine possession?"
The Zhǎngzhě said,
"Just promise it to me."
He said, "I can do that."
(The Zhǎngzhě) then gave him five hundred ounces of gold. The worthy one received the gold
and widely offered Dàna.
The Buddha taught him the Dharma,
and he immediately attained the Path.
The Buddha was in Píshèlǐ.
At mealtime, he put on his robes and took his bowl,
bringing Ānán into the city to beg for food.
At that time, in the city of Píshèlǐ,
there was a householder named Píluósīnà.
He had dismissed his guests
and was enjoying himself with the five desires for seven days.
He told the doorman, "Do not permit anyone through the outer gate."
At that time, the Buddha was begging for food,
and gradually approached Píluósīnà's house.
At that moment, he heard the sounds of music being played.
He then addressed Ānán, his attendant.
Ānán answered according to the situation.
The Buddha said,
"This elder
will surely die after seven days have passed.
When he dies, he will be born in the Tíkū Dìyù (Crying Hell).
The reason for this is
that the roots of goodness he originally cultivated are now severed;
he is no longer cultivating new ones.
Because of this, when his life ends, he will be born in hell."
Ānán said to the Buddha,
"Is there perhaps a means
by which this householder can pass these seven days without his life ending?"
The Buddha told Ānán,
"There is no means to prevent his life from ending.
There is only a means to avoid hell.
If that elder
shaves off his beard and hair, puts on the three Dharma robes,
and with resolute faith leaves home to practice the Way,
the elder will then be able to avoid falling into hell."
Ānán said to the Buddha,
"I shall now go and persuade him to leave home."
At that time, all the Śākya clan members in Píshèlǐ
commonly made a pact with Ānán, saying:
"When Ānán's words reach our home,
if there are people
sleeping inside,
or engaged in various activities,
they must all allow the person sent by Ānán to enter directly.
The reason for this is
that his speech is gentle and his words harm no one."
At that moment, Ānán spoke to the doorman:
"You may go in and inform him."
The doorman immediately entered
and fully explained the matter.
The elder immediately stopped his enjoyment, quickly came out, and paid respects at Ānán’s feet.
He said to Ānán,
"Please enter my house and bless my sons and daughters."
Ānán replied,
"The Tathāgata knows the time and does not speak falsely.
He predicted that you, elder, would perish in seven days,
and upon the end of your life, would be born in the Tíkū Dìyù."
Hearing this, the elder was terrified and wept.
He said to Ānán,
"Is there perhaps a means to prevent my life from ending?"
Ānán replied,
"There is no means by which your life can be saved.
There is only a means to avoid hell."
When the elder asked the reason,
Ānán replied,
"If you leave home, you will avoid hell."
At that time, this elder thought of arranging his family affairs
and then going to the Buddha to leave home and practice the Way.
He then made this statement:
"Seven days is still far away.
I will enjoy myself with the five desires today,
and I will go early tomorrow morning."
When it was time,
Ānán put on his robes and took his bowl, entering the city to beg for food.
He went to the householder's home and said to the householder,
"One day has now passed; six days remain.
You should leave home immediately."
The elder replied,
"I will go later."
In the same manner, he repeatedly said,
"I want to enjoy myself further;
I will go the day after tomorrow."
Thus, he procrastinated and could not resolve himself.
Ānán went every single day to persuade him.
When the sixth day was complete,
on the morning of the seventh day,
Ānán spoke to him again.
Finally, he arranged his family affairs,
bid farewell to his family great and small,
and went to the Buddha’s place.
The World-Honored One commanded Ānán
to administer the full monastic precepts to him.
Having completed the receiving of the precepts,
he passed away during the last watch of that seventh day,
and was born in the Four Heavenly Kings Heaven (Sìwángtiān).
Ānán asked the Buddha,
"Where was he
born?"
The Buddha told Ānán,
"Bhikṣu Píluósīnà,
upon his death, was born in the Sìwángtiān.
When his life there ended,
he was born in the Heaven of the Thirty-Three (Sānshísāntiān).
Thus, he cycled through human and celestial realms,
passing through nine *kalpas*.
Receiving rebirth alternately in the heavens and among humans, in his very last body,
he returned again to the human realm,
shaved off his beard and hair,
and with resolute faith,
left home to practice the Way,
achieving the state of a Pratyekabuddha,
named Píluósīnà.
The reason for this is
that this Bhikṣu Píluósīnà,
having received the full precepts and diligently practiced until the end of his life, achieved this result."
As for Ānán's pure conduct and its reward,
wherever he is born, he receives blessings.
The Buddha was dwelling in the Vihāra (Jīngshè) in the wilderness outside Wángshěchéng.
There were five hundred bhikṣus
all begging for funds to build dwellings.
There was a merchant who, seeing the bhikṣus approaching,
immediately closed his shop and returned home to avoid them.
A bhikṣu encountered him on another road, accosting him.
He then preached about retribution (guǒbào),
instructing him to generate faith.
He even went so far as to seize him by the head
and forcibly urged him to make offerings (bùshī).
The reason for this was
to enable him to gain appearance, strength, and long life,
to increase his merit and virtue, and attain the fruit of Amṛta (Gānlù Guǒ).
The merchant heard this and generated faith,
making a small offering.
Later, he saw Shèlìfú
and fully recounted the incident to Shèlìfú.
Shèlìfú, having heard this,
preached the Dharma to delight him,
and then returned and fully informed the Buddha.
The Buddha told the bhikṣu managing the affairs (Yíngshì Bhikṣu),
"In a past world,
there was a bhikṣu
named Bápìn.
He dwelt in a forest.
At that time, Śījūnduō birds
also nested in this forest.
They cried out noisily morning and evening, disturbing Bápìn. Bápìn went to the World-Honored One's dwelling,
bowed his head at the Buddha's feet,
and stood to one side.
The World-Honored One consoled and inquired,
"Are you free of sickness and vexation, living contentedly in the forest?"
The bhikṣu replied,
"I am free of sickness and vexation and live happily there.
However, the Śījūnduō birds
squawk and create a disturbance, preventing me from meditating (sīwéi)."
The Buddha told the bhikṣu,
"Do you wish that these birds would never come at all?"
He replied,
"I do."
The Buddha said, "Bhikṣu,
when these birds come,
you should beg one feather from each of the birds."
The bhikṣu followed the instruction and begged for feathers.
The birds each dropped one feather.
When they left each morning, he begged again in this manner.
The birds then moved and stayed elsewhere for one night.
Finding no peace, they immediately returned.
At that time, the bhikṣu begged feathers from them again,
and they each gave him one again.
The flock of birds spoke among themselves:
"The Śramaṇa keeps begging for feathers ceaselessly.
We fear that soon our coat of feathers will be completely exhausted,
and we will be unable to fly again."
They then further discussed, saying,
"This bhikṣu permanently dwells in the forest.
We ought to leave
and seek other nesting places."
The various bhikṣus fully reported this to the Buddha, saying,
"The bhikṣu in the forest is timid and weak,
easily disturbed and fearful of the harsh bird sounds."
The Buddha said,
"It is not only today that he is timid and weak.
In a past age, there was a Dragon Elephant (Lóngxiàng)
dwelling in the forest.
A great wind suddenly arose,
blowing and breaking the trees.
The elephant heard the snapping sound
and fled in terror.
When its fear subsided slightly,
it took shelter under another tree.
That other tree also broke,
whereupon it fled again.
At that time, a god (Tiān) saw the elephant and thought,
"This elephant is randomly running wild."
He immediately spoke a *gāthā* (verse):
'The forest trees break in the windstorm, The Lóngxiàng flees in shock and fear.
Even if the whole world turns to chaos, Where can the Lóngxiàng hide?'"
Fó said.
The elephant at that time
was the Bhikṣu (Bǐqiū) in the forest.
Fó (Buddha) again addressed the Bhikṣus (Bǐqiū):
In a past lifetime,
there were five hundred Immortals (Xiānrén),
dwelling within the Xuěshān (Snow Mountain).
At that time, one Immortal (Xiānrén)
resided in a separate place.
There was excellent spring water,
and flowers and fruits were luxuriant.
Not far from this place,
there was Sàluó Shuǐ (Sàluó Water).
In the water lived a Nāga (Lóng).
The Nāga (Lóng) saw the Immortal's (Xiānrén) dignified and orderly demeanor,
and affection arose in his heart; he came to visit the Immortal (Xiānrén).
It happened that he arrived just as the Immortal (Xiān) was sitting in the full lotus posture.
The Nāga (Lóng) encircled the Immortal (Xiānrén) seven times.
He covered the top of his head with his own head and stayed there.
Daily it was like this.
Only during mealtime did he not come.
Because the Nāga (Lóng) encircled his body,
the Immortal (Xiānrén) sat upright day and night, unable to rest.
His body became emaciated and weak, and immediately developed sores and scabies.
At that time, people resided nearby,
offering provisions to the Immortal (Xiānrén).
They went to the place of the Immortal (Xiānrén)
and saw his weakness, sores, and scratching.
They immediately asked,
"Why is it like this?"
The Immortal (Xiānrén) fully recounted the aforementioned events.
They further asked,
"Do you wish the Nāga (Lóng) never to return?"
He replied, "Indeed."
They then told the Immortal (Xiānrén):
"Upon this Nāga's (Lóng) throat there is a precious pearl forming a necklace.
You may demand the pearl from the Nāga (Lóng).
The nature of Nāgas (Lóng) is stinginess; they will ultimately not give it to anyone."
When the Nāga (Lóng) came, the Immortal (Xiānrén) immediately demanded the pearl.
The Nāga (Lóng) heard this request;
his heart immediately became displeased, and slowly he departed.
The next day, the Nāga (Lóng) came and recited a verse from afar:
“The lustrous Maṇi (Móní) jewel, a necklace adorning my body—
If a Nāga (Lóng) can bestow it upon me, only then is he a truly good friend.”
The Nāga (Lóng) replied with a verse:
“Fearing the loss of the Maṇi (Móní) pearl, it is like holding a stick and calling a dog.
The precious pearl cannot be obtained; I will not come back to see you again.
Superior food and all treasures are due to this venerated Maṇi (Móní).
This ultimately cannot be obtained. Why do you earnestly seek it?
Excessive demands separate affection and love; because of this, I will not come again.”
At that time, a Deva (Tiānrén)
spoke in the empty sky,
reciting a verse:
“The reason for dislike and abandonment arises
entirely due to excessive demands. When the Brahmacārin (Fànzhì) showed signs of greed, the Nāga (Lóng) then sank into the abyss.”
Fó (Buddha) addressed the Bhikṣus (Bǐqiū) who were involved in many activities:
“Nāgas (Lóng) and elephants are mere animals,
yet they detest excessive demands.
How much more so should humans?
You Bhikṣus (Bǐqiū),
do not engage in many activities, extensively seeking without satiety,
causing those faithful Brāhmaṇas (Póluómén) and householders (Jūshì)
to suffer distress while giving up their wealth.”
At that time, the Buddha (Fó) was with five hundred Bhikṣus (Bǐqiū).
They arrived in the country of Vṛji (Báqí Guó).
They resided in the city of Vaiśālī (Píshèlǐ Chéng).
The people suffered famine, and the five grains did not ripen.
The dead lay everywhere, and alms food was difficult to obtain.
A wealthy elder (zhǎngzhě) in the city was named Yaśas (Yēshè).
Yēshè, having left the household life, found alms food difficult to obtain.
He frequently returned home looking for food.
His mother told him:
"You are suffering greatly.
Our family wealth is considerable.
You may use whatever you wish.
Your wife is still here.
You should live together.
You are free to perform giving (bùshī) and make offerings to the Three Jewels (Sānbǎo)."
This was repeated up to three times.
Yēshè did not comply.
His mother further told him:
"If you do not delight in the five desires (wǔyù),
then at least beg for a seed from me to continue the lineage.
So that after I die, our property will not be confiscated by the government."
Yēshè replied:
"Since you wish to leave a seed,
I now respectfully obey this command."
The mother quickly went in and announced it.
The new wife (xīnfù) said, "Good."
He adorned himself, and they met just once.
The wife immediately became pregnant.
Later she bore a son, who was consequently named Xùzhǒng (Continuation of the Seed).
People of the world spoke of this,
even referring to the property as belonging to Xùzhǒng.
When Yēshè heard this,
he felt greatly ashamed.
He immediately reported it to Śāriputra (Shèlìfú).
Śāriputra, in turn, reported it to the World-Honored One (Shìzūn).
Yēshè went with Śāriputra to the place of the Buddha.
He reported the complete matter to the Buddha (Fó).
The Buddha said:
"Bhikṣu Yēshè,
such a thing has never occurred within the Saṅgha (sēng).
You ignorant person!
You have opened the gate to a great offense."
The Buddha continued:
"It is not only today, in my Dharma, that he has suffered this kind of wretchedness.
In a past lifetime,
he was born in the Radiant Sound Heaven (Guāngyīn Tiān).
When this world first formed,
there was one person,
who was restless, agitated, and greedy for desire.
He came first and ate the flavor of this earth.
The remaining sentient beings then followed suit and imitated his practice.
Their minds became attached and indulged.
Their bodies became heavy, and desire arose because of this.
Their transcendent powers (shéntōng) departed, and their radiance immediately vanished.
Because of this, the sun and moon subsequently arose.
That restless sentient being was Yēshè.
His mother did not only today deceive and mislead her son.
In the past, she had previously informed the various Bhikṣus.
At that time, the country was named Kāśi (Jiāshī).
The city was named Vārāṇasī (Bōluónài).
The crown prince (wángzǐ) was named Dàmíngchēng (Great Renown).
He practiced generosity (bùshī), maintained the precepts (chíjiè), and transformed the world through the Way (Dào).
The first Queen (fūrén) observed the constellations.
She saw a golden Deer King (lù wáng),
coming from the south, traversing the sky, and heading north.
The Queen thought:
"If I obtain this skin and make a mat from it, I will die without regret."
If she did not obtain it, she would remain the King’s Queen (Wáng Fūrén).
She immediately took off her necklace (yīngluò) and put on dirty, worn-out clothes.
She entered the Chamber of Distress (Yōunǎo Fáng).
The King sought her out, observing her intentions.
He immediately asked the attendant.
The attendant replied:
"The Queen has just entered and is staying in the Chamber of Distress."
The King then went and asked, "Who has offended you?"
She remained silent and did not answer.
The King sent someone to question her.
Again, she did not answer.
He then ordered an old, trusted female servant (qīngyī),
who was skilled in various clever methods, to speak to and persuade her in various ways.
She replied:
"No one has offended me.
I simply have something else on my mind, which is why I haven't spoken."
She then described seeing the golden deer.
She wished to obtain its skin and use it as a mat.
The qīngyī reported this to the King.
The King asked his officials:
"Who can obtain it?"
He then assembled the various hunters and commanded them:
"Seek it urgently."
The hunters all said:
"We have never heard its name,
let alone seen it."
The King commanded that they be chained in prison.
At that time, there was one hunter,
named Nàishé (Nàishé).
He was brave, strong, and ran as fast as a bounding beast.
He shot arrows at flying birds and never missed.
He thought to himself that he was innocent yet was being imprisoned.
He grasped the principle and asked:
"Are there any who have seen or heard of it?"
The King said:
"You can go ask the Queen yourself."
The Queen replied:
"I saw it from the top of the tower.
It came from the south, traversed the sky, and headed north."
The hunter was skilled in observing beasts.
He then knew that the deer rested in the south and fed in the north.
He sought it out at its feeding ground.
The hunter, carrying his bow and arrows, gradually walked north.
He eventually reached the Snow Mountain (Xuě Shān).
On the mountain were Immortals (Xiānrén),
who concealed all hunting equipment.
At the Immortals' residence,
he paid his respects and inquired after their well-being.
They ordered him to take a seat.
They offered him various drinks and fruits.
The hunter asked:
"How long have you lived here?"
The Immortal replied, "For many years."
The hunter said:
"Have you ever experienced any unusual or strange things?" He replied:
"South of this mountain there is a tree,
named Nyagrodha (Nígūlǜ).
A golden Deer King (Lù Wáng) frequently
flies here and eats its leaves from above."
The Immortal showed him the way.
He arrived beneath the tree and saw it.
The tree was sparse, but its covering of leaves was very wide.
Suddenly, he saw the deer.
Like a King of Geese, it came traversing the sky.
It landed atop the tree and ate the leaves.
When it was full, it flew away again.
He returned and reported this to the King:
"It is not reachable by net or arrow.
There is no means to obtain it."
"You should go yourself and report this to the Queen."
The Queen said to the hunter:
"You can take honey and smear it on the highest leaves.
Next time, move downward, and set up a net and snare (wǎng xuǎn) there.
The deer will search for the honey.
Lured by the fragrance, it will gradually eat the leaves,
descending until it reaches the snare location,
and be captured by the snare.
Then drive it away alive."
The Immortal saw this from afar and said:
"Alas! How terrible this calamity is!
Although it can traverse the sky,
it cannot escape the hands of the wicked."
The Immortal spoke a Gāthā (Jì):
The greatest evil in the world is none other than fragrance and flavor (xiāngwèi).
It deceives ordinary people and all the beasts of the forest and plains.
Due to the attachment to fragrance and flavor, one suffers this painful affliction.
The hunter smeared honey on the tree leaves.
After [the deer] ate, he brought it back.
The King heard the deer had arrived.
He burned incense and welcomed it.
The Queen saw it.
She stepped forward and embraced the Deer King.
Because of the serious nature of her defiling attachment (wūrǎn qíng zhòng),
the golden color of the Deer King immediately vanished.
The King told the Queen, "The golden color of this deer has suddenly changed and disappeared.
What should be done?"
The Queen said:
"This golden thing is now useless.
Release it and let it go."
The golden deer
was Yēshè.
The Queen (Fūrén) was Yēshè’s mother.
They have suffered various miseries and greedy attachments even until today.
(Śrāvastī City). There was a Bhikṣu named Nántí
. Whether walking, standing, sitting, or lying down, his mind constantly focused on samādhi (concentration)
. After seven years had passed, he lost his Dhyāna concentration
. He again relied beneath a tree and resumed practicing *zhèngshòu*, desiring to regain his original concentration
. Māra watched for his opportunity and transformed into a woman of incomparable beauty
. She stood before him and spoke to him, saying
: "Bhikṣu, come commit fornication with me
." Nántí said
: "Evil delusion, quickly vanish
! Evil delusion, quickly vanish
!" Although his mouth spoke the words, his eyes did not look
. The second and third times were also like this
. The Heavenly Maiden then took off her clothes, exposing her form, and stood before Nántí
. Nántí saw her form and his mind became stained by lust
. At that time, the Heavenly Maiden gradually backed away and left
. Nántí called out, saying
: "You may wait a little
!" The Heavenly Maiden swiftly reached the moat of the Qíhuán
(Jetavana). In the moat there was a dead horse
. The Heavenly Maiden concealed her form there and disappeared
. Nántí’s desire was fiercely intense
. He immediately fornicated with this dead horse
. After his lust subsided, he reflected that this was unwholesome
. He immediately took off his monastic robes and went to Qíhuán
. He spoke to the Bhikṣus, saying
: "I have committed a heavy transgression
." The Bhikṣus immediately asked for the circumstances
. Nántí recounted the full story
. The Bhikṣus reported the matter to the Buddha
. The Buddha ordered him to be expelled
. The Bhikṣus reported to the Buddha, saying
: "Nántí practiced the holy life (brahmacarya) for a long time
. How was he seduced by a woman
?" The Buddha said
: "Nántí was not only seduced by a woman now
; it was the same in the past
. In a past life, in the southern country of Āpóntí Guó (Avanti), there was one of the Kāshè Shì
(Kāśyapa clan). He was an outsider (Tīrthika) who renounced the household life, intelligent and widely knowledgeable
. He assisted the king in governing the nation
. The king enforced the national laws, torturing and punishing criminals and bandits
. The Tīrthika reflected, saying
: 'I have already renounced the household life
. How can I share with the king in judging and deciding these matters
?' He immediately reported to the king, saying
: 'I wish to leave the household life.' The king said
: 'Master, you have already left the household life
. Why do you still say, "I wish to leave the household life"
?' He replied
: 'Now that I participate in these various kinds of punishments
, how can I be called one who has left the household life
? I now wish to leave the household life according to the way of the Immortals
.' The king said, 'So be it
.' He immediately built a monastery on Bǎiyán Shān (Hundred Crags Mountain)
. He practiced the way of the Immortals and obtained the Five Supernatural Powers
. Suddenly, due to a minor physiological need, impurities flowed out
. At that time, there was a female deer
. It drank this urine and licked its vulva
. It immediately became pregnant and gave birth to a small child
. The Immortal went to look and saw the deer giving birth to a child
. He was astonished and reflected, saying
: 'How can a beast give birth to a human
?' He entered concentration to observe it
. Knowing it was his son, he took him in and raised him
. Because he was born dependent on the mother (deer), his body was spotted like a deer
. Therefore, he was named Lùbān
(Deer Spot). The Immortal thought, saying
: 'Nothing ruins uprightness and destroys virtue more than women
.' Thereupon, he taught him Dhyāna concentration
. He guided him with the Five Supernatural Powers
. And for him, he spoke a gāthā (verse), saying
: 'All classes of living beings
inevitably return to death; Following where their karma leads,
they personally receive their retribution. Those who do good are born in heaven;
those who commit evil deeds enter the hells. Practicing the Way and cultivating the holy life,
when defilements cease, one attains Nirvāṇa.' At that time, the Immortal immediately passed away
. Thereupon, the boy purely cultivated the holy life
. He obtained the Five Supernatural Powers
. Shìtí Huányīn
(Śakra Devānām Indra), riding a white dragon-elephant, traveled around the world observing
: 'Who is filial and obedient to parents,
making offerings to Śramaṇas and Brāhmaṇas, and who is capable of practicing generosity, observing precepts, and cultivating the holy life
?' While traversing the world, he then saw this Immortal boy
. The Heavenly Emperor (Śakra) reflected, saying
: 'If this boy
seeks to become Shìtí or Brahma King, he will surely be able to achieve it
. He should be corrupted early
.' Thus, he devised a skillful means and struck the Dharma drum
. Hundreds of thousands of heavenly beings (Devaputras) all gathered
. Shìtí announced, saying
: 'In Yánfútí (Jambudvīpa) there is an Immortal boy
, named Lùbān
. He possesses great merit
. I wish to corrupt him
.' The heavenly beings were unhappy upon hearing this
. They then reflected, saying
: 'If this person is corrupted
, it will diminish the multitudes of Devas
and increase the Asuras
.' One heavenly being then proclaimed these words
: 'Who should go
?' At that time, there was a reply, saying
: 'This Heavenly Maiden should go
.' They immediately summoned her
. Immediately, hundreds of thousands of Heavenly Maidens all gathered
. There was one Heavenly Maiden
, named Ālánfú
. Her hair was multi-colored, having four colors
. Blue, yellow, red, and white—thus she was called Multi-Colored
. This Heavenly Maiden was selected to go to Yánfútí
to corrupt the boy Lùbān
. The Heavenly Maiden then reported to Shìtí, saying
: 'Since times long past
, I have frequently corrupted the holy lives of humans
, causing them to lose their Supernatural Powers
. I wish that you would instead send another Heavenly Maiden who is more beautiful and attractive to delight people
.' Then Shìtí again spoke various verses among the assembly to encourage the Heavenly Maiden
. Thereupon, the Heavenly Maiden immediately corrupted the Immortal boy
." The Buddha informed the Bhikṣus
: "At that time, was the Immortal boy someone different
? He is none other than the present Dhyāna Nántí
. As for the Heavenly Maiden Ālánfú
, she is this Heavenly Maiden now
The Buddha lived in Kùshēmí Guó.
At that time, the elder Chǎntuó
had a wicked nature and was difficult to address.
All the Bhikṣus, even after triple admonition within the Saṅgha,
still could not make him cease.
The Bhikṣus reported to the Buddha.
The Buddha said:
In the past, there was a son of an elder.
He had a slave named Āmóyóu.
His nature was fierce and evil.
At that time, the elder’s son and the sons of various Brahmins were playing in the garden grove.
All the followers stayed outside the garden gate.
Then Āmóyóu, outside the garden gate, beat the followers.
The followers who were beaten
each reported to their masters.
Then all the sons of the Brahmins came out and reprimanded him.
But Āmóyóu did not accept their words.
He answered the sons of the Brahmins, saying:
"I will not follow your words.
If my master's son comes to reprimand me, then I shall accept his words."
Consequently, the beating did not stop.
(The beaten slaves) immediately came and told Āmóyóu’s master.
Āmóyóu’s master possessed the divine eye from birth.
He observed the fighting location.
Below it was a hidden treasury of gold and silver.
"It is the fierce nature of the ground that causes this fighting!"
He immediately went and reprimanded him.
At that time, the slave immediately stopped.
The Buddha told the Bhikṣus,
"Was the elder’s son at that time anyone else?
It was myself.
As for Āmóyóu at that time,
it is Chǎntuó Bhikṣu now. Also, in a past age,
there was a great scholar Brahmin named Fúlúxī.
He was the king’s teacher and constantly taught the children.
At that time, a slave was born in the Brahmin's house.
Named Jiāluóhē.
He was usually tasked with supplying the needs of the children.
This slave had sharp faculties; hearing the Dharma spoken, he could remember and retain it all.
Once, this slave had a small resentment against the children,
and then ran away to another kingdom.
He falsely claimed, saying:
"I am the son of the Brahmin Fúlúxī.
My personal name is Yěruòdáduō."
He spoke to the Brahmin who was the teacher of this kingdom’s king, saying:
"I am the son of Fúlúxī, the king’s teacher in Bōluónài Guó.
I have intentionally come here
wishing to take refuge under the Great Master to study the Brahmin Dharma."
The Master answered, "That is acceptable."
This slave was intelligent, and had heard the teachings before.
Now hearing them again, he was able to retain everything he heard.
The Master was extremely pleased.
He immediately ordered him to teach the five hundred young disciples, saying:
"You teach them in my place.
I must attend to the royal family."
This Master Brahmin had no sons.
He had only one daughter.
He then formed this thought:
"I can now give my daughter in marriage to Yěruòdáduō.
If he stays in my house, he will be like my son."
He immediately told him, saying:
"Yěruòdáduō, do not return to that kingdom.
I shall now give my daughter in marriage to you."
He answered:
"I follow your instruction."
He immediately stayed home with the daughter.
They lived together and made a life like son and father.
The household gradually became wealthy.
But Yěruòdáduō, if the food and drink were not good,
would immediately become greatly angry.
His wife respected him greatly.
She sought information about that person, but was unable to obtain it.
At that time, the Brahmin Fúlúxī fully heard that his slave was there.
He formed this thought:
"My slave Jiāluóhē
escaped to another kingdom.
I should go and seize him.
Perhaps I can recover the slave."
He immediately went straight to that kingdom.
At that time, Yěruòdáduō,
along with his disciples, went to the garden grove to play.
While on the road, he encountered his original master.
He was immediately terrified and secretly instructed his disciples:
"O children!
You should all go back
and recite and practice by yourselves."
After the disciples left,
he immediately went before his master.
He prostrated his head and face to the master’s feet and spoke to him, saying:
"When I came to this kingdom,
I said my master was my father.
I then took refuge under the great scholar Brahmin, the master of this kingdom, as my teacher.
Because I possess the great scholarly scriptures,
the Master Brahmin gave me his daughter as my wife.
I beg your honor today not to expose my identity.
I will offer you the price for a slave."
The master Brahmin (Fúlúxī) was good at understanding worldly affairs.
He immediately answered, "You are truly my son.
What else is there to say?"
He simply created a pretense
and was quickly sent on his way and brought back to the house.
He told his family,
"My relative has arrived."
His wife was happy.
She prepared various kinds of food and drink.
After the food was offered and finished,
when there was a short period of free time,
she paid respect to the guest Brahmin’s feet,
and asked him, saying:
"When I serve my husband, Yěruòdáduō,
the food and drink offerings are constantly unsatisfactory to him.
I wish you would now instruct me what food he used to eat when he was at home.
I will prepare the food and drink according to his former custom."
The guest Brahmin immediately became angry.
And he formed this thought:
"This fellow! This fellow!
Tormenting the daughter of another household!"
He spoke to the daughter, saying:
"Just send me away quickly.
When I am about to leave,
I will teach you a verse.
When you recite this verse,
it will make your husband speechless."
After sending off the guest Brahmin,
when he was about to depart,
he spoke one verse for her, saying:
Having no relatives, roaming other lands, deceiving people under heaven.
Rough food is the norm; what is there to dislike about merely eating it?
"I now give you this verse.
If he gets angry and complains that the food is poor,
then stand near him, turn your back, and softly recite it,
letting him hear it."
Having given this instruction,
he then returned to his own kingdom.
As for Yěruòdáduō,
after sending his master away,
every time it came to mealtime,
he would again become angry.
His wife tested reciting the verse near her husband.
When the husband heard this verse, his heart was immediately displeased.
He then formed this thought:
"Alas! This old one
exposed my shameful affair!"
From this point onward, he always spoke gently.
He feared his wife would tell others his private secrets.
The Buddha told the Bhikṣus:
"At that time, the Brahmin Fúlúxī
of Bōluónài Chéng,
was he anyone else?
It was myself.
As for the slave Jiāluóhē at that time,
he is Chǎntuó Bhikṣu now.
At that time,
he already relied on me to abuse others.
Now, it is likewise so.
He relies on my influence
to abuse others."
In Śrāvastī City (Shěwèichéng) there were two Mahāras (Móhēluó).
They both abandoned their wives and children and left home to follow the Way (become monks).
After traveling among people for a long time,
they both returned to Śrāvastī (Shěwèi),
sharing one room.
Each contemplated
temporarily returning home to see their wives and children.
They immediately went to their original homes.
When the wife saw him, she angrily said,
"You, being deficient in virtue and without principles, abandoned your family to study the Way!
Our daughter is grown and cannot be married off.
Why have you come now? I ought to break your legs."
The younger Mahāra (Móhēluó)
immediately returned to the room, sorrowful and unhappy.
The older Mahāra (Móhēluó) was also driven out.
They returned to the room together.
He asked his younger companion,
"Why are you suffering from worry?"
He replied,
"Why is there a need to ask?"
(The elder) asked again,
"We two
share one room.
If you do not share your good and bad affairs with me,
and don't tell me,
then who should you tell?"
(The younger) immediately explained the whole matter.
The older Mahāra (Móhēluó) said,
"What is there to worry about in this?
My family is also like that.
Your son and my daughter can be a matching couple."
(The younger) replied, "That can be done."
The younger Mahāra (Móhēluó) returned and told his wife,
"I have found a son-in-law for our daughter."
The wife replied, "That is excellent."
The older one also returned
and reported to his wife,
"I have found a wife for our son."
She asked, "Who is it?"
He answered, "A certain girl."
Thus, the two Mahāras (Móhēluó) arranged the marriage.
Each rejoiced as if the poor had obtained treasure,
and they loved and respected each other even more.
The Buddha (Fó) told the Bhikṣus (Bǐqiū),
"These two Mahāras (Móhēluó) did not only perform such deeds today.
In the past, in the Kingdom of Kāśī (Jiāshīguó),
there was a Brāhmaṇa (Póluómén).
He possessed old, ground, sandy beans
which were impossible to cook thoroughly,
and he could not sell them commercially."
Furthermore, there was another family that kept a vicious, stubborn donkey.
It also could not be sold.
The bean owner thought,
"I will now exchange these beans for that donkey."
So he went and spoke to him.
The donkey owner also thought,
"I will use this stubborn donkey to exchange for those beans."
He replied, "That can be done."
They were both happy.
The bean owner recited a verse, saying:
"It is the way of the Brāhmaṇa (Póluómén) to skillfully market these old, frozen beans, sixteen ages old;
You will waste all your firewood trying to cook them, and they still won't soften, breaking the teeth of everyone in your family, young and old."
Then the donkey owner
also composed a verse, saying:
"What joy do you, Brāhmaṇa (Póluómén), possess? Although it has four legs and fine hairy coat,
when carrying heavy loads on long roads, you will know that even being stabbed by an awl or burned by fire, it absolutely will not move."
Then the bean owner
spoke another verse, saying:
"I will live alone for a thousand years, carrying a four-inch awl fixed to the tip of my staff.
Since I can subdue this useless, stubborn donkey, what worry is there that it cannot be managed?"
Then the donkey addressed the master
and spoke a further verse, saying:
"I will firmly plant my two front feet and double-kick with my two hind hooves,
breaking your front molars; then you will naturally know."
The bean owner again addressed the donkey
with a verse, saying:
"When flies, mosquitoes, and venomous insects sting you, you rely only on your tail to protect yourself.
I shall cut off your tail, and then you will know suffering and bitterness."
The donkey replied again, saying:
"From my ancestors onward, we have practiced this stubborn, violent manner.
I inherit and practice this unto death; I will never abandon it."
At that time, the bean owner,
knowing that its vile temperament could not be managed through harsh words,
immediately praised it with a verse, saying:
"Your voice is resonant and clear; your face is beautiful, like white shell-snow.
I shall find a wife for you, and you can travel together through all the forests and marshes."
When the donkey heard these gentle, loving words,
it immediately spoke a verse in return, saying:
"I can carry eight *hú* and travel six hundred *lǐ* daily!
Brāhmaṇa (Póluómén), you should know that upon hearing of a wife, my heart rejoices!"
The Buddha (Fó) said,
"Those two people then
are the two Mahāras (Móhēluó) of today.
That donkey then
is the son of the Mahāra (Móhēluó) now.
They had previously cheated each other, causing the Brāhmaṇa (Póluómén) householder distress and loss of property."
The Buddha (Fó) told Śāriputra (Shèlìfú),
"In the past, there was a Buddha
whose title was Jìnshèng.
There were two Bhikṣus (Bǐqiū):
one named Wúshèng,
and the second named Chánghuān.
Bhikṣu (Bǐqiū) Wúshèng possessed the Six Supernatural Powers.
Bhikṣu (Bǐqiū) Chánghuān had not yet eliminated the bonds and defilements.
There was a certain Elder (Zhǎngzhě)
named Dà'ài.
His wife was named Shànhuàn.
She was peerlessly beautiful.
These two Bhikṣus (Bǐqiū) relied on them as Dānapatis (Tányuè).
The wife Shànhuàn provided offerings to Wúshèng,
managing everything so that nothing was lacking.
Chánghuān received extremely scant provisions.
Chánghuān became jealous and slandered (Wúshèng), saying,
'Bhikṣu (Bǐqiū) Wúshèng is having an affair with Shànhuàn.
He only receives offerings due to affection and love.'
The Buddha (Fó) said to Śāriputra (Shèlìfú),
'Do you know who Chánghuān was?
He was my present self.
The wife Shànhuàn
is the Brāhmaṇa (Póluómén) woman, Cañcā (Zhānshā).
At that time, by slandering Wúshèng, who was an Arhat (Luóhàn),
(I spent) countless thousands of years in hell.
Although I have attained Buddhahood now, due to the residual karmic retribution,
that talkative girl used a wooden bowl, pretended to be pregnant, and danced,
coming before me and saying:
"Śramaṇa (Shāmén), why do you not speak about family matters,
but rather speak about the affairs of others?
You rejoice alone now, unaware of my suffering.
You first had relations with me, and now I have a child in my body.
When the time comes, I need ghee and oil
to nourish the infant.
You must provide everything for me."
At that time, the assembly bowed their heads and remained silent.
Śakro Devānām Indra (Shìtíhuányīn), who was standing behind and fanning the Buddha (Fó),
transformed into a rat.
It entered her clothing
and gnawed the wooden bowl, causing it to fall to the ground.
Then the four assemblies of disciples and the six teachers
raised their voices in celebration, rejoicing and laughing boundlessly. They all cursed her together, saying:
"You creature deserving of death!
You dared to slander the Supreme and True One!
This ground is senseless
to be able to bear such an evil creature!"
The earth immediately split open, and fierce flames burst forth.
The woman immediately fell into the Mahāniraya (Dànílí).
When the great assembly saw this,
King Ajātaśatru (Āshéshì Wáng) was terrified, his hair standing on end.
He immediately rose and reported,
"Where is this woman now?"
The Buddha (Fó) replied,
"Great King,
the place where this woman has fallen
is called Avīci Niraya (Ābínílí)."
The King asked the Buddha (Fó) again,
"Did this woman not kill or steal, but merely lie
to fall into Avīci (Ābí)?"
The Buddha (Fó) replied to the Great King,
"The Dharma I teach
includes actions of body, mouth, and mind, categorized as superior, medium, and inferior."
The King asked the Buddha (Fó) again,
"Which is the most serious (heavy)?
Which is medium?
Which is the inferior (lightest)?"
The Buddha (Fó) told King Ajātaśatru (Āshéshì Wáng),
"Action of the mind (yì xíng) is the most serious.
Action of the mouth (kǒu xíng) is medium.
Action of the body (shēn xíng) is the inferior."
In the Kingdom of Kāosàluó there were two Bhikṣus.
One man violated the precepts.
One man upheld the precepts.
They wished to go together to see the Buddha.
On the road, they encountered water containing insects.
The one who violated the precepts said to the one who upheld the precepts:
"We can drink this water together."
The one who upheld the precepts said:
"There are insects in the water.
How can we drink it?"
The one who violated the precepts said:
"If I do not drink, I will die,
and I will not be able to see the Buddha, hear the Dharma, or see the Saṅgha."
The upholder of the precepts refused to drink, even unto death.
At that time, the violator of the precepts drank.
The upholder of the precepts died because he did not drink.
He was immediately reborn in the Thirty-Three Heavens (Trāyastriṃśa).
He obtained a complete heavenly body.
He first arrived at the Buddha's place and bowed his head and face to the Buddha’s feet.
He stood to one side.
The Buddha taught the Dharma to him in various ways, and he attained the purification of the Dharma Eye.
Immediately, he bowed to the Buddha’s feet and said:
"I take refuge in the Buddha, I take refuge in the Dharma, I take refuge in the Saṅgha.
I shall be a Yōupósāi (Upāsaka) for the rest of my life."
After the Buddha taught him the Dharma again, he became silent.
At that time, the deva finished bowing to the Buddha,
and suddenly disappeared.
At that time, the one who drank the water arrived later at the Buddha’s place.
The Buddha was surrounded by countless beings, teaching the Dharma. The Buddha saw the Bhikṣu approach.
The Buddha immediately uncovered his Yōuduōluósēng (upper robe).
He showed his golden-colored hand.
"You foolish man, you desire to see my physical body.
Why are you not like the one who upheld the precepts,
who first saw my Dharma body?"
The Buddha spoke a verse (gāthā):
"The mind does not observe well, and the seeing is not truly discerning;
Foolish like a moth plunging into fire, craving to observe my body.
The material body is merely impure; what do you seek to see?
Within it are fat, blood, and flesh, outwardly covered by thin skin.
That one, though scorched by thirst, still practiced and honored the precepts;
Until death, he guarded my teachings. He saw Me; you did not."
When the Buddha had finished speaking this verse,
he addressed all the Bhikṣus:
"From now on, traveling is not permitted if one does not carry a water strainer (filter bag).
If one does not carry it, one transgresses.
Non-transgression applies if there is clear flowing water,
or a great river or spring water,
[and one is traveling] from this monastery to that monastery,
within twenty *lǐ* (miles)."
In Jiāluó Guó.
At that time, there was a hungry ghost (preta).
It stood leaning against the city gate.
The Bhikṣu Mǎnyuàn asked the hungry ghost:
"What are you seeking here now?"
The ghost said:
"Do you see me now?"
The Bhikṣu said, "Yes, I see you."
The ghost said:
"My husband entered the city and has not returned until now.
Therefore, I am standing here waiting for my husband to come out."
The Bhikṣu asked:
"What did your husband seek upon entering the city?"
The ghost answered:
"In this city today there is a great elder (Zhàngzhě).
He has been suffering from a chronic abscess.
Today it is about to burst.
Pus and blood will flow out.
My husband is bringing it back,
so the two of us can eat it together to sustain our lives."
The Bhikṣu asked again:
"How long ago did your husband enter the city?"
The city walls were close to a river.
She raised her finger and pointed to the city,
saying to the Bhikṣu:
"Since this city was founded and destroyed on this and the opposite bank,
this is now the seventh time.
My husband entered the city that long ago."
The form and lifespan of hungry ghosts are immeasurable and limitless.
Formerly, there were five hundred Bhikṣus.
They were traveling in a great marsh when they encountered robbers and bandits.
[The bandits] stole their robes.
They bound all the Bhikṣus,
making them all sit on the ground.
They gathered wild grass,
tied their hands with it, and then left.
These monastics realized that if they killed the grass in order to get up, they would violate the Buddha's precepts.
Each one reflected:
"I would rather destroy my own body,
than violate the precepts."
They remained bound for four days.
The King went out hunting.
He saw the monastics
sitting in the wilderness.
He dismounted, paid homage, and asked the reason for their condition.
They immediately answered fully.
The King unbound the monastics and took them back to offer them sustenance.
In the mountains, there was a Buddhist shrine (Fótú).
There was a separate room.
Inside there was an evil ghost (guǐ).
It habitually came to harass people.
All the monks had abandoned the place.
A guest monk came.
The Wéinà (Prior) instructed him to stay in this room,
and said to him:
"This room has a ghost that habitually comes to harass people."
The guest monk, relying on the power of his precept observance,
replied:
"What can a small ghost do?
I can subdue it."
He immediately entered the room and stayed there.
As dusk approached,
another monk came asking for lodging.
The Wéinà also instructed him to stay in this room
and also told him about the ghost.
That man also said:
"I shall subdue it."
The one who entered first
closed the door and sat properly, waiting for the ghost, which did not come.
The later arrival,
during the night, knocked on the door, asking to enter.
The one who entered first thought it was the ghost
and did not open the door for him.
The later arrival hammered vigorously on the door.
The monastic inside forcefully resisted.
The one outside prevailed,
pushed the door open, and managed to enter.
The one inside hit him,
and the one outside also hit him back violently.
When they saw each other the next morning,
they were in fact old classmates.
The monastics apologized to each other in shame.
The crowd gathered, laughing at and marveling at the incident.
The Buddha was in Shèwèi Guó.
There was a Bhikṣu
who lived in a dirt cave among the rocks in Cānguó.
His hair, beard, and nails were long, and his robes were ragged and worn.
At that time, King Yōutián Wáng
wished to go out on a pleasure tour and commanded that the roads be cleared.
The King, accompanied by his beautiful women, arrived at the foot of the mountain.
One of the beautiful women looked and saw the dirt cave.
Inside was a Bhikṣu,
whose beard, hair, and nails were long, and whose clothes were torn and tattered.
His appearance resembled a ghost.
She immediately cried out loudly:
"Son of Heaven!
There is a ghost in there!"
The King then asked from afar:
"Where is it now?"
The beautiful woman said:
"Close by, in the dirt cave among the rocks."
The King immediately drew his sword and followed.
He saw the Bhikṣu in that state.
He immediately asked: "What kind of person are you?"
He replied:
"I am a Śrāmaṇa (Shāmén)."
The King asked:
"What kind of Śrāmaṇa are you?"
He replied:
"I am a Shìjiā Śrāmaṇa."
The King said:
"Are you an Arhat (Yīngzhēn)?"
He replied, "No."
"Do you possess the Fourth Chán (Dhyāna)?"
He replied again, "No."
"Do you possess the Third Chán or the Second Chán?"
He replied again, "I do not possess them."
"Have you reached the First Chán?"
He replied:
"Truly, I practice the First Chán."
The King, becoming angry and unconvinced,
turned and said to his attendants:
"This eunuch has lustful intentions!
This Śrāmaṇa is merely an ordinary person without true practice.
How dare he look upon my beautiful women?"
He then commanded the attendant to quickly execute him.
The attendant immediately went away.
The mountain spirit (shān shén) thought:
"This Bhikṣu is without fault.
He is now in danger of death.
I should protect him and allow him to escape this calamity."
The spirit then transformed into a large pig
and slowly ran near the King.
The attendant immediately reported to the King:
"A large pig is close by the King."
The King immediately abandoned the Bhikṣu,
drew his sword, and chased the pig.
The Bhikṣu, seeing the King was already far away,
immediately ran out.
There was a Bhikṣu
who recited the Sūtra of Ēmítuó Fó
and the Great Bōrě Bōluómì (Prajñāpāramitā).
When this man was about to die, he told his disciples:
"Ēmítuó Fó has come with his great assembly."
He moved his body to take refuge and died within a moment.
After he died, his disciples cremated him.
The next day, upon collecting the ashes, they found his tongue unburnt.
The country of Jiāosàluó.
There was a Bhikṣu.
He lived alone in the deep mountains.
In the forest there was a female non-human (spirit).
She spoke to the Bhikṣu, proposing sexual relations.
The Bhikṣu said,
"Do not speak such words.
I am one who has severed sexual desire."
The woman said,
"If you do not come (agree),
I will destroy your livelihood (offerings) and cause you suffering and distress."
The Bhikṣu said, "Do as you wish."
In the middle of the night, while the Bhikṣu was sleeping,
the female ghost used a coarse robe to carry the Bhikṣu.
She placed him lying next to the Queen inside the King's palace.
When the King awoke, he asked,
"Who are you?"
The Bhikṣu said,
"I am a Śrāmaṇa."
"What kind of Śrāmaṇa are you?"
He replied,
"I am a Shìzi Śrāmaṇa."
The King said,
"Why have you come here now?"
The Bhikṣu fully recounted the events to the King.
The King said,
"Why do you need to dwell in deep forests and mountains?
Thus you are harassed by evil spirits.
Leave.
Because I understand the Buddha's Dharma, I will not interrogate you."
The Bhikṣu, having escaped, fully related the incident.
Because of this, the Buddha established a rule:
Do not enter the deep mountains.
Furthermore, in the country of Jiāosàluó,
there was a Bhikṣu
dwelling in an Āraṇya area.
There was a female Píshèzhē ghost.
She came and spoke to the Bhikṣu, saying,
"Come, let us engage in sexual activity."
The Bhikṣu said,
"Do not speak such words.
I am one who has severed sexual desire."
The female ghost said,
"If you do not agree,
I will destroy your livelihood (offerings) and cause you suffering and distress."
The Bhikṣu said,
"Do as you wish."
When the Bhikṣu slept at night,
the female ghost wrapped him up in a coarse robe and carried him.
She placed him inside a wine jar at a tavern.
The tavern keeper, the next day, saw the Bhikṣu inside the wine jar.
He asked,
"Who are you?"
He replied,
"I am a Śrāmaṇa."
"What kind of Śrāmaṇa are you?"
He replied,
"A Shìzi Śrāmaṇa."
He asked,
"Why are you inside this?"
The Bhikṣu fully recounted the events.
The tavern keeper said,
"You must leave."
Because of this, the Buddha said,
"Bhikṣus must not dwell in deep mountains, forests, solitary places, frightening places, or uninhabited places."
There was a Bhikṣu.
He went everywhere seeking alms (pindapāta).
By chance, he entered a brothel.
The prostitute saw him enter and was overjoyed and leaped up.
She immediately welcomed him, bowing her head to his feet.
She invited him out and offered him a seat.
She further asked the Bhikṣu,
"Venerable Sir, where have you come from?"
The Bhikṣu replied,
"I am mainly seeking alms, thus I came to beg."
She immediately prepared various delicious dishes and foods for him.
Filling his bowl to the brim, she offered it to him.
The Bhikṣu received it and departed.
Having obtained this fine food,
his heart was filled with delight, which he could not control.
He repeatedly went to visit her.
At that time, the woman thought to herself,
"I reckon this Bhikṣu,
who adheres to the Dharma, is unparalleled." She frequently prepared for him
sweet, crispy, rich, and delicious food,
and gave it to him.
His coming and going was ceaseless.
His studies (of the Dharma) were not yet clear;
his practice was not yet established.
Having not yet subdued his senses,
upon seeing the woman’s beautiful appearance, sexual desire immediately stirred.
His mouth uttered gentle, sweet, loving words.
His heart cherished attachment.
The Bhikṣu, hearing and seeing, was confused and led astray by lust,
unable to awaken himself.
At that time, the World-Honored One said,
"Although seeing women,
the elders should be regarded as mothers,
those in the middle as sisters,
the young as daughters
or sons and daughters.
One should contemplate the body internally,
reflecting that it is all foul discharge, having nothing lovable about it.
Externally it is like a painted jar filled internally with impurities.
Contemplate that this body is a temporary combination based on the Four Great Elements,
and fundamentally owns nothing." At that time, that Bhikṣu did not understand the contemplation of emptiness (Śūnyatā).
He only performed the contemplation of form (Rūpa).
His mind was confused by sexual desire.
He spoke a verse to the woman, saying:
"O good lady, young in years, your form is pure, your face and appearance are upright, especially graceful and wonderful.
I hope you will yield to your virtue and follow my wish; my heart is overcome, desiring to keep you as a companion."
The prostitute recited a verse, saying:
"Even if you had wealth and resources, why establish your mind on seeking that which is difficult to obtain?
Since your actions show no shame, run quickly, flee, and leave my house!"
At that time, the Bhikṣu, having been driven out,
followed (others) until he reached Jīshù.
He asked the other Bhikṣus.
Immediately, they came to approach the Buddha.
They reported to the World-Honored One,
fully relating the beginning and end of the matter.
The Buddha said,
"This Bhikṣu,
in a past life, was once a water turtle.
The woman was a monkey.
They also desired each other, but their wishes were not fulfilled.
He turned back and deceived himself, failing to enter the proper teaching,
increasing his suffering and vexation.
Now it is again like this.
His wish was not followed.
Instead, he was rebuffed and insulted.
He left in shame.
The Buddha said,
"In the past world, there was a turtle.
By the river bank, the trees and vegetation were flourishing.
Among that thicket of trees was a monkey
residing in those trees.
The turtle came out of the water.
He saw the monkey in the tree from afar
and exchanged words with her.
He advanced closer and grew intimate.
Day after day it was like this.
He gazed upon her unceasingly.
Consequently, a mind of defilement arose.
He spoke a verse, which she answered by cursing him and avoiding him. That monkey is now this prostitute.
That turtle is the Bhikṣu seeking alms."
In the past, there was a pure believer (Qīngxìnshì).
His name was Yōuduōluó.
He respected the Buddha, delighted in the Dharma, and was close to the virtuous and the holy assembly.
He observed the six days of purification (liùzhāi) each month, upheld the eight precepts, abstained from misfortune-bringing acts, and practiced benevolence.
He protected the lives of all creatures.
His reputation was called Zhēnzhòng (Precious and Weighty).
Glory and luxury could not turn his heart.
Beautiful women or national treasures could not disturb his resolve.
His loyal faith was hard to overturn.
Liquor never passed his lips.
