Filial piety was his constant duty.
He did not eat after the proper time.
He maintained a receptive mind to receive the Way.
Fragrant flowers, rouge, and powder never clung to his body.
Weapons and vicious tools were not used to damage virtue.
He kept distance from the foolish and befriended the virtuous.
He used the Buddha's divine influence to enlighten his mother's heart.
But his mother believed in perverse and heterodox views.
She was stingy and did not give charity.
After her life ended,
the son became a Śramana (shāmén).
His mind eliminated defilement and achieved tranquility.
He sat upright beneath a tree,
observing the ten directions.
He constantly thought to himself:
“My mother died more than twenty years ago.
I shall try to find where she is
to repay the kindness of being born and nurtured.”
In a moment, a hungry ghost appeared.
He was ugly, black, and repulsive.
His long hair was matted around his body.
It wrapped around his feet and dragged on the ground; he stumbled back and forth, crying out and lamenting, having no salvation.
He came to the Śramana and said:
“I kept company with a gang of foolish and wicked people.
I did not believe in the Buddha’s teachings.
I indulged my mouth in whatever it desired.
Now I am a hungry ghost.
For twenty-five years, I have not seen a Śramana.
Today I have met one!
I am dying of hunger and thirst.
I pray that you use heavenly moisture
to grant me water and grain
to save my meager life.”
The Śramana replied:
“Is the clear water of the great sea not enough for you to drink?”
The ghost said:
“Just as I was about to approach and drink,
the water transformed into pus.
The stench was immeasurable.
If I obtained rice,
the food transformed into scorching coals
that burned my mouth down to the bottom.”
“Wicked ghosts also use iron chains to bind my neck,
and iron staffs glowingly hot,
to beat my body indiscriminately.
How heavy are my sins
to have reached this state?”
The Śramana said:
“When you were human in the past,
you violated the Buddha’s teachings.
You banded together with the deaf and the blind.
You pursued foolish delusions yourself.
You mistook calamity for fortune.
You guarded your stinginess and refused to give.
You greedily took what was not your due.”
The ghost wept tears and said:
“Indeed, it is just as you say.
Moreover, when I lived in the world
and was human, I had a son.
He upheld the five precepts of the Buddha.
He specialized in guarding the ten virtuous deeds.
He was a pure believer (Qīngxìnshì).
He never failed in keeping the six days of purification or the eight precepts.
He served his parents with filial piety.
He served the saints with wisdom.
He sought out the paths of the lofty and pure Śramanas.
Like a shadow chasing form,
he encouraged me to give charity
and make offerings to the holy assembly.
Because I lacked the wisdom of true reality
and believed in the insane and wicked words of the foolish,
I now reap this calamity.
The torture and agony are hard to describe.”
Weeping, he said:
“Śramana, have pity on me and save me.”
The Śramana said:
“Since you have reached this transgression,
by what virtue can you ward off this misfortune?”
The ghost said:
“Take a bottle and fill it with water.
Put a willow branch inside.
Cover it with a monastic robe (fǎfú).
Present it to the Bhikṣu (bǐqiū) monks.
Have food prepared and offered to them.
Call out my name and recite a vow (zhòuyuàn) for me.
This will allow me to obtain clothing and food.
This will not take long.”
“Those who have died
and are in the realm of hungry ghosts—
when a Śramana recites a vow,
they all obtain release at that very moment.”
The Śramana followed his words.
He prepared a bottle of water with a willow branch in it.
He fed the Bhikṣu monks.
He presented the monastic robes to the monks.
He called out the ghost's name and recited a vow.
Immediately, there appeared a great pond with lotus flowers growing in the water.
Their fragrance touched his body.
Fruit trees provided cool shade.
His wishes were realized according to his heart.
His companions, five hundred people,
were astonished and said:
“What singular merit and aid
allowed this fellow to be quickly released from such heavy guilt?
Did his wish come true immediately?”
In the past, there was a Śramana.
He crossed the sea, accompanying merchants.
Halfway, the ship turned back
and could go no further.
The assembly all declared:
“There must be someone unclean or impure on board the ship.”
They drew lots to find the person and put him out.
The Taoist man (dàorén, referring to the Śramana) drew the lot three times.
He threw himself into the sea.
The Dragon King immediately received him on a seven-jeweled lotus flower and carried him into the sea.
He reached the Dragon Palace.
He saw the high towers, jeweled residences, and halls.
The Dragon King invited him in.
The King bowed down, touching his head to the Śramana's feet, and said:
“I have suffered from a headache.
For more than six hundred years I have sought a Taoist man.
Now I have finally obtained one.
Taoist man, you must cure my illness.”
The Taoist man said:
“I do not know medicine.
How can I treat you?”
The Dragon King said:
“In this sea of mine, there are many divine medicines.
But they do not cure my illness.
I have only not yet obtained the medicine of the Dharma.”
The Taoist man preached the Dharma for a short while.
The Dragon King immediately felt himself cured and recovered.
The Dragon was greatly delighted.
He provided for the Taoist man for ninety days.
He spoke to the Taoist man, saying:
“I have burdened you for a long time, and I imagine you feel wearied and depressed.
The earlier ship has just arrived, and now I shall send you off.”
The Dragon King selected three maṇi pearls.
One he gave to the Buddha above.
One he gave in charity to the Sangha (Sēng, the monastic assembly).
One he gave to the Taoist man.
He sent a spirit to escort him.
Suddenly, he arrived at the ship.
His shipmates were surprised and joyful.
Together they returned to their native land.
The assembly all followed the Taoist man to the Buddha.
The Buddha preached the Dharma for them.
They all resolved to attain the Way.
The number they saved was immeasurable.
In the past, Ānán related an incident.
There was a Śramana who attained the state of Ānàhán (Anāgāmin).
He was boiling plants on a mountain to dye his robes.
At that time, a man who had lost his cow was searching everywhere.
Seeing the smoke, he went toward it.
He looked into the cauldron, and the plants had all turned into cow bones.
The bowl had transformed into a cow’s head.
The kāsāya (jiāshā, monastic robe) had transformed into cowhide.
The man then tied the bones and head to the Śramana
and led him around the country for public humiliation.
When the masses saw this,
a Śrāmaṇera (shāmí, novice monk)
who saw that the time was noon
hit the bowl (or gong) but did not see his master arrive.
He then entered his cell and used full contemplation (sīwéi).
He saw that his master was being humiliated by men.
He then went to the master, bowed, touching his head to his feet,
and asked: “When did you say this would happen?”
The master replied: “It is the sin from a long time ago.”
The Śrāmaṇera said:
“You may return temporarily to eat.”
The two men then released the master.
They departed together using spiritual power (shénzú).
The Śrāmaṇera had not yet attained the Way.
He still had anger that was not extinguished.
He looked back and saw the pure believers (qīngxìnshì) and the countrymen.
They treated my master like this!
He caused the dragons to rain sand and stones and shake the country,
filling them with terror.
Just as he finished this thought,
sand rained down from the four directions.
The inner and outer walls and all the houses and rooms were completely destroyed.
The master said:
“In a previous life, I made a living slaughtering cows.
Thus, I incurred this calamity.
Why do you commit sin?
Go away! You must not follow me again.”
The master said:
“Sin and blessing are like this.
Should one not be careful?”
In a foreign country, there was a Śrāmaṇa.
He traveled begging for alms and arrived at the house of a pearl merchant.
The host prepared food and drink for him.
There was a large pearl, the price of which was counted in the hundreds of millions.
Someone carried it back
and placed it next to the Śrāmaṇa.
At that time, there was a parrot.
It immediately went out and swallowed the pearl.
The host did not see this.
He subsequently asked the Śrāmaṇa.
He replied,
“I did not take it.”
The host asked again,
“Was there anyone else here?”
He answered, “There was nobody.”
The host angrily said,
“I just brought the pearl here.
Since there was no one else,
and only the Śrāmaṇa is here,
yet you say you did not take it.
Where is the pearl now?”
Then he beat the Śrāmaṇa.
Blood flowed out onto the ground.
The Śrāmaṇa still said,
“I am not concealing the pearl.”
A moment later, the parrot came out and drank the blood on the ground.
It encountered the staff.
The parrot immediately died.
The host was again about to raise his hand to beat the Śrāmaṇa.
The Śrāmaṇa said,
“Stop. Listen to my words.”
The parrot swallowed it.
He immediately cut open the parrot and retrieved the pearl.
The host said to the Śrāmaṇa,
“Why did you not say so earlier,
to prevent things from becoming like this?”
The Śrāmaṇa said,
“I observe the precepts of the Buddha, and am not permitted to kill living beings.
I immediately wanted to tell you,
but I feared killing the parrot.
Now that the parrot is dead,
I can finally tell you.
If the parrot were alive,
even if you beat me to death,
I would ultimately not have spoken.”
The host then severely reprimanded himself, repented his fault,
and offered his apologies.
The Śrāmaṇa was not angry.
His expression did not change.
There was a Śrāmaṇa
meditating on the Dao in the mountains.
There was a ghost
which transformed itself into a headless person and walked around.
The Śrāmaṇa said,
“Ah, how fortunate to be headless!
Then one does not know the pain of a headache.
Also, without eyes and ears, one does not know sounds.”
The ghost then transformed itself into a body without a torso.
The Śrāmaṇa said,
“Ah, how fortunate to be a person without a head!
You do not know pain and itchiness.
Without the five viscera, you do not fall ill.”
The ghost then transformed itself into a person without hands or feet.
The Śrāmaṇa said,
“Ah, how fortunate to be without hands and feet; you cannot walk,
nor can you take other people's property.”
The ghost knew the Śrāmaṇa was steadfast in his resolve,
and immediately vanished.
In a foreign country, there was a Śrāmaṇa practicing the Dao.
He encountered a man-eating ghost.
The ghost quickly embraced him.
The Śrāmaṇa said,
“Although I have encountered you now,
your heart and mine are as far apart as heaven and earth.
Your heart delights in killing,
my heart delights in saving lives.
You are opposed to the Dao.”
The ghost then released the Śrāmaṇa,
not daring to embrace him again.
It immediately withdrew, apologized, and said,
“I am foolish and ignorant; I did not understand.”
In the past, there was a Daòrén.
He practiced the Dao day and night,
never slackening.
Furthermore, being under the stress of bodily needs
he required food and drink.
So he went out to beg for alms.
Suddenly, he arrived at a hunter's dwelling and begged.
The hunter was immoral
and became greatly enraged.
He intended to shoot the Daòrén.
The Daòrén said,
“Stop, stop.
Do not shoot me anywhere else,
just shoot my belly.”
Then he opened his clothes and exposed his belly,
calling out for him to shoot.
The hunter immediately lowered his bow and released his arrow.
He went forward and asked the Daòrén,
“When people exist in the world,
there is no one who does not fear death.
Why then did the Daòrén tell me to shoot your belly?”
The Daòrén told him,
“This belly desires food.
Because of this,
I do not avoid danger.
Therefore, shoot it.”
The hunter immediately understood.
“I rely on the mountain ridges,
not avoiding tigers and wolves,
also for the sake of this belly.”
His past karmic fortune arrived,
and suddenly he became enlightened.
The Daòrén spoke to him about the suffering of the Sāntú and the joy of Níhuán.
The hunter realized that his sin of killing and hunting was heavy.
He immediately received the precepts
and developed the heart of Bodhi.
The Buddha resided in Śèwèichéng
There was an elder
named Nántí
. He left home and abandoned secular life, moving, standing, sitting, and lying down.
His mind constantly focused on concentration,
and he was named Chán Nántí (Concentration Nántí).
At that time, Nántí built a thatched hut in the Forest of Opening Eyes (Kāiyǎnlín).
In it, he practiced his discipline during the first, middle, and last watches of the night, attaining mundane absorption (shìsú zhèngshòu).
After seven years had passed,
he lost his meditative concentration (chándìng).
He then sat beneath a tree again, seeking to regain his original absorption.
At that time, the dependents of Māra often created skillful means to watch for his vulnerability.
One transformed into a woman of unparalleled beauty,
adorned with flowers, perfume, and pearl necklaces (yīngluò).
She stood before Nántí and said,
“Bhikṣu,
come, let us enjoy each other and engage in sexual acts.”
Nántí said,
“Evil wickedness, quickly perish!
Evil wickedness, quickly perish!”
Although his mouth spoke these words, his eyes did not look.
The celestial maiden spoke a second and a third time, saying the same things as above.
Nántí responded the same way on the second and third occasions.
As she spoke, the celestial maiden stripped off her yīngluò and clothes, exposing her body.
She stood before Nántí
and said to Nántí,
“Come, let us commit fornication.”
When Nántí saw her form and features,
desire arose in his mind, and he answered, “Agreed.”
At that moment, the celestial maiden gradually backed away.
Nántí called out,
“Wait a moment so we can enjoy each other!”
Nántí went toward her.
The celestial maiden quickly departed.
Nántí pursued her until he reached the ditch of the Zhǐyuán (Jetavana).
There was a dead horse belonging to the royal family.
The celestial maiden reached the horse and concealed herself, disappearing from sight.
At that time, Nántí’s mind was blazing with desire, and he immediately fornicated with the dead horse.
When his desire subsided, he thought thus:
“I am truly unwholesome, and this is not the dharma of a Śrāmaṇa.
I left home based on faith, yet I have committed the offense of Pāráyì (defeat).
Why should I wear the dharma robe and consume the offerings given by others in faith?”
He immediately stripped off his dharma robe and held it in his right hand.
With his left hand covering his private parts, he hurried toward the Zhǐyuán.
He said to the Bhikṣus,
“Elders, I have committed Pāráyì.”
At that time, the Bhikṣus were practicing walking meditation between the gates of the Zhǐyuán.
They spoke to one another, saying,
“This is the meditating Nántí (Zuòchán Nántí), a practitioner of the holy life (fànháng rén).
He should not have committed Pāráyì.”
Nántí replied again,
“Elders, it is not so.
I truly committed Pāráyì.”
The Bhikṣus asked him for the details.
Nántí immediately recounted the entire affair.
The Bhikṣus reported this matter fully to the World-Honored One (Shìzūn).
The Buddha told the Bhikṣus,
“This good man Nántí has confessed the serious offense he committed; he should be expelled.”
Then the Bhikṣus expelled him as instructed.
The Bhikṣus reported to the Buddha, saying,
“World-Honored One,
how is it that Elder Nántí, who has long practiced the holy life,
was deceived and confused by this celestial maiden?”
The Buddha told the Bhikṣus,
“It is not only today that this Nántí was confused by the celestial maiden and lost the holy life (fànháng).
In a past life, he was also confused by her and lost the holy life.”
In a past life,
in the southern country of Āpántí, there was a man of the Kāyè clan.
He was an outside path (wàidào) ascetic, intelligent and widely knowledgeable.
He thoroughly mastered the classics and understood everything.
This wàidào assisted the king in governing the state.
At that time, the king arrested adulterers and criminals.
He inflicted various severe punishments, such as cutting off ears and noses, treating them with great cruelty.
At that time, the wàidào reflected deeply:
“I have already left home.
How can I participate in these affairs with the king?”
He then reported to the king, saying,
“Permit me to leave home [properly].”
The king immediately replied,
“Master, you have already left home.
Why do you now say you wish to leave home?”
He replied,
“Great King,
now that I am involved in these various punishments,
afflicting sentient beings with suffering, how can this be called leaving home?”
The king then asked,
“Where do you wish to leave home now, Master?”
He replied,
“Great King,
I wish to leave home and study to become an Immortal (Xiānrén).”
The king said, “It may be so.
Leave home as you wish.”
Not far from the city was the Mountain of a Hundred Crags (Bǎiyánshān).
There were flowing springs, clear pools, and lush flowers and fruits.
He went immediately to that mountain and established a quiet dwelling place.
In the mountain, he cultivated the outside path practices,
attained mundane concentration (shìsú dìng), and manifested the five supernatural powers (wǔ shéntōng).
In the later days of spring, having eaten various fruits, his four great elements (sì dà) were unbalanced.
Due to this, impurities (urine/semen) flowed out during his minor bodily function.
At that time, a thirsty female deer seeking water drank this urine.
The impurity stuck to her tongue, and she licked her birth canal.
The karma of sentient beings is inconceivable.
Because of this, she became pregnant.
She constantly stayed near the hermitage, eating grass and drinking water.
When her months were complete, she gave birth to a small child.
At that time, the Xiānrén went out to gather grass.
Because the deer had a difficult birth, she cried out greatly in distress.
The Xiānrén heard the deer crying urgently,
assuming it was being harmed by an evil insect,
and wished to go and rescue it, but instead saw the newborn child.
When the Xiānrén saw this, he was surprised and thought:
“How can an animal give birth to a human?”
He immediately entered concentration (dìng guān) and saw the root cause: it was my son.
He immediately developed affection for the small child.
He wrapped him in a deerskin garment and carried him home to raise him.
The Xiānrén held the child up, and the deer mother nursed him.
Because he was born dependent on his mother, his body was spotted, resembling a deer.
Therefore, he gave him a name,
calling him Lùbān (Deer Spot).
Gradually, he grew up until he reached the age of seven.
Being benevolent, loving, dutiful, and compassionate, he gathered fruit and fetched water to serve the Xiānrén.
At that time, the Xiānrén thought:
“In the world, nothing is more terrifying than a woman.”
He immediately instructed and cautioned his son, saying,
“There is nothing more extremely terrifying than a woman.
The downfall of righteousness and the destruction of virtue are always caused by them.”
Thereupon, he taught him meditative concentration (chándìng)
and transformed him using the five supernatural powers (wǔ tōng).
Then he recited a verse for him, saying.
Humans have seven reservoirs.
First is called the reservoir of wind (Fēngzàng).
Second, the reservoir of birth (Shēngzàng).
Third, the reservoir of maturity (Shúzàng).
Fourth, the reservoir of cold (Lěngzàng).
Fifth, the reservoir of heat (Rèzàng).
Sixth, the reservoir of sight (Jiànzàng).
Seventh, the reservoir of desire (Yùzàng).
Among these various reservoirs,
the reservoir of desire (Yùzàng) is the strongest.
It relies on mucus and saliva,
thin fluids, pus, and blood,
sinews, bones, skin, and flesh,
the heart, the liver, and the five viscera,
the intestines, stomach, feces, and urine.
At that time, among the assembly, there was an Upāsaka,
named Xuǎnzé.
His wife was named Miàosè.
Her countenance was dignified and beautiful,
and her appearance was exceptionally striking.
The Upāsaka loved her intensely, and his passions were burning fiercely.
Having heard the Buddha speak this,
he immediately addressed the Buddha, saying,
“World-Honored One,
do not speak thus!
How can the mind of desire arise from feces and urine?
My wife is dignified and beautiful, without any foul odor or impurity.”
At that time, the Buddha miraculously manifested a woman.
She was dignified, beautiful, and pure, resembling Miàosè in form.
With a composed face and slow steps, she came and entered the assembly.
The Upāsaka asked,
“Why have you come?”
She replied,
“I wish to listen to the Dharma.”
The Upāsaka immediately pulled her and seated her upon his robe.
The Buddha, using spiritual power,
caused this woman to defecate and soil the robe.
This made the Upāsaka unable to bear the stench.
He covered his nose with his hand
and looked around at those nearby, asking,
“Who did this?”
Bánántuó could not tolerate it.
He spoke to the Upāsaka, saying,
“Why are you covering your nose and looking at me?”
He replied,
“The stench is extremely great.”
By the Buddha’s spiritual power,
Bánántuó and the entire assembly
saw this woman soiling the Upāsaka’s robe.
At that time, Bánántuó said to the Upāsaka,
“Just look at the foul impurity created by your wife!”
The Upāsaka replied,
“My wife is pure and clean.
Her body has no impurities.
If anyone doubts this, they should look for themselves.”
He continued, speaking to Bánántuó,
“I suspect that you were the one who created this filth.”
Bánántuó became extremely angry.
Rising from his seat, he said,
“You should now be named ‘Upāsaka of Excrement’!
While your wife was sitting, feces came out upon your robe.
You are smeared with feces,
yet you feel no shame.
Instead, you wish to slander others.”
Furthermore, he cried out,
“This Upāsaka of Excrement should be sent out of the assembly!”
Immediately, he grabbed him by the hand and forced him outside the assembly.
The Upāsaka said to his wife,
“Because I respected you,
I allowed you to sit upon my robe.
As a grown person,
is this how one should behave?”
The wife immediately replied,
“Since you are close to a bag of excrement, this is naturally how things must be.”
The Upāsaka, at that moment, immediately generated a sense of revulsion.
Wishing to remove the feces from the robe,
he soiled his body further.
He addressed Bánántuó,
“What method should I employ to be rid of this filth?”
Bánántuó said,
“It is not just this excrement that soils your body.
There are various further calamities
that are your lot.
If you wish to escape, you must distance yourself from this.
It is because of your wife's feces
that this great assembly is suffering headaches and agitation.”
The Upāsaka replied,
“All the Shìzǐ are generally very compassionate.
Are you truly such a foul-mouthed person
as this?”
Bánántuó said,
“How can someone like you be deserving of pity?
Look at yourself now—are you clean and pure?
Yet you wish to slander me.”
At that time, the Upāsaka said to his wife,
“You should go back home.”
After he had dismissed her,
he spoke to Bánántuó,
“I now clearly see that women are deceitful
and full of many faults.
They are filled with impurity.
My heart has generated aversion and detachment.
I wish to leave home and seek the Way in the Buddha’s Dharma.”
Bánántuó said,
“Your physical body is now so foul and filthy.
If you were to apply perfume and wait for years,
then perhaps you might be fit to leave home.”
The Upāsaka replied,
“If I were to apply perfume and wait for years,
perhaps my body would already have perished,
or perhaps the Buddha would have entered Nirvāṇa.
That would destroy my opportunity to leave home and seek the Way.
If I could now earnestly be granted permission to leave home,
I would no longer dwell in cities, towns, villages, monastic cells, or temples (Jīngshè).
I would practice Ālánruò, beg for food, wear rags,
and stay in solitary places.
Who then would smell my stench?”
The Buddha heard him and called out, “Well come!
You shall be a Shāmén,
practicing Fànxíng.”
The Upāsaka’s beard and hair immediately fell away,
the Jiāshā robe was placed upon his body,
and he carried the begging bowl (Yìngqì),
appearing like a Bǐqiū.
The Buddha taught him the Dharma:
suffering, accumulation, extinction, and the path.
Distant from dust and separated from defilement,
he attained the purity of the Dharma Eye,
becoming a Xūtuóhuán.
The Buddha taught the Dharma again until he attained the state of Ānàhán.
Having passed that night,
holding his robe and carrying his bowl,
he went to Wángshěchéng.
Proceeding sequentially on his alms round,
he eventually arrived at his former residence
and stood outside the gate.
At that time, his wife Miàosè saw her husband
with shaven head and Dharma robes, having left home to seek the Way.
She immediately spoke to him, saying,
“Was it proper according to the Dharma to abandon me and become a Shāmén?”
Xuǎnzé replied,
“Was it proper according to the Dharma yesterday for you
to discard filth onto my robe and soil my body?”
Miàosè replied,
“As a Bǐqiū, should you slander others?
From my father’s house, I came to your home.
I have never even seen the outer gate,
much less reached the Zhúyuán.
At that moment, an evil Māra
spoke to the Upāsaka, saying,
“The one you saw yesterday was never Miàosè.
She was a manifestation made to appear so,
meant to deceive and confuse your mind.
Now you can return and amuse yourself with the five desires.
The Shāmén Qútán is merely deceiving you.
You are now fraudulent, not a real Bǐqiū.
The Shāmén Qútán
constantly uses magic to confuse many people,
causing them to leave home,
just as he is now deceiving you.”
Bǐqiū Xuǎnzé, having verified the True Dharma,
immediately realized this was Māra.
He addressed him, saying,
“Wicked one! You are a manifestation, and I
am also a manifestation of the sister Miàosè.
Both are mere transformations.
The Dharma taught by the Buddha is entirely empty, like a transformation.”
At that time, Miàosè heard this Dharma.
Distant from dust and separated from defilement, she attained the purity of the Dharma Eye.
She removed doubt and regret and did not follow the words of others.
In the Buddha's Dharma, she attained the Dharma of Fearlessness.
She said to Xuǎnzé,
“What you have done is extremely good,
to be able to
happily practice Fànxíng in the Buddha’s Dharma.
I also wish to leave home and seek the Way in the Dharma.”
In the past, there was a man given to lewd indulgence.
His mind was solely focused on female beauty.
His thoughts could not separate from it.
He wished to converse with her and communicate even in dreams.
At that time, his wife encountered sickness.
Her bones wasted away and her flesh was exhausted.
There was an acquaintance, a *dàorén*, who frequently visited the household.
The wife informed the *dàorén*, saying:
The affliction I currently suffer causes me to be weak and distressed day and night.
I intend to express my feelings about the cause of this condition.
Is it permissible or not?
The *dàorén* said:
Just speak; there is no harm.
Should there be matters needing concealment,
I will cover and hide them, preventing disclosure.
The woman replied:
My husband is excessively lustful.
He pressures and harasses me day and night, not allowing me time to eat or rest.
Because of this, sickness arose, and I fear I cannot recover myself.
The *dàorén* said:
If your husband approaches you,
tell him this message:
Is the conduct of a *Xūtuóhuán*
properly supposed to be like this?
The wife immediately told her husband.
The husband felt greatly ashamed.
He reflected internally,
“I am a *Xūtuóhuán*.
Should I not instantly cease this intention?”
In a quiet place, he contemplated the attainment of *Ānàhán* fruition.
Knowing himself to have attained the trace of the path,
he thereafter no longer engaged in sexual relations with women.
The woman asked her husband:
Why have you now forever ceased your lustful intentions?
The husband said:
I have truly seen you.
How could I possibly interact with you again?
His wife said to her husband:
You say you have truly seen me.
What fault do I have?
I have always been chaste and pure.
I have not violated the duties of a woman.
Why do you insult me?
Even to this extent?
The woman immediately gathered her relatives and clan members.
She informed them, saying:
Now my husband treats me with indifference.
He has forever ceased affection and closeness, and moreover insults me,
claiming that he has 'seen' me.
Now, in front of the assembly, he should explain this.
The husband said:
Wait a moment. I must bring forth evidence to clarify myself.
The husband returned home.
He decorated a beautiful vase.
He filled it completely with feces and filth.
He firmly sealed its opening.
He scented it with fragrant flowers.
Returning to the assembly,
he addressed his wife, saying:
Do you truly love me or not?
If you love me, please embrace and fondle this vase,
as you love my own body.
The wife followed his instructions.
She embraced the vase and fondled it, her mind unwilling to let it go.
The husband, seeing his wife attached to this vase,
immediately struck the vase, breaking it.
Foul stench and filth flowed out, and maggots emerged.
He then asked his wife:
Are you still able to embrace this broken vase now?
She replied:
I would rather die than go near this.
I would rather enter a pit of fire,
throw myself into deep water,
or cast myself down from a high mountain,
with my head and feet separated,
I absolutely cannot approach this.
The husband: Now you have correct insight.
I view your body as worse than this vase.
From head to foot,
analyzing and contemplating,
the thirty-six constituents.
What is there worth desiring?
He again spoke verses (*gè*):
The brave one enters concentration and contemplates the body and the dust with which the mind interacts;
Having seen it, disgust arises, like that decorated vase.
There was a *Bǐqiū*
who attained the concentration of cessation (*Mièjìn Dìng*).
When begging for food,
he put on his robe and went to the dining hall.
That day, the monastery struck the *qiánchuí*.
Later, that *Bǐqiū*,
diligently made this thought:
Why should I waste this time in vain?
Not observing the future,
When will the *qiánchuí* be struck?
He immediately made a solemn vow,
and entered the concentration of cessation,
vowing that he would arise only when the *qiánchuí* was struck.
At that time, a difficult situation arose at the *sēngqiélán*.
Then the *Bǐqiū*s
abandoned the *sēngqiélán* and left.
After three months passed,
the difficult matter was resolved.
Then the *Bǐqiū*s returned and assembled, and struck the *qiánchuí*.
At that moment, the *Bǐqiū* arose from concentration and immediately died.
Later, there was another *Bǐqiū* begging for food,
who attained the concentration of cessation.
In the early part of the day,
he wished to go begging for food.
At that time, there was heavy rain.
He made this thought:
If I enter the village, the color of my robes will be ruined.
If I do not go, why should I return empty-handed?
At this time, not observing the future, he immediately made a vow and entered concentration,
vowing that he would arise only when the rain stopped.
Some say
the rain lasted half a month.
Others say the rain lasted one month.
When the rain stopped, that *Bǐqiū* arose from concentration and immediately died.
In the kingdom of *Mótóuluó*,
in the *Nígūlèi* Park,
there was a *Bǐqiū*.
He sat in meditation in a quiet place.
Furthermore, there was a poisonous snake
coiled and lying under the couch.
The *Bǐqiū* slept,
sometimes lowering his head, sometimes lifting it.
The poisonous snake thought to itself:
This person, seeing me, will surely want to kill me in fear.
It immediately reared its body and struck.
The *Bǐqiū* died and was reborn in *Dāolì Tiān*.
Various heavenly maidens came to serve and attend him.
The heavenly son (Devaputra) told them:
All of you sisters, do not come near my body.
If you should approach, you will surely violate the precepts.
The maidens thought to themselves:
This deity, in his previous life, must have been a *Shāményuán*.
That is why he was born here to receive heavenly blessings.
Then the heavenly maidens each held a mirror forward to reflect the heavenly son's face.
Seeing his heavenly robes and crown,
he then realized he had been reborn in heaven.
He immediately arose from his seat,
and seeing all the attendants following him,
he walked to the park.
He sat beneath a tree,
sitting upright and contemplating, seeking concentration and *Sānmèi*.
In the pool water, there were birds of different species.
They cried sadly to each other,
their sounds mournful and harmonious.
He wished to attain the path,
but was unable to accomplish it.
At that time, the heavenly son,
descended from the Thirty-three Heavens (*Sānshísān Tiān*) to *Yánfú Tí*.
He arrived at the abode of the World-Honored One (*Shìzūn*).
He reported:
When my heavenly blessings are exhausted,
I will descend into *Tàishān* Hell.
This cycle of rebirth continues endlessly.
May you mercifully save and deliver me so I may attain liberation.
The Buddha preached the Dharma for him.
Immediately, while sitting there, all the dust and defilements were purified, and he attained the pure Eye of the Dharma (*Fǎyǎnjìng*).
According to the customary etiquette of the inner teaching:
Those who enter the temple to hear the Dharma and venerate the Buddha
must all remove their head coverings and caps.
At that time, there was a *Guówáng*.
He had naturally sparse hair on his head.
Moreover, he had sores.
He was also wearing leather sandals on his feet.
Relying on his grandeur and nobility,
he wrapped his head with folded cloth.
He entered the hall to listen to the scriptures.
The king addressed a *Bǐqiū*:
Preach the Dharma for me.
The *Bǐqiū* replied:
The *Rúlái* has an instruction:
The Dharma is not preached for those wearing leather sandals on their feet.
The king, hearing this, harbored resentment.
He immediately removed his leather sandals and said to the *Bǐqiū*:
You must quickly preach the Dharma to satisfy my feelings.
If you disobey my original intent, I will hang your head.
The *Bǐqiū* informed the king:
Moreover, the *Rúlái*'s prohibition states that the Dharma cannot be preached for those who cover their heads.
The king became furiously angry and brandished his divine authority, saying:
You wish to humiliate me!
I will now intentionally remove the covering and expose my head.
Listen to you preach the Dharma.
If you cannot resolve my knot of ignorance,
I will cut your body into three pieces.
The *Bǐqiū* spoke verses (*gè*):
Do not show the impure intention, nor the angry person,
He who desires to know the Dharma is spoken of by the *Sānyēsān fó*.
All those who eliminate pride, whose minds are extremely pure,
and who can abandon harmful intentions, only they may hear the Right Dharma.
The king was ashamed of his face and disgraced by his reflection.
He immediately rose from his seat.
He prostrated himself, throwing his five limbs to the ground.
He sought refuge, begging forgiveness for the transgressions of his body, speech, and mind.
He knelt respectfully, joined his hands, and said to the Bhikṣu:
"I wonder whether this verse
came from the divine mouth of the Rúlái (Tathāgata),
or whether this honorable person (you) knew my thoughts and intentions and then spoke it?"
The Bhikṣu informed the king:
"This verse was indeed spoken by the Rúlái.
It has existed for a long time."
The king thought to himself:
"Excellent, Great Sage (Dàshèng)!
The wisdom of the Three Knowledges (Sāndázhì) leaves nothing unpenetrated.
You even knew that there would be followers like me in the future,
who harbor hateful and harmful intentions."
Now he deeply regretted his actions and vowed never to create new [evil karma].
The Bhikṣu preached the Dharma.
While the king was sitting, all the dust and defilements were purged, and he obtained the pure Dharma Eye (Fǎyǎnjìng).
The Buddha was in the country of Shèwèi (Śrāvastī).
There was a certain Bhikṣu,
who daily traveled the path between the wilderness tombs outside the city.
He had to pass through someone else's field to reach that place.
When the owner saw this, he became angry and resentful.
"What kind of Daoist (Dàoshì) is this?
He comes and goes daily but does not cultivate virtue or the Way (Dàodé)."
He immediately asked the Daoist:
"What kind of beggar (Qǐshì) are you?
You traverse back and forth across my field,
creating a definite path."
The Daoist replied:
"I have a dispute and have come to seek witnesses."
At that time, that field owner,
whose past karmic ties were connected and who was destined to achieve salvation,
followed the Daoist.
He secretly hid and accompanied him.
He saw [the Daoist] in the midst of the tombs.
Corpses and skeletons were strewn about everywhere.
They were swollen, rotten, and foul-smelling.
Birds and beasts were eating them.
[The remains] were scattered in that place.
Some were completely eaten, others not.
Some looked like gray pigeons.
Maggots and worms were biting and wriggling.
The stench was foul and difficult to approach.
Crows, magpies, foxes, and dogs,
old vultures, owls, and screech owls,
were devouring the corpses of the dead.
The Bhikṣu raised his hand
and said to that man:
"All these birds and beasts
are my witnesses."
[The owner] asked:
"Why are these birds and beasts
your witnesses?
Bhikṣu, with whom are you disputing now?"
The Bhikṣu replied:
"The mind (xīn) is a source of sickness;
it has many flaws and defilements (lòuhuàn).
I observe these skeletons,
analyzing the foul excretions.
I then return to my chamber
and contemplate my own body.
From head to foot,
it is no different from those [corpses].
Yet this mind and intention
gallops and rushes toward countless extremes,
chasing illusory falsities:
forms, sounds, smells, tastes, and tactile sensations (xìhuá zhī fă).
Now I want to recognize the true origin (yuánběn) of the mind.
Your mind must now generate this thought:
'Do not let [the mind] lead me into the hells or among the hungry ghosts.'
I am now an ordinary person (fánfū) and have not yet escaped all fetters.
However, this mind-thief does not obey orders.
Because of this, I go to the wilderness daily
to preach the contemplation of foul excretions and impurity (bùjìng zhī xiăng).
Moreover, I arouse the mind to speak to the mind,
addressing the sudden, violent, chaotic, erroneous, and unstable mind.
It must now reform and cease creating evil karmic causes."
At that time, that field owner,
having heard the Daoist's instruction,
wiped away his tears with his hand.
His throat choked up, and he found it difficult to speak.
That field owner,
during the ten thousand years of Kāshèfó's (Kāśyapa Buddha's) Dharma period,
had cultivated the contemplation of impurity (bùjìng xiǎng).
He immediately analyzed
the thirty-six components [of the body],
recognizing the foul excretions and impurity.
At that time, the Bhikṣu and that field owner
attained the Path of Sūtuóhuán (Sotāpanna, Stream-Enterer) right there in the great, desolate cemetery wilderness.
There was a blind Bhikṣu.
His eyes could see nothing.
He was sewing his robe by hand.
The thread slipped out of the needle.
He then said:
"Who loves merit (fúdè)?
Thread this needle for me."
At that time, the Buddha came to his place.
He said to the Bhikṣu:
"I am the one who loves merit.
I have come to thread it for you."
This Bhikṣu recognized the Buddha’s voice.
He quickly rose and performed obeisance.
He said to the Buddha:
"The Buddha's merits (gōngdé) are already complete.
Why do you say you still love merit?"
The Buddha replied:
"Although my merits are already complete,
I deeply understand the cause and effect (yīnguǒ) of merit.
Among all sentient beings,
I have attained the highest and most supreme position.
[This is] due to merit.
Therefore, O Bhikṣu, I praise merit."
He then preached the Dharma for him.
At that time, this Bhikṣu attained the pure Dharma Eye (Fǎyǎnjìng).
His physical eyes (ròuyǎn) also became clear.
A Tripitaka Bhikṣu from Jìbīn (Kashmir),
following the Ālǎnyě (Arañña, forest dwelling) method,
arrived at a king's monastery.
A grand assembly (dàhuì) was being held.
The gatekeeper saw his coarse and worn-out robes and barred the gate, preventing him from entering.
This happened repeatedly.
Because his clothes were worn out, he was always unable to advance.
He then devised a skillful means (fāngbiàn).
He borrowed fine clothes and returned.
The gatekeepers did not stop him.
Once he reached the assembly seat,
he received various kinds of good food.
He first offered [the food] to the robe.
The crowd asked:
"Why do you do that?"
He replied:
"When I, a Bhikṣu, came repeatedly, I was always unable to enter.
Now, because of these robes, I am able to sit here
and receive various kinds of good food.
Therefore, I first offer it to the robes."
At that time, there was a son of a noble family (zúxìngzǐ).
He abandoned his home, gave up his wife, and left all his relatives.
He went forth and became a Śamána (Shāmén).
His wife was beautiful and exquisitely charming.
Seeing her husband had left home,
she went and married again.
When the son of the noble family heard this,
a thought immediately arose in his mind:
[He wished] to enjoy pleasure with his wife again.
At that time, he became sad, worried, and distressed.
He no longer delighted in cultivating the pure Brahmā practices (Fànhéng).
He then arose and returned home.
The Bhikṣus heard about this,
and went to inform the Buddha.
The Buddha summoned him and, in order to remove the filth of ignorant attachment and worldly affliction (chénláo zhī huì) and bring rest to his troubled thoughts, [preached the Dharma].
At that time, the son of the noble family immediately realized the Dharma of the Sages (Xiánshèng zhī fă).
Then the Bhikṣus said to the World-Honored One (Shìzūn):
"If not for the Rúlái, who could have done this?"
[The Buddha] addressed the Bhikṣus:
"This Bhikṣu
has not only in this life had his mind constantly attached to desire.
Long ago, in a distant past world,
there was a king
named Fāngjì.
The palace women and attendants (cǎinǚ) were countless.
They were lascivious, loose, and contentious, unwilling to live in harmony.
After they quarreled,
they left the palace.
Fāngjì searched for them but did not know where they had gone.
He became sad, worried, and unhappy, unable to console himself.
At that time, there was an immortal (xiānrén)
who possessed the Five Supernormal Powers (wŭ shéntōng).
His miraculous powers allowed him to fly, and his divine might was endless.
His name was Wúlè.
He flew in the air,
and suddenly descended.
Why? He preached about the difficulty of separating from sensual desire (àiyù zhī nán) and the virtue of detachment,
[urging him] to leave home and cultivate the Way (Dào).
[The king] cultivated the Four Brahmā-Vihāras (sì Fànhéng).
After his life ended,
he was reborn in the Brahmā Heavens (Fàntiān).
The Buddha told the Bhikṣus:
"The King Fāngjì of that time
is precisely this Bhikṣu now.
And the immortal Wúlè
is myself."
Formerly, a Zhāntuólì family gave birth to seven sons.
Six elder brothers attained the path of Xūtuóhuán dào.
The youngest one still remained an ordinary mortal (fánfū).
The mother, Zhāntuólì, attained the path of Ānàhán dào.
The seven brothers all received the five precepts.
It was the established custom of that country
that the Zhāntuólìs carried out executions.
If men or women in the country
committed murder, theft, sexual misconduct, or other heavy crimes,
they were all made to be executed by the Zhāntuólìs.
At that time, the King summoned that eldest son and said:
"There is a criminal who deserves death.
You go and execute him."
He bowed and explained himself:
"I especially beg for great leniency.
I have received the five precepts.
I guard my person cautiously.
I dare not kill even an ant.
I cannot commit this wrong.
I would rather kill myself,
than dare to violate the precepts."
The King then burst forth in anger.
He ordered them to execute him publicly in the marketplace.
Again he addressed the King:
"My body is the King's subject.
My mind is my own possession.
If you wish to kill me, then kill me.
I cannot comply with your command."
The King immediately ordered his decapitation.
Next, he summoned the younger brothers.
The six men all said:
"Having received the precepts, we dare not carry out executions."
The King’s anger and rage flared greatly.
He executed them all.
Next, he summoned the youngest brother.
The mother and son came together.
When the King saw the mother coming, his anger doubled.
"Earlier, when I executed the six sons,
the mother did not come to attend them.
Now I summon the youngest son,
why do you come immediately?"
The mother replied:
"I beg you to listen to my humble words so that I may explain the reason.
Regarding the previous six sons,
they all attained the path of Xūtuóhuán dào.
Even if the Great King were to take those six men and shatter their bodies like dust,
they would ultimately not arouse malice, not even a single hair's worth.
But this youngest one,
remains an ordinary mortal (fánfū).
Although he cultivates goodness in his body,
he has not yet been blessed by the Dharma path.
For this reason, I worry about my son.
Since he has not yet attained the path,
he might lose his resolve,
fear the King’s commands,
cherish his physical life,
violate the precepts and carry out execution,
and when his body perishes and life ends,
enter the Tàishān Hell (dìyù).
It is out of pity and concern for my son
that I have brought him here."
The King then asked the mother:
"The six sons who died earlier,
did they all attain the path of Xūtuóhuán dào?"
She replied:
"They all did."
The King further asked the mother:
"What path have you yourself attained?"
The mother replied:
"I have attained the path of Ānàhán dào."
When the King heard these words,
he threw himself onto the ground.
He cried out in distress and reproached himself:
"I have created the root of sin!
I willfully intended and executed six Xūtuóhuáns."
His body and mind were distressed, and he was restless; he immediately prepared aromatic oil, clarified butter, and wood fuel.
He took the six corpses and cremated them (shéwéi).
He erected six stūpas (tōupó) and offered reverence to those who were slain.
He confessed three times a day,
wishing in his heart to extinguish the sin.
Gradually, the sin lessened.
He also distributed wealth and goods,
providing for that old mother.
When the observance days (zhāirì) arrived,
he repeatedly confessed,
hoping that his sin would lessen,
and he would be spared from hell.
At that time, Diàodá (Devadatta),
harbored malice in his heart and slandered the Tathāgata (Rúlái).
He claimed to possess the Way.
The multitude rebuked him.
Devas, Nāgas, Ghosts, Spirits, Shì, Fàn, and the Four Heavenly Kings,
all jointly enlightened him, saying:
"You wish to destroy the Buddha.
This is like raising your hand to throw stones at the sun or moon."
Diàodá heard this,
but his heart remained unchanged.
At that time, the Bhikṣus (bǐqiū),
fully informed the Buddha:
"What serious grievance and hatred does Diàodá hold that causes him to act this way?"
The Buddha told the Bhikṣus:
"Diàodá has not only done this in this life,
but it has been like this life after life.
In a past life,
there was a Fànzhì woman,
exquisitely beautiful, whose appearance was peerless.
It was the custom of the Fànzhìs that when a virgin was to be given to one who understood the scriptures,
they would invite five hundred of his fellow students,
provide them offerings for three months, and observe their knowledge.
Among these five hundred men,
one man was widely learned and knowledgeable,
but he was old and frail, ugly of face, and had blue eyes.
The parents were worried and grieved.
The daughter also harbored distress,
asking, 'How can I become the wife of this man?
He might as well be a vengeful ghost!
What should be done?'
At that time, there was a Fànzhì from a distant place,
young of age,
whose appearance was extraordinarily fine,
intelligent and wise.
He heard that Fànzhì had invited fellow students, intending to bestow the daughter.
He immediately went there,
and posed difficult questions to all the Fànzhìs.
They were all exhausted and speechless.
The knowledge of the five hundred men was all inferior to his.
At that time, the girl's parents and the girl herself,
seeing him, were all greatly delighted.
'We sought a son-in-law, and now we have achieved our wish.'
The elderly Fànzhì (Niánzūn Fànzhì) said:
"Since I am already old, she was promised to me long ago.
Let this woman be my wife.
Furthermore, the offerings and gifts I have received,
I will give all to you.
Pity my advanced age.
Do not insult or ruin me."
The young man replied:
"One cannot transgress the established law (Fǎ) to follow human sentiment.
I am the one who ought to take her."
When the three months came to an end,
they immediately gave the virgin to the young man.
That old man,
harbored poisonous hatred in his heart.
(He thought:) 'He immediately insulted and ruined me, and seized my wife.
Life after life, wherever I am born, I will be your enemy.
I will never let you go."
The young Fànzhì always practiced loving-kindness (cíxīn).
But the other one solely harbored malice.
The Buddha told the Bhikṣus (bǐqiū):
"The elderly Fànzhì (Niánzūn Fànzhì) at that time
is Diàodá today.
The young Fànzhì
is myself.
And the woman is Qúyī."
Diàodá and King Āshéshì
jointly planned to destroy the Buddha and all his disciples.
The King commanded the people of the kingdom not to venerate the Buddha.
At that time, Shèlìfú and others,
and Bōhétí Bhīkṣūnī and others,
each took their disciples and departed for other countries.
Only the Buddha, along with five hundred Luóhàn,
remained on Gúshān.
Diàodá went to the King and said,
"All the Buddha's disciples have now dispersed.
There are still five hundred disciples remaining beside the Buddha.
I request that tomorrow, Your Majesty invite the Buddha into the city.
I shall cause five hundred great elephants to drink [alcohol],
make them drunk, and command them to trample and kill them.
I shall then become the Buddha who teaches the world."
The King heard this and was delighted.
He immediately went to invite the Buddha.
The Buddha knew their scheme,
and replied,
"Excellent."
The King withdrew and left.
He returned and reported back to Diàodá.
The next day, at mealtime,
the Buddha and the Luóhàn entered the city gate together.
The drunken elephants trumpeted with their noses and advanced.
They charged against the walls,
breaking trees; the entire city trembled.
The five hundred Luóhàn flew up into the air.
Only the Venerable Ānán remained at the side.
The drunken elephants advanced straight ahead, aiming for the Buddha.
The Buddha raised five fingers, which transformed into five lions,
all roaring simultaneously.
The sound shook heaven and earth.
The drunken elephants lay prostrate on the ground, not daring to raise their heads.
Their drunkenness lifted, they shed tears and repented of their actions.
The King, his ministers, and the people all observed with solemn respect.
The Shìzūn slowly advanced to the King’s palace hall.
After finishing the meal with the Luóhàn, he offered blessings.
The King addressed the Buddha, saying,
"My natural disposition was unclear.
I believed those malicious words
and perpetrated wicked, rebellious acts.
I pray you extend great compassion
and pardon my confusion and ignorance."
The Buddha addressed Āshéshì and the entire great assembly,
saying, "There are eight conditions in the world
that give rise to increased slander.
All of them, originating from seeking reputation, lead to great sins.
What are these eight?
Gain, loss, defamation, praise, renown, ridicule, suffering, and joy.
From antiquity until today, few have avoided being deluded by them."
The Buddha then spoke a verse, saying:
"In the past, there was a King
who was fond of eating goose meat.
He constantly dispatched hunters
to set nets and catch geese.
Every day, one goose was sent
to provision the King's meal.
At that time, there was a Goose King,
who led five hundred geese flying down to forage.
The Goose King fell into the net and was seized by the hunter.
The remaining geese flew up in alarm, circling and refusing to depart.
At that time, there was one goose that pursued him continuously,
not shunning bow and arrow, crying mournfully and spitting blood.
It did not stop day or night.
The hunter saw this
and was touched by its loyalty.
He immediately released the Goose King, allowing them to go together.
The flock of geese, having recovered their King, rejoiced and circled around him.
At that time, the hunter
reported the whole matter to the King.
The King was moved by their loyalty
and permanently ceased catching geese.
That Goose King then
is my present body.
The one goose is Ānán.
The five hundred geese
are the present five hundred Luóhàn.
The King who ate geese
is the present great King.
The hunter at that time
is the present Diàodá. Since former lives,
he has constantly desired to harm me.
I, through the power of great compassion,
have subsequently been able to save him.
By not dwelling on resentment or wickedness,
I naturally attained Buddhahood."
The King and his ministers,
all rejoiced.
Formerly there was a Bhikkhu,
named *Diàodá*.
He was clever and widely learned.
For twelve years, he sat in meditation, entering concentration with an unwavering mind.
The twelve austere practices (*dhūta*) were never once incomplete.
He initiated the meditation on impurity.
He understood the in-and-out breath.
He practiced the Highest Dharma in the World,
and even the Summit Dharma, discerning each individually.
The Buddhist sūtras he recited totaled sixty thousand,
a load which elephants could not carry.
Later, his intention reversed, and gradually evil thoughts arose.
He yearned for others' offerings and worldly gain.
He went to the place of the World-Honored One, paid obeisance by touching his head to the feet,
stood to one side, and addressed the Buddha, saying:
“Indeed, *Shìzūn*, I request you to speak on the path of supernormal powers (*shenzú*).
Once I have heard this, I will cultivate it well,
so that when I obtain supernormal powers,
I may travel to other regions and teach everywhere.”
*Shìzūn* told him:
“You should put aside supernormal powers for now.
Why don't you study the Four?
The meaning of Impermanence,
the meaning of Suffering, the meaning of Emptiness, and the meaning of Non-self.”
At that time, the Bhikkhu *Diàodá*
generated this thought:
“The reason the *Rúlái* does not explain supernormal powers to me
is that he fears someone might surpass him and that he would feel ashamed of his inferiority.”
*Diàodá* immediately left the *Rúlái*
and went to the place of *Shèlìfú*,
seeking the path of supernormal powers.
Then *Shèlìfú* said to *Diàodá*:
“You should put that aside for now.
Why do you not cultivate the Four Impermanences?”
*Diàodá* pondered:
“This *Shèlìfú*'s wisdom is foremost,
but in my estimation, he is like a firefly compared to the sun and moon.
Among all that I have recited and practiced, none is equal to me.
If I still do not understand the path of supernormal powers,
how could *Shèlìfú* possibly understand it?”
He then immediately left
and went to *Mùlián*'s place,
seeking the path of supernormal powers.
*Mùlián* said:
“Stop, stop, *Diàodá*!
A beginner must first study the Four Impermanences,
and then they must diligently cultivate the Four Dhyānas (*sì chán*).
Only then will you attain the path of supernormal powers.”
*Diàodá* became angry:
“This *Mùlián* boasts that his supernormal powers are unequaled.
The reason he won't give them to me
is that he fears he might be inferior to me.
If I obtain them, he will lose his reputation.
Now I have sought the path of supernormal powers everywhere,
and none has taught me.
My younger brother *Ānán* is widely heard and broadly learned,
possessing all virtues. I shall go and ask him now.”
He spoke to *Ānán*, saying:
“I hear that you understand the path of supernormal powers well.
You should explain it to me.
Once I obtain supernormal powers, I shall travel to other regions
and teach everywhere.”
At that time, *Ānán* then explained it to him.
When *Diàodá* heard this,
he went to a secluded place and concentrated with a focused mind.
He entered the subtle from the coarse, and rising again from the subtle, he returned to the coarse.
He lifted the body with the mind, and the mind with the body.
Body and mind united, and he gradually left the ground.
First, he was the size of a sesame seed, then he turned into the size of a walnut.
Gradually leaving the earth, he went from the ground to the couch,
from the couch to the roof, and from the roof to the sky.
In the empty sky, he performed the Eighteen Transformations.
He appeared and vanished freely.
He transformed himself into a newborn baby,
whose appearance was handsome
with five tufts of hair on the head and a face like a peach blossom.
He sat on the lap of Crown Prince *Āshéshì*.
He laughed sometimes and cried sometimes, exhibiting the behaviors of a baby.
However, the Crown Prince knew it was *Diàodá*'s body,
and he played with it all day long without tiring.
Sometimes he fondled it,
or lifted its body and passed it from his left hand to his right.
The Crown Prince thought:
*“Diàodá*'s supernormal powers surpass those of *Qú Tán*.
He can perform countless transformations.”
Prince *Āshéshì* supplied five hundred pots of food daily,
offering provisions timely, ensuring he lacked nothing.
At that time, many Bhikkhus,
seeing *Āshéshì* provide for *Diàodá*,
fully informed the *Shìzūn*.
The Buddha instructed the Bhikkhus:
“You should not covet *Diàodá*'s* offerings.
*Diàodá* entraps himself and also entraps others.
Both fall into transgression.
Just like the banana tree:
A foolish person seeks its fruit but cannot obtain it.
The bamboo and reed are also like this.
The *jùxiū* mule, when pregnant, loses both lives.
Formerly, there was a flock of eagles, each incubating eggs.
The eagle told its chicks:
‘If you learn to fly and hang in the empty sky,
seeing the earth like a plate, be careful not to fly past the limit above.
There is the *Suílán* wind which will harm you,
scattering your head, brain, limbs, and joints in different places.’
At that time, a chick did not follow its father's instruction,
flew past the limit, was blown by the wind, and died in another place.
Bhikkhus, you should not entertain such intentions.
Bhikkhus should know that it is like a flock of turtles.
They told their children:
‘Guard yourselves, and do not go to a certain place.
There is a hunter there who will certainly capture your bodies and cut them into five parts.’
The turtle children at that time did not follow their words
but went to that place to amuse themselves together.
They were then captured by the hunter.
Some were safe and managed to return home.
The turtle asked its children, ‘Where have you come from?’
The children replied to their parents:
‘We went together to view that place.
We did not see the hunter.
We only saw a long thread chasing after us.’
The turtle told its children:
‘This thread has been pursuing you for a long time.
Our ancestors, your grandparents, all perished because of this thread.’
Bhikkhus should know
that it is like a *gǔhú* jackal, which waits day and night seeking excrement.
After it has finished eating the waste of livestock and beasts,
it produces its own excrement again.
The Bhikkhu *Diàodá*,
in his greed for offerings, is also like this.
In the past, in the *Dàyuèzhī Guó*,
it was the custom and rule that they must feed pigs with wheat fried in butter (*sū jiān mài*).
At that time, a foal belonging to the official stables said to its mother:
‘We exert ourselves for the King, regardless of distance,
and all fulfill his command.
Yet we are fed coarse grass
and given rainwater to drink.’
The mare told her son:
‘You should be careful not to develop this intention of envying that butter-fried wheat.
Before long, the verification will appear by itself.’
When the festive season approached and the New Year was near,
every household tied up their pigs and threw them into cauldrons of boiling water,
screaming loudly.
The mare told her son:
‘Do you still remember the butter-fried wheat?
If you want to know the proof, you can go and observe it.’
The foals knew it was exactly true.
They then understood the circumstances of frying and governing.
When they ate grass and encountered wheat again,
they protected the wheat and did not eat it.
The Buddha spoke a verse, saying:
The banana dies by bearing fruit; the bamboo and reed perish the same way by fruition.
The *jùxiū* perishes by conception; the practitioner loses himself through greed.
The Buddha told the Bhikkhus:
*“Diàodá* is evil and dangerous.
They praise each other unjustly.
The Bhikkhu *Jūjiālì* praises *Diàodá*,
and *Diàodá* in turn praises *Jūjiālì*.
These two persons lack morality and principle.”
The Bhikkhus heard this.
“Indeed, Great Sage,
we observe the Bhikkhu *Jūjiālì*
relied for a long time on the orthodox scriptures and followed the disciplinary rules and teachings,
and left home life out of faith.
Yet he praises *Diàodá* unjustly,
and *Diàodá* praises *Jūjiālì*.
Together they take wrong to be right
and right to be wrong.”
The Buddha said:
“This group is foolish and ignorant.
It was the same in previous ages.
In a past age,
a eunuch died and was abandoned among the *chū* trees.
At that time, a *gǔhú* jackal and a bird came together to eat the flesh
and praised each other in turn.
The bird said:
‘Your body is like a lion, your head is like an immortal!
The fat is like the King of the deer; how excellent, like a beautiful flower!’
The *gǔhú* jackal praised him, saying:
‘You, Honored One, up in the tree, your wisdom is supreme and foremost!
It illuminates the ten directions like accumulated refined gold!’
They went back and forth like this.
At that time, the Great Immortal said:
‘They praise each other unjustly, speaking emptiness without reality.’
The *gǔhú* jackal is *Diàodá*.
The bird is *Jūjiālì*.
The Immortal is the Bodhisattva.”
Dàivádá.
Went to the location of the Shìzūn (World-Honored One).
Bowed his head to the ground, performed the head-and-foot prostration (lǐ zú), and stood to one side.
He addressed the Fó (Buddha), saying:
“I observe the Rúlái (Tathāgata).
Your complexion is changing, and your faculties are fully mature.
You have passed the prime of youth and are now declining into old age.
I only wish, Shìzūn,
that you would retire yourself to a quiet room and enjoy meditation.
I wish that the four assemblies [of disciples] be entrusted to me.
I shall teach and admonish them, just as the Fó does, without difference.
I will provide the four necessities (sì shì) as needed, without fail.”
The Fó said:
“Alas, you ignorant and foolish person!
You do not consider your future retribution (yāng).
The bhikṣus Shèlìfú and Mùlián
I still do not entrust [the community] to—
how much less you, a lazy, depraved, and wicked person,
can be entrusted with the assembly of the noble ones (shèng zhòng)!”
Dàivádá internally aroused jealousy.
Hearing the Shìzūn’s words,
his anger and resentment doubled.
“Today, the Rúlái praises the bhikṣus Shèlìfú and Mùlián,
but furthermore belittles and despises a junior disciple [like me].
I must seek an opportunity to destroy the master and disciples,
so that living beings in this country will neither see their forms nor hear their voices.”
At that time, the bhikṣu Dàivádá
immediately rose from his seat, performed the lǐ zú, and departed.
Everywhere he went, he used smooth talk and deceitful words,
deluding secular people and enticing several dozens [of followers].
In every place, they encouraged one another.
To put it concisely:
When the Fó was surrounded by the great assembly, speaking the Dharma,
Dàivádá addressed his own disciples, saying:
“Do not listen to what Qú Tán (Gautama) teaches; it does not follow the true Dharma (zhèng fǎ).
I have deep sūtras and excellent meanings, one by one,
which I ought to teach you.”
He merely sought opportunities to destroy the assembly of the noble ones.
The Fó said: “Stop! Stop!
Dàivádá!
Be careful not to arouse the intention to ruin and disturb the noble assembly.
Later, you will receive retribution, the pain of which will be unbearable.”
Dàivádá stubbornly held firm and did not change, knowing his intention was firm.
The Fó observed the past causes and conditions and the karmic retribution (sù duì) and knew it could not be averted.
Dàivádá led five hundred disciples.
The Rúlái also led five hundred disciples.
Both groups traveled together near Bǎojī shān (Precious Heap Mountain).
The disciples of the Púsa (Bodhisattva) were generous, benevolent, gentle, and harmonious.
They were taught the zhèng fǎ.
They cultivated and upheld the precepts; in their coming, going, advancing, and stopping, they did not overstep their bounds.
Dàivádá’s assembly spoke coarse words.
Their speech always aroused resentment.
When speaking with his disciples, it was like mutual resentment, fighting, and litigation.
The disciples became weary and disgusted, and all abandoned him.
They went to join the Púsa.
Dàivádá arrogantly boasted, saying:
“I have a thousand disciples.
They possess all virtues completely,
and are uniquely separate from the world—who can surpass them?”
Dàivádá was enraged.
He immediately made a vow (shì yuàn):
“This person, today,
has enticed my disciples and ruined my followers.
Even if he achieves Buddhahood, I will destroy his assembly
just as I do now, without difference.”
The Rúlái observed and knew that Dàivádá
would certainly ruin the noble assembly; there was no doubt about it.
The Rúlái immediately rose from his seat,
left the assembly, and departed.
There are five conditions
under which the Saṅgha (zhòng sēng) cannot be ruined or disturbed.
First, while the Rúlái is present,
due to the Rúlái’s divine power (wēi shén) and his non-abandonment of his original vow (běn shì).
Second, after the Rúlái enters Parinirvāṇa (Bānnihuán),
if someone says,
“I have now achieved Buddhahood and attained the Supreme Right Enlightenment (Zuì Zhèng Jué),”
they should be asked,
“When Shìjiāwén Fó was alive, where were you?”
Third, when there has not yet been a time of evil (è shí).
Fourth, when bhikṣus do not compete for offerings (lì yǎng).
Fifth, when disciples possessing wisdom (zhì huì) and spiritual powers (shén zú) are harmonious.
The Rúlái observed using the wisdom of past lives (sù mìng zhì).
He certainly knew that Dàivádá was about to ruin and disturb the Saṅgha.
The Rúlái immediately left and departed.
Dàivádá remained behind and spoke the Dharma to his assembly:
“If there are living beings
who serve me as their revered one and accept my teachings and precepts,
they should practice five specific dharmas. Any bhikṣu who cultivates these five dharmas
will quickly attain liberation (jiě tuō), exhaust the outflows (yǒu lòu), and achieve the non-outflows (wú lòu).
Why rely on Qú Tán’s Eightfold Noble Path (bā zhí xíng)?”
[He also] spoke to Shèlìfú and Mùlián, saying:
“I have attained great benefit and have become a venerated image of the Three Realms (Sān Jiè Zūn xiàng) like the Rúlái.”
The Rúlái informed Shèlìfú and Mùlián, saying:
“I suffer from back pain and wish to sleep peacefully for a short while.
You two should speak the Dharma to the noble assembly.”
Dàivádá lay down on his right side, wishing to sleep.

A heavenly spirit (tiān shén) compelled Dàivádá to lie on his left side. The heavenly spirit then tormented him with deceitful speech; snoring sounds appeared externally, and foul odors permeated far.
Mùlián used his power of shén zú
to fly up into the void, performing eighteen kinds of transformations.
He sat, lay down, walked, surged up, and sank down with perfect freedom.
Shèlìfú addressed the members of the assembly:
“The Rúlái’s divine virtue (shén dé) is immeasurable.
He completely possesses omniscience (yī qiè zhì).
He reaches infinitely forward and reaches infinitely backward.
The Rúlái’s Dharma
leads to the present realization of karmic reward, happiness, and non-action (wú wéi).
It is what the wise cultivate and study,
not what the foolish practice.
The Rúlái’s noble assembly
has all accomplished the Five-Part Dharma Body (Wǔ Fēn Fǎ Shēn).
They are worthy of respect and veneration, service and offerings.
They are the excellent protectors and field of merit (fú tián) for living beings.”
At that time, all the bhikṣus generated this thought:
“We are foolish and deluded, not recognizing the truly correct path.
We abandoned the real and followed the superficial; we discarded the root and chased the branch.
Now we observe the teaching of the two noble ones (Shèlìfú and Mùlián)—it is rare in the world.
Wouldn't it be better for us to abandon this Dàivádá and join the Rúlái’s assembly?
Isn't that joyful?”
Shèlìfú knew their thoughts.
He immediately rose from his seat.
The five hundred bhikṣus all followed him.
Mùlián followed behind and departed.
The bhikṣu Qúpōlí
stepped on Dàivádá with his right foot and said:
“Wicked Dàivádá, why are you indulging in sleep?
Shèlìfú and Mùlián, the two of them,
have taken all your disciples away!”
Dàivádá woke from his sleep, feeling greatly distressed and sorrowful.
In ancient times,
there was a youth (mónà) who was reciting a Kṣatriya text (chà lì shū) in a mountain cave.
There was a wild fox that came near him.
It listened attentively to the recitation and gained some understanding in its heart.
It thought:
“If I understand the words of this text,
I am fit to be the king among all beasts.”
It then arose and traveled.
It encountered a skinny wild fox
and immediately intended to kill it.
The fox said, “Why kill me?”
It replied:
“I am the King of Beasts.
You do not submit to me.”
The fox said:
“Please do not kill me.
I will follow you.”
Thereupon, the two foxes traveled together.
They encountered another fox.
The questioning and answering were the same as above.
In this manner, through successive steps, it subdued all the foxes.
Then, using the multitude of foxes, it subdued all the elephants.
Furthermore, using the host of elephants, it subdued all the tigers.
Furthermore, using the host of tigers, it subdued all the lions.
Thus, it temporarily managed to become the King of Beasts.
It further generated this thought:
“Since I am the King of Beasts,
I should not take a beast as a wife.”
It then rode a white elephant,
and made all the multitude of beasts surround the kingdom of Jiāyí guó (Kāyi country).
They encircled it hundreds and thousands of times.
The King sent an envoy to ask:
“Why are you doing this?”
The wild fox replied:
“I am the King of Beasts.
I should marry your daughter.
If you do not give her to me, I will destroy your kingdom.”
The envoy returned and reported to the King.
The King gathered his ministers for deliberation.
Except for one minister,
all said that she should be given:
“The reliance of the country is solely upon our elephants and horses.
We have elephants and horses, but they have lions.
When the elephants and horses smell the lions, they are terrified and collapse to the ground.
We will certainly lose the battle.
Why regret giving up one daughter and lose an entire kingdom?”
At that time, there was one great minister who was intelligent, sharp, and possessed foresight.
He addressed the King, saying:
“Your servant observes that from ancient times until now, it has never been heard or seen that the daughter of a human king married a base creature.
Although your servant is weak and dim-witted,
if we kill this fox, the multitude of beasts will scatter and flee.”
The King immediately asked him [how].
The minister replied:
“Your Majesty need only send an envoy to set a date for battle
and request one condition:
Let the lions fight first and roar afterward.
The fox, thinking we are afraid, will certainly order the lions to roar first and fight afterward.”
When the day of battle arrived,
the King commanded everyone inside the city to block their ears.
The King followed his words, and then led out the army.
As the armies were about to clash,
the wild fox indeed ordered the lions to roar first.
When the wild fox heard it, its heart broke into seven pieces,
and it immediately fell from the elephant onto the ground.
The multitude of beasts scattered and fled.
The Fó spoke a verse (gè yán):
“The wild fox, full of arrogance, sought to possess a royal family.
Traveling to the city of Jiāyí, it proclaimed itself the King of Beasts.
Human arrogance is also like this, presently leading followers
in the kingdom of Mógē zhī guó, proclaiming oneself the Master of Dharma.”
He told the Bhikṣus (Bīqiū).
At that time, the King of Jiāyí (迦夷) was I.
The astute and sharp minister was Shèlìfú (舍利弗).
The King of the Wild Foxes was Diàodá (調達).
Diàodá was in Luōyuèchéng (羅閱城).
He aroused the intention to murder and harm.
Later, the matter was exposed.
At that time, King Āshéshì (阿闍世)
said to Diàodá:
"You ought to leave the country; you should not remain here.
The sixteen great kingdoms have all heard and know this.
Diàodá has committed evil against the Tathāgata (Rúlái)."
Diàodá heard this and harbored worry and distress within.
He then returned to his own country, wrapped in anger and resentment.
He burst into the palace of the Bodhisattva (Púsà).
He said to Qúyī (瞿夷):
"I wish to appoint you as the first consort (Fūrén).
May I ask, saintly woman, whether this is acceptable?"
Qúyī replied:
"First, I wish to grasp your right hand."
Diàodá stretched out his hand, allowing her to grasp and clench it.
His wrist bones were crushed, and blood issued from his five fingers.
At that moment, he was dazed and faint, and only revived after a long time.
At this time, Diàodá proceeded further into the palace,
and sat upon the Bodhisattva's bed.
The palace attendants saw him, seized him, and threw him beneath the bed.
Immediately, his left hip (iliac bone) was injured, rendering him unable to walk or move.
He was carried back to his original dwelling.
All the Śākyas (Shì) resented him and came to tell him:
"You should now go to the Buddha (Fó) and repent."
Diàodá heard this.
He secretly devised a cunning scheme.
He secretly made iron claws.
He smeared deadly poison upon them.
His outer appearance was gentle and compliant, but internally he harbored hatred and rage (chēnhuì).
At that time, Diàodá recalled what the Buddha had said:
"Śramaṇa (Shāmén) Gautama (Qútán) constantly maintains this statement:
'If a body has no wounds or sores, it cannot be harmed by poison.'
'Poison can do nothing against a wound.'
There is no evil that has not been committed."
"I should now go and pretend to repent,
and use the claws to gouge and damage his feet.
The poison will spread and overflow, and he will naturally die."
The people carried him in a sedan chair toward the World-Honored One (Shìzūn).
When they were twenty-one *rèn* (paces/fathoms) away, he told the people around him:
"Set me down on the ground; I wish to walk the rest of the way."
Immediately, he was set down on the ground.
At that moment, raging fire boiled forth and enveloped his body,
carrying him into Avīci Hell (Dìyù).
The Buddha was staying in Rājagṛha (Wángshěchéng).
At this time, Devadatta (Típódáduō)
wished to destroy the harmony of the Saṅgha (Sēng).
The Bhikṣus repeatedly admonished him three times, but he still did not stop.
The Buddha said:
"In a past life,
in the country of Vārāṇasī (Bōluónài),
there was a Brāhmaṇa (Póluómén).
He built a charity well in the wilderness,
providing water for travelers.
When the sun was setting toward evening,
a group of wild jackals came to drink the remaining water.
There was a King of the Jackals who did not drink the water on the ground.
He put his head into the jar and drank the water.
After drinking, he raised the jar high upon his head and smashed it.
The other jackals kindly spoke to him, but he did not accept their advice.
Thus, it was not just once; he smashed fourteen jars.
The Brāhmaṇa waited and watched the jackals.
Then he made a wooden jar, sturdy and difficult to break.
It was easy to enter but difficult to exit; he placed it by the well.
Holding a staff, he waited.
The jackals gathered in a group.
The king drank as before.
He threw it to the ground but could not break it.
At that moment, the Brāhmaṇa came out holding the staff
and beat the jackal to death.
That King of the Jackals
is now Típódáduō.
That group of jackals
are now the Bhikṣus who admonish Típódáduō."
The Buddha was staying in Wángshěchéng.
At that time, the Bhikṣus
performed the act of censure (*karma*) against Típódáduō.
The six groups of Bhikṣus immediately shared Típódáduō's words and views.
The Buddha told the Bhikṣus:
"In a past life,
in a deserted place,
there were five hundred monkeys roaming through the forest.
They arrived at a Nyagrodha tree (Nígùlǜshù).
Beneath the tree was a well, and the moon's reflection was in the well.
The King of the Monkeys saw this moon reflection.
He said to his companions:
'The moon has now died and fallen into the well.
We must pull it out together, lest the world remain in long-lasting darkness.'
They discussed together how they could pull it out.
The King of the Monkeys said:
'I know the method for pulling it out.
I will grasp a tree branch, and you grasp my tail.
By linking up one after the other, we can pull it out.'
The monkeys immediately followed the king's instruction.
Linking up one after the other, they had almost reached the water.
The weight of the linked monkeys caused the weak branch to break, and all the monkeys fell into the well water.
That King of the Monkeys
is now Típódáduō.
The rest of the monkeys at that time
are now the six groups of Bhikṣus."
The Buddha told Ānán (阿難):
"If any sentient being arouses a single malicious thought
toward the Buddhas of the three ages,
or toward a Pratyekabuddha (Pìzhī), an Arhat (Luóhàn), or those who wear dyed robes, and all Śramaṇas,
they acquire measureless offense.
Why is this?
The dyed robe is the distinguishing mark (biāoshì) of the noble sages.
If one can arouse the mind to revere the wearer of the dyed robe,
the merit acquired is immeasurable.
Because I respectfully maintained faith in them, I was able to attain Buddhahood (Chéngfó)."
Ānán submitted:
"In the past, how was this respectful devotion accomplished?"
The Buddha told Ānán:
"In ancient times, measureless *kalpas* (jié) ago,
in this Jambudvīpa (Yánfú Tí), there was a great king named Típí (提毘), who ruled eighty-four thousand minor kings.
There was no Buddhadharma (Fófǎ) in the world.
There was a Pratyekabuddha
who dwelt among the mountains, practicing meditation and the path (xíngdào).
At that time, all the wild beasts came and attached themselves to him.
There was a lion
named Shìjiāluóbī (尸迦羅毘), whose body was golden and whose radiant marks were brilliant.
He ate fruit and consumed grass, and did not harm sentient beings.
At that time, there was a hunter.
He shaved his head and wore a *kaṣāya* (jiāshā),
internally bearing a bow and arrows, and walked in the marshlands.

He saw the lion sleeping and shot it with a poisoned arrow. The lion awoke in shock and immediately intended to rush and harm him, but seeing him wearing the *kaṣāya*, he thought to himself, 'This wearer of the dyed robe is the distinguishing mark of a virtuous person.
If I harm him,
I would be directing evil intent toward the noble sages.'
He pondered and ceased (his intention).
The arrow poison traveled internally, and his life would not last long.
He then spoke a verse (gè) saying: 'Yēluópóshāshābāhē (耶羅婆奢沙婆呵).'
When he spoke these words,
the heavens and earth greatly shook, and blood rained down without clouds.
All the *devas* (tiān) were terrified and alarmed.
