They immediately observed with their heavenly eyes
that the hunter had killed the lion.
They rained down heavenly flowers to make offerings to its corpse.
At this time, the hunter skinned the lion
and presented the skin to King Típí.
The King then thought:
"The scriptures say:
'Any beast with golden color must be a Bodhisattva.'
He asked the hunter:
"When the lion died, what auspicious signs appeared?"
The answer was as described above.
When the King heard these words,
sorrow and joy intermingled in his heart, and his faith intensified fiercely.
He immediately summoned all his ministers, elders, and wise men,
instructing them to interpret this meaning.
At that time, there was an immortal (xiānrén) in a quiet forest named Shēmó (奢摩).
He interpreted the meaning of the words
'Yēluó' for the King.
The meaning is: Only by shaving the head and wearing the dyed robe
can one quickly attain liberation from the cycle of birth and death (shēngsǐ).
'Póshāshā' means:
all are marks of noble sages, close to Nirvāṇa (Nièpán).
'Bāhē' means:
they shall be revered and admired by all *devas* and people of the world."
When the immortal had interpreted these words,
Típí rejoiced.
He immediately summoned all the kings to assemble at this place.
He built a seven-jeweled chariot and displayed the lion skin upon it,
indicating to everyone that they should revere and respect it together.
They burned incense and scattered flowers to make offerings.
Afterward, he molded gold into a coffin,
placed the lion skin inside, and built a *stūpa* (tǎ) for it.
That lion at the time,
because it generated a benevolent heart toward the wearer of the dyed robe,
became a Cakravartin (Zhuǎnlún Shèng Wáng) for ten hundred million *kalpas*.
The Buddha told Ānán:
"That lion at that time
is my present body.
That king at that time is now Maitreya (Mílè).
That immortal at that time is now Shèlìfú.
That hunter at that time is now Típódáduō."
Bhagavā was in Shèwèi Chéng.
In Qíshù Jǐgūdú Yuán.
He addressed the Bhikṣus:
“There are four great Nílí (Hells).
The first is the great Nílí of Tíshě.
Flames emerge from his body, twenty cubits long.
The second is the great Nílí of Qúpōlí.
Flames emerge from his body, thirty cubits long.
The third is the great Nílí of Tiáodá.
Flames emerge from his body, forty cubits long.
The fourth is the great Nílí of Mòqúlí.
Flames emerge from his body, sixty cubits long.
If there were people who desired peace and tranquility,
and sought to seize this meaning—
if twenty great seas of water were poured over his body,
that seawater would be exhausted, yet the fire would still not be extinguished.
It is comparable to molten copper.
If someone were to take twenty drops of seawater,
and pour them onto the molten copper, the water drops would quickly vanish.
The flames of Bhikṣu Tíshě are not extinguished.
Furthermore, if there were people who desired peace and tranquility and sought to seize this meaning,
and again used twenty great seas of water
poured over his body, that water would quickly be exhausted.
Bhikṣu Tíshě, the fool,
obstructed the Saṅgha of Bhikṣus, causing them to go without food for one day.
This caused Bhikṣu Tíshě to enter the great hell.
Bhikṣu Qúpōlí.
If someone desired to bring peace and tranquility and seize this meaning,
and poured great seawater over his body,
that seawater would quickly be exhausted.
This is like copper melted by two suns.
If there were a person
who took thirty seas of water
and put them into the molten copper, they would vanish completely.
Bhikṣu Qúpōlí, the fool.
If someone arose desiring to seize the meaning of peace and tranquility,
and poured thirty great seas of water
over his body,
the great seawater would quickly be exhausted.
Bhikṣu Qúpōlí, the fool,
slandered Bhikṣu Shèlìfú and Mùjiànlián.
When his body perished and his life ended, he was born into the three evil paths (dào),
falling into the Pàtóumó Hell.
Bhikṣu Qúpōlí entered the great Nílí.
The great Nílí of Tiáodá.
Furthermore, if there were people who desired to achieve the meaning of peace and tranquility,
and again used forty great seas of water
poured over his body,
those great seas would quickly be exhausted, yet that fire would not be extinguished.
For example, copper melted by three suns.
If someone were to take forty drops of water,
and place them into the molten copper,
they would instantly vanish without residue.
Tiáodá, the fool.
If someone arose desiring to achieve the meaning of peace and tranquility,
and poured forty great seas of water over his body,
those great seas would quickly be exhausted, yet that fire would not be extinguished.
The reason is this:
Tiáodá, the fool,
desired to harm the Tathāgata and killed an Arhat Bhikṣuṇī,
destroying and confusing the Saṅgha of Bhikṣus.
When his body perished and his life ended, he was born into the three evil paths, entering the Ābí Hell.
Bhikṣu Tiáodá entered the great hell.
Flames emerge from his body, forty cubits long.
All Bhikṣus,
that great Nílí of Mòqúlí.
If there were a person who desired to bring peace and tranquility,
and poured sixty great seas of water over his body,
the seawater would quickly be exhausted, yet that fire would not be extinguished.
For example, copper melted by four suns.
If someone were to take sixty drops of water,
and place them into the molten copper, they would instantly vanish completely.
Mòqúlí is also like this.
Sixty great seas of water poured over his body,
the great seawater would quickly be exhausted, and this fire would not be extinguished.
This Mòqúlí, the fool,
instructed and accepted one hundred Jūlí people,
causing them to practice heretical views (xiéjiàn).”
The Buddha said.
Once, at a certain time,
I resided in Rājagṛha (Wángshě Chéng).
The Bhikṣu Shànxīng served as my attendant.
In the first watch of the night,
I expounded the essentials of the Dharma to Śakra (Tiāndì Shì).
The duty of a disciple is to sleep after the master.
At that time, Shànxīng,
because I sat for a long time, conceived wicked thoughts in his mind.
At that time, the young boys and girls in Rājagṛha (Wángshě Chéng),
if they did not stop crying, their parents would say,
“If you do not stop,
we will hand you over to the ghost Bó Jūluó.”
At that moment, Shànxīng felt restrained (as if seized by the ghost)
and said to me,
“Hurry and enter the meditation chamber! Bó Jūluó has come!”
Śakra (Dìshì) said,
“World-Honored One,
can such people
also enter the Buddha Dharma?”
I said,
“They also possess Buddha Nature,
and shall attain unsurpassed Bodhi.”
Although I taught the Dharma to this Shànxīng,
he had no mind of faith or acceptance whatsoever.
When I was in Śivapura (Shīpó Fùluó Chéng) in the Kāśi (Jiāshī) country,
Shànxīng served as my attendant.
I entered the city seeking alms.
Innumerable sentient beings, with open minds and longing thirst, desired to see my footsteps.
Shànxīng followed behind, trying to erase them.
Since he could not erase them,
he caused sentient beings to develop unwholesome thoughts.
After I entered the city,
I saw a Nirgrantha (Nígān) in a wine house,
hunched over and squatting on the ground, eating wine dregs.
Shànxīng said,
“If there is an Arhat (Āluóhàn) in the world,
this man is the most superior.
Why?
This man proclaims that there are no causes and no effects.”
I said, “Ignorant man,
do you not constantly hear
that an Arhat (Āluóhàn) does not drink alcohol, does not kill, does not deceive, nor does he steal or commit immorality?
How can such a person,
who kills his parents and eats wine dregs,
be called an Arhat (Āluóhàn)?
When this person abandons his body,
he will certainly fall into the Avīci Hell (Ābí Dìyù).
An Arhat (Āluóhàn)
forever severs the three evils (of body, speech, and mind).
How can he be called an Arhat (Āluóhàn)?”
Shànxīng immediately said,
“If the nature of the Four Great Elements can still be shifted,
it is impossible
to mandate that this person will certainly fall into Avīci (Ābí).”
I said, “Ignorant man,
do you not constantly hear that the truthful words of all Tathāgatas (Rúlái) are never double-tongued?”
Although I taught the Dharma to him,
he had no mind of faith or acceptance.
“Good men,
when Shànxīng and I resided in Rājagṛha (Wángshě Chéng),
there was a Nirgrantha (Nígān),
named Kǔdé (Suffering Attained).
He constantly made this statement:
‘The afflictions of sentient beings have no cause or condition.
The liberation of sentient beings also has no cause or condition.’”
Shànxīng said,
“If there is an Arhat (Āluóhàn) in the world,
Kǔdé is the foremost.”
I said,
“Ignorant man, the Nirgrantha Kǔdé
is truly not an Arhat (Luóhàn).
He cannot understand the way of the Arhat (Āluóhàn).”
Shànxīng replied,
“Why does an Arhat (Luóhàn)
give rise to jealousy toward another Arhat (Āluóhàn)?”
I said, “Ignorant man,
I do not give rise to jealousy toward Arhats (Luóhàn).
Rather, you yourself give rise to wicked, false views.”
“If you say Kǔdé is an Arhat (Luóhàn),
then seven days hence,
he will suffer from undigested food, die of abdominal pain,
and be born among the spirits that vomit what they eat (Shítǔ Guǐ).
His companions will carry his corpse and place it in the charnel ground (Hánlín).”
Shànxīng immediately said to the Nirgrantha (Nígān),
“Elder,
think carefully and employ all means
so that the World-Honored One will fall into the error of false speech.”
Kǔdé ceased eating
from the first day until the sixth day.
When the seventh day was complete, he ate black honey.
He then drank cold water, died of abdominal pain,
and his companions carried his corpse and placed it in the charnel ground (Hánlín).
Immediately taking the form of a starving spirit that vomits what it eats (Shítǔ Èguǐ),
it stood beside its corpse.
Shànxīng went to the charnel ground (Hánlín),
saw Kǔdé’s body,
and spoke to him,
“Great Virtuous One, are you dead?”
Kǔdé replied,
“I am dead.”
“How did you die?”
He replied,
“I died due to abdominal pain.”
“Who brought out your corpse?”
He replied,
“My companions.”
“Where was it placed?”
He replied, “Ignorant man,
do you not recognize this charnel ground (Hánlín)?”
“What kind of body did you obtain?”
He replied,
“I obtained the body of a spirit that vomits what it eats (Shítǔ Guǐ Shēn).”
Shànxīng said,
“World-Honored One,
the Nirgrantha Kǔdé was born in the Trāyastriṃśa Heaven (Sānshísān Tiān).”
I said, “Ignorant man,
an Arhat (Āluóhàn) has nowhere to be born.
How can you say
that Kǔdé was born in the Trāyastriṃśa Heaven (Sānshísān Tiān)?”
The Tathāgata (Rúlái), along with Kāśyapa (Jiāshè),
went to where Shànxīng was.
Shànxīng saw them from afar and conceived a wicked, false mind.
While still alive, his physical body sank down and fell into the Avīci Hell (Ābí Dìyù).
It is like a person who has sunk into a latrine.
A good friend (Shàn Zhīshì) stirs around with his hand,
hoping to grab the hair on his head and pull him out.
After long seeking and failing to find anything,
he finally gives up the idea.
I am also like this:
I sought and searched for a trace of wholesome roots in Shànxīng,
intending to save him and pull him out.
I sought for him all day long,
yet I could not obtain anything, not even the measure of a single hair.
Therefore, I could not pull him out of hell.
Shèwèiguó.
There was a village of mountain people.
Fifty or sixty households.
It was five hundred *lǐ* distant from the capital.
In the village there was one poor family.
The wife was pregnant for ten months and bore two sons (twins).
They were extremely handsome and incomparable.
Their parents loved them.
They gave names to their sons.
One was named Shuāngdé.
The second was named Shuāngfú.
When they were fifty or sixty days old.
Their father was resting on the bed after tending the cattle.
Their mother was picking up firewood and had not yet returned.
These two children mutually questioned and reproached each other.
One said: "Previously we were about to attain the Way (Enlightenment).
Merely because of a foolish thought that life could be permanent,
we fell back into the cycle of rebirth (samsāra) for immeasurable *jié* (kalpas).
Now we are born into this poor family.
Objects made of straw and grass serve as our blankets and coarse cloth.
Our food and drink are crude and bad, barely sustaining our lives.
If this continues for long, how can we survive?
This is all due to our previous lives, when we yearned for wealth and nobility.
We indulged our bodies and scattered our minds, finding pleasure for a fleeting moment.
Since then, we have suffered on a long path.
Now that we are anxious and distressed, what reliance can we have?"
The other replied,
"At that time there was a minor difficulty, and we did not persevere entirely in our diligence for that one moment.
And now, for several generations, we have encountered all these evil troubles.
This was done by ourselves, not by our parents.
We must simply face it together; what else is there to say?"
The father heard this, thought it strange, and supposed they were ghosts.
While they are still small and not grown up, it is fitting that they should be killed.
The father, alarmed, went to the fields.
He gathered firewood and bundles of kindling, intending to burn and kill them.
The mother returned and asked her husband,
"What are you using this firewood for?"
The husband told her the situation.
The mother, hearing this, was stunned.
The next day, the husband and wife both went out and secretly listened.
The two sons were reproaching each other as before.
They then gathered the firewood together, secretly intending to burn them.
The Buddha, seeing this with his divine eye (Tīnyǎn),
went to the village and universally emitted a bright light (guāngmíng).
Heaven and Earth greatly shook.
Mountains, rivers, and trees all became golden-colored.
He arrived at the home of the twin children.
The two children saw the Buddha's light
and rejoiced immensely.
The parents were also startled, and each held one child.
They brought them to the place of the Buddha and asked the World-Honored One (Shìzūn).
"These children have been born for forty or fifty days.
What they say is as described, and we find it extremely strange.
Fearing they might cause misfortune or harm, we intended to burn them with fire.
We do not know what kind of ghosts or sprites (guǐmèi) they are.
We only pray that you will explain."
The children, seeing the Buddha, leaped up happily.
The Buddha, seeing the children, laughed loudly.
From his mouth came five-colored light (guāng),
universally illuminating Heaven and Earth.
The Buddha proclaimed,
"These two children are not ghosts or sprites.
They are Sons of Merit and Virtue (Fúdé).
Previously, during the time of Kāyèfó (Kassapa Buddha), they were *shāmény* (Śramaṇas).
They were friends from their youth.
They shared the same aspiration, left home, and practiced diligence individually.
Just as they were about to attain the Way, they suddenly gave rise to improper thoughts.
They mutually discouraged each other and delighted in worldly glory and splendor.
Relying on their merit, they were reborn in the heavens.
They descended and became marquises, kings, rulers of states, and elders (*zhǎngzhě*).
Upon suddenly arising such thoughts, they retreated on their own.
They did not attain Nirvāṇa (*Níhuán*) but rather underwent this cycle of life and death (samsāra).
For countless years, they have constantly been connected and drawn to each other.
They always share birth as twins, and now they encounter my era.
Now they have just been born.
Because they previously offered provisions to the Buddha, their remaining merit allows them to be saved.
They were born with knowledge of their past lives (sùmìng), and now I have come to save them.
If I had not saved them, they would have been wrongly burned by fire."
He then spoke a *gè* (verse):
The great man’s body is without desire, in his presence, he brightly illuminates what is seen.
Although he may encounter suffering or pleasure, he does not elevate and display his wisdom.
The great worthy has no worldly concerns, he does not wish for sons, wealth, or state.
He should maintain the path of precepts and wisdom, and not covet wicked wealth and nobility.
The wise man’s wisdom wavers, like a tree in the sand.
Friends whose aspirations are not strong are easily stained, just as plain silk is dyed by color.
The Buddha spoke.
These children saw the Buddha.
Their bodies leaped up and became the size of eight-year-old children.
Immediately they became *shāmís* (Śrāmaṇeras) and attained the Way of the Arhat (Luóhàndào).
The villagers, young and old, saw the Buddha’s light and signs.
They also saw the children’s form change and leap up (grow).
They were all greatly rejoiced and attained the Way of the Stream-Enterer (Xūtuóhuándào).
The parents’ doubts were dissolved, and they also attained the Dharma Eye (Fǎyǎn).
There was a king
whose name was Zhāntuóyuè.
He revered the way of the Brāhmaṇa.
He also employed them to govern the nation justly.
The king highly favored a minor consort.
The other consorts hated and envied her.
They gave gold to the Brāhmaṇas and slandered her to the king,
saying that the son she bore would surely bring calamity to the state.
The king heard this and was displeased.
He asked the Brāhmaṇas,
"What should be done?"
They replied,
"The only thing to do is kill both mother and child."
The king said,
"Human life is precious; how can they be killed?"
They responded,
"If you do not kill them, you will certainly lose your kingdom and perish yourself."
The king then wrongfully killed the child.
Afterward, the child was born in a grave.
Half of his mother's body did not decay.
The child drank her *tǒng* (milk).
*Tǒng* means breast milk.
This continued up to three years.
The grave collapsed and sank.
The child managed to get out.
He played together with birds and beasts.
In the evening, he returned to the grave.
When he reached six years of age,
the Buddha thought of his suffering, living in the company of birds and beasts.
He immediately transformed himself into a Śramaṇa (monk).
He went and called out to the child and asked him,
"Whose son are you?"
"Where do you live?"
The child happily replied,
"I have no home.
I only reside and sleep in this grave."
"I beg to follow the Daoist (monk) away."
The Buddha said,
"What do you wish to do?"
The child replied,
"Whether good or bad, I will ultimately follow the Daoist now."
The Buddha then brought him to the Qíhuán (Jetavana Vihāra).
Seeing the dignified manners and rules of the Bhikṣus (monks),
he was extremely delighted.
He then reported to the Buddha,
"I wish to request to become a Bhikṣu."
The Buddha immediately permitted him.
He rubbed the top
of his head with his hand, and the hair fell off by itself, and a *jiāshā* (robe) clothed his body.
He was named Xūtuó.
He kept the precepts diligently, and his mind was not lax.
After seven days, he attained the path of Arhatship (Luóhàn).
The Buddha said to Xūtuó,
"You should go and convert King Zhāntuóyuè."
Xūtuó went there.
The King of the state said,
"I am greatly worried in my heart; what should I do?"
The Daoist said,
"What are you worried about?"
The king said,
"I am already old.
Time is passing, and I have no heir, which is why I am grieving and worried."
The Daoist heard the king's words.
He did not respond at all but merely laughed silently.
The king then angrily said,
"I am speaking with the Daoist,
yet he does not answer me at all,
but instead just laughs silently!"
He immediately intended to kill him.
Xūtuó knew his intention,
so he lightly rose up, flew, and remained hovering in the air.
He divided his body and scattered his form, appearing and disappearing without obstacle.
The king saw this divine transformation and immediately repented, saying,
"I am truly foolish, unable to distinguish between true and false.
I only wish that the Great Spirit would return for a moment,
allowing me to take refuge."
Xūtuó immediately descended from the air and stood before the king.
He addressed the king, saying,
"If you are able to take refuge, that is excellent.
You should take refuge in the Buddha.
The Buddha is my master,
the most honored of the Three Realms, who delivers and liberates sentient beings."
Xūtuó, in the time it takes to stretch an arm,
led the king and his people
to the place where the Buddha was.
They took refuge in the Three Jewels (Saṅgha) and requested to receive the Five Precepts, thereby becoming Upāsakas (Yōupósāi).
The Buddha fully explained
that Xūtuó was the king's son.
When the king heard the Buddha's words,
he became even more terrified, unable to restrain himself.
The Buddha said,
"Long ago, during the time of the Buddha Kūxiānní,
there was a king named Fúshědá.
The people of the state all made offerings to the Three Jewels.
At that time, there was an ordinary man who was poor and jobless.
He
was usually hired by the wealthy and noble people in the state to herd and care for several hundred cows.
He saw the king and the people making offerings to the Bhikṣu Saṅgha.
He immediately asked,
"What are you doing?"
The people replied,
"We are making offerings to the Three Jewels.
Afterward, wherever we reside, we will be peaceful, happy, and noble, without suffering or toil."
He immediately thought to himself,
"I am poor, so I can only boil cow's milk to make curds and butter
and offer them to the Bhikṣus with a pure heart."
The Bhikṣu Saṅgha gave him blessings, saying,
"May you receive blessings life after life."
Afterward, he transmigrated through life and death.
He always received that merit.
Sometimes he ascended to become one of the various Devas (Heavenly Beings),
sometimes he descended to become a king or a noble.
When he was a king
or noble, he went out hunting. He saw a fine cow that was pregnant with a calf and killed it.
The consort said to the king,
"Do not kill her son."
At that time, the cowherd (owner of the cow) cut open the cow, took the calf, and raised it.
The owner angrily said,
"May the king suffer the fate of this cow!"
Afterward, that soul became the son of the king.
Before he was born,
his mother was killed by the king—that is Xūtuó.
Xūtuó's mother was the king's consort at that time.
The Brāhmaṇas are the cowherd.
Xūtuó was born in the grave,
and half of his mother's body did not decay,
allowing him to drink her milk
and grow up—
this was due to his past life, when he offered curds and butter to the Bhikṣu Saṅgha.
The king heard this, his mind was freed,
and he attained the fruit of Srotāpanna (Xūtuóyuán).
The Buddha was in the state of Shèwèi (Śrāvastī).
At that time, the Venerable Shèlìfú (Śāriputra),
used his divine eye to observe three times, day and night.
Whoever ought to be converted, he immediately went and converted them.
At that time, there was a merchant who wished to travel to another country. His fellow merchants brought a dog with them, and they arrived halfway along the road.
The group of merchants stopped to rest, and the dog stole meat.
Thereupon, the group beat the dog together.
They broke its leg, abandoned it in the wilderness, and departed, leaving it behind.
At that time, Shèlìfú saw the dog with his divine eye,
lying lame and crippled on the ground, starving, exhausted, and close to death.
He flew to the dog's location and gave it food.
The dog saved its remaining life and was extremely joyful in its heart.
At that time, Shèlìfú
then preached the profound Dharma to this dog.
The dog then died
and was reborn into a Brāhmaṇa family in the state of Shèwèi.
At that time, Shèlìfú
was walking alone, begging for food.
The Brāhmaṇa saw him and asked,
"Venerable One, are you traveling alone without a Śrāmaṇera (Shāmí)?"
Shèlìfú said,
"I do not have a Śrāmaṇera.
I hear you have a son.
You should give him to me to serve."
The Brāhmaṇa said,
"I have one son.
His name is Jūntí.
Since he is only an infant,
he is not fit to be employed or ordered around.
Wait until he is older, and I shall give him to you."
At that time, Shèlìfú
kept this in mind.
When the boy reached seven years of age, he returned and requested him.
The Brāhmaṇa then allowed his son to leave home (become a monk).
Shèlìfú brought him to the Qíhuán.
Gradually, he preached the Dharma to him.
His mind opened and was freed, and he attained Arhatship. Jūntí Shāmí, having just attained the path,
used his power of wisdom to observe his past lives.
He saw that his previous life was that of a starving dog.
Through the kindness of his Upādhyāya (spiritual teacher), he now obtained a human body
and also achieved the fruit of the Way.
Joy arose inwardly,
and he thought to himself,
"I received my master's kindness and was delivered from all suffering.
Now I must devote my entire life to providing whatever he needs, remaining a Śrāmaṇera forever."
Going back to the time of the previous Buddha Jiāyè (Kāśyapa),
there were several Bhikṣus assembled in one place.
At that time, a young
Bhikṣu had a clear and refined voice and was skilled at chanting and singing praises.
There was another Bhikṣu
who was aged and elderly, whose voice was coarse and dull.
He could not chant the sutras.
He frequently made sounds to entertain himself.
The old Bhikṣu had already attained Arhatship.
Thereupon, the young Bhikṣu scolded him, saying,
"Your voice now, Elder, sounds like a dog barking."
The old Bhikṣu
then called the young man.
"Do you recognize me?"
The young man replied,
"I fully recognize you.
You were the chief Elder Bhikṣu during the time of the Buddha Jiāyè."
The old Bhikṣu answered,
"I have now attained Arhatship."
The young man was terrified, blamed himself, and confessed his sin.
Nevertheless, for five hundred lifetimes, he continually received the body of a dog.
Because he left home and maintained pure precepts,
he was able to see me now and receive deliverance.
Formerly there was a small kingdom.
Not far from the city was a fine forest grove.
There were five *dàoshì* studying the Way within it.
There was one *Bǐqiū* who had attained the Six Supernormal Powers (*liù shéntōng*).
There was one *Shāmí* (novice monk), eight years of age.
They were together in the mountains.
Each sat facing a direction, contemplating the scriptures and the Way.
The master knew that the *Shāmí* had only seven days of life remaining.
Should this one die here, his parents would blame me, saying,
“You did not look after him well and thus caused his death.”
They would harbor resentment.
He immediately spoke to the *Shāmí*.
“Your parents are missing you.
You may return home, but come back early on the eighth day.”
The *Shāmí* was delighted, bowed his head, and departed.
On the road, he encountered heavy rain; the runoff was torrential.
There were ant holes in the ground, and the running water was about to rush into them.
The *Shāmí* reflected, saying,
“I am a disciple of the Buddha.
Firstly, I must possess a compassionate heart.
Secondly, I must save lives.”
He immediately blocked the flow with earth, diverting the water away.
The *Shāmí* returned home, and nothing else changed.
On the eighth day, he returned in the morning.
The master saw him from afar.
He was astonished as to the reason.
“He should have perished after seven days.
What cause or condition is this now?
Perhaps a ghost or spirit has transformed itself and appeared?”
He immediately entered *sānmèi* (samādhi).
He saw that because the *Shāmí* had saved the ants, his lifespan was extended in this present life.
The *Shāmí* arrived.
He bowed his head, performed the proper rites, and sat down on one side.
The master addressed him, saying,
“You have performed a great meritorious deed (*gōngdé*).
Do you know it yourself?”
The *Shāmí* replied,
“During my seven days at home, I performed no other meritorious deeds.”
The master said,
“Your life ought to have ended.
Yesterday, because you saved the ants,
your life has been increased by eighty-odd years in this present world.”
The *Shāmí* rejoiced, believing that good deeds have retribution (reward).
He immediately dedicated himself to further diligent practice, striving ceaselessly.
He attained *Āluóhàn* (Arhatship).
In the kingdom of Shèwèi, there was an old man.
He had lost his wife early.
He lived alone with his son.
Afflicted by a lack of wealth and treasures,
and perceiving the impermanence of the world,
he left home to become a monk under the Buddha.
His son was still young.
He also became a *Shāmí*.
He went begging for food with his father.
As dusk approached, they were returning.
The father walked slowly.
The son feared venomous beasts.
He quickly supported his father, pushing him forward along the path.
He did not hold him firmly.
He pushed his father, who fell to the ground and died instantly.
The son arrived alone at the place where the Buddha was.
At that time, the various *Bǐqiū*s reprimanded the *Shāmí*.
They then informed the Buddha.
The Buddha told them, saying,
“Although this master died, it was not done with malicious intent.”
He then asked the *Shāmí*.
“Did you kill your master?”
He replied,
“I did indeed push him.
It was not with malicious intent.”
The Buddha said,
“I know your heart held no malicious intent.
It was also like this in a past lifetime.
They killed each other without malicious intent.
Formerly, a father and son lived together in one place.
At that time, the father was extremely ill.
While he was sleeping,
many stinging flies repeatedly came and bothered him.
The father told the son to keep the flies away,
hoping to gain peaceful sleep.
The son diligently chased the flies, but they did not stop coming.
The son then became angry.
He took a large staff and waited to kill a fly; just then, many flies clustered upon his father’s forehead.
He struck them with the staff, and his father instantly died.
The father then was this *Shāmí*.
The son then was the deceased *Bǐqiū*.
Because there was no evil mind and no malicious intent,
it was also not intentional killing.
The *Shāmí* practiced diligently without slacking.
Consequently, he attained the Way of *Luóhàn* (Arhatship).
The Buddha was traveling in the Jīshù Jǐgūdú Yuán in Shèwèi.
At that time, there was another *Bǐqiū*.
He had a disciple whose disposition was gentle and refined, and whose actions were benevolent and virtuous.
He constantly served his *Héshang* (preceptor) with sincerity, caution, and diligence.
He respectfully followed the Dharma teachings and did not violate his master’s commands.
His lifespan was short, and he died while still young.
He was born in the Dāolì Palace and observed the heavenly realm.
But he only saw a great fire.
The vows he had originally made could not be fulfilled.
He could not remain with his virtuous friends.
Now, having abandoned a good master, he followed evil companions.
Thus, he departed far from his revered *Héshang*,
and the assembly of *Āyílí* (teachers).
And all those who practiced pure conduct.
The disciples of the Four Assemblies.
There is one who possesses omniscience,
whose title is *Rúlái* (Tathāgata).
Now he has departed far from all of them.
One who is difficult to encounter and difficult to see for countless eons,
has arisen in the world, teaching profound and subtle scriptures, things previously unspoken.
Yet, he calmly and peacefully taught and explained the various conditions of origination.
Each person understood the causes from which things arise.
What had not been seen or heard for countless eons
was all solved for him.
Having encountered these scriptures and Vinaya (precepts),
he abandoned home for the Way.
What he ought to have established did not reach final completion.
Now, on the contrary, he had become unrestrained.
He first went to the World-Honored One (*Shìzūn*) and bowed his head at the Buddha’s feet.
The Buddha saw his mind,
that it was genuinely joyful in the Way and purely focused on the Dharma.
He preached the [Four Noble Truths of] suffering, accumulation, cessation, and the Way.
The disciple immediately perceived the truths.
The *Héshang* was sorrowful, weeping tears like rain.
The Buddha called him and asked,
“Why are you troubled and distressed?”
He replied,
“My disciple has died.”
The Buddha said,
“Why this sorrow and worry?”
He replied,
“My *Shāmí* disciple was extremely virtuous and excellent.
He had not yet reached completion but died prematurely.
Therefore, I am depressed and cannot comfort myself.”
The Buddha said,
“Do not worry. He has already reached completion.
He gained rebirth in the heavens.
At midnight today, he will distinguish the Noble Truths.”
The *Bǐqiū* stopped weeping.
Shèlìfú had a śrāmaṇera (novice monk).
Named Chúntóu.
He was eight years old and attained the Six Supernatural Powers (liù shéntōng).
Flying through the air, he reached the Ānòuqúan (Anu Spring).
There was a Brahmin who possessed the Five Supernatural Powers (wǔ tōng Fànzhì).
Named Xū Bá.
He also arrived at that spring.
At that time, above the spring,
there was a spring-guarding green-clad ghost (qīngyī guǐ).
It chased away the wǔ tōng Fànzhì.
Throwing tiles and stones, it prevented him from approaching the spiritual spring.
The śrāmaṇera Chúntóu arrived soaring through the sky.
The hundreds of green-clad ghosts all came forward to greet him.
Some came forward to straighten his robe.
Some carried pure water to wash his hands and feet.
Some used clean towels to wipe his head and face.
Some used fragrant water (xiāng tāng) to bathe his body.
The Brahmin Xū Bá spoke aloud, saying:
"I have now attained the Five Supernatural Powers, and my spiritual virtue is immeasurable.
My strength can move mountains and stop flowing water.
I can turn the heaven and earth around just like turning a pearl in my palm.
Since I started studying the Way (Dào), it has been over one hundred and twenty years.
I have toiled my form and tormented my body, exhausting my physical and spiritual selves.
Sometimes serving the Five Knowledges (wǔ míng).
Lighting fires in four places
with the sunlight shining down from above.
Sometimes lying on ashes and dung.
Sometimes lying among thorns and dangerous precipices.
There is no practice of the Way (Dào) that I have not studied.
Yet, I am chased away and not allowed to reach the spring.
But this small child in black robes,
only seven or eight years old,
not yet weaned from nursing,
whose body is dirty and smelly, is treated with excessive respect.
For what reason is this?"
At that time, the green-clad ghost said to the Brahmin:
"This scholar now,
though small in form and age, his conduct surpasses the Three Realms (sān jiè).
He has attained the Eight Ranks of the Way of the Worthy and the Sagely (xián shèng bā pǐn dào).
You do not possess this now, hence we do not show respect."
There was a Brahmin.
Named Yuèchā.
He established a temple.
Also named Yuèchā.
He constantly supplied butter (sū) and oil to light the temple lamps.
At that time, Brahmins from distant regions
came to that temple.
They also heard that the Brahmin Yuèchā possessed high talent and bright virtue.
He strongly believed in the Buddha Dharma (Fó Fǎ), established spiritual shrines (shén miào), and met with them.
At that time, a śrāmaṇera
came to collect the oil and butter
to light the temple lamps.
The multitude of Brahmins
said to the Brahmin Yuèchā:
"Do you indeed bow to this man in colored robes?"
Before their words were finished, the śrāmaṇera had already arrived.
[Yuèchā] immediately bowed to him again.
The multitude of Brahmins
said to this Brahmin:
"You come from the Four Castes, your talents and skills surpass others.
There is nothing in astronomy or geography that you have not examined and mastered.
By means of spiritual incantations (shén zhòu) and moving the spirits, there is no endeavor you cannot conquer.
Now, this person in colored robes
originates from common castes.
His lineage is not pure.
Why do you violate your original dharma (fǎ) and respectfully bow to him?
Furthermore, you, sir Brahmin, practice pure conduct.
You cultivate yourself in the Inner Repository, the diagrams, prophecies, and secret records.
Practicing the Way (Dào) achieves blessings; what vow can you not fulfill?
There is nothing concerning texts, seals, or talismans that you do not fully comprehend.
The conduct of the Buddha (Fó) is rare and slight; what is there to value?
Abandoning the root and grasping the branch is what we deplore.
We generally hear that Śramaṇas (shā mén) are lowly and base.
They are full of clever tricks and deception, deluding the people of the world.
Their practices are short-lived, aimed only at glorifying their own person.
They cannot prolong the attainment of Brahmic blessings (fàn fú).
Even if you meet them, you should only slightly lift your robes as a courtesy, and nothing more.
Why do you cast your five limbs to the ground (wǔ tǐ tóu dì), respectfully performing a bow?
We personally witness this and find it very strange.
Moreover, the previously learned great men (dà rén)
how could they possibly forgive you for this transgression?"
Yuèchā replied to the multitude of Brahmins, saying:
"Sirs, be silent and listen to what I say:
The virtue of the Worthy and the Sagely is hard to measure; the Eight Straight Paths (bā zhí) are the unsurpassed Way (Dào).
This is the Brahmic Śramaṇa, declared by the mouth of the Tathāgata (Rúlái)."
"Seeing that this form is small, he has achieved the Way (Dào) of the Worthy and the Sagely.
Therefore, I now take refuge. Brahmins, why do you ridicule this?"
"Those who attain [the Way] are able to reach the ultimate end.
Srotāpanna (Xūtuóhuán) and Sakṛdāgāmin (Sītuóhán)
are able to sever the bonds of the desire realm (yù jiè), the various mental defilements (chán), skandhas (yīn), and āyatanas (rù).
Therefore, it is said that those who attain [the Way] are able to exhaust the root of Māra (mó yuán).
Those who enter absorption (dìng) and practice seated meditation (zuò chán)
delight in quiet and secluded places, their will devoted to a singular purpose.
Counting the breaths (jì chū rù xī), their intention is firmly held.
They are able to sever Māra’s bonds,
and also bind Māra himself.
A person who enters absorption
can employ ghosts and spirits, and they arrive instantly as desired.
You ought to seek skillful means (fāng biàn) to sever Māra's firm fetters."
In the past, there was a small child.
His age began at seven years old.
He greatly loved the Buddha Way (Fó Dào) and became a śrāmaṇera.
He followed his Arhat (Luóhàn) master and studied in the mountains.
He was diligent and tireless.
By the time he was eight years old,
he attained the Four Penetrations (sì tōng).
The first is the unobstructed sight (divine eye).
The second is the unobstructed hearing (divine ear).
The third is flying and transformation.
The fourth is knowing his previous lives and where he came from.
Sitting down, he contemplated.
He immediately saw the experiences of his past lives.
He had been the son of five mothers (wǔ mǔ).
He then laughed to himself.
The master asked, "Why do you laugh?"
The śrāmaṇera said:
"How would I dare to laugh at the Master?
I only look at my own body, which has had five mothers.
Day and night they weep, wounded by sorrow and grief.
They constantly say:
'Thinking of our son, we have never forgotten him, not even for a moment.'"
"I think to myself:
one body has caused sorrow and grief for five households.
That is why I laughed."
"When I was the son of the first mother,
a neighbor had a child born at the same time as me.
After I died, the child born on the same day would come and go, walking.
My mother saw this and would say:
'If my son were alive, he would also be coming and going, walking like this.'
She was then sorrowful, grieved, and pained, thinking of me."
"I was again the son of the second mother.
I was born, and soon after, I died again.
My mother saw people who were nursing and raising their children,
and she was pained and thought of me.
She was sorrowful, anxious, and wept."
"I was again the son of the third mother.
Soon after, I died again.
When my mother was eating, tears would fall as she thought of me and said:
'If my son were alive, he would be eating with me.
He abandoned me and died.'"
"I was again the son of the fourth mother.
Soon after, I died again.
When my contemporaries were getting married,
my mother would think of me again and say:
'If my son had not died, he would also be marrying a wife now.'"
"I was the son of the fifth mother, and I am still existing now.
I left home to study the Way (Dào).
My mother cries every day, saying:
'My son is lost.
I do not know where he is.
In hunger, cold, life, or death, we will never see each other again.'"
"She is distressed and heartbroken.
Now the five mothers are gathered together.
Each speaks of her lost son, facing one another.
They weep and think of me, this single person.
That is why I laughed."
"People in the world do not know that there are lives hereafter.
They only speak of death.
When a person does good, they gain blessings; when they do evil, they incur calamity.
People in the world are afraid of good and evil themselves
They have no fear of later suffering the pain of evil.
When they enter the evil paths (è dào), regret is useless.
I am weary of the world, and thus I left my family to seek the Way (Dào)."
"I look upon the suffering of hells (dì yù), animals (chù shēng), hungry ghosts (è guǐ), and poverty.
I am terrified on their behalf.
I received the kindness of my master and accepted the Buddha’s (Fó) scriptures and precepts.
Now I am delivered and freed.
I think of my five mothers.
They are unable to gain deliverance,
and furthermore, they worry about me."
There was a Bǐqiū.
He had few desires and was content.
At that time, in the kingdom of Āntuó Guó, there was a Yōupósāi
who respected and believed in the Three Jewels and offered lifelong support.
He sent offerings every day.
In that kingdom, there was a Zhǎngzhě
who had a son.
Wishing for him to leave home life, he sought a good master.
He immediately went and addressed the Bǐqiū, saying:
“I wish for this son of mine to leave home life.
I only hope, Virtuous One, that you will compassionately accept and save him.”
At that time, the Bǐqiū, observing with the eye of the Way, knew:
“If this person leaves home, he will be able to maintain pure precepts.”
He ordained him as a Shāmí. At that time, the Yōupósāi had a close, kind lay person (Jūshì) friend.
The next day, there was a gathering of guests.
In the morning, the father thought:
“Since we must attend the gathering today, who will stay behind to guard the house?”
His daughter immediately addressed her father:
“Please, Father and Mother, take all the servants with you.
Just go to the invitation; I am capable of guarding the house alone.”
The father said, “Very good.”
The whole family went.
The daughter then locked the door and stayed alone inside the house.
That day, the Yōupósāi, being hurried, forgot to send the food.
At that time, the Venerable One thought to himself:
“It is getting late.
Lay people are busy with many things.”
He immediately sent the Shāmí to fetch the food.
The Shāmí maintained his dignified manner perfectly, just as the Fó taught.
The Shāmí knocked on the door.
The girl asked, “Who is it?”
He replied,
“The Shāmí has come to fetch food for his master.”
She immediately opened the door for him.
This girl was beautiful and her countenance was exquisite.
She was sixteen years old, and the fire of lust was burning within her.
In front of the Shāmí,
she performed various seductive and charming actions, deeply displaying signs of desire.
The Shāmí saw this and thought:
“Does this girl have a wind or epilepsy illness?
Is she perhaps driven by the bonds of desire, wishing to destroy my pure conduct?”
He firmly controlled his dignified manner, and his expression did not change.
The girl then threw her five limbs to the ground and addressed the Shāmí, saying:
“I have a constant wish that I want to express.
The storage houses of precious treasures in this dwelling
are like the treasury of Píshāmén Tiān’s palace,
but they have no owner.
You should condescend to become the master of this house.
I will be your maidservant, attending to and serving you, thus fulfilling my wish.”
The Shāmí thought:
“I would rather give up my life than violate the monastic precepts.
In the past, when a Bǐqiū visited the house of a prostitute,
he preferred to throw himself into a fire pit rather than violate desire.
Furthermore, there were Bǐqiū who were robbed by bandits and bound with grass ropes.
The wind blew, the sun exposed them, and insects bit and ate them.
Because they guarded the precepts, they did not break the grass rope to escape.
Just like the bird that swallowed a pearl—
although the Bǐqiū saw it,
due to maintaining the precepts, he endured extreme suffering and did not speak.
Like when a sea ship was wrecked,
the junior Bǐqiū,
in order to guard the precepts, gave the plank to the senior monk (Shàngzuò) and drowned in the sea, dying.
Only the disciples of the Fó can maintain the monastic precepts like these individuals.
I am not a disciple who cannot uphold them.
The Tathāgata, the World-Honored One, is the master of those others, and he is also my master.”
He used an expedient means and said:
“Lock the doors securely. I will enter a room to do what must be done.
Then we shall unite.”
The girl immediately locked the door.
The Shāmí entered a room, closed and bolted the door.
He found a razor.
He removed his robes and placed them on a rack.
He pressed his palms together and knelt, facing Jūshīnà Chéng, the place of the Fó’s Nirvāṇa.
He established his vow:
“I do not now abandon the Fó, the Dharma, or the Saṅgha.
Nor do I abandon the precepts; it is precisely for the sake of upholding the precepts
that I give up this life. May my subsequent rebirth
be marked by pure conduct in the homeless life, the elimination of all defilements, and the attainment of the Way.”
He immediately cut his own throat and died.
The girl, surprised by the delay, went to the door to look.
She saw that he was dead and that his original appearance was gone.
Her desirous mind instantly ceased; she was afflicted by shame, remorse, sorrow, wailing, and she fainted.
When her father returned from the gathering and saw his daughter in this state, he asked why.
She fully replied with the truth.
The father immediately entered the room and saw the Shāmí.
His body was stained red with blood, like sandalwood.
He bowed and praised him, saying:
“He guarded the Fó’s precepts and was able to give up his life.”
The law of that kingdom at the time stipulated:
If a Śramaṇa (Shāmén) died in a layperson’s (báiyī) house,
a fine of gold currency must be paid.
The Yōupósāi placed one thousand pieces of gold currency on a copper tray and carried it to the royal palace.
He addressed the king, saying:
“Great King,
I have incurred a penalty
that should be paid to the King.
I ask that you accept it.”
The King said:
“In my kingdom, you are the sole person who respects and believes in the Three Jewels, and whose words and conduct are flawless.
What fault could you possibly have
that requires you to pay a fine?”
The Yōupósāi then fully recounted the preceding events,
denouncing his daughter and praising the Shāmí.
When the King heard this, he was awestruck and said to him:
“The Shāmí guarded the precepts and gave up his own life.
You bear no fault or guilt.
Just take the money back home.
I myself now wish to go to your house to make offerings to the Shāmí.”
The King went and saw him.
He approached and performed a reverence.
He used a tall chariot adorned with various treasures to carry the deceased Shāmí to flat ground.
He piled up various fragrant woods and performed a *Jīpí* (cremation) offering.
He heavily adorned the girl in the most exceptional worldly manner
and placed her in a high, conspicuous place so that everyone at the gathering could see her.
He addressed the multitude, saying:
“This girl is so uniquely exquisite and radiant.
Among those who have not escaped desire, who would not have a defiled mind?
Yet this Shāmí, although he had not attained the Way,
used his mortal body to uphold the precepts and give up his life. This is extremely remarkable and rare.”
The King then sent someone to request the Shāmí’s master,
who extensively spoke the subtle and wonderful Dharma for the great assembly.
Everyone present at the gathering who saw and heard this event
was inspired; some sought to leave home life,
and some generated the unsurpassed Bodhi mind.
In the past, there was an Arhat (Luóhàn)
who practiced the Way in the mountains with a Shāmí.
The Shāmí went daily to people’s houses to beg for food and drink.
He walked across a raised embankment.
The path was rough and dangerous, and he stumbled and fell to the ground.
The rice became soiled with mud. The Shāmí took the rice that was not soiled
and put it in his master’s bowl.
He washed the soiled rice and ate it himself.
This happened more than once.
The master asked:
“Why do you wash away and abandon the flavor of the rice?”
He replied:
“When I went begging, the sky was clear.
When I returned from begging, it rained.
I stumbled on the embankment and spilled the rice.”
The master was silent and reflected on this.
Knowing that a dragon was harassing the Shāmí, he got up and went to the embankment.
He held his staff and struck the dense thicket.
The dragon transformed into an old man and came out,
bowing and placing its head and face on the ground.
The Śramaṇa (Shāmén) said:
“Why do you harass my Shāmí?”
He replied:
“I truly love his appearance.”
“Starting today, come to my room every day to eat.”
The Śramaṇa accepted the invitation and went to eat every day.
Sometime later, the Shāmí saw in his master's bowl
two or three grains of rice that were not worldly rice.
He asked his Upādhyāya (Héshàng).
The master remained silent and did not respond.
The Shāmí then got under the master's bed and held onto the bed frame.
When the Héshàng completed his meditation, the Shāmí followed him,
and they both flew to the top of the dragon’s palace.
The dragon and his wife both bowed to the Śramaṇa and then bowed to the Shāmí.
The master then became aware
and called the Shāmí out, speaking to him:
“These are not goddesses (cǎinǚ).
They are merely animals (beings of the animal realm).
You are a Shāmí.
Although you have not yet attained the Way,
you will certainly be reborn in the Dāolì Tiān (Trāyastriṃśa Heaven),
which is a hundred times superior to this place.
Do not harbor impure thoughts.”
The Shāmí said:
“This dwelling place of the dragon is rarely seen in the world.”
The master said:
“They endure three sufferings.
First, although the rice has a hundred flavors, when it enters the mouth, it immediately turns into toads.
Second, although the attendants are incomparably beautiful,
when they desire to be husband and wife, two snakes intertwine instead.
Third, the dragon’s back has inverted scales,
and sand and stones grow beneath them.
The pain reaches their heart and chest.
This is great suffering.
Why would you follow them?
Since you have not yet attained the Way,
I should not have allowed you to see the realms of ghosts or the inner affairs of kings.”
The Shāmí did not respond.
He thought about it day and night,
and, unable to eat due to his longing, he fell ill and died.
His spirit was reborn as the dragon's son.
(It was) like one Śrāmaṇa.
His heart always loved dairy products (cheese/yogurt). All the Dānayuè presented dairy products to the Saṅgha.
At that time, the Śrāmaṇa always received the leftovers.
Joy and delight in his heart clung to him without departing.
After the end of his life, he was born inside the jar of leftover dairy products.
The master of the Śrāmaṇa attained Āluóhànship.
When the Saṅgha divided the dairy products,
he said slowly,
"Do not harm this Śrāmaṇa who loves dairy products."
Everyone said,
"Why do you speak of the Śrāmaṇa who loves dairy products?"
He replied,
"This was originally my Śrāmaṇa.
Solely because of his greedy attachment to the leftover dairy products,
he was born inside this jar."
When the master received his portion of the dairy product,
a worm came out from within it.
The master said,
"O lover of dairy products, why have you come here?"
He immediately gave the dairy product to it.
The Pójiāpó was in Luóyuèchéng.
At that time, the Bhīkṣuṇī Bàtuóluó,
having left the bhikṣus’ park, sat beneath a tree.
Sitting upright and focusing her mind, she recognized her past lives and then laughed.
The other Bhīkṣuṇīs saw this and immediately asked her.
Bhīkṣuṇī Bàtuóluó said,
"I have recognized my past lives."
Ninety-one kalpas in the past,
there was the Rúlái Pípóshì,
who appeared in the world.
There was a youth,
named Bàluómótípó,
who possessed abundant wealth and many goods, infinitely rich.
The youth held a jeweled canopy and emerged from his house.
There was an elder's wife,
whose beauty was unparalleled,
who also passed by there.
Many people all observed (the woman).
At that time, the youth then had this thought:
"I am now holding a jeweled canopy,
assembled from many treasures, and passing along this road,
yet there is no one who observes me.
This elder’s wife!
I must now devise a means to make the people observe me."
At that time, the youth, holding the jeweled canopy in his hand,
then left that area,
and proceeded to the place of Rúlái Pípóshì.
He stood behind the Rúlái and held the jeweled canopy
for seven days and seven nights.
He made this vow, saying,
"By the merit of my offering to the Shìzūn,
may I be born as a woman whose beauty is unparalleled,
such that any who see me become confused and fall prostrate upon the ground."
When the youth's life ended,
he was born in the Thirty-three Heavens as a celestial maiden.
She was superior in five ways.
What are these five?
Celestial lifespan, celestial appearance, celestial joy, celestial spiritual power, and celestial superior merit.
When the celestial beings saw this woman, they all held hope and desired to be with her.
At that time, the Thirty-three Heavens all contended with each other.
When the celestial maiden's life ended, she came to be born among humans as the daughter of the Queen Ruòdátuō Póluómén.
She was extraordinarily beautiful and wonderful.
Going back and forth between the human and celestial realms, she always attained perfect beauty.
She met many Buddhas and served and made offerings to all of them.
She sought to be a woman.
Afterwards, she was born among humans in the home of a low-status Brāhmaṇa.
She became the maidservant of the youth Yuèguāng Tóngzǐ.
Her name was Jǐluó.
The wife of Yuèguāng Tóngzǐ was named Mónúhēlā.
Her beauty was unparalleled.
At that time, Yuèguāng's wife said to that maidservant,
"You go outside the house.
If you see any Śrāmaṇas or Brāhmaṇas, bring them here.
I wish to give offerings."
At that time, the maidservant left the house.
There was a Pìzhīfó
begging for food upon the doorstep.
Jǐluó the maidservant said to him, "Please come in,
I wish to give you offerings."
The wife saw that his physical form was not beautiful.
She said to Jǐluó,
"Send the Śrāmaṇa away. I will not give offerings."
The maidservant said,
"I pray, Venerable One, open your mind. Do not dislike the Śrāmaṇa's appearance.
The merit of making offerings is incalculable."
At that time, the wife replied,
"Quickly drive this Śrāmaṇa out.
I am unable to make offerings."
The maidservant replied,
"If the Venerable One does not give offerings to this Śrāmaṇa,
then please do not begrudge the food portion that I am due today."
At that time, the wife immediately gave the food to the maidservant.
Jǐluó the maidservant
immediately placed her portion of food into the Pìzhīfó's bowl.
Having eaten, his body ascended into the empty sky.
At that time, the maidservant was overwhelmingly joyful upon seeing this.
She then made a vow:
"By this merit, may I not fall into evil destinies,
and may I always encounter this worthy sage in the long future to come.
May he preach the Dharma for me so that I may quickly attain liberation."
At that time, King Fànmódáduō of Bōluónàichéng,
saw that Pìzhīfó ascending into the empty sky.
He said to his ministers,
"That offering was made..."
At that time, the elder Yuèguāng,
leading five hundred merchants, gathered in the great lecture hall.
They saw the Pìzhīfó holding his bowl and ascending into the sky from afar.
Some merchants said this:
"This worthy sage must have received food at my house."
At that time, the wife of Elder Yuèguāng,
seeing Jǐluó the maidservant, said,
"The merit you have obtained,
give it to me as a gift.
This way, it will be an offering made by me.
I will now give you food again."
The maidservant said, "I will not give it."
The wife spoke again,
"I will now give you two portions of food."
(Jǐluó) replied,
"I also do not need it."
The wife spoke again,
"I will give you three portions, five portions, ten portions, twenty portions, up to one hundred portions, or even one thousand portions."
Jǐluó the maidservant said,
"I will not give it to you."
The wife replied,
"If you do not give it to me,
I will cut off your ears, nose, and hands."
Jǐluó the maidservant said,
"I will not give it to you."
At that time, the elder's wife
beat the maidservant with a stick.
When the beating was finished,
Elder Yuèguāng returned.
He saw Jǐluó the maidservant,
whose head was broken and clothes were torn, weeping sorrowfully and shedding tears.
He asked for the full story.
She reported the matter in full.
At that time, the youth Yuèguāng
took that wife and made her a maidservant.
He made Jǐluó the maidservant his first wife,
surrounded by five hundred court ladies,
and adorned her body with hundreds of thousands of rare treasures.
At that time, King Fànmódáduō,
heard that Yuèguāng’s maidservant had fed that Pìzhīfó.
At that time, King Fànmódáduō
presented hundreds of thousands of ounces of rare treasures to Yuèguāng the Elder's wife.
Furthermore, he gifted fields and property to Yuèguāng the Elder.
Now, King Fànmódáduō
is Gāpíluómóshēluó.
Yuèguāng the Elder is Dàjiāyè.
Jǐluó the maidservant is this very body of mine.
Now, I have met the Buddha and attained Āluóhànship.
At that time, in the kingdom of Shèwèiguó, there was the wife of an elder.
She gave birth to a daughter.
She was exceptionally beautiful, rarely matched.
When she was first born,
she emerged wrapped in a fine, soft white cloth.
Her parents found this strange.
They observed her appearance, which was very auspicious.
Because of this, they gave her a name.
She was named Shūlí. When Shūlí grew up,
the cloth grew with her body.
This girl was excellent and magnificent.
People near and far throughout the country competed to seek her hand in marriage.
The girl informed her parents,
“I wish to leave home and become a renunciant.”
Her parents loved her and did not go against her wish.
They immediately took out the cloth
wanting to make the five robes (Buddhist garments).
The girl informed her parents,
“The garments I am wearing are already complete.
There is no need to make any more.
I only request that you permit me to go to the Buddha at this time,
approach the Buddha, pay homage, and request to leave home.”
The Buddha said, “Welcome.”
Her hair fell off by itself.
The white cloth she was wearing immediately transformed into the five robes.
She was entrusted to Dà Àidào to become a Bhikṣuṇī.
Through diligent practice, she soon attained the path of an Arhat.
Ānán addressed the Buddha, saying,
“What merit did Shūlí originally cultivate,
that she was born with the cloth, left home, and attained the Way?”
The Buddha said,
“In the past, there was a Buddha
named Pípóshī.
At that time, kings, ministers, and common people frequently made offerings.
At that time, there was a woman
named Tánnìqū.
She was extremely poor.
The husband and wife shared only one cloth (garment).
If the husband went out, he would wear it and leave.
The wife would then remain naked.
If the wife wore the cloth,
the husband would sit naked.
A Bhikṣu who was propagating the Dharma
traveled to their house.
Seeing the woman,
he urged her, saying,
“The era of the Buddha is difficult to encounter; a human body is difficult to obtain.
You ought to listen to the Dharma, and you ought to give alms.”
The woman returned and told her husband,
“A Śramaṇa is outside,
urging me to see the Buddha, listen to the Dharma, and give alms.”
The husband replied to her, saying,
“Our family is poor.
Although we have the intention, what should we use for alms?”
The wife said,
“My intention is to use this cloth for alms-giving.”
The husband said, “You and I
share this one cloth.
We go out and seek sustenance with it to maintain our lives.
If we use it for alms now, we will both face death.”
The wife said,
“Humans are born to die; we will die even if we do not give alms.
If we give alms and then die, there will be hope for the next life.
If we die without giving alms, the subsequent life will be even more miserable.”
The husband happily said,
“We accept death in order to give alms.”
The wife immediately went back out
and told the Bhikṣu,
“Virtuous One, please write down the request
and include my name.”
The Bhikṣu replied,
“If you wish to give alms, you must give them face to face,
so that I may recite blessings for you.”
Shūlí replied,
“I only have this cloth I am wearing, and I have no other clothes inside.
A woman’s body is impure and ugly; it is not appropriate to remove it here.”
She immediately went back inside,
and from afar, she removed the cloth she was wearing,
reaching down and passing it to the Bhikṣu.
The Bhikṣu recited blessings for her, took the cloth, and carried it to the Buddha.
The Buddha said,
“Bhikṣu, bring this cloth here.”
The Bhikṣu handed it to the Buddha,
and the Buddha received it with his own hands.
This cloth was soiled and dirty.
At that time, the King and the assembly
secretly felt dislike that the Buddha accepted this dirty cloth.
The Buddha knew the thoughts of the assembly and addressed them, saying,
“Looking at this assembly,
there is no greater pure offering than this,”
— referring to the giver of the cloth.
When the great assembly heard this, none were not awed.
The Queen (Fūrén) rejoiced.
She immediately removed the ornamented clothes, necklaces, and precious garments she was wearing
and sent them to Tánnìqū.
The King also felt delighted.
He removed the clothes from his body, sent them to her husband, and ordered him to attend the assembly.
The Buddha told Ānán,
“If you wish to know who the poor woman Tánnìqū was at that time,
she is the Bhikṣuṇī Shūlí now.
Because she offered the cloth with a pure heart at that time,
for ninety-one *jié* (kalpas), in all places where she was born,
she was always born with cloth,
and lacked nothing.”
In the kingdom of Jùsàluó,
King Bōsīnì
heard that Bàtuójiāpíluó had left home (to become a nun).
He immediately invited her into the palace
to stay together in one place during the three months of the summer retreat (*Ānjū*).
The King went to the garden,
and instructed the gatekeeper, saying,
“Guard the gate well.
Do not allow this Bhikṣuṇī to leave.”
The gatekeeper thought thus:
“This Bhikṣuṇī enjoys staying here and will not run away.”
At that time, the gatekeeper had other business.
The Bhikṣuṇī put on the Queen’s (Fūrén) garments and robes and exited through the gate.
She went far away to Qíhuán
to listen to the Buddha preach the Dharma.
The Buddha saw her from afar and said,
“Welcome, Bàtuójiāpíluó.”
Immediately, she lost the Queen’s garments and robes.
Her hair fell off by itself, the *jiāshā* (kasaya) was put upon her body, and she became a Bhikṣuṇī.
She approached the Buddha and paid homage to the Buddha with her head and face (prostration).
The Buddha preached to her about the power of the Four Bases of Spiritual Power (*Sì Rúyì Zú Lì*).
At that time, the Bhikṣuṇī gained spiritual power.
At that time, the King heard that the woman Bàtuójiāpíluó had run away.
He immediately led his troops to surround the assembly of Bhikṣus
and also surrounded the Bhikṣuṇī residence (fang).
This Bhikṣuṇī then flew into the air.
The King looked up
and immediately generated a heart of repentance.
“How could I dare to defile an Arhat Bhikṣuṇī?”
He was distressed and fell to the ground, repenting to the Bhikṣuṇī.
The Bhikṣuṇīs in the monastery drove her out.
She replied,
“I have no mind for lust or desire.”
The Bhikṣuṇīs said,
“You stayed with the King in the palace for the four months of summer.
How can you be without lust?”
They reported the matter to the Buddha.
The Buddha, though knowing, intentionally asked,
“Bhikṣuṇī,
did you truly experience the softness (of the palace life)?”
She replied,
“World-Honored One, how could I accept it?
I perceived that softness as hot iron entering my body.”
The Buddha said,
“If you had no mind to accept that softness, you are without fault.”
Shèwèi Chéng.
At that time, in Yōushànnà Yì,
there was a young householder
who went out for recreation.
He saw a woman
named Liánhuāsè.
Her beauty was like the plum blossom
and she possessed all the qualities of a woman.
They deeply respected and loved each other,
and he immediately married her as his wife.
Soon after, the wife became pregnant.
She was sent back to her parents' home.
When the month was full, she gave birth to a daughter.
Because the wife was in childbirth, he no longer went near her.
Consequently, he secretly had relations with her mother.
When Liánhuā realized this, she abandoned them and left.
The path of husband and wife was broken, and fearing she would burden her parents,
she looked compassionately upon the infant and swallowed the shame and disgrace.
She returned to her husband's family
and raised the daughter for eight years before finally leaving.
She arrived at Bōluónài.
Extremely hungry, thirsty, and weary,
she sat down by the water's edge.
At that time, a certain elder
was traveling for sightseeing.
He saw her, was deeply attracted, and immediately asked,
"Whom do your current family and parents belong to,
and why are you alone here?"
Liánhuāsè replied,
"I am the daughter of a certain clan,
but now I belong to no one."
The elder asked again,
"If you belong to no one,
could you be my principal wife?"
She answered, "If a woman has a husband,
why should she not?"
He immediately brought her home and installed her as the principal wife.
Liánhuāsè managed the household,
harmonizing the old and the young.
Husband and wife respected each other for eight years.
At that time, the elder said to his wife,
"I have outstanding debts in
Yōushànnà Yì. They have not been collected
for eight years now.
Accounting for the interest accrued, the amount is in the hundreds of millions.
I am going now to collect them and must temporarily leave you."
The wife said,
"The women in that town are known for being reckless and loose.
If you go yourself now, you might lose your integrity as a husband."
He replied,
"Although I am dull and ignorant, I would not descend to such immorality."
The wife said again,
"If you must go, then go.
But I wish to hear one vow."
He answered,
"Very well.
If I harbor any improper thoughts, may that thought perish simultaneously with its arising."
Thereupon, he departed.
He arrived at that town.
As there were many accounts to settle, he spent a full year there.
His longing for his wife gradually deepened.
He thought, "If I commit adultery, I will have broken my original vow.
Taking a separate wife would not be a breach of faith."
Thereupon, he sought around and encountered a young woman.
Her face was elegant and beautiful, and her gaze was proper.
He greatly respected and loved her,
and went to seek marriage.
Because the elder was intelligent and very wealthy,
the father happily gave her to him.
Once the collections were completed, he brought her back to his homeland.
He settled her in a separate residence,
and only then did he return home.
He went out in the morning and returned in the evening, unlike his usual routine.
Liánhuā found this strange.
She secretly questioned his attendants.
The attendants answered,
"He has a young wife."
Her husband returned late.
Liánhuāsè asked,
"You have a new wife.
Why do you hide her and not let me see her?"
He replied,
"I feared you would resent her, so I kept her outside."
The wife said,
"I harbor no jealousy or envy.
The Divine Spirits watch over us.
You may call her home.
She can help you manage things."
He immediately brought her back.
It turned out to be her daughter.
Mother and daughter met but did not recognize each other.
Later, while washing her hair, she carefully observed her features
and suspected it might be her daughter.
She then asked about her native village, parents, clan, and family name.
The daughter answered everything fully.
Only then did the mother know.
The mother was startled and sighed mournfully,
"Before, I shared a husband with my mother;
now, I share a son-in-law with my daughter.
The confusion of life and death reaches such an extent!
If I do not sever loving desire and leave home to study the Way,
how can such distorted delusion ever cease?"
She then abandoned everything and departed.
She arrived at the gate of the Jìhuán.
Hungry, thirsty, and extremely weary, she sat beneath a tree.
At that time, the World-Honored One
was surrounded by a great assembly, teaching the Dharma.
Liánhuāsè saw the great crowd
and thought it was a festival gathering
where food and drink would be available.
She then entered the monastery.
She saw the Buddha, the World-Honored One, teaching the Dharma to the assembly.
Hearing the Dharma, her mind opened, and her hunger and thirst vanished.
Thereupon, the World-Honored One
surveyed the entire assembly to see who should be saved.
Only Liánhuāsè was found to be capable of attaining the fruit of the Way.
He immediately spoke of Suffering, Accumulation, Cessation, and the Way.
She immediately, while seated, became distant from defilement and dust, obtaining the purity of the Dharma eye.
Having attained the fruit,
she stood with focused mind, palms joined, facing the Buddha.
After the Buddha had finished teaching the Dharma,
the assembly dispersed.
Then Liánhuāsè stepped forward, paid homage to the Buddha's feet, knelt, joined her palms, and addressed him,
"I request to leave home and enter the Dharma of the Buddha."
The Buddha immediately granted her permission.
He instructed Bōshépōtí Bhikṣuṇī,
"You may now initiate this woman into the Way."
She was immediately initiated, left home, and received the full precepts.
Diligently practicing perseverance, she attained Āluóhànship,
possessing the Eight Liberations.
Her appearance shone, twice as glorious as before.
She entered the city to beg for food.
A Brāhmaṇa saw her and conceived impure desire.
He thought to himself,
"This Bhikṣuṇī is unobtainable now.
I must find her dwelling place and contrive a way to get her."
Later, when she was again out begging for food,
that Brāhmaṇa sneaked in afterwards and hid beneath her bed.
That day, the Bhikṣuṇīs
were extremely weary from discussing the Dharma all night.
Returning to her room, she lay down on her back and fell into a deep sleep.
Thereupon, the Brāhmaṇa emerged from beneath the bed
and engaged in impure conduct.
At that moment, the Bhikṣuṇī immediately soared up into the empty sky.
The Brāhmaṇa immediately sank through the bed, while alive, into Hell.
The Buddha was on Qíshéjué Shān in Luóyuèzhī.
There was a courtesan
named Liánhuā.
A good thought spontaneously arose in her, and she abandoned worldly affairs
to become a Bhikṣuṇī.
She then went to the mountain and walked toward the Buddha's location.
Before reaching the halfway point, there was a running spring.
The woman drank the water, washed her hands, and looked at herself.
Seeing her face and figure were peerlessly beautiful,
she immediately thought,
"Why should I abandon myself and become a Shāmén?"
"I should rather indulge my private desires for a little while."
She immediately turned back toward home.
The Buddha knew that Liánhuā should be saved.
He manifested as a woman, exquisitely beautiful and unrivaled in the world,
surpassing the courtesan Liánhuā.
She came along the road.
Liánhuā saw her
and felt great love and admiration.
She immediately asked the manifested person,
"Where do you come from?
Where are your husband and relatives?
Why are you traveling alone without attendants?"
The manifested person answered,
"I came from the city and wish to return home.
Though we do not know each other, let us return together to the spring."
Liánhuā said, "Good."
The two returned together to the spring.
They conversed intimately.
The manifested person slept,
resting her head on Liánhuā's lap.
In a moment, she suddenly died.
She became swollen, stinking, and putrid; her belly distended and worms emerged.
Her teeth fell out, her hair dropped off, and her body disintegrated.
Liánhuā saw this and was greatly shocked and terrified.
"How can such a beautiful person suddenly be impermanent?
If this person is already like this, how long can I last?"
Frightened, she determined to go to the Buddha and diligently study the Way.
She immediately went to where the Buddha was located.
She cast her five limbs on the ground in homage and confessed her thoughts.
The Buddha told Liánhuā,
"Women have four things
that cannot be relied upon."
"First: Youth and vigor will inevitably turn to old age.
Second: Strength and health will inevitably turn to death.
Third: The joy and company of six kinds of relatives will inevitably lead to separation.
Fourth: Accumulated wealth and treasures must inevitably be dispersed."
Liánhuā heard the Dharma and was happily enlightened,
attaining Āluóhànship.
East, southeast of Shèwèiguó, there was a terrace.
Above it, there were fragrant flowers and trees, clean and pure.
There were five hundred Brāhmaṇa women.
They served heterodox paths with extremely diligent intent, but they did not know of the Fó (Buddha).
At that time, these women said to one another:
"We have received our forms and were born as women.
From youth to old age, we are constrained by three matters and cannot be free.
Our lifespan is also short; our forms are like illusions and we must eventually die.
It would be better if we went together to the fragrant flower terrace.
Let us gather fragrant flowers and diligently maintain abstinence.
We must beseech Fàntiān (Brahma) to descend and ask him for our wishes.
We wish to be born in Fàntiān, to live long, and not to die.
Moreover, we wish to gain self-mastery, without constraints or taboos.
We wish to leave all karmic retribution and no longer have worries."
Immediately, they carried offerings and went up to the terrace.
They gathered flowers and fragrances to serve Fàntiān.
With concentrated minds, they maintained abstinence, wishing the Venerable Spirit to descend.
The Fó, seeing their minds were ready to be converted and delivered,
immediately flew into the sky with his great assembly.
He went to the terrace and sat beneath a tree.
The women rejoiced, thinking:
"This is Fàntiān! We congratulate ourselves—we have obtained our wishes!"
At that time, a celestial being said to the women:
"This is not Fàntiān.
He is the most honored in the three realms.
His title is Fó (Buddha).
He delivers immeasurable beings."
The women said to the Fó:
"We are heavily defiled and are now women.
We seek to be free from constraints and wish to be born in Fàntiān."
The Fó said:
"Women, it is a good advantage that you have generated this wish.
In the world, there are two matters whose retribution is clear and certain:
doing good receives fortune; doing evil receives calamity.
There is the suffering of the mundane world and the joy of the heavens.
There is the affliction of conditioned phenomena and the stillness of unconditioned phenomena.
Who among you can choose and seek the true reality?
Excellent, women!
You have noble resolve."
Thereupon, the Shìzūn (World Honored One)
immediately spoke this verse (gāthā):
"Who can choose the ground, renounce constraints, and attain heaven? Who speaks the Dharma phrase,
like choosing fine flowers, knowing the world to be corrupting, discussing that illusory phenomena appear abruptly?
Cutting off Māra’s flowers, when the path opens, one sees neither death nor birth."
When the women heard the verse,
they wished to study the true path and become Bhīqíunī (nuns).
Their hair fell off by itself, and they were fully equipped with Dharma robes.
They contemplated the stillness and concentration.
Immediately, they attained the path of Luóhàn (Arhat).
Yōutuóyí (Udayin)
went to Jūsàluóguó (Kauśala Kingdom).
He arrived at the mango grove belonging to the Brāhmaṇa woman of the Píniǔjiādànyán (Viṣṇuka-Kātyāna) clan and stayed there.
The nun's disciples were walking around collecting firewood.
They came to the mango grove.
They saw Yōutuóyí sitting under a tree; his appearance was proper and his senses were calm and still.
His mind was peaceful and stable, having achieved the foremost discipline.
They went forward to his location, asked about his welfare, and sat down respectfully.
At that time, Yōutuóyí preached various aspects of the Dharma to these young people.
After exhorting them, he became silent.
Those young people, having heard the Dharma, rejoiced.
Carrying bundles of firewood, they returned to the nun.
They reported, saying, "Venerable Master,
there is a Śamána (monk) in the grove.
His clan name is Qútán (Gautama).
He preaches the Dharma extremely well."
The nun said to her disciples:
"You may go and invite him for the meal tomorrow."
At that time, the disciples received the instruction and went to invite him.
The Zūnzhě (Venerable One) remained silent.
They returned and reported to the Venerable Master:
"The Zūnzhě has accepted the invitation."
When the night had passed, Yōutuóyí
put on his robe, carried his bowl, and went to the nun's dwelling.
The nun saw him approaching from afar.
She arranged a seat and invited him to sit.
She prepared various foods and drinks.
She personally served the offerings, which were abundant and satisfying.
After rinsing his mouth and washing his bowl, he returned to his original seat.
The Brāhmaṇa woman wore fine leather sandals,
covered her head with a cloth, and provided herself with a separate, high seat.
She displayed an arrogant demeanor.
She said to Yōutuóyí:
"I have something I wish to ask.
Do you have the leisure to answer me or not?"
He replied:
"Sister, now is not the time."
The next day, the disciples
returned to the grove, collected firewood, and listened to the Dharma.
They returned and reported to the Venerable Master.
The nun again sent them to invite him for food, exactly as before, three times.
Even when she asked for the Dharma,
he replied, "It is not the time."
The disciples said:
"Venerable Master, the nun sits without respect.
How can he preach?"
The Venerable Nun said:
"If that is the case, then invite him again for me."
They received the instruction and invited him again.
The offerings were as before.
At that time, the Venerable Nun,
knowing he had finished eating,
removed her leather sandals and upper garment, and sat on a lower seat instead.
Respectfully, she reported, saying:
"I have something I wish to ask.
Can you please answer me or not?"
He replied:
"Just ask. I shall preach to you."
She immediately asked:
"How is it that some say suffering and joy are self-made?
Others say suffering and joy are made by others.
Others say suffering and joy are made by self and others.
Others say suffering and joy are made neither by self nor by others."
He replied:
"Sister, the Āluóhē (Arhat) teaches
that suffering and joy arise differently."
She asked again:
"What does that mean?"
He replied:
"Suffering and joy arise dependent on causes (conditions).
He continued:
"Now I ask you.
Answer me according to your understanding.
Are there eyes?
She replied, "There are."
Are there forms?
She replied, "There are."
Are there eye-consciousness, eye-contact, and resulting internal feelings—whether suffering, joy, or neither suffering nor joy—born from contact as the cause?
She replied, "It is so."
Yōutuóyí said:
"This is what the Āluóhē teaches:
suffering and joy arise dependent on causes (conditions)."
When the Zūnzhě preached this Dharma,
