the Brāhmaṇa woman departed from dust, became free from defilement, and gained the pure eye of the Dharma.
She rose from her seat and straightened her garments.
She respectfully pressed her palms together and addressed the Zūnzhě, saying:
"Today, I have crossed over into certainty.
From this day forward, I take refuge in the Fó, the Fǎ (Dharma), and the Sēng (Saṅgha).
For the rest of my life, I rely upon the Three Jewels (Sānbǎo)."
Formerly, in the city of Shèwèichéng (Śrāvastī),
belonging to the kingdom named Jūsàluóguó (Kauśala),
there were many dissolute and disorderly people.
They were devoted solely to violence and wickedness.
At that time, the Bhīqíunī (nuns) in the kingdom
diligently and sincerely contemplated the right path beneath the trees, never abandoning their resolve.
The foremost among the Bhīqíunī in wisdom
was named Chàmó (Kṣamā).
The foremost in spiritual power (iddhi)
was named Liánhuáxiān (Utpalavarṇā).
Each had virtuous conduct and majestic spiritual authority.
As the weather was slightly hot, they went together to bathe.
They approached the side of a flowing stream.
The wicked multitude saw them from afar and immediately generated evil intent.
Their lustful thoughts soared high, and they wished to violate them.
Waiting for the Bhīqíunī,
just as they took off their clothes and entered the water to bathe,
they rushed forward, snatched their clothes, and carried them far away.
They intended to drag them away and violate them.
At that moment, the Bhīqíunī felt sorrowful pity for them.
Thereupon, she removed both her eyes and placed them in her palm.
She showed them to the transgressors.
"You who love me,
only love the color of my face.
Now that I am blind and without eyes,
what is there left to love?"
She further displayed her belly and stomach.
She separated her body, five organs, hands, and feet.
She threw them to one side.
She said to the wicked multitude:
"Where is the beauty now?"
The perverse and wicked ones saw this,
and were instantly terrified.
They realized that the world is impermanent and the three realms are merely borrowed.
They realized that her body was transformed into bone, blood, and impurity,
and nothing was worth clinging to.
They immediately returned her clothes.
They bowed their heads, repented their vile actions,
saying they were rebellious and unjust, and wished to renounce their karmic retribution.
Kneeling with clasped hands, they each received the Five Precepts (Wǔjiè).
They led them to the place of the Fó.
They bowed their heads to the ground,
and confessed their sins.
. Named Pí Dī Luó
. Diligently managing the household affairs, holding charge of the treasury, everything was entrusted to her
. The Elder Xu1 Dá
, invited the Buddha and the Saṅgha, supplying their needs
. The monks nursing the sick requested many things
. The old mother was stingy and greedy, harboring resentment toward the Buddha, the Dharma, and the Saṅgha
. And she spoke thus
: "My family's Elder is foolish, deluded, and confused
. He accepts the methods of these *shāmén* whose begging is never satisfied. What sort of Dào is this
?" Having spoken these words, she further made an evil vow
: "When will I finally be able not to hear the names of the Buddha, the Dharma, and the Saṅgha
?" Mòlì Fūrén heard of this
, and spoke thus
: "How is it that Xu1 Dá, who is like a beautiful lotus flower
, has four poisonous snakes standing around him
?" She immediately ordered Xu1 Dá
, "Send your wife here
." The wife arrived
. [Mòlì Fūrén] said to her
: "That old maidservant in your house
uses foul language and slanders; why do you not drive her out
?" The wife said
: "The Buddha's emergence benefits and enriches many
. How much more so should we tolerate an old maidservant
?" The Queen, hearing this, was greatly delighted in her heart
. "I wish to invite the Buddha
. You send the maidservant here
." The next day, the Buddha arrived
. The Elder sent the maidservant
, carrying a full jar of gold, a *mó ní* jewel, and a canopy
, to encourage and assist the Royal Household in offering support to the Saṅgha
. When the Buddha entered the gate
, the old maidservant saw him and was displeased in her heart
. She immediately wished to retreat and exit through the dog hole
. The dog hole and the small alleys in all four directions were immediately blocked
. Only the main path was open
. The old mother covered her face with a fan
. The Buddha was in front of her
. He caused the fan to be like a mirror, obstructing nothing
. She turned her head and looked in all four directions, and everywhere she saw the Buddha
. She lowered her head and prostrated on the ground, and her ten fingers all transformed into the Buddha
. The old mother saw the Buddha and the various miraculous displays
. [Her ignorance] removed eighty million *yì*
. Although she did not give rise to faith, she was still able to repel the sin of birth and death
. The Buddha saw that [her attitude toward] him had changed
. The maidservant ran back home and entered a wooden cage
. She wrapped her head with white felt, fearing she would see the Buddha again
. The Buddha said
: "This maidservant's sin is heavy, and she has no affinity with the Buddha
. Róuhóu Luó has a great affinity with her
. He should be commanded to transform her
." At that time, Róuhóu Luó, relying on the majestic spiritual power of the Buddha
, entered the *Rúyì* Samādhi
. He transformed his body into a *Zhuǎnlún Shèng Wáng*
. The twelve hundred and fifty *bǐqiū* transformed into a thousand sons
. Ā Nán became the Minister of the Treasury
. Nán Tuó became the Minister in charge of the Army
. The Seven Treasures and the Four Armies were all fully equipped
. At that time, the Golden Wheel Treasure was in the sky
, riding a lotus pedestal
, and went directly to the house of the Great Elder Xu1 Dá
. A *yè chā* proclaimed
: "The Holy King has appeared in the world
! He expels all evil people
and propagates the virtuous Dharma
." The old mother heard this and was greatly delighted in her heart
. "When the Holy King appears, there is the *Rúyì Zhū*
. He seeks nothing and asks for nothing; this is truly worthy of praise
." At that time, the Holy King struck the bell and beat the drum, riding a great jeweled carriage
. He arrived at Xu1 Dá's house
. The old mother saw him and was extremely happy
. "The Holy King’s appearance in the world benefits and enriches many, and he distinguishes good from evil; surely he will not be
deceived by the *shāmén*." She came out of the wooden cage
. She respectfully bowed to the Holy King
. The Holy King immediately sent the Minister in charge of the Treasury
, to go to the woman's place and announce
: "Sister, you have the signs of stored merit from past lives
. The Holy King, who possesses the marks of royalty
, now wishes to take you, Sister, as the Jewel Maiden
." The old mother replied
: "My body is lowly, like filth and refuse
. The Holy King's inquiry brings boundless joy and celebration
. How could I be qualified to become the Jewel Maiden
? If you would kindly consider me
, please instruct my Master
, to release me and free me
. The gifts bestowed are already many
." At that time, the Holy King
, addressed Xu1 Dá, saying
: "The old woman of your house possesses many lofty characteristics
. I now wish to appoint her as the Jewel Maiden
." Xu1 Dá replied
: "Your command is the only thing we obey
. I wish to present her to the Great King
." The old maidservant, hearing she was released, rejoiced immensely
. The Holy King immediately used the *Rúyì Zhū* to illuminate the woman's face, causing her to see herself
as being like the Jewel Maiden
. She was doubly delighted
, and spoke thus
: "All those *shāmén* speak lofty and grand words
. They claim they possess the Dào, but there is not a single proof
. The Holy King's appearance in the world spreads benefits widely
. He caused me, old and wretched as I am, to be like the Jewel Maiden
!" Having spoken these words, she cast her five limbs to the ground and bowed to the Holy King
. At that time, the Minister of the Treasury
, proclaimed the King's excellent decree
, and opened (explained) the Ten Virtuous Deeds
. The woman heard the Ten Virtuous Deeds and was greatly delighted in her heart
. She immediately spoke thus
: "What the Holy King has spoken
is in principle entirely good
." She paid homage to the King, confessed her past errors, and blamed herself
. Since her mind was already subdued
, Róuhóu Luó then returned to his original form
. The old mother raised her head
. She saw the twelve hundred and fifty *bǐqiū*
. She immediately spoke these words: "The Buddha's Dharma is pure and does not abandon living beings
. Even someone as wretched and wicked as myself is still transformed and saved
." Having spoken these words
, she sought to receive the Five Precepts
. Then Róuhóu Luó
, spoke for her the three refuges and the method for receiving the Five Precepts
. The mother, hearing this Dharma
, before she could raise her head, attained *Xū Tuó Huán*
. Then Róuhóu Luó
, led this old mother to *Qí Tuó Lín*
. Having arrived, she saw the Buddha
. Joyfully, she clasped her hands, bowed, and repented
. She sought the Buddha to become a monastic
. The Buddha told Róuhóu Luó, "You take this mother to *Jiāo Tán Mí*
." Before they reached the destination
, Róuhóu Luó
, preached to her the Dharma concerning suffering, emptiness, impermanence, and non-self
. The old mother, having heard this
, her hair fell out by itself, and she became a *Bǐqiū Ní*
. She possessed the Three Knowledges, the Six Supernormal Powers, and fully attained the Eight Liberations
. King Bō Sī Nì
, and Mòlì Fūrén
, were greatly delighted in their hearts and said
: "World-Honored One
, this old mother
, what sins did she commit in past lives
? And what meritorious fortune
enabled her to attain the path of the Arhat
?" The Buddha replied
: "Great King
, in a past *jié*
, there was a Buddha, the World-Honored One
, named Bǎo Gài Dēng Wáng
. After that Buddha passed into extinction, during the Semblance Dharma Period
, there was a king named Zá Bǎo Huā Guāng
. That king had a son
, named Kuài Jiàn
, who sought to become a monastic
. His father immediately consented
. The prince arrived at the monastery
, seeking to leave home life
. At that time, there was a *bǐqiū*
, who was intelligent, highly knowledgeable, and deeply understood the ultimate reality
. [The prince] received him as his master
. Furthermore, there was another *bǐqiū*
, named Dé Huā Guāng
, who was skilled at explaining the essentials of the Dharma and encouraging beginners
. Although the prince-monk had left home
, he still harbored arrogance
. His preceptor preached to him the profound and wondrous Dharma—the meaning of the Great Emptiness of *Bōrě Bōluómì*
. The prince, having heard it, misinterpreted it and spoke wrongly
. After the *bǐqiū* passed away, he immediately said
: 'My great *Héshàng* was empty and lacked wisdom
. He was only capable of praising void, empty matters
. I vow that in future lives, I will not enjoy seeing him
. My *Āshélí* has wisdom and eloquence. I vow that in this life, he will be my good friend
.' Having spoken these words
, the prince-monk called the Dharma non-Dharma and non-Dharma the Dharma
. He instructed his followers
to all engage in wrong views
. Although he upheld the prohibitions and his deportment was flawless
, because of his misinterpretation, after the end of his life
, in the time it takes to shoot an arrow, he fell into *Ā Bǐ Yù*
. For eighty million *jié*, he perpetually underwent great suffering
. Upon emerging, he became a poor and humble person
, deaf, foolish, and blind
, and served as a maidservant for others
. The *Héshàng* at that time is myself
. The *Āshélí* at that time is Róuhóu Luó
. The prince-monk is this old mother
There was a Brāhmaṇa, Sìzhà Bóluómén.
His mother had six sons.
They died successively; grieving for her sons, she went mad.
Naked and disheveled, she walked along the road.
Distantly seeing the Shìzūn, she immediately regained her senses.
Ashamed and humiliated, she gathered herself and squatted down.
The Fó told Ānán:
“Take your Yùduōluósēng (uttarasanga), give it to her to wear, and let her listen to the Dharma.”
Ānán gave her the robe to wear.
She came before the Fó, bowed her head, and paid homage to the Fó.
The Fó preached the Dharma for her, demonstrating instruction, bringing benefit and joy.
She accepted the Three Refuges and became a Yōupóyí.
Joyfully, she departed.
Later, her seventh son died.
She did not weep or cry.
Her husband, holding her, asked her with a verse, saying:
“When your sons died before, you grieved and were troubled;
Day and night you ate and drank not, even going mad.
Now you mourn your seventh son, yet you alone show no sorrow.”
The wife said:
“Sons and grandsons are countless, born from the harmony of causes and conditions;
Through the long night they pass away; you and I are likewise.
Where they are reborn, in place after place, they further kill and devour each other.
If one knows the necessity of birth, why should one grieve again?
I have already recognized liberation, therefore I am troubled no more.”
The husband said:
“I have never heard this Dharma, but now I hear you speak of it.
Where did you hear the Right Dharma, that you do not sorrow for your son?”
The wife said:
“The Děngzhèngjué (Perfectly Enlightened One) today, eternally free from all suffering,
preached Suffering, Origin, Cessation, and the Path, which leads safely to Nièpán.
I have understood the Right Dharma, which dispelled my sorrow for my son.”
The husband said:
“I should now also go to Mítí Ānluó Yuán,
and from that Shìzūn seek to dispel the suffering of grieving for my son.”
The wife said:
“You must behold the Děngzhèngjué’s gentle, soft, golden body;
He tames those who are untamed, and widely saves all people.”
The husband went and saw the Fó.
The Fó recited a verse, saying:
“Suffering, Origin, Cessation, [and the] Path are not directed toward Nièpán.
He immediately saw the Dharma and achieved the incomparable result.”
Hearing the Dharma, his mind was liberated, and he left home under the Fó.
Contemplating quietly alone, he achieved Āluóhànship.
The wife and the daughter, Sūntuópánlí,
all also left home and ultimately reached the end of suffering.
In Shèwèi Chéng.
There was a poor and solitary mother.
She had given birth to a daughter.
The girl was seventeen years old.
Her appearance was dignified and solemn, though her clothes did not conceal her form.
The mother begged for food to sustain them.
The daughter was virtuous, wise, and highly perceptive.
She extensively read the sūtras and upheld her chastity, never leaving their door.
She lived near the Royal Way, and her heart wished for the King.
She also wished to serve a god as she would the Fó.
The King was traveling throughout the country.
He saw a crow calling above the poor maiden’s door.
The King immediately raised his bow and shot the crow.
The crow, carrying the King's arrow, flew into the girl's house.
The King’s attendants pursued the crow into the dwelling.
The girl did not show her face.
She merely pulled out the arrow, released the crow, took the arrow, and threw it outside.
The King's men saw her fingers and knew she was extraordinary.
In the following year,
the King’s principal consort died.
They sought a new consort through marriage proposals.
No one matched the requirements.
They searched widely among the people.
The attendants reported, saying:
“The poor and solitary mother’s daughter, the one from when you shot the crow before,
is sixteen or seventeen years old. Although we did not see her face,
seeing her hand and hearing her voice, she seems to be a noble person.”
The King immediately went to see her, called for her, and brought her along.
He sent diviners to interpret signs, and they arrived at the girl’s door and went straight inside.
The girl's mother was absent; only the girl lived there alone.
The messenger called for the girl to come out, but she did not answer after three calls.
The messenger said:
“Girl of the poor household, come out!”
The girl replied, saying:
“Whether talented or untalented, each is the child of a family.
Who are you, sir, to barge rudely into my house?
Hurry and get out of the door!”
The messenger said:
“The King sent me to call you.
You are the child of a humble family; how dare you speak thus?”
The girl said:
“What business does the King have in sending you here?
If he seeks me to be a maidservant,
my family has not violated the King’s law.
If he seeks me to be his wife,
then you people are my servants.
How dare you lightly disregard a poor household,
taking advantage of your authority to trespass, bully, and threaten a woman?
Although a woman may be humble,
she has her own destiny and will not yield to coercion.
You people must inform the King.”
The messenger dared to respond.
He reported everything to the King.
The King then commanded his hundred officials,
prepared the carriages, and furnished the full ceremonial requirements.
Accompanied by five hundred palace women (cǎinǚ), he went to welcome her.
The messenger carried offerings and tokens of respect: cattle, sheep, pigs, wine, and betrothal provisions.
The messenger rode in a black-canopied carriage.
Five horses drew the carriage to welcome the girl.
Leading the way were one hundred thousand elite soldiers.
Following them were one thousand chariots,
ten thousand fine horses,
and one hundred twenty thousand common retainers.
The ringing of bells and the beating of drums shook heaven and earth.
Countless onlookers gathered and went to the girl’s door.
The messenger descended from the carriage and went forward to convey his greetings and respect.
The girl ordered respectfully, saying:
“I thank the messenger and all the officials, officers, and people.
You have all labored greatly on the road.
This solitary, poor, and lowly girl
has caused far-off attendants to follow.
You have subjected yourselves to this humble service, the King’s weighty command.
Though I am of humble birth, by mistake due to past merit,
I am to stand on the King's steps and in his hall. I measure myself as ugly:
I lack the virtue of a royal consort.
My looks lack the color of peach blossoms or udumbara flowers.
My voice lacks the agreeable sound of strings and pipes.
My wisdom lacks the brilliance of the divine and great Sages.
My perception lacks the thousand-mile vision of the Saints.
My body lacks the sheen and luster of purple gold.
My fragrance lacks the scent of sandalwood and musk.
My speech lacks the beauty of loyalty, harmony, benevolence, and goodness.
My conduct lacks the propriety of measured advance, retreat, high, and low.
I have erroneously burdened myself with the King’s command and fatigued the viewers in vain.”
The messenger and the hundred officials sighed repeatedly.
She addressed the cǎinǚ:
“You, born with meager fortune, have fallen into this lowly service.
From now on, we shall serve together.
You should all correct your hearts and cultivate virtuous conduct.
Do not violate the King’s decorum.”
The five hundred cǎinǚ all assented readily.
She then called the two thousand five hundred female servants (qīngyī).
She spoke to them, saying:
“Among people, there is no high or low rank; the one who possesses the Way is honored.
You are all children of good people.
Changes throughout history have placed you in humble positions.
Do not feel inferior, but strive to do good.”
All replied, “We obey your instruction.”
The hundred officials came forward with the royal gifts.
One thousand catties of gold.
Two thousand catties of silver.
Jewels, auspicious blossoms, crystal, and lapis lazuli.
Luminous moon pearls, divine gems, coral, and amber.
One thousand bolts of white silk and one thousand bolts of imperial silk.
Brocade, fine silk, cotton, gauze, crimson embroidery, purple, and green.
Garments of plain, yellow, red, white gauze, and crepe.
Sandalwood perfume, one thousand measures of various kinds.
The hundred officials presented a hundred sets of robes, the consorts’ attire.
The girl accepted them. When her adornment was complete,
she came out and paid obeisance to those of higher rank.
When the hundred officials saw her, none failed to rejoice.
They all shouted, “Ten thousand years! The country will surely have Great Peace (Dàpíng)!
We have gained the mother of our hundred clans and ten thousand people!”
The cǎinǚ and qīngyī felt close to her, clinging to her as children find their mother.
She adjusted her robes and ascended the carriage; the carriage became steady and secure.
The horses were well-controlled, and the sky became clear.
White elephants gathered like clouds, chasing each other and trumpeting sadly.
The hundred officials, ministers, and people all said:
“A heavenly person has descended; the country will surely be protected and safe.”
When they reached the gate of the royal palace, it opened naturally.
The five hundred attendants entered the palace and descended from the carriages.
Inside the palace, five-colored light spontaneously arose.
The hall was bright, illuminating both inside and outside.
She entered the hall and paid respects to the King.
The King was shocked and bewildered by the sight.
He descended from his seat to respond to her.
The great consort (dà fūrén) bowed to the King
one hundred times, kneeling like flowing water.
She knelt and rose, only ceasing after a hundred bows.
The King knelt deeply in response.
She issued instructions within the palace:
Be gentle, harmonious, benevolent, and kind; do not harm the intentions of others.
The King loved and revered her.
Her speech was gentle and spare, and what she said was always in accordance with justice.
Inside and outside the palace, people respected and obeyed her.
She was in the palace for seven days and seven nights without closing her eyes or sleeping.
She engaged in shared entertainment with the other consorts and cǎinǚ.
The King wished to see her.
The consort’s intentions were pure and her heart clean, not dwelling in defilement.
Her original intention was purity; she would not speak to the King
nor meet with him.
The King said:
“The duty of a family and the relationship between husband and wife
are based on affection and love for closeness.
The consort has entered the palace for seven days and seven nights
without meeting me.
What is the meaning of this?
Is this according to the Law (Dharma)?”
The consort sent a cǎinǚ to answer the King, saying:
“I made two vows in my youth.
One has now been achieved.
One has not yet been achieved.
Therefore, we have not yet met.”
The King said:
“Which one has been achieved?
Which one has not yet been achieved?”
The consort replied:
“I made a solemn vow when I was young:
to have a husband like the King, and to serve a spirit (god) like the Fó.”
The King said:
“You can meet me once.
Afterward, I shall go and summon the Fó for you.”
The consort said, “No.
Until I have seen the Fó,
I will never meet with the King.”
The King was greatly angered and said:
“You are inherently of humble and base origin, the seed of a beggar.
How dare you defy the will of the Lord of Ten Thousand Chariots?”
The consort said:
“A woman’s fate is tied to her husband.
I will obey whatever command you give.
However, I have a solemn vow from a past life that cannot be broken.
Although the King is honored,
he may not unjustly question an innocent person.”
The King said:
“I am the Lord of Ten Thousand Chariots.
A transgressor shall be immediately executed.
Why should I inquire whether the deed was just or unjust?”
The consort said:
“The King is the father and mother of the people.
Judgments must be based on principle (dàolǐ).
How can one act according to one’s own pleasure and anger?
This is behavior that common people ought not to practice,
let alone the King!”
The King said:
“He who follows my heart shall be pardoned.
He who does not follow shall be executed.”
The consort said:
“A woman also has her own subtle will.
Only when my will is followed can we meet.
If my will is not followed,
I will never meet you.”
The King said:
“How shall I invite him?”
The consort said:
“The Fó is in our country. If you invite him, he will surely come.”
The King said:
“I fear the hundred officials will laugh at me.”
The consort said:
“Let the King invite the Fó into the palace.”
Ascending the hall, the hundred officials naturally rejoiced.
Receiving blessings generation after generation, they would not be ridiculed by the Wáng.
The Wáng said:
Greatly excellent.
Immediately that day, he commanded the kitchen to prepare food for one hundred thousand people.
He sent a maidservant to inform the Fūrén, saying:
The feast prepared for one hundred thousand people, intended for inviting the Fó, is ready.
You may go and invite the Fó.
The Fūrén said:
A woman only obeys commands.
Regarding the matter of inviting the Fó, Your Majesty (Dà Wáng) should personally trouble your chariots and riders.
Go for a moment, meet the Fó, and show him profound respect.
The Wáng said:
If I invite him, I will go myself.
If you invite him, you must go yourself.
I will not go.
The Fūrén said:
The Wáng is noble and revered, and he is my husband (master).
A woman's power is not equal to even a minor word from the Wáng.
Wáng, please humble your prestige and briefly go to meet the Fó.
If not, I am not a member of Your Majesty’s family.
The obligations of husband and wife, of house and family, have not yet been established.
Therefore, I am merely another person.
The Wáng said:
If husband and wife are not yet established, then the lack of duty and righteousness rests on your will alone.
The Fūrén remained silent, speaking nothing.
Her brilliance shone brightly, and her countenance was extraordinary.
The Wáng suspected that the Fūrén feared she might want to kill herself.
Or perhaps he feared she might suddenly depart.
He commanded the internal and external patrols (Yóujiào Sīhòu) to monitor.
Guards, officials, and soldiers were deployed to close the palace gates.
A net of infantry was continuously linked so that a flying bird could not pass through.
Inside the palace, court ladies (Cǎi Nǚ) followed one after another so closely that a needle could not drop to the ground.
The Fūrén knew the Wáng's intent was not to go and invite the Fó.
And that he did not trust the Fūrén.
The Fūrén immediately vanished (huà miè) from the hall.
Her body was utterly nowhere to be seen.
One thousand court ladies, along with the seventy-one other Fūrén,
were all astonished, looking at each other, and scattered to search for her.
Inside and outside the nets and barriers, she was utterly nowhere to be seen.
The Wáng was greatly ashamed and terrified, choking back tears as he rose.
The Wáng said:
What shall I do? What shall I do?
This was caused by my rigidity and obstinacy, and I regret it deeply now.
By what means can I cause her to return?
The second Fūrén reported to the Wáng, saying:
The Dà Fūrén (Chief Lady),
is not one of our common, vulgar sort.
The Wáng should have praised and followed her wishes.
Instead, you suddenly refused her, treating her with annoyance and harsh words.
This person is truly a celestial being (tiān rén).
Wáng, if the Dà Fūrén leaves,
upon whom shall we seventy-one others
rely?
The court ladies (Cǎi Nǚ) and servants (Qīng Yī) all wept bitterly.
It was as if someone had died.
The dukes and ministers, men and women, were also grieved and resentful.
Now, in our kingdom, who shall we depend upon?
A hundred birds cried out, and heaven and earth greatly shook.
The Wáng was so deeply moved he wished to die.
He sighed deeply toward heaven, and his tears fell like rain.
The common people stopped their work, and the markets were deserted and abandoned.
In groups of ten, five, and five, they followed each other in sorrow.
For seven days and seven nights, the Wáng lay restlessly, cutting off grain and refusing to eat.
The second Fūrén said:
You should first go and meet the Fó for a while,
and invite them to come together.
The Wáng arrived at the Fó’s location and bowed down his head in reverence (tóu miàn wéi lǐ).
He addressed the Fó, saying:
I am Hégādáliú, the Wáng of the kingdom of Āqíluónài.
Having done this three times, he presented the Xūbūtì homage.
I have been continuously burdened by state affairs, not waiting for morning or evening.
The Fó said:
Being troubled and distressed by state affairs, and constantly being bothered by the common populace, truly exhausts your spiritual energy.
Are your officials, people, and boundaries all at peace?
The Wáng said:
All receive the Fó’s grace.
I only wish that you would condescend
to briefly visit my humble dwelling.
The Fó remained silent.
In a moment, the Fó arrived in the hall.
The Dà Fūrén,
together with the various Fūrén and three thousand five hundred seventy-one court ladies (Cǎi Nǚ), bowed to the Fó.
The Wáng initially did not see the Fūrén.
The court ladies also did not see her.
Only the Fó saw her.
After the Wáng finished bowing to the Fó, his heart was worried and unhappy.
The Fó spoke to the Wáng, saying:
The Dà Fūrén for whom you are searching,
is precisely this person here.
The Wáng saw her and rejoiced.
The hundred officials, Fūrén, and court ladies (Cǎi Nǚ), great and small, all rejoiced as well.
The Wáng arranged a meal.
After the meal, the Fó gave a great blessing (zhòu yuàn).
Each sought what they desired in their hearts.
The Wáng addressed the Fó, saying:
My Dà Fūrén,
was originally the daughter of a poor, lowly, solitary mother.
Now she is the Dà Fūrén.
Furthermore, she is able to make her body vanish and perform such illusions (huàn huà).
What sin or merit caused this?
She is noble and revered above all others.
She has attained the position of the mother of the common people.
Her benevolence, virtue, wisdom, and compassion, and her gentle speech do not harm people's feelings.
She concealed her form for seven days, and humans, ghosts, spirits, or dragons did not know her whereabouts.
The Fó informed him, saying:
The Dà Fūrén,
was previously a great Jiāluóyuè (Gṛhapati, householder).
He had immeasurable wealth but was miserly, greedy, and did not give alms.
Therefore, she is now poor.
The Jiāluóyuè nature was fond of lust and dissipation (yín zhí).
He enjoyed dealing with women.
Therefore, she is now reborn among women.
Furthermore, he enjoyed associating with learned scholars (dàoshì).
Due to this learning, she possesses wisdom.
She has already met five hundred Fó.
Now she has met me.
In the past, she was a good friend (shàn zhī shì) of the Wáng.
Therefore, they have become husband and wife.
The Dà Fūrén, in former lives, served five hundred Fó.
But she did not maintain a firm mind (in practice).
And she disturbed and troubled worldly people, hence she fell into the realm of women.
The Dà Fūrén, after thirty-nine kalpas (jié),
will attain Buddhahood (zuò Fó).
The Wáng will also be born in heaven seven times.
And born in the human world seven times.
When the Wáng is born in heaven,
the Dà Fūrén will be a heavenly maiden (tiān nǚ).
Serving by the Wáng’s side.
Always pleasing the Wáng.
The Wáng and the Dà Fūrén made a vow to die together.
And life after life, they will accompany each other and both attain liberation.
The Wáng, by acting haughtily, extravagantly, and controlling his temper (i.e., being difficult),
will never see such things (magical displays) again.
The Wáng’s heart was greatly joyful.
He immediately attained the path of Āwéiyuèzhì (Avaivartika, non-retrogression).
The Fó then administered the Five Precepts (wǔ jiè) to the Wáng.
The Fūrén, court ladies (Cǎi Nǚ), great and small officials, dukes, ministers, and all the people of the entire country observed the Five Precepts.
The Dà Fūrén had previously received the Ten Precepts (shí jiè).
She observed the Three Fasts (sān zhāi) yearly.
And the Six Fasts (liù zhāi) monthly.
She guided the three thousand five hundred seventy-one court ladies (Cǎi Nǚ) of the inner palace
to engage in good conduct and lead each other in virtue.
The Wáng’s righteous governance was vast and expansive, bringing great peace to the country.
The stupas and monasteries established were all made of the Seven Treasures (qī bǎo).
They respected each other, and there was no sense of separation inside or outside.
When the people died, it was always at the completion of their lifespan.
The Dà Fūrén, realizing and contemplating the impermanence of the world,
that people indulge day and night in lust, attachment, and ignorance, resulting in defilement and pollution (zhuó huì).
When alive, they lack a virtuous reputation.
When dead, they become unclean ghosts.
She then sighed deeply, changed her clothes, disheveled her appearance, and ruffled her hair.
She came forward and addressed the Wáng, saying:
Everything under heaven is impermanent and must ultimately return to death.
The reason the Wáng is greedy for me
is because I am young, my complexion is radiant, my skin is smooth and lustrous, and my breath is fragrant and pure.
These are all impermanent and must all return to death.
The union of husband and wife is fundamentally unremarkable; it is all impure.
From this attachment and love, old age and sickness must follow.
Their arrival has no fixed date; who can hold them back for me?
I am now sorrowful and afraid that sudden disaster will strike, and I will be unable to escape.
All people, noble or humble, because of this one matter (death and decay),
will eventually swell up, rot, stink, and become unclean.
What benefit is there in clinging to and cherishing such emptiness?
Wáng, please contemplate this yourself:
What is remarkable about the union of man and woman?
My words are the true reality; they do not fall short of the facts.
The Wáng said:
You are of the lineage of celestial beings (tiān rén).
What you say is not false.
Everything attains its reality; nothing is impossible.
The people of the country, men and women, great and small, all rely upon you.
Please be mindful and remain for their sake.
The Dà Fūrén said:
I am a woman.
I cannot control myself, thus I address the Wáng.
Your Majesty (Dà Wáng) may send me forth to fulfill my fundamental vows from past lives (sù mìng).
The Wáng said:
I am about to grow old.
Although I have other Fūrén, court ladies (Cǎi Nǚ), and children,
there is not one who pleases my heart.
You should see out my remaining years.
After I pass away, the affairs of the state should be entrusted to you.
The Tàizǐ (Crown Prince) is still small.
Why must you abandon me and leave?
Where will you go?
The Fūrén said:
Birth and death for me are impermanent, and I am weary of these transformations.
I wish to request of the Fó to become a Shāmén (monastic).
The Wáng said:
You are the mother of the nation, the supreme Fūrén.
The Fūrén of all states, and the court ladies (Cǎi Nǚ), great and small, in the palace, all rely on you.
How can you suddenly propose and establish this plan?
When gentlemen (shì fū) near and far hear of this, they will laugh at such people. This class of Shāmén is not what you, a Fūrén, should aspire to be. You ought to reconsider.
The Fūrén said:
All the Fó of the ten directions have come from the ranks of the Shāmén.
Fó Jiāshā Wáng (Kāśyapa Buddha),
abandoned the Fūrén and court ladies (Cǎi Nǚ)—eight or nine thousand people—of ninety-nine small kingdoms,
and sought to become a Shāmén.
In the past and future, those, male and female, who seek to become Shāmén are not few.
I am not the only woman.
O King, out of affection, lustful desire, and attachment to beautiful appearance, you cherish my body.
My body is full of pus, blood, foul secretions, and impurity.
It is difficult to deal with women.
Whoever deals with women invariably falls into sin.
A woman's body is hotter than boiling water or fire.
It burns people, causing them to fall into grave sins,
from which they cannot escape for a thousand *jié*.
In my previous life, I was also a man.
Merely because I dealt with women,
and had excessive affection, I left the form of a man and became a woman.
Women are terrifying.
The King merely does not perceive this.
If the King intends not to separate from women,
your *Fūrén* and palace maidens already number over three thousand, enough for your enjoyment.
The King should intend to send me away, without causing distress or worry.
Even if I become a *Shāmén* and die repeatedly, I will not stop.
The King should encourage me and ought not to obstruct me.
The King said,
"If you are like that, what use is the kingdom to me?"
The *Fūrén* said,
"If the King can realize impermanence (*wúcháng*), that is the King's highest aspiration.
The lands, the royal throne, the officials, the palace maidens, the treasures, the palaces, and the cities are none of them truly yours.
Even the King's body, skeleton, head, brain, and five viscera—
all will eventually scatter and disperse.
What is there to cherish?"
The King said,
"Today I will permit you alone.
I fear that my *fūrén* and palace maidens will follow you and all depart together."
The *Fūrén* said,
"Everyone has their own predestined fate and meritorious power.
It is not something that humans can stop.
Even if you apply knives and staves to everyone, things should remain thus.
You ultimately cannot stop them.
I merely wish that my body may be sent forth.
The King should use affection and compassion to comfort all the others.
They will naturally draw near and cling to the King."
The King said,
"These people admire and delight in your virtue.
How can I, one man, extend good intentions throughout all of them?
I rely only on you to properly govern them.
Now you abandon me.
These women will only fear me if I take a knife and slaughter them."
The *Fūrén* said,
"Not so.
Women simply regard men as their proper guidance.
If the King pays attention and approaches them, they will remain at peace naturally."
The King said,
"It depends on you."
The *Fūrén* then summoned the three thousand *fūrén* and palace maidens.
She admonished and addressed them, saying,
"All you women,
take care to approach the Great King with reverence and honor; do not treat him with contempt.
I now separate from you all.
Each of you strive diligently day and night.
Personally uphold the Sūtra teachings and practice zealous effort (*jīngjìn*).
I pray that I may quickly attain the Way of the Buddha.
Then I shall return to save you."
The *fūrén* and palace maidens immediately raised their voices and wept loudly.
(The sound) was heard in the *Dāolì Tiān*.
*Dìshì* (Śakra) immediately descended and bestowed the *jiāshā* (robe).
It naturally covered her body, and her hair fell to the ground.
She was given the five hundred precepts and became a *Bǐqiūní*.
The *fūrén* and palace maidens were all greatly delighted.
*Dìshì* further bestowed the *jiāshā* and alms bowl to make her a *Shāmén*.
The King achieved contentment (*zhīzú*), was serene, and no longer angry.
Joyfully, he laughed loudly and said,
"How majestic are the merits of these noble people! Is this not delightful?"
He immediately attained the trace of the Way. The King returned to the inner palace.
He was deeply perplexed in his heart.
He came out and called the Crown Prince (*Tàizǐ*), entrusting the kingdom to him.
The King then made a vow, saying,
"I now wish to become a *Shāmén*. Who will recognize me?"
*Dìshì* then shaved the King's head.
The *jiāshā* clothed his body, and the appropriate utensils were spontaneously provided.
He then followed the Buddha.
The kings of the twelve minor kingdoms,
all abandoned their states and entrusted them to their Crown Princes,
and followed the King to become *Shāmén*.
At the same time, they all attained the path of *Āluóhàn*.
The person who was *Ājiādáliú* is me.
The Great *Fūrén* is *Qúyī*.
The Buddha dwelt in *Píshànlí*.
He addressed the *Bǐqiū* (monks), saying,
"I heard that among the *Ní* (nuns), the one whose meritorious virtue is foremost
is *Shīlìmó*.
At that time, the world suffered famine, and obtaining alms food was difficult.
At that time, the *Bǐqiūní Shīlìmó* entered the city to beg for food.
Seeing a *Bǐqiū*, she immediately asked,
'Venerable Sir, have you obtained food?'
The *Bǐqiū* immediately showed her his empty bowl.
She then took the food in her own bowl and gave it to the *Bǐqiū*.
The *Bǐqiū*, having obtained food, returned to the monastery (*jīngshě*).
He called the other *Bǐqiū* to eat together.
The *Bǐqiū* asked,
'Elder, where did you obtain this excellent food?'
He replied,
'I obtained it from the *Bǐqiūní Shīlìmó*.'
When the *Bǐqiū* heard this, they each went to ask for it.
Proceeding thus sequentially, up to five hundred *Bǐqiū*
all obtained food.
Afterward, she sought food for herself.
The time of day had already passed.
Having missed her meal, she returned to the monastery.
The following morning,
the *Bǐqiū* again put on their robes and carried their bowls.
They went and stood at the gate of the *Bǐqiūní* monastery.
When the *Bǐqiūní* saw them, she immediately went inside.
She told *Shīlìmó*, saying,
'The *Bǐqiū* are now waiting outside the gate.'
When *Shīlìmó* heard this, she told her disciples,
'Bring my robe and bowl.
I will beg for food for the highly revered ones.'
After sequentially supplying the five hundred people thus, she then sought food for herself.
The time of day passed again, and she returned, having missed her meal.
On the third day, it was also like this.
Until she sequentially supplied five hundred people.
Only one person had not yet obtained food.
This *Bǐqiū* followed behind *Shīlìmó* and entered a household.
Because he had missed his meals for the preceding three days,
his body was weak and frail, and he fainted and fell to the ground.
There was a *Bǐqiūní* named *Bàozhì*,
who, on the contrary, harbored wicked beliefs, slandered the Buddha, and defamed the Sangha.
The Buddha said,
"Not only in this present life,
but in the innumerable *jié* of the past,
there was a Monkey King (*Míhóuwáng*) who lived among the forest trees, eating fruit and drinking water.
At that time, he thought of all creatures that crawl, walk, breathe, and live,
wishing to save them all and lead them to *wúwéi* (Nirvāṇa).
At that time, there was a tortoise (*biē*) whom he regarded as a close friend.
The tortoise frequently came and went to the Monkey's abode.
They would eat, drink, talk, and discuss righteous principles.
His wife saw this.
Supposing there was licentiousness, she asked,
'Husband, where have you been going?'
He replied,
'I have formed a close friendship with a Monkey King.
He is extremely intelligent and wise, and also understands righteous principles.'
The wife still did not believe him.
She then feigned illness.
She lay weakly on the ground, and refused to recover despite treatment.
She told her husband,
'My sickness is very severe.
Only if I obtain the liver of the Monkey King whom you befriended,
will I be able to live.'
The husband replied,
'I have entrusted my body and life (to him in friendship).
How can I use that to save you?'
The wife said,
'Husband and wife share one body; do you not think of assisting me,
but instead side with the monkey?' The husband respected and valued his wife.
He went and invited the Monkey King to eat together.
The Monkey King replied,
'My home is on the land,
you are in the water.
How can I follow you?'
The tortoise said,
'I shall carry you on my back.'
The Monkey King agreed and was carried by the tortoise. Halfway across, the tortoise told the Monkey King, saying,
'My wife is sick and needs your liver.'
The Monkey King said,
'Why didn't you say so sooner?
My liver is hanging on the tree; I did not bring it along.
We must return to retrieve the liver before I can follow you.'
He immediately returned to the tree, leaping and swinging joyfully.
The tortoise asked,
'You ought to go get your liver
and come to my house,
but instead you are leaping around. Why?'
The Monkey King replied,
'There is none more foolish in the world than you.
We became close friends and entrusted our bodies and lives (to each other).
Yet you turned around and sought to endanger me.'
The tortoise's wife is *Bàozhì*.
The tortoise is *Diàodá*.
The Monkey King is me."
The [Fó] traveled in [Shèwèi] in the [Qí] country (Jeta Grove).
[Bō Sī Nì Wáng] (King Prasenajit)
invited the [Fó] and the Saṅgha
to set up a meal within the palace.
When they were about to go to the King’s palace,
there was a [Bǐqiūní]
named [Bào Zhì].
She tied a wooden bowl (or casque) to her belly, appearing as if pregnant.
Then she demanded the [Fó]'s robes:
"You were my husband, and from you, I conceived this body (child).
Why do you not provide clothing and food? What is the meaning of this matter?"
At that time, the great assembly—humans, celestial beings, [Shì] (Indra), [Fàn] (Brahmā), the Four Heavenly Kings, various deities, ghosts, and spirits—
and the people of the country, were all greatly astonished and alarmed.
The [Fó] is the most honored of all the Three Realms.
His mind is purer than the [Móní] gem.
The radiance of his wisdom surpasses the sun and moon.
He walks alone through the three ages; none can reach him.
He subdues all evil.
The ninety-six kinds [of heterodox views] all submit to him.
His virtue and principle are lofty and cannot be compared.
Empty space is formless and cannot be defiled.
The [Fó]'s mind surpasses that, having no equal.
Since this [Bǐqiūní] is a disciple of the [Fó],
why does she harbor malice and seek to slander the [Rúlái]?
The [Fó], seeing the minds of the assembly and wishing to resolve their doubts, looked up towards the heavens.
Immediately, [Tiān Dì Shì] (Śakra) descended.
He transformed himself into a mouse and gnawed the rope that tied the bowl.
The bowl immediately fell to the ground.
The assembly witnessed this.
Anger and joy mixed together, marveling at the reason behind it.
At that time, the King was angry.
“This [Bǐqiūní] abandoned her home and renounced her livelihood to become a disciple of the [Fó].
Not only is she unable to praise the boundless merits of the [Rúlái],
but she turns back to slander him out of jealousy.” Upon this, the Great King
immediately ordered his attendants,
to dig a pit in the earth and intended to bury her upside down.
The [Fó] then explained and admonished, "Do not do that.
This is my own past karma (sin), not solely her misfortune.
Long ago, in a distant past life,
there was a traveling merchant
selling many fine pearls.
They were round, bright, and beautiful.
At that time, there was a woman who wanted to buy them all.
Just as the transaction was about to be concluded,
a certain man came along.
He offered double the price, took the pearls, and left alone.
The woman, unable to obtain them, harbored anger and resentment.
She approached him and asked for them, but he still refused to give them up.
Since her anger was intense,
she thought: 'I was buying the pearls just now,
and you came and took them away.
I asked you again, and you still refused to give them up.
You have disgraced and insulted me.
In whatever life I am reborn, I shall repay this enmity of yours.'
The man who bought the pearls at that time is my current self.
The woman's body is [Bào Zhì].
This is a condition from a past life.
It is not confined only to this present life."
When a kalpa is about to form,
the disaster of water arises, destroying the Second [Chán] Heaven.
The disaster of wind blows and forms, and the world is established.
When the merits and lifespans of the [Guāng Yīn Zhū Tiān] (Abhāsvāra Devas) are exhausted,
they are reborn as humans, taking joy as their food.
Their bodies shine by themselves, and they fly by means of spiritual power.
There is no distinction between male and female, high or low.
Therefore, it is said that living beings had natural earth flavor.
It was like fine cream ([tíhú]).
Its color was like fresh butter.
Its taste was sweeter than honey.
They took it with their hands and tasted it.
Then they developed attachment to the taste.
Those who ate a lot had rough and sallow complexions.
Those who ate little had bright and glossy skin and features.
Consequently, there were winners and losers, and they began to judge each other.
The earth flavor then disappeared.
Then earth skin (earth membrane) grew.
Its appearance was like a thin membrane.
Its color, flavor, and fragrance were excellent, and they ate it together again.
They gradually slighted and disparaged one another, and the earth skin disappeared again.
Then earth flesh (earth moss) grew; due to eating more or less, various evil practices arose.
The earth produced cultivated rice, which the multitude ate together.
The forms of male and female arose, leading finally to the establishment of kings. The world became wealthy and joyful, and the earth produced green grass.
Like the tails of peacocks, [the countries] gradually spread and divided.
There were eighty thousand countries.
The villages and settlements of the people were close enough that the sound of rooster crows could be heard between them.
In the world, there was no sickness, intense heat, or intense cold.
They governed the country with the Dharma and practiced the Ten Virtues.
They loved and cared for all beings as if they were their parents.
Human lifespans were long.
Later, the virtue of the kings gradually diminished, and lifespans slowly decreased.
It decreased until ten thousand years.
Now it reaches one hundred years.
When a king died, his son succeeded him.
Named [Zhēnbǎo].
He was a [Zhuǎnlún Shèng Wáng] (Wheel-Turning Holy King, Cakravartin).
The reason he obtained the Golden Wheel is that
[Dì Shì] constantly ordered the Four Heavenly Kings
to inspect the world six days a month
to observe the good and evil deeds of people.
The Four Heavenly Kings and the envoys of their great sons,
if they saw a Great King governing the world using the Ten Virtues and the Four Immeasurables,
working diligently for the welfare of the people, with a heart surpassing a benevolent father,
reported this matter to [Tiān Dì Shì].
When [Dì Shì] heard this,
he rejoiced that the King was able to do so.
He immediately ordered [Píshǒu Jiémó] (Viśvakarma)
to grant him the Golden Wheel.
[Píshǒu Jiémó] immediately brought it out and handed it over to [Píshāmén Tiānwáng] (Vaiśravaṇa, King of the Devas).
[Píshāmén Tiānwáng] handed it over to a flying [Yèchā] (Yakṣa).
The flying [Yèchā] brought it and gave it to the Great King.
[Píshāmén Tiānwáng] ordered this [Yèchā]:
"You must always hold this Golden Wheel for the King.
It must remain above the King's head until the end of his lifespan.
You must not abandon it halfway."
This [Yèchā] constantly held it for him.
Whether advancing, resting, coming, or going, it followed the will of the Holy King until the end of his lifespan.
Afterwards, he returned it to [Píshāmén Tiānwáng].
[Píshāmén Tiānwáng] returned it to [Píshǒu Jiémó].
[Píshǒu Jiémó] returned it and placed it within the treasure vault. The King whose species [of karma] is the Way and whose virtue is firm rides the Golden Wheel and rules the four continents.
The King whose species [of karma] is natural disposition rides the Silver Wheel and rules the three continents.
The King whose species [of karma] is acquired practice rides the Copper Wheel and rules the two continents.
These [kings] obtain sovereignty based on the Ten Virtues.
The King who rides the Iron Wheel rules one continent.
He achieves the Seven Treasures.
He possesses four divine virtues (sì shén dé).
First, the Golden Wheel Treasure.
Second, the White Elephant Treasure.
Third, the Blue Horse Treasure.
Fourth, the Divine Pearl Treasure.
Fifth, the Jewel Woman Treasure (Yùnǚ Bǎo).
Sixth, the Householder Treasure (Jūshì Bǎo).
Seventh, the General Treasure (Zhǔbīng Bǎo).
When the Cakravartin King (Zhǎnlún Wáng) appears in Jambudvīpa (Yánfú Tí),
all the Kṣatriyas (Chàlì) sprinkle water upon the King’s crown, bathing him in fragrant water when the moon is full.
He ascends the high palace hall, where music and entertainment are assembled.
Suddenly, the Heavenly Golden Wheel Treasure (Tiān Jīnlún Bǎo) appears before him.
The wheel has a thousand spokes, fully endowed with brilliance and color.
It is made of heavenly gold, not belonging to this world.
The diameter of the wheel is fourteen zhàng.
The King sees it and a thought arises:
"I have heard from ancient times that when this wheel appears, there will be no opposition."
"Now, I should test this Wheel Treasure."
The King immediately summons his four divisions of troops
and faces the Golden Wheel Treasure.
He bares his right arm and places his right knee upon the ground.
Using his right hand, he rubs and touches the Golden Wheel, saying:
"Turn toward the East according to the Dharma (fǎ), and do not violate the usual principle."
The wheel immediately turns eastward.
The King, leading his four divisions, follows behind it.
Four spirits (shén) precede the wheel, guiding it to where it should stop.
The King then stops his carriage.
Small countries in the East bring silver grain contained in gold bowls,
and gold grain contained in silver bowls.
They come to the King's location.
They bow their heads and report, saying:
"Excellent, O Great King (Dà Wáng).
Now, the land in this eastern region is fertile and joyous, possessing many rare treasures, and the population is flourishing.
We wish the Great King to remain here to rule and transform us."
The Great King replies:
"You yourselves should simply govern the people by the Right Dharma (Zhèngfǎ).
Do not allow partiality or injustice, and ensure that no unlawful conduct exists within your domains.
Personally, abstain from killing.
Teach people not to kill, steal, commit sexual misconduct (xié yín), engage in double-tongue (liǎng shé), harsh speech (è kǒu), or false speech (wàng yán).
[Teach people not to engage in] flowery speech (qǐ yǔ), greedy misconduct (tān xié), jealousy (jídù), or harbor wrong views (xié jiàn).
This is what is called my governance."
Then all the minor kings,
followed the Great King and toured the various countries.
They traveled to the East, South, West, and North,
following wherever the wheel went.
All those kings offered the level and expansive parts of their lands.
The wheel traveled completely around, demarcating and measuring the boundaries.
East to West, twelve Yóujùn (Yojana).
North to South, seven Yóujùn.
Heavenly spirits (Tiānshén) built the city walls.
The city had seven layers.
Seven layers of railings, seven layers of netting,
and seven layers of trees forming rows, surrounding and intersecting as decoration.
It was constructed of the Seven Treasures (Qī Bǎo), extending even to countless flocks of birds singing in harmony.
Furthermore, inside the city, various palaces and halls were constructed.
The palace walls had seven layers, constructed of the Seven Treasures.
At that time, the Golden Wheel Treasure (Jīnlún Bǎo) stayed in the empty space above the palace.
The King sat in the main hall (Zhèngdiàn) early in the morning.
Suddenly, the Natural Elephant Treasure (Xiàng Bǎo) appeared before him.
Its hair was pure white, and its seven stationary parts were level.
Its strength allowed it to fly, and its head was multi-colored.
Its six tusks were slender and sharp, inlaid with true gold.
The King saw it and thought:
"This elephant is virtuous and good.
If it is properly trained, it can be driven and ridden."
He immediately tested and trained it, and all its abilities were fully prepared.
Then the Cakravartin King (Zhǎnlún Wáng) wished to test the elephant himself.
He immediately mounted it.
Early in the morning, he left the city and traveled around the Four Seas (Sì Hǎi).
He returned by mealtime.
Then, early in the morning, the King sat in the main hall.
Suddenly, the Natural Horse Treasure (Mǎ Bǎo) appeared before him.
It was a deep blue color, with crimson hair on its tail and head.
It arched like a horse, and its strength allowed it to fly.
The King saw it and thought:
"This Horse Treasure is excellent.
If it is properly trained, it can be driven and ridden."
He immediately tested and trained it, and all its abilities were fully prepared.
The King wished to test the horse.
He immediately mounted it himself and left the city early in the morning.
He traveled around the Four Seas and returned by mealtime.
Then, early in the morning, the King was in the main hall.
Suddenly, the Natural Divine Pearl (Shén Zhū) appeared before him.
Its substance and color were pure and penetrating, without any flaw or impurity.
The King saw it and thought:
"This pearl is wondrous and fine.
If it has brightness, it can illuminate the interior of the palace."
The King wished to test the pearl.
He immediately summoned his four divisions of troops.
He placed this precious pearl upon a high banner pole.
In the deep darkness of the night, he carried the banner outside the city.
The pearl’s radiance illuminated one Yóujùn (Yojana).
The people within the city were seen rising and performing their duties,
believing it to be daytime.
The Jewel Woman Treasure (Yùnǚ Bǎo) suddenly appeared by itself.
Her countenance was poised, and her face was beautiful and proper.
She was neither too tall nor too short, neither coarse nor fine.
Neither too pale nor too dark, neither hard nor soft.
In winter, her body was warm; in summer, her body was cool.
Sandalwood (zhāntán) fragrance issued from the pores of her entire body.
From her mouth issued the scent of the Utpala flower (Yōubōluó Huā).
Her speech was gentle and tender, and her movements were graceful and composed.
She rose before the King and sat down after him, never failing in propriety.
At that time, the King had no attachment, and did not harbor lustful thoughts even for a moment,
much less approaching her intimately.
The Householder Treasure (Jūshì Bǎo) suddenly appeared by itself.
Within his treasury, his wealth was immeasurable.
Due to the merit accumulated by the householder in former lives (sù fú), his eyes could penetrate and see clearly.
Submerged treasures in the earth, whether ownerless or owned,
he was completely able to see and know.
Those that had owners, he was able to protect.
Those that were ownerless, he retrieved for the King’s use.
Then the Householder Treasure went and reported to the King, saying:
"Great King (Dà Wáng),
you need not worry about any supplies or provisions.
I am personally capable of obtaining them."
The King then wished to test this Householder Treasure.
He immediately ordered a boat to be prepared to play upon the water.
He announced to the householder:
"I require gold treasures; quickly give them to me."
The householder replied:
"Great King,
please wait a little until I reach the shore."
The King then insisted, saying:
"I require them now, Householder Treasure."
The Householder reached his right hand into the water.
Treasure vases from the water emerged following his hand,
like insects crawling up a tree.
The King saw this.
He spoke to the householder, saying:
"Stop, stop. I require nothing.
I was merely testing you just now."
He immediately threw the treasures back into the water.
The General Treasure (Zhǔbīng Bǎo),
suddenly appeared.
His wisdom and strategy were heroic and fierce, and his brilliance in planning was decisive and unique.
He immediately went to the King's location and reported, saying:
"Great King (Dà Wáng), you need not worry about any military expeditions or punishments.
I am personally capable of managing them."
The King then wished to test the General Treasure.
He immediately assembled the four divisions of troops and announced to him, saying:
"You are now managing the troops.
Assemble those who are not assembled.
Dismiss those who are already assembled.
Equip those who are not equipped.
Disarm those who are already equipped.
Cause those who have not gone to go.
Cause those who have already halted to halt."
The General Treasure carried out everything exactly as the King commanded.
The King saw this and rejoiced, saying:
"I am now truly the Cakravartin Holy King (Zhǎnlún Shèngwáng)!
First, I have longevity and do not die prematurely; none can compare.
Second, my body is strong and without sickness; none can compare.
Third, my face and appearance are proper and beautiful; none can compare.
Fourth, my treasures overflow; none can compare."
These are the four merits (sì gōngdé) possessed by the Holy King (Shèngwáng).
On the far shore of the Great Sea,
there is also the Pàtóumó Pond (Padma/Lotus Pond).
The Jùwùtóu Pond (Kumuda/Water Lily Pond).
The Fēntuólì Pond (Puṇḍarīka/White Lotus Pond).
Beyond this empty space of land,
within that empty land, there is great sea water.
Named Yùchánnà.
Beneath this water is the path of the Cakravartin Holy King (Zhǎnlún Shèngwáng Dào).
It is twelve Yóujùn wide.
Along both sides of the path, there are seven layers of walls, seven layers of railings, seven layers of netting, and seven layers of trees in rows.
They are constructed of the Seven Treasures (Qī Bǎo).
When the Cakravartin Holy King (Zhǎnlún Shèngwáng) appears in the world on the continent of Jambudvīpa (Yánfú Tí),
the water naturally recedes, and the path becomes level and straight.
The Cakravartin Holy King (Zhǎnlún Shèngwáng),
then orders his carriage to take him out to tour his private garden.
He immediately instructs the charioteer:
"You must drive skillfully and proceed carefully.
The reason for this is that I wish to observe closely,
that the people of the country are peaceful, happy, and without distress."
At that time, the people of the country,
who were watching by the roadside,
spoke in turn to their attendants: "You must proceed slowly.
I wish to observe closely the dignified countenance of the Holy King (Shèngwáng)."
At that time, the King nourished the people and things with kindness, just as a father loves his son.
The citizens admired the King, just as a son looks up to his father.
All their rare treasures, they entirely presented to the King,
requesting that he kindly accept them.
The King replied:
"Wait, all of you.
I possess my own treasures; you may use yours yourselves."
When the King governed this Jambudvīpa (Yánfú Tí),
the ground was level and straight.
There were no brambles, thorns, pits, hollows, mounds, or hills.
Nor were there mosquitoes, horseflies, bees, regular flies, snakes, vipers, or other noxious creatures.
Stones, sand, broken tiles, and rubble naturally sank away.
Gold, silver, precious jewels, and jade appeared on the ground.
The four seasons were harmonized, neither cold nor hot.
The earth was soft and moist, without dust or filth.
It was clean and glossy, like oil spread upon the ground.
Flowing springs emerged from the earth, pure and inexhaustible.
Trees and shrubs flourished greatly, and flowers and fruits were abundant.
Soft grass grew on the ground, eternally green in winter and summer, its color like that of a peacock's feathers.
Naturally grown *jīngmǐ* (polished round-grain rice) lacked husks and chaff, and was complete with all flavors.
At that time, there were fragrant trees whose flowers and fruits flourished profusely.
When their fruits ripened, they naturally split open, giving off a rich, fragrant aroma.
Moreover, there were clothing trees whose flowers and fruits flourished profusely.
When their fruits ripened, the skin and shells naturally split open, yielding various kinds of clothing.
Moreover, there were adornment trees.
When their fruits ripened, they produced various kinds of adornments.
Moreover, there were garland trees.
When their fruits ripened, they produced various kinds of garlands.
Moreover, there were vessel trees.
When their fruits ripened, they produced various kinds of vessels.
Moreover, there were fruit trees.
Their flowers and fruits flourished profusely; when their fruits ripened, the skin and shells naturally split open, yielding various kinds of fruit.
Moreover, there were musical instrument trees.
When their fruits ripened, they produced all manner of musical instruments.
When the *Zhuǎnlún Shèngwáng* (Wheel-Turning Sage King) governed the world,
the Dragon King Ānòu Dá (Anavatapta),
after midnight,
caused great, dense clouds to arise, filling the world,
and sent down a great rain for the duration of a bull’s urination.
And the water of the eight excellent flavors moistened everything thoroughly and universally.
The land was without stagnant water or muddy mire.
The moisture was pervasive and adequate.
After midnight, the sky was clear and bright.
Pure, without clouds or shadows.
A cool breeze arose from the sea, pure, gentle, and soothing, causing pleasure to the body.
The Sage King ruled the country justly, without bias or oppression, practicing the ten good deeds.
At that time, all the people also cultivated right view and possessed the ten good actions.
After a long time, the King felt slightly unwell, like a joyful person eating food.
And then he passed away, being reborn in the Brahmā heavens.
At that time, the golden wheel, the white elephant, the deep-blue horse, and the brilliant pearl all vanished.
Then the Jewel Woman, the Jewel Householder, and the Jewel General of the Troops,
along with the officials and common people of the country,
performed songs, dances, and music, and washed the King’s body with fragrant water.
They wrapped five hundred layers of fine cloth with cotton.
Layer by layer they wrapped him.
They reverently lifted the King’s body and placed it inside a golden coffin.
They poured fragrant oil over him.
They placed that inside an iron coffin.
Then they covered the outside with a wooden sarcophagus, piled up heaps of fragrant firewood, and covered the top deeply.
And then they cremated him (*zhāwéi*).
At the head of the four major crossroads, they erected a Seven Jewels stupa.
Its length and width were one *yóuxún* (yojana).
Built from the Seven Jewels, interwoven with variegated colors.
The Jewel Woman, the Jewel Householder, the Jewel General, and all the officials and common people throughout the country,
all came to make offerings to this stupa.
They gave charity to all the poor and needy.
Those who needed food were given food; those who needed clothing were given clothing.
Elephants, horses, and precious carriages.
They supplied whatever the multitude required, giving according to their wishes.
In the past, during measureless, boundless *āsēngqí jié* (asamkhyeya kalpas),
this world was named Rìyuè Léi.
There was also a time of the Five Corruptions (*Wǔ Zhuó Shì*).
At that time, I acted as a *Zhuǎnlún Wáng* (Wheel-Turning King).
Ruling over Yánfútí (Jambudvīpa).
Named Dēng Guāngmíng.
I educated *āsēngqí* people, causing them to abide in good *Dharma*.
I saw a person whose body was bound and restrained.
I immediately asked,
"What crime has this man committed?"
The minister replied,
"One-sixth of the grain and wheat produced in the fields must enter the royal office.
This man has not obeyed the royal law, therefore he is bound."
I commanded that he be released.
The minister replied,
"Now, all the provisions needed by Your Majesty’s various sons and the members of the inner palace are taken forcibly from others.
There is not a single person who gives them with a pure heart."
The King was greatly distressed.
He divided this land into five hundred portions.
And equally distributed them among his sons.
Then he left home (became an ascetic).
He went to the forest of *Yùtóumó* (Udumbara) trees by the shore of the Southern Sea.
Eating various kinds of fruit.
Gradually, through cultivation and study, he attained the Five Spiritual Powers (*Wǔ Shéntōng*).
At that time, there were five hundred merchants in Yánfútí.
Who entered the sea to gather treasures.
There was a chief merchant.
Named Mǎnyuè.
Having obtained what they wished,
they immediately desired to set off for return.
A *Nāga* (dragon) harbored anger in its heart and wished to harm the merchants.
Furthermore, there was another Dragon King.
Named Mǎ Jiān.
Who was a great *Púsà* (Bodhisattva).
Due to his original vow, he had been born among the *Nāgas*.
He aroused a heart of compassion and rescued all the merchants.
Causing them to safely cross the great sea and reach the shore.
The Dragon King then returned to his original dwelling place.
At that time, there was a great evil *Luóchà* (Rākṣasa).
Following the merchants like a shadow follows a form.
Intending to inflict cruel harm.
This evil *Luóchà*,
on that very day, raised a great evil wind.
At that time, the merchants became confused, disoriented, and lost their way.
They gave rise to great fear, crying and weeping aloud.
Calling out to all the Heavenly Devas, Móxī Shǒuluó (Maheśvara), the Water God, the Earth God, the Fire God, and the Wind God.
And invoking their fathers, mothers, wives, children, and family members,
praying, "Please save us!"
Good man,
I, at that time,
heard their voices with my pure divine ear.
I immediately went to their location.
And consoled and comforted them with a gentle voice:
"Do not give rise to fear. I will show you the way,
enabling you to return safely to Yánfútí."
Good man,
I, at that time,
wrapped a piece of white cloth around my arm, poured oil over it,
lit it as a wick, and spoke words of truth:
"I previously cultivated diligently for thirty years
the Four Immeasurable Minds in the *Yùtóumó* forest.
I ate fruit for the sake of all sentient beings,
and persuaded and transformed eighty-four thousand *Nāgas*, *Yèchā* (Yakshas), and other spirits,
causing them not to regress from *Ānòuduōluō Sānmiǎo Sānpútí* (Anuttara Samyak Sambodhi).
By virtue of these roots of goodness, I now burn this arm,
in order to show the way.
So that these merchants may safely return to Yánfútí."
My arm burned for seven days and seven nights.
These merchants,
immediately returned safely to Yánfútí.
Good man,
I, at that time,
further made a good vow:
"If Yánfútí lacks precious treasures,
and if I am destined to achieve *Ānòuduōluō Sānmiǎo Sānpútí*,
and having achieved my own benefit, I shall act as the chief merchant.
In every single world, I shall rain down treasures seven times.
Moreover, I shall enter the great sea to retrieve the Wish-Fulfilling Pearl (*Rúyì Zhū*).
And in every single world, I shall again rain down various mixed and assorted treasures.
In this sequence, I shall traverse this world completely.
And similarly throughout the measureless, boundless *āsēngqí* worlds in the ten directions."
Good man,
all the vows I made in the past have been accomplished.
Throughout great *jié* (kalpas) equal to the sands of the Gangā (Ganges),
I constantly acted as the Supreme Chief of the Caravans (*Sàbó*).
In *Wǔ Zhuó È Shì* equal to the sands of the Gangā, I rained down various treasures.
Raining them down seven times in a single day.
Causing them to be fully satisfied.
Thereafter, I persuaded and transformed them, causing them to abide in the Three Vehicles (*Sān Chéng*).
In the past, in Yánfútí.
There were four rivers and two great kings.
One was named Póluómén Típó, who unilaterally controlled three rivers.
His people were prosperous but also weak.
The other king was named Fáshé Jiàntí, who only possessed one river.
His population was also small, but the people of his country were all brave and robust.
At that time, Jīngāng Jù was residing in the main palace.
The king thought:
"My troops are brave and fierce, but the water we possess is little.
That country is weak, yet it monopolizes three rivers.
I should now send an envoy to demand one river.
If he gives it to me, we will be close friends.
We will mutually offer gifts of good things from our countries.
If there are difficulties, we will mutually come to aid each other.
If he does not comply, I will take it by force."
He immediately sent an envoy to the Fàntiān Guó.
The envoy fully conveyed the king’s intention.
The Fàn Wáng said:
"My country is rich and substantial, and the population is also large.
Furthermore, this border territory belonged to my father,
who transferred and granted it to me.
Regarding a conflict of strength, I am not inferior to him."
The reply stated:
"This country was granted by my father.
My strength is not diminished compared to yours.
If you wish to settle this by force,
I do not fear you."
The envoy returned and reported fully to the king (Jīngāng Jù).
He immediately mobilized his army and attacked the Fàntiān Guó.
After one engagement, the Fàntiān army was routed.
Seizing the advantage, he pursued them directly to the edge of the city wall.
The multitude, terrified, retreated and dared not come out again.
All the ministers gathered and went to the Fàn Wáng's location.
They said to the Great King:
"The army of the other country is strong, while our country is weak.
By begrudging one river, we have incurred this defeat.
If this continues, we fear we will lose the kingdom soon.
We only wish that you open your mind and grant him one river,
and by becoming close friends, we can secure safety."
The king (Fàn Wáng) sent an envoy to grant one river.
He also promised his daughter to be his consort.
They agreed to mutually present rare objects from their countries.
In times of urgent difficulty and danger, they would mutually rush to aid each other.
At that time, Jīngāng Jù immediately welcomed the daughter and installed her as his consort.
They settled their conflict and withdrew their armies back to their respective countries.
After several days, the king's consort felt that she was pregnant.
After conceiving the embryo,
there was constantly a large, naturally formed canopy of Seven Treasures
resting over her body.
Whether sitting, lying down, walking, or standing, it never left her side.
When ten months were complete, she gave birth to a male child.
His body was purplish-gold in color, and his hair was deep dark blue.
His brilliance and appearance were outstanding, rarely matched in the world.
As soon as the child left the womb, the canopy was over him.
He summoned all the physiognomers to examine the child.
The physiognomers reported to the king:
"The crown prince's virtues and signs are rare in the world."
The king and the assembly of ministers were overwhelmed with joy.
They immediately gave him a name.
His name was Chàluó Gālí, and he grew up until he reached adulthood.
His parents then passed away, and the young king
was installed by the ministers and the populace, due to the Canopy Sign (Gàishì).
After ruling for several years, he went out to tour and observe.
He saw all the people toiling and suffering through farming.
He asked his attendants:
"What are these people doing?"
They replied:
"The state is based on the people, and the people depend on grain for life.
If they do not farm, the lives of the people cannot be sustained.
If the lives of the people cannot be sustained, the state will perish."
The king then said:
"If my fortune and signs qualify me to be a king,
let my people acquire spontaneous grain."
As soon as he finished speaking,
the granaries and baskets of the people were full, and they possessed all sorts of grain according to their wishes.
Later, he went out touring again.
He saw people fetching water, pounding, grinding, and performing tasks.
He again asked his ministers:
"Why are these people doing this?"
The ministers reported to the king:
"Having received the king’s grace, they acquired spontaneous grain.
But the matters still require processing and cooking.
Therefore, the common people are preparing food provisions."
The king then said:
"If my merit and virtue qualify me to be a king,
let all the people in my country possess spontaneous food."
As soon as he finished speaking,
the entire realm acquired spontaneous food.
Later, he went out touring again.
He saw people weaving and making clothes preparations.
He asked:
"Why are these people undertaking this work?"
The ministers replied:
"They are preparing clothing."
The king said:
"If my merit and virtue qualify me to be a king,
cause all the trees in my country to produce spontaneous clothing."
Immediately upon uttering this command,
all the trees in the country produced exquisite clothing.
They were extremely fine and soft, in blue, yellow, red, and white, according to whatever people preferred.
Later, he went out touring again.
He saw all the people competing to make musical instruments.
The king again asked his ministers:
"Why is this so?"
The ministers said:
"They are crafting instruments for entertainment and music."
The king said:
"If I possess fortune and qualify to be a king,
let the trees in my country grow musical instruments, all available according to desire."
After a little more time,
kings, ministers, and people all came to pay respects and offer congratulations.
Finding it was time for the King’s meal, he invited them to stay and partake of food and drink.
At that time, all the ministers,
having received the king's food and drink, which was complete with a hundred flavors,
all reported to the king:
"The food and drink at our homes is meager in flavor.
But the food we have received from the King today is extraordinarily delicious."
The king informed them:
"You ministers and people,
if you wish to always obtain food like mine,
then when I take my meal, those who also eat
will all obtain food like this."
He immediately commanded the attendant official:
"When my mealtime arrives, always beat a large drum,
so that all the people may hear and know.
Those who eat at my mealtime will receive the finest provisions of a hundred flavors."
From then on, the drum was beaten when he ate.
All the people, hearing the sound, thought of food,
and the finest dishes of a hundred flavors appeared spontaneously before them.
The people lived in prosperity and joy.
At that time, King Fàntiān sent an envoy
who came to the kingdom of King Gàishì.
He said to Gàishì:
"When your father was alive,
I granted the river water to your father.
Since your father has passed away, it should be returned to me."
King Gàishì replied to that envoy:
"My present territory and the river water,
were not forcefully taken from you by my own strength.
However, since I became king, I do not burden the people or resources.
Halt for now; I must meet with your king later."
The envoy returned and reported to his king (Fàn Wáng).
The king consented to this idea.
A date was fixed for their meeting.
Both kings advanced, surrounded by their armies.
Each established a large camp on one side of the river.
The two kings boarded boats and met in the middle of the river.
When King Fàntiān first saw Gàishì,
his body color was brilliant, like a mountain of purplish-gold.
His hair was shiny, like deep dark blue lapis lazuli.
His eyes were broad and long, rarely seen among men.
Respect arose within his heart, and he thought Gàishì was Brahmā (Fàntiān).
They arrived, greeted each other, and sat opposite one another in one place.
They discussed the territories of the two countries and deliberated on the matter of reclaiming the water.
Gàishì replied:
"Whatever the people of my country desire appears spontaneously.
There is also no burden of taxes, levies, or royal service."
Before he finished speaking, mealtime had arrived.
King Gàishì's army beat the drum, ready to eat.
Fàntiān thought they intended to kill him, and terrified, he rose to apologize.
He spread out a sheepskin and placed his abdomen on the ground before him.
Gàishì rose himself, pulled him, and made him sit back down.
He said to him again:
"Great King, why are you so terrified?
When my army eats, we always beat the drum.
The reason for this is:
those who eat at my mealtime all obtain the finest provisions of a hundred flavors."
Fàntiān rose again and reported to Gàishì:
"We only wish, O Great King,
that you universally look upon and govern me and my people.
I sincerely wish to surrender and submit.
Cause all the common people to receive your grace and favor."
Consequently, Gàishì ruled over Yánfútí.
All the people obtained peace and happiness entirely.
After ascending the throne, he was seated in the main palace.
The officials and all the various officers stood by as guards and attendants.
When the sun first rose, a Golden Wheel Treasure came from the east.
