Thus, the Seven Treasures arrived in succession, and he ruled the Four Continents (Sì Tiānxià).
All sentient beings received the king's grace and virtue, freely attaining whatever they desired.
The king taught and commanded them all to practice the Ten Virtues (Shí Shàn).
After the end of their lives, they all attained rebirth in the heavens.
The Buddha told Ānán:
"The king Chàluó Gālí was my present self.
King Fáshé Jiàntí was my present father (Śuddhodana).
His mother was Māyé."
At that time, the Cakravartin (Zhuanlún Shèng Wáng).
Seeking the Buddhadharma (Fófǎ), he thoroughly questioned all of Jambudvīpa (Yánfútí),
asking who understood the Buddhadharma.
The Great Cakravartin wished to learn and practice it.
At that time, everyone said:
"In a small, boundless country,
there is a Brāhmaṇa (Póluómén)
who understands and knows the Buddhadharma."
He immediately invited him into the palace,
saying, "Explain it for me."
The Brāhmaṇa said:
"O King, you are extremely foolish.
I studied the Buddhadharma and endured hardship and toil for a long time before achieving success.
How can you now simply wish to hear it immediately?"
The King reported to the master, saying:
"What do you require?"
The Brāhmaṇa said:
"Provide me with an offering (gōngyǎng)."
The King said:
"What kind of offering is required?"
The Brāhmaṇa said:
"If you can carve a thousand sores into your body,
fill them completely with oil, and insert wicks to make lamps as an offering,
then I shall explain the Buddhadharma to you."
Before the King could answer, he quickly stepped down from the high seat.
Thereupon, the Great King
immediately stepped forward, embraced him, and replied:
"Wait a little while and let me consider it; I shall certainly make the offering."
Thereupon, the Great King
entered the palace and informed his various consorts (fūrén):
"I now separate myself from you.
I intend to carve my body to make a thousand lamps as an offering to the Great Master."
The consorts said:
"That which is most valued in the world is one's own body.
How can you damage and harm it?"
The King replied:
"I seek the Buddhadharma for the sake of all sentient beings.
I wish to light the lamp of wisdom in the great dark room
to illuminate your ignorance and the darkness of cyclic existence (shēngsǐ),
cutting off all fetters and attachments so that you may attain Nirvāṇa (Nièpán)."
"How can you people
now oppose my intention?"
At that time, the consorts remained silent and did not respond,
their hearts choked with sadness and sorrow.
The King took leave of everyone, both inside and outside the palace.
He returned to the hall and went to the Great Master's location.
He removed his body ornaments, sat up straight,
and addressed the assembled people, saying:
"Who can carve a thousand sores into my body?"
They all replied in unison:
"We would rather gouge out our own two eyes;
we can never dare to carve the King's body with our hands."
There was a Caṇḍāla (Zhāntuóluó), whose nature was wretched and evil.
Following the sound, he went toward the crown princes (tàizǐ) and said:
"Do not worry or suffer. I have a means
to ensure the Great King’s deed will not be accomplished,
and he will return to govern the country just as before."
The crown princes were delighted upon hearing this.
Then the Caṇḍāla said:
"If you want someone to carve the body, I can do it."
The King said:
"You are now my supreme companion on the Path (dàobàn)."
Then the Caṇḍāla
took a knife shaped like an ox tongue and went to the King's body.
In the blink of an eye, he quickly carved a full thousand sores.
Thinking the King might withdraw his resolve, he threw down the knife and fled.
[The King's attendants] filled [the sores] completely with refined oil, using fine cloth as wicks.
Then the Brāhmaṇa addressed the King, saying:
"Such diligence is truly difficult, yet you accomplished it.
You cultivated this ascetic practice (kǔxíng)
in order to hear the Buddhadharma."
He then spoke half a verse (bànjì):
"All born must die;
the cessation of this is joy."
The King said:
"Those who have compassion for me
ought to memorize and uphold this teaching.
In all kingdoms where people reside, propagate the King’s command."
"Everyone must know:
The Great Cakravartin,
seeing all sentient beings drowned in the sea of suffering
and unable to find the way out, conceived great compassion (dàbēixīn).
He carved a thousand lamps on his body to seek this half verse."
"Everyone should now transcribe this verse,
read and recite it, practice it, contemplate its meaning, and cultivate practice according to its teaching."
The people, though having different mouths, spoke with one voice, praising the Great King, saying:
"Excellent, O Great King!
You are truly a compassionate father,
cultivating this ascetic practice for the sake of all sentient beings."
"We ought to quickly go and transcribe it,
either onto paper or silk, or onto stone,
or onto trees, tiles, gravel, grass, or leaves.
In gorges, paths, major roads, and places where many people walk, we shall all transcribe it."
Those who see or hear it all developed the mind of the Way (dàoxīn).
The King lit the thousand lamps as an offering to the Great Master.
Their light shone far, illuminating the worlds in the ten directions.
From the lamp light, sounds also emerged, reciting this half verse.
Those who heard the Dharma
all developed the mind of the Way.
The light shone upwards until it reached the Trāyastriṃśa Heaven (Dāolì Gōng),
concealing the light of the devas (tiān).
The Lord of Trāyastriṃśa Heaven (Dāolì Tiān Wáng) immediately generated this thought:
"For what reason is there such bright light?"
He immediately used his divine eye to observe the world.
He saw the Cakravartin, who, having cultivated his mind with great loving-kindness and compassion (dà cí'bēi),
had carved a thousand lamps on his body for the sake of sentient beings,
offering them to the Great Master in order to save sentient beings.
"We ought to go and encourage him, advise him, and assist him."
He immediately descended to the world, transforming himself into an ordinary person (fánrén).
He went to the King’s location and asked the Great King:
"You carved a thousand lamps on your body and cultivated this ascetic practice
to seek half a verse—what are you striving to achieve?"
The King replied:
"Good man,
I do this for the sake of sentient beings, so that they may generate the mind of the Way."
Thereupon, the transformed person immediately resumed the body of Śakra (Shì) [Indra].
He replied:
"You made this offering.
Do you seek the position of Heavenly King (Tiān Wáng), Demon King (Mó Wáng), or Brahmā King (Fàn Wáng)?"
[The King] said:
"I do not seek these.
I seek only Bodhi (Pútí) for the sake of sentient beings."
"To bring peace to those who are unpeaceful,
to bring understanding to those who do not understand,
to save those who have not yet been saved,
and to enable those who have not yet attained the Way to attain the Way."
Śakra, the Heavenly King, said:
"Great King,
are you not foolish now?
To seek Bodhi
requires enduring toil and hardship for a long time before success can be achieved."
"How can you desire to seek the supreme Way (wúshàng dào)?"
The King replied to Śakra, the Heavenly King, saying:
"Even if a hot iron wheel were rotating on top of my head,
I would never allow this suffering to diminish my resolve for the supreme Way."
[Śakra] said: "Although you have spoken these words, I absolutely do not believe you."
Then the Cakravartin,
before Śakra, the Heavenly King, made a vow.
"If I am not truly seeking Samyaksaṃbodhi (Sānbódí)
and am deceiving Śakra, the Heavenly King,
may my thousand sores never heal.
If this is not the case,
may my blood turn to milk and the thousand sores be instantly restored."
As soon as these words were spoken, the sores were immediately restored to their original state.
Śakra, the Heavenly King, said:
"Excellent, O Great King!
You truly possess great compassion.
With such ascetic practice, you shall soon attain Anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi (Wúshàng Pútí)."
"When you attain Bodhi, you must first save me."
Then Śakra, the Lord of Devas (Tiāndì Shì),
emitted a great bright light that illuminated the King’s entire body.
He and hundreds of thousands of devas generated the mind of Bodhi (pútíxīn).
The five hundred crown princes, seeing their father’s body sores restored, were immensely joyful and generated the mind of Bodhi.
The twenty thousand consorts and hundreds of thousands of palace maidens did likewise.
In the past, there was a king.
His name was Módiào.
He was known at the time as the Zhējiāyuè wáng (Chakravartin King).
He ruled the four continents (the whole world).
He governed by the True Dharma, and did not oppress the populace.
He constantly practiced compassion, viewing the people as newborn infants.
Human lifespans were eighty thousand years.
The king possessed the seven treasures.
Moreover, he had a thousand sons.
Whips and canes were not used.
The people had no lawsuits or disputes.
No one failed to be transformed (by his virtue).
When the king wished to travel to the four directions, he arrived immediately as he wished.
Tens of millions of people followed behind him, flying.
They carried no swords or weapons.
The people, ghosts, and spirits were all naturally joyful.
He spoke to his attendants:
"If white hairs grow on my head or beard, you must inform me."
The attendant said, "White hairs have grown."
The king summoned the Crown Prince and announced:
"White hairs have grown on my head, and senescence is approaching.
I now establish you as king.
The four continents now belong to you.
You, too, should later tire of worldly pleasures and pursue the Way."
The king then abandoned his kingdom, shaved his head, and studied the Way.
At that time, all the ministers and people wept loudly.
Módiào’s descendants inherited the nation in succession.
A thousand and eighty-four kings, upon their hair turning white, studied the Way.
A thousand and eighty-four generations after King Módiào,
he was born again as a human and continued the royal lineage.
His name was Nán.
He again upheld the True Dharma.
He immediately commanded the central palace (the queen) and all the nobles,
to observe the eight precepts and perform the six monthly fasts.
Ministers, citizens, men, and women all likewise adhered to them.
If *Shāméng dàorén* (monks and practitioners of the Way) lacked clothing or food,
he provided everything, even medicine.
The Tiāndì (Heavenly Emperor) spoke:
"Would you like to meet the various Heavenly Kings in Dāolì Heaven (Trāyastriṃśa)?"
King Nán immediately replied:
"I wish to see them."
Dìshì (Sakra) said:
"I will send a carriage drawn by a thousand horses to welcome the king.
The carriage is named Cài Yùduō."
The fame of King Nán spread far and was heard in Dāolì Heaven.
He was respected and honored by the various Heavenly Kings, who wished to meet him.
Upon seeing the carriage, he exclaimed in surprise:
"This is not something of this world!
Our King's goodness and charity caused a heavenly chariot to be sent to welcome the King."
King Nán mounted the chariot.
The chariot and horses immediately flew.
He immediately instructed the charioteer:
"You must pass by two paths.
I wish to see the path of evil people.
And I also wish to see the path of good people."
Mó replied:
He immediately led him past to view the Nílì Dìyù (Naraka Hell), the place where evil people are tormented and scourged.
Then he ascended to Dāolì to observe the heavenly bliss.
The King arrived at Shì’s (Sakra’s) palace.
The Tiāndì spoke again:
"The various Heavenly Kings greatly desire to meet you."
King Nán consistently preached the doctrine of merit and virtue.
He immediately stepped forward, took his arm, and sat beside him.
King Nán's body transformed to resemble a heavenly being's form.
It was no longer foul like a mortal body.
Celestial music was played, flowers were scattered, and incense was burned.
Dìshì spoke to King Nán, saying:
"Do not be anxious or sorrowful.
You may amuse yourself here with the various performers and music.
They are quite sufficient to make you forget your worries."
King Nán did not consider the heavenly music and entertainment as happiness.
King Nán then spoke to Shì:
"Just as a person borrows an object and must eventually return it,
due to my original vows, I do not take joy in heavenly entertainment."
The King Nán of that time is now my present body.
The Bodhisattva in a past *kalpa*.
This Buddha-world was named Nàdīlán.
The *kalpa* was named Shàntí.
There was a Wheel-Turning King named Wú Zhēngniàn.
He ruled the four continents.
There was a minister named Bǎohǎi.
He was of the Brahmin caste.
He was skilled in divination and physiognomy.
At that time, a son was born [to him].
He possessed the thirty-two marks and eighty minor characteristics.
The marks were perfected by a hundred blessings, and his constant aura extended one *xún*.
Hundreds and thousands of *devas* came together to make offerings.
They gave him the name Bǎozàng.
Afterwards, when he grew up,
he shaved off his hair and beard, donned the Dharma robes, left home life, and attained *Sānbùtí*.
He was still named Bǎozàng, possessing the ten epithets in full.
He immediately turned the Wheel of Dharma.
He caused all sentient beings to attain rebirth in the heavens.
All received liberation, benefiting both *devas* and humans.
The *Shēngwén* great assembly respectfully surrounded Ānzhōuluó City.
This was the place governed by the Sacred King.
Not far from the city was a garden park.
It was named Yánfú.
At that time, the Buddha and the *Shēngwén* great assembly resided in this park.
When the King heard this,
he, along with countless masses, went to where the Buddha was.
Having arrived at the Buddha's location, they bowed their heads to His feet.
They circumambulated three times to the right and withdrew to sit on one side.
The Buddha immediately preached the Right Dharma for the King.
He used various skillful means to instruct, transform, benefit, and bring joy.
The King addressed the Buddha, saying:
"I only wish that the *Rúlái* and the venerable assembly
accept my offerings of robes, food, bedding, and medicine during these three months."
At that time, the Buddha remained silent.
The King bowed his head to the ground, circumambulated the Buddha three times, and returned.
He instructed the lesser kings, ministers, people, and relatives to prepare all the necessary offerings.
At that time, the Minister of Treasures,
in the Yánfú Park, made the ground out of pure gold.
Upon this ground, he constructed a tower of seven treasures.
The four gates of the tower were made of the seven treasures.
Rows of jewel trees stood, and upon these trees were hung jeweled robes and necklaces.
Various jeweled canopies and all kinds of precious vessels [were also prepared].
Furthermore, they scattered various perfumes and precious flowers.
Fine silks, satins, and layered floss served as coverings and furnishings.
They hung silken streamers and the King's golden wheel.
Seven *chǐ* above the ground, in front of the tower observation deck,
the Jewel Woman held a canopy.
Mani jewels were placed together before the Buddha.
The light of the two jewel wheels constantly illuminated the park, making no difference between day and night.
Ox-head *zhāntán* was used for beds and couches.
Seats and white elephants [were prepared].
Jewel trees and various decorations were placed before and behind the Buddha and the Saṅgha.
The Jewel Maiden held seven Mani jewel canopies before the Buddha.
Ox-head *zhāntán* and black *chénshuǐ* [were used],
scattered as offerings.
They played various musical instruments.
Outside the park, the Four Armed Forces Jewel surrounded it completely.
The King arrived at the Buddha's location, performed a reverence, and circumambulated three times to the right.
He personally performed the washing water service and poured the liquids himself.
He offered superior and delicious food to the Buddha and the Saṅgha.
When they finished eating, he put away the bowls, provided water, and rinsed their mouths.
The King held a precious fan and fanned the *Rúlái* and every single *Shēngwén*.
At that time, the King's thousand sons and the eighty-four thousand lesser kings,
all made offerings to every single *Shēngwén*.
Just like the Wheel-Turning King.
Immediately after the meal,
countless beings entered the park to listen to the Dharma.
The *devas* scattered flowers and performed heavenly music
to make offerings to the Buddha.
In the empty sky, heavenly robes, necklaces, and various jeweled canopies
revolved on their own.
Forty thousand blue-clad *Yèchā*
used ox-head *zhāntán* to prepare food for the assembly.
At that time, the Wheel-Turning King
lit hundreds, thousands, countless *yì* and *nàyóutuō* lamps before the assembly at night.
The King wore one lamp on his head,
carried two lamps on his shoulders,
and held four lamps in his left and right hands.
He placed one lamp on each of his two knees,
and one lamp on each of the tops of his two feet.
He made offerings day and night.
Due to the Buddha's divine power, his body felt no extreme fatigue.
It was as if he had entered the Third Dhyāna.
The happiness experienced by the Holy Wheel-Turning King was also like this.
When the three months were completed,
he presented the Jewel Minister of Treasures to the *Rúlái* as a tribute.
He offered eighty-four thousand dragon-head necklaces made of *Yánfútán* gold,
the excellent Golden Wheel Jewel, the White Elephant, the Dark Horse, the Mani Jewel, and the exquisite Fire Jewel.
He offered the Jewel Minister of Treasures, the Jewel Minister of Arms, and all the lesser kings.
He offered Ānzhōuluó City and the smaller cities and towns.
Robes made of the seven treasures, jeweled flowers, piles of jewels, jeweled canopies, and exquisite clothing that was worn.
Flower garlands, necklaces, jeweled chariots, and jeweled weapons.
Jeweled head ornaments, intertwining nets, and all kinds of jeweled nets.
*Yánfú* gold chains and strung pearls.
Superior and exquisite sandals, fine silks, and embroidered furnishings.
Subtle and exquisite seats and seven-jeweled vessels.
Bells, drums, musical instruments, jeweled bells, and *kēbèi*.
Gardens, forests, banners, streamers, vases, jars, lamps, and candles.
Birds and beasts made of the seven treasures, intertwined [with decorations], and exquisite fans.
All kinds of medicines—objects such as these,
each numbering eighty-four thousand,
were given as charity to the Buddha and the Saṅgha.
Having performed this act of charity,
he addressed the Buddha, saying:
"World-Honored One,
there were many affairs in my kingdom,
and some things were deficient; now I repent.
I only wish the *Rúlái* would long reside in this park,
so that I may frequently pay homage and respect."
The King's various sons likewise invited the Buddha and Saṅgha [to accept offerings].
When the three months were concluded,
the *Rúlái* remained silent.
"Good men,
at that time, among the King's thousand sons,
the first Crown Prince was named Bùxùn.
He completed three months [of service].
His offerings were the same as the King's,
except he lacked the Wheel and the other Seven Treasures.
The great minister Bǎohǎi, the Brahmin,
proclaimed throughout Yánfú Tí to all men and women:
"Those who seek and beg for something
must first take refuge in the Three Jewels and generate the Bodhi Mind.
Only then shall they receive your charity."
At that time, throughout Yánfú Tí,
there was no one who did not follow the Brahmin,
receive the Three Refuges, and generate the Bodhi Mind.
Then they received the objects of charity.
At that time, all the various princes each generated an aspiration.
Some wished to become the King of Dāolì Heaven,
some sought to become the Brahmā King,
or sought to become the Māra King,
or sought to become the Holy Wheel-Turning King,
or wished for great wealth,
or sought the level of a *Shēngwén*.
Each one repented before the Buddha and the Saṅgha.
The Holy Wheel-Turning King,
due to his past charity, sought to remain [in the Dharma] now.
past lifetime.
The king was named Jiāngù.
He possessed the four kinds of armies
and served as a Zhuǎnlún Wáng.
He governed the world
and ruled by means of the Dharma.
He was accompanied by the Seven Treasures and the Four Excellences of the Human Realm.
Later, the king lost the Heavenly Wheel.
He summoned Crown Prince Dǐnglái and said,
“I formerly heard from old men
that if a Zhuǎnlún Wáng loses the Heavenly Wheel,
the king surely will not live long.
Crown Prince,
I have already consumed the desires of the human realm,
and now I seek heavenly desires.
I wish to shave my head, put on the robes of the Dharma, and faithfully rejoice in leaving home (becoming a monk).
I now give you the land of the great ocean.
You must teach and command according to the Dharma, making sure no wrongdoing is committed.
If you do so, the Heavenly Wheel will return to its place for you.”
After Jiāngù Wáng had studied the path for seven days, the Heavenly Wheel suddenly vanished during the day.
Dǐnglái Wáng
reported to his father, the king, saying,
“If I cannot be king, what should be done?”
The father king said,
“Perform meritorious deeds corresponding to the Wheel, and it is possible that it will appear.
On the fifteenth day, during the recitation of the precepts,
wash your head and ascend the main hall.
A Heavenly Wheel will arrive from the East.
It is not made by human skill or labor.
Its brilliance is extraordinarily wondrous.
On the fasting day, wash your head and ascend the east side of the main hall.”
Jiāngù Wáng said,
“My son, you should observe and act according to the Dharma toward your sons, daughters, wives, and ministers and citizens,
not just those who are Śramaṇas or Brāhmaṇas—
down to the birds and deer.
You must keep the fast on the eighth, fourteenth, and fifteenth days of the month.
Give charity to Śramaṇas, Brāhmaṇas, the poor, the lonely and elderly, and beggars.
Provide them with food, drink, clothing, blankets, flower garlands, various incense, couches, beds, and dwellings.
Treat them as clear witnesses (of merit).
If there are Śramaṇas or Brāhmaṇas recognized within your domain,
you should go to them and question them in due course
about what constitutes good and bad, and the white and black retribution.
What is the meaning of this present world?
What is the meaning of the world hereafter?
How does one act so as to receive the good and avoid the bad?
You must realize this.
If there are poor people within your domain,
you must bestow
wealth and goods upon them. This is the conduct required to obtain the Wheel.
If your conduct corresponds with this, you will obtain it.
If, on the fifteenth day, during the recitation of the precepts,
you wash your head and ascend the east side of the main hall,
a Heavenly Wheel will come to you, and it will remain thereafter.”
Dǐnglái Wáng
ruled according to the Dharma
and bestowed wealth within his domain.
He became a Zhuǎnlún Wáng, accompanied by the Seven Treasures
and the Four Excellences of the Human Realm.
What are these excellences?
They are the Seven Treasures described above and the Four Excellences described above.
Later, his Wheel,
the Heavenly Wheel, also changed its position
until the Wheel was not visible.
Dǐnglái Wáng, however, did not worry or grieve at first.
He was devoted to pleasure and lust, ignorant of downfall.
He governed the world by force, and the population decreased daily, never increasing.
The former king ruled according to the Dharma, and the population only increased, never decreased.
The wise Brāhmaṇas then addressed him, saying,
“Heavenly King, you must know:
governing the people with desire only causes decrease, never increase.
Like the previous Zhuǎnlún Wángs,
those whose actions corresponded to the law of the Wheel only saw their population increase, never decrease.”
The king asked,
“What must I do?”
They replied,
“Heavenly King, within your domain, there are those skilled in calculation
and among your ministers are those skilled in incantations who know the law of the Wheel.
The King must ensure his conduct corresponds to the law of the Wheel.
If you are in correspondence, it is possible
that the Wheel can be obtained.
On the fifteenth day, during the recitation of the precepts,
bathe and ascend the high hall on the east side,
and you shall obtain the Heavenly Wheel.”
The King asked,
“What is the conduct of the Wheel
that will cause my actions to correspond?”
They replied, “You must act and observe the Dharma toward your wives and children, and down to the giving of material goods.
This is the conduct of the Heavenly Wheel for a Heavenly King.
If you conform to this conduct,
it is possible that the Wheel can be obtained.”
Dǐnglái Wáng
later practiced the Dharma toward his wives and children and down to the poor people.
He hoarded wealth and did not give, so when people became poor and had nothing,
they resorted to stealing.
They were brought before the king for punishment.
The king said,
“Have you, living being, truly taken what was not given?”
He replied,
“Indeed.
If I do not steal, I have no means to sustain my life.”
The king then gave him goods
and told that person,
“You may go, and do not do this again later.”
When other poor people heard that if they stole and appeared before the king, he would bestow goods upon them,
they thought, “Shouldn’t we take what is not given?” and they went stealing again.
Stealing gradually increased greatly.
Human lifespan gradually decreased,
starting from 84,000 years and finally reaching 100 years.
At that time, if anyone transgressed,
the king said,
“If anyone in my domain steals again,
they shall all be placed under a tree and beheaded with a sword.”
The Buddha told the various Bhikṣus:
“In the future, the human lifespan will be ten years.”
In ancient times, there was a king
named Wéntuójié.
He was born from his mother’s head.
Later, he became the Zhējiāyuè Wáng.
East, west, south, and north were all subject to him.
He possessed the Seven Treasures completely.
The king had a thousand sons.
He ruled the Four Continents
for thousands of years.
He contemplated in his heart:
“I possess the Four Continents.
The population is prosperous, and grain prices are low.
My thousand sons are handsome, highly talented, strong, and brave.
Would it not be pleasing if Heaven rained gold and silver for seven days and seven nights?”
Heaven immediately did so for the king,
raining coins, gold, and silver for seven days and seven nights.
The king’s heart rejoiced.
Hearing that the populations in various regions were prosperous,
the king mobilized the Seven Treasures and the four kinds of armies.
The multitudes flew together, successively reaching various countries.
They all submitted, and he governed the world with the true Dharma.
This lasted for thousands of years in each case.
The king then conceived another thought:
“I possess Yánfútí Guó, 280,000 *lǐ*.
I possess Jùyēní Guó, 320,000 *lǐ*.
I possess Fúyú Dài Guó, 360,000 *lǐ*.”
The king heard only that in the north was Yùdānyuè,
where the world was greatly joyous and the populace prosperous.
The king intended to go there.
There were no poor, no tyrannical, weak, or strong
people; there were no slaves, nor differences in status.
All were of the same rank.
“I will let my retinue feast on their naturally grown refined rice,
and their naturally available clothes, coverings, garments, and various treasures.”
So they flew together and entered Yùdānyuē.
The earth was emerald green, and as they proceeded forward,
they saw naturally grown rice, white as snow.
“You all must eat this.”
As they proceeded forward again, they saw various jeweled trees.
A hundred kinds of clothing trees, and gold and silver garlands were all hanging on the trees.
The king asked his close ministers,
“Have you seen these things?”
The close ministers replied,
“Yes, we have seen them.” Having entered the country,
the people were all subdued.
The king ruled the land of Yùdānyuè, 400,000 *lǐ* wide,
for thousands of years.
He thought again,
“I possess the Four Continents.”
The king intended to ascend the precious Mount Xūmí Bǎoshān
to the dwelling place of Dāolì Tiānwáng Shì (Śakra).
He mobilized the Seven Treasures and his entire bureaucracy
and flew together to Mount Xūmí.
He entered the palace of Tiānwáng Shì.
Tiānwáng Shì saw him from afar and welcomed him, saying,
“I have often heard of the King’s virtues and have long desired to meet you.
It is excellent that you, benevolent one, have come.”
He then pulled him to sit together,
giving half of his seat to Wéntuójié Wáng.
As soon as he sat down, the king looked around.
There were celestial jade maidens.
His heart immediately thought,
“I possess the Four Continents and have the power to cause rain of treasures.
If I could cause Tiānwáng Shì to die,
I would like to replace him
and rule Heaven just as I rule the world.”
As soon as this thought arose, he was awakened and departed, immediately returning to the world.
He then contracted a severe illness and was confined to his bed.
The ministers asked the king,
“Did you perhaps harbor the intention of seizing the place of Tiānwáng Shì?”
He replied, “As soon as that thought arose,
I descended to the ground
and immediately suffered this grievous illness.”
He regretted in his heart, saying,
“Humans are never satisfied.
Those who know contentment are few.
I am that Wéntuójié Wáng.”
The king's name was Shànzhù.
At that time, this king managed affairs as the Crown Prince.
And after ascending the throne, he ruled for eighty-four thousand years.
At that time, a fleshy tumor grew atop the king's head.
The tumor was soft.
Like fine, soft Kàibèi cotton.
It gradually grew, but he did not regard it as a distress.
When a full ten months had passed, the tumor split open.
A boy was born.
His form was perfect and handsome.
Foremost among men.
The royal father was joyful.
He was named Dǐngshēng.
King Shànzhù at that time
immediately entrusted the affairs of the state to him.
He abandoned his wife and son, entered the mountains to study the Way (Dào).
A full eighty-four thousand years.
At that time, King Dǐngshēng,
on the fifteenth day [of the month],
while bathing and observing the precepts in a high tower,
immediately, the Golden Wheel Treasure arrived from the East.
The wheel had a thousand spokes, and the hub and rim were complete.
It was not made by craftsmen but achieved spontaneously.
And came forth in response to him.
The king formed this thought:
"I once heard the Wǔtōng Immortal say:
If a Chàlì king,
on the fifteenth day, while in a high tower, bathing and observing the precepts,
if a Golden Wheel comes forth in response,
he should know that he is destined to become a Zhuǎnlún Shèngdì."
He immediately tested it by raising it with his left hand,
holding an incense burner in his right [hand],
with his right knee touching the ground,
and he made this vow:
"If this Golden Wheel Treasure is real and not false,
it should act like the Zhuǎnlún Shèngwáng of the past."
It immediately flew up into the void, circling the ten directions.
It returned to the king's left hand, and the king knew in his heart he would become a Zhuǎnlún Shèngwáng.
Not long after that, the Elephant Treasure appeared again.
It was like a white lotus flower.
With seven limbs resting on the ground.
The king thought,
"This is also just as the Immortal said:
on the fifteenth day, while in a high tower, bathing and observing the precepts."
The king tested it by lifting the incense burner and placing his right knee on the ground.
And he made this vow:
"If this White Elephant Treasure is real and not false,
it should act like the elephants ridden by the Zhuǎnlún Shèngwáng of the past."
Immediately, from morning until evening, it traveled throughout the eight directions,
reaching the edge of the great ocean, it returned and stood in its original place.
The king was greatly joyful.
And again he spoke these words:
"I am now certainly a Zhuǎnlún Shèngwáng."
Not long after that,
the Horse Treasure followed.
The king acted just as before.
Next, the Female Treasure (Jewel Woman) appeared.
Her appearance was upright, subtle, and foremost.
When she touched the king's clothes with her hand,
she immediately knew the suffering and happiness of the king's body.
She also knew the objects contemplated by the king's mind.
Then, the Móní Pearl Treasure spontaneously appeared.
It was like pure azure Liúlí.
As large as a carriage wheel, illuminating one Yóuxún.
If the sky rained down drops as thick as carriage axles,
the power of this pearl could create a great canopy.
Covering one Yóuxún, blocking the heavy rain and preventing it from falling through.
The king considered it just as before.
Next, the Zhǔzàng Chén
spontaneously appeared.
Possessing abundant wealth and treasures, lacking nothing.
His eyes could see hidden treasures.
Whatever the king wished for, he could accomplish it.
They immediately rode a ship together and entered the great ocean.
The king told the Minister of the Treasury:
"I now wish to obtain rare and exotic treasures."
Having heard this, the minister immediately stirred the great ocean water with both hands.
At that moment, ten treasure repositories emerged from his ten fingertips,
to present to the Holy King.
And he addressed the king, saying:
"Great King,
use whatever you need according to your wish.
Those remaining shall sink into the great ocean."
The king was greatly joyful.
Next, the Zhǔbīng Chén
spontaneously appeared.
He was brave, robust, strategic, and foremost in planning.
He was skilled in understanding the four branches of the army.
He could command them to defeat enemies.
And those who were already subdued, he had the power to protect.
The king addressed his ministers:
"You should know
that this Yánfú Tí is peaceful, secure, rich, and joyous.
I now have the Seven Treasures achieved and the thousand sons complete.
What more is there left to do?"
The ministers replied:
"Yes, Great King.
Eastern Fú Pótí, Western Jū Yēní, and Northern Yùdān Yuè
have not yet submitted to your virtue.
The King should now proceed there."
At that time, the King, together with the Seven Treasures and all his retinue, flew through the air and proceeded.
The people of the four directions joyfully submitted to his virtue.
He again addressed his chief ministers:
"My four continents (Four Dīpas) are peaceful, secure, rich, and joyous.
The people are prosperous and have all submitted to my transformation.
What more is there left to do?"
The ministers replied:
"Yes, Holy King.
The Sānshísān Tiān Devas have long lives, are secure and happy.
Relying on their celestial fortune, they have not come to submit to your transformation.
You should now proceed to suppress them and make them submit."
The king again flew into the air and ascended to the Dāolì Tiān.
He saw a tree whose color was verdant green.
He immediately asked his chief ministers:
"What is this?"
The chief ministers replied:
"This is the Bōlì Zhìduōluó Shù.
The Devas of Trāyastriṃśa, during the three summer months,
constantly amuse themselves and enjoy pleasure beneath it."
He also saw a white color, like a white cloud.
He again asked his chief ministers:
"What is this?"
The chief ministers replied:
"This is the Shànfǎ Táng.
The Trāyastriṃśa Devas constantly gather within it to discuss matters of men and heavens."
Thereupon, the Lord of Heaven, Shìtí Huányīn,
knowing the king was outside, came out to welcome him.
Upon seeing him, they held hands, ascended the Shànfǎ Táng, and sat in divided seats.
At that time, the appearances and features of the two kings were equally indistinguishable.
The only difference was that one blinked (the human king). The King said:
"May I now dwell here and be the King of Heaven?"
At that time, Tiān Dìshì
accepted, maintained, read, and recited Dàshèng Sūtras and proclaimed them to others.
Only, he had not yet fully penetrated the profound meanings.
The King then generated wicked thoughts toward Shìtí Huányīn.
He immediately fell down and returned to Yánfú Tí.
Separated from those he loved, both human and celestial, he generated great suffering and distress.
Furthermore, he encountered sickness and immediately died.
Śakra Devānām Indra was Kāshè Fó.
The Cakravartin Holy King is precisely my current self.
The king of Wēizhālìfúduō Guó had the family name Kǒngquè.
His personal name was Píntóusuōluó, and he had a son.
Named Āshūkē, his body was rough and coarse, and his father did not love or cherish him.
Then, later in time,
he sent for skilled physiognomists to examine
which of his sons was fit to be king.
He summoned Āyù’s mother and secretly informed her:
“You should go back to your residence.”
Āyù petitioned his mother,
“The Royal Father is displeased.”
His mother said, “Just go.”
The minister Chénghù asked,
“Why are you going now?”
He answered with the truth of the matter.
Chénghù drove the finest elephant
and provided it for his conveyance.
When providing meals for all the sons, all the vessels were made of treasure.
But not for Āyù.
His mother secretly prepared food and vessels, all of which were excellent.
The physiognomist said,
“Āyù is the most excellent and is fit to be king.”
The great king said,
“I do not value him.
He will certainly be killed. You must search again.”
The physiognomist replied again,
“He who now possesses the fine mount, the fine food, and the fine vessels—
this one is fit to be king, and there is none superior.”
Later, a small kingdom within the territory,
named Déchāshīluó,
intended to rebel.
The king commanded Āyù,
“You are to gather the four kinds of troops and seize that kingdom by surprise.
I will not provide you with weapons, resources, or materials.”
Āyù accepted the command.
He immediately contemplated,
“If I possess merit and ought to be king,
may vessels and food appear spontaneously from the earth, and may the earth immediately tremble and split, producing countless vessels and food.”
The kingdom of Déchāshīluó, hearing of Āyù’s arrival,
decorated the roads and came forth to welcome him upon hearing the news.
All the people eagerly raised up offerings.
He was not disliked at the beginning.
Secondly, the king sent envoys to Qiéshī Guó
to seek two mighty heroes who could crush mountains and overturn peaks.
At that time, the devas spoke,
saying to the two men,
“This is the quarter-ruling Zhuǎnlúnwáng.
He rules Yánfútí and cannot be opposed.
There is no hero or worthy man who does not respectfully pay homage.”
The devas placed the celestial jeweled crown upon his head.
The great king heard this
and immediately dispatched his eldest son, Xiūsīmó.
He heavily mobilized military forces, but ultimately failed to punish him.
The great king
contracted a severe illness and became even more enraged.
When he heard that they were unsuccessful,
he vomited hot blood and immediately died.
Āyù then ascended the great throne.
He appointed Chénghù as the first minister
to manage the affairs of the state.
Xiūsīmó and others, hearing that their father had passed away and that Āyù had been installed as king,
felt intolerable resentment in their hearts.
They immediately gathered troops to attack Āyù.
The two mighty warriors and Chénghù each guarded one gate.
The king stationed himself at the Eastern Gate.
He set up a large fire pit and covered it with material,
ensuring there was no smoke or flame.
He built wooden mechanical men.
The king rode a large wooden elephant,
moving slowly to show weakness.
Xiūsīmó led his sharp troops,
intending to kill Āyù immediately.
Seeing the mechanical wooden men moving sluggishly,
he urged his army straight forward, fell into the great fire pit, and was burned to death.
A distance of 280,000 *lǐ* all became his subjects.
Land dragons and Yakṣas were all subdued.
However, there was one place where a dragon resided,
spanning over three hundred *lǐ*.
He first established a stūpa to hold the Buddha’s *śarīra*.
It was in Luómó Cūn.
It possessed great merit
and alone refused to submit to transformation.
Āyù subsequently recruited and acquired a Zhāntuóluó servant
named Qílìkē.
He was skilled in carrying out slaughter.
He immediately established a prison to punish those who did not submit.
He adorned the prison gate, making it extremely beautiful and magnificent.
Those who saw it loved it, but once they entered, they could not leave.
At that time, a Bǐqiū at the Jīsì recited the Xiūduōluó.
The Xiūduōluó spoke of the matters of hell.
Qílìkē heard it
and accordingly constructed cauldrons of boiling liquid, charcoal furnaces, knife mountains, and sword trees, etc.
There was a Bǐqiū named Hǎiyì.
Early in the morning, he put on his robes, took his alms bowl, and entered the city to beg for food.
By chance, he entered the gate of the hell-prison.
Qílìkē seized him.
The Bǐqiū wept and told him,
“A human body is difficult to obtain, and taking tonsure is hard to encounter.
I have already attained the Dharma.
I beg to be granted one month [of life].”
He replied,
“I have received the king's command.
This absolutely cannot be granted.
I will allow you seven days.”
The Bǐqiū diligently cultivated day and night.
He also saw a prince
speaking with an inner palace woman.
The king commanded that they be handed over to the prison.
Qílìkē immediately pounded them to pieces with an iron mortar and pestle.
The Bǐqiū’s heart was filled with increasing terror.
On the night of the seventh day, he contemplated and attained the stage of Arhatship.
The next day, Qílìkē
placed the Bǐqiū in the iron cauldron.
It contained boiling feces, urine, mixed filth, pus, and blood.
He cooked him with fierce fire, but the Bǐqiū was not damaged even after a period of time.
The Bǐqiū sat alone upon a lotus flower.
The king heard about it and went with all the people to observe him.
The Bǐqiū immediately used his spiritual power to ascend into the sky.
He displayed eighteen kinds of miraculous transformations.
The king was greatly delighted and said,
“Your body is the same as a human body,
but your power surpasses human power.
You should let me know of this [miracle].
I will create divine powers for you.”
He replied,
“The King should praise the Buddha's words, extensively build stūpas and temples, and make offerings to the *śarīra*.
For the benefit of the Dharma, destroy the shortcomings of the Buddha’s extinction,
show incomparable compassion, and triumph over the masters of heterodox teachings (Xiéshī).
I am a disciple.
The Buddha prophesied that the Zhuǎnlúnwáng
would take my *śarīra* and erect eighty-four thousand stūpas,
extensively carrying out all the Buddha’s work.
The king previously established the hell-prison and carried out countless severe killings.
You must eradicate all these wicked deeds and bestow fearlessness.”
The king immediately joined his palms
and confessed his repentance to the Bǐqiū.
He then entered the prison himself and came out.
Qílìkē said,
“I first received the royal command that nothing could be excluded, and once one entered, one could not leave.”
The king said,
“Do you wish to kill me?”
He replied, “That is the rule.”
The king asked,
“When this prison was first established, who entered first?”
He replied,
“Qílìkē entered first.”
The king told the prison guards,
“Place Qílìkē in the shellac house and burn him with fire.
Then destroy the hell-prison and leave.”
Thereupon, he provided the five monastic sections
with a thousand gold, silver, and lapis lazuli jars,
filled with perfumed water,
and made offerings of various foods, fragrant flowers, etc.
After receiving the Eight Precepts,
holding an incense burner in his hand,
he ascended the high palace and invited the monks of the four directions.
He spoke, saying,
“May the disciples of the World-Honored One who are in the four directions
all come here for the sake of accepting and protecting me.”
Then he recited this verse:
“May all the Arhats come to accept and protect me,
I invite the Arhats to all come to this place.”
There were three hundred thousand Bhikṣus (monks).
One hundred thousand Āluóhàn (Arhats).
Two hundred thousand trainees (Śikṣamāṇā).
Countless common people (Pūthagjana).
In one location reserved for the foremost seats,
there was no one sitting.
The king asked Yěshè, saying:
“Why is the seat of the foremost position unoccupied?”
He replied, saying:
“The Buddha said,
‘Among my disciples, there is one who is capable of the lion’s roar,
named Bīntóulú (Pindola).
He is the foremost elder (Sthavira).’”
When the king heard this, his hair stood on end,
like the Kēdànbá (Kodambaka) flower. He further asked:
“Are there any now living
who saw the Buddha before he entered Níhpán (Nirvana)?”
He replied, saying:
“That is none other than Bīntóulú.”
He further asked:
“Can I see him now?”
He replied, saying:
“He should be arriving presently.”
At that time, the king was greatly delighted upon hearing this.
He immediately recited verses of praise.
He joined his palms and gazed upward into the sky,
his eyes not leaving the sight for a moment.
At that moment, Bīntóulú,
accompanied and surrounded by countless Āluóhàn,
descended from the sky and sat in the foremost seat.
The whole assembly rose.
They saw Bīntóulú:
his hair and temples were snow white, his forehead skin and eyebrows
were all merged, covering his face, like the body of a Yuánjué (Pratyekabuddha).
They prostrated with five limbs (five-point prostration) and paid homage to Bīntóulú.
The king licked his (Bīntóulú’s) feet with his tongue, weeping, and recited verses
praising Bīntóulú.
Bīntóulú lifted his eyebrows with both hands and addressed Āyù (Aśoka), saying:
“I have repeatedly seen the Rúlái (Tathāgata) and therefore praise the Buddha’s virtues.”
Āyù further asked:
“Where did you see the Buddha?”
He replied:
“The Buddha, together with five hundred Āluóhàn,
went together to Wángshě Chéng (Rājagṛha) for the rainy season retreat (Vassā).
I was in the assembly at that time.
Also, in Shèwèi Guó (Śrāvastī),
he manifested various supernatural powers in order to overcome the external paths (non-Buddhist doctrines).
Also, he spent the retreat in the Trāyastriṃśa Heaven (Thirty-Three Heavens).
After concluding the dharma teaching for his mother, he descended.
He also went to Āsēngkēshē Guó (Saṃkāśya).
Also, the solitary woman Xiūmótuógā (Sumāgadhā)
invited the Buddha and five hundred Āluóhàn.
The Buddha, by divine power, went to Fēntuóbá tuó Guó (Puṇḍravardhana).
I, by divine power, lifted a mountain
and also reached that country from the empty sky.”
At that time, the Rúlái strictly commanded:
“You must not enter Níhpán.
Guard and maintain my Dharma.”
Āyù further asked:
“Venerable Bīntóulú,
how many people are following you?”
He answered in verse, saying:
“Six tens of thousands of Āluóhàn, all having exhausted the poison of afflictions (Klesha).
Great King, why are you suddenly doubtful? Quickly provide food for the monastic assembly.
When the monastic assembly has finished eating,
I shall speak further with the King.”
The King answered, “So be it.”
All kinds of desired offerings
were provided as offerings.
At that time, the King spoke to the Bhikṣu
named Yīqiè Zhī:
“I shall bestow upon the Sangha one hundred thousand pieces of gold and one thousand silver liúlí (Lapis Lazuli) vases.
Offer them in my name within the great assembly.”
Āyù’s Prince, named Jiūnàluó (Kuṇāla),
went to his father’s side.
Fearing his father, he dared not speak.
He raised two fingers and pointed, proclaiming,
“That Bhikṣu indicates that his merit cultivation (will be) double his father’s aspect.”
The assembly burst into loud laughter.
The King saw the crowd laughing.
He spoke to the high minister Chénghù, saying:
“What you did was not right, that is why people laughed.”
Chénghù replied:
“Many people wish to create merit.
They certainly wish for double.”
Āyù replied:
“I shall present three hundred thousand pieces of gold to provision the monastic assembly,
and three thousand vases filled with fragrant water.”
The King further said:
“Venerable Sir, I will now create a treasury of seven precious jewels.
All the officials and ministers across the great earth,
along with my own body and Jiūnàluó,
I shall bestow all upon the Sangha.”
Formerly, there was a King in Yánfútí (Jambudvīpa),
named Qiánshénnípólí (Khaṇḍavālarāja).
He governed eighty-four thousand villages.
He was compassionate to all; grains were abundant and cheap.
Everyone attained peace and joy, but his mind was not yet satisfied.
“I should seek the wondrous Dharma to benefit them.”
He issued a proclamation to all: “Whoever possesses the wondrous Dharma,
if you speak it for me, you shall receive whatever you desire.”
There was a Brahmin (Pōluómén),
named Láodùchā (Raudrākṣa).
He said, “I possess the Dharma.”
The King welcomed him, paid reverence, and said:
“May the Great Master graciously expound the Dharma for us to hear.”
Láodùchā said:
“Great King,
if today you can cut open your body and ignite a thousand lamps as an offering,
then I shall speak it for you.”
The King issued a command throughout Yánfútí:
“Seven days hence, I will cut my body and light the lamps.”
The common people, bearing sorrow, came to the King’s location, saying:
“Our lives rely on the King, just as an infant relies on its mother.
If the King dies, upon whom shall we rely?
How can you abandon everything for the sake of this one Brahmin?”
The King said: “You all must strictly avoid discouraging my mind set on the Unsurpassed Way.
I swear to seek Buddhahood for this matter.
When I later achieve Buddhahood, I will certainly save you first.”
The masses wept, prostrated on the ground, and felt remorse.
The King then cut his body and placed fat wicks upon it.
He said to the Great Master:
“Please pity me and teach the Dharma
before lighting the lamps.
If my life is severed, I might not get to hear it.”
Láodùchā said:
“That which is permanent must all perish; that which is lofty must also fall.
Assemblies must separate; those who are born must die.”
The King’s joy was immeasurable.
He then commanded the lighting of the lamps.
“The Dharma I seek is for the attainment of the Buddha Way.
I shall illuminate and awaken the multitude with the light of wisdom.”
When he uttered this vow, heaven and earth greatly shook.
Up to the Niṅgjū (Śuddhāvāsa) Heavens, all were also shaken.
Seeing this Great Being (Mahāsattva) disregard his body and life,
they all descended together, filling the sky,
weeping and shedding tears like heavy rain.
The Heavenly Thearch (Śakra) said:
“Such pain and distress—does your mind regret it?”
He replied, “No regret.”
Thereupon, he made a vow, saying:
“If my mind has not regretted this from beginning to end,
may my body be completely restored to health.” Upon thinking this, it was restored.
That King was the body of the Buddha in a former life.
Formerly, in Yánfútí,
there was a Great King,
named Pílèngjiélí (Vilaṁgaka).
His mind loved the wondrous Dharma.
There was a Brahmin,
named Láodùchā,
who went to the palace gate and said:
“I am able to preach the Dharma.”
“If you can nail your body with a thousand spikes,
then I shall preach it for you.”
The King said:
“In Saṃsāra, I have killed my body countless times.

Whether due to the calculation of the Three Poisons (Saṃdūṣa), the gathered white bones were higher than Mount Xūmí (Sumeru), the flowed blood surpassed the Five Lakes, and the weeping tears exceeded the azure sea.
I have carelessly wasted my body and life, but never before for the sake of the Dharma.
Now, I strike the nails to seek the Way.
When I later achieve Buddhahood,
I shall use the sword of wisdom to sever the knots (afflictions) of you all.
Do not hinder my mind set on the Unsurpassed Way.”
The multitude remained silent.
At that time, Láodùchā then spoke verses himself:
“All things are impermanent; all that is born entails suffering.
All Dharmas are empty and non-arising, truly not possessed by the self.”
The King immediately nailed his body with spikes.
Thereupon, he made a vow, saying:
“If I have no eternal regret,
may my body be restored to its former state.”
His body was immediately restored to its original condition.
In the past, there was a kingdom.
Named Bōluónài.
The King was named Dàguāngmíng.
His heart was compassionate to all, and he never went against people's wishes.
There was a minor king who constantly harbored malice and rebellion.
On the monthly observance day (Zhāi day),
the great King used five hundred large elephants loaded with treasures, clothing, and food.
He placed them in the major marketplace and outside the four city gates.
Distributing them as gifts to everyone.
At that time, enemies of the kingdom heard
that the King gave alms and indulged the wishes of others.
Jealousy arose in their hearts.
They immediately gathered their ministers and asked:
"Who can beg for the head of King Dàguāngmíng?"
The reward will be a thousand *jīn* of gold.
A Brāhmaṇa (Póluómén) said, "I can."
The King immediately supplied him with provisions.
When the Brāhmaṇa reached the border,
the ground trembled in six ways.
Birds and beasts scattered, the sun and moon lost their light, and the constellations deviated from their courses.
Red, black, and white rainbows constantly appeared day and night, and meteors crashed down.
Within his kingdom, all the springs and bathing pools dried up.
The Brāhmaṇa went toward the city gate.
At that time, the gate-keeping deity (shén) told the gatekeeper:
"This person is extremely wicked.
He has come from a distant land intending to beg for the great King’s head.
Do not let him enter."
The Brāhmaṇa was delayed for seven days, unable to proceed.
He told the gatekeeper:
"I have come from afar hoping to see the great King."
The gatekeeper immediately went in to inform the King.
The King heard this and immediately went out to receive him with reverence.
He performed a ritual bow before him, as a son bows to his father, and asked where he had come from.
"Did you endure the journey along the dusty road without becoming weary or fatigued?"
The Brāhmaṇa replied:
"I heard in other lands
that Your Majesty gives alms and never goes against anyone's wishes.
Your fame is heard far and wide, reaching up to the azure sky and down to the Yellow Springs (Huángquán).
Therefore, I have come from afar, hoping to gain something."
The King said:
"I give everything; if you seek something, do not hesitate or have doubts."
The Brāhmaṇa said:
"Is that truly so?
I do not need other things.
Now I wish to perform a great sacrifice (Sì).
I beg Your Majesty for your head."
The King pondered to himself:
"Since time without beginning, I have never acted for the Dharma (Fǎ).
I have vainly suffered birth and death, exhausting my spirit.
Now that I possess this body, I seek Bodhi and have vowed to save all sentient beings.
If I do not give it now, I violate my original intention.
By what means shall I then achieve Unsurpassed Bodhi (Wúshàng Pútí)?"
The King said, "Excellent!
I must inspect and arrange the transfer of the nation, the throne, the Queen, and the Crown Prince.
After seven days, I shall give it to you."
At that time, the great King
immediately entered the palace and informed his Queens, saying:
"There is a Brāhmaṇa
who wishes to beg for my head, and I have already promised it to him."
When the Queens and the Crown Prince heard these words,
they threw themselves upon the ground, cried loudly, tore out their hair, and ripped their clothes.
And they spoke these words:
"Your Majesty, of all things valued in the world, nothing is more important than one's own body.
How can you use it today to give away as alms to another person?"
Then five hundred ministers said to the Brāhmaṇa:
"What use do you have for this stinking, rotting head of pus and blood?"
The Brāhmaṇa replied:
"I begged for it myself; why do you ask me?"
The ministers said:
"Since you have entered our country, we ought to question you, and you ought to answer us."
The Brāhmaṇa,
though he truly wanted to answer, was frightened in his heart, fearing his life would be cut short.
The ministers then said:
"We now grant you fearlessness (Wúwèi) for the sake of the great King.
Poor Brāhmaṇa, why do you need this head?
We five hundred people
will each create a head made of the seven jewels (Qībǎo).
We will exchange them with you, and also give you whatever else you require."
The Brāhmaṇa said:
"I do not need them."
Since the ministers could not fulfill their wish,
they cried out sorrowfully and appealed to the great King:
"How can you bear to abandon the kingdom, the Queens, and the Crown Prince,
eternally forsaking us for the sake of one Brāhmaṇa?"
The King said:
"I am now giving up this body for the sake of all."
The First Minister, hearing the King's resolute words,
immediately thought to himself:
"How can I bear to see the great King abandon his body and life?"
He immediately entered a quiet room and killed himself with a knife.
At that time, the great King
went into the rear garden and called the Brāhmaṇa to him.
"You begged me for my head.
Out of compassion for you, I will not oppose your wish.
May I, in future lives, gain the head of wisdom and give it to you all."
Having spoken these words, he arose and pressed his palms together (Hézhǎng).
He bowed toward the Buddhas (Fó) of the ten directions and said:
"May the awesome spiritual power of the Buddhas and the revered Bodhisattvas (Púsà) of the ten directions guard and assist me, ensuring that this deed is accomplished."
He told the Brāhmaṇa, "Take it away as you wish."
The Brāhmaṇa said:
"Your Majesty has the strength of a powerful warrior. Should the pain become unbearable, you might change your mind or even harm me instead.
If Your Majesty can truly do this, why not tie your hair to a tree branch?"
When the King heard these words, compassion arose in his heart.
"This Brāhmaṇa is old and weak; if he cannot sever my head, he will lose a great benefit."
He immediately followed his suggestion and tied his hair to the tree.
He told the Brāhmaṇa:
"After you sever my head, place it in my hand.
I shall then use my hand to present it to you."
The Brāhmaṇa then approached, holding the knife.
At that moment, the tree deity (shù shén) immediately grabbed the Brāhmaṇa, who fainted and fell to the ground.
At that time, King Dàguāngmíng said to the tree deity:
"Instead of assisting me, you create an obstacle!"
The tree deity heard this and felt sorrow in its heart.
It immediately cried out, "Alas, suffering!"
In the empty sky, blood rained down without clouds.
Heaven and earth greatly trembled, and the sun lost its brilliant light.
The Brāhmaṇa then severed the King’s head and carried it back to his home country.
At that time, the five hundred Crown Princes and all the ministers
collected the remaining body and bones of the great King and erected a stūpa (tǎ) for offerings.
The Buddha (Fó) instructed Ānán:
"The First Minister who, upon hearing that King Dàguāngmíng gave his head as alms,
could not bear it in his heart and immediately abandoned his life, is now Shèlìfú.
The King Dàguāngmíng at that time is now Shìjiā (Śākya)."
The King was greatly diligent
and regarded all sentient beings as a mother loves her child.
There was no Buddha in the world.
When Shìtí Huányīn (Sakra Devānām Indra) was about to die, he thought to himself:
"Where can I find an omniscient person (Yīqiè Zhì Rén)?"
He traveled everywhere asking difficult questions but could not resolve his doubts, so he sat down in sorrow.
The master of skillful transformation, the deity named Píshǒu Jiémó Tiān,
asked:
"Lord of the Devas,
why are you sorrowful?"
He replied:
"I am searching for an omniscient person but cannot find one, which is why I am sorrowful."
Píshǒu Jiémó said:
"There is a Bodhisattva who, through giving (bùshī), upholding precepts (chíjiè), meditation (chándìng), and wisdom (zhìhuì), will soon achieve Buddhahood.
Dìshì (Indra) asked, "Who?"
He replied:
"It is King Shībǐ (Śibi) of the Yōushīnà lineage."
Shìtí Huányīn said to Píshǒu Jiémó:
"Let us now test him."
Píshǒu Jiémó transformed himself into a pigeon with red eyes and red feet.
Shìtí Huányīn transformed himself into an eagle.
The eagle swiftly chased the pigeon, which flew straight in and nestled beneath the King's armpit.
Its entire body trembled with fear, its eyes fluttered, and its voice was strained.
At that time, many people spoke amongst themselves:
"The King is compassionate and benevolent, and he ought to protect all beings.
The pigeon, being a small bird, seeks refuge with him just as a person enters their house."
At that time, the eagle was perched on a nearby tree.
It said to King Shībǐ:
"Give me back my pigeon; this is what I should consume."
The King then spoke to the eagle:
"I accepted this refuge first; it is not yours to consume.
When I first conceived the intention [of Buddhahood], I vowed to save all sentient beings."
The eagle said:
"Your Majesty wishes to save all sentient beings.
Am I not included in 'all'?
Why do you alone show me no pity and deprive me of my food?"
The King replied:
"What food do you require?
I have made a solemn vow that any sentient being who comes to seek refuge with me must be saved and protected.
Whatever food you require, I shall provide it to you."
The eagle said:
"I require fresh, hot meat."
The King thought to himself:
"Such a thing is hard to obtain; it cannot be acquired without killing a living creature.
How can I kill one being and give it to another?"
After his reflection was settled, he said:
"The flesh of this body of mine
is constantly subject to old age, sickness, and death; it will soon rot. If the eagle requires it, I shall give it."
Having thus reflected,
he called for a person to bring a knife and cut the flesh from his thigh to give to the eagle.
The eagle said to the King:
"Although Your Majesty gives me hot meat,
you must, according to principle, ensure that the weight of the meat equals the weight of the pigeon."
The King said:
"Bring the scales, and weigh the meat against the pigeon."
He continued cutting the King's flesh until it was entirely gone, and only then did the weight equal that of the pigeon.
He reprimanded his own heart, saying:
"You must remain resolute; you must not become confused or faint.
I have vowed to ferry all sentient beings who have fallen into the great sea of suffering.
Why are you languid and faint? This suffering is minimal, but the suffering in the hells is far greater.
I possess wisdom, diligence, precept-keeping, and meditation, yet I suffer this pain.
How much more so those in hell who have no wisdom?"
When his mind was determined, heaven and earth trembled in six ways.
The great sea surged, and withered trees sprouted flowers.
Heaven rained fragrant showers and scattered famous flowers.
Celestial maidens sang praises, declaring that he would certainly achieve Buddhahood.
Dìshì said to the King:
"Did your heart not become vexed or depressed from the pain and hardship of cutting your flesh?"
The King said:
"My heart is joyous, neither vexed nor depressed."
Dìshì said:
"Who would believe you?"
The King then spoke a vow:
"If, when I cut my flesh and blood flowed, I did not feel anger, vexation, or mental depression, and if I did this solely in search of Buddhahood,
I pray that my body shall immediately be restored to normal."
Immediately, it became as it was before.
had a separate dwelling place. The ground was
exceedingly flat and spacious. At that time, the Buddha went
and sat down. Fàntiān (Brahmā), Dìshì (Indra),
and the Four Heavenly Kings, various kings of the human realm, such as Píngshā Wáng (King Bimbisāra),
and others, each spoke to the Buddha, saying:
"We wish to prepare a high seat for the World-Honored One." The Buddha said:
"Wait a moment. I myself know the time." At that time, among the lay devotees,
there were those who believed in external paths. They each established seats worth hundreds of thousands
[of currency]. There were also those who joyfully believed in making offerings to the Buddha. From the first day of the month up to the fifteenth day,
the kings of Mógēdī (Magadha), Píngshā, and others took turns setting up offerings. In the center of all the seats, naturally appeared a lion seat made of seven jewels.
The Rúlái (Tathāgata) sat upon it. At that time, everyone took their seats.
At that time, there was a Dānyuè (donor/patron). On that subsequent day, he set up an offering and presented the Buddha with a toothbrush twig (Yángzhī).
The World-Honored One chewed it and threw it behind him. It immediately became a great tree, its roots, stems, branches, and leaves flourishing and luxuriant.
At that time, the great assembly witnessed the Buddha’s spiritual power, rejoiced, praised him, and found it unprecedented. The Buddha, the World-Honored One,

used countless expedients and various methods of preaching the Dharma, causing them to rejoice. At this moment, countless hundreds of thousands of people in the assembly removed dust and impurity and attained the pure Dharma Eye.

In this way, the manifestation of spiritual transformations continued until the fifteenth day, varying greatly. The great assembly saw the Buddha's divine powers and transformations and were all greatly joyful.
The Buddha preached the Dharma for them, and they attained the pure Dharma Eye. At that time, Mógē Wáng (King Magadha) and Píngshā Wáng (King Bimbisāra),
on the fifteenth day, offered food to the Buddha and the Saṅgha, along with Bōluóshūtí Wáng,
Yōutuóyán Wáng, Fànshī Wáng, Bōsīnì Wáng (King Prasenajit) and Mòlì Fūrén (Queen Mallikā),
the elder Líshīdáduō, Fùluónà, and the entire great assembly
all set up offerings. When they were finished eating, the bowls were put aside, and water was passed around. Píngshā Wáng then took a low seat and sat in front of the Buddha.
At that moment, the World-Honored One
undid his cross-legged (meditation) posture and stretched his foot onto a footstool. At that time, the earth shook six times,
in eighteen ways. At that moment, the mark of the wheel (Cakra) beneath the Buddha's foot—a wheel with a thousand spokes, its rim perfectly formed—
the characteristics of the spoked wheel were complete. Brilliant light shone
and illuminated the Three Thousand Worlds. Mógē Wáng,
seeing this, immediately rose from his seat, bared his right shoulder, knelt with his right knee on the ground, and spoke, saying:
"World-Honored One, what merit did you perform in the past
to attain these auspicious marks?" The Buddha addressed Píngshā:
"In the past ages, on the land of Yánfú Tí (Jambudvīpa), there was a king named Lìzhòngshēng (Benefiting Sentient Beings).
At that time, the kingdom was rich and fertile, and the populace was thriving. He governed 84,000 cities and 5.5 billion villages.
The city where the king resided was named Huìguāng (Wisdom Light). The king's first consort was named Huìshì (Wisdom Affair).
Initially, they had no children. In order to seek an heir, they paid homage to all the devas, mountains, rivers, ghosts, and spirits, seeking wishes everywhere.
Later, she became pregnant. She reported to the king, saying:
'I am now pregnant.' The king doubled the offerings and services of food, drink, clothing, and medicine.
Later, she gave birth to a son whose appearance was upright and handsome. On the day the child was born,
84,000 hidden treasures naturally sprung forth, lining up according to the items they contained. The king said to the mother:
'Name the child Huìdēng (Wisdom Lamp).' Later, the king passed away.
The Crown Prince was eight or nine years old. His mother taught him skills, arts, writing, calculation, riding, and driving.
When he reached fifteen years old, the ministers petitioned, saying:
'The Great King has passed away; you should now ascend the throne.' The Crown Prince replied:
'In my previous life, I was a king for six years. Afterward, I fell into hell for 60,000 years.
Because of this, I cannot be king.' The ministers said:
'Is there any expedient way for you to become king?' He replied:
'If all the speaking beings in Yánfú Tí, male or female, practice the Ten Virtues (Shí Shàn), then I shall be king.'
When the ministers and people heard the Crown Prince's decree, they immediately announced the order in the four directions:
'The people of Yánfú Tí shall all practice the Ten Virtues and refrain from killing sentient beings.'
The ministers then reported fully to the Crown Prince: 'You may now ascend the throne.'
The Crown Prince immediately succeeded to the throne. The ministers petitioned the King, saying:
'When the King was first born, 84,000 hidden treasures naturally sprung forth.
They should now be collected and placed in the royal treasury.' The King said:
'They do not need to be stored in the treasury.' He immediately ordered that, wherever they appeared,
at the heads of the four crossroads, they should be given as alms to Śrāmaṇas (Shāmen), Brahmins (Póluómén), the poor, the lonely, and the old.
The ministers immediately followed the King's decree. According to where the treasures were located,
at the gates of the 84,000 cities and the heads of the four crossroads, they were distributed as alms.
At that time, Dìshì (Indra), transformed into a man, spoke to himself, saying: 'The King ordered me to practice the Ten Evils.'
The ministers reported to the King: 'Was there such a decree?'
The King answered: 'My previous order
was that all speaking beings within Yánfú Tí shall practice the Ten Virtues. I never issued such a statement [as practicing Ten Evils].'
He immediately rode his jeweled elephant to where the man was. The King asked:
'Did you say that Huìdēng taught you to practice the Ten Evils?' The transformed man replied: 'That is truly so.'
The King asked further: 'Can you practice the Ten Virtues?'
He replied:
'If you wish to achieve the path of a Bódàosà (Bodhisattva), I must eat your flesh raw and drink your blood raw.
Only then will I practice the Ten Virtues.' The King thought thus:
'Since beginningless time, I have gone through all kinds of suffering, revolving through the Five Paths and fully experiencing slaughter and cutting.'
He immediately took a knife, cut the flesh from his thigh, put the blood into a vessel, and handed it to the man, saying:
'Man, you may eat the flesh and drink the blood.
Diligently practice the Ten Virtues.' The transformed man immediately vanished
and did not reappear. He returned, manifesting the body of Dìshì, and asked:
'Was your act of giving for the sake of one world or for the sake of the Four Great Continents?'
The King said: 'It was to seek the unsurpassed path and to deliver those who have not yet been delivered.'
Dìshì poured divine sweet dew upon the wound, and it immediately healed, benefiting sentient beings. The father king at that time is my father king now.
The first consort is my mother now. King Huìdēng is myself."
"In the past, there was a king
named Dàlì (Great Strength). He possessed great roots of goodness.

He lavishly established gatherings for giving (Dāna), fulfilling whatever desires were sought. If food was needed, he gave food; even elephants, horses, cattle, sheep, land, and property, he gave all of it away.
At that time, Mùlián (Maudgalyāyana) said:
'Your charity is great.' At that time, Dìshì transformed into a Brahmin (Póluómén).
He went to the King's place and said: 'O King, since your charity is so great,
I now require a part of your body.' The King thought to himself:
'This Brahmin does not require wealth or goods. He has come now purely to ruin my great act of charity.
If I do not give him a part of my body,
I will destroy my own great assembly of giving.' Having thought this, he spoke to the Brahmin, saying:
'I will give you a part of my body; you may cut it off and take it away. But today, many beggars have gathered here, coming from the four directions.
I should ensure that they are all satisfied.' The Brahmin said:
'I, alone, am still not satisfied.
What talk is there of others?' The King immediately took a knife and cut off his own arm,
and gave it to the Brahmin, without any regret.
Because he gave everything away with a single heart, the arm was restored to health. Since Dìshì acted as an obstacle and cause [of difficulty],
his celestial blessings immediately ended, and he fell into the Ābí (Avīci) hell. King Dàlì is myself.
Dìshì is Tiáodá (Devadatta)." The Buddha was in Shèwèi Guó.
At that time, Ānán (Ānanda), after the midday meal, was meditating in the forest.
He thought: "The Rúlái appeared in the world, and all kinds of sentient beings have received peace and joy.
Furthermore, what roots of goodness did Jiāochénrú (Kondañña) and the others plant
so that when the gate of the Dharma first opened, they were the first to enter?" He used his thoughts to report to the Buddha.
The Buddha told him:
"Jiāochénrú and the others, in distant past kalpas, on this Yánfú Tí,
there was a great king named Míluó. He had 20,000 consorts and 10,000 ministers. The King possessed the Four Immeasurables (Sì Děng) and never tired or grew weary.
He taught the people the Ten Virtues, and the four directions admired him, and the kingdom was peaceful and joyous. The various plague demons constantly consumed human blood.
At that time, the people restrained their body, mouth, and mind, diligently practicing the Ten Virtues. The evil plagues dared not invade, and the demons became hungry, weak, and distressed.
At that time, five Yakṣas (Yèchā) came to the King's residence. 'We rely on the blood and vital essence of humans to maintain our lives.
Due to the King's instruction and guidance, everyone practices the Ten Virtues. We are hungry and thirsty, with no way to survive.
O Great King, since you possess kindness and compassion, how can you not pity us?' The King harbored pity and sorrow.
He immediately let blood flow by piercing five parts of his body. The five Yakṣas collected the blood and drank it, experiencing immeasurable joy.
The King said:
'Remember to cultivate the Ten Virtues. I now use the blood of my body to relieve your hunger and thirst.
When I later achieve Buddhahood, I shall use the Dharma body's blood of morality (Jie), concentration (Dìng), and wisdom (Huì) to eliminate your three poisons and settle you in Nirvāṇa.'
King Cílì (Compassionate Power) at that time is myself now. The five Yakṣas are Jiāochénrú and the others now.
I vowed in life after life that I would deliver them first."
. This king diligently maintained the precepts
, always relying on truthful speech
. In the morning, he rode in a carriage, taking his palace women into the park to play
. As he exited the city gate, a Brāhmaṇa (Póluómén) came begging
. The king replied, "Yes" (Nuò)
. "I shall respectfully heed your request
. Wait until I return from my outing, after I have entered the park to bathe and amuse myself"
. At that time, there was a king with two wings named Lùzú
. He flew down from the sky, seized the king from among the palace women, and carried him away
. The women wept and wailed grievously; the entire country was shocked, and the city, inside and out, was agitated and terrified
. Lùzú carried the king, soaring through the air, until they reached his dwelling mountain
. He placed him among ninety-nine other kings
. King Xūtuóxūmó wept, his tears falling like rain
. Lùzú spoke to him
. "Great Kṣatriya (Chàlì) king
, why do you weep like a small child
? Life ends in death; meetings end in separation"
. King Xūtuóxūmó replied
. "I do not fear death; I regret having broken my promise
. Since I was born, I have never spoken falsely
. This morning, when I left the gate
, a Brāhmaṇa (Póluómén) came to beg from me
. I promised him then that I would bestow charity upon my return
. I did not foresee impermanence, thus disappointing his expectation
. I have brought the guilt of deception upon myself; that is why I weep"
. King Lùzú said
. "If you fear false speech
, I permit you to return
. After seven days, finish giving charity to the Brāhmaṇa (Póluómén), and then immediately return here
. If you do not return after seven days, I have the power of wings, and seizing you will not be difficult"
. King Xūtuóxūmó
, upon returning to his original country, wholeheartedly practiced giving (bùshī)
. He established the crown prince as the new king
. He gathered the people and apologized, saying
. "My wisdom was insufficient for governing, and my administration did not accord with the Dharma; please forgive me
. As of today, this body is no longer mine, and I must immediately return"
. The people of the entire country and all his relatives kowtowed, begging him to stay
. "We beg the King to reconsider and protect this country; do not worry about Lùzú, the Ghost King (Lùzú Guǐwáng)
. We will set up iron fortifications and elite soldiers
. Even if Lùzú is supernatural, we will not fear him"
. The king said
. "This cannot be done"
. And he spoke a verse (jì)
. "Truthful speech is the foremost precept; truthful speech is the ladder to heaven
. Whether humble or great, great falsehood leads to entering hell (dìyù)
. I now uphold truthful speech, preferring to abandon my body and life
. My heart will hold no regret"
. Having thought thus
, the king immediately departed and arrived at the place of King Lùzú
. Lùzú saw him from afar, was joyful, and said
. "You are a person of truthful speech who did not fail the covenant
. However, all people cherish life
. To escape death and still return to keep your promise, you are a great person"
. At that time, King Xūtuóxūmó praised truthful speech
. "Truthful speech is the essence of being human
. Untruthful speech is not human"
. He thus praised truthful speech and condemned false speech in various ways
. Lùzú heard this, and his faith became pure
. He spoke to King Xūtuóxūmó
. "Now I release you, and the ninety-nine other kings shall also return to their native countries
. This is the fulfillment of Sīla Pāramitā (Shīluóbōluómì)"
. In the past, there was a king
. His title was Sàwòtán (Dāna); whatever was sought, he would not deny people's wishes
. The king's name spread and was heard in the eight directions
. Mañjuśrī (Wénshūshīlì) wished to go and test him
. He transformed into a young Brāhmaṇa (Póluómén) who came from a distant country and arrived at the palace gate
. The king was extremely pleased
. He immediately came out to greet him, asking the practitioner where he had come from
. The Brāhmaṇa (Póluómén) said
. "Hearing of the King's merits and virtues, I have come to see you and now wish to beg
." The king said, "Excellent
. Whatever you wish to obtain, do not hesitate
." The Brāhmaṇa (Póluómén) said
. "I wish to obtain your body to serve me as a slave
, and the Queen (fūrén) to serve me as a maidservant
." The king was greatly delighted
. He replied, "Excellent
. My body can certainly be taken
. I wish to belong to the practitioner to serve and obey
. As for the Queen, she is the daughter of a great king
. I must go and ask her
." Thereupon, the king entered and spoke to the Queen
. At that time, the Queen (fūrén) immediately followed the king out
. She personally spoke to the practitioner, saying
. "I wish to dedicate my body to serve the practitioner
." The Brāhmaṇa (Póluómén) said
. "You must follow me
. Both of you must be barefoot, not wearing shoes
, following the custom of slaves and maidservants
." They both said, "Yes, we obey the master's instructions"
. So he took the slaves and walked away down the road
. He used a transformed person to replace the king and the Queen (fūrén)
, to manage the affairs of the state, maintaining everything as before
. The Queen (fūrén), having long dwelled deep within the palace, was unused to arduous labor
. Furthermore, she was heavy with child, being several months pregnant
. Walking and following the master, her whole body ached, and the soles of her feet were wounded and broken
. Unable to go on, exhausted, she lagged behind
. Then the Brāhmaṇa (Póluómén) turned back and scolded her
. "You are now a maidservant, and must abide by the rules of a maidservant
