. You cannot display the demeanor you had before
." The Queen (fūrén) knelt and reported, "I dare not be lazy or neglectful
. I am merely a little exhausted and have stopped to rest"
. He called out, "Come quickly
! Hurry and follow behind me until we reach the national marketplace
." He sold the slave and maidservant separately, each to a different master
. They were separated by several *lǐ*
. At that time, an elder (zhǎngzhě) bought the slave and made him guard the charnel house
. He was ordered to collect taxes from all those who came to bury the dead, but he was not allowed to tax unfairly
. The maidservant, at that time, belonged to a great family
. The mistress (fūrén) was very jealous and made her work day and night without rest
. Several months later
, the maidservant gave birth to a baby boy in her hardship
. The mistress (fūrén) angrily said
. "You are a hired maidservant, how can you have this child
? Seize him and kill him
." Following the great master's instruction, she immediately killed her child
. She carried him away to bury him
. She went to the place where the slave was kept, and they met
. They did not speak of their arduous suffering, and neither held resentment in their hearts
. After speaking thus
, in an instant (xūyú), they suddenly felt as though they were dreaming
. They were back in their own country, sitting upon the main throne, exactly as before
. And all the officials, the secondary palaces, and the palace women were all as they had been
. The crown prince who had been born was also naturally alive
. The King and the Queen (fūrén) wondered internally what circumstances had caused this
. Mañjuśrī (Wénshūshīlì)
sat in the empty sky upon a jeweled lotus flower, manifested his body and characteristics, and praised them, saying
. "Excellent
. Your giving (bùshī) is now utterly sincere like this
." The King and the Queen (fūrén) leaped up with joy
. They immediately stepped forward and bowed
. Mañjuśrī (Wénshūshīlì) spoke the sutra Dharma for them
. The three-thousand great thousand world system (sānqiān chàtǔ) was completely shaken
. All the people covering the entire country developed the intention for the unsurpassed true and correct Way (Dào)
. The King and the Queen (fūrén) simultaneously attained the realization of the Unborn Dharma (Bùqǐ Fǎrěn)
. The Buddha told Ānán
. "The King at that time was myself
. The Queen (fūrén) at that time is now Qúyī
. The Crown Prince at that time is now Luóyún
." In the past, in Jambudvīpa (Yánfútí), there was a great king
named Qúlóupó
. He ruled eighty-four thousand small countries
. He sheltered and nourished the people and creatures
. He thought to himself
. "I only provide everyone with wealth and goods
. I have never provided the teaching of the Way (Dào); this is truly my fault
." He issued a decree throughout the country: "Whoever possesses the Dharma and can speak it for me, I shall provide for all their needs"
. Vaiśravaṇa (Píshāmén Wáng) transformed into a Yakṣa (Yèchā) and came to the palace gate
. He said, "Whoever wishes to hear the Dharma, I will speak it for them
." The king personally came out, welcomed him, and performed the rite
. He first gathered his officials and requested to hear the Correct Dharma (Zhèngfǎ)
. The Yakṣa (Yèchā) announced
. "Learning the Dharma is difficult
. I require the King's beloved wife and son
. Give them to me to eat
." The king immediately ordered the Queen (fūrén) and the Crown Prince to be given to the Yakṣa (Yèchā) as food
. All the officials wept
. The king's resolve did not waver
. The Yakṣa (Yèchā) finished eating
. He immediately spoke a verse (jì), saying
. "All conditioned phenomena (xíng) are impermanent; all who are born experience suffering; the Five Aggregates (Wǔyīn) are empty and without characteristic
. There is no self (wǒ) and nothing belonging to the self
." The king's heart was joyful and without regret; he proclaimed the verse to all devas and humans, urging them to memorize and maintain it
. Vaiśravaṇa (Píshāmén Wáng) returned to his original form
. The Queen (fūrén) and the Crown Prince were perfectly intact, as before
. He praised the king's remarkable distinctness
. The Buddha said
. "The King of that country at that time is myself now"
Formerly there was a man-eating ghost.
It became a king among men.
It constantly ate human flesh and used it for its cooking provisions.
Neighboring countries were conquered, and ninety-nine kings were captured.
The ninety-nine kings addressed the Rólàchà Wáng (羅剎王) saying:
"In a neighboring country there is a king,
named Shànxù (善宿).
He loves to practice charity and cultivate the virtue of a Bodhisattva; whatever is sought or requested, he never opposes people's wishes.
If Your Majesty can manage to capture him, we shall willingly accept death without regret."
At that time, the Rólàchà Wáng immediately raised ghost troops.
He went to seek his opportunity.
He happened upon Shànxù strolling in his outer garden, viewing the bathing pond.
There was a Fànzhì (梵志) who took leave of his family to study abroad.
Now, the custom of a Fànzhì, when taking leave to depart,
is to inform his parents, saying:
"I am now leaving home to join companions in study.
The day of my return is yet uncertain.
Should I become utterly lacking in wealth or goods, I will borrow a loan from the King.
When I return, I shall certainly repay it."
This man's studies were successful and completed.
When he came home, he only saw empty houses and no people.
He immediately asked the neighbors:
"Where are my parents, brothers, and sisters now?"
The neighbors informed him, saying:
"After you left to study, they borrowed the King's goods and wealth, and had nothing with which to repay the debt.
They were seized by the King and are now in prison."
The man thought to himself:
"My family is poor and in dire straits, possessing no treasures.
If I go to the prison to personally see my parents, I will also be arrested.
Suffering the same distress, I will not escape the King's law.
It is fitting that I stay outside for now, change my appearance, switch my clothes, and secretly seek resources.
Only after fully repaying the government's debt can they be released."
The man further thought:
"In a neighboring country there is a king,
named Shànxù.
He cultivates virtue and constantly practices charity.
I should go there and sincerely appeal to him.
He will certainly not refuse me, allowing me to fully repay the King's goods."
He immediately went there and begged the King for the required sum.
The King said, "Excellent!
I shall provide for you.
Wait until I have finished bathing.
Then I shall bestow the gift upon you.
Wait a little longer, do not worry; I will not break my word."
When the King went to the bathing pond, he was seized by the ghost troops.
The King immediately looked back, sorrowful and weeping.
The Ghost King asked:
"We hear that the King is benevolent, gentle, and universally loving, helping everyone without exception.
Though you face distress and difficulty, why are you sorrowful?"
The King replied to the ghost, saying:
"I have practiced giving throughout my life and have never had remorse.
Just now, there was a Fànzhì outside begging for a request.
I promised but have not yet given it to him.
This is why I am sorrowful."
The Ghost King addressed the King:
"The King maintains sincerity and trustworthiness, which has never changed throughout his life.
I shall now release the King. When you return after completing the charity, then I shall know the King's heart."
The King was able to return to his palace.
He opened the treasury and bestowed charity, fully satisfying the man's needs.
He immediately honored his promise and went to the location of the Ghost King.
The Ghost King said:
"Do you not fear me?
Why have you come to accept death?"
Shànxù replied in verse:
"Practicing merit and not practicing evil, all results from the law of past deeds.
I ultimately do not fear the path of death, like a boat crossing a swift current."
When the Ghost King heard this, he felt shame and remorse internally.
He changed his heart, reformed his conduct, and thought of cultivating good roots.
He immediately told King Shànxù:
"What I have heard today is rare among men.
I now release the ninety-nine kings.
I relinquish this position.
I request that the King take charge, governing and transforming them with the Dharma; I shall lead the multitude of ghosts back to their dens and caves.
If we both maintain the precepts, I shall naturally visit you frequently."
They then parted ways, and each returned to his place.
The ten thousand people hailed it with rejoicing, and the country was peaceful and prosperous.
They jointly practiced the Ten Virtues and cultivated no evil deeds.
Shànxù accumulated practices ceaselessly.
Afterwards, he achieved Buddhahood.
Under the King of Trees, he recited the previous verse again.
Formerly there was a king,
named Yuèhēi (惒黑).
He resided in a border region and had not yet seen the sacred transformation (of the Dharma).
He served external doctrines, and the entire country held wrong beliefs.
They killed living creatures for sacrifices. The King's mother was taken ill.
They sought all kinds of doctors and spirits over the course of years.
But she did not recover or improve.
He then summoned two hundred Bóluómén (婆羅門) within the country,
and addressed them, saying:
"My great Lady has been gravely ill for a long time, and I do not know the cause."
The Bóluómén said:
"The stellar mansions are inverted, and the Yīnyáng is unbalanced; this is the cause."
The King said:
"What method should be employed to make her recover and be cured?"
The Bóluómén said:
"You must level and cleanse a spot outside the city walls.
Offer suburban sacrifices to the Four Mountains, the Sun, the Moon, and the stellar mansions.
You must obtain one hundred head of livestock of various different types, and one small child, kill them, and sacrifice them to Heaven.
The King must personally lead his mother to kneel and bow and plead for her life; only then will she be cured."
The King immediately obeyed the command.
He drove out people, elephants, horses, cattle, sheep, and all types of creatures, including insects.
Their mournful cries along the road shook heaven and earth.
They went out through the eastern gate to approach the sacrificial altar, where they were to be killed for the sacrifice to Heaven.
The Buddha, bearing great compassion, pitied the King's stubborn foolishness.
He immediately led his disciples and proceeded toward that country.
The King saw the Buddha from afar.
He was like the rising sun or the full moon, his glorious form shining brilliantly.
All the common people who saw him felt love and respect.
The sacrificial victims all wished and prayed for release.
The King paid homage to the Buddha, joined his hands in respect, knelt for a long time, and inquired of him, saying:
"My mother has been ill for a long time, and good doctors and spirits have been consulted everywhere without exception.
Now I am about to perform rituals to apologize and give thanks to the stellar mansions, the Four Mountains, and the Five Peaks.
I am pleading for my mother's life, hoping that she may recover."
The Buddha said:
"If you desire grain and food, you must practice plowing and sowing.
If you desire great wealth, you must practice charity.
If you desire long life, you must practice great compassion.
If you desire wisdom, you must practice study.
If you perform these four matters, you will obtain the fruit according to what you sow.
Sacrifices are frivolous and chaotic, mistaking evil for righteousness.
Killing life in order to seek life is far removed from the path of life."
Then he spoke in verse:
"If a person lives a hundred years, diligently serving all gods under heaven,
using elephants and horses for sacrifice, it is not equal to performing a single act of compassion."
The Buddha released a dazzling, bright light that illuminated Heaven and Earth.
All beings in the Three Evil Paths and Eight Difficulties were filled with joy.
When the King heard the Dharma and saw the light, he immediately attained the Path (Dào).
When the mother heard this, her heart was delighted, and her illness was eliminated.
The two hundred Bóluómén felt shame and remorse, repenting their errors, and all became Shāmen (沙門). Thereafter, the King loved his people as if they were his own children.
The five grains ripened abundantly, and there were no disasters or plagues in the country.
People lived to be eighty thousand years old, and he protected all sentient beings with compassion, like Tiāndìshì (天帝釋, Indra).
He believed in and respected the Three Treasures, constantly practiced the Ten Virtues, and led and transformed all the people in the four quarters.
At that time, there was a poor person who stole someone else's property.
The owner caught him.
The King asked, "Why did you steal?"
He replied:
"Because I am poor and cannot sustain myself, I reluctantly violated the sacred law."
The King said sorrowfully:
"When the people are hungry, it means I starved them.
When they are cold, it means I left them naked.
It is within my power to ensure there are no poor people in the country.
The suffering and happiness of the people rests entirely with me."
He immediately declared a great amnesty throughout the country.
He brought out the hidden treasures and bestowed them upon the hungry and cold.
Carts, horses, medicines, and food were taken as desired.
The King also gave charity to flying birds, running beasts, down to insects and fish.
Afterwards, the country was abundant, and the people were wealthy, guiding each other by the Dào.
There was no mention of the Ten Evils.
Ghosts and spirits aided them with joy and protected the country.
The five grains yielded bumper harvests, and families had surplus wealth.
They immediately attained the Five Blessings:
First, long life.
Second, a better complexion.
Third, virtue moving the eight directions.
Fourth, being without illness and increasing strength.
Fifth, peace and tranquility within the borders, with minds constantly joyful and content.
In the past, there was a king.
He offered a *jiāshā* (monastic robe) to the Buddha.
Thereby, he generated the intent for the unexcelled and equal deliverance.
When the Buddha entered *Pánníhuán* (Nirvana), his body was incinerated,
but the *jiāshā* was not burned.
The Buddha’s *shèlì* (relics) were collected, and a stupa was erected.
Everything perished, but the *jiāshā* remained.
Later, the practice of offering to the stupa ceased.
The *jiāshā* accumulated years and seasons.
The Dharma was no longer heard.
Whenever a fasting day arrived,
the king, ministers, and countless common people
offered incense, flowers, banners, and canopies to the *jiāshā*.
This tradition was passed down continuously, and they imitated the practice, never letting it lapse.
Later, there was a king.
He thought,
“The former kings and I have reverently served this robe.
What merit should be gained?
What kind of robe is this?”
No one knew.
People from the Buddha’s land came for trade and livelihood.
They informed the king, saying,
“In our country, there is a king
named Yuè tóu tán.
He gave birth to a sage son, whose courtesy name was Xī dá.
He left home to study the Way, and his title is called the Buddha.
He possessed the thirty-two marks.
He specifically wore this robe.”
When the king heard this, he rejoiced.
He dispatched an envoy to invite the Buddha.
The merchant said,
“If you invite the Buddha, you need only burn incense, bow, and invite him from afar.”
The king immediately burned incense, making an offering to invite the Buddha.
“I wish the Buddha would, tomorrow,
condescend his spirit.”
The smoke of the incense traveled toward the Buddha, encircling the Buddha seven times.
It immediately transformed in the empty sky into a floral canopy.
At that time, the Buddha smiled.
The radiance of his breath illuminated countless *chà* (Buddha-fields).
He ascended into the empty sky and merged with the incense.
They combined to form a floral canopy, which returned together into the crown of his head.
Ā nán questioned the Buddha,
“From which direction did this incense smoke come?”
The Buddha fully informed Ā nán.
Immediately, the three thousand great thousand worlds experienced a great tremor.
The city gates of that country all turned to gold.
Musical instruments like the *kōnghóu* played without being struck.
The pearl bracelets of the women all made sounds.
Hundred-year-old dead trees grew again.
The king was greatly terrified and called out, asking his people,
“What strange calamity is this
that causes my kingdom to shake?”
The merchants informed the king,
“Wherever the World-Honored One goes, auspicious signs appear first.
This is all due to the merit of the King.”
The king immediately leaped with joy,
and proclaimed to his ministers and people,
“Burn incense to welcome the Buddha!”
The king wished in his heart,
“Let me become a *Luóhàn* (Arhat), a personal attendant of the World-Honored One.”
The king presented the *jiāshā* to the World-Honored One.
The Buddha could not support it.
It sank down into the earth, passing through countless Buddha-fields in the lower direction.
It then hovered in the empty sky.
The *Púsà* (Bodhisattvas) in the lower fields asked their Buddhas,
“Where did this *jiāshā* come from?
It does not fall to the ground.”
The Buddha said,
“Wait a moment, and there will naturally be a response.”
Shìjiāwén Fó
instructed Mùlián, Shèlìfú, and five hundred other disciples to go and retrieve the *jiāshā*.
Though they used all their divine powers, none could reach it.
The Buddha told Wénshū to go retrieve it, but he too could not support it.
The Buddha said,
“This *jiāshā*
was offered to a previous Buddha by a person in a former life,
who generated the Great Way intention.
After countless lifetimes,
it has again come to belong to this king.
Now he offers it to me again.
However, in the middle of this process, he desired to obtain realization,
wishing to become a *Shēngwén* (Śrāvaka).
Therefore, the *jiāshā* cannot be supported.
Why is this?
The former intent was profound, so the *jiāshā* was light.
The later ambition was small, so the *jiāshā* became heavy.”
When the king heard the Buddha’s teaching, he immediately repented,
saying, “I am a king.
I do not wish for the people in my kingdom to desire my position.
If they have such an intention,
I call it rebellious.
The Buddha is the World-Honored One,
therefore I did not dare to aspire for the fruit of Buddhahood.”
The king and his ministers all generated the intention for the unexcelled and equal deliverance.
The *jiāshā* naturally leaped up from the earth.
The king lifted the *jiāshā*,
held it up, and presented it to the Buddha.
He vowed, “May all crawling beings in the ten directions
receive this *jiāshā*.”
Thereupon, the Buddha preached a sutra for him.
The king and his ministers were all established in the stage of non-retrogression.
In a past *kalpa* (eon), there was a great king named Sàhédá. He offered gifts to all *shā mén* (ascetics) and all people, never contradicting their wishes.
A *Bóluómén* (Brahmin) boy from another country lost his father when he was young.
He lived alone with his mother, elder sister, and younger siblings in extreme poverty.
His mother said,
“Now we are poor and cannot support ourselves.
You should go to King Sàhédá and beg.”
The boy replied to his mother,
“I do not know anything yet.
I must first acquire knowledge, and only then should I go.”
His mother did not permit it.
The boy first borrowed one ounce of gold on credit.
This was enough to provide a year’s worth of grain.
He then left home to travel and study. After one year, he returned.
His mother saw him and immediately asked,
“Have you gone to see King Sàhédá?”
The boy replied to his mother,
“What I have studied is not yet complete. I must study further.”
The mother said,
“The previous gold is already exhausted.”
He immediately went back to the house where he had previously borrowed the money.
He borrowed one more ounce of gold.
The owner of the gold said to the boy,
“The gold you took before has not yet been returned to me.
If you want to borrow more,
you must bring your mother and sister to sign the bond, and only then can you get it.
If you cannot repay it when the time comes, you shall become my slaves.”
The boy then made the bond, took the gold, and gave it to his mother.
He left home again to study.
Another year passed.
His knowledge was roughly complete, and he wished to return.
He traveled toward King Sàhédá.
On the road, he was seized by the creditor.
He, his mother, sister, and younger siblings were taken back, chained and bound.
The Brahmin boy said to the creditor,
“Your chaining me now is ultimately useless.
It would be better to release me to go to King Sàhédá.
I can beg for something and use it to pay you back.”
The owner allowed him to leave.
At that time, a foreign country raised an army
to seize King Sàhédá.
When the King heard this, he reflected,
“Human life is short and inevitably returns to impermanence.
I have always enjoyed practicing generosity.
I possess compassion and forbearance without injury. I do not wish to engage in conflict with that country.
Why is that?
We simply must not prepare for defense,
nor should we be afraid.
We should merely prepare to go out, meet them, perform the ritual salute, show respect, and serve them.
We shall receive their command and let it supersede mine.”
The ministers asked the king,
“If another country enters the border, how can we not prepare?”
The king remained silent and did not respond.
This happened three times.
The king said,
“There is no need to resist.
Do as I said before.”
The ministers accepted the instruction.
The king said, “Very good.
Everyone settle your families and be careful not to cause alarm or disturbance.”
In the middle of the night, the king removed his seal and sash and quietly vanished and left.
That king entered the country and immediately took the throne.
He then offered a reward to seek Sàhédá.
The reward was extremely heavy.
King Sàhédá traveled five hundred *lǐ* outside the country and saw a Brahmin boy from afar.
The two met.
The king asked,
“Where are you going now?”
He replied,
“I wish to go to Sàhédá.
I lost my father when I was young,
and my family is extremely poor.
I used my mother, sister, and younger siblings
to act as collateral for debt.
I want to beg to redeem them
and save myself as well.”
The king said,
“I am Sàhédá.
Another king wants my country.
I do not wish to cause harm, so I am avoiding him.”
The Brahmin boy threw himself onto the ground and wept loudly,
unable to control himself.
The king then counseled him to rise and told him there was no need to weep again.
“I shall give you what you seek right now.”
The Brahmin boy said,
“The king has now lost his country.
What can you use to save me and fulfill my begging?”
The king replied,
“The king of that country offers a very heavy bounty for me.
You can cut off my head and take it to him.
You can obtain whatever you ask for there.”
Thereupon, the Brahmin boy recited a verse, saying:
“Killing one’s mother and father in the world leads certainly to *Nílì* (hell).
If I were to now harm the King, the sin would be no different.
I truly cannot bear to commit evil against the Great King.
I would rather my life end now than commit a rebellious act.”
Sàhédá Wáng.
Again, he spoke to the son of the Brahman, saying:
"If you are unwilling to take my head,
then you may cut off my nose and ears and send them (to the other king).
This is not because I regret (my promise to) the king."
The son of the Brahman said:
"I also cannot bear to do that."
The king said:
"Then binding and sending me is also acceptable."
The son of the Brahman replied:
(I only agree because I) know that king will do no harm (to you).
Thereupon, the king and the son of the Brahman journeyed together to return.
When they were approaching the country, about twenty *lǐ* away,
the king said:
"You should bind me."
The son of the Brahman then bound the king.
All the people of the country, men and women, old and young, wept uncontrollably and were heartbroken.
It was worse than losing their parents, as they proceeded before the palace gates.
The ministers immediately went in
and reported to that king, saying:
"The Sàhédá whom you previously solicited has already been bound and sent by the son of the Brahman.
He is now at the palace gate."
That king immediately ordered:
"Hurry and present him."
When all the officials and commoners saw Sàhédá Wáng,
there was no one who did not fall to the ground and weep.
That king, Jié Rén Wáng, also shed tears.
He then asked his ministers:
"Why are you all weeping?"
The ministers reported, saying:
"We see Sàhédá Wáng,
who abandoned his kingdom and gave it to Your Majesty,
and further offered his body as a gift to the son of the Brahman.
He does not regret what he has done, and that is why we weep."
When that king, Jié Rén Wáng, heard all the officials and commoners say this,
he immediately fell to the ground and wept loudly, unable to control himself.
He immediately asked the son of the Brahman:
"How did you originally obtain this king?"
The son of the Brahman answered the king, saying:
"I was truly poor.
My mother, older sister, and younger brother had incurred debts.
Hearing that this Sàhédá Wáng greatly loves giving charity,
I came from far away, hoping to beg for resources to redeem my mother, older sister, and younger brother, and thus sustain our lives.
I met him on the road, and we exchanged greetings.
Sàhédá Wáng said to me:
'I have now abandoned my kingdom and given it to another king.
I have nothing with which to grant your request.'
At that time, I was terribly distressed, heartbroken, and helpless.
Then Sàhédá Wáng
instructed me to cut off his head and bring it to Your Majesty.
At the time, I dared not.
He again ordered me to cut off his nose and ears and send them.
I again refused.
Consequently, we journeyed together back, and he ordered me to bind him and send him.
The essence of what you asked is exactly this."
Regarding that king, Jié Rén Wáng,
upon hearing what the son of the Brahman said,
immediately fell to the ground again, shedding tears.
He spoke,
commanding his ministers:
"Quickly undo the king's bonds, bathe him, clothe him, give him back his royal seal and ribbon, and reestablish him as king."
Immediately, he ascended the throne and ruled the country as before.
Thereupon, that king knelt down, clasped his hands, and praised him.
He spoke in verse, saying:
"While residing in my original kingdom, I heard from afar of the Great King's virtue;
Now having come here, seeing Your Holiness surpasses what I heard.
Majestic are the merits you have accumulated, like a mountain of pure gold;
Your strength is so firm, there is none who can shake it.
The conduct I now witness the King performing is truly unparalleled in the world.
I request to return the kingdom to you, and further offer the domain where I reside.
I pray to return to my native land, practice reverence, and perform the duty of a minister.
I dare not be arrogant again, and I shall serve the King as I would the revered heavens."
The Buddha said:
"Sàhédá Wáng at that time was I myself.
The king of that country was Shèlìfú.
The son of the Brahman was Tiáodá.
The completion of my Six Pāramitās,
the Thirty-Two Marks, the Ten Strengths, and the fulfillment of various merits—
all were due to Tiáodá's kindness.
Tiáodá is my worthy spiritual friend (kalyāṇa-mitra).
He is also a worthy teacher."
In the past, in the kingdom of
Mótianluó, there was a king named
Rì Nán. He studied and mastered spiritual understanding, and nothing hidden remained unseen.
Realizing the impermanence of the world, he said:
"My body will inevitably decay and become waste matter in the world.
What kingdom can be protected?"
He renounced honor and abandoned pleasure, putting on the supreme monastic robes.
A single bowl of food was sufficient.
He received the precepts of a Śramaṇa (monk) and lived in the mountains and forests for thirty years.
Beside his tree residence, there was a pit thirty *zhàng* deep.
At that time, a hunter, while riding in pursuit of a deer, fell into the pit. There was also a crow and a snake.
They were all startled and fell at the same time, their bodies severely injured.
They cried out to heaven mournfully with the sound of the desolate and destitute.
The ascetic, saddened, shone a light and saw them.
Tears streamed down his neck.
Approaching the pit, he announced:
"You need not worry; I shall pull you out."
He immediately lowered a long rope, and they either held onto it with their mouths or grasped it.
Thus, they regained their full lives.
They all thanked him at the same time, saying:
"We have received the boundless benevolence and kindness of the ascetic,
allowing us to see the light of day.
We vow to spend the rest of our lives providing for the needs of the multitude."
The ascetic replied:
"I was a king.
My kingdom was great, my people numerous, my palaces wealthy, my consorts beautiful, and I was superior to all other states.
Whatever I wished for was instantly answered, and nothing was unobtainable.
Yet I regarded the kingdom as enmity and the six sense objects (*liù chén*) as six swords,
constantly slicing my body.
Six arrows shot my form.
Because of these six evils,
one cycles through the three miserable realms (*sāntú*).
These are unbearable in their cruelty, and I am greatly disgusted by them.
Therefore, I gave up the kingdom to become a Śramaṇa.
I desire to attain the Buddha Way and enlighten all sentient beings, allowing them to return to their original source.
How can I be satisfied with saving merely your three lives?
Return now to your former dwelling places and see your kin.
Instruct them to take the Three Refuges and not violate the Buddha's teachings."
The hunter said:
"I have lived in this world for many years and have seen good people,
but none like the disciple of the Buddha.
You forgive yourself and save the multitude, hiding your good deeds without broadcasting your name.
If the ascetic ever lacks anything, please come to my house and beg for a small offering."
The crow said:
"My name is
Bō. If the ascetic faces difficulty, please call my name.
I will surely rush to you."
The snake said:
"My name is
Zhǎng. If the ascetic is troubled,
please call my name, and I will certainly come to repay your kindness."
After saying their farewells, they each departed.
One day, the ascetic went to the hunter's dwelling.
The hunter saw him approaching from afar
and told his wife:
"That inauspicious person is coming.
I order you:
Prepare food, but set it out slowly.
He must not eat after noon."
The wife saw the ascetic.
She put on a false face, deceitfully kept him waiting while pretending to set out the meal, and engaged in empty talk until noon had passed.
The ascetic departed and returned to the mountain.
He saw the crow and called its name, saying, "Bō."
The crow asked:
"Where have you come from?"
He replied: "I came from the hunter's place."
The crow asked: "Have you eaten yet?"
He replied: "He was setting out the meal, but it wasn't finished, and noon had passed, so I left without waiting."
The crow said:
"Such ominous and ill-fated creatures are difficult to save with compassion!
They violate benevolence and betray kindness—a treacherous person!
I have no food or drink to offer you in support.
Just wait and sit down patiently.
I will fly instantly to the kingdom of Bānzhē.
I saw the King's consort sleeping, and among her headdresses was a bright Moon Pearl."
The crow carried it back in its beak and offered it to the ascetic.
When the consort awoke, she sought it but did not find it.
She immediately reported this matter to the top.
The King commanded his officials and people:
"For anyone who finds it,
the reward will be one thousand *jīn* of gold and silver each, and one thousand head of oxen and horses each.
If anyone obtains it and fails to report it, the crime will extend to the extinction of his entire clan."
The ascetic gave the pearl to the hunter.
The hunter tied up the ascetic, tortured him, and reported to the King,
saying:
"Where did you obtain it?"
The ascetic pondered deeply:
"If I reveal its owner, the crow of an entire kingdom will surely die.
This is not the way of a Buddha's disciple."
He remained silent and endured the torture, suffering a thousand blows from the staff.
He neither resented the King nor hated the hunter.
He made a vow of compassion, saying:
"May I attain Buddhahood and deliver all beings from suffering."
The King buried the ascetic, leaving only his head exposed, intending to execute him the next day.
The ascetic then called the snake, saying, "Zhǎng."
The snake replied: "No one in the world knows my name
except the ascetic.
When he raises his voice to call me, there must be a reason."
It rushed forward and saw the ascetic.
It asked:
"How did you come to this?"
The ascetic then narrated the entire cause of the event.
The snake wept, saying:
"O ascetic, though you possess benevolence and compassion, even between heaven and earth, you still meet with disaster!
How much more so for the wicked—who will protect them?
I shall enter the palace and bite the Crown Prince to death."
The snake gave the ascetic a magical medicine to apply, and his wounds immediately healed.
The snake night entered the palace and bit the Crown Prince, who instantly expired.
After leaving the body for three days, the King issued an order, saying:
"Whoever can revive the Crown Prince
shall be granted half the kingdom to rule."
The entourage carried the body toward the mountains and passed near the ascetic's location.
The ascetic said:
"I can revive him."
The King heard this and was overjoyed.
The ascetic applied the medicine to the Prince's body.
Suddenly, the Prince spoke, saying:
"Why am I here?"
The attendants fully explained the situation.
The Prince returned to the palace, and everyone, great and small, rejoiced and danced. The King granted the ascetic half the kingdom as reward.
The ascetic accepted nothing.
The King realized, saying:
"If he refuses half the kingdom, how could he possibly have committed theft?
Ask him how he obtained the pearl.
His virtuous conduct is so lofty, yet he suddenly suffered this calamity."
The ascetic fully recounted the entire story.
The King's face was bathed in tears.
He announced to the hunter:
"You have performed a meritorious service for the state.
Summon all your nine degrees of kin
immediately; I wish to reward them heavily."
All the kin, great and small, proceeded to the palace gate.
The King said:
"This unbenevolent, ungrateful head of wickedness shall be completely executed."
The ascetic entered the mountains to practice the Way, striving diligently without tiring,
and eventually was reborn in heaven.
The ascetic at that time is my present self.
The crow is
Qiūlùzǐ. The snake is
Ānán. The hunter is
Diàodá. And the wife is
Huáipán Nǚzǐ."
In the past, in Jambudvīpa, there was a great king
named Xiānyù.
He greatly revered the Mahāyāna, and his heart was utterly pure and good.
He was free of crudeness, wickedness, jealousy, and stinginess.
His mouth constantly spoke loving and virtuous words.
His person constantly protected the poor, the isolated, and the solitary.
His acts of giving and diligence never ceased.
At that time, there was no Buddha, Śrāvaka (hearer), or Pratyekabuddha (solitary enlightened one).
The King loved and delighted in the Mahāyāna Vaipulya (Fāngděng) scriptures.
For twelve years, he served the Brāhmaṇas.
After providing for all their needs for more than twelve years,
and concluding the offering and settling arrangements,
he then made this declaration:
"Masters, you should now give rise to the Bodhi mind (awakening mind)."
The Brāhmaṇas replied:
"Great King,
the nature of Bodhi is non-existent.
The Mahāyāna scriptures are likewise.
Great King,
why do you wish to make people the same as empty space?"
When the King heard the Brāhmaṇas slander the Vaipulya teachings,
he immediately cut off their lives.
Because of this cause and condition, he did not fall into hell.
The power of safeguarding and upholding the Mahāyāna scriptures
is thus.
In the past, the King of the kingdom of Tiānluó had a Crown Prince
who wished to ascend the throne.
His name was Bānzú.
He received instruction from the outsider teacher, Luótuó,
who said he should take the heads of a thousand kings to offer sacrifice to the tomb spirit, after which he could ascend the throne.
He had already obtained nine hundred and ninety-nine kings,
lacking only one king.
He then traveled ten thousand *lǐ* north and captured King Pǔmíng.
Pǔmíng told Bānzú:
"I request permission to spend one day feeding Śramaṇas and paying homage to the Three Jewels."
Bānzú permitted it.
Pǔmíng then relied on the Dharma of the Seven Past Buddhas.
He lectured the eight thousand verses of the Prajñāpāramitā twice that day.
The First Dharma Master spoke a verse to the King:
"When the kalpa-fire concludes, heaven and earth burn through. Mount Sumeru and the vast oceans
are all reduced to ashes and smoke. The blessings of the gods and dragons perish therein, fading away.
If the dual realms of heaven and earth still perish, what permanence can a kingdom possess? Birth, aging, sickness, and death
turn ceaselessly without boundary. Deeds run contrary to wishes, and sorrow and grief bring harm.
Desire is deep, misfortune is heavy, and sores and tumors are everywhere. The three realms are all suffering;
what reliance can there be in a kingdom? Fundamentally, existence comes from non-existence, and conditions create all things.
Those that flourish must decline; the substantial must become empty. Sentient beings are foolish and ignorant,
all dwelling as if in a phantom illusion. Sound and echo are both empty; the homeland is likewise.
The conscious spirit is formless, falsely riding the four snakes. Ignorance is the precious elephant
taken as the chariot of pleasure. The body has no fixed master; the spirit has no fixed home.
If the body and spirit are separated, how can there be a kingdom?"
King Pǔmíng.
Together with his retainers, attained the emptiness of the Dharma Eye.
The King personally realized the space-equal concentration, heard the Dharma, and attained awakening.
He returned to the place of King Bānzú in the state of Tiānluó Guó.
He informed the nine hundred and ninety-nine kings, saying:
When the time of death approaches, everyone should recite the Gāthā of the *Rénwáng Bōrě Bōluómì* of the Seven Past Buddhas.
Bānzú asked:
What Dharma should be recited?
King Pǔmíng immediately answered the King with the above Gāthā.
The King heard this Dharma and attained emptiness samādhi.
The nine hundred and ninety-nine kings also, having heard the Dharma,
all realized the concentration of the Three Gates of Emptiness.
At that time, King Bānzú was exceedingly joyful.
He spoke to all the kings, saying:
I was misled by heterodox teachers.
The fault is not yours.
All of you should return to your respective countries.
Each of you should invite a Dharma Master
to lecture on the names, flavors, phrases, and assemblies of the *Bōrě Bōluómì*.
Then King Bānzú entrusted the kingdom to his younger brother.
He left home to practice the Way and attained the patience of non-arising Dharma.
This is spoken of in the chapter on the Ten Kings' Stages.
King Ājāshì said to Wénshū Shīlì, “I only wish that you would extend your kindness and grace, and condescend to come to my palace to eat.”
Wénshū Shīlì replied: “What is sufficient can be considered an offering.”
Moreover, the Buddha Dharma is not based on clothing and food.
The King said:
“By what, then, should I give alms?”
He replied:
“If you penetrate deeply into the profound subtlety of the matter, and examine it closely and sincerely,
without defilement and without attachment,
without doubt,
and without fear or difficulty.
Furthermore, contemplate all dharmas, and do not contemplate existence or non-existence, nor contemplate past, future, or present completion.
Also, you should not contemplate that all visible beings should receive pity.”
The King said:
“Everything you have said is contained within the Dharma; there is no difference.
But solely for the sake of the body, you ought to show compassion and accept my invitation.”
Wénshū Shīlì said:
“Stop now.
The Way is not for the sake of this [body].
If you drink or if you eat,
if the King does not contemplate the existence of a self, a being, a life, or a person,
by contemplating thus, you obtain compassion.” The King was greatly joyful and asked:
“How many people are there?”
Shèlìfú said:
“Five hundred people.”
He ordered them all to eat at the palace.
Returning to the city, he commanded the preparation of food of a hundred flavors and arranged his palace hall.
He set up various banners, pennants, curtains, canopies, and flower parasols.
Flowers were strewn upon the ground, and everything was scented with perfume.
He set up five hundred high seats.
The palace, the city, and the inner neighborhoods were all thoroughly swept clean.
They were spread with flowers and incense, and the people came to receive them reverently.
Wénshū Shīlì, in the time it takes to extend an arm, arrived in the East.
Passing eighty-two thousand Buddha-lands.
The Buddha's title was Cháng Míngwén.
That Buddha’s name was Wéijìngshǒu.
He is now present in the world.
There was an assembly of Bodhisattvas, with no other paths.
That realm constantly turns the Āwéiyuèzhì Dharma wheel.
From that land constantly issues the sound of the Three Jewels.
Wénshū Shīlì addressed the Buddha:
“I wish that you would fully command all
Bodhisattvas to go to the Shāhē Chàtǔ (Sahā realm),
to eat at the palace of Ājāshì.”
The Buddha said:
“Those who wish to go, go.” When the King heard this,
Wénshū Shīlì arrived, followed by twenty-two thousand five hundred Bodhisattvas.
The number of Bhikṣus was five hundred. The King thought to himself:
“I have only prepared provisions for five hundred people; how shall I make the offering now?”
At that time, the Heavenly King named Xiūxīxīn,
together with the venerable Yèchā named Jīnpí,
both came and met the King, saying:
“Do not fear, do not worry, and do not consider this a difficulty.”
The King asked: “How is it not difficult?”
They replied:
“Wénshū Shīlì manifests ōuhéjūshěluó (Skillful Means) and boundless wisdom.
He comes fully endowed with the light of merit and virtue.
If one single meal is given to Wénshū Shīlì and his company,
it is as if all beings in the entire three thousand great thousand worlds,
who seek food, can be fully satiated, and the food will not be exhausted.
Why should twenty-three thousand people be cause for worry?
The merit and virtue of Wénshū Shīlì are extremely venerable
and inexhaustible.”
The King was delighted and leaped for joy.
Leading his musicians, he personally went out to greet and receive them, and at the same time, they entered the palace.
There was one Bodhisattva,
named Pǔshì Xījiàn.
Wénshū Shīlì commanded Sānmótuó Ālóutuó,
to strictly arrange the place so that it could accommodate those who came.
The Bodhisattva accepted the command.
He observed and surveyed the four directions, and immediately everything was prepared.
Furthermore, there was a Bodhisattva,
named Fǎlái Zédé.
He was commanded to prepare the seats.
In the snap of a finger, there were twenty-three thousand seats, variously adorned.
The Bodhisattvas and Śrāvakas all took their seats.
The King said to Wénshū Shīlì:
“The provisions I have prepared are very meager.
Please bear with me for a moment while I prepare more provisions.”
He replied:
“What has been prepared is already sufficient. Do not trouble yourself further.”
The Heavenly King Píshāmén (Vaiśravaṇa),
with his family, household, and servants, all came to pay their respects.
They respectfully attended on the left and right.
Shìtí Huányīn (Śakra Devānām Indra),
personally, along with the great lady,
named Shǒuyē,
and the celestial maidens,
all carried famous incense as offerings.
They scattered them upon Wénshū Shīlì, the various Bodhisattvas, and the Bhikṣu Saṅgha.
The Bodhisattvas were not moved or affected by the flowers and incense.
Fàntiān (Brahmā),
transformed himself into a young Brahmin,
beautiful and perfectly upright.
He stood to the right of Wénshū Shīlì, attending and fanning him.
All the sons of Brahmā
fanned all the Bodhisattvas and Bhikṣus.
The Ānòudá Lóngwáng (Anavatapta Dragon King),
was in the empty space, unseen by anyone.
He held strings of pearls hanging down like banners.
Eight-flavored scented water flowed down from the strings.
In front of every person, there were hanging pearls.
Water issued from within them, supplying everything required.
The King considered that the assembly did not carry alms bowls; with what utensils would they eat?
At that moment, Wénshū Shīlì said:
“Bodhisattvas do not carry bowls when they travel.
But wherever they eat, bowls spontaneously come into their hands.”
The Bodhisattvas thought of bowls.
The bowls flew in by themselves, arriving in ranks.
King Ānòudá
personally washed them clean and filled them completely with water.
The Dragon attendants and court ladies
all carried the twenty-three thousand bowls.
They handed them to every single Bodhisattva.
Wénshū Shīlì said to the King:
“You may distribute the food; it will be complete and not diminished.”
Wénshū Shīlì said:
“Is it exhausted now?”
The King replied: “It is not exhausted.”
“The reason it is not yet exhausted is because you have doubt.”
When the Bodhisattvas had finished eating,
they threw their bowls into the empty space, where they remained in rows.
They neither fell to the ground nor swayed.
The King asked again:
“How do these bowls remain? On what do they rely?”
Wénshū Shīlì said:
“The dwelling of these bowls is like the dwelling of the King’s doubt.” The King replied:
“These bowls have no dwelling place.
Nor are they on the ground.
Nor do they have any [reliance].
They neither rely on anything nor have a location.”
Wénshū Shīlì said:
“Just as the King’s suspicion (doubt) has no dwelling place,
all dharmas are like the bowls: they have no dwelling place and no falling.”
When the meal was finished,
the King took a seat
and said to Wénshū Shīlì:
“I beg you to resolve my doubt.”
He replied:
“Even Buddhas equal to the sands of the Gaṅgā River cannot speak to the King about this suspicion.”
The King was immediately startled and terrified.
He fell from his seat like a great tree being felled.
Móhē Jiāyè (Mahākāśyapa) said to the King:
“Do not be frightened, do not be afraid.
Why is this so?
Wénshū Shīlì has entered the extremely profound ōuhéjūshěluó (Skillful Means).
Slowly, slowly, ask him.”
The King said:
“Buddhas equal to the sands of the Gaṅgā cannot speak of my doubt.”
Wénshū Shīlì said:
“You suppose that [doubt] can be seen resulting from the causes and conditions of the mind.”
The King said:
“Because the mind is not born, therefore the Buddha can be seen.
Neither Saṃsāra nor liberation hold these two aspects that create a Buddha.
My suspicion is such that Buddhas equal to the sands of the Gaṅgā cannot speak of it.
Why is this so?
If a person says:
‘Can I defile the empty space with dust?’ Can he really do it?
If a person says:
‘Can I remove the filth from empty space?’ Can he surely remove it?
The King said: “He cannot.”
Wénshū Shīlì said:
“The Buddha knows that all dharmas are like empty space.
Why is this so?
Because they are fundamentally detached.
Nor is the root of any dharma seen.
If there is anything to be said, the King’s suspicion is something that Buddhas equal to the sands of the Gaṅgā cannot speak of.”
At that moment, the King attained the realization of faith (assurance).
Joyfully leaping, he said:
“Excellent! Excellent!
You have resolved my suspicion.”
Wénshū Shīlì said:
“This great doubt is related to the Dharma that states that all dharmas are fundamentally unrooted (without origin). How, then, can doubt arise?”
The King said:
“I have received this great kindness and have obtained a small relief.
Now, even when my life ends, I will not worry about not reaching Nirvāṇa.”
Wénshū Shīlì said:
“That which the King hopes for is also fundamentally unrooted.
Why is this so?
Because all dharmas are fundamentally Nirvāṇa; therefore, nothing is born.”
The King then rose from his seat.
He took a famous cloth worth billions and thousands [of coins] and wrapped it around Wénshū Shīlì’s body.
Wénshū Shīlì’s body did not appear.
The cloth remained suspended in empty space.
Only his speech was heard, his form was not seen, yet hearing his speech was like seeing him.
The King himself saw his doubt, thus seeing all dharmas as they are seen [in ultimate reality].
A voice in the air spoke, addressing the King’s sight [realization]:
“Then take the cloth and give it to him.”
The next Bodhisattva seated was named Déshàngyuàn.
The King then took this cloth again, intending to offer it to him.
Déshàngyuàn said:
“One who seeks liberation and Nirvāṇa,
does not receive anything from a basis of existence.
Nor do I accept the possessions of common people.
Why?
Because common people
believe there are worldly affairs; therefore, I do not accept it.
Nor does one receive from those who seek Arhatship or Pratyekabuddhahood.
Those who give and receive
receive without a dualistic mind.
They also have no dualistic mind.”
Therefore, it is said that what is received exceeds what is relinquished.
The king immediately took the robe, wishing to place it upon the Bodhisattva.
Suddenly, [the Bodhisattva] vanished, and [the king] no longer knew where [he was].
He only heard the sound but did not see the form.
[The voice] said:
Give the robe to the body that appears.
Following this sequence, he gave the robe to each one individually, but they all vanished.
Even the couch, the stand, and the seat also vanished.
He only heard the voice.
It said to give the robe to the one who appeared.
Even the five hundred Śrāvakas also did not accept it.
The king deeply contemplated.
All the Bodhisattvas, Bhikṣus, and Saṅgha have vanished.
To whom should I give my robe?
He decided to give it to the Queen and the Great Ladies.
The Ladies also vanished at that moment.
The king then attained Samādhi (sānmèi).
He did not see any forms.
Nor did he see women.
Nor did he see men.
Even walls, trees, houses, chambers, cities, and outer walls.
He still had a lingering thought, saying:
There is my body, and the consciousness of forms.
All ceased.
Again, he heard the voice.
Just as everything that is seen should be seen as doubt of the self.
Just as the doubt is seen, seeing all phenomena is also like this.
He then took the robe back, intending to put it on himself.
Not seeing his body, he mentally spoke to Wénshū:
I once heard the Buddha say that those who commit heinous crimes must enter the Great Naraka, is that not so?
The king said, "I have heard."
Do you know yourself whether you must enter Naraka?
The king said:
Is there any phenomenon attained by the Buddha that leads one to ascend to Heaven or enter Naraka?
Is there any peaceful phenomenon that leads one to Nirvāṇa (níhuán)?
Wénshū said, "There is none." The king said:
I know that all phenomena are empty (kōng).
Why is that?
Naraka, Heaven, and peace are all empty as well.
All phenomena cannot be destroyed or ruined.
Therefore, [one] enters the Dharma-body (fǎshēn).
The Dharma-body also contains no Heaven, human realm, Naraka, animals, Pretas (bìlì), and the like.
Worldly kings and those who commit heinous acts, having purified themselves, attain this endurance.
The king said:
All phenomena are entirely pure and undefiled.
When he spoke these words, he quickly attained the Faith Endurance (xìnrěn).
Ānán knew what the assembly was thinking.
He stepped forward and addressed the Buddha, saying, "World-Honored One,
from what cause did you first generate the Bodhi-mind (dàoxīn)?"
The Buddha said:
In a distant kalpa in the past,
in this Jambudvīpa (Yánfú Tí), there was a great king.
His name was Dà Guāngmíng.
He was virtuous, meritorious, and intelligent.
At that time, a neighboring king was close friends with him.
They exchanged gifts of the treasures of their countries.
At that time, that king hunted and obtained two elephants.
They were white like crystal (pōlí) and their seven limbs touched the ground.
They were adorned with various gems and the most precious worldly treasures.
He dispatched someone to send them over.
When King Guāngmíng saw the elephants, his heart rejoiced.
He entrusted them to the elephant trainer Sànshé.
Sànshé received the decree.
Before long, they were trained and obedient.
He went and addressed the king, saying:
The elephants are now trained.
I request the king to observe the test.
The king gathered his ministers and ordered them to observe the testing of the elephants.
When the great assembly was gathered,
the king first mounted the elephant and went out of the city to sport.
The elephant's spirit was strong and fierce.
It saw a herd of elephants by a lotus pond.
It ran after a female elephant and consequently reached a deep forest.
At that time, the king's body was injured and bleeding.
He thought to himself that he would surely die.
He grasped a tree branch, and the elephant departed, leaving the king behind.
He climbed down the tree and sat on the ground, generating great suffering and distress.
The elephant trainer kowtowed and said:
May the king not worry or suffer.
When the elephant's lustful mind ceases and it becomes disgusted with filth,
and it yearns for good grass and food, it will return by itself in this manner.
The king immediately declared:
I shall not use it again.
The elephant indeed returned afterwards.
The elephant trainer reported to the king:
The elephant has now returned.
The king said:
I have no need of you, nor do I need the elephant.
Sànshé appealed to the king:
If the king does not need it,
I only request that you observe my method of training elephants.
The king consented.
He immediately ordered the trainer to make seven iron balls and burn them until they were extremely red.
Having done this, he thought:
If the elephant swallows these balls, it will certainly die.
The king later felt somewhat regretful and someone addressed him, saying:
"Great King,
this precious white elephant is only obtained by a Cakravartin King (zhuǎnlún wáng).
Since it has only a small fault, it should not be destroyed."
The king's anger surged greatly, and he commanded:
"Go far away!"
The elephant trainer told the elephant:
"Swallow these iron balls.
If you do not swallow them, I shall tear your brain apart with an iron hook."
The elephant knew his intention.
[It thought,] "I would rather swallow this hot ball and die."
It bent its knees toward the king, shedding tears, hoping for salvation.
The king, still angry, slowly looked on. Sànshé told the elephant, "Why do you not swallow the balls?"
The elephant then took the balls, placed them in its mouth, and swallowed them.
Entering its belly, they scorched and melted it, and it immediately died.
When the balls fell to the ground, they were still red.
When the king saw this, he finally repented.
He immediately addressed Sànshé:
"You train elephants thus!
Why, when we were in the forest, were you unable to control it?"
At that time, the Pure Abode Deva (Jìngjū Tiān), knowing that King Guāngmíng should generate the Bodhi-mind (pútíxīn),
immediately caused the elephant trainer to kneel and reply to the king, saying:
"I can only train the body, but I cannot train the mind.
Only the Buddha is capable of training the mind."
The king said:
"Of what lineage is the Buddha?
What is his birth lineage?"
[He] replied, "He is born of two kinds of lineage:
First, wisdom (zhìhuì);
Second, great compassion (dàbēi).
He diligently practices six matters,
which are the Six Pāramitās (liù bōluómì).
When merit and wisdom are fully complete,
he is titled the Buddha."
When the king heard this, he leaped for joy.
He immediately arose, washed, changed into new clothes, and performed prostrations facing the four directions.
He generated a mind of great compassion toward all sentient beings, burned incense, and took an oath.
"May all the merit I possess be dedicated toward the path of Buddhahood (fódào).
I shall train my own mind, and I shall also tame all sentient beings.
If there is benefit to be had in Naraka (dìyù), I shall enter that prison.
I shall never relinquish the Bodhi-mind."
Having made this vow,
the earth shook in six ways.
Among the mountains, the great seas, and in the empty space, musical sounds naturally arose.
The Buddha told the Bhikṣus:
The white elephant that swallowed the iron balls at that time was Nánduó.
The elephant trainer at that time was Shèlìfú.
King Guāngmíng was my current body.
At that time, seeing the elephant disciplined and obedient, I first generated the Bodhi-mind.
In the past, there was a king.
His name was Duōfú.
His crown prince was named Zēngfú.
The king revered the Six Teachers (liù shī).
His son served the Buddha.
There were no Śramaṇas (shāmén) in the world.
There was only one layman who served as the chief teacher.
Five hundred Non-Buddhist Practitioners (wàidào) were jealous of his reputation and virtue.
They immediately addressed the king, saying:
"The affairs of the country follow two doctrines, causing minds to be unsettled.
We request that our teacher and the Buddha's teacher each demonstrate their wondrous virtue.
We agree that whoever fails shall be made servants and slaves."
The king consented.
The Non-Buddhist Practitioners and the [lay] teacher set a date and made a pact.
Before the king, they each tested their skills and arts.
The Brahmacārins (fànzhì), skilled in archery, immediately went into the mountains.
The five hundred people each shot a large deer.
They all pierced the left eye, carried the deer back, and used them to demonstrate their craft.
The worthy man (xiánzhě) entered the mountain and meditated earnestly upon the Buddha.
He sought the mighty assistance of the Buddha to display the Great Way.
A five-colored deer sprang forth from the ground.
He joyfully took it and returned.
The Non-Buddhist Practitioners learned of this.
Waiting for the worthy man to go out,
they went to his wife and said:
"Your husband has abandoned his family to become a Śramaṇa.
It is only because of this deer.
It ruins your family customs."
The wife heard this, became angry, and gave the deer to them.
When the worthy man returned and did not see the deer,
he immediately asked where it was.
His wife said:
"This inauspicious thing has now been lost."
The husband was greatly saddened and worried.
He returned to the mountain and sincerely repented his fault.
A radiant moon pearl (míngyuè shénzhū) suddenly sprang forth from the ground.
He immediately took this pearl and observed the movements of the Brahmacārins.
He went to their gate, advertising the sale of marvelous objects.
The Brahmacārin's wife said:
"My family also has extraordinary things that can be compared [to yours]."
She immediately brought out the five-colored deer.
The worthy man then said:
"The king ordered me to bring this deer.
Now you have stolen it; your crime is immeasurable."
The wife hurriedly returned it.
When the day of the test arrived,
the Brahmacārins each presented their deer; all were wounded in the left eye, and they were both filthy and stinking.
The king greatly lamented this.
The worthy man arrived, presenting the divine deer and carrying the radiant moon pearl into the king's palace hall.
The two objects flew and leaped, playing together, shining like streaking stars and flashing lightning.
The entire palace praised the wonder.
The five hundred Brāhmaṇas (póluómén),
knowing that their magic arts were inferior,
were immediately made servants and slaves.
Their wives were made maidservants.
The worthy man guided them by teaching the Sūtras and made them his disciples.
. During the heat of summer
, he resided in a high tower. Sitting upon a seven-jeweled bed, he ordered a maidservant to massage him
. His body was anointed with Niútóu Zhāntán (Ox-Head Sandalwood) fragrance
. The maidservant’s arms wore many bracelets
while massaging the King’s body. The sound of the bracelets filled his ears, and the King was greatly troubled by it
. He instructed her to take off the bracelets one by one
. When only one bracelet remained
, there was complete silence. The King then became enlightened and said
. "The state, ministers, people, and palace women—many activities lead to much vexation—it is exactly like this
." Immediately, he detached from desire, dwelled alone, contemplated, and attained Pratyekabuddhahood (Pìzhī Fó)
. His beard and hair fell off naturally, and he wore the robes of nature
. Leaving the tower, he used his divine power
to renounce the world and enter the mountains. This cause and condition resulted in a middling-grade Pratyekabuddha
. If someone wishes to become a Pratyekabuddha
, they cultivate this root of goodness
. When there is no Buddha in the world
, when their goodness has matured
, they become weary of the world, renounce home, and attain the Way
. They are called a Pratyekabuddha
. The King of Yuèshì
, wishing to seek the path of the Buddha, built thirty-two stūpas
. He made offerings, creating them one by one, until the thirty-first
. At that time, a wicked person touched the King
. The King's aspiration retreated
. "How can such a wicked person be saved
?" Immediately, he turned his mind, abandoned samsāra (birth and death), and aimed for Nirvāṇa (Nièpán)
. He built the thirty-second pagoda (fútú) in order to seek liberation
. Due to this cause and condition, he achieved the path of an Arhat (Luóhàn)
. Therefore, this monastery is named Bōluódìmùchā
, and less than two hundred years have passed since that time. This monastery is still standing
. I also saw it
. The King of Shèwèi (Śrāvastī) was named Bōsīnì (Prasenajit)
. At that time, there was a kingdom in the south
, named Jīndì (Golden Land)
. Its king was titled Jiébīnníng
. The Crown Prince was named Móhē Jiébīnníng
. When the father died, the Crown Prince immediately ascended the throne
. His nature was wise and courageous
. He commanded thirty-six thousand small states
. His formidable presence spread far and wide
, and none failed to submit. However, he did not communicate with the Central Lands
. Afterwards, a merchant traveled to Jīndì
. He presented four lengths of fine linen to that King
. The King asked the merchant
, "This item is excellent; where does it originate
?" He replied
, "It originates in the Central Lands
." The King asked again
, "What is the name of that Central Land
?" He replied
, "It is named Luóyuèqí
. It is also named Shèwèi
." The King asked further
, "For what reason does the King of the Central Lands not come to pay tribute to me
?" He replied again
, "They each rule their own territory, and their renowned power is equal to yours
. Therefore, they do not come
." The King thought to himself
, "Now I must increase my might and compel them to submit
." He asked the merchant again
, "Among the kings of the Central Lands, who is the greatest
?" He reported
, "The King of Shèwèi is the greatest
." Immediately, he dispatched an envoy to the Kingdom of Shèwèi
. He carried a letter instructing them, detailing his complete justification, and delivered it to their King
. It said to Bōsīnì
: "My awe-inspiring power covers all of Jambudvīpa (Yánfú Tí)
. What do you rely upon to cut off diplomatic relations
? I now intentionally send an envoy to communicate with you
. Seven days from now, meet with me
. If you fail to do this, I will raise an army and destroy your state's borders
." Bōsīnì heard this and was deeply alarmed and terrified
. He immediately went to the Buddha and fully reported this matter
. The Buddha told the King
, "Return and tell the envoy
, 'I am not the greatest; there is an even greater King
.' " The King followed the Buddha's instruction
. He told the envoy
, "There is a Sagely King in the world
. He is nearby, residing here
. You should go to him and convey your King's command
." The envoy immediately went to the Jìhuán (Jetavana) Monastery
. At that time, the World-Honored One
transformed his own body into a Cakravartin (Zhǎnlún Wáng, Wheel-Turning King)
. The Seven Treasures and his retinue were all completely present
. The envoy advanced and entered the transformed city
. Having seen the Great King, he was extremely astonished and fearful, and presented the letter to him
. The transformed King received the letter and trampled it under his feet
. He addressed the envoy, saying
: "I am the Great King who oversees and rules the four continents
. Your king is foolish and deluded, daring to defy me
. You must quickly return to your kingdom and proclaim my teaching
. The day the message arrives, he must rush here to pay court
. If lying down when he hears it, he must stand up
. If sitting when he hears it, he must stand
. The appointed time is seven days; there must be no delay
. If he dares to violate this decree, the penalty will be swift and unbidden
." The envoy returned to his native kingdom and fully reported what he had heard and seen to the King of Jīndì
. The King accepted this account and deeply blamed himself
. He gathered all the minor kings he commanded, intending to pay homage to the Great King, but he did not immediately set out
. First, he dispatched an envoy to report to the Great King
, "Your servant commands thirty-six thousand kings
. Should they all go
? Or should half of them go
?" The Great King sent back a reply
, "Allow half to remain, and only bring the other half
." At that time, the King of Jīndì brought eighteen thousand minor kings, and they arrived simultaneously
. After they had seen the transformed King and finished their audience and bowing
, a thought arose in his mind
: "Although the Great King's physical appearance surpasses mine
, his strength must be inferior
." The transformed King then commanded his minister in charge of military affairs to give the bow to the King of Jīndì
. The King of Jīndì could not hold it in his hand
. The transformed King took it back and drew the bow with his finger
. He handed it back and commanded him to pull the string
. The King of Jīndì was completely unable to draw it
. The transformed King took it back and twanged the bowstring
. The Three Thousand Great Thousand Worlds all shook
. Furthermore, he took an arrow, bent the bow, and shot
. After leaving his hand, it transformed into five shots
. All the arrowheads emitted brilliant light
. At the tip of each beam of light, there was a lotus flower as large as a carriage wheel
. On every single flower, there was a Cakravartin King
. Possessing the Seven Treasures, they shone forth with brilliant light
, illumining universally the Three Thousand Great Thousand Worlds
. All sentient beings in the Five Paths received benefit
. Beings in the heavenly realms, upon seeing the light and hearing the Dharma preached
, their bodies and minds became pure, and some gave rise to the aspiration for the unsurpassed, correct, and true Way
. Furthermore, some attained the stage of non-retrogression
. Sentient beings in the human path—some attained the First Stream, the Second Return, or the Third Return
. Those who renounced home and entered the essentials attained the state of the Worthy One (Arhat)
. Those who gave rise to the aspiration for the unsurpassed, correct, and true Way
and those who attained the stage of non-retrogression were countless
. Sentient beings in the Three Evil Paths were freed from suffering, liberated, and reborn among humans and devas
. Then King Móhē Jiébīnníng
and all the minor kings of Jīndì
saw this divine transformation and their hearts became believing and submissive
. They discarded the dust, departed from defilement, and attained the pure Dharma Eye
. All eighteen thousand minor kings simultaneously experienced this
. In an instant, the Buddha withdrew his divine power and returned to his original form
, surrounded by the multitude of Bhikṣus (Bǐqiū)
. The royal company of Jīndì requested to renounce the world
. Their beards and hair fell away naturally, and kāṣāya (jiāshā) robes appeared on their bodies
. Contemplating the subtle Dharma, they all attained Arhatship
. In remote kalpas (jié) past
, a Buddha appeared in this city of Kūshī
. His title was Huānxǐ Zēngyì (Joy and Increase)
. He lived in the world for measureless time, and after transforming sentient beings
, he then entered Parinirvāṇa (Bān Nièpán) between the twin Śāla (Suōluó) trees
. After the Buddha’s Nirvāṇa, the residual Dharma remained in the world for measureless hundreds of millions of years
. When the Dharma had forty years remaining before its extinction
, there was a Bhikṣu who upheld the precepts
, named Juédé
. He had many disciples and family members surrounding him, and he could sound the lion's roar and widely explain the scriptures
. He prohibited the Bhikṣus from owning slaves, maids, cattle, sheep, or any unlawful possessions
. At that time, many Bhikṣus who violated the precepts
heard this teaching and all conceived evil intentions
. They held knives and staves and pressed upon this Dharma Master
. At that time, the King
, named Yǒudé (Virtuous)
, hearing about this matter
, in order to protect the Dharma, immediately went to the place where the Dharma was being preached
. He fought fiercely
, causing the preacher of the Dharma to escape harm
with these evil Bhikṣus who had broken the precepts
. The King was wounded all over his body
. Juédé then praised the King, saying
, "Excellent! Excellent
! The King is truly a protector of the Correct Dharma
. In future generations, this body shall become a vessel for measureless Dharma
." The King, having heard the Dharma at that moment
, his heart greatly rejoiced, and he immediately died
. He was reborn in the land of Akṣobhya Buddha (Āchù Fó) as the foremost disciple
. The King’s retinue, including the common people and family members
, those who had fought
and those who had rejoiced
—none of them retreated from the resolve for Bodhi (Pútí)
. When they died, they were all reborn in the land of Āchù Fó
. The Bhikṣu Juédé, when he later reached the end of his life
, was also reborn in the land of Āchù Fó
, becoming the second disciple among the assembly of Śrāvakas (Shēngwén)
. When the Correct Dharma is about to perish
, one ought to receive, uphold, and protect it in this manner
. The King at that time was I myself
. The Bhikṣu who preached the Dharma was Jiāshè Fó (Kāśyapa Buddha)
, hearing the verses taught by the Buddha and witnessing the divine transformations
, increased and strengthened his heart set on Bodhi
. He paid homage at the Buddha's feet and addressed the Buddha, saying
: "We only wish, O World-Honored One
, and the assembly of Bodhisattvas and disciples
, to accept my invitation for eighty-four thousand years
." Pǔmíng Wáng Rúlái
agreed: "I vow to provide clothes, food and drink, bedding, medicine, and all necessary services
." That Buddha and the great assembly immediately accepted the invitation
. When the King knew the Buddha had accepted his invitation
, he departed joyfully
. The Crown Prince Shīzǐ Jìn, along with twenty thousand other princes, relinquished worldly glory and position
. In the Dharma of the Buddha, they shaved off their beards and hair, left home, and cultivated the Way
. They diligently practiced vigorous effort, delighting in seeking the good Dharma
. At that time, Shīzǐ Jìn attained the Five Supernatural Powers (Abhijñā) and became firm and non-regressing
. That Buddha added his awesome divine power to him, and he constantly revealed and taught the subtle Dharma for sentient beings
, performing the works of the Buddha throughout the three-thousand great-thousand world system
. Countless sentient beings became firm and non-regressing in the unsurpassed Mahāyāna
. Gōngdé Zhuāngyán Wáng, during the eighty-four thousand years
, offered all kinds of pleasurable necessities to the World-Honored One and the great assembly
. Along with all his ministers, leading the procession before and after, he formed the assembly listening to the Dharma
. And he conceived this thought
: "My sons have shaved off their beards and hair, left home, and cultivated the Way
. They constantly receive offerings and cannot personally practice giving
. Nor have I seen them attain transcendent Dharma
. It would be better for them to return home, renounce their wealth, practice giving, and cultivate various merits
, just like the good roots that I have sown
?" At that time, Pǔmíng Wáng Rúlái
immediately knew the thoughts in the heart of Gōngdé Zhuāngyán Wáng
, and addressed Shīzǐ Jìn Púsà, saying
: "Good man
, manifest your sovereign meritorious divine power
. Let the transformations manifested by the Great Bodhisattva enable this great assembly to universally see and hear
, and turn their wrong thoughts so that they attain right view
." Shīzǐ Jìn Púsà immediately entered Samādhi and manifested such signs
. The great-thousand world system shook
. In the sky above, it rained flowers, incense, silk canopies, banners, pennants, musical instruments, fine delicacies, food and drink, and necklaces
, clothing, and all kinds of precious treasures
. They fell abundantly, filling the great-thousand world system
. The sentient beings attained what they had never had before and were all greatly joyful
. At that time, from the Earth Gods and all the Devas up to the Ājiānìzhà heaven
, all proclaimed these words
: "This Great Bodhisattva may be named Xūkōngzàng
. The reason is
, he is able to rain jewels from the empty sky, fully satisfying everyone
." The Buddha immediately ratified this
. The King, seeing this, leaped for joy, gained what he had never had before, and abandoned his mind of arrogance
. He joined his palms towards the Buddha
and spoke these words
: "Rare indeed, O World-Honored One
. The merit and wisdom of the Bodhisattvas can truly be like this
. World-Honored One
, those who practice giving while staying home gain little benefit
. But those who leave home give boundlessly through the power of supernormal abilities
. Householders who give do not satisfy the recipient's intention
. Even when giving, they still cling (or are stingy), which leads to suffering and distress
. Those who leave home do not cling and do not generate suffering and distress
." The King renounced his throne
, handing it over to his son Jíyì
. With true faith, he shaved off his beard and hair
, left home, and cultivated the Way in the Dharma of the Buddha
. He increased his good Dharma, constantly practiced vigorous effort, and attained the Four Dhyānas, the Four Immeasurable Minds, and the Five Supernatural Powers
. Then Jíyì Wáng
governed the kingdom according to the Dharma, and there were no enemies
. He vigorously and tirelessly made offerings to the World-Honored One
. As for Gōngdé Zhuāngyán Wáng
, he was Jūliúsūn Rúlái
. As for Shīzǐ Jìn Púsà
, he was Xūkōngzàng Púsà
. As for Jíyì Wáng
, he was Mílè
In Śàwèi there was a king.
His name was Lándá.
The land was fertile and the people were pure and faithful.
Rulers, ministers, fathers, and sons led one another according to the Way (Dào).
Later, a king ascended the throne.
The laws and customs became diminished, and governance was unfair.
He oppressed the populace and executed the innocent recklessly.
Righteousness and chaos brought misfortune; rain fell out of season.
The five grains were not abundant, and strange calamities arose repeatedly.
Consequently, devastation resulted, and fear of peril and ruin spread.
They served over five hundred practitioners of heterodox ways (xiédào).
They also sacrificed to malevolent spirits (yāoshén); those above and those below imitated each other,
like grass bending in the wind.
The common people delighted in disorder and competed to commit crimes and villainy (jiān guǐ).
The strong bullied the weak, and they injured and killed one another.
They robbed others of their wealth, disregarding reason (dàolǐ).
They violated other men's wives, and the ruler and ministers indulged excessively in dissipation.
Delusion increased daily, and the drought exceeded three years.
They prayed repeatedly, but initially obtained no rain.
The various masters told the King:
"Now we must perform a great sacrifice (dà cí).
We must use seven young boys, and ten heads each of white oxen and white horses, burning them to sacrifice to Heaven.
Only then can rain be obtained."
The King immediately prepared the items.
Inside the country, great fear arose, and everyone, high and low, was agitated.
The Buddha (Fó) instructed Mùlián:
"The country of Lándá is devastated, and the people are suffering hardships.
There are three hundred million people who should obtain release through you.
You may go and enlighten them."
Mùlián went and taught the Dharma (shuō fǎ) to clarify their minds.
Initially, none of the people in the country accepted it.
Mùlián
transformed himself into the body of a great ghost deity (guǐ shén).
He was dozens of *zhàng* tall.
He sat right by the city gate.
With a booming voice, he called for the King and his close ministers to come out.
The ruler and ministers were terrified and bewildered, fearing for their lives.
The King immediately led his close ministers, knocking their heads (kòu tóu) and declaring himself.
"We only beg to be spared!"
The deity said to the King:
"Quickly seek out those ministers who are disloyal and sons who are unfilial and bring them here.
I wish to eat them."
The King immediately investigated and asked.
They replied, "There are none."
The deity again said to the King:
"Quickly seek out thieves,
those who commit debauchery,
and those with a double tongue and wicked speech.
I wish to eat them."
The King immediately investigated and asked.
Again, they replied, "There are none."
The deity again said to the King:
"Quickly seek out those who drink alcohol.
I wish to eat them."
The King immediately investigated and asked.
Again, they replied, "There are none."
Thereupon, Mùlián returned to his true form (zhēnshēn).
He went and spoke with the ghost deity.
When the King saw Mùlián,
he knocked his head and earnestly pleaded with him to interpret/explain to the great deity.
Mùlián said to the King:
"What does this deity seek?"
The King said:
"He wishes to eat wicked people."
Mùlián asked:
"Are there truly such people in the country?"
The King replied, "There are none."
He begged earnestly that he dispatch the deity.
"I shall dedicate my life to submitting to the man of the Way (Dào Rén)."
Mùlián spoke to the great deity:
"The people in this country do not possess those whom you seek.
You may pardon their offenses.
If anyone offends again,
you may return and eat them."
The deity immediately complied with his words
and suddenly departed.
The King and his ministers and subjects
immediately knocked their heads together, expressing gratitude and begging to take refuge (guī mìng).
Mùlián told him:
"If the King wishes to take refuge,
he should first take refuge in the Buddha (Fó)."
The King asked about the merit and virtue of the Buddha (Fó Gōngdé).
Mùlián spoke of the Dharma (Fǎ) preached by the Buddha (Fó), who is solely honored in the Three Realms (Sān Jiè), and whose śrāvakas (shēngwén) numbered three thousand.
The King said:
"I am now fortunate to have obtained this extraordinary teaching."
He then addressed Mùlián:
"I humbly wish to invite the Buddha (Fó) to receive his honored Dharma words and observe them throughout my life."
Mùlián told the King:
"If you can truly do this,
your merit (fú) will be immeasurable.
You must simply purify your mind and contemplate the Buddha (Fó)."
The King immediately accepted the instruction, bathed, and fasted (zhāijiè).
