Facing the Buddha Land (Fó Guó) from afar, he bowed his head and performed the rites,
saying: "I, due to my ignorance (ànmèi), mistakenly presided over the people.
I was unable to cleanse my heart and guide them,
thus causing the country to become desolate; the fault lies with me.
I only wish that the Heavenly Honored One (Tiān Zūn) may descend and shed light,
universally enabling the common people to obtain inexhaustible blessings (fú)."
The Buddha (Fó) and the various bhikṣus (bǐqiū),
while still a hundred *lǐ* away, traveled through the air.
Five-colored lotuses supported their feet.
The devas (tiān) attended him with wings, holding jewel banners and ornamented canopies, welcoming them along the path.
They played various renowned musical instruments, filling the air.
Observing the majestic spiritual power (wēishén) of the Buddha (Fó) illuminating Heaven and Earth,
the King and his ministers bowed their heads at his feet.
At the intersection of the four roads, they broadly set up curtains and coverings, swept and purified the area.
The Buddha (Fó) sat upon the naturally manifested Lion Seat (Shīzǐ zhī Zuò).
The seat was fully covered with celestial silks and embroidered mats (tiān zēng wǎn yán).
The King personally poured the food and drink and personally performed the ablutions.
When the incantation and blessings (zhòuyuàn) were finished,
the Buddha (Fó) then taught the essence of suffering (kǔ), emptiness (kōng), impermanence (wúcháng), and the Four Noble Truths (Sì Dì).
The King was immediately overjoyed and begged to receive the Five Precepts (Wǔ Jiè).
His bonds and defilements were dissolved
and removed, and he attained Sūtra-to-be-entered (Xūtuóhuán).
At that time, the five hundred externalists (wàidào) whom the King served begged to become bhikṣus (bǐqiū).
The Buddha (Fó) immediately permitted this.
He touched their heads with his hand; their hair fell off, and kasayas (jiāshā) clothed their bodies.
Seven days later, they all attained Arhatship (Luóhàn).
The assembled people attained Sūtra-to-be-entered (Xūtuóhuán),
or received the Five Precepts (Wǔ Jiè) and diligently practiced the Ten Virtues (Shí Shàn).
They took refuge in the Three Jewels (Sān Zūn).
They fasted six days a month (liù zhāi),
and three days a year (sān zhāi).
They guided one another to make this a regular practice.
Ānán reported to the Buddha (Fó):
"What kind of connection
did this King and his people have with Mùlián in a past life (sù)?
The Buddha (Fó) said:
"Formerly, during the time of Wéiwèi Fó,
Mùlián was an Upāsaka (Yōupósè).
He lived in poverty and maintained the precepts, keeping his resolve undefiled.
While picking flowers in the mountains, he saw a Xūwén tree.
Just as he was about to climb the tree to gather flowers,
he did not know there was a beehive in front of him.
Several thousand bees were startled, scattered, and chased him.
He immediately thought in his heart:
'If I attain the Way (Dào), I shall deliver you all.'
Those who have attained the Way (Dào) today are all those very bees from that time."
In the past, there were five kings of states.
Their state borders were close, and they became good friends, frequently visiting each other.
The greatest among them was named Pǔ'ān.
He practiced the way of a Bodhisattva.
The other four minor kings habitually practiced evil conduct.
The great king pitied them.
He summoned them to the palace hall and entertained them.
This lasted for seven days.
Day and night, when the seven days were complete,
the minor kings addressed the great king, saying:
"State affairs are many, please allow us to retire and return home."
The great king saw them off.
Upon reaching the road, he spoke to the minor kings:
"Tell me what each of you enjoys."
One king replied:
"The bright spring third month, when trees bloom gorgeously, playing and enjoying the open fields."
Another king replied:
"I wish always to be a king.
With saddles, horses, fine clothes, and decorations, surrounded by officials and subjects on all sides.
Shining brightly and gloriously, striking bells and beating drums, coming and going, making passersby turn their gaze."
Another king said:
"I wish my wife and children were uniquely beautiful,
and that we might enjoy each other, satisfying our desires to the utmost."
Another king said:
"I wish my parents were always present,
and that friends, brothers, wives, and children were arrayed around.
With good clothing and delicious food to indulge body and mouth.
Playing the plain zither and wearing simple clothes, enjoying each other."
Together, they asked the great king what he enjoyed.
The great king replied:
"I enjoy not being born, not dying, having no suffering, no vexation, no hunger, no thirst, no cold, no heat, and being free in existence and non-existence."
The four kings together said:
"Such joy must require an enlightened teacher."
The great king replied:
"My teacher is titled the Fó.
He is currently nearby at the Jìhuán Jīngshě."
The kings were delighted and went together to the Shìzūn.
The great king addressed the Fó, saying:
"These men, having attained human form, are ignorant and unwise, deeply attached to the world.
They enjoy things without knowing sin or merit.
We beg the Fó to speak of the Truth of Suffering for these disciples."
The Fó said:
"You should listen carefully.
I shall speak of it for you.
When a person lives in the world, many sufferings oppress the body.
Briefly, there are eight sufferings.
First, the suffering of birth.
When a person dies, the spirit does not know which path it is heading toward.
Before attaining a birthplace, it universally receives the form of the intermediate state.
Up to three seven-day periods (21 days).
When the father and mother harmonize, it comes to receive the embryo.
The first seven days, it is like thin curds.
The second seven days, like thick curds.
The third seven days, like congealed butter.
The fourth seven days, like a lump of flesh.
In the fifth period, the embryo completes its form, and the clever wind enters the abdomen.
It blows upon the body, and the six senses open up.
It is in the mother’s womb, below the undigested food storage and above the digested food storage.
When the mother eats one grain of hot food,
it pours over the infant’s body, like plunging into boiling water.
When the mother drinks one cup of cold water,
it is also like sharp, cold ice slicing the body.
When the mother is full,
the squeezing pressure on the body causes indescribable pain.
When the mother is hungry,
the infant is disturbed in the abdomen, suffering measureless pain, like being hung upside down.
When the month is complete and birth is imminent,
the head faces the birth canal.
The extreme pain is like two rocks crushing a mountain, or falling onto grass during birth.
Since the body is fine and soft, the grass touching it is like treading on swords and blades; suddenly, it loses its voice and cries out loudly.
Is this not suffering?
They all said it is suffering.
Second, the suffering of old age.
Parents raise and nurture (the child) until it grows up.
When hungry, it is extremely hungry; when full, it is extremely full.
There is no restraint or moderation.
Gradually, they reach old age, their heads become white, and teeth fall out.
Eyesight is blurry, and hearing is dull.
Vigor departs, decline arrives, skin sags, and the face wrinkles.
All joints ache painfully, and walking is extremely difficult.
Sitting down and getting up is accompanied by groans, worry, sorrow, and distress.
Consciousness gradually fades, and death is imminent.
The days of life shorten and end; speaking brings tears, and sitting or rising requires assistance.
Is this not suffering?
They replied: "Truly, it is suffering."
Third, the suffering of sickness.
Earth, Water, Fire, and Wind harmonize to form the body.
If one great element is unbalanced, 101 diseases arise.
If the four great elements are unbalanced, 404 diseases act simultaneously.
If the Earth element is unbalanced, the entire body aches.
If the Water element is unbalanced, the entire body swells grossly.
If the Fire element is unbalanced, the entire body suffers heat.
If the Wind element is unbalanced, the entire body is stiff and rigid, and the painful aching of the hundred joints is like being struck by a rod or cane.
As the four great elements advance and recede, the hands and feet become useless.
Strength is exhausted, and sitting or rising requires assistance.
The mouth is dry, the lips are cracked, tendons break, and the nose collapses.
The eyes cannot see colors, and the ears cannot hear sounds.
Impurities flow out, and the body lies upon them.
The mind harbors pain and vexation, and every word spoken is sorrowful.
Relatives are at the bedside, watching over them day and night without rest.
Sweet and delicious food tastes bitter upon entering the mouth.
Is this not suffering?
They replied: "Truly, it is suffering."
Fourth, the suffering of death.
When a person dies, 404 diseases act simultaneously.
As the four great elements are about to scatter, the soul and spirit are unsettled.
At the moment of imminent death, the "knife-wind" dismembers the form; there is no place that does not ache.
White sweat flows out, and the two hands grope at the emptiness.
The family, both inside and outside the house, surrounds them.
Worry, sorrow, weeping, and wailing pierce to the bone marrow, unbearable even for themselves.
The wind departs, the breath dissipates, the fire is extinguished, the body is cold, and the soul is gone.
The body stiffens and straightens, losing all knowledge.
Within ten days, the flesh decays, blood flows, the body swells, rots, and stinks, making it extremely difficult to approach.
If abandoned in the wilderness, birds and animals devour it; the flesh is gone, the bones dry out, and the skull lies elsewhere.
Is this not suffering?
They replied: "Truly, it is suffering."
Fifth, the suffering of separation from what is loved and cherished.
Family members, brothers, wives, and children are together,
loving and longing for one another, but in a single morning, they are scattered and lost.
Being plundered and robbed by others, they are scattered, the father going east, the son west, the mother south, the daughter north—not remaining in one place.
Becoming slaves and bondservants, each harbors sorrow in their heart.
Their cries cease abruptly; distant and obscure, there is no time when they will meet again.
Is this not suffering?
They replied: "Truly, it is suffering."
Sixth, the suffering of not obtaining what is sought.
Having wealth in the family, they spend it to seek official positions.
Hoping to achieve wealth and nobility, they seek it ceaselessly.
If they happen to obtain it, and gain a border post,
before much time has passed, they greedily take the people's possessions.
They are reported by others, and suddenly an incident occurs.
They are brought back loaded in a cage-cart, suffering measureless distress, not knowing if they will live or die, or on what day.
Is this not suffering?
They replied: "Truly, it is suffering."
Seventh, the suffering of encountering what one hates.
Worldly people are shallow; living amidst love and desire, they quarrel over unnecessary matters.
They mutually injure and kill each other, thereby creating great enmity.
Each tries to avoid the other, hiding where there is no ground (to hide).
They sharpen knives and arrows, carry bows, and hold staves.
If they meet on a narrow road, they draw their bows and ready their arrows.
The two blades face each other, not knowing whose victory or defeat it will be.
At that moment, the fear is measureless.
Is this not suffering?
They replied: "Truly, it is suffering."
Eighth, the suffering of anxiety, sorrow, and vexation.
A person living in the world—
the longest lives a hundred years; the short-lived ones die in the womb (stillbirth).
Even if one manages to reach a hundred years, the night consumes half of it. The remaining
fifty years:
they are drunk, sick, and do not know how to conduct themselves as human beings.
When young, they are foolish and ignorant for fifteen years, not knowing propriety or righteousness.
When they pass eighty years, they are old, dull, and unwise.
The ears are deaf, the eyes are dim, and they have no principles left.
If the world is about to fall into chaos, there may be drought, fire, or severe frost, and the crops in the fields do not ripen.
Inside and outside the family, there are many illnesses and pains.
When running a business, they frequently suffer losses; government officials demand hundreds of fines, and they are imprisoned in jail, not knowing when they will be released.
Brothers and sons travel far and have not returned.
At home, they are poor and cold, lacking clothing and food.
The surrounding households and villages cannot manage their local affairs.
Family members die, and there is nothing available for shrouding or burial.
When planting in spring, there is no ox for the plow.
When gathering together on festival days, where there should be joy, they face each other with shared sorrow.
Is this not suffering?
They replied: "Truly, it is suffering."
At that time, the five kings and all the assembled officials, tens of thousands of people,
heard the explanation of the Truth of Suffering, and their hearts opened and their minds awakened.
They immediately attained the Sūtuóhuán Dào.
They then viewed their palaces as looking at a foul latrine; there was nothing enjoyable about them.
They immediately abandoned their royal thrones, handed them over to their younger brothers, and left home to follow the Way.
They cultivated all merits, never growing weary day after day.
The kingdom of Duōmèi.
There was a Brāhmaṇa (Pólúomén) king.
He relinquished his royal stipend and dedicated himself largely to alternative paths (heterodox teachings).
Suddenly, one day, the king generated a benevolent intent and desired to give great charity (bùshī).
Following the method of the Brāhmaṇas.
He piled up treasures like a mountain, and whoever came begging was permitted to take them himself.
A handful measured out by weight. Thus, for several days, the pile did not diminish.
The Buddha knew this king had accumulated merit (sùfú) and ought to be saved.
He transformed himself into a Brāhmaṇa student (Fànzhì).
He went to that kingdom.
The king came out to meet him.
He bowed and inquired about his well-being, saying:
“What do you seek? Do not hesitate or feel difficulty.” The Fànzhì replied:
“I have come from afar, desiring to beg for treasures to build a residence.”
The king said, “Excellent!”
“Take one handful by weight yourself.”
The Fànzhì took a handful and walked.
After seven steps, he returned and placed it back in its original spot.
The king asked:
“Why do you not take it?”
The Fànzhì replied:
“This is barely enough to build a simple hut.
I would still need to take a wife, and together it would be insufficient for use. Therefore, I did not take it.”
The king said:
“Take three handfuls more.”
The Fànzhì immediately took them.
After walking seven steps, he returned and placed them back in their original spot.
The king asked the Fànzhì:
“Why do you do this again?”
He replied:
“This is enough to take a wife.
But I still have no fields, servants, cattle, or horses.
Calculating this, it is still insufficient.
Therefore, I abandoned the thought.”
The king said:
“Take seven handfuls more.”
The Fànzhì immediately took them.
After walking seven steps, he returned and placed them back in their original spot.
The king said:
“What is your intention now?”
The Fànzhì replied:
“If I have sons and daughters,
I would again have marriage expenses and funeral costs.
Calculating this, it is insufficient for use. Therefore, I did not take them.”
The king said:
“I will give you all these treasures as a gift.”
The Fànzhì accepted them and then discarded them, leaving.
The king found this extremely strange.
He asked again for the reason behind his intention.
The Fànzhì replied:
“Originally, I came begging, desiring to use this for my life.
But reflecting carefully, human life in this world is brief.
All things are impermanent (wúcháng), and the future is uncertain, even from dawn till dusk.
Karma (yīnyuán) accumulates, worries and suffering deepen daily. Piling up treasures like a mountain does not benefit the self.
Greed and schemes are merely striving for difficulty in vain.
It is better to cease all intention and seek the path of non-action (wúwéi dào).
Therefore, I did not take them.”
The king’s mind was enlightened.
He requested to follow the illuminating teachings.
Thereupon, the Fànzhì,
revealed the luminous form of the Buddha, leaped up, and stood in the air.
He spoke verses for the king, saying:
“Though one may gather treasures, piling them high up to heaven,
filling the world in such a manner, it is not equal to seeing the essence of the Way.
Evil seems like good, attachment seems like non-attachment.
Taking suffering for joy—like a madman, one does not feel aversion.”
The king saw
the Buddha’s light illuminating heaven and earth afar.
Hearing these verses again, he jumped up with joy.
The king and his ministers immediately accepted the Five Precepts (wǔjiè).
They attained the path of the Stream-Enterer (Xūtuóhuán dào).
There was a king,
named Mórá.
He led an army to conquer, selecting several million commoners.
At that time, there was a Bhikṣu (Bǐqiū) who had attained Arhatship (Luóhàn dào).
He entered the kingdom for alms (fēnwèi).
He was seized along with the others and taken to the royal palace.
The king ordered him to tend the official horses.
He labored hard for seven days.
The king personally came to observe him.
When the Bǐqiū saw the king,
he lightly rose, flew up, and stood in the air, manifesting his awe-inspiring spiritual power (wēishén).
The king was immediately terrified, kowtowed, and confessed his error.
“I was truly ignorant, unable to distinguish the genuine from the false.
I will investigate among all within and without who caused this divine person to perform this task.
Today, there must be punishment or execution.”
The Bǐqiū addressed the king:
“The fault lies neither with the king nor the people of the kingdom.
In my previous life, while practicing the Way, I always made offerings to my teacher.
At that time, I prepared a drink for my teacher.
The teacher said to me:
‘First, wash your hands, and then drink.’
My ignorant mind thought:
‘The teacher doesn't even tend the official horses;
why doesn’t he wash his hands beforehand?’
The teacher immediately said to me:
‘You think this thought lightly now, but how heavy will the consequence be later?’
Hearing these words, I became worried and distressed.
The teacher knew my intention,
and then thought:
‘I am destined for Nirvāṇa (Níhuán).
Why should I cause distress to this person?’
That very night, during the third watch,
the teacher entered parinirvāṇa (bō Níhuán).
Since then, a long time has passed, and we have each undergone rebirth (shēngsǐ).
Because of that karma from the past, I now received its consequence (sùyāng),
of tending horses for seven days.
Indeed, good and evil deeds immediately result in suffering or blessings, just as a shadow follows the form.”
The king heard the Bǐqiū speak of sin and blessings.
His mind was enlightened and joyful, and he begged to dedicate his life to the divine person.
The Bǐqiū informed him:
“You should take refuge in the Buddha.
The Buddha is the teacher of the Three Realms (Sānjiè).”
The king and the people of the kingdom
all followed the Bǐqiū out to the place where the Buddha was.
They bowed their heads to the ground, performed obeisance, and reverently accepted the Five Precepts.
They became Upāsakas (Yōupósè, lay devotees).
The Buddha then, for the king and the people of the kingdom,
manifested the auspicious signs (xiànghǎo), and his awe-inspiring spiritual power shone forth, illuminating heaven and earth.
Furthermore, he spoke to them about impermanence (wúcháng), suffering (kǔ), and emptiness (kōng).
The king at that time attained the Xūtuóhuán dào.
The people throughout the kingdom all accepted the Five Precepts and the Ten Good Deeds (shíshàn).
They dedicated their lives to the Three Jewels (Sānzūn) and observed fasts and precepts monthly.
This became their fixed practice.
At that time, there was a king,
named Jiàntuó.
He devotedly served a Brāhmaṇa (Pólúomén) who lived in the mountains.
The Brāhmaṇa had planted many fruit trees, but woodcutters damaged them.
The Pólúomén then
led the woodcutters to the king, stating they had behaved outrageously,
ruined the fruit trees, and requested the king to punish and kill them. The king revered and served the Pólúomén,
and immediately executed them.
Not long thereafter,
a cow ate someone’s rice plants.
Its owner then struck the cow, breaking one of its horns.
Blood flowed over its face, and the pain was unbearable.
The cow went directly to the king’s place and appealed, saying:
“I truly behaved outrageously by eating a little of that person’s rice.
Now he has struck and broken my horn.”
The king understood the language of birds and beasts.
He told the cow:
“I shall punish and kill that person for you.”
The cow said:
“Even if you kill this person, it will not stop my pain.
You should only admonish and command him not to cause pain to others in the future.”
The king was moved and reflected:
“I serve the Pólúomén.
Merely over fruit trees, he caused me to kill people.
He is not equal to this cow!”
He immediately summoned the Pólúomén and asked:
“By serving this path now, what merit (fú) can be gained?”
The Pólúomén replied:
“One can avert disaster, attain blessings, wealth, high status, and long life.”
The king further asked:
“Can one escape rebirth (shēngsǐ)?”
He replied:
“One cannot be freed from rebirth.”
The king went to the Buddha’s abode.
He prostrated with five limbs touching the ground (wǔtǐ tóudì), performed obeisance to the Buddha, and reported, saying:
“I have heard that the Buddha’s Way is supremely honored.
Your teachings guide the world, and those saved are countless.
I wish to receive the Dharma words to reform myself.”
The Buddha immediately conferred the Five Precepts and the Ten Good Deeds upon the king.
He spoke to him about how all things—heaven, earth, people, and objects—are neither born nor perish.
Giving charity (bùshī) and maintaining precepts (chíjiè) brings blessings in this life.
Those who practice patience (rěnrǔ), diligence (jīngjìn), mental cultivation, and wisdom (zhìhuì)—their virtues are immeasurable.
In a future life, being born in heaven, one may also become a Cakravartin King (Zhējiāyuè wáng).
One can attain the Way of non-action (wúwéi) and transcend the world.
The Buddha manifested the auspicious signs, and his awe-inspiring spiritual power shone forth.
The king was joyful and enlightened in mind.
He attained the Xūtuóhuán dào.
Seven days later, the cow reached the end of its life,
and was born in heaven.
There was a king of the state of Fūyán.
His name was Pǔdá.
He personally upheld the Buddha Dharma, never being partial or unjust.
He always possessed compassion.
The foolish people in his country did not know the Three Jewels (Sān Zūn).
Whenever he observed the precepts and fasts (zhāijiè), he would ascend a high place to observe them.
Upon returning, he would certainly bow his head and face, performing the kowtow (jī shǒu wéi lǐ).
The ministers and common people in the country were puzzled by the King's behavior.
They discussed among themselves, saying:
“The King holds the honored position of ten thousand people.
Those far and near respect and submit to him, and he is looked upon as the leader of men.
What request could cause him to ruin his dignified appearance by putting his head and face upon the ground?”
The assembled officials wished to remonstrate but dared not.
When he went out of the palace with several thousand officials and common people, not far away, they saw a dào rén.
The King descended from his carriage, drew back the canopy, and stopped.
His followers paid their respects to the dào rén.
They immediately followed the King back.
They arranged a meal, and thus the planned journey was not accomplished.
The assembled officials remonstrated, saying:
“Your Majesty is the most honored one.
How is it proper to put your head and face upon the ground in the road for this begging dào rén?
The most honored parts in the world are the head and face.
Moreover, as King of the country, you are not the same as others.”
The King commanded his subordinates:
“Seek the heads of dead people and the heads of the six types of domestic animals.”
The subordinates searched everywhere, and after days passed, they finally obtained them.
The King said:
“Sell them in the marketplace.”
The subordinates sold them.
The heads of cows, horses, pigs, and sheep were all sold.
Only the human heads remained unsold.
The King said:
“Sell them regardless of price; if they remain unsold,
then have people take them as gifts.” In this way, days passed, but they were still unsold.
When offered as gifts, no one would take them, and the heads became swollen and rotten.
The King then became greatly enraged.
He spoke to his subordinates, saying:
“You said
that the human head is most noble and must not be disgraced.
Why is it now that when human heads are offered as gifts, no one will take them?”
He immediately commanded the royal chariot to be prepared, intending to go out into the desolate marshes to question them further.
The assembled officials trembled and left, reaching outside the city.
The King informed his officials, saying:
“Do you perhaps remember that during the time of my late predecessor (Xiān Jūn),
there was a young boy who constantly held the canopy?”
The subordinates replied, “We certainly remember him.”
The King said:
“Where is this boy now?”
They replied:
“He has been dead for seventeen years.”
The King said:
“What kind of person was this boy, good or evil?”
They replied, saying:
“We often observed him serving the late King (Xiān Wáng).
He observed the precepts, was respectful and solemn, maintained honesty and self-restraint, and spoke no improper words.”
The King told the officials:
“Now, if you were to see the clothes this boy wore when he was alive,
would you recognize them?”
The officials replied:
“Although it has been a long time, Your servants still recognize them.”
The King had the clothes of the former deceased boy brought.
He said:
“Is this it?”
The subordinates replied, “It is.”
The King said:
“Now, if you were suddenly to see the boy himself, would you recognize him?”
The subordinates paused for a long time.
Then they replied:
“Your servants fear our own ignorance and dullness; if we saw him suddenly, we could not distinguish him.”
The dào rén they had previously seen arrived.
The King was greatly delighted.
He also told the dào rén how they tried to sell the heads or give them away, but no one would take them.
“Now I wish to show them the origin and the result (běnmò).
I am fortunate to have met you.
I request that you enlighten and guide them.”
The dào rén immediately spoke to the subordinates:
“The King was originally the young boy who held the canopy during the time of the previous King (Xiān Wáng).
He constantly followed the previous King.
He observed the precepts and fasts, practiced the righteous Dharma purely, guarded his mind, and committed no evil deeds.
After his life ended, he was reborn as a prince.
His present attainment of honor and nobility is entirely due to his past deeds (sù xíng) and adherence to the precepts.”
All the subordinates, great and small, unanimously said:
“We are fortunate to have met and seen the dào rén.
We pray that you pity our ignorance and blindness and request to become your disciples.”
The dào rén told the officials and common people:
“I have a Great Master (Dà Shī).
You should receive instruction from him.”
The officials replied:
“We wish to spend the rest of our lives receiving the words of the Dharma.”
The dào rén said:
“My Master is called Fó (the Buddha).
His body can fly, and light shines from the crown of his head.
He can separate his body, scatter his form, and manifest ten thousand kinds of transformations.
He walks alone through the Three Realms (Sān Jiè); no one can equal him.
His followers are pure and all are Śramaṇa (Shā mén).
His teachings and methods of deliverance are never in vain.
The subordinates immediately addressed the dào rén:
“Can the Buddha (Fó) be seen?
How far is he from here?”
The dào rén replied:
“Very well.
I shall inform the World-Honored One (Shì Zūn).
He is over six thousand *lǐ* away.”
The dào rén immediately flew to Shèwèi.
He fully informed the Buddha (Fó).
The Buddha (Fó) said:
“Tomorrow I shall arrive at the state of Fūyán. Upon my arrival, I shall manifest divine power (wēi shén).”
The King and his assembled officials took flowers and incense and went out of the city to welcome the Buddha (Fó).
Seeing the Buddha’s (Fó) majestic power and spiritual efficacy, joy and fear were intermingled, and they cast their five limbs (wǔ tǐ tóu dì) to the ground, bowing their heads in reverence.
They reported to the Buddha (Fó), saying:
“We apologize for troubling the World-Honored One (Shì Zūn),
and the multitude of Saṅgha (Sēng), to travel so far to this land.”
The King devotedly prepared offerings.
He personally poured the drinks and offered water for washing.
When the blessings were concluded,
the Buddha (Fó) smiled, and five-colored light shone from his mouth.
Ānán said:
“The Buddha (Fó) never smiles without reason.”
The Buddha (Fó) replied:
“Formerly, in the time of the Buddha Móhēwén Fó,
this King was the son of a prominent family.
His father made offerings to the Three Jewels (Sān Zūn).
The father commanded the son to transmit incense.
At that time, there was a serving attendant (shì shǐ).
The son felt contempt for the attendant and did not give him the incense.
The resulting consequence of sin and merit momentarily led him to receive the karmic reward of servitude (yì bào).
Because his adherence to the Dharma was unfailing, he now attains kingship.
When I attained the Way (Dào), I was obligated to deliver this person.”
Upon understanding the origin and outcome, the King immediately attained the fruit of Sūtuóhuán (Sotāpanna).
The people in the country
all received the Five Precepts (Wǔ Jiè) and practiced the Ten Virtues (Shí Shàn).
In the past, Píngshā Wáng.
had a high official (minister).
He committed a crime and was banished to the middle of Nánshān, a thousand *lǐ* away from the capital.
Traditionally, no one could cultivate the five grains there.
When the minister arrived there,
spring water flowed freely, and the five grains flourished greatly.
Those who were starving and cold from various surrounding kingdoms came to this place.
Within a few years, there were three or four thousand families.
He provided land to the newcomers so they could make a living.
Among them, the three elders and senior respected figures (elders) of long standing
collectively discussed the kingdom’s lack of a ruler.
Since they themselves lacked a prime minister, they went to the minister's residence.
They nominated the minister to be their king.
The minister replied to the elders, saying:
“If you take me as king,
I must follow the laws of all other kings.
Ministers on the left and right, civil and military officers and generals,
upward and downward court tribute, sending women to open the palace, and collecting taxes in grain and silk must conform to the people’s laws.”
The state elders replied:
“Yes, we respectfully follow your command.
We shall adhere entirely to the king’s law.”
He was immediately installed as king.
He appointed various officials.
The civil and military establishment, high and low, requisitioned and mobilized the people.
They built walls, constructed houses, palaces, and lofty towers.
The people suffered severely and could no longer endure it.
They all began to conceive the idea of plotting against the king.
The wicked officials led the king out hunting.
They went thirty or forty *lǐ* away from the city.
In the open wilderness and marshland, they cornered the king intending to kill him.
The king asked his attendants:
“Why are you killing me?”
They all replied:
“The people desired prosperity and joy and honored you as king with rites.
The people are distressed and desire chaos; you destroy families and plot against the state.”
The king told them:
“You yourselves caused this; I did not fundamentally create it.
If you wrongfully murder me, the spirits and gods will know it.
Allow me to make one vow so that I die without resentment.”
He immediately vowed, saying:
“I originally opened up the wilderness, cultivated the land, and supported the people.
All who came lived, and their wealth and joy were boundless.
Since you raised me to be king,
I followed the systems of other nations, which you collectively agreed upon. Now you turn back and kill me.
I truly have done no evil to these people.
If I die, I vow to become a Luóchà.
I will return and enter my former body and surely repay this vengeance.”
Thereupon, they strangled him, abandoned the corpse, and left.
After three days, the king’s spirit returned to the body.
He named himself Āluópō.
He immediately arose and entered the palace.
He killed the new king, along with the palace women, maids, and the wicked officials around him.
He wished to kill all the people.
The three elders of the state bound themselves with grass ropes and came,
confessing before the Luóchà.
“This was the work of wicked officials.
It was not something the ordinary people could possibly know about.
We beg for pardon and forgiveness and wish you to return to govern the state.”
He said: “I am a Luóchà.
To conduct affairs among men, I must consume human flesh as food and drink.”
The Luóchà was quick-tempered and furious, not considering difficulties.
The three elders said:
“The kingdom belongs to the king; therefore, things must be as before.
What is needed for your food and drink will be supplied in sequence.”
The state elders went out together and issued an order to the people.
From now on, they established a sequence:
each household must provide one small child
alive, to be used as food.
The Luóchà king was fed by three or four thousand families.
There was exactly one household that was a disciple of the Buddha.
They maintained diligence within their home and upheld the Five Precepts of the Buddha.
The wise man and his family, great and small, were distressed and wept.
Facing the distant Juéshān, they performed a ritual greeting (sālām) to the Buddha.
They repented their faults and blamed themselves.
The Buddha saw their distress through his wisdom eye.
He then spoke to himself, saying:
“Due to this small child, countless people shall be saved.”
He then flew alone and arrived at the gate of the Luóchà.
He manifested transformed light forms, illuminating the interior of the palace.
The Luóchà saw the light and suspected it was an unusual person.
He immediately came out and, seeing the Buddha, conceived a poisonous intent.
He tried to leap forward to swallow the Buddha, but the light stung his eyes.
He carried mountains and spat fire, but all transformed into dust.
After a long time, exhausted, he was finally subdued and converted.
He invited the Buddha to enter and sit, and bowed with his head to the ground in reverence.
The Buddha preached the Dharma for him, and he listened wholeheartedly.
He immediately received the Five Precepts and became a Yōupósè (lay Buddhist follower).
The village official rushed the food collection, seized the child, and returned.
The family cried loudly and followed along the road.
Countless onlookers felt sorrow for them.
The official held the child, presented the food, and placed it before the Luóchà.
The Luóchà held the child in his hand.
Kneeling solemnly, he addressed the Buddha:
“The people of the state are taking turns providing children as food.
Now that I have received the Buddha’s Five Precepts, I can no longer eat people.
I ask to give this small child in charity to the Buddha,
to serve as the Buddha’s attendant.”
The Buddha accepted him.
He preached the Dharma and offered blessings.
The Luóchà was joyful and attained the path of Xūtuóhuán (Stream-Enterer).
The Buddha placed the small child in his alms bowl.
He carried him out the palace gate and returned him to his parents.
And he instructed them, saying:
“Raise the child well; do not worry or grieve anymore.”
When the people saw the Buddha, none were not astonished and surprised.
“What kind of spirit is this? What merit does this child have,
that he alone was rescued?
The one whom the Luóchà was to eat was taken back and returned to his parents.”
The Buddha then spoke a verse (gātha), saying:
The virtue of precepts can be relied upon; karmic reward constantly follows oneself.
Seeing the Dharma brings growth to humanity and eternally removes one from the three evil paths.
Vigilance and caution remove suffering and fear; karmic reward brings honor throughout the three realms.
Ghosts, dragons, and evil, poisonous harms do not violate the person who upholds the precepts.
Seeing the Buddha’s light and form, they all became disciples of the Buddha.
Hearing the verse, they rejoiced and all attained the trace of the path.
In the kingdom of Shèwèi Guó, there were two merchants.
One person thought, saying:
The Buddha's body is *zhànglǐu*, its magnificent color like purple gold.
On his crown is the *ròujì*, and light shines from his neck and back, majestic and hard to describe.
The Buddha is like an Emperor or King; the *shāmén* are like loyal ministers.
The Buddha explains the clear Dharma, and the *shāmén* recite and proclaim it. This King is enlightened.
He knows the Buddha is worthy of reverence.
The Buddha knew his intention and regarded him closely.
That person's heart and mind rejoiced as if he had gained a treasure.
The other one thought, saying:
The Buddha is like an ox; disciples are like a carriage.
That ox drags the carriage east, west, south, and north.
The Buddha is also just like that.
The Buddha knew he held an evil thought and would surely receive calamity. He was mournfully sorry for him.
That person’s heart was evil. The two men both departed.
After thirty *lǐ*, they reached a rest station and stayed overnight, bought wine, and drank it.
They argued vehemently over shared belongings and contested matters.
As for the one with the good thought:
The *Sì Tiānwáng* sent good spirits to protect him.
As for the one with the malicious thought:
The ghost spirits of Tài Shān made the wine enter his belly.
It was like fire burning his body.
He left the rest station, lay exposed, tossed and turned, and fell into a carriage rut.
At dawn, five hundred merchant carriages passed by and ran over him.
His companion saw this and said:
I am now disgraced.
If I return to the kingdom and am suspected of taking his possessions and leaving, it will be called unrighteousness.
Thus, he disregarded his own life and abandoned his wealth, and departed.
Turning and advancing afar, he traveled tens of thousands of *lǐ* away from Shèwèi.
There was a country.
The King had passed away, and there was no crown prince.
The prophecy book said:
A humble man from the central kingdom (*Zhōngguó*) shall be King of this land.
The officials discussed, saying:
A country without a ruler is like a body without a head.
It is difficult to maintain for long.
The former King had a horse that always performed a salute for the King.
If it meets the designated King, the horse will surely bend its knee.
All agreed, saying, "Excellent!"
Immediately, they prepared the grand carriage, placing the royal seal and ribbon upon it.
People and horses filled the roads, and all observers shed tears.
At that time, that merchant also came out to watch.
The Grand Astrologer (*Tàishǐ*) of the kingdom said:
"He has a canopy of yellow cloud above him; this is the aura of a King."
The divine horse went straight toward him, bent its knee, and licked his feet.
The ministers were delighted. They gave him a fragrant bath.
They appointed him as the ruler of the kingdom.
All unanimously acclaimed him as their sovereign.
The King said:
"I was originally a merchant.
I possess no virtue toward the people, and I am not fit for the Heavenly Position."
The officials said:
"Heaven grants it to the virtuous, and the divine horse bent its knee."
Thereupon, he took up residence in the royal palace.
He listened to and examined the state administration.
He deeply considered to himself, saying:
"I have no minute goodness; by what affinity did I obtain this?"
"It must be the Buddha's grace that caused this to happen."
In the morning, seated on the throne, he sighed about the Buddha’s unsurpassed sanctity.
Leading the officials of the land, he faced Shèwèi Guó.
He bowed his head to the ground, saying:
"This humble person, having received the Venerated One's (*Shìzūn*) grace, obtained the position of ruler.
This land, throughout the generations, has not known of the Buddha.
Even popular books contain no record of him.
I wish that with your great illumination, you might open the deafness and blindness of the people of this country.
Tomorrow, I wish that together with the multitude of *Yìngzhēn* and saints,
You would graciously favor this place for a period of three months."
The Buddha instructed Ānán:
"Command all the *bǐqiū*.
The King invites tomorrow.
All must follow the transformation and manifest divine, venerable virtue.
So that his countrymen may all witness it together."
The *Zhū Tiān* heard the Buddha's teaching there.
They led each other, followed, made music, and sang of his virtue.
Jeweled canopies, banners, and streamers were profuse, their brilliant colors dazzling the eyes.
The Buddha and the *Yìngzhēn* all sat in the main hall.
The King personally poured and served until finished.
He took a small chair and sat before the Buddha.
The Buddha extensively spoke the Dharma.
The King said:
"I was fundamentally a humble person.
My actions contained no immediate virtue; by what affinity did I obtain this?"
The Buddha informed the King, saying:
"In the past, when you were feeding the Buddha,
Your heart thought, saying:
The Buddha's heart is like a King.
The *shāmén* are like ministers.
You planted this seed, and now you obtain its fruit.
That other person said:
The Buddha is like an ox; the disciples are like a carriage.
That person himself planted the seed of being run over by a carriage.
He is now on Tài Shān, being run over by a carriage of fire.
He receives his own fruit.
It was not achieved by the King's valor.
Good deeds are followed by blessing; evil conduct is pursued by disaster.
Just as an echo answers a sound, good and evil follow like sound.
It is not bestowed by *Tiānlóng*, ghosts, or spirits.
Nor is it done by ancestors.
That which creates it is the mind.
That which completes it is the body and speech."
The Buddha chanted a *gè*, saying:
The mind is the root of phenomena, the mind is honored, the mind controls. If the mind holds evil thoughts,
then words and deeds follow, and suffering pursues one, like a carriage track following the wheel.
The mind is the root of phenomena, the mind is honored, the mind controls. If the mind holds good thoughts,
then words and deeds follow, and blessing and joy pursue one, like a shadow following the form.
The *Shìzūn* further informed the King, saying:
Among the multitude of wicked sins, there are five that are the gravest.
Being unfilial, being disloyal, killing one's parents, killing one's sovereign; the family is destroyed and the country is in chaos.
This is the first grave sin.
An *Luóhàn* practices, attains emptiness, does not desire the meditation of non-thought.
He shares the Buddha's intent to save sentient beings.
Yet, foolishly harming him.
This is the second grave sin.
The Buddha has exhausted all sins, and auspicious blessings have amassed and matured.
He possesses the marks of perfection and the *Shílì*, using the Dharma to guide sentient beings.
His loving-kindness, compassion, sympathetic joy, and equanimity surpass a compassionate mother's heart.
Yet, foolishly and maliciously slandering him. This is the third grave sin.
Pure and clean *shāmén* whose aspiration is peaceful and conduct is lofty.
Their inner feelings embrace the Sutras and Dharma, helping the Buddha convert the foolish.
All Buddhas succeed one another; sentient beings attain liberation, all through the assembly of monks.
Flattering slander causes contention and disharmony.
Because of disharmony, the Right Dharma (*Zhèngfǎ*) is ruined.
If the Right Dharma is ruined, the people run astray wildly.
When the people run astray, the *Sān È Dào* flourish.
Disturbing the assembly of *bǐqiū* monks.
This is the fourth grave sin.
The Buddha's venerable temples, treasures, resources, water, and land.
Sentient beings offer them with pure hearts to the Three Venerated Ones (*Sān Zūn*).
Foolish people destroy or steal them.
This is the fifth grave sin.
Those who violate these five have unforgivable sins.
It is called suicide, self-destruction of one's lineage, and self-casting into the fires of Tài Shān.
The gravity of these five sins is heavier than Xūmí. Be careful not to commit them."
When the Buddha finished speaking the Sutra.
The King and his ministers all attained the stage of *Xūtuóhuán*.
They received the *Wǔ Jiè* and became pure believing laymen (*qīngxìn shì*).
Among the countrymen, some became *shāmén*.
Others guarded the precepts and became pure believing laymen.
Consequently, they used the *Wǔ Jiè* and the *Shí Shàn* as the basis for governing the country.
The *Zhū Tiān* protected and assisted them, and the country flourished.
King Bō Sī Nì.
He had previously planted the root of virtue, and the resonance of blessing naturally responded.
In his backyard garden, a sugarcane tree naturally grew.
Sweet juice flowed forth from it ceaselessly day and night.
Furthermore, a stalk of polished non-glutinous rice grew.
It hung with hundreds of ears, and gathering them never exhausted the supply.
The King received this blessing and ate the food without limit.
His body became heavily fat; his breathing was extremely labored, and he could not turn over.
He went to the Buddha's residence, lowered his body, bowed respectfully,
and sat to one side.
The Buddha then spoke a verse:
If a person can focus their intention on food and know when to stop and be satisfied,
he seeks only to support his form, sustain his life, nourish his longevity, and guard virtue and the Way.
The King was delighted and leapt for joy.
He immediately arose from his seat, bid farewell to the Buddha, and returned to the palace.
He commanded the food-bearers: "Those who approach me,
must first recite this verse, making it a permanent rule."
The King gradually reduced his food intake.
His body decreased, and his frame became light.
He could move about without difficulty.
King Bōsīní.
While sleeping at night, he had ten kinds of dreams.
First, a small tree bore flowers.
Second, he saw a small tree bearing fruit.
Third, he saw a cow seeking milk from its calf.
Fourth, he saw a person cutting a rope, and a sheep followed and ate it.
Fifth, he saw ten cauldrons stacked, and the topmost cauldron boiled over and poured into the lowest cauldron.
Sixth, he saw a horse with one body and two heads eating grain.
Seventh, he saw blood flowing and forming a ditch.
Eighth, he saw clear water that was pure around the four edges but muddy in the center.
Ninth, he saw a dog urinating in a gold vessel.
Tenth, he saw four oxen coming from the four directions, colliding with each other, then scattering and returning whence they came.
The king felt terrified, and the hairs on his body stood up.
He immediately woke up from his sleep and formed this thought:
"Am I about to die and lose this royal position?"
He immediately went to ask the Buddha (Fó).
The Buddha (Fó) said:
"Great King (Dàwáng), harbor no fear.
You will not lose your royal position because of these dreams."
Regarding the dream of the small tree bearing flowers:
In the future, sentient beings will desire to practice non-Dharma (fēifǎ) acts.
They will constantly harbor greed and envy and align themselves with false doctrines (xiéfǎ).
At that time, people who are unfilial toward their parents
and do not serve Śramaṇas (shāmén) or Brahmins (Póluómén)
will obtain offerings
just like those who are filial toward their parents and offer to Śramaṇas (shāmén) today.
Regarding the small tree bearing fruit:
In the future, sentient beings will desire to practice non-Dharma (fēifǎ) acts.
They will constantly harbor greed and envy and align themselves with false doctrines (xiéfǎ).
At that time, people will return (home) not long after getting married
while holding a child, knowing no shame or remorse.
Regarding the cow seeking milk from its calf:
In the future, sentient beings will desire to practice non-Dharma (fēifǎ) acts.
They will constantly harbor greed and envy and align themselves with false doctrines (xiéfǎ).
The mother will guard the gate while the daughter engages in promiscuity (pángtōng) to support herself and live.
Regarding the person cutting the rope and the sheep following and eating it:
In the future, sentient beings will desire to practice non-Dharma (fēifǎ) acts.
They will constantly harbor greed and envy and align themselves with false doctrines (xiéfǎ).
They will give their own wealth and treasures to outsiders (wàirén) for illicit dealings.
Regarding the dream of ten stacked cauldrons, where the topmost cauldron overflows and pours into the lowest cauldron:
In the future, sentient beings will desire to practice non-Dharma (fēifǎ) acts
and align themselves with false doctrines (xiéfǎ).
Children will speak to their parents, saying:
"Quickly leave this house and go to the mountains, wilderness, or marshes.
I want to live in this village."
Regarding the horse with one body and two heads eating grain:
In the future, sentient beings will desire to practice non-Dharma (fēifǎ) acts.
They will constantly harbor greed and envy and align themselves with false doctrines (xiéfǎ).
They will rely on the king (Guówáng) to rob and seize from Brahmins (Póluómén) and elders (zhǎngzhě),
or rely on Brahmins (Póluómén) and elders (zhǎngzhě) to rob and seize the royal treasury.
Regarding the dream of blood flowing and forming a ditch:
In the future, there will be kings (Guówáng) who are not content with their own territories.
They will assemble four types of troops to invade and seize other territories.
They will also be unrestrainable and disobedient to the Dharma teachings.
At that time, the number of people who die will be numerous.
Regarding the dream of clear water that is pure around the four edges but muddy in the center:
In the future, sentient beings will desire to practice non-Dharma (fēifǎ) acts.
They will constantly harbor greed and envy and align themselves with false doctrines (xiéfǎ).
Sentient beings in the central regions (Zhōngguó) will love conflicts and turmoil.
The people in the border countries (biānguó) will have no disputes or lawsuits.
Regarding the dream of the dog urinating in a gold vessel:
In the future, sentient beings will desire to practice non-Dharma (fēifǎ) acts.
They will constantly harbor greed and envy and align themselves with false doctrines (xiéfǎ).
The Dharma treasures (Fǎbǎo) that I diligently collected over three great Kalpas (ā sēng qí jié)
will all be slandered.
They will strike my disciples (shēngwén) with knives, staves, tiles, and stones, saying:
"What this type of Śramaṇa (shāmén) teaches is non-Dharma (fēifǎ).
They are good at composing songs and praises."
Regarding the dream of four oxen coming from four directions, colliding and butting each other, then scattering and returning whence they came:
In the future, sentient beings will desire to practice non-Dharma (fēifǎ) acts.
They will constantly harbor greed and envy and align themselves with false doctrines (xiéfǎ).
At that time, great clouds will arise from the four directions.
There will be thunder, lightning, and crackling, but they will disperse without raining.
These are the interpretations of the ten dreams.
Great King (Dàwáng), these ten dreams
have these ten interpretations.
For this reason, the king should harbor no fear; you will neither die nor lose your royal position.
These are all phenomena that will occur in the future Latter Age (mòshì).
Great King (Dàwáng), you should study this.
The king was greatly delighted.
King Bōsīní's
daughter, Pótú, had passed away.
He loved and cherished her intensely.
She was never far from his sight.
After the funeral was completed,
he personally went to see the Tathāgata (Rúlái), bowed his head and face to the feet, and sat down to one side.
The Buddha (Fó) said:
"Why is the king's clothing soiled with dust and why is he so melancholy and worried today?"
The king said:
"A daughter whom I dearly loved just passed away.
The funeral rites have just been completed. I wished to redeem my daughter's life with elephants,
even down to carriages, horses, and hidden treasures.
Worry, sorrow, distress, and affliction all arise from affection and love (ēn'ài)."
The reason for this is,
"In ancient times, Great King (Dàwáng),
in this city of Shèwèi,
there was a man whose daughter died.
Because he loved and cherished his daughter, he never let her out of his sight.
He became confused and bewildered, recognizing nothing.
He wandered everywhere, asking the populace:
'Who has seen my daughter?'
Great King (Dàwáng), you should realize through this incident
that worry, sorrow, distress, and affliction all arise from affection and love (ēn'ài).
Great King (Dàwáng), harbor no worry or sorrow.
All affection and love must eventually lead to separation.
Everything that is produced must eventually decay and perish."
Thus, he extensively preached the Dharma for him.
The king accepted the teaching and departed.
At that time, in the city of Shèwèichéng.
There was a Brāhmaṇa of great lineage,
named Yéruòdá.
He possessed much wealth and treasure.
One of his maids, named Huángtóu,
regularly guarded the Mòluó Yuán.
At that time, the maid was constantly anxious and sorrowful, saying,
“When will I be able to be freed from being a maid?”
One morning,
having eaten her portion of dry rice, she carried it toward the garden.
At that time, the World-Honored One (Shìzūn) entered the city to beg for food.
The maid Huángtóu saw the Tathāgata (Rúlái) from afar.
She thought to herself,
“I would rather take this rice now and offer it to that Śramaṇa (Shāméng).
Perhaps I might be freed from this servitude as a maid.”
She immediately presented the rice as an offering to the Buddha.
The World-Honored One compassionately accepted it and returned to the Vihāra (Jīngshě).
The maid Huángtóu,
then advanced and entered Mòluó Yuán.
King Bōsīnì [Pasenadi],
having deployed the four types of troops, went out hunting.
His entourage dispersed to chase herds of deer.
The weather was extremely hot, and he saw Mòlì Yuán (Malla Garden) in the distance.
He immediately turned his carriage and entered the garden on foot.
Huángtóu saw Bōsīnì approaching from afar.
His manner of walking and his bearing were not that of an ordinary person.
She immediately came forward to welcome him, saying,
“Welcome, great man. Please sit here.”
She immediately took off one of her garments and spread it out for the King to sit upon.
Huángtóu asked,
“Do you need water to wash your feet?”
The King said, “Yes, I do.”
She immediately fetched water and gave it to the King,
and rubbed the King’s feet for him.
She asked the King again,
“Would you like to wash your face?”
She then fetched more water for the King to wash his face.
She asked the King again,
“Would you like a drink?”
She then went to the pond, washed her hands again,
took a fine lotus leaf, filled it with water, and gave it to the King.
She asked the King again,
“Do you wish to lie down and rest?”
She then took off another garment and spread it out for the King.
Seeing the King lying down, she knelt before him
and massaged his feet and other limbs,
relieving the King’s fatigue.
Huángtóu’s body was fine, soft, and excellent, like that of a celestial being.
The King felt how smooth and soft she was [when she touched him].
He thought to himself,
“There has never been a woman so intelligent!
She has done all these things without my instruction.”
The King then asked,
“Whose daughter are you?”
She replied,
“I am the maid of Yéruòdá’s household.
He assigned me to guard this garden.”
While they were speaking thus,
the King’s ministers,
following the tracks of the King’s carriage, arrived at the garden.
They knelt and bowed at the King’s feet and stood to one side.
The King commanded one person,
“Go summon the Brāhmaṇa Yéruòdá.”
The Brāhmaṇa came to the King’s location.
The King asked,
“Is this woman your maid?”
He replied, “She is.”
The King said,
“I now wish to take her as my wife.
What is your opinion?”
He replied,
“She is merely a maidservant; how can she become a wife?”
The King said,
“No matter.
We shall just discuss the price.”
The Brāhmaṇa said,
“If you wish to discuss the price—
a hundred thousand measures of gold—
how could I accept a price from the King?
I will simply present her to the King now.”
The King said,
“That is not right.
I am taking her as a wife.
How can I not give a price?”
He immediately took out a hundred thousand measures of gold
and gave it to the Brāhmaṇa.
He then welcomed her and had her conveyed into the palace.
The ministers escorted them.
Because she came from the Mòlì Yuán (Malla Garden), she was named Mòlì Fūrén (Malla Lady).
The King cherished and respected her greatly.
Subsequently, at another time,
among the five hundred women of the King,
she was established as the First Lady (Queen).
While in the high palace, she thought to herself,
“Due to what karmic retribution was I freed from being a maid and now enjoy such happiness?”
She thought again:
“Perhaps it was because I previously offered my portion of dry rice mixed with honey to the Śramaṇa (Shāméng).
Due to this cause and condition, I am now freed from being a maid
and receive such happiness.”
In ancient times, there was a Buddha
whose title was Shǐwú.
At that time, there was a king
named Hǎoxìn.
He delighted in the Buddha Dharma and never tired of viewing the Buddha.
He planted a Níjùlèi (Nyagrodha) tree,
and beneath the tree, he laid out a sandalwood couch and seat for the Buddha.
The Buddha sat upon it.
King Hǎoxìn listened to the Sūtra.
After the Buddha entered Nirvāṇa (Níhuán),
the King could no longer see the Buddha.
He then named the Níjùlèi tree the Buddha Tree.
Seeing it was like seeing the Buddha.
He went and sat under the tree every day,
imagining that he heard the teachings and precepts at the place where the Buddha used to sit.
The King had a favored attendant (Qīngyī)
named Jūlù.
She always served by the King’s side.
The Queen (Fūrén), out of jealousy, hired a Brāhmaṇa to use incantations to kill the Buddha Tree.
This Brāhmaṇa,
on the night of the seventh day of the fourth month, took the brain of a large venomous serpent from the Southern Mountains and smeared it on the tree.
The tree immediately withered and died.
The King was immediately overcome with grief and tears.
On the night of the eighth day of the fourth month, when the morning star appeared, he took fragrant water of five colors and gathered flowers to sprinkle upon the tree.
It immediately revived and grew again.
The King then made a vow, saying,
“May all Buddhas in the ten directions use this day for their birth,
use this day for achieving the Way (enlightenment),
and also use this day for entering Parinirvāṇa (Bānnīhuán).”
From this time forward, when Buddhas appear in the world,
it is always on this day.
Therefore, the eighth day of the fourth month is used for bathing the Buddha.
Jìyù, the King of Medicine,
invited the Buddha and the Saṅgha,
except for Pántè (Panthaka).
Pántè spent four months reciting the name of the broom,
but was ultimately unable to succeed.
The Tathāgata and the Saṅgha went and sat in Jìyù’s dwelling.
When the pure water was served, the Tathāgata did not accept it.
Jìyù reported to the Buddha,
“I do not understand the reason why the Tathāgata does not accept the water.”
The Buddha informed Jìyù,
“Pántè Bhikṣu is not among this assembly today.
Therefore, I do not accept it.”
Jìyù reported to the Buddha,
“This Pántè is foolish and dull.
Even herdsmen of cows and sheep are superior to him.”
The Buddha told Jìyù,
“If you do not invite Pántè, I will not accept the pure water.”
Thereupon, Jìyù, following the Buddha’s instruction, immediately sent someone to summon Pántè.
The Buddha told Ānán,
“Give the bowl to Pántè.
Have him remain seated and remotely present it to me.”
Jìyù, seeing this spiritual power, immediately repented and rebuked himself.
“Alas, what a great mistake! I have humiliated a Worthy and a Sage.
Today I realize I committed a great fault of the mouth.”
He immediately developed a sense of reverence toward Pántè Bhikṣu,
surpassing that for the five hundred monks.
The World-Honored One elaborated:
In a past life, Jìyù was a general involved in trade and exchange.
He once drove a thousand horses to another kingdom.
Midway, one horse gave birth to a foal.
He gave the foal to someone as a gift and proceeded to the other kingdom.
He met with the ruler of that kingdom.
The King told the horse general,
“These thousand horses of yours are all common horses.
But one horse that cried out sounded different; it must have given birth to a prized foal.
When that foal grows up, its value will be equal to a thousand horses.”
“If you can obtain that foal, I will buy all your horses; otherwise, I do not want them.”
The horse general pursued the person to whom he had given the foal.
Before ten days had passed, the foal was speaking human language.
It told its owner,
“If the horse general comes seeking me,
you can give me to him for five hundred horses.”
The horse general sought to redeem it for one ordinary horse.
That person replied,
“I did not originally ask you for it by force.
I diligently nourished and kept it alive.
Now you want it,
so redeem it with five hundred horses, and I will return it to you.”
Thus, he agreed.
Previously, he scorned and despised the foal.
Now, [in this life] he excluded Pántè.
Later, both were highly valued.
The karmic cause involving Pántè is ancient;
it did not arise only today.
In the past, the ancestors of King Bǐngshā.
The law for governing criminals was:
If one committed robbery, they had to slap their own head.
The thief felt great shame, which was no different from death.
Afterward, they did not commit the crime again.
When it reached the reign of his father king, the rule was:
If one committed robbery, they were driven out of the city as a strict instruction.
The thieves all felt shame, which was no different from death.
Afterward, they did not commit the crime again.
Píngshā succeeded to the throne.
If one committed robbery, they were driven out of the country.
At that time, there was a thief who was driven out seven times.
Yet he still returned to rob and kill in villages and cities.
Finally, he was bound and sent forth.
The King said:
Take him away and sever his little finger.
At that time, the official quickly severed it, fearing the King might regret his decision.
The King tried biting his own finger, finding the pain exceedingly difficult to bear, and immediately called to stop the severing.
The minister answered the King, saying:
It has already been severed.
The King was greatly distressed and regretted it.
He then pondered to himself, saying:
I am the last of the kings who governed by law,
and the beginning of those who govern without law.
A true king should worry and care for the people below him,
yet I have severed a person's finger.
He immediately commanded his carriage
and went to the Buddha, saying:
My great-grandfather, ancestors, and father king,
all governed the people by law.
But when it reached my person,
evil daily increases, and righteous transformation gradually weakens.
I have wrongly attained kingship and injured and severed a person's body part.
I truly feel profound shame and fear, deeming myself without the Way.
The Buddha addressed the Great King:
Regarding the law for governing the nation,
how much money stolen merits the death penalty, and how much merits exile from the country?
How much marks the threshold for applying punishment?
The King said:
World-Honored One,
nineteen ancient coins make up one fraction of a jìlìshāpán (Karshāpaṇa).
One jìlìshāpán is divided into four parts.
If one steals one part, the crime merits death.
The Buddha then preached the Dharma for him.
The King bowed to the Buddha and withdrew.
At that time, the Bhikṣus said:
How is it that King Bǐngshā fears sin to such an extent?
The Buddha said:
He does not only fear sin in this life.
In the past, there was a country named Jiāshī (Kāśi).
The king’s royal title was Míngchēng.
The people of that country at that time,
all possessed craftsmanship and artistic skills to earn their livelihood.
If one lacked craftsmanship or skill, they were called foolish.
If one committed robbery, they were also called foolish.
At that time, there was a man who committed robbery and was bound and sent to the King.
The King said:
Stop, stop.
That man lost property, and this man committed robbery.
Why should I participate in creating evil with them?
He reflected:
Since ancient times, there has only been this one foolish person.
If these foolish people do not reach one thousand, I ought to meet my end (die).
He immediately handed the foolish person over to a high minister, saying:
I need one thousand foolish people to prepare for a great assembly.
Gather them until the number is complete, and report it to me so I may know.
The minister took the foolish person and detained him in one place.
The King then pondered, saying:
Will this foolish person suffer hardship?
He then instructed the minister:
Take good care of this person; do not let him become emaciated.
Place him in my Wúyōu (Asoka) Garden.
Provide him with the five pleasures, entertainment, and music.
The minister obeyed the command.
Wishing to please the King, he took extra care in watching over them.
Not long afterward, the number reached one thousand.
The minister reported that the number was complete.
If anything else is needed, it should be prepared quickly.
When the King heard this,
he was greatly worried and anxious.
For a long time in the past, there was only that one person.
How is it that now the number has suddenly reached a thousand?
Perhaps this means the wicked Dharma is increasing in the latter age.
The King commanded his officials:
Sweep and clean the garden, burn incense, and hang silk banners.
Prepare all sorts of delicious foods and drinks.
The King, together with his officials and the eighteen groups of attendants, went to the Wúyōu Garden.
He commanded the foolish men to be brought forward and saw that their clothes were torn, dirty, their nails long, and their hair disheveled.
He immediately commanded them to be bathed, their hair cut, and their nails trimmed.
New clothes were provided to them.
Afterward, they were brought forward, and each was given various foods, drinks, and treasures.
They were allowed whatever they desired.
He instructed them to return home and support their parents,
work diligently in their professions, and never commit robbery again.
The foolish men heard the command, rejoiced, and obeyed.
At that time, the King ceded his throne to his crown prince,
left home, and entered the mountains to learn the methods of the immortals.
The king of that country at that time was Píngshā.
He always feared karmic retribution for sin.
The Buddha said:
O King Píngshā,
not only in this life have you ordered a finger severed and immediately regretted it afterward.
In a past life, there was a Brahmán (Bōluómén).
He had no wealth and lived by begging.
This Brahmán’s wife did not give birth to a son.
The household originally had a nakulá (mongoose).
Then she bore a son.
The Brahmán thought of the mongoose as his son.
The nakulá son also thought of the Brahmán as its father.
A short time later, the wife bore a son.
When the Brahmán went out begging for food, he instructed his wife, saying:
If you go out, you must take the child with you.
The wife fed the child and went to a neighbor’s house to borrow their mortar for pounding rice.
The child had the scent of ghee and curds.
A poisonous snake opened its mouth, spitting venom, intending to kill the baby.
The nakulá thought:
My parents are not here.
How can this poisonous snake try to kill my younger brother?
It immediately killed the poisonous snake and severed it into seven parts.
It smeared blood on its mouth and stood at the door.
It wanted its parents to see this and be happy.
At that time, the Brahmán,
just arriving from outside, saw his wife far away outside the house.
He immediately became angry and said:
I told you that when you go out, you must take the child with you!
Why did you go alone?
When the father was about to enter the door, he saw the nakulá with blood on its lips.
He immediately thought:
My wife and I were absent.
The nakulá, behind our backs, must have killed and eaten my son.
He struck and killed the nakulá with his staff.
Entering the door, he saw his son,
sitting in the courtyard sucking his finger and playing.
He also saw the poisonous snake in seven pieces and felt exceedingly great sorrow and regret.
This nakulá saved the life of my son.
I did not observe carefully but rashly killed it. How painful and pitiable!
He immediately fainted and fell to the ground.
At that time, a deity in the air
immediately spoke in verse, saying:
It is proper to observe carefully; do not act with sudden fierce anger.
Good friends and loved ones are lost, unjustly harmed, and trust is hurt and painful.
The Brahmán at that time
is the present King Píngshā.
King Bǐngshā asked Mùlián (Maudgalyāyana):
Which heaven has excellent food?
Mùlián praised, saying:
The Heaven of the Four Great Kings (Cāturmahārājika).
Bǐngshā ought to be reborn in Dōushuài (Tuṣita Heaven).
He immediately thought to be born in this heaven first,
and later be born in Dōushuài.
When his life ended, he became the Crown Prince of King Píshāmén (Vaiśravaṇa),
named Zuìshèngzǐ.
As stated in the instructions given by Mùlián:
The first people who walked on their chests were named Móhóulè (Mahoraga).
Beings born with three hands were named Xiàng (Elephants).
Question:
Why are people mentioned
as either Móhóulè
or Xiàng?
Answer:
It is evidence that those beings, having finished their lives in the Guāngyīn Heaven (Abhāvara or Radiant Sound Heaven), came to be born here.
At that time, they were born among the beasts.
But their appearance was like that of humans.
Their food was wicked, their intentions evil, and their cunning and deceit increased greatly.
Thus, the form of humans gradually vanished and they became beasts.
Their form was like that of frogs.
At that time, the King of Wángshěguó,
whose name was Píngshā,
when he was young as Crown Prince, constantly sought five vows.
Firstly, that when I am young, I may become king.
Secondly, that a Buddha may appear in my kingdom.
Thirdly, that I may constantly go and come (to see him).
Fourthly, that I may constantly hear the Sūtras expounded.
Fifthly, that upon hearing them, my afflictions may dissolve, and I may attain the level of Sūtuóhuán (Stream-Enterer).
The King attained all of them.
At that time, the King traveled north from Wángshěguó to another country.
The country's name was Déchāyīluó.
The king's name was Fújiāshā.
He held himself in very high esteem.
In a previous life, he had seen the Buddha and received the Buddha's Sūtra teachings.
He studied the Sūtra concerning the six constituents of the body,
which are called Earth, Water, Fire, Wind, Space, and Mind.
However, King Píngshā
and King Fújiāshā had never met in person.
From afar, they loved and respected each other as if they were brothers.
They constantly exchanged letters and inquired after each other.
A lotus flower grew in King Fújiāshā's kingdom,
which had a thousand petals, all rendered in a golden color.
He sent it as a gift to King Píngshā.
King Píngshā
saw the flower and rejoiced greatly, saying,
"King Fújiāshā
has sent me something truly extraordinary and rare."
King Píngshā
wrote a letter to King Fújiāshā, saying,
"My country has much gold, silver, and rare treasures.
I do not consider these to be treasures.
Now a human flower has grown in my kingdom,
named Fó (Buddha).
His body is of purplish-yellow gold color and possesses thirty-two characteristics."
King Fújiāshā
heard the word 'Buddha' and leaped for joy.
He wrote a letter to King Píngshā,
fully relating his intentions concerning the Buddha's teachings, precepts, and practice.
King Fújiāshā,
a few days later, thought to himself,
"Human life is unpredictable, lasting only the span of a breath.
I cannot wait any longer for Píngshā's reply."
He commanded the kings of the smaller countries and his ministers
to prepare carriages and set out, intending to go to the Buddha's residence.
On the way, he encountered a letter from King Píngshā.
The letter stated:
"The Buddha teaches people to abandon their homes, renounce their wives and children, and cut off all attachment and desire.
They should remove their hair and beard, put on the Dharma robes, and become a Shā mén."
It also detailed the Twelve Links of Dependent Origination,
and sent it to King Fújiāshā.
King Fújiāshā,
having finished reading the letter, contemplated by himself.
After nightfall, when the ministers, officials, and crowd had all gone to sleep, he left.
Silent and without a sound, he secretly arose and fled.
He entered the grave mounds and shaved his head himself.
He put on the Dharma robes and became a Shā mén.
The Buddha, with his divine sight, saw that Fújiāshā
had arrived at Wángshěchéng and was staying at a pottery kiln house.
The Buddha thought,
"King Fújiāshā's life will end tomorrow."
He immediately flew to the kiln house and requested to stay for one night.
The owner of the kiln house replied,
"You may be accommodated."
The Buddha sat upright in one place.
He then thought to himself,
"This Fújiāshā is truly tranquil and serene."
He arose and went before Fújiāshā,
asking him,
"Whose disciple are you, and whose doctrine did you receive to become a Shā mén?"
He replied,
"I heard there is a Buddha, and I am now serving him as my teacher."
The Buddha thought,
"This worthy man became a Shā mén because of me.
I should explain the Sūtra concerning his past lives that I know.
Only then will he attain understanding."
The Buddha said,
"I will speak the matter of the Sūtra for you.
Listen carefully."
Fújiāshā said, "Good."
The Buddha expounded the Dharma for him.
He attained the Third Path, Ānàhán (Non-Returner).
He was able to recognize that this was the Buddha.
He immediately arose and made obeisance to the Buddha.
The next day, not far after entering the city,
a young horned ox gored and attacked Fújiāshā.
The Bhikṣus reported to the Buddha, saying,
"The Shā mén for whom the Buddha expounded the Sūtra yesterday at the kiln house
was gored and killed by an ox.
To what destination will he go?"
The Buddha said,
"When I expounded the Sūtra for him, he immediately attained Ānàhán.
He will be reborn in the sixteenth heaven and attain Āluóhàn."
The Buddha ordered the Bhikṣus to retrieve Fújiāshā's body
and gather and bury it properly.
They raised a Stūpa over it.
At that time, there was the celestial being Chìmǎ Tiānzǐ,
whose appearance and color were exceedingly marvelous.
In the latter part of the night, he came to the Buddha's residence.
He addressed the Buddha, saying,
"World-Honored One,
is there anyone who can travel beyond the edge of the world
and reach the place of no birth, no aging, and no death?"
The Buddha told Chìmǎ,
"There is none who can reach it."
Chìmǎ Tiānzǐ again addressed the Buddha, saying,
"Wondrous, World-Honored One!
You have spoken this meaning well.
As the World-Honored One says,
Why is this so?
I remember my past life.
My name was Chìmǎ.
I was an external path Xīan Rén (immortal).
I attained spiritual powers and was separated from all desires and attachments.
At that time, I thought,
'I possess such swift spiritual feet
that are like a strong warrior shooting a sharp arrow horizontally.
In the space of a moment, the shadow of a Tāluó tree shifts.
I can ascend Mount Xūmí,
reach one Xūmí,
step on the Eastern Sea, and leap across to the Western Sea.'
I thought about my swift spiritual power and wanted to seek the edge of the world.
I then set off.
Except for eating, resting, and excretion,
I reduced sleep and traveled constantly for a hundred years.
I died on the road and ultimately did not reach it."
He immediately disappeared and vanished.
In a foreign country, there was an evil rain.
If it fell into rivers, lakes, wells, or ponds,
people who drank it would become mad and intoxicated for seven days.
There was a king
who was very wise and knew about the evil rain; he knew it by looking at the clouds.
He ordered one well to be covered so that the rain would not enter.
At that time, the officials and ministers drank the evil rainwater.
The entire court went mad.
They stripped off their clothes, sat naked on the royal palace floor, smeared mud on their heads.
Only the King alone did not go mad.
All the ministers did not know they were mad.
Instead, they called the King mad.
"Why is he wearing clothes, alone and different from the rest of us?"
They all said to each other,
"This is no small matter; we should think about how to deal with him."
The King feared that the ministers wanted to rebel and became frightened himself.
He spoke to the ministers, saying,
"I have a good medicine that can cure my illness myself.
Please wait a moment while I take the medicine."
The King then went inside, stripped off his clothes to join them, and came out.
All the ministers saw this and were greatly pleased.
After seven days, the ministers awakened and were greatly ashamed.
Each put on their clothes and caps and came to the morning assembly.
The King was still sitting naked, as before.
The ministers were all startled and asked,
"Your Majesty is usually very wise.
Why is it like this?"
The King answered his ministers, saying,
"My mind has always been steady and unchanging.
Because you were mad, you instead called me mad.
This was not my true intention."
In the past, the King of Jiāshīguó
governed according to the correct Dharma.
The people were peaceful and happy, free from all troubles and difficulties.
At that time, the King had no son.
The queen suddenly became pregnant.
After ten months, she gave birth to a child with no eyes or nose.
Seven days after birth, a great assembly was arranged, gathering all the ministers.
Physiognomists and Daoists were consulted to name the child.
According to the law of that country,
names were given based on auspicious features, constellations, or parents.
A Brāhmaṇa asked,
"What unusual features does the Prince's body have?"
Someone nearby replied,
"This Prince's face is completely flat, without any eyes or nose."
The Brāhmaṇa said,
"He should be named Jìngmiàn (Mirror-Face)."
Four wet nurses were appointed to serve and raise him:
one person for bathing and rubbing,
one person for removing impurities,
one person for holding and embracing,
and one person for suckling.
These four wet nurses served him day and night.
Like a lotus flower, he grew day by day.
When he reached adulthood, his father, the King, died.
Jìngmiàn was immediately installed in the honored position of King.
However, this Prince had cultivated the roots of virtue in past lives.
Although born without eyes, he possessed the celestial eye.
He was capable of being king.
His power of merit and virtue was great.
