The people of the country, upon hearing that Crown Prince Jìngmiàn was King, were all struck with wonder.
At that time, a minister wanted to test him.
He could not find an opportunity.
It happened that the King issued a command,
commanding all the ministers
to erect a new palace hall,
with carved patterns, engravings, and various colored paintings.
The minister tested the King.
He brought a macaque, dressed it in clothes, put it into a leather bag,
and slung it over his shoulder, bringing it before the King.
"The skilled artisans have arrived; please, Your Majesty, give instructions."
The King knew he was being tested.
He then spoke a Gāthā (verse), saying:
Observing this class of beings—glaring eyes, wrinkled faces,
their nature is frivolous and restless; when accomplishing tasks, they are capable of destruction.
Receiving their due fate is like this. How can they raise palaces?
They mutilate and break flowering and fruit trees, and are unfit to approach people.
How much less are they able to build palaces! Urge them and send them back to the wild forests.
At that time, Jìngmiàn wáng (King Mirror-Face).
Now it is I myself.
Púlíxiānní wáng (King Prasenajit)
dreamt ten things while sleeping at night.
First, he dreamt of three jars side by side. The jars on the two sides were full, emitting vapor and interacting [with each other],
but not entering the empty jar in the middle.
Second, he dreamt of a horse whose mouth ate, and its buttocks also ate.
Third, he dreamt of a small tree
flowering. Fourth, he dreamt of a small tree bearing fruit.
Fifth, he dreamt of a person twisting a rope.
Behind the person was a sheep.
The sheep owner ate the rope.
Sixth, he dreamt of a fox eating on a gold bed and in gold vessels.
Seventh, he dreamt of a large cow drinking milk back from its calf.
Eighth, he dreamt of four oxen bellowing and coming from four directions, rushing toward each other, wanting to fight.
Just as they were about to clash but had not yet clashed, the oxen vanished [lit., their location was unknown].
Ninth, he dreamt of a large pond whose water was turbid in the center and clear on the four sides.
Tenth, he dreamt of the water flowing in a large ravine, being entirely red.
The king woke up greatly frightened,
(fearing) the ruin of his kingdom and his own person.
He immediately summoned the Duke Ministers and various Dàorén (ascetics) who understood and interpreted dreams, and questioned them.
There was a Fúluómén (Brahman)
(who said): "These are all inauspicious matters.
You must take your dearly beloved queen and crown prince,
as well as attendants, servants, and maidservants close to you,
and kill them all to sacrifice to the King of Heaven.
As for bedding and precious jewels and fine things worn on your person,
you must burn them all to sacrifice to Heaven.
If you can do this, the king's person will avoid misfortune."
The king heard this and was unhappy.
The queen asked the king,
"Why are you troubled and worried?"
The king told her,
"Last night I dreamt ten things,
fearing the ruin of the kingdom and myself.
A Fúluómén
interpreted the dreams as all inauspicious."
The queen said,
"O King, do not worry.
Now the Buddha is nearby in the Jīngshè (vihāra),
not far from the capital.
Why do you not go and ask the meaning of the dreams?
Whatever the Buddha explains,
the King should follow it."
The king immediately went to the Buddha's location.
He prostrated his head and face at the Buddha's feet and reported everything to the Buddha, saying,
"I fear the ruin of the country, myself, and my wife and children.
I wish to hear your teachings and precepts."
The Buddha said,
"Do not fear.
O King, your dreams
pertain to people in later ages, who will not fear legal restraints.
They will be greedy, licentious, and jealous, never knowing satisfaction.
They will lack righteousness, be without compassion, and know no shame or guilt.
The first dream means that the powerful and noble will follow each other,
disregarding the poor and lowly.
The second dream, seeing a horse eat with both ends,
means that in later ages, emperors and various high ministers
will receive salaries and emoluments but will also extort the common people, never knowing satisfaction.
The third dream, a small tree flowering, means
that in later ages, people whose age has not yet reached thirty
will grow white hair on their heads.
They will be greedy, licentious, and full of desires, young in years but prematurely old.
The fourth dream, a small tree bearing fruit, means
that in later ages, people whose age has not yet reached fifteen
will marry and return home carrying a baby.
They will know no shame or guilt.
The fifth dream, a person twisting a rope, and behind the person there is a sheep,
and the sheep owner eats the rope, means
that in later ages, when a husband travels abroad,
the wife will commit adultery with others and consume his property and goods.
The sixth dream, a fox eating on a gold bed and in gold vessels, means
that in later ages, base and lowly people will become esteemed and noble.
They will possess wealth and property, and everyone will respect and fear them.
The descendants of dukes and marquises will instead become poor and lowly,
occupying the lower seats and eating last.
The seventh dream, a large cow drinking milk back from its calf,
means
that in later ages, people will have no propriety or righteousness.
A mother will act as a matchmaker for her daughter to entice other men,
engaging in intercourse with her daughter and demanding money,
thereby enriching herself, knowing no shame or guilt.

The eighth dream, four oxen bellowing and coming from four directions, rushing toward each other, wanting to fight, but just as they were about to clash but had not yet clashed, the oxen vanished [lit., their location was unknown], means
that in later ages, emperors, high officials, and the common people
will all lack sincerity in their hearts.
They will mutually deceive, be foolish, and harbor hatred.
They will not respect Heaven and Earth. Because of this, the timely benefit of rain will be absent.
High officials and the common people will pray and request rain.
Heaven will raise clouds, thunder, and lightning from the four directions, making noise.
High officials and the common people will all say,
"It is about to rain." But in a moment, the clouds will disperse and the rain will depart, failing to fall.
Why is this?
Because the emperors, high officials, and the common people possess no loyalty, uprightness, benevolence, or compassion.
The ninth dream, a large pond whose water is turbid in the center and clear on the four sides, means
that in later ages, Zhōngguó (the central state) will be in turmoil, and governance will be unjust.
The common people will be unfilial toward their parents and disrespectful toward their elders.
The border kingdoms will, however, be peaceful and clear.
Their people will be harmonious, loving, and obedient to both parents.
The tenth dream, the water flowing in a large ravine being entirely red, means
that in later ages, various kingdoms will dispute angrily, raising armies and gathering masses to mutually attack and conquer.
They will use chariot troops, infantry, and cavalry.
Fighting together, the killing and wounding will be countless.
The blood of those who die on the road will flow entirely red.
The king knelt down and reported,
"Having received the Buddha's teachings and precepts, my heart is immediately joyful."
He paid homage to the Buddha and returned to the palace.
He highly honored the principal queen.
He confiscated the emoluments of all the high ministers,
and no longer trusted external paths or the Fúluómén.
In Yuèzhī guó (the Yuezhi Kingdom) there was a king,
named Èshǎo wáng (King Evil Young).
There was nothing in this world that did not submit to him.
His mother instructed the king, saying:
"Should there be a difficulty leading to death, strictly avoid circumambulating the Buddhist temple counter-clockwise (left-turn).
You must remember to circumambulate clockwise (right-turn). Strictly avoid violating this teaching of mine."
At that time, Èshǎo wáng
extensively deployed troops and masses to attack Chúnxuè chéng (Pure Blood City).
He personally wielded a sword and killed three hundred million people.
Later, the battle went poorly for him.
Riding an elephant, he fled. He looked back at the Fótú (stupa/Buddha image).
Remembering his mother's instruction, he turned the elephant and circumambulated clockwise.
The enemy states saw this and scattered and submitted.
The king saw the bandits retreat and immediately followed up, pressing forward.
He gained control of his original city and captured the enemy king.
He then remembered the Buddha's words:
"One who takes refuge in the Buddha is the most respected and the highest; none can surpass him."
(He thought) "If I had not circumambulated clockwise, how could I have defeated these bandits?"
Shèwèiguó. There was a king of Nànguó,
named Fēnhétán.
He greatly loved virtue and the Way.
Daily, he fed more than a thousand monks (dàoshì).
The King believed of himself
that his wisdom was unparalleled, and he bound his stomach with iron,
constantly fearing his wisdom might improperly escape.
He wished to arrange a marriage for his son.
He asked his ministers,
"Is there anyone in the world as wise as I am?"
"If there is such a person,
I wish to take his daughter for my son."
There was none within his kingdom.
The King dispatched messengers to search in other regions.
They arrived in Shèwèiguó and asked the people there about the Buddha.
The messenger said,
"Does the Buddha have a daughter?"
They replied,
"A man of the Way does not have daughters."
The messenger said,
"Next, who is there?"
They replied,
"Ānándàndǐ is wise, good, and loves the Way, and his daughter is foremost."
The messenger said,
"Why is she considered foremost?"
They replied,
"He once argued with Prince Jī over a garden and field, holding them up [in value] to offer to the Buddha.
The elephants carried tens of millions of billions of gold, but he did not covet the heavy treasure, only aspiring to do good."
The messenger immediately went to Ānándàndǐ's residence.
He returned and reported this to the King.
The King immediately rushed to meet him.
The King of Nànguó
was completely without clothing. Naked, dark, and ugly, his appearance resembled a ghost.
Ānándàndǐ asked,
"What do you seek?"
The King said,
"I heard that you are wise, good, and love the Way, and that your daughter is foremost.
Therefore, I have come to request your daughter for my son."
Ānándàndǐ called him forward and seated him, saying,
"I must consult the Buddha."
He fully reported the matter to the Buddha.
The Buddha said, "Give her to him."
Ānándàndǐ said,
"This will terrify my daughter to death!"
The Buddha said, "It will not."
He then immediately gave her to him.
The daughter's name was Sānmógé.
She was destined to save and liberate eighty thousand people in Nànguó.
Ānándàndǐ dared not question the Buddha again.
His heart truly held resentment.
He returned and told the King of Nànguó,
"The girl shall be given to you."
The King immediately offered the wedding gifts, welcomed her, and returned to his kingdom.
The Crown Prince went to Sānmógé's dwelling that night.
Sānmógé kicked the Crown Prince with her foot, pushing him back onto the ground.
This happened for four or five days.
The Crown Prince dared not go again.
The King's Madam (Queen) asked him,
"Why do you not go?"
The Crown Prince remained silent.
The Madam immediately went to Sānmógé's dwelling.
"I sought a wife for my son; you should now serve him.
Why did you insult my son?"
Sānmógé said,
"Madam, the Crown Prince, and all the people in the kingdom,
their bodies are all like dogs, no different from beasts."
The Madam reported to the King,
"Your wisdom is unparalleled, and you sought a wife for your son from afar.
She has no fear of difficulty and insults my son.
Moreover, she scolded me to my face."
When the King heard this,
he immediately went to Sānmógé's dwelling.
Sānmógé did not come out to pay respects.
The King said,
"I married a new wife from afar.
Is it acceptable that she scolds the Madam to her face and insults my son?"
Sānmógé said, "Indeed.
The people in your kingdom are all like dogs and beasts."
The King was greatly astonished and said,
"I constantly feared that wisdom might improperly escape from my stomach,
so I bound it with iron.
I feed more than a thousand monks daily.
Who can surpass me?
Yet, I am scolded in return."
Sānmógé said,
"Men and women, old and young, are naked facing each other.
Even if they cultivate merit, they are still contemptible and lowly."
The King went to his teacher's door and fully stated the above matters.
The teacher said,
"Go back and question her again.
Be careful not to become angry."
The King immediately returned and asked,
"What makes the people of your country superior?"
Sānmógé said,
"The men and women of my country all have clothing.
The noble and the humble have different positions, and their bodies do not appear before one another.
There is a Great Man named Fó (Buddha).
He teaches and transforms hundreds of thousands of millions of people, enabling them all to attain the Way.
They enter fire without being burned, and enter water without
drowning. He can control and encompass the Three Thousand Suns and Moons and the Twelve Thousand Heavens and Earths.
He knows the affairs of the Three Times (past, present, future).
His body possesses the Thirty-two Marks and Eighty Minor Characteristics.
His virtue and the Way are universally known, and all the devas respect and visit him."
The King said,
"Can the Buddha be seen?"
Sānmógé said,
"If you request him from afar, he can be brought here."
The King said,
"Excellent!
How should I make the request?"
Sānmógé said,
"Just burn incense yourself, and the King should follow me.
The Madam and the Crown Prince should all follow
me." Sānmógé immediately ascended a high platform and requested, saying,
"The King of Nànguó has just heard the name of the Rúlái (Tathāgata).
We pray that the Buddha will accept the King's meal offering tomorrow."
The Buddha told Mùlián,
"Instruct all the Bhikkhus.
Tomorrow, they are all to go to Nànguó."
Sānmógé
ordered the King, the Madam, and the Crown Prince to purify themselves, burn incense, spread mats, and arrange the food vessels,
to wait upon and offer food to twelve hundred and fifty people.
Sānmógé
immediately stayed in the central courtyard together with the King, the Madam, and the Crown Prince.
She commanded that when the Arhats arrived, they should come first, and the Buddha should come last.
"Be careful not to be startled or afraid; follow what I do."
The Buddha and the Bhikkhus each transformed themselves.
Shèlìfú appeared as a pair of white elephants.
Mùlián transformed into a lion.
All the great Bhikkhus changed their forms.
Various displays were shown.
Some were geese; all were different, descending from above.
The people of Nànguó were greatly alarmed.
Sānmógé said,
"Do not be afraid.
The Buddha is the very last, with water and fire issuing from his body."
Sānmógé stepped forward and paid homage to the Buddha.
The King, the Madam, and the Crown Prince also paid homage.
The Arhats took their seats, ranked by seniority.
Sānmógé, the King, the Madam, and the Crown Prince
proceeded to offer water for ablutions and place the food vessels down.
The people in the kingdom found it strange that the King had closed the palace gates.
Greatly angered, they each took an axe, intending to chop down the palace gate.
The Buddha said,
"I wish all people to perform good deeds."
He immediately caused the palace walls to transform into crystal.
When the people saw what was inside from the outside, they immediately stopped and dared not chop again.
At that time, Bīntóulú was sitting on a mountain.
Suddenly, he left and went to Nànguó.
He pricked the ground with a needle.
The thread connected to his clothes.
He used divine power to walk to Nànguó.
The mountain followed behind him.
A pregnant woman in the kingdom saw the mountain coming and feared
she would fall. In her fright, she immediately miscarried.
The Buddha ordered Mùlián to ask Bīntóulú,
"What is that behind you?"
Bīntóulú looked back.
The mountain was flung back to its original location, eight thousand *lǐ* away.
The Buddha said,
"I taught you the means of liberation.
Now, by missing the timing, you have caused the death of another person.
The grave importance of human life is something I am displeased by.
From now on, you shall not follow me during the time
of offering food (meal time). Only when the Mílè Fó (Maitreya Buddha) appears will you be allowed to attain *bānníhuán* (parinirvāṇa)."
Bīntóulú was silent and grieved bitterly.
The King reported to the Buddha, saying,
"Would you be willing to compete in spiritual power?
The one who loses must jump into a well."
The Buddha said, "Excellent.
Three questions; the one who loses must jump into a well."
The King said, "Agreed."
The Buddha asked,
"When you recite scriptures, how do you do it?"
The King said,
"When I recite scriptures,
I crawl on my hands and knees; when exhausted, I immediately lie prone on the ground."
The Buddha said,
"When I recite scriptures, I sit; when exhausted, I walk [meditative walking].
If you crawl while reciting scriptures, that is the way a dog walks.
The King is inferior."
The King attempted to jump into the well, but his two hands clung to the ground and he refused to enter.
The Buddha said, "Let him be."
The King immediately returned to his kingdom and practiced the Way of the Buddha.
Sānmógé
then served the King, the Madam, and the Crown Prince.
In Nànguó, she taught and transformed eighty thousand people.
All attained the Four Stages of Śrāvaka fruit.
At that time, there was a king.
His name was **Āzhì**.
The region he governed extended ten thousand *lǐ* around.
The people flourished greatly.
The king was extremely brave but understood nothing of the Dharma.
He invaded neighboring states and unjustly tormented good people.
All the neighboring states suffered because of him.
The Buddha, with the great assembly, went to that state.
**Āzhì** heard of this.
With his thirty-two sons, all of whom were valiant and robust, he raised troops with wicked intent.
He gathered several million people.
They advanced upon the main road, intending to meet and repel the Buddha.
The Buddha spoke to **Ānán**.
"King **Āzhì** and his sons
tomorrow will direct malice toward me and the great assembly.
How will you subdue them?"
The great *bodhisattvas* and heavenly beings laughed, shaking heaven and earth.
The Buddha asked, "Why the laughter?"
**Ānán** replied,
"We are laughing at King **Āzhì**, that is all."
The Buddha said,
"**Āzhì** is foolish and raises this wicked intent,
causing his people to acquire sin.
Having already mobilized a great army, relying on the strength of men and horses,
even if they filled the four continents, they could not move a single hair of mine.
How much less can a mere few million men do so?
The Buddha instructed **Ānán**:
"Command the wise disciples to all carry their *bō* (alms bowls) and set out.
Tomorrow, we shall take our meal from within the army of King **Āzhì**."
The king, his sons, and the vast army—even ghosts and spirits were alarmed.
At this time, the Buddha's body moved forward, emitting a great light.
He passed through the army and crossed into the state of **Āzhì**.
The king's drums ceased to sound.
Bows and crossbows could not be deployed; swords and weapons could not be drawn.
Elephants and horses stumbled, and the infantry suffered muscle cramps.
Heaven and earth grew dark; the sun and moon lost their light.
The king and his sons
were all bewildered, breathless, immediately subdued, and fled.
The Buddha and the great assembly paused and took their meals, filling their bowls.
They then arrived at the king's capital.
The city gates opened by themselves.
The Buddha advanced to the royal palace, entered the hall, and sat down.
It was silent and still.
Eight hundred and seventeen thousand heavenly beings all took their seats.
The palace spontaneously became vast, high seats appeared naturally, jeweled canopies interwove and sparkled, and the five musical tones played themselves.
The king and his sons said to one another,
"The power of a king is not equal to the power of virtue and the Way."
The soldiers were startled and terrified.
The princes said,
"We have now heard that the Buddha has entered and is already inside the palace.
We ought to return and meet the Buddha."
The king said,
"What face do I have left to meet the Buddha?
Above, I am ashamed before the spirits, and below, I have failed the people."
His sons said,
"The Buddha is benevolent and merciful and does not harm people's feelings."
The king then gathered his soldiers and slowly returned to the palace.
He met the Buddha.
He bowed his head to the ground, performed reverence to the Buddha, and offered an apology.
[He said:] "I am base, crude, and and ignorant; I studied little in my youth and know nothing of propriety or righteousness, comparable to a wolf or beast.
Foolish and bewildered, I have offended heavenly beings and humans.
The Great Sage does not regard remote, petty states.
Yet, now the **Shìzūn** unjustly traveled afar to this wretched land, and your ruler and ministers showed violent rebellion.
I only pray that the **Tiānzūn** will pity this lack of wisdom.
Now that you have profoundly favored and transformed the people..."
The king again prostrated his head to the ground, clasped his hands, and stood back.
The king's thirty-two sons, the dukes, ministers, numerous officials, and the common people
all repented their faults, blamed themselves, and focused their hearts upon the Buddha.
The king saw the eight hundred and ten thousand divine beings all seated in rows on lion thrones.
Within the sparkling canopy, celestial music played spontaneously.
He knew the Buddha was miraculous and divine.
The king commanded the ladies and concubines of the inner palace
to all come out and pay reverence to the Buddha.
The king prepared a meal of a hundred flavors.
He served the queen and his thirty-two sons.
He walked on his knees, offered water for washing, and personally served the food and drink.
When the meal was completely served, everyone, high and low, was respectful, solemn, focused, and joyful until they finished eating.
The king stepped forward, bowed his head, and addressed the Buddha, saying:
"I have received the grace of the **Tiānzhōngtiān** (Heaven of Heavens).
It is due to the depth of my former merits and the aid of my ancestors that I am placed above the common people.
**Tiānzūn**, Great Sage,
you ought to pity the people of my state. We beg for the precepts, which we shall uphold and practice for the rest of our lives.
What Dharma should I use to govern the people justly and peacefully?
I should form alliances with neighboring states, abandoning evil and embracing goodness.
May the Buddha give us guidance."
The Buddha said,
"Your conquests and invasions were neither righteous nor what is sought
by one who seeks long life and peace for the altars of the state (the nation)."

"The King must practice kindness and trust, benevolence and righteousness, compassion and filial piety, fidelity and purity, broadness and gentleness, patience and humility, generosity, nurturing the people, sheltering them, and forgiving others as you would yourself.
If you practice all these things,
you can long preserve the altars of the state.
If you lack these nine, the altars of the state will be difficult to preserve."
The king said, "How should I accomplish this?
I beg you to kindly bestow your compassionate teachings."
The Buddha said,
"Sentient beings are pitiable; human life is precious.
The treasures of the state and territory are not worth relying upon.
The King must cherish human life as parents pity their own children.
When the people regard the King more dearly than their own parents,
all the ten thousand states under heaven can be secured,
not just this one state.
Although the King has several million soldiers, chariot troops, and cavalry,
they are only sufficient to repel small enemies.
When I practiced the *Bodhisattva* Path and sat in meditation beneath a tree,
the **Mówáng** (Demon King) came with ghost and spirit soldiers, one hundred eighty million of them.
They all transformed their shapes into various beasts and animals, attempting to destroy my resolve.
I used my divine power and pointed my right finger toward the ground,
and heaven and earth violently shook, and they all stumbled and fell,
unable to return to their original forms.
The **Mówáng** was subdued.
How can the strength of the King's several million people
compare to the strength of hundreds of millions of ghosts and spirits?"
The king said,
"Indeed, it is because I was foolish and ignorant."
The king immediately bowed his head, confessed, apologized, and begged to change and reform himself.
The Buddha said,
"I use great compassion, contemplating the salvation of all beings in the ten directions, causing them all to attain liberation.
Those who have not yet been saved, I save, so they may quickly attain the Buddha Path.
This is not done solely for the King and his sons."
The king again expressed deep remorse and self-reproach.
"I pray the Buddha will pity me, and I will once again receive the teachings and precepts, observing them throughout my life,
so that the people of the state may be safe and peaceful."
The Buddha said,

"The King must lighten punishments, abolish excessive taxes, broaden kindness and trust, provide for the orphaned and the widowed, frequently pardon prisoners, rescue the destitute, enrich the poor, and feed the hungry.
If the King acts thus, he can preserve his reign from beginning to end."
The king resolved upon the Path and ordered his attendants and ministers
to fetch treasures from the vault and present them to the **Shìzūn**.
When the Buddha finished reciting the *dhāraṇī* (blessings),
he returned them all to the King, and the attendants and ministers all became prosperous and wealthy.
The king's thirty-two sons said to one another,
"If we live as unrighteous men
and die as unrighteous ghosts,
it is better, brothers, to seek to become *Shāmén* (monks)."
They all said, "That is excellent."
They immediately went together to the Buddha and fully explained their resolve.
The Buddha knew their intent was deep in wisdom of the Way.
**Tiāndìshì** (Śakra, Lord of Heaven) shaved their heads and beards, and they all became *Shāmén*.
The queen and concubines of the inner palace, three thousand people,
the dukes, ministers, numerous officials, and all the common people
all received the Five Precepts and observed the Six Fasts every month.
The state attained great harvests and prosperity.
Neighboring states heard of this and revered and admired him from afar.
From that time onward, the King
governed the state with broad benevolence, and there were no thieves or robbers.
Men and women respected each other, were free of greed and desire, and were entirely harmonious and good.
The king used the seven treasures to build a great *Jīngshè* (Vihāra/monastery).
The people within the state together practiced the Ten Virtues.
When their lives ended, they were born into heaven; none entered the evil paths.
The Buddha said,
"When I sought the Way for humanity, I sought only liberation.
Neither *tiānlóng* (devas and nāgas), ghosts, nor spirits could overthrow me.
When you practice the Way,
you should be like me."
At that time, King Yōutián
said to the Buddha:
“How many practices must a king accomplish,
O World-Honored One,
before he does not long remain in the world, external enemies rise in contention,
and before he can achieve cultivation, he dies and enters the evil paths?”
The Buddha replied: “Ten practices.”
“What are these ten?”
First, his mind is not focused solely on various affairs.
Second, he craves and clings to food, like a hungry tiger.
Third, he craves and clings to wine and meat, neglecting state affairs.
Fourth, he frequently harbors anger and resentment, leading to much sorrow and worry.
Fifth, he constantly practices ignorance and does not accept the remonstrance of others.
Sixth, he relies only on his own strength to manage what he undertakes.
Seventh, he constantly delights in taking life and oppressing the weak.
Eighth, he frequently dispatches troops to invade the borders of other states.
Ninth, he speaks much, but his words lack genuine importance.
Tenth, he is not compassionate towards the people.
If he accomplishes these, he will not long remain in the world, and external enemies will rise in contention.
If he dies, he will enter the three evil paths, and his bad reputation will spread far.
The King said:
“How many practices must he accomplish to long remain in the world, so that external enemies do not rise,
and when he dies, he is reborn in the good abode of heaven?”
The Buddha replied: “Ten practices.
He will long remain in the world, and external enemies will not rise.
When he dies, he will be reborn in the good abode of heaven.”
“What are these ten?”
First, his mind is not confused regarding various actions and deeds.
He treats all equally, removes unrighteous conduct, and approaches virtuous deeds.
Second, the King does not crave or cling to food.
He sustains life moderately and distinguishes the categories of precepts.
Third, he does not crave flavors or indulge in wine.
He sees all faults and transgressions and knows that finding the path to liberation is joy.
Fourth, he is not stingy or greedy; he delights in acts of charity and observes all actions and deeds.
Fifth, he possesses wisdom, understands the meaning [of the teachings], and constantly cultivates goodness
and eliminates evil.
Sixth, he does not rely on his own strength or act solely on his own will.
When there are Śramaṇas, Brāhmaṇas, ministers, or people who are intelligent and insightful,
he explains the meaning of whatever they ask and follows their instruction and guidance.
Seventh, he does not tyrannically kill the people.
He examines their deeds before applying punishment.
Eighth, he does not frequently dispatch troops to invade the borders of other states.
He constantly maintains peace and harmony with all other kings.
Ninth, what he speaks is genuinely important, and his words are not burdensome or excessive.
He examines the words of others before speaking about affairs.
Tenth, he constantly harbors compassion and mercy toward his ministers and people, and frequently examines the affairs of the state.
If he accomplishes these ten practices, he will long remain in the world, and external enemies will not rise.
When his body breaks and his life ends, he will be reborn in the good abode of heaven.
Moreover, after his life ends, his reputation will spread far, transmitted by gods and humans.
Rule [the people] with righteous laws, not with unreasonableness.
At that time, the King replied:
“If I rule the people with righteous laws,
when my body breaks and life ends, I will be reborn in the good abode of heaven.
If one practices unrighteous conduct,
when his body breaks and life ends, he enters the three evil paths, and his bad reputation spreads far.”
The people of the country presented a beautiful woman to King Yōutián.
The King was greatly delighted.
He appointed the woman’s father as Tài Fù.
He built a palace for the woman.
A thousand musicians and entertainers were provided to serve her.
The King’s principal consort served the Tathāgata (Rúlái) as her teacher and attained the path of Srotāpanna (Xūtuóhuán).
Later, the consort was slandered before the King.
The King shot the consort with a hundred arrows.
The consort, seeing this, was neither afraid nor angry at all.
She focused her mind on the Buddha, turning a compassionate heart toward the King.
All the arrows circled the consort three times and stopped before the King.
All hundred arrows did the same.
The King was instantly alarmed and fearful.
He immediately harnessed a white elephant and a golden chariot and rushed to the Buddha’s location.
He prostrated himself at the Buddha’s feet and confessed, saying:
“I have committed grievous faults concerning the Three Venerables.
I indulged in lustful charm and gave rise to evil desires.
I harbored a malicious and wicked mind toward the Buddha’s noble assembly.
The power of compassion of a lay disciple is already like this—
how much more so that of the Tathāgata!
I now confess my faults and take refuge in the Three Treasures.
I only wish that your vast compassion may pardon my transgressions.”
In the past, in the kingdom of Pōhuántí,
its king was named Tánnà.
Within the country, there was expected to be a torrential flood.
After the flood subsided,
suddenly a massive snake coiled around the city once, resting its head at the city gate.
The inhabitants of the city, over three hundred million people,
could not exit for many days.
Many were starving.
The snake did not show any anger,
but if anyone attempted to leave, it would devour them.
All the people in the entire country were terrified.
At that time, there were two ascetics (dàorén) practicing the path purely in the mountains near the King’s border.
One was named Móhēdiào.
The other was named Shāhēdiào.
They sat and reflected, saying:
“The snake is a poisonous creature,
but now it circles the city and endangers human lives.”
Immediately, they both went.
Upon entering the country, they met the King.
The King, upon seeing the two ascetics, said:
“Because my governance is unjust and unequal, this disaster has occurred.
The entire country is grieving and desolate, having lost their morale.”
The two ascetics immediately informed the King:
“We shall now devise a skillful means to remove it for the King.”
The King and his ministers all bowed their heads repeatedly and sincerely requested:
“If we receive the grace of the two ascetics,
the people of this country will be reborn.”
Shāhēdiào immediately transformed into a large toad.
It walked past the snake, which, unable to bear its hunger,
ran after the toad.
Móhēdiào then transformed into a kind of weasel (Qiúnài).
He chased after the snake from behind.
When the snake saw the Qiúnài, it ran in fright into the deep mountains.
After the snake left, the people gained peace.
The King and his ministers immediately sought out the two ascetics and reached their location.
Bowing their heads, they expressed their gratitude and apology, saying:
“The two ascetics have been nearby here,
but I was truly ignorant and did not serve you earlier.
When disaster struck, the ascetics rescued us.
We only wish that the ascetics would return and stay in the palace,
so that we and the people may offer extensive support.”
The ascetics replied:
“Our practice of the Way is pure and without desire.
We do not enjoy offerings.
The King should restrain himself and personally lead [the kingdom] with the Way.
If the people uphold and practice the righteous Dharma, they can achieve peace from beginning to end.”
The King then requested and accepted the Five Precepts and the Ten Virtuous Deeds.
He took refuge in the Three Venerables.
Observing monthly purification and abstinence became his permanent rule.
From then on,
the country was prosperous, the people were peaceful, and surrounding regions carried burdens and came to submit.
Thus, Great Peace was achieved.
Shāhēdiào was the body of the Buddha.
Móhēdiào was Mílè.
The King was Jiumó Jiāyè.
The Great Snake was Tiáodá.
In the past, there was a king
who enjoyed drinking wine and hunting.
Upon returning, he would light lamps, burn incense, place them on a tray, and pay reverence.
The attending servants said:
“Your Majesty drinks wine and hunts;
when you return and place offerings on a tray and pay reverence, what merit could there be?”
The King heard this,
and immediately ordered someone to light a great kettle.
The water boiled vigorously.
He placed a bottle of gold inside.
The boiling water surged and leaped.
He then called the attendant to try and retrieve the gold.
The attendant said: “The water is hot, and I cannot approach it.”
The King said: “You must use a skillful means to retrieve it.
Why can you not get it?”
The attendant said:
“I do not know what skillful means I should use to obtain it.”
The King said:
“Go remove the fire and add water to the soup.”
The attendant immediately followed the King’s order
and retrieved the gold.
The King said:
“When I drank wine and hunted, it was like the boiling water.
When I placed the tray and paid reverence, it was like removing the fire and adding water to the soup.
Why is it
that I should not gain merit?”
In the past, a king possessed a wish-fulfilling luminous pearl.
He kept it hidden in his topknot.
He cherished it day and night.
Later, the king died.
The custom of the country was first to place the body in the fields until the flesh had fully decomposed,
and then collect and bury the remains.
When the King’s form decayed and his topknot loosened, the luminous pearl was exposed.
At that time, the wife of a soldier,
named Zhētuólì,
was walking by, saw the pearl, and took it home.
The royal household, when collecting and burying the remains, forgot and lost this pearl.
The crown prince inherited the throne.

It was then that he realized the loss and sought it, offering a reward: whoever recovered the divine pearl would be granted an enfeoffment of ten thousand households and given a thousand catties of gold.
The soldier’s wife then brought the pearl to answer the proclamation.
She was immediately granted the enfeoffment.
The King wore the pearl upon his head.
had a king.
(He) raised troops to attack his enemy country.
The ministers of the enemy country informed their king, saying:
"That country has raised troops and is now approaching.
We request that Your Majesty prepare himself so we can fight them together."
The king said to his ministers:
"This is an insignificant matter, why must I be involved?"
The bandits attacked the city gates.
The ministers informed the king:
"The bandits are now outside."
The king told the ministers:
"Although the bandits are outside, it is not worth worrying about for long.
Just focus on your private gain; why worry about public affairs?"
At that time, the cruel bandits advanced further and entered the city.
His attendants reported, saying:
"The bandits have already entered the city."
The king told the ministers:
"This matter is trivial, why is it worthy of being reported to me?"
The great king of the neighboring country advanced further and reached the palace hall.
The ministers reported, saying:
"The king of the neighboring country has now ascended the hall.
We wonder what considerations the Shèngzūn has?"
That king replied, saying:
"My existence in this world is subject to continuous change.
That which flourishes must decline.
Meeting and gathering implies separation.
It is difficult to preserve things forever.
I shall change my appearance, following the way of a beggar (qǐshì).
I will retire (móhé zìtuì) and go to dwell in the deep mountains.
I will contemplate the Dào and virtue (dàodé) to find my own enjoyment.
Even if this cruel king wishes to harm my body, I will not decline his fault (I will accept the consequence).
The reason for this is:
The loss of the kingdom and the land is all due to one person.
If I accept death now, the myriad people will suffer no calamity.
Is this not a great blessing for me?"
The king of the enemy country sighed at what was unprecedented (tàn wèicéngyǒu).
Raising his voice, he proclaimed, saying:
"Excellent! Great King!
From ancient times until now, there has been nothing comparable to this.
Although I achieved victory, I am not equal to Your Majesty.
You have embraced the Great Dào (Dàdào) and disregard worldly glory.
From now onward, I will restore Your Majesty to your kingdom.
I will establish Your Majesty and complete the transformation.
We shall receive each other and become close friends."
In the past, there was a king.
He selected a wise person from the country
to be his auxiliary minister (fǔchén).
At that time, the king,
exercising expedient means (quán fāngbiàn) and immeasurable wisdom,
selected one person.
(He was) intelligent and broadly knowledgeable, and his ambition was lofty and refined (hóngyǎ).
He was awe-inspiring but not cruel, and fully possessed fame and virtue (míngdé).
The king wished to test him.
Therefore, he imposed a heavy penalty: filling a bowl (bō) completely with oil and making him carry it for twenty *lǐ* (miles).
If he dropped one single drop, he would be executed without need for further reporting.
The court official set forth.
Spectators filled the road.
Just as when water is still and the wind blows it, the water ripples,
(his) heart was uneasy and insecure.
That person thought in his heart, "I am certainly going to die now.
If I can carry the bowl so the oil doesn't fall and reach that country, then I will live."
He only focused on the oil bowl (yóubō), walking steadily and slowly.
At that time, his ministers, soldiers, parents, relatives, and countrymen all gathered
and followed him to watch.
He also encountered a greatly drunken elephant that dashed into the road, roaring and bellowing violently,
like thunder.
It trampled and killed elephants, horses, cattle, sheep, pigs, and calves on the road.
It smashed various carriages, scattering them everywhere in disorder.
People saw this and fled in terror, running east and west,
like clouds blown by the wind.
People also shot at the elephant.
But the person carrying the bowl
initially did not know the elephant had arrived,
nor did he notice the elephant leave.
A fire broke out in the city, burning various palaces and halls.
Furthermore, various stinging insects (fúfēng) released venom and bit people, while official soldiers fought the fire.
Also, five-colored clouds arose, and the sky thundered greatly.
Wild winds swept the ground, filling the king's road with dust, sand, tiles, and stones.
It uprooted trees, broke branches, and knocked down flowers and fruits.
Lightning flashed and thunder rolled (pīlì), peacocks cried out, and various celestial disasters (hail) fell.
Despite these disturbances, that person neither noticed nor heard them.
He carried the full bowl of oil and successfully reached that country,
without dropping a single drop.
The king was then delighted and installed him as a high minister (dàchén).
In the past, there was a king
who had the body of a man but the head of a donkey.
The Buddha (Fó) told the king:
"On Xuěshān (Snow Mountain), there is a medicine
called Shàngwèi (Superior Taste).
If the king goes and eats it, he can regain a human head."
The king went to Xuěshān, selected the medicine, and ate it.
Yet his head did not change.
The king returned and reported to the Buddha:
"Why did you speak falsely?"
The Buddha replied to the king, saying:
"Do not pick and choose the herbs; then you will regain your human head naturally."
The king returned to the mountain.
(He realized that) whatever grew on the mountain naturally cured disease.
He no longer picked and chose.
He ate a mouthful of the grass and immediately recovered his human head.
In the past, there was a king
who did not sleep day or night.
If the person on duty (zhí) beside him slept, he would kill them.
He had killed four hundred and ninety-nine people previously.
There was a son of an elder (zhǎngzhě zǐ) whose turn it was to enter duty.
His family cried and wept as they sent him off.
A young man asked,
"Why are you weeping?"
(The family) answered him truthfully.
(The young man said) "If you can hire me,
I can take your place."
The elder was greatly pleased.
He gave him a thousand *liǎng* (taels) of gold and sent him to enter duty.
The king said:
"Why have you entered (duty)?"
(He) replied, "I am standing duty in place of the elder's son."
The king said:
"Be careful not to sleep, or I will kill you."
At that time, the young man slept.
The king intended to kill him.
(The king) said, "Why did you sleep?"
(He) replied, "I wasn't sleeping, I was just thinking about something."
The king said:
"What were you thinking about?"
(He) replied, "Making a one-shēng (pint) container hold two *shēng* of material,
and putting one *shēng* of sand in it, yet still having room for one *shēng* of water."
The king tested it, and it was true.
(The young man) slept again, face down on the ground.
The king again intended to kill him.
(He) replied, "I was just thinking about something."
(The king) said, "What were you thinking about?"
(He) replied, "Digging a one-chǐ (foot) hole, then filling it with the earth taken out, but it still doesn't fill up to eight *cùn* (inches)."
The king again sent someone to make it, and it was indeed true.
(The young man) slept again, prostrate on the ground.
The king again intended to kill him.
(He) asked, "Why are you sleeping again?"
(He) replied, "I was just thinking about something.
If the King pardons my crime, I will tell you."
The king said, "Go ahead and speak."
The young man said:
"The King looks exactly like a ghost (guǐ)."
After speaking, he left immediately.
The king pondered:
"Why did this person call me a ghost?"
He immediately reported and asked his mother.
The mother said:
"You are truly a ghost.
When I was pregnant with you, I dreamt at night of meeting a ghost,
and when we were together, you were conceived."
The king then awoke (to realization).
He stopped killing people, regretted his faults, and committed to doing good.
He subsequently studied the Dào.
The king at that time was myself.
The four hundred and ninety-nine people are the present five hundred foremost disciples.
The young man who caused me to awaken is
Wénshū Shīlì."
In the past, King Āyù Wáng
had not yet understood the Buddha Dharma.
He established various hells (jails),
and those who entered were certainly punished.
He tortured them using various poisons.
Later, he gained faith,
and consequently abandoned all non-virtuous deeds and served the Enlightened One (Buddha).
The people suffered from plagues.
The King decreed that the inner and outer areas were not permitted to communicate,
fearing the disease would reach the palace.
He sent a messenger to inform the assembly of Sages (Bhikkhus),
begging for distant blessings and incantations.
He asked that one Bhikkhu might be sent into the palace
to perform the Dà Chèn rites (giving and receiving offerings) so that the world might be peaceful and diseases eliminated.
The assembly of monks (Seng) accepted this duty,
wishing to grant his request.
At that time, the assembly of Sages sent a Śrāmaṇera who was eight years old.
His name was Miàoyán.
He had already attained Arhatship and possessed complete divine powers.
He flew to the King's palace and addressed the Queen and the palace women,
speaking of their shortcomings and revealing the Tao and virtue, and explaining that the Buddha is supremely honored, how much more so his disciples?
Miàoyán accepted the instruction.
He flew into the King's palace and stood before the Queen.
The Queen paid homage and raised her hand, wishing to embrace him.
She said, "Child Miàoyán, how could you condescend to manifest your divine powers?"
Miàoyán said to the Queen,
"Step back, step back!
It is not appropriate to approach a Śrāmaṇa closely."
The Queen replied,
"You are but a young child, only eight years old.
My heart cherishes you as if you were my own son.
If I approach you closely, what harm could there be?"
The Śrāmaṇa replied,
"If we discuss closeness based on sentiment, it is as the Queen says.
But sentiment arises from the minute.
It is like a fire starting from a grain of millet that can burn ten thousand *lǐ* of wilderness.
It is like water dripping from a finger that can wear through jade and stone, and yet also fill a vessel.
All matters proceed gradually,
accumulating much from little,
achieving greatness from smallness.
Therefore, the wise keep far from suspicion and avoid doubt,
in order to prevent what has not yet happened."
The Śrāmaṇa and the Queen debated back and forth, and their voices grew high.
The sound reached the main hall.
The King asked those nearby,
"Whose voices are those? It sounds as if there is a dispute."
A nearby minister replied,
"The Śrāmaṇa Miàoyán has arrived in the palace,
and he is speaking with the Queen.
Their voices are loud and clear, and can be heard from here."
The King immediately rose and went to meet him.
He performed a reverence and inquired what the dispute was about.
The Śrāmaṇa replied,
"The noble Queen saw my appearance and showed compassion for me,
wishing to approach me, but the Dharma does not allow it.
Therefore, I have firmly refused her."
King Āyù Wáng said,
"You are still young, just like my son.
If she holds you affectionately, what suspicion could there be?
Why do you counter her with such strong words?"
The Śrāmaṇa replied,
"That is not correct, Your Majesty.
The ancient Sages established rules of conduct, preventing things before they manifest, and cautioning against beginnings and endings.
A daughter seven years old does not play near her father's desk.
A son eight years old does not stand proudly on his mother's bed.
Below a fruit tree, one does not adjust one’s head covering.
In a melon field, one does not touch one’s foot.
The reason for this is
to keep far from suspicion, avoid doubt, stop small evils, and eliminate beginnings.
This serves as guidance for the future and prevents what has not yet happened.
My mind is already pure and has no minor impurities remaining.
I am like a lotus flower, unpolluted by muddy water.
I am like a vessel of crystal or lapis lazuli.
Indeed, according to the Tathāgata's teaching,
I am equal to a son and mother, so there is no difference.
However, although I know I am faultless, I must set an example for those who cannot achieve this.
When the King and Queen heard his words, they were greatly astonished and valued them highly.
"As Miàoyán says,
if a young child of eight years still regards potential difficulties,
how much more should those who are grown up and have not yet destroyed the three poisons!"
Thereupon, the Śrāmaṇa spoke the Sūtra Dharma to them.
The Queen and the five hundred palace women all attained the stages of the Path.
Furthermore, the Queen, the surrounding ministers, and the Crown Prince all conceived the intention for the Path,
and immediately attained the ground of non-retrogression (Avaivartika).
In the past, the Queen of Bōluónàiguó conceived.
The Queen knew herself that she was pregnant,
and she told the King.
The King immediately provided for her, caring for her and ensuring everything was comfortable and fitting.
When the month was full, she gave birth to a piece of flesh,
red like a rose mallow flower.
Other wives gave birth to handsome sons,
but she had given birth to a piece of flesh without hands or feet.
She felt deep shame.
Thinking that if the King saw it, he would surely despise and reject it,
she stored it carefully in a vessel, beat out gold foil, and inscribed it with cinnabar:
"This was born of the Queen of Bōluónàiguó."
She covered the vessel's lid and sealed it with the King's seal.
She placed the written gold foil outside the vessel
and sent it to be abandoned in the river.
After the messenger had cast it away,
various spirits and deities guarded it, ensuring there were no winds or waves.
At that time, a Taoist (Dàoshì)
lived by the riverbank, staying with cattle herders.
In the morning, while bathing, he saw the vessel in the distance.
He picked it up and saw the characters written on the gold foil.
He also saw that it was sealed with the King's seal.
He opened the vessel and looked inside, seeing only the piece of flesh.
He thought to himself:
"If this were dead flesh, it would have rotted and stunk long ago.
It must possess some unusual sign."
He took it back to his dwelling and carefully placed it in a secluded spot.
After half a month passed, it split into two pieces.
After that, another half a month elapsed.
Each of the two pieces grew five sacs.
Yet another half a month later, one piece turned into a boy,
and the other piece turned into a girl.
The boy's complexion was like gold,
and the girl's complexion was like silver.
The Taoist saw this,
and felt deep love and affection, treating them as his own children.
Milk naturally flowed from the thumbs of his two hands.
One thumb fed the boy,
and one thumb fed the girl.
When the milk entered the children's bellies, they were bright and transparent inside and out, like a clean water pearl (Maṇi jewel).
The Taoist named the children,
calling them Lí Chēzǐ. The Taoist struggled greatly to raise these two children.
Every morning he entered the village to beg for food,
and he did not return until late in the day, taking care of the two children.
At this time, the cattle herders,
seeing the Taoist suffering so much for the sake of the two children,
said to him:
"Great Virtue (Dà Dé),
those who have left home should focus solely on practicing the Way.
Why do these two children hinder and abandon your spiritual work?
You can entrust them to us; we will raise them and provide for them."
The Taoist replied, "Excellent!"
These cattle herders all returned to their homes.
The next day, they and their companions leveled the roads,
erected banners and flags, and scattered various colored flowers.
They beat drums and came to welcome the two children to the Taoist's place.
They said to the Taoist,
"It is now time for these two children to depart."
The Taoist instructed them:
"These two children possess great, immeasurable fortune.
You must manage them well.
You must sustain them with five kinds of food: milk, curds, ghee, and raw and cooked butter.
When these two children grow up, they should marry each other.
Find a good, flat, and spacious location for them to settle and reside.
The boy may be enthroned as King and the girl as Queen."
The cattle herders accepted the instruction and departed.
When the two children reached sixteen years old,
they found a flat and spacious place measuring one hundred *yóujùn* in width and length.
They built a dwelling in the center.
They married the girl to the boy,
establishing them as husband and wife.
Afterward, she gave birth to two children—one boy and one girl.
In this manner, sixteen generations passed,
and the cattle herders saw that the number of royal children gradually increased.
They further expanded the residences and created various parks and grounds,
resulting in thirty-two residences altogether.
Since they thus expanded the city three times,
it was therefore named Píshèlǐ.
The Buddha, along with twelve hundred and fifty Bhikṣus.
Traveled to the Měiyīn Jīngshè in the kingdom of Kūlánní.
When his feet trod upon the threshold, the heavens and earth shook.
Jewels, pearls, and musical instruments sounded without being struck.
Voodoo and poisons lay hidden; auspicious signs were harmonious and pure.
In the region, there was no person who did not yearn for him.
The king's name was Yōu Tián.
He was fiercely oppressive and exploitative, accepting flattering words and indulging excessively in feminine music and entertainment.
He established two queens, one on the left and one on the right.
Their looks were supremely marvelous.
The left one was named Zhào Táng.
She was haughty, arrogant, slanderous, and jealous.
The right one was styled Yàn Róng.
She constantly practiced kindness and compassion.
The king cherished her integrity and consulted her privately on every matter.
Yàn Róng had an old maidservant.
Named Duó Shèng.
She constantly traveled about distributing incense.
She reduced and saved [the money] and gathered it together.
To feed the Buddha and the Saṅgha.
The Buddha spoke the Dharma for her.
She dedicated her mind entirely and did not forget it.
When the offering was finished, she returned to the palace.
Holding the incense she had distributed.
Because of this merit.
The fragrance, pursued by her fundamental conduct, spread far and wide.
The weight was doubled, and the scent was doubled.
Yàn Róng officially questioned her.
She explained that she had first saved the money for the incense.
And used it to feed the Buddha and the Saṅgha.
The Dharma was profound and its meaning marvelous, unlike anything heard in the world.
When Yàn Róng heard about the Buddha.
Joy arose in her heart.
She thought to herself that she had no chance to hear the true Dharma.
She immediately informed Duó Shèng.
“You must speak it for me.”
Duó Shèng replied.
“My body is lowly, and my mouth is impure; I dare not immediately proclaim the honored words of the Tathāgata.”
“I beg permission to go to the Buddha, receive his command, and then return.”
Yàn Róng immediately sent her out of the palace.
She further instructed her, saying.
“Receive the ritual forms fully.”
When Duó Shèng had not yet returned.
The Queen and her maids gathered closely, filling the central courtyard.
The Buddha instructed Duó Shèng.
“When you return and speak the Dharma, there will be many who attain liberation.”
“The proper form for speaking the Dharma is first to arrange a high seat.”
Duó Shèng fully conveyed the Holy Edict.
Yàn Róng was joyous and delighted.
She opened her clothes chest, took out her garments, and piled them up to make a high seat.
Relying on the majestic spiritual power of the Buddha, she spoke the Dharma as appropriate.
Queen Yàn Róng and all her maids had their doubts resolved and attained the Way.
Duó Shèng attained Dhāraṇī (total retention).
Zhào Táng, out of jealousy, often blamed and slandered Yàn Róng, not just once.
The King refused to follow her advice.
Later, she spoke of it again.
The King's mind was then misled.
She waited until Yàn Róng was observing the fast and urged the King to play music.
And summoned the Queen.
The King then summoned everyone universally; those ordered arrived.
Yàn Róng, observing the fast, alone did not respond to the command.
She was summoned three times repeatedly, but she maintained her integrity and did not move.
The King’s rage swelled mightily; he had her bound and dragged before the palace hall.
Intending to shoot and kill her.
Yàn Róng, with the slightest part of her heart, returned to the Buddha.
The King personally shot two arrows, both of which returned and pointed towards himself.
The King was terrified and released her.
He asked her, saying.
“What magic or power do you possess to bring this about?”
She replied, saying.
“I only serve the Tathāgata and take refuge in the Three Honored Ones.”
“I uphold the Buddha’s precepts of fasting in the morning and not eating after noon.”
“I further practice the Eight Precepts and maintain purity, avoiding proximity [to sensuality].”
“It must be that the World-Honored One pities me in this manner.”
The King said.
“Excellent!”
“How can this be spoken of merely in words?”
“We ought to proceed to the Vihāra to respectfully see the World-Honored One.”
It happened that an enemy state raised troops and entered the borders.
The King personally went out to campaign, and entrusted his orders to a Brahmin.
Whose name was Jí Xīng.
To temporarily govern the state.
Zhào Táng rejoiced, saying.
“My father (the Brahmin) is leading the government; Yàn Róng's death is certain!”
The woman conspired with the Brahmin and consequently burned and killed Yàn Róng and all her maids.
They falsely claimed it was an accidental fire, thinking they could cover it up.
After the event, the truth was revealed.
The King was greatly enraged by this.
He exiled Jí Xīng far away and abandoned him beyond the borders.
Zhào Táng and her accomplices were confined to an underground cave.
He suppressed and drove out heterodox ways.
And widely promoted the Buddha’s transformation.
The Buddha was in the kingdom of Shèwèi Guó.
The king and all the officials of the state had none who did not take refuge and look up to him.
At that time, there was a merchant.
Named Bō Lì.
He entered the sea with five hundred merchants seeking treasures.
At that time, the Sea God emerged and presented the "Tinkling Water."
He asked Bō Lì, saying.
“Is the seawater greater in quantity?”
“Or is the Tinkling Water greater in quantity?”
Bō Lì answered, saying.
“The Tinkling Water is greater.”
“Although seawater is vast, it cannot save a person who is hungry or thirsty.”
“Although the Tinkling Water is small, it can save the life of one exhausted by thirst.”
“Thus, the rewards received lifetime after lifetime are measureless and countless.”
The Sea God was delighted.
He immediately took off the eight kinds of fragrant necklaces (Yīng) on his body.
And compared them to the Seven Treasures, offering them to Bō Lì.
Bō Lì returned to his kingdom.
He took these fragrant necklaces and presented them to King Bōsīnì.
The King valued them greatly as rare wonders.
He immediately lined up all his consorts.
Saying that he would give the fragrant necklaces to the one who was best.
The sixty thousand consorts all dressed splendidly and emerged.
The King asked.
“Why has Queen Mòlì not come out?”
The attendants replied, saying.
“Today is the fifteenth day (of the lunar month); she is upholding the Buddha’s Dharma fast, wearing plain clothes and not dressing splendidly.”
The King said.
“Should upholding the fast today mean disobeying the King’s command?”
This happened three times repeatedly.
Queen Mòlì came out in plain clothes.
Among the crowd of people, she shone like the sun and moon, appearing twice as beautiful as usual.
The King’s heart was reverently awestruck; he increased his respect and asked her, saying.
“What virtue or power do you possess that makes you shine so extraordinarily?”
The Queen addressed the King.
“I reflect that I have little merit, having been born into this female form.”
“My emotional defilements accumulate like mountains day and night.”
“Human life is brief and short; I fear falling into the Three Lower Realms (Tus).”
“Therefore, every lunar month I observe the fast of the Buddha’s Dharma.”
“I sever attachment and follow the Way, hoping to receive blessings life after life.”
The King heard this and was pleased.
He then gave the fragrant necklaces to her.
The Queen declined, saying.
“I am currently upholding the fast; it is improper for me to wear this.”
“You may give it to another person.”
The King said.
“My original intention was to give it to the most excellent one.”
“You are now the most excellent.”
“Furthermore, you uphold the Dharma fast, and your aspiration for the Way is singularly noble.”
“Therefore, I give it to you.”
“If you do not accept it, where shall I place it?”
The Queen answered, saying.
“Great King, do not worry.”
“I wish that Your Majesty would kindly consent to go together to the Buddha’s abode.”
“And present these fragrant necklaces to the World-Honored One.”
“And gather the holy teachings, thus accumulating merit for countless kalpas.”
The King immediately agreed.
He immediately ordered the carriage prepared and went to the Buddha’s abode.
He addressed the Buddha, saying.
“These fragrant necklaces from the Sea God were presented by Bō Lì.”
“The sixty thousand consorts all coveted them.”
“Queen Mòlì was given them but would not accept them.”
“Upholding the Buddha’s Dharma fast, her mind is without greed or desire.”
“I respectfully present them to the Buddha above.”
“I pray that you condescend to accept them.”
“It is hard to match the resolve maintained by the World-Honored One's disciple.”
“With such upright faith, must she not have great blessings?”
Thereupon, the World-Honored One accepted the fragrant necklaces for them.
And immediately spoke a verse, saying.
Much making of jeweled flowers and binding them in silk to sway; widely accumulating the fragrance of virtue.
That which is born becomes ever better. The fragrant flowers of rare grasses do not diffuse against the wind.
But when spreading near the Way, the virtuous person's scent pervades everywhere. Sandalwood has abundant fragrance.
The fragrant flower of the blue lotus, though called true, is inferior to the fragrance of precepts (Śīla).
The fragrance of flowers is slight and cannot be called true; the fragrance of upholding the precepts.
Reaches the heavens and is singularly sublime. Those who fully accomplish the precepts and act without negligence.
With concentrated minds, attain deliverance and eternally abandon the path of Māra.
The king of the Pántí guó [state/kingdom] was named Yōudá.
During the time of Jiāshè Fó, he left home to cultivate the Way.
Later, relying on Shìjiā, they all attained the traces of the Way [enlightenment].
His kingdom was wealthy and the people prosperous.
The king had twenty thousand fūrén [concubines/ladies].
The chief fūrén,
whose cognomen was Yuèmíng,
was refined in appearance, and the king loved and respected her deeply.
In less than half a year, the signs that the fūrén was about to die appeared.
The king was extremely worried and distressed.
Yuèmíng asked him about it.
The king said:
"Your life is coming to an end.
The grief is due to the impending separation of our love and affection."
Yuèmíng replied:
"Since there is life, there is death.
This is the normal course of the world.
Why worry particularly about this?
If you truly care for me, just permit me to leave home [and become a nun]."
The king permitted her to enter the Way.
"If you leave home, even if you do not achieve enlightenment, you will certainly be born in Heaven.
If you are born in Heaven, you must return to me."
"Then I permit you to leave home."
Yuèmíng immediately agreed to his oath.
She summoned the bhikṣuṇī.
She immediately abandoned the five desires.
Because many people came to inquire, show respect, and offer support, hindering her cultivation of the Way,
she therefore traveled throughout various kingdoms.
Counting from the day she left home, six months passed.
She upheld the precepts purely and felt aversion toward the world.
She attained the state of Ānàhán.
She passed away in a certain village and was immediately born in the Rūpa-dhātu Heaven.
She observed the past conditions and the promise she had made with the king.
She desired to fulfill her original vow.
Observing that the king was immersed in the five desires, rebellious, difficult to transform,
and that simply going to him would not inspire him,
it was necessary to frighten and coerce him so that he would submit.
She then transformed herself into a great Luóchà.
Her clothes and hair stood up rigidly, and she held a five-foot knife.
While the king was sleeping that night, she hovered in the air not far from him.
The king was extremely terrified.
She immediately spoke to the king, saying:
"Although your warriors and multitude are in the thousands,
now you belong only to me and have no freedom.
The time of your death has arrived; how can you save yourself?"
The king immediately replied:
"I have no means, except to maintain my original good deeds,
and cultivate a pure mind, so that when I die, I may be reborn in a good place."
The goddess said:
"This is the most reliable thing; there is no other principle."
The king then asked:
"What spirit are you that makes me so afraid?"
The goddess answered:
"I am Yuèmíng Fūrén.
The king permitted me to leave home, and by contemplating detachment from desire, I was born in the Rūpa-dhātu Heaven.
Now I have come to fulfill the promise."
The king said:
"Although you say this, I still do not believe it.
Return to your original form; only then can I believe you."
The goddess immediately transformed into her former appearance.
Her clothes and ornaments were as they were originally, and she stood there.
The king's desire arose, and he instantly rushed forward intending to seize her.
Yuèmíng immediately ascended into the sky and spoke the Dharma to the king, saying:
"This body is impermanent; it cannot be guaranteed even for the snap of a finger.
It is like the morning dew, which vanishes when the sun rises.
Why do you not consider impermanence and cling greedily to my body?
Oh King, do you not see?
The splendor and beauty of youth are consumed and extinguished by old age.
All faculties decay.
The eyes cannot see clearly.
The ears cannot hear acutely.
The form collapses and rots away, becoming useless.
It is like brewing wine: once the pure flavor is taken, the dregs are worthless.
Once this body is old, there is nothing to greedily enjoy.
Only death remains.
Since the body is born, death and impermanence accompany it.
Oh King, do you not see?
Whether in the womb, or as infants, youths, or strong adults, all die.
This body is fragile and imperiled; the thief of death constantly follows it.
The body and mind are aflame with fire, which is just a collection of sufferings.
The mind has the three poisons; the body has cold, heat, hunger, and thirst.
Yet you do not generate revulsion but cling greedily to my body?
The palace women, the dancing girls, the beautiful forms, the five desires,
state wealth, wives, and children—none of these belong to me.
When the time of death arrives, not one thing follows you.
You must abandon even the body itself, let alone other things!
Deluded and submerged in the five desires, you revolve in the cycle of birth and death, knowing no way out.
You, Oh King, are a wise person; why do you not grow weary of this, leave home, and seek the Way?"
The king's good mind arose, and he permitted her to leave home.
Yuèmíng further converted him, saying:
"I should leave home, seek the profound Dharma, receive and practice it, and diligently strive day and night without slackening."
Having said these words, she suddenly disappeared.
The king immediately abdicated the throne to the Crown Prince.
He abandoned the five desires.
He went to Jiāzhānyán and left home to follow the Way.
The people of that time, seeing that he had abandoned great glory and profit,
and sought the true Way,
ministers, officials, and common people came frequently to offer support, reverence, and greetings, thus hindering his cultivation of the Way.
Thereupon, he traveled to the Mójié guó.
The Buddha preached the Dharma for him, and he attained the state of Āluóhàn.
Carrying his clay bowl, he entered Wángshèchéng.
After begging for leftover overnight rice, he returned to the forest and sat down to eat.
Píngshā wáng came out for a stroll and proceeded to the forest.
He greeted him and said:
"You were formerly a king, entering and leaving in glory with a retinue.
Now you act like a beggar, walking alone and soliciting food.
Is this truly enjoyable?
You should return, abandon the Way, and rule half of the kingdom."
The man of the Way replied:
"I was the king of a great state with many settlements.
Why should I now abandon the great for the small? This is not proper for me."
Píngshā wáng said:
"You formerly ate the finest delicacies served in jeweled vessels.
Now you hold a clay bowl and beg for stale, leftover food. Is this not difficult?
You were formerly guarded by brave warriors as a king.
Today you are alone. Are you not afraid?
Previously, in the deep palace, concubines and dancers, beautiful forms, filled and pleased your eyes and ears.
You sat on a jeweled throne covered with fine embroidered silks.
Today you sleep alone in the wilderness, lying on grass. Is this not miserable?"
He answered:
"I am now content and have nothing I greedily enjoy."
Píngshā wáng said:
"You are pitiful now."
He replied:
"You are the one who is pitiful, not me.
Why is that?
You are entangled by the five desires and driven by affection and attachment, possessing no freedom.
I am now happy, with a mind free of obstruction."
Píngshā, having heard this, immediately returned.
Formerly there was a man
who saw a Fótú sì.
He intended to build one.
But his money and silk were insufficient.
He made a vow to enter the sea to gain gold and jewels,
saying, "I will build a temple that is the finest in the kingdom."
He returned having acquired gold and silver and reflected deeply.
"Who can agree to collaborate with me to build the temple?"
The king of the state often said,
"I wish to build a temple and stūpa,"
but so far had not begun the work.
He decided to present the pearls, jewels, and jade he had acquired to the king.
The king was delighted and asked,
"Where did you obtain these?"
The worthy man said:
"I vowed to build a temple, but I cannot accomplish it alone.
I went to sea to acquire treasures in order to build the temple.
Returning safely now is my first benefit.
Successfully acquiring gold and jewels is my second benefit.
Not clinging greedily to these, but establishing a temple is my third benefit.
Relying on the merit of these three benefits, I now wish to build a temple.
However, I lack the manpower and resources.
Therefore, I have come to inform Your Majesty."
The king said:
"I also have three benefits.
Desiring to build a temple and stūpa, and having attained the body of a king, being supreme among men, is my first benefit.
Having abundant wealth, treasures, people, and soldiers is my second benefit.
Having the four directions all submit is my third benefit.
I shall collaborate with you to build the temple."
The king summoned his five hundred fūrén and gave them pearls.
The five hundred fūrén all adorned themselves, each desiring to receive the pearls.
Only the principal fūrén did not adorn herself or comb her hair.
The king asked why.
She replied, "I also have three benefits.
Therefore, I am able to be the king's fūrén.
Being respected by the entire palace is my first benefit.
Giving birth to a son who is the Crown Prince is my second benefit.
Always taking pleasure in the sutras and the Way, and desiring to build a Fótú sì is my third benefit."
The king said, "Excellent!"
He gave her the pearls.
The principal fūrén used hundreds and thousands of taels of gold to assist the king in establishing the temple.
The king, together with the worthy man in the kingdom, built a temple one thousand paces wide.
It was all carved and engraved with gold and silver.
The king said:
"Only we three possess this merit.
Shall the people in my kingdom not receive this blessing?"
He sent messengers through the streets to announce the decree:
"Whoever possesses great virtuous intent will gain immeasurable fortune."
There was a poor woman who owned only a small hut and begged for clothes and food.
Hearing this, she reproached herself:
"In previous lives, I failed to give charity, which is why I am now afflicted with poverty."
She untied the linen skirt from her body and threw it toward the messenger, asking him to use the skirt to assist the king.
"My form is naked; I have no clothes to go out in."
The king heard this and was astonished, realizing that such virtuous intent existed.
He immediately commanded her to be brought.
The messenger said:
"This woman has no clothes to wear."
The king commanded his five hundred fūrén,
"Each of you take one garment and give it to her.
Go quickly and fetch her."
The king saw her and appointed her as the second Fūrén.
He ordered her to instruct the palace [women].
. He disliked glory and luxury, and dwelled in seclusion among the mountains and marshes
. At that time, in the depths of a valley, there was a starving tiger
. She had just given birth to seven cubs when heaven sent down snow
. The mother tiger had been holding her cubs for three days, unable to seek food
. Fearing her cubs would freeze to death, she guarded them, starving herself, while the snow fell ceaselessly
. The mother and cubs were suffering from hunger and exhaustion; death was imminent
. Since the mother was so tormented by hunger, she was even planning to eat her cubs
. At that time, the immortals said
: "Who can abandon his body to save these creatures?"
. The Crown Prince said
: "Excellent! My vow is fulfilled!"
. He went to the cliff edge and looked down
. Seeing the mother tiger holding her cubs, covered by the snow, he developed great compassion
. Standing atop the mountain, he silently entered samādhi (meditation)
. He immediately attained the pure forbearance of the Uncreate Dharma (Wúshēng Fǎrěn)
. He observed the events of countless past *kalpas* (eons), and the future was likewise clear
. He immediately returned and informed his master and five hundred fellow students
: "I am now abandoning my body; I wish you all to rejoice in this act"
. The master said
: "Your time studying the Way is short, and your insight is not yet extensive
. Why do you suddenly resolve to abandon your beloved body?"
. The Crown Prince replied
: "In the past, I made a vow that I should abandon a thousand bodies
. Previously, I have already abandoned nine hundred and ninety-nine bodies
. The body I abandon today will complete the thousand bodies. This is why I abandon it
. I pray, Master, rejoice in this"
. The master said
: "Since your ambition and vow are lofty and wonderful, you will surely attain the Way first. Do not forget us"
. The Crown Prince bade farewell to his master and departed
. The master and five hundred *shénxiān* (divine immortals), with tears streaming from their eyes, escorted the Crown Prince to the mountain cliff edge
. At that time, there was the elder Fùlán
. Bringing five hundred followers, both men and women, with offerings, he ascended the mountain
. Seeing the Crown Prince preparing to abandon his body, they were moved with sadness and wept
. They also followed the Crown Prince to the mountain cliff edge
. The Crown Prince, before the crowd, made a great vow
: "I now abandon my body to save the lives of these creatures
. May all the merit I gain quickly lead to the attainment of Bodhi
. May I attain the Vajra Body (Jīngāng Shēn), the eternal, joyous, true-self, pure, unconditioned Dharma Body (Wúwéi Fǎshēn)
. May those who are not yet delivered be delivered; those who are not yet enlightened be enlightened; and those who are not yet at peace be brought to peace
. This body of mine is impermanent, full of suffering and distress, and collected from all poisons
. This body is impure, with nine apertures overflowing, and is bitten and stung by the four great poisonous snakes
. It is chased, wounded, and cut by the five drawing-knife thieves
. Such a body, though nourished with sweet, delicious foods and the pleasures of the five desires, is ungrateful
. After this body dies, it offers no good return or recompense
, but rather falls into the hells, suffering immeasurable pain
. Indeed, this human body should only be subjected to suffering, not pleasure
." He further made this vow
: "Now, I use my flesh and blood to save that starving tiger
. The remaining *shèlì* (relics/bones)
—my parents will surely erect a *tǎ* (stupa) for them later
. If all sentient beings whose physical illnesses and suffering, caused by past karmic sins, cannot be cured by medicine, acupuncture, or moxibustion
, come to the site of my stupa and sincerely make offerings
, then regardless of the severity of the illness, within one hundred days they will surely be healed and relieved
. If this is truly not false, may the various *tiān* (deities) rain down fragrant flowers"
. Immediately, in response to his words, *Mantuóluó* flowers rained down, and the earth shook
. The Crown Prince then unwrapped his deerskin garment and wrapped it around his head
. He threw himself before the tiger
. The mother tiger ate the flesh of the *Púsà* (Bodhisattva)
. Both the mother and the cubs were saved
. At that time, the people on the cliff edge looked down and saw the Crown Prince
. His flesh and bones were scattered, having been devoured by the tiger
. They wailed and cried out loudly, their voices shaking the mountains
. Some beat their chests, threw themselves down, and rolled on the ground
. Some entered meditative thought
. Some knocked their heads (kowtowed) in repentance
. The *tiān* of the Shǒutuóhuì (Śuddhāvāsa heaven), and Shì (Indra), the Lord of Heaven (Tiāndì Shì), and the Four Heavenly Kings (Sì Tiānwáng), et cetera
, along with the Sun and Moon *tiān*, numbering tens of millions
, all aroused the mind of unsurpassed Bodhi
