. They created music and song, burned incense, and scattered flowers to make offerings to the Crown Prince
. And they proclaimed these words
: "Excellent, *Móhēsàduǒ* (Mahāsattva)
! Not long from now, you shall sit upon the Bodhimaṇḍa (Dàochǎng)"
. The five hundred immortals all aroused the mind toward the unsurpassed, true, and correct Way
. The great master of the divine immortals attained the forbearance of the Uncreate (Wúshēng Rěn)
. The Lady (the Crown Prince's mother) sent a messenger with provisions
. The messenger only saw the clothes, parasol, bowl, tin staff (*xī*), and bottle inside the stone dwelling
. He thoroughly questioned the immortals
. In groups of ten or five, they faced one another and wept
. He went to the place of the Great Master
. He only saw the immortal master sitting, supporting his cheek with his hand, tears streaming from his eyes, groaning
. He questioned all around, but none would answer or reply
. The messenger was terrified
. He immediately offered the food and drink to the immortal gentlemen, ran back, and fully reported the preceding events to the Lady
. The Lady said
: "Alas! My son is dead!"
. She beat her chest, cried loudly, and rushed toward the King
. The King heard and swooned
. The ministers admonished the King
: "The Crown Prince is on the mountain
. We pray that Your Majesty rests a while"
. The King, the Lady, the consorts, the palace women, the ministers, officials, and common people rushed up the mountain
. The elder Fùlán came to meet the King and informed him
: "Yesterday, the Crown Prince threw himself beneath the cliff to feed the tiger with his flesh
. Now only scattered bones remain on the ground. Let us go together to the site of the body"
. The King, the Lady, the consorts, the palace women, the ministers, officials, and common people raised their voices in sorrowful cries, shaking the mountain valleys
. The King and the Lady collapsed onto their son's remains, their hearts broken, and they were confused and unable to recognize people
. A consort came forward, held his head, arranged the Crown Prince's hair, and said
: "I would rather have my body shattered into dust than have my husband suddenly perish like this"
. At that time, the ministers reported to the King
: "The Crown Prince made this great offering, vowing to save all sentient beings
. He was not seized and taken by the demon of impermanence
. While the body has not yet decayed, it is fitting to prepare offerings
." They immediately collected the bones and brought them out to the mouth of the mountain valley
. On a flat piece of ground, they piled fragrant sandalwood firewood
, along with fragrant *sū* (sesame/ghee) oil, and performed the *shéwéi* (cremation)
. They collected the *shèlì* (relics) and erected a *Qībǎo Tǎ* (Stupa of Seven Treasures)
. That Crown Prince at that time was my current body
. The King, his father, is now my father, Shūtóudán
. The Lady (Fūrén) is my mother, Móyé (Māyā)
. The consort (Hòufēi) is now Gūyī (Gopā)
. The cremator (*Shéwéizhě*) is Ānán (Ānanda)
. The great master of the divine immortals on the mountain is Mílè (Maitreya)
. Formerly, in Yánfú Tí (Jambudvīpa), there was a king named Fàntiān
. The King had a Crown Prince whose courtesy name was Tánmógān
. He greatly loved the True Dharma
. Dì Shì (Indra) transformed himself into a *Póluómén* (Brahmin) and said
: "I can teach the Dharma"
. The Crown Prince touched his feet in reverence and requested to hear it
. The Brahmin said
: "I have studied for a long time
. How can you expect to hear it immediately?
. If you can spare neither your body nor life, nor your wife and children
, and enter a great fire pit to make offerings to me
, then I shall bestow the Dharma upon you"
. The Crown Prince did exactly as he was told
. He prepared a great fire pit
. The King, the Lady, and the palace women
went to the palace to advise the Brahmin
: "We beg that the kingdom, the capital, the wife, and children all serve you
. Please do not allow the Crown Prince to throw himself into this fire"
. The Brahmin said
: "I am not forcing him; he follows his own will
. The King decreed throughout the nation that in seven days, the Crown Prince would burn his body
. "Those who wish to witness it should come early on that day"
. Nobles and commoners from the entire kingdom assembled at once
. They begged piteously and insisted, repeating everything that had been said before
. The Crown Prince spoke to the crowd
: "During the long ages of transmigration, I have lost countless bodies
. As humans, due to greed, we alternately cut and harm one another
. In heaven, when life ends, we lose desire and suffer distress
. In the hells, there is burning, boiling, skinning by knives, dismemberment, and the pain of the Ash River and Sword Trees piercing the heart and marrow
. Among the hungry ghosts (Èguǐ), a hundred poisons bore through the body
. As animals (Chùshēng), the body feeds the masses, eats grass, and bears heavy burdens
. I have held onto this life, filled with all these sufferings, in vain
. I have never, with a good heart, devoted it to the Dharma
. Now I abandon this foul and impure form to seek purity and excellence
. Why do you all wish to prevent this?
. When I attain the Way of the Buddha (Fódào), I will bestow upon you the five-part Dharma Body (Fǎshēn)"
. The Crown Prince then stood above the fire pit
. The Brahmin said
: "Constantly practice the mind of loving-kindness, removing thoughts of anger and malice
; With great compassion, pity sentient beings, weep tears for their pain
; Cultivate the mind of great joy (sympathy), sharing the Dharma one has attained
; Protect them with the mind of the Way—this is fitting for the practice of a Bodhisattva (Púsà)"
. The Crown Prince heard this and was about to throw himself into the fire
. At that moment, Dì Shì and Fànwáng (Brahma King) grabbed one of his hands
, and addressed him, saying
: "All living creatures within Yánfú Tí
rely on the Crown Prince’s kindness, and none are left without support
. If you throw yourself into the fire now, the world will lose its father. Why do you destroy yourself and abandon everyone?"
. The Crown Prince replied
: "Do not obstruct my unsurpassed resolve for the Way"
. He cast himself into the fire pit
. Heaven and earth shook greatly
. The various *tiān* in the sky cried out simultaneously, their tears falling like heavy rain
. Instantly, the blazing fire pit transformed into a pool of flowers
. The Crown Prince sat upon a lotus flower pedestal
. The *tiān* rained down flowers until they reached his knees
. King Fàntiān is now Jìngfàn (Śuddhodana)
. The mother is now Fūrén Móyé
. The Crown Prince is now the Shìzūn (World-Honored One)
The king of the Bōluónài kingdom was wise, benevolent, and virtuous, but had no son or heir.
He served a mountain spirit for twelve years, praying tirelessly.
Later, his primary wife gave birth to a boy.
His nature was good, he harbored no anger, and he possessed a complete human form.
He summoned all his ministers
to divine his fortune. They immediately gave him a name, calling him Rěnrǔ.
When he grew up, he loved practicing *bùshī* (giving).
He treated all sentient beings equally with compassion.
The kingdom had six ministers.
They were treacherous, deceitful, flattering, wicked, lawless, hated by the people, and they envied
the crown prince. At that time, the king fell gravely ill, his life hanging by a thread.
Prince Rěnrǔ spoke to his father's ministers, saying:
"My father the King is critically ill; what should be done now?"
The ministers replied:
"The wondrous medicine is hard to obtain, and his life will not last long." The Prince, grieving, fell to the ground.
The wicked ministers immediately plotted to eliminate the Prince.
They petitioned the Prince, saying:
"The King's illness requires medicine, but the medicine is unobtainable."
The Prince asked:
"What sort of thing is it?"
They replied:
"It is the eyes
and marrow of a person who harbors no anger.
If this medicine is obtained, the King's life will certainly be saved."
The Prince said:
"My body seems to fit this description."
That person then took leave of his mother,
and gathered all the kings of the smaller nations.
He personally issued a proclamation, saying:
"I now part with this body and the assembly."
He immediately summoned a *zhāntuóluó* (caṇḍāla) to crush his bones to extract the marrow and gouge out his two eyes.
The ministers immediately pounded and mixed the ingredients and offered them to the Great King.
The King ingested it, and his illness was cured.
He asked the ministers:
"This medicine is extraordinary; it has removed my suffering."
The ministers replied:
"This medicine was provided by the Crown Prince."
The King said:
"Where is he now?"
They replied:
"He is outside. His body is mutilated, and his life will not last long."
The King wept bitterly.
When he arrived where his son lay, the Prince's life had already ended.
His mother, heartbroken, threw herself upon the corpse.
"Due to my accumulated past transgressions, I deserve
this ultimate fate, my body turning to dust. It has caused my son to lose his body and life."
They used *Niútóu Zhāntán* (Ox-Head Sandalwood) to perform the cremation.
They built a *qībǎo* (seven-jeweled) stupa
over his bones. Formerly, there was a king in Yánfúlì named Zhìlì.
He constantly protected the Buddhist Dharma with deep sincerity.
A *bǐqiū* (monk) was close to the King.
He was respected by the King and highly revered by the people of the kingdom.
The King desired to see him without ever being satisfied.
A large, malignant sore appeared on the *bǐqiū*'s thigh.
The medicine and doctors in the kingdom could not cure it.
The King and his twenty thousand consorts were all deeply saddened.
At that time, the King had a dream while sleeping.
A celestial being came and spoke to the King, saying:
"If you wish to cure this *bǐqiū*,
you must use the flesh and blood of a living person for him to eat and drink; then he will be cured."
The King awoke, feeling distressed.
He thought that because the *bǐqiū*'s illness was so severe, it required this medicine.
He commanded his officials and subordinates, asking:
"Where can the flesh and blood of a living person be obtained?"
At that time, the Crown Prince, named Zhìzhǐ,
reported to the King:
"Your Majesty, do not worry or grieve.
Human flesh and blood are the cheapest of things.
What the world values does not contradict the Way."
The King said, "Excellent!"
The Prince remained silent.
He returned to his dwelling, held a blade, cut meat from his thigh,
and sent the meat and blood to the *bǐqiū*.
The *bǐqiū* ingested it, the sore was immediately cured, and his body achieved tranquility.
The King heard that the *bǐqiū* had recovered.
He was overwhelmed by joy and delight.
The Prince's wound healed naturally.
All the treasures of the kingdom were bestowed upon the Prince.
At that time, the one of utmost sincerity was Tíhégēluó Fó.
King Zhìlì was Mílè.
Prince Zhìzhǐ was myself.
There was Prince Yuèguāng.
He went out touring and observing.
A person suffering from leprosy saw him, stopped his carriage, and reported, saying:
"My body is heavily diseased, and I suffer torment and grief.
Should the Prince amuse himself and rejoice alone?
Out of great compassion, I beg you to save and treat me."
The Prince heard this and asked his doctors.
They said: "You must use the blood and marrow of a person who has never harbored anger from birth to adulthood, applied externally and consumed internally; only then can he be cured."
The Prince thought:
"Even if such a person exists, how can they be obtained, given that they cherish life and cling to longevity?
Aside from my own body, there is nowhere else it can be obtained."
He immediately summoned a *zhāntuóluó*.
He ordered him to cut the flesh from his body, break the bones to extract the marrow to apply to the sick person, and give the blood for him to drink.
In like manner, he practiced giving, including giving his wife and son, giving without regret.
It was like casting away grass or trees; he viewed the objects given as having arisen due to conditions.
Seeking the reality of the self, nothing at all was found.
Everything was pure, like the mark of Nirvāṇa.
He even attained the realization of the non-origination of all phenomena.
This is the practice of *Dànboluómì* (Dānapāramitā), manifesting the body formed by accumulated karma.
In the time of the semblance dharma of Pípóshī Fó.
The king of Bōluónài Guó,
named Luóshé,
had only three sons,
each administering a small state.
At that time, the King was intelligent and wise, ruling by the True Dharma, and did not mistreat his people.
The King possessed virtue and power; the wind and rain arrived seasonably, and the five grains ripened abundantly.
A trusted minister of the King, named Luóhóuluó,
conceived malicious rebellion and suddenly raised an army of four divisions to attack Bōluónài Guó.
He took the life of the Great King.
Next, he attacked the first and second princes,
and then sought out the third.
The third prince was handsome and tall in stature, upright and exceedingly beautiful, naturally gentle and well-spoken.
He always spoke with a smile, benefiting others and not harming people's feelings.
He ruled the people according to the True Dharma, and the land was abundant and joyous.
The national treasury was full, and the four directions praised him.
The various devas in the heavens and all spirits and ghosts likewise respected and loved him.
He had one crown prince, named Xūchǎntí.
He was intelligent, compassionate, and fond of generosity (dāna).
His body was golden yellow, perfectly formed in the seven places, possessing all the auspicious marks of a human being.
He was seven years old, and his father loved him dearly, never forsaking him even for a moment.
At that time, the spirit protecting the palace spoke to the King, saying:
"Luóhóu is a malicious traitor, plotting to seize the throne and intending to kill the royal father.
He quickly raised armies to hunt down your two elder brothers, and has already ended their lives.
His troops will soon arrive here."
The King heard these words,
and was so grieved and distressed that he could not control himself.
His heart and liver seemed to burst; he writhed and fell to the ground.
After a long time, he revived.
In a faint voice, he spoke toward the empty sky, saying:
"Who are you?
I only hear your voice,
but do not see your form.
Was what you just announced truly so?"
The voice immediately replied to the King, saying:
"I am the spirit protecting the palace. Because the King is wise, upright, and does not mistreat his people, I inform you of this.
The King should quickly leave; his arrival is imminent."
The King thought to flee to a neighboring state, but there were two paths.
One path required seven days of travel, and the other required fourteen days of travel.
He immediately prepared seven days' worth of provisions for one person.
Entering the palace, he called Xūchǎntí and held him on his lap.
The Queen stepped forward and asked:
"Your Majesty appears to be afraid."
The King said:
"This is not something you need to know."
The Queen replied:
"My body and the King are like two wings of a bird.
How can you say that I am not concerned or involved?"
The King informed her of the situation as stated above.
He immediately embraced the Crown Prince and set out on the road.
The Queen followed behind, confused and distraught, and mistakenly entered the fourteen-day path.
That path was perilous and difficult, lacking water and grass.
After traveling for several days, the provisions shared by the three of them were completely exhausted.
The journey was still long.
The King and the Queen cried aloud,
saying: "Alas, what suffering! Since birth until now, we have never heard of such distress!
How is it that today we personally experience this?"
They deeply regretted and blamed themselves.
Pressed by hunger and thirst, their lives hung by a thread.
[The King] thought of a means (upāya).
Not wishing all three to die together, he considered killing the Queen to save himself and the child.
Xūchǎntí saw the King's strange appearance.
He stepped forward, grabbed his father's hand, and asked:
"What are you intending to do?"
The father, eyes full of sorrowful tears, faintly said to his son:
"I intend to kill your mother and take her flesh and blood to sustain your life."
Xūchǎntí choked back his tears and replied to his father:
"Where is there a son who eats his mother's flesh?
If I do not eat the flesh, both the son and mother will die.
I pray that you only kill the son to save the lives of the parents."
The King heard his son's words
and immediately fainted. He revived and faintly said to his son:
"You are like my own eyes. Where is the person who plucks out his eyes and then eats them?
I would rather lose my life than kill my son and eat his flesh."
Xūchǎntí further said:
"If I simply die now, the flesh and blood will rot.
Before many days pass, I wish to request one thing.
If you refuse it, you are not compassionate parents."
At that time, the royal father said to the Crown Prince:
"I will not oppose your wish."
Xūchǎntí said:
"I only wish that every day you cut three *jīn* (catties) of flesh from my body.
Two parts shall be offered to sustain the parents,
and one part I shall eat myself to sustain my life."
The parents, weeping, agreed to this.

They managed to advance on the road for the remaining two days. The flesh on his body was gradually exhausted, but his limbs, joints, sinews, and bones remained connected, and his remaining life was not yet severed.
His parents held him and cried aloud: "We are worthless!
We have wrongfully eaten your flesh and caused you such bitter pain.
The road ahead is still long; we have not yet reached our destination.
Now that your flesh is finished, our lives will end together, and our corpses will gather in one place."
At that time, Xūchǎntí faintly remonstrated, saying:
"You have already eaten your son's flesh and progressed this far.
Parents, now do not act like ordinary people.
Do not refuse this out of compassion and let our lives end together in one spot.
You may cleanly cut the remaining flesh between the joints of my body.
Use it to save the parents so that you may reach your destination."
The parents followed his words, and after eating, they cried out and parted ways.
Xūchǎntí stood up and watched his parents.
The parents wept bitterly and continued down the road.
When the parents had gone far and could no longer see Xūchǎntí,
the Crown Prince, yearning for his parents, did not turn his gaze away even for a moment.
After a long time, he fell to the ground. The scent of the fresh blood and flesh from his body perfumed the ten directions.
There were mosquitoes and gadflies around.
Smelling the scent of the blood and flesh, they came and covered his body.
They sucked and ate all over his body; the excruciating pain was beyond description.
While his remaining life was not yet severed, he spoke, establishing a vow:
"May the accumulated evils and misfortunes of previous existences be utterly eliminated from this point onward.
From now on, I dare not commit them again.
I have used this body of mine to serve and nurture my parents.
May my parents always gain eleven excess blessings.
May the remaining blood and flesh, which I offer to these mosquitoes and gadflies, allow them all to be satisfied."
When he made this vow,
the earth shook in six ways.
The sun lost its luster, and birds and beasts scattered and fled.
The great seas surged, and Mount Xūmí rose and sank.
All the devas of the Six Desire Heavens were terrified and descended to Yánfú Tí,
transforming themselves into lions, tigers, and wolves.
They glared, scratched their whiskers, roared loudly at the earth, jumped, stomped, and leaped, coming forth intending to attack and devour him.
Xūchǎntí saw the great terrifying display put on by these creatures.
He faintly spoke, saying:
"If you wish to eat me, take and eat as you please. Why do you try to frighten me?"
At that time, the King of Heaven, Dìshì, immediately resumed his divine form.
The Crown Prince saw him and rejoiced immensely.
Dìshì then asked the Crown Prince:
"You have renounced what is difficult to renounce.
Is this merit intended for rebirth in heaven, to become a Demon King (Mówáng), or a Brahma King (Fànwáng)?"
The Crown Prince replied:
"I vow to achieve unsurpassed Bodhi (enlightenment)."
Dìshì said:
"These are empty words. Who would believe you?"
The Crown Prince swore an oath:
"If I am deceiving you, may the wounds on my body never heal, from start to finish.
If not so, may I be completely restored."
His blood immediately turned into milk, and his body was restored, becoming twice as handsome as before.
At that time, the King of Heaven, Dìshì, bowed down his head and worshipped his feet, exclaiming, "Excellent!
I am not equal to you.
Your courageous diligence will certainly achieve Bodhi. I pray that you save me first."
Then the King of Heaven, Dìshì,
immediately vanished in the empty sky.
Meanwhile, the King and the Queen reached the neighboring state.
The neighboring king heard of it
and traveled far out to welcome them. Upon meeting, they fully recounted the previous events.
He provided them with everything they needed, fully meeting their expectations.
The neighboring king was moved by
the Crown Prince's compassion and filial piety.
He immediately deployed an army of four divisions and returned the kingship to the deposed King.
They proceeded to attack Luóhóu and returned along the road.
When they were approaching the spot
where they had previously parted from the Crown Prince, intending to collect his remains and mourn before his coffin,
as they drew nearer, they saw from afar that the Crown Prince's body was completely restored.
They immediately went forward and embraced him, overwhelmed by sorrow and joy combined.
Xūchǎntí then fully recounted the preceding events to his parents.
The parents were overjoyed.
They rode together on a great elephant and returned to their native state.
Due to the profound merit of the Crown Prince, they successfully returned to their home country.
They immediately established the Crown Prince as the Great King.
The royal father at that time is now King Shūtóután.
The mother at that time is now Lady Móyé.
Xūchǎntí is the Buddha himself now.
The King of Heaven, Dìshì, at that time is now Āruòjiāochénrú.
Formerly, the king of Yèbō Guó was titled Shīsuí.
The crown prince was named Xūdànà.
He universally protected with the Four Immeasurables; his speech did not harm people.
He constantly desired to practice dāna (giving) to save and relieve all sentient beings.
Wishing that in his later generations he would receive endless fortune.
The foolish do not see the impermanent transformations and think that [things] can be maintained.
The wise illuminate the presence of the Five Houses (sources of loss).
To those desiring clothes, food, gold, silver, various treasures, carriages, horses, fields, or residences, there was nothing asked for that he would not give.
His radiance and renown spread far, reaching the Four Seas, eliciting sighs of praise.
His father, the king, had a white elephant.
Its fierce might and martial prowess could resist sixty hostile states; whenever they came to battle, the elephant was invariably victorious.
The various kings held a joint discussion.
They sent eight Brahmins to request the white elephant from him.
The crown prince joyfully asked what they desired, and they replied,
"We wish to beg for the white elephant that walks upon lotus flowers."
The elephant's name was Luóshéhétán.
The crown prince said, "Good."
"Gold, silver, and various jewels, whatever your heart desires, take freely."
He immediately commanded his attendants,
"Quickly adorn the white elephant with saddles and bridles of gold and silver."
Holding the elephant's reins in his left hand,
And holding a golden vase in his right hand,
He cleansed the Brahmins' hands.
With compassionate joy, he handed over the elephant.
The Brahmins were greatly delighted.
They immediately finished reciting their blessings and rode the elephant away.
The Prime Minister and all the officials were universally distressed.
They all said,
"This elephant possesses fierce strength; in battle, it is always victorious.
Now he has bestowed it upon an enemy state.
What shall we rely upon?"
They reported the entirety of the matter to the king.
The king heard this, looked distressed, and after a long time said,
"The crown prince loves and delights in the Buddha's Way.
His actions are to assist the poor and relieve the destitute with compassionate nurturing; there is no way to stop him.
Should we subject him to confinement and punishment,
That would be unrighteous."
All the officials said,
"In the matter of admonishing and educating, the deliberation must not be faulty.
Confinement and punishment would be tyranny.
We, your servants, dare to suggest:
Chase him out of the kingdom and place him in the wilderness.
Within ten years, let him come to regret this himself.
This is the desire of your servants."
The king immediately sent an envoy.
He instructed him, saying,
"The elephant is a national treasure, yet he bestowed it upon an enemy?
I cannot bear to inflict punishment, but he must quickly leave the kingdom."
The envoy received the command and proclaimed it thus.
The crown prince replied,
"I dare not disobey the heavenly decree (the royal command).
I request to use my private wealth for seven more days of dāna, so as not to encroach upon the state's resources."
The envoy reported this.
The king immediately consented.
The crown prince joyfully performed a great act of dāna for the poor and destitute.
He proclaimed that they should come quickly and take whatever their hearts desired.
When the seven days were finished, the poor were all wealthy.
His wife was named Mándī.
She was originally the daughter of a various king.
Her countenance was splendid and graceful, unmatched in the entire kingdom.
From her head to her feet, she was adorned with precious ornaments of the seven treasures.
He spoke to his wife, saying,
"Arise and listen to my words.
The Great King is banishing me to Tántè Shān for a limit of twelve years; do you know this?"
The wife looked at the crown prince in astonishment, weeping tears, and said,
"For what crime are you being banished, abandoning the honor of the state to reside in the deep mountains?"
He replied,
"I used the elephant, famed throughout the nation, and bestowed it upon a king who is our enemy.
Consequently, the officials became angry and banished me."
The wife immediately made a vow:
"I wish the kingdom rich harvests, and the king, officials, and populace endless wealth and longevity.
I shall only establish my resolve in the mountains and swamps and vow to achieve the Way."
The crown prince said,
"That mountain swamp is a place of terror.
Tigers, wolves, and harmful beasts make it difficult to reside there.
Moreover, there are poisonous insects, sprites, mountain goblins, and evil spirits.
Thunder and lightning flash, and wind, rain, clouds, and fog are extremely frightful.
Cold and heat are extreme; trees are difficult to rely on; caltrops and gravel stones cannot be endured by the soles of the feet.
You are the child of a king.
Born into glory and joy, raised within the palace.
Your clothes are fine and soft; your food and drink are sweet and delicious.
When sleeping, you have curtains and screens, and various music fills your ears.
Your every wish has been indulged.
Now, residing in the mountain swamps,
Sleeping on straw mats and eating fruits and vegetables is what ordinary people cannot endure.
How can you bear it?"
His wife said,
"What good are fine clothes, various treasures, curtains, screens, or sweet delicacies
if they benefit me but cause me to be separated alive from the crown prince?
Now, a king is recognized by his banner.
Fire is recognized by its smoke.
A woman is recognized by her husband.
I rely on the crown prince just as I rely on my two parents.
When the crown prince was in the kingdom giving dāna far and wide, I always shared his vow.
Now you must pass through danger; how could I remain behind guarding glory? That would not be the path of benevolence!
If, perchance, someone were to come begging and I were not present, the crown prince's heart would be troubled and tied up, and I would certainly die without doubt."
The crown prince said,
"If someone from a distant land comes to beg for my wife and children, I have no intention of refusing.
If you, out of sentimental attachment, should happen to violate the Way of Generosity, you would pluck away the great blessings and ruin my weighty obligation."
His wife said,
"The dāna of the crown prince is rarely seen in the world; you should fulfill your great vow and take care not to tire.
For hundreds of thousands of generations, there has been no one like you establishing the Buddha’s weighty mission; I dare not oppose it."
The crown prince said, "Good."
He immediately took his wife and children to his mother to say farewell.
He bowed his head to the ground and tearfully bid farewell, saying,
"I wish you to cast aside heavy worries and keep your noble body safe and tranquil.
When burdened with state affairs, frequently offer compassionate counsel.
Do not use self-will to coerce the common people.
You must endure what is unendurable."
His mother said,
"When I had no son, I formed a vow seeking an heir.
The day I became pregnant was like a tree bearing blossoms, day by day awaiting its maturity.
Heaven did not deny my wish and allowed me to have a son.
Now that you have been raised to maturity, we must separate while living."
The ladies and concubines no longer showed respect to each other.
The crown prince, his wife, and children bowed their heads and retreated.
Within the palace, great and small, none were without choked sobs.
He went out and tearfully bid farewell to the officials, and together they left the city.
There was no one who did not secretly whisper,
"The crown prince is the sacred spiritual essence of the nation, the most honored of all treasures.
What heart do his parents have to banish him?"
The crown prince sat outside the city, thanked all those who had escorted him, and sent them back to their homes.
The common people bowed down in prostration, all collectively raising a lamentation of grief.
Some fell down and leapt up, calling out to heaven, their voices echoing and shaking the kingdom.
Having traveled far from the kingdom, they sat down beneath a tree.
There was a Brahmin who had traveled far, begging for the ornaments and clothes on his body, and his wife and children.
He bestowed all his pearls and jewels upon him.
He ordered his wife and children to mount the carriage, and holding the reins, they departed.
Just as they were about to set off on the road,
They again met a Brahmin who begged for the horse.
He bestowed the horse upon him.
He then pulled the carriage himself from between the shafts to advance on the road.
Again, he met a Brahmin who came begging for the carriage.
He immediately bestowed the carriage upon him.
The crown prince's carriage, horse, clothes, ornaments, and various possessions were entirely given away, leaving nothing remaining.
He ordered his wife to carry the daughter, and he himself carried the son.
After twenty-one days, they finally arrived in the mountains.
The crown prince saw the mountains where the trees were lush, running springs provided sweet water, and delicious fruits were plentiful.
Ducks, geese, and mandarin ducks played among them.
The crown prince said to his wife,
"The trees reach the sky, and few are broken or damaged.
Flocks of birds sing sorrowfully, and the springs and fruits are abundant.
They are sufficient for food and drink; we must only focus on the Way."
The Daoists (hermits) in the mountains all maintained their chastity and loved learning.
There was one hermit named Āzhūtúo.
He had lived in the mountains for a long time and possessed excellent virtue.
The crown prince immediately went to him with his wife and children.
He bowed his head and said,
"I have brought my wife and children here to learn the Way.
I beg you to extend your great compassion and instruct me to fulfill my ambition."
The hermit instructed them.
The crown prince then built a hut from wood and grass, knotted his hair, wore rush-woven clothes, ate fruits, and drank spring water.
The son was named Yēlì.
He wore small grass clothes and followed his father in and out.
The daughter was named Jìnúoyán.
She wore deer-skin clothes and followed her mother in and out.
After residing in the mountains for one night, Heaven increased the springs for them and caused medicinal trees to grow anew.
Later, there was a poor, elderly Brahmin named Jiūliúsūn.
His wife was still young and her countenance was beautiful and proper.
Carrying a vase, she went out to draw water.
On the road, she met a young man who stopped her and taunted her, saying,
"Are you poor? You covet the wealth of that old man, hoping to return to a settled life.
That old man is studying the Way, hoping to become one of the accomplished.
He is solely foolish, obstinate, and cruel. Is this what you desire?
His face is ugly and dark, his nose is crooked and flattened.
His body is contorted and strange, his face is wrinkled, and his lips are overly thick.
His speech is stuttering and harsh, and his two eyes are also blue; his appearance resembles a ghost.
He has no virtues in his entire body. Who would not dislike and despise him?
Being his wife, do you feel no shame or disgust?"
The woman wept tears and departed.
The old man's beard and temples were pure white, like frost covering the trees.
Though he had not yet died, morning or evening, there was nothing she could do about it.
She returned and reported this matter in full detail to her husband.
"If there are no servants to wait on me, I will leave you."
Her husband said,
"I am poor. How can I suddenly obtain servants?"
His wife said,
"I heard that Xūdànà, possessing great compassion, aids the populace and has been banished to reside in the mountains.
He has two children; if you beg for them, he will bestow them upon you."
Since his wife spoke repeatedly, and the affection for his wife was hard to violate, he immediately followed her suggestion.
Seeking out the road, he encountered a hunter.
The hunter already knew the reason for the crown prince's banishment.
He flared up and cursed, saying,
"I shall chop off your head!"
[The Brahmin] asked if the crown prince was being moved for the Brahmin's benefit, and being frightened, he said,
"The king and his officials have ordered me to call the crown prince back to the kingdom to be king."
[The hunter] replied,
"Excellent! I am happy to show you his location."
They soon saw the small hut.
The crown prince also saw them approaching.
The two children saw them, and their hearts were deeply frightened.
The brother and sister together stated,
"Our father loves giving, and this person has traveled far.
His wealth is exhausted and he has nothing left; he will certainly bestow us, his brother and sister, upon him."
They held hands and fled together.
Their mother had previously dug a sheltered pit large enough to hold people.
The two children entered it and covered the top with firewood.
They cautioned each other, saying,
"When Father calls, do not answer."
The crown prince spoke to comfort and reassure them, saying,
are weary and exhausted from traveling far.
(The man) replied,
"Since I came from that place, my entire body has ached painfully.
Moreover, I am extremely hungry and thirsty."
The Crown Prince (Tàizǐ) offered fruit juice.
"Therefore, I now return in distress, hoping to prolong my meager life."
The Crown Prince (Tàizǐ) said compassionately,
"I have nothing left to regret having exhausted my wealth."
The Brāhmaṇa (Fànzhì) said,
"You can give me your two children to provide for my old age."
(Tàizǐ) answered,
"My heart holds no refusal."
The Crown Prince (Tàizǐ) called for his children.
The brothers were afraid.
They said to each other,
"Our father is calling and asking for us.
He surely intends to bestow us upon this demon.
(We decide) to disobey the command and not answer."
The Crown Prince (Tàizǐ) knew they were hiding among the bushes.
He moved aside the brushwood and saw them.
The children came out, embraced their father, trembling, weeping, and wailing, saying,
"This is a demon! He is not a Brāhmaṇa (Fànzhì).
We have often seen Brāhmaṇas (Fànzhì), but none look like this.
Do not make us food for the demon.
Why is our mother, who went gathering fruit, so late returning?
Today we are certainly going to die, eaten by the demon.
When mother returns and seeks us,
like a cow seeking its calf,
she will run wildly, grieving bitterly.
Father will surely regret this."
The Crown Prince (Tàizǐ) said,
"In my life, I have never felt the slightest regret about giving alms (bùshī).
I have already promised him. You must not refuse."
The Brāhmaṇa (Fànzhì) said,
"I am old and weak, and the children are running away toward their mother. Crown Prince (Tàizǐ), in your great generosity, bind them and hand them over to me."
The Crown Prince (Tàizǐ) held his children and allowed the Brāhmaṇa (Fànzhì) to bind them, while he himself held the end of the rope.
The two children fell down, writhing before their father, wailing sorrowfully and calling to their mother, saying,
"Heavenly spirits, earth spirits (dìqí), and all mountain and tree deities, please, sorrowfully tell our mother,
that her two children have been bestowed upon someone, and that she should come to see us just once."
The sorrow moved Heaven and Earth (èryí), and the mountain spirits responded with a sound like a thunderclap.
At that moment, the mother (Mǔ) was gathering fruit, and her heart felt heavy.
She looked up at the azure sky but saw neither clouds nor rain.
Her right eye twitched, her left sole itched, and milk flowed from both breasts.
The mother (Mǔ) reflected, saying,
"This omen is extremely strange. I must return and see my children."
She abandoned the fruit and rushed back, frantic as if mad.
Śakra, the Lord of Heaven (Dìshì), contemplated, saying,
"The Bodhisattva's (Púsà) resolve is lofty, and he wishes to accomplish a heavy responsibility.
If his wife arrives, she might undermine his high resolve."
(Śakra) transformed into a lion (shīzǐ) and squatted in the middle of the road.
The wife (Fù) said,
"You are the king among hunters.
I am the daughter of a king among men, and we both reside on this mountain.
I have two children who are still very young.
Since morning, they have not eaten and are waiting for me."
The lion (shīzǐ) avoided her, and the wife (Fù) was able to proceed.
(Śakra) returned and transformed into a white wolf (báiláng) ahead of her.
The wife (Fù) pleaded as before, and the wolf (láng) again avoided her.
(Śakra) then transformed into a tiger (hǔ), and only upon calculating that the Brāhmaṇa (Fànzhì) had gone far did he finally withdraw.
The wife (Fù) saw the Crown Prince (Tàizǐ) sitting alone and said, distraught and afraid,
"Where are my children? Why are you sitting alone now?
Whenever the children saw me return, they would run toward me.
They would jump and laugh happily, saying, 'Mother is back!'
Now, their toys—clay elephants, clay oxen, clay horses, clay pigs, and various cleverly made objects—are scattered all over the ground.
Seeing this makes my heart ache, and I feel like going mad.
Surely they haven't been devoured by tigers (hǔ), wolves (láng), demons (guǐmèi), or robbers?
Quickly resolve this anguish for me, or I will certainly die!"
The Crown Prince (Tàizǐ) was silent for a long time and then said,
"A Brāhmaṇa (Fànzhì) came and requested the two children.
He said,
that his life was ending and his years were few, and he wished to save himself, so I bestowed them upon him."
The wife (Fù) heard these words, was heartbroken, leaped, and fell to the ground, writhing, grieving sorrowfully, weeping, and saying,
"This is exactly like the dream I had last night!
I dreamed I saw an old, poor Brāhmaṇa (Fànzhì),
cutting off my two breasts, seizing them, and rushing away.
This must have been for this moment."
Her bitter lamentation and crying out to Heaven shook the entire mountain region.
The Crown Prince (Tàizǐ) watched his wife's sorrowful lamentation.
It was extreme.
He said to her,
"I originally worried that because you so highly valued filial piety and respected your elders, if someone asked for a gift, you would not refuse, as your vows were very clear.
But now your sorrowful lamentation is disturbing my mind."
The wife (Qī) said,
"Your Highness (Tàizǐ), how great is the effort you put into seeking the Way (Dào)!"
Śakra, the Lord of Heaven (Dìshì), and all the devas (zhūtiān) unanimously discussed, saying,
"The Crown Prince's (Tàizǐ) Way (Dào) is vast, and his boundless almsgiving (bùshī) will never cease. Let us test him by asking for his wife."
Śakra (Shì) transformed into a Brāhmaṇa (Fànzhì) and said,
"Sir, you possess the benevolence of Heaven and Earth (qiánchuān).
You universally save sentient beings through unobstructed almsgiving (bùshī), which is why I have come to put my faith in you.
Your wife (Qī) is virtuous and chaste, and her reputation for virtue is far-reaching, which is why I have come to beg for her."
(Tàizǐ) answered, "Excellent!"
Heaven and Earth suddenly shook violently, and all devas (tiānrén), ghosts, and spirits (guǐshén) praised his goodness.
The Brāhmaṇa (Fànzhì) said,
"I am Śakra, the Lord of Heaven (Tiāndì), not a common person of this world.
I came specifically to test you.
Your reverence for the wisdom of the Buddha (Fóhuì) sets an unparalleled example.
What wish do you have now? Ask freely, and it will surely be granted."
The Crown Prince (Tàizǐ) said,
"I wish to attain great wealth and constantly enjoy giving alms (bùshī) without attachment or transgression.
Also, my Royal Father (Fùwáng) and the ministers and citizens of the kingdom wish to see me."
The Lord of Heaven (Tiāndì) said,
"Good!" and immediately vanished.
The Brāhmaṇa (Fànzhì), delighted to have obtained his livelihood.
Traveled without feeling fatigue, dragging the two children as if they were fugitive slaves.
The children were grandsons of the King (Wáng), accustomed to glory, pleasure, and freedom.
Separated from their two parents, they were bound by rope.
Where the knots were tied, they were all wounded, and they wailed sorrowfully, calling for their mother.
(Fànzhì) whipped them, forcing them to walk, and their blood flowed, staining the ground red.
The heavenly spirits (Tiānshén) took pity, unbound them, and healed their wounds.
They caused sweet fruits to grow for them and made the ground soft.
The brothers picked the fruits, handed them to each other, and ate them, saying,
"They are as sweet as the fruits in the royal garden (yuànzhōng)."
"And the ground is as soft as the King's (Wáng) felt carpet."
The brothers supported each other, looked up at the sky, and called for their mother.
(Fànzhì), with tears streaming down his body, returned to his home, laughing joyfully and saying,
"I have obtained two male and female slaves (núbì) for you to employ as you wish."
His wife (Qī) saw the children and said,
"They are not slaves (núbì)!
These children are handsome, their hands and feet are refined; they are not fit for labor.
You must go and peddle them and buy people suited for labor instead."
(Fànzhì) intended to travel to a different country.
Heaven (Tiān) confused his path, and he instead went to his native country.
The millions of people recognized them and all said,
"These are the great grandsons of the King (Wáng)!"
They immediately informed the King (Wáng).
The King (Wáng) called them into the palace (gōng).
All the palace staff, both high and low, sighed in lament.
The King (Wáng) wished to embrace the two children, but they refused to approach.
The King (Wáng) asked, "Why?"
The children said,
"Previously we were grandsons of the King (Wáng), but now we are as lowly as slaves (núbì).
How can we sit on the King's (Wáng) lap?"
The King (Wáng) asked the Brāhmaṇa (Fànzhì),
"How did you obtain these children?"
He answered truthfully.
(The King) said, "How much money do you want for selling the children?"
The Brāhmaṇa (Fànzhì) had not yet answered.
The grandson (Nánsūn) preemptively said,
"The boy is worth one thousand silver coins (yínqián) and one exceptional bull,
and one hundred head of cows and oxen.
The girl is worth one thousand gold coins (jīnqián), one exceptional bull, and two hundred head of cows and oxen."
The King (Wáng) said,
"The boy is older but cheaper, and the girl is younger but more expensive. Why is that?"
(The grandson) replied,
"The Crown Prince (Tàizǐ) is both sage and benevolent, a person everyone relies upon.
Yet he was driven far away; therefore, we know the boy is cheap.
A commoner's daughter, simply because of her beauty, is able to dwell in the deep palace.
Therefore, we know the girl is expensive."
The King (Wáng) said,
"An eight-year-old child already possesses the arguments of a high scholar!
How much more so must his father be!"
All the palace staff, both high and low, heard his satirical admonishment and burst into mourning.
The King (Wáng) paid the Brāhmaṇa (Fànzhì) all the demanded amounts, and the Brāhmaṇa (Fànzhì) withdrew.
The King (Wáng) embraced his two grandsons, sat them on his lap, and said,
"Just now you refused my embrace, yet now you come so quickly?"
(The grandson) replied,
"Just now we were slaves (núbì); now we are grandsons of the King (Wáng)."
(The King) asked, "What does your father eat to sustain himself in the mountains?"
Both children said,
"He eats vegetables and tree fruits to sustain himself.
Every day he enjoys himself with the beasts and the birds; he has no worried heart."
The King (Wáng) dispatched messengers (shǐzhě) to welcome them.
As the messengers (shǐzhě) took to the road,
the trees in the mountains bent and swayed, seeming to offer the ritual of kneeling and rising.
The multitude of birds cried sorrowfully, moving human emotions.
The Crown Prince (Tàizǐ) said,
"What kind of auspicious sign (ruì) is this?"
His wife (Qī), who had been lying on the ground, said,
"The King's (Wáng) intent has cleared up, and messengers (shǐzhě) are coming to welcome us. The spirits (shénqí) assist goodness, hence these auspicious signs (ruì) arise."
Since losing her children, the wife (Qī) had been lying on the ground.
When the messengers (shǐzhě) arrived, she finally rose and bowed to the King's (Wáng) command.
The messengers (shǐzhě) said,
"The King (Wáng) and the Queen (Hòuhuáng) have reduced their food intake and choked back tears. Their bodies and lives weaken daily, and they long to see the Crown Prince (Tàizǐ)."
The Crown Prince (Tàizǐ) looked left and right, gazing longingly at the trees and flowing springs in the mountains, wiped away his tears, and ascended the carriage.
From the moment the messengers (shǐzhě) departed, the whole kingdom was joyous.
They repaired the roads, swept them clean, and set up curtains and canopies in advance.
They burned incense, scattered flowers, and prepared musicians, banners, and parasols.
The entire kingdom rushed out, hailing longevity without measure.
The Crown Prince (Tàizǐ) entered the city, bowed his head to apologize for his faults, and retreated to inquire about the King's health and daily life.
The King (Wáng) once again handed over all the national treasures to the Crown Prince (Tàizǐ) and urged him to perform almsgiving (bùshī).
Distressed people from neighboring countries gathered like rivers flowing into the sea.
Long-time enemies saw this, bowed, approached, and declared themselves vassals.
Tributes followed one after another. Robbers and invaders cherished benevolence, thieves competed to give alms (shī), weapons were put away, and prisons (língyǔ) were destroyed.
All sentient beings found eternal joy, the ten directions celebrated the goodness, and the accumulation of virtue never ceased.
Although he initially endured suffering, he now became the Honored One (Zūn) without end.
Later, the Crown Prince (Tàizǐ) died and was born into the Tuṣita Heaven (Dōushùtiān).
From Heaven, he descended and was born into the palace of King Śuddhodana (Báijìng Wánggōng).
I am that person today.
The Royal Father (Fùwáng) was Ānán.
The wife (Qī) was Guyī (Qúyī).
The son was Ráhula (Luóyún).
The daughter was the mother of the Arhat Zhūchí (Luóhàn Zhūchí Mǔ).
Śakra, the Lord of Heaven (Tiāndì Shì), was Maitreya (Mílè).
The hunter was Udāyin (Yōutuóyē).
Zhūtuó was Mahākāśyapa (Dàjiāyè).
The Brāhmaṇa (Fànzhì) who sold the children was Devadatta (Tiáodá).
The Bodhisattva's (Púsà) compassionate generosity (cíhuì) and almsgiving (bùshī) were thus.
In the past, there was the kingdom of Wéiyēlī (維耶離).
In the royal park, a nài (奈) tree grew.
Its branches and leaves were luxuriant, and it possessed extraordinary luster, color, fragrance, and beauty.
The king greatly cherished and loved it.
Unless they were honored nobility within the palace, they were forbidden from eating its fruit.
At that time, there was a Fànzhì (梵志) [Brahmin].
His family was exceptionally wealthy, unmatched in the entire kingdom; he was intelligent, broadly learned, and his talent and wisdom surpassed the common crowd.
The king employed him as a chief minister (dàchén).
The king invited him for a meal, and after serving the Nài fruit, he presented him with one Nài fruit.
The Fànzhì saw that the Nài fruit was extraordinarily fragrant and beautiful, and then asked:
“Is it possible to beg for a small sapling from beneath this Nài tree?”
The king said:
“If you wish to obtain one sapling, I will give it to you.”
The Fànzhì planted it.
Watering it day and night, the branches grew vigorously and well, and after three years, it bore fruit.
Its brilliance and size were exactly like those found at the royal household.
The Fànzhì was greatly pleased and thought to himself:
“My assets are countless and no less than the king’s.”
“The only thing I lacked was this Nài fruit. Now that I have obtained it, I lack nothing.”
He immediately took one and ate it, but it was extremely bitter and astringent.
He then retreated and pondered:
“This must be because the soil is not fertile.”
He then obtained milk, feeding one hundred cows in succession, and boiled the resulting milk down into crème de la crème (tíhú).
He watered the tree with it every day, until the next year.
The fruit was indeed sweet and delicious.
However, a knot grew on the side of the tree.
It was as large as a clenched fist.
It grew larger day by day, and he feared it would hinder the fruit production.
Just as he intended to chop it away,
he again feared injuring the tree.
He hesitated and remained undecided.
The knot sprouted a branch.
It was robust, straight, and well-proportioned, towering above the treetop.
Seven zhàng (丈) above the ground,
it spread out branches, forming a shape like an inverted canopy.
The flowers and leaves were beautiful and luxuriant, surpassing the original tree trunk.
He immediately built a scaffold (zhàngé) to climb up and look at it.
He saw that within the inverted canopy, there was a pond of water.
It was both clear and fragrant, and the many flowers were vibrant and bright.
He parted the flowers and looked underneath.
There was a young woman (nǚ'ér) in the pond water.
The Fànzhì embraced her, took her home, and raised her.
He named her Nàinǚ (奈女).
When she reached the age of fifteen, her appearance was exquisitely beautiful, unmatched in the world, and her fame reached distant kingdoms.
There were seven kings.
They all arrived at the Fànzhì's residence simultaneously, seeking to marry Nàinǚ and make her their madam (fūrén).
The Fànzhì did not know whom to give her to.
He erected a tall tower in his garden and placed Nàinǚ on top of it.
He said to the kings:
“This girl was not born of me.”
“She spontaneously appeared atop the Nài tree.”
“Now seven kings all seek her hand.”
“If I give her to one, the other six will surely be angered.”
“I dare not selfishly withhold her.”
“The girl is now on the tower in the garden.”
“O Kings, please simply discuss and decide among yourselves.”
“Whoever is worthy should take her; this is not for me to decide.”
The seven kings argued fiercely among themselves, unable to reach a decision.
That night, King Píngshā (洴沙王) entered through a hidden passage, climbed the tower, and slept with her.
The next morning, as he was about to leave,
Nàinǚ said:
“Great King, you have graciously lowered your majestic dignity to visit me.”
“If I should bear a child, who is of the royal lineage, to whom should it be entrusted?”
The king replied:
“If it is a boy, he returns to me; if it is a girl, she returns to you.”
The king immediately removed the gold ring seal (jīnhuán zhī yìn) from his hand, gave it to Nàinǚ, and said:
“Use this as proof.”
When he came out, he spoke to his ministers:
“I have already obtained Nàinǚ and spent the night with her.”
Píngshā’s soldiers all shouted, “Long live the King!” and said:
“Our King has already obtained Nàinǚ.”
The six [other] kings heard this and each returned to his home.
Nàinǚ gave birth to a boy.
When he was first born, he held a bag of acupuncture needles and medicines (zhēnyàonáng) in his hand.
The Fànzhì said:
“This son of the King, holding medical instruments, must certainly be the King of Physicians (yīwáng).”
His name was Qíyù (祇域). When he reached the age of eight,
he was intelligent, learned, and his writings surpassed his peers.
When playing with neighboring children, he often looked down upon them in his heart.
The children cursed him, saying:
“Son of no father, born of a promiscuous woman! How dare you look down on us?”
Qíyù was stunned and remained silent, unable to reply.
He immediately returned home and asked his mother:
“I see that all these boys are inferior to me.”
“Yet they insult me, saying I am the son of no father.”
“Where is my father now?”
His mother said:
“Your father is King Píngshā.”
Qíyù said:
“King Píngshā is in the kingdom of Luóyuèzhī (羅悅祇 Guó).”
“It is five hundred *lǐ* (里) from here.”
“How did he come to father me?”
He immediately took the ring and traveled to the kingdom of Luóyuèzhī.
He walked straight through the palace gates and went directly before the king.
He performed a ritual greeting to the king, knelt down, and reported:
“I am the prince (wángzǐ), born of Nàinǚ.”
“I am now eight years old and only recently learned that I am of the Great King’s lineage.”
“Therefore, I offer this finger ring seal as proof, having traveled far to return to my home.”
The king saw the inscription on the seal.
Recalling the oath he had sworn long ago, he knew this was his son.
He was deeply moved and compassionate, and he appointed him as the crown prince (tàizǐ).
Two years passed, and King Āshìshì (阿闍世 Wáng) was born.
Qíyù then addressed the king, saying:
“When I was first born, I held a bag of needles and medicine in my hand.”
“I am destined to be the King of Physicians.”
“Although you have made me the crown prince, this is not my desire.”
“The King’s rightful son has just been born.”
“He should inherit the noble succession.”
“I wish to travel and study medicine.”
The king immediately granted his request.
He commanded the kingdom’s chief physicians to teach him everything.
However, Qíyù just enjoyed himself and never formally received instruction.
The various masters admonished him, saying:
“Medical arts are humble and indeed not suitable for the supremely honored Crown Prince to study.”
“However, the Great King’s command cannot be ignored or disregarded.”
“Many months have passed since we received the order.”
“Yet, the Crown Prince has not accepted a single word of instruction.”
“If the King asks us,”
“what shall we reply?”
Qíyù said:
“I was born with the proof of medicine in my hand.”
“Therefore, I informed the Great King that I would abandon honor and luxury to seek medical knowledge; how could I be lazy?”
“It is simply because the methods of the masters here are not worth learning.”
He then took up the classics on herbal medicines (běncǎo), acupuncture methods (zhēnfāng), and pulse diagnosis (mài), and thoroughly questioned the masters.
The masters were unable to answer.
Instead, they bowed to him, saying, “The Crown Prince is divine and sacred, far beyond our reach.”
“We beg the Crown Prince to explain the medical doubts accumulated over the generations.”
He then explained the meanings [of the difficult passages].
The doctors were delighted, paid their respects, and followed his teachings.
Qíyù then proceeded to treat patients.
Everyone he treated was immediately cured, and his fame spread to distant kingdoms.
Returning to the palace gates, he encountered a boy carrying a load of kindling (kěi); Qíyù looked and saw the threads of the boy’s Five Organs (wǔzàng) clearly defined.
Qíyù thought to himself:
“The Běncǎo Scripture says:
‘There is a King of Medicine Tree (Yàowáng Shù) that shines illumination from the outside inwards.’”
“This boy’s bundle of kindling must contain the Yàowáng Shù.”
He immediately asked:
“How much are you selling this bundle for?”
The boy replied, “Ten coins.”
He paid the agreed ten coins.
The boy lowered the bundle of kindling to the ground.
Immediately, it became dark, and Qíyù could no longer see inside the boy’s abdomen.
Qíyù reflected:
“I do not know which piece in the bundle is the Yàowáng wood.”
He then untied the two bundles and placed the pieces one by one on the boy’s abdomen.
Nothing shone through, and he continued this until both bundles of kindling were exhausted.
The last small twig illuminated the boy’s interior.
Qíyù was greatly delighted.
He knew that this small twig was definitely the Yàowáng.
He returned all the kindling to the boy.
The boy happily departed.
At that time, the daughter of a Jiāluōyuè (迦羅越) family in the kingdom, aged fifteen,
suddenly died from a headache just before her wedding day.
Qíyù heard of it, went to her home, and asked:
“What illness did the girl normally have that led to her premature death?”
Her father replied:
“The girl had suffered from headaches since childhood, and they grew worse day by day, becoming fatal this morning.”
Qíyù used the Yàowáng wood to illuminate the girl’s head.
He saw boring worms (yǎnchóng).
Hundreds of them, reproducing continuously, were boring and consuming the brain tissue; since the brain was exhausted, she had died.
He then used a golden scalpel (jīndāo) to cut open her head.
He removed all the worms and sealed them inside a jar.
He applied three kinds of wondrous ointment to the wound.
One kind repaired the damage between the bones eaten by the worms.
One kind regenerated the brain tissue.
One kind healed the external wound caused by the scalpel.
He instructed the girl’s father:
“Ensure she remains completely calm; be extremely careful not to startle her.”
“In seven days, she will recover.”
“I will return on that day.” Just as Qíyù departed,
the girl’s mother began weeping again, saying:
“My daughter will die a second time!”
“How can someone whose head has been split open and whose brain has been dug out possibly come back to life?”
The father stopped her, saying:
“Qíyù was born holding needles and medicine.”
“He abandoned his honored position to become a physician.”
“He protects and cures the lives of all people.”
“This Heavenly King of Physicians (Tiān Yīwáng)—how could he act recklessly?”
“He specifically instructed you to be careful not to startle her.”
“Yet now you weep and cry, frightening her.”
“Do you want to prevent this girl from reviving?”
The mother heard this, stopped crying, and carefully attended to and protected her.
After seven days of silence and stillness,
the girl sighed and awoke, as if waking from sleep.
She said:
“My head no longer hurts at all.”
“My body is completely at ease. Who protected me so that I could become like this?”
The father said:
“You had previously died.”
“The King of Physicians, Qíyù, came specifically to save you.”
“He split open your head and removed the worms so that you could be reborn.”
He then opened the jar, brought out the worms, and showed them to her.
When the girl saw them, she was greatly astonished and amazed.
She considered herself deeply fortunate and said:
“Qíyù is truly divine!”
“How can I repay such kindness?”
A short while later, Qíyù arrived.
The girl was overjoyed.
She went out the door to welcome him, performed a ritual greeting, knelt down, and said:
“I wish to be your maidservant for the rest of my life, thereby repaying the kindness of my rebirth.”
Jìyù said:
I am a physician, traveling everywhere healing illnesses, and having no fixed abode. Why would I need a servant girl?
If you truly wish to repay my kindness, give me five hundred liǎng of gold.
I will not use it myself; I must thank my teacher for his kindness.
Although my teacher had nothing with which to instruct me,
I saw that he still maintained disciples.
Now, upon receiving your gold, I shall give it to them.
The woman then presented five hundred liǎng of gold.
Jìyù received it and gave it to his teacher.
Consequently, he informed the king that he was briefly returning home to visit his mother.
He arrived in the country of Wéiyēlī.
There was the son of a Jiāluóyuè family.
He was fond of learning and made a wooden horse more than seven chǐ high.
He practiced vaulting upon it. At first attempt, he succeeded in mounting the horse.
Afterwards, he lost his footing, fell to the ground, and died.
Jìyù heard of this.
He immediately went and shone his King of Medicine (skill) upon him.
He saw that the liver was twisted backward, and the qì (vital breath) was knotted and obstructed, which was the cause of death.
He again used his gold knife to cut open the abdomen and probed inside with his hand to set things right.
He finished turning the liver back toward the front.
He applied three kinds of wondrous ointment.
One kind restored the area where his hand had protected and held things in place.
One kind smoothed and circulated the breath.
One kind was specifically for closing the knife wound.
He instructed the father, saying:
Be careful not to let him be startled; he will recover in three days.
The father received the instruction and mandate, quietly observing and nursing him for three days.
The boy then breathed out and woke up, just as if waking from sleep.
He immediately rose and sat up.
Soon thereafter, Jìyù came.
The boy came out to greet him and bowed, saying:
I wish to become your slave and serve you for the rest of my life to repay the kindness of saving my life.
Jìyù said:
I am a physician, traveling everywhere healing illnesses.
The families of the sick all compete to work for me. Why would I need a slave?
My mother raised me through diligence and hardship.
I have not yet been able to provide for her.
If you wish to thank me,
give me five hundred liǎng of gold,
to repay my mother’s kindness.
He took the gold and presented it to Nàinǚ.
He then returned to the country of Luóyuèzhī.
Because Jìyù had saved these two people, his name quickly spread throughout the world, and everyone heard of it and knew him.
Furthermore, to the south, there was a great country eight thousand lǐ from Luóyuèzhī.
Píngshā and all the other small countries were its vassals.
Its king had been ill for many years without recovery.
He constantly suffered from rage and anger, glaring sideways and killing people.
If someone raised their eyes to look at him, they were killed.
If someone lowered their head and did not look up, they were also killed.
If he commanded someone to walk slowly, they were killed.
If they walked quickly, they were also killed.
The attendants around him did not know where they should put their hands or feet.
If a physician compounded medicine, the king would immediately suspect it was poisoned and would also kill them.
The number of ministers, palace women, and physicians killed before and after could not be counted.
The illness only increased daily. The poisonous qì attacked his heart.
He felt agitated and bloated, his breath was short, and his body felt like it was burning in fire.
Upon hearing Jìyù's name, he immediately issued a document
mandating King Píngshā to summon Jìyù.
Jìyù, hearing that this king had killed many physicians, was extremely frightened.
Píngshā also pitied him for his youth and feared he would be killed.
Although he wanted not to send him, he feared punitive execution.
The father and son stayed together, worrying day and night.
They finally took Jìyù and went together to ask the Fó.
The Fó instructed Jìyù:
In your past life, you and I made a vow that we would both save and protect the illnesses of the people of the world.
I treat internal illnesses, and you treat external illnesses.
Now I have attained Buddhahood (Fó), and in accordance with your original vow, you have coincidentally been born before me.
This king is severely ill and has sent a long way to welcome you. How can you not go?
Hasten to go and protect him.
Find ways and means to ensure his illness is certainly cured.
He will not kill you.
Jìyù then relied upon the awesome spiritual power of the Fó.
He went to the king's location.
He examined and investigated the pulse theory,
and illuminated the king with his King of Medicine skill.
He saw that within the king's five viscera and hundreds of vessels,
the blood and qì were violently agitated, and he clearly saw
that it was the poison of a snake or scorpion covering the entire body.
Jìyù reported to the king:
Your Majesty's illness can be treated.
If treated, recovery is assured.
However, it is necessary to meet with the Grand Queen (Tàihòu) to consult about compounding the medicine.
If I do not meet the Grand Queen (Tàihòu), the medicine will ultimately not be successful.
The king heard these words and did not understand the reason.
He was very inclined to become angry.
However, he suffered from his bodily illness.
Having previously heard Jìyù's name, he had welcomed him from afar.
Hoping there would surely be a benefit, and moreover, seeing that the young boy seemed to have no deceitful private agenda, he endured and agreed.
He immediately sent blue-robed eunuchs to lead him in to see the Grand Queen (Tàihòu).
Jìyù reported to the Grand Queen (Tàihòu):
Your Majesty's illness can be treated, and I must now compound the medicine.
It is appropriate to secretly reveal the prescription; it must not be publicly disclosed.
I request that the attendants be dismissed.
The Grand Queen (Tàihòu) immediately complied and sent the blue-robed eunuchs out.
Jìyù then asked the Grand Queen (Tàihòu):
Just now, when I examined the king's illness,
I saw that the blood vessels within the king’s body were entirely filled with the poison of a snake or scorpion, seeming not to be of human kind.
Whose son, exactly, is the king?
If the Grand Queen (Tàihòu) tells me the truth,
I can treat him.
If you do not tell me,
I will not know how to treat him.
The Grand Queen (Tàihòu) said:
Formerly, I was once lying down during the day in the Hall of Golden Pillars.
Suddenly, something came and rubbed itself upon me.
At that time, I was in a daze, and in a dream I interacted intimately with it.
I suddenly woke up.
I saw a huge scorpion, more than thirty zhàng long, crawling away from me, and immediately felt I was pregnant.
The king is truly the son of this scorpion.
Out of shame, I have never spoken of this.
That the young man can now perceive this—how wondrous and divine!
If the illness can be treated,
I wish to entrust the king's life to the young man.
Now, what medicine should be used to treat him?
Jìyù said:
Only clarified butter (tíhú) is needed.
The Grand Queen (Tàihòu) said:
Hey, young man, be very careful not to say that!
This king intensely hates smelling the scent of clarified butter (tíhú).
He also hates hearing its name.
Thousands of people have previously died merely for mentioning clarified butter (tíhú) out loud.
If you mention it now, he will certainly kill you.
If you try to make the king drink this, he will never swallow it.
Please use another medicine instead.
Jìyù said:
Clarified butter (tíhú) treats poison sickness.
That he hates hearing the name clarified butter (tíhú) is precisely why (it is the cure).
If the king's illness were minor, or if it were another type of poison, there would be other medicines that could cure it.
Since the scorpion poison is severe,
and has already covered the whole body,
if it is not clarified butter (tíhú), it can ultimately not be dissolved.
I must now boil and extract its essence, transforming it into water.
He then went out and saw the king, saying:
I just went in and saw the Grand Queen (Tàihòu).
I have already presented the prescription, and I must now compound the medicine.
It will be completed in fifteen days.
Now I have five requests.
If Your Majesty grants them, the illness can be cured immediately.
If you do not grant them, the illness cannot be cured.
The king asked: What are these five requests?
Jìyù said:
First, I request to wear new clothes from the king's treasury box that have never touched a body.
Second, I request permission to enter and exit the palace gates alone without being prohibited or challenged.
Third, I request permission to enter and see the Grand Queen (Tàihòu) and the Queen (Wánghòu) alone every day, without prohibition or challenge.
Fourth, I request that when the king drinks the medicine, he must swallow it all in one gulp, without stopping midway.
Fifth, I request to ride the king’s eight-thousand-lǐ white elephant.
The king heard this and became greatly enraged, saying:
Young man, how dare you request these five things?
Begin by explaining them!
If you cannot explain, I will beat you to death now.
Jìyù said:
When compounding medicine, one must be pure, clean, and observe the fast.
But I have traveled for many days,
and my clothes are covered in dust and dirt. Therefore, I wish to wear the king's clothing when compounding the medicine.
Furthermore, all the physicians the king employed before and after were suspected and distrusted, and none were treated with confidence or caution.
Moreover, after they were executed, their medicine was not taken.
All the ministers, great and small, say that the king will kill me again.
But the king's illness is already severe.
I fear that outsiders might become suspicious and cause disturbance.
If you allow me to enter and exit freely without being prohibited or challenged,
then all outsiders, great and small, will know that the king trusts me without doubt.
He will surely take my medicine, and the illness will surely be cured.
Then they will not dare to harbor rebellious and disruptive thoughts.
Furthermore, it is said that the king has killed many people before and after.
All the subordinates, great and small, harbor fear.
None of them desire the king’s peace and stability.
There is no one who can be trusted.
Now, when compounding the medicine together,
I fear that in the instant I turn my head away,
they might throw poison into the medicine.
If I do not notice it, that would not be a minor matter. I reflected:
Those who can be trusted in the world, whose kindness and affection are inexhaustible,
are only the mother and the wife.
Therefore, I wished to go in and see the Grand Queen (Tàihòu) to compound the medicine with her, which must be decocted.
Since it takes fifteen days to complete, I request to enter daily to monitor the timing of the heat.
Furthermore, medicine has fixed proportions; the qì (essence) and flavor should be kept continuous.
If there is a stop in the middle, the qì will not be connected.
Moreover, there are marvelous medicinal herbs in the Southern Mountains,
four thousand lǐ from here.
When the king takes the medicine, he should immediately obtain these herbs
and take them again. Therefore, I want to ride this elephant to go and gather them.
Going in the morning and returning in the evening will ensure the medicinal properties are continuous.
The king’s anger greatly subsided.
He granted all the requests entirely.
Thereupon, Jìyù boiled and extracted the clarified butter (tíhú). After fifteen days, it was completed, transformed into clear water.
He obtained five shēng in total, and presented it to the Grand Queen (Tàihòu) and the Queen (Wánghòu).
They both came out to present the medicine and reported that it could be administered.
He requested that the white elephant be covered (saddled) and placed in front of the palace hall.
The king immediately granted this.
The king saw the medicine was only like clear water, and he drank it all in one draft.
Jìyù then rode the elephant and immediately departed, heading toward his native country’s road.
After traveling just three thousand lǐ, being young and frail and unable to endure the rapid pace, he became dizzy and utterly exhausted, and lay down to rest in the mountains.
After noon, the king belched, emitting the scent of clarified butter (tíhú).
Angrily, he said:
That young boy dared to poison me with clarified butter (tíhú)!
No wonder that young boy asked for my white elephant.
He simply wanted to escape and flee!
The king had a brave warrior
named Wū,
who could travel with divine speed.
Immediately, he commanded [his servants] to pursue and bring the child back.
I will beat him to death right before my eyes.
Wū (Wū) caught up to him and said:
Why did you give fresh cream (tíhú) to the King
and yet claim it was medicine? The King has ordered me to pursue and call you back.
You must hurry back with me, confess and apologize; perhaps you can hope to live.
If you insist on running away now, I will certainly kill you, and you will never escape.
Qíyù (Qíyù) thought to himself: Although I have cleverly used strategies (fāngbiàn) to obtain this white elephant,
I still cannot escape.
Now I must use another strategy (fāngbiàn); how can I just go back with him?
He then spoke to Wū (Wū), saying:
I have not eaten since this morning, and if I return, I will surely die.
Could you perhaps grant me a moment in the mountains
to eat some fruit and drink some water before I resign myself to death?
Wū (Wū) saw that Qíyù (Qíyù), being a young boy, was terrified of death and spoke mournfully.
Pitying him, he consented, saying:
Eat quickly and then we must leave; you may not remain long.
Qíyù (Qíyù) then took one pear and ate half of it.
He placed poison under his fingernail and used it to taint the remaining half, which he then set on the ground.
He also took a cup of water and first drank half of it.
He then applied the poison under his nail to the remaining water and also set that on the ground.
Then he sighed, saying:
This water and this pear are both divine medicines.
They are pure, fragrant, and delicious.
Whoever consumes them will be at ease.
All hundred diseases will be cured, and one's strength will be doubled.
It is a pity that they are not within the capital city,
so that the common people could all share them.
Since they are deep in the mountains, no one knows about them.
He then entered the mountains to search for other fruits.
Wū (Wū), whose nature was greedy, could not resist the food and drink.
Moreover, hearing Qíyù (Qíyù) praise them as divine medicine,
and also seeing that Qíyù (Qíyù) had already eaten and drunk,
he assumed there was certainly no poison.
He immediately ate the remaining pear and drank the remaining water.
He was instantly seized by diarrhea.
The flux was like pouring water.
He fell down and lay on the ground.
Whenever he tried to stand, he became dizzy and collapsed.
He could no longer move.
Qíyù (Qíyù) went over and spoke to him, saying:
The King took my medicine and his illness will surely be cured.
However, currently, the medicine's power has not yet circulated, and the remaining poison has not been fully expelled.
If I go now, he will certainly kill me.
You knew nothing,
and merely wanted to capture me to fulfill your duty, thus causing your illness.
The illness itself is not severe; be careful not to move or shake; you will recover in three days.
If you try to stand up and pursue me, I will certainly die, without a doubt.
He then mounted the elephant and left.
Passing a village elder (Wǔzhǎng) of a settlement (xūjù), he said:
This man is an envoy of a great king.
He has suddenly fallen ill.
You must quickly go and carry him back
and take good care of him at home.
Provide thick bedding and soft gruel (mǐzhōu). Be careful not to let him die.
If you allow him to die, the King will destroy your country.
Having finished speaking, he departed and returned to his native country.
The Wǔzhǎng (Wǔzhǎng) received the order.
They welcomed and cared for [Wū (Wū)]; after three days, the poison subsided.
He was able to walk and returned.
Seeing the King, he kowtowed and stated:
I am truly foolish and violated Your Majesty’s command.
I trusted Qíyù’s (Qíyù) words and consumed
the remaining fruit and water.
I was struck by the medicine and suffered diarrhea for three days; only now am I recovering, but I know I deserve death.
During the three days before Wū (Wū) returned, the King’s illness was already cured.
He regretted sending Wū (Wū) out.
Seeing Wū (Wū) return,
he was both happy and sorrowful, saying:
I am relieved you did not bring the boy immediately.
When I was angry, I certainly would have beaten him to death.
I received his kindness and now have life.
To kill him in return would be utterly perverse and unthinkable.
All those whom he had previously unjustly killed were given a proper, elaborate burial.
Their family lines were restored, and they were granted money and property.
He longed to see Qíyù (Qíyù) to repay his kindness.
He immediately sent an envoy to respectfully welcome Qíyù (Qíyù).
Although Qíyù (Qíyù) knew the King's illness was
cured, he still harbored fear and did not want to go back.
The Buddha (Fó) informed Qíyù (Qíyù):
In your past lives, you have already made great vows and achieved merit (gōngdé).
Why should you stop? You ought to go again.
You have treated his external illness, and I shall also treat his internal illness.
Qíyù (Qíyù) then followed the envoy.
The King was greatly overjoyed to see Qíyù (Qíyù).
He invited him to sit with him, held his arm, and said:
Relying on the kindness of you, benevolent one (rénzhě), I have now been reborn.
How should I repay you? I should divide the territory and give you half.
Half of the palace maidens (cǎinǚ), treasuries, and precious objects shall also be divided and given to you.
Qíyù (Qíyù) said:
I was originally a Crown Prince (Tàizǐ).
Although my country is small, it still has people.
It is fully stocked with treasures.
I do not enjoy ruling a country, which is why I sought to be a physician, traveling to treat illnesses.
What use would I have for territory, palace maidens, or treasures? They are all useless to me.
Your Majesty previously listened to my five wishes,
and your external illness was cured.
Now, if you listen to one more wish of mine,
your internal illness will also be removed.
The King said:
I obey only the instructions of the benevolent one.
Please ask for it.
Qíyù (Qíyù) said:
I wish Your Majesty would invite the Buddha (Fó) and receive the bright Dharma (míngfǎ) from him.
[Qíyù (Qíyù)] spoke to the King about the Buddha’s (Fó) merit (gōngdé).
The King heard this and was greatly pleased, saying:
Now I wish to send the minister Wū (Wū) with a white elephant to welcome the Buddha (Fó); can this be done?
Qíyù (Qíyù) said:
A white elephant is not necessary.
The Buddha (Fó) knows your thoughts from afar.

Just observe ritual fasting (zhāijiè) and purification, prepare all the offerings, burn incense, perform a distant prostration (yáolǐ), and kneel long (chángguì) to invite the Buddha (Fó); the Buddha (Fó) will surely come himself.
The King followed his words.
