The Buddha (Fó) came together with twelve hundred and fifty bhikṣus (bǐqiū). After the meal was finished,
[the Buddha (Fó)] preached the Sūtra (jīng) to the King.
The King immediately attained enlightenment and generated the mind of unsurpassed awakening (wúshàng dàoxīn).
Everyone in the country, great and small, observed the Five Precepts (wǔjiè).
When Nàinǚ (Nàinǚ) was born, there were already strange and unusual signs.
As she grew, she was intelligent and studied under her father.
She widely understood the Sūtra teachings (jīngdào), astronomy (xīnglì), and various arts, surpassing her father.
Moreover, she mastered music, and her voice was like that of Brahmā-deva (Fàntiān).
Five hundred women, combining those from Kālāvati (Jiāluóyuè) and Brahmin (Fànzhì) families, all went to study under her, taking her as their great teacher (dàshī).
Nàinǚ (Nàinǚ) often led her five hundred disciples in teaching Sūtras and arts.
Sometimes they played together in gardens and pools, or created music.
The people of the country did not understand the reason,
so they started slandering her, calling her an adulteress (yínnǚ).
The five hundred disciples were all labeled the "Adulterous Faction" (yíndǎng).
When Nàinǚ (Nàinǚ) was born,
there were also two other girls born in the country at the same time:
one was Sūmànnǚ (Xūmànnǚ),
and the second was Pōtánnǚ (Pōtánnǚ).
Sūmànnǚ (Xūmànnǚ) was born in a Kālāvati (Jiāluóyuè) family that often pressed [oil].
Sūmàn (xūmàn) was used to make fragrant ointment.
Beside the stone used for pressing the ointment, a nodule suddenly formed,
as large as a pellet,
and as long as a hand scroll.
The stone then burst open.
Inside the stone's knot, a glow like a firefly was seen.
It shot out and fell to the ground, and three days later, Sūmàn (xūmàn) grew.
Three more days later, it bloomed into a flower (huā).
Inside was a small girl.
The Kālāvati (Jiāluóyuè) took her and raised her,
naming her Sūmànnǚ (Xūmànnǚ).
When she grew up, her talent, brilliance, and wisdom were second only to Nàinǚ (Nàinǚ).
Pōtánnǚ (Pōtánnǚ) came from a Brahmin (Fànzhì) family.
Inside their bathing pond, a blue lotus (qīng liánhuā) grew.
Day by day it grew as large as a five-pint jar.
When the flower opened, a small girl was seen inside.
The Brahmin (Fànzhì) raised her and named her Pōtánnǚ (Pōtánnǚ).
When she grew up, her talent, wisdom, brilliance, and understanding were equal to Sūmànnǚ (Xūmànnǚ).
Kings from various countries heard that the beauty of these two girls surpassed the world,
and they came one after another to seek marriage.
The two girls said:
We were not born through the womb
but emerged from grass and flowers (cǎohuā).
We are different from ordinary people.
How could we properly follow common custom and marry?
Having heard that Nàinǚ (Nàinǚ) was wise and without equal in the world,
and that her birth was also of the same nature as ours,
they both bade farewell to their parents and went to serve Nàinǚ (Nàinǚ), asking to become her disciples.
Their brilliance, wisdom, learning, and understanding surpassed all five hundred people.
At that time, the Buddha (Fó) arrived at the country of Wéiyēlì Guó.
Nàinǚ (Nàinǚ) and her disciples went out of the city to respectfully welcome and prostrate before the Buddha (Fó). Kneeling, she said:
We wish the Buddha (Fó) to eat in my garden tomorrow.
The Buddha (Fó) silently accepted.
The King came out of the palace to welcome [the Buddha (Fó)].
He also requested that [the Buddha (Fó)] eat in the palace the next day.
The Buddha (Fó) said:
Nàinǚ (Nàinǚ) invited me first; the King is second.
The King said:
I am the ruler of the country, and I sincerely invite the Buddha (Fó); I surely hope for compassionate permission.
Nàinǚ (Nàinǚ) is merely an adulteress (yínnǚ).
Every day she leads five hundred disciples to behave improperly.
Why would the Buddha (Fó) abandon me and accept her invitation?
The Buddha (Fó) said:
This woman is not an adulteress.
In her past lives, she possessed great merit (gōngdé) and has already made offerings to three hundred million Buddhas (Fó).
In the past, she was constantly sisters with Sūmàn (Xūmàn) and Pōtán (Pōtán).
Nàinǚ (Nàinǚ) was the eldest, Sūmàn (Xūmàn) was next,
and Pōtán (Pōtán) was the youngest. They were born into a family of great lineage.
They were rich in wealth and treasures. The sisters, guided by a teacher, jointly made offerings to five hundred Bhikṣuṇīs (Bǐqiūní).
They provided food, drink, and made clothing, supplying everything lacking throughout their entire lives.
The three people swore an oath:
We vow that in our next life, we will encounter a Buddha (Fó) and be born spontaneously through transformation (huàshēng).
We will not be born through the womb, thus remaining far from impurity and defilement (huìzhuó).
Now, according to their original vow, they have been born and have encountered me.
Although they formerly made offerings to five hundred Bhikṣuṇīs (Bǐqiūní),
because they were born into great wealth, their speech was arrogant and unrestrained.
At that time, they jested with the nuns (ní), saying:
All you practitioners have been secluded and repressed for a long time; surely you must wish to marry.
It is only because we pressure you with offerings that you cannot follow your desires.
Therefore, now they receive this remaining negative karma (yúyāng).
Although they lecture on the Sūtra teachings (jīngdào), they are falsely slandered as adulteresses.
These five hundred disciples, at that time, united their efforts and shared the same mind, and in this life, they are again able to follow them.
Qíyù (Qíyù) was at that time a poor family's small boy. Nàinǚ (Nàinǚ) saw his intent to make offerings, and he greatly longed to do so, but he lacked resources.
So he often swept and cleaned for the Bhikṣuṇīs (Bǐqiūní).
He would frequently think:
I vow that I may be able to cure the illnesses of all people under heaven.
Nàinǚ (Nàinǚ) pitied his poverty
and praised his diligence, often calling him 'son'.
When those Bhikṣuṇīs (Bǐqiūní) were sick...
Qíyù to fetch doctors and prepare medicinal decoctions.
All said:
"May you in future lives together with us obtain this blessing." All those treated by the doctors Qíyù fetched
were completely cured.
Then he made a vow, saying:
"May I in my future life be a great Physician King, always treating the diseases of the Four Great Elements in all human bodies, and wherever I turn, all are cured." The King,
hearing the words of the Fó,
then repented his faults.
He postponed the meeting until a subsequent day.
The Fó the next day went with all the Bhikṣus to Nàinǚ Yuán.
He fully explained to them the merit of the fundamental vow.
The three women, hearing the scripture, all attained enlightenment.
And the five hundred disciples all attained the path of Āluóhàn.
Śākyà Wénní Fó in his previous body acted as a great king of medicine.
He cured all illnesses.
He did not seek fame or profit, but solely pitied and commiserated with living beings.
There were exceedingly many sick people, and his strength was insufficient to save them all.
He worried about and thought of everyone, but could not satisfy his heart's desire.
Filled with regret and vexation, he died and was immediately born in the Dāolì Heaven.
He pondered to himself, saying:
"Now that I am born in Heaven, I merely consume the reward of merit, gaining no lasting benefit."
He immediately devised a skillful means to terminate this body [of a Deva].
He abandoned this heavenly life span.
He was born in the palace of the Pójiātuó Dragon King.
He became the Dragon Crown Prince.
His body grew large, and his parents loved and treasured him greatly.
Desiring to willingly court death, he approached the Jīnchì Bird King (Garuda King).
The bird immediately seized this Dragon Son and swallowed him upon the Shěmólì Tree.
His parents wept loudly, crying and filled with grief.
After the Dragon Son died, he was born in the middle of Yánfú Tí (Jambudvīpa).
He became the Crown Prince of a great kingdom.
His name was Néng Shī.
He was able to speak immediately upon birth.
He asked those around him:
"What kind of things are there in this country now?
Bring them all so I may use them for bùshī (giving/charity)."
The people, finding this strange and frightening, all abandoned him and fled.
His mother, out of affection, guarded him alone.
He said to his mother:
"I am not a luóchà (rākṣasa/demon); why do the people flee?
In my previous lives, I always delighted in bùshī.
I am the tányuè (patron/donor) of all people."
The mother heard his words and relayed them to the crowd.
The people then returned.
The mother raised him well, and when he grew up, he exhausted all his own possessions.
He went to his Father King and asked for things to give away.
His father gave him an allowance, and he exhausted that too in giving.
Seeing the people of Yánfú Tí poor, struggling, and suffering, he desired to provide and give to them.
But because his wealth and resources were insufficient, he began to weep.
He asked the people:
"What skillful means should I employ so that everyone may be satisfied with wealth?"
The elderly people replied:
"We have heard before
that there is a Rúyì Bǎozhū (Wish-Fulfilling Pearl).
If one obtains this pearl, then whatever one wishes for in their heart, they will certainly receive."
He informed his parents that he wished to enter the Great Sea to seek the Rúyì Bǎozhū from the Dragon King's head.
His parents replied, saying:
"We have only you, one son.
If you enter the Great Sea, there are many dangers difficult to traverse.
If we suddenly lose you, what purpose will our lives serve?
In our current storehouses, we still have resources that we should give you."
The son said:
"What is in the storehouses is limited, but my intention is boundless.
I want to fully satisfy everyone so that there is no scarcity or lack.
I pray that you grant me permission so I may fulfill my original intention,
allowing the people of Yánfú Tí to be completely satisfied."
The parents knew his ambition was great and dared not restrain him, so they let him go.
At that time, five hundred merchants were all happy to follow him.
Knowing the day of his departure, they gathered at the entrance to the sea route.
The Crown Prince asked the crowd, saying:
"Who knows the way to reach that Dragon Palace?"
There was a blind man named Tuóshě.
He had previously entered the Great Sea seven times and thoroughly knew the sea route.
The Púsà (Bodhisattva) immediately ordered him to travel together.
He replied, saying:
"Since I am already old and both my eyes are blind,
although I have entered [the sea] many times, I cannot go now."
The Púsà said:
"This journey I undertake now is not for myself.
It is universally for all [beings] that I seek the Rúyì Bǎozhū.
I wish to provide sufficiently for living beings so their bodies suffer no lack.
Furthermore, I will instruct and convert them through the reasons and conditions of the Dharma Path.
You are a wise man; how can you refuse?
If my wish is achieved, will it not be due to your strength?"
Tuóshě bowed deeply and replied, saying:
"If I enter the sea now, my life will certainly not remain safe.
Place my remains upon the Golden Sand Island.
The boat will depart as if flying.
When you reach the Island of Many Treasures,
the many merchants will scramble to load up enough treasures.
They will ask the Crown Prince:
'Why do you not take anything?'
You should answer:
'What I seek is the Rúyì Bǎozhū.
These are perishable objects; I do not need them.
You all must know contentment and know moderation. Do not overload the boat and fail to escape [danger]."
At that time, the many merchants addressed the Púsà, saying:
"Great Virtuous One, please recite an incantation and make a vow so that we may obtain peace and safety."
Thereupon, they took their leave and departed.
Tuóshě then said to the Púsà:
"Set aside a separate small boat and follow a separate path.
Wait for the wind for seven days, reach the south coast of the sea, and you will arrive at a dangerous spot.
There will be sheer cliffs and jujube tree branches covering the water.
A great wind will blow the boat, and the boat will be destroyed.
You must reach up and grasp a jujube branch; this way you can save yourself.
My body is sightless; I shall die here.
Past this narrow shore, there will be a Golden Sand Island.
You can place my body on that sand.
Pure golden sand is my wish."
It was immediately as he said; the wind came, and they departed.
When they reached the sheer cliff, it was just as Tuóshě had said.
The Púsà reached up and grasped a jujube branch, thereby saving himself.
He placed Tuóshě's corpse and laid it to rest upon the golden ground.
Thereupon, he went on alone.
Following the instructions given previously:
He floated in deep water for seven days.
He walked in water up to his throat for seven days.
He walked in water up to his waist for seven days.
He walked through mud for seven days.
He saw beautiful lotus flowers, fresh, pure, and soft.
He pondered to himself, saying:
"These flowers are soft and fragile; I should enter the Xūkōng Sānmèi (Void Samādhi)."
He made his body light and walked upon the lotus flowers for seven days. Then he saw many venomous snakes.
He thought:
"Creatures bearing poison are extremely fearsome."
He immediately entered the Cíxīn Sānmèi (Loving-Kindness Samādhi).
He walked upon the heads of the venomous snakes for seven days.
The snakes all lifted their heads and presented them to the Púsà, allowing him to step over and pass.
After passing this difficulty,
he saw seven layers of treasure cities and seven layers of moats.
The moats were all filled with venomous snakes.
There were two great dragons guarding the gate.
The dragons saw the Púsà's appearance, which was handsome, adorned with auspicious marks, majestic in deportment, and capable of overcoming many difficulties to reach this place.
They thought:
"This is no ordinary mortal.
He must be a Púsà, a person of great merit."
They immediately allowed him to advance and directly enter the palace.
The Dragon King and his wife had not long lost their son and were still weeping mournfully.
Seeing the Púsà approach, the dragon possessed spiritual insight and knew this was their son.
Milk flowed from both her breasts.
She bade him sit down.
And asked him, saying:
"You are my son.
When you abandoned me and died, where were you born?"
The Púsà also recognized his past lives and knew these were his parents.
He answered his mother, saying:
"I was born upon Yánfú Tí.
I became the Crown Prince of a great kingdom.
Out of pity for the poor people who suffer from hunger, cold, and toil, and who lack freedom, I have come here.
I wish to seek the Rúyì Bǎozhū."
The mother said:
"This precious pearl is on your father's head as an ornament, and it is difficult to obtain.
He will surely take you into various treasure hoards, and whatever you desire, he will certainly want to give you.
You must reply, saying:
'I do not need the other miscellaneous treasures.
I only wish to obtain the precious pearl from the Great King's head.
If you pity me, I pray that you give it to me.'
In this way, you can obtain it."
He immediately went to see his father.
The father was greatly compassionate and rejoiced immeasurably.
He pitied his son for traveling far and encountering hardships to reach this place.
He pointed out wonderful treasures, saying, "I will give them to you according to your wish; take whatever you need."
The Púsà said:
"I have come from afar, hoping to see the Great King and request the Rúyì Bǎozhū from the King's head.
If you pity me, you should give it to me.
If you do not give it, I do not need the other objects."
The Dragon King replied, saying:
"I have only this one pearl, which constantly serves as my head ornament.
The people of Yánfú Tí have shallow merit and are base and humble; they should not see it."
The Púsà pleaded, saying:
"It is for this very reason that I have traveled far, crossed difficulties, risked death, and come from afar.
It is for the people of Yánfú Tí who are shallow in merit, poor, and humble,
that I wish to use the Rúyì Bǎozhū to satisfy their needs.
Afterwards, I will instruct and convert them through the reasons and conditions of the Buddha Path."
The Dragon King gave him the pearl but stipulated, saying:
"I give this pearl to you now.
When you pass away, you must return it to me."
[The Púsà] replied:
"I shall respectfully follow the King's instructions."
The Púsà obtained the pearl.
He flew up into the void, arriving at Yánfú Tí in the time it takes to flex and extend an arm.
The Human King and Queen saw their son return safely.
Joyful and excited, they embraced him and asked, saying:
"What did you obtain?"
He answered, saying:
"I obtained the Rúyì Bǎozhū."
They asked:
"Where is it now?"
He replied:
"It is inside the corner of this garment."
His parents said:
"Why is it so small?"
He replied:
"Its divine efficacy matters, not its size."
He informed his parents, saying:
"You should command that inside and outside the city be swept and purified, incense be burned, silk banners and canopies be hung, and that [people] maintain fasting and observe the precepts.
Tomorrow morning, use a tall wooden pole as a standard and place the pearl on top of it."
The Púsà then established a vow:
"If I am destined to achieve the path of Buddhahood and deliver all beings,
may the pearl, according to my wish, produce all kinds of treasures,
so that whatever people require is fully provided."
At that time, dark clouds spread everywhere and rained down various treasures, clothing, food, bedding, bath materials, and medicine.
Whatever people spoke of needing was entirely provided.
This continued perpetually and without interruption until the end of their lives.
Such [actions] are called the Púsà's practice of bùshī (giving) generating jīngjìn bōluómì (Vīrya Pāramitā, the perfection of vigor).
In the past, in Yánfútí,
at one time there were two kings.
The King of Lìshībá Guó was named Yuè.
The King of Bōluónài Guó was named Yuègài.
They were agreeable in their interactions and held no grudges or enmity.
They jointly established a pact:
If sons were born, they would establish an excellent marital relationship between the two families.
King Yuègài had neither sons nor daughters.
Wishing to seek a son,
he offered sacrifices to the Water God and various other spirits and deities.
By the Xiūluózhà Hé were two divine Immortals possessing the Five Supernatural Powers (Wǔtōng Shénxiān).
The River God informed the King:
“If the two Immortals wish to be born into the royal house, the King will certainly have sons.”
The King went to the place of the Immortals and said,
“If you are born into my house, you will indulge in the five desires, enjoying endless happiness.”
The Immortals replied,
“It shall be so.”
Seven days later, one of the Immortals died and immediately entered the womb of the First Queen.
After another seven days, the other Immortal also died,
and took residence in the womb of the Second Queen.
When the First Queen completed nine months,
she bore a son whose appearance was handsome and upright.
On the day he was born, five hundred merchants returned from the sea.
Five hundred hidden treasures unexpectedly revealed themselves.
Five hundred death row inmates were released from prison.
When the Second Queen gave birth,
there were many strange occurrences: jackals howled,
Asuras seized the sun,
and five hundred people who were supposed to die went and died naturally. The King was extremely pleased.
He immediately summoned the physiognomists to predict their fortune and assign names.
The physiognomists asked,
“What auspicious signs were there when these children were born?”
He replied,
“The mother of the First Prince had always been rude, jealous, arrogant, and self-important.
Since she conceived the child, her temperament has become gentle, her countenance soft, her words pleasing, and she is compassionate toward all beings.”
The physiognomists replied,
“This is caused by the meritorious virtue of the child.”
He shall be named Shànyǒu (Good Friend).
Regarding the son born to the Second Queen, they asked about the auspicious signs.
He replied,
“His mother had always been gentle, and her words pleased everyone’s heart.
Since becoming pregnant, her temperament has become suddenly violent and her speech crude and malicious.”
The physiognomists replied,
“It is the karma of this child that causes the mother to be this way.”
He shall be named Èyǒu (Bad Friend). When they reached the age of fourteen,
Prince Shànyǒu was intelligent, benevolent, compassionate, and loved giving charity.
His parents favored him, valuing him as their own eyes.
Èyǒu was violent and malicious, hated by his parents, who did not enjoy seeing him.
He was jealous of his elder brother and constantly wished to destroy and harm him.
In every matter, he was disobedient, contrary, rebellious, and perverse.
The Prince, escorted by attendants, preceded and followed by singers and musicians,
was surrounded by a crowd as he went out of the city to observe.
He saw a farmer cultivating the earth, and worms were brought up, which birds followed and pecked to eat. He felt pity and sorrow for them.
He asked his attendants,
“What are they doing, mutually harming one another?”
They replied,
“The kingdom relies on the people; the people rely on food and drink; food relies on cultivation and planting.”
The Prince said,
“How miserable! How miserable!”
Going further, he again saw men and women spinning and weaving.
He asked again,
“What are they doing?”
They replied,
“They spin and weave to make various clothes, to cover shame and protect the five parts of the body.”
The Prince said,
“This labor and toil is also not insignificant.”
Moving further forward, he saw people butchering oxen and skinning sheep.
He asked again,
“And what is this?”
They replied,
“They slaughter and sell meat to supply clothing and food.”
The Prince said,
“Strange and miserable!
The strong harm the weak, accumulating calamities for countless kalpas.”
Moving further forward, he saw people netting birds and baiting fish.
He asked again.
They answered again,
“They set nets for birds and catch fish.”
Tears of sorrow filled the Prince’s eyes.
“Sentient beings in the world create the roots of all evil, and their suffering never ceases.” Filled with anxiety and displeasure, he immediately turned his carriage and returned to the palace.
The King asked,
“Why are you sorrowful?”
The Prince answered fully with the above information.
The King said,
“These things have always existed; why should they be cause for sorrow?”
The Prince said,
“I now wish to ask one request from the King:
I wish to obtain the national treasury’s wealth and use it to give charity to all.”
The King said, “Do as you wish.”
The Prince immediately ordered his attending ministers to open the royal treasury.
Using five hundred great elephants, they loaded up the precious treasures and exited the four city gates.
He proclaimed throughout the land that anyone who had needs could freely take whatever they desired.
The renown of Prince Shànyǒu reached the eight directions, and everyone gathered.
In a short time, one-third of the treasury was used up.
The treasury official reported to the King,
“Your Majesty should reconsider.”
The King said,
“I do not wish to thwart him.”
After a short time passed again,
the officials consulted together,
“The state relies on the treasury; if the treasury is depleted, the state will also be empty.”
They went again to inform the King,
“Two-thirds of the total wealth has been used up.
Your Majesty should deeply consider this.”
The King said,
“I do not wish to thwart him.
You should delay slightly and not allow him to fulfill his wishes completely.”
The Prince wished to open the treasury.
At that time, the treasury official happened to be absent due to travel.
The Prince repeatedly tried to pursue him, but they missed each other and he failed to achieve his goal.
The Prince said,
“How dare a mere official disobey my intention?
This must be the instruction of my royal father!
A filial son should not completely empty his parents’ treasury.
I should now seek wealth myself to satisfy sentient beings.
I if I cannot sufficiently provide clothing, food, and drink to all sentient beings exactly as they wish,
how can I be called a Great Prince?”
The Prince immediately gathered all the officials and magistrates and consulted with them, saying,
“Among the endeavors to seek wealth and profit, which undertaking is the most excellent?”
Some said cultivation; others said animal husbandry.
One great minister said,
“Among seeking profit in the world, nothing surpasses going to sea to gather marvelous treasures.
If one obtains a wish-fulfilling jewel (Maṇi jewel), one will be able to satisfy the needs of all sentient beings as desired.”
The Prince said,
“Indeed.” He then informed the King.
When the King heard this, he choked and could not speak.
Later, he said to the Prince,
“The kingdom is yours.
The treasury’s precious jewels can be taken and used as you wish. Why go to sea?
You are my son, raised in the deep palace.
When you sleep, it is under fine curtains; when you eat, it is to satisfy your palate.
Now, traveling far on dangerous roads, who will know your hunger, thirst, cold, or heat?
In the great ocean, there are countless dangers:
there might be evil spirits, poisonous dragons, fierce winds, great waves, mountains the color of water, and Makara great fish.
Of the thousands who go, only one or two reach their destination.
How is it that you now wish to enter the great ocean?”
The Prince immediately prostrated with his five limbs touching the ground, spreading his hands and feet, and made this declaration:
“If my parents do not permit this, I will sacrifice my life and never rise again.”
The King and the Queen stepped forward to remonstrate, but the Prince refused all food and drink until the sixth day.
The parents were anxious and fearful that he would not survive.
On the seventh day, they took his hand and gently coaxed him.
The Prince said,
“If my parents do not consent, I shall surely perish here.”
The First Queen said to the King,
“The resolve of our son is difficult to shake and must not be disregarded.
How can we bear to see our son sacrifice his life here?
I beg Your Majesty to show compassion and permit him to enter the great ocean.
In doing so, there is still one chance in ten thousand of success.
If we do not consent now, he will certainly perish here.”
The King then granted permission.
The Prince rejoiced and bowed his head to the King.
The Great King proclaimed an order: “Who wishes to enter the sea?”
When the crowd heard this, they happily gathered.
Five hundred of these people all said,
“Great King, we shall now follow the Prince.”
There was a sea master who had entered the great ocean several times before,
and was skilled at knowing the characteristics of the open and blocked parts of the route,
but he was eighty years old and both eyes were dim and blind.
The King spoke to the guide,
“I have only this one son, who has never left the gates before.
I ask the esteemed Master to exert yourself and accompany him into the great ocean.
I beg you to follow him.”
The guide immediately replied,
“The great ocean holds countless dangers and hardships.
Of the thousands who go, only one or two reach their destination.
How can the Great King allow the Prince to travel far upon this perilous path?”
The King informed the guide,
“It was out of deep compassion that I reluctantly granted permission for him to follow his wish.”
The guide said,
“I dare not refuse.”
The Prince equipped himself, and the five hundred followers loaded their provisions and journeyed to the seashore.
Èyǒu thought to himself,
“Shànyǒu is dearly loved and favored by our parents.
Now he is going to the great ocean to gather marvelous treasures.
If he returns successfully, the parents will certainly abandon me.”
He reported to his parents,
“I wish to follow Shànyǒu into the sea to gather treasures.”
His parents replied,
“Do as you wish. When the path becomes perilous and difficult, may the brothers follow each other and surely help and protect each other.”
When they reached the great ocean, they locked their ship with seven iron chains.
The ship remained moored for seven days.
When the sun first rose, the Prince beat the drum and issued a decree,
“All of you people, who wishes to enter the sea?
Those who enter should remain silent.
If you long for your loved ones, you may return home now.
In the great ocean, there are countless dangers.”
The crowd remained silent.
The Prince then broke one chain and lifted it onto the ship.
Daily, he issued this decree until the seventh day.
He then broke the seven chains and hoisted the sails, relying on the wind.
Due to the power of the Prince’s compassionate heart and merit, they encountered no obstructions or difficulties.
They reached a sea island where there was a mountain of precious jewels.
The Prince beat the drum and proclaimed,
“The journey is long and distant! Load the precious jewels quickly!”
They stopped for a maximum of seven days.
He then spoke again,
“Some of these jewels are very heavy,
and they are not worth much in Yánfútí.
Do not overload the boats and ships until they sink, failing to reach the destination.
Yet, do not take too little, such that the long and distant journey is not sufficiently compensated for the toil.”
The preparation was completed, and he bid farewell to the people.
And spoke these words:
"You all should now return safely and peacefully.
I am currently intending to advance forward to gather the Móní jewels."
The Crown Prince and the blind guide
proceeded forward in sequence.
They traveled for seven days where the water reached their knees.
They again advanced for seven days where the water reached their neck.
Again they proceeded for seven days, floating, they managed to cross and immediately arrived at the place of the treasure.
The guide asked, saying:
"What is this substance on the ground?"
The Crown Prince replied, saying:
"The ground is purely white silver sand."
The guide said:
"Looking in the four directions, there should be white mountains. Have you seen them yet?"
The Crown Prince said:
"To the southeast there is a white silver mountain. We have reached the foot of this mountain."
The guide said:
"Next, we should arrive at golden sand."
The guide, exhausted and faint, collapsed onto the ground and spoke to the Crown Prince, saying:
"My life will not last long; I shall surely perish here.
The Crown Prince, therefore, should travel eastward for seven (days); there will be a golden mountain.
Advancing again for seven (days) from that mountain, the ground will be purely green lotus flowers.
Advancing again for seven (days), the ground will be purely reddish-crimson lotus flowers.
Passing yet another seven (days), there is a great jeweled city,
adorned purely with seven treasures, where the Dragon King resides.
In the Dragon King's ear is a Móní wish-fulfilling jewel.
You must go and beg for it.
If you obtain this jewel, it can fulfill (the needs of) all Yánfú Tí, raining down the seven treasures, clothing, food and drink, medicine, and music, producing whatever is wished for.
It is named the Wish-Fulfilling Jewel (Rúyì Zhū)."
Having spoken, the guide stopped breathing and died.
The Crown Prince embraced him, crying loudly in sorrow.
"Alas, how unfortunate I am to have lost you while still alive!"
He immediately buried him in the ground,
covering him with golden sand.
He circumambulated him seven times clockwise, paid homage, and departed.
He proceeded past the golden mountain and saw the green lotus flowers.
Beneath them were green snakes.
These snakes possessed three kinds of poison:
namely, biting poison, touching poison, and breath/hissing poison.
These venomous snakes coiled their bodies around the lotus flowers,
staring at the Crown Prince with wide eyes and gasping breaths.
The Crown Prince immediately entered the Samādhi of Loving-Kindness (Cíxīn Sānmèi).
He arose and advanced, stepping upon the lotus leaves.
At that time, the venomous snakes neither damaged nor injured him, and he arrived at the Dragon King’s dwelling place.
Seven layers of moats were filled with poisonous dragons, which intertwined together, raising their heads and crossing their necks, guarding the city gate.
The Crown Prince arrived outside the city gate.
Seeing the poisonous dragons, he immediately cultivated loving-kindness.
He thought of all sentient beings in Yánfú Tí:
"If my body were harmed by these poisonous dragons now,
you sentient beings would all lose a great benefit."
He immediately raised his right hand and announced to the poisonous dragons, saying:
"You should all know:
I wish to see the Dragon King for the sake of all sentient beings."
The poisonous dragons opened the path and allowed the Crown Prince to enter.
He saw two jade maidens spinning crystal threads.
The Crown Prince asked, saying:
"Who are you?"
They replied, saying:
"We are the maids guarding the outer gate of the Dragon King."
Entering through the middle gate, he saw four jade maidens spinning white silver threads.
The Crown Prince asked again:
"Are you the wives of the Dragon King?"
They replied: "No.
We are merely the maids guarding the middle gate of the Dragon King."
The Crown Prince entered the inner gate and saw eight jade maidens spinning golden threads.
The Crown Prince spoke to them:
"Who are you?"
They replied, saying:
"We are merely the maids guarding the gate of the Dragon King."
The Crown Prince said:
"Please announce to the Great Sea Dragon King that
Shànyǒu, the Crown Prince of the Kingdom of Pōluónài in Yánfú Tí, wishes to come and meet him and is now waiting at the gate."
At that time, the gate guard immediately informed the King.
The King was greatly puzzled and wondered:
"If he were not a person of pure goodness and merit (Fúdé), he would have no means of traveling such a distant, perilous road."
He immediately invited him into the palace, and the King came out to welcome him respectfully.
The floor was dark lapis lazuli, and the seven treasures emitted various kinds of light, dazzling the eyes.
The Crown Prince preached the Dharma, providing instruction and joyful benefit.
He praised and spoke on the doctrine of generosity (shī lùn), the doctrine of precepts (jiè lùn), and the doctrine of humans and heavens (rén tiān zhī lùn).
The Dragon King was delighted in his heart.
"You have humbled yourself to travel so far. What do you require?"
The Crown Prince said:
"Great King,
all sentient beings in Yánfú Tí suffer endless hardship for clothing and food.
I now wish to beg the Móní jewel from the King's left ear."
The Dragon King said:
"Please accept my humble offerings for seven days. Then I shall present it to you."
The Crown Prince accepted the Dragon King's invitation.
After seven days, taking the jewel, he returned to Yánfú Tí. The Dragon King ordered various dragon spirits to fly through the air and escort him.
He arrived safely at this shore.
He saw his younger brother, Èyǒu, and asked:
"Where are your followers and companions now?"
He replied, saying:
"The ship sank; everyone died completely.
Only I, your younger brother, survived entirely by holding onto the corpses.
All the property and goods are now totally lost."
Shànyǒu said:
"Among the great treasures under heaven, none is more important than one's own body."
The younger brother said: "It is not so.
People desire to die rich, not to live poor.
How do I know this?
I once went to the burial grounds and heard the ghosts of the dead discussing this."
Shànyǒu was truly straightforward and told his brother the truth:
"Although you have lost your treasure, that is of minor concern.
I have now obtained the Dragon King's Wish-Fulfilling Jewel."
The younger brother asked:
"Where is it now?"
Shànyǒu said:
"It is now in my topknot."
The brother heard this, and jealousy arose in him. He said to Shànyǒu:
"How splendid, truly excellent!
Having obtained this precious jewel, you should guard it carefully."
Shànyǒu unwound the jewel and gave it to his brother, instructing him with these words:
"If you lie down weary, I shall stand guard.
When I sleep, you should stand guard."
Then it was Èyǒu's turn to guard the jewel.
When his elder brother was fast asleep,
he arose, took two dry bamboo thorns, stabbed his brother's eyes, seized the jewel, and departed.
Shànyǒu called out to Èyǒu:
"A thief is here! He stabbed both my eyes and has taken the precious jewel away!"
Èyǒu did not respond.
The elder brother was distressed and worried that the thief might kill him.
He cried out loudly, his voice shaking the spirits and deities (shénqí), but after a long time, there was no response.
The tree spirit spoke out, saying:
"Your younger brother Èyǒu is your evil thief.
He stabbed your eyes and took the precious jewel away."
The Crown Prince was greatly dismayed, worried, angered, and tormented.
Èyǒu carried the jewel back to the kingdom and reported to his parents, saying:
"By my own merit (fúdé) I was entirely saved.
Shànyǒu and his companions drowned and all perished."
The parents cried loudly, fainted, and fell to the ground.
They spoke to Èyǒu, saying:
"How could you possibly bring that face back here?"
When Èyǒu heard these words, remorse arose in his heart.
He immediately buried the precious jewel in the ground.
Shànyǒu, having been stabbed, had no one to pull out the thorns.
He wandered about, staggering, not knowing where to go.
At that time, he suffered terribly from torment, great affliction, hunger, and thirst.
He could neither find life nor find death.
Gradually advancing, he arrived at the Kingdom of Lìshībá.
The King of that place had a daughter,
who had previously been promised to Shànyǒu, the Prince of Pōluónài.
There was a herdsman who tended five hundred cattle for the King, following water and grass.
The Crown Prince was sitting on the road.
The cattle herd was about to approach closely.
The King Bull stood upon the Crown Prince, allowing the other cattle to pass.
Afterwards, it moved its feet, circled clockwise, looked back, turned its neck, stuck out its tongue, and licked the Crown Prince's two eyes, pulling out the bamboo thorns.
The herdsman saw this and asked, saying:
"Who are you?"
Shànyǒu did not reveal his true identity.
He replied, saying:
"I am merely a blind beggar boy."
The herdsman thoroughly observed him.
Seeing that he had an unusual appearance, he said:
"My home is nearby.
I will provide for you."
He immediately brought him home and gave him various kinds of food and drink.
He instructed his family,
"You must treat him no differently than you treat me."
After more than a month passed, the family grew weary of him.
Shànyǒu was dejected. The next morning, he reported to the master, saying:
"I wish to leave now."
The master asked:
"What is unsatisfactory?"
Shànyǒu said:
"According to the norms between host and guest, one cannot stay long."
Shànyǒu continued:
"If you care for me,
please give me a singing zither (míng zhēng) and escort me to a populous settlement."
The master immediately provided for him as requested and escorted him to the densely populated area of the city of Lìshībá.
Shànyǒu played the zither.
Its sound was harmonious and refined, pleasing the hearts of the multitude.
All the people jointly provided him with food and drink.
The King had an orchard.
The orchard was lush, but constantly suffered from birds.
At that time, the orchard supervisor spoke to Shànyǒu, saying:
"Protect the birds for me,
and I will provide for you.
I have tied ropes to the tops of the trees and placed copper bells there.
You sit beneath the tree; when you hear the sound of the birds, pull the end of the rope."
Shànyǒu said:
"Very well.
I can settle down under the tree, and also play the zither to entertain myself."
At that time, the daughter of the King of Lìshībá, accompanied by attendants, entered the garden.
Seeing this blind man, she immediately went up to him and asked:
"Who are you?"
He replied, saying:
"Merely a blind beggar."
Love and affection arose in the Princess's heart, and she could not bear to leave him.
The King again sent an envoy to summon his daughter home.
The daughter said, "I will not go. Send food here for me."
After she finished providing the blind man with food and drink,
she reported to the Great King, saying:
"If the King would now give me to this blind man, it would greatly fulfill my wish."
The King said:
"A demon has possessed you! Your mind is deranged and confused! How could you wish to live with a blind man?
Your parents previously promised you to Crown Prince Shànyǒu of Pōluónài.
Shànyǒu went into the sea and has not yet returned.
How can you now become the wife of a beggar?"
The woman said, "Although it is so, even if I must abandon my life, I will ultimately not leave you."
The king heard these words and could not refuse or oppose her.
He immediately sent an emissary to welcome the blind man, brought him, and confined him in a quiet chamber.
The royal woman spoke to the blind man, saying:
"I shall now become husband and wife with you."
Shànyǒu replied:
"Whose daughter are you, wishing to become my wife?"
She answered:
"I am the daughter of King Lìshīpō."
Shànyǒu replied:
"You are a king's daughter.
I am a beggar. How can you show me respect?"
The wife said:
"I will serve you with all my heart."
Later, the wife went out without informing her husband, and only returned after a long time.
Shànyǒu reproached her: "You privately went outside without informing me. Where did you go and return from?"
The wife said:
"I did not go out privately."
The husband said: "Whether it was private or not, who would know besides you?"
The wife swore an oath:
"If I went out privately, may your two eyes never be cured from beginning to end.
If it is not so, may one of your eyes be restored to its former condition."
Having made this vow, it was immediately restored to its former full state, shining brilliantly and clearly.
The wife said:
"Do you believe me or not?"
Shànyǒu smiled slightly.
The wife said:
"You do not recognize my kindness and care.
I am the daughter of a great king.
You are a man of low standing, yet I serve you with all my heart.
Yet regarding me, you do not trust me."
The husband said:
"Do you recognize me or not?"
She answered, "I recognize you. You are a beggar."
The husband said: "No, that is not so.
I am Prince Shànyǒu, the son of King Bōluónài."
The wife said:
"You are a greatly foolish person. Why do you utter such words?
The Prince of King Bōluónài went to sea and has not yet returned.
Now you speak falsely. I do not believe you."
Shànyǒu said: "Since I was born, I have never spoken falsely."
The wife said:
"Who should believe whether that is false or true?"
The husband said:
"If I am deceiving you, may my one eye never be healed.
If I speak truly, may my other eye be restored to its former condition, allowing you to see it."
Immediately, as he had vowed, the pupil shone brightly, just as it was originally, without difference.
Prince Shànyǒu's two eyes were fully recovered; his face and head were handsome, and his magnificent appearance was peerless.
The wife saw this and rejoiced.
It was as if she had met a sage or saint; she gazed upon his entire body, her eyes not leaving him for a moment.
She immediately entered the palace and reported to her royal father:
"My husband now is none other than Prince Shànyǒu."
The king said: "Foolish person!
Shànyǒu has not yet returned. How can you call a beggar the Prince?"
The daughter said: "No, that is not true.
If you do not believe it, you may go and look at him once."
The king immediately went and looked.
He recognized that it was Shànyǒu.
He was immediately filled with fear and spoke thus:
"King Bōluónài,
if he hears of this matter, will certainly resent me greatly."
He immediately went forward, confessed, and apologized to Prince Shànyǒu, saying, "I truly did not know."
The Prince said:
"No trouble. Bring provisions for me,
and deliver them to this herdsman."
The king immediately gave gold, silver, jewels, clothing, and food,
and also gave the five hundred cattle that had been released.
That man was infinitely joyful and praised his goodness.
"Although I have not yet repaid this small kindness,"
he proclaimed loudly thus:
"The retribution for secret charity is vastly great and infinite."
When the multitude heard this, they all generated the mind of charity.
Before Shànyǒu went to sea, he raised a white goose.
It was always with him in clothing, food, travel, dwelling, sitting, and lying down.
His wife spoke to the goose, saying:
"When the Prince was here, you were always with him.
Now, life and death are separated, yet you show no feeling or remembrance for the Prince?"
The goose immediately cried sadly, weeping and turning its head, replying:
"I want to seek the Prince."
The wife personally wrote a letter and tied it around the goose's neck.
Its body rose into the empty sky and flew away.
It flew to the great sea, searched for him, but did not find him.
Following the sequence, it arrived at the country of Lìshīpō.
It saw Shànyǒu from afar, standing in front of the palace.
The goose flew towards him, crying sadly but joyfully.
The Prince immediately took the mother's letter, respectfully placed it on his head, opened the seal, and read it.
He immediately knew that his parents were weeping sadly day and night, thinking of him.
(The letter mentioned that) the Prince had lost sight in both eyes.
The Prince wrote a letter detailing the previous matters, tied the letter around the goose's neck, and sent it back to Bōluónài.
The parents received the letter, were infinitely joyful and delighted, and praised the goodness immensely.
They were fully informed that the Prince had suffered hardship from the wicked friend, who had stolen the precious pearl.
The parents chained and shackled the wicked friend and confined him in the prison.
They sent an emissary to inform King Lìshīpō:
"Why do you now keep the Prince hidden, causing me worry and suffering?"
King Lìshīpō felt fear in his heart.
He immediately arrayed the Prince in fine clothes and sent him to the border.
He sent an emissary to report:
"I have given my daughter to him as a wife and sent him back to his country."
The parents mounted great famous elephants.
They prepared singers, musicians, swept the path, burned incense, hung silk banners and canopies, and traveled far to welcome the Prince.
The people of the kingdom, men, women, husbands, and wives, heard the Prince had returned and all went out to respectfully welcome him.
The Prince stepped forward and bowed to his parents.
The parents' eyes were dark, and they could not see the Prince.
They felt him with their hands, saying, "Are you Shànyǒu? We have suffered so greatly worrying about you."
After the Prince finished inquiring about his parents' daily well-being,
the Prince addressed his royal father, saying:
"Where is the wicked friend?"
The king said:
"He is now in prison."
The Prince said:
"I request that you release the wicked friend so that I may see him." He repeated this request up to three times.
The king could not bear to refuse and immediately ordered his release.
[The Prince] immediately went forward, embraced him, used kind words and gentle persuasion, and softly inquired:
"You have suffered greatly carrying my precious pearl. Where is it now?"
This was repeated up to three times.
Only then did [the wicked friend] reply:
"It is in that mound of earth."
The Prince recovered the precious pearl.
He went before his parents, knelt, burned various wonderful incense, and immediately made a sacred vow:
"If this pearl is truly the Wish-Fulfilling Jewel,
may my parents' two eyes become bright and clear as before."
Immediately, they were restored to normal, and seeing their son, they rejoiced.
On the morning of the fifteenth day of the month, the Prince
purely bathed himself, put on fresh and clean clothes, and burned precious incense.
In a high tower, holding the incense burner, he bowed his head and face to the Maṇi precious pearl.
He made a solemn vow, saying:
"I sought this precious pearl by enduring this great suffering
for all sentient beings of Yánfú Tí."
At that time, a great wind arose in the east.
It blew away the clouds and mist, making everything bright and clear.
Moreover, all the filth, dung, urine, ashes, soil, and wild grass existing in Yánfú Tí were swept clean and purified by the clear wind.
By the awesome power of the pearl,
over Yánfú Tí,
it rained naturally ripened rice everywhere.
It was fragrant, sweet, soft, fine, and complete in color and flavor.
The ditches and channels were full, piled up to the knees.
Next, it rained clothing, jeweled rings, hairpins, and bracelets.
Next, it rained the seven treasures and all wonderful musical instruments.
Everything needed by sentient beings was fully supplied.
Afterwards, King Gài Wáng died, and [Shànyǒu] immediately succeeded to the throne.
The wicked friend reported:
"I shall sustain my life by begging for food."
The King said:
"You guard my neck, and I will give you food."
The King then fell asleep.
[The wicked friend] drew a knife, intending to cut off the King's head, but the head fell off by itself.
The King awoke and asked about it.
[The wicked friend] replied:
"Heaven accomplished this deed."
The father at that time is now Yuètóután.
The mother at that time is now Móyé Fūren.
The wicked friend is Típódáduō.
The daughter of King Yuè is Qúyī.
Shànyǒu is myself.
In the past, there was a Bodhisattva,
who became the king of a great country,
named Chángshòu.
The king had a crown prince,
named Chángshēng.
The king governed justly; the suffering of swords and cudgels was not inflicted upon the officials or the people.
Wind and rain came in season, and the five grains were abundant.
There was a king of a neighboring country,
whose established conduct was cruel and harmful, who did not govern correctly, and whose people were impoverished.
He said to his attendant ministers:
"I hear that King Chángshòu is rich, prosperous, and joyous, and lacks preparations for war. I wish to seize his country."
The ministers said, "Excellent."
They raised an army and attacked.
King Chángshòu told his gathered ministers:
"They covet my wealth.
If we engage in battle, my people will surely be harmed.
Indeed, struggling for a kingdom and killing the people is something I cannot bear."
The gathered ministers did not follow his advice.
They dispatched troops outside the borders to meet and resist the invaders.
The king and the crown prince climbed over the city wall and hid themselves.
The greedy king entered the country and issued a bounty for Chángshòu: a reward of one thousand *jīn* of gold and ten million coins.
Later, the king came out by the roadside beneath a tree.
He met a Brāhmaṇa and asked where he had come from.
He replied:
"I am a poor ascetic.
Hearing that King Chángshòu is fond of charity, I traveled far to beg from him."
The king thought silently:
"I have encountered this time when I have lost my country."
He shed tears and said:
"I am that king.
Meeting me in such a state, I have nothing I can bestow upon you."
The two wept.
The king said:
"I hear that the new king seeks me very urgently.
If you take my head and go to him, you will surely obtain a lavish reward."
The Brāhmaṇa said:
"With my meager blessings, I dare not accept this command."
The king said:
"You traveled far to come here and met me in destitution.
Life eventually leads to death.
I wish to give this to you as a gift; why do you refuse?"
He replied:
"How could I bear to kill you?
If you truly wish to give charity, I ask that you follow me back to the country."
Thereupon, they returned together, arriving at the city gate.
The king ordered the Brāhmaṇa to bind him and report to the greedy king.
The greedy king immediately rewarded him with gold and money and sent him away to return home.
At the intersection of the four streets, he intended to burn and kill Chángshòu.
Within the outer city, the villages, and the countryside, none failed to cry out to Heaven.
The Crown Prince heard of this.
He came out and stood before his father, his heart grievously pained.
The father, fearing his son would seek revenge for the enmity,
looked up to Heaven and sighed, saying:
"This death is what I desire.
If you wish to show utmost filial piety, let your father die without regret; do not seek revenge."
Chángshēng could not bear to watch his father die and returned back into the mountains.
After the king had died, Chángshēng reflected.
"My father's benevolence and righteousness were deep and sincere, unwavering even unto death.
The greedy king is lawless and cannot distinguish good from evil.
He unjustly killed my father; I cannot endure this.
If I do not kill him, I shall certainly not continue to live dishonorably."
So he came out and worked as a hired laborer for the chief minister, borrowing a piece of land to grow vegetables, and the vegetables were excellent.
The chief minister asked the garden supervisor.
The supervisor replied:
"We hired a man who is very diligent and capable."
The chief minister called Chángshēng and asked him:
"Can you prepare food and drink?"
He replied, "Yes, I can."
Afterward, [the minister] invited the king to eat and drink, and the meal was delicious.
The king asked who had prepared it.
He replied, "A servant."
The king immediately summoned him back to the palace to prepare food and drink.
Later, the king asked:
"Can you study military strategy?"
He replied, "I am very proficient."
The king appointed him to attend him constantly.
He told him:
"I have an enemy and I am constantly afraid of encountering him.
Now I rely on you to assist and protect me."
He replied, "Yes.
I shall exert my strength and dedicate my life for Your Majesty."
A few days later, the king asked:
"Do you happen to enjoy hunting?"
He replied:
"Your servant has enjoyed hunting since youth."
The king then commanded his attendants to prepare the chariot, and consequently went out hunting together with Chángshēng.
Just as they entered the mountains and forests, they spotted running beasts.
The king and Chángshēng rode swiftly to pursue them.
They turned and entered the deep mountains, losing the path for three days.
Consequently, they became hungry and exhausted.
The king then dismounted, removed his sword, and handed it to Chángshēng, saying:
"I am extremely exhausted. Sit down; I wish to rest my head on your knee and sleep."
Chángshēng drew the sword, intending to kill the greedy king.
He thought of his father's command, returned the sword to its sheath, and stopped.
This occurred three times.
The king then woke up startled and asked Chángshēng:
"I dreamed that Chángshòu's prince intended to come and harm me."
Chángshēng said:
"That was merely a strong ghost coming here to frighten you."
Finally, [Chángshēng] revealed his true intention to kill.
Chángshēng said:
"I am indeed the Crown Prince of King Chángshòu, and I came here specifically to kill the Great King.
But my father, upon his death, urgently commanded me not to avenge this enmity upon the king.
I reflected upon my father's teaching and cast the sword onto the ground, obeying my father's instruction.
Although I have done this, I still fear that later I might become confused and lose my resolution.
I beg the Great King to kill me immediately."
The king then repented, saying:
"I have acted wickedly and rebelliously.
I could not distinguish good from evil.
The worthy father and son practiced benevolence sincerely and firmly, unwavering even unto death.
Yet, I was greedy and cruel, completely unaware [of their virtue].
Today my life belonged to your hand.
You still harbor benevolence.
You only remember your father’s words
and would rather not harm me.
I am truly moved by your great kindness.
Now that I wish to return to the country, by which path should we go?"
Chángshēng said:
"I know the path well. I deliberately confused Your Majesty earlier because I wished to avenge my father's enmity."
They then both emerged from the forest and immediately saw their troops.
The king returned to his original country, restored this country to the Crown Prince, and they formed a bond of brotherhood, vowing never to invade or seize [each other's lands].
They offered gifts to one another and helped each other through times of hardship.
King Chángshòu was myself.
The Crown Prince was Ānán.
The greedy king was Diàodá.
In the past, the king of Zhēluó guó.
He happened to have a queen but no heir.
The King was deeply distressed by this.
He commanded, saying:
“You shall return to your clan to seek the means of having an heir.”
The Queen wept, took her leave, and departed.
She swore an oath to sacrifice herself by plunging into the steep, rugged mountain forests.
Dìshì (Śakra) was moved, saying:
“This Queen of the King was my elder sister in a former life.
Now, because she lacks an heir, she sacrifices her body in the dangerous mountains.”
He felt sorrowful compassion for her.
Suddenly, he descended.
He handed her a vessel containing fruit, saying:
“Sister, if you swallow this fruit, you will certainly have a holy heir.
He will become a hero to the world.
If the King has doubts, show him this vessel.
This is the divine vessel of the Heavenly King, a supreme, clear proof.”
The Queen looked up to heaven and swallowed the fruit; suddenly, she could not see (the deity), and she felt a stirring in her body.
She returned to see the King and truthfully recounted everything she had heard.
When the months were full, she gave birth to a boy.
His appearance was hideous and ugly, rarely seen in the world.
When he was a young child, he was profoundly intelligent and widely knowledgeable, his strategies surpassing calculation.
His strength enabled him to trip elephants, run down and capture flying eagles, and his voice, when extended, resonated like the roar of a lion.
His fame spread far and wide, and the eight directions all praised him.
The King sought a daughter from a neighboring state to be his wife.
Her name was Yuèguāng; she was upright, graceful, beautiful, and possessed all the qualities favored by the world.
She also had seven younger brothers.
They were also handsome and fair.
The Queen feared that Yuèguāng would detest the Prince’s appearance.
She falsely stated:
“It is an old custom in our state that husband and wife do not meet in daylight.
To look upon him is a grave matter.
My Lady, do not violate this custom.”
She replied:
“I respectfully assent.
I dare not disregard your venerable instruction.”
After this, the Prince never revealed his true appearance when entering or leaving.
The Prince deeply reflected: “My state is hostile to seven other states; there are violent conflicts, leaving the populace unrestful and groaning in lamentation.
I shall use stratagem to bring peace to them.”
He thought to himself:
“My body is utterly ugly; if the consort sees it, she will surely flee.”
He petitioned his mother, wishing to see the consort’s features.
The Queen said:
“Your appearance is repulsive, while the consort’s face is glorious and radiant.”
The Prince reiterated his request.
The Queen, pitying him, led the consort to observe him.
The Prince pretended to be a herdsman.
The consort saw him and said:
“Is that herdsman ugly?”
The Queen said:
“That is the late King’s herdsman.”
Later, when they went to observe the elephants,
the consort saw him again.
She suspected, saying:
“Could this person I keep seeing be the Prince?”
The consort said:
“I wish to see the radiant countenance of the Prince.”
The Queen then used a stratagem, ordering the Prince’s younger brothers to go out walking,
accompanied by the Prince’s officials as attendants.
The consort observed them, and her heart felt a slight pleasure.
Later, when she entered the garden again,
the Prince climbed a tree and threw fruit at her back.
The consort said:
“This must certainly be the Prince.”
That night, she waited while he slept, secretly illuminated him with a lamp, and saw his appearance; terrified, she fled back home.
The King and Queen angrily said:
“How did you let the consort return?”
He replied:
“The consort’s flight is the foundation of peace under Heaven, and the people will ultimately be able to cherish their loved ones.”
He bowed, took his leave, and searched for her, arriving at the consort’s state.
He pretended to be a potter, hiring himself out to make clay vessels.
He then entered the city and hired himself out as a dyer.
He next worked for the prime minister, hired to fatten horses.
Finally, he served as the Supervisor of the Imperial Kitchens, managing all dishes, and brought soup into the inner chambers.
The King had eight daughters; they were all delighted by his service, but Yuèguāng did not look at him.
Dìshì sighed in admiration, saying:
“A Bodhisattva’s concern for saving sentient beings extends even to this degree.”
“I shall use stratagem to assist him.”
He provoked the seven enemy states by transforming into handwritten letters from Yuèguāng’s father, the King,
promising Yuèguāng as a wife to each of them.
The seven states all prepared rituals and sent envoys to personally welcome her back to their states.
They all declared:
“We are betrothing the King’s daughter named Yuèguāng.”
The disputes were chaotic.
Each presented the handwritten letter.
Their complaints were heard in unison, saying:
“We must exterminate your heir.”
They were unwavering in this.
They sent back letters, all severely criticizing, saying:
“Because of your one daughter, you have incurred the enmity of seven states.
With combined forces launching a massive attack, we believe the loss of your state is imminent.”
The King heard this and said fearfully:
“This impending disaster must have been incurred by deeds in a past life.”
He said to Yuèguāng:
“You became a consort.
Whether your husband is wise or foolish, fortunate or disastrous, handsome or ugly—this is determined by past karma. Who can avert it?
Instead of remaining faithful and dutifully serving and honoring him, you returned to this state with your meager intellect, bringing disaster upon us to this extent.
I must now cut your corpse into seven parts to apologize to the seven kings.”
Yuèguāng wept, saying:
“I beg you to grant me just a moment of life.
If we recruit wise men, there must be someone capable of repelling the threat of the seven states.”
The King immediately offered a reward, saying:
“Whoever can avert this calamity,
I will give him Yuèguāng as his wife and grant him immense prosperity.”
The Prince said:
“Quickly build a high tower; I can repel them.”
When the tower was completed,
the Prince feigned illness, stumbling and falling to the ground.
“You must have Yuèguāng carry you on her back, and then you will repel the enemy.”
Yuèguāng, greatly terrified of being slaughtered, helped him climb the tower.
The Prince spoke in a loud voice, saying:
The sound reached the kings of the seven states, shaking them far away.
It was like the roar of a lion, explaining that the Buddha’s teaching is supreme.
“To govern the people, one must use the path of benevolence.
But now you rise up in mighty anger, and calamity will ensue.
If calamity ensues, your persons will perish and your states will be lost.
Is this due to mere names and appearances?”
The commanders and heroes of the seven states were all utterly shocked and collapsed.
A moment later they revived and desired to return to their home states.
The Prince petitioned the King: “Regarding marital alliances, there is nothing better than joining these kings.
Why not marry off your seven daughters to those seven princes?
With them as sons-in-law and outer defenses, the King will enjoy great peace.
The ministers and people will be at rest.
And the relatives will receive support.”
The King said:
“Excellent! This joy is great indeed.”
He then commanded the seven kings to marry his daughters.
The eight sons-in-law showed ritual reverence, and the ruler and ministers were joyful.
The King, down to his ministers and people, finally realized that the Prince was Yuèguāng’s original husband.
He immediately selected excellent counselors and warriors to accompany each of the kings, who all returned to their respective states.
The nine states were peaceful and harmonious, and the populace danced for joy.
They all sighed in admiration, saying:
“Heaven has sent a holy strategist; his wisdom is not matched by ordinary men. His virtue accumulated, his merit achieved, everything is peaceful and beyond reproach.”
After returning to his state for many years, the Great King passed away.
The Prince ascended the throne and issued a great pardon for all criminals.
He taught and transformed the populace with the Five Precepts, Six Pāramitās, Eight Abstinence Precepts, and Ten Goods.
Disasters and evils ceased completely, the state prospered, the people were secure, and the great teaching spread widely; all revered the Three Jewels.
Virtue flourished, blessings returned, and all diseases vanished.
The reason for this was:
In a past life, the Bodhisattva was a layman who farmed with his wife and ordered her to fetch food.
He waited, expecting his wife’s return, when he saw her walking with a Pìzhīfó (Pratyekabuddha) who then disappeared into the mountain cliff.
After a long time, she had not arrived, and doubt arose in his mind.
He became angry, grabbed his hoe, and intended to go and strike her.
When he arrived, he saw his wife offering a portion of her food to the śramaṇa.
He stepped back, stood respectfully with folded hands.
When the śramaṇa finished eating, he raised his bowl into the air; magnificent light shone brilliantly as he flew away and departed.
The husband felt regret and shame, considering his wife’s virtue.
“She was able to bring forth such a venerable one.
I, possessing profound foolishness, was about to suffer calamity.”
He immediately said to his wife:
“I shall share in the merit of your offering.
Let us eat the remaining rice together; do not refuse.”
When their lives ended, they were each born into royal families.
Because the wife possessed the grace of pure compassion,
she was born upright and beautiful.
Because the husband was first angry and later compassionate, he was initially ugly but later became handsome.
The Prince was myself.
The wife was Jūyí.
The royal father was Báijìng Wáng.
The mother was my mother, Shèmiào.
Dìshì (Śakra), the Lord of Heaven, was Mílè.
Bodhisattvas worry about sentient beings throughout endless lives and rescue them from deep suffering.
At that time, the crown prince of the kingdom of Bōluónài
was named Mùpò.
He was incomparably handsome.
He recalled the countless kalpas of his past lives,
and all the good and evil, long and short lives, beauty and ugliness he had experienced, he completely knew and saw.
When he reached thirteen years old, he closed his mouth and spoke not.
The king had only this one son, whom the entire country loved and respected, and who was destined to inherit the throne.
He spoke neither of hunger nor cold, being calm, simple, and rustic, his mind like dry wood.
Although he had ears and eyes, he paid no attention to looking or listening.
Though his wisdom and thoughts were profound, he seemed to have no heart or will.
He was like the blind and the deaf, not speaking of direction.
He appeared dull and foolish, unlike ordinary people.
His father worried greatly and suffered immensely because of it.
He was deeply ashamed before neighboring states, fearing they would scorn him.
Therefore, he summoned the Brāhmaṇas (Póluómén) of the kingdom and asked them:
“Why is this child unable to speak?”
The Brāhmaṇas replied:
“Although this child’s appearance is upright, inwardly he harbors misfortune.
He intends to harm his parents, endanger the state, and destroy the lineage; this will happen soon.
Those who are unable to conceive sons are all obstructed by this wicked child; he should be buried alive.
Then the king’s own life can be preserved, and the state and lineage secured.
Only then can you again have a noble son.
If not, the danger is immense.”
The king believed the madness and folly, thinking it was surely true, and was immediately filled with anxiety.
He was restless whether sitting or standing; entertainment music was not utilized, and delicious clothing and food brought no pleasure.
He immediately discussed it with the elders and ministers; some suggested abandoning him far away in the deep mountains.
Others suggested casting him into deep water.
One minister said:
“Just build a deep pit.
The side entrance should be like a chamber.
Provide him with provisions and assign five servants to attend him.
Place him alive inside, and let fate decide his future.”
The king immediately followed this suggestion.
The Crown Prince felt sadness, distressed by their foolish delusion.
His mother, loving him, was heartbroken and cried out:
“My son, ill-fated, has met this calamity!”
Weeping and sobbing, since the matter was unavoidable, she bowed and yielded him up.
She took all the Prince’s clothes, jewelry, and treasures, and sent them along with him.
The servants were outside.
They then began digging the pit. Before the digging was finished,
Mùpò, alone in the chariot, deeply pondered to himself.
His heart spoke to his mouth:
“The king and the people all truly believe me to be foolish and mute.
The reason I have not spoken is that I wish to abandon worldly ties, secure my body, avoid vexation, save my spirit, and leave suffering.
Now, conversely, I am endangered by mad deception.
If I perish and fall victim to those people,
I should silently take my jewelry and treasures and leave.”
The people digging the pit did not notice.
Mùpò took the items and departed.
Then Mùpò immediately went to the water’s edge.
He thoroughly bathed himself and applied fragrance to his body.
He put on all his clothes, coverings, and jewelry.
He went to the place where the pit was being dug and asked:
“What is this pit being made for?”
The servants replied:
“The king has a crown prince named Mùpò.
He is mute, dumb, deaf, and foolish, thirteen years old, and cannot speak.
We are digging this pit to bury him alive.”
The Crown Prince answered:
“I am Mùpò.”
The workers were terrified and ran to look in the chariot but did not see him there.
Returning to the pit, they carefully observed him; they heard his words, which were exceptionally clear.
His radiance was like the moon, rarely heard of in the world.
He moved among them, and those walking stopped, and those sitting rose for him.
Flying birds and running beasts all gathered and assembled, prostrating themselves before the Crown Prince to listen to his words.
He further said:
“Look at my hands and feet, observe my appearance.
How can this mass of deluded people believe this mad deceit, resulting in me being buried alive and abandoned?”
His speech was eloquent, startling those around him.
They all bowed and knocked their heads, begging for mercy and forgiveness.
The Crown Prince said:
“Now that I have been abandoned, it is not suitable to return.”
The servants immediately rushed off to report to the king.
The king heard the news, feeling both grief and joy.
He immediately rode out with the Queen (Fūrén) to welcome him.
Before the king arrived, Mùpò thought to himself:
“I ought to go practice the Way (Dào).”
Shì Tì (Indra) transformed a garden tree, incomparably pleasant.
The king saw the Crown Prince sitting under the tree from afar.
When Mùpò saw the king, he immediately rose to greet him.
The king performed a ritual bow for him; Mùpò then advised the Great King to take a seat.
The king heard the Prince’s voice and speech.
His awesome spiritual power was immeasurable, shaking heaven and earth, incomparably unique.
The king was extremely delighted.
He then circled Mùpò, and they returned together to the country.
The king said: “Occupy the throne and manage the government. I ask to step aside.”
Mùpò said:
“It must not be done.
I am ashamed of and weary of the myriad sufferings, anxieties, and poisons of the hells.
I once served as a king
named Qǐngniàn.
I governed the country with righteous law and practiced all manner of goodness.
For twenty-five years, no whip or staff was applied, no weapons were used, and there were no detainees in prisons.
I bestowed kindness, love (rén'ài), and universal grace, saving the poor and stranded without greed or regret.
Despite these practices, I still committed a minor offense and eventually fell into hell for over sixty thousand years.
I was boiled, peeled, and split—the agonizing pain was unbearable.
I sought death but could not find it; life offered no relief.
At that time, my parents were wealthy and noble, enjoying boundless pleasure.
Could they possibly know how intense my torment and punishment were in that hell?
Could they possibly come and share my suffering?
The reason I fell into sin was that in the past, when I was king, minor states were subject to me.
My nature was extremely compassionate and kind, my precepts and virtue were upright, but my laws were not strict.
All the kings of the smaller states regarded me lightly and easily, and they all conspired together, saying:
‘This Great King,
being both benevolent and weak—his authority and strategies are inadequate, and his virtue is insufficient to govern a great state—should be punished, deposed, and removed.’
They immediately raised troops and came to attack the great state.
At that time, King Qǐngniàn sent them rare gems and treasures, which he bestowed upon them.
He further comforted and soothed them with high office and generous salaries, thus settling them.
They immediately returned to their own states.
Before long, they came again to attack and punish, repeatedly, not just once.
The ministers of the great state reported to the Great King:
‘These small vassal states are foolish, dark, and unrighteous.
They disregard their offenses and frequently act with arrogance and aggression.
They plot murder and rebellious disobedience, violating the high sovereign.
They cause the people to be alarmed and disturbed, forcing us to constantly defend ourselves. They ought to be executed and slain to eliminate this banditry.’
The King said:
‘Being the parents of the people, one must devote oneself to benevolent transformation.
We must forgive others, nurture creatures, risk our lives, and save the masses.
They are like infants; pity their ignorance, guide them gradually, and do not bear to harm them.’
The King universally loved all living beings and forever refrained from punishment.
The ministers of the great state could not endure being repeatedly
scorned by the small vassal states; they grew angry and disregarded the danger.
They raised troops to suppress and slaughter the people.
The Great King wept tears.
He immediately mourned the dead people of those states as if they were his own sons, having boundless compassion for them.
When the kings of the small states saw the Great King’s merciful heart and compassion for the people,
they all surrendered and came to submit.
The Great King universally arranged precious feasts, which required the cooking and killing of oxen, sheep, and other six types of domestic animals to prepare various delicacies.
They always first sought permission from the King.
Though the King’s heart was compassionate, the matter was unavoidable.
He nodded his head, and because of this, he incurred sin and suffered such hardship.
Every time I think of this, my heart trembles greatly, my body feels empty and cold; I recall the good and bad fortune, safety and danger, success and failure I went through in past lives.
I fear meeting them again, and hope through silent stillness
to escape impurities and exit the world of toil.
I want to forever renounce the secular world and avoid calamities.
It just occurred to me that if I had persisted in closing my mouth and not speaking, and had been buried alive by the King,
I feared that the King would eventually incur this calamity and consequently enter hell without any hope of exit.
My intention was not to allow the King to incur sin, thus I spoke again.
I maintain the resolve of non-action (wúwéi) and take no pleasure in being king.
The world of human beings is fleeting, like a dream.
The joys of family last only for a moment.
Life is reckoned to be short, while worry and fear are prolonged.
Pleasure is little, suffering is much, and vexations are manifold.
Therefore, the wise person
regards the treasures of the state and familial affection as burdens,
and all desires as dust.
If I were made king, I would become arrogant, indulgent, and greedy for gratification,
causing the people anxiety and annoyance.
This is the great affliction of the world.
Now I wish to eliminate and abandon it.
I wish to trace the stream back to its source and save those who have not yet crossed over.
Living in this world is like being a guest; there is nothing to rely upon.
I do not crave wealth and nobility, nor value treasures.
I discard worldly glory and contemplate the Great Way (Dàdào).
I will soar high and travel far, extracting myself from the world.”
The Father King said:
“Since you are a wise person, you must not act like this.”
Mùpò replied:
“How can a father and son, having been born, abandon each other?
When flesh and blood have separated, their conduct is exceedingly flawed.
To struggle to welcome each other back only increases trouble and annoyance.”
The father, seeing his resolve was firm,
was at a loss and had no words to reply.
He then said:
“When you were king in your previous life, you practiced all manner of goodness.
You had a small lapse concerning possessions, something you did not consciously know,
yet you still suffered hardship and sin like this.
Now, when I govern the country, I do not adhere to righteous laws.
I have no small measure of goodness; instead, I commit transgressions and faults.
If I continue in dangerous behavior, what punishment will I deserve?”
He then released the Crown Prince, allowing him to leave and practice the Way.
The Crown Prince then abandoned the state, renounced the kingship, and did not engage in worldly affairs.
He focused wholeheartedly, dedicated himself to contemplating the Way and cultivating virtue, accumulating meritorious deeds
until the present time. Mùpò is my own body.
The Father King is Yuètóután.
The Mother is Móyé.
The counselor (Xiàngshī) is Tiáodá.
The servants at that time were Āruòjūlín and the other five people.
He practiced virtuous deeds, and his kingdom was without enemies.
The king had three sons.
The eldest was named Mahēbōnuólúo.
The second was named Mahēdítuó.
The youngest was named Mahēsàduǒ.
Together they went out touring until they reached a bamboo grove where they stopped their carriages and rested.
Moving forward again, they saw a tiger.
It had given birth seven days prior, and seven cubs surrounded it.
Extremely starved and distressed, its body was weak and wasted, and its life was about to expire.
The first prince said:
"Alas! This tiger cannot seek food.
Compelled by hunger, it will inevitably turn back and eat its cubs."
The third prince said:
"What does this tiger normally eat?"
The first prince replied:
"It eats warm blood and flesh."
The third prince replied:
"Who can give this tiger food?"
The second prince replied:
"Its remaining life is short; even if others seek food, they surely won't reach it in time.
Who can offer their body and life without regret?"
The first prince replied:
"Nothing is harder to abandon than one's own body."
The third prince replied:
"Those whose wisdom is shallow are deeply attached and possessive.
They cannot abandon their body and are terrified merely upon hearing of it.
Only Great Beings [Dàshì], whose hearts hold compassion,
find it no hardship at all to abandon this body and life for the sake of benefiting others."
