All of them, holding these worries in their thoughts, gazed intently at the tiger and departed.
The third prince thought to himself:
"The time for me to abandon my body has arrived.
Since time immemorial, this body has been pointlessly abandoned without achieving anything.
I constantly protect it like a dwelling or clothing,
nurturing it with all kinds of food and drink so that it lacks nothing.
It does not recognize kindness or affection but instead generates resentment and harm.
Ultimately returning to impermanence, since it brings no benefit,
it is detestable like a thief and like a moving latrine.
I shall now use this body to serve as a great bridge over the ocean of Saṃsāra.
This body of limitless abscesses and sores, hundreds and thousands of diseases and fears,
held together by sinew, blood, skin, and marrow, containing urine and feces.
I should now abandon it in order to seek the tranquil and supreme Nièpán.
[I shall gain] limitless concentration, wisdom, and merit.
I shall fully attain the subtle Fǎshēn,
and grant all sentient beings the various joys of the Dharma."
Fearing that his two older brothers might hinder him,
he immediately addressed his brothers:
"Please take the retinue and return to the place where we rested."
Sàduǒ returned to where the tiger was.
He removed all his clothes and hung them on the bamboo.
"I do this for the wisdom of Pútí, to forever leave the three realms of existence."
He immediately threw himself down, lying before the starving tiger.
The tiger was unable to eat him.
He used a dry bamboo splinter to pierce his own neck.
He threw himself down from a height; the great earth shook, and the sun lost its radiance.
Heaven rained down mixed flowers and various wondrous fragrances.
A voice in the air praised him, saying:
"This is unprecedented!"
The tiger immediately licked the blood and gradually was able to consume the flesh.
It regained the strength to eat.
Only bones remained.
In a past life,
the people of Yánfútí,
when the Kalpa of Sickness arrived, were universally distressed by disease.
At that time, the king of Yánfútí
was named Móxīsīnà.
He ruled over eighty-four thousand great cities,
and his authority was unrestricted.
Since his chief consort became pregnant,
whoever her hand touched who was sick was cured and recovered.
When the time was full, she gave birth to a son.
Immediately upon birth, he spoke, saying:
"I am able to cure sickness."
Also, at the time of his birth,
all the devas and spirits within Yánfútí announced together, saying:
"What the King has now produced is truly the medicine for humanity."
Because this announcement was widely heard, he was named Rènyào (Medicine for Humanity).
At that time, sick people were brought to see this prince.
When the sick people arrived,
if the prince touched them with his hand or touched them with his body, they were immediately all cured,
finding peace and joy.
Prince Rènyào cured sickness in this manner for a thousand years.
Afterward, he died.
The sick people came and, hearing that he had died,
were worried and wept, saying, "Who will save me now from the suffering and distress of sickness?"
The sick people asked:
"Where was Prince Rènyào's body cremated?"
They asked and learned the location and hurried to the cremation site.
They took out the bones, crushed them into powder, smeared it on their bodies, and were immediately all cured.
After the bones were used up, those who went to the place where the body was burned were all cured of their sickness.
"Prince Rènyào was none other than myself."
There was a prince who wanted to know his past lives.
So he asked the Fó.
The Fó said:
"There is no need to know it; it will cause you worry and sorrow."
The prince still insisted on knowing.
This happened up to three times.
The Fó then imparted the precepts, allowing him to know his past lives.
Thereupon the prince viewed his past affairs.
He saw that at age fifteen he was destined to die, and his sorrow was inexpressible.
When he reached the age of fifteen, he died.
The royal family buried him and planted a cypress tree that grew large.
A root grew down into the ground and went directly into his heart.
His consciousness was still in the body, watching the cypress root grow,
exactly piercing his heart.
Then, escaping from the root among the cypress leaves, he saw a sheep coming.
He thought to himself:
"If this sheep eats the cypress, it will certainly harm me again."
It happened that the sheep came and ate.
He was inside the sheep's belly.
He came out through the sheep's feces, attached to them.
A gardener gathered it up to fertilize chives.
He was attached between the chive leaves.
It happened that the queen craved chives.
She ordered her attendant to send for them.
The gardener held a knife, intending to cut the chives.
He feared being killed by the knife.
His worries concerning every matter became even more indescribable.
The gardener cut and bundled the chives and sent them to the royal household.
He was inside the bundle of chives.
When the royal household received the chives, the queen immediately ate them.
He entered her belly along with the chives and became a fetus.
When the months were full, he was born.
As he gradually grew up, he again recalled his past lives.
He then went to the Fó's presence and said:
"I no longer need to know my past lives.
It causes me sorrow and worry.
Having now known my past lives, I return this knowledge to the Fó."
The Fó said to the prince:
"At that time, I did not want to give it to you,
but you insisted on getting it.
Now that you regret it, you may cease."
In Rájashèchéng, there was a maiden.
Her courtesy name was Pólúobátí.
The king commanded that a courtesan house be established for her.
Those who spent the night with her paid two hundred taels of gold for a day and night.
People from the four directions gathered to view her, as she was exceedingly beautiful.
At that time, Prince Píngshā’s son, named Wúwèi,
slept with this courtesan and subsequently became pregnant.
The courtesan then commanded the doorkeeper, saying:
"If anyone asks to see me, reply that I am ill."
Later, when the months were full, she gave birth to a male child.
His appearance was handsome and proper.
That courtesan
immediately wrapped the child in white cloth and commanded a maidservant to discard him in the alley.
Prince Wúwèi saw it and asked a bystander:
"What is this thing?"
They replied:
"This is a small child."
He asked:
"Dead or alive?"
They replied:
"Still alive."
He sent someone to pick him up, take him back to his residence, and give him to a wet nurse to raise.
He immediately gave him the name Jípó Tóngzǐ (Jīva the youth).
Afterwards, he gradually grew up.
The prince loved him, called him, and spoke to him, saying:
"If you wish to remain in the royal household for long,
without possessing talent or skill,
you cannot consume the royal emoluments in vain.
You should study arts and skills."
He replied, "Yes."
He then studied under a physician in the country of Déchāshīluó.
His surname was Ātílî
and his courtesy name was Bīngjiāluó.
After seven years, he reported to his master, saying:
"When will my learning and practice be complete?"
The master then gave him a basket and tools for digging herbs.
"You must search for herbs in the country of Déchāshīluó,
within an area of one yóuxún (league),
and bring back anything that is not medicine."
Jípó Tóngzǐ
followed his master’s instructions and searched everywhere but could find nothing that was not medicine.
All the grasses, trees, and everything he saw,
he was skilled at distinguishing and knowing their uses; there was nothing that was not medicine.
He returned and reported to his master.
The master replied:
"You may now leave; your medical training is complete."
"Amongst Yánfútí, I am the first.
After I die, you shall be next."
He returned to the city of Pógātuó.
The wife of a great Zhàngzhě (elder) in that city
had suffered from headaches for twelve years.
Many physicians had treated her but could not cure her.
Jípó heard about this.
He immediately went to her house and spoke to the doorkeeper, saying:
"Inform your Zhàngzhě,
there is a physician outside the gate."
The doorkeeper informed the Zhàngzhě.
The Zhàngzhě’s wife asked:
"What is the doctor’s appearance like?"
He replied:
"He is young."
She thought to herself:
"The old, experienced doctors could not cure this,
much less a young man."
(She decided:) "If there is no harm, call him in."
Then Jípó approached the Zhàngzhě’s wife.
He immediately took fine medicine and boiled it with oil (sū).
He poured it into the Zhàngzhě’s wife's nose and mouth.
The oil and mucus came out together.
He ordered a servant to catch it in a vessel.
The oil was collected and saved.
The mucus was separated and discarded.
Jípó then said:
"This small amount of impure oil is still so frugally treasured,
how can you reward me?"
The Zhàngzhě’s wife replied:
"It is not easy to obtain things for the household.
What good is it to throw it away?
It can be used to light a fire, that is why we saved it.
Just cure the illness; why worry about such things?"
Afterwards, the illness was cured.
Then the Zhàngzhě’s wife
gave him four hundred thousand taels of gold,
along with male and female servants, cattle, and horses.
Jípó returned to Rájashèchéng and arrived at the gate of Prince Wúwèi.
The Prince called him in.
He fully reported the preceding circumstances to the Prince.
He offered all the wealth he had obtained to the Prince, saying:
"This is Jípó Tóngzǐ’s first successful treatment."
There was a king
whose title was Fànmónán.
He made offerings to the Buddha and the Sangha.
Whenever the fast day arrived,
the King would customarily lead his entourage to the place where the Buddha resided.
Whenever the Buddha preached the Dharma,
the King would listen to the scriptures with joy and reverence.
His crown prince, named Jūnlínrú,
with sincere diligence, awakened to the impermanence of the world.
He sought neither birth nor death and did not crave worldly glory.
He reported to the King, saying:
"It is hard to encounter a Buddha age, and difficult to hear the Dharma scriptures.
I beg to become a Shāmén (monk)." The King immediately granted permission.
Jūnlínrú then bade farewell to the King and went to the Buddha's place.
He requested to become a Bhikkhu (monk).
The Buddha then rubbed his head with his hand.
His hair spontaneously fell off and the kāṣāya robe clothed his body.
He upheld the serious precepts and diligently cultivated his practice.
Without growing tired, day and night, after three months,
he attained Arhatship (Luóhàn).
The King, at that time, did not know that he had attained the Way.
Seeing his arduous effort and coarse diet of vegetables,
he frequently went to offer him unique provisions, different from the other monks.
His heart was troubled (due to the hardship).
He usually addressed him, saying:
"In my kingdom, there is no shortage of rare treasures, the seven precious things, or sweet and savory foods.
Why are you happy to be a Shāmén?"
Jūnlínrú immediately lifted himself lightly up and resided in the air.
He flew, transformed, divided his body, scattered his form, and passed through things without obstruction.
When the King saw this,
sorrow and joy converged; he prostrated himself, touching the ground with five parts of his body, and paid reverence to Jūnlínrú.
The Buddha instructed Jūnlínrú to preach the Dharma of the Four Noble Truths (suffering, emptiness, and impermanence) to the King.
The King immediately understood the meaning
and attained the path of Sūtuóhuán (Stream-Enterer).
When Āyù Wáng (King Aśoka) first ascended the throne,
he established his younger brother Dìxū as Crown Prince,
and spoke to him, saying:
"You should cultivate good countenance and faith in the Buddhadharma."
Later, the brother went hunting and entered a forest.
He saw an ascetic (Xiānrén) roasting his body with five fires.
He immediately developed profound faith.
He bowed his head to the ground and revered his feet, asking:
"How long have you lived here, and what do you wear and eat?
How can you peacefully rest and yet give rise to greedy desires?"
He replied:
"For twelve years, I have constantly eaten the roots of trees and fruits,
twisted thatch for clothing,
and slept on grass mats.
But seeing deer engaging in cohabitation, I gave rise to thoughts of desire."
Dìxū was doubtful.
"If this hardship-practitioner still gives rise to the mind of desire,
how can the Buddha’s disciples, who speak of peace and practice pleasure,
see desire and be able not to give rise to the mind?
Since the mind of desire arises, how can they achieve aversion and departure?"
He then spoke a verse:
"The Xiānrén suffers in vain, ingesting air and eliminating foul food,
living in emptiness, eating roots, leaves, and fruits, yet love and desire cannot be extinguished.
The sons of Shìjiāmóuní (Śākyamuni) have sufficient, warm, and sweet clothing and food,
not abandoning human provisions. In Píntóu Shānfútí."
Dìxū further said:
"Śākyamuni’s disciples deceive the King to make him perform merit."
The King heard this and told his ministers:
"My younger brother has developed faith in external paths.
We must use skillful means to let him attain correct understanding."
"I wish to bathe
and must enter the bathing room.
You should adorn my brother with the heavenly crown and royal attire,
and let him ascend my throne."
When the King was bathing,
the ministers persuaded Dìxū.
Dìxū complied.
The King saw him and said:
"I have not yet perished,
and yet you have already assumed kingship!"
He then ordered his execution.
Many men carrying weapons surrounded him.
The ministers reported to the King:
"This is Your Majesty’s younger brother.
We beg Your Majesty to endure this and not generate anger."
He replied:
"I shall practice endurance."
"For seven days, I shall temporarily give him the kingdom and let him act as king.
Provide him with all kinds of music, entertainment, and court maidens.
All ministers and common people shall go and pay respects.
The executioners shall stand at the gate holding knives."
Day after day, the events were reported to the King until the seventh day.
On the seventh day, Āyù Wáng’s ministers and various people, having adorned (him) with royal regalia, accompanied Píduōshūkē (Vītāśoka) to jointly pay their respects to Āyù Wáng’s minister.
Then the King asked:
"You were king for seven days.
Did you enjoy hearing and seeing the various kinds of entertainment and music?"
He replied with a verse:
"During these seven days, I neither saw nor heard sounds,
nor smelled or tasted delicious flavors, nor perceived any tactile sensations.
My body’s ornaments and the court maidens
were not engaged with, because I was thinking about the fear of death.
The sound of singing and dancing maidens, the palace, and the bedding,
and the various treasures of the earth—I never experienced joy in them.
Because I saw the executioners standing at the gate holding knives,
and also heard the sound of the bell shaking, which caused me to harbor the fear of death.
Death pierced and nailed my heart, making me unaware of the subtle five desires.
Having contracted the disease of fearing death, I could not sleep peacefully.
Thinking only of death approaching, I did not notice the night had passed."
The King (Wáng) spoke again to his younger brother.
If you contemplate the suffering of death throughout your life,
even though you attain the most exquisite five desires, you will not generate attachment.
A monk (Bǐqiū) who has left home, regarding the twelve sensory fields (shí'èr rù),
contemplates the measureless suffering of endless rebirth (shēngsǐ) and the three evil paths.
Furthermore, he contemplates that the frenetic pursuits in the human and celestial realms, reaching to the four cardinal directions (sì wéi), ultimately lead to ruin and decay.
It is like an empty village without inhabitants.
The fire of impermanence burns all the worlds.
The disciples of the Buddha constantly practice this contemplation.
How then could afflictions (fánnǎo) arise?
The King used expedient means (fāngbiàn) of the Buddhadharma (Fófǎ) to instruct him.
Víduōshūkē said,
“From this day forward, I take refuge in the Buddha (Fó), the Dharma (Fǎ), and the Saṅgha (Sēng).”
The King embraced his younger brother’s neck with both hands,
and spoke to him, saying,
“I do not reject you; I merely wished to cause you to believe in the Buddhadharma.
That is why I displayed this expedient method.”
At that time, Víduōshūkē used various flowers, incense, and performing arts (jì yuè) to make offerings to the stupa of the Buddha (Fótǎ).
He used various foods and drinks to make offerings to the Saṅgha. On another day, he again went out hunting.
He arrived at an āraṇya (Āliànyě) dwelling place
and saw a monk (Bǐqiū) sitting.
His name was Tánwúdé.
There was a bird that broke off a wooden branch and remotely brushed the monk with it.
Dìxū (Tìxū) was delighted in his heart and made a vow, saying,
“When will I be able to be like that monk?”
The monk Tánwúdé knew Dìxū’s vow beforehand.
He immediately used his divine power (shénlì) to fly into the empty sky,
allowing Dìxū to see him.
He went to the Āyù (Āyù) Saṅghārāma (Sēngqiélán) and sat/stood in the pond water.
He removed his clothes, placed them in the empty sky, and entered the pond to wash.
Dìxū saw this and said,
“I must leave home (chūjiā).”
Returning to the palace, he reported to the King, saying,
“I earnestly request your compassion to permit me to leave home.”
The King said,
“With performing arts and a hundred flavors of delicacy, why must you leave home?”
The King used various expedient means to stop his intention.
But Dìxū’s resolve was firm, and he would absolutely not comply.
He replied to the King, saying,
“Joys are temporary, and separation will eventually occur.”
The Great King sighed and said, “Excellent! You should first practice begging for food, and then you may leave home.”
At that time, there was a large tree in the King’s rear garden.
He spread grass on the ground and made him dwell beneath it.
He gave him an earthenware bowl (wǎ bō) and ordered him to enter the palace to beg for food.
Víduōshūkē immediately took the bowl and walked into the palace grounds.
Various excellent foods were then given to him.
The King spoke to the palace attendants:
“How could you give the beggar such excellent food?
From now on, you must give him coarse food as alms,
even barley rice.”
At that time, Víduōshūkē received and ate it without considering it bad.
The King spoke to him, saying,
“Do not eat this food.
I permit you to leave home.
After leaving home, you must always come and see me.”
Immediately, garments and the bowl were prepared.
With a thousand chariots and ten thousand cavalry, he was escorted to Jīsì (Chicken Temple).
Thinking that being constantly active (dòng) would prevent him from cultivating the Way (xiūdào),
he then went to the country of Pítí
to leave home under the monk Tánwúdé.
One thousand sons of powerful and wealthy elders (zhǎngzhě zǐ) in that country also followed him and left home.
All the people were suspicious
and spoke among themselves, saying,
“Even he abandoned the royal throne.
What purpose do we have?”
Countless people all left home.

The King’s nephew, the son of a brāhmaṇa (pólúomén) named Āshì, also left home. All the feudal lords (zhūhóu), hundred officials, male and female servants, and retainers (pú shǐ) universally upheld the Five Precepts (Wǔjiè), observed the six fast days (liù zhāi) monthly, and fully practiced the Eight-Section Dharma (Bāzhīfǎ).
Because of this, many Kṣatriyas (Chàlì) left home, and the Buddhadharma flourished.
The external paths (wàidào) declined, completely losing offerings. When they universally begged for food, they received nothing.
They falsely entered the Buddhadharma and acted as śramaṇas (shāmén).
However, they still clung to their original doctrines while instructing the people.
The good monks did not associate with them in their work.
At that time, Mùliánzǐ Dìxū entrusted his disciples to Móxǐntuó
and withdrew to the tranquil Āxiūhé Mountain.
The monks of the external paths wished to use their scriptures to mix up and corrupt the Buddhadharma.
Thus, filth and impurity arose.
Some worshiped fire.
Some scorched their bodies with the five fires (wǔ rè).
Some immersed themselves in water during severe cold.
Some destroyed the Buddhadharma.
In this way, this confusion continued until for seven years the recitation of the Precepts (shuōjiè) could not take place.
Āyù sent a great minister into the royal Saṅghārāma.
He reported to the Elder (Shàngzuò), saying,
“The King orders the assembly of monks to reconcile and recite the Precepts.”
The Elder replied, saying,
“The good monks will not recite the Pōṣadha (Bùsà) together with the external path monks.”
The minister then proceeded to execute them one after another, reaching Dìxū.
The minister asked,
“Who are you?”
He replied,
“I am the King’s full brother.”
Upon this, the execution stopped.
The minister immediately reported to the King.
The King, hearing this, was astonished and dismayed, his heart filled with regret.
He immediately went to the monastery and asked,
“Monks, who is guilty of sin?”
One monk said,
“Both parties are guilty.”
Another monk said,
“Since there was no intention to kill,
the King himself is without sin.”
The King’s heart was filled with doubt.
He asked the monks,
“Is there anyone who can resolve my doubt?
If my doubt is resolved, I shall re-establish the Buddhadharma.”
The monks said,
“Dìxū can resolve it.”
He sent a messenger to welcome Dìxū.
The envoy transmitted the King’s intention, saying,
“Now the Buddhadharma has perished.
We humbly ask the Great Virtuous One (Dàdé)
to come and help re-establish it.”
Dìxū replied, saying,
“I left home precisely for the sake of the Buddhadharma; now the time has come.”
During the night, the King dreamed that a white elephant rubbed the King’s head with its trunk and held the King’s right hand.
The next morning, he asked the physiognomist.
The physiognomist replied, saying,
“The one who holds the King’s hand is the image of a śramaṇa.
He then asked the messenger, saying,
“Dìxū has now arrived.”
The King went out to welcome him.
Dìxū took the King’s hand and drew swords from his left and right sides, intending to harm him.
The King saw the shadow of the swords in the water and said,
“Previously, I commanded you to go to the monastery and ensure the assembly of monks reconciled and recited the Precepts.
You misinterpreted my intention and killed the monks.
Do you now wish to kill me as well?”
The King led Dìxū into the garden.
He personally washed his feet and rubbed them with oil.
He requested, saying,
“I wish to see the Great Virtuous One’s divine power.”
Dìxū circled the four directions, each distance being one yojana (yóuxún), and marked the boundary with a cord.
He placed carriages in the east, horses in the south, people in the west, and copper in the north.
He caused the water to swirl, making each of them ride the boundary; the area outside the boundary shook.
All the outer legs shook, but the inner legs did not move.
The King rejoiced, saying,
“My former doubts are resolved.
The evil doctrines within the Buddhadharma shall be eliminated.”
Dìxū preached the Jātaka Sūtra (Běnshēng Jīng) for him, saying,
“The Buddha told the monks,
‘First measure the mind, and then undertake the action.
All karma (yè) arises from the mind.’” Afterward, he attained the path of Arhat (Āluóhàn) and received the joy of liberation.
Remembering the King’s former promise,
“After leaving home, always come to see the King,”
he thought, “I must now fulfill my original promise.”
He then proceeded successively to travel to Pāṭaliputra (Bōzhālìfúduō) Country.
He rose early, put on his robes, held his bowl, and entered the country to beg for food.
Traveling in sequence, he arrived at the royal city and spoke to the gatekeeper:
“Go in and report to the King, saying,
‘Víduōshūkē is now outside the gate and wishes to see the Great King.’”
The gatekeeper immediately reported to the King.
The King said, “Lead him in.”
He immediately rose and performed a prostration, like a great tree falling.
He rose, joined his palms, and gazed at him without tiring.
He wept mournfully and said:
“All living beings should rejoice in harmony,
but you have now cast aside harmony and savor the tranquil mind.
I now know your mind: your wisdom is never satisfied.”
The minister Shànhù saw
Víduōshūkē wearing rag robes (fèn sǎo yī), holding an earthenware bowl, begging for food successively, receiving both coarse and fine food, his mind making no distinction.
The minister then reported to the King, saying,
“Víduōshūkē has few desires, is content, and his task is accomplished.”
The King then lifted him and placed him upon a fine seat.
He personally gave him various foods and drinks.
When he finished eating, he washed the bowl and placed it aside.
He preached the Dharma for the King:
“The King has now gained sovereignty; he should cultivate diligence (bù fàng yì).
The Three Jewels (Sānbǎo) are extremely rare to encounter; the King should diligently make offerings to them.”
He ascended into the empty sky, and all the common people saw him.
The King and the great multitude observed him, joining their palms,
their eyes not leaving him for an instant. The King asked him:
“You no longer cherish the love of relatives and friends, like a bird flying in the void.
I am bound by the chains of greed and defilement (tānrǎn), unable to depart freely.
Dhyāna (Chándìng) has superior fruits, entirely without obstruction.
Those blinded by desire and attachment cannot see this Dharma.
You now use your divine power to mock my arising of sensual love.
I formerly held arrogance regarding wisdom, but now you are the most victorious.
We are attached to worldly dharmas (shìfǎ); only upon seeing the noble ones (shèng) do we first know fear.
Now we weep because you abandon us.”
Pǐduōshūkē went to the frontier region.
Having arrived, he contracted a disease.
Because the illness was severe, his entire head developed sores.
At that time, the King heard of it.
He immediately sent attendants, doctors, and medicine for treatment.
Later, he achieved a slight recovery.
The doctors and attendants were all sent back.
The nourishment for his body relied solely on drinking cow's milk.
To beg for food, he went to a place where there were many cows.
There was another kingdom named Fēnnà Pódànuó, where everyone believed in heterodox doctrines.
A Buddhist disciple saw this and reported it to the King.
He commanded a Yèchā that, in the space of a single thought,
to immediately bring the heterodox disciples and their painted images.
He generated great anger.
Regarding all the heterodox practitioners in the kingdom of Fēnnà Pódànuó,
he killed them all.
In a single day, he killed 108,000 heterodox practitioners.
Furthermore, there was a heterodox disciple.
He loved the heterodox doctrine and served a naked god.
He drew the Rúlái bowing down to the god's feet.
At that time, the King heard of this matter again.
He immediately ordered others,
to seize this man and his relatives.
They were placed inside a house and burned with fire.
At that time, the King issued a command:
"If anyone can obtain the head of one Níjiàn,
I shall give him one gold coin."
Pǐduōshūkē, having entered the cattle-rearing place, had been ill for many days.
The hair on his head and temples, and his nails, had all grown long and sharp.
His clothes were worn out, ugly, and lacked luster.
At that time, the cowherd woman secretly generated this thought:
"Now this Níjiàn has come into my house."
She immediately spoke to her husband:
"You should kill this Níjiàn, take his head, and give it to the King.
You will certainly receive a gold reward."
Her husband drew his knife and went.
Pǐduōshūkē immediately reflected to himself,
seeing his karmic retribution, there was no way to escape.
He then accepted death.
He brought the head to the King's place, desiring to seek the gold.
The King was suspicious and immediately asked his doctors and attendants.
They replied: "This is the head of Pǐduōshūkē."
The King fainted and was unconscious for a long time.
A great minister addressed the King:
"A person free from defilements does not eliminate this suffering.
Great King, you should bestow fearlessness upon all sentient beings."
The King followed his words and proclaimed to all that they must not kill Níjiàn again.
The Bǐqiū became doubtful.
They asked Yōupójíduō.
"What karma did Pǐduōshūkē create in the past that caused him to receive this retribution now?"
He replied:
"In a past life, there was a hunter who killed many herds of deer.
In a great forest, there was a spring of water.
At that time, this hunter stretched nets and placed snares by the water's edge, killing many deer.
At this time, the Buddha had not yet appeared in the world.
There was a Yuánjué who ate by the water's edge.
After finishing his meal, he washed and returned to sit beneath a tree.
At that time, those deer smelled the Yuánjué’s scent and did not go to the water's edge.
The hunter waited but did not see the deer come.
He immediately followed their tracks to the place of the Pìzhīfó.
He thought:
'Because of this person sitting here, the deer have not come.'
He immediately used his knife to kill the Pìzhīfó.
The former hunter is Pǐduōshūkē.
Because he killed the deer, he now suffers great pain from illness.
Furthermore, because he killed the Pìzhīfó, he remained in hell for countless years.
He endured all kinds of suffering and affliction for five hundred lifetimes.
Whenever he was reborn in the human realm, he was constantly killed by others.
Now this is his final guǒbào.
Although he attained Luóhàn, he was still harmed by others.
He had previously left home during the Dharma of Jiāshè Fó.
He joyfully practiced bùshī.
He constantly exhorted people to make offerings to the Sēng.
There was a stūpa containing the Buddha’s hair and nails.
He made offerings to it with incense, flowers, banners, parasols, and various kinds of music and entertainment.
Due to this karmic reward, he was born into a great family.
For 100,000 years, he constantly practiced fànxíng.
He further generated a vow:
"May I, through this karmic condition, attain Āluóhàn."
Prince Jítuó addressed the Buddha, saying:
"Formerly I received the Five Precepts.
The precept against alcohol is difficult to uphold, and I fear that I might incur an offense.
Now I wish to abandon the Five Precepts and accept the Ten Virtuous Actions."
The Buddha said:
"When you drink alcohol, what evil deeds do you commit?"
He replied:
"The powerful and influential figures in the kingdom occasionally gather together.
Bringing alcohol and food, we entertain each other.
We achieve happiness, but personally, I commit no other evil.
When I receive alcohol, I remember the precepts and do not commit evil."
The Buddha said:
"If a person can be like you, what harm is there in drinking alcohol for the rest of his life?
One who acts like this should instead generate fú and will not have committed a sin.
In general, there are two types of good deeds performed by people:
First, those with outflows (yǒulòu).
Second, those without outflows (wúlòu).
Those whose goodness is yǒulòu receive the joys of humans and heaven.
Those whose goodness is wúlòu transcend the suffering of shēngsǐ.
The fruit and reward of Nièpán.
If a person drinks alcohol but does not give rise to evil karma,
due to the condition of a good mind, he receives a good reward.
Why should you lose the upholding of the Five Precepts?"
In the city of Shèwèi, there were powerful clans, Chàlì Dukes, and Kings.
Due to minor contention, a great enmity arose.
They each formed plots and raised troops to attack one another.
Both families were heroes and strongmen in the country.
They were all also relatives, and it was not possible to arrest and confine them.
They fought chaotically and would not listen to rational advice.
(The King) was deeply worried about this.
He further thought to himself:
"In the past, the great minister of the former king, named Tíwéiluó,
relied on his noble family's wealth, status, and power.
He was dismissive and arrogant toward me, ridiculing and playing tricks on me.
At that time, filled with anger and resentment, I truly wanted to execute and eliminate him.
I reported the matter to my father.
But my father did not listen.
Harboring malice and holding onto hatred, there was nothing I could do.
Distressed and melancholy, I could neither eat nor drink.
The Queen Mother saw my distress and suffering.
She gave me various kinds of counsel, but my mind was still troubled.
She thereupon sought good alcohol and urged me to drink it.
At that time, I addressed my mother, saying:
'Our ancestors have continuously served Nàluóyán Tiān.
If I drink alcohol now, I fear the Deva will certainly be angry.
The Póluómén will surely criticize and punish me.'
The mother, during the stillness of the night,
secretly opened the palace gate so that no one would know.
She pressed me repeatedly, and though reluctant, I complied.
After having drunk the alcohol, I forgot my sorrow and hatred.
I gathered the palace women and engaged in singing, entertainment, and music for twenty-one days.
From this, I gained relief."
Having reflected on this,
he immediately ordered his loyal ministers,
to prepare good wine and various sweet delicacies.
He summoned all the ministers to gather in the King's hall.
The loyal minister prepared a liúlí bowl.
The bowl held three shēng.
The King first poured a bowl.
Everyone prepared a bowl of sweet, marvelous medicine.
Afterward, they discussed state affairs and simultaneously performed various musical and theatrical acts.
As the men received the wine and heard the music, their hearts were joyful; they forgot their enmity, and were completely free of worry.
The King again held his bowl and addressed the gentlemen, saying:
"Gentlemen, the cultivation of virtue has been passed down through generations.
One should follow and respect the sacred teachings without divergence.
Why, gentlemen, do you become angry and contentious over minor matters like this?
If you are not forbearing, I fear the ancestral shrines of the kingdom will perish.
Therefore, I strongly advise you to please bring this to an end."
The ministers addressed the King:
"We respectfully accept your solemn command and dare not disobey."
Thus, peace resulted—this was the merit of the wine.
The Queen of Āyù Wáng,
named Bōmó Pódǐ, gave birth to a son.
His physical form and color were handsome, and his eyes were supreme.
There was no one who saw him who did not love and delight in him.
A palace servant reported to the King:
"The Queen has given birth to a son."
The King was greatly delighted.
Therefore, this child was named Dá Mópódànuó. [The servant] immediately embraced the child and showed him to Āyù Wáng.
When the King saw him, he joyfully spoke a gè:
My son's eyes are handsome and majestic, created by merit;
their radiance is intensely bright, like a Yōubōluó flower.
With these meritorious eyes adorning one side,
his face is handsome and proper, like the full moon in autumn.
When Jiūnàluó grew up, a consort was taken for him.
The consort's name was Yúzhēnàmóluó. At that time, Āyù Wáng,
led Jiūnàluó to the Kī-Sì.
In the monastery, there was a Shàngzuò who was a Luóhàn possessing the Liù Tōng.
Named Yěshě.
At that time, Yěshě saw Jiūnàluó.
Before long, he was destined to lose his eyes.
He immediately addressed the King, saying:
"Do not let Jiūnàluó cease his self-cultivation."
Then Āyù Wáng said to Jiūnàluó:
"Great Virtuous One, remember what you have done.
You must follow it."
Then Jiūnàluó paid homage at Yěshě's feet.
Saying:
"Great Virtuous One, please teach me what to do."
Yěshě replied:
"The eye is not permanent. You must contemplate this."
He immediately spoke a verse:
You, Jiūnàluó, constantly contemplate the impermanence, sickness, and suffering of the eye.
It is the accumulation of various sufferings; due to it, ordinary people give rise to faults and confusion.
Then Jiūnàluó sat alone in a quiet place within the palace, contemplating,
that the eyes and other sense bases are suffering and impermanent.
At that time, Āyù Wáng's First Queen,
named Wéishāluòqǐduō,
went to Jiūnàluó's location and saw him sitting alone.
Looking at his eyes, she generated lustful desire.
She embraced him with her hands.
And spoke a verse:
The fire of powerful love now burns my heart;
Like fire burning firewood, you must satisfy my desire.
Jiūnàluó covered his ears,
and spoke a verse:
Now you are my mother; this unrighteous love ought to be abandoned.
It opens the gate to the evil path.
The Queen's heart grew angry and furious.
She spoke another verse:
Love goes to your place, but you have no love.
If your heart possesses evil, it will perish shortly, in a moment.
Jiūnàluó said:
I would rather die now than give rise to an impure mind.
If one generates evil thoughts, they lose the wholesome Dharma of humans and devas.
Since wholesome Dharma is not complete, upon what can one rely to be born?
Wéishāluòqǐduō
constantly waited for his faults and desired to kill him.
To the north there was a country
named Déchāshīluó.
It had rebelled against the king.
Āyù Wáng commanded Jiūnàluó:
You go to that country.
[Jiūnàluó] answered the king, "So be it."
The king thought in his heart,
therefore he doubly embellished and carefully repaired the roads,
ensuring that the old, the sick, and the dead were all kept out of sight.
At that time, the King and Jiūnàluó rode together in one carriage to send him off.
Near the road, as they were about to part,
[the King] embraced his son’s neck with his hand.
Seeing Jiūnàluó’s eyes,
he wept and said:
If anyone sees Jiūnàluó’s eyes, because their heart rejoices,
all illnesses are removed.
The physiognomist saw the King.
He looked only at the son's eyes and paid attention to nothing else.
He immediately spoke a verse, saying:
The prince’s eyes are pure; when the King looks, his heart rejoices.
All the people of the country, seeing them, are delighted as if in heaven.
If these eyes are lost, everyone will suffer distress.
Subsequently, Jiūnàluó
proceeded step by step until he reached the country of Déchāshīluó.
The people of that country, hearing [of his arrival], repaired and adorned all the roads extending half a yojana [outwards].
Water was placed everywhere awaiting the arriving assembly.
Thereupon, the people spoke a verse:
The people of Déchāshīluó hold jeweled ewers filled with water
and various offerings to welcome Prince Jiūnàluó.
When the Prince arrived,
the people put their palms together and made this statement:
We welcome the Prince.
We do not do this for contention, nor
do we bear resentment toward the Great King.
Rather, the minister sent by the King who is in our country,
has acted lawlessly.
We wish to depose him.
At that time, the people
honored Prince Jiūnàluó with various offerings and welcomed him into the country.
At that time, Āyù Wáng contracted a severe illness.
Feces issued from his mouth, and impure fluids oozed from his pores.
All excellent physicians were unable to cure him.
The King then spoke to his officials:
Summon Jiūnàluó to return.
I shall consecrate him and bestow the throne upon him.
I no longer cling to my body or life.
At that time, Wéishāluòqǐduō addressed the King:
I can cause the King’s illness to be cured.
The King accepted her words and dismissed the physicians.
Wéishāluòqǐduō told the physicians:
Go outside and inquire if there is any man or woman whose illness is like the King's; if so, bring them in.
At that time, there was a person in Āpíluó Guó whose illness was exactly like the King's.
The sick person's wife sought a physician for him.
The physician replied:
Bring him; I want to see him.
I will then prescribe medicine.
The wife sent him to the physician.
The physician sent him to the King’s Lady (Wéishāluòqǐduō).
Then the King’s Lady placed the sick person in a solitary location
and had his abdomen cut open, examining the two types of intestines (raw and cooked).
There was a large worm.
If the worm moved upward, feces came out of the mouth.
If the worm moved downward, discharge came out below.
If it moved left or right, it came out of the pores.
Then the King’s Lady placed Málízhē next to the worm,
but the worm did not die.
She again placed Bìbō next to the worm,
but the worm also did not die.
She again placed dry ginger next to the worm,
but the worm also did not die.
Finally, she placed garlic next to the worm,
and the worm immediately died.
Then the King’s Lady fully reported this matter to the King:
The King should now eat garlic.
The illness will immediately be cured.
The King replied:
I am a Kṣatriya and cannot eat garlic.
The Lady again said:
For the sake of your body and life, consider it medicine and eat it.
The King then ate it; the worm died and the illness was removed.
His elimination was as it was formerly.
The King washed and bathed cleanly, and spoke to the Lady:
What do you seek now? I shall grant it according to your wish.
The Lady addressed the King:
I request that the King permit me to be King for seven days.
The King said to the Lady: If you become King, you will surely kill me.
The Lady replied again:
After seven days have passed, I will return the rule to the King.
At that time, the King permitted it.
The Lady falsely acted as King.
She wrote a letter to the people of Déchāshīluó,
commanding them to take Jiūnàluó's eyes. After the letter was written,
she needed the tooth seal to stamp it.
While the King slept,
the Lady approached the King to stamp the letter.
The King suddenly awoke with a start.
The Lady addressed the King:
Why are you startled?
The King said:
I dreamt that vultures desired to take Jiūnàluó's eyes.
The Lady replied:
Prince Jiūnàluó is now very safe and sound.
He dreamt a second time.
The King again arose startled: I have dreamt again.
The Lady asked:
What was the dream like this time?
The King replied:
I saw Jiūnàluó's head, beard, hair, and nails all grown long and sharp,
but he could not speak.
The Lady replied:
He is safe now; please do not worry about it.
The King slept again.
The Lady secretly stamped [the letter] with the Great King’s tooth seal.
She dispatched a messenger to send it to the people of Déchāshīluó.
The King again dreamt that all of his own teeth had fallen out.
When the bright clear morning arrived, after bathing and washing were complete,
he summoned the physiognomist and informed him of the dream.
The physiognomist replied:
If a person has this dream,
their son will lose his eyes;
it is no different from losing the son.
When the King heard this,
he immediately stood up, put his palms together,
and, facing the Gods of the West, pronounced this vow:
Now I single-mindedly take refuge in the Buddha, the pure Dharma, and the Saṅgha.
All sages and immortals in the world are supreme in the world.
May all the noble assemblies protect Jiūnàluó.
The messenger carrying the letter arrived at the country of Déchāshīluó.
When the people there saw this letter arrive,
thinking of Jiūnàluó, they collectively concealed the letter and did not give it to him.
These people thought further:
Āyù Dà Wáng is very dreadful and not respected in his heart.
He desires to take the eyes of his own son;
how much more will he commit evil against us?
They gave the letter to Jiūnàluó.
When Jiūnàluó received the letter,
he said to the people:
If you are able to take my eyes, now follow your intention.
At that time, the people summoned a Zhāntuóluó:
You must gouge out Jiūnàluó's eyes.
The Zhāntuóluó put his palms together and spoke:
I cannot comply now.
If a person can remove the light from the full moon,
that person will be able to remove the bright moon-like eyes from your face.
At that time, Jiūnàluó
immediately removed his jeweled crown and spoke to the Zhāntuóluó:
If you gouge out my eyes, I will give [the crown] to you.
There was another person whose appearance was repulsive,
having eighteen kinds of ugliness.
He spoke to Jiūnàluó:
I can gouge out the eyes.
At that time, Jiūnàluó quickly recalled what the great virtuous Yéshè had taught.
He then spoke a verse:
Remembering the good friend's true teachings and contemplating this meaning,
I know the eye is impermanent. My good friend, the benefactor,
has already spoken of the cause and condition of the suffering of the eye. I always contemplate
that all things are impermanent—I deeply recall and hold fast to the teacher's instruction.
I do not fear suffering, seeing that the Dharma is non-abiding. Constantly relying on the King’s command,
you may take my eyes.
He spoke to the ugly person:
You should take one of my eyes and place it in my hand. I
want to observe it.
When this ugly person wished to take his eye, countless
people scolded each other angrily
and spoke a verse:
His eyes are pure and stainless, like the moon in the sky.
Your gouging out these eyes now is like pulling a lotus from a pond.
These countless people wept and cried mournfully.
At that time, the ugly person immediately took out the eye and placed it in Jiūnàluó’s hand.
Then Jiūnàluó received it with his hand and spoke a verse toward the eye:
You were previously able to see all forms, but now,
why do you not see? Previously, those who saw you gave rise to love.
Now, looking, [you are] unreal, merely illusion, like water foam.
You are empty and have no reality, no power, and no self-mastery.
If a person sees this, they will not endure suffering.
Contemplating that all phenomena are impermanent,
he attained the Xūtuóhuánguǒ (Sotāpanna result).
He further said to the ugly person:
Take the remaining eye as you wish.
At that time, that ugly person gouged it out again
and placed it in Jiūnàluó's hand.
Having lost his physical eyes, he gained the Eye of Wisdom.
He spoke a verse again:
I now abandon these fleshly eyes. The Eye of Wisdom is hard to obtain,
but I have now obtained it. The King has now abandoned me; I am no longer a prince.
I have now attained the Dharma and become a Prince of the Dharma. From now on, I am free.
Leaving the palace of suffering, I ascend the palace of the self-mastering Dharma King.
Jiūnàluó knew that the one who took his eyes was Wéishāluòqǐduō.
He spoke a verse, saying:
May the King’s Lady live long in prosperity and happiness. May she exist forever when her life ends,
without exhaustion or destruction. By means of her expedient action, I have accomplished what needed to be done.
The wife of Jiūnuóluó heard that her husband had lost his eyes.
When she saw him, she immediately fainted and only revived after being sprinkled with water.
Weeping, she spoke a verse:
The bright light of your eyes was lovable; seeing them in the past gave rise to joy.
Now seeing them separated from your body, great anguish arises in my heart.
Jiūnuóluó spoke to his wife, saying:
Do not weep.
I created the karma myself, and I receive this retribution myself.
He spoke another verse, saying:
All beings in the world receive a body through karma; their bodies are composed of various sufferings.
You ought to know that all things that combine must separate.
You should understand this matter and ought not to weep.
Jiūnuóluó, accompanied by his wife,
returned from the Dé chā shī luó Guó to the court of Āyù Wáng.
These two people had never trod the ground since they were born.
Their bodies were soft and weak, unfit for labor.
Jiūnuóluó was skilled at playing the zither.
Furthermore, he could sing and play wind instruments.
Following their former route, they begged for food to sustain their lives.
Gradually traveling, they arrived at their home country.
When they wished to enter the palace gate,
the gatekeepers at that time
did not permit them to proceed.
Since they were not allowed to proceed, they went back out
and took up residence in the stable yard for chariots and horses.
During the latter part of the night, he played the zither and sang.
The song said:
My eyes are already lost;
the Four Noble Truths (Sì Dì) have already been seen.
He spoke another verse, saying:
If a person has wisdom, he can perceive the Twelve Sense Bases (shí èr rù).
By means of this lamp of wisdom, one achieves release from the suffering of life and death.
If you wish to seek supreme joy, you ought to contemplate this.
The King heard the singing voice
and his heart was greatly rejoiced.
He immediately spoke a verse, saying:
The speaking of this verse and the sound of the zither now seem like they belong to my son
Jiūnuóluó. If this voice is indeed his, why does he not come to see me?
The King commanded a man to listen.
(He said:) "That sounds like Jiūnuóluó's voice.
It is clear, wonderful, sorrowful, and charming, and it causes my heart to be distraught.
Like an elephant that has lost its young, I pace anxiously and am uneasy.
You may go and look.
If it is him, bring him here."
The messenger saw a man with no eyes,
his skin exposed and rough, making him unrecognizable.
He returned and reported to the Great King:
"It is a solitary blind man and his wife dwelling together in the stable yard."
The King heard this, became distressed, and pondered,
speaking a verse, saying:
"As I dreamed in the past, I saw Jiūnuóluó losing his eyes.
I have no doubt that this blind man now is Jiūnuóluó.
You may go back there again, and simply bring this person.
Because I am thinking of my son, my heart is restless."
The messenger received the command and went back to his location.
He spoke to Jiūnuóluó, saying:
"Whose child are you? What is your name and lineage?"
Jiūnuóluó replied with a verse:
"My father's name is Āshū kē, increasing the lineage of the Peacock Clan (Kǒngquè).
All the great lands are governed by him.
I am his Prince, named Jiūnuóluó.
He is of the solar lineage, a Dharma King Buddha (Fǎ Wáng Fó), and I am now a Dharma Prince (Fǎ Wáng Zǐ)."
The messenger brought Jiūnuóluó and his wife into the palace.
When the King saw Jiūnuóluó,
exposed to the wind and sun, his clothing was a mixture of straw and ragged cloth.
His appearance was so changed that he was unrecognizable.
The King felt doubt in his heart and spoke to him, saying:
"Are you Jiūnuóluó or not?"
He replied, "I am."
The King fainted and fell to the ground.
The attendants surrounding the King
spoke a verse, saying:
The King sees Jiūnuóluó, who has a face but no eyes.
Anguish burns his heart; he falls from his seat onto the ground.
The attendants sprinkled the King until he regained consciousness.
He returned to his seat,
held Jiūnuóluó and placed him on his knees,
then embraced his neck, weeping and shedding tears.
He wiped his head and face, recalling his former appearance,
and spoke a verse, saying:
"Where are your beautiful and dignified eyes now? You must
now speak of the cause of losing your eyes. You are now eyeless, like the sky without the moon.
Who caused your appearance to change? Your former countenance
was like that of an Immortal. Who lacked compassion and destroyed your eyes?
Who in the world is your enemy? The root of my suffering
arises from this. Who destroyed the wonderful color of your body?
The fire of regret and anguish now burns my body, like a thunderbolt
that crushes and breaks a tree. The thunder of regret shatters my heart.
Quickly tell me this cause."
Then Jiūnuóluó
answered with a verse:
"Does the King not hear the Buddha's words? Retribution is inexpressible.
Even a Pratyekabuddha (Pìzhīfó) cannot escape it.
All ordinary people (fán fū) are entirely created by karma.
When the time for the consequences of good and evil karma arrives, they must be received.
All sentient beings create their own retribution and receive it themselves.
Because I know this cause, I do not speak of the person who destroyed my eyes.
I created this suffering myself; there is no other creator.
This cause relating to the eyes did not originate from a human action.
The suffering of all sentient beings is likewise thus;
it all originates from karma. The King ought to know this matter."
The King spoke another verse:
"You must speak only of the person; I will not generate anger (chēn xīn).
If you do not speak, my heart will be agitated and uneasy."
At that time, the King realized that this was the work of Wēishāluòqǐduō.
He summoned Wēishāluòqǐduō
and spoke a verse, saying:
"You have committed a great evil now; why does the earth not swallow you?
Now, you have acted contrary to the Dharma (fǎ), and this is a great fault against me.
Since you have committed evil now, I abandon you from this day forward,
just as a person practicing good abandons profit that is contrary to the Dharma."
The King, burned by the fire of anger,
looked at Wēishāluòqǐduō
and spoke another verse, saying:
"Now I wish to tear out her eyes, and I wish to use an iron saw
to dismember her body, use an axe to break her body, and use a knife to cut her tongue,
use a knife to sever her neck, use fire to burn her body, and force her to drink poison
to end her life."
The King spoke of these measures,
desiring to punish Wēishāluòqǐduō.
Jiūnuóluó heard this
and generated deep compassion.
He spoke another verse:
"The various evil karmas committed by Wēishāluòqǐduō—
Great King, you ought not to kill her now.
Of all great strengths, none surpasses patient endurance (rěnrǔ).
What the World-Honored One (Shìzūn) spoke of, that is the most foremost."
At that time, the King did not accept his son's words.
He placed Wēishāluòqǐduō
in a hut made of dry material and burned it with fire.
He also ordered the execution of the people of Dé chā shī luó.
At that time, a Bhikṣu felt doubt
and asked the Elder Yōupōjíduō, saying:
"What karma did Jiūnuóluó create previously that he now receives this retribution?"
He replied:
"In the past, in the Bōluónài Guó, there was a hunter.
He went into the Snow Mountains and killed many herds of deer.
Another time, he went to the Snow Mountains and encountered thunder and lightning.
There were five hundred deer.
Due to fear, they entered a stone cave.
The hunter captured all of them.
If he killed them all, the meat would rot.
He had no choice but to
immediately gouge out both their eyes, so that they would not die, but they would not know how to leave.
Later, he gradually killed them.
That former hunter is Jiūnuóluó.
For countless years, he was constantly in hell.
After leaving hell, he was born among humans.
Within five hundred lifetimes, he was constantly having his eyes gouged out.
This is now the last remaining retribution."
The Bhikṣu asked again:
"For what reason was he born into a great lineage and possessed dignified and beautiful eyes?"
He replied:
"In the distant past, when human life spanned forty thousand years,
a Buddha named Jiāluójiūcūndà
appeared in the world and entered Nirvāṇa without remainder (wú yú niè pán).
At that time, there was a King
named Shūpō, who erected a stupa of four jewels for the Buddha.
Later, when that King died,
his younger brother, who did not believe in the Buddha,
dug up and took all the objects from beneath the stupa, leaving only earth and wood.
All the people, seeing the stupa destroyed,
lamented aloud with sorrow.
At that time, a son of an elder (zhǎng zhě zǐ) asked,
'Why are those people grieving?'
The people replied,
'The stupa of the World-Honored One originally contained four treasures.
Unexpectedly, now they have all been destroyed.'
That elder's son immediately restored the four treasures as originally adorned.
Furthermore, he made it taller and broader, surpassing the original structure.
He also erected a golden image and placed it inside the stupa.
Having completed what was done,
he then made a vow, saying:
'The Buddha Jiāluójiūcūndà was formerly the teacher of the world.
May my future teacher also be like the one today.'
Bhikṣus ought to know
that the son of the elder in the past is Jiūnuóluó.
Because he repaired and maintained the stupa of the Tathāgata (Rúlái) Jiāluójiūcūndà, he was able to be born into a great lineage.
Because he created the image of the Tathāgata, the body he has now obtained is supremely beautiful and dignified.
Because he vowed to meet a good teacher, he now encounters Shìjiā
and sees the Four Noble Truths."
Formerly, the Buddha (Fó) was upon the Deer Park (Lùyěchǎng) in the kingdom of Bōluónài.
He preached the Dharma (Fǎ) to the assembly.
At that time, the crown prince of a great kingdom, leading more than five hundred sons of minor kings,
went to the place of the Buddha (Fó).
They paid homage to the Buddha (Fó), retired, and sat on one side,
listening to the Dharma (Fǎ).
The princes then addressed the Buddha (Fó), saying:
"The path of the Buddha (Fó Dào) is pure, marvelous, profound, distant, and difficult to attain.
Since ancient times,
have there truly been kings, crown princes, high ministers, or sons of elders
who have abandoned their kingdom, officials, populace, affection, glory, and joy, and gone forth to practice as Śrāmaṇas (Shāmén)?"
The Buddha (Fó) said:
"The glory, joy, affection, and love associated with worldly kingdoms
are known to be like illusions, transformations, dreams, and echoes,
quickly arriving and quickly departing, impossible to maintain permanently.
He further said:
Kings and crown princes cannot attain the Way (Dào) due to three matters.
What are these three matters?
First, they are arrogant and willful, failing to study the profound principles of the Buddhist Sūtras (Fójīng) in order to save the root of the spirit (shén běn).
Second, they are grasping and greedy, failing to contemplate giving charity (Bùshī) to relieve the distress of the poor and those in danger.
The wealth and treasures possessed by their ministers and generals
they do not share with the populace, thereby failing to cultivate the root of wealth (cái běn).
Third, they cannot keep far away from matters of sexual desire and pleasurable love,
and abandon the vexations and distress of this imprisonment,
going forth to practice as a Śrāmaṇa (Shāmén) to extinguish all suffering and hardship, and thereby cultivating the root of the body (shēn běn).
Therefore, when a Bodhisattva (Púsà) is born as a king,
he removes these three matters and naturally attains Buddhahood (Fó).
Furthermore, there are three matters [to be done]:
First, in youth and vigor, they study and manage the kingdom,
leading and transforming the populace so they practice the Ten Good Deeds (Shí Shàn).
Second, in middle age, they use wealth to give charity (shī) to the poor, orphaned, and widowed, and they share joy with their ministers, warriors, and the populace.
Third, they constantly consider impermanence (wúcháng)—that life does not remain long.
They should properly renounce home and practice as a Śrāmaṇa (Shāmén),
severing the causes and conditions of suffering, and not undergoing Saṃsāra (shēngsǐ) again.
If these three matters are not practiced, they receive the death of an ordinary being."
The World-Honored One (Shìzūn) said:
"Formerly, in my previous life, I acted as a Cakravartin (Zhuǎnlún Shèngwáng).
My name was Nánwáng Huángdì, and the Seven Treasures followed me.
I thought to myself:
'Human life is short and temporary, impermanent, and hard to safeguard.
One must only perform merit (fú) to seek the truth of the Way (Dào zhēn).'
I resolved to constantly practice charity (Bùshī).
All the wealth and goods possessed by the people of the world,
I shared with the populace, thereby planting meritorious virtue (fúdé).
I must only renounce home and practice as a Śrāmaṇa (Shāmén),
severing greed and desire in order to extinguish suffering."
He combed his hair, and finding white hairs, plucked them and placed them on the table.
The King wept, saying:
"The first messenger has suddenly arrived again.
It is proper now to renounce home, practice as a Śrāmaṇa (Shāmén), and seek the natural Way (Zìrán Dào)."
He held the hairs in his palm,
and spoke a Gāthā (Jì) himself, saying:
"Now white hairs have grown upon my body and head, serving as proof.
The Heavenly Messenger has summoned me; now is precisely the time to renounce home,
practice as a Śrāmaṇa (Shāmén), enter the mountains, and cultivate the Way (Dào)."
After completing his human lifespan, he was immediately reborn in the Second Heaven,
becoming the crown prince of the Deva King Śakra (Tiāndì Shì).
Afterwards, he managed the world, just like the great king.
He again saw white hairs and went forth to practice as a Śrāmaṇa (Shāmén).
He successively acted as father and son.
Above, he was the Deva King (Tiāndì).
Below, he was the Sage King (Shèngwáng).
In the middle, he was the Crown Prince (Tàizǐ).
Each role occurred thirty-six times.
For tens of thousands of years, the cycle ended and then began again.
By practicing these three matters, he naturally attained Buddhahood (Fó)."
"At that time, the father is my present self.
The crown prince is Śariputra (Shèlìfú).
The grandson king is Ānanda (Ānán).
They were successively born from each other, continually becoming kings to transform the world."
At that time, the kings, crown princes, and all the populace
were all greatly delighted.
They accepted the Five Precepts (Wǔ Jiè) of the Buddha (Fó), becoming Upāsakas (Yōupósè),
and attained the path of the Sotāpanna (Xūtuóhuán Dào).
Formerly, King Bīxiānnì
had two consorts.
The son of the first consort was named Liúlí.
The son of the second consort was named Jí.
On the day Jí was first born,
treasures from the four directions arrived simultaneously as offerings.
The King said:
"None of my sons have ever been born like this.
He may be named Jí."
When he grew up and studied, there was no Sūtra (Jīng) he did not master.
The King established a separate dwelling for him, constructed of the Seven Treasures, with golden and silver statues of men and women flanking the gate.
He carried a jeweled bowl filled with the Seven Precious Things (Qī Zhēn).
Though he took from it day and night, it would immediately refill as before.
The crown prince (Liúlí) was jealous and sent troops to seize it.
At that time, there were more than five hundred Deva-soldiers (Tiānbīng) on horseback
guarding Jí’s residence.
Liúlí’s troops saw them, were frightened, retreated, and returned.
The Crown Prince (Tàizǐ) was angry.
He sent for Jí and questioned him, saying:
"Last night I sent troops to comfort you.
Did you conceal troops inside, intending to rebel?"
Jí replied:
"I dare not, and I do not keep civilian or military followers.
Inside, there is not an inch of weaponry."
Liúlí sent men to check, and there was nothing inside or outside.
Liúlí's mind was cleared, and he reported the full matter to the Buddha (Fó).
The Buddha (Fó) said:
"Jí cultivated virtue and encountered strong conditions;
therefore, his treasure cannot be seized.
In the time of the Buddha Vipaśyin (Wéiwèi Fó),
there was a person who went to the temple, offered food to the monks (sēng), and subsequently offered one male and one female servant to sweep the temple.
Since then, in the heavens and among humans, he has received immeasurable blessings.
This is precisely Zuìshèng (Jí)."
The King of the Bōluónài [Vārāṇasī] state and his wife gave birth to a daughter.
Her body was golden yellow.
Her hair was deep blue (kòngqīng).
When she reached the age of sixteen,
her parents saw that the daughter had grown up
and wanted to seek a husband for her.
The daughter said,
"I do not need a husband.
If you wish to seek a husband for me,
he must also have a golden yellow body and deep blue hair.
Only such a person would be acceptable."
Her parents then sought [such a man] for her,
but utterly failed to find one.
At that time, the Buddha was in the Shèwèi [Śrāvastī] state.
There was a man from the Shèwèi state
who went to the Bōluónài state for hired work.
The King immediately invited the hired man to meet him and exchanged greetings.
He showed the daughter to him and said,
"I am seeking a husband for this daughter.
Are there any good people in the world [suitable for her]?"
The hired man answered,
"There is a person in my state
who surpasses even this daughter."
The King heard this and was delighted.
He ordered the hired man to welcome and fetch the Buddha.
The hired man then wrote a letter to the Buddha.
The letter stated that this daughter was extremely beautiful, excellent, and unparalleled,
and sought to take her as a wife for the Buddha.
The Buddha was in the Qíhuán [Jetavana] [monastery],
teaching scriptures to several thousand Bhikṣus.
The man carrying the letter went straight up to the Buddha.
The Buddha already knew what the letter contained.
Upon receiving it, he tore and destroyed it.
He wrote a letter in reply to the golden-colored woman, saying,
"The suffering of people all arises from love and affection (ēn'ài).
After birth, one must grow old.
After old age, one must become sick.
Sickness leads to death.
Death leads to sorrow and weeping.
The suffering in the world all arises from love and affection."
The woman received the letter and contemplated it herself.
Immediately, she attained the Five Supernormal Powers (wŭtōngdá).
The first was that her eyes could see through [all things].
The second was that her ears could hear through [all sounds].
The third was knowing the minds and thoughts of others.
The fourth was knowing the sources of her births.
The fifth was the ability to fly.
She then took leave of her parents and flew before the Buddha.
The Buddha immediately smiled.
A five-colored radiance emerged from his mouth.
Ānán [Ānanda] stepped forward and asked.
The Buddha said,
"Ānán,
do you see how capable this woman is?
If you wish to know who she is:
In the time of Jiāshè [Kāśyapa]
Buddha,
this golden-colored woman was the wife of a poor family.
Her husband's hands and feet were contracted, and he could not walk.
At that time, the King was named Jīlì.
He had a daughter
who was beautiful.
Adorned in gold and silver yīngluò [jewelry],
she went directly to the place of Jiāshè Fó to receive the scriptures and precepts.
At that time, the wife of the poor man,
whose body was covered only by a coarse linen cloth,
also followed and arrived at the Buddha's place.
Outsiders did not allow her to proceed forward.
The poor man's wife thought to herself,
"Why am I alone not allowed to go forward?
And why does the King's daughter go forward alone?"
The Buddha immediately knew this.
He ordered someone to call her forward.
The woman immediately bowed and stated,
"Why is this King's daughter alone so noble and wealthy?
And why am I alone so poor?"
The Buddha said to the woman,
"This King's daughter,
in her previous life, liked to read scriptures and donated clothing to the Śrāmaṇas.
Therefore, in this life, she has obtained nobility, venerability, dignity, and beauty.
In your previous life, you did not delight in the Dharma.
You were stingy and greedy, unwilling to practice giving (bùshī).
When you saw Śrāmaṇas, you did not respect or serve them.
This caused you to be poor like this in the present life."
The poor woman said,
"I pray that the Buddha will pity my ignorance and teach me the Dharma."
Jiāshè Fó then taught her.
She read the scriptures beneath a tree.
Sitting and contemplating by herself,
she then picked tree leaves, sewed them together to make a garment,
and covered her body with it.
She intended to offer the coarse linen cloth she was wearing to the Buddha.
Shì [Śakra, or Indra], the King of Heaven, saw that she was utterly sincere.
He then bestowed heavenly robes, gold coins, food, and drink upon her.
The woman received the robes and immediately made offerings using the cloth.
When her lifespan ended, she was born in heaven.
When her lifespan in heaven ended, she came to be born in the world [of humans].
She became the King's daughter.
Because she delighted in reading scriptures and practicing giving,
her body is golden yellow and her hair is deep blue.
Fó was in Shèwèi Guó.
At that time, the major consort of Bōsīní Wáng,
named Mòlì,
gave birth to a daughter.
She was named Pōshéluó Nǚ (Vajrā), but her face was ugly, and her skin and body were rough
like camel hide.
Her hair was like horsehair. When the King observed this daughter, he felt no joy.
He immediately commanded those in the palace:
“Guard her carefully. Do not let outsiders see her.”
When the daughter grew older and reached the age for marriage,
the King told his officials:
“You must search for a noble family who is poor, and bring the man here.”
The official immediately followed the instruction.
He found a poor scholar from a noble lineage
and brought him to the King’s residence.
The King spoke to that man:
“I have a daughter whose appearance is hideous,
and she has not yet found a suitable partner.
I will provide for you.
I hope you will not refuse,
and will accept her.”
The elder’s son knelt and said:
“I shall obey the King’s command.”
The King immediately gave his daughter in marriage to that poor man.
He built a residence with seven layers of gates and chambers.
The King commanded his son-in-law:
“Hold the door bolt yourself.
If you wish to go out, close it yourself.
Do not let anyone see your wife’s appearance.”
The King provided his son-in-law with everything so that he lacked nothing.
He also appointed him as a great minister (dàchén).
This man was wealthy,
and held gatherings together with other noble clans.
Each month, when it was their turn to gather,
the couples would attend the assembly.
Everyone brought their wives.
Only this Dàchén always went alone.
The crowd grew suspicious and wondered,
“Perhaps this man’s wife is extremely beautiful,
or perhaps she is extremely ugly.
That is why he does not bring her.”
They secretly discussed it among themselves.
They plied him with wine until he was drunk, removed the door bolt,
and opened the gate.
At that moment, the daughter felt distressed and blamed herself for her offenses.
“What sin did I sow that makes my husband hate me
and keep me constantly secluded, never letting me see other people?”
She then thought to herself:
“The Fó is currently in the world,
benefiting all sentient beings and saving them from suffering and calamity.”
She immediately paid homage to the World-Honored One (Shìzūn) from afar with a sincere heart,
“I only wish that you, out of compassion,
would come before me and briefly grant me instruction.”
Since the daughter was truly sincere, the Fó knew her intention.
He immediately went to her home
and appeared before the daughter,
springing forth from the ground.
When the daughter saw the Fó, joy arose in her heart.
Her hideous appearance immediately vanished.
Her body became beautiful and stately,
like a celestial maiden (tiānnǚ).
Her extraordinary beauty surpassed the world.
Out of compassion for the daughter, the Fó preached the wondrous Dharma for her.
She immediately eliminated all evils and attained the path of Xūtuóhuán Dào (Sotāpanna).
At that time, those five men,
opening the door and entering, saw that the wife was beautiful.
They were surprised that the husband had not brought her before.
They closed the gate again,
tied the key to the original belt (of the husband).
When the man awoke and returned home after the assembly,
he saw his wife's appearance, which was rare among humans.
Joyfully, he asked:
“Who is this person?”
The daughter answered her husband:
“I am your wife.”
The husband said:
“Before, you were extremely ugly, but now you are beautiful.”
The wife explained all the matters described above.
Her husband immediately went to inform the King.
“She has now received the miraculous grace of the Fó
and has become beautiful,
no different from a celestial maiden.”
The King commanded her to be brought, and welcomed the daughter into the palace.
The King saw her and rejoiced.
The King and the consort,
along with the daughter and her husband,
went together to the Fó’s place and paid homage, saying:
“We do not understand how this daughter,
though planted with merit in a past life to be born into wealth, received such an ugly form.”
The Fó told the King:
“In a past age,
there was a kingdom called Bōluónài
where a great elder (zhǎngzhě) lived.
His wealth was immeasurable.
The entire family constantly provided offerings to a Pratyekabuddha (Pìzhīfó),
whose body was coarse and ugly in appearance.
At that time, that Zhǎngzhě had a young daughter.
When she saw the Pìzhīfó,
she spoke ill of him with malicious contempt, scolding and disparaging him:
‘Your face is hideous, and your skin is coarse and evil—how hateful!’
This Pìzhīfó,
having accepted their offerings, was about to enter Nirvāṇa.
He performed the eighteen transformations (shíbā biàn) for his donor (dānyuè).
He immediately descended from the sky and returned to the family’s home.
The Zhǎngzhě was doubly joyful.
The daughter immediately repented of her error:
‘I only wish that the Venerable One would forgive me.’
The Pìzhīfó then accepted her repentance.”
The Fó told the Great King:
“The daughter of that time is now your daughter.
Because she disparaged this wise saint, she received the ugly form.
Later, having seen the spiritual transformation,
she reformed and repented, and thus regained her beautiful appearance.
Because of the offerings made to the Fó, she was wealthy throughout successive generations, leading to liberation (jiětuō).”
The Fó went to the home of Jiāluóyuè to eat.
He entered without closing the door.
All those who came after were given food until they were satisfied.
The younger brother conceived an evil thought:
“I will not allow them to enter.
If any freely moving Bhikṣus (Bǐqiū) come, I will break their legs.”
The two brothers then parted ways
and both slept beneath trees.
The younger brother, having conceived an evil thought,
had his leg broken when a frightened ox ran over it.
The older brother, having conceived a virtuous thought,
remained under the tree where the shadow of the setting sun still covered him.
The son-in-law of Bōsīní Wáng died.
The King cherished his daughter deeply.
He summoned a Brāhmaṇa (Póluómén) for his daughter,
to seek out a man of merit to be her new husband.
The Póluómén went out surveying and saw a man lying beneath a tree.
The setting sun’s shadow still covered the spot.
The Póluómén said,
“This is a man of merit.”
He immediately reported this to the King.
The King said,
“How do you know?” (The Póluómén recounted the circumstances described above.)
The King summoned the man, bathed him, and dressed him in fine clothes.
Then he married his daughter to him.
In the past, there was a city in a foreign country.
Named Tóujiāluó.
Inside there was a layman.
Every day, he invited a Śramaṇa to return home to eat.
The Śramaṇa was an Arhat.
While the Śramaṇa was sitting and eating, there was a dog inside.
When the Śramaṇa ate, he always molded a piece of rice and shared it with the dog.
The dog, upon receiving and eating the rice, developed goodwill toward the Śramaṇa.
The Śramaṇa went there daily, and the dog became accustomed to waiting for him.
When the Śramaṇa ate, the dog longed to see the Śramaṇa.
When the Śramaṇa arrived, he would again take a molded piece of rice and give it to the dog.
The dog had goodwill toward the Śramaṇa.
After many years, it died.
It was then reborn as the daughter of the king of Ānxī state.
Upon birth, she recognized her past life and knew she had originally been a dog.
She said, "I abandoned the body of a dog and obtained the body of a king's daughter."
In the state, there were no Buddhist temples or Śramaṇas.
At that time, the king of Yuèzhī dispatched an envoy to visit the king.
Seeing that the envoy was capable and wise, the king intended to give his daughter to him as a wife.
The envoy took the daughter away.
When the daughter saw the Śramaṇas, her heart rejoiced greatly.
She recalled previously being a dog, how the Śramaṇa gave her food, and the goodwill she felt toward the Śramaṇa.
Now she had obtained a human body.
Now she ought to make great offerings to the Śramaṇas.
In the state of Yuèzhī, there were many Śramaṇas.
The wife regularly provided food for three or five hundred people daily.
She personally served the food and did not rely on others.
As soon as the meal was finished,
she personally swept the floor.
The women, maidservants, and slaves in the house all developed goodwill and said:
"This wife is actually a king's daughter.
She came to live in this place.
She constantly sweeps and makes offerings to the Śramaṇas.
We too should apply ourselves wholeheartedly."
The maidservants and slaves then hid the broom.
They wanted to sweep the floor themselves.
When the lady looked for the broom, she could not find where it was.
She then took the rolls of new clothes she had brought in her basket upon arrival and used them to sweep the floor.
When the husband saw his wife sweeping the floor with new clothing,
he said:
"Although you venerate the Buddhadharma, why must you sweep the floor with new clothes?
You should look for the broom."
The wife said:
"I merely held goodwill toward one Śramaṇa.
In two years, I obtained these clothes.
What harm is there in sweeping with these very clothes?
In my former life, initially,
I had nothing available for *dāna*.
But because I had goodwill and believed in the Buddhadharma, I obtained this merit.
I did not earn these clothes through livelihood either."
The husband spoke to his wife, saying:
"Although you believe in the Buddhadharma and make offerings to Śramaṇas,
I have never seen a Śramaṇa give you one or two coins.
These clothes were all acquired through my own strength and labor."
The wife then personally explained her past life to her husband, saying:
"In my former life,
I was born among dogs.
The master of the house frequently invited Śramaṇas.
The Śramaṇa molded rice and gave it to me.
Because I had goodwill toward the Śramaṇa,
I abandoned that dog body and was born as the daughter of a royal house."
When the husband heard this, he rejoiced.
He said to his wife:
"You merely held goodwill toward one Śramaṇa,
and obtained blessings to such an extent!"
The husband was previously stingy and greedy.
Hearing what his wife said, he immediately practiced great *dāna*.
He spared nothing.
He kept the precepts, was diligent, and established Buddhist temples.
The husband thought in his heart:
"Merely by having goodwill, such merits were obtained."
The wife then replied:
The mind can enable a person to attain Buddhahood, to be born in Heaven, to become a Pìzhīfó, or to attain Āluóhànship.
All these are the power of the mind.
If the mind contemplates evil,
it causes one to fall into the hells.
The Bodhimaṇḍa in Bōluónài state.
From the bottom of the earth upwards, it was entirely golden in color.
Like fish scales and tortoise shells, layer upon layer succeeding each other.
All the Buddhas of the past sat upon it.
The king was named Zhīxúnní.
He was a Upāsaka.
He was enlightened regarding the scriptures and the path.
He established a monastery for the Buddha.
He adorned it with extreme splendor.
The king had seven daughters, all equally beautiful.
They all maintained the Five Precepts, held fast to their principles, and did not marry.
The first daughter was named Shūdiào.
The second was named Yìmiào.
The third was named Chútān.
The fourth was named Qīngshǒu.
The fifth was named Xīxīn.
The sixth was named Jìngyǒu.
The seventh was named Sēngbì.
They regularly observed the eighth, fourteenth, fifteenth, twenty-third, twenty-ninth, and thirtieth days of the month.
They diligently received the Eight Precepts and upheld the fasts of the Proper Dharma.
They cultivated the practices of their faith: upholding the precepts, practicing *dāna*, gaining reputation, and cultivating wisdom.
When the seven daughters completed their fast,
they sought permission to go outside the city to the tombs to wander and observe.
The king told the seven daughters:
“The tombs are detestable; there are only dead people there.
Skeletons are strewn about, and foxes, jackals, owls, and carrion birds consume the flesh.
Those who are crying and weeping fill the place.
What is there to observe?
