I have gardens, parks, and bathing ponds in my palace.
Within them are lotuses of five colors.
Night herons, kingfishers, mandarin ducks, and many birds fly and gather there.
Plants that double in brilliance are arrayed there.
Exotic trees provide cool shade, and sweet fruits satiate the mouth.
You can go there and play."
The seven daughters replied:
"Great King, how do sweet fruits and diverse beauties benefit us?
We see that the lifespan of people in the world is short.
Life approaches death daily, and the body is illusory transformation.
It cannot last long.
We are free from the burdens of husbands and children,
and are not tempted by sweet pleasures.
We only wish to observe the impermanent nature of things,
and thereby repel the mind of greed.
We pray the King graciously grants permission."
The king immediately consented.
The seven daughters all left the city.
They went to the burial grounds, a place of great stench.
They heard the sounds of crying and weeping.
Their hair stood on end with dread.
Thereupon, they walked straight ahead together and observed the dead bodies.
They saw severed heads, severed arms, and hands and feet lying in separate places.
Some rigid corpses were covered with grass or wrapped in mats.
Others were exposed, restrained, and lying on the ground.
There were guilty people who were not yet dead, tied up with fresh ropes.
Their families wept and begged for their release.
Furthermore, there were people carrying dead bodies out of the city.
The seven daughters looked far and wide to the left and right.
They saw a great many dead people.
Birds and beasts of prey fought to eat their flesh.
Some animals dragged and pulled corpses out of the soil.
The bodies were bloated and generating worms, their stench making them difficult to approach.
Thereupon, the seven daughters circled the area once.
They spoke among themselves, saying:
"Our bodies will soon be the same way."
Each then recited a verse.
The first daughter said:
People value their bodies, adding fine clothes and precious fragrance;
They look charmingly, their elegant gait desiring others' gaze.
Dead, all are abandoned in the tomb—what use are these decorations and splendors?
The second daughter said:
It is like a house inhabited by a person who leaves, and the dwelling collapses.
The spirit wanders away and the body is discarded; nothing can control its form.
The foolish and greedy believe it can be kept safe, but how do they know it must later perish?
The third daughter said:
Observe when the spirit carries the form, it is like a horse pulling a carriage.
When the carriage breaks down, the horse departs; thus, we know this (form) is impermanent.
The fourth daughter said:
Originally, we saw the city intact and good, and the people inside enjoyed peaceful living.
Their desires were far from fully satisfied, so why did they suddenly become empty and void?
The fifth daughter said:
If one crosses the water by boat, upon arrival, the boat must be abandoned.
The body is not the permanent abode of the spirit; how can it reside there forever?
The sixth daughter said:
When a person dies and lies relying on the earth, the physical form is still fresh and fair.
Standing firm and unmoving, where does the spirit reside?
The seventh daughter said:
It is like a sparrow inside a jar, with fine silk covering the opening.
When the silk tears, the sparrow flies away; the spirit proceeds on its way.
At that time, Dìshì [title] heard this below and praised them.
Excellent! Excellent!
What wishes do you desire?
I shall grant them to you now.
The seven women asked,
“Are you Fàntiān [deity]?
Or are you a terrestrial spirit?
Could it be that you are Dìshì [title]?”
He replied, “Indeed.
I am Dìshì of the Trāyastriṃśa Heaven (Dāolì Tiān [heaven name]).”
The first woman said,
“I wish to obtain a tree without root, without branch, and without leaf,
and be born within it.
That would be swift (or: excellent).”
The second woman said,
“I wish the place where I am born
to be pure, without desire, without yin and yang,
silent, and without dependence.”
The third woman said,
“I wish to be like an echo of a voice called out in the mountains,
without going and without returning,
naturally formless.”
The fourth woman said,
“I wish to be like the void (space), without beginning and without end, without arising from anything, and thoroughly connected with the Way (Dào [concept/term]).”
Dìshì [title] said,
“Stop! Stop! The wishes of you ladies are extremely subtle.
If you wished to become a king among the sun and moon, that could be attained.
But as for emptiness, non-existence, and non-thought, that is not within my jurisdiction.”
The seven women said,
“Tīandì [title],
your spiritual power is so lofty and great, why can you not accomplish this?
The Buddha (Fó [title]) said that those who consume merit, when their merit is exhausted, cannot escape fear.
It is like an old ox that cannot be used by men.
How could that benefit us?”
Dìshì [title] said,
“Ladies, practice purity and observe the precepts. I also worship the Buddha (Fó [title]).
We should become Dharma siblings.
How excellent are these wondrous wishes!”
Having finished speaking, he disappeared.
King Bōsī'nì [ruler name]
had a daughter who was a widow,
named Jīngāng [name].
She returned beautifully adorned.
The father-King, grieving and pitying her,
established a separate palace for her,
and provided her with five hundred singing girls to entertain her.
There was an elderly servant (qīngyī [servant class]),
named Dùshèng [name].
She constantly went to the market to buy cosmetics, powders, incense, and flowers.
Suddenly, she saw countless men and women in a great crowd, each carrying incense and flowers, leaving the city.
She immediately asked,
“Where are you intending to go?”
The crowd replied,
“We intend to visit the Buddha (Fó [title]).”
“The Buddha (Fó [title]) has appeared in the world, the Honored One of the Three Realms (Sānjiè [term]),
He grants liberation,
allowing all sentient beings to attain Nirvāṇa (Níhuán [term]).”
When Dùshèng [name] heard this,
her heart was joyous and her mind delighted.
She immediately thought to herself,
“To meet the Buddha (Fó [title]) in old age is the merit of past lives.”
She then divided the price of the perfume she was carrying and bought fine incense and flowers.
She followed the crowd and arrived at the place of the Buddha (Fó [title]).
After performing the reverence, she stood aside,
scattering flowers, burning incense, and listening to the Dharma (Fǎ [term]) wholeheartedly.
She went past the market to fetch one perfumed object while listening to the Dharma (Fǎ [term]).
The fragrance, obtained through merit and practice in past lives,
was twice as potent as before.
The attendants, complaining of her delay, jointly questioned her.
Dùshèng [name] said,
“In the world there is a Sage Master, the Honored One of the Three Realms (Sānjiè [term]),
who speaks the unsurpassed Dharma (Fǎ [term]).
I listened and received it according to the person.
That is why I was delayed.”
Jīngāng [name], hearing this, was overjoyed,
and sighed to herself,
“What sin have we committed that we alone are separated and cannot hear it?”
She immediately instructed Dùshèng [name],
“Try to tell it to me.”
Dùshèng [name] accepted the command.
She first sent out and prepared the full ceremonial arrangements for receiving the teaching.
Before Dùshèng [name] returned,
Jīngāng [name] and her maidservants waited attentively in the central courtyard,
like children waiting for their mother.
The Buddha (Fó [title]) instructed Dùshèng [name],
“When you return, the proper ceremony for teaching the Dharma (Fǎ [term])
is first to set up a high seat.”
Dùshèng [name] received the instruction.
She fully proclaimed the sage decree, and all were greatly delighted.
Each stripped off one upper garment and piled them up to form the high seat.
Dùshèng [name] washed herself,
and relying on the majestic spiritual power of the Buddha (Fó [title]),
she preached the Dharma (Fǎ [term]) as appropriate.
Jīngāng Nǚ [name] and the more than five hundred others
had their doubts resolved, destroyed evil, and attained the Path of Srotāpanna (Xūtuóhuán Dào [path]).
The Dharma (Fǎ [term]) was taught so beautifully that they did not notice a fire starting.
They were burned to death at once and immediately ascended to heaven.
The King (Wáng [title]) provided coffins, collected the remains, and finished the funeral rites.
He then went to the Buddha's (Fó [title]) location.
The Buddha (Fó [title]) asked,
“Where has the King (Wáng [title]) come from?”
The King (Wáng [title]) replied,
“Jīngāng [name], unfortunately, did not notice the fire.
The major and minor servants were all burned up. I have just returned from providing coffins and collecting the remains.
I do not understand what sin caused them to meet this fire calamity.
I only wish that the World-Honored One (Shìzūn [title]) would reveal what I have not yet heard.”
The Buddha (Fó [title]) informed the Great King (Dàwáng [title]):
In a past age, there was a city
named Bōluónài [city name].
There was an elder’s wife,
who, leading five hundred maids,
went outside the city for a great sacrificial ritual.
The rules of that rite were difficult to violate.
People of other surnames were not allowed near it.
Regardless of whether they were close or distant,
anyone who approached was thrown into the fire.
At that time, there was a Pratyekabuddha (Pìzhī Fó [title])
named Jiāluó [name].
He lived in the mountains, coming down in the morning for alms,
and habitually returning to the mountains in the evening.
Jiāluó [name] came for alms and approached the suburban sacrifice.
The elder's wife saw him.
She was suddenly filled with anger.
Together they seized Jiāluó [name] and threw him into the fire.
Though his whole body was scorched and ruined,
he immediately displayed his spiritual powers,
flying up into the void.
The women were terrified, crying tears and repenting their faults.
They knelt down, raised their heads, and addressed him, saying:
“We women are ignorant and foolish, not recognizing the utmost truth.
As a group of evil, stupid, and wild creatures, we have defiled and insulted a spiritual being.
We realize our faults and sins are piled up like mountains.
We pray that you descend, Honored Virtue, to eliminate our severe calamity.”
Following their cry, he immediately descended and attained Parinirvāṇa (Bō Nièpán [term]).
The women erected a stūpa and made offerings to the relics (Shèlì [term]).
The Buddha (Fó [title]) then recited a verse for the Great King (Dàwáng [title]):
“The ignorant and foolish commit evil, unable to free themselves, calamity pursues and burns them up.
When the sin is complete and fiercely burning, the places sought by the foolish are not called happiness,
but only when approaching the descent into calamity do they realize the non-goodness.”
The Buddha (Fó [title]) informed the Great King (Dàwáng [title]):
The elder's wife at that time
is now the King's daughter, Jīngāng [name].
The five hundred maidservants
are now Dùshèng [name] and the five hundred maidservants.
In the past, there was a king's daughter
who was deeply loved by the King (Wáng [title]) and was never out of his sight.
At that time, rain fell from heaven and there were bubbles on the water.
The daughter saw the bubbles and conceived a strong love and reverence for them.
The daughter told the King (Wáng [title]), saying,
“I wish to obtain the bubbles on the water to use as a flower garland (huāmán [object]) for my head.”
The King (Wáng [title]) informed his daughter, saying,
“The bubbles now on the water cannot be grasped and held.
How can they be taken to be used as a flower garland (huāmán [object])?”
The daughter said,
“If I cannot obtain them, I will kill myself.”
The King (Wáng [title]) heard the daughter's words
and commanded the skilled artisans, saying,
“You possess extraordinary skill and there is nothing you cannot accomplish.
Quickly fetch the water bubbles and make a garland (mán [object]) for my daughter.
If you fail to do this, I shall have you executed.”
They replied,
“We are incapable of catching bubbles and making a garland (mán [object]).”
One elderly craftsman said,
“I am able to catch the bubbles.”
The King (Wáng [title]) was greatly pleased,
and immediately told his daughter,
“Now there is a person capable of making the garland (mán [object]).
You may go yourself and personally oversee it.”
The daughter followed the King's (Wáng [title]) words and looked on outside.
At that time, the elderly craftsman addressed the King's (Wáng [title]) daughter, saying,
“I inherently cannot distinguish between good and bad water bubbles.
I humbly request that the King's (Wáng [title]) daughter personally take the bubbles, and I will make the garland (mán [object]).”
The daughter then sought to catch the bubbles, but they broke and were destroyed as soon as they touched her hand, and she could not obtain them.
Thus, throughout the day, she failed to obtain a single bubble.
The daughter became exhausted and disgusted and abandoned the effort and departed.
The daughter told the King (Wáng [title]), saying,
“Water bubbles are illusory and cannot remain long.
I pray the King (Wáng [title]) will make me a garland (mán [object]) of pure purple gold (zǐmó jīn [metal name]),
which will never wither, day or night.
Water bubbles deceive and confuse the eyes of men.
Although they have form and substance, they arise and immediately perish.
The intense heat haze (yě mǎ [mirage term]) is also like this.
Those who thirst for desire grow weary and lose their lives.
The human body is illusory; pleasure is scarce and suffering is abundant.
Things subject to decay cannot remain long.
Transformation and change occur constantly, and one’s time in the world is short.
In the past, there was a king.
His name was Jìn Mèi.
He had a daughter.
She wore a natural golden floral wreath (màn).
She was titled Mó Lín Ní.
The king summoned five hundred girls born on the same day in the country,
to serve as attendants.
Mó Lín Ní grew up,
and offered sacrifices to five hundred Brāhmaṇas every day without fail.
At that time, Kē Shè Fó (Kāśyapa Buddha) lived in a park.
[Mó Lín Ní] regularly went out traveling and approached the park where the Buddha lived.
The charioteer would not enter.
The girl asked:
"I enter every park, why do you avoid this one?"
He replied:
"This park only contains a bald-headed Śramaṇa (Shā Mén),
named Kē Shè.
It is not proper to see him.
That is why I am not entering."
The girl said:
"You may enter."
Seeing the Buddha's golden body, her heart was filled with great joy.
She bowed her head to the ground in reverence, and the Buddha preached the profound Dharma; she received the Three Refuges and the Five Precepts, paid her respects, and departed.
The girl reflected to herself:
"The Brāhmaṇas are not a good field of merit (fú tián).
They should not receive offerings."
She turned [her devotion] to making offerings to the Buddha instead.
At that time, the Brāhmaṇas heard that Mó Lín Ní had become a disciple of Kē Shè.
They offered her even finer delicacies (to win her back).
Jealousy arose in their hearts.
King Jìn Mèi, late at night,
had eleven kinds of dreams.
In the morning, he gathered his ministers and described the dreams he had perceived.
The ministers ordered him to ask the prognosticating Brāhmaṇa.
The Brāhmaṇa said:
"These dreams are inauspicious.
You might either lose your kingdom or lose your life."
The king said:
"Can I avoid it?"
The soothsayer replied:
"You must have various kinds of cattle, sheep, elephants, and horses,
along with the king's daughter Mó Lín Ní,
and her five hundred attendants.
After seven days, sacrifice them to the heavens by killing them at the crossroad.
This calamity can then be averted."
The king heard the command.
He immediately made preparations, called Mó Lín Ní, and told her the situation.
He told her that within the next six days, she could do whatever she desired.
She replied:
"I certainly do not fear death.
I wish on the first day to go with the men and women of the city to Kē Shè Fó's location,
and for all of them to receive the Three Refuges and the Five Precepts."
The king immediately permitted it.
"I wish on the second day to go with the king's ministers to the Buddha's location.
I wish on the third day to go with all the princes to the Buddha's location.
I wish on the fourth day to go with all the princesses to the Buddha's location.
I wish on the fifth day to go with the king’s ladies and palace women (cǎi nǚ) to the Buddha’s location.
I wish on the sixth day to go with the King to the Buddha's location."
The king permitted all of it.
And so, she and all the people went to the Buddha’s location.
The Buddha preached the Dharma for them, and they achieved attainment.
All received the Three Refuges and the Five Precepts.
The king reported his eleven dreams to Kē Shè Fó.
The Buddha said:
"The significance of these dreams relates to the future, not the present.
The dream of a small tree bearing flowers:
In the future, there will be a Buddha named Shì Jiā Wén (Śākyamuni).
People of that age will begin growing white hair and having sons when they are only twenty years old.
The dream of a calf plowing: The ten-year-old child will manage household affairs,
and the parents will lose their freedom.
The dream of three cauldrons boiling rice together, where the side cauldrons leap into the central one but do not fall down:
The rich will give gifts back and forth to each other, but the poor will receive nothing.
The dream of seeing a two-headed camel eating grass:
Ministers will consume the king’s salary and also seize the people’s property.
The dream of seeing a mare mother drinking her foal's milk:
At that time, mothers who marry off their daughters will instead seek food from them.
The dream of seeing a golden bowl moving in the empty sky:
Rain will fall out of season. The dream of seeing a wild fox urinating into a golden bowl:
People will marry for wealth, disregarding lineage.
The dream of a macaque sitting on a bed:
At that time, the kings will use unlawful and tyrannical methods, acting without the Way.
The dream of seeing an ox head wearing a sandalwood turban being of equal value to rotten grass:
Members of the Śākya clan (Shì zhǒng) will preach the Dharma for the sake of avarice.
The dream of seeing water that is turbid in the center but clear around the four sides:
The Buddha Dharma will first perish in the central kingdom, while the border countries will flourish instead.
Regarding the king himself, there is no inauspiciousness."
The king immediately issued a decree to his ministers from his seat, saying:
"All the livestock intended for the sacrifice to heaven are now safe.
From now on, I would rather forfeit my own life
than intentionally kill a living being, much less a human being."
There was a king who had a daughter
named Gǒu Tóu.
There was a fisherman
named Shù Pó Qié.
While he was walking along the road,
he saw the princess from afar on a high tower.
Seeing her face through the window, he became attached to her image.
His heart could not forget her even for a moment; days and months passed, and he could not eat or drink.
His mother asked him the reason.
He replied to his mother with his feelings:
"I saw the princess, and my heart cannot forget her."
His mother restrained him, saying:
"You are a humble person, and the princess is noble.
You cannot have her."
The son said:
"My heart desires her joyfully and cannot forget her even briefly.
If my wish is not fulfilled, I cannot live."
For the sake of her son, the mother entered the royal palace.
She regularly delivered choice fish and choice meat
as gifts to the princess without taking payment.
The princess was surprised and asked:
"What do you seek?"
The mother said to the princess: "Please dismiss your attendants, and I will report my feelings to you."
"I have only one son.
Because of his reverence and admiration for the princess, his longing has become a sickness, and his life is not far from ending.
I beg you to take pity and grant him his life."
The princess said:
"On the fifteenth day of the month, you shall stay behind the divine image in a certain temple dedicated to the heavens."
The mother returned and told her son:
"Your wish has been granted."
She informed him exactly as above.
He bathed, put on new clothes, and stayed behind the divine image.
When the time came, the princess reported to her royal father:
"I have had an ill omen and need to go to the Heavenly Temple to seek good fortune and blessings."
The king said, "Excellent."
He immediately prepared five hundred carriages and escorted her out to the Heavenly Temple.
Having arrived,
she commanded her followers:
"Stop at the gate."
She entered the Heavenly Temple alone.
The celestial deity reflected:
"This should not happen.
The king is a benefactor, and this humble person must not be allowed to defile and disgrace the princess."
Immediately, the deity struck this person, causing him to fall into an unconscious sleep.
When the princess entered,
she saw that he was in a heavy sleep, and although she pushed him, he did not wake up.
She immediately left behind a jeweled necklace (yīng luò) worth one hundred thousand taels of gold and departed.
After she left, the man awoke.
He saw the jeweled necklace.
He also asked the bystanders and learned that the princess had come.
His sexual desire was not satisfied.
In his sorrow, hatred, remorse, and distress, the fire of lust erupted within him, and he spontaneously combusted and died.
Based on this evidence, we know
that the heart of a woman does not distinguish between noble and humble;
she only follows her desire.
Furthermore, in the past, there was a princess
who chased after a Cāṇḍāla (Zhān Tuó Luó) and committed impurity with him.
Also, there was a hermit's daughter
who followed and pursued a lion.
In the city of Bō Luó Nài (Vārāṇasī), there was an elder
named Ā Jù Lì Zǐ.
His personal name (zì) was Shé Tuó, and he was twenty-four years old.
He had crystal sandals (liú lí jī) that adhered to his feet since birth.
His parents held them in high regard as unusual.
His personal name was Shé Tuó.
They built him a separate residence.
He moved places depending on the season, and singing girls and entertainers were constantly by his side.
Bǎo Chēng, in the middle of the night, suddenly saw all the singing girls appearing as if they were dead.
Pus and blood flowed profusely, their limbs were broken and destroyed, and the residence and all its contents resembled a grave.
The doors suddenly opened by themselves, and the sky and earth became completely dark.
He only saw a faint light moving toward the East City Gate.
The gate then opened by itself, brightly illuminating Lù Yuán (Deer Park).
Following the light, he saw the Buddha and gazed upon his physical marks.
His fear ceased, his confusion dissolved, and he lifted his voice and exclaimed:
"Long have I been imprisoned in the jail of desire, bound by the fetters of form and color.
Now that I approach the Divine Venerable, may I attain liberation?"
The Buddha said:
"Welcome, young man! You are awakened.
In this place, there is no sorrow, and all practices are completed."
He advanced and bowed at the Buddha's feet.
The Buddha preached the Dharma for him, and he attained the Stainless Dharma Eye.
He immediately rose and addressed the Buddha:
"I wish to become your disciple."
The Buddha said:
"Welcome, Bhikṣu!" And immediately he became a Śramaṇa.
The next morning, the singing girls searched everywhere in distress.
The family was shocked and frightened, not knowing where he was.
The elder dispatched horses in all directions to search.
The father rode his son’s carriage and traveled east, searching for him.
On the way, he encountered a river.
The river was named Bō Luó Nài.
Crossing the water, he saw his son’s precious sandals cast off on the bank.
He immediately followed the footprints directly toward Lù Yuán.
The Buddha used skillful means to prevent the father and son from seeing each other.
The elder asked the Buddha:
"The footprints of my son Bǎo Chēng lead here.
Did Gautama (Qú Tán) see him?"
The Buddha told the elder:
"If your son is here, why worry that you will not see him?"
The Buddha preached the Dharma for the elder, and he attained the Stream-Enterer stage (Xū Tuó Huán).
Bǎo Chēng's mind was liberated, and he attained Arhatship (Luó Hàn).
The father and son then saw each other, but their affection and attachment had grown weak.
The elder reported to the Buddha:
"Today my heart is delighted, and my feelings contain two joys:
First, the joy of meeting the Buddha and achieving understanding;
second, the joy of being free from attachment.
At that time, Bǎochēng's relatives included four people.
The first was named Fùnòu.
The second was named Wéimóluó.
The third was named Qiáoyánbō.
The fourth was named Xūtuó.
Having heard that Bǎochēng had already become a Śramaṇa (monk),
they were astonished and delighted, their hair standing on end. They said:
We shall go together to the Buddha and also visit Bǎochēng.
Thereupon, they traveled together.
When they saw the Buddha's form, they immediately fulfilled their original vows.
They bowed and reported to the Buddha:
We have been thirsty for the Dharma teaching and empty-hearted for a long time.
Do not consider us lowly, we wish to become disciples.
The Buddha said:
Welcome, Bhikṣus (monks). You have all attained monkhood (Śramaṇa).
He explained the innate purity of the mind; when they heard the meaning, their minds were enlightened.
They immediately attained Arhatship.
If there were those who heard [the Dharma] and started seeking it,
they all attained the fruit of the Way.
In Zhānpó Chéng (Campā City) lived the son of a great elder.
His courtesy name was Shǒulóngnà.
His parents had only this one son,
and cherished him dearly.
Since birth, accustomed to luxury, he had never stepped on the ground; hair grew on the soles of his feet.
At that time, the King of Mójié Guó (Magadha Kingdom) heard about the great elder's son in Zhānpó Chéng and desired to see him quickly.
He immediately ordered the City Lord,
to command all the elders to bring their sons.
The City Lord of Zhānpó Chéng followed the command.
He proceeded to the King of Mójié.
He stood on one side.
The King permitted him to spread clothes upon the ground,
and then approach the King.
The King saw the hair on his feet,
and was greatly pleased in his heart.
He immediately spoke to him:
You should go to see the Buddha, perform prostrations, and inquire after his health.
This will benefit you in future generations.
At that time, the City Lord of Zhānpó Chéng and the various elders
together went to Qízhéqū Shān (Gṛdhrakūṭa Mountain).
At that time, there was the Elder Pógétuó,
who served the Buddha and was seated on a large rock.
The City Lord of Zhānpó Chéng
went to where the Elder Pógétuó was and said:
We wish to see the Tathāgata (Rúlái).
Then Pógétuó instantly vanished from the rock and sprang up before the Buddha.
He reported, saying:
The elders from Zhānpó wish to see the World-Honored One (Shìzūn).
The Buddha said:
Go and spread a seat in the shade of the house.
I will go there to sit.
Then Pógétuó spread the seat and returned to the Buddha's location.
He reported to the World-Honored One, saying:
The seat has been spread.
After the World-Honored One was seated,
He instructed Pógétuó, saying:
Tell the elders to come.
Then Pógétuó vanished before the Buddha and sprang up onto the rock.
At that time, the elders exclaimed, "This is unprecedented! If the World-Honored One's disciple possesses such spiritual power,
how much greater must the Tathāgata be!"
Pógétuó said:
Elders, you should know this.
At this time, the City Lord of Zhānpó came to the Buddha's location.
The World-Honored One then,
immediately preached the Dharma and exhorted the sons of the elders and the City Lord of Zhānpó.
They immediately attained the Purity of the Dharma Eye while seated.
They reported to the World-Honored One, saying:
O Great Virtuous One,
from now on, we take refuge in the Three Jewels,
and become Upāsakas (lay devotees).
Later, Shǒulóngnà subsequently left home (became a monk).
He went to the Śīdhā grove (cemetery forest) beside the Wēnshuǐ Hé (Warm Water River).
He diligently practiced vigorous effort (Vīrya).
Where he paced in meditation, blood flowed and stained the ground,
appearing as if smeared with blood.
At that time, Shǒulóngnà contemplated in silence:
Among the Buddha's disciples, there is none who surpasses me in diligent effort.
Why have I still not attained the Uncontaminated (Wú Lòu)?
I should abandon the precepts, return home, indulge in the five desires, and make offerings to generate merit.
The Buddha knew his thoughts.
He arrived where Shǒulóngnà was.
I will ask you now.
Answer me as you wish.
When you were at home, you played the zither (qín).
If the zither strings were slack or taut, was the sound good?
Only if it is neither slack nor taut can one obtain a good sound.
The Buddha said:
A Bhikṣu is also like this.
If the mind is neither slack nor taut, it will accord with the Way.
Following this teaching and practicing, he attained Arhatship.
Formerly, inside Shèwèi Chéng (Śrāvastī City),
there was an elder,
named Zuìshèng (Most Excellent).
There was also another elder,
named Nánjiàng (Hard to Subdue).
These two men were the foremost in stinginess in the country.
They possessed immeasurable wealth and countless treasures.
Both men had seven layers of doors, and they commanded the gatekeepers:
Do not allow any beggar to enter our courtyards or inner rooms.
Iron nets completely covered the courtyards to keep out flying birds.
On all four sides, there were iron walls to prevent rats from burrowing and gnawing through instruments and goods.
At that time, the Five Great Śrāvakas (Hearers), one after another, went there to teach and transform them.
They sprang up from the ground and taught them the giving of the Dharma.
The two elders heard it but each refused to be transformed.
Later, the Buddha went there himself, sitting and lying in empty space, emitting great light.
The Buddha spoke the subtle and wonderful Dharma to the elders.
Although the elders heard it, their minds were still not penetrating (unmoved).
They thought internally:
Since the Buddha has come, we cannot let him return to the Vihāra (Jīngshè) empty-handed.
It is proper to enter the storehouse and take one white woolen blanket (zhān) to give to the Tathāgata.
He immediately rose and entered the storehouse.
He selected an inferior one, but it turned out to be better.
He discarded it and took another, obtaining one that was twice as good.
His mind and will contended with each other, and he could not decide for himself.
On that very day, the Asuras (Āxūlún) and the Trāyastriṃśa Heavens (Dāolì Tiān) were fighting together.
Sometimes the Devas won and the Asuras lost.
Sometimes the Asuras won and the Devas lost.
At that time, the World-Honored One, using his Divine Eye, observed the elder's mind.
Sometimes the miserly mind prevailed, and the giving mind lost.
Sometimes the giving mind prevailed, and the miserly mind lost.
At that time, the World-Honored One then spoke this verse (gāthā):
Giving is like a battlefield; those who gain wisdom here are not praised [by the world].
The moment of giving is also the moment of battle; these two things are equally balanced.
The elder heard this from afar and felt shame internally.
What the Tathāgata spoke was precisely about me.
He immediately brought out a fine woolen blanket and used it as an offering.
The Elder Nánjiàng,
brought out five hundred liǎng of gold and used it for generous giving.
Their hearts opened and their minds understood, and they each saw the path.
If one releases men and women, or if one releases male and female slaves.
If one allows common people (to enter the path), or if oneself
leaves home and enters the Way, the merit is immeasurable.
The reward of generosity (Dāna) is returning and dwelling among the Six Heavens and humans for ten lifetimes.
The blessing of leaving home is boundless and immeasurable.
It surpasses erecting a Stūpa of seven treasures, extending up to the Thirty-Three Heavens (Trāyastriṃśa).
Because of greed, people can destroy (those merits).
The virtue of leaving home cannot be ruined.
It is as high as Xūmí.
Deeper than the great ocean, wider than empty space.
If someone creates hindrance for those leaving home,
their sin is extremely heavy.
They enter deep hell, dark and sightless.
There was an elder,
named Shīlìbìtí. He was a hundred years old and sought to leave home.
His family, both old and young, found him useless.
Shīlìbìtí went toward the Jiālántuó Zhúlín.
He sought Shèlìfú, wishing to leave home.
Because he was old, he was not allowed to leave home.
He asked five hundred Luóhàn (Arhats), and all agreed.
Shèlìfú exited the gate of the Bamboo Garden.
(Shīlìbìtí) raised his voice and wept loudly.
Yōubōlí was a low-caste person who cut hair.
Nítí was a vile person who cleared away filth.
Yāngjué Móluó killed countless people.
And Tuósèjī, a great villainous thief.
Such people were still able to leave home.
What sin have I committed that I alone cannot?
The Fó immediately appeared soaring up.
He asked Fúzēng,
"Why are you crying?"
Hearing the Fó’s pure voice, he was delighted and performed a ritual bow.
He reported to the Fó,
"All sinful and evil people were able to leave home.
What sin prevents me from being allowed to leave home?
The young and old (in my family) no longer have use for me.
Furthermore, I cannot leave home in the Fó's Dharma.
If I return home, I certainly won't see the future.
Where should I go?
Today, I shall certainly abandon my life here."
The Fó comforted him, saying,
"Do not worry or grieve.
I permit you to leave home."
He instructed Dà Mùlián,
"Permit him to leave home."
Immediately, he was allowed to leave home.
He received the complete precepts.
Day and night, he diligently practiced, gathered, read, and recited, widely penetrating the Sūtra Piṭaka.
Because of his old age, he could not constantly respect, greet, send off, or inquire of the senior Bhikṣus.
The younger Bhikṣus, acting as superiors, constantly used harsh and sharp words against him.
He again thought thus:
"I would rather die now."
He went to the bank of the great river, took off his Kasāya, and placed it on a tree branch.
Weeping, he swore an oath,
"I am not abandoning the Fó, the Dharma, or the Saṅgha.
I only wish to abandon my life.
If there is any reward for my practice of generosity, upholding the precepts, diligence, and Sūtra recitation in this body of mine,
if there is any reward for this,
I vow that after abandoning this body, I will be born into a rich and happy family.
May my dependents be obedient.
May they not create hindrance for my good Dharma practices.
May I constantly encounter the Sānbǎo (Triple Gem) and meet excellent masters,
who demonstrate and enlighten me to Nièpán (Nirvāṇa)." He then threw himself into the torrent.
Before he reached the water, Mùlián reached out and placed him back on the bank.
He made him grasp the corner of his robe and soared up into the empty sky.
Just like a fierce eagle carrying a small bird in its mouth.
In the time it takes to flex and extend an arm, they arrived at a large ocean island.
By the sea, there was a recently deceased person.
She possessed the complete features of a woman.
They saw a worm coming out of her mouth, re-entering through the nose, coming out again through the eyes, and entering through the ears.
Bìtí asked,
"What woman is this?"
He replied,
"The time has come; I will explain."
Walking further, they saw another woman.
She carried a copper cauldron on her back, lit a fire, and blew on it until it boiled.
Taking off her clothes, she entered the cauldron herself.
Her hair and nails first fell off, her flesh cooked and separated from the bones. The boiling blew the bones out.
Outside, the wind blew, and immediately she returned to being human.
She took her own flesh and ate it.
Next, walking forward, they saw a great tree.
Many worms surrounded and chewed its trunk, branches, and leaves.
There was no empty space, not even the size of a needle head.
It screamed loudly, shaking, like the sound of Di Yù (Hell).
Furthermore, they saw a man.
Around him were vicious ghost spirits with animal heads.
In their hands they held bows and crossbows, repeatedly firing poison arrows whose tips were all burning with fire.
They competed to shoot him.
His body was completely scorched.
They also saw a great mountain.
Below it were placed swords and knives. They saw a person.
He threw himself down from the top; knives, halberds, swords, and spears pierced and damaged his body.
He immediately collected and pulled them out, setting them back up in their original place.
This going and returning never stopped.
Ahead, they saw a mountain of bones.
Seven hundred Yóuxún (Yojanas) high.
Mùlián explained to Bìtí concerning the mountains:
In Shèwèichéng, the wife of the great Sàbáo (Caravan Leader).
Her husband loved and adored her deeply.
When he wanted to enter the great sea (for trade), he was reluctant to leave his wife.
He immediately took her with him into the sea.
The wife held a mirror to illuminate her face.
She viewed her own beauty and correctness.
She immediately gave rise to arrogance and deep attachment.
At that time, they encountered a great turtle that stepped on the boat and sank it into the sea.
Everyone died.
Five hundred merchants all died.
The sea did not accept the corpses.
Yèchā and Luóchà brought them out and placed them on the shore.
Driven by her attachment, after death she was reborn as the worm.
After abandoning this worm body, she will fall into the Great Hell.
In Shèwèiguó, the maidservant of a Yōupóyí. The Yōupóyí invited a Bhikṣu (to attend).
For the ninety days of summer retreat, she served and provided offerings.
She instructed the maidservant to deliver the food.
When the maidservant arrived at a secluded place, she selected the best parts and ate them herself.
The remainder she gave to the Bhikṣu.
When the mistress found out and asked her,
the maidservant replied,
"If I ate it first, may I, lifetime after lifetime, eat my own flesh."
Now she is first receiving the "flower reward" (the lighter immediate retribution) and later will fall into Di Yù.
The great tree, being chewed by all the worms, emitted a great evil noise.
This was Bhikṣu Lèilìzhà, who handled Saṅgha affairs.
He used Saṅghika (property belonging to the Saṅgha community)—flowers, fruits, rice, and food—
and gave them to lay people.
He is receiving this flower reward.
Later, he will fall into Di Yù.
The worms chewing the tree,
are the people who received the stolen goods.
The one who cried out loudly, whose body was shot by many arrows,
this person in his previous life was a great hunter.
He killed many birds and beasts; due to this sin, he receives this bitter suffering.
When his life ends here, he will fall into the Great Hell.
The one who throws himself down onto knives and swords from the great mountain,
was a great, strong general of Wángshěchéng.
Because of his fierceness and bravery, his body was always at the vanguard.
Because he injured and destroyed the lives of creatures using knives, swords, spears, and shields, he receives this retribution.
There was a king named Tánmófúdì.
He practiced generosity, upheld the precepts, was compassionate, and did not harm the lives of creatures.
He governed the country with righteous laws for twenty full years.
He played a game of chance with a person.
At that time, a person committed murder.
The ministers reported to the King.
He replied,
"Judge him according to the national law."
The person was immediately executed according to the law.
When the King finished his game, he asked,
"Where is the criminal?"
The ministers replied, "He has been executed."
Hearing this, the King wept and said,
"The seven treasures all remain, but I alone will enter Di Yù!"
He immediately abandoned the throne, entered the mountains, and practiced self-cultivation.
When his life ended, he became a Mógé Yú (Makara fish).
Its body was seven hundred Yóuxún long.
The King's ministers relied on their power and wrongfully oppressed the common people.
When their lives ended, they also became great Mógé Yú.
The worms inside their bodies caused itching, so they rubbed against the crystal mountain.
They crushed and killed the worms, whose blood flowed for a hundred Lǐ, all red.
They were destined to fall into the Great Hell.
This fish slept for a hundred years before awakening.
When it awoke, it was extremely hungry and thirsty.
It immediately opened its mouth, and the seawater poured in like a rushing great river.
There were five hundred merchants who entered the sea to gather treasures.
Their ship happened to be drawn toward the fish's mouth.
The merchants invoked Námó Fó (Homage to the Buddha).
The fish heard and closed its mouth.
The merchants survived.
The fish, dying of hunger, was reborn in Wángshěchéng.
A Yèchā brought the body out and placed it by this seashore.
"The former king is your body (meaning, the bone mountain represents the former king and his ministers)."
(The crime was) ordering the killing of a person, which caused him to become the fish.
Bìtí achieved spiritual understanding through impermanence and detachment from the world.
He eradicated all defilements and attained the fruit of a Luóhàn.
In the country of Shèwèi Guó, there was a great elder (Zhǎngzhě).
His name was Xūdáduō. He regularly gave alms to orphaned and solitary beggars.
People used this as his appellation.
Previously, he had land and property in Wángshè Chéng.
Every year, he traveled there for business and lodged at the house of the elder Hùmí.
He rose up at night, swept and cleaned the dwelling, and prepared food.
Xūdá asked him about it.
He replied:
In Jiāpíluó Chéng, there is a son of the Śākya clan,
named Xīdáduō.
His family name is Qútán.
Not long after his birth, physiognomers divined about him.
They determined he would certainly become a Cakravartin (Zhǎnlún Wáng).
His heart did not desire this pleasure.
He abandoned it and left home (to become a monk).
Without a teacher, he spontaneously attained Anòuduōluó Sānmiǎo Sānpútí.
Because his mind is equal towards all sentient beings, he is called the Fó.
Tomorrow, he will accept my invitation.
He asked again:
Where is he now?
He replied:
He is in the Jiālántuó Zhúlín Jīngshě. Xūdáduō concentrated his mind upon the Fó and all his merits.
Suddenly, there was a great light.
Following the light, he went out and reached the city gate of Shīhē Chéng.
Due to the Fó’s spiritual power, the gate naturally opened, and as he exited, there was a heavenly shrine (Tiāncí).
Xūdá paid respects, and immediately the darkness returned.
Fear arose in his heart.
He wanted to return to the city gate.
There was a great heavenly spirit (Tiānshén),
who spoke to Xūdá, saying:
Worthy one, seeing the Fó will certainly bring good fortune.
The merit obtained throughout all of Yánfútí,
is not equal to setting forth the mind and taking one step toward the Rúlái.
Xūdá asked:
Who are you?
He replied:
I am Xìnxiāng, the son of a Brāhmaṇa (Póluómén), and I am your good friend from former existences (Shànzhīshí).
In the past, because I saw Shèlìfú and Dàmùjiànlián, paid respects, and rejoiced,
I abandoned my body and obtained rebirth as a son of the Northern Heavenly King Píshāmén.
I specifically oversee the protection of this city. How much more merit is there in seeing the Rúlái, paying respects, and making offerings!
Xūdá paid reverence to the Fó.
The Fó preached the Dharma according to his needs.
He attained the path of Xuītuóhuán.
The elder Xūdá experienced seven subsequent periods of poverty, the last being the most severe.
In a mound of dung, he found a wooden peck (dǒu).
It was actually made of Zhāntán.
He took it to the market and sold it.
He obtained four pecks of rice.
He told his wife, "Cook one peck immediately.
I will go fetch vegetables."
At that time, the Fó thought:
"I must deliver Xūdá and cause his fortune to be reborn."
Just as the rice was cooked,
Shèlìfú arrived.
The wife saw him and rejoiced.
She poured all one peck of cooked rice into his bowl (bō).
She cooked another peck.
Mùlián arrived again.
She also joyfully gave it to him.
She cooked another peck.
Jiāshè arrived again.
She also gave it to him.
There was just one peck left.
Immediately, she cooked it thoroughly.
The Rúlái himself came.
The wife thought to herself:
"Our remaining food for days
should not be diminished."
"Now we have this rice.
The Rúlái himself has condescended to visit.
May it be that our karmic offenses are finished and fortune is being born?"
She offered all one peck of cooked rice to the Rúlái.
The Fó pronounced blessings.
"The destruction of offenses and the generation of fortune begins this very day."
Xūdá returned immediately.
The wife, fearing his anger,
then asked:
"Just now, the Fó came, as did Shèlìfú and Mùlián.
Jiāshè also came, all seeking food.
Should I have given it to them?"
He replied, "You should give it to them.
Fields of merit (Fútián) are hard to encounter.
If they come seeking, this is a valuable meeting."
The wife said:
"I used all four pecks of rice we had just now for offerings."
The husband greatly rejoiced.
They drank the remaining rice water together, husband and wife.
After a moment, as they lingered,
all the rooms were filled with treasures, and the storehouses with grain and cloth,
naturally and completely filled.
He was rich again, just as in former times.
Xūdá leaped for joy,
knowing that the Fó had taken pity on him.
He further invited the Fó and the Saṅgha (Sēng) and made offerings until his stores were exhausted.
The Fó preached the Dharma to them, and all attained the traces of the Path (Dàojì).
The most excellent elder (Zhǎngzhě) heard the wondrous Dharma preached.
Immediately, while seated, all defilements were exhausted, and he attained the purification of the Dharma Eye (Fǎyǎnjìng).
He accepted the Three Refuges (Sān Zìguī) and became an Upāsaka (Yōupósè).
For the rest of his life, he would not kill.
Not long after the Fó departed,
the wicked Māra Pāxún transformed himself into the image of the Fó, complete with the major and minor marks (Xiànghǎo),
and came to the elder's house.
The elder thought:
"How quickly the Rúlái has returned after having just departed!"
The false Fó told him:
"I thought the elder possessed high talent, broad wisdom, and could discern various doctrines.
But upon reflection, elder,
you are foolish, deluded, and lack wisdom.
What I previously taught regarding the Four Noble Truths (Sì Dì) is actually not the true doctrine.
This is merely perversion.
It is what non-Buddhist doctrines (Wàidào) practice."
The elder immediately realized the truth himself.
He immediately retorted, saying:
"Stop, stop! Speak no more!
I have obtained the Eye of Wisdom (Huìyǎn) and stand on firm ground.
Even if you transformed yourself into hundreds of millions of bodies,
I would not regress.
Why does the light of a firefly compete with the brightness of the sun?
The dirt mound of a tenant farmer wishes to compare itself to Xūmí.
Owls, vultures, crows, and magpies attempt to fly alongside Jīnchì."
Pāxún felt shame, reverted his form, and departed.
At that time, in Wángshěguó.
There was a chief elder of the four castes.
His courtesy name was Shēnrì.
His wealth was exceedingly great.
He possessed countless amounts of gold, silver, and rare treasures.
Shēnrì served other Daoists (ascetics).
He only did not serve the Buddha.
All the heterodox Daoists were jealous of him.
They discussed together with Shēnrì, saying:
“The Buddha is now respected by the King, his ministers, the chief elders, officials, and the common people.
But we alone are not treated with such importance.”
“The Buddha constantly claims, saying:
‘He knows the past, future, and present affairs.’
‘He knows what others are thinking.’
Now, why don’t we test him,
to see if this is truly so or not?”
Shēnrì said:
“How shall we test him?”
The heterodox Daoists said:
“Invite the Buddha, putting poison in the food.
Dig a pit five *zhàng* deep inside the gate.
Put fire inside and cover it lightly on top.
Let the Buddha walk over it.
If he knows, he will surely not accept the invitation.
If he accepts the invitation, then he does not know.”
Shēnrì agreed.
He immediately went to invite the Buddha.
The Buddha said: “Very well.”
The heterodox Daoists said:
“He already knows nothing!
Just continue digging the ground.”
Shēnrì had a son.
His courtesy name was Zhānlúofǎ.
He was sixteen years old.
He was thoroughly versed in past lives, diligently studied the Buddhist path, and could know the affairs of the past, future, and present.
He advised his father, saying:
“The Buddha already knows this.
Do not follow the words of wicked men and throw yourself into scalding fire.”
Shēnrì did not believe him.
He dug the pit, lit the fire, and placed poison in the food.
He told the *bhikṣus*:
“Follow behind me as I walk.”
When the Buddha set out on the road,
he emitted a brilliant light causing Shēnrì’s dwelling to be entirely gold-colored.
At that time, Zhānlúofǎ immediately told his father:
“Now the Buddha has set out on the road.
The ten directions are bright as the sun.”
When the Buddha arrived at the city gate,
his foot trod upon the threshold,
and the entire great city immediately shook violently.
The sick were instantly healed.
Musical instruments (*kōnghóu*) played by themselves without being struck.
When the Buddha arrived at Shēnrì’s gate,
the five *zhàng* deep fire pit transformed into a bathing pond.
Lotus flowers grew within it.
Each flower had a thousand petals.
The *bhikṣus* trod upon these lotuses.
One flower produced a hundred more flowers.
They all walked upon the flowers.
Shēnrì saw the fire had turned into a water pond with lotuses growing in it.
He became greatly frightened and terrified.
He bowed his head and face to the ground and confessed sincerely, saying:
“The meal I prepared for the Buddha now all has poison placed within it.
I beg leave to cook again.”
The Buddha said:
“There is no need to cook again.
Bring the poisoned food to eat.”
He commanded the *bhikṣus*:
“Do not eat yet.
Wait until I instruct you, then eat.”
The Buddha immediately recited a *mantra*, saying:
“In the world, there are generally three poisons:
The first is greed and lust (*tānyín*).
The second is anger and hatred (*chēnhuì*).
The third is ignorance and delusion (*yúchī*).
If the Buddha is without these three poisons, then the poison will not act.
If one is supremely sincere and possesses the Dharma Sutras,
the poison will likewise not act.”
The poisoning in the food immediately vanished by itself.
The Buddha said: “Now, eat all the food.”
Shēnrì bowed his head and face, knelt at the Buddha’s feet, and said:
“I was greatly improper.
I used the words of wicked men.
I beg the World-Honored One to pity me and pardon my transgression.”
The Buddha preached the Sutras for him.
He attained the path of *Suòtuóhuán*.
In Shèwèiguó, there was a chief elder’s son.
His name was Biànyì.
Hearing the Buddha preach the essence of fifty matters,
he attained the Dharma Patience.
Five hundred chief elders’ sons obtained purity of the Dharma Eye.
Biànyì said:
“I only wish that the World-Honored One and the great assembly
would condescend to dine at my humble dwelling at noon tomorrow.”
The Buddha and the great assembly went to his home to eat.
Before the grace was recited,
a beggar came
going around the seats asking for alms.
No one dared to give him anything, and having gone everywhere, he received nothing.
He left in anger.
He immediately conceived a wicked thought:
“These *śramaṇas*
are indulgent, foolish, and deluded.
What path do they follow?
When a poor person begs, they have no heart to give.”
“If I become king,
I will use a chariot with iron wheels to crush their heads.”
Having said this, he departed.
After the Buddha finished reciting the grace,
another beggar came.
He begged food from the assembly.
Each person gave him something.
He obtained a great amount of food, and happily departed.
He immediately conceived a thought, saying:
“These *śramaṇas* have compassionate hearts.
If I become king, I will offer support to the Buddha and the Saṅgha.
Even for seven days,
I could not repay the kindness of relieving my current hunger and thirst.”
Having said this, he departed.
The two beggars wandered about seeking alms.
They reached another country and lay down by the roadside in deep grass.
At that time, the ruler of that country suddenly died without an heir.
The physiognomists judged, saying:
“The written records state that a lowly person shall become king.”
The officials and civil servants, with a thousand chariots and ten thousand horsemen, patrolled the borders of the country.
They looked up and saw a cloud-like canopy above the grass.
The physiognomist said:
“There is a divine person within.”
They immediately found the beggar.
All the officials bowed and paid respects.
The beggar was astonished and claimed:
“I am lowly and not of royal lineage.”
They all said:
“You should be bathed with fragrant water,
and dressed in royal robes.”
With brilliant adornments, they escorted him into the capital.
The beggar with the wicked thought
was lying asleep deep in the grass, unaware.
The chariot crushed and severed his head.
Formerly there was a chief elder,
whose courtesy name was Tánmóliúzhī, who came to inquire after the Buddha.
The Buddha said:
“Tánmóliúzhī,
it has been a very long time since we last met and are now able to see each other again.”
Someone asked about this.
The Buddha replied:
“Long ago, during the time of an *asáṃkhyeya* *kalpa*,
there was a Buddha in the world,
named Dìngguāng.
I was then a Brāhmaṇa (*fànzhì*),
whose courtesy name was Chāoshù.
At that time, Dìngguāng Fó
was about to enter the city.
I immediately encountered him midway along the road.
I unbound my hair and spread it upon the mud, allowing the Buddha to step over it.
The Buddha immediately made a prediction, saying:
‘Your courage is thus great!
After the passing of an *asáṃkhyeya* *kalpa*, you shall attain Buddhahood.’
You at that moment conceived a thought of anger, saying:
‘This person is no different from an animal;
to actually step over another person's hair and pass by.’
Since that thought arose, for an *asáṃkhyeya* *kalpa*,
you were continually reborn among animals.
Later, you were in the great sea,
as a *makara* fish (*mójiéyú*).
Its length was seven thousand *yóuyán*.
At that time, there were five hundred merchants
who sailed into the sea to gather treasures.
They encountered this great fish which sucked in their boat, nearly taking it into its mouth.
The five hundred people each called out the deeds they had done.
Then the chief merchant spoke to the multitude, saying:
‘In this age, there is a Buddha named Shìjiāwén.
He rescues people from peril and distress like no other.’
‘Let us call upon his name, hoping to gain deliverance.’
They immediately cried out in unison.
When the fish heard the Buddha’s name, its essential consciousness remained.
It immediately reflected, saying:
‘Shìjiāwén Fó has already appeared in the world.
Why then is my body still in the form of a fish?’
It immediately submerged back into the water.
The five hundred merchants returned safely.
The fish then threw itself out onto a sandy bank.
It neither drank nor ate for fourteen days, and then died.
It was born as the son of a chief elder’s family,
named Tánmóliúzhī.
Now he has come to meet me.
That is why I spoke of ‘a long time.’”
Liúzhī heard this full account.
He immediately went to the seaside to seek his former corpse.
He saw the bones of the great fish; the skin and flesh were all gone. He walked upon the rib bones.
He reflected, saying:
“This is my former corpse.”
He immediately scattered flowers upon the former corpse.
Meditating upon this, he immediately departed.
Suddenly, he attained the Dao.
In the past, there was a man who was very wealthy but stingy.
His wife loved the Dharma and wished to practice giving, but she did not dare.
The husband was about to embark on a voyage across the sea.
First, he used three layers of iron caltrops (ji li) to encircle his dwelling.
His wife was obstructed by them and could not get out.
She focused her mind on invoking the Buddha.
All the iron obstacles turned into swan feathers.
She took a bolt of silk cloth and entrusted it to someone to give to the Buddha.
The Buddha accepted it and recited blessings (zhòu yuàn).
The husband and five hundred companions were together in the middle of the sea.
They were eaten by demons.
Only the husband was spared.
The demons spoke among themselves:
“This man’s wife serves the Buddha;
he must not be approached.”
When his companions had all perished, he alone returned with treasures.
He asked his wife what she had done.
The wife told him everything.
The two of them rejoiced.
They immediately invited the Buddha and the Saṅgha, held an assembly (shè huì), and attained the Way (dédào).
In the past, when the Buddha was alive, there was a great elder (zhǎng zhě).
His name was Xiūluótuó (修羅陀), and he had countless riches, believing in and heading toward the Way and Virtue (dào dé).
He vowed
always to invite the Buddha and the Saṅgha on the eighth day of the twelfth lunar month (là yuè),
and that he and his descendants would uphold this practice without ceasing for the rest of their lives.
When the elder passed away,
he instructed his son not to abandon it.
The son’s name was Píluótuó (毘羅陀).
Later, he gradually became poor.
When the time arrived, he had nothing with which to prepare the offerings (gōng bàn) and was sorrowful, anxious, and unhappy.
The Buddha sent Mùlián (目連) to ask, saying:
“The month for your father's offering is approaching; what plan should you make?”
He replied,
“I only pray, O World-Honored One (Shìzūn),
that you do not suddenly neglect and abandon me.”
When the eighth day was nigh,
he took his wife to his in-laws’ house
to mortgage one hundred taels of gold.
He returned and prepared the offerings.
The Buddha and the assembly of twelve hundred and fifty monks went to his dwelling and sat down.
Water was served, the food was distributed, and when the purity rite was finished, they departed.
That night, in the middle of the night, all the old treasure storerooms spontaneously filled with jewels.
The couple saw this,
and were both happy and afraid,
fearing that the officials (guān) would question [them].
They immediately went and reported to the Buddha.
The Buddha said:
“Rest your minds at ease and use them happily; do not have any doubts or difficulties.
You have practiced faith (lǚ xìn) and have not deviated from your father’s teaching.
Having heard the Way of Giving and Wisdom (shī huì dào), the Seven Treasures (qī cái) are fulfilled.”
The Buddha was in the country of Luóyuèqí (羅閱祇).
There was an influential elder (háo zhǎng zhě)
named Shīlìzhì (尸利躓).
He was extremely rich, overflowing with wealth.
His wife gave birth to a son whose appearance was majestic and wonderful.
They invited a master to read the omens, and he praised the child's blessings and virtues (fú dé).
He asked, saying:
“What auspicious signs occurred since this child was conceived?”
The elder said:
“His mother was slow of speech and clumsy of phrase (nè kǒu dùn cí).
As soon as she conceived this child, her speech became clever and skillful.”
They named him Póshìzhì (婆世躓).
When he was grown up, he traveled around to observe things.
He saw a girl from the home of a Nàluó (那羅) performer
and his heart became attached, wishing to take her in marriage.
He returned and informed his parents, requesting them to seek her hand for him.
His parents told him:
“The high and the low are not a match; how can we arrange a marriage?”
The son replied again, saying:
“Do not ask about the family background, only consider her person.
Please seek her for me; if my wish is not fulfilled, I will take my own life.”
His parents complied with him
and arranged the marriage.
The son was so infatuated by her beauty that he was not ashamed of degrading matters.
He went immediately to her house
and studied performance arts (xì yì), mastering all of them.
At that time, the King gathered many Nàluó performers for various acts.
The elder’s son, in turn, was supposed to present his skill by running along a rope high up.
The King happened not to see it.
He commanded him to go up again.
His strength gradually weakened, and he was about to fall midway.
In his heart, he was panicked and had nowhere to turn for reliance.
Mùlián, hovering in the void (líng xū), called out to him, saying:
“As you are today, would you rather preserve your whole life and body to leave home and study the Way (chū jiā xué dào),
or would you rather fall to the ground and marry that woman?”
He replied:
“I wish to save myself; I do not need the woman.”
Mùlián immediately transformed the area into flat ground, allowing him to save his whole body and head (quán shēn shǒu).
He was overcome with joy.
He followed Mùlián
and went to the World-Honored One (Shìzūn) to prostrate and make offerings.
The Buddha then extensively expounded the wondrous doctrines (miào lùn).
His mind became enlightened, and he attained the first fruit (chū guǒ).
He then requested to leave home, and the World-Honored One consented.
His hair and beard fell off by themselves, and the Dharma robe (fǎ yī) was upon his body.
He focused diligently on meditation (chán sī) and became an Arhat (Āluóhàn).
The Buddha said:
“In a past age, in the country of Bōluónài (波羅奈),
there was a great elder (zhǎng zhě).
He first had a son who was incomparably handsome.
Someone came from the sea carrying a bird’s egg, which he presented to the elder.
The elder accepted it.
After a short time,
the egg hatched, and a bird chick emerged.
Its feathers were glossy and bright.
The elder accepted it and gave it to his son to play with.
The son rode on the bird’s back, flying around and observing things.
He heard that the king of another country was holding a Nàluó performance.
He rode the bird there.
The bird perched on a tree.
He happened to see the king's daughter and his heart became attached in love.
He sent a messenger to convey his feelings (téng qíng).
The daughter then engaged in relations with him.
The King came to know of this.
He was pursued, captured, bound, and was about to be executed.
The elder’s son said:
‘Sirs, why bother exerting yourselves to kill me?
Allow me to climb the tree and throw myself down to die.’
The people consented.
He then climbed the tree, mounted his bird, and soared away into the void.
He managed to prolong his life (yán shòu suì mìng).
That elder's son is the current Póshìzhì.
The king’s daughter is the current performer’s daughter (jì jiā nǚ).
The bird at that time is the current Mùlián.
In the past age, he was troubled by lust and nearly faced difficulty, but was saved by the bird.
Now he was about to die,
but thanks to Mùlián, he gained peace and safety.”
In the country of Shèwèi (舍衛), there was a great elder (zhǎng zhě).
He had a son
who was handsome, and who could speak from birth.
He asked his parents:
“Are the World-Honored One, Śariputra (Shèlìfú), Ānán (阿難), and the others all alive?”
His parents replied that they were.
Seeing that he could speak, they took him to be non-human.
They immediately went to ask the Buddha.
The Buddha said:
“This child has an auspicious appearance (yǒu xiāng).”
His parents rejoiced.
The child then requested, saying:
“I pray that you invite the Buddha and the Saṅgha.”
They replied:
“We suddenly have nothing for offerings (gōng yǎng).”
The child requested again, saying:
“Just sweep and sprinkle the hall and dwelling (táng shě) and arrange the beds and mats attractively (zhuāng yán chuáng xí).
Set up three high seats (gāo zuò).
A hundred flavors of food (bǎi wèi fàn shí) will naturally fill the hall.”
“Moreover, my mother from my previous life is still alive.
She resides in the country of Bōluónài.
I wish to look up and repay her (yǎng bào).”
The parents sent a messenger on an elephant to welcome her.
Regarding the three high seats,
one was intended for the Tathāgata (Rúlái),
one for his current father,
and one for the mother who bore him in the former life.
When the Buddha and the multitude of monks entered his dwelling,
sweet-flavored food (gān wèi fàn shí) naturally appeared, various kinds in great abundance.
The Buddha taught the Dharma for them.
The whole family, great and small, all attained the first fruit.
Shèwèi Chéng was Ānàbīndǐ.
He had seven sons whose hearts lacked true faith.
Toward the Dharma and the Saṅgha, they did not maintain the Five Precepts.
The elder Ānàbīndǐ said:
"I will grant you a thousand taels of gold.
You must take refuge in the Sānbǎo and receive the Five Precepts."
The seven sons heard this
and immediately desired to take refuge in the Sānbǎo and uphold the Five Precepts.
The father granted each a thousand taels of gold.
Together they went to the place of the Shìzūn
and fully reported it to the Buddha, saying:
"How is it, Shìzūn?
Do those seven sons perhaps possess good fortune, various merits, or virtuous deeds?"
The Buddha said:
"Excellent, elder!
You benefit sentient beings and bring peace to gods and humans.
Those seven sons, because of this cause, have perfectly accumulated various good merits.
The karmic results they have obtained, I shall now declare.
To the north there is a kingdom.
The city is named Shíshì.
The land is fertile and abundant, and the people are flourishing and prosperous.
There, there is the treasure of Yīluópōduōluó,
containing countless hundreds of thousands of gold, silver, and precious jewels.
Among the seven treasures of the people of that Jiàntuólài Guó,
whatever they desire, they can all spend
without any decrease, even including this great treasure of Yīluópōduōluó.
Those seven thousand taels of gold, multiplied a hundredfold, a thousandfold, countless times,
all together cannot equal the merits obtained by your seven sons."
The Shìzūn preached the subtle Dharma to Ānàbīndǐ.
[Ānàbīndǐ] immediately rose from his seat and spoke to the Shìzūn, saying:
"May you accept my invitation,
along with the Saṅgha of Bhīqiu,
as I wish to prepare nectarous food and drink
for the sake of the seven sons."
The Shìzūn silently accepted.
The Shìzūn, knowing the time,
entered Shèwèi Chéng surrounded by the Saṅgha of Bhīqiu, front and back.
They proceeded to the house of Ānàbīndǐ and all immediately took their seats.
The elder and his sons paid reverence to the Shìzūn.
The Shìzūn preached the Dharma, and they immediately attained right view.
He declared it to be so.
The elder's seven sons provided sweet and exquisite food and drink.
They fed the Buddha and the Bhīqiu.
When the meal was finished, the bowls were removed.
The Buddha preached the Dharma to the seven sons.
While still in their seats, all their defilements and impurities were eliminated.
Without flaw or taint, the Dharma Eye was born.
They had truly seen the Dharma,
having neither confusion nor doubt, nor hesitation.
The Elder's Son, Liúshuǐ.
In the kingdom of King Tiānzìzàiguāng,
he healed countless sufferings and ailments of all living beings,
causing their bodies to recover.
Because the illnesses were cured, many good deeds were performed.
They spoke thus:
"Excellent, Elder's Son!
You are able to increase the limitless lifespans of living beings.
You must be a *Púsà* who understands all medicinal remedies."
At that time, the Elder's Son, together with his two sons, Shuǐkōng and Shuǐzàng,
took the two sons and traveled sequentially through cities, towns, and villages.
Finally, they arrived in a large empty marsh.
They saw tigers, wolves, dogs, birds, and beasts,
all rushing and fleeing in one direction.
The Elder's Son followed and observed, seeing a pond.
Its water had dried up.
Within the pond were many fish.
Seeing these fish, he gave rise to great compassion.
At that time, a tree spirit (shùshén) appeared, showing half its body,
and spoke thus:
"Great good man,
these fish are pitiable; you should give them water.
This is why you are named Liúshuǐ (Flowing Water).
You should now make the reality conform to the name."
Then the Elder's Son asked the tree spirit,
"How many heads (fish) are there in this count?"
The tree spirit replied,
"A full ten thousand."
(This) further increased his great compassionate heart.
At that time, this empty pond was exposed to the sun;
only a little water remained.
These ten thousand fish,
about to enter the gates of death, writhed in all directions.
Seeing the Elder's Son, their hearts gave rise to dependence.
They followed whichever direction the Elder's Son went,
following and gazing at him, never leaving sight.
At this time, the Elder's Son rushed in four directions,
searching and seeking water, but could not find any.
Seeing a great tree, he quickly took branches and leaves.
He returned to the pond's edge and provided shade for them.
He searched further, trying to discover where the water in the pond originally came from.
He went out in four directions, searching everywhere,
but could not locate the source of the water.
He quickly ran again and saw a great river,
named Shuǐshēng.
There were evil people who, in order to catch these fish, had diverted and abandoned the water at a steep and dangerous place upstream,
preventing it from flowing down.
The Elder's Son reported the circumstances to the King:
"I only wish, Great King, that you would lend me twenty great elephants,
so they may carry water to save the lives of those fish,
just as I extend the lifespans of various sick people."
The King commanded his ministers to quickly provide the supplies:
"You may now go personally to the elephant stables and select whatever you wish for the benefit of living beings."
At this time, Liúshuǐ and his two sons
took the twenty elephants, borrowed ropes and leather bags,
rushed to the river, filled the water, and had the elephants carry it.
The water quickly became abundant and returned to its former state.
Then the Elder's Son walked slowly around the four sides of the pond.
The fish also followed, moving along the bank.
Then the Elder's Son had this thought:
"These fish must be tormented by the fire of hunger.
They must be seeking food and drink from me again.
I should now give it to them."
Then the Elder's Son told his sons,
"Take one elephant, the strongest one,
and quickly go home.
All the edible items
that are the portion of your parents for eating and drinking,
as well as the portions for your wives, children, servants, and maids—
gather everything together and load it all onto the elephant.
Return quickly."
At that time, the two sons went home.
They reported the above events to their grandparents
and gathered the edible items in the house.
Loading them onto the back of the elephant, they quickly returned to their father at the empty marsh pond.
When the Elder's Son saw his sons return,
his heart gave rise to measureless joy and excitement.
He took the food and drink items from his sons.
After scattering them into the pond and feeding the fish,
he contemplated to himself:
"I have now been able to give these fish physical food,
allowing them to be full.
In future generations, I should bestow the Dharma food."
I once heard that in a quiet, vacant place, there was a *Bhikkhu* who recited the *Mahāyāna Fāngděng* Sūtras.
In the Sūtras it said:
"If any living being, when approaching the end of their life,
is able to hear the name of *Bǎoshèng Rúlái* (Tathāgata Jewel Victory),
they will immediately be reborn in heaven."
I must now, for the sake of these ten thousand fish,
explain the extremely profound Twelve Links of Dependent Origination (Shí'èr Yīnyuán).
I should also recite the name of the Buddha *Bǎoshèng*.
He immediately entered the water
and spoke thus:
"Námó (Homage to) *Bǎoshèng Rúlái* of the past."
"In previous ages, while practicing the *Púsà* path,
he made this solemn vow:
'If there are any living beings in the realms of the ten directions,
who hear my name when approaching the end of their lives,
I vow that these beings shall immediately ascend and be reborn in the Thirty-Three Heavens (*Sānshísān Tiān*).'"
He again explained such extremely profound and subtle Dharma to the fish,
namely, the Twelve Links of Dependent Origination (Shí'èr Yīnyuán).
Having finished speaking the Dharma,
he immediately returned home with his sons.
Later, the Elder's Son
was lying down, drunk, during a gathering of guests.
At that time, the ground suddenly shook greatly.
The ten thousand fish died on the same day and were reborn in the *Dàolì Tiān*.
Having been born in heaven, they thought thus:
"By what good *karma* were we able to be born in heaven?"
They then said to each other:
"We were previously within *Yánfú Tí*,
fallen into the animal realm, receiving the body of fish.
The Elder's Son, Liúshuǐ, gave us water and food and drink,
and explained the Twelve Links of Dependent Origination to us,
and also recited the name of *Bǎoshèng Rúlái*.
Because of these causes and conditions, we were able to be born in this heaven.
We should now repay his kindness and make offerings."
At that time, the Elder's Son was sleeping exposed on the upper floor of his house.
These ten thousand sons of heaven (Tiānzǐ)
placed ten thousand heavenly exquisite pearl necklaces (*yīngluò*) by his head.
They placed another ten thousand by his feet.
They placed another ten thousand by his right side.
They placed another ten thousand by his left side.
They rained down *Mantuóluó Huā* and *Móhē Mantuóluó Huā*, piling them up to his knees.
Various heavenly instruments produced subtle and wonderful sounds.
All those sleeping in *Yánfú Tí* were awakened and enlightened.
The Elder's Son, Liúshuǐ, also awoke from his sleep.
These ten thousand sons of heaven flew through the upper sky, traveling about.
In every place within the kingdom of King Tiānzìzàiguāng, they rained down exquisite heavenly lotus flowers.
These sons of heaven returned to their original location, the empty marsh pond,
and again rained down heavenly flowers.
Then they vanished from there and returned to the *Dàolì Gōng* (Trāyastriṃśa Palace),
freely enjoying the five heavenly desires as they wished.
When that night had passed,
King Tiānzìzàiguāng
asked his ministers,
"What was the cause for such a pure and wonderful auspicious sign to appear last night?"
The ministers replied:
"Great King, you should know that
the Devas of *Dàolì* Heaven, at the home of the Elder's Son, Liúshuǐ,
rained down forty thousand pearl necklaces and countless *Mantuóluó Huā*."
The King immediately commanded his minister:
"You may go to the home of that Elder's Son and summon him to come."
The minister immediately went to his home and proclaimed the King's command.
At this time, the Elder's Son quickly went to the King's location.
The King asked the Elder's Son,
"What was the reason for this auspicious sign to appear?"
The Elder's Son replied,
"I know for certain
that the lives of those ten thousand fish have ended."
Then the Great King said,
"Now, send someone to verify the truth of this matter."
At that time, Liúshuǐ immediately sent his sons to the pond
to see whether the fish were truly dead or alive.
At that time, his sons went to the pond.
They saw that in the pond there were many *Móhē Mantuóluó Huā*,
piled up like a mound in the middle.
All the fish had died.
They returned and reported to their father:
"Those fish have all died."
At that time, Liúshuǐ again went to the King's location
and confirmed that the ten thousand fish had all died.
The King heard this and rejoiced.
At that time, the World-Honored One (*Shìzūn*) addressed *Shànnǚ Tiān* (the Good Woman *Devī*):
"The Elder's Son Liúshuǐ of that time is My present body.
The eldest son, Shuǐkōng, is *Luóhóuluó* (Rāhula).
The younger son, Shuǐzàng, is the present *Ānán* (Ānanda).
The ten thousand fish of that time are the present ten thousand sons of heaven.
Therefore, I now give them a prediction (of their Buddhahood).
The tree spirit (*Shùshén*) who showed half his body at that time is your present body."
In the past, there was an elder (*zhǎngzhě*).
His name was Shùtígā.
His storehouses were overflowing, and he possessed ample gold and silver.
Slaves and maids formed long lines; he lacked nothing.
There was a white cotton handkerchief hanging by the pond.
By chance, a divine wind arose and blew it to the front of the King’s palace.
The assembled ministers discussed and divined the reason.
All the ministers said:
"The kingdom is about to flourish, and Heaven has bestowed this white cloth."
The subject Shùtígā remained silent and did not speak.
The King asked:
"Why are you, noble sir, saying nothing?"
Tígā replied:
"I dare not deceive the King.
This is a cloth from my house used for wiping the body.
It was hanging by the pond.
By chance, a divine wind arose and blew it to the front of the palace."
After several days,
a flower of nine colors, as large as a carriage wheel,
was again met by a divine wind and blown to the front of the King’s palace.
The King again discussed and divined the matter with his assembled ministers.
Tígā replied:
"This is merely a flower that withered and fell in my garden, blown here by the wind."
The King asked Tígā:
"Your household is truly like that?
I wish to lead an army of 200,000 to your house to see."
Tígā replied:
"I wish the King would follow me immediately."
The King then led the 200,000 troops
and arrived at Shùtígā’s house.
Entering directly through the south gate,
there were thirty youths whose countenances were handsome and upright.
The King asked Shùtígā:
"Are these your sons and grandsons?"
He replied:
"They are the slaves who guard my gates."
Proceeding into the central pavilion,
there were twenty young maidens whose countenances were handsome and upright.
The King asked:
"Are these your wives and daughters?"
Tígā replied:
"They are the serving maids who guard the pavilion."
Proceeding to the main chamber,
the walls were made of silver and the floor of crystal.
The King saw what appeared to be flowing water and hesitated to advance.
Shùtígā immediately guided the King into the chamber.
The couch was made of yellow gold and the table of white jade.
Shùtígā's wife, covered by a hundred and twenty layers of gold and silver curtains, was peerlessly beautiful.
She performed a ritual bow for the King, and tears streamed from her eyes.
The King asked:
"Seeing me, why is it that your wife cries and sheds tears?"
She replied:
"The King’s clothes carry the smell of smoke, and that is why the tears flow."
The King said:
"Commoners burn grease/fat.
Feudal lords burn wax.
The Son of Heaven burns lacquer.
None of these produce smoke.
Why, then, do tears stream forth?"
Shùtígā replied:
"My household possesses a
'Bright Moon Divine Pearl' (*Míngyuè Shénzhū*).
It hangs in the main hall.
Day and night are indistinguishable, and we do not require firelight.
The King is a king who uses smoke.
Therefore, she smells the fumes."
In front of Shùtígā’s family hall
stood a twelve-story tall tower.
He led the King to the top.
Looking east, one forgot the west.
Looking south, one forgot the north.
It was immense and silent.
The King felt that even a brief moment there was bearable.
They went to the back garden, where there were flowing springs and bathing pools.
They ate various fruits and melons, enjoying the sweetness.
It was exceedingly delightful, and this lasted for a whole month.
The chief minister informed the King:
"You should now return to the kingdom."
Shùtígā then distributed gifts of gold, silver, jewels, brocade, silk, and colored silks.
The 200,000 men, horses, and carriages returned to the kingdom simultaneously.
The King immediately assembled his ministers, astonished by the situation.
"Shùtígā is my subject,
