yet his wives, daughters, and residences far surpass mine.
I want to attack him.
Is it appropriate to seize his possessions or not?"
All the ministers said:
"It is right to seize them."
The King then led 400,000 troops, beating bells and drumming, surrounding Tígā’s residence.
They destroyed hundreds of layers of walls.
At Tígā’s gate stood a strong warrior (*lìshì*).
Holding a golden staff, he faced the 400,000 troops.
At once, they all fell down and lay on the ground, unable to rise.
Tígā, riding a carriage of flying cloud wheels in the empty sky, asked:
"You people, why, when you arrived, are you lying on the ground, unable to rise?"
Everyone answered regarding the matter above.
Shùtígā asked:
"Do you wish to get up or not?"
They all replied that they wished to.
Shùtígā projected great divine sight and glanced at them.
The 400,000 troops all stood up immediately
and returned to their native kingdom.
The King immediately sent an envoy to summon Shùtígā.
They went together to the Buddha’s place and asked:
"World-Honored One (*Shìzūn*),
Shùtígā is my subject,
yet what merit did he possess in a previous life
that his wives, daughters, and residences far surpass mine?"
The Buddha replied:
"Shùtígā’s merit comes from giving (*bùshī*).
Seeing the joys of Heaven,
five hundred merchant leaders, taking various merchants,
carrying precious treasures, rushed into the empty mountains.
They encountered a sick Daoist practitioner (*dàorén*).
They provided him with a grass hut and thickly laid bedding.
They gave him water, gruel, cooking utensils (*wūyù*), and grain.
They provided him with lamps and candles.
At that time, they prayed for the offerings of the Heavens.
Now he has received such retribution (*guǒbào*)."
The Buddha said:
"The one who gave gifts at that time
is now Shùtígā and his wife.
The sick Daoist practitioner at that time
is now myself.
The five hundred merchants all attained the path of the Arhat (*Āluóhàn*)."
In the kingdom of King Aśoka (*Āyù Wáng*) of old,
there was a householder (*Jiāluóyuè*).
He provided offerings to 20,000 Bhikṣus (*bǐqiū*).
He requested offerings for a full year.
His fame reached the King.
The King summoned him for an audience.
"I hear you are extremely wealthy.
What exactly do you possess?"
He replied:
"In truth, I possess nothing."
The King did not believe him.
He detained Jiāluóyuè and sent someone to look at his house.
The envoy saw that his gates had seven layers of houses, residences, and halls.
They were all made of the Seven Treasures (*qībǎo*).
They surpassed the royal palace.
His wives and daughters were also superior.
However, there was no grain, silk, money, or goods.
The envoy then returned and reported to the King, and the King's skepticism gradually dissipated.
Jiāluóyuè immediately laughed.
The King asked, "What are you laughing at?"
He replied:
"The King simply did not believe me."
Jiāluóyuè pointed his finger to the East,
and immediately the area was filled with the Seven Treasures.
Pointing South was the same.
The King then sent him back.
The monastery (*jīngshè*) of the assembled monks was not far from the palace.
The King then went to the monastery.
He saw the community of Bhikṣus.
He performed a respectful bow and asked the Senior Monk (*Shàngzuò*):
"That Jiāluóyuè, what fortune did he possess in a previous life that divine treasures appeared merely by thinking of them?"
The Senior Bhikṣu entered *Sānmèi* (samadhi).
He observed objects up to four hundred *yóuxún* away through mental concentration.
He saw that this elder
was, in the time of the Buddha Vipaśyin (*Wéiwèi Fó*), one of four men who together erected a stupa and monastery.
Among them, one person devoted himself with great sincerity.
After the stupa and monastery were completed, he mixed gold, silver, the Seven Treasures, and many beautiful flowers together.
He scattered them over the three uppermost tiers of the stupa,
scattering them towards the four directions,
praying that his reward of food would never cease afterward.
The one who now possesses naturally appearing treasures
is this one person.
When the King heard this, he greatly cultivated merit.
In the past, there was a householder elder (*Jiāluóyuè zhǎngzhě*),
who was intelligent, well-read, and possessed massive wealth.
He lived near the seaside.
He planted many trees that flourished, reaching up to the sky.
At that time, on a small island in the sea, there were great treasures.
Their value was hundreds of billions, but people could not approach them.
Only birds flew back and forth.
They ate only the 'Bright Moon Pearls' (*Míngyuè Zhū*).
They flew in in the morning and left in the evening,
roosting and sleeping in the elder’s groves.
The elder, possessing great wisdom, devised a skillful plan (*fāngbiàn*) concerning them.
He immediately prepared food of a hundred flavors
and used it to feed the birds.
When the birds ate and were full, they spit out the pearls, covering the ground.
The elder acquired them
and consequently became extremely wealthy.
In the country of Shèwèi-guó there was a *jūshì* (householder/layman).
He lost his fields and residences; his family members were convicted, died, and were all exhausted (gone).
Only one son remained, with nothing left upon which to rely.
The son heard people say:
"Those who feed the Buddha and the Saṅgha are reborn in the Dāolì Heaven."
He thereupon vowed to feed the Buddha and the Saṅgha.
He decided he must work as a hired laborer to fulfill this vow.
There was a *jūshì* who had many fields and residences.
Although this child was small, he possessed many skills.
He sought to be hired.
The *jūshì* asked:
"What can you do?"
He replied:
"I can write, calculate, understand literary meaning, distinguish gold, silver, pearls, shells, money, tie up feathers (manage accounts/records), and supervise fields.
Sitting in a marketplace, there is nothing I cannot understand."
He (the *jūshì*) asked how much he requested per year.
He replied:
"One thousand gold coins per year."
The *jūshì* said:
"Since the world is currently suffering famine, I will only hire you for five hundred.
When the year is full, I will pay it back entirely." The child said:
"My talent is not worth that little, but since my need is urgent,
I will agree to it for you now."
He was immediately made to sit in the marketplace.
After exactly one month,
the tallied profit already exceeded three times the original amount.
He ate only one meal per day, saving the portion for the other meal.
He was then sent to supervise the fields; by the time of the winter harvest, he had gained another threefold profit.
When the year was full, he requested the gold and the food (savings).
The *jūshì*, fearing he would immediately leave, repeatedly made excuses, saying he was not present.
Later he said to him:
"Why do you urgently seek to do this work?"
The child said:
"I wish to feed the Buddha and the Saṅgha."
When the *jūshì* heard this, he immediately generated faith.
He further asked where he intended to do this.
He replied:
"I wish to go to Qíhuán (Jetavana)."
The *jūshì* said:
"Just stay at my door; I will help you with the vessels and utensils."
The child informed the Buddha:
"I pray that tomorrow you will accept my offering of food."
The Buddha and the Saṅgha remained silent (assenting). It happened to be a festival day.
Many laypeople (in white clothes) sent pork, dried cakes, and various foods and drinks.
The assembly of monks received them and spoke among themselves, saying:
"Today this poor child exhausted his effort to organize this assembly (feast).
Everyone should eat only a small amount for his sake."
When they arrived at the *jūshì*'s residence,
he personally served the food with his own hands.
They all said to give them less.
Consequently, the food was not diminished.
The poor child asked the monks:
"Is the food coarse and difficult, or do you pity my poverty?"
They replied:
"Today is a festival day.
People sent food early this morning.
Although at first we only gave them a little,
since the number of families was great,
we consequently became completely full."
The poor child was distressed and worried that his intention would not be fulfilled.
Weeping, he questioned the Buddha.
The Buddha preached the Dharma to him, saying he would surely be reborn in heaven.
"Hurry back now."
The poor child was overjoyed.
He once again served the monks, letting them take according to their wishes.
"I supplied everything with the last of my savings obtained through hard work.
Now, even if the Venerable Ones cannot eat it,
please take it away as you wish."
At that time, five hundred traveling merchants (*shāngkè*),
coming from the country of Yōunàchán-guó, arrived in the late afternoon.
The road was extremely long,
and they had been without food for three days.
They entered the city to buy food.
Because the world was suffering famine and the weather was intensely hot, they could not obtain anything at all.
The merchant leader sighed, saying:
"There is no lack of goods at sea, yet in this great city, there is no food!"
"We should search everywhere again, regardless of what we need."
The poor child was weeping toward the Buddha.
At that time, many people saw this and said to the merchants (*gǔkè*):
"In a certain house, there is food."
They immediately went to the *jūshì*'s house.
They said to the child:
"We need food."
The child asked:
"How many people are there?"
They replied:
"There are five hundred."
"You may call them all here.
Why need we discuss the price?"
When they arrived, food was immediately served, and all were satisfied.
There was a large copper bowl (*yú*).
One merchant leader,
untied the pearl from the corner of his clothing.
It was worth one hundred thousand gold coins.
He placed it in the bowl.
The remaining merchants all untied their pearls
and threw them into the bowl.
The child said:
"I did not sell the food.
Why have you suddenly given me pearls?
Gentlemen, wait a moment while I ask the Buddha."
The Buddha said:
"Just take them; it is not detrimental to gaining rebirth in heaven.
This is the flower-retribution; the full fruit-retribution will come later, and you will still receive the treasures."
The merchants further asked:
"The *jūshì* named Mǒujiǎ who was previously in this city, where is he now?"
He replied:
"He has already passed away."
They asked again:
"Does he have descendants?"
He replied:
"The donor who was just serving you is his son."
The merchants said to the child:
"Your father was our [equal] master."
They gave him another hundred thousand *liǎng* of gold to strengthen their old friendship.
At that time, the (hiring) *jūshì* had no son,
only one daughter who was upright, beautiful, and wonderful.
He sought to make the child his son-in-law.
He gave him a dowry of a hundred thousand *liǎng* of gold.
After the *jūshì* died,
King Bōsīnì (Prasenajit) asked:
"Does he have a son?"
"Who will manage his affairs?"
They replied:
"He only has one son-in-law."
The judge ruled that the property should all belong to the son-in-law.
He was appointed as a high minister (*dàchén*).
The king then commanded that he take the office of the Great Elder (*dàzhǎngzhě*) within Shèwèi City. At that time, the people of the country called him the Suddenly-Arisen Elder (*Hūqǐ Zhǎngzhě*).
At that time, in the kingdom of Shèwèi, there was a great elder (Zhǎngzhě).
His wealth was immeasurable, but he had no sons.
He only had five daughters, who were virtuous, intelligent, and perceptive.
While his wife was pregnant, the elder passed away.
By the law of the state, if there was no son, the property went to the King.
The King dispatched a high official to seize and record the assets.
The daughters thought to themselves:
"Our mother is pregnant, and we do not yet know the sex.
If she bears another girl, the property should belong to the King.
But if she bears a boy, he should become the owner of the wealth."
They went and informed the King.
King Bōsí Nì at that time governed fairly under the law.
He immediately approved what they reported.
Soon after, the mother completed her months and gave birth to a child.
Its body was chaotic (Húndùn), lacking ears and eyes.
It had a mouth but no tongue, and also no hands or feet.
It possessed only male genitalia.
They immediately gave it a name: Màn Cí Pí Lí.
At that time, the daughters
fully presented this matter and went to ask the King.
The King told the daughters:
"The wealth belongs to your brother.
I shall not take it."
At that time, the eldest daughter
married into another family and served her husband,
showing humility, respect, and diligence, just as a servant would.
The master of the house, the elder, seeing her conduct thus,
was surprised and questioned her.
The young woman replied:
"When my father died, his family wealth was immeasurable.
Although there were five daughters, the property was still expected to revert to the King.
Fortunately, my mother was pregnant and gave birth to my brother.
He lacked all human features, possessing only male genitalia,
but he was able to become the master of the wealth.
Although there were many daughters, they were not equal to one son."
The elder, having heard this,
immediately went with the daughter to the place where the Buddha resided,
and spoke, saying:
"World-Honored One,
by what cause and condition did that elder’s son [suffer such a fate]?"
The Buddha said:
"In the distant past, there were two brothers who were great elders.
The elder brother was named Tán Ruò Shì Zhì.
The younger brother was named Shī Luó Shì Zhì.
The elder brother, from his youth,
was trustworthy, sincere, and honest, and always enjoyed giving charity; the whole country praised him.
The King entrusted this man to be the national arbiter (Píngshì).
According to the national law, all loans, receipts, and payments made without a contract were brought before the arbiter.
At that time, a merchant borrowed a large sum of money from the younger brother, Shī Luó Shì Zhì.
The younger brother, the elder,
had only one son, who was young.
He took his son, along with the money lent,
and went to the arbiter's office.
He reported, saying:
'Elder Brother,
this merchant's son borrowed money from me.
When he returns from sailing the sea, he should owe this amount.
Should I die, let this serve as proof so that my son may obtain it.'
The arbiter replied, 'So be it.'
The younger brother, the elder, soon died.
The merchant sailed the sea, encountered a storm, and lost his cargo.
The merchant himself survived.
When the elder's son heard of his return empty-handed,
he thought to himself:
'Although he owes me, how can I collect it?
I must wait until he has the means to repay the debt.'
This merchant again borrowed other capital.
He subsequently sailed the sea again and obtained great treasures.
He returned safely.
He thought to himself:
'Although the elder's son previously did not ask me for the money I borrowed,
perhaps because he was young then he does not remember?
Or perhaps he saw that I was poor before and therefore did not press the debt?
Now I shall test him.'
He immediately prepared fine horses and clothing adorned with many jewels.
The elder's son saw him and immediately sent a person to speak, saying:
'You owe me money; you should repay it now.'
The merchant replied, 'It can be done.'
The merchant thought to himself:
'The sum borrowed was huge, and the accrued interest has compounded.
There is no way I can settle it.
I must devise a plan to resolve this.'
He took a precious pearl and went to the arbiter's wife.
He reported, saying:
'Madam,
I originally borrowed money from Shī Luó Shì Zhì.
His son has come to demand payment.
I now present this pearl, valued at a hundred thousand.
If he presses me for the debt, please instruct the arbiter [to deny the claim].'
His wife replied:
'The elder is truly honest and will surely not consent to this.
Nevertheless, I shall try to speak to him.'
She accepted the pearl. When the arbiter returned in the evening,
the wife reported everything fully.
The elder replied:
'How can such a thing be?
Because of my loyalty, sincerity, and refusal to utter false words, the King established me as the national arbiter.
If I utter one falsehood, this position is untenable.'
'Tomorrow, when the merchant comes, inform him fully of the situation.'
He immediately returned the pearl.
At that time, the merchant offered another pearl, valued at two hundred thousand,
requesting that she ensure the message was passed on.
He said: 'This is a small matter,
yet by merely speaking one word, you gain three hundred thousand.'
At that time, the woman, greedy for the precious pearl, accepted it for him.
In the evening, she again reported to her husband:
'Please grant my wish concerning the matter I told you about yesterday.'
The elder replied:
'Absolutely impossible!'
At that time, the elder had one son.
His wife wept and said:
'If you do not comply, I will first kill our son and then kill myself.'
When the elder heard this,
he was like a person choking.
He thought to himself:
'I have only this one son.
If he should die, there will be no one to whom the wealth can be transferred.
If I comply with this request, people will lose faith in me.
I shall suffer endless persecution and hardship in the future.'
He immediately consented.
The wife told the merchant:
'The elder has agreed.'
The merchant was delighted.
He prepared a magnificent elephant adorned with many jewels, put on precious robes, and rode the elephant into the market.
The elder's son saw him and immediately went and spoke, saying:
'You should now repay the money you previously owed.'
The merchant feigned surprise and said:
'I do not recall owing you anything, nor when I did so.'
They immediately went together to the arbiter's place.
The elder's son said:
'This man personally borrowed a certain amount of money from my father in the past.
Uncle, were you the arbiter at that time, or not?'
He replied, 'I do not know.'
His nephew was astonished and said:
'Uncle, are you sure you did not see or hear it at that time?'
He replied again, 'No, I did not.'
The nephew said angrily:
'Because of your loyalty and goodness,
the King appointed you as arbiter.
The people of the country trust you.
If even for your own kin and disciple, you violate the law like this,
how many outsiders must be wronged?
The truth of this matter will be known in the afterlife.'
The Buddha told the elder:
"Do you wish to know who the arbiter elder of that time was?
He is Màn Cí Pí Lí today.
Because of that single false word spoken at that time, he fell into the great hells and endured much agonizing suffering.
After emerging from the hells, he was forced to endure this kind of body for five hundred lifetimes.
Because he cultivated good charity,
he is always born wealthy and is able to become the owner of property."
There was an elder named Yīn Yuè.
He possessed countless wealth but was old and childless.
He considered this a source of distress and sorrow.
Although, owing to the accumulation of merit from previous lives,
four rewards manifested.
First, his wife gave birth to a son.
Second, five hundred white horses simultaneously gave birth to colts.
Third, the King sent an envoy to confer a golden seal upon him.
Fourth, five hundred treasure ships arrived at the same time.
The Buddha told Ānán:
In a previous life, the elder Yīn Yuè,
sent five hundred men aboard ships into the sea.
After obtaining various treasures, they safely returned home.
Therefore, the Rúlái proclaims that these four blessings universally converged simultaneously.
The elder thought:
“Heaven has sent good fortune and blessings to my courtyard.
I should prepare fine delicacies so my family and relatives can celebrate.”
At that time, the Four Heavenly Kings, Shì, Fàn, and all the various Devās, dragons, spirits, ghost kings, Āxūlún, and others,
each with their retinues, filled the surrounding sky.
The Rúlái, perceiving this elder's immense joy,
went to him because of his happiness and praised him.
If he could be enlightened, he could cultivate further merit.
At the appropriate moment, [the Buddha] sang the Eight Auspicious Sounds.
The elder rejoiced and addressed Qū Tán, saying:
“This is truly miraculous!
You knew that my family and relatives received boundless auspiciousness.
You graciously condescended, Venerable Spirit, to come and praise me.”
Using fine white silk worth ten thousand measures of gold,
he offered it to the Rúlái. The Buddha immediately accepted it.
The Buddha told the elder:
“Wealth is subject to five calamities.
If you can manage them now, you will surely receive a subsequent reward.
Wherever you are born, blessings will naturally attach themselves to you.”
The elder replied to the Buddha:
“What are these five calamities?”
The Buddha said:
“First, destruction by fire.
Second, washing away by flood.
Third, seizure by the authorities (county officials).
Fourth, profligate sons who spend without limit.
Fifth, robbery by thieves. These five matters,
once they arrive, cannot be controlled.”
The elder, hearing this, became even more joyful.
Thereupon, the Rúlái suddenly returned to Qíshéjué Shān.
At that time, there was a Ní Jiàn heretic in the kingdom,
named Bùlán Jiāshè.
He heard that the Rúlái had gone to the elder's house, sung one verse (gāthā),
and received ten thousand measures of gold from the elder.
He thought: “If a Śrāmaṇa can obtain gold,
how much more should I receive if I go and beg?”
He also thought to himself:
“I should go and ask Qū Tán, the Śrāmaṇa, for the verse he spoke.
If I then go and beg, I will surely obtain precious treasures.
My praises will certainly surpass Qū Tán’s.”
Bùlán Jiāshè,
harboring this foolish and jealous intention,
went to ask the Buddha.
“I heard that Qū Tán,
went to the elder’s house, sang one verse, and obtained great treasures.
Would you perhaps take pity on me and grant me the verse you recited,
so that I may chant it, hoping to gain treasure?”
The Rúlái, possessing the Three Insights, knew that after a certain period, this elder’s wealth would be dispersed.
Bùlán Jiāshè did not know the right time or situation.
If he were to proclaim auspiciousness at a house struck by calamity,
he would surely receive countless blows from the elder’s stick.
The Rúlái said:
“I do not begrudge you this verse, but you do not know the time.
If you recite this verse, you will certainly suffer pain.
Therefore, I refuse you.
If you wish to obtain a timely explanation and a truly marvelous phrase,
I shall give it to you.”
This would both allow the elder to hear the true Dharma
and save him (Bùlán Jiāshè) from the pain of being beaten.
Bùlán Jiāshè thought to himself:
“Qū Tán, the Śrāmaṇa, does not want me to go and beg for treasures.
That is why he is stingy and unwilling to give it to me.”
He immediately reiterated his request:
“Just give it to me! How can you know what else will happen?”
The Rúlái compassionately admonished him three times, but he ultimately did not believe or understand.
The Buddha also foreknew that Bùlán Jiāshè was due to suffer this pain due to karmic causes from previous lives.
The Rúlái then said:
“Karma cannot be averted.”
The Buddha immediately recited the Auspicious Verse for him.
The Ní Jiàn chanted it for a whole year before he memorized it.
Afterward, the elder suffered a fire that burned his house, and all his valuable treasures were completely destroyed.
The five hundred colts were burned to death simultaneously.
The excellent son who was born suddenly died.
The King sent an envoy to seize and revoke the golden seal.
Later, he again took ships to sea to gather treasures and returned safely.
While moored at the shore, the five hundred treasure ships suddenly drifted away and sank.
All members of his family, young and old, were afflicted with deep sorrow.
Bùlán Jiāshè went to his gate,
and chanted the Rúlái’s Auspicious Verse, as mentioned above.
When the elder heard it, his whole household became furious.
“There is no disaster or calamity in the world greater than mine!
Why does this naked, shameless person,
stand here performing this sorcery,
saying I am auspicious, thereby increasing my grief and worry?”
He immediately came out and beat him.
From head to foot, [Bùlán Jiāshè] crawled back home.
The followers of the Six Teachers asked him why this happened.
He replied:
“This calamity came directly from Qū Tán.”
Inwardly, he failed to examine himself, but instead resented the World-Honored One.
The Buddha addressed the assembly:
“Previously, Bùlán Jiāshè sought one verse from the Rúlái,
wishing to go to the elder and chant it to beg for treasure.
The Rúlái warned him,
but he did not believe.
Now he has been there and suffered the pain and affliction.”
Ānán asked the Buddha:
“What karmic connection did Bùlán Jiāshè have with this elder that caused him to suffer this affliction?”
The Buddha told Ānán:
“In the long, distant past, during an Asaṃkhyeya kalpa,
there was a king also named Yīn Yuè.
There was also a bird
named Parrot (Yīngwǔ).
It landed on the King’s palace and sang a pleasant, harmonious sound.
The King was sleeping during the day and, hearing the bird's song, awoke in surprise.
He asked his attendants:
“What bird is this? Its sound is wonderfully beautiful.”
The attendants replied:
“There is a marvelous bird,
resplendent with five colors, which just sang upon the palace and then departed.”
The King sent infantry and cavalry to pursue and search for it.
After searching for a long time, they captured it and brought it to the King.
He immediately adorned its body with a necklace of the Seven Treasures and kept it constantly by his side.
He watched it day and night, never letting it leave.
A moment later, another bird arrived,
named Tūxiāo (Owl).
It came upon the palace.
Seeing that the Parrot alone received preferential favor,
it asked the Parrot:
“How did you achieve this?”
The Parrot replied:
“I came upon the palace and sang a wonderfully sad and beautiful song.
The King loved and respected me, took me, and keeps me constantly by his side.”
The Tūxiāo heard this,
and harbored jealousy.
It thought to itself:
“I shall also sing a sound superior to yours.
The King will then also favor and love me.”
While the King was sleeping, the Tūxiāo immediately cried out.
The King immediately awoke in shock.
His hair stood on end, appearing terrified.
The King asked his attendants:
“What is that sound that startled and frightened me?”
The attendants replied:
“It is an evil-sounding bird named Tūxiāo.”
The King sent a large group to spread out and search for it.
They immediately found it and brought it to the King.
The King ordered his attendants to pluck its feathers alive.
Its entire body in great pain, it walked away.
The other birds asked it:
“How did this happen?”
The Tūxiāo angrily replied to the other birds:
“It is entirely because of the Parrot that I received this misfortune!”
The Buddha said:
“A good voice attracts fortune; an evil voice invites disaster.
The consequence of his transgression was his own doing, yet he resented the Parrot.
The King of the past is the elder Yīn Yuè today.
The Parrot is my current body.
The Tūxiāo is Bùlán Jiāshè.”
In the past, there was an elder named Jiū Liú.
He did not believe in the retribution of good and evil deeds in this life or the next.
He traveled with five hundred men to conduct business.
Before reaching the foreign kingdom, they had been without food for three days.
Moving forward, they saw a dense forest in the distance.
They imagined it must be a dwelling.
Upon arrival, they saw a tree spirit.
They immediately bowed to it.
The man (Jiū Liú) was starving and exhausted.
The spirit immediately raised its hand.
From the tips of its five fingers naturally came forth food, drink, and sweet water, which it gave to him. After Jiū Liú was full, he cried out loudly again.
The spirit asked why.
He replied:
“My five hundred companions are all extremely hungry and thirsty.”
The spirit ordered them to be called over.
It again provided them with food and drink.
Both the men and the horses were satisfied.
Jiū Liú asked the spirit:
“What merit did you originally possess that allowed you to achieve this?”
The spirit said:
“I was originally a poor person during the time of Jiāshè Fó.
I constantly polished mirrors at the city gate.
Whenever a Śrāmaṇa entered or exited,
I was always happy to point out the places for begging food (piṇḍapāta),
as well as the Buddhist stupas and monasteries.
I did this more than once.
When my life ended, I was born here,
and naturally received blessings without any lack or shortage.”
The elder became enlightened in his heart and practiced great charity (dāna).
Every day he fed eight thousand people.
The water used to wash the rice flowed out of the city gate,
enough to sail a boat on.
Later, he was born into the Second Heaven,
as a devaputra who scatters flowers.
Formerly, there was a respected elder (zhǎngzhě) in the kingdom of Bōluónài
named Rìnán.
He was extremely wealthy and possessed rare treasures.
He was notoriously stingy and jealous.
Before sunset, he always ordered the gatekeeper,
"Do not let beggars pass."
Rìnán's son, Zhāntán,
was also stingy and greedy.
After Rìnán reached the end of his life, he was reborn in that same kingdom,
as the son of a blind woman.
Her husband told the woman,
"You are severely ill and now pregnant again.
I have no clothes or food; you should leave."
The woman left home and found a large pile of stacked straw/rubble (jùqiáng).
She stayed there.
After nine months, she gave birth to a son, and both her eyes were also blind.
She begged for food to raise him.
When he reached the age of seven, his mother said sorrowfully,
"If only someone would beg for me a little rice to relieve my hunger, like rain to one who thirsts."
The child heard his mother's words and went begging for food, arriving at his (former) son's house.
At that time, the gatekeeper had stepped out briefly, allowing the child to enter the central courtyard.
Zhāntán heard voices
and called the gatekeeper to question him.
The gatekeeper, fearing punishment,
immediately seized the blind boy and threw him violently outside the gate, injuring his head and breaking his arm.
The mother heard the commotion and rushed over, crying, "Who is this wicked person?"
At that moment, the deity above the gate spoke to her,
"The pain you suffer now is small;
the great suffering is yet to come.
Because you, in a former life, possessed wealth but refused to give, you now suffer toil and hardship.
Greater suffering and pain await you after death." The observers heard the sound.
The Buddha asked Ānán,
"What kind of sound is that?"
Ānán fully explained,
and requested the Buddha to have compassion.
Having gone to the child's location and shared his meal,
he went to see the blind child and stroked his head with his hand.
His eyes immediately opened and became bright.
His broken injuries instantly healed.
Consequently, he recalled his past life.
The Buddha asked,
"Are you not the respected elder named Rìnán from a former life?"
He replied, "I am."
The Buddha told Ānán,
"People living in the world are extremely afflicted and foolish.
Father and son in one lifetime do not recognize each other."
Then the Buddha preached a sutra to enlighten their minds.
Some seek sons, others seek wealth; in these two matters,
they suffer great worry, toil, and pain, yet others reap the fruits.
If one cannot even preserve the body one possesses, how much less can one preserve sons and wealth?
It is like stopping to rest under a cool tree in the heat of a summer month;
after a moment, one must leave, for nothing in the world is permanent.
Formerly, there was a respected elder
who cultivated the Bodhisattva mind.
He gathered all the poor people, totaling five hundred,
and supplied them with clothes and provisions.
He entered the sea to gather treasures and stayed overnight on a great mountain.
The others were drowsy and dull, but only the elder sat alone,
gazing upon something.
At night, he saw a person emerge from the side of the mountain,
whose radiant light was extraordinary and whose face was handsome,
but whose mouth resembled a pig's mouth, and who entertained himself with music and performance.
He circled the mountainside.
The elder asked,
"Who are you?"
Hearing the voice, the figure was startled and said,
"I am one who enjoys blessings and have chosen to reside here."
The elder asked,
"Your body is handsome, but why is your mouth uniquely like that?"
He replied,
"It is because I committed faults of the mouth, always delighting in revealing secrets (xièyǔ)."
The celestial being (Tiānrén) asked,
"Who are you?"
He replied,
"I am a respected elder in the kingdom.
I worry about the impoverished and desire them to be secure, so I brought the multitude into the sea to gather treasures.
I also intend to transport the treasures to benefit Yánfú."
The celestial being said,
"Are you perhaps a Bodhisattva?"
The elder replied,
"I have cultivated the Bodhisattva mind.
I rescue and relieve all those suffering from the diseases of lust, anger, and delusion (yín nù chī bìng).
Those who have not yet crossed over, I shall ferry across."
The celestial being said,
"Excellent!"
Thereupon, he led them to the place of treasures, and they returned heavily laden.
Formerly, in the kingdom of Jìbīn, there was a respected elder
who was originally very wealthy.
After his parents died,
he consistently offered sustenance to several practitioners (dàorén).
Within a few years, his household was nearing poverty.
He had nothing left.
Worrying intensely about generating merit for his parents, he became deeply distressed.
The wife said to her husband,
"It is better to toil hard for one lifetime and achieve eternal liberation later,
ensuring our distant parents gain immeasurable blessings."
The elder agreed.
"Let us temporarily borrow one hundred taels of gold for the two of us.
We agree that when the gold is used up, we will work until the debt is paid."
As soon as they obtained the gold, they gave it away entirely, and then went to work.
He was sent to plow the fields, and his wife cooked in the kitchen.
While plowing, he found a large stone resembling a mill cover.
When he uncovered and looked, he saw a thousand cauldrons (dǐng) of gold.
He covered it back up immediately and did not return to eat.
The elder's wife sent food to her husband.
The husband then carried the gold and returned home himself.
The next day, he weighed the gold and returned it to the creditor.
The borrowing couple returned home.
They used the gold for acts of generosity (bùshī) for the benefit of their parents of seven previous generations.
It never ran out throughout their lives.
Formerly, there was a king
who was greedy for lust and committed unrighteous deeds.
Whenever he heard of a beautiful woman, he immediately went and seized her.
The whole country suffered because of him.
There was a respected elder
whose wealth was uncountable, and who was highly talented and broadly knowledgeable.
His wife had a beautiful and proper appearance.
A subordinate informed the king.
The king heard this, his heart was moved, and he sent envoys to forcibly seize her.
Her husband was grief-stricken and vexed.
He abandoned his home and went forth to become a monastic (shā mén).
From his mouth came forth a fragrance that wafted for forty *lǐ*.
His entire body carried the scent of sandalwood (zhāntán qì).
The king saw this person.
Since he had no descendants,
the king confiscated all his household assets.
The king established the man's wife as the primary Queen (Zhènghòu).
Beautiful lotuses grew throughout the kingdom,
blue, yellow, red, and white, very large, fragrant, and pure.
The king, respecting the Lady, first took some and gave them to her.
When the Lady received the flowers, she became even more deeply mournful and emotional.
The king asked,
"You are now the mother of the entire kingdom.
I respect you and we are not estranged.
What is unacceptable in your mind?
Why are you so unhappy?"
The Lady replied,
"I dare not be unhappy.
But I recall that the fragrance of my former husband’s body and mouth surpassed these many flowers.
Reflecting privately on the past, I cannot help but feel sorrow."
The king did not believe her words and therefore sent for him.
The former husband had already attained Arhatship (Luóhàn).
With spiritual powers, he flew through the air, and the fragrance emitted from his body filled the entire kingdom.
The king had him bathed and heavily scrubbed.
But the fragrance of his body intensified.
The king tested him by asking the Buddha.
The Buddha said,
"In the past, there was a poor man
who was destitute and jobless, earning a living by selling firewood.
When he returned after gathering wood, he had not yet reached the city gate,
and the city gate was already closed.
Outside the gate there was a monastery where monks recited scriptures at night.
The man lodged there and sat listening to the scripture recitation.
He burned incense and offered praise until dawn."
Because of this, for five hundred lifetimes he did not fall into the evil realms.
He was continually reborn in heaven, and his body and mouth were fragrant and pure.
Formerly, there was a respected elder.
His wife became pregnant.
A lovely fragrance came from her mouth, filling the entire kingdom.
King Āshìshì
sent an envoy to search, and they found the elder's home.
The envoy asked the elder about this.
The elder fully answered.
The envoy reported to the king.
The king was extremely delighted and summoned the elder, saying,
"If you give birth to a boy, you must bring him to me." The child born later was a girl,
and she naturally wore a golden-threaded garment (jīnlǚyī).
The mother found this strange and removed it.
As soon as she was born, another layer immediately reappeared on her body.
Thereupon, the elder went to ask the Buddha.
The Buddha said,
"Formerly, there was a poor family.
The wife went out and encountered rain.
She saw an aged monastic (shā mén), who was a Pratyekabuddha (Pìzhīfó).
He slipped and fell in the mud, cutting his knee so that blood flowed out.
She immediately helped the monastic up and washed off the mud.
She tore a piece of her own clothing and used it to wrap the injured knee."
Although the woman had not yet fully observed the dharma precepts,
she always enjoyed praising and commending the Buddha Path (Fódào).
After death, she was born into the second heaven.
When her life span there ended, she was reborn below.
Therefore, she possesses the garment that appears naturally,
and a lovely fragrance comes from her mouth.
In the city of Shèwèichéng, there was a rich Elder (Zhǎngzhě).
When he died, he had no sons.
All his money and possessions were confiscated by the government.
When the Elder was alive, he ate coarse food and wore ragged, worn-out clothing, using tree leaves for a coverlet.
The Fó said:
Although he attained a high position, he did not sustain himself,
nor did he raise his children, nor support his parents.
He did not associate with friends, nor give charity to Shāmén.
Today, dying, he enters the Tíkū Dìyù (Crying Hell).
The Fó said:
In the past, he gave food to a Pìzhīfó (Pratyekabuddha).
After giving, he regretted it, saying:
I should not have given it to slaves or servants,
but instead, I gave it to a shaven-headed Shāmén.
Because of this good retribution (Shànbào),
he was born in heaven seven times and born among men seven times, always achieving high nobility.
Because of the regretting heart, this was the retribution of his karma:
He did not eat good food, nor wear good clothes.
He also did not covet the five desires.
King Bōsīnì Wáng:
You should diligently practice exertion and remove laziness.
There was an Elder (Zhǎngzhě) who wanted to build a pagoda and monastery (Tǎsì).
The timber was all prepared,
but only one stone was missing.
It was needed to hold down a pillar.
There was an Elder
who, although he did not worship the Fó, still knew about merit.
He then donated a stone from his home used for pounding clothes.
The monastery (Sì) was thus completed.
When the person who donated the stone died,
he was immediately reborn in the second heaven in a palace of seven treasures.
Divine maidens attended him, and clothing and food appeared spontaneously.
After a long time, the country was destroyed.
No one repaired the monastery, and it fell completely into ruin.
Only the one stone remained, buried in the ground.
The people were plowing the land, and the stone hindered the plow.
They decided to dig it up.
The Heavenly Being (Tiānrén) who owned the stone felt a disturbance in his heart.
Using his divine sight, he observed the man digging up the stone.
He thought to himself:
I was born in heaven because of the merit from this stone.
If this man takes it away now, will my merit not run out?
He immediately descended and transformed into a mortal, standing before the man who was digging the stone.
He asked:
Sir, do you intend to take this stone away?
The man answered:
I want to plow the land, but finding the stone obstructs the plow, so I intend to remove it.
The Heavenly Being asked:
Even if you plow this land, you will only harvest a few dozen *hú* of seeds.
The Heavenly Being said:
Sir, do not take this stone.
I will give you five hundred *liǎng* of gold.
The man asked:
Are you perhaps a spirit?
He answered:
I am a Heavenly Being.
He immediately resumed his heavenly body and said to the man:
I was originally a person of this land.
In a previous life, I gave this stone to a Daoist (Dàorén) to build a monastery.
I was able to be born in heaven and receive spontaneous abundance because of this merit.
Just now, my heavenly palace vibrated, and I wondered why.
I saw you, and that is why I came.
This stone is the root of my merit.
Sir, do not take it.
When the man heard this, he said:
Originally, I did not know.
This is a sacred, bright pagoda and monastery.
It is the field of merit of a Heavenly Being; I dare not violate it. The Heavenly Being returned to heaven. The man reflected:
This Heavenly Being merely donated this stone and obtained such great merit.
I should also build a pagoda and monastery.
He immediately began work and repaired the pagoda as it was before.
Formerly, Jǐgēlǔdú Shì had three sons.
All turned their backs on the correct path, facing the deviant; they wasted themselves on wine and women.
They indulged in galloping, hunting, throwing dice (Chūpú), and gambling (Bóyì).
They departed from light and entered darkness, becoming increasingly foolish day by day.
The father pitied and grieved for them.
He compassionately instructed them, pointing out misfortune and fortune, doing so every single day.
But the sons alone did not change, their wild behavior worsening daily.
The father then clothed them in coarse grass garments and fed them beans and wheat.
Suffering destitution, they repented.
The father said:
Since you have committed unwholesome deeds, you now suffer such extreme misery in this present life.
How much more so the pain of burning and boiling in the Hells? Who will save you then?
The sons knocked their heads on the ground, saying:
We were led astray by wicked friends, indulging in reckless habits.
It was like a pig in the mire, unaware of the stench.
From now on, we dedicate ourselves to serving the Three Venerable Ones (Sānzūn).
The father said, "Excellent!"
If you cleanse your minds, serve the Fó, and observe the Five Precepts (Wǔjiè) without transgression for the rest of your lives,
I will give you fifty million gold pieces annually.
If you take refuge in the Three Refuges (Sān Zìguī), [I will give you] thirty million.
The sons replied:
Yes! We shall obey the venerable teaching.
He immediately had them washed, led them to the place of the Fó.
They bowed their heads, received the precepts, retired, and cultivated virtue.
They purified their intentions, assisted the poor, and relieved the needy.
Their compassion reached all beings; the scholars of the kingdom praised their virtue.
Their names were equal to the sages of antiquity.
Formerly, in the city of Luóyuèqíchéng,
there was an Elder,
named Xūtán.
He was extremely rich and possessed great wealth.
His son was named Xūmótí.
When the father died,
the younger brother was named Xiūyěshěmótí.
[Xūmótí] planned not to share the inheritance with his brother,
intending instead to kill him.
The elder brother said to the younger brother:
Let us go together up Mount Qíshéjuéshān (Vulture Peak) to discuss something.
He then grabbed his brother’s hand and led him up to a sheer cliff.
He then pushed him to the bottom and piled stones upon him.
The younger brother immediately died.
Xūtán was none other than King Zhēnjìng (Śuddhodana).
Xūmótí at that time was I (the Fó).
Xiūyěshě was none other than the current Tuóbōdádōu (Devadatta).
King Bōsīnì Wáng.
There was a high official,
named Líqímí.
He took a wife for his seventh son.
He married the beautiful daughter of Tánmóhē, the younger brother of King Bōsīnì Wáng.
This woman was intelligent, sharp-witted, and possessed many virtues and skills.
After ten months of pregnancy, she laid thirty eggs.
From the eggs hatched one male child.
His form was exceptionally outstanding, peerlessly courageous and strong.
The strength of one man exceeded that of a thousand men.
His parents loved him, and the entire kingdom respected and feared him.
There was a rich Elder.
His son was foolish.
He took a boat to start a business, loading only sinking incense (Chénxiāng).
The incense was refined and expensive,
but buyers were few.
It remained unsold for a long time.
His companions returned home, but he alone was unable to leave.
Fearing he would miss his company,
he looked everywhere in the market and saw that charcoal was the fastest selling commodity.
He immediately burned the incense to make charcoal, hoping to sell it quickly.
When the people saw this,
they all criticized and mocked him, saying:
"This wildly foolish person! Even if selling incense is slow, the profit is substantial.
Now that you have burned it into charcoal, what will you gain?"
The country of Āshīmójiā Āpándì Guó.
There was a chief of the village,
named Sàbó.
In the village, there was a great wealthy householder.
His wealth and treasures were abundant, but he lacked sons and heirs.
He sought from various deities but could not obtain one.
When the time came for a son to be conceived, his wife perceived that she was pregnant.
This woman was sharp-witted and possessed four exceptional insights.
First, knowing whether the husband loved her.
Second, knowing whether the husband did not love her.
Third, knowing the exact time of conception.
Fourth, knowing the cause from which the child was obtained.
She told this to the householder.
The householder rejoiced.
After the full months, she gave birth to a boy whose ears bore golden rings.
This child was handsome, and those who saw him were delighted.
Brahmins were assembled.
They examined him and said:
"This child truly possesses merit and spiritual power."
They created two names for him.
[Because of his] previous life as an ascetic (one who left home),
he was immediately named Shāmén Ěrhuán (Śramaṇa Earring).
[Since the rings] were not man-made and were worth one hundred million [coins],
he was also called Shāmén Yì'ěr (Śramaṇa Billion Ears).
He was cared for by five types of nurses:
First, the body-washing mother.
Second, the filth-removing mother.
Third, the wet nurse.
Fourth, the auspicious mother.
Fifth, the playful mother.
Due to the child's meritorious power, he grew up rapidly.
He was then taught writing, calculation, arithmetic, and sealing.
He was skilled in understanding the costs and relative values of all goods.
This royal village was a gathering place for merchants and travelers.
At that time, people from the four directions came to the village.
They asked, saying:
"Who among these people is virtuous and trustworthy, to whom we may entrust messages and who can advise us on profit and loss?"
Everyone pointed out Shāmén Yì'ěr.
The merchants then went to see him.
They welcomed him as their leader.
These merchants saw his great power.
They thought thus:
"If he acts as Sàbó and leads many people to enter the sea, they will surely return safely."
The people said:
"Shāmén Yì'ěr,
why do you not go into the great sea?"
He replied:
"What would I do if I entered the great sea?
There are many terrors there.
When a hundred or a thousand people go, perhaps only one returns."
The merchants stirred him up and encouraged him, saying:
"What kind of person relies on others to live?"
Shāmén Yì'ěr believed them, accepted the idea, and wished to go.
He went to his parents to bid farewell, wishing to enter the sea.
At that time, his parents spoke of all the terrifying things, hoping to make him change his mind, regret his decision, and restrain him from leaving.
But he did not follow his parents' words.
His parents told the dignitaries, "Help us detain Yì'ěr."
At that time, all the high officials, elders, and householders helped detain him.
He ultimately did not follow [their advice].
When his parents knew his resolve was fixed, they permitted him to go.
Thereupon, riding an elephant and shaking a bell, he broadly announced to the village:
"Shāmén Yì'ěr intends to enter the great sea.
I will act as Sàbó. Who wishes to go together?"
Due to his merit, five hundred merchants were all happy to follow him.
They decorated the ship and lowered it into the water, cutting one rope each day.
On the seventh day, they encountered the Yīlèfēng wind and cut the seventh rope.
The ship was faster than an arrow and went straight to the Jewel Island.
He told the merchants:
"Take jewels to fill the ship, but do not make it too heavy."
Having obtained the Yīlèfēng wind, the ship traveled at a speed faster than an arrow.
They returned to Yánfútí, heading toward the royal village of Sàbó.
There were two paths.
Shāmén Yì'ěr said to the merchants:
"Which path do you wish to take?"
Everyone said:
"It is better to take the land route."
They stopped for the night in an empty marsh.
He told the merchants:
"I once heard that robbers come to plunder merchants.
If they first kill the Sàbó,
then the merchants will achieve nothing.
If they do not kill the Sàbó,
then whether by the strength of money and goods, or by one's own strength,
or by the strength of others, one will certainly be able to capture the robbers.
I should sleep in a different place.
When you leave, you must call me."
The people said, "Yes."
Yì'ěr drove his donkey and went to lodge elsewhere.
These merchants set off around midnight.
Though everyone woke up, they ended up not calling Yì'ěr.
Later that night, there was a great storm with wind and rain.
Yì'ěr woke up and called out, but there was no reply.
Immediately, he pursued them. The road had much sand and dust.
The wind and rain washed away the tracks, so he relied on his donkey to sniff the trail and proceed.
Yì'ěr was extremely hungry. Proceeding forward, he saw a city.
Thinking he might get food, he stood by the city gate.
Following his thought, he involuntarily cried out:
"Food! Food!"
At that moment, countless hundreds of thousands of hungry ghosts came out.
They all said:
"What food? Who will give it?" Yì'ěr said:
"There is no food.
I traveled and became extremely hungry, thinking I might get food.
That is why I uttered this word. I have no food."
The hungry ghosts said:
"This is the City of Hungry Ghosts.
We have lived for hundreds of thousands of years, and only today have we heard the cry for 'food.'
Because we did not practice giving (dāna),
and were overly stingy and greedy, we fell into the realm of hungry ghosts."
"Where do you intend to go?"
Yì'ěr replied:
"I want to go to the royal village of Sàbó."
The ghosts said:
"Go by this path."
Thereupon, he proceeded forward and again saw a city.
Following his thought, he cried out for "water," and the circumstances were the same as before.
Not long after proceeding forward, he again saw a tree.
Named Bōluó.
He lodged beneath it for the night.
He shook the tree, and leaves fell. He ate the finer ones himself and gave the coarser ones to his donkey.
Just as the sun set,
a couch appeared, bearing a man and a woman.
Their appearance was handsome and proper. They wore heavenly jeweled crowns and were engaging in entertainment together.
He thought this:
"I should not stare at others'
private matters."
When the night passed and day came,
the couch immediately vanished, and dogs came to devour the man's flesh until only bones remained.
Yì'ěr thought:
"What deeds did this person perform previously to now receive this retribution?
Good at night, evil during the day.
I must wait and ask him."
When night arrived, there was again a beautiful couch,
with the man and woman engaging in entertainment.
He immediately went and asked the man.
The man said:
"Do you know a certain butcher in the royal village of Sàbó in Āshīmójiā Āpándì Guó?
There was the elder Jiāzhānyán
who constantly came and went from my house.
I always supplied him with food, drink, clothing, and medicine.
He often told me:
'Do not commit evil deeds, or later you will suffer great pain.'
I replied at that time:
'From previous generations until now, we have taken this as our profession.
If I do not do this now, how can I sustain myself?'
Jiāzhānyán said again:
'Do you commit this evil more often during the day or more often at night?'
I said, 'More during the day.'
He then told me:
'If you observe the Five Precepts at night, you may obtain a small amount of goodness.'
I immediately accepted and observed them.
Now I receive this retribution."
Not long after proceeding forward, he again saw two trees.
Named Bōluó.
He stopped beneath them to lodge and ate the leaves as before.
The man and woman came during the day to entertain each other.
In the evening, the couch and the woman both vanished.
Centipedes emerged and devoured the man's flesh.
Only bones remained.
Yì'ěr asked, saying:
"What deeds did you perform to obtain this retribution now?"
The man said:
"In Āshīmójiā Āpándì Guó,
in the royal village of Sàbó,
there was a certain man who committed adultery with another's wife.
There was the elder Jiāzhānyán who frequented my house.
He instructed me, saying:
'Do not commit evil deeds, or you will later receive painful retribution.'
I replied, saying:
'If I cannot restrain myself, what can be done?'
He spoke to me again, saying:
'When do you commit this act most frequently?'
I said, 'More often at night.'
Jiāzhānyán then told me:
'If you observe the Five Precepts during the day, you may obtain a small amount of goodness.'
Because I followed his words, I obtained this retribution."
He again saw a grove and a pond of clean water.
Yì'ěr bathed in it and gave his donkey water to drink.
By the side of the pond was a hall adorned with all kinds of jewels.
Yì'ěr looked up.
He immediately thought:
"I am dying of hunger and thirst. Where should I go?"
He then ascended the hall.
He recited the verse from the Buddhist scripture:
"Hunger is the foremost sickness; compounded existence (samsāra) is the foremost suffering.
He who thus knows the reality of the Dharma [knows that] Nirvāṇa is the foremost happiness."
(He) saw a woman sitting on an ivory bed.
Tied to the legs of the bed were two hungry ghosts (èguǐ).
This woman recognized Yì'ěr.
She therefore asked, saying:
"Śramaṇa Yì'ěr, was your journey not difficult, or were you not thirsty or hungry?"
Yì'ěr replied:
"Noble lady, please give me food."
The woman said she would give it to him.
"But do not give any to these two hungry ghosts."
The woman immediately gave him water to wash his hands and gave him food.
Wishing to let Yì'ěr know the cause (of her condition), the woman briefly stepped outside the hall.
At that time, the two hungry ghosts stretched out their hands and said:
"Please give me a mouthful!"
"Please give me half a mouthful!"
"We are currently burning with hunger in our stomachs like fire."
Yì'ěr, being charitable, gave each of them a mouthful.
It turned into pus and blood; they swallowed much of it, but then spat out the foul, stinking contents.
The woman said:
"I told you not to give it to them.
Why did you give it to them?"
Yì'ěr said:
"Sister,
I gave it because I did not know."
At that time, another woman came and spoke:
"Noble lady,
give me food."
The woman (on the bed) said:
"Eat your usual food."
Having said this,
immediately there were three marvelous cauldrons of boiling, fiery liquid.
This woman took off her clothes and entered the cauldron, where her skin and flesh completely rotted away.
Only her bones and marrow remained; a cold wind came and blew her out of the cauldron, and she revived.
She put on her clothes and ate her own rotting flesh.
After eating, she departed.
Yet another woman came and said:
"Noble person,
give me food."
The woman (on the bed) said:
"Eat your usual food."
When she finished speaking this,
the woman transformed into a ram (gǔyáng) and ate grass.
Yì'ěr said to the woman (on the bed):
"What kind of affair is this?"
The woman said:
"Do you recognize the Sàbó Wáng settlement in the kingdom of Āshīmójiā Āpándì?
Yì'ěr said, "I recognize it."
The ghost tied to the bed leg near my head,
is my husband, the Upāsaka Mǒu Jiǎ.
The one tied to the bed leg near my feet,
is my son.
The Elder Jiāzhānyán used to enter and leave my house.
He received my offerings of clothes, soup, and medicine.
These two people angrily told me:
'We struggled hard when we sought (these things),
but you take them and give them to others, exhausting yourself for nothing.'
Because of this stinginess (qiāntān) and dislike of giving dāna (bùshī), they fell into the realm of hungry ghosts (èguǐ zhōng).
Due to the karma (yè) of their malicious speech (èkǒu), when given food, it turns into pus and blood."
Yì'ěr said:
"Why does that woman eat her own flesh?"
The woman said:
"She is my daughter-in-law.
I gave her goods to keep.
She either consumed them herself or gave them to others.
When I asked for them,
she replied:
'I did not consume them, nor did I give them to others.'
'If I consumed them myself or gave them to others,
then I shall eat my own flesh.' Therefore, she eats her own flesh.
The second woman is my maidservant (bì).
I ordered her to pound and grind grain.
She either consumed it herself or gave it to others.
When I questioned her, she said:
'I neither consumed it myself nor gave it to others.'
'If I consumed it myself or gave it to others, then in a future life I shall become a sheep eating grass.'
Because of this condition (yīnyuán), she is now a ram eating grass."
Yì'ěr said:
"What deeds did you perform?"
The woman said:
"I had a small offense and was born here.
I will not dwell here long, but will be reborn in the Heaven of the Four Great Kings (Sì Tiān Wáng Tiān).
Can you perhaps go for me to the Sàbó Wáng settlement
and tell my daughter that
'I saw your parents, sister-in-law, and maidservant.
Only your mother alone enjoys blessings.
The rest are suffering punishment.'
Your mother, through me, tells you:
'Do not commit evil deeds, or in a future life you will receive painful retribution.'
If you do not believe these words of your mother,
there is a large amount of wealth hidden in a certain location.
Take it and perform meritorious deeds (zuò fú) on my behalf.
Make offerings to the Saṅgha (zhòngsēng) and to Jiāzhānyán.
The remainder you may use for your own livelihood."
She asked Yì'ěr:
"Do you wish to go?"
He answered, "I wish to go."
The woman said:
"Sleep and close your eyes."
In a moment, he arrived at the Sàbó Wáng settlement.
The merchants (jiǎkè) had already arrived earlier.
People were asking:
"Did you see Śramaṇa Yì'ěr?"
They replied:
"He was lost at sea."
The entire town wept as if they had lost their parents.
When Yì'ěr heard this,
(He thought) "If they see me now, they will surely be disturbed again, so I should not return immediately."
He gradually went to the woman's house.
They exchanged greetings.
He related the mother's message to the daughter.
The daughter said:
"Alas, man!
You are a madman (chīkuáng rén)!
My parents gave dāna (bùshī) and performed meritorious deeds (zuò fú); after death, they must have been born in heaven.
How could they be among the hungry ghosts (èguǐ zhōng)?"
Yì'ěr immediately told the daughter:
"Your mother said:
'There is a large amount of money and goods hidden in a certain location.
She instructed you to take it and make offerings.'"
When the daughter heard this, she opened the hiding place and found a large amount of wealth.
She was thus able to generate faith.
Following her mother's command,
she invited Jiāzhānyán and followed him to hear the Dharma preached.
Immediately, while sitting, she attained the pure, stainless Eye of the Dharma (fǎyǎn) concerning all phenomena and achieved fearlessness (wú suǒ wèi).
She bowed to Jiāzhānyán and said:
"Venerable Sir (Dàdé),
I take refuge in the Three Jewels and become an Upāsaka.
I wish to leave home and receive full ordination (shòu jùzú) within the excellent and victorious Dharma."
Jiāzhānyán said:
"Have your parents allowed you to leave home?"
He replied, "They have not yet allowed it."
Jiāzhānyán said:
"According to my Dharma, if parents do not permit it, one cannot leave home and receive full ordination."
He immediately returned home and paid respects to his parents.
Previously, due to sorrow and distress, they had both gone blind.
Hearing that Yì'ěr had returned safely from the great sea,
tears of sorrow and joy came forth, and their eyes regained sight.
After five or six days passed,
he reported to his parents, saying:
"Please permit me to leave home."
His parents said:
"We originally prayed sincerely and wished to obtain you.
When you entered the sea and we received news of your death, we became sorrowful and blind.
Now that you have returned, we are extremely joyful, and our eyes have opened and can see.
You are now, as it were, reborn.
If you accept our words, that will be offering to us.
How much longer can our lifespan last?
If you can complete our remaining lifespan (before leaving),
and do not leave home, we will have no regret when we die."
Yì'ěr answered, "Yes."
In the past, there was an Upāsaka.
He lived temporarily in the kingdom of Shèwèi guó.
His wife's appearance was so beautiful that the whole country heard of it.
When friends wished to see her, he consistently refused to show her.
People informed the King of this.
The King desired to see her but did not know how.
One minister advised,
“The couple both uphold the Five Precepts and offer sacrifices to Daoist priests, personally serving them food and drink.
The King could falsely disguise himself as a Daoist priest, carry an alms bowl, and go to their door.
He will certainly be able to see her.”
The King immediately followed his minister’s advice.
He temporarily changed his appearance and robes and secretly arrived at their home.
The wife saw the Daoist priest and performed a full bow.
When the King had observed her, he returned and spoke to his ministers:
“This woman is truly beautiful and has entered my heart.
I do not know how I can obtain her.”
The assembled ministers replied,
“Although this man is merely a resident, he should come and have an audience with the King.
His arrogance in not coming can be considered a crime.”
There was a large pool of water over a thousand *lǐ* away from Shèwèi chéng.
In this pool grew five-colored lotus flowers.
It was known that the pool had three dangers:
vipers, ghosts and spirits, and fierce beasts.
Criminals sentenced to death were sent to retrieve the flowers.
They would inevitably perish there.
The King then called him and asked,
“What kind of man are you?” He bowed twice and replied, “I am a subject of the Great King.”
The King said,
“Why have you not come for an audience?”
He replied,
“My ignorance prevented me from doing so.”
“I know I have committed a fault.”
The King said,
“I sentence you to go to the pool and retrieve the flowers. You must return within seven days.
If you violate the deadline, I shall punish you severely.”
He accepted the order and withdrew.
He returned home and informed his wife fully.
The wife said to her husband,
“Your current predicament is due to my beauty.
You recognize the Buddha’s luminous teaching: in the Three Realms, there is no one to rely upon; only the precepts are dependable.
On the day you set out on the road, constantly hold the Sānzūn (Three Reverences) in your heart and recite the Shí Shàn (Ten Virtuous Deeds); do not forget them for a moment.
If you do not return, I shall leave home, find happiness in the precepts, and not marry a second man.”
She provided provisions for her husband.
After bidding farewell, he set out on the road, and halfway there,
a man-eating ghost appeared and asked,
“Who are you?” He replied,
“I am a disciple of the Buddha.”
The ghost said,
“All criminals are sent to us.
They lie and say they are retrieving flowers.
You, worthy man, must truly be a criminal,
slandered by wicked people.”
He replied to the ghost,
“Human life is hard to obtain, relying solely on the Great Spirits.”
The ghost said,
“Since you are a disciple of the Buddha and furthermore are without crime,
I will not harm you.
There remain two other dangers which I fear you cannot escape. What should you do?”
The ghost further said,
“I will retrieve the flowers on your behalf to save your life,
so that I may obtain immeasurable merit throughout the long night.
You, xiánzhě, stay here quickly.” The ghost then departed.
In a moment, it returned.
It gave the beautiful five-colored flowers to the xiánzhě.
The xiánzhě found them too heavy to lift.
The ghost then picked up the flowers and helped the xiánzhě.
In the time it takes to bend and extend an arm, they arrived at the palace gate.
The ghost bid farewell and departed.
The xiánzhě approached the gate and announced himself.
The King was surprised by his speedy return.
He fully inquired about the circumstances.
The Upāsaka recounted the truth exactly.
The King was greatly astonished and ashamed, saying,
“A ghost has no human righteousness and harms living beings,
yet today it saved a good man. I, conversely, lack righteousness.
I cannot distinguish between good and evil, making me inferior to a demon.”
He immediately blamed himself, prostrated his head in repentance, and sought refuge.
He requested to become a disciple.
He accepted and observed the Five Precepts and extensively practiced the Liù dù (Six Pāramitās).
The kingdom achieved Great Peace.
The xiánzhě and his wife both increased their diligence,
and attained the stage of non-retrogression.
A hundred years after the Buddha’s Níhuán (Nirvāṇa),
the King served the heaven gods.
For the great sacrifice, they used a hundred heads each of cattle, sheep, swine, dogs, and chickens.
He ordered the chief cook (chúshì) to kill them all.
At that time, the chúshì said,
“I have received the Buddha’s precepts, and I cannot kill living things.”
The kitchen supervisor (chújiān) was enraged and reported him to the King for punishment.
The King said,
“Those who disobey the order shall die.”
The chúshì replied,
“I am a disciple of the Buddha, observing and upholding the Five Precepts.
I would rather kill myself than violate the Buddha’s teachings by slaughtering living beings.
If I follow the King’s order and commit murder,
I will die and enter the hells, and after my sins are exhausted and I emerge, I will always be short-lived.
If I die while upholding the precepts,
I will immediately be born in the heavens, where the blessings and joys I desire will manifest naturally.
Even if I were to die now, my human body would transform, and I would receive a celestial form.
For this reason, I will not kill, even if I must die.”
The King said,
“I will grant you a seven-day period.
You shall be crushed to death by an elephant trampling you.
If you do not die,
your words are true.”
Seven days later, the King viewed the Upāsaka’s body as being like the Buddha’s body.
He drove five hundred elephants toward him to crush him to death.
The Upāsaka, following the Buddha’s method, raised five fingers.
They transformed into five mountains.
From between each mountain, a lion emerged.
The elephants saw the lions and were terrified, crouching on the ground.
Just as when the Buddha was alive,
the King then believed in the Buddha.
He subsequently abolished the sacrifices.
He immediately received the Buddha’s Five Precepts from this man.
Officials and common people, both inside and outside [the court], also received the Dharma.
He consequently became the National Preceptor (Guóshī).
There was an Upāsaka
who traveled far out to seek livelihood with a group of merchants.
They encountered bitter cold and snow.
Traveling at night, he became separated from his companions and stayed in a stone chamber.
At that time, a mountain spirit (shānshén) transformed into the appearance of a woman,
and came to test him, saying:
“White snow covers Heaven and Earth, birds and beasts are all hidden.
I alone have no one to rely upon.
I only ask that you take pity on me and show compassion.”
The Upāsaka covered his ears with both hands and said:
“Shameless, vile, and wicked woman! Speaking these impure words!
I would rather be swept away by water or burned by fire than see or hear you.
I am unwilling to have [impure thoughts toward] my own wife,
how much less would I commit wrongful sexual conduct!
The feelings of sexual pleasure are shallow and fleeting; the great suffering [that results] is deep and terrifying.”
When the shānshén heard this,
it lifted him with both hands and sent him back among his companions.
An Upāsaka married his daughter to a worldly man.
When she was about to leave,
the parents wished to take away their daughter’s precepts.
The daughter said,
“Why should you take away the precepts?”
The parents said,
“The custom is to marry a daughter to a secular person.
It is like throwing gold into cow dung.
What use are the precepts then?”
The daughter said,
“It is like a person making a long journey through a vast, empty wilderness where there are no people.
Should they not increase their provisions and supplies?
Since worldly families serve ghosts, and I fear the ghosts might find an advantage over me,
I should increase my adherence to the precepts to strengthen my resolve.
If gold is in cow dung,
it can still be washed and used.
How can it be the same as the cow dung?”
The parents were moved by her words.
They gave her an image of the Buddha.
The daughter placed it in a solemn vessel.
Morning and evening, she bowed toward the vessel.
The son-in-law asked about it.
The wife answered,
“This is the Buddha, who can prevent the head from turning white and keep one’s complexion perpetually good.”
The son-in-law joined in the offerings.
Afterward, they were both born in Heaven together and did not experience the Sān tú (Three lower realms).
In the past, there was a devoted layman (qīngxìn shì).
When he first received the precepts, his diligence was unsurpassed.
In later years, he grew old and infirm, separating himself from virtuous assemblies.
He dwelt alone on a mountain ridge, and his resolve weakened further.
He became engrossed in his fields and gardens, forgot the Buddha, and abandoned the Dharma.
He reverted to being an ordinary person.
In that mountain lived a Fànzhì (Brahmin) Daoist.
He was thirsty and sought a drink.
The farmer’s family was busy with their affairs and gave him nothing.
The Fànzhì felt resentment and departed in hatred.
The Fànzhì could raise the dead and command ghosts and spirits.
He immediately summoned a killer-ghost and commanded it, saying,
“That man insulted me. Go and kill him.”
An Arhat (Luóhàn) in the mountains knew of this and traveled to the farmer’s house.
The farmer saw the Śramaṇa and happily prostrated his head.
He prepared a meal for him.
The Śramaṇa said,
“Tonight, light the lamp early and diligently take the Sān Zìguī (Three Refuges), reciting the verse on guarding the mouth and controlling the mind.
If you compassionately contemplate all sentient beings, you may enjoy lasting peace and security.”
After the Śramaṇa left, the owner did as instructed.
He spent the whole night reciting the Buddha’s name and the precepts without ceasing.
The killer-ghost arrived before dawn, watching for the slightest opening, intending to kill him.
But seeing his compassionate heart, the ghost had no way to kill him.
It is the law of ghosts and spirits that if they are sent to kill someone,
but that person possesses the virtue that makes them unkillable,
the law dictates that the killing intent must rebound and kill the sender instead.
The killer-ghost became angry and sought to harm the Fànzhì.
The Luóhàn concealed the Fànzhì with his divine power,
so that the ghost could not see him.
The farmer awakened to the Way.
The Fànzhì was saved.
The ghost therefore avoided the sin of killing.
The farmer immediately took the Sān Zìguī.
He recited the Buddha's name tirelessly,
saving the lives of his whole family.
There was a pure lay believer (Upāsaka).
He upheld the precepts, making vigorous progress without slackening.
There was a Śrāmaṇa (monk) who had already cast off the heavy burden,
permanently ended Saṃsāra (birth and death), and attained spiritual powers (abhijñā).
They were close friends.
At that time, the pure lay believer suddenly became gravely ill.
Medicine could not cure him, and his wife suffered great sorrow.
She said to her husband:
"We are husband and wife; why do you alone bear this suffering?
By what means can we divide the sickness to make it lighter?
If you should pass away, upon whom shall I rely?
And upon whom will our lonely son depend?"
When the husband heard this, he became even more attached and affectionate.
When his great life was ending, he died immediately.
His spirit immediately returned, residing inside his wife's nose,
transformed into an insect.
The wife wept greatly and could not stop herself.
At that time, the Dàorén (monk) went to meet the wife,
intending to admonish her and persuade her to discard her worry and grief.
When the wife saw the Dàorén arrive, her sorrow intensified.
"Alas, Hélàng (Venerable Master), my husband is dead!"
The insect suddenly fell to the ground from her nasal mucus.
The wife immediately felt disgusted and was about to step on it with her foot.
The Dàorén instructed her, saying:
"Stop! Stop! Do not kill it!
This is your husband, transformed into this insect."
The wife said, "Dàorén,
my husband revered the Sūtras, upheld the precepts, and achieved unsurpassed diligence.
Why, upon the end of his lifespan, did he transform into this form?"
The Dàorén replied:
"He made the mistake of giving rise to attachment (love and affection), and thus in this life, he was born as an insect."
The Dàorén preached the Sūtra to the insect:
"Your diligence in revering the Sūtras and upholding the precepts earned you the merit that should have led you to be born in heaven and see the various Buddhas.
But merely due to the thought of affection, love, and attachment,
you fell into this form of an insect.
You should immediately feel shame and regret."
The insect listened and understood the meaning.
It immediately reproached itself.
Soon thereafter, its life ended.
It was immediately born into heaven.
Formerly, there was a man
who had only one son,
named Bójuèlú.
The boy was seven years old.
When his wife died, the man took a second wife.
The stepmother hated the son of the previous wife and steamed rice gruel in a steamer.
The boy asked his mother (stepmother) for some.
The mother held him and placed him inside the steamer,
covering the opening with an earthen basin, intending to kill the boy.
The boy ate the rice gruel inside the steamer but did not die.
Afterwards, she held him and placed him on a hot iron pan.
He ate the rice gruel on the pan and suffered no harm.
Later, while washing clothes by the riverbank,
she threw him into the deep water where he was swallowed by a fish.
After seven days passed,
the father invited the assembly of monks to hold a great Dharma gathering.
He bought a fish, carried it home by cart,
and intended to cut open the fish belly.
The boy said,
"Gently, gently! Do not injure the child's head."
This boy had previously received the single precept of non-killing.
Now he obtained five kinds of immortality (or survival).
Formerly, there were five brothers.
Their father instructed them to uphold the precepts.
Only the eldest son was unwilling to uphold the precepts.
He took five coins and went to consult a physiognomist (Xiàngshī).
The Xiàngshī said:
"You will live for about a hundred years and become greatly rich and noble."
Then he added, "But destiny is certainly ill-omened."
And further said, "It is not good."
"Fixedly, thirteen days from now,
you shall die."
That man was greatly frightened and said:
"This is not something that ordinary worldly masters can cure or treat.
Only the Buddha can foresee what has not yet happened.
He is nearby in Qíshéjú Shān (Gṛdhrakūṭa Mountain).
I should go and ask him."
Thereupon, he immediately went to ask the Buddha.
The Buddha said:
"You have antagonistic enemies from a past life who wish to come and claim you.
If you wish to escape,
you must uphold the Five Precepts (Wǔjiè); only then can you be freed."
"When you return, prepare lamps and candles, burn them, and pass the thirteen days."
He immediately accepted the refuge (guī) and the precepts (jiè), lit lamps, and maintained the light.
Day and night, he recited Sūtras and Gāthās,
saying, "Námó Fó (Homage to the Buddha),"
and "Guīmìng Fó (I take refuge in the Buddha)," diligently without rest.
After the thirteen days passed, he was naturally saved.
On that night, two ghosts went to kill him together.
One ghost stayed a hundred steps away,
sending the other ghost to go and kill him.
(The second ghost) saw the bright light of the lamps and fire,
and only heard the sound of calling, "Námó Fó! Guīmìng Fó!"
He did not dare to advance. He countered and told the first ghost,
"We cannot approach this person anymore.
He is only calling 'Námó Fó! Guīmìng Fó!'
I hate hearing this sound; it makes my head ache."
Thereupon, the two ghosts held each other and fled, never going near him again.
From that point onward, he enjoyed long-lasting peace and safety.
Formerly, in the kingdom of Jiāluónài (Kālānā),
there was a son of a Brāhmaṇa,
named Zhíchí (Dharaṇa).
He received the prohibitions and precepts of the Buddha and violated nothing.
After a long time, Zhíchí traveled to another kingdom.
Seeing people committing killing, stealing, and sexual misconduct (yín), he became covetous of them.
Seeing people doing good or bad, he would discuss it.
Seeing those who drank alcohol, he wished to pursue them (and drink).
He was never settled for a moment.
He then thought to himself:
"I regret having received the oath of the precepts; I should return them to the Buddha."
He immediately went to the place of the Buddha and said:
"The Five Precepts I previously received contain many prohibitions, preventing me from following my desires.
The Dharma of the Buddha is too revered for an ordinary person like me to respectfully serve.
May I renounce them?"
The Buddha remained silent and did not respond.
Before his words were fully concluded,
naturally (from the law of karma), ghosts and spirits appeared from his mouth.
They held iron maces and pounded Zhíchí’s head.
Furthermore, there were ghosts and spirits who stripped off his clothes and hooked his tongue.
There was a lustful female ghost who used a knife to cut his genitals.
There was a ghost pouring molten copper into his mouth.
Before and behind him, and to the left and right, were various ghosts and spirits.
They rushed to tear him apart, taking his flesh and blood
and devouring it.
Moreover, there was a spontaneous fire burning his body.
He could not find life, nor could he find death.
The multitude of ghosts held him tightly, preventing him from moving.
The Buddha saw this and asked,
