"Zhíchí, why are you now speechless, unable to speak again?"
He could only beat himself with his hands.
The Buddha, using his spiritual majesty, rescued the elder.
When the kings of the ghosts and spirits saw the World-Honored One (Shìzūn),
they each stood on one side.
Thereupon, he revived.
He arose, knocked his head (in prostration), and reported to the Buddha:
"My body has five thieves,
who seized me and dragged me into the Three Evil Paths (Sān'è Dào).
Because I wished to commit sins and renege on what I had received,
I pray that the Buddha may pity me.
From now on, I will reform my past and cultivate my future, reverently receiving the Dharma of the precepts.
I will observe the six monthly days of purification (liù zhāi) and the three yearly long fasts (sān cháng zhāi).
I will burn incense, scatter flowers, and hang various streamers and canopies.
I will make offerings to the Three Jewels (Sānbǎo) and dare not violate them again."
The Buddha said:
"What you have said now is excellent.
Since you saw with your own eyes, the suffering was self-inflicted and self-obtained; the sin was not bestowed by Heaven."
Formerly, there was a man who did not believe in sin or blessing.
When he was fifty years old,
he dreamed of killing ghosts who were coming to claim him.
Waking up terrified, he sought a master to interpret the dream.
The master made a divination sign and said:
"Killing ghosts certainly intend to harm you within ten days.
If you wish to ward this off,
for the period of ten days starting from now,
receive the Five Precepts of the Buddha, burn incense, light lamps, and hang silk streamers and canopies.
Trusting and tending toward the Three Jewels, you can avoid this death."
He immediately followed this method, sincerely trusting and tending toward them.
When the killing ghosts arrived at the door, they saw him performing meritorious deeds and could not harm him.
The ghosts immediately ran away.
Due to this karma, the man lived to the full age of one hundred years.
Upon death, he was born into heaven.
Formerly, there was a greatly wealthy family.
There were six family members (including dependents/servants) whom they supported,
and their gold, silver, jewels, and treasures were countless.
The Buddha and Ānán (Ānanda) were gathering alms in the neighborhood.
When the Buddha arrived at their gate,
the parents, sons, wives, and grandsons
leapt up joyfully and invited the Buddha to enter and sit.
They spread wool blankets on the ground, and all their eating utensils were gold and silver.
The Buddha said:
"In a previous life, this person encountered an era of famine.
His family was poor and destitute.
They could only gather various vegetables to sustain their lives.
As soon as the soup was cooked,
a Dàorén was outside begging for alms. They saw the Śrāmaṇa.
The parents immediately said,
'I will give him my share.'
The sons, wives, and grandsons each gave their share to him.
They deferred to the mother, asking her to eat.
The six people simultaneously made the resolve and each went without eating for one day.
They only regretted their family's poverty and lack of good offerings. Because of this blessing, they were born into heaven and amongst humans.
They constantly attained peace, stability, and abundant wealth.
Because their resolution was equivalent (made together),
they created karmic connections together lifetime after lifetime.
Now they have met again.
The parents, sons, young and old, all upheld the Five Precepts at the same time.
When their lives ended, they were born into heaven and received immeasurable blessings.
If they had met the Buddha (in that life), they would all have attained Arhatship (Luóhàn)."
A person was walking along the road.
He saw a dead person beside the road.
A *guǐshén* was whipping him with a staff.
The traveler said,
"This person is already dead; why are you whipping him?"
The *guǐshén* said,
"This was my former body (self).
While it was alive, it was unfilial toward its parents and disloyal in serving the ruler (*jūn*).
It did not venerate the Three Jewels (*Sānbǎo*).
It did not follow the words of its masters (*shīfù*).
Now, I am compelled to live according to these sins.
The suffering is hard to describe.
In anger (*chēn*), I whip him."
He walked a little further.
Again, he saw a dead person.
A *tiānrén* came down,
scattered flowers upon the corpse, and stroked it with their hand.
The traveler asked, saying,
"Looking at you, Sir, you appear to be a *tiānrén*.
Why do you stroke this dead person?"
They replied, saying,
"This was my former body.
While it was alive, it was filial and obedient to its parents.
It was loyal and faithful in serving the ruler (*jūn*).
It venerated the Three Honored Ones (*Sānzūn*).
It received and accepted the teachings of its masters (*shīfù*).
This allowed my spirit (*shén*) to be born in heaven.
All this is due to the kindness (*ēn*) of this former body.
Therefore, I have come to repay it."
He walked a little further.
Again, he saw a *tiānrén*.
Their clothes were bright, beautiful, dignified, fragrant, and pure.
They were picking sour jujubes (*suānzǎo*) by the side of the road and eating them.
The traveler asked,
"I observe you, Sir, to be a *tiānrén*.
Why are you eating sour jujubes?"
The *tiānrén* replied,
"When I was in the world, I was filial and obedient to my parents.
I was loyal and faithful in serving the ruler (*jūn*) and venerated the Three Honored Ones (*Sānzūn*).
I performed all kinds of meritorious deeds (*gōngdé*).
The only thing was that I did not enjoy offering food and drink to guests (*rénkè*).
Now that I am a *tiānrén*, I constantly eat, but I am never satisfied.
Therefore, I eat sour jujubes."
In one day, the traveler witnessed these three transformations.
He immediately returned, devotedly upheld the Five Precepts (*Wǔjiè*), and practiced the Ten Virtues (*Shíshàn*).
He was filial and obedient to his parents, and loyal and faithful in serving the ruler (*jūn*).
He narrated this to later generations, showing how sin and merit follow people.
There was a certain *yōupósāi* who originally practiced heterodox ways (*wàidào*), tired of suffering, and often made offerings and sacrifices.
He abandoned those practices, entered the Dharma (*fǎ*), upheld the precepts, and was diligent.
He diligently recited scriptures, enjoyed giving alms (*bùshī*), and was responsible.
He practiced patience (*rěnrǔ*) and constantly maintained a compassionate heart (*cíxīn*).
He died suddenly; just before he died, he instructed his parents, saying,
"If my sickness proves fatal, do not inter me for seven days."
He suddenly appeared dead, and the body was kept for eight days.
All the relatives said,
"We must quickly hold the funeral and collection rites (*bìnliǎn*)."
The parents said,
"The body is not swollen or rotten, so we wish to keep it until the tenth day."
While they were speaking, they saw his eyes open.
He was not yet able to move.
His parents were delighted and watched over him until the tenth day.
He then stood up, sat down, and was able to speak clearly.
They asked where he had been and everything he had seen.
He replied,
"Official soldiers (*lìbīng*) came and led me to a great city.
Within the city was a prison (*yù*).
The prison was utterly black, a city of iron on all four sides.
The city gates were entirely of iron, burning bright red.
The people imprisoned sat in the midst of fire.
They were burned completely, top to bottom, with blue smoke rising.
Some people had their flesh cut off with knives and were eaten.
The Prison King (*Yùwáng*) asked me, saying,
'What kind of person are you?
What crime have you committed that you have come here?
Here, we punish the Five Grave Sins (*Wǔnì*), those unfilial toward their parents, and those disloyal and unfaithful in serving the ruler (*jūn*).'
I replied,
'When I was young, I was misled by wicked people.
I practiced heterodox ways (*wàidào*) foolishly.
Moreover, I drank alcohol, killed living beings, and sacrificed to Heaven and Earth (*Tiāndì*).
Furthermore, in the marketplace, I seized wealth and profit.
I manipulated measures hoping to enrich myself.
Afterwards, I met a good master (*shànshī*).
He led me into the Buddhist path (*Fódào*).
I saw a *shāmén* and a *dàorén*.
They administered the Five Precepts (*Wǔjiè*) to me, and I upheld the Ten Virtues (*Shíshàn*).
From that time until today,
I have not committed evil again.'
I look up to the Illumined King (*Míngwáng*); may he pity me before it is too late."
I immediately kowtowed.
The King stood up, clasped his hands, and said to me,
"Stop! Stop!
A person of pure faith should not be treated like this.
He then provided me with a seat.
He called the officials (*lì*) and asked them,
'This is a disciple of the Supreme True Dharma (*Wúshàng Zhèngzhēn*).
All of you should obtain deliverance (*dù*) through people like him.
It is only when this person's lifespan is naturally exhausted
that he should die.
His soul (*húnshén*) follows his actions.
If he is reborn in heaven, the *tiānshén* welcome him.
If he is reborn among humans, the human realm welcomes him.
How dare you bring such a person
into this place of the Five Grave Sins (*Wǔnì*)?'
The officials replied to the King, saying,
'There are many such people in the world.
They do not fear the King's law (*wángfǎ*).
They do not fear the four seasons.
They are not restrained by the Five Phases (*Wǔxíng*).
They ignore Heaven, Earth, ghosts, and spirits (*tiāndì guǐshén*), running rampant across the land.
They must be interrogated.
There are masters called *shāmén*.
They shave their heads and wear coarse and simple clothing.
They use this to make themselves great.
They lead many disciples everywhere, east, west, south, and north.
These acts are too severe; they ought to be punished.'
The King said,
'Stop! Stop! Those who wear the robes of the Dharma (*fǎfú*) are valued and respected by others, and difficult for others to threaten.
All the Śakra-Brahma gods (*shìfàn*), the sun, the moon, and the kings (*wáng*),
down to emperors, kings, ministers, and common people,
who honor and serve these people gain immeasurable blessings (*fú*).
Those who disrespect them bring sin and suffering (*zuìkǔ*) upon themselves.
Quickly check the register of names—has his lifespan ended yet?'
The official said,
'He should not have died yet.
He still has twenty years remaining in his calculation of life.
He was taken because of some prior sins he committed.
This was to make his peers humble themselves a little.'
The King said,
'A Son of the Buddha (*Fózǐ*) who upholds the precepts and is diligent is honored by the *tiānshén*.
The Buddha (*Fó*) uses great compassion (*dàcí*) to save and protect all creatures, whether flying, crawling, or wiggling.
The *tiānshén*, the Earth Spirits (*Dìqí*), all ghosts, and dragons (*lóng*) all respect and value them.
How could they be restrained by the King's appearance, the four seasons, or the Five Phases (*Wǔxíng*)?
The Buddha's grace (*Fó'ēn*) is like the four seas, without measure.'
The official said, 'Great King (*Dàwáng*),
do you also uphold the Buddha's precepts?'
The King replied,
'It is because I did not uphold the Buddha's Dharma that I was punished and made this Prison King (*Yùwáng*).
If a person has already entered the True Dharma (*Zhèngfǎ*),
but later regrets and returns to heterodox ways (*wàidào*),
even if he lives for a thousand years, he will still encounter the Nine Sudden Calamities (*Jiǔhèng*).
As for the *bǐqiū* who maintain the precepts, and all the disciples,

they must diligently practice the Six Perfections (*Liùdù*), sever the Six Decays (*Liùshuāi*), cut off the twenty (hindrances), and contemplate the Buddha's merit (*Fógōngdé*), which is like the great ocean—it cannot be matched.'
The official said,
'It is truly as the King says.
We failed to distinguish the genuine from the false.
Quickly release him; bid him farewell and send him away.'
I fell from a height and suddenly revived.
Together with his parents, he went to *Qíhuán*.
He reflected on himself and disciplined himself.
He devotedly received the Five Precepts (*Wǔjiè*) and practiced the Ten Virtues (*Shíshàn*)."
Greatly believed in heretical views.
There was no Buddha, Dharma, or Saṅgha.
There was a woman,
named Yōupō Sīnà, who, due to some business, went to the state of Shèwèi.
After the business with King Bōsīnì was concluded,
she heard of the Buddha's merits from various deeply devoted Upāsakas.
Wishing to see the Buddha,
she immediately went to Qíhuán.
She happened upon the Buddha teaching the Dharma of the Five Precepts to the great assembly.
Yōupō Sīnà requested to receive them from the Buddha.
She immediately received the Five Precepts.
The Buddha also gave her the Fǎjù Jīng (Dharmapada Sūtra) and told her to recite it.
At midnight, while she was reciting the Fǎjù Jīng,
Vaisravana, the Heavenly King Píshāmén,
traveling with several thousand Yakṣas, intending to go to the south where Vaisravana Pílóulèchà resided,
heard the sound of the sūtra recitation and all immediately stopped to listen.
They praised her, saying,
"Excellent, sister! You skillfully speak the essentials of the Dharma."
Yōupō Sīnà immediately asked,
"Who are you?
I only hear a voice in the air but see no form."
They replied,
"I am Píshāmén Tiān, the King of Ghosts.
I stopped in the sky to listen to the Dharma."
She asked again,
"You are a god (deva) and I am a human.
Why do you call me sister?"
He answered,
"The Buddha is the King of Dharma and the father of humans and devas alike.
Sharing the same flavor of the Dharma, we call each other sister."
At that time, Yōupō Sīnà's heart was greatly delighted.
She constantly sent people into the woods to gather firewood.
The next morning, climbing a tree,
she saw Sàlìfú and Mùlián, along with five hundred Bhikṣus, diligently practicing meditation and recitation in the woods.
She sent a person back to inform her mistress.
Yōupō Sīnà was infinitely joyous and took off two golden bracelets to reward the messenger.
The messenger further said,
"The World-Honored One has good words to entrust to the mistress."
He fully related the Five Kinds of Giving (Wǔ Shī).
She again took off her necklace and bestowed it upon him.
The messenger said,
"Now, quickly get up, wash your hands, and prepare the food and drink.
I already took the liberty of using the mistress's words
to invite the two Venerables and the five hundred disciples
to come today for a meal."
She immediately released the messenger and provided him with jewels.
She informed all her family members and neighbors
to set up the offerings.
The Venerables and the Bhikṣus put on their robes, took their bowls, and sat down in their seats.
After making the prostration, she personally served water and offered various kinds of food.
The fragrance and taste were complete.
She said to Shèlìfú,
"There is a spirit in this house who is close to me.
When I make offerings, he tells me:
'This is an Arhat,
this is a Noble One, this is an ordinary person,
this one observes the precepts, this one breaks the precepts,
this one is wise, this one is foolish.'"
She further said to Shèlìfú,
"I have four sons and a husband,
all of whom cling to wicked, heterodox views.
If I make offerings to the Three Jewels or give charity to the poor,
they become jealous and angry.
But I continue cultivating goodness and giving charity without ever retreating, and I have attained the state of Sūtuóhuán (Sotāpanna)."
Shèlìfú said,
"This is truly rare."
"The World-Honored One will, this evening,
come to the woods of Píqián to stay.
We must now return to our abode."
After the Saṅgha had left,
she immediately prepared what was needed and went to the Buddha’s location.
She observed where the various monks were staying overnight.
She saw one sick monk lying in a grass hut.
She asked what his illness was and what he needed.
He replied,
"The four elements (Dà) are unbalanced, causing extreme suffering.
The doctor ordered me to take fresh meat broth." Sīnà said,
"Do not seek elsewhere.
I will deliver it tomorrow."
The next day was the fifteenth, and the national law forbade killing.
She sought everywhere but could not find any.
So, she sent away all her attendants.
In a quiet room, she bathed herself and cut the flesh from her thigh.
She wrapped it in cloth, mixed it with various herbs,
cooked it into a soup, and sent it to the sick Bhikṣu.
After the Bhikṣu ate it, his illness immediately vanished and he recovered.
Her husband soon returned and saw his wife’s complexion had changed.
He immediately asked,
"Why are you so haggard?"
She replied,
"I am ill."
He immediately called a doctor, but the doctor could not diagnose it.
He pressed the servants and maids until they told him everything.
The husband went into the streets and loudly proclaimed,
"The śramaṇas, the sons of Śākya, eat human flesh, just like King Jùnzú!"
Because of this, the Buddha instituted a rule:
"Monks,
all impure meat must not be eaten."
The Upāsikā said,
"Because of me, the eating of meat was prohibited."
She immediately said to her husband,
"If you can invite the Buddha and the Saṅgha to come here and set up offerings for me, it would be wonderful.
If you cannot, I will end my life."
For the sake of his wife, the husband entered the forest and invited the Buddha.
The next day, food was prepared at the house.
The Buddha and the assembly of monks took their seats.
The Buddha asked, "Where is Sīnà?"
They replied, "She is ill."
The Buddha said, "Call her here."
The husband said,
"Your Master is calling you."
She replied,
"The pain of the illness prevents me from getting up."
The Buddha told Ānán,
"You go and tell her to get up."
Ānán immediately went and called her in the Buddha's name.
She was carried to the Buddha’s presence along with her bed.
Upon encountering the Buddha's light, her painful illness was immediately eradicated, and she was restored as before. She immediately rose and prostrated to the Buddha.
The Buddha preached the Dharma for her, and she attained the way of Ānàhán (Anāgāmin).
Her husband and family members abandoned their heterodox views
and received the Five Precepts, becoming disciples of the Buddha.
In the city of Wéiyēlǐ (Vaiśālī),
there was a woman
named Āfánhélì.
Hearing that the Buddha was traveling there, she was infinitely joyful.
Together with five hundred women, she went to the Buddha's location.
Hearing the Buddha preach the Dharma, her heart became enlightened.
She invited the Buddha for food and drink.
At that time, there were also five hundred sons of elders in the city
who also invited the World-Honored One.
The World-Honored One said,
"I have already accepted Āfánhélì's invitation for tomorrow."
Then the sons of the elders
said to Hélì,
"The supremely Honored Buddha has come to transform our country.
We should feed him first.
You should temporarily postpone your offering."
The woman said,
"Do not use the power of the strong against the weak woman.
If you can grant me four wishes, I shall yield to you."
"First, let my heart preserve goodness and never change.
Second, let my life be preserved and not perish.
Third, let my wealth not decrease.
Fourth, let the Buddha reside in this country permanently."
The elders' sons said, "Good!
You are now able to comprehend impermanence.
But the wishes you hope for are not things we can accomplish.
We will let you feed the Buddha first."
Among them, a few youths were ashamed to be secondary.
They obstinately refused to desist.
They then commanded the city market officials to stop all trade and commerce.
Hélì sent people to seek various goods,
but found nothing at all.
However, the various provisions in her storeroom were naturally filled.
Only firewood and charcoal were lacking.
She used oil-soaked white cloth in place of them.
Furthermore, the inner city gates were ordered shut so she could not leave.
She sent a message requesting the Buddha to come.
She immediately sent a parrot to report that the food was ready.
The elders’ sons shot at it.
Through the Buddha's spiritual power, the arrows transformed into flowers.
It reached the Buddha's location.
It flew and chirped, reporting to the Buddha, the Blessed One (Zhòngyòu), and the Saṅgha.
When the Buddha set his foot on the city gate, heaven and earth trembled.
The five hundred elders' sons,
Āfánhélì, and the various women,
seeing and hearing this event, attained the Eye of the Dharma and received and upheld the Five Precepts.
The Elder Xūdá in the Kingdom of Shèwèi.
He had a young daughter born later.
Her name was Sūmàn.
Her face and head were most exquisite.
Her father loved her dearly.
He took her to the place of the Buddha.
When the girl saw the Buddha, her feelings swelled with double joy and excitement.
She wished to obtain good perfume and smear it upon the Buddha's dwelling chamber.
This girl had Bīnpóluò in her hand.
The Buddha requested it from the girl.
She immediately gave it to the Buddha.
He wrote "fragrance" upon it and returned it to her.
The girl and her father returned to the city to seek and purchase.
They brought what the Buddha required and proceeded to Qíhuán.
She personally pounded and ground (the ingredients).
Day after day it was like this.
At that time, the King of Tèchā Shīlìguó,
sent one of his sons as an envoy to Shèwèi to travel widely and observe.
He arrived at the monastery and saw the girl Sūmàn.
He immediately took her as his wife.
Later, she became pregnant and gave birth to ten eggs.
After the eggs opened, there were ten sons.
Their appearance was beautiful, and they were brave and strong, quite extraordinary.
However, they enjoyed hunting.
Their mother instructed them not to do this.
The sons reported to their mother,
"Shooting and hunting are the greatest pleasures."
When the mother ordered them to stop, they took her efforts at hindrance as hatred (towards them).
The mother again told them,
"Because I love you, I constrain you in this way.
If I hated you, I would certainly never say such things.
The sin of killing living beings will cause you to enter the hells.
After immeasurable kalpas, how will you be freed?"
The sons asked their mother,
"Did this come from your own heart, or did you hear it from another source?"
The mother again told them,
"I heard it from the Buddha."
The sons again asked the mother,
"Who is the Buddha?
We humbly request you to explain fully."
The mother told her sons,
"He is the Prince of Jìngfàn Wángzǐ of the Kingdom of Jiāwéiluóyuè.
He grew weary of aging, sickness, and death, left home to study the Way, and attained the unsurpassed fruit.
His great body is sixteen feet tall (zhàng liù), he possesses the Three Insights and the Six Supernatural Powers, and his far-reaching contemplation knows no bounds."
The sons petitioned their mother, seeking to go and pay homage to the Buddha.
The mother immediately consented.
They went to Qíhuán and paid reverence to the Rúlái.
The Buddha preached the Dharma for them.
All ten men simultaneously obtained the pure Dharma Eye.
They then requested to leave home (become monks).
The Buddha consented to their following the Way.
Their beards and hair spontaneously fell off, and the robes of the Dharma appeared on their bodies.
They diligently pursued the great task.
They all attained Luóhànship, exhausting the bounds of suffering.
Ninety-one kalpas ago, there was Pípóshī Fó.
After his Parinirvāṇa, his relics (shèlì) were distributed, and innumerable stupas were erected.
At that time, one stupa had decayed, rotted, and collapsed.
There was an old woman who repaired and maintained it.
Ten young men happened to be passing by and saw it.
They joyfully helped, and the task was completed.
They vowed to be mother and sons.
Since then, for ninety-one kalpas,
they have constantly been born together in the heavens and among humans, enjoying blessings and happiness.
The old woman then is now the girl Sūmàn Nǚ.
The ten youths then are now the ten Luóhàn.
The Buddha was in the Jǐgūdú Yuán in the Kingdom of Shèwèi.
There was a solitary mother who had lost a son.
Distressed, anxious, and deeply troubled, she embraced the corpse, weeping and running.
She was like a mad person.
She went out and arrived at Qíhuán.
She heard that the Buddha was a Great Sage, revered by devas and humans.
He preached the sutras and the Way, causing worry to be forgotten and misfortune to be removed.
The solitary mother saw the Buddha, made obeisance, and knelt down for a long time.
She begged to be released from her bond of sorrow.
The Buddha told the solitary mother,
"You must quickly enter the city and walk throughout the streets and lanes.
Beg for fire from a family that has not experienced death and bring it back."
The solitary mother searched but could not find one.
She returned empty-handed.
The Buddha told the solitary mother,
"A person living in the world has four conditions that cannot be maintained forever:
First, permanence must lead to impermanence.
Second, wealth and nobility must lead to poverty and lowliness.
Third, gathering together must lead to separation.
Fourth, strength and good health must lead to death.
Why are you now acting so?
Why do you not worry for yourself?
Why not broadly practice giving (bùshī), uphold the precepts, observe the six fast days (liùzhāi) monthly, and provide charity to the solitary and the poor according to your capacity and ability?
The solitary mother reported to the Buddha,
"The love I bear my son has penetrated my bones and marrow.
How could I begrudge my body or life?"
At that moment, the Buddha wished to transform her and enable her to awaken.
He immediately manifested four great fire pits surrounding the solitary mother.
The heat of the fire pressed against her body, and she used her son to shield herself.
The Buddha said to the solitary mother,
"You just now stated that your love for your son was so heavy it penetrated your bones and marrow,
and that you would rather destroy yourself than allow your son to perish.
Now that the heat of the fire presses against you, and the aching pain is unbearable,
you merely choose to endure it yourself while using your son as a shield?
The small fire of the human realm is truly not worth mentioning.
When the fires of hell burn, the pain is immeasurable.
Animals suffer from delusion.
Hungry ghosts suffer from hunger and thirst.
Those who can benefit themselves ought to cultivate generosity (bùshī), uphold the precepts, and practice patience (rěnrù).
Then they will not be reborn in the hells or as hungry ghosts.
They will receive the blessings of devas and humans, gradually approaching Níhuán."
At that moment, the solitary mother blamed herself internally and grew weary of the suffering caused by affection.
Right there before the Buddha, she eliminated all worldly defilements.
She achieved Xūtuóhuánship.
In Tiānzhú, there was a man.
He traveled to Shèwèiguó.
His wife bore two sons.
The elder son was seven years old.
The younger son was an infant in arms.
The mother was pregnant again.
She was nearing the time of delivery.
According to the custom of Tiānzhú,
when a woman approached her month, she returned to her parents' house.
At this time, the couple rode together in a cart, carrying their two sons.
They proceeded toward Shèwèichéng.
Halfway there, they let the ox graze.
Then, a poisonous snake coiled around the ox's leg.
The ox thus broke loose from its tether.
When the husband went to retrieve the ox, the snake abandoned the ox and killed the husband.
The wife saw this, was terrified, and wept bitterly.
The day was already approaching darkness.
They were not far from home.
A river separated them (from the destination).
Fearing bandits in the darkness,
she immediately abandoned the cart and led her two sons.
She arrived at the river bank.
She left the elder son at the water's edge,
embraced the younger one, and crossed. When she was only halfway across the water,
a wolf devoured her son, who cried out for his mother.
The mother heard the sound, turned back, and saw this.
Shocked and terrified, she unintentionally dropped the child she held into the river.
He was carried away by the current and perished.
The mother became increasingly remorseful, vexed, bewildered, and lost her will.
She stumbled in the water and miscarried the child she carried.
She finally crossed the water and asked a traveler on the road,
"Are my parents at home safe?"
He answered,
"There was a fire yesterday, and they were all burned to death."
She then asked the traveler,
"Have you heard if my husband's family, my mother-in-law and father-in-law, are safe?"
He answered,
"They were attacked and killed by robbers; both your in-laws died."
Grieved, terrified, bewildered, and faint, she could not distinguish East from West.
She ran wildly, naked.
Those who saw her thought her strange.
They thought she was afflicted by an evil sickness.
She ran quickly until she saw the Buddha.
The Buddha was preaching the Dharma to a great assembly.
When the woman saw the Buddha, her mind immediately attained concentration.
She was no longer troubled or worried.
She looked at her naked body, felt shame and remorse, and prostrated herself on the ground.
The Buddha called Ānán to fetch clothing and give it to her.
The woman put on the clothing and paid her respects.
The Buddha then preached the sutra for her, revealing karma and blessing.
She immediately gave rise to the Unsurpassed Bodhi Mind.
She was established in the stage of non-retrogression.
Her grief and worries dispersed like the sun breaking through the clouds.
She gave rise to the Unsurpassed Mind.
In Péi shànshé Guó.
There was a woman.
Named Tíwéi.
Of the Brāhmaṇa (Pólómén) caste.
Her family was very wealthy, but she had lost her husband and had no children.
She remained a desolate widow, poor, with no one to rely upon.
According to the Brāhmaṇa (Pólómén) doctrine (dharma),
if things were not satisfactory, they would immolate themselves.
All the Brāhmaṇas (Pólómén) went and taught her, converting her.
They directed her to wish to be reborn in the realm of Nàluóyán Tiān (Nārāyaṇa Heaven).
She invited exactly one hundred Brāhmaṇas (Pólómén).
She prepared a great feast, and after they had eaten,
each was presented with a cow.
Moreover, all possessions
that were in the houses of those who accompanied the calf (the donors)
were given to five hundred Brāhmaṇas (Pólómén).
By the side of the Héng Shuǐ (Ganges River), she piled up firewood to burn herself.
The Brāhmaṇas (Pólómén) offered prayers and incantations for you,
causing all your sins, light or heavy, to be extinguished instantly.
When you are reborn in a future life, your immediate family and relatives shall have measureless lifespan and endless happiness.
Tíwéi followed their advice.
She immediately chopped down firewood
intending to burn herself.
A Śramaṇa (Shāmén) in the kingdom, named Bōdǐpó,
was vigorous, upheld the precepts, and possessed great learning and wisdom.
He constantly taught and converted the world with compassion.
He caused people to abandon evil ways and turn to righteousness, giving up wickedness and cultivating goodness.
He went and asked Tíwéi, saying, "Why are you using the firewood and fire?"
She replied,
"I wish to burn my body to eradicate my misfortunes and sins."
Biàncái said:
"Truly, the karma (zuìyè) from previous lives follows the spirit.
It is not attached to the physical body.
Vainly burning yourself—how can that extinguish sin? Misfortune arises according to the mind.
If the mind thinks of good teachings, the retribution received will also be good.
If the mind thinks of evil teachings, the retribution received will also be evil.
All other retributions are the same.
How, amidst suffering and vexation,
can you seek to destroy sins and hope for good retribution?
Fortunately, you do not need to proceed with something illogical.
It is like a sick person who is tormented by pain.
If they are further subjected to scolding and beating by wicked people,
will that sick person maintain a kind heart without anger and vexation?"
Tíwéi said,
"They would only generate anger and vexation."
Biàncái said,
"You are now like this.
Due to the sins of your past life, if you burn your body now,
when the fierce flames rise, your body will be scorched and decayed, but your breathing will not yet cease.
Because the mind is not yet destroyed,
at that time, both body and mind will be tormented.
Because the consciousness has not yet left, you will suffer bitter pain, distress, and mental anguish.
Dying from this, you will be reborn in the hells.
The suffering and vexation there will be thousands, hundreds of thousands, and millions of times more intense.
Furthermore, it is like an ox burdened by a cart, weary of the cart.
If it wishes the cart to be destroyed—if the front cart is destroyed, the rear cart will attach itself (to the yoke) again.
If your sinful karma is not exhausted, even if you burn and destroy
a hundred million bodies, the causes and conditions of your sinful karma will continue endlessly.
It is like the Ābǐ Hell, where within a single day, one dies eighty thousand times and is reborn eighty thousand times.
Only after the passing of a single kalpa will those sins finally be completed.
How much less can you, by burning your body just once, hope to extinguish your sins?"
She asked,
"I wish to hear the method for extinguishing sins."
Biàncái replied,
"The evil committed by the former mind is like clouds covering the moon.
The goodness arising from the later mind is like a torch dissolving the darkness.
The source of rising sin is the physical actions of the three [types of] body, the four [types of] speech, and the mind.
Now you must wholeheartedly, sincerely repent, change what is deviant, and turn toward what is righteous.
Renounce the body you receive, until you achieve the path to Buddhahood."
Biàncái imparted the ten good precepts.
Tíwéi was delighted.
She offered various foods and beverages, as well as treasures,
and requested him to remain and teach.
Biàncái said,
"By receiving the teachings of the ten good precepts, you have become a vessel of the Dharma.
Furthermore, converting others is your way of reciprocating.
You have already attained liberation.
It is inappropriate for me to remain.
I must go convert other places."
He accepted nothing of the offerings.
And thus, he departed.
There was a woman.
She was several months pregnant.
She saw the Buddha (Fó) and the Saṅgha (Sēng).
She vowed, "After my son is born, may he leave home and become a Śramaṇa."
When the son was born, however, her affection for him grew intense, and she did not fulfill her original vow.
When the child was seven years old, her intention suddenly returned and awakened. She prepared food for two people and the three Dharma robes.
Carrying a jar, she took her son and went to the place of the Buddha (Fó).
She said to the Buddha,
"I pray you pity my son and let him become a Śramaṇa.
May he later attain the Way and his form be like that of the Buddha (Fó)."
The Buddha immediately consented.
The mother poured water from the jar to wash her child.
Immediately, nine dragons emerged from the jar.
They spat water and anointed the child.
After bathing, the remaining water was scattered over the child’s head.
Above and below his head, it transformed into a flowery canopy.
Jeweled netting interwove,
and on the lion throne were various Buddhas (Fó).
The Buddha (Fó) then smiled.
He emitted five-colored light, illuminating ten billion realms.
It returned, encircled the body of the Buddha (Fó), and entered the child’s crown.
The mother immediately stepped forward, offered the rice to the Buddha (Fó), and fed her son.
The son generated the supreme, equal aspiration for the Way.
The ten billion Buddha realms shook six times.
All the Buddhas (Fó) in the numerous realms spontaneously appeared.
The Buddha (Fó) used the rice offered by the mother to satisfy them.
The Buddha (Fó) and all the Bhikṣus were equally satisfied.
Yet the rice remained undiminished.
The mother was immediately overjoyed.
And all the gods and humans attained the state of non-retrogression (Āwéiyuèzhì).
At that time, the child's hair fell out, and he became a Śramaṇa.
He was established in non-retrogression.
I am that person.
The Buddha (Fó) was traveling and residing in the Jī Gūdú Jīngshě (Jetavana Vihāra).
King Bōsīnì (Prasenajit) offered provisions to the Buddha (Fó) and all the great Saṅgha assembly and their dependents.
The Jīhuán (Jetavana) extended one hundred and sixty *lǐ* in length and breadth.
King Bōsīnì (Prasenajit) lit lamps everywhere, and the common people rushed to see them.
The poor woman Nántuó (Nandā) had no permanent dwelling.
She asked passersby and learned
that King Bōsīnì (Prasenajit) had used one thousand measures of oil to light lamps for the Buddha (Fó).
Nántuó blamed herself,
saying, "Why am I alone so poor?"
She immediately went into the streets.
She begged from house to house and obtained a little mixed rice.
She thought to herself,
"I must sell this to pay for a lamp."
Having sold it and obtained one coin, she carried it to the oil vendor's house.
The oil vendor asked the woman, "What merit are you trying to accomplish with one coin's worth of oil?"
Nántuó answered,
"I want to light a lamp for the Buddha (Fó)."
When the oil vendor heard this,
rejoicing, he gave her the oil for one lamp
as a donation.
The poor woman happily received it and went to the Qíhuán (Jetavana).
The Buddha (Fó) instructed Ānán (Ānanda), saying,
"There is a great elder generating supreme merit.
He cannot come himself; open the gate and let him proceed."
King Bōsīnì (Prasenajit) heard this instruction from the Buddha (Fó).
He immediately pondered,
"I am the sovereign of Shèwèi (Śrāvastī).
How could the offering I initiated for the Way be inferior to others?
Why has the Buddha (Fó)
not praised me but instead speaks of an elder?"
In a moment, the poor woman arrived at the Buddha's (Fó) place.
She lit the lamp she carried before the Buddha (Fó).
She now made a great vow,
encompassing all beings,
seeking the knowledge and vision of the Buddha.
She wished that this light would penetrate the ten directions,
and that all dark, miserable realms would find peace.
Having done this, she retreated, waiting until the next morning.
The Venerable Mùlián (Maudgalyāyana) inspected all the lamps.
Only the light of the lamp lit by Nántuó remained unchanged.
Mùlián immediately blew upon it.
He could not extinguish it by blowing.
He then used his spiritual power, pouring the water of the five Héng Shuǐ (Ganges Rivers), but still could not extinguish it.
He blew upon it using the great wind of Suílán (Samanta), but could not extinguish it.
He exhausted his spiritual power but ultimately could not extinguish it.
His heart was filled with dread.
The Buddha (Fó) told Mùlián (Maudgalyāyana),
"The person who lit this lamp possessed a deeply earnest heart.
Because of this, the lamp remains perpetually bright.
Even if Arhats like Shèlìfú (Śāriputra), and Pratyekabuddhas,
used their spiritual transformative merit together to extinguish this lamp, they could not extinguish it.
Even if the Golden-Winged King scooped up the great sea water,
or if the King of Lions roared and surged forth to extinguish this lamp,
the lamp would be impossible to extinguish."
When the sun rose, the woman Nántuó
personally went to examine the lamp she had lit the night before.
The lamp was still not extinguished.
Its light was not diminished.
She was greatly delighted and bowed her head at the Buddha's (Fó) feet.
The Buddha (Fó) knew the woman's mind sought the Supreme Way.
He emitted five-colored light from his mouth.
Whenever the Buddha (Fó) preached the Dharma regarding the actions of the Three Vehicles (Sān Chéng zhī yè), he would bestow [teachings for] the Śrāvakas;
the light enters the crown [of the head].
He would bestow [teachings for] the Pratyekabuddhas;
the light enters between the two eyebrows.
He would bestow [teachings for] the Bodhisattvas—the light enters the mouth.
The Buddha's (Fó) majestic light ascended up to the Thirty-Three Heavens.
It reached everywhere unobstructed.
Then it returned,
circled the Buddha's (Fó) body three times, and entered his mouth.
At that time, Ānán (Ānanda) rose and asked.
The Buddha (Fó) said,
"Ānán (Ānanda),
did you see the woman who lit the lamp last night?
When this woman's life ends, due to this merit,
she will transform her woman’s body and become a man.
For the subsequent twenty kalpas, she will not fall into the miserable realms.
She will be born among the various gods and as a Golden Wheel-Turning King.
After twenty kalpas,
she will attain Buddhahood.
Her title will be Sānmàntuó Yōuhē."
The Buddha was in Shèwèi Guó.
At that time, there was a householder’s daughter,
named Shànxìn.
Her age began at fifteen.
She was benevolent and filial.
Her wisdom was broad and profound.
Since childhood, she constantly held a great vow,
having no delight in worldly affairs.
She sat and contemplated,
“All things are impermanent and must return to death.
Even those who live ten thousand years must all die.
Heaven and Earth must decay and fail, how much more so the human body?
I contemplate that I must receive such culpability and condemnation,
with suffering and pain difficult to describe.
After death, the spirit must enter the evil paths.
Cruel poisons and intense suffering must be endured alone.
Where do I fundamentally come from?
Suddenly there are anger, fear, and sorrow,
or sometimes happiness.
These impermanent matters exist,
unseen when they arrive.
Where do they go when they depart?
These comings and goings are without rest or cease.
I contemplate my parents, my family members, brothers, and the five types of relatives both internal and external,
who do not know sin or merit, and whose greed and desires are never satisfied.
I, at the age of three-fives (fifteen), have already been promised to another man.
My family members and brothers receive food, drink, wine, and meat, and accept silk cloth.
I contemplate that my body must go and endure difficulty and disaster,
being constrained, bound, and shackled, unable to escape.
What should I do?
For this reason, birth and aging are not as good as myself
today purifying myself and sending forth the supreme vow,
seeking the tranquil and long-lasting palace of joy where I can amuse myself,
and not suitable for sinking in filth and drowning in the Three Evil Paths.
I shall not see the bright light, but remain long associated with suffering.”
Then, concentrating her mind, she swore an oath to herself,
“I dedicate my body and life to take refuge.
May the gods and spirits know the sincerity of my heart.”
At that time, a celestial deity appeared in the void,
speaking to Shànxìn, saying, “If you wish to take refuge in the tranquil and pure Dharma Realm of the West,
you must first bow and pay homage toward the ten directions.
With a compassionate heart and reverence, your aspiration will certainly be realized.”
Having finished, he disappeared.
At that time, Shànxìn leaped up with joy.
She immediately purified herself, burned incense, scattered flowers, paid homage to the ten directions, and clasped her hands.
She contemplated to herself.
Then, the celestial deity spoke from the air to all the people,
“You must correctly direct your minds toward the West.”
He spoke this one verse,
using it to praise Āmítuó Fó.
Shànxìn immediately faced the West,
just as the deity had commanded.
Heaven and Earth shook greatly.
All who were in distress obtained release.
Illnesses were immediately removed, agonizing pains became tranquil, and sorrow turned to joy.
The blind and deaf were cured, and the mute could speak.
The unwholesome all became wholesome, and the faithless all gained faith.
Humans and non-humans alike each attained their wishes.
Shànxìn burned incense, scattered flowers, and spoke a verse, saying,
“I correct my mind, close my eyes, count my breaths, and contemplate the matters within my body.”
Dìshì transformed himself into a handsome young man,
aged eighteen or nineteen,
holding yellow gold in his hand, and stood before Shànxìn.
He teased her with a verse.
Shànxìn, with a correct mind, replied with a correct verse,
reproving the faults of men and women.
Dìshì leaped up with joy, clasped his hands, and praised her,
asking, “What do you seek?
Your merit is boundless throughout the world, vast and immeasurable.
I wish you would tell me.”
Thereupon, Shànxìn heard the praise of Dìshì.
Her faith rejoiced, and the earth shook greatly.
She immediately spoke a gāthā (verse).
“I wish to uphold the Buddha Dharma.”
Dìshì was greatly delighted.
He then dissolved his transformation.
Shànxìn burned incense and took refuge in the Buddhas.
The Buddha, accompanied by the great assembly, immediately flew to Shànxìn’s house.
Her parents and brothers saw the Buddha flying in the sky,
and there was no one who was not joyful.
Shànxìn stepped forward, bowed, and circumambulated the Buddha one hundred times.
The Buddha then smiled, and countless rays of light emerged.
He spoke the precepts and Dharma to her.
The light circled her body one hundred times and then re-entered through the crown of her head.
He immediately bestowed the twenty-four precepts.
The Buddha said,
“These are the twenty-four precepts (three times eight) of high conduct for my Upāsikā (female lay practitioner).”
Shànxìn rejoiced and attained the Seventh Stage (Bhūmi).
She then transformed her body into a male form before the Buddha.
Her parents and brothers all received the Five Precepts.
The Buddha told Wénshū,
“Do you wish to hear about the establishment of the external paths (heterodox teachings) in the world?”
In a past time world, there was a Buddha
named Jūsūntuó Pótúluó.
He arose and flourished in the world.
At that time, that world had no gravel or sand,
and no name for external paths (heterodoxies).
There was only the Great Vehicle (Mahāyāna).
After the Buddha entered Nirvāṇa, when the Dharma was about to perish,
there was an āraṇya Bhikṣu (monk dwelling in solitude),
named Fóhuì.
A good person offered him a priceless robe.
The Bhikṣu accepted it.
Some hunters conceived the desire to rob him.
At night, they took the Bhikṣu deep into the mountains,
harmed his body, stripped him naked, suspended him by the head, and tied him to a tree.
At that time, a flower-gathering Brahmin arrived at the āraṇya dwelling place.
Seeing a tiger, he fled toward the mountain in terror.
He saw that Bhikṣu,
harmed in body, naked, suspended by the head, and tied to a tree.
He exclaimed in shock, “Alas!
This Śramaṇa previously wore a *kāṣāya* (saffron robe),
but now he is naked.
It must be known that the *kāṣāya* is not the cause of liberation.
Hanging oneself in asceticism is the true way of learning the Dao.
How could that person abandon the good Dharma?
It must be clearly known
that this is the path to liberation, which destroys the True Dharma.”
He immediately cast off his clothes, plucked out his hair, and became a naked Śramaṇa.
The naked heterodox path arose from this.
At that time, the Bhikṣu managed to free himself from the bonds.
He immediately took tree bark,
dyed it with red earth,
using it to cover himself.
He tied up grass to sweep away mosquitoes.
Again, a flower-gathering Brahmin saw him
and reflected,
“This Bhikṣu has abandoned his former good robe
and wears such clothing
and holds such a whisk.
How could he abandon the good Dharma?
It must be clearly known
that this is the path to liberation.”
He immediately studied this method.
The house-leaving Brahmin arose from this.
At that time, that Bhikṣu went into the water to bathe in the evening.
While washing a wound on his head,
he immediately took his bathing garment to cover the wound.
He took an old worn-out garment discarded by a cowherd to cover his body.
At that time, someone saw him and reflected,
“This Bhikṣu previously wore a *kāṣāya*,
but now he has completely abandoned it.
It must be known that the *kāṣāya* is not the cause of liberation.
Therefore, he wears disheveled hair and tattered clothes, bathes three times day and night, and practices bitter asceticism.
How could he abandon the good Dharma?
It must be clearly known
that this is the path to liberation.”
He immediately studied that method.
The ascetic Brahmin arose again from this.
After the Bhikṣu bathed, his body had many sores, which flies and bees ate and stung.
He immediately applied white ash to the sores everywhere
and covered his body with his bathing garment.
At that time, someone who saw him claimed,
“This is the Dao (Path),” and studied that method.
The ash-smeared Brahmin arose from this.
The Bhikṣu lit a fire to warm his sores.
The sores became increasingly painful, and he could not bear it.
He threw himself into a cliff to kill himself.
At that time, someone who saw him said,
“This Bhikṣu previously wore good robes,
but now he is like this.
How could he abandon the good Dharma?
He correctly knew that throwing oneself into a cliff is the path to liberation.”
The path of cliff-jumping and fire-worship arose from this.
In this sequence, there arose ninety-six types,
all due to the different forms and appearances of this Bhikṣu.
They conceived various delusions
and each generated their own views.
It is like when people in a country look at each other
and conceive coarse notions.
Once coarse notions are generated,
they start killing each other.
The birth of differences among the external paths is also like this.
In the past, the Six Teachers (Liù Shī) were in the world.
They greedily clung to gain and support, calling themselves the Solely Honored Ones.
Hearing that the Buddha (Fó) had appeared in the world, whose divine virtue surpassed humanity,
they gathered and took a joint oath.
"We should unite our minds and deliberate together.
If our words do not contradict each other, then we can overcome him."
They immediately dispatched one person to go and observe the Tathāgata (Rúlái).
"Is he truly human or not?"
He gazed at him, never tiring of the sight.
Returning, he reported to the Six Teachers (Liù Shī):
"Qú tán's appearance is rare in the world; his majestic, divine light surpasses the sun and moon.
As far as I have seen, he is beyond comparison."
The six men pondered again.
"That man comes from a royal lineage.
Naturally, he should be handsome.
Why should we be surprised by this?
Now, let us send another person to observe him again.
Is he tranquil (non-acting) or restless and hasty?"
Returning, he informed the Six Teachers (Liù Shī):
"Qú tán, when in a gathering, is like the king among beasts.
He has nothing to fear or dread."
The six men pondered again.
"Ignorant people seldom experience such things,
so they covet his radiance.
This is a common phenomenon.
Why should we be surprised by this?
He came out of the royal palace, where six myriad court ladies entertained him day and night; he has not yet studied under a master.
Let us send someone else to listen.
Does he perhaps speak with principles and reasons, or is he like a common mortal?"
They immediately sent one knowledgeable person to observe what the Buddha (Fó) said.
Returning, he reported to the six men:
"What he speaks reaches antiquity and knows the present.
He knows the limitlessness of the past and sees the endlessness of the future.
He judges meanings and analyzes principles clearly without being tedious or redundant."
The Six Teachers (Liù Shī) then thought.
"In the world, there are many people whose rhetorical skills are quick and pleasing to the hearts of men.
However, the underlying principles may not be there and cannot be sought out."
They again sent someone to observe.
"When the crowd hears him speak, do they listen quietly or are they chaotic?"
Returning, he reported to the Six Teachers (Liù Shī):
"What Qú tán reveals tastes like sweet dew.
The assembly listens with thirst and reverence, never having their fill."
The six men pondered again.
"When people gather initially, they are bound to scatter after a long time."
They again sent one highly superior person to go and examine.
"Are his doctrines profound and subtle, or are they shallow?"
Returning, he reported to the Six Teachers (Liù Shī):
"What Qú tán reveals is like the shoreless ocean.
What we know is like water in a cow's footprint.
Now, I myself,
wish to go and request to be his disciple."
The messengers, both earlier and later, all accompanied each other to the place of the Tathāgata (Rúlái).
Furthermore, countless sentient beings competed to arrive.
The Buddha (Fó) spoke a verse, saying:
"Having attained the Most Perfect Enlightenment (Zuì Zhèng Jué) oneself, not defiled by any dharma;
complete wisdom and fearlessness, naturally without a teacher or protector."
When the disciples of the Six Teachers (Liù Shī) heard the Buddha (Fó) recite the verse,
those whose minds were firm immediately requested the Way.
Those whose minds were hesitant returned to report to their masters, saying:
"He is the Solely Honored One of the Three Realms (Sān Jiè), ruling over the ten directions.
He truly has no equal.
We should all disperse quickly and seek our own tranquility."
"Since I have neither teacher nor protector, and am without companions,
by accumulating oneness, I attained Buddhahood (Fó), naturally accessing the holy path."
There was a king named Duō Fú.
His crown prince was named Zēng Fú.
The King served the Six Teachers (Liù Shī).
The son served the Buddha's (Fó) Way.
What they followed differed.
At that time, there were no Śramaṇas (Shāmén).
Only one layman served as the head master.
Five hundred external practitioners (Wàidào) envied the master's reputation and virtue.
They reported to the King, saying:
"The nation serving two separate laws prevents people from having single-minded devotion.
We request that the master of the Buddha's (Fó) Way and we each display our wondrous virtues.
The one who fails the contest shall be enslaved."
The King agreed to this.
The external practitioners (Wàidào) fixed a date with this master
for the agreed contest.
Before the King, they would each test their skill and art to verify their capabilities.
The Brāhmans (Fànzhì) were all skilled in archery and charioteering.
They immediately went into the mountains.
The five hundred men each shot one deer.
They all pierced the left eye to demonstrate their skill.
The virtuous man also entered the mountains, concentrating diligently on reciting the Buddha's (Fó) name, seeking divine aid to manifest the Great Way (Dà Dào).
Immediately, a five-colored deer calf suddenly emerged from the ground.
Joyfully, he took it home.
The external practitioners (Wàidào) knew about this.
They watched for when the virtuous man went out,
and went to his house.
They deceitfully said to his wife:
"Your husband intends to abandon his home and become a man of the Way.
Merely because of this deer, your family will be ruined."
When the wife heard this, she became angry.
She gave the deer to them.
When the virtuous man returned home and did not see his deer,
he asked his wife.
"The inauspicious thing has now been lost."
The husband was greatly troubled.
He returned to the mountains and sincerely repented.
Immediately, a bright moon spirit pearl (shén zhū) suddenly emerged from the ground.
He took this pearl and presented it to the Brāhmans (Fànzhì).
He went to their gate and walked around, selling rare objects.
The Brāhman's (Fànzhì) wife said:
"My family also has an extraordinary object with which we can compare."
She immediately brought out the deer calf.
The virtuous man then reported to the King:
"This deer calf was entrusted to me.
If you have now stolen it, your crime is immeasurable."
The wife, fearing, returned it.
When the day of the contest arrived,
the Brāhmans (Fànzhì) presented dead deer, all injured in the left eye, both foul and smelly.
The King greatly detested them.
The virtuous man stepped forward, leading the divine deer,
bringing the bright pearl to the King's palace hall.
The two objects flew and leaped, playing like stars streaming and electricity shining.
The entire court found it marvelous.
The five hundred Brāhmans (Póluómén), knowing that their magical arts could not compete,
were immediately relegated to slavery.
Their wives all became maids.
In Southern India (Nán Tiānzhú), there was a master of discourse.
He wrapped his abdomen with copper sheeting
and lit a fire on his head.
He came into the country of Shèwèi.
The people of the time asked him,
"Why are you like this?"
He replied,
"My knowledge is so great that I fear my belly will split open.
I wear fire because I want to illuminate the darkness."
The people then said,
"O foolish Brāhman (Póluómén)!
The sun illuminates the world; why do you speak of darkness?"
He replied,
"You do not know.
There are two kinds of darkness.
One is the absence of the sun, moon, fire, or lamp.
The second is foolishness, the lack of the light of wisdom."
The people also said,
"You have not yet seen the Bhikṣu (Bǐqiū) Hēduō Shìzǐ.
How dare you speak like this?"
He replied, "If I meet and speak with him, it will be like seeing the sun rise in the dark night."
The city inhabitants immediately summoned the Bhikṣu (Bǐqiū) Hēduō Shìzǐ,
wishing him to hold a discussion.
When Hēduō heard this,
his heart was troubled as he entered the city.
On the road, he saw two rams fighting fiercely.
He immediately took it as an omen.
"One ram is the Brāhman (Póluómén).
One ram is me.
I am the inferior one."
He became even more worried.
Walking further, he saw two bulls fighting.
He again thought:
"One bull is the Brāhman (Póluómén).
One bull is me.
I am again the inferior one."
Arriving at the main gate,
he saw two people wrestling.
He again thought:
"I am also the inferior one."
When he was about to enter the debate venue,
he saw a person carrying a full pitcher of water.
The water pitcher immediately broke.
He again thought:
"I have seen many inauspicious signs."
He had no choice but to enter the dwelling.
He saw the Brāhman (Póluómén).
Judging by the appearance of his eyes and mouth, he knew himself to be inferior.
He took his seat for a moment.
The people then said,
"You may begin the discussion."
He replied,
"I am slightly unwell right now.
I must wait until tomorrow," and then returned to his lodging.
In a past age,
there was a great kingdom
located in the northern borderlands,
named Zhì Huàn.
The people of Zhì Huàn brought crows
to the country of Bōzhēlǐ Guó.
Within the boundaries of that country, there were no such crows,
nor were there any other kind of marvelous birds.
When the people saw the crows,
they were overjoyed and ecstatic.
They offered them food, drink, fruits, and melons,
and cared for them.
Crows from distant lands all gathered, countless in number.
The entire nation widely served and revered them boundlessly.
Later, at another time, a merchant came from a foreign country, bringing peacocks.
The assembly saw their outstanding feathers and wings, their grand and elegant gait, which they had never witnessed before.
Hearing their voices, their hearts were filled with joy.
They all abandoned the crows and loved the peacocks.
All the provisions previously used to nourish the crows were supplied to the peacocks.
They revered them and relied upon them.
All the crows disappeared, their whereabouts unknown.
At that time, a god praised them in verse, saying:
"Before the sunlight is seen, a candle flame is the only light.
Originally, they served the crows, offering water, drink, and fruits and melons.
When the beautiful sound is complete, it is like the sun rising between the trees.
The crows lost their offerings, revealing who is honored and who is lowly."
Ānán’s praise says:
If the Buddha had not appeared, the Brahmins would have received offerings.
Now that the Buddha is perfected, the external heterodox schools lose their offerings.
The peacock is my own body.
The crow is the various external heterodox followers.
The celestial being is Ānán.
Formerly, in Shèwèiguó, there was a Brahmin master.
Named Pùlán Jiāshè.
He was accompanied by five hundred disciples.
The king and the people all served him.
When the Buddha first attained the Way (Enlightenment).
He and his disciples traveled from Luóyuèqí to Shèwèiguó.
His physical form was radiant, and his teachings were pure and beautiful.
The king, the royal court, and all the people in the land showed him reverence.
Jiāshè, feeling jealous, wished to slander the World-Honored One.
He said to Bōsīní Wáng:
"We elders are the former masters of this kingdom.
The Śramaṇa Qú tán,
appeared later seeking the Way, and truly possesses no divine sanctity.
Yet the King abandons us. Now, I wish to compete with the Buddha in a trial.
Whomever excels in virtue and the Way, the King should serve."
The King said, "Excellent."
The King informed the Buddha.
The Buddha said, "Very good."
They set a date seven days hence to compete in spiritual transformations.
The King chose a spacious, level, and good piece of ground east of the city.
He erected two high seats.
The King, the officials, and the great multitude gathered like clouds.
Wishing to observe the two men competing in the Way.
Jiāshè and his disciples arrived first at the location of the seats and ascended by ladder.
The spirits and kings (devotees) of the *bānshī*.
Seeing his falsehood and jealousy.
Immediately raised a great wind.
Blowing away his sitting mat, overturning his banners and streamers.
Sand, gravel, and stones flew up and rained down.
Making it impossible to see.
The World-Honored One’s high seat remained solemn and unmoved.
The Buddha and the great multitude came slowly and gracefully.
Facing the high seat, he suddenly ascended it.
All the monks sat down silently in order.
The King and the officials showed increased reverence, bowed their heads, and said:
"We pray that you will graciously display divine transformations to subdue heterodox views.
And further, cause the people of the kingdom to clearly believe in the true righteousness."
The World-Honored One suddenly vanished from the seat.
He immediately ascended into the void, emitting a great radiance.
He vanished in the east and appeared in the west, and similarly in the four directions.
Water and fire issued from his body, alternating above and below.
Sitting and lying down in the air, performing twelve transformations.
He vanished completely and reappeared upon the seat.
Devas, nāgas, ghosts, and spirits offered flowers and incense.
The sounds of praise shook heaven and earth.
Pùlán Jiāshè knew himself to be without the Way.
He lowered his head in shame and fear, not daring to raise his eyes.
A Vajra Attendant (Jīngāng Lìshì) held a vajra club.
Fire issued from the club's tip, aiming at Jiāshè.
He asked, "Why do you not display transformations?"
Jiāshè, panicked and fearful, threw himself down and fled.
His five hundred disciples scattered and dispersed.
The World-Honored One’s majestic demeanor showed neither joy nor sorrow.
He returned to Qíyuán (Jetavana).
The King and the officials happily took their leave.
Thereupon, Jiāshè and his disciples departed, having suffered humiliation.
While traveling down the road, they met an old Upāsikā (female lay devotee).
Named Móní.
She cursed them harshly, saying:
"You foolish group, you do not measure yourselves!
Yet you wished to compare magical skills and the Way with the Buddha.
Mad, foolish, deceitful, and lacking shame!
You should not carry these faces around in the world!"
Jiāshè was ashamed before his disciples.
He went to the riverbank and deceived his disciples.
"If I now throw myself into the water, I will certainly be born in the Brahmā heaven.
If I do not return, then I have found bliss."
Those disciples waited, but he did not return.
They conferred among themselves, saying:
"Our Master must have ascended to heaven.
Why should we remain here?"
One by one they threw themselves into the water, hoping to follow their Master.
Unknowing that they were pulled by their sins, they all fell into hell.
On a later day, the King heard of this situation.
Greatly astonished, he went to the Buddha and said to the Buddha:
"For what reason did Jiāshè and his followers act like this?"
The Buddha replied to the King:
"Jiāshè and his followers had two serious offenses.
First, the Three Poisons were intensely burning, yet they falsely claimed to have attained the Way.
Second, they slandered the Tathāgata, hoping to receive reverence and service.
Due to these two offenses, they should fall into hell.
Misfortune and calamity compelled them to drown in the river.
When their bodies died and their spirits departed, they suffered immeasurable torment.
In the past, there were two monkey kings (Míhóu Wáng).
Each led five hundred monkeys.
One king developed feelings of jealousy.
He wished to kill the other king, planning to rule alone.
He then went and fought with him.
He was unequal in combat.
Ashamed, he retreated.
He arrived at the seashore, in the curve of the sea.
There was a large accumulation of foam.
Blown by the wind, the accumulation was several hundred *zhàng* high.
The foolish Míhóu Wáng believed it was the Snow Mountain.
He spoke to his followers, saying:
'I have long heard that there is a Snow Mountain in the sea.
Where there is bliss and sweet fruits to indulge in.
Today I see it at last. I should go first and check.
If it is truly blissful, I will not be able to return.
If it is not blissful, I shall return and tell you.'
Thereupon, he climbed a tree and jumped with all his strength.
He plunged into the accumulated foam and drowned in the bottom of the sea.
The others, astonished that he did not come out.
Believed it must be great bliss.
One by one they plunged in, breaking the group and drowning.
The jealous Míhóu Wáng is Pùlán Jiāshè.
The followers are the current five hundred disciples of Pùlán.
Chàntí Xiānrén (Kṣānti Rishi) was in a great forest.
Cultivating patience and practicing loving-kindness.
At that time, King Jiālì Wáng led his palace women into the forest to amuse themselves.
After the meal was finished.
The King took a small rest (slept briefly).
The palace women gathered flowers in the woods.
They saw this Xiānrén.
They respectfully bowed and stood to one side.
The Xiānrén then preached to the palace women about loving-kindness and patience.
His words were beautiful and wonderful; those who heard them never tired.
They remained for a long time and did not leave.
King Jiālì Wáng awoke and did not see the palace women.
He drew his sword and followed their tracks.
He saw them in front of the Xiānrén.
Swollen with arrogance and jealousy, he glared angrily and brandished his sword.
And asked the Xiānrén:
"What are you doing?"
The Xiānrén replied:
"I am here cultivating patience and practicing loving-kindness."
The King said:
"I will now test you.
I shall use this sharp sword to cut off your ears and nose, and chop off your hands and feet.
If you do not become angry, then I will know you cultivate patience."
The Xiānrén said, "As you wish."
The King immediately drew his sword, cut off his ears and nose, and severed his hands and feet.
And asked him:
"Does your heart waver (or become agitated)?"
He replied:
"I cultivate loving-kindness and patience; my heart does not waver."
The King said:
"You are alone here, without any power.
Although you verbally say your heart does not waver, who will believe you?"
At that moment, the Xiānrén immediately made a vow:
"If I truly cultivate loving-kindness and patience,
may my blood turn into milk."
Immediately, the blood changed into milk.
The King was greatly startled and overjoyed.
He led the women away.
At that time, the nāgas and spirits in the forest caused thunder, lightning, and sharp peals for the sake of the Xiānrén.
The King was afflicted by a poisonous curse (or retribution) and sank down, unable to return to his palace.
Formerly, there was a Xiānrén.
Named Luówén, whose energetic progress was pure and complete.
There were some who, when residing in a lay household, did not maintain the pure practices (brahmacarya).
Some would say:
"Though Luówén had pure practices,
while residing in a lay household, he was not entirely pure."
Luówén wrote scriptures.
Wind and rain could not damage them.
To cultivate pure practices in the secular world,
like an Ānàhán (Anāgāmin).
Surrounded by family members at home.
Is this not a pure practice?
The realm of spiritual power is inconceivable.
The Fó was dwelling in Luóyuèqí.
He proclaimed the True Dharma.
All the Níjiān and others were distressed and worried in their hearts.
On Líyí Shān there were five hundred Xiānrén (Immortals/Sages).
The Níjiān sent messengers, saying:
"Here there is a Fó.
He boasts of having attained the Way and being supreme in spiritual transformations (shénbiàn).
He is inferior to us, yet he elevates himself highly.
We request that the Great Masters,
condescend to come and assist us.
We must discuss the essential points of the Way and destroy his teaching.
This will cause the fame and merit of all our masters to shine forth even brighter."
They replied, "Excellent.
We shall first send four people to challenge Qú Tán (Gautama)."
The Níjiān proclaimed throughout the country:
"Seven days hence, there will be four Fó entering the country to deliver sentient beings."
When that day arrived,
the four people displayed spiritual transformations visible to all.
They came from the sky, each entering from one side of the city.
The multitude saw them and believed them to be the True Fó.
The Níjiān sent a messenger to inform the Fó:
"You may come now to discuss the Way."
The Fó said:
"I will come at mealtime."
The Níjiān rejoiced and said:
"Qú Tán is probably unable to face us,
pretending he will not arrive yet."
Everyone agreed.
The Fó commanded fire to rise in the sky.
It came from the west side.
The four people flew south, and the fire also came south.
Heat radiated from the four directions, and the four people were terrified.
They fell down and lay on the ground.
The Fó manifested in a cool place.
Immediately, seeking coolness, they came before the Fó.
The Fó spoke the Dharma for them.
They all became Shāmén (monks) and attained the path of the Arhat (Yìngzhēn).
The Fó entered the city.
The people in the city said:
"In the morning, there were four Fó in the empty sky."
The Fó said:
Immediately pointing to his left and right,
"These four Luóhàn are those ones."
For example, the Yùtuóluógā Xiānrén.
He attained the Five Supernatural Powers (Wǔ Shéntōng).
He flew to the king's palace to eat.
The Queen (Wáng Dà Fūrén), according to the custom of her country,
greeted him by touching his feet.
As soon as the Queen's hand touched him, he lost his supernatural powers.
He requested a carriage from the King.
He rode out and returned to his original place.
Entering the woods and trees, he again sought the Five Shéntōng.
He was focused intently, about to achieve them,
but a bird atop a tree urgently cried out, disturbing his concentration.
He abandoned the tree and went to the waterside to seek concentration (Dìng).
Again, he heard the sound of fish fighting and stirring the water.
This person could not attain Chan (meditation).
He immediately generated anger and resentment.
"I must kill all the fish and birds."
Long after, this person pondered and attained Dìng.
He was reborn in the realm of Neither Thought nor Non-thought (Fēi Yǒu Xiǎng Fēi Wú Xiǎng Chù).
When his lifespan there ended,
he was reborn below as a flying civet.
He killed all the fish and birds.
Having committed immeasurable sins, he fell into the Evil Path (È Dào).
Yōutuóyán Wáng,
taking all his palace attendants and court ladies (cǎinǚ),
went to Yùdú Bōtuó Shānlín.
He removed all men and entertained himself solely with women and the five pleasures (Wǔ Yuè).
Their music was pure and exquisite, and famous incense was burned.
At that time, among the court ladies,
some danced in the nude.
At that time, five hundred Xiānrén passed through that place.
When the Xiānrén saw the sights, heard the sounds, and smelled the fragrances, they immediately lost their divine powers (Shénzú).
Like birds without wings, they fell into that forest.
The King asked:
"Who are you?"
The Xiānrén answered:
"We are Xiānrén."
The King asked again:
"Have you attained the concentration of the realm of Neither Thought nor Non-thought?"
They replied, "We have not."
He asked further:
"Have you attained the First Chan (Chū Chán)?"
They replied:
"We attained it once, but now we have lost it."
The King then angrily said:
"Lustful people seeing my palace women—this is utterly unacceptable!"
He then drew his sharp sword and cut off the hands and feet of the five hundred Xiānrén.
Yōutuóluómó Zǐ
had a King
who regularly provided him with food.
When mealtime arrived,
he would use his divine powers (Shénzú lì) to fly up into the void and go to the King's palace.
The King would receive him, embrace him, and seat him on a golden couch.
He would be offered provisions made of the flavors eaten by the Xiānrén.
When that Xiānrén finished eating,
he would remove the utensils, rinse his mouth, recite a Gāthā (verse), offer blessings (Zhù Yuàn), and fly away into the sky.
Later,
the King had state affairs that required him to travel elsewhere.
There was no one to serve the Xiānrén.
The Xiānrén was quick-tempered.
[The King thought:] "He might become angry and curse me,
causing me to lose my throne or cutting short my life."
So, he asked his daughter:
"If the Xiānrén comes, can you attend to him according to my usual custom?"
The daughter replied, "I can."
The King then solemnly commanded the daughter to serve him wholeheartedly,
and only then did he depart
to attend to state affairs.
On a subsequent day, at mealtime, the Xiānrén flew in.
The princess followed the King's custom:
she personally received him, embraced him, and seated him on the golden couch.
The princess's body was delicate and soft.
When the Xiānrén touched the daughter, he lost his divine powers.
After eating,
he removed the utensils, rinsed his mouth, recited a Gāthā, and offered blessings.
He wished to fly but could not.
At that time, there was a private garden forest in the King's palace.
He immediately entered it, desiring to cultivate his divine powers.
Hearing the sounds of elephants, horses, and carriages, he could not successfully cultivate them.
At that time, the city dwellers constantly had this thought:
"If the Great Xiān were to walk on the ground,
we could approach him and bow at his feet."
The Xiānrén was clever, sharp-witted, and knowledgeable of expedient means (Fāngbiàn).
He spoke to the princess, saying:
"You must now announce to the people of the city:
'Today, the Great Xiān will walk out from the King's palace.
All you people, do everything that ought to be done.'"
The princess then acted according to his command.
She immediately announced it.
The streets and lanes were cleaned, free of broken tiles, pebbles, dung, and filth.
Banners were hung, incense was burned, and various flowers were scattered.
The adornments were fresh and pure.
The Xiānrén walked out, and not far from the city,
he entered the woods and trees, desiring to cultivate his divine powers.
Hearing the sounds of many birds, he could not successfully cultivate them.
He then abandoned the woods and went again to the riverbank.
Using his original method, he wished to cultivate his divine powers.
Again, he heard the sounds of fish and turtles turning and stirring the water,
and he could not successfully cultivate them.
He then climbed a mountain and contemplated:
"The reason I have now lost my good Dharma is entirely due to sentient beings.
I swear by all the good Dharma and pure practices I possess:
May I become a sentient being like this:
one who can destroy all creatures in the world—those walking on land, flying in the sky, and swimming in the water—
none shall escape me."
Having made this evil vow, he saw [the way].
He departed from the eight levels (Bā Dì) and wished to be reborn in the summit realm of Neither Thought nor Non-thought (Fēi Xiǎng Fēi Fēi Xiǎng Yǒu Dǐng Chù).
He opened the gate of Sweet Dew (Gānlù Mén) and entered the tranquil garden (Jìngjìng Yuántián).
For eighty thousand Kalpas (jié), he enjoyed quiet happiness there.
When his Karmic reward was exhausted, he returned to this realm,
to the Dábō Shùlín Tánmó Ālánrě Chù (Dábō Forest Dhamma Aranya).
He was reborn as a winged civet (zhù chì lí).
Its body was fifty Yóuxún (yojana) wide.
Both wings were each fifty Yóuxún wide.
Its total size was one hundred fifty Yóuxún.
With this massive body, he killed and harmed creatures walking in the air, in the water, and on land.
None could escape him.
When his body perished and his life ended, he was reborn in the Ābí Dìyù (Avīci Hell).
Before the Fó appeared in the world,
Tiāndìshì (Sakra) often went to the Típōyánnà Xiānrén's dwelling to hear the Dharma.
Later, at one time, he was riding a jeweled carriage, intending to visit the Xiānrén.
Shèzhī thought:
"Now Tiāndìshì is abandoning me and wants to go to another court lady."
She immediately concealed her form and got onto the carriage.
Tiāndìshì did not know until he was about to reach the Xiānrén's place.
He looked around and saw her.
He asked her:
"Why have you come?"
"The Xiānrén does not wish to see women.
You must return to the palace."
Shèzhī did not want to leave.
Tiāndìshì struck her with a lotus stem.
Shèzhī apologized to Tiāndìshì using a woman's soft and lovely voice.
When the Xiānrén heard it,
he generated sensual desire (Yù Ài).
His spiral hair (luófà) immediately fell off, and his ear consciousness retreated.
In the past, there was an ascetic (xiānrén) on the Snowy Mountain (Xuě Shān).
His name was Bágēpó.
He subsisted on fruits and grass roots, practicing loving-kindness (cí xīn).
However, he could not eliminate all the bonds of affliction (fánnǎo jié).
At that time, there was a tigress living in that place.
She coupled with him, and consequently became pregnant.
When the months were fulfilled, she came to the xiānrén's dwelling and gave birth to twelve sons.
The xiānrén took pity, immediately took them, bathed them, and nursed them.
The tiger mother, out of love and remembrance, nursed them as the time required.
The xiānrén gave each of them a name.
The first was Jiégē.
The second was Bábāgē.
The third was Hǔ (Tiger).
The fourth was Shīzǐ (Lion).
The fifth was Dànzhòng (Bearer of Burden).
The sixth was Póluóduòshé.
The seventh was Bùxíng (Walker).
The eighth was Póluónú.
The ninth was Jiànshí (Strong Eater).
The tenth was Èxìng (Vicious Nature).
The eleventh was Shīzǐ Dàn (Lion's Burden).
The twelfth was Jiànxíng (Strong Walker).
When they reached the age of seven, they were able to eat roots, flowers, and fruits.
When both parents died, the sons' hearts were filled with sadness and distress.
They looked up to heaven, cried loudly, having nowhere to rely.
A tree spirit (shù shén) spoke:
“Do not cry loudly yet.
You should, during the six periods (shí) of day and night, cleanse yourselves, bathe, face the empty space (xū kōng), pay homage with utmost sincerity, and implore Fàntiān for compassion.
When Fàntiān hears this,
he will come to your dwelling, destroy your ignorance (chī àn),
bestow upon you the light of wisdom, and render offerings to you.”
They acted according to the instruction for twelve years.
At that time, Fàntiān and Dìshì (the Lord of Heaven) of Sānshísāntiān (Thirty-three Heavens),
together with countless retinues, all came to offer provisions.
They spoke to the youths, saying:
“Why have you practiced diligent asceticism for twelve years?
What do you seek by making offerings to me?”
They all replied:
“We only wish, Great Being (dàshì), that you bestow wisdom upon us.
So that now we may recognize and know the deeds (yè) of good and evil, and the matters of suffering and pleasure.”
In the past, during a remote former age,
there was a xiānrén.
His name was Bōjié.
He had attained the five supernormal powers (shéntōng).
At that time, he was revered and served by the king of the country.
