Using his divine feet (shén zú), he flew back and forth to the royal palace.
The king provided offerings and gave him every comfort.
The king would spread his hair and, holding the xiānrén, would assist him in walking.
He personally poured and prepared a hundred kinds of food and drink.
This accumulated over many years.
At that time, the king had duties elsewhere.
The king had a daughter.
She was beautiful and excellent, rare in the world.
The king respected her greatly.
The daughter had never left the gates.
The king instructed his daughter, saying:
“I serve the xiānrén and dare not incur his displeasure.
Now that I am traveling far, you must provide offerings to him.
You must act as if I were present.”
At that time, the xiānrén flew down from the sky and entered the palace.
The princess saw him arrive.
She lifted him with her hands and placed him upon a seat.
Upon touching the girl's soft body, immediately a desire arose in him.
As love and desire flourished, he instantly lost his divine feet (shén zú).
He thought and practiced walking meditation, wishing to restore his divine feet, but could not achieve it.
He walked out of the palace.
At that time, countless people gathered to watch.
The king, having completed his journey, returned and heard that the xiānrén had fallen due to lust and could no longer fly.
The king went to the palace at night, walking alone in secret.
He went to see the xiānrén and bowed his head at his feet.
He recited a verse (gè sòng), saying:
“I heard that the great Brahman (fàn zhì) inherently consumed different foods and drinks,
from what teaching did you come, and for what reason did you fall into carnal desire (sè yù)?”
Bōjié replied:
“It is indeed so, Great King, just as you, the holy one, have heard.”
The king said:
“I do not know where wisdom resides; it is what virtue contemplates.
Even if the mind of desire arises, one should not fail to subdue one's fundamental nature.”
Bōjié replied:
“Loving desire destroys righteousness and benefit; the lustful mind burns fiercely.
Having heard the king's words today, I ought to abandon this loving desire.”
The xiānrén felt shame, restrained his heart, and reproached himself.
He diligently practiced day and night and soon recovered his supernormal powers (shéntōng).
That xiānrén at that time is now Shèlìfú.
The king at that time is my present self.
At that time, in the mountains of the Bōluónài Guó (Varanasi), there was a xiānrén.
During the middle month of autumn,
he urinated into a washing basin.
Seeing two deer copulating, a lustful mind instantly arose.
His semen flowed into the basin, and a deer drank it.
Immediately, a body was conceived.
When the moon was full, a son was born, largely resembling a human.
He had one horn on his head and his feet resembled those of a deer.
When the deer was about to give birth, she went to the xiānrén's dwelling and delivered the son in front of it.
She entrusted the child to the xiānrén and departed.
When the xiānrén came out, he saw this deer-child.
He recalled the original circumstance and knew it was his own son.
He took him and raised him.
When he grew older,
the xiānrén diligently instructed him in learning.
He mastered the eighteen great scriptures (dà jīng).
He also studied seated meditation (zuò chán).
Practicing the four immeasurables (sì wúliàng xīn), he attained the five supernormal powers (shéntōng).
Once, when he was ascending the mountain,
he encountered heavy rain and slippery mud.
His feet were unsteady, and he slipped, injuring his foot.
He immediately became greatly angered.
He cursed, commanding that there be no rain.
Due to the xiānrén's merit (fú dé), all the dragons, ghosts, and spirits caused the rain to cease.
Because there was no rain, grain and fruits did not grow.
The people became impoverished and had no means to live.
The King of Bōluónài was worried, sorrowful, and vexed.
He commanded all the great officials to gather and discuss the matter of the rain.
The wise ones deliberated and said:
“We have heard that the One-Horned Xiānrén,
having injured his foot while ascending the mountain, angrily cursed, causing no rain for twelve years.”
The king immediately announced a reward.
“If there is anyone who can cause the xiānrén to lose his five supernormal powers (wǔ shén tōng) and make him subject to me as a citizen,
I shall share half of the country's rule with them.”
In this Bōluónài Guó, there was a courtesan.
Her name was Shàntuó.
She was beautiful and extremely wealthy.
She came to answer the king's recruitment.
The courtesan said:
“If he is human, I am able to ruin him.” Having said this,
she took a gold basin and filled it with fine treasures.
She said to the king:
“I shall ride this xiānrén when I return.”
The courtesan immediately requested five hundred carriages.
They carried five hundred beautiful women.
Five hundred deer carts carried various "joy pills" (huān xǐ wán).
These were all compounded with various medicinal herbs.
She also brought various kinds of powerful fine wine.
The color and taste were like water. She wore tree-bark clothes and traveled among the woods.
This was done to resemble an xiānrén.
She built a thatched hut near the xiānrén's dwelling and stayed there.
The One-Horned Xiānrén was walking about and saw her.
All the women came out with beautiful flowers and exquisite incense to make offerings to the xiānrén.
The xiānrén was pleased.
The women respectfully greeted the xiānrén with pleasing words.
They led him into the room and seated him on a fine bed and cushion.
They gave him fine, pure wine, claiming it was pure water.
They gave him the "joy pills," claiming they were fruits and melons.
After he had eaten and drunk his fill,
he spoke to the women, saying:
“Since I was born, I have never obtained such fruits and water.”
The women replied:
“Because we single-mindedly practiced virtue (xíng shàn), heaven granted our wish and gave us these fruits and water.”
The xiānrén asked the women:
“Why are your complexions so plump and flourishing?”
They replied:
“We regularly eat these fine fruits and drink this wonderful water.”
The xiānrén said:
“Why do you not stay here?”
They replied:
“It is indeed possible to stay.”
The woman called him to bathe together.
When he touched the woman’s soft hand,
his mind was stirred, and he fell into lust.
Instantly, he lost his supernormal powers.
Heaven caused heavy rain for seven days and seven nights.
He was allowed to enjoy the food and drink for seven days.
When the wine and food were all consumed,
they were replaced by water and tree fruits.
The taste was not pleasant.
He asked for the former items again.
She replied that they were finished.
“Now we must go together to fetch them.
Not far from here is a place where they can be obtained.”
The xiānrén said:
“As you wish.”
They went out together, not far from the city.
The woman then lay down on the ground and said:
“I am exhausted and cannot walk anymore.”
The xiānrén said:
“If you cannot walk, ride upon my neck.
I shall carry you.”
The woman had previously sent a messenger to inform the king.
“The king should briefly come out and observe my skill and intelligence.”
When the king saw them, he asked:
“How did this happen?”
The woman replied: “Using the power of skillful means (fāngbiàn lì), he is no longer capable of anything [supernormal].”
The king ordered the xiānrén to stay in the city, provided him with good offerings, and showed him respect.
He fulfilled all the xiānrén’s desires and appointed him as a high official (dà chén).
After staying in the city for a few days, the xiānrén's body gradually grew thin and weak.
He remembered meditative concentration (chán dìng) and felt aversion toward the desires of this world.
The king asked the xiānrén:
“Why are you unhappy?”
He replied:
“Although I have obtained the five desires (wǔ yù), I constantly long for the forest.”
The king said:
“Originally, the goal was to eliminate the drought disaster. Why should I forcefully take away his will?”
Immediately, he sent the xiānrén away.
Once he returned to the mountains and diligently practiced, he soon recovered the five supernormal powers (wǔ tōng).
The One-Horned Xiānrén is my present self.
The courtesan is Yēshūtuóluó.
In the past, Dìngguāng (定光), the protector of the multitudes, appeared.
In the great nation of Bōmó (鉢摩).
With the four divisions of the assembly, who were countless.
All came to make offerings and provide what he needed.
At that time there was a Brāhmaṇa,
named Yěrěnuódá (耶若達).
He resided on the side of the Xuěshān (雪山),
observing all secret prophecies, astronomy, and geography, which he comprehensively mastered.
Writings and letters he also thoroughly understood.
The Brāhmaṇa Yěrěnuódá had a disciple,
named Léiyún (雷雲).
(Léiyún) was intelligent and widely knowledgeable, skilled in everything.
He was constantly cherished and taught by Yěrěnuódá, never leaving him for a moment.
The Brāhmaṇa Léiyún reflected,
"All that I should study is now complete.
I ought to repay my teacher's kindness.
However, I am poor and destitute.
I should go to the border of the country to seek what is needed."
The teacher thought,
"He is my beloved.
If I were to die, he still could not bear to leave me,
much less today when he wishes to abandon me and depart."
(Yěrěnuódá) composed five hundred verses and gave them to him to recite.
Before many days passed, he recited them all fluently.
At this time, Yěrěnuódá the Brāhmaṇa
announced to his five hundred disciples:
"This Brāhmaṇa Léiyún's mastery of the arts is complete."
He immediately conferred a name upon him,
calling him Chāoshù (超術).
The Brāhmaṇa Chāoshù, after several more days,
spoke to his teacher again, saying:
"What I have studied is known.
However, it is recorded in the scriptures that those who surpass all academic studies must repay their teacher’s kindness."
The teacher replied,
"You know that you know."
Chāoshù bowed and departed.
At that time, in the great nation of Bōmó,
not far from the city, there was an assembly of Brāhmaṇas.
They were gathering at one house to hold a great sacrifice,
and also intended to hold a debate.
There were eighty-four thousand Brāhmaṇas gathered together.
The foremost elder (Shangzuò) could recite writings and scriptures, knowing everything.
They had set aside five hundred taels of gold, one gold staff, one gold washing vessel, and one thousand head of cattle,
to present to the teacher.
They would first test the arts of the foremost elder,
and whoever surpassed him would receive them.
The Brāhmaṇa Chāoshù thought to himself,
"Why should I now beg from house to house?
It is better to go to that great assembly and compete in the arts."
Chāoshù went there.
The multitude of Brāhmaṇas called out from afar, saying:
"Excellent, O Lord of the Sacrifice! Today you have gained a great benefit!
It is none other than Brahmā Heaven (Fàntiān) himself who has personally descended!"
At that moment, the eighty-four thousand Brāhmaṇas,
all rose together to welcome him.
With different mouths but the same voice, they spoke these words:
"Welcome, great Brahmā, celestial deity!"
The Brāhmaṇa Chāoshù said:
"I am not Brahmā Heaven.
Stop, noble sirs!
Have you not heard
that north of the Xuěshān there is the great master of the Brāhmaṇa multitude,
named Yěrěnuódá?
I am his disciple,
named Chāoshù."
He then spoke to the elder, saying:
"If you know the arts, please explain them to me."
At that time, the foremost elder of that assembly
immediately recited the Three Pitakas (Sānzàng) and the arts without any omission or error.
Then Chāoshù addressed the elder, saying:
"The five hundred words of a single sentence
—can you speak them now?"
The elder replied,
"I do not understand them."
Chāoshù then recited the Three Pitakas, the five hundred words of a single sentence, and the Marks of a Great Man (Dàrén zhī Xiàng).
At that moment, the eighty-four thousand Brāhmaṇas
exclaimed, "This is unprecedented, extremely wonderful and unique!
We have never before heard of the Marks of a Great Man.
Now, Your Holiness ought to sit as the elder (Shangzuò)."
Chāoshù moved to the elder's seat and became the first among them.
At that time, the former elder of the assembly harbored extreme anger and rage.
He made this vow:
"This man has seized my seat.
In whatever place this person is born and whatever deeds he wishes to accomplish,
I shall perpetually undermine and destroy his success."
Then the patron immediately offered the legal donations to the elder (Chāoshù).
Chāoshù addressed the host, saying:
"I now return the gold coins and silver coins to you as an offering.
I shall only accept five hundred pieces of each.
The gold vessel shall be used to provide offerings to women,
and the thousand head of cattle shall be returned to the host.
I do not habitually indulge in desires, nor do I accumulate wealth."
Having finished, he went to the great nation of Bōmó.
Its king was named Guāngmíng (光明).
Outside the city’s east gate, he saw five hundred Brāhmaṇas who were aged and highly virtuous.
At that time, the king of that country had invited Dìngguāng Rúlái (定光如來) to be exposed to the sun and scorched by fire.
(The king) immediately gave five hundred gold coins, one coin each, to the community of Bhikṣus (Bǐqiū zhòng).
(The king provided) clothing and food offerings, sweeping and cleaning the area.
He ensured there was no pollution from earth or sand,
hung silk banners and canopies, and smeared the ground with fragrant liquid.
The musical instruments were countless.
(Chāoshù) saw a woman,
named Shànwèi (善味),
carrying seven lotus stems (flowers) and drawing water with a vase.
He immediately asked the woman,
"I wish to buy the flowers."
The woman replied,
"I am carrying them to offer to the Buddha."
(Chāoshù) immediately offered five hundred silver coins and requested five flower stems.
The woman, coveting the silver coins, gave him five flower stems.
After walking several dozen paces, the woman thought to herself,
"This man has a dignified appearance and does not begrudge the silver coins."
She chased and called out to the man, asking what he intended to use them for.
He replied, "To offer to the Buddha."
The woman said,
"I beg you, take the remaining two flower stems and offer them to the Buddha also.
I vow that in future lives we shall always be husband and wife."
Chāoshù said,
"A Bodhisattva cherishes nothing.
If you become my wife, you will certainly corrupt my mind."
The Brāhmaṇa woman said,
"I shall never corrupt you.
Even if you offer me as a gift to others,
I shall certainly endure the practice (of the Bodhisattva path)."
Dìngguāng Buddha said,
"What the Bodhisattva practices is to cherish nothing."
The Brāhmaṇa (Chāoshù) replied in verse:
"Parents, venerable Buddhas, the sun and moon traversing the world
cannot be given away to others; everything else is certainly easy to give up."
He spoke another verse, saying:
"I should endure the suffering of countless eons, giving away my head, body, ears, and eyes,
my wives and children, nation, treasures, carriages, horses, and attendants."
(He was a) Mónà (摩納, young Brāhmaṇa student).
Mónà replied again in verse:
"If a great mountain burns like fire, I can endure carrying it on my head for countless eons,
but I cannot destroy the will for the Way (Dào yì). I only wish that you would now grant a prophecy."
He immediately unbound his hair and spread it on the ground,
and spoke this verse:
"Having destroyed the mind of craving and arrogance, and being able to extinguish desire, anger, and delusion,
the First Radiant Mark, the foot (of the Buddha)—I only ask the Buddha to illuminate my mind.
The vow I sought in the past, today I have seen the Buddha.
Now I scatter these five flower stems, wishing to attain the state of non-retrogression (bùtuìzhuǎn).
The remaining two are not my flowers; the royal daughter entrusted them as an offering to the Buddha.
O supreme Great Guide, look upon me with compassion and step upon my hair!"
The Buddha replied again in verse:
"Mónà, you have aroused the great mind, widely saving countless beings.
Your vast vow is not for yourself, but to plant the root of manifold merits.
After countless eons, in the era of the Five Corruptions (Wǔzhuó shì),
you shall become a Buddha and deliver sentient beings, bearing the name Shìjiāwén (釋迦文).
Your radiance shall have thirty-two extraordinary marks, the venerable among men."
The Buddha passed by, stepping upon his hair with his feet.
Furthermore, using his spiritual power, he held the five flower stems.
And my body (Chāoshù's body) was lifted into the empty air.
The remaining two flowers rested upon the Buddha's two shoulders.
Since the time when I destroyed the Brāhmaṇa sacrifices and the Fire of the Heavenly Lord (Tiāndì Huǒ),
I practiced right view and utilized the Dharma of equality.
I never again fell into the three lower realms or the eight difficult circumstances.
At that time, Chāoshù was me (Shìjiāwén).
The flower-selling woman was Qúyí (瞿夷).
There was a *Bǎohǎi Fànzhì* (Brahmaṇā).
He reported to the Buddha:
“I wish that the *Rúlái* (Tathāgata) and the *Bǐqiū* Saṅgha
would accept my four kinds of offerings for seven full years.”
The *Rúlái* permitted it.
The *Fànzhì* later thought thus:
“I have now caused hundreds of thousands of millions of *nayutas* of sentient beings to arouse the *Pútí* (Bodhi) mind.
However, I do not know what the wishes of the *Zhuǎnlún Shèngwáng* (Chakravartin Holy King) are.
The kings of men, the kings of devas, the *Shēngwén* (Hearers), and the *Yuánjué* (Pratyekabuddhas)—
do they seek the unsurpassable *Pútí*?
If I am certain to achieve the path of the Buddha in a future life,
then while I sleep at night, various Devas, Māras, Brahmās, and *Zhū Fó Shìzūn* (World-Honored Buddhas) will appear to me in a dream.”
In his sleep, he saw light.
He immediately saw the *Zhū Fó Shìzūn* throughout the worlds numbering as the sands of the Gaṅgā in the ten directions.
Each one bestowed a lotus flower upon him from afar.
The flowers were exquisite, and on the calyx of each flower, the image of a sun disk was seen.
Above the sun disk was a canopy made of seven treasures.
Every single sun disk emitted sixty billion rays of light.
All of them came and entered the mouth of the *Fànzhì*.
He saw the light filling a thousand *yóuxún* (yojanas).
It was as clear as a bright mirror, and he saw inside his abdomen
sixty billion *nayutas* of hundreds of thousands of *Púsà* (Bodhisattvas).
They were seated cross-legged on lotus flowers, entering into correct concentration (*sānmèi zhèngshòu*).
Furthermore, he saw sun rays encircling their bodies.
From the various flowers, all sorts of musical entertainments emerged.
He also saw that King
with blood flowing out, defiling his body, running wildly in the four directions.
His face and head resembled a pig, devouring various insects.
He sat beneath an *Yīlán* tree.
Innumerable sentient beings came and ate his body.
Only fragmented bones remained.
Repeatedly taking rebirth, it was also like this.
He further saw the various princes.
Some had faces like pigs, elephants, water buffaloes, lions, foxes, wolves, tigers, leopards, or monkeys, etc.
Their bodies were defiled with blood, and they all devoured sentient beings.
They sat beneath an *Yīlán* tree.
Again, there were innumerable sentient beings
who came and ate their bodies.
When the fragmented bones were separated,
repeatedly taking rebirth, it was also like this.
Or he saw a prince
wearing *Xūmànnà* (Sumana) flowers as a garland.
Riding in a small, dilapidated carriage, drawn by a water buffalo,
traveling rapidly southward on an improper path.
Furthermore, he saw the Four Great Heavenly Kings, *Shìtí Huányīn* (Śakra Devānām Indra), and the *Dàfàn Tiānwáng* (Mahābrahmā King) come to him.
They addressed the *Fànzhì*, saying:
“The lotus flowers that you now have on all four sides,
you should first take one flower and give it to the *Zhuǎnlún Wáng* (Chakravartin King).
Give one flower to each prince.
The rest of the flowers should be given to the minor kings.
Next, give (them) to your sons.
And distribute them all to the remaining people as well.”
Suddenly he awoke.
He recalled all the things he had seen in the dream.
He realized that the Holy King's wishes were base, loving and delighting in the cycle of life and death.
He further realized that the princes, having aroused the mind,
were seeking the *Shēngwén* vehicle (Śrāvakayāna), which is why he dreamed of them wearing *Xūmànnà* flowers as garlands,
riding in a water buffalo carriage, rushing southward on an improper path.
“What was the reason I dreamed of this?”
The *Zhū Fó Shìzūn* (World-Honored Buddhas, conveyed this realization):
“Because I previously instructed and encouraged innumerable sentient beings within *Yánfútí* (Jambudvīpa),
causing them all to dwell in the three grounds of merit, thus arousing the *Pútí* mind.
And invited the Buddha and the Saṅgha
to provide them with everything they needed for seven full years.”
In the country of *Shèwèi* (Śrāvastī), there was a *Fànzhì*.
Who was extensively cultivating fields and crops near the *Qíshù* grove.
He went to look at it and was delighted.
He told himself that his wishes were fulfilled.
Immediately that night, the sky rained large hailstones.
All the crops died.
His daughter also died.
Grief-stricken, distressed, and worried, he cried uncontrollably.
At that time, the *Bǐqiū* entered the city for alms distribution.
They saw his two misfortunes, returned, and fully reported to the Buddha.
The *Xū Xiàng Fànzhì* personally arrived at the Buddha's location.
After completing the prostration.
The Buddha knew his thoughts
and spoke to the *Fànzhì*, saying:
“In the world, there are five things that cannot be avoided or escaped:
First, there must be depletion and diminution.
Second, there must be loss and abandonment.
Third, there must be sickness and emaciation.
Fourth, there must be old age and decay.
Fifth, there must be death.
Only the Noble Truth of the Path can lead to separation (from these),
by practicing generosity (*bùshī*) and maintaining the precepts (*chíjiè*).”
The *Fànzhì*'s mind softened, and he subsequently perceived the Four Noble Truths.
“From now on, I take refuge in the Buddha, the Dharma, and the Saṅgha,
and become a pure lay believer (*qīngxìn shì*).”
The *Bǐqiū* reported to the Buddha:
“World-Honored One,
the *Fànzhì* had his worries resolved and left happily.”
The Buddha said:
“It is not only now that his worries have been resolved.
In the past, the land of *Yánfúli* (Jambudvīpa) had five rulers.
One of these rulers was named *Jiétān* (Rapacious Greed).
He governed the country improperly.
The high officials and the people,
with mobilized troops and bearing white banners, all arrived before the King.
They collectively addressed the King, saying:
‘Do you not know that your greed harms the populace?
You must quickly leave the country.
If not, we will harm you.’
The King trembled greatly.
He left the country with his chariots and cavalry.
He wove grass sandals and sold them to support himself.
The high officials and the people then appointed the King's younger brother as king.
He governed without oppressing the people.
The former king sent up a memorial, stating his case.
He begged the King for one small area to support himself.
The King immediately granted it.
Having obtained the one area, he immediately governed it properly.
He requested two more areas,
and eventually requested half the kingdom.
The King gave it all to him.
After such a long time,
*Jiétān* developed a thought:
He raised the army of half the kingdom, attacked his brother, was victorious, and recovered his former country.
He then raised the army of one country and attacked the second (king).
He then doubled the troops and attacked the fifth country.
He was victorious everywhere he went.
At that time, the Four Seas all submitted to him, and he changed his title to *Dàshèng* (Great Conqueror).
*Dìshì* (Indra/Śakra) tested him,
asking if he knew contentment or not.
He magically transformed into a young boy *Fànzhì*,
whose surname was *Jūyíshì*.
With disheveled hair, carrying a golden staff and holding a golden vase, he stood at the palace gate and sent word to the King.
The King then came forward, sat down, and finished the customary exchange of pleasantries.
He then spoke to the King, saying:
‘I came from the seaside.
I saw a great country
whose people were flourishing and had many treasures.
You can go and attack it.
I wonder if you are already satisfied,
or if you wish to obtain this as well.’
The King said he wished to obtain it.
The Heavenly King (*Tiānwáng*) said:
‘You should prepare more ships and mobilize your army to wait.
Seven days later, I will lead the King there.’ Having spoken, he vanished.
When the day arrived, the King mobilized the army and prepared the ships.
The *Fànzhì* did not come, and the King became worried, distressed, and unhappy.
At that time, the people of the whole country turned and sat facing the King.
When the King wept, they also wept.
When the King worried, they also worried.
The King then thought:
‘Increasing thoughts follow desires; having one wish fulfilled leads to stronger wishes daily for happiness.
From this comes self-mastery.’
‘Whoever can explain this will be rewarded with one thousand gold coins.’
At that time, there was a youth named *Yùduō* (Uttara).
He said he could explain it and asked for seven days to come and answer.
When the seventh day arrived, he told his mother:
‘I wish to resolve the King's worry.’
The mother said to her son:
‘Son, please stop.
Do not go.
Rulers are difficult to serve.’
The son said:
‘I have the power to stop (the troubles).’
He went to the King and said:
‘I have now come to answer the meaning.’
And thereupon recited a verse.
*Dàshèng Wáng* then bestowed one thousand gold coins.
*Dàshèng* was precisely that *Fànzhì* of various kinds.
The youth *Yùduō* at that time was myself.”
Formerly, there was a *Móyīndí Fànzhì* (Māgaṇḍiya Brahmaṇā).
Who had a beautiful daughter.
Kings, crown princes, ministers, and elders came seeking her but were refused.
He saw the Buddha, who had a golden hue and the thirty-two marks (of a great man).
He then thought to himself:
“To a person like this, I will give my daughter.”
He returned home and told his wife:
“Today, I have found a son-in-law who surpasses my daughter.”
He immediately adorned his daughter with various jeweled necklaces (*yīngluò*).
And led his daughter out of the city.
The mother saw the footprint marks of the Buddha, clearly visible.
She said to the father:
“Do you not realize that if these footprints appeared in the void, you would ultimately not obtain a son-in-law?”
The wife recited a verse, saying:
“Lascivious people walk dragging their heels; hateful people walk clenching their toes;
Foolish people stumble their feet on the ground. These footprints belong to the Honored One of Devas and Men.”
The father said:
“Foolish woman, you are making trouble for your daughter.”
He immediately took his daughter to the Buddha's location.
Holding her arm with his left hand and carrying a vase with his right hand.
He then spoke to the Buddha, saying:
“I now present this daughter to you as a gift, to be your wife.”
The daughter saw the Buddha's form, and her lustful intentions became attached.
Her mind was set ablaze.
The Buddha then recited a verse, saying:
“I have seen the three daughters of *Xié* (Māra) and yet did not desire their wicked lust.
Now, would I embrace this container of feces and urine? Even touching your feet is improper.”
In the past, there was a Brāhmaṇa (Pólúomén) who left home to study while young.
He reached sixty years of age but could not attain the Way (Dào).
According to custom, he should return home,
take a wife, and become a householder (Jūshì).
He fathered a son,
who was handsome and lovable.
When the boy reached seven years old, he suddenly contracted a severe illness.
He died overnight. The Fànzhì grieved for him,
and collapsing onto the corpse, he passed out and then revived.
His relatives advised him, forcefully took the body, prepared it for burial, and interred it outside the city.
The Fànzhì thought to himself,
“My weeping now achieves nothing.
It would be better to go to the residence of Yánluó Wáng and beg for my son’s life.”
He bathed, kept the fast, and carried flowers and incense.
He set out from his house and departed.
Wherever he went, he asked people,
“Where is the seat of power of Yánluó Wáng?”
He traveled thousands of *lǐ* forward until he reached deep mountains.
He saw several Fànzhì and asked them the same question as before.
They replied,
“Why do you ask for the location of Yánluó Wáng’s seat of power?”
He replied,
“I had a son who recently died suddenly.
I wish to go to Yánluó Wáng’s residence and beg for my son’s life.”
The Fànzhì pitied his ignorance
and immediately told him,
“The seat of Yánluó Wáng’s rule is not a place living people can reach.
I will show you the direction.
You should go west from here for over four hundred *lǐ*.
There is a great river valley, and within it, there is a city.
This is the resting city for the celestial spirits (Tiānshén) who inspect the world.
Yánluó Wáng always passes through this city on the fourth day of the month during his inspection. If you maintain the fast and precepts and go there, you will certainly see him.”
He left happily.
Arriving in the river valley, he saw a beautiful city wall, palaces, and buildings,
like those of Dāolì Tiān.
The Fànzhì approached the gate,
burned incense, stood on tiptoe, and chanted prayers (zhòuyuàn), begging for his son.
Yánluó Wáng commanded the gatekeepers to bring him in.
The Fànzhì reported,
“I begot a son late in life, hoping he would support me in old age.
I raised him for seven years, but he recently died.
I only wish that the Great King would bestow grace and return my son’s life to me.”
The King said, “Excellent.
Your son is now playing in the Eastern Garden.
Go and take him yourself.”
He immediately went and saw his son,
playing with several other children.
He stepped forward, embraced him, and wept, saying,
“Thinking of you day and night, my food and sleep have been tasteless.
Do you ever think about the hardship of your parents?”
The boy shouted back and scolded him, saying,
“You stupid, foolish old man! You do not understand principle (dàolǐ).
I stayed there for a short time and was named your son.
Do not speak nonsense anymore.
It is better that you leave quickly.
I now have my own parents here.”
The Fànzhì was heartbroken and wept as he departed.
He immediately thought to himself,
“I have heard that Qútán Shāmén knows the Way (Dào) of the transformations of human soul and spirit.
I should go and ask him.”
He immediately returned to Fó’s place, prostrated himself, and performed the rite.
He fully recounted the entire story to Fó.
“[My son] truly refused to return.
He called me a stupid, foolish old man,
saying he only stayed there for a short time and was named my son.
There is absolutely no feeling of father and son.
Why is this so?”
Fó told the Fànzhì,
“You are truly ignorant.
When a person dies, the spirit departs and takes another form.
Parents, wives, and children gather together due to karmic conditions (yīnyuán).
It is like staying with a guest—when they rise to leave, they scatter.”
When the Fànzhì heard this, he suddenly understood the meaning, bowed, and submitted himself,
requesting to become a Shāmén.
Fó said, “Excellent.”
His beard and hair naturally fell out, and the dharma robes appeared on his body.
He immediately became a Bǐqiū.
Immediately, while seated, he attained the Way of the Luóhàn Dào.
In the past, there was a Fànzhì
who was wealthy and learned but did not believe in the Correct Way (Zhèng Dào).
He often argued with Shāmén and refuted them.
Whenever he heard that Shāmén ate the charity offered by believers but were unable to progress diligently,
he thought that after death they must become oxen and horses to repay the donors.
So he secretly made a plan to prepare a meal
and take them in a future life,
using them for his livelihood.
His nature was usually stingy and greedy, but suddenly he went to the monastery.
In the monastery there were five hundred monks (dàoren), and he invited them all.
He respectfully prepared a rich and superior meal, better than others,
certainly intending to capture five hundred oxen and horses.
The senior monk (Shàngzuò) had already attained the four paths of Luóhànship.
He knew the Fànzhì’s thoughts.
He immediately called the Wéinà and instructed the Bǐqiū,
“Each person must focus their minds and recite one *gāthā* (jì) while accepting the respectful offering.”
The Shàngzuò then said,
“The debt has been fully repaid.
You will no longer acquire oxen or horses.”
The Fànzhì exclaimed in surprise,
“The monks (Dàoren) are divine and holy! They knew my intentions beforehand.”
The Shàngzuò then fully informed the Bǐqiū,
“When you have received the food,
recite one phrase of the Dharma (fǎ yán) with a compassionate mind focused on the Way (Dào).
This alone can digest even Xūmí Shān,
let alone this small meal.”
The Fànzhì was extremely ashamed.
The Shàngzuò then spoke the Dharma for him, extensively laying out the essential meanings.
His heart opened, he accepted the Way (Dào), and immediately understood the Path (Dào Jì).
In the past, there was a Fànzhì
who was determined not to see Fó and secretly entered someone else's house.
The Great Sage (Dàshèng) took pity on him and appeared before his eyes.
He tried to flee quickly but could not move himself;
he came to Fó’s residence.
At that time, the Shìzūn
spoke the *sūtra* Dharma for him, and a joyous heart arose in him.
He took refuge in the Dharma Saṅgha (Fǎ Sēng), accepted the precepts, and circumambulated Fó before departing.
He immediately took a begging bowl (yìng qì) and filled it entirely with honey.
Holding it up with both hands, he wished to offer it to Fó.
Fó told the Bǐqiū,
“Take this bowl of honey and distribute it among the assembly of monks (Zhòng Sēng).”
At that time, Fó and the entire assembly of monks were satisfied by the one bowl of honey,
yet the bowl remained full as before.
The Fànzhì immediately offered it to Fó again.
Fó told the Fànzhì,
“Pour it into the great water, into the boundless stream.”
The Fànzhì again asked why.
Fó said,
“All the insects, mollusks, turtles, alligators, fish, and soft-shelled turtles in the water will fully receive its taste.”
The Fànzhì accepted the instruction.
The Shìzūn smiled joyfully and emitted a five-colored light.
It ascended up to Fàntiān and universally illuminated the five paths (Wǔ Dào).
It then returned, circling Fó’s body three times.
When conferring the assurance (jué) of a Púsà, the light entered through the crown of his head.
When conferring the assurance of a Yuánjué, the light entered through his mouth.
When conferring the assurance of a Shēngwén, the light entered through his arm.
When speaking of the blessings of the higher heavens, the light entered through his navel.
When speaking of granting a human body, the light entered through his knees.
When speaking of the hells (dìyù), hungry ghosts (è guǐ), and animals (chùshēng), the light entered through his feet.
Ānán rose from his seat, clasped his hands, and addressed Fó, saying,
“Fó does not laugh randomly;
when he laughs, there is always a purpose.”
Fó told Ānán,
“Did you see the Fànzhì offer honey to Fó?”
Ānán replied, “Yes.”
“This Fànzhì, in future lives hence,
will traverse twenty *kalpas* (jié) without falling into evil realms.
After twenty *kalpas*, he shall attain Yuánjuéship.
His name will be Mìjù.”
The Bǐqiū said,
“This Fànzhì gained great benefit from one bowl of honey, thereby attaining Yuánjuéship.”
Fó told the Bǐqiū,
“Regarding this Fànzhì, not only in this life,
but in previous past lives, it was also thus.
In the past, there was a Pólúomén living in quiet solitude.
He saw a divine immortal (Shénxiān).”
Someone said,
“This immortal now is wonderfully auspicious and hard to reach.
We should go and receive his teaching.”
Someone else replied,
“Why would you use him? He merely preserves the physical body (Yǎng Shēn zhī Zhǒng).”
There was one immortal possessing the Five Supernatural Powers (Wǔ Tōng Xiān).
He saw what the Pólúomén was thinking.
He immediately leaped up into the air between the trees
and stopped before that person.
Seeing this, the Pólúomén rejoiced greatly.
He immediately filled a bowl with honey and offered it to the immortal.
The immortal received it and flew away into the void.
Due to the merit of this charity (Shī Dé), the Pólúomén later became a king.
His name was Mìjù.
He ruled the country by the Proper Dharma (Zhèng Fǎ) and, upon the end of his life, was born in heaven (Tiān).
Fó told the Bǐqiū,
“If you wish to know who the Wǔ Tōng Xiān of that time was,
then it was my body.
The Fànzhì of that time is the present Fànzhì.
At that time, the offering of honey led to the blessing of celestial and human rebirths (Tiān Rén Fú).
Due to that condition, he again made an offering to Fó in this present life,
and later attained Yuánjuéship.”
There was a Fànzhì.
He was in Luóyuèqí.
Hearing that the people of Shèwèiguó were mostly filial, upheld the scriptures, cultivated the Way, and served the Sānzūn,
he desired to seek knowledge, and immediately went to consult and receive instruction.
Not far from the kingdom,
he saw two people, father and son, tilling the ground and sowing seeds.
A poisonous snake came out and bit his son to death.
The father did not stop tilling and sowing, nor did he look back.
The Fànzhì questioned him.
The tiller asked in return,
“Whence have you come?”
The Fànzhì replied,
“I have come from Luóyuèqí.
I heard that the people of this country are mostly filial, support and serve the Sānbǎo, and thus I came to seek learning.”
“The one who just died, whose son was he?”
He replied, “My son.”
The Fànzhì asked, “If he is your son, why are you not grieved, and instead continue tilling and sowing?”
That man replied,
“Life entails death; things that form must decay.
It is not something that sorrow, worry, crying, or weeping can remedy.
If I do not eat or drink, what benefit is that to the deceased?
When you enter the city, please pass word to my family.
My son has died.
Do not bring food portions for two people anymore.”
The Fànzhì secretly thought,
“People are faithless.
The child lies dead on the ground,
yet he is calmly without worry and instead demands food.”
He entered Shèwèichéng and went to the tiller's home.
He saw the dead child's mother and told her,
“Your son has died.
His father said,
‘Just bring food portions for one person.’”
The child's mother said,
“It is like a guest who comes to stay.
Coming is not difficult; leaving is not delayed.
This child is just like that.
When born, he came by himself; when dying, he also leaves alone.
It is not within my power to advance or retreat him.
He follows his original actions (karma) to seek rebirth.”
He also spoke to the child's elder sister.
The sister also spoke of impermanence (wúcháng) using parables.
The Fànzhì spoke to the woman.
“Your husband has died.”
The woman told the Fànzhì a parable.
He also spoke to the slave boy.
“Your master has died.”
The slave boy also told a parable.
When the Fànzhì heard this,
his heart was affected and his eyes were dark; he could not distinguish east from west.
“I heard that the people of this country are filial and serve the Sānbǎo, so I came to seek instruction.
I have not yet achieved good intentions.
I see five people who are faithless and whose bodies and minds labor in vain.”
He then asked a passerby, “Where is the Buddha?”
The person replied,
“He is nearby, at the Qíshù Jǐgūdú Yuán.”
The Fànzhì immediately went to the Buddha's location.
He bowed his head to the Buddha’s feet and withdrew to sit on one side.
He was sorrowful and unhappy,
lowering his head, silent, and said nothing.
The Buddha knew his thoughts
and spoke to the Fànzhì, saying,
“Why are you unhappy?”
The Fànzhì replied,
“Because I have gone against my original vow, I am sorrowful.”
The Buddha asked again,
“How so?”
He answered fully concerning the events.
The Buddha said, “Not so.
It is not as you say.
These five people are the most consistent.
They know that life is impermanent and cannot be remedied by sorrow and worry.
They return to self-determination, and thus have no worry or sorrow.
Common people do not recognize impermanence.
They regret, worry, cry, and weep, unable to release themselves.
It is like a person whose body contracts a fever.
They are unaware, frantic, sudden, and speak falsely.
When a good doctor gives medicine,
the fever is immediately removed and cured, and they no longer speak falsely.
Common people’s sorrow and worry, caused by the fever of foolish delusion, cannot be naturally resolved.
If they understood impermanence, they would no longer be sorrowful,
just as the fever is cured.
These five people can all attain realization of the Way.”
When the Fànzhì heard these words, he immediately blamed himself, saying,
“I have been foolish and ignorant, not knowing the great principle.
Now that I have heard the Buddha’s words,
it is like the blind gaining sight, seeing light in the darkness.”
He immediately accepted the Five Precepts, bowed his head, and withdrew.
The Fànzhì had four brothers.
Each had attained the Five Supernatural Powers (Wǔtōng).
After seven days, they were all scheduled to die.
They discussed it among themselves, saying,
“The power of the Wǔtōng can overturn heaven and earth.
We can touch the sun and moon with our hands, move mountains, and stop rivers.
There is nothing we cannot do.
Surely we can avoid this retribution of death?”
One person said,
“I shall enter the great ocean.
I will not appear on the surface nor reach the bottom,
but stay exactly in the middle.
How will the death demon of impermanence know my location?”
Another person said,
“I shall enter into Xūmí Shān.
I will close up its exterior so that no border appears.
How will the death demon of impermanence know my location?”
A third person said,
“I shall lightly ascend and hide in empty space.
How will the death demon of impermanence know my location?”
A fourth person said,
“I shall hide in the middle of the great market.
If the death demon of impermanence manages to capture one person, why must it seek me?”
When the four people had finished their discussion,
they went together to bid farewell to the king.
“Our remaining lifespan is seven days.
We now wish to flee death,
hoping to escape. If we return, we will personally pay our respects.
We only ask that you continue to advance virtue.”
Thereupon, they separated and left.
When the seven-day period was fulfilled, they all died,
just like ripe fruit falling.
The market administrator reported to the king,
“One Fànzhì suddenly died in the market.”
The king then understood and said,
“Four people tried to evade retribution, and one has already died.
How can the remaining three possibly be spared?”
The king immediately prepared his carriage and went to the Buddha's location.
He made an obeisance, withdrew and sat down, and reported,
“Recently, there were Fànzhì,
four brothers, each having attained the Wǔtōng.
Knowing their lifespan was ending, they all tried to evade it.
I wonder whether they were able to escape now?”
The Buddha informed the Great King,
“There are four matters concerning humanity that cannot be escaped.
First, being in the Zhōngyīn (intermediate state) inevitably leads to accepting rebirth.
Second, being born inevitably leads to accepting aging.
Third, aging inevitably leads to accepting sickness.
Fourth, sickness inevitably leads to accepting death.”
There was a Qīngxìnshì (lay devotee).
His wife was proper and virtuous, peerless in majesty.
Her speech was eloquent, and she was respected by all people.
However, her husband did not esteem her and was not pleased to see her.
Instead, he loved his maidservant.
The wife, seeing her husband's mind,
spoke to him, saying:
“Since you are not pleased with me,
I request permission to leave home.”
The husband immediately agreed to it.
She immediately left home and became a Bǐqiūní (nun).
She progressed diligently day and night.
Before long, while practicing the Way, she attained Luóhàn (Arhatship).
Afterward, the woman whom the Qīngxìnshì respected died.
The Qīngxìnshì called the Bǐqiūní to return home.
The nun completely refused.
The Bǐqiūní reported to the Buddha,
narrating the entire history.
The Buddha said:
“In a former life, this Qīngxìnshì already scorned and insulted this virtuous person.
This woman had unique and special aspirations.
This man constantly sought to corrupt and confuse her.
Having already entered the Great Path, he still wishes to ruin her.
He cannot succeed.”
The Buddha said:
“In a past life, there was a Fànzhì (Brahmin) and his wife,
named Liánhuá.
She was exceedingly beautiful.
The Fànzhì did not like her.
The one he loved was a maidservant.
Following the maidservant’s words,
he abandoned his wife in the mountains.
He climbed a Yōubōtánshù tree, picked the ripe fruit,
and threw the unripe ones down to his wife.
The wife asked:
‘My lord, you eat the ripe fruit alone,
and throw the unripe ones down for others.’
The husband said:
‘You may climb the tree.’
The wife immediately climbed the tree.
The husband took thorny shrubs and surrounded the tree four times,
intending to cause her death so that she could not descend.
At that time, the King of the country was hunting.
He saw the woman’s beauty
and immediately asked the woman,
‘Who are you?’
The wife fully recounted her entire story.
The King reflected that the Fànzhì
was foolish, ignorant, and not a real man.
He immediately removed the thorny shrubs.
He carried her back to the palace in a chariot and established her as the Queen.
She possessed many arts and crafts, and her intelligence and eloquence were unmatched.
She was also skilled at playing chūbó (a board game).
Women from near and far came to play the game with her.
The Queen always won, and no one could contend with her.
The Fànzhì was skilled at board games.
Hearing remotely of the Queen’s victories,
he thought:
‘That is my former wife, not some other person.’
He then sought to visit the King to display his skill.
When the Queen heard the description of the Fànzhì's appearance, she knew it was her former husband.
She informed the King and revealed his presence.
They remotely tested him with the board game.
The Queen answered with a gāthā (verse).
The Fànzhì’s heart was filled with shame and regret.
He immediately blamed himself, but regret was useless.
The Fànzhì of that time is the Qīngxìnshì of today.
The wife of that time is the wife of today.
The King of that country is myself.”
There was a Fànzhì who possessed countless wealth.
He had exactly one son, twenty years of age,
for whom he had recently taken a wife.
Less than seven days had passed.
It was the third month of spring.
The couple went together to the back garden to play.
There was a tall pear tree with beautiful flowers.
The wife wished to have them, but there was no one to pick them for her.
The husband knew his wife’s desire and immediately climbed the tree.
He picked just one flower.
When he wished to pick a second,
the branch broke, and he fell to the ground and died.
The entire family rushed forward to the location of the boy.
Crying out to heaven, they fainted and then revived.
His innumerable relatives all shared in the grief and pain.
Hearing of it caused heartache; seeing it caused sorrow.
The parents complained against Heaven, saying it failed to protect them.
When the funeral rites and burial were completed,
they returned home, weeping and unable to stop themselves.
Thereupon, the Shìzūn (World-Honored One),
pitying their ignorance, went to visit them.
The whole family saw the Buddha
and tearfully expressed their hardship and sorrow in full detail.
The Buddha said to the Elder:
“Stop your sorrow and listen to the Dharma: all things are impermanent and cannot be preserved for long.
Where there is birth, there is death; crime and blessing follow one another.
This child is being wept for in three places,
and the despair and heartache are difficult to bear.
Whose child is he ultimately?
Who are his relatives?”
Thereupon, the Shìzūn immediately spoke a verse (gāthā), saying:
“Life is like ripe fruit or blossoms, always feared to fall and wither.
All that is born possesses suffering; who can attain deathlessness?
From the beginning, enjoying love and desire, capable of lust, entering this fragile scene,
The form received—life is like lightning, flowing day and night, difficult to halt.
This body is a dead thing; the spirit is formless Dharma.
It acts, causing death and rebirth; crime and blessing never perish or cease.
Beginning and end are not just one lifetime; they come from prolonged foolish love.
One creates and receives suffering and joy; though the body dies, the spirit is not lost.”
When the Elder heard the verse, his mind opened, and he forgot his sorrow.
Kneeling, he addressed the Buddha:
“What crime or offense did this child commit in his past life
that, in the prime of his beautiful life, he met with untimely death?
I sincerely wish you would explain the sins he originally committed.”
The Buddha said:
“A long time ago, there was a young boy
who took a bow and arrow and entered a sacred tree to play.
Nearby were three men watching a sparrow in the tree.
The boy wanted to shoot it.
The three men encouraged him, saying:
‘If you can hit it, the world will call you a brave boy.’
The boy was delighted and drew his bow and shot.
He hit the sparrow, and it immediately died.
The three men laughed together, helped him celebrate, and then each went their way.
Through countless kalpas of rebirth,
wherever they met, they came together to receive their karmic retribution.
Among those three men, one who had merit is now in heaven.
One was born into the sea as a miraculously born Dragon King.
The third is the body of the Elder today.
As for the young boy, in his previous life, he was born in heaven as the son of a deity.
When his life ended, he descended to become the son of the Elder.
After falling from the tree and dying, he was immediately born into the sea as a miraculously born dragon’s son.
On the very day he was born, the King of the Garuḍa (Jīnchìniǎo) birds took and ate him.
Can you describe the heartache and weeping in these three places today?
Because in that former life, they assisted in his joy (at the killing),
these three men repaid it with weeping.”
The King, ministers, and people of Shèwèiguó (Śrāvastī)
revered the Shìzūn and offered the four requirements (sìshì gōngyǎng).
They abandoned the Fànzhì (Brahmins).
The Fànzhì deliberated together, saying:
“We must seek a beautiful woman, kill her, and bury her among the trees,
so that the followers of Qútán (Gautama) will have a notorious bad name spread far and wide,
and we will find people who will wait upon us.”
They immediately coerced and instructed a beautiful woman, saying:
“From now on, you shall visit the Buddha morning and evening so that all people may see and know.”
The young woman followed the instruction.
Then they killed her and buried her among the trees.
The Fànzhì then gathered and went to the palace gates,
crying out complaints, saying:
“In our school, there was a woman
who was uniquely most beautiful.
Her flowery color was unmatched, and no one knows whether she is alive or dead.”
The King said to them:
“Where did she usually go?”
They replied:
“She went to the vicinity of Qútán.”
The King said:
“She must be sought there.”
Messengers went to the Qíshù (Jetavana) Grove.
They dug out the woman’s corpse and placed it on a bed.
They cried out complaints throughout the streets, saying:
“The Śramaṇa Qútán always claims that his precepts and virtue are vast and unsurpassed.
How can he privately share intimacy with a woman
and then kill and hide her?
What Dharma and precepts does he have?”
At that time, the various Bǐqiū (monks) entered the city to beg for food.
The people cursed them, saying:
“If the offenses committed by these Śramaṇa are like this,
how can they receive clothing and food?”
The Bǐqiū left the city holding their empty bowls.
They returned and reported to the Buddha.
The Buddha told the Bǐqiū:
“This slander directed at me will not last more than seven days.”
At that time, a woman named Wéiyán in the city heard
that the Bǐqiū seeking food had all returned with empty bowls.
She went to the Buddha’s location and bowed her head to the ground in reverence.
Clasping her hands, she said to the Buddha:
“I request that the Buddha and the Sangha dine at my house for seven days.”
The Buddha silently accepted.
The Buddha told Ānán (Ānanda):
“You and the assembly of monks should enter the city streets
and recite this verse (gāthā):
‘One who constantly deceives and leads astray, secretly speaks of acts which the body does not commit,
The actions committed in heavy darkness will certainly be fully realized, and one will inevitably receive sorrow and suffering.’”
Wéiyán then provided food for the Buddha and the Sangha at that time.
In the capital city of Shèwèi.
There was a Brahmin, Bīntóulú Duǒzhē.
His wife was ugly and malicious, both eyes piercingly blue/green.
They had seven daughters but no sons.
He was poor, his daughters destitute, and his wife wicked and fond of scolding.
When the daughters came asking for necessities, she glared angrily and wept.
He had ripe grain in the field, so he borrowed an ox from another person.
He took it to tread the grain, but lost it in the marsh.
At that time, the Brahmin sat down and pondered.
“What sin have I sown?
I am pressured by my women, and now I have lost another man's ox.”
Searching for it until he was physically exhausted, he happened to reach a forest.
There he encountered the Rúlái.
Gazing upon him, a thought arose:
“The śrāmaṇa Qútán is now the most peaceful and happy.
He is free from the troubles of the self.”
The Buddha knew his heart.
Then he spoke to him, saying,
“It is just as you have pondered.”
The Buddha told him, saying,
“Do you wish to leave home (to become a monk)?”
He immediately replied to the Buddha, saying,
“World Honored One (Shìzūn),
To be allowed is most fitting to my humble wish.” The Buddha said,
“Welcome, Bhikṣu (Bǐqiū).”
His beard and hair fell off by themselves.
The clothes he was wearing transformed into a kāṣāya (Jiāshā) robe.
The Buddha taught him the Dharma.
He attained Arhatship (Āluóhàn).
The Buddha told Ānán:
“In the past, there was a king,
named Āpōluódìmùqié.
He transformed beings through the Way.
At that time, there was a Brahmin,
named Tánnìchuō.
His family was desolate and poor, and he had a small amount of ripe grain.
He borrowed an ox to tread the grain, drove it back to its owner,
but forgot to formally inform him.
Although the ox owner saw it, he assumed the work was not yet finished,
and thus did not take it in. Both families intentionally abandoned it.
The ox owner took Tánnìchuō to the king to settle the matter.
Leaving, he ran into the king’s stable keeper.
He called out to Tánnìchuō, “Stop this horse for me!”
Tánnìchuō picked up a stone and threw it.
It hit the horse’s leg, and it immediately broke.
Next, walking to a river, he did not know the crossing place.
He met a carpenter.
The carpenter held his hatchet in his mouth, hitched up his clothes, and was about to cross.
At that moment, Tánnìchuō asked that person, saying,
“Where can I cross?”
As the man opened his mouth to reply,
his mouth opened, and the hatchet fell into the water.
Distressed by his creditors and moreover hungry and thirsty,
he begged for a little white wine from a liquor seller’s house.
He sat on the bed to drink it.
Unexpectedly, there was a small child lying asleep beneath the bedding.
He crushed the child, and its belly ruptured.
He went to the side of a wall.
Thinking about and fearing his sin,
he threw himself and jumped over the wall.
A weaver was below.
He fell on him, and the weaver died instantly.
Then the weaver's son caught hold of him again.
He took him, along with the crowd, before the king.
“This man publicly killed my father!”
At that time, all the creditors brought him before the king.
Then the ox owner stepped forward and said to the king,
“This man borrowed an ox from me.
He did not return and formally hand it over.
It was lost, and he refuses to compensate me.”
The king asked, “What is the reason?”
Tánnìchuō said,
“I truly borrowed the ox, and when I finished using it, I quickly returned it.
The owner also saw it.
Although I did not verbally hand it over, the ox was at his gate.”
The king said to that person,
“Both of you are in the wrong.
Because Tánnìchuō did not verbally hand it over to you,
his tongue should be cut off.
Because you saw the ox and did not take it in yourself,
your eyes should be gouged out.”
That man said to the king,
“I request to abandon this ox; I do not desire to have my eyes gouged out or his tongue cut off.”
The king immediately allowed the reconciliation.
The stable keeper again spoke,
“That man is ruthless; he broke my horse’s leg.”
The king then asked,
“This is a royal horse; how dare you break its leg?”
He knelt and said to the king,
“The creditor was taking me along the road.
That man called out to me, asking me to stop the royal horse.
I picked up a stone and threw it.
I accidentally broke the horse's leg.”
The king said,
“Because you called out to him, your tongue should be cut off.
Because he hit the horse, his hand should be cut off.”
The stable keeper said to the king,
“I beg for everyone to be reconciled.”
The carpenter stepped forward and said,
“Tánnìchuō caused me to lose my hatchet.”
The king said to the carpenter,
“Because he called out to you, his tongue should be cut off.
The proper method for carrying tools traditionally uses the hand.
Because you held it in your mouth,
your two front teeth should be broken.”
The carpenter said to the king,
“I would rather abandon the hatchet than have this punishment carried out.”
Then the liquor seller's mother again came forward, saying to the king, “He unjustly killed my son!”
Tánnìchuō knelt and said to the king,
“I was afflicted by hunger and thirst.
I begged for a little wine to drink.
I did not know there was a small child lying under the bedding.
May the King observe this.”
The king said to the mother,
“You sell liquor in your house, and many guests gather.
Why did you put a sleeping child in a place for sitting?
Both of you are at fault.
Since your child is already dead,
Tánnìchuō shall be given to you as a son-in-law.
Only when you have another child shall he be released.”
The mother kowtowed and said,
“Please allow us to reconcile.
I do not need a husband (or son-in-law).”
Then the weaver's son stepped forward again.
“This man, in his madness and violence, stepped on and killed my father!”
The king asked, saying,
“You killed his father.”
Tánnìchuō said,
“The crowd pressured and blamed me.
In fear and panic, I jumped over the wall and happened to fall upon him.
It was truly not intentional.”
The king said to that person,
“Both of you are in the wrong.
Since your father is already dead,
Tánnìchuō shall be given to you as a father.”
That man said to the king,
“My father is now dead.
I absolutely refuse to take this Brahmin as my father.”
The king granted permission for everyone to reconcile.
The king then permitted it.
At that time, Tánnìchuō, having all his affairs concluded, remained before the king.
He saw two mothers arguing over one child.
The king, being wise and clever, devised a resourceful plan.
“Now there is only one child.
Two mothers are fighting over it.
I permit the two of you to each pull one of its arms.
Whoever can acquire him will take him.”
The one who was not the true mother had no maternal love for the child and pulled hard with all her might.
The one who gave birth to the child, having deep maternal love for her son,
could not bear to yank and pull him.
The king discerned the truth from the falsehood.
He interrogated and exposed the fraud who tried to forcefully claim the other person’s child.
He immediately had the child returned to its mother and arrested the other.
Then they were released.
At that time, Tánnìchuō said to the king,
“When I was by the side of the road,
a poisonous snake requested me to speak to the King on its behalf.
It does not know why, when it comes out of its hole, it changes and becomes soft and supple.
But when it returns to its hole, it is hindered and suffers pain.”
The king answered him, saying,
“When it comes out of its hole, it is free from all afflictions.
Its mind is harmonious and gentle, and its body is likewise.
Outside, it is provoked by birds, beasts, and various circumstances,
and its anger flourishes, causing its body to swell and become coarse.
You may tell it,
‘If you maintain a mind without anger, you will not have this problem.’”
Next, Tánnìchuō said, “I saw a woman.
She asked me to tell the King:
‘When I am at my husband’s home, I miss my parents’ house.
When I am at my parents’ house, I miss my husband’s home again.’
The king said,
“You may tell her,
‘It is because of your evil intentions.
At your parents’ house, you keep a side lover.
When you are at your husband’s house, you miss that side lover.
When you get to him, you quickly tire of him and miss your lawful husband.
That is why this is so.
If you maintain a mind that abandons evil, you will not have this problem.’”
Next, Tánnìchuō said, “I saw a pheasant up in a tree.
It asked me to tell the King:
‘When I am in other trees, my cry is unpleasant.
But if I am in this tree, my cry is sorrowful and harmonious.
I do not know the reason.’
The king told that person,
“It is because under that tree there is a large cauldron of gold.
Therefore, when it is above, its cry is sorrowful and beautiful.
In other places, there is no gold,
so its sound is unpleasant.”
The king instructed Tánnìchuō,
“You have committed many faults, but I have already absolved you.
Being poor and distressed, take the cauldron of gold under the tree.
I give it to you.”
Tánnìchuō respectfully received the king’s order, dug the ground, and took the gold.
He traded it for what he needed, and enjoyed happiness without want.
“The Great King at that time was my present self.
As for Tánnìchuō,
he is the present Brahmin Bīntóulú Duǒzhē.”
In the Kingdom of Bāliánfú there was a brāhmaṇa,
named Āqínídáduō.
He was conversant with the Sūtras and Śāstras.
Shortly after he married a wife, she conceived.
During the pregnancy, she greatly desired discussion and debate.
The husband consulted a physiognomer.
The physiognomer replied:
"The child in the womb will be skilled at debate."
When the months were completed, she bore a boy,
who mastered various Sūtras and Śāstras.
He became a teacher to brāhmaṇas,
and also instructed people in medical arts.
At that time, the people of Luóyuè Chéng,
according to their clans, invited the Buddha (Fó) and the Saṅgha (Sēng).
Then all the brāhmaṇas
gathered like clouds from the four directions and set a limitation among themselves.
Each was to contribute one hundred coins for the Buddha and the Saṅgha.
At that time, Jītóu, a brāhmaṇa, knew he was poor and had no money
and could not obtain the means to make offerings to that assembly.
The people said to him:
"You have no money."
Jītóu then returned to his wife and said:
"Everyone drove me out of the assembly
because I have no money."
The wife then replied:
"You should go into the city and borrow one hundred coins on credit."
He searched everywhere but could not obtain it.
He returned and told his wife.
The wife further said:
"Go to the house of the Elder Fúshāmìduōluó
and borrow from him."
He immediately went and requested, saying he would repay within seven days.
"If I do not repay, my body and my wife shall become slaves."
The Elder then lent him one hundred gold coins. He obtained them and returned to tell his wife.
The wife responded, saying:
"Take them and go to the assembly and say,
'I have obtained the money; allow me to participate.' "
The assembly said to Jītóu:
"It is already prepared; we do not need your money."
Jītóu returned.
The husband and wife went together to the World-Honored One (Shìzūn).
They inquired about each other's health.
Then Jītóu's wife bowed at the World-Honored One's feet,
and fully reported the matter to the Buddha.
The Buddha said to Jītóu:
"You may now invite the World-Honored One and the Bhikkhu Saṅgha (Bǐqiū Sēng)."
Then Jītóu's wife said to her husband:
"My lord, follow the Buddha's instruction."
At that time, Jītóu immediately rose from his seat and bared his right shoulder.
He clasped his hands and addressed the Buddha, saying:
"May the World-Honored One accept my invitation,
and the Bhikkhu Saṅgha."
The World-Honored One remained silent.
Śakra Devānām Indra (Shìtíhuányīn) spoke to Vaiśravaṇa Heavenly King (Píshāmén Tiānwáng), saying:
"Kubera (Jūpíluó)! Assist this brāhmaṇa
in preparing the third meal."
He replied, "I obey the instruction."
Then Vaiśravaṇa Heavenly King concealed his true form.
He transformed into a human and commanded five hundred Rākṣasas (Luóchà), saying:
"You must quickly go to the Sandalwood Forest (Zhāntán Lín)
and fetch fragrant firewood.
He planned to feed the Buddha and the Saṅgha in the Bamboo Grove (Zhúyuán).
He materialized an iron stove.
The five hundred Rākṣasas each carried Ox-head sandalwood (Niútóu zhāntán) fragrant firewood and placed it inside the iron stove.
At that time, Jītóu used the iron stove to cook the food.
The aroma was smelled throughout twelve Yóuyán (Yojanas).
Then Śakra Devānām Indra (Shìtíhuányīn) spoke to the Deva-putra (Tiānzǐ) Píshīpōjiāmó:
"You should transform and create a tall and spacious lecture hall,
so that the Buddha and the Saṅgha may sit and eat."
He replied, "I obey the instruction."
Just like a strong man bending and extending his arm,
he descended from the Trāyastriṃśa Heaven (Sānshísān Tiān) to the middle of the Bamboo Grove (Zhúyuán).
Next to the iron stove, he materialized a lecture hall,
constructed of the Seven Treasures.
He created one thousand two hundred and fifty seats,
which were embroidered and patterned.
Holding censers, they burned various famous incenses.
They caused Tāla trees (Duōluó shù), made of the Seven Treasures, to appear.
A gentle breeze blew, causing the sound of bells to be heard far away.
At that time, King Pínpísuōluó of the Kingdom of Magadha (Mójié Guó) heard this
and asked his officials.
The officials replied:
"It is Jītóu the brāhmaṇa
who is cooking food for the Buddha and the Saṅgha in an iron stove using Ox-head sandalwood.
This is the source of the fragrance."
The King then went to the Buddha's location
and addressed his officials:
"In ancient times, there was no such lecture hall.
Who made it now?"
The officials reported to the King, saying:
"We do not know."
The World-Honored One then extensively explained the matter to the King, as described above.
The King then shed tears, unable to control himself.
He reflected: "Sentient beings today have little merit and short lifespans.
They do not recognize the names of these treasures, much less see them.
Now, through the Buddha's grace, I see this lecture hall.
It has never appeared before."
The World-Honored One said:
"Sentient beings in the future will not even hear of the Seven Treasures,
much less see them with their own eyes.
Now, through the Buddha's grace, you behold such a sight."
The World-Honored One preached the subtle Dharma (Fǎ) for the King,
causing his heart to rejoice.
The King said:
"Jītóu the brāhmaṇa has quickly obtained excellent benefit."
The King said:
"I wish to return to the palace."
The Buddha said:
"Now is the right time."
The Buddha said to Jītóu:
"You should invite the King to share the meal for the day."
He replied, "So be it."
He immediately went to the King, raised his right hand,
and addressed the King, saying:
"O Heavenly King (Tiānwáng),
I wish you to accept the invitation and gather in this lecture hall tomorrow."
The King remained silent.
On the next morning, Píshāmén Tiānwáng bathed,
presented Jītóu with splendid clothing,
and held the censer.
Facing the World-Honored One's location,
he bowed his head to the ground and had this thought:
"Now is the right time.
The meal is ready.
I pray you honor us with your presence."
The Buddha, encircled by the Saṅgha, proceeded to the lecture hall.
The Saṅgha took their seats in order.
At that time, the King prepared his carriage and, surrounded by his officials, proceeded to Jītóu's location.
He brought delicious food and drink, each of a hundred flavors,
encouraging and assisting Jītóu in feeding the Buddha and the Bhikkhu Saṅgha.
At that time, the World-Honored One entered the city of Shěwèi Chéng (Śrāvastī).
There was a certain brāhmaṇa,
who was old and whose faculties were mature.
Holding a staff and carrying an alms bowl, he begged food from house to house.
The World-Honored One asked:
"Why are you doing this?"
He replied:
"Gautama (Qútán),
I have handed over all my wealth to my son.
After taking a wife for him, I was abandoned.
So I carry this bowl and beg for food."
The Buddha further said:
"Can you receive and recite one verse (gāthā) from my Dharma (Fǎ),
and then recite it to your son?"
He replied to the Buddha that he could receive it.
Then the World-Honored One spoke the verse:
"With a joyful heart when a son is born, gathering wealth for the son,
moreover taking a wife for him, only to be cast aside and driven from home.
The sons, heirs to fields and houses, turn against and disobey their father;
having the heart of a Rākṣasa (Luóchà) in a human form, they abandon the aged and revered.
When an old horse is no longer useful, they take away its flour and wheat.
The son is young while the father is old, begging food from house to house.
His staff is the supreme reliance, not the son lacking in love and affection.
It guards me against aggressive oxen and ensures safety in dangerous places.
It repels vicious dogs and supports me walking in dark places,
avoiding deep pits, empty wells, and thorny thickets.
Relying on the staff's power, I stand upright without falling."
The brāhmaṇa then received the verse from the Buddha.
He returned home and reached the gate.
First, he addressed the great assembly (his family):
"Listen to what I have to say,"
and then recited the verse as above.
His son felt shame and fear.
He immediately embraced his father and brought him back into the house.
He massaged his body, bathed him, covered him with clothing and blankets,
and established him as the head of the household.
The brāhmaṇa then thought:
"That I have now gained victory over my household is due to the grace of the Śramaṇa (Shāmén).
My Sūtras state
that if one acts as a teacher, one should be honored as a teacher.
I shall now take this superior and wonderful garment
and go to the World-Honored One's location. I will greet him and report to the Buddha, saying:
'I pray you accept this garment,
out of compassion for me.' "
The World-Honored One immediately accepted it.
He further preached various aspects of the Dharma,
demonstrating the teaching, illuminating it, and bringing joy.
In a past lifetime,
there was a young Brāhmaṇa
named Sǎnjì (散若).
He went to an archery master seeking to learn the art of shooting.
The master said, "You may learn."
Sǎnjì studied this craft constantly for seven years.
Afterwards, he asked the master,
"When may I stop?"
The master replied,
"Take up your bow and fix an arrow.
I will briefly enter the village; wait until I return, then shoot."
The master then entered the village.
Sǎnjì waited for the master for a long time, but he still did not return.
He shot at a large tree in front of him; the arrow passed through and wounded a snake.
When the master returned, he asked,
"Did you not shoot the arrow yet?"
He replied, "I have already shot it."
The master said,
"If you had not shot it,
you would be the foremost Grand Master in Yánfú Tí (閻浮提).
Since you have already shot the arrow,
after I die, you shall succeed me."
At that time, the master adorned his daughter
and gave her to him, along with five hundred arrows and a horse-drawn carriage.
Sǎnjì received them.
When he was crossing the wilderness,
there were five hundred bandits
eating in the wilderness.
Sǎnjì sent his wife to beg food from the bandits.
The bandits said,
"Judging by the one who sent her, he is no ordinary person.
We should give him food."
One bandit said,
"Are we still alive only to allow this person to take his wife and carriage and leave?"
Sǎnjì shot him.
He died immediately from a single arrow.
As quickly as they rose up, he shot them, and none failed to perish.
Only the bandit chief remained. He spoke to the wife, saying,
"Take off your clothes and put them on the ground."
She immediately took off her clothes.
When he saw her, Sǎnjì shot him again, and he died immediately from the arrow.
The five hundred bandits were precisely the five hundred Bhikkhus
(monks), and Sǎnjì (散若) was Shèlìfú (舍利弗).
The Buddha entered Shèwèi Chéng (舍衛城) for alms.
His robe had small tears and damage.
There was a Brāhmaṇa
who saw the Buddha's damaged robe.
He immediately obtained a small piece of white muslin from his home
and offered it to the Buddha.
He petitioned, "May the Tathāgata use this cloth to mend your robe."
The Buddha accepted it immediately.
The Buddha gave him a prophecy,
that in the coming age,
within the period of two Asaṃkhyeya and a hundred kalpas, he would attain Buddhahood.
The man departed joyfully.
The local nobles, worthy elders, and householders said,
"How can the World-Honored One give such a great reward for such a small offering?"
They all damaged fine muslin and made various robes for the Tathāgata.
In the past, there was a Buddha
named Pípōshī (毘鉢尸).
The king at that time was named Pántóu (槃頭).
There was a minister
who invited the Buddha and the Saṅgha for a three-month offering.
The Buddha immediately consented.
King Pántóu (槃頭) then said to the Buddha,
"I desire to obtain the three-month offering for the Buddha and the Saṅgha."
The Buddha informed Pántóu (槃頭),
"I have already accepted the invitation of that minister first."
The king told the minister,
"The Buddha is residing in my kingdom.
Since you have invited him, you should now yield the offering to me."
The minister replied to the king,
"If Your Majesty guarantees my life
and further guarantees that the Tathāgata will permanently reside here,
and that the kingdom will always be peaceful, then I will relinquish my intention."
The king then enlightened him, saying,
"You invite him for one day, and I will invite him for the next day."
The minister then agreed to it.
Each fulfilled their vow.
The king prepared the three robes for the Tathāgata.
Furthermore, he made the seven-striped robe for ninety thousand Bhikkhus.
That minister offered robes and food to the Buddha and the Saṅgha.
That person is myself (the Buddha).
There was a Brāhmaṇa
who asked his wife,
"Do we have food prepared in the house?
I wish to follow the company and make an offering to the śramaṇa Qútán (瞿曇)."
His wife said, "We do."
He immediately prepared it and took it with him.
He happened upon the King, ministers, Kshatriyas, Brāhmaṇas, and the chiefs of eighteen large villages seated together.
The Brāhmaṇa did not dare to advance.
He thought,
"The Buddha is the All-Knowing One; he should know my heart."
The Buddha called him from afar and asked,
"What is in the vessel?"
He replied, "It is cake."
The Buddha said,
"You should take it and give it to the multitude of monks."
He replied, "It is too little; it cannot satisfy everyone."
The Buddha said,
"Just take it and distribute it."
Even after one round, the amount was still undiminished.
Even after three times, it was still not depleted.
The Buddha knew his heart.
Following this, the Buddha taught him the Dharma, and he attained the path of Sūtuóhuán Dào (須陀洹道).
In the past, there was a Dragon King
named Bádǐ (拔抵).
His temperament was violent and cruel.
He frequently used wind, rain, thunderbolts, and hail to kill people.
Countless birds, beasts, and creeping creatures died.
Ten thousand venerable Arhats consulted together.
"If one kills a single person, the sin of falling into hell for one kalpa is still not exhausted.
Now, this dragon is harming sentient beings
ceaselessly,
becoming increasingly difficult to save.
We should go together and remonstrate with him and stop him."
At that time, the Buddha knew this
and praised them, saying, "Excellent!"
The ten thousand Arhats proceeded together.
The dragon released wind, rain, lightning, and thunderbolts.
The ten thousand people were shocked and terrified, and immediately prostrated themselves and returned.
At that time, the Buddha was on Jīshéjué Shān (耆闍崛山).
He went to the dragon's abode accompanied by ten thousand Bodhisattvas and ten thousand Arhats.
The dragon immediately became furious,
releasing fierce winds, sudden rain, thunder, hail, and thunderbolts.
The size of the hailstones he released caused the walls
to measure forty *zhàng* wide.
If they reached the ground, they would penetrate four *chǐ* into the earth.
He intended to harm the Buddha and the assembly of Bodhisattvas and monks.
When the Arhats saw the dragon's destructive transformation,
they were all terrified and moved forward to cling close to the Buddha.
The dragon himself saw the hailstones turn into flower canopies.
He reflected again, saying to himself,
"I will solidify my own body and coil it up to forty *zhàng* in size.
I intend to strike the Buddha and the assembly of monks from above."
He immediately struck himself, but could not hit anything.
He raised his head, opened his eyes, and gazed intently, seeing the Buddha.
He suspected that the Buddha was a venerable, wonderful, and supreme divine person.
Thereupon, the smaller dragons also struck themselves, but nothing was moved.
At that moment, the Dragon King immediately exhausted his life and was reborn in heaven.
All the other smaller dragons also died and attained the status of Sons of Heaven (Devaputras).
They all descended and stood near the Buddha.
The Buddha told Ānán (阿難),
"Do you know the origin of these Devas?"
He replied, "I do not know."
The Buddha said,
"These were the dragons who harbored evil intentions just now.
They struck themselves on the ground and generated a single benevolent thought, recognizing the Buddha as the Venerable One.
Having exhausted their lives, they became Devas—this is the reason."
The Devas heard the Buddha's words,
and the Sons of Heaven all generated the supreme intention for universal deliverance and equality.
The Buddha said,
"In the past, the Dragon King Bádǐ (拔抵) and Śìjiāwén Fó (釋迦文佛) were Brāhmaṇas together.
Bádǐ’s disciples,
who numbered ten thousand at the time,
abandoned their master and served Śìjiāwén.
Bádǐ harbored resentment and was reborn as a dragon.
Since the Buddha’s virtue was accomplished, he saved many beings.
The ten thousand disciples all attained Arhatship.
The dragon harbored evil poison and thus wished to harm them.
Although the ten thousand people had attained the four stages (of sainthood),
they still suffered his humiliation.
If they were Bodhisattvas, the dragon would not dare to do this."
In the past, there was a Brāhmaṇa.
He took no pleasure in worldly affairs.
He hid himself deep in the mountains, focusing purely on the Way.
He immediately entered meditation (samādhi) for over three hundred years.
Dust covered his body, and grass and trees grew upon him.
Down the mountain lived several hundred Brāhmaṇa families who raised livestock and had wives and children.
Young and old went together to gather firewood high in the trees,
breaking off dead branches and roots.
They accidentally touched the forehead of the Brāhmaṇa, and as the tree shook,
the Brāhmaṇa woke from meditation and emerged from the ground.
He saw the firewood gatherers and asked them,
"Who are you?"
