They replied,
"We are Brāhmaṇas."
"And who are the others?"
They replied,
"They are our wives and children."
The Brāhmaṇa laughed and said,
"I have been in meditation for over three hundred years,
yet I still do not dare to call myself a Brāhmaṇa.
How can you dare to call yourselves Brāhmaṇas?"
Long ago, east of Shèwèichéng.
There was a very wealthy Bóluómén.
His son married a wife
who happened to be a woman of the Buddhist faith.
She observed the Five Precepts and upheld the Six Fasting Days.
She always enjoyed giving charity to Shāmén monks and Daoist priests.
She urged her husband to practice giving.
Her husband immediately understood and accepted.
He reported this to his parents.
His parents became greatly enraged,
saying that he was destroying their family house.
The wife took money and silk to her husband.
The husband took it and gave it to the maid who guarded the inner rooms.
The maid took it and gave it to the slave who guarded the gate.
The slave took it and went to the Buddhist temple.
They gave charity to the Shāmén, burned incense, and lit lamps.
The couple swore a joint oath:
“Even if giving charity brings no fortune to ourselves,
yet if there is fortune,
may all the people under heaven jointly witness it.”
At that time, according to the national custom, on the third day of the third month,
all the people of the country went to the waterside to make merry, sing, and play.
At that time, in the southeast corner, there was a Deva.
He rode a white horse and passed by flying through the air.
The crowd looked up and asked what spirit this was.
He answered,
“Ask the one who comes later.”
A moment later, there appeared a seven-jeweled palace.
There was a Yùnǚ sitting alone atop it.
Four Great Heavenly Spirits (Sì Dà Tiānshén) carried the palace flying.
The crowd asked again,
“What merit or virtue do you possess?”
The Yùnǚ also said,
“Ask the one who comes later.”
After a short while, there was a four-pillared jeweled palace.
A Deva and a Yùnǚ were sitting together inside it.
In the front, back, left, and right were four groups of musicians.
Twelve Heavenly Spirits jointly carried the palace.
The crowd asked again,
“What merit and virtue do you possess?”
They also replied,
“Ask the one who comes later.”
A moment later, there were two preta ghosts (bìlì guǐ).
They were thirty feet tall.
They were black, emaciated, ugly, afflicted by hunger and thirst, and suffering intense pain.
Their bodies were scorched internally.
Each grasped a large club and repeatedly beat each other.
The crowd asked again.
They replied,
“Gentlemen, have you heard of the very rich Bóluómén east of Shèwèichéng?
The one riding the white horse is the gate-guarding slave.
The Yùnǚ in the smaller palace is the room-guarding maid.
The two people in the great palace are my son and my son’s wife.
The two ghosts are the Bóluómén husband and wife.
In their previous lives, they were foolish and did not believe in the True Dharma.
Now, encountering this calamity, what can be done?”
The Buddha traveled to the Bóluómén city.
The Bóluómén kings,
knowing that the Tathāgata's (Rúlái) divine virtue could move the hearts of the multitude,
said: “If one eats his food, who would still accept our words?”
Consequently, they jointly established a regulation:
“If anyone gives food to the Buddha or listens to the Buddha’s words, they shall be fined five hundred pieces of gold.”
At that time, the Buddha entered the city begging for food.
People all closed their doors, and he came out with an empty bowl.
There was a servant
who came out the door to discard foul, rotten slop contained in a broken earthenware vessel.
Seeing the Buddha with an empty bowl, his faith became pure.
He wished to make an offering but had no way to fulfill his wish.
He said, “If you require this inferior food now, you may take it.”
The Buddha knew his intention, immediately accepted the donation, and spoke:
“The woman who gave food will receive fortune and happiness in the heavens and among humans for fifteen kalpas, and will not fall into evil paths.
Later, she will obtain a male body, leave home to study the Way, and achieve Pratyekabuddha (Pìzhīfó) attainment.”
Next to them was a Bóluómén
who used a verse to accuse the Buddha of lying about food,
saying, “How could the reward for such foul food be so profound?”
The Buddha immediately put out his tongue, covering his face up to his hairline.
He said to the Bóluómén,
“Have you seen in the scriptures anyone with a tongue like this who speaks falsehoods?”
The Bóluómén said,
“One with such a tongue certainly does not speak falsehoods.
I just do not understand how a small donation can result in such a great reward.”
The Buddha said,
“Have you ever seen a Nyagrodha tree (Nígùtuó shù) whose shade covers five hundred merchant carts, yet still not be fully utilized?”
He replied, “I have seen it.”
He asked again,
“How large is the seed of this tree?”
He replied,
“About one-third the size of a mustard seed.”
He asked again,
“Who would believe this?”
He replied,
“It is visible to the eye.”
He asked again,
“I am also like this.
This elderly woman obtained a great reward.
This is due to the excellent quality of the Tathāgata’s field of merit (fú tián).”
At that time, the Bóluómén’s mind opened and he understood; he prostrated himself completely before the Buddha and repented.
The Buddha spoke the Dharma for him, and he attained the fruit of the first path.
He immediately let out a loud cry and announced to the crowd,
“The gate of sweet dew (Gānlù Mén) is open, why do you not come out?”
The Bóluómén begged to pay the fine money
and invited the Buddha for offerings.
The Bóluómén king and his officials and citizens also took refuge in the Buddha Dharma.
The men and women in the city all gained pure faith.
In the past, there was an elder named Xūdá.
He invited the Buddha and the Saṅgha and organized a large assembly.
On the road, he encountered a person offering a jar of fermented milk.
He saw a Bóluómén and asked him to carry it back.
Upon arriving and seeing the Buddha and the Saṅgha, the Bóluómén was delighted and stayed.
He listened to the sūtra and observed the fast until evening before returning home.
His wife was extremely suspicious of him.
She also had not eaten until evening and strongly pressured him to eat.
Because he failed to complete the fasting observance (zhāi fǎ), after his life ended,
his spirit was reborn as a great marsh tree spirit in Yùnduōluó Guó.
At that time, there were five hundred scholars
who wished to go to the Shen Chí (Divine Pool) of the three shrines to bathe and aspire for immortality.
Their provisions were exhausted and they had no water or drink.
They were utterly distressed and exhausted.
They looked toward that tree from afar, imagining it to be a spring of water.
They all arrived at the tree, but there was no spring water below it.
They were about to fall into great distress.
They jointly raised their voices, begging the tree spirit to save their lives.
The tree spirit immediately manifested its upper body.
It lifted the tip of its right hand.
Naturally, a hundred flavors of food appeared.
In its hands, it offered honey drinks and all kinds of provisions.
They all ate their fill.
The five hundred men then discussed among themselves, saying,
“We intended to go to the Shen Chí to bathe and aspire for immortality.
How could the lofty path of this immortal be surpassed?”
They asked the tree spirit again,
“What merit and sacred virtue did you cultivate to be like this?”
The tree spirit replied,
“I once saw the Buddha at the Shèwèi Jīngshè.
I upheld the Eight Precepts (bā guān zhāi).
But I was defeated by my wife and did not complete the fasting observance.
My spirit should have been born in heaven.”
The five hundred men immediately dedicated themselves to upholding the precepts of the fasting observance.
Later, they attained the path of Sūtuóhuán Dào.
In the past, there was a Bóluómén.
The husband and wife had no son.
They possessed countless wealth.
When approaching the end of their lives, they said to each other,
“We should each swallow money to use as provisions.”
It was the custom of that country
not to bury the dead but just to place them beneath a tree.
Each swallowed fifty pieces of gold and died.
When their bodies decomposed, the money came out.
A virtuous man (xián zhě) in the country was traveling and saw this.
He wept pitifully, grieving their stinginess and greed.
He took the money to perform meritorious deeds for them.
He sincerely prepared offerings and invited the Buddha and the Saṅgha.
He held the food before the Buddha and recited the names, making wishes.
At that time, the stingy husband and wife,
who were suffering as hungry ghosts, were immediately reborn in heaven.
To perform the meritorious deeds, he broadly invited the four kinds of followers.
The one who had been reborn in heaven immediately obtained the divine eye and knew that merits were being made for him.
He descended from heaven, transformed himself into a young man, and helped the donor (Tán yuè).
The Buddha said,
“This young man in the kitchen is the true Tán yuè.”
When he arrived, the Buddha spoke the Dharma, and the young man immediately attained the path.
The virtuous man also attained the path.
The assembled crowd was joyful, and they all attained rebirth in heaven.
When the Buddha was in the world, there was a Bóluómén.
He had two daughters, both of whom were beautiful and proper.
He deliberately hung up gold
and sought bids for ninety days from anyone who could criticize his daughters as ugly.
He would then give them the gold.
In the end, there was no one who answered the call.
He brought them to the place where the Buddha was.
The Buddha then criticized them, saying,
“These girls are all ugly; there is not a single beautiful thing about them.”
Ānán reported to the Buddha, saying,
“These girls are beautiful, but the Buddha says they are bad.
What is wrong with them?”
The Buddha said,
“For a person's eyes not to look upon sights is considered beautiful.
The eyes, ears, nose, and mouth are also the same.
For the body not to cling to fine smoothness is considered beautiful.
For the body and hands not to steal the wealth of others is considered a beautiful hand.
Not committing these deeds is truly beautiful.
If the eyes look upon sights, the ears listen to sounds, the nose smells fragrance,
the body delights in fine smoothness,
and the hands delight in stealing the wealth of others,
then such things are all not beautiful.”
In the past, there was the city of Duō Shòu Yì.
There was a Brāhmaṇa.
He was the Royal Grand Astrologer (Tàishǐ).
He was the foremost in the state.
He had a son.
On his head, he naturally had a fiery garland (huǒ mán).
Because of this, it was taken as his name, Huǒ Mán.
His appearance and features were upright and possessed thirty marks.
There was a potter's son.
Named Nán Tí Pó Luó.
He and Huǒ Mán were close friends from childhood and respected each other deeply.
The potter's son was diligent, brave, compassionate, benevolent, and filial.
Both his parents were blind, and he provided for them without lack.
Although he was a potter, his hands did not dig the earth.
He only took broken walls, collapsing riverbanks, and earth piled by rats, mixed it, and used it to make vessels.
If there were buyers,
they would place grains, wheat, hemp, or beans on the ground and take the vessels.
He never argued over the price.
Nor did he accept gold, silver, wealth, or silk.
He only accepted grains to sustain his parents, and nothing more.
The monastery where Jiā Shè Rú Lái resided,
was not far from Duō Shòu Yì.
There were twenty thousand great Bhikṣus with him.
All of them were Luó Hàn.
Hù Xǐ spoke to Huǒ Mán, saying:
"Let us go together to see Jiā Shè Rú Lái."
Huǒ Mán replied:
"Why should we go see this Daoist?
He is just a shaven-headed man.
What way (Dào) does he possess?
The Buddha's Way is hard to attain!"
He spoke thus up to three times.
Hù Xǐ spoke again to Huǒ Mán,
"(Saying,) 'Shall we go to the water together to bathe?'"
Huǒ Mán replied, "That can be done."
So they went together to the water to bathe.
Hù Xǐ raised his right hand, pointed into the distance, and said:
"Jiā Shè’s monastery is not far from here.
We could go see him briefly together."
Huǒ Mán replied:
"What is the use of seeing him?"
Hù Xǐ immediately grabbed Huǒ Mán’s clothes and pulled him.
Huǒ Mán stripped off his clothes and ran away.
Hù Xǐ then grabbed him by the head and pulled, saying:
"Come with me just once to see the Buddha."
According to the custom of the kingdom, touching someone's head was taboo, punishable by execution (beheading).
Huǒ Mán was shocked and terrified, thinking:
"Does this potter's son risk death just to grab my head?"
Hù Xǐ said:
"If I die,
I will not let you go even in death.
I must certainly make you see the Buddha."
Huǒ Mán thought:
"There must definitely be something good (about this),
which causes this man to risk death to hold onto me."
Huǒ Mán said:
"Release my head, and I will go with you."
He then tied up his hair and put on his clothes again.
They followed each other and went to Jiā Shè Fó.
Hù Xǐ reported to the Buddha, saying:
"This Huǒ Mán is my close friend from childhood.
However, he does not recognize or believe in the Three Jewels (Sān Zūn).
We pray the World-Honored One enlighten and transform him."
The youth Huǒ Mán beheld the excellent marks of the Buddha.
He thought:
"The excellent marks recorded in the scriptures are all present,
except for two things."
Then Jiā Shè Rú Lái,
extended his wide and long tongue and covered his face.
He covered his uṣṇīṣa (fleshy protuberance) and both ears, seven times.
He licked his head, retracted his tongue, and put it back in his mouth.
A brilliant light shone forth, illuminating the trichiliocosm (Great Thousand World).
It obscured the brightness of the sun and moon, reaching up to the Ā Jiā Nì Zhà Tiān.
The light returned, circled his body seven times, and entered through the crown of his head.
With his supernatural power (Shénzú lì), he manifested the retractable male organ (Yīnmǎ zàng).
He caused Huǒ Mán alone to see it.
Others did not perceive it.
The youth Huǒ Mán fully beheld the thirty-two marks of the Buddha.
He leaped with joy and could not restrain himself.
Jiā Shè Rú Lái,
preached the merits of abandoning the Bodhisattva path to the youth Huǒ Mán.
What is the merit of abandoning the Bodhisattva path?
The Dharma body (Fǎshēn) cannot be practiced, yet one practices it.
The mouth cannot speak, yet one speaks.
The mind cannot conceive, yet one conceives.
These are the three wicked practices of a Bodhisattva (Sān è xíng).
Thereupon, Huǒ Mán advanced, bowed at the Buddha's feet, and said:
"I now repent, and I pray the Buddha permit and accept it.
From this day forward, I dare not commit transgressions again."
He spoke thus up to three times.
Jiā Shè Rú Lái silently accepted it.
The youth Huǒ Mán and the youth Hù Xǐ,
both bowed at the Buddha's feet, took their leave, and returned.
Huǒ Mán said:
"You have experienced loss, not gain.
I do not like seeing your face.
I do not like hearing your name."
Hù Xǐ replied:
"Why is that?"
Huǒ Mán said:
"You heard the profound Dharma from the Buddha long ago.
How can you still remain in a lay household?"
Hù Xǐ replied:
"My parents are old and both are blind.
If I must provide for my two parents, how can I leave home?
If I were to leave home, my parents would then die.
It is for this reason that I cannot leave home."
Huǒ Mán said to Hù Xǐ:
"Since I heard the three causes of wicked practice of the Bodhisattva path from Jiā Shè Fó,
I no longer enjoy lay life.
I wish to return from here to the Buddha's residence and request to become a Bhikṣu."
Hù Xǐ responded:
"Excellent, Huǒ Mán.
Have you gained the power of contemplation?
Then you should return immediately.
The reason is that a Buddha world is difficult to encounter."
The youth Huǒ Mán immediately embraced Hù Xǐ,
circumambulated him three times, joined his hands, and apologized, saying:
"If I have committed any offense against you in body, speech, or mind,
I pray you pardon and forgive me.
You have pointed me toward the righteous, true Great Way (Dà Dào)."
Thereupon, Huǒ Mán spoke a verse of praise:
"You are my benevolent friend, my Dharma friend, without greed for anything;
You guided me onto the right path—this is the friend praised by the Buddha."
Having spoken this verse,
he circumambulated Hù Xǐ three times and returned to the monastery.
He reported to the Buddha, saying:
"May I enter the path and receive the full precepts (Jù Jiè)?"
The Buddha immediately ordained Huǒ Mán and bestowed the complete precepts upon him.
The Buddha spoke to Shè Lì Fú:
"The youth Huǒ Mán at that time was I myself.
Huǒ Mán’s father is the present King Zhēn Jìng (Śuddhodana).
Hù Xǐ, who frequently urged me to leave home,
is therefore a Good Spiritual Advisor (Shàn Zhīshì) on the path.
Previously, I spoke wicked words toward Hù Xǐ, saying:
'What Way (Dào) does Jiā Shè Fó, that bald-headed Śramaṇa, have?'
Therefore, for six years, I suffered by eating one sesame seed, one grain of rice, large beans, and small beans daily, like this.
In the past, there was a Brāhmaṇa.
He served external paths (Wàidào).
His wife served the Buddha.
She said to her husband:
"Allow me to be a maidservant to the Buddha.
I will hang banners and canopies, burn incense, and light lamps."
The husband did not permit it.
She then made one banner and hung it inside the house.
Morning and evening, she bowed toward it.
The husband killed oxen and sheep and summoned his teacher to perform a ceremony.
When the teacher arrived at the gate, he said:
"There is a Buddha banner/canopy in your house,
I dare not enter."
The husband immediately went in and questioned his wife.
He searched and found the banner.
The husband was angry and beat his wife.
The wife immediately jumped into the river.
Because her heart was sincere, the river spirit was moved, and the river water dried up.
A seven-jewel flower canopy naturally appeared above her.
The husband saw this auspicious sign and realized the Buddha should be revered.
He immediately abandoned the external paths (Wàidào) and served the Great Dharma.
In Bá Tí Chéng, there was a great Householder (Jū Shì).
His given name was Mín Tuó. He was extremely wealthy in treasures and possessed great influence.
He liberally distributed supplies to people according to whatever they desired.
In his granary, there was a hole as large as a chariot axle.
Grain and rice flowed out spontaneously.
His wife used eight dòu (pecks) of rice to make meals.
She fed the troops of the four divisions and those who came from the four directions.
The food was never exhausted.
His son gave a thousand ounces of gold to the troops of the four divisions and beggars from the four directions.
The amount was never exhausted, regardless of how much was desired.
His daughter-in-law used one packet of aromatic paste.
She satisfied the needs of the troops of the four divisions and those who came from the four directions to beg, according to their desire.
The aromatic paste was never exhausted.
His servant, using one plow, cultivated seven furrows daily.
The rice produced was extremely abundant.
His maidservant used eight dòu of grain.
She fed the horses of the four divisions of troops.
The horse feed was never exhausted.
The family members argued among themselves, each one saying:
"The power of fortune is mine."
Mín Tuó went to the Buddha and bowed down, touching his head and face to the ground.
[He/They] said.
Whose power [is this]?
The Buddha said.
You all share it.
Formerly, in Wángshě Chéng, there was a weaver.
The weaver had a wife, and also a son, and the son also had a wife.
[They] had one male servant and one female servant.
Once, they were eating together.
A Pratyekabuddha came seeking alms food.
Each one wished to give away their due share.
The Pratyekabuddha said.
Your benevolent hearts have each already given [the offering].
Each person may slightly reduce [their offering].
For you, it is not too little.
For me, it is sufficient.
They immediately complied together.
After the Pratyekabuddha ate, he manifested various miraculous transformations in the empty sky.
Only then did he depart.
The weaver's family, upon abandoning their lifespan (dying).
Were born in the Heaven of the Four Great Heavenly Kings, up to the Heaven of Controlling Others' Enjoyments (Tāhuà Zìzài Tiān).
After cycling [through these heavens] seven times, the remaining merit caused them to be born here.
Méntuó heard this.
He immediately invited the Buddha and the Saṅgha and practiced unlimited giving.
If anything is needed, regardless of time or amount, take it from me.
The Bhikṣus did not dare to accept.
They reported to the Buddha.
The Buddha said.
I permit [you] to accept according to your need.
Afterwards, when the Bhikṣus traveled and requested provisions.
[Méntuó] dispatched messengers carrying gold and silver to follow their route.
When much was left over, they brought it back to the Elder.
The Elder said.
I have already given it away completely; you should not bring it back.
Yùjiā, being drunk, was surrounded by court ladies.
[He was] in the great forest of Píshèlǐ (Vaiśālī).
He saw the World-Honored One seated among the trees from afar.
[The Buddha was] handsome and wondrously excellent, his senses and mind resting in concentration.
His radiance was like a heap of gold.
Upon seeing [this], his intoxication cleared.
He went to where the World-Honored One was and sat down respectfully on one side.
The Buddha explained the Four Noble Truths for him.
He attained the Dharma of Fearlessness.
He bowed his head to the Buddha's feet.
I take refuge in the Three Jewels.
[I will] become a Upāsaka (lay follower) and uphold the Five Precepts.
He returned to his residence and addressed his family, saying.
You should now know.
I have received the precepts from the World-Honored One.
If you wish [to remain] happy, practice giving and accumulate merit.
If you are not happy [with this path], each return to your own relatives.
I will release you.
At that time, the principal wife said.
[If] you have received the precepts from the World-Honored One for the remainder of your life.
There is a certain person; you should give me to him to be his wife.
At that time, the householder immediately called that man.
He held the principal wife's right hand with his left hand.
Holding a golden water vessel, he spoke to that man, saying.
I give this principal wife to you to be your wife.
That man was terrified, and his hair stood on end.
He said to Yùjiā.
Householder, do you not wish to kill me?
[Yùjiā] answered, saying, No.
I have undertaken the pure practice (Brahmacarya) for the remainder of my life, following the Buddha.
Therefore, I give my principal wife to you.
I will never change or regret this.
Formerly, there was a great clan.
They were always fond of charity and giving.
Later, a son was born.
He had no hands or feet.
His body resembled a fish.
His name was Yúshēn (Fish-Body).
After his parents died, he inherited and maintained the family business.
He lay down in his room and did not see visitors.
At that time, there was a strong man (Lìshì).
He relied on the king's kitchen for food.
He constantly suffered from hunger and lack.
He single-handedly pulled sixteen carts of firewood.
He sold [the wood] to sustain himself.
Yet, it was still often insufficient.
He went to this great clan seeking what he lacked.
Yúshēn requested to meet him.
[Yúshēn] showed him his physical form.
The strong man thought to himself.
My strength is merely such.
I am inferior to the man without hands and feet.
He went to the Buddha's place and asked about his doubts.
The Buddha said.
Formerly, during the time of Jiāshè Fó (Kāśyapa Buddha).
Yúshēn and this king were offering food to the Buddha.
You, at that time, were poor and helped them with their chores.
Yúshēn prepared the provisions and went with the king.
But [the king] told Yúshēn, saying.
Today, I have duties, and we cannot go together.
If I go, it will be no different than cutting off my hands and feet.
The one who went then is the king now.
The one who said he wouldn't go is Yúshēn now.
The one who assisted at that time is you now.
The strong man's mind was awakened.
He immediately became a Śramaṇa (monk).
He attained the path of Arhatship (Āluóhàn Dào).
Formerly, within the city of Shíshì Chéng (Stone Chamber City), there were three householders.
The first name was Shélì.
The second name was Pūtuómǎn.
The third name was Pópōnuó.
These three people were blood brothers.
[They possessed] many treasures, elephants, horses, and the seven precious jewels.
There was a Brāhmaṇa.
He observed the fast of Yīluóbō Dragon.
Hoping for wealth and honor.
The dragon manifested its body and spoke to the Brāhmaṇa.
Why do you labor and suffer now?
Cutting off grains and eliminating flavors while observing the fast here.
What are you seeking?
The Brāhmaṇa said.
I hope for great wealth.
The dragon said.
I have two names.
The first name is Yīluóbō.
The second name is Wealth-Without-Satiation (Cái Wúyàn).
Since my name is Without-Satiation.
Do you still seek from me?
The Brāhmaṇa said.
If you do not grant it, I will immediately die.
The dragon produced refined purple gold to repay him.
Near the city gate, there was a wealthy and powerful elder.
He originated from Tiānzhú (India).
You should give him the gold and seek riches from him.
The elder saw it and informed [the Brāhmaṇa], saying.
Conceal it; do not let anyone see it.
He informed his five close relatives.
While eating, drinking, and enjoying, they concealed the gold inside a vault.
All the miscellaneous items inside the vault went back into the earth.
They returned to that dragon's treasury.
The property of the seven families surrounding [the Brāhmaṇa] was like this.
The three householders heard of this.
They spoke among themselves, saying.
The wealth obtained by our three families through the Dharma is certainly not in vain.
[We will not be] wrongly robbed like the five families.
The people of the kingdom heard this and called it an arrogant boast.
They gathered at the three householders' residences.
They asked the householders, saying.
You claim that the wealth obtained through the Dharma is not wrongly lost.
What do you use as proof?
Then the three householders each produced ten catties (jin) of gold.
They divided it into six portions.
They led the populace and the owners of the lost property of the seven families.
They went to the Dragon Spring and tossed the gold into the water.
The water all surged and boiled, like soup in a cauldron.
The Dragon King was startled and frightened.
He immediately dispatched a dragon maiden to take the gold out and return it.
[The Dragon King] expressed gratitude and sent them back.
What is obtained through the Dharma is achieved through principle.
It will ultimately not be encroached upon by [forces that harmed] the five families.
Those who deceitfully hoard wealth obtained illegitimately will be like those seven families.
In the past, there was a kingdom.
Named Huānlè Wúyōu.
The King's title was Guǎng Cí'āi.
In the kingdom, there was a householder.
Named Móhētán.
His wife was named Zhāntuó.
They had a son.
His appearance was upright and handsome, rarely matched in the world.
Upon falling to the ground (at birth), he spoke.
He issued a solemn vow, saying:
"I shall practice giving (Dāna) throughout the world, saving and helping the people. To those who are lonely, solitary, or poor,
I shall provide and protect them, allowing them to attain peace and safety."
His parents thus named him Dàyì.
Seeing his extraordinary appearance, unlike that of others,
they feared he might be a celestial being (Tiānlóng), ghost, or spirit (guǐshén).
They intended to seek divination.
Dàyì knew this.
He then told them,
"I am certainly a human, not a Tiānlóng, ghost, or spirit.
I merely think of the distressed and afflicted people of the world,
and wish to protect and care for them, that is all."
Having spoken this intention,
he did not speak again.
When he reached the age of seventeen, he finally told his parents,
"I wish to practice giving to suffering people, allowing them to attain peace and safety."
His parents thought,
"When our son was first born, he already had this vow."
They then told their son,
"Our wealth is countless; you may give as you please, without constraint."
Dàyì replied,
"Although the wealth of my parents is abundant, it is still insufficient for my needs.
I must only enter the sea to gather treasures to provide and give to the people of the world, that is all."
He repeated these words several times.
His parents finally consented.
Dàyì entered the sea route, passing through another kingdom.
In that kingdom, there was a Brāhmaṇa (Bóluómén).
His wealth was immeasurable.
Seeing Dàyì's radiant and handsome appearance,
he was greatly pleased and delighted, and told him,
"I hold you in high respect.
I now have a young daughter whom I wish to offer you.
I hope you will remain here."
Dàyì replied,
"I left home to enter the sea to gather the Seven Treasures (Qībǎo).
I do not yet dare to accept your offer.
Please wait until I return."
Thereupon, he proceeded to gather the treasures.
He immediately sent a messenger carrying the treasures back to his home kingdom.
He then traveled further to the seaside, seeking extraordinary objects.
Suddenly, he saw a great tree.
It was eighty Yóuyán (Yojanas) tall and wide.
Dàyì then climbed the tree and saw, in the distance, a Silver City.
The palaces, towers, halls, and residences were all made of white silver.
Celestial maidens attended at the sides, and music played naturally.
There was a venomous snake coiling around the city three times.
Seeing Dàyì, the snake immediately raised its head. Dàyì thought to himself,
"People who are harmed by poison are all afflicted due to a lack of good intent."
He then sat down and contemplated.
After a moment, the snake immediately lowered its head and lay asleep.
Dàyì wished to enter the city.
The gatekeepers immediately went in and informed the king, saying,
"A worthy man outside wishes to see Your Majesty."
The king personally came out to welcome him.
Happily, he said,
"We only wish, Benevolent One, that you would stay here.
For a period of three months, you may receive the offering."
Dàyì replied, "I am traveling to gather treasures, and it is not fitting for me to stay long."
The king replied,
"I will not attend to state affairs.
I only wish that you would stay."
Dàyì then stayed.
The king immediately provided offerings: clothing, food, drink, music,
and sleeping arrangements.
After ninety days had passed,
Dàyì bid farewell to the king, wishing to depart.
The king then took precious and rare Qībǎo, intending to give them to him as a gift.
Dàyì said,
"I do not have much need for these Qībǎo.
I hear that Your Majesty possesses a Luminous Moon Pearl (Míngyuè Zhū).
I intend to ask for it."
The king said,
"I do not begrudge this pearl,
but I fear that the journey is harsh and difficult for you to carry it yourself."
Dàyì said,
"Indeed, when good fortune is about to follow a person, they do not fear harsh difficulties."
The king said,
"This pearl carries along with it twenty *lǐ* of treasures, following your wishes.
I vow to become your disciple, receiving the opportunity to provide offerings
that surpass what I offer today."
Dàyì then accepted the pearl and departed.
Thereupon, Dàyì traveled onward and saw a Golden City.
The palaces, towers, halls, and residences were all of gold.
Trees of the Qībǎo, and spontaneous music.
The celestial maidens attending were double the number of the previous place.
There was also a venomous snake coiling around the city six times.
When the snake saw Dàyì, it raised its head and looked at him.
Dàyì again sat down and fixed his mind (in contemplation).
The snake again lowered its head and lay down.
Dàyì wished to enter the city.
The gatekeepers immediately went in to inform the king.
The king then came out to meet him and invited him forward.
He asked him to stay.
"For a period of three months, you may receive the offering."
Dàyì then stayed.
The king treated him as before.
After sixty days passed, he bid farewell, wishing to leave.
He told the king,
"I hear Your Majesty possesses a Míngyuè Zhū.
I wish that you would bestow it upon me."
The king replied as before.
"Forty *lǐ* worth of treasures will follow it."
He then offered it up (to Dàyì).
"When you attain the Way later, Benevolent One,
I vow to become your disciple.
My spiritual powers (shénzú) shall be unmatched,
and I shall have the opportunity to provide offerings exceeding those of today."
Dàyì accepted the pearl and departed.
Dàyì traveled onward again.
He saw another Crystal City (Shuǐjīng Chéng).
The palaces, towers, halls, and residences were all just like before.
There was also a venomous snake.
It coiled around the city nine times, its head lowered and sleeping.
The king came out to welcome him.
He requested Dàyì stay for three months.
Dàyì immediately stayed.
The king again provided offerings wholeheartedly,
setting out food, drink, clothing, and music.
After forty days had passed, he bid farewell to depart.
He told the king,
"I hear Your Majesty possesses a Míngyuè Zhū.
I wish that you would bestow it upon me."
The king then replied,
"This pearl carries sixty *lǐ* of treasures.
They will follow it naturally."
He then offered it up.
"If you attain the Way later, Benevolent One,
I vow to become your disciple.
My wisdom shall be unmatched.
I shall again provide offerings exceeding those of today."
Dàyì then accepted the pearl and departed.
Traveling forward, he saw another Lapis Lazuli City (Liúlí Chéng).
He also saw a venomous snake.
It coiled around the city twelve times, its head lowered and sleeping.
The king welcomed and invited him, begging him to stay for three months.
Dàyì immediately stayed.
The king personally provided offerings of food, drink, clothing, and music to entertain him.
After twenty days had passed, he bid farewell to depart.
He told the king,
"I hear Your Majesty possesses a Míngyuè Zhū.
Might you bestow it upon me?"
The king said,
"This pearl carries eighty *lǐ* of treasures following it."
He then offered it up.
"When you attain the Way later, Benevolent One,
I vow that I shall be your disciple,
providing pure-hearted offerings exceeding those of today,
and thus gaining lasting wisdom."
Dàyì accepted the pearl and departed.
He thought,
"I originally came to seek treasure.
Now that my wish is fulfilled, I should return from here."
He then followed his former route, intending to return to his home kingdom.
While passing through the great sea,
the divine kings (shénwáng) then consulted together, saying,
"Although our sea has many rare treasures and famous jewels,
none are like these pearls."
They immediately commanded a Sea Spirit (Hǎishén) to intercept him and seize the pearls.
The spirit then transformed into a man and met with Dàyì.
He asked,
"I hear you have obtained extraordinary objects.
Would it be possible to borrow them for viewing?"
Dàyì stretched out his hand and showed him the four pearls.
The Hǎishén then shook his hand, causing the pearls to fall into the water.
Dàyì thought to himself,
"The kings told me
that these pearls are difficult to keep safe. Fortunately, I had already obtained them.
Now, to have them seized by this fellow is not right."
He immediately said to the Hǎishén,
"I exerted myself, traveled through dangerous obstacles, and came to obtain these pearls.
Yet you unjustly seized them from me.
If you do not return them to me now,
I shall scoop out all the seawater!" The Hǎishén knew his intention and asked,
"Your resolve is wonderfully high.
The sea is three million, three hundred thirty-six thousand Yóuyán deep,
and its vastness has no boundaries.
How will you exhaust it?
It is like the sun, which ultimately does not fall to the earth.
It is like the great wind, which cannot be grasped and bound.
The sun might still be made to fall to the earth,
and the wind might still be grasped and bound,
but the water of the great sea cannot be scooped out and exhausted."
Dàyì smiled and replied,
"I reflect that,
in countless lives past, receiving bodies, being born and dying, ruined and destroyed,
my accumulated bones have exceeded Mount Xūmí (Sumeru).
My blood has flowed into the Five Rivers (Wǔ Hé).
The Four Seas are insufficient to compare to it.
I still wish to sever the root of birth and death (Samsara).
But how could this small sea be insufficient to scoop out?
In the past, when I made offerings to various Buddhas, I swore this vow:
May my resolve and conduct be courageous in the Path, ensuring that wherever I turn, there is no difficulty.
I shall move Mǐshān and drain the great ocean water, but I will never retreat.
With determination, he then focused his mind entirely and used a vessel to bail the seawater.
Due to the sincerity of his utmost devotion,
the Four Heavenly Kings came to assist Dàyì.
He had bailed two-thirds of the water.
Thereupon, the various Spirit Kings in the sea,
all greatly trembled with fear and discussed, saying:
"If we do not return his pearl now, the consequence will not be small."
"When the water is exhausted, the mud will appear and destroy our palaces."
The Sea Spirits then brought forth numerous treasures and offered them to Dàyì.
Dàyì did not take them.
He announced, saying:
"I have no use for this kind of thing."
"I only want to get my pearl."
"Unless you return my pearl, I will never stop bothering you."
The Sea Spirits knew his resolve was strong, so they brought out the pearl and returned it to him.
Having obtained the pearl, Dàyì went and married the Brāhmaṇa woman.
He returned to his native country and gave great alms according to his wishes.
From then on, within his domain, there were no longer any who suffered from hunger, cold, poverty, or lack.
Scholars and commoners from the four directions all abandoned their former superiors.
Carrying their children on their backs, they returned to his benevolence.
He gave alms like this for years, and his kindness extended to all.
Those that crawled, flew, walked, or squirmed—none failed to receive succor.
Afterwards, when his life ended, he ascended to become Dìshì.
Sometimes he descended to become a Flying Emperor.
Having accumulated merits and virtues, he naturally achieved Buddhahood.
His unique supremacy in the Three Realms was entirely due to his past actions.
It was not spontaneous.
The Buddha addressed the Bhikṣus:
"Dàyì was myself."
"The layman Móhētán at that time is now Yuètóután."
"His mother, Zhāntuó, at that time is now the consort Móyē."
"The king of the Land of Joy and Worrylessness at that time is Móhējiāyè."
"The Brāhmaṇa woman at that time is Qiúyí."
"The woman’s father at that time is Mílè."
"The king in the Silver City at that time is Ānán."
"The king in the Golden City at that time is Mùjiànlián."
"The king in the Crystal City at that time is Shèlìfú."
"The king in the Lapis Lazuli City at that time is Xūtuó."
"The Fourth Heavenly King who helped Dàyì bail the seawater at that time is Yōutuó."
"The one who stole his pearl at that time is Tiáodá."
"The guards of the four city gates at that time are Xūbá Pántè Sūhépī Jūliú."
"The poisonous snakes surrounding the four cities at that time are Shìgòng Chàsuāntuólì, the Four Ministers."
Ānán addressed the Buddha:
"By what merit did he obtain the four bright moon pearls, accompanied by numerous treasures?"
The Buddha replied:
"Long ago, during the time of Wéiwèi Buddha,
Dàyì once used four treasures to erect a stūpa for the Buddha."
"He made offerings to the Three Jewels and observed the precepts (fasting) for seven days."
"At that time, there were five hundred people."
"They simultaneously built monasteries together."
"Some hung silks and lit lamps."
"Some burned incense and scattered flowers."
"Some made offerings to the Bhikṣu Saṅgha."
"Some chanted sūtras and taught the Way."
"All of them have now come together here."
"In the past, there was a merchant."
"Named Bōlì."
"He went to sea with five hundred men to seek treasure."
"At that time, a Sea Spirit came out holding a handful of water."
"He asked Bōlì, saying:"
"Is the ocean water more, or is the handful of water more?"
Bōlì answered, saying:
"The handful of water is more."
"Why is this so?"
"Although the ocean water is vast, it is of no use at the moment."
"It cannot save those who are hungry and thirsty."
"Although the handful of water is small, if it is encountered by someone thirsty, offering it saves their life."
"The recipient gains merits throughout successive lifetimes that cannot be measured."
The Sea Spirit rejoiced and praised him, saying, "Excellent!"
Immediately, he removed the eight kinds of scented necklaces from his body, adorned with seven treasures.
He gave them to Bōlì.
The Sea Spirit escorted him.
Bōlì returned safely to Shèwèiguó.
He presented this scented necklace to King Bōsīní.
He fully explained how he obtained it and requested the King graciously accept it.
The King received the scented necklace and considered it a wonderful rarity.
He immediately summoned his consorts to line up and stand before him.
He intended to give the scented necklace to the one who was the best.
Sixty thousand consorts adorned themselves entirely and came forth.
The King asked:
"Why has Lady Mòlì not come out?"
A servant replied, saying:
"Today is the fifteenth day. She is observing the Buddha’s precepts (fasting) and is dressed plainly, not adorned."
"That is why she has not come out."
The King became angry and sent a person to call her, saying:
"Even if you are observing the precepts, you must not disobey the King’s command!"
This happened three times.
Lady Mòlì, dressed plainly, came out.
Among the assembled people, she shone brightly like the sun and moon.
She was twice as beautiful as usual.
The King was awestruck and added respect, asking:
"What virtue or Way do you possess that makes you shine so brilliantly and differently?"
The Lady replied to the King:
"I reflect that my fortune is small."
"I have assumed this female form, and my emotional state is defiled."
"My transgressions accumulate daily, yet human life is fleetingly short."
"I fear falling into the Three Evil Paths."
"Therefore, month after month, I observe the precepts (fasting) of the Buddha Dharma."
"I renounce attachment and follow the Way, so that in life after life I may receive blessings."
The King heard this and was delighted.
He immediately offered the scented necklace to her.
Lady Mòlì replied, saying:
"I am now observing the precepts, and I ought not to wear this."
"It can be given to someone else."
The King said:
"My original intention was to give it to the most superior person."
"You are now the most superior."
"Moreover, you observe the Dharma fast, and your aspiration for the Way is exceptionally lofty."
"Therefore, I give it to you."
"If you do not accept it, where shall I place it?"
The Lady replied, saying:
"Great King, do not worry."
"I wish the King would condescend to go with me to the place of the Buddha."
"We can present this scented necklace to the World-Honored One."
"And gather his sacred teachings."
"This will accumulate merit for countless eons."
The King immediately agreed.
He immediately ordered his carriage prepared and went to the Buddha's place.
He prostrated himself on the ground, then withdrew and took the seat reserved for the King.
He addressed the Buddha, saying:
"This scented necklace from the Sea Spirit was presented by Bōlì."
"None of the sixty thousand consorts failed to covet it."
"Lady Mòlì, when offered it, did not take it."
"She observes the Buddha Dharma fast and her heart is without greed or desire."
"I respectfully present it to the Buddha above."
"I pray that you graciously accept it."
"It is difficult for the disciples of the World-Honored One to maintain such resolve."
"Such straightforward faith is like this."
"Are there not blessings in this?"
"We only wish, World-Honored One, that you would accept the scented necklace for her."
The Buddha spoke a gāthā, saying:
"Though many form treasures and flowers, tied with pendants and silks, and widely accumulate fragrant virtues,
that which arises becomes better. Rare grasses and fragrant flowers do not diffuse against the wind."
"When approaching the Way and hearing the teaching, the person of virtue spreads fragrance everywhere. Though these things are said to be true,
they are not as good as the Fragrance of Precepts."
In former times, in Yánfú,
there was a country named Bōluónài.
At that time, there was a Sàbáo,
named Móhē Yèyí.
His wife became pregnant.
Naturally kind and good, her disposition was gentle and harmonious.
When the month was complete, she bore a son,
whose body was proper and upright.
The parents loved and cherished him.
They prepared fine foods,
invited relatives,
and all the physiognomists to celebrate together.
They held the child up to show the gathering and named him.
The physiognomists asked,
"What auspicious sign was there when this child was conceived?"
The father replied,
"During conception, the mother was naturally harmonious and good."
The physiognomists named him Shànqiú.
He grew up, nursed and nurtured, delighting in accumulating virtues and showing compassion to sentient beings.
Subsequently, she became pregnant again.
When the term was complete, she bore a son,
whose appearance was ugly.
The physiognomists asked,
"What corresponding manifestation was there when this child was conceived?"
She answered,
"While carrying the child, the mother was naturally wicked and malicious."
The physiognomists named him Èqiú.
He grew up, nursed and nurtured, delighting in doing evil deeds.
He constantly developed greed and harbored jealousy.
When they were both grown up,
they traveled together into the sea to seek and procure treasures.
Each had five hundred attendants.
The road was extremely long, and halfway they ran out of provisions.
After seven days, they were not far from death.
At that time, Shànqiú and all the merchants
sincerely prayed together to all the deities, wishing to be rescued from the danger of starvation.
In the empty marsh, they saw a tree from afar,
whose branches and foliage were luxuriant.
They immediately hurried toward it.
There was a spring of water.
Shànqiú and the multitude all jointly pleaded for mercy.
The tree spirit manifested itself and spoke to them:
"If you cut away one branch, what you require will appear."
Everyone was delighted.
They then cut one branch, and sweet beverages flowed out.
They cut the second branch, and various kinds of food came forth, complete with a hundred flavors.
They all received and accepted it, and each gained satisfaction.
They cut the third branch, and various wonderful clothes came forth, fully provided.
They cut the fourth branch, and various treasures were all fully provided.
Their pack animals were fully loaded, and everything they required was prepared.
Èqiú arrived later.
The crowd, as before, gained complete sufficiency.
He then thought to himself,
"Now, if the branches of this tree can produce these various good things,
how much more so its root?
I shall now cut it down,
and certainly obtain exceedingly wondrous and excellent goods."
He ordered men to fell it.
Shànqiú spoke to Èqiú, saying,
"We were suffering from hunger and lack, and thanks to the kindness of this tree, we were able to save our remaining lives.
Why do you want to cut it down?"
Èqiú immediately dug up its root.
Shànqiú, feeling deep gratitude, could not bear to witness it.
He led his followers home.
When the felling of the tree was complete,
five hundred Luóchàs seized this Èqiú and the multitude of merchants and entirely devoured them.
Their wealth and goods were lost.
The Buddha told Ānán:
"Shànqiú is now my present self.
The father is now King Jìngfàn.
The mother is now Móyé.
Èqiú is Dípó Dáduō.
In the past, I often met with him and constantly taught him the good Dharma,
but he did not use it.
On the contrary, he took me as his enemy."
In the land of Yánfúlì, there were many traveling merchants.
They gathered together and sailed into the sea to collect treasures.
Just then, they encountered fierce, swirling winds which wrecked their large ship.
Moreover, there were several other people.
They traveled on the broken, damaged ship, floating along with the wind until they were cast into the Ràchà (Rākṣasa) realm.
The Ràchà women, whose appearances were extremely beautiful, came forward to welcome the merchants, saying:
"There are many treasures here.
The brilliant pearls are priceless; take as many as you wish.
We have no husbands, and you have no wives or concubines.
You may stay here and we can enjoy pleasure together.
Later, when the favorable winds come, good companions will return home.
Gentlemen, you must know:
If you see on the left
side people who are on the path,
be careful not to follow them."
At that time, among the merchants, there was one wise man who said:
"What these women say cannot be followed."
He immediately proceeded along the left path for several *lǐ*.
Along the way, he heard millions of people inside a city crying out in lamentation and calling names.
They were saying, "Why did we abandon Yánfútí only to end our lives here?"
The merchant went forward to the base of the city and observed all around.
He saw that the city was cast from iron, the walls were also iron, and there were no gates or places for entry or exit.
Not far from the city, there was a Shīlíshī tree.
He immediately went and climbed the tree, seeing the millions of people inside the city.
He asked the people inside the city from afar, saying:
"Why are you
calling out the names of your fathers, mothers, and brothers?"
The people inside the city replied, saying:
"We entered the sea to gather treasures but were drifted by the wind.
Furthermore, we were deceived by the Ràchà women and imprisoned in this iron city.
Previously, five hundred men were gradually taken and killed.
Now there are two hundred and fifty people remaining.
Sir, do not call these women human.
They are all Ràchà ghosts!
That man descended the tree and told his companions.
'They advised me to return home and diligently seek a plan.
What do you gentlemen intend to do today?'
The group replied, saying:
'Why did you not ask again last night?
Did those people have any temporary or expedient plan,
so that all of us, including myself, might return home safely?'
The wise man immediately replied, saying:
'Tonight I will get up and go ask them again.'
Waiting until the women were asleep, he secretly got up and climbed the tree.
He asked the people inside the city if they had any plan
so that all you gentlemen and I,
might be able to return to Yánfú Dì?"
The people inside the city answered.
"When the thought arose in us that we wished to return,
this iron city immediately transformed into multiple indestructible layers.
Those who die here are taken in sequence, and there is no way for us to escape.
Only you, being an outsider, have a slight opportunity for an expedient measure.
You might be saved and return to your native land.
On the morning of the fifteenth day, there is a Horse King
who comes from Yùdān Yuè to this realm.
He resides on the peak of a high mountain.
The King himself calls out,
'Who wishes to return home to the land of Yánfúlì?'
If you gentlemen hear the horse's voice,
all go and pay reverence, seeking to return to your homeland."
That man told his companions, detailing the situation.
The group replied, saying:
"Can we leave now?"
He answered, saying:
"We must wait until the fifteenth day, when the Horse King
arrives; then we can leave."
Before many days had passed, the Horse King arrived.
The merchants, having heard this, went to the place of the Horse King.
They stated:
"We all wish to seek return to our homeland.
We pray that you will take and receive us."
The Horse King announced, saying:
"You gentlemen, listen with intelligent minds to what I say.
Those who wish to return to their native land and home,
if their minds are truly focused, they will be able to return home.
If their minds are not truly focused, they cannot return.
These women will be holding their sons and daughters,
following you gentlemen, weeping and crying out.
If any of you raise a mind of attachment and longing,
even if they are already on my back, they still cannot leave.
If you can abandon affection and love,
maintain an upright mind, and have no attachments,
hold onto a single hair of mine with a sincere heart, and you will be able to return home."
At that time, the women each spoke to their husbands, saying:
"You can certainly abandon my lowly body.
Why must you cast away your children?
They first instructed the children to go and embrace their fathers' necks,
weeping and calling out:
'Where do you wish to go by abandoning us?'"
Those whose minds were attached and longed for them were unable to return.
Only Dàzhì Shīzǐ, one man of great wisdom,
returned safely.
At that time, the Ràchà women,
holding their sons and daughters, pursued Shīzǐ.
They told the villages:
"This man Shīzǐ is my husband.
We bore these children together.
He abandoned me and fled, and we do not know where he went."
When people heard this, they asked Shīzǐ, saying:
"Looking at your wife,
her character and appearance are among the most outstanding and marvelous of humans.
Your children are pitiable; why did you abandon them?"
Shīzǐ replied, saying:
"This is also not a human; she is a Ràchà ghost.
In the sea islands, she killed and devoured countless merchants.
Several hundred of my companions are imprisoned in the iron city.
Only I alone was fortunate enough to be saved and escape.
Now this female ghost is pursuing me again,
planning to harm me. I fear I may not escape alive."
He continued traveling onward.
He returned to his native country.
The ghost still followed him, arriving at his kingdom.
The ghost went and reported to the King (Wáng):
"Shīzǐ and I were married as husband and wife.
We bore these children.
We hoped to gain strength later, but unexpectedly, today he has abandoned us forever."
The King summoned Shīzǐ and asked him for the truth of the situation.
Shīzǐ reported the entire situation detailed above to the King.
The King told Shīzǐ:
"Even if you do not want her, you can take her and give her to me."
Shīzǐ replied, saying:
"This is truly not a human; she is a Ràchà ghost.
If great disaster follows, do not blame me later."
He further spoke to the surrounding officials:
"If this ghost arrives here, there will certainly be harm.
The King now does not believe me and wishes to take her into the inner palace.
If this continues, before long, the King and the inner palace will all be destroyed."
The King became angry again and said to Shīzǐ:
"Her feminine beauty is like a celestial maiden (yùnǚ).
Why do you repeatedly call her a Ràchà ghost?
Quickly leave and stay outside; I will observe her myself."
The King took the female ghost into the palace for one night.
The next morning, at mealtime, the palace gate did not open.
The officials discussed it together.
"The King has newly taken a wife and is desirous of pleasure, so the gate is not open."
Shīzǐ said:
"This discussion is incorrect.
The King, his Queen, and all the palace women
must have been completely devoured by the Ràchà, which is why the gate is not open."
They immediately erected a tall ladder and climbed over the wall to enter the interior.
They saw dead human skeletons filling several rooms.
The officials rebuked Shīzǐ, saying:
"It is exactly because of you that you brought this Ràchà ghost,
killing the King, losing the country, and destroying the palace.
What do you intend to do now?"
Shīzǐ replied, saying:
"I had a previous agreement with the King: do not blame me later.
Why do you gentlemen now criticize and blame me again?"
The officials and the common people came forward and stated to Shīzǐ:
"The King is now dead, and there are no successors.
We humbly request that Shīzǐ ascend the throne and govern the people."
Shīzǐ announced, saying:
"If you wish to elevate me as King,
you must follow my teachings." The people, regardless of rank, unanimously praised this as good.
The King (Shīzǐ) told his officials:
"We must gather soldiers and enter the sea to attack.
Kill all the Ràchà men and women; leave none behind.
Afterwards, break open the iron city and release the people inside."
The common law of the land was:
"If there is one person who does not serve the Buddha (Fó), they shall be sent west of the mountain and handed over to the ghosts to be devoured."
Since then, the Dharma (Fófǎ) flourished, and countless people attained the Way (Dào).
Therefore, it is said:
Those who believe in Fó, like these beings who returned safely, all did so because of the Horse King (Mǎ Wáng).
Moreover, the constant ritual in that country was:
When the King had sons,
whether ten, one hundred, or even countless,
all would leave home to practice the Way (zuò dào) and recite and study the Buddhist scriptures (Fójīng).
They fully mastered the Three Baskets (Sānzàng).
They would then return and retire from the Way (bà dào).
They would then ascend the throne.
Generally, those who had not mastered the scriptures and had not been nominated were not allowed to ascend the throne.
Formerly, there were five hundred merchants.
One, named Mílián,
was the most respected elder.
The five hundred men shared a boat and entered the sea.
Their boat was struck and broken by a *Mójiéyú* (Makara fish).
All five hundred died.
Mílián survived by clinging to a plank.
He was in *Bímódì*.
To avoid the fish, he walked east and west.
He saw a small path.
Entering it, he saw a Silver City.
The trees reached the sky.
Interspersed were bathing pools.
The city was square and regular, surrounded by flowing water channels.
Four women came out from the city.
They were as beautiful as jade.
The women together welcomed Mílián and said,
"You must be extremely exhausted.
We greatly congratulate your arrival.
We have long desired to meet you.
We shall serve the Benevolent One.
This Silver City now belongs to the Benevolent One.
Inside the city, happiness is abundant; the trees reach the sky.
There are channels of water, bathing pools, places for recreation, and residences.
In the city, there is a hall of seven treasures,
named *Luómàn*.
It is built of gold, silver, crystal, lapis lazuli, coral, amber, and agate.
We four shall supply and serve you.
We shall sleep late, rise early, and diligently follow your instructions.
You may reside here.
There is no need to go to other places."
Mílián immediately entered the city with the four women.
He ascended the hall of seven treasures and indulged his desires every day.
He remained in this city for more than a thousand years.
Later, Mílián thought to himself,
"These four women do not want me to travel elsewhere.
What is their intention?"
Mílián waited until the four women were sleeping.
He secretly arose, descended the hall, and left the city, traveling onward.
He saw in the distance a Gold City.
The trees and bathing pools were exactly like the previous city.
There were eight women.
Their beauty and their welcoming words were all the same as before.
Mílián indulged his desires and enjoyed pleasure with the eight women for several thousand years.
Later, Mílián pondered,
"I suspect these eight women
also do not want me to go to other places.
What is their intention?"
Mílián waited until the eight women were asleep during the day.
He secretly arose and traveled onward.
He saw in the distance a Crystal City.
The trees, bathing pools, and all matters were as before.
Sixteen women came out of the city to greet him, speaking the same welcome as before.
Mílián immediately indulged his desires and enjoyed pleasure
with the sixteen women for several thousand years.
Mílián departed again and saw a Lapis Lazuli City.
The circumstances were also as before.
Thirty-two women came out of the city to greet him.
Mílián indulged his desires and enjoyed pleasure with the women for several thousand years.
Afterward, he left the city and traveled onward.
He saw in the distance an Iron City.
Inside, there was no one to welcome him.
Mílián entered the city gate.
A ghost questioned him.
Mílián asked about the way of travel.
Inside the city, he saw a man
named *Jùyǐn*.
A burning iron wheel rolled over his head.
He said, "Because I entered various cities and sat without being satisfied,
this burning iron wheel rolls over my head."
Mílián thought of
the *Luómàndiàn*, the *Xièmòdiàn*, the *Luómódiàn*, and the *Fànyùdāndiàn*.
Tears came out, and he said,
"Why have I come into this place?"
Mílián spoke to the ghost of the Iron City and said,
"If I enter and the burning iron wheel rolls over my head, when will I be released?"
The ghost replied,
"Only when someone like you comes will you be released."
The Buddha said,
"The iron wheel rolled over Mílián's head.
He was released only after six hundred million years.
Mílián was myself.
Before seeking the Way,
I was foolish, and after bathing and donning new clothes, I stepped on my mother's head.
Therefore, my head was burned for one day.
However, I kept the Eight Vows of Purification (*Bāguānzhāi*) for four months, and my heart was joyful,
hence I received the Four Treasure Cities of gold, silver, crystal, and lapis lazuli.
My lifespan was tens of millions of years.
Therefore, worldly people are never satisfied with the five desires until death.
Those who are driven by desires
and are unfilial to their parents and teachers
will have a wheel roll over them,
and they will become like Mílián."
In the kingdom of *Luóyuèzhīguó*, there was a merchant.
He and his younger brother lived together in one place.
The elder brother sought the daughter of an elder to be his wife.
The girl was young and not yet suitable for marriage.
The elder brother, with the company of merchants, traveled far to another country.
Many years passed, and he was delayed, failing to return in time.
When the girl came of age, the elder spoke to the younger brother:
"Your brother traveled far and has perished there, not returning.
You should now take my daughter."
The younger brother replied,
"How can such a thing happen?"
The elder insisted repeatedly.
The younger brother's resolve was firm and he never changed his mind. The elder falsely wrote a letter from afar,
entrusting it to several merchants, claiming the elder brother had died.
He then announced,
"Your brother is dead.
What will you do now?"
The younger brother married the girl, and after some time,
the woman became pregnant.
The elder brother returned from afar.
The younger brother was frightened and fled to *Shèwèi*.
Thus traveling far, he arrived before the Buddha.
He requested to renounce the world.
The Buddha immediately consented.
He became a *Shāméng* named *Yōupōsī*.
He upheld the disciplinary conduct and attained *Āluóhàn*.
The elder brother learned this and was furious.
Intending to kill him, he traveled to *Shèwèiguó*.
He immediately posted a heavy reward of five hundred ounces of gold.
Those who answered the summons advanced together.
When they saw the younger brother sitting in meditation, a thought of compassion suddenly arose.
"How can I kill this *Bǐqiū*?"
"But if I don't kill him, they will take away my gold."
He tried to shoot the *Bǐqiū*, but instead hit his own elder brother.
The elder brother, filled with hate and resentment, died suddenly.
He received the form of a poisonous snake
and was born inside the pivot hole of the *Dàorén*'s door.
When the door was constantly opened and closed,
his body was crushed, and he died.
He returned with a vow to become a small poisonous insect again,
dwelling in the *Dàorén*'s house.
It fell from the roof onto the *Bǐqiū*'s crown.
The fierce, malignant poison immediately caused him to die.
The Buddha told *Shèlìfó*:
"A long time ago in the past, there was a *Pìzhīfó* (Pratyekabuddha)
who appeared in the world and lived in the mountain forests.
At that time, there was a hunter who constantly captured birds and beasts.
He set up traps and schemes, hoping to catch them.
The *Pìzhīfó* startled the birds and beasts, so the hunter failed to catch them.
He then harbored anger and hatred and used a poisoned arrow
to shoot the *Pìzhīfó*.
The *Pìzhīfó* at that time,
pitying this person, wished for him to repent.
He displayed his spiritual powers for him.
At that moment, the hunter felt reverence and awe.
Terrified, he repented, returned his allegiance sincerely, and apologized for his fault.
The *Pìzhīfó* accepted his repentance and atonement.
He died due to the poison's attack.
When that man died, he immediately fell into *Dìyù* (hell).
After he emerged from *Dìyù*,
he was constantly killed by poison for five hundred lifetimes.
Up until today, having attained the *Luóhàn* way,
he still died after being stung by a poisonous insect.
Formerly, in *Yánfútí*,
five hundred merchants
traveled together through the wilderness, passing along a perilous road.
The great mountain caves were extremely dark.
At that time, the merchants were distressed and worried,
fearing the loss of their wealth.
This place had many bandits, which also caused fear.
They all resolved together
to cry and pray for mercy
to Heaven and Earth, the Sun and Moon, the mountains and seas, and all the deities.
At that time, the *Sàbó* (leader of the caravan),
pitying the merchants,
told them not to fear.
"I shall create a great light for you to see."
At that moment, the *Sàbó* immediately wrapped his two arms with white cloth.
He poured oil (*sūyóu*) onto them.
He lit them to serve as torches.
He led the merchants.
After seven days, they finally crossed the darkness.
The merchants were immensely grateful for his kindness, and their reverence was boundless.
Each found peace and security, overjoyed beyond control.
The *Sàbó* was myself.
The merchants are the five hundred *Bǐqiū* today.
In the past, there was a Sàbó.
He heard that in a foreign country there were even rarer treasures.
He wished to go there to conduct business.
However, in the middle between the two countries lay a Ròuchà difficulty (danger).
It was impossible to cross.
The Sàbó traveled around and saw, at the western gate of the market,
a Dàorén sitting on an empty bed saying he was selling the Five Precepts (Wǔjiè).
The Sàbó asked, "What are the Five Precepts?"
He replied:
"They have no form or substance.
You receive them by mouth and hold them in your heart.
Afterwards, you can be reborn in Heaven.
In this life, they can repel the Ròuchà ghost calamity."
The Sàbó wished to buy them.
He asked how much money was sought.
He replied, "One thousand gold coins."
He immediately approached and, after giving the money, finished receiving the Five Precepts.
[The Dàorén] spoke to him:
"When you go toward the foreign country and reach the boundary edge,
if the Ròuchà comes, you must only say:
'I am a disciple of the Five Precepts of Shìjiā.'"
A short while later, the Sàbó reached the middle between the two countries.
He saw the Ròuchà.
Its height was one *zhàng* and three *chǐ*.
Its head was yellow like ginger.
Its eyes were like red studs.
Its entire body was covered in scales and armor.
It alternately opened its mouth like a fish puffing its gills.
It looked up to catch flying swallows, and when it stepped on the ground, the earth sank up to its knees.
Hot blood flowed from its mouth.
A crowd of several thousand rushed to seize the Sàbó.
[The Sàbó] spoke:
"I am a disciple of the Five Precepts of Shìjiā."
When the Ròuchà heard this, it absolutely refused to let him go.
The Sàbó tried to poke it with both his fists.
His fists entered the scales and armor and could not be pulled out.
He then used his foot to stomp on its head.
He kicked it, but again his foot could not be pulled out.
His five limbs were submerged within the scales and armor.
Only his back could move.
The Ròuchà said to him:
"Your body, hands, and feet are all bound at once.
You should just go and face death; why jump about in vain?"
The Sàbó's resolve remained firm.
He spoke to the Ròuchà, saying:
"Although my body, hands, and feet are bound at once,
I gather my mind like metal and stone; I will never be killed by you."
The Ròuchà again spoke to the Sàbó, saying:
"I am the king among ghosts, and I possess great physical strength.
The number of your kind I have eaten since the past cannot be counted.
You should just go and face death; why speak such boastful words?"
The Sàbó was tempted to curse in anger.
He thought to himself:
"This body has circulated through the Sānjiè (Three Realms) of Saṃsāra.
I have never begged from anyone before.
I should now use this body to beg,
offering this Ròuchà one satisfying meal."
He immediately spoke:
"I have long wished to be separated from this foul-smelling, putrid body.
The Ròuchà takes me and uses all of me as an act of Dāna (charity/giving).
I aspire to seek the fruit of the Móhēyāna (Great Vehicle) and achieve omniscience."
The Ròuchà was intelligent;
it understood the Sàbó's words.
It immediately felt shame in its heart.
It released the Sàbó and let him go.
It knelt down with palms pressed together and apologized to him, saying:
"You are a master who saves people, rare in the Sānjiè.
Aspiring to seek the Móhēyāna, you will soon achieve Buddhahood.
Therefore, I take refuge in you, bowing my head and paying homage."
The Ròuchà repented of its faults.
Finally, it escorted the Sàbó to the foreign country.
[The Sàbó] obtained great treasures.
[The Ròuchà] then escorted him back home.
[The Sàbó] greatly cultivated merit and virtue.
And consequently achieved the path to enlightenment (Dàojì).
Regarding animals and humans, and all four modes of birth (*Sìshēng*):
Question:
"How do we know that among humans there are egg-born (*Luǎnshēng*)?"
Answer:
"As is recounted:
In the land of Yánfúlí,
many merchants entered the sea to gather treasures.
They obtained two swans (or geese).
According to their desire, they transformed (or disposed of) them, leaving one of each sex.
They played with them.
They slept in one room and engaged in union with them.
Consequently, two eggs were laid.
The eggs gradually warmed and matured.
Then two boys were born.
Later, they grew up, left home, and studied the path.
They achieved the fruit of Āluóhàn.
One name was Shīpīluó.
The second name was Yōubōshīpóluó."
Question:
"How do we know that among humans there are moisture-born (*Shīshēng*)?"
Answer:
"As stated in the Sūtras:
There was Dǐngshēng Wáng.
The Venerable Zhēluó.
The Venerable Yōupózhē.
The Luólì Maiden."
Question:
"How do we know that among humans there are transformationally-born (*Huàshēng*)?"
Answer:
"The people of the beginning of the *kalpa* (eon) were such.
Those who have already attained the holy Dharma will no longer be egg-born or moisture-born."
Question:
"Why will they no longer be egg-born or moisture-born?"
Answer:
"Egg-born and moisture-born are included in the realm of animals (*Chùshēng qù*)."
In the past, there was a Dǎoshī (guide/leader).
He traveled with five hundred merchants to conduct business and reached
a great wilderness completely devoid of water or liquid.
Extremely afflicted by hunger and thirst, they searched in all directions.
They climbed a height and looked into the distance, seeing some trees.
They supposed there must be water there.
They all rushed toward it together.
When they arrived, they saw that under the tree
grass grew all around, and the ground was clean.
They all dug and excavated.
At that time, a Tiānrén (Heavenly Being) saw the Dǎoshī from afar.
In the time it takes to extend an arm, he arrived at their location.
He stood on the tree and extended his right hand.
From between his five fingers flowed the eight-flavored, sweet, and delicious water.
And it was inexhaustible.
Everyone was satisfied and full.
Buddha resided in a great forest town south of Shèwèi Chéng.
A merchant drove eight oxen,
arriving at the northern kingdom of Jùduō Guó.
There was another merchant
who was jointly grazing oxen in the marsh.
At that time, a Líche captured a dragon maiden (nǚ).
He pierced her nose and led her away.
The merchant saw this
and immediately felt compassion.
He asked the Líche,
"What do you intend to do, leading her like this?"
He replied,
"I want to kill and eat her."
The merchant said, "Do not kill her.
I will give you one ox
to trade for her release." The captor refused,
even up to eight oxen.
Finally, the captor said,
"Now, for your sake, I shall release her."
He immediately took the eight oxen and let the dragon maiden go.
Then the merchant thought again,
"This is an evil man; I fear he might pursue her again and recapture her."
He immediately followed her himself, watching where she went.
When they reached a pond,
the dragon transformed into human form.
She spoke to the merchant,
"Noble Sir (tiān), you granted me life, and now I wish to repay your kindness.
Please come with me into the palace.
I shall repay your noble grace."
The merchant replied,
"Your dragon nature is volatile, prone to sudden anger (chēnhuì), and impermanent.
You might kill me."
She replied,
"When that man bound me,
I had the power to kill him.
But because he had accepted the precepts of the Bùsà Dharma,
he had no killing intent whatsoever.
How much less would I harm
you, Noble Sir, who have now granted me longevity?
Wait here briefly.
I shall enter first and tidy up."
By the dragon gate, he saw two dragons bound together in one place.
He asked them,
"What crime did you commit?"
They replied,
"This dragon maiden observes the fast (zhāi fǎ) for three days out of the half-month.
We brothers guarded this dragon maiden,
but we were not diligent, and she was captured by the Líche.
For this reason, we are bound.
We only beg for your noble compassion (tiān cí) to tell her to release us.
If this dragon maiden asks what kind of food you wish to eat,
you must ask for human food from Yánfútí."
The dragon maiden finished tidying up
and immediately called him in.
He sat on a precious couch and mat.
The dragon maiden said,
"Noble Sir, what food do you wish to eat now?"
He replied,
"I need human food from Yánfútí."
She immediately served various types of food.
He asked the dragon maiden,
"Why are these persons bound?"
The dragon maiden said,
"They committed a fault, and I intend to kill them."
The merchant said,
"Do not kill them."
She replied, "If not, I must definitely kill them."
The merchant said,
"If you release them, then I shall eat."
She replied,
"I cannot simply release them as they are.
I must punish them by banishing them to the human realm for six months."
The merchant asked,
"Do you observe the Bùsà [precepts] despite such dragon adornments?"
She replied,
"In the Dharma of dragons, we suffer five calamities.
What are these five?
When born, we are dragons.
When sleeping, we are dragons.
When engaging in sexual activity, we are dragons.
When angry, we are dragons.
Three times in a half-day,
our skin and flesh fall off, and our bodies are scorched by hot sand."
He further asked,
"What do you seek?"
She replied,
"I wish to be reborn in the human realm."
He asked, "If I have already obtained a human body, what should I seek?"
She replied,
"Leaving home (becoming a monastic) is hard to attain."
He further asked,
"From whom should I take monastic vows?"
She replied,
"The Rúlái, the Worthy One (Yìnggòng), the Perfectly Enlightened One (Zhèngbiànzhī), is now in Shèwèi Chéng.
He frees those who are not yet free.
You should go and leave home under him."
He then said,
"I wish to return home."
The dragon maiden immediately gave him eight gold pieces and said,
"This is dragon gold.
It is sufficient for your parents
and family members to use for the rest of their lives without being exhausted." She said,
"Close your eyes."
She immediately used divine power (shén biàn) to transport him to his homeland.
His traveling companions had arrived earlier
and told his family,
"He went into the dragon palace."
His parents believed their son was dead.
Relatives and family gathered in one place, weeping and crying mournfully.
At that time, the herdsmen and the people gathering firewood and grass
saw him and returned first to tell his family,
"So-and-so has returned."
When the family heard this, they were extremely happy.
They went out to greet him, brought him into the house, and held a feast celebrating his life.
When the feast was held, he took the eight gold pieces and presented them to his parents.
"This is dragon gold.
If it is cut, it regenerates.
Use it for the rest of your lives."
There was a merchant leader
who led a group of merchants into a dangerous region.
They encountered a Luóchà Guǐ.
The demon blocked them with its hand and said,
"Stop and do not move! I will not let you leave."
The merchant leader immediately struck it with his right fist.
The fist immediately stuck to the demon and could not be pulled away.
He struck it again with his left fist.
That also could not be separated.
He kicked it with his right foot.
It was the same again.
He rammed it with his head.
His head also became stuck.
The demon asked,
"Now that you are like this, what do you intend to do?
Has your resolve rested yet?"
He replied, "Although five parts of my body are bound,
my resolve shall never rest.
I shall use the power of diligence (jīngjìn lì) to fight you."
The demon thought,
"This man's courage and strength are immense."
It immediately said,
"Your power of diligence is great and you will certainly not rest.
I shall let you go now."
There was a merchant leader
named Jílì.
He entered the sea to retrieve great treasures.
He returned safely.
Altogether, he had eighty billion Mani jewels.
Each one was worth ten billion liǎng of gold.
He gave many precious items to a beggar.
Without entering his home, he returned again to the sea
to gather precious treasures.
After entering the sea, he gained twice the amount of treasures.
After eighty years, he returned to his homeland.
As he was about to enter the city, he saw a criminal.
The executioners had tied him up and were beating a harsh-sounding drum.
They were announcing throughout the streets that he was being led to the execution ground
to be subjected to punishment and killing.
The man who was supposed to die met Jílì
and said this:
"Merchant leader,
save me from the death penalty!
Grant me life!
You are a great Dàntuō, a wise, good person."
When Jílì heard this, he spoke to the condemned man,
"Halt, man!
I now grant you fearlessness
and save you from the death penalty."
He immediately went to the executioners.
He gave each person a Mani jewel worth one hundred million liǎng of gold.
[He said,] "Wait here briefly.
I shall go to the King and return."
At that time, Jílì quickly reached the King's location
and reported,
"Great King,
I wish to use fine treasures to purchase this man's life."
The King answered,
"Jílì,
this man's crime cannot be pardoned and cannot be bought. If you must buy it,
you must give me everything you own
and substitute yourself for him in death; only then can he be freed."
Jílì was delighted.
"I have achieved great profit and fulfilled my vow!
To be able to save this person truly satisfies my intention."
He immediately took all the wealth he possessed at home and the treasures he had obtained from the great sea,
countless thousands of millions of gold, silver, and precious objects,
and sent them all to the King, saying to the Great King,
"You may release this person.
Everything I own is now here."
[The King] ordered the executioners,
"Go and kill Jílì."
They immediately bound Jílì and led him to the execution ground.
The executioner raised his right hand holding the knife, intending to chop Jílì,
but his hand went stiff and would not descend.
Astonished, bewildered, and terrified, he immediately reported it to the King:
"Please see for yourself."
When the King heard this,
