he immediately took the knife himself, intending to kill Jílì.
As he raised the knife, both of his hands dropped off, and overcome by great distress and anguish, he cried out and died.
At that time, Jílì was precisely my present body.
At that time, the King was Diàodá.
A countless *asaṃkhyeya*-kalpas ago,
there were two groups of merchants, five hundred men in each.
They were in Bōluónài.
They gathered their funds, prepared their ships, and crossed the sea.
They untied the moorings, hoisted the sails, and traveled straight on the wind.
They soon reached Bǎozhǔ (Treasure Isle),
where there were supreme, wonderful, beautiful women, and nothing was lacking.
The leader of one group of merchants said,
"We have endured hardship to arrive here for the sake of wealth.
We ought to remain and enjoy ourselves."
The second Sàbó (caravan leader) said,
“Although this place is rich in many treasures, we should not stay long.”
At that time, a celestial maiden (Tiānnǚ), feeling compassion for this group,
spoke to the assembled people from the air, saying,
"Although this place is pleasant, it is not safe to remain long.
In seven days, this land will sink."
Having spoken, she vanished.
Furthermore, there was a demoness (Mónǚ) who wished to cause the merchants to be completely drowned here.
She announced from the air, saying,
"You all need not prepare your vessels and return.
This land has no water; even if water were to come,
how could these many treasures, many women, and five forms of pleasure exist?
What the previous celestial being said was all false."
Having spoken, she vanished.
The first Sàbó commanded his followers,
"You all must not leave. Do not believe the previous celestial being."
The second Sàbó then told his group,
"You must not be greedy; quickly prepare and fix the ships.
What the previous celestial being said is absolutely true and not false.
If the water does not come, we can enjoy ourselves here and then slowly return.
If the water truly comes, we will already be prepared and gone."
The Buddha told Shèlìfú,
"Seven days later, just as the previous celestial being had said,
water flooded the land.
The second Sàbó immediately boarded the ship with his group.
The first Sàbó had not prepared beforehand.
On the day the water arrived, they put on armor and weapons and fought with each other."
The second Sàbó, from atop the ship, used a spear to pierce the first Sàbó’s leg.
It passed through, and he immediately died.
The Buddha told Shèlìfú,
"Do you know who the first Sàbó was? He was Dévádádoù (Devadatta).
The second Sàbó was none other than I.
The five hundred people who were the first group of merchants are now Dévádádoù’s five hundred disciples.
The five hundred people who were the second group of merchants are now the five hundred Arhats.
The first celestial maiden was Shèlìfú.
The second celestial maiden is now the *Bǐqiū* and *Bōluómén* disciple named Mǎnyuè.
During the time of Dìngguāng Fó (Dīpaṁkara Buddha),
there were five hundred merchants who entered the sea seeking treasure.
One among them, harboring ill intentions, thought,
"I will now kill all the merchants and take the treasures alone."
At that time, in Yánfútí (Jambudvīpa), there was a great guide (Dàoshī),
named Dà'āi (Great Compassion).
While he was sleeping and dreaming, the sea spirit spoke to him:
"Among the group of merchants, there is a thief
who intends to kill his five hundred companions and take the treasures alone.
If this deed is accomplished, he will fall into the hells.
Now, the benevolent guide must employ expedient means (*quánbiàn*)
to ensure the merchants do not die and the thief does not incur the offense."
The guide contemplated for seven days,
finding no other expedient means.
He realized that he must kill this malicious person.
If he told the assembled merchants, they would surely become angry and kill him together,
and both would fall into the evil realms.
"If I kill him alone,
I will incur the offense.
I would rather endure the suffering of hundreds of thousands of kalpas myself
than allow the merchants to be universally harmed
and furthermore, allow one thief to fall into the hells."
First, he preached the Dharma to him,
making his heart joyful and ecstatic, so he lay down to sleep.
The Buddha said,
Dà'āi, the guide, relying on great compassion toward the merchants, killed this one thief using expedient means.
After the end of his life, he was born into the Twelfth Guāngyīn Heaven (Heaven of Radiance and Sound).
That Dà'āi was none other than I.
By this expedient means, he transcended thousands of kalpas of life and death.
The five hundred merchants on the same ship
are the five hundred Buddhas who will arise in this Xián Jié (Bhadrakalpa).
In the past, there were five hundred merchants
who sailed ships into the sea.
They encountered a *Mójié* fish (Makara) that emerged, opened its mouth, and intended to devour sentient beings.
At that time, the sun was faint and the wind slight, yet the ship moved like an arrow.
The Sàbó leader said to the assembly,
"The ship is going too fast; we should lower the sails."
They lowered them as instructed.
The ship traveled even faster and could not be stopped.
The Sàbó leader asked the man on the upper deck,
"What do you see?"
"I see two suns above,
a white mountain below,
and a black mountain in the middle."
The Sàbó leader exclaimed in alarm,
"This is a great fish! What are we to do?
You and I have now met with distress and disaster.
Entering the belly of this fish, there is no chance of survival.
You should each focus sincerely on what you usually worship and pray to it."
Thereupon, the assembled people each prayed to what they worshipped.
They wholeheartedly took refuge and sought release from this calamity.
The more devotedly they prayed, the faster the ship moved.
In a moment, it would not stop, and they would enter the fish’s mouth.
Thereupon, the Sàbó leader announced to everyone,
"I have a great deity whose title is Fó (Buddha).
You should all abandon the deities you originally worshipped and call upon this name wholeheartedly."
At that moment, the five hundred people together cried out in a loud voice, invoking "Námó Fó" (Homage to the Buddha).
The fish heard the name of the Buddha
and contemplated to itself, saying,
"Today, in this world, there is actually a Buddha!
How can I bear to harm sentient beings?"
It immediately closed its mouth.
The water flowed backward, causing the ship to turn and escape far away from the fish.
The five hundred merchants generated good thoughts.
All gained liberation.
In one district there were people.
All practiced the Five Precepts (Wǔ Jiè) and the Ten Good Deeds (Shí Shàn).
Within the district boundaries, there were no brewers of alcohol.
Among them was the son of a prominent family (dà xìng jiā zi).
He wished to trade and hawk far away.
As he was about to depart, his parents told him:
"You must diligently keep the Wǔ Jiè and practice the Shí Shàn.
Take care not to drink alcohol, thereby violating the Buddha’s grave precept."
He traveled until he reached another state and met an old classmate.
Happily, the classmate returned home and brought out grape wine, wanting to drink it with him.
He declined, saying:
"My country honors the Buddha's precepts; none dare violate them.
Moreover, I have taken leave of my parents, and they further instructed me upon parting. Although we meet after a long separation, and our hearts are joyful,
it is improper to cause me to violate the precepts and disobey my parents' teachings."
The host said:
"We and you studied under the same teacher; by favor, we are like brothers.
My parents are therefore your parents.
If parents offer a drink, how can one refuse it?
If I were in your home, I would certainly obey your parents."
Seeing no other option, he yielded and drank it.
When the affair was finished, he returned home and confessed (bái) to his parents.
His parents replied:
"You have disobeyed our teaching and furthermore violated a precept.
This is the start of disrupting the Dharma; you are not a filial son (xiào zǐ).
You must not speak of this."
They then took the possessions he had obtained and banished him, ordering him out of the state.
Because the son had violated the precept, he was expelled by his parents.
He then went to another state and stayed at an inn.
The host served three ghost spirits (guǐ shén).
They could transform into human shapes.
They ate and drank facing people, and spoke human language.
After serving them for many years, the host's wealth was completely exhausted.
Moreover, illnesses, deaths, and funerals in the family were incessant.
They privately discussed the matter.
The ghosts knew what the people were thinking.
The ghosts conferred, saying:
"This person's wealth is finished.
We have never brought them any benefit.
Now they resent and worry about us.
We ought to seek out treasures and give them to him."
They then went and stole fine treasures from the royal treasury (wáng kù cáng) of another state, piling them up in the garden.
They reported:
"You have served us faithfully for many years and suffered greatly.
We now wish to bestow fortune upon you, so that you may become rich."
The host said:
"I accept the great spirits' grace."
The ghosts said:
"There is gold and silver in your garden; you may go and take it."
The host was delighted.
He entered the garden, saw the objects, carried them back home, loaded (liǎn) them, and returned to his dwelling.
He thanked the ghosts, accepting their grace.
The next day, he wanted to prepare food and drink (fàn shí).
He invited them, saying, "I beg you to descend and favor me with your presence."
All the preparations were made.
The ghost spirits approached the gate.
They saw a man from the state of Shèwèi Guó (Śrāvastī) in the host's dwelling.
They immediately ran away.
The host chased and called out:
"Since you have already favored me with your presence,
why do you abandon the feast and leave?"
The spirits said:
"Your dwelling has an honored guest; how dare we approach?"
They ran away again in alarm.
The host contemplated:
"Within my house, there is no one unusual.
It is only this person."
He immediately went out and spoke, explaining that the offerings were ready.
Then he asked him, saying:
"What merits or virtues do you possess that the spirits I serve fear you and run away?"
The guest thoroughly explained the merits (gōng dé) of the Buddha, the Wǔ Jiè, and the Shí Shàn.
He admitted that he had violated the precept against alcohol and was consequently driven out by his parents.
But I still maintain the remaining four precepts, thus I am protected by the heavenly spirits (tiān shén).
Your spirits dare not confront them."
The host spoke:
"I wish to observe the Wǔ Jiè."
Consequently, he received the Three Refuges (Sān Zì Guī) and the Wǔ Jiè from the guest.
He proceeded with single-minded diligence, daring not to slacken.
He asked where the Buddha resided and whether he could meet him.
The guest replied:
"He is in Shèwèi Guó, at the Jǐgū Dú Yuán (Jetavana Monastery)."
The host proceeded there wholeheartedly, passing by a rest stop (tíng).
Inside was a woman.
She was exactly the wife (fù) of a man-eating ghost (dàn rén guǐ).
The road ahead was long, and dusk was approaching.
He requested lodging from the woman.
The woman immediately warned him:
"Take care not to stay here.
You should hurry on your way."
The man asked:
"What reason is there for this advice?"
The woman replied:
"I have already told you; why ask again?"
The man thought to himself:
"Previously, the man from Shèwèi Guó maintained four of the Buddha's precepts, and my spirits still feared him.
I have already received the Sān Guī and Wǔ Jiè.
My mind is not slackening.
What is there to fear?"
Consequently, he stayed overnight.
At that time, the dàn rén guǐ saw the powerful spirits guarding the precepts forty *lǐ* (li) away from the rest stop.
For one night, the ghost did not return.
The next day, the man advanced and saw the bones and skeletons of people eaten by the ghost scattered about.
His heart became fearful, and he regretted turning back.
He reflected:
"In my home state, I had sufficient clothing and food.
I was vainly converted by that man
who said the Buddha was in Shèwèi Guó.
Before seeing anything marvelous, I instead see scattered skeletons.
It would be better to take this woman and return to my homeland to live as before."
He immediately turned back.
Consequently, he asked the woman to stay another night.
The woman said to the man:
"Why have you returned again?"
He replied:
"My travel plans did not work out, so I merely returned."
He stayed one more night.
The woman said, "Sir, you will die!
My husband is the dàn rén guǐ.
He will be coming soon.
You must urgently leave this place."
The man did not believe her, so he stopped and did not leave.
He became confused, and lustful thoughts arose again.
He no longer believed in the Buddha's Sān Guī and Wǔ Jiè.
The heavenly spirits immediately left, and the ghost was able to return.
The woman feared the ghost would eat the man,
so she hid him inside a jar (wèng zhōng).
The ghost smelled human scent and said to his wife:
"Did you get meat?
I want to eat it."
The wife said:
"I haven't been out; how could I have gotten meat?"
The wife asked the ghost:
"Why didn't you return last night?"
The ghost said:
"Because of that honored guest you housed
who caused me to be driven away.
The man in the jar became increasingly terrified.
He no longer remembered the Sān Zì Guī.
The wife said:
"Why couldn't you get meat?"
The ghost said:
"It is exactly because you housed a disciple of the Buddha (Fó Dìzǐ).
The tiān shén chased me out forty *lǐ* away.
I slept in the open, shaking with fear, and am still uneasy now, so I couldn't get meat."
The wife then asked her husband:
"What are the Buddha's precepts (Fó Jiè)?"
The ghost said:
"I am extremely hungry; quickly bring me meat! You don't need to ask about that.
These are the supreme, true, and real precepts.
They are not something I dare speak of."
The wife said:
"Tell me about them,
and I will give you meat."
The ghost, being of a greedy and cruel nature, wanted food endlessly.
The wife pressed him with questions.
Consequently, he then spoke to her about the Sān Guī and Wǔ Jiè.
When the ghost first spoke one precept, the wife immediately received it.
By the fifth precept, she held it in her heart and recited it with her mouth.
The man in the jar recognized the Wǔ Jiè and received them accordingly.
Shì Tī Huán Yīn (Śakra, the Lord of Heaven) knew that these two people had taken refuge in the Buddha in their hearts.
He immediately dispatched fifty good spirits (shàn shén) to protect the two people.
The ghost then ran away.
When morning came,
the wife asked the man:
"Were you afraid?"
He replied, "Greatly afraid.
Thanks to your kindness (rén zhě),
my heart was awakened, and I recognized the Buddha."
The wife said to the man:
"Why did you turn back yesterday?"
He replied:
"I saw the scattered skeletons of recently and long-dead people and was afraid, so I just returned."
The wife said:
"Those bones are what I discarded.
I was originally a daughter of a good family (liáng jiā zhī nǚ),
but I was abducted by the ghost and taken as his wife.
Grieved and desperate, I had no recourse.
Now, thanks to your kindness,
I have heard the Fó Jiè and have been separated from this ghost."
She further said:
"Where do you, enlightened one (xián zhě), intend to go?"
The man replied:
"I wish to go to Shèwèi Guó to see the Buddha."
The wife said, "Excellent!
I will accompany the xián zhě to see the Buddha."
They then traveled forward together and met four hundred and ninety-eight people.
They then greeted each other and asked:
"Venerable sirs, where have you come from, and where are you going?"
They replied:
"We have come from the Buddha's presence."
They asked:
"Since you have already seen the Buddha, why are you leaving again?"
They replied:
"The sūtras spoken by the Buddha are confusing (wǎng wǎng) to our minds, so we still do not understand and are returning to our homelands."
The two xián zhě fully explained the whole story,
about how ghosts feared those who upheld the precepts (jiè) and were highly virtuous.
Their minds were then enlightened, and they all returned together to see the Buddha.
When the Buddha saw them from afar, he smiled.
Five-colored light emanated from his mouth.
Ānán (Ānanda) knelt respectfully.
"The Buddha does not smile capriciously; there must be something he intends to say."
The Buddha said to Ānán.
Did you see those four hundred and ninety-eight people return?
These people have now obtained their original teacher.
Those who come to see the Buddha shall all attain the Way.
At that time, five hundred people came to the Buddha's residence and listened to the scripture with concentrated minds.
Their minds opened and their understanding cleared; they all became Shāmen.
They attained the Way of Āluóhàn.
However, these two people were the teachers of the four hundred and ninety-eight people in a previous life.
If people seek the essentials of the Way,
they must obtain their original teacher and their good friends.
Only then will they understand.
In Wángshěchéng,
there was a magician.
Named Bátuó.
He clearly understood the scriptures, mastered techniques, and his creations were skillful and clever; he was multi-talented and rejoiced in a lofty and widespread reputation.
The people of Mójié could not match him.
Everyone, great and small, in the country followed him and received his teachings.
Bátuó happened to see the World-Honored One, whose physical form was majestic and wonderful.
He conceived the idea of testing him.
So he sent an invitation to the Buddha.
He thought: If he knows my intention, he certainly will not accept the invitation.
If he does not know it, he will certainly accept without doubt.
The Buddha knew his intention and desired to convert him.
He silently accepted.
Bátuó thought:
The Buddha has no penetrating wisdom and does not see my intention.
He entered Wángshěchéng.
In a clean place, he miraculously created a lecture hall.
Silk banners and flower canopies were hung.
Beneath every tree,
he spread Lion Seats (simhāsana) for the various Bhikkhus.
Inside the lecture hall,
he specially set up a Lion Seat for the Tathāgata.
It was forty-nine feet high.
He prepared meals of a hundred flavors.
At that time, the Four Heavenly Kings and Tiāndìshì,
along with thirty-two thousand heavenly beings, said to Rénxián:
You have truly obtained great merit.
To invite the Tathāgata to the lecture hall for offerings.
We shall help provide what is lacking.
Immediately, they transformed the structure into a palace like the Trāyastriṃśa Palace (Dāolìgōng).
The Buddha, the Bodhisattvas, and the various Bhikkhus went to the lecture hall.
They saw the Buddha seated on the seat that had been created.
Tiāndìshì also saw the Tathāgata seated on the majestic seat he had created.
Rénxián listened to what the Buddha taught.
He cast away his arrogance and bowed his head at the Buddha's feet.
He spoke to the Buddha, saying:
I only wish that the Tathāgata would forgive my offenses.
He wanted to dissolve the miraculous creations he had made.
The Buddha ordered that they not change.
The Buddha then spoke to him again, saying that all phenomena are like illusion and transformation.
Ānándǐnbó,
lived at the foot of Érliánshān.
He was extremely rich in treasures.
Merchants from the four directions borrowed money from him.
Beggars who went to him never left empty-handed.
At that time, there were five hundred merchants.
While traveling by sea, their ship was destroyed, and all their treasures sank.
Not a few died; some survived by clinging to planks.
They all went to Ānándǐnbó.
The host prepared a meal.
The host drew water from the well and obtained chests and baskets of treasure.
Each item had a dedication listing the names and surnames of the owners.
After the merchants finished eating, they were all sorrowful.
The host asked the reason.
They answered, saying:
We were a company of five hundred people.
We traveled together on the sea; our ship overturned and sank.
Not a few died.
Clinging to small planks, we barely managed to survive.
We lost our treasures and mourn for our companions.
Just now we saw the treasure chests obtained from the well.
They all belong to us, but we do not know how they got there.
The host said:
You gentlemen conduct your livelihood through trade and commerce.
If you had acted with utmost sincerity, you would not have lost them.
It is only because you lacked utmost sincerity that you lost them.
Since innumerable kalpas ago,
I have never failed to be utterly sincere and have never once cheated or encroached upon others.
All those who lose treasure find their way to my well.
You gentlemen may each examine the names and surnames and take them away.
In the past, there was a man named Xiánzhí.
He had attended the Eight Precepts Retreat (Bāguān) three times and listened to and recited scriptures.
He claimed that his heavenly eye did not blink, and he never forgot what he recited or pondered.
However, this Xiánzhí
was skilled at stealing things from others without them noticing it right before their eyes.
The king lost a pearl.
He summoned his ministers to measure the situation and deliberate.
The ministers answered the king, saying:
We have heard that there is Xiánzhí, who is extremely capable of theft.
The king ordered him brought in and questioned, hoping he would confess, but he denied the theft.
Since the king possessed the Way, how could he wrongfully punish someone?
He again summoned the ministers to deliberate together.
A minister said:
We should use a skillful means to make him confess and submit.
We should put heavy cangues and fetters on him, parade him through the marketplace, and announce that he is to be killed.
Then, give him wine until he is drunk, remove the fetters, carry him onto a platform, and have courtesans perform music.
The king instructed the courtesans:
When Xiánzhí is drunk, ask him:
You must reply, saying:
This is Heaven, and I am a celestial maiden.
You should attend to me here.
Because you stole the king's pearl in your previous life, you were able to be born here.
The king acted according to this plan.
When Xiánzhí heard this, he thought silently and turned to leave.
He thought: I heard the scriptures say
that the heavenly eye does not blink, but this woman blinks constantly.
Furthermore, if I stole the pearl, I should have fallen into Diyù.
Is it not the case that the king is trapping me to make me confess?
He immediately spoke, saying:
My rebirth in heaven is because I did not steal the pearl.
The courtesan reported this to the king.
Relaying Xiánzhí's words.
The king then laughed heartily.
This fellow certainly did not steal my pearl.
He immediately released him and allowed him to go.
He heavily rewarded him with gold and treasures.
This man had actually stolen the pearl.
By reciting one verse (gāthā), he was exempted from punishment and received a reward.
In the past, there was a man named Cíluó.
He saw someone selling a turtle and felt pity in his heart.
He wept toward the turtle.
The seller of the turtle said:
Why are you weeping toward the turtle?
Cíluó replied, saying:
I cannot bear to see it.
The destitute turtle seller laughed heartily.
You are mad and foolish!
Cíluó replied:
I intend to request to buy this turtle from you.
The owner said:
The turtle is worth a million [coins].
Cíluó then took it back home.
He emptied his resources and borrowed from his family, obtaining eight hundred thousand.
Cíluó said:
My money ends here; I have no place left to borrow.
The turtle seller said:
Since your money is finished, you can work my field to pay the remaining cost.
Cíluó agreed.
He loaded the turtle onto a cart and released it into a pond.
The turtle immediately began to speak.
It said: When a great flood comes, you must climb a tree and call out to me.
Later, a great flood arose, and all the people died.
Cíluó climbed a tree and called the turtle.
The turtle immediately came to him.
Cíluó sat upon the turtle's back.
They proceeded for several *lǐ*.
They saw a woman floating on a raft, distressed and near death.
She begged Cíluó for a ride.
Cíluó addressed the turtle:
This person is pitiful; let us please give her a ride.
The turtle said:
Go ahead and take her on.
They traveled forward for ten *lǐ*.
They saw the son of the turtle seller floating on a raft.
He begged Cíluó for a ride.
The turtle said: I am already heavily burdened.
I fear I will be utterly exhausted and unable to cross over myself.
Absolutely do not take him on.
Cíluó said:
He is pitiful now; whether right or wrong, we must carry him.
Cíluó took him on as well.
They traveled forward for several dozen *lǐ*.
They saw several *shēng* of ants (or moths) floating on a raft.
Cíluó again told the turtle to take them on.
They reached the country of Nàjié.
The woman then gave gold to Cíluó as thanks.
The turtle seller (father) said:
This turtle was originally sold by me.
Now that you have obtained gold, you should give it back to me.
Cíluó did not give it to him.
The turtle seller’s son then went to the King of Nàjié and claimed:
Cíluó stole someone’s wife and is trafficking her.
He has now brought gold and silver and come into this country.
The King of Nàjié immediately summoned Cíluó and ordered an official to behead him.
The official ascended and reported the matter, and as he was about to write the decree,
the ants immediately crawled up the brush, making it impossible to form characters.
The king heard of this and asked Cíluó:
What meritorious virtue do you possess?
Cíluó answered fully.
The king executed the turtle seller.
The city of Pújiāluō in Dàyuèzhī.
There was a painter.
His name was Qiānnà.
He traveled frequently to the eastern country of Duōchà Shīluó.
He worked as a hired painter for twelve years.
He obtained thirty liǎng of gold and took it back to his home country.
He met a Saṅgha whose faith was pure and clean.
He immediately asked the Karmadāna (Wéinà).
"How much material wealth does this assembly need to make one day's meal?"
He replied:
"Thirty liǎng of gold would suffice."
The painter handed it all over to the Karmadāna (Wéinà),
requesting that one meal be prepared.
"I will come tomorrow."
He returned home empty-handed.
His wife asked:
"What did you earn after working for twelve years?"
He replied:
"I obtained thirty liǎng of gold.
I have already sown a field of merit.
I gave it to the Saṅgha to hold a gathering."
The wife tied up her husband and handed him over to the officials,
fully recounting the aforementioned matter.
The official asked:
"Why did you not provide for your wife and children but instead give it to others?"
The painter replied:
"In my past life, I lacked merit, so I was poor and constantly suffered hardship.
Meeting the Saṅgha is meeting a good field of merit.
If I do not sow good deeds, I will be poor again in the next life.
Poverty and suffering would continue without a time for release.
Therefore, I gave it all to the Saṅgha."
The person ruling the case was a Upāsaka (Yōupósè).
He immediately removed his pearl necklace, and gave the horse he was riding and his village to the painter.
He said to him:
"You gave to the Saṅgha.
The Saṅgha has not yet eaten,
but it is like the grain seed has not yet been sown, yet the sprout has already emerged,
and the great fruit is still to come."
Formerly, there was a man.
After he died, his spirit returned to stroke the side of his former bones.
People asked him:
"You are already dead.
Why do you again stroke these dry bones?"
The spirit said:
"This was my former body.

It did not kill living beings, did not steal, did not commit adultery, did not speak with a double tongue, did not curse with evil words, did not lie, did not use ornate speech, did not envy, did not get angry, and was not ignorant.
After death, I was able to be born in heaven.
My desires are naturally fulfilled, and my joy is limitless.
Therefore, I love and cherish it."
Formerly, in Northern Tiānzhú,
there was a skillful artisan.
He made a wooden woman.
She was peerlessly beautiful, dressed and adorned with ornaments, no different from a woman of the world.
She could come and go, pour wine, and attend to guests.
Only she could not speak.
At that time, in Southern Tiānzhú, there was a painter.
He was also very skilled at painting.
When the artisan heard about him,
he prepared fine food and drink and invited the painter.
He then made the wooden woman pour wine and serve the food.
From dawn until night,
the painter did not realize and thought she was a real woman.
His lustful desires became extremely intense, and he thought of her constantly.
By this time, the day was drawing to a close.
The artisan went in to sleep.
He asked the painter to stay.
He had the wooden woman stand attendant at the painter's side.
Then he spoke to the guest, saying:
"I intentionally left this woman here; you may sleep with her."
After the host had gone inside,
the wooden woman stood by the lamp.
The guest immediately called her,
but the woman did not come.
The guest then went forward and pulled her.
Only then did he realize it was wood.
He immediately felt shame and remorse.
"The host deceived me!
I must repay him."
Thereupon, the painter again devised a plan.
He immediately painted his own image on the wall.
The clothing he wore was no different from his actual body.
He tied a rope around the neck, depicting the appearance of being strangled to death, and painted the image of the rope holding his mouth closed.
Having finished, he closed the door and hid himself under the bed.
At dawn, the host came out and saw the door was not open.
He immediately looked inside.
He only saw the image of the guest strangled to death on the wall.
The host was greatly terrified and assumed he had actually died.
He immediately broke the door down and entered, using a knife to cut the rope.
Thereupon, the painter emerged from under the bed.
The artisan was extremely ashamed.
The painter immediately said:
"You were able to deceive me.
I am able to deceive you.
The matter between guest and host is settled, neither has wronged the other."
The two men believed and understood the nature of delusion and confusion.
They each abandoned their relatives and attachments, left home, and cultivated the Way.
There was a certain king.
His body was afflicted by a severe illness.
For twelve years, he did not recover.
All the great physicians were unable to cure him.
At that time, a small border country subject to the great king
had a physician who was skilled at curing illness.
The king immediately summoned him to treat his ailment.
Before long, he was cured.
The king then considered wanting to repay this master's kindness.
He ordered an envoy to proclaim an order to that country:
"This master who achieved the cure should be suitably rewarded."
Elephants, horses, carriages, cattle, sheep, fields, dwellings, servants, slaves, and all sorts of adornments were all to be given to him.
That small country's king respectfully executed the superior order.
The master was at the side of the great king, and no one spoke of this matter.
The master then reflected:
"I put forth great effort in treating the king's illness.
I wonder whether the king will reward me or not."
After several more days, the king had fully recovered.
The master requested permission to take leave and return to his home country.
The king permitted it.
He was given one emaciated horse, and the riding equipment was also worn out.
The master laughed bitterly, regretting, "I treated the king's illness
with great effort,
but the king did not recognize the magnitude of the kindness.
He did not take care of me
and let me leave empty-handed."
Along the way, he grieved and sighed, taking it as a perpetual regret.
Just as he arrived in his home country, he saw a herd of elephants.
He asked the elephant driver:
"Whose elephants are these?"
The elephant driver replied:
"These are the elephants of a certain master."
He again asked the elephant driver:
"How did that master obtain these elephants?"
He replied:
"That master cured the great king's illness.
These were obtained as the reward for his achievement."
He proceeded a little further.
He saw herds of horses, cattle, and sheep.
He asked:
"Whose property is this?"
The shepherd replied:
"It belongs to that master."
He proceeded a little further.
He saw his former dwelling: high halls and storied pavilions, vastly different from his original house.
He asked the doorkeeper:
"Whose house is this?"
The doorkeeper replied:
"This is the house of that master."
He then entered the inner chambers.
He saw his wife, whose appearance was plump and cheerful, and whose body was clad in precious robes.
Surprised, he asked:
"Whose lady is this?"
The attendant replied:
"This is the wife of that master."
Since seeing the elephants and horses
and entering the house,
he knew that all these things were obtained as the reward for the achievement of curing the king's illness.
He then regretted that originally,
his effort in treating the king's illness had been minimal.
Formerly, there was a Gāluóyuè (Gṛhapati).
He prepared a great altar and invited the Buddha and the Saṅgha.
At that time, there was a man selling fermented milk.
The host kept him to eat,
persuading him to observe the fast and listen to the sutra.
He returned home only when night fell.
His wife said to him:
"I have waited for you since morning, not having eaten until now,
thus ruining my husband's observance of the fast."
The merit of even half a day's fast is sufficient to be born in heaven for seven lifetimes.
When born among humans, one constantly obtains things naturally.
Observing the fast for one day yields sixty myriad years of naturally provided provisions.
Furthermore, there are five blessings:
First, few illnesses.
Second, the body and mind are peaceful and secure.
Third, little lust.
Fourth, little sleep.
Fifth, after the end of life, the spirit obtains birth in heaven and constantly remembers past lives.
In the past, there was a man tilling and sowing in the fields.
The sun was already nearing noon.
The meal from home had not yet arrived.
A Dàorén, having lost his way, arrived at his field.
He begged for the midday meal.
The ploughman assented, saying, "Yes."
"Please wait a little while."
"The meal from home is late."
The Dàorén said,
"Since the food has not arrived, I would still like to rinse my mouth."
The ploughman untied his belt and gave him one Hēlìlè fruit.
The Dàorén immediately accepted it and ate.
Furthermore, [the ploughman] offered one coin as a gift (chèn) to the Dàorén.
The Dàorén said,
"If my heart is moved [by your kindness], I have nothing with which to repay you."
"I wish to transmit the Five Precepts (Wǔjiè)."
"Can you accept them?"
[The ploughman] replied,
"As your disciple living in the secular world, the Wǔjiè are difficult to keep perfectly."
"I will only accept not killing (bù shā)."
When the ploughman's life ended, he was born into a Guówáng's (King's) family.
The Huánghòu (Queen), with her entourage, went to the edge of a flowing stream.
They sang, danced, and made music. Holding the infant, she approached the water.
She accidentally dropped the child into the water, and a fish immediately swallowed it.
Inside the belly for seven days, the child was neither hungry nor thirsty.
Following the current, it drifted down for over a thousand *lǐ*.
Entering the border of a lower Guó (State), people caught the fish and traded it in the market.
At that time, the ruler (Zhǔ) of the lower Guó sent someone to buy the fish in the market.
Bringing it back inside the city, they used a knife to prepare the fish.
The child, inside the belly, cried out,
"Slowly, slowly! Do not harm me!"
They immediately cut open the fish's belly and saw a small child.
The child was peerlessly handsome, and the entire Guó rejoiced.
The ruler (Zhǔ) of the upper Guó heard of this and said,
"This must be my son."
He sent an envoy to request him.
The ruler (Zhǔ) of the lower Guó replied,
"Found in the fish's belly, he is a gift bestowed by Heaven."
"I am unwilling to give him up."
The two Guó contended with each other, and the dispute reached a Dàguó (Great State).
The Dàwáng (Great King) judged, saying,
"If the upper Guó had not given birth to this child and he had not fallen into the water, how could the lower Guó have obtained him?"
"If the lower Guó had not obtained this child,"
"where would the upper Guó have sought him?"
"These two states have an affinity [with the child]."
"You two Guó,"
"should build a Gōngdiàn (palace) in between, where this child may reside jointly."
"He shall be titled the Tàizǐ (Crown Prince) of Both Guó."
He then followed this intention and stayed there,
adhering to the ceremonies and laws of a Tàizǐ.
The Fó (Buddha) told his disciples,
"The ploughman of former days,
by giving one fruit and one coin in Dāna (bù shī) to the Dàorén,
consequently obtained the position of the Tàizǐ of Both Guó."
Formerly there was a lame-footed Dàorén.
He upheld the precepts (chíjiè) and begged for food, happening upon a certain household.
A believer in the Great Dharma (Dàfǎ), having long seen his afflicted foot,
felt compassion in his heart and offered Gōngyǎng (support) for one year.
The Dàorén took his leave.
The master of the house said,
"I hope you will often honor me with your presence."
At the time of parting, the guest and host wept sadly.
After the Dàorén left,
the master of the house lifted up his couch and saw only gold and treasures (jīnbǎo).
Because of this, he became extremely wealthy.
A neighboring household saw his great wealth
and asked for the cause (yīnyuán).
That man truthfully answered.
The neighbor, having evil thoughts, wished to obtain rare treasures (zhēnbǎo).
He immediately sought a lame person to offer Gōngyǎng to.
After searching everywhere, there was none.
Coincidentally, a Dàorén whose body was whole arrived.
[The neighbor] tied him up, broke his leg, and offered Gōngyǎng for a short time.
He then forcibly drove him away.
After the Dàorén left, [the neighbor] lifted up his couch.
Due to the influence (gǎn) of his evil intention (èxīn),
venomous snakes, bees, and scorpions came and stung the entire family.
He received wicked retribution (èbào) in this life and later entered Dìyù (Hell).
The one who obtained the rare treasures was upright and benevolent in his heart (zhēnjí).
The one who was stung by the poison was unkind in his heart (bù rén).
In the past, there were two people, a sister and a younger brother.
The sister had one son.
Both he and his maternal uncle worked for the government (or imperial court).
They wove silk brocade with gold thread, fine silk, gauze, and magnificent, unique garments, stored among precious silks and treasures.
Then they discussed, saying:
"We have worked diligently and tirelessly at weaving.
We know the quality and quantity of all the stored goods.
Is it not better that we take and use some together to relieve our poverty?"
That night, they dug a hole in the ground and crept in to steal the goods.
The next morning, the keeper of the treasury noticed that the goods were diminished.
He reported the matter to the King (Wáng).
The King (Wáng) commanded that it should not be widely publicized.
He ordered that the thieves should think the King (Wáng) was preoccupied and unable to detect them.
They would certainly return again in the coming days.
Furthermore, the guards must be strictly vigilant; those who catch the thieves must arrest them and not let them escape.
The treasury keeper received the order.
He immediately increased security.
After some time, the men indeed returned to steal again.
The nephew instructed the maternal uncle (jiù):
"Your age is advanced, your body is weak, and your strength is small.
If you are caught by the guards, you will be unable to escape.
So, enter the hole walking backward.
Should we be seen and caught,
my strength is great, and I will be able to rescue and free you."
The maternal uncle (jiù) hesitated and then entered the hole, whereupon he was seized by the guards.
The captors called out.
The nephew feared being recognized.
He cut off his maternal uncle's (jiù) head and fled.
At dawn, the treasury keeper fully reported the events.
The King (Wáng) again issued an edict, saying:
"Carry out the corpse and place it openly at the crossroads.
Anyone who weeps over it or takes the dead body, we will know is the thief."
Many days passed like this.
A merchant (gǔkè) from a distant land arrived.
People and horses blocked the road, rushing forward and crowding together aggressively.
That person loaded two carts of firewood and placed them on top of the corpse.
They reported the situation fully to the King (Wáng).
The King (Wáng) commanded:
"If anyone sets it alight, capture and bind him and send him here."
The nephew was about to instruct the young servants to hold torches and dance playfully.
The crowd gathered and threw fire onto the firewood.
The flames became raging and intense.
The guards did not notice.
They reported the situation fully to the King (Wáng).
The King (Wáng) again issued an edict, saying:
"Increase the number of guards.
Strictly watch for his bones."
The nephew then brewed pure wine.
He specifically made it thick and strong.
He went to the guards
and sold it quietly.
The guards had been hungry and thirsty for many days.
Seeing the wine, they drank it together.
Having drunk too much, they all fell into a drunken sleep.
The nephew then used the wine jars to collect the bones
and departed.
The guards did not notice.
The next morning, they reported again to the King (Wáng).
The King (Wáng) again issued an edict, saying:
"Despite the previous alerts and guards, they have failed to capture him.
This thief is cunning and clever; we must devise another plan."
The King (Wáng) then presented his daughter, adorned with splendid jewels, pearl necklaces, and precious ornaments.
He built her chamber beside a great river.
Many people served as guards, watching carefully for anything unusual.
There must be someone attracted by her beauty who comes to her.
The daughter had been previously instructed that if she caught hold of him, she should call people to seize and arrest him.
Another night, the nephew secretly approached.
He released a log (or wooden float) into the water, letting it flow downstream.
He shouted and raced to hide.
The guards were startled and hurried out, thinking there was an intruder.
But they only saw the log.
This continued repeatedly for several nights.
The guards fell asleep.
The nephew then rode the log to the daughter's chamber.
The daughter immediately grabbed his clothing.
The nephew told the daughter:
"You may seize my arm."
The nephew had previously taken a dead person's arm and handed it to her.
The daughter released the clothing, seized the arm, and shouted loudly.
When the guards woke up, the nephew had managed to escape and run away.
The next morning, they reported fully to the King (Wáng).
The King (Wáng) again issued an edict, saying:
"This person’s ingenious methods are unrivaled among hundreds.
We have sought to capture him for a long time without success.
What should we do?"
The daughter immediately became pregnant.
Ten months later, she gave birth to a boy.
He was extremely handsome and proper.
He commanded the wet nurse to carry the child and travel throughout the kingdom.
If anyone made a soothing sound (or cooed) to the child, they were to be bound and brought in.
She carried the child all day long.
The nephew was a pastry maker, living near the bread oven.
The little child cried from hunger.
The wet nurse carried the child toward the bread oven.
She bought a cake (or biscuit) and fed the child.
The nephew saw the child being soothed.
She immediately returned and reported to the King (Wáng), saying:
"The child walked all day, and no one came near him.
When he was hungry and passed the bread oven,
the seller of the cakes gave him a cake and only then did he coo."
The King (Wáng) again issued an edict, saying:
"Why did you not bind him?"
The wet nurse replied:
"The little child cried from hunger, and the pastry maker gave him a cake and soothed him; this should not mean he is the thief."
The King (Wáng) ordered the wet nurse to carry the child out again, along with all the observers.
Anyone seen approaching the child was to be bound and brought in.
The nephew sold fine wine.
He invited the wet nurse and the observers to the wine shop and urged them to drink wine.
When they were greatly drunk and asleep, he stole the child and left.
When they awoke and realized the child was missing,
they reported fully to the King (Wáng).
The King (Wáng) again issued an edict, saying:
"You are dull, foolish, and greedy for this wild liquid (wine)! Not only did you fail to capture the thief, but you also lost the child!"
The nephew, having obtained the child, carried him to another country.
He presented himself before the King (Guówáng).
He presented divination and expressed thanks, answering questions, citing classics, and explaining doctrines.
The King (Wáng) was greatly pleased.
He immediately bestowed upon him a high position and salary, making him a great minister (dàchén).
And he said to him:
"In my entire country, there is no one whose wisdom and ingenuity can match yours.
I wish to match you with either the daughter of a court official or my own daughter—you may choose whatever you desire."
He replied: "I dare not presume."
"If the King (Wáng) pities me, I wish to seek the daughter of a certain King (Wáng) from another country."
The King (Wáng) said, "Excellent!
I will grant your wish."
The King (Wáng) adopted him as his son.
He sent envoys to request the daughter of that other King (Wáng).
That King (Wáng) consented.
The King (Wáng) then thought:
"This might be that charming thief, who was so cunning before and after."
He immediately sent an envoy
to welcome his daughter.
He sent his crown prince (tàizǐ) with five hundred cavalry, all strictly organized and prepared.
The nephew felt fear.
He feared that upon arriving in that country,
the King (Wáng) would surely seize him.
He then reported to his King (Wáng):
"If the King (Wáng) sends me,
you must provide five hundred riders and horses, complete with clothing, saddles, and bridles, without any difference among them.
Only then can I welcome the bride."
The King (Wáng) agreed to his words.
He immediately went to welcome the bride.
The King (Wáng) ordered his daughter to offer food and drink to receive the guest.
Two hundred and fifty riders were in the front,
and two hundred and fifty riders were in the rear.
The nephew was in the middle, sitting astride his horse, not dismounting.
The bride's father personally went among the riders,
seized the nephew, and said:
"Were you that person who used clever tricks before and after, whom we could not capture?
Was it you, or was it not?"
He bowed his head and replied:
"It was."
The King (Wáng) said:
"Your wisdom and cleverness are unmatched throughout the world.
According to your wish, I will betroth my daughter to you so that you may become husband and wife."
The nephew is Wú (I, the Buddha).
The bride's father, the King (Wáng), is Shèlìfú.
The maternal uncle (jiù) is Tiáodá.
The King's (Guówáng) adoptive father is Shūtóután.
The mother is Móyé.
The wife is Jūyí.
The son is Luóyún.
In the past, there was the kingdom of Qíshéjúe Guó.
There was a young woman.
Her appearance was beautiful, and her talent and intelligence were unmatched.
Her temperament was gentle and harmonious, and she never became angry.
Her household, her nine generations of kin, and all distant and near acquaintances loved and respected her.
Suitors from various kingdoms, numbering hundreds and thousands of people,
ultimately did not succeed in marrying her.
At that time, there was a young man from the kingdom of Luōyuè Guó.
His natural disposition was brilliant and outstanding, and his intentions were lofty and transcendent.
The citizens of the country all feared and respected him.
Although he had concubines and wives, he never favored or approached them.
He often thought:
"The woman in Qíshéjúe Guó
is truly my match.
I just haven't gone there yet."
Immediately
that day, he declared: "All those filling the hall were acquired through influence and wealth; they are not my proper companions."
In an instant, he sent them away and cleared everyone out.
He then rode a white elephant, accompanied by two servants, and set out for that kingdom.
He crossed mountains and traversed grasslands, traveling thousands of miles.
Only after five years did he arrive.
The woman, dwelling in her deep palace, felt her heart strangely stirred.
Thus, she went out to stroll freely.
She attempted to peer into the outer chambers.
Suddenly, she saw this man.
She was both sorrowful and joyful, unable to restrain herself.
"This is my husband.
The suitors I saw before were not my destined partners."
She immediately became personally attached to him, her feelings of wifely affection clinging to him.
The woman's parents were worried and distressed, having no plan, saying:
"We raised our daughter until adulthood, but we never expected this to happen."
They urgently increased surveillance and isolation, preventing communication.
The woman was frustrated and didn't know what to do.
The man was sorrowful and distraught, both harboring feelings of melancholy confusion.
Thereupon, the woman devoted herself to ascetic practice, keeping vegetarian fasts and following the path day and night.
She gave away and scattered her wealth, donating to the Buddha and the Saṅgha.
Her mind was weary and her body withered; five years passed.
No news reached the other party, though both held affection for each other.
Ultimately, nothing materialized.
Then, on the eighth day of the fourth month,
she personally bound her body and went to the Buddha's stūpa.
Burning incense and bowing, she made this vow:
"I will carve and cut my flesh to make offerings to the World-Honored One.
I dare not spare myself.
I only wish that this resolve may find fruition."
The Buddha ordered a Bhikṣuṇī to create the conditions for her.
Then they were able to be harmoniously coupled.
The Buddha told Ānán:
"Why is this so?
It is because, since countless kalpas (Asaṃkhyeya Kalpas) ago,
they have long established their vow and commitment, which is why they attained this result."
In the past, there was a couple.
They shared three fruits (Lí).
Each person took one piece.
The remaining one they wished to break and divide.
The wife said:
"Do not divide it.
Let us bet on it.
We will both remain silent.
The first to speak loses.
The one who speaks later wins."
Thereupon, they closed their mouths until midnight.
A thief (Dòu Tǔ) broke in secretly.
He saw the two of them sitting without speaking.
Thinking they were greatly afraid, he dared not make a sound.
He gathered their belongings, put them on his shoulders, and started taking them out the door.
The wife shouted loudly:
"You are the husband! Why do you allow him to take our belongings away?"
The husband said:
"I win! I win!
Now I get the big fruit!"
Everyone criticized and laughed at them, calling them utterly crazy and foolish.
In the past, there was a man.
He saw that another man's wife's nose was well-shaped.
He thought to himself:
"My wife's face is peerless,
but I only regret that her nose is ugly.
I shall now take this nose and replace my wife's nose with it."
He immediately led the woman to a secluded spot,
cut off her nose, and took it back.
He also cut off his own wife's nose and attempted to attach this other woman's nose.
Both women lost their noses, and the two noses did not fit.
Everyone found this strange and cursed him, saying he was truly crazy and mad.
In the past, there was an extremely poor man.
He was skilled in understanding the language of birds.
He was hired by a merchant (Jiǎ Kè) to carry burdens.
As they passed a waterside, they stopped to drink.
A crow cried out.
The merchant was frightened,
but the hired man laughed instead.
When they arrived home, the merchant asked:
"I was drinking there.
When I heard the crow cry out,
I was greatly frightened, yet why did you laugh instead?"
He replied:
"The crow was speaking to me, saying:
'The merchant has a beautiful white pearl on his body.
You should kill him and take the pearl,
and I want to eat his flesh.'
That is why I laughed."
[The merchant] said: "Why did you not kill me?"
He replied:
"Because in a former life, I was poor and earned a living carrying burdens due to my greed for other people's wealth.
If I kill someone again and take their property, I will suffer in the next life.
When will that ever end?
I will not do this, even unto death."
A great flood suddenly engulfed the land.
All living beings relied on mounds to avoid it.
When the mounds were also on the verge of submerging,
suddenly there was a Fènghuáng (Phoenix).
It arrived at the wise man's location, and he clung to its wings.
Consequently, they ascended to high ground and escaped the calamity of the water.
The remaining people who had not yet left [the mound]
suddenly saw a Lúcí (Cormorant) and entrusted themselves to its feathers.
However, this Lúcí immediately plunged into the deep water,
and they all drowned at once.
In the past, there was a man.
He was poor and useless.
To earn a living, he entered the sea to gather treasures and returned to his country.
He met a good spiritual advisor (Shàn Zhīshì) and said:
"I have always been poor, but now I have obtained this treasure.
It is enough for me to settle down.
If my mother is against this,
I intend to abandon my mother and leave.
If my wife is against this,
I intend to seek another."
The advisor replied:
"Nearby, there are highly wise people filling the city.
You can go and buy wisdom from them.
It will cost no more than a thousand ounces of gold.
They will naturally tell you the method of wisdom."
The man followed his words.
He entered the village where the Buddha's followers dwelled.
He fully questioned the people there.
They replied:
"When in doubt about a matter,
walk forward seven steps and walk backward seven steps.
If you repeat this three times, wisdom will naturally arise."
The man returned home that night.
He saw his mother sleeping next to his wife.
He thought it was another man.
He drew his knife, intending to kill.
He felt unsettled in his heart.
He lit a large lamp, shone it from afar, and contemplated.
"I bought wisdom this morning."
Thus, he walked forward and backward three times.
His mother then woke up.
The man exclaimed:
"This is truly wisdom!
How can it only be worth a thousand ounces of gold?"
He immediately gave them three thousand ounces of gold.
In the past, there was a man walking in the mountains.
He met a man-eating ghost (Dànrén Guǐ).
The ghost grabbed him, intending to eat him.
The man pleaded for mercy, saying:
"Allow me a moment to ask one question.
If you eat me afterward, I will have no regrets."
The ghost believed the man, thinking it was a sincere request.
It granted his wish.
He immediately asked the ghost:
"Why is your face white, and your legs, knees, and abdomen white,
while the rest of your body is all black?"
The ghost immediately replied:
"My nature is evil and avoids the essence of the sun.
I can move with my back to the sun, but I cannot face the sun.
This is why it is so."
The man ran toward the sun.
The ghost was left with empty regret and could not catch him.
In the past, there was a man engaged in two trades.
He had two wives, and he went to visit the younger wife.
The younger wife spoke to him:
"I am young,
but my husband is old.
I am not happy here.
You should go and live at the elder wife's place."
The husband plucked out his white hairs.
When he arrived at the elder wife's place,
the elder wife spoke to him:
"I am old, and my head is already white.
My husband's head being black is unsuitable for me."
Thereupon, he plucked out the black hairs to make the rest white.
He did not stop,
and consequently, his head became completely bald.
Both wives disliked this.
So they both abandoned him and left.
Overwhelmed by grief, he died.
In a past life, he became a dog living in a monastery.
There was one monastery east of the water and one monastery west of the water.
When the wooden fish drum (jiànchuí) sounded, the dog would go and receive food.
On a later day, both monasteries simultaneously sounded their stone chimes (qìng).
The dog floated on the water, wanting to cross.
Just as it wanted to reach the west, it feared the food at the eastern monastery was better.
Turning toward the east, it again feared the food at the western monastery was better.
Thus, caught in this hesitation, it drowned in the water.
In the past, there was a man.
He heard that a foreign country had immortal water (Xiān Shuǐ), and entering it granted immortality (Xiān).
So he went toward that foreign country and lodged at someone else’s house.
The host asked the guest,
“Where do you intend to go?”
He replied, “To learn the way of immortality (Xué Xiān).”
The host harbored malicious intent.
He said to the guest,
“I possess an immortal tree (Xiān Shù).
If you can work hard for me for one year,
I will grant you immortality (Xiān); why trouble yourself to go far away?”
The guest said, “That is excellent.”
He worked hard for one year, constantly without any expression of resentment.
When the year was complete,
the host intended to deceive him.
Since he did not possess an immortal tree (Xiān Shù),
he led him deep into the mountains, pointed to a tree near a cliff, and said, “This is the immortal tree (Xiān Shù).
Climb to its top.
When I call out for you to fly, you should leap out and fly in response.”
The guest’s heart was sincere.
He immediately flew high into the empty sky from that tree,
and thus attained the Way of Immortality (Xiān Dào).
The host saw, “I meant for him to die,
but how did he attain immortality (Xiān)?”
He deeply respected this tree, believing it truly to be sacred (Shèng).
After a short time passed,
the father and his son went together beneath the tree.
The son deferred to his father to climb first.
The son then called out, “Ā Yé (Father), you can fly!”
The father immediately tried to fly,
but fell onto the rocks below.
His body was shattered.
In the past, there was a man
who was selling a *Pí Yé* demon (Guǐ) in the marketplace.
The person wishing to buy the demon (Guǐ) asked how much he sought.
The demon master (Guǐ Zhǔ) said,
“Two hundred *liǎng* of gold.”
He said,
“What is so strange and wonderful about this demon (Guǐ),
that you seek so much gold?”
He replied,
“This demon’s (Guǐ) skill is such that there is nothing it cannot do.
We calculate that one day’s work equals that of a hundred men.
It only has one fault (Bìng).
You should guard against it first.”
He asked, “What kind of fault is it?”
He replied,
“When this demon (Guǐ) needs to be made to work,
you must employ it day and night;
do not allow it to stop and rest.
If there is nothing for it to do, it will instead harm its master.”
The master (Zhǔ Rén) took the demon (Guǐ) for the price of the gold and returned home.
He ordered it to plant the fields.
When the planting was finished, he ordered it to do carpentry.
When the carpentry was finished, he ordered it again to level the ground.
It built houses, pounded grain, milled flour, and cooked meals, never resting for a moment.
Within a few years, he became greatly wealthy.
The master (Zhǔ Rén) had some business and had to travel.
He forgot to give the demon (Guǐ) instructions, and the demon (Guǐ) wanted to work again, but there were no orders for it to follow.
It took the master’s (Zhǔ Rén) son, placed him inside a pot, lit a fire, and boiled him.
By the time the master (Zhǔ Rén) returned, his son was thoroughly cooked.
Grieved and remorseful, he did not know what more to say.
In the past, there was a rich man (Fù Rén).
The king (Wáng) commanded him to list his property.
He immediately prepared a list:
“In a certain year, I spent X tens of millions to construct Buddhas (Fó).
I spent X to hold vegetarian feasts (Zhāi Huì) and copy scriptures.
Furthermore, I used X to provide relief for the poor and elderly.
Currently, I possess 89 million.”
He presented the list to the king (Wáng).
The king (Wáng) was greatly enraged and furious and asked,
“You suddenly listed property that has already been spent, not what you currently possess.”
The rich man (Fù Rén) replied,
“What has been spent is the greatest treasure (Bǎo Zàng).
It provides for one’s spiritual consciousness (Shén Míng), and that is why I humbly present it.
Wealth that has not yet been used is shared by the five families (Wǔ Jiā).
It does not belong exclusively to your subject.
Therefore, I dared to list it thus.”
The king (Wáng) then became enlightened:
Virtuous merit (Gōng Dé) is truly reliable.
In the past, there was a man who committed a crime against the king (Wáng).
The king (Wáng) was greatly enraged and furious.
He ordered men to cut five *jīn* of flesh from his back.
He was placed in a lower dwelling.
This man’s painful cries reached the king (Wáng).
The king (Wáng) asked, “Why are his cries unceasing?”
He replied,
“Truly, it was not my crime.”
The king (Wáng) reflected and was ashamed of his action.
He commanded that one hundred *jīn* of meat be given to him.
Yet, the man still groaned and cried out.
The king (Wáng) said,
“He has been given a sudden replacement of a hundred *jīn*; why is he crying so loudly?”
The various officials replied,
“He does not perceive this as a remedy.
What good is giving him a thousand *jīn* for his pain?
If a man’s one son has died,
and another person gives him a hundred [sons]—
can this person fail to mourn his own son?”
There were two men who were acquaintances (Zhī Shì).
Their wives were both pregnant.
They immediately made a mutual pledge
that if they produced a boy and a girl, they would be joined in marriage (Hūn Yīn).
After separating, one family bore a boy and the other bore a girl.
The boy’s father died early, and the boy grew up without having married.
He traveled, selling various goods, and happened to arrive at the girl’s family home.
The girl’s father (Gōng) asked, “Son, where do you come from?
Where do you reside? What are your parents’ surnames and given names?”
The boy answered fully.
The father (Gōng) heard this and was greatly surprised.
He then said to the boy,
“When your father was alive, he and I arranged a prenatal marriage (Tāi Hūn).
I have constantly sought you but did not know where you were.
My daughter (Chǔ Nǚ) has not dared to marry yet.”
The boy said,
“I knew nothing about the girl.”
The father (Gōng) said,
“Ask your close relatives.”
The boy returned and asked his wet nurse, and indeed it was true.
The boy traveled to the girl’s house.
On the road, he saw ditch water flowing
into a skull (Dú Lóu), but there was no time when it was full.
The boy, afraid, walked forward and saw ripe fruit on a tree.
He wanted to pick and eat it.
The fruit then said,
“Take me, take me!”
The boy was greatly terrified and ran quickly, tripping and falling to the ground.
He arrived at the girl’s house.
A dog came forward, knelt upright, and licked his two feet.
The puppies inside the dog’s belly cried out loudly and came forward,
trying to injure and bite him.
He immediately fell back to the ground and revived only after a long time.
The girl’s father (Gōng) came out, and the boy recounted everything.
The father (Gōng) was very surprised and went inside to tell his daughter.
The daughter replied to her father (Gōng): “As for seeing the ditch water flowing into the skull (Dú Lóu) without ever being full—
in a future generation (Hòu Shì), people will gather
all the wealth, goods, treasures, and jewels (Zhēn Bǎo) of the world, supplying them to one person, yet he will never be satisfied.
As for seeing the ripe fruit on the tree, wanting to pick and eat it,
and the fruit saying, ‘Take me, take me!’—
In a future generation (Hòu Shì), people will seek older daughters,
but the younger daughters will say,
‘Why don’t you seek me? Why don’t you seek me?’
As for the dog coming forward, kneeling upright, and licking his two feet,
and the puppies inside the dog’s belly crying out and coming forward trying to bite him—
In a future generation (Hòu Shì), people will speak to each other
with mouths like lard (Zhī Gāo, meaning smooth and oily speech), but hearts like awls and knives.
They satisfy each other with their words, but inwardly plot against one another.
All these things are predictions for a future generation (Hòu Shì), not for the present.”
The father immediately married the girl to the boy,
thus fulfilling their original intention (Běn Zhì).
In the past, a prestigious family (Dà Xìng) had two sons.
He gave each two million coins to engage in trade (Xíng Gǔ).
The elder son spent it all on gambling (Chū Pú).
His clothing was worn and ragged when he returned and reported to his father.
The father said,
“I am content just to have you back.
What use is wealth?”
He provided him with clothing, bedding, food, and drink,
and comforted him kindly.
The younger son returned and reported to his father:
“I have gained a profit of two million.”
The father said,
“Bring the receipts.”
He examined the accounts with him, and finding a discrepancy of several thousand,
he immediately bound and flogged him.
This happened three times.
He accumulated a profit of six million,
but whenever he returned, he was beaten.
The elder son, in three trips, lost six million.
He stayed in a foreign country (Tā Guó) and did not return.
He associated with a scoundrel.
He said to that man,
“My father has one casket each of gold, silver, and white pearls,
placed at the head of the main bed.
You go back and tell my father,
‘I was not foolish enough to lose the money and goods;
I dare not return.’
When you have the opportunity, kill my father and bring the goods here,
so we can share them.”
This man arrived at the house and met the father.
He relayed the son’s message.
The father heard this, wept, and said,
“What use are objects and wealth?
Why does my son not come back?”
He choked with grief when eating and breathing.
The traveler (Kè) said,
“Your son (Jūn Zǐ) is unfilial; he used the money to commit evil
and lost it all immediately.
He ordered me to come and kill you and take your gold and silver.
But I see how much you miss your son and how kindly you treat me,
which moves my heart.”
The father said,
“The boy is still foolish.” He immediately sent someone to welcome him back.
He told his son,
“You lost the money, but return quickly.
Why did you speak such foolish words?”
He made new clothing and bedding and gave it to him.
The Master (Shī) said:
“The younger son was repaying a debt.
The elder son was seeking a debt.”
In the past, there were three men who traveled together as merchants.
Each divided and obtained over five million [units of wealth].
If one coin were to be given to one person,
then it would be unfair.
If they wanted to break it apart and divide it,
that matter was not feasible.
At that time, a Shāmén was begging for food.
The three men together spoke of giving alms to the Shāmén, and each said it was excellent.
They held it together in their hands and gave it.
The Shāmén pronounced a blessing,
saying, "May you obtain this merit in this life and subsequent lives."
They were reborn together in Luóyuèguó, and each attained great wealth.
One man specialized in mining gold in the mountains.
One man specialized in plowing fields to obtain gold.
One man specialized in drawing gold from the water.
This was due to receiving the merit of the alms given in their previous lives.
The Wáng heard of this.
He thought, "The people and goods of my country are all mine."
He then led his soldiers and went to the mountains to mine it.
The gold transformed into stone.
Next, he went to the land of the second family,
which yielded gold when plowed.
The gold transformed into earth.
Next, he went to the well of the third family to draw the gold.
The gold transformed into tiles.
He could not obtain any of it.
The Wáng asked the Fó,
saying, "I calculated that the gold of these three men belongs to me.
When I went to take it, it all transformed, and I could not obtain the gold.
What merit did these men have in their previous lives to achieve this fortune now?"
The Fó fully explained it,
saying, "It is not the property of the Wáng.
The Wáng should not take it."
In the past, there was a poor family who made offerings to a Daorén (cultivator).
After one year, the Daorén left.
He used a bronze vase and requested the host, saying,
"This vase is struck by a spirit.
Whatever is requested from the mouth of this vase will be obtained.
Do not invite the Wáng."
After they parted, the family struck the vase.
The family gradually became immensely rich.
They forgot the Daorén's instruction,
and consequently invited the Wáng.
The Wáng asked the cause of their wealth.
They answered the Wáng truthfully.
The Wáng immediately seized the vase.
The family then became extremely impoverished.
Only then did they recall the Daorén and searched everywhere until they found him.
They reported the facts to him.
The Daorén said,
"I deliberately required this vase.
I beg you for one earthen pot filled with trees and stones.
Take it and go to the Wáng's gate to ask for the vase."
When he reached the Wáng's gate, he loudly demanded the vase.
The Wáng heard this and became greatly enraged.
He dispatched dozens of people to try and capture him.
When the pot was opened, trees and stones flew horizontally through the air, driven by the wind.
The Wáng's servants, being hit by these trees and stones, had their heads broken, and quickly one thousand people perished.
The corpses of those broken by the force of the wind blocked the gate.
The Wáng was greatly terrified and distressed.
He begged to return the vase.
That man obtained the vase.
His family was again greatly wealthy.
He extensively performed meritorious deeds.
When he died, he gained rebirth in heaven.
The Fó and Ānán entered Wángshěchéng.
At that time, there was heavy rain.
The water washed out hidden treasures, revealing various valuables.
The Fó said, "Poisonous snake."
Ānán said, "Evil, poisonous snake."
A man cutting wheat beneath the mountain heard this and thought,
"I have never seen a Shāmén's poisonous snake."
He immediately went and saw the treasures.
He used a cart and cloth bags to collect them and store them inside his house.
He displayed signs of wealth and built a new large residence.
Jealous people informed the Wáng,
saying, "There was formerly a poor and lowly man who suddenly showed signs of wealth.
This person must have obtained a great treasure hoard."
The Wáng immediately summoned him and questioned him.
He replied that he had not obtained anything.
The Wáng immediately commanded that he be tortured.
This man recalled that the Fó and Ānán had called it an evil, poisonous snake.
Who, having obtained a treasure hoard, would not speak of it?
He wholeheartedly invoked the Fó.
The Wáng spoke these words:
"The Fó called it a poisonous snake.
Ānán called it an evil, poisonous snake."
The Wáng immediately called and questioned him.
The man replied,
"Great Wáng,
if you grant me fearlessness, I shall speak the truth."
The Wáng agreed.
He fully recounted the previous matter.
"What can it do to my body now?
It must devour my life."
The Wáng rewarded him with five hundred gold coins,
for being able, in his distress, to speak the words of the Fó and Ānán.
In the past, there was an old man, poor, cold, and solitary.
His family had no independent livelihood.
He happened upon an axe in the market.
It was the essence of all jewels,
but he did not recognize it.
He used it to chop firewood and sell it to sustain his meager life.
The use of the axe was nearly finished.
He happened to meet a great merchant from a foreign country,
named Sàbó.
Sàbó saw the axe and recognized it.
He then asked the old man,
"Will you sell this axe?"
The old man said,
"I rely on this axe to live; I will not sell it."
Sàbó further said,
"I will give you a hundred bolts of silk; why will you not sell it?"
The old man did not agree.
Sàbó further said,
"I will give you two hundred bolts."
The old man became dejected and unhappy.
Sàbó further said,
"If you think it is too little, I will increase it.
Why are you unhappy?
I will give you five hundred bolts."
The old man then wept bitterly.
Sàbó further said,
"If the silk is too little, I will increase it.
Why are you weeping?"
The old man said,
"I do not resent the small amount of silk; I resent my foolish ignorance.
This axe was originally one and a half cubits long.
I have used it up by chopping wood, and only five inches remain.
Yet, I still received five hundred bolts of silk.
This is what I regret."
Sàbó further said,
"Do not hold onto regret.
Now I will give you a thousand bolts of silk."
He immediately broke the agreement [by increasing the payment] and took it away.
When he burned it in firewood, it all transformed into precious jewels.
The Shìzūn entered Shèwèichéng in the morning.
The Zūnzhě Ānán followed him.
There were two old husband and wife,
aged, with senses fully developed, and hunched backs like hooks.
They went to the street corner where refuse was burned.
They both squatted facing the fire, like old cranes.
They looked at each other with desire in their hearts.
The Fó told Ānán,
"Do you see that couple?"
Ānán replied,
"Yes."
The Fó said,
"This old husband and wife,
if, during their youth and vigorous prime,
they had diligently sought wealth, they would have become the richest people in Shèwèichéng.
If they had left home to study the path and diligently cultivated practice, they would have attained Āluóhànship.
If, during their second period of vigor and prime,
they had diligently sought wealth, they would have become the second richest people in Shèwèichéng.
If they had left home to study the path, they would have attained the fruit of Ānàhán.
If, during middle age, they had diligently sought wealth,
they would have become the third richest people in Shèwèichéng.
If they had left home to study the path, they would have attained the fruit of Sītuóhán.
But now, today, they are old and their senses are fully declining.
They have no money, and they have no means.
They are no longer capable.
They painfully search for money,
but they also cannot attain the Dharma that surpasses humanity."
He further spoke a verse, saying:
Because they did not practice pure conduct, they did not obtain wealth in their youth,
thinking of ancient matters, sleeping on the ground like a bent bow.
Not having cultivated pure conduct, nor obtained wealth in their youth,
they are like old cranes, guarding death in an empty pond
In the kingdom of Yēlì Guó there was Jiāluóyuè.
He offered provisions to the Buddha, and after the invocation and vows were finished,
he requested to hear the meaning of the Dharma.
The Buddha smiled, and a light issued from his mouth, circling his body three times, and then re-entered through the crown of his head.
Ānán asked the reason.
The Buddha said,
“In that country, there were five hundred men
who entered the sea to gather treasures, placed them on a ship, and returned on foot.
They traveled through deep mountains and stopped to rest when dusk fell.
They prepared early to depart at dawn.
Four hundred ninety-nine men all left.
One man slept deeply.
He lost his companions.
Then he encountered snow falling from the sky.
He lost the trail.
Stranded and distressed in the mountains, he cried and called upon Heaven.
There was a Zhāntán tree spirit.
It spoke to the stranded man, saying,
‘You may stop and remain here.
I will provide you with clothing and food.
You may leave when spring arrives.’
The stranded man stayed for three months.
He addressed the tree spirit, saying,
‘I have received your kindness and was able to save my life.
I have not yet been able to offer a small recompense.
I recall that my two parents are now in my homeland.
I truly wish to see them.
I pray that you will graciously send me forth.’
The tree spirit said, ‘Good.’
It bestowed golden cakes upon him.
‘Not far from here,
you will reach a country and city.
You will then be able to return to your village and hometown.’
As the stranded man was about to leave, he asked the tree spirit,
‘This tree is fragrant and pure, rarely seen in the world.
Now that I am leaving far away, I wish to know its name.’
The spirit said,
‘You do not need to ask.’
The stranded man replied again,
‘I have relied on the shade of this tree for three full months.
Now that I must depart far away, my heart is regretful and sorrowful.
If I reach my native country, I shall proclaim the tree’s kindness.’
The spirit then said,
‘The tree’s name is Zhāntán.
Its roots, trunk, branches, and leaves cure all diseases of men.
Its fragrance travels far, and people covet it; you do not need to speak of it.’
The stranded man arrived in his country.
His inner and outer relatives happily celebrated and consoled him.
Later, the king of the country fell ill with a headache.
Prayers and sacrifices offered to the gods of Heaven, Earth, mountains, and water could not alleviate the sickness.
Famous doctors examined him and determined that only the fragrance of Zhāntán could cure the disease.
The King immediately sought it out, but none was available among the people.
He then issued a decree throughout the country:
‘Whoever obtains Zhāntán fragrance,
will be appointed and granted the title of Marquis, and I shall give him my youngest daughter in marriage.’
At that time, the stranded man heard that the reward was heavy.
He then said,
‘I know the location of the Zhāntán fragrance.’
The King then commanded a close official to take the stranded man and go cut down and retrieve it.
They went directly to the tree’s location.
The envoy saw that the tree was vast and straight,
its branches and twigs lush and abundant, and its flowers and fruits resplendent.
It was rarely seen by men, and he could not bear to cut it down.
If he did not cut it down, he would violate the King's command.
The disease would not be cured.
If he cut it down, his heart would ache slightly.
He hesitated and paced back and forth, not knowing what to do.
The tree spirit spoke from the air,
‘Go ahead and cut it down.
Just leave the roots.
After cutting, smear it with human blood.
Cover it with the liver and intestines.
The tree will naturally grow,
and return to its former state.’
When the envoy heard the spirit’s words,
he immediately ordered men to cut it down.
The stranded man stood by the tree.
A branch of the tree sprang up from the ground and struck him dead.
The envoy and his men discussed it together.
They butchered the stranded man, taking his liver and blood.
As commanded by the spirit, the tree immediately grew again.
They loaded the cut wood onto carts and returned to the country.
The doctor immediately administered the medicine.
The King’s illness was cured.
The whole country rejoiced.
The King ordered the people throughout the country:
‘All those who are sick shall go to the palace gate.’
The King offered the fragrant medicine to them.
Their illnesses were all cured.
The King’s body was healthy and joyful, and the common people were free from sickness.
The whole country was happy and celebrated, thereby achieving Great Peace.
Once, there was a man walking in an empty marsh.
He saw a black elephant.
The man thought,
‘This elephant will surely come and harm me.
I must kill it.’
The elephant also thought,
‘This man will certainly kill me.
I must constrain him.’
The man immediately left.
The elephant pursued him from behind.
He ran several miles ahead and fell into a deep valley.
The valley was steep and bottomless.
He immediately grasped a tree root at the edge of the cliff.
It was shaped like a finger.
Following the root down,
he hung suspended by the cliffside.
