The elephant, from the top of the valley, reached for him with its trunk.
It almost reached him, but did not quite touch him.
Looking downwards, he saw that the bottom was only poisonous snakes and venomous creatures, and furthermore, two mice were gnawing on the tree root together.
Moreover, three black snakes thrust out their heads, ready to bite him.
Furthermore, mosquitoes and gadflies came to sting his eyes.
The man thought,
‘Today I shall die.’
He looked up to Heaven and pleaded for help.
His voice was sorrowful, and his sincerity reached its peak.
Heaven sent down sweet dew, which dripped into his mouth.
As soon as he received one drop, the two mice departed.
When he received the second drop, the venomous snakes abandoned him.
When he received the third drop, the black elephant turned back on its own.
When he received the fourth drop, the mosquitoes and gadflies disappeared.
When he received the fifth drop, the deep valley leveled itself, and he stood on flat ground.
Heaven transformed and guided him, leading him back to Heaven.
Five hundred young boys formed a group of companions.
Every day they played games together by the river.
They gathered sand to build a stūpa, each saying their stūpa was good.
Although they had good hearts, their fortune from past lives was meager.
At that time, the sky suddenly rained, and the river water surged violently, washing them away and drowning them.
The Buddha told the assembly,
“The five hundred boys were born in Dōushù Tiān.
They all unanimously roused the intention to practice the path of a Bodhisattva.”
The Buddha emitted a bright light, allowing their parents to see where their children were.
The Buddha called the five hundred youths from afar to come.
They immediately arrived and stood in the empty sky.
They scattered flowers below the Buddha, bowed their heads in reverence, and spoke,
“We have received the kindness of the World-Honored One.
Although our bodies perished, we were able to see Mílè.”
The Buddha said, “Excellent!
You decided resolutely to know the ultimate truth (Dào) and established stūpas and monasteries.
Because of this, you were born in heaven, saw Mílè, and received the guidance of the Dharma.
The Buddha preached the sūtra to them, and all were joyful and attained Non-Retrogression.
Each addressed their parents, saying, “Do not grieve or suffer anymore.
Strive diligently and cultivate yourselves through the Dharma.”
The parents all aroused the intention for the Way (Dào-yì).
They bowed their heads to the Buddha’s feet and circumambulated the Buddha three times.
Suddenly, they disappeared and returned to Dōushù Tiān.
Once, there were several boys.
They were playing together on the road and encountered the Buddha.
One boy performed a reverence.
He had five beans in his hand and offered them to the Buddha.
Four beans entered the bowl, and one fell to the ground.
The Buddha said,
“May you attain blessings generation after generation.”
When the boy died, he was immediately born in heaven.
Later, for eighty generations, he became a Wheel-Turning King (Cakravartin).
One hundred years after the Buddha’s Nirvāṇa,
the fields and marshes in the mountains were covered with lush vegetation.
Not far outside the mountain, there was a village where people lived. Cattle and horses entered a pond.
Five-colored lotus flowers grew there.
A cowherd boy entered the pond and picked them.
He filled his vessel with lotuses, carried them out to the edge of the mountain, intending to present them to the Buddha (at the stūpa).
Before he reached the monastery,
he encountered a herd of cattle on the road, which gored and killed the boy.
His spirit was immediately born in Dāolì Tiānshàng.
He had a naturally formed palace and five-colored lotuses.
When he was first born in heaven, he thought to himself,
“My palace alone has unusually colored lotuses.”
But the rule among the gods is:
One must first observe the causes and conditions of past lives before enjoying the blessings.
He then saw the gods who were previously there.
They said to each other, “This god has just arrived. Why is he so terrified and unsettled when he should be enjoying entertainment with us?”
They went and asked him.
He replied,
“I was originally a cowherd boy.
I gathered lotuses, intending to scatter them upon the Buddha’s stūpa.
Impermanence struck me on the way.
Due to this blessing, I came to be born here.
Therefore, I am now plucking flowers, intending to go to the former stūpa again to scatter them before the Buddha, thus completing my original vow.”
At that time, five hundred celestial beings held lotuses,
and followed him to scatter them upon the Buddha’s stūpa.
Because of this blessing, when Mílè descends, they shall collectively attain the Way.
In the past, there was a man.
He used three coins for *bùshī* (giving alms/charity).
He begged for three wishes.
The first was that he would become a *guówáng* (king) in the future.
The second was to understand the speech of all living beings.
The third was to possess great wisdom.
When that man died, he was reborn into a commoner's family.
His appearance was upright and proper.
The *wáng* (king) recruited men for his attendants.
This boy responded to the recruitment and was allowed to serve beside the *wáng*.
He saw a swallow in its nest.
He raised his head, looked at it, and laughed.
The *wáng* asked why he laughed.
He replied:
The swallow said:
'I have obtained a *lóngnǚ* (dragon daughter)'s hair, ten *zhàng* long, and I am calling my companion to look at it.'
The *wáng* said:
If this is truly so, good.
If it is not so, you shall be killed.
He sent someone to check and it was indeed obtained.
The *wáng* wished to take the woman as his wife.
He spoke to the young boy, saying:
Since you understand bird speech, you must have many strategies.
I will give you provisions.
Find this woman.
If you succeed, you will be heavily rewarded.
If you do not succeed, I will kill you and your entire household.
The young boy risked death and headed toward the shore of the *Dōnghǎi* (East Sea).
He saw two people arguing over an invisibility cap, water-walking boots, and a life-and-death staff.
The young boy said:
Why do you argue endlessly?
I will shoot one arrow, and the two of you chase it.
The one who reaches it first will receive the three items.
They replied, "Good."
He drew the bow and released the arrow.
The two men scrambled away.
The young boy took the cap, put on the boots, and grabbed the staff.
He went straight into the sea to the abode of the *lóng* (dragon).
He took off the invisibility cap, allowing the *lóngnǚ* to see him.
The woman was sensual.
Consequently, she took a [Huìjīn] gold item with the young boy and returned to the foreign state.
The *wáng* sent people to welcome her.
He commanded the woman to enter alone.
The woman then went forward.
The young boy put on the invisibility cap and followed the woman inside.
The woman saw that the *wáng* was ugly.
She threw the gold item at the *wáng*, breaking his forehead, and he died.
The young boy took off the cap.
He ascended the hall with the woman.
He cried out loudly, saying:
I should be the *wáng*, and this woman the *huánghòu* (empress).
I shall reign over the land.
In the past, there was a group of merchants.
They traveled through a treacherous path and encountered robbers (*jié*).
They lost a great amount of clothing and goods.
Among them was one garment.
It was woven from soft, smooth, and lustrous deer fetal hair to make a cloak.
Its price was a hundred times [that of the others].
But its color was dark purple-black and displeased the eye.
The robbers did not value or recognize it, but used it as a bag.
They used it to hold rough clothes and shared them elsewhere.
Each took various items, thinking they were strange and excellent.
This one bag remained, yet to be divided and spread out.
Among the band of robbers was a weak and distressed person.
He alone was not given a share.
After bitter arguing, they collectively gave him the bag.
He immediately sold it himself.
At that time, a great noble (*guìrén*) knew it was a valuable item.
He paid the stipulated price.
Compared to the equal shares the other robbers had gained,
When the robbers heard this, they were greatly shamed and vexed.
In the past, there was a woman.
She was upright and beautiful, with black hair as long as her body.
The *guówáng fūrén* (king's consort) asked for the hair and offered a thousand *liǎng* of gold, but she refused to give it.
Seeing the *Fó* (Buddha), she was joyful and wished to offer support.
She asked her parents to invite him for her.
Her parents said:
"Our family is poor and has nothing with which to offer him a meal."
The woman said:
“Take the price of my hair and use it for the offering.”
The parents reported to the *Fó*, wishing that the *Fó* would momentarily accept their humble meal the next day.
The woman cut her hair and gave it to the *wáng fūrén*.
The *fūrén*, knowing her urgent need, only gave her five hundred *liǎng* of gold.
The woman took the gold, bought food, and felt boundless joy.
She regretted her previous stinginess and greed which resulted in poverty in this life.
She prayed that she would not encounter this suffering again in the future.
The woman saw the *Shìzūn* (World-Honored One).
A five-colored golden light shone within her gate.
She bowed her head to the ground and circumambulated the *Fó* three times.
Her hair immediately returned to its former state.
The *Fó* said:
This woman, in previous existences, was poor and had nothing to offer.
She constantly placed her head and face on the ground to pay homage.
For eighty-one *jié* (kalpas) thereafter, she was always born among humans.
This merit has now run out, and she is born into a poor family in this life.
Yet, remembering her meritorious deeds, seeing me brought her boundless joy and blessing.
When her life ends, she will be reborn in the second *Dāolì Tiānshàng* (Trāyastriṃśa Heaven).
When her celestial [merit and] life are exhausted,
she shall develop the *Púsà dàoxīn* (Bodhisattva aspiration).
The woman's parents and siblings were all filled with joy, and when their lives ended, they were born in heaven.
In the past, there was a single mother (*dúmǔ*).
She was hired to guard a field and garden.
The master had business, so the meal was delivered past the usual time.
When the food arrived and she was about to eat,
a *shāmén* (monk) asked for alms.
She put all her portion of food into his bowl.
She also respectfully offered one stalk of lotus flower.
The *dàorén* (man of the Way) immediately displayed miraculous powers.
The mother rejoiced and exclaimed:
“Truly a *shèngrén* (sage)!”
“I wish that in my next life, I may have a hundred sons like this.”
When the mother died, she became the successor (*sì*) of a *Fànzhì* (Brahman).
Her spirit gathered at the spot where the *Fànzhì* urinated.
A deer licked the urine and consequently conceived.
When the time was due, she gave birth to a daughter.
The *Fànzhì* raised her.
When she reached over ten years old,
she guarded the dwelling and tended the fire.
The girl was playing with a deer and did not realize the fire had gone out.
Her father ordered her to seek fire.
Wherever the girl stepped among people, a lotus flower sprang up with every step.
The owner of the fire said:
“If you circumambulate my dwelling three times, I will give you the fire.”
The girl immediately obeyed the command.
Lotus flowers grew on the dry earth, encircling the house three times.
The *guówáng* heard of this.
He summoned and questioned the physiognomist (*xiàngshī*).
The *shī* said:
“There must be a sacred successor who will endlessly transmit transformation.”
The *wáng* commanded a virtuous minister.
He sent gifts to propose marriage and welcomed her back to the palace.
When she was full term in pregnancy, she gave birth to a hundred eggs.
The *hòufēi* (queen and consorts) and the concubines all envied her.
They put the eggs in a bag and secretly sealed the opening.
They threw them into the river current.
The *Tiāndìshì* (Sakra, King of Devas) descended and sealed the opening with an impression.
The various *tiān* (devas) protected it and caused it to stop flowing.
It was carried by a post planted in the ground to the country downstream.
The *wáng* of that place looked out from his terrace and remotely sighted something in the water.
There was a bag flowing down.
It radiated bright splendor, appearing to contain spiritual power.
He took it and examined it.
He saw the seal of *Dìshì*.
He opened the bag of a hundred eggs, nurtured them, and kept them warm.
When the time was due, bodies formed, and they were born as a hundred sons.
Born with sacred wisdom, they were enlightened without instruction.
Their appearance was rare and excellent, and their strength matched a hundred men.
The *wáng* provided a hundred white elephants to serve the sacred successors.
When they campaigned against neighboring states, none failed to submit.
They also attacked the state of their biological father, the *wáng*.
The *wáng* said:
“Who can repel this enemy?”
The mother said:
“Great *Wáng*, do not fear.
I will cause them to submit for Your Majesty.”
She immediately ascended the observation tower and spoke loudly to them, saying:
“The greatest rebellious acts are three.
First, not staying away from evil crowds, which invites suffering in two worlds.
Second, being born yet not knowing one's kin and acting contrary to filial piety.
Third, relying on power to kill kin and poisoning the Three Jewels (*Sānzūn*).”
“Those who harbor these three rebellious acts, their evil is endless.”
“Are you showing your lack of faith by gaping?”
“Now, the mother will retract her milk.”
By celestial command, milk spurted out and covered the mouths of the hundred sons.
Moved by her sincerity, drinking the milk, they felt sorrow.
They all said together:
“This is our mother!”
They kowtowed and repented their faults.
Kin and successors gathered, and none failed to mourn sadly.
The two states became peaceful and harmonious, and everyone praised the goodness.
The various sons perceived the impermanence of the world.
They bid farewell to their parents to learn the *dào* (way) and kept far from the defilements of the world.
Ninety-nine sons all attained *Yuánjué* (Pratyekabuddha status).
One son governed the state; when the father died, he became the *wáng*.
He granted a great amnesty for all crimes and opened the treasuries for *bùshī*.
The common people lacked nothing.
He transformed the state by governing it with the Ten Virtuous Deeds (*shíshàn*) and proper goodness.
He founded stupas and monasteries and made offerings to *shāmén*.
He recited scriptures and discussed the *dào*; his mouth committed none of the Four Evils.
The *Tiāndì* (Heavenly Emperor) nurtured and protected him, like a parent raising a child.
The one who remained to be the *wáng* is precisely my present body.
The father is now *Báijìng Wáng*.
The mother is *Shèmiào*.
There was a woman who was pregnant for several months.
Seeing the Fó and the Saṅgha, she thought to herself,
"If my son is born like this,
I will let him become a Shā mén, a disciple of the Fó."
When the month was full, she gave birth to a handsome boy, extraordinary among the multitude.
When he reached the age of seven,
her family was poor, but she prepared food for two people and three Dharma robes.
Holding a water vase in her hand, she led her son to the Fó and said,
"I beg compassion for my son; let him become a Shā mén."
The Fó immediately consented.
He instructed her to wash the boy's hands with the vase.
Immediately, nine dragons emerged from the mouth of the vase.
They spouted water to bathe the boy.
The remaining water sprinkled onto the boy's head,
transforming into a canopy of flowers (huágài).
Within it was a lion's seat (shīzǐ zuò).
On the seat sat a Fó.
The Fó smiled, emitting five-colored light.
It illuminated countless koṭis of Buddha-kṣetras (fó chà),
returned, encircled the Fó's body, and entered through the boy's crown.
The mother offered the food vessel to the Fó,
and also fed her son.
She generated the supreme aspiration for enlightenment (wú shàng dào xīn).
Ten koṭis (shí yì) of Buddha-kṣetras vibrated six times.
All the Fós manifested themselves.
The mother used the food to make offerings to all those Fós and the Bhikṣu Saṅgha.
All were satisfied, and the food was not diminished at all.
The boy's hair fell out naturally, and he became a Shā mén.
He immediately attained the ground of non-regression (bù tuì zhuǎn dì).
Formerly, east of Rājagṛha (Wángshě Chéng), there was an old woman.
She was stingy, greedy, and lacked faith.
Her maidservant, however, was diligent and always practiced loving-kindness (cí xīn).
She kept in mind two practices for the benefit of living beings:
First, she never poured hot water onto the ground.
Second, she always gave leftover grains from washing dishes to others.
The old woman fell ill but still breathed.
Her spirit (hún shén) was led into the hells (dì yù).
She saw chariots of fire, charcoal furnaces, boiling cauldrons of soup, mountains of knives, and forests of swords, enduring endless forms of suffering.
The old woman saw them and asked what these things were.
The hell wardens (yù zú) replied,
"This is the hell
where the stingy and greedy old woman east of Rājagṛha (Wángshě Chéng)
is due to enter."
The old woman, realizing this was her fate, was terrified and distressed.
She moved forward a little further.
There were palaces (gōng shě) made of the seven treasures (qī bǎo), thousands of celestial maidens (jì nǚ), and all kinds of rare and precious things.
She asked what this was.
They replied,
"The Heavenly Palace (tiān gōng).
The diligent maidservant of the stingy and greedy old woman east of Rājagṛha (Wángshě Chéng), upon the end of her life, will be born here."
The old woman suddenly revived and recalled the previous events.
She spoke to the maidservant, saying,
"You are due to be born in heaven.
You are my maidservant;
how can you enjoy it alone? You must share it with me."
The maidservant replied,
"If such a principle exists, I shall certainly obey your command.
But I fear that good and evil follow their form, and we cannot share the reward."
The mother immediately ceased to be stingy and greedy,
and performed great meritorious deeds (gōng dé).
Formerly, the Fó Vipaśyin (Wéiwèi Fó),
accompanied by sixty-two thousand Bhikṣus,
first emerged from the mountains and returned to his father, the king's, state.
The king ceded land outside the city and established a vihāra (jīng shě).
Each Bhikṣu received a plot of land.
A Bhikṣu spoke to a neighboring family,
wishing to request them to build a hut.
The man of the house did not consent.
The old woman of that family built it herself by hand, and the hut was completed.
Her ten fingers were all pierced (from the labor).
The Bhikṣu sat inside in dhāraṇa and samādhi (chán dìng).
Entering samādhi, he manifested the samādhi of fire-light (huǒ guāng sānmèi), and the hut appeared to be engulfed in a great fire.
The mother saw it from afar.
She thought, "The hut I built has already burned down. How shallow is my fortune (bó fú)!"
When she entered, the hut was still there,
but she saw the Bhikṣu within the firelight.
She was extremely delighted.
When her life ended, she was born in heaven.
When Śākyamuni (Shìjiā) attained Buddhahood, her heavenly lifespan had not yet ended.
She descended and informed the Fó,
"Tomorrow I will offer a meal to the Fó and the noble assembly (shèng zhòng)."
The Fó accepted it silently.
King Prasenajit (Bōsīnì Wáng) also sent a messenger to invite the Fó.
The Fó said,
"I have already accepted an invitation from a heavenly being."
The King said,
"I have never seen a heavenly being descend to make an offering.
How can this be?"
The next day, he sent someone to watch, but no preparations for the offering were seen.
Even until midday (yú zhōng), it remained completely quiet.
The King commanded that food and delicacies be prepared,
saying, "If no one provides, I will make the offering."
At noon, the heavenly being arrived, bringing no food whatsoever.
She merely brought various celestial maidens (yù nǚ),
played various musical instruments, paid homage to the Fó, and stood there.
She announced that the time (for the meal) had arrived.
As soon as she lifted her hand towel, everything was prepared.
After the water service was finished,
she lifted her hand again.
One hundred flavors of sweet dew (gānlù) came forth from the kitchen and settled on the ground.
She personally poured (the food and drink), and the entire assembly was satisfied.
The King was astonished and overjoyed upon seeing this.
After the hand washing was complete, he addressed the Fó,
"I am unsure what merit
this heavenly being accumulated in a past life (sù), that her hand can produce one hundred flavors—her merit is so great!"
The Fó spoke to the King.
"In a former life, she built a hut for a Bhikṣu with her own hands.
Because of this, she was born in heaven for ninety-one kalpas (jié).
The merit that allows her hand to produce all these things has not yet ended."
A mother gave birth to two sons.
One did not know how to swim.
He fell into the water and died.
The mother did not weep at all.
The other one knew how to swim but also fell into the water and perished.
The mother wept sorrowfully for him.
People said,
"You did not weep for the first son,
but you weep for the second son. Why is this?"
The mother said,
"The first did not know how to swim, so his death was fitting.
The second was skilled at swimming, so his death is a wrongful injustice (wǎng)."
Formerly, there was a man who lacked faith.
His wife greatly served the Fó.
The wife addressed her husband, saying,
"Human life is impermanent; you should cultivate merit and virtue (fú dé)."
The husband was indifferent and lazy.
The wife feared he would eventually enter the hells (dì yù).
She then addressed her husband again,
saying she wished to hang a bell and attach it above the door.
"When you enter or exit,
hit the bell to make a sound and recite 'Námó Fó' (Homage to the Fó)."
The husband said, "Very well."
After a long time,
the husband died.
The hell wardens (yù zú) stabbed him and threw him into a cauldron of boiling soup.
The stabbing hit the cauldron and created a sound.
He thought it was the sound of the bell,
and recited "Námó Fó."
The hell official (yù guān) heard this
and said, "This person serves the Fó."
He released him and allowed him to leave.
He gained rebirth in the human realm (rén zhōng).
The people of Zhānbó country served the Six Masters (Liù Shī).
Previously, they had never heard the names of the Buddha, the Dharma, or the Saṅgha.
They committed extremely evil deeds.
At that time, the Buddha,
for the sake of sentient beings, went to the city of Zhānbó.
At that time, there was a great elder (Zhàngzhě) in that city
who had no heir.
He jointly served the Six Masters, seeking a son.
Not long after, his wife became pregnant.
When the elder knew this, he went to the place of the Six Masters.
Joyfully, he asked,
"Will it be a boy or a girl?"
The Six Masters replied,
"When born, it will certainly be a girl."
The elder was sorrowful and distressed.
Furthermore, a friend came and spoke to the elder, saying,
"Have you not heard that the brothers, Yoūlóupínluó Jiāyè and others,
are disciples of whom?
If the Six Masters were the Omniscient Ones,
why did Jiāyè abandon them and follow the Buddha?
Moreover, Shèlìfú, Mùjiànlián, and others,
as well as kings such as Pínpósuōluó and other royal wives,
Fūrén Mòlì,
and elders of various countries like Xūdá,
all such people are disciples of the Buddha.
The Tathāgata, the World-Honored One (Rúlái Shìzūn), has unimpeded knowledge and vision regarding all phenomena.
Therefore, he is named the Buddha.
The Tathāgata is dwelling nearby right now.
If you wish to truly know, you should go to the Buddha's place."
At that time, the elder immediately went to my (the Buddha's) location
and asked the Buddha about the matter.
The Buddha said, "Elder,
the child your wife is carrying is undoubtedly a boy.
His merit and virtue are unparalleled."
The elder was delighted.
The Six Masters, harboring jealousy, mixed poison with an āmalaka fruit and brought it to the elder.
They said, "Excellent! Qú Tán (Gautama) spoke well of its characteristics.
When your wife is approaching the delivery month, she should take this medicine.
The child will be handsome, and the birth will be without distress."
The elder received it and had his wife take it.
After taking it, she immediately died.
The Six Masters rejoiced.
They went all over the city proclaiming,
"The Śramaṇa Qú Tán predicted
that the elder's wife would bear a boy.
Now, the child has not yet been born, but the mother has already died!"
At that time, the elder again developed a lack of faith in me.
He immediately prepared the corpse, covered it in a coffin, and cremated it.
When I saw this matter, I looked and commanded Ānán,
"Bring my robe. I wish to go there and destroy these erroneous views."
At that time, the Six Masters, seeing the Buddha approaching from afar, said to each other,
"Has the Śramaṇa Qú Tán come to this burial ground because he wants to eat meat?"
Those Upāsaka who had not yet attained the Dharma Eye were all ashamed and afraid,
and they reported to the Buddha,
"That woman is already dead; we beg you not to go there."
At that time, Ānán said to everyone,
"Wait a moment.
The Tathāgata will soon widely reveal the realm of the Buddhas."
When the Buddha arrived,
the elder challenged him, saying,
"Your words are never false.
But since the child's mother has died, how can a son be born?"
I said, "Elder,
at that time, you did not ask about the length of the mother's life.
You only asked whether the child she was carrying was male or female.
The statements made by the Tathāgatas, the Buddhas, are never false.
Therefore, you must know that you will certainly obtain a son."
At that moment, the corpse was burned by the fire, the abdomen split open, and the son emerged from within.
He sat upright in the fire, like a lotus pedestal.
When the Six Masters saw this, they called it magic arts.
When the elder saw it, his heart was again filled with joy.
He scolded the Six Masters,
"If you call it magic, why can't you do it?"
At that time, I immediately told Jīpó,
"Go into the fire and bring this child here."
Jīpó stepped into the pile of fire as if entering a cool, great river.
He held the child and returned to my location.
He handed the child to me.
After I received the child, I told the elder:
"The lifespan of all sentient beings is unstable,
like bubbles on water.
If a sentient being has the karmic retribution of heavy karma,
fire and poison cannot harm them.
This was not done by me."
Then the elder said,
"Excellent, World-Honored One.
If this child is able to fulfill his natural lifespan,
I only request that the Tathāgata give him a name."
The Buddha said,
"Elder,
this child was born in a fierce fire.
The name for fire is Shùtí.
Therefore, he shall be named Shùtí."
The Buddha was in Shèwèi country,
speaking the essence of the Dharma to innumerable multitudes.
At that time, there was a female disciple of external paths, Mónàqí Nǚ,
whose accumulated sins were extremely heavy. She wore a wooden bowl on her body, covered with clothes.
She left the city of Shèwèi and went to the Qíhuán Temple.
She saw the World-Honored One from afar, speaking the Dharma to the countless assembly.
She rejoiced and leaped, unable to contain herself (with malice).
[She thought:] "Today, I must disgrace Qú Tán among this assembly
so that my masters may receive offerings."
She then went into the assembly and recited a verse, saying:
"This Dharma Speaker made this body of mine pregnant with a child!"
At that time, among the great assembly, there were many externalists and naked Brahmacārya.
Those who believed in the Buddha were few; those who practiced falsehood were many.
Hearing the woman's words, they all believed her.
Those who believed in the Buddha reflected internally:
"Formerly, when the Buddha was in the palace,
he abandoned his weighty royal position and cast aside the palace ladies.
He left home to study the Way and achieved the Most Supreme Enlightenment.
How could he harbor the intention to engage in such activity with this vile and ugly woman?"
At that time, Shìtíhuányīn was behind the Tathāgata, holding a fan and fanning, and reflected internally:
"How dare this wicked Brahmacārī woman conceive this intention to slander the Buddha?"
He transformed himself into a white mouse.
It gnawed the rope attaching the wooden bowl, which broke with a huge resounding noise.
There was no one in the assembly who did not see it.
Those among them who did not firmly believe were all astonished.
"What kind of sound is this that resonates so far in all four directions?"
Those among them who believed in the Buddha heard this sound and were joyful and ecstatic.
They were unanimously delighted.
Immediately, a person rose from his seat,
holding the wooden bowl in his hand, and said to the woman,
"Is this your child?"
At that moment, the ground opened by itself, and her whole body immediately entered Ābí Hell.
Then, the woman's clan mourned, cried, and could not bear to leave.
Those who had not believed the Buddha immediately arose and repented.
Those who believed (in the Buddha) among them told each other, saying,
"The retribution for slander is such a sin.
The proof is evident right here.
Why speak of the future life?"
There was a great Kaluóyuè.
His wealth was countless.
His son was handsome, intelligent, and greatly loved the path of the scriptures.
He left home to follow a master and observe the canonical Dharma.
The master first ordered him to go begging for seven days.
In the country, there was an immoral and wanton housewife.
She called him and ordered him to enter.
Once he entered, she immediately closed the door and began dragging the Śramaṇa forward.
The Śramaṇa would not follow.
The wife was greatly enraged.
She called her maidservants to come and dig a fire pit ten feet deep.
She ordered four maidservants to tightly seize his body so that he could not move.
They held him over the fire pit.
The Śramaṇa said,
"Stop for now.
I must reflect and calculate."
The Śramaṇa thought to himself,
"If I enter the fire, it is but one death.
Dying while upholding the precepts allows me to be born in heaven.
If I die having broken the precepts, I will enter Nirí (hell) with no time of exit." He then entered the pit.
The fire transformed into water up to the Śramaṇa's waist.
He slowly and calmly came out.
Formerly, there was an elder named Shàn Shī.
His family had an unmarried daughter.
She was facing the fire at home.
The warm vapor entered her body, and she consequently became pregnant.
Her parents were astonished and questioned her about the circumstances.
The girl truthfully answered that she did not know the reason.
Her parents questioned her repeatedly,
inflicting various beatings and torments, but her statement did not change.
They consequently reported it to the king.
The king also interrogated and reproached her, but her statement was still the same.
He promised her death.
The girl immediately cried out in grievance, saying,
"Is there then to be an unprincipled ruler in the world who unjustly executes the innocent?
If I were wicked, I would surely be tested.
I am being wronged like this!"
The king then investigated and verified the matter.
It was exactly as the girl had stated, without addition or omission.
He said to her parents,
"I wish to take her."
The mother replied,
"Take her as you wish.
What use is this condemned woman to us?"
The king then brought her into the palace.
He provided care for her according to the time, and the months and days were completed.
She gave birth to a son who was handsome and exceedingly beautiful.
As he grew older,
he left home to study the Way, becoming intelligent and widely accomplished.
Through diligent effort, he soon attained the Way of Arhatship.
He then returned and converted his parents.
In the past, there was a Bhikṣu (monk) who was diligent and kept the Dharma.
He strictly observed the prohibitions and precepts, never violating them.
What he could recite was the Bānruò Bōluómì (Prajñāpāramitā).
Whoever heard the voice of this Bhikṣu was invariably joyful.
There was a small child, seven years old, herding cattle outside the city, who heard the sound of the Bhikṣu chanting the Sūtra from afar.
He immediately went to the Vihāra and bowed to the Bhikṣu.
He listened to the words of the Sūtra.
At that time, the topic of form (matter, *sè*) and emptiness (*kōng*) was being discussed.
Hearing it suddenly, he immediately understood.
The child was greatly delighted.
He then questioned the Bhikṣu.
The Bhikṣu's reply did not satisfy the child.
At that moment, the little child, in turn, explained the meaning to the Bhikṣu.
The Bhikṣu was joyful, as this was something he had rarely heard before.
He marveled that this small child’s wisdom was extraordinary.
At that time, the child immediately left and returned to where the cattle were.
The calves he was herding had scattered and run into the mountains.
The child searched for their tracks, pursuing and seeking them.
At that moment, he encountered a tiger, which harmed this small child.
The child died and was reborn into the house of a respected elder (zhǎngzhě).
When the mistress of the house was pregnant,
her mouth was already able to speak the Bānruò Bōluómì.
From morning till night, she never paused or rested.
The family of the zhǎngzhě found this strange.
They thought the mistress's mouth was speaking wildly, calling it a demonic illness.
They consulted divination and sought to banish the evil influence, but no one could understand it.
At that time, the Bhikṣu entered the city for alms and arrived at the zhǎngzhě's gate.
Hearing the voice from afar, his heart was extremely delighted.
He immediately asked the zhǎngzhě,
"Who inside is speaking this profound Sūtra?"
The zhǎngzhě replied,
"My wife has a demonic illness; she speaks wildly day and night, her mouth never resting."
The Bhikṣu replied,
"This is not a demonic illness.
She is merely speaking the honored Sūtra, the great path of the Buddha.
I request permission to enter and meet her."
The zhǎngzhě said, "Good."
He immediately went to his wife's location.
The Bhikṣu posed difficult questions, and she repeatedly analyzed and explained them.
They immediately detained the Bhikṣu and prepared food and drink for him.
The news spread from person to person.
The mistress, while pregnant, was reciting the honored Sūtra.
Her voice was exquisite and wonderful.
On a later day, the zhǎngzhě again invited the Bhikṣu.
He arranged for all (the monks) to come to his house and prepared the implements for the meal.
At that time, the mistress came out, paid respects to the assembly of Bhikṣus, and again preached the Dharma to them.
All matters of doubt and difficulty that they could not comprehend were fully explained by her.
The Saṅgha (monastic community) rejoiced.
When the months were full, she gave birth to a male child.
Immediately upon birth, he joined his hands, knelt upright, and spoke the Bōluómì.
After the mistress gave birth, she returned to her normal state.
The zhǎngzhě asked,
"What manner of being is this?"
The Bhikṣu replied,
"He is a true disciple of the Buddha; take good care of him.
When this child grows up, he will become the teacher of all people.
All of us must seek instruction and acceptance from him."
When the child was seven years old, the Way and the Dharma were all complete in him.
He surpassed the entire assembly, and his perfection of wisdom was infinite.
Errors and omissions in the Sūtras,
or anything that was lacking,
he corrected and rectified, completing what was deficient.
Wherever the child's mother went, she immediately enlightened people.
The zhǎngzhě’s household, inside and out, totaling five hundred people, young and old, all learned from the child.
Those whom he enlightened numbered eighty-four thousand people.
All of them gave rise to the Unsurpassed True Way (zhèngzhēndào).

Five hundred Bhikṣus, hearing what the child preached, extinguished all defilements, attained spiritual understanding, focused their minds on seeking the Mahāyāna (Great Vehicle), and attained purity of the Dharma Eye.
That child at the time was myself.
The Bhikṣu was Jiāyè Fó (Kāśyapa Buddha).
There were a husband and wife who had no son.
They offered sacrifices to the heavenly spirits to seek an heir.
The spirit immediately granted their wish.
Subsequently, she became pregnant.
She gave birth to four kinds of things:
First, a Chándán (sandalwood) measure filled with rice;
second, an Amṛta (nectar) vase;
third, a sack of jewels;
and fourth, a divine staff with seven joints.
The man sighed, saying,
"I sought a son, but instead gave birth to these other objects."
He then went to the spirit and reiterated his request.
The spirit then spoke to him, saying,
"If you wanted to obtain a son, how would he profit you?"
He replied,
"A son should be able to serve and provide for us."
The spirit said,
"This rice measure can be used without ever being exhausted.
The Amṛta vase, when eaten from, does not diminish,
and it cures a hundred ailments. The sack of rare jewels, when used, shows no loss or reduction.
The divine staff with seven joints can guard against violence and brutality.
How could a son accomplish all this?"
The man was greatly pleased.
Returning home, he tested them, and they were truly as the spirit had said.
Consequently, he became immeasurably wealthy, beyond calculation.
The king heard of this.
He immediately sent an army to attack and seize (the objects).
The man lifted the staff, flew about, struck the enemies, and crushed them.
The strong assembled forces all retreated and dispersed.
The man was joyful and had no further worries or troubles.
The person blinded and infatuated by lust,
would rather lose his relatives,
than rest his mind from acts of lust.
Near the city of Shèwèichéng (Śrāvastī), there was a woman.
Carrying her child and holding a vase, she went to the well to draw water.
There was a man whose appearance was handsome and proper,
sitting on the right side of the well, playing the sè (zither) and entertaining himself.
The woman, being greatly lustful, became deeply attached to the man.
The man also took pleasure in the woman. The woman, confused and infatuated,
tied a rope around her child's neck and lowered him into the well.
She soon pulled him back out.
The child was already dead.
Grieving and distressed, she cried out to heaven and shed tears.
And she spoke a verse to herself.
The Buddha gathered the great assembly and informed the Bhikṣus:
"The fire of lust is raging and can burn away the root of goodness.
A person infatuated by lust does not distinguish between good and evil, cannot tell purity from impurity, and knows nothing of bondage or liberation.
Such people are utterly without shame.
They would rather lose their relatives and share in punishment and disgrace.
Some, because of adultery and lust, kill their parents, brothers, and six types of relatives.
Those executed by the king die and receive evil retribution.
Life after life, without end."
In the past, there was a man
who was obsessively fond of adultery and lust.
He was the only son born to his parents.
One night, at an improper hour,
the sky was dark with thunder and lightning. Carrying a knife and holding arrows, he wished to go to the village of the lustful woman.
His mother realized this.
She immediately grabbed him and admonished him,
"The night is already dark; you might be harmed by someone.
I have little merit from past lives and only this one son.
If you encounter evildoers, I will have no one to rely on."
The son replied to his mother,
"I must go; I cannot stay."
The mother knew his intention was fixed (on leaving).
She then blocked the path where her son was going.
He immediately drew his knife and stabbed his mother to death.
He then knocked on the door of the lustful woman.
The woman responded, saying,
"Who are you?" He answered with a recitation (verse):
"Lust and anger weaken the roots (senses); I am mistaken by thoughts and delusions.
I do not consider many activities, being covered by foolish darkness.
Now I have taken my mother and killed her, overcoming her like a slave.
I stand outside the door, waiting like a guest waiting for service."
The woman replied with a verse:
"Alas! You turn your back on nurturing kindness and kill your mother, creating catastrophic sin!
How could I bear to look upon your face? You should quickly go far away from my house.
Parents embrace, rear, and nurture their child, enduring all kinds of suffering for him.
Having killed your mother and walking upon the earth, why does the earth not swallow you and kill you?"
The man then replied to the woman, saying,
"For your sake, I harmed my mother and created boundless sin.
Please grant me a little grace and forgiveness.
Open the door so we may talk briefly.
Then I will return home."
The woman replied,
"I would rather jump into a charcoal furnace, or leap from a mountain into a dark valley,
or tread upon a seven-pacer snake while alive, than associate with a fool like you."
The man returned home.
On the road, he met vicious bandits and was killed by them.
He entered Ābí Yù (Avīci Hell) to suffer punishment.
In the past, there was a zhǎngzhě whose wealth was limitless.
He had only one younger sister who married a poor husband.
The elder brother frequently sent her gifts.
When the sister eventually felt embarrassed to keep coming (for aid),
she borrowed flour from her brother.
The brother said,
"Go and take it yourself."
The sister then deceitfully took the flour.
She took it and returned as if she had repaid it.
The brother did not notice, and this happened repeatedly, more than once.
When the sister died, she was reborn as a calf in her brother’s household.
The brother loved it very much and fed it until it was fat.
He was about to slaughter it to sacrifice to the spirits.
At that time, five hundred merchants wanted to borrow money from the master (the zhǎngzhě) for a short rest.
Outside, they discussed among themselves, asking each other,
"How much money will you take?" Each stated his amount.
The last person said,
"Just take more.
Later, we will all fail to repay, so what does the quantity matter?"
At that moment, the calf was nearby.
It immediately spoke human language,
"Gentlemen, why do you harbor such intentions?
I am the master's younger sister.
Because I borrowed flour and cheated my brother,
I am now in the body of an ox, coming to repay my brother's debt."
At that time, the five hundred merchants,
hearing these words, were all trembling with fear.
They all refrained from borrowing the money and departed.
Pìzhīfó arrived at the elder’s house to beg for food.
The wife saw that his appearance was dignified and upright.
She said to Pìzhīfó:
“If you follow my wishes, I shall offer alms.”
Pìzhīfó said:
“I may not.”
Since what the wife had requested was not accepted,
she immediately felt shame and anger, and sent him away.
The elder’s maidservant (qīngyī) complained about the wife, saying:
“Why did you speak of inappropriate things to him?”
She took her own portion of food and gave it to Pìzhīfó.
After finishing the meal, she returned to her room to sleep and rest. When she awoke,
her dirty and dark skin had naturally peeled off.
Her face was dignified and beautiful, surpassing ordinary people,
like a heavenly maiden (yùnǚ).
The elder was astonished and asked her the whole story.
He immediately appointed her the first wife (dìyī fūrén).
In the state of Shèwèi,
there was a wealthy elder (fù zhǎngzhě).
His name was Chénjū.
His household had a maidservant.
Her name was Fúníchí.
She had a large head, bald hair, and perfectly blue eyes.
Her mouth and nose were distorted (liǎolì), scarcely resembling a human.
She usually managed outdoor labor, gathering firewood and grass.
A few miles from the house there was a spring.
It was both fragrant and sweet.
The maidservant carried a jar to fetch water.
At that time, a woman from a nearby dwelling
had hanged herself from a tree, and her shadow fell into the spring.
The maidservant saw the reflection of the face and thought it was her own form.
She immediately became greatly enraged and cursed,
“My appearance is so dignified!
Yet I am driven to labor in the fields and gardens, suffering such hardship!”
She immediately smashed the jar, returned home, ascended the hall,
and sat upon the wife’s seven-jeweled throne (qībǎo zuò), inside the fringed canopy.
The family was greatly astonished and strange, assuming the maidservant was mad.
They asked her what she was doing.
She replied:
“I saw myself reflected in the water as dignified.
The Master (dàjiā) does not distinguish me and only treats me as inferior.”
They immediately gave her a mirror to look into.
She saw her ugly appearance but still refused to believe it.
They took her to the water's edge and showed her the dead woman's shadow.
Only then did the maidservant’s mind understand, and she was ashamed of her presumption.
The Great Asura King (Dà Āxiūluó Wáng) was named Luóhē.
He resided at the bottom of the great ocean, north of Mount Xūmí.
The water hung suspended above his palace, supported by the Four Winds. The city walls extended eighty thousand yóujūn in length and breadth.
It had seven layers, both inner and outer, three thousand yóujūn high, with golden walls, silver gates, cool gardens and pools, and harmonious bird songs.
It was ten thousand yóujūn away from Mount Xūmí.
His body was twenty-eight thousand *lǐ* long. He ate kneaded food, bathed, and wore clothes (made) of fine, smooth material.
On the fifteenth day of the month,
he entered the middle of the sea.
He transformed his body (shape).
With the lower half of his body in the water up to his navel, the upper half mounted Mount Xūmí, and his fingers covered the sun and moon.
The Devas (Tiānzǐ) of the Sun (Rì) and Moon (Yuè),
seeing his ugly form, were all greatly afraid.
They lost their brilliance.
When he wandered about, there was a natural wind
that blew the gates open and shut, and blew the ground clean.
It scattered the flowers.
He had five great ministers.
The first was named Zhuōchí.
The second was named Xiónglì.
The third was named Wǔyí.
The fourth was named Tóushǒu.
The fifth was named Cuīfú.
They attended and guarded him.
Suddenly, he thought to himself,
“I possess such awesome virtue and divine power,
yet I allow the King of Dāolì and the Devas of the Sun and Moon to travel above my head.
I swear I will capture the sun and moon and use them as earrings.”
He gradually grew very angry and desired to strike them.
He then recalled
the two Asura Kings, Shèmólí and Pímózhìduō.
Along with his various ministers, each prepared weapons and went to fight against the Devas.
At that time, the two great Dragon Kings (Lóng Wáng), Nántuó and Bánántuó,
wrapped their bodies around Mount Xūmí seven times.
The mountain shook, clouds spread, and they struck the water with their tails.
The great ocean surged, waves cresting high above Xūmí.
The Dāolì Devas said:
“The Sūlún want to fight!”
The various Nāgas, Garuḍas (Jiālóuluó), and Guǐ (ghosts) in the sea, who bear flowers and enjoy eternal pleasure,
along with the two categories of Guǐshén (ghosts and spirits), each took their troops and engaged in successive battles.
If they were not victorious, they all fled.
The palaces of the Four Heavenly Kings (Sì Tiān Wáng) were strictly prepared for the attack.
They first reported to Dìshì.
Dìshì informed the Devas above him.
The Devas, from Yánmó up to Tāhuà,
innumerable masses of Devas, along with the Nāgas and Guǐ, encircled them in front and behind.
Dìshì commanded:
“If our army wins, use the Five Bindings
to bind Pímózhìduō.
Bring him back to the Hall of Excellent Dharma (Shànfǎ Táng).
I want to observe him.”
The Sūlún also said:
“If our multitude wins, use the Five Bindings
to bind Dìshì and bring him back to the Hall of Seven Leaves (Qīyè Táng).
I want to observe him.”
They engaged in a great battle simultaneously. Although their weapons clashed, neither side was injured.
They only caused pain and suffering by touching the opponent’s body.
Dìshì manifested a body with a thousand eyes.
He held a vajra staff (jīngāng chǔ), and smoke and flames issued from his head.
When the Sūlún saw this, their forces retreated and failed.
Pímózhìduō was immediately captured, bound, and brought back.
Seeing Dìshì from afar, he immediately hurled abusive language.
Dìshì replied:
“I merely wish to discuss the principles of the Way (dàoyì) with you.”
(Dìshì continued, speaking about the Asura:) "His lifespan is one thousand celestial years, rarely more, often less.
He has an evil mind and loves fighting, yet he does not break the precepts.
Because he greatly cultivated dāna (bùshī, giving), he received this body."
Regarding Pímózhìduō:
Formerly, at the beginning of the kalpa,
the Devas entered the water and their bodies experienced tactile pleasure.
Their essence flowed therein and naturally formed an egg.
From the egg was born a daughter, whose form was dark blue/black.
She entered the great ocean, splashed the water, and enjoyed herself.
The essence of the water entered her body, and she conceived.
She then gave birth to a son.
He had nine heads, and each head had a thousand eyes; fire issued from his mouth.
He had nine hundred ninety-nine hands and eight legs.
He squatted in the middle of the sea, feeding on blue mud and lotus roots.
He took a female deity (Shénnǚ) of the Gandharvas (Gāntàpó) from Fragrant Mountain as his wife.
Her appearance was exquisitely beautiful, her complexion surpassing white jade.
Later, she gave birth to a daughter.
She was singularly dignified and extraordinary, peerless between Heaven and Earth.
Jiāoshījiā sent an envoy to request her hand.
The Āxiūluó said:
“If you can enable me to ride in a seven-jeweled palace, I shall give her to you.”
Dìshì immediately took off his jeweled crown and offered it as the reward for the Ten Virtuous Deeds (shí shàn).
This allowed the Āxiūluó to sit in the Victorious Hall (Shèng Diàn).
He rode a platform of six kinds of jewels to welcome her.
He placed her atop the Shànfǎ Táng.
He renamed her Yuèyì.
All the Devas and assisting ministers were joyful.
Later, Dìshì visited the Garden of Joy (Huānxǐ Yuán).
He entered the pond to play games with the various celestial maidens (cǎinǚ).
Yuèyì became jealous.
She sent five Yakṣas (Yèchā) to report back to her father.
Her father immediately grew greatly enraged.
He raised the four kinds of troops and went to attack Dìshì.
Standing in the great ocean, he squatted on the summit of Mount Xūmí.
His nine hundred ninety-nine hands acted simultaneously.
He clawed the City of Joyful Sight (Xǐjiàn Chéng), causing Mount Xūmí to shake.
The waters of the Four Great Oceans surged into waves at once.
Shìtí Huányīn was alarmed, fearful, and distraught, not knowing where to turn.
At that time, a deity in the palace
spoke to the Heavenly King (Tiān Wáng):
“The Buddhas of the past taught
that the King of Mantras of the Prajñāpāramitā (Bānruò Bōluómì) should be recited and upheld.
The army of spirits will shatter on its own.”
Then Dìshì gathered the assembly in the Shànfǎ Diàn, burned fragrant incense, and made a great vow:
“The Prajñāpāramitā is the Great Bright Mantra (dàmíng zhòu), the Supreme Mantra (wúshàng zhòu), the Unequalled Mantra (wúděngděng zhòu). This is certainly true and not false.
By upholding this Dharma, I shall attain the path of the Buddha.
May the Āxiūluó naturally retreat and scatter.”
As he spoke these words,
four great wheels of knives appeared in the void.
They naturally descended upon the Āxiūluó.
His ears, nose, hands, and feet fell off simultaneously.
The waters of the great ocean turned red like crimson pearls.
The Āxiūluó was greatly shocked and terrified.
Having nowhere to flee, he escaped into a lotus root hole.
In the past, the Āxiūluó
raised troops and fought against the Heavenly Emperor (Tiāndì).
Shìtí Huányīn was not successful (defeated).
Riding his thousand-spoked jeweled chariot, he retreated in fear.
Midway, he saw a Tánsuōluó tree.
A bird's nest held two fledglings.
He immediately commanded his charioteer:
“This tree holds two birds.
You must turn the chariot to avoid it.
I would rather allow (the enemy) to come and harm me,
than harm these.”
He immediately turned the chariot.
The Sūlún saw this from afar and said to one another:
“Dìshì is turning his chariot; he must intend to return and fight.
He cannot be withstood!”
They immediately retreated and scattered. Thus the Devas gained victory. The Sūlún surpass Yánfútí in three things:
First, their palaces are tall and extensive.
Second, their palaces are decorated beautifully.
Third, their palaces are pure and clean.
In a past lifetime,
there was an Asura King,
named Luóhóuluó,
who begot a daughter.
She was exceptionally beautiful and proper.
She possessed all sixty-four kinds of feminine virtues,
complete without fail.
The breath she exhaled while speaking was like the *Utpala* flower.
Her body emitted the fragrance of ox-head *candaná* (sandalwood).
Her facial complexion was rosy and white, delighting all who saw her.
At that time, Shìtíhuányīn
thought, "The many women in this palace are beautiful,
but compared to the daughter of Xūlún (Vimacitra), they all fall short.
Now I shall gather troops, go conquer her, and take her to serve me."
He immediately summoned the gods and fully informed them of this matter.
The gods reported,
"If you go, you should send the musical deities
holding the ninety-one-stringed lapis lazuli lute, singing of the blessings and happiness enjoyed by us heavenly beings."
He immediately commanded the musical heavenly prince, Bānzhāyì, and others,
to prepare their instruments, go before Póxīhē, and play the lute.
He stated his intention, saying:
"I desire Póxīhē to serve me.
If she is not given, I shall take her by force of arms."
Xūlún became greatly enraged.
"I also possess sufficient strength to match and resist you."
Bānzhāyì and the others immediately reported this to the Heavenly Monarch (Dìshì).
At that time, Xūlún gathered his troops and arrived at the side of Mount Xūmí.
They destroyed the crooked-foot heavenly palace.
Next, they destroyed the palaces of the Wind God, the Horse God, and Zhuāngyán, and other heavenly palaces,
reaching the four gates.
Dìshì recalled the mantras he had previously recited and chanted them.
The Xūlún armies gradually retreated.
Leading their four kinds of armies, they entered the holes of the lotus stems in the Jūxīluó pond.
A certain scholar saw this.
He thought to himself,
"I must be mad or lost my wits, witnessing such strange events."
The Buddha told the *bhikṣus*,
"This is the truth."
At that time, Shìtíhuányīn gathered all the heavenly hosts and exited through the four gates.
They only saw swords, armor, bows, and arrows on the ground,
but did not see the Xūlún forces.
They pressed forward, straight into the palace of the Asuras.
They saw tens of millions of Póxīhē maidens,
but did not see the Asuras.
(Dìshì) led the maidens back to the Trāyastriṃśa (Dāolì) Palace.
At that time, all the Asuras
sought mercy and refuge, addressing Shìtíhuányīn, saying:
"We were foolish and confused, failing to recognize the majestic divine power of the Buddha's disciples.
Our ancestors faithfully served the Tathāgata.
We heard that the Buddha's precepts forbid taking others' possessions.
Yet today, the Heavenly King Shì has taken all our family members to fill his heavenly palace.
This is not an action suitable for a Buddha's disciple."
Dìshì, hearing this, became regretful and displeased.
"I should rather observe the prohibition and not commit theft."
He immediately returned the maidens.
The Asura King then offered his most beloved daughter to the Heavenly Monarch Shì.
Dìshì immediately repaid him with sweet dew (*gānlù*).
Xūlún and the heaven dwellers made peace
and together upheld the Tathāgata's Three Refuges and Eight Precepts.
In a previous lifetime, the Asura
had been a poor man.
He lived near the river and often crossed it, carrying firewood.
At that time, the river was deep and the current swift.
This man was frequently swept away by the water.
Having lost his burden,
his body would sink and drown.
He was carried by the current and barely escaped death.
At that time, there was a Pratyekabuddha (*Pìzhīfó*).
Assuming the form of a *śramaṇa* (monk), he went to the poor man's house to beg for food.
The poor man joyfully gave him rice and food.
After eating, the *Pìzhīfó* threw his bowl into the air and flew away.
Seeing this, the poor man made a vow:
"May my body be large in my next life,
so that no deep water can ever pass my knees."
Because of this cause and condition, he obtained an immensely large body.
The water of the four great oceans could not pass his knees.
Standing in the great ocean, his body was taller than Mount Xūmí.
Resting his hand on the mountain peak, he looked down upon the Trāyastriṃśa (Dāolì) Heaven.
The King of the Gandharvas (Qiántàpó)
lives in a city to the right of the Snow Mountains (Xuéshān),
named Píshèlǐ.
When the world first formed, a wind wheel arose,
named Zhuāngyán.
It constructed this palace city.
North of the city are seven black mountains.
North of the mountains is the Fragrant Mountain,
situated between ten jeweled mountains.
There is always the sound of musical performance. The mountain has two caves:
one named Zhòu,
and the second named Shànzhòu.
They are made of seven treasures, soft, fragrant, and pure,
like heavenly garments.
The King of the Gandharvas,
along with five hundred Gandharvas, dwells within them.
The Buddha was on Mount Pítuó.
Shìtíhuányīn instructed the musical deity
Bānzhāyì to hold the lapis lazuli lute and sing before the Buddha.
The Buddha said,
"You have been able to use the lute song to praise the Tathāgata.
The tone is sorrowful, harmonious, plaintive, and moving to the heart.
In this sound, it says:
'The meaning of Nirvana, which binds pure practicing *śramaṇas* and sentient beings, is fully contained.'"
Dìshì looked at him and said,
"You shall fill your father's position.
You shall be supreme among your kind,
and I will give you a daughter in marriage."
The Kinnaras (Jǐnnàluó) live north of Mount Xūmí.
Passing beyond the small Iron Ring Mountain, there is a great black mountain,
also located among the ten jeweled mountains.
There are no Buddhadharma, sun, moon, or stars there.
Due to the power of past charity,
they now dwell in palaces of seven treasures.
Their lifespans are extremely long.
This king was originally a human.
A great elder was building a stupa for the Buddha.
This Kinnara offered one temple mast, thus completing the temple.
Furthermore, he provided pure food to the craftsmen.
When his life ended, he became a chest-spirit,
residing between the two mountains.
Previously, while human, he was a great elder possessing immeasurable wealth.
When a *śramaṇa* came begging for food,
his wife held out the rice to give him.
The elder became greatly enraged and said,
"What beggar is this, staring at my wife?
May this person's hands and feet be broken and ruined!"
After his life ended, he received this ugly form.
For eighty-four *kalpas*, he constantly lacked hands and feet.
Whenever the gods held banquets, they all shared shifts with the Gandharvas, alternating above and below.
When the gods wanted to play music,
filth flowed from their armpits,
and they ascended to heaven by themselves.
There was a Kinnara
named Tóulóumóqín
who sang of the true nature of all phenomena to praise the World-Honored One.
At that moment, Mount Xūmí and all the forest trees vibrated.
Jiāyè (Kāśyapa), seated, could not remain still.
Five hundred *ṛṣis* (immortals) became ecstatically drunk
and lost their divine powers, falling to the ground simultaneously.
There are four great heavenly spirits: first, Earth;
second, Water;
third, Wind;
fourth, Fire.
The Earth spirit thought,
"The Earth is without Water, Fire, and Wind."
The Buddha said,
"Water, Fire, and Wind exist within the Earth,
but because Earth is predominant, it receives that name."
The spirits of Water, Fire, and Wind each felt the same way.
The Buddha preached the Dharma to them.
They all accepted the Five Precepts and became *Upāsikās* (female lay devotees).
All houses and dwellings where people live
have spirits and deities; none are empty.
Streets, alleys, roads, slaughterhouses, markets, shops, and all mountains and tombs
all have spirits and deities; there is no empty place.
Generally, all spirits and deities are named according to what they rely on (or guard). When a person is first born, there are spirits and deities who follow and protect them.
When a person is about to die, the spirits collect their vital essence.
A hundred or a thousand people who practice the Ten Evils are guarded by just one spirit,
just as a king assigns hundreds or thousands of people to guard one minister.
If sentient beings are born among the hungry ghosts (*èguǐ*),
due to constant hunger and thirst, their eyes are sunken and their hair is long.
They run wildly east and west, sometimes eating vomit, grease, flesh, pus, blood, feces, urine, snot, or saliva, or the residual liquid from cleansing.
Their lifespan is immeasurable, hundreds of thousands of years.
They have never heard the name of sauce or water.
Should they see it, they rush toward it urgently.
It transforms into raging fire, pus, and blood.
Sometimes, even if it does not transform, many people holding weapons prevent them from approaching.
Sometimes, when rain falls in summer, it turns into fire on their bodies. This is called the retribution of evil deeds.
By the side of the Gaṅgā (Hénghé) River, there were many hungry ghosts,
five hundred in number.
For immeasurable years, they had never seen water.
Although they reached the riverbank, they only saw flowing fire.
Driven by hunger and thirst, they cried out loudly.
The hungry ghosts reported to the Buddha,
"We are hungry and thirsty, and our lives will not last long."
The Buddha said,
"The Gaṅgā River is flowing with water."
The ghosts replied,
"The Tathāgata sees water, but we only see fire."
The Buddha said,
"I shall remove your delusion and allow you to see the water."
He extensively explained the fault of avarice and greed.
The ghosts said,
"We have been thirsty for so long that even upon hearing the Dharma, it does not penetrate our minds.
We must first enter the river and drink our fill."
Due to the power of the Buddha, they immediately gained access to the drinking water.
The Buddha preached the Dharma to them, and they all aroused the Bodhi Mind
and abandoned their ghostly forms.
Some hungry ghosts are constantly being burned by fire,
like when the *kalpa* ends and fire erupts from all the mountains.
Some are emaciated, run wildly, their bodies covered by their tangled hair.
Some stand by latrines, watching for filth.
Some constantly seek the residual blood of women in childbirth to drink.
Their bodies are like burned trees and their throats are like needles.
If given water to drink, they cannot be satisfied for a thousand years.
Some break open their own heads, taking out the brains to lick them.
Some have forms like black mountains, their necks bound by iron chains,
kowtowing, begging for mercy, and surrendering to the prison guards.
Some, in previous lives, had foul mouths and enjoyed using coarse language to insult others, who hated seeing them as enemies.
Because of this sin, they fell into the realm of hungry ghosts.
Such is the retribution for sin, causing immeasurable suffering.
There was a person who made a living by selling liquor.
A *guǐ* appeared and came to drink the liquor, but had not paid the price.
And [it] told the owner, saying:
"Tomorrow, there will be a man carrying flowers, wearing a white robe both inside and out, and tied with a dark green sash (*téng*)."
"Inside the sash, there will be a thousand *jīn* of gold and silver."
"He will bathe in the lake and suddenly die, failing to emerge."
"You go and retrieve the gold and silver, ensuring you have no worries afterward."
The next day, the owner waited.
He saw the man come, enter the water, wash and bathe, go ashore, put on his clothes, wash his feet, and then collapse dead onto the ground.
The liquor seller (*jiǔ shī*) went and retrieved the gold and silver as predicted.
The day after, the *guǐ* came.
The owner prepared food and brought out liquor, and reported to the spirit (*shén*), saying:
"I saw the man die just as he was dressed and about to leave."
"Why did you not kill him in the water, allowing him to reach the shore?"
The *guǐ* said:
"I cannot kill people or make them sick."
"I merely know the time when a person's lifespan diminishes and ends."
The master (*Shī*) said:
"The *guǐshén* in heaven and on earth,"
"know when a person's lifespan, sins, or blessings are due or not yet due,"
"but they cannot bring people to life, nor can they kill people."
"They cannot make people rich, noble, poor, or lowly."
"They merely desire to cause people to commit evil and homicide,"
"and take advantage of a person's decline to go and mislead them."
"They speak of their misfortunes and blessings, causing people to worship and sacrifice to them."
The king of the kingdom of *Jiāyī* [was] named *Fànmódá*.
At that time, he went out hunting in the wilderness.
He saw a house and immediately went towards it.
Inside was a woman.
He requested food and drink from her, but she had none to give.
The king requested to see her clearly.
The woman was completely nude.
The king took off his clothing and gave it to her, but as soon as she wore it, it instantly burned up.
This happened three times.
The king asked the woman about this.
The woman replied:
"In the past, I was the king’s wife."
"The king fed *Shāmén* and also gave robes."
"At that time, I advised [him]:"
"‘Giving food is sufficient; there is no need to give robes as well.’ Therefore, I incurred this sin."
"If the king wishes to enable me to wear clothes,"
"he must make clothing for me and first give it to *Shāmén* and those who understand the *Jīng* (sutras)."
The king sought a *Shāmén* but was unable to find one.
"It is acceptable to give [it] to a worthy person who keeps the Five Precepts."
The worthy person invoked a blessing, saying:
"May the woman of the golden couch (*Jīnchuáng Nǚ*) obtain measureless blessings and be able to wear the king's clothes."
The king asked the woman:
"What kind of spirit (*shén*) are you?"
She replied:
"I am superior to humans."
"Slightly inferior to *Tiān* (devas/gods)."
"Therefore, I am in the path of *guǐshén*."
"After abandoning this life, I shall be born in the First Heaven."
Long ago, a traveler went far away and stayed alone overnight in an empty house.
During the night, a *guǐ* carrying a dead person arrived and placed it in front of him.
Then another *guǐ* pursued it, coming with angry shouts.
[It said:] "That dead person is my property! Why have you suddenly carried it away?"
The first *guǐ* said:
"It is my property; I carried it myself." The second *guǐ* said:
"This dead person was truly carried here by me."
The two *guǐ* each grasped one foot and one hand and argued over it.
The first *guǐ* said:
"There is a person here who can be asked."
The second *guǐ* immediately asked [the traveler]:
"Who carried this dead person here?"
The man pondered:
"These two *guǐ* have great power."
"Whether I speak the truth or lie, I cannot escape death."
He said:
"The first *guǐ* carried him here."
The second *guǐ* became greatly enraged.
It grabbed the man’s arm, ripped it off, and threw it onto the ground.
The first *guǐ* took one arm from the dead person and fitted it [onto the traveler].
It immediately attached. Just like this,
both arms, both legs, the head, and ribs—his entire body was replaced.
Thereupon, the two *guǐ* shared and ate the body parts they had exchanged [from the dead person].
They wiped their mouths and departed.
The man pondered:
"The body given to me by my parents,"
"I saw with my own eyes was completely eaten by the two *guǐ*."
"Now this body of mine is entirely someone else's flesh."
"Do I definitively possess a body now, or do I have no body?"
He traveled to a Buddhist stupa and asked the *Bǐqiū* (monks).
He extensively related the foregoing matters.
The *Bǐqiū* said:
"From the very beginning, there has always been no self (*wú wǒ*)."
"It is only because the Four Great Elements are combined that [you] mistakenly regard [it] as your body."
"Whether your original body or your current one,"
"there is no difference."
The *Bǐqiū* ordained him into the path.
He attained *Āluóhàn* (Arhatship).
There was a certain *guǐshén*.
His body was extremely large and he had hands of golden color.
From his five fingers, sweet dew (*gānlù*) constantly flowed.
If there were practitioners who needed anything—
food, drink, or articles necessary for life—
everything flowed forth from his fingers, and he freely gave it to them.
*Mùlián* asked, saying:
"What kind of *Tiān* (deva) are you?"
"Your karmic reward and merit (*gōngdé*) are so exceptionally remarkable."
[He replied:] "I am not a heavenly king or *Fàntiān Wáng* (Brahma King)."
"I am a *guǐshén*."
"I reside near a great city in a certain country."
"I came here for the purpose of traveling around and observing."
*Mùlián* asked:
"What good deeds did you perform to receive such a reward?"
[He] replied:
"The great city in that country is named *Luólóu*."
"In the past, I was a poor woman living there."
"I also wove wool yarn bags and sold them to support myself."
"My financial situation became poorer, and my house eventually collapsed completely."
"So, I moved to the side of the road."
"Near the house of a very wealthy and generous *Zhǎngzhě* (elder), I wove yarn to support myself."
"When the sun was about to reach noon,"
"if there were any *Shāmén* or *Póluómén* (Brahmins)"
"carrying bowls and begging for food,"
"who asked me,"
"‘Where is the house of the wealthy *Zhǎngzhě*?’"
"My heart was sincere and without falsehood."
"Joyfully, I raised my hand and pointed to his house, saying:"
"‘Go to that place.’"
"‘The time is about to pass; do not seek elsewhere.’"
, there was a ghost.
Named Píshā, he was extremely ferocious and violent.
He killed countless people.
Daily, continuously, several dozen people (were killed).
All gathered together and made this statement:
"We should flee this country and go far away to another region."
The ghost knew what was in the hearts of the people, so he spoke to them, saying:
"You must not leave this place and go to other lands.
You will never escape my grasp.
If you offer one person daily to sacrifice to me, then I will not trouble you."
At that time, the people of Báqí daily took one person as a sacrifice
to that evil ghost.
The bones of the people eaten by this ghost filled the ravines and valleys.
At that time, there was a householder’s son named Shànjué.
He lived there, possessing great wealth and many treasures.
His son was named Nāyōuluó.
He had only this one son.
There was this limitation (by lot or turn):
The son, Nāyōuluó, was due to be sacrificed to this ghost.
After the parents bathed this young child,
dressed him in fine clothes, and brought him to the location of that ghost,
their weeping and wailing were immeasurable.
And they spoke thus:
"All spirits and Earth Deities, bear witness together!
This one son of ours—we pray you protect this child and allow him to be rescued and spared!
Shìtíhuányīn and Fàntiānwáng,
all disciples of the Rúlái, the Āluóhàn who have exhausted their outflows, and the Pìzhīfó,
even the Rúlái, the most honored, the most supreme, the excellent protector, the field of merit (fútián)—
there is none superior to the Rúlái!
May you observe and inspect this!
We pray the Rúlái will illuminate this sincere heart!"
They handed the child over to the ghost and then retreated and departed.
At that time, the Shìzūn, with his divine eyes and ears, completely heard and saw (the events).
Using his spiritual power, he arrived north of Xuěshān.
He entered the ghost’s dwelling place and sat cross-legged (in meditation).
At this time, the young child arrived at the ghost’s dwelling place.
He saw the Rúlái from afar, radiating brilliant color and light.
His body was adorned with the thirty-two marks and eighty minor characteristics.
He felt joy and approached the Rúlái.
(He approached), believing this was the evil ghost who would eat him at will.
At that time, the Shìzūn declared:
"Nāyōuluó, as you have said,
I am now the Rúlái, the Utterly True, the Perfectly Enlightened One (Děngzhèngjué).
Therefore, I have come to save you and subdue this ghost."
Nāyōuluó rejoiced and prostrated himself, bowing his head to the feet (of the Rúlái).
Then the Shìzūn explained the subtle meaning of the Dharma to him.
Immediately, in that seat (where he sat), all his defilements were exhausted, and he attained the pure Eye of the Dharma (fǎyǎnjìng).
Having perceived the Dharma, he took refuge in the Buddha (Fó), the Dharma (Fǎ), and the Saṅgha (Shèngzhòng), and received the Five Precepts (wǔjiè).
The evil ghost returned to his original place and saw the Shìzūn sitting properly, motionless, from afar.
He immediately grew enraged.
He rained down thunder, lightning, and bolts, and sometimes rained down knives and swords.
Before they fell to the ground,
the Rúlái transformed them into Utpala Lotuses (Yōubō Liánhuá).
He further rained down various spiritual powers, but the Rúlái proceeded to subdue them accordingly.
(The ghost thought): "The robes and hair of this Shāmén have not stirred! I must now go and ask him profound questions.
If you cannot answer me, I will grab your two legs and throw you into the Southern Sea."
The Fó said:
"Neither man nor non-man is able to grab my two legs and throw me into the Southern Sea.
If you wish to ask, then ask."
Then the ghost asked:
"What are the Old Actions (gùxíng), the New Actions (xīnxíng), and the Cessation of Actions (xíngmiè)?"
The Shìzūn declared:
"You should know that the eye is the Old Action.
Conditions created in the past (which result in) affliction/suffering become the basis for action (xíng).
The ear, nose, mouth (tongue), body, and mind—these are the Old Actions.

The three actions created by the body, the four by the mouth, and the three by the mind in the present life—these are the New Actions (xīnxíng). You should know that the Old Actions are extinguished and exhausted.
They do not arise again, nor do they create further actions (xíng).
One who is able to grasp this action (xíng) will never be born again; they are utterly and permanently exhausted, without remainder.
This is called the Cessation of Actions (Xíngmiè)."
The ghost said to the Fó:
"I am extremely hungry now; give the young child back to me."
The Shìzūn declared:
"Formerly, when I was a Bodhisattva (Púsà),
a dove sought refuge with me. I still did not begrudge my body and life to save that dove from peril.
How much less now that I have achieved Rúlái-hood,
could I abandon this child and allow you to eat him?
During the time of Jiāshè Fó, you were once a Shāmén.
You cultivated the pure practice (fànxíng), but later violated the precepts.
(Because of this), you were born as this evil ghost."
At that moment, the evil ghost, relying on the Fó's spiritual power and majesty,
immediately recalled all the actions (xíng) he had committed in the past.
He immediately approached the Shìzūn's location,
and prostrated himself, bowing his head to the feet.
"I am now foolish and confused, unable to distinguish truth from falsehood.
I dared to harbor such intentions toward the Rúlái.
I only pray, Shìzūn, that you accept my repentance."
He did this three or four times.
The Shìzūn declared:
"I accept your confession of transgression."
And he preached the Subtle Dharma (Màofǎ) for him.
At that time, the evil ghost held up several thousand *liǎng* of gold in his hands and respectfully presented them to the Shìzūn.
"I now take this valley
and donate it to the Saṅgha (Zhāotísēng).
I only pray, Shìzūn, that you accept it on my behalf."
The Shìzūn immediately accepted.
Then he spoke this verse (jì):
"Giving orchards and fruits to the pure, and building wooden bridges;
If one is able to construct great boats, and various means of sustenance;
Day and night, without laziness or slackness, the merit gained is immeasurable.
When the Dharma, meaning, and precepts are fulfilled, after death, one is born in heaven."
The ghost asked: "What other teachings are there?"
The Shìzūn declared:
"Abandon your original form, wear the three Dharma robes, and become a Shāmén.
Enter the city of Báqí and teach and command everywhere:
‘The Rúlái has appeared in the world to save those who are unsaved,
and enable them to attain liberation.
The most honored, the most supreme, the excellent protector, the field of merit (fútián),
has now saved the young child Nāyōuluó
and subdued the evil ghost Píshā.
You should all go there and receive transformation (by the Dharma).’"
Then the ghost Píshā, in the kingdom of Báqí,
proclaimed these words.
At that time, the householder Shànjué,
having heard these words, was overwhelmed with joy.
Leading a multitude of eighty-four thousand people,
he proceeded to the location of the Shìzūn.
Formerly, there was a woman.
She had very many children.
Her nature was wicked and merciless.
She delighted in stealing other people's children, killing, and eating them.
Families who lost children did not know who had taken them.
Walking in the alleys, weeping and crying, this was not uncommon.
When Ānán went out, he frequently saw the weeping and crying.
After returning, they discussed the matter together.
They lamented the families who had lost children.
The Fó, knowing this, asked deliberately:
“What are the assembly discussing?”
Ānán reported to the Fó, saying:
“While I was out seeking alms just now, I saw people weeping and crying.
When asked, they all said:
‘We have lost our child; we do not know where the body is.’”
The Fó then explained to Ānán:
“The one who is stealing children in this country is no ordinary person.
It is the Guǐzǐ Mǔ.
Having been born as a human in this life, she delights in stealing people's children.
This mother has a thousand children.
Five hundred children are in the heavens.
Five hundred children are in the human realm.
All thousand children are Ghost Kings.
One King is followed by tens of thousands of ghosts.
Thus, five hundred Ghost Kings are in the heavens disturbing the various devas.
Five hundred Ghost Kings are in the world disturbing emperors, kings, and common people.
Even the devas have no way to deal with these five hundred Ghost Kings.”
Ānán said:
“The Guǐzǐ Mǔ is in this country.
Can she perhaps be commanded not to steal people's children?”
The Fó said, “That is excellent.”
Ānán said:
“What means should be used?”
The Fó told Ānán:
“Go to where this mother resides. After watching for her to go out,
gather up her children and place them inside the monastery (Jīngshè).”
He immediately went, watched, and gathered up ten or so children and hid them inside the Jīngshè.
When the mother returned and did not see them, she stopped killing other people’s children and dared not do so again.
She walked about searching for her children everywhere but did not know their location.
She walked the roads weeping and crying like this for ten days.
The mother then beat her chest and struck herself, crying out loudly toward heaven, and stopped eating or drinking.
The Fó sent a Shāmén (monk) to go and ask her.
She immediately reported to the Shāmén, saying:
“I am crying because many of my children are missing.”
The Shāmén further said:
“Do you wish to get your children back?”
She replied, “I wish to.”
The Shāmén said:
