“If you truly wish to get them back, you should go ask the Fó, and you may receive your children.”
When the mother heard these words,
she was happy and relieved, and immediately went to the Fó’s place.
She bowed to the Fó.
The Fó immediately asked the mother:
“Why are you weeping and crying?”
The mother replied, saying:
“Because my children are missing.”
The Fó asked:
“Did you abandon your children?
Where did you go when you lost them?”
The mother immediately fell silent.
This happened up to three times.
The mother realized that stealing other people’s children was an evil act.
She immediately rose and bowed.
“It is because of my ignorance.”
The Fó further asked:
“If you have children, do you love them?” The mother said:
“When I have children, whether sitting or rising, I always want them close beside me.”
The Fó further asked:
“You have children and know to love them.
Why then do you daily go and steal the children of others?
Other people also love their children just as you love yours.
Families who lose children also walk the roads weeping and crying, just like you.
Yet you steal people’s children, kill them, and eat them.
After death, you will enter the Tàishān Dìyù (Hell of Mount Tài).
Do you still wish to retrieve your children?”
The mother immediately touched her head and face to the ground.
“I pray the Fó takes pity on me.”
The Fó said:
“If your children are returned, will you truly be able to repent?”
“If you can repent, I shall return your children.”
The mother said:
“I am able to repent.”
The Fó said:
“If you are able to repent, what kind of repentance will you perform?”
The mother said:
“I will listen to the Fó’s teachings and commandments, and I will follow the Fó’s words.
Please, Fó, return my children.” The Fó said:
“If it is truly as you say.”
He conferred the Five Precepts upon her.
“All your thousand children, I shall explain their names.
Five hundred children are in the heavens.
Five hundred children are in the world.
They disturb the devas and humans.
Your children act as Ghost Kings leading tens of thousands of ghosts.
Such ones are innumerable.
Some falsely claim to be Tree Spirits, Earth Spirits, Water Spirits, or Spirits of boats and carts,
of houses, of darkness and shadows, of terrifying dreams and waking states, and various strange and monstrous spirits.
They thus falsely claim (divinity) and make people offer sacrifices.
They slaughter, cook, and eat; they cannot protect human lives.
They merely increase wickedness.
These ignorant people do not know how to reflect on poverty (the cause of suffering).”
The Guǐzǐ Mǔ heard the Fó’s discourse.
She repented wholeheartedly.
She immediately attained the Xūtuóhuán Dào (Stream-Enterer Path).
Kneeling for a long time, she reported to the Fó, saying:
“I pray the Fó pities me.
I wish to reside beside the Fó Jīngshè.
I wish to summon my thousand children.
I wish to make them form a covenant with the Fó.
I wish to repay the kindness of those in the heavens and those in the world.”
The Fó said, “Excellent indeed!
That you have such an intention is truly excellent.”
The Fó said:
“Then reside beside the Fó Jīngshè.
For those people in this country who are childless,
when they come seeking children, you shall give them children according to their wishes.
I shall command your children to go and follow people, protecting them.
They must not recklessly disturb them again.”
Those who wish to seek a boon from the Guǐzǐ Mǔ,
her name is Fútuó Móníbō.
Her elder sister is named Zhì Nì.
All the ghosts in heaven and earth are subject to Móníbō.
All boats, carts, business affairs, and wealth within the four seas belong to Móníbō.
Móníbō made a covenant with the Fó and received the precepts.
She is responsible for protecting people's wealth and belongings.
Zhì Nì is responsible for households; if someone is giving birth, she shall go and assist them.
At that time, the Qūmó Yèchā ghost
came to the place of the Fó, bowed its head to the Fó’s feet, and withdrew to stand on one side.
Then the Qūmó ghost reported to the Fó, saying:
“Shìzūn,
I now invite the Shìzūn and the great assembly
to stay here for the night.”
The Shìzūn remained silent.
At that moment, Qūmó transformed five hundred multi-storied houses, sleeping mats, sitting beds, and cross-legged seats.
He prepared five hundred sets of bedding and pillows.
He also magically created five hundred lamps,
which had no smoke or flame.
At that time, Mùlián (Maudgalyāyana) was practicing walking meditation in the deep night.
The wicked Māra magically transformed himself into a shadow and entered Mùlián’s abdomen.
Mùlián entered samādhi to observe its origin.
He immediately spoke to the wicked Māra:
“Please come out! Please come out!
Do not disturb the Fó’s disciple.
You will gain prolonged suffering.”
Māra thought in his heart, saying:
“This Shāmén has never seen me before.
He is recklessly fabricating lies.
Even if it were his master, he still would not know me,
let alone his disciple.”
Mùlián replied:
“I know exactly what you are thinking in your heart.”
Māra immediately became frightened, thinking, “He has detected me!”
He immediately transformed his entire body, came out, and stood before him.
Mùlián told Māra:
“In a past age, during the time of Jūlóuqín Fó,
I was once Māra.
My title was Míng Hèn.
I had an elder sister.
Her name was Yǎn Hēi.
You were born as her child.
It is because of this that I know you are the child of my elder sister.”
At that time, a Fó appeared in the world.
He had two disciples.
One was named Hóng Yīn.
The second was named Zhī Xiǎng.
Why was he named Hóng Yīn?
Residing in the Brahmā Heaven, the sound of his clearing his throat
was heard throughout the three thousand (great thousand world systems).
Zhī Xiǎng lived alone in solitude, sitting beneath a mountain tree.
While he was absorbed in right concentration (samādhi), cowherds, shepherds, and people carrying firewood or grass,
said to each other:
‘This person has already passed away; let us cremate him together.’
Zhī Xiǎng arose from samādhi and entered the city to seek alms.
There was once a woman
who was possessed by a hungry ghost.
He immediately used an incantation to question the ghost, saying:
‘Why are you tormenting this woman?’
The ghost answered him, saying:
‘This woman is my enemy.
She constantly killed me for five hundred lifetimes.
I, too, for five hundred lifetimes,
have severed her life-root.
If she can relinquish the heart of old enmity,
I can also relinquish mine.’
At that time, the woman spoke thus:
‘I have now relinquished the heart of enmity.’
The ghost observed the woman: although she said she had relinquished it with her mouth,
her heart had not released it.
It immediately severed her life.”
Mó prepared a feast.
He transformed into forty thousand Bǐqiū.
They wore dirty, worn-out clothes and held broken bowls.
Their chests and backs were completely exposed, and their faces were hideous.
They were lame, crippled, hunchbacked, and their hearts were filled with fear and agitation.
They received various kinds of food.
Wénshū caused the bowls of all these transformed people to remain constantly full.
They stuffed the food into their mouths, but gagged and could not swallow it.
Their bodies were uneasy, and they spontaneously fell to the ground and asked Mó:
"Bǐqiū, why do you not eat?"
Mó replied:
"They are about to die."
Wénshū said:
"How can a person without poison still generate defiled poison?
People possessing lust, anger, and delusion—this is the poison.
Because I preach the Dharma, I do not possess this poison."
The five hundred devas who had followed Mó
arose the aspiration for Bodhi.
Mùlián arrived at the bank of the Hénghé (Ganges River).
He saw five hundred hungry ghosts gathering toward the water, where there were guardians of the water.
They drove them away with iron staffs, preventing them from approaching.
Thereupon, the ghosts went directly to Mùlián.
They bowed at Mùlián’s feet and each asked about their respective sins.
One ghost said:
"I have received this body and constantly suffer from heat and thirst.
I previously heard that the water of the Hénghé is clear and cool.
Joyfully heading toward it, it became boiling hot and destroyed my body.
I tried to drink one mouthful.
My five viscera were scorched and rotten, and the stench was unbearable.
For what cause and condition do I endure such a sin?"
Mùlián said:
"In your former life, you were a physiognomist (fortune teller).
You predicted people's fortune and misfortune.
There was little truth and much fabrication.
Sometimes criticizing, sometimes praising.
You claimed your readings were precise in order to stir up people's minds.
You used deceit, confusion, and fraud to seek wealth and profit.
You confused sentient beings, causing them to lose things they desired."
Another ghost said:
"I am constantly being eaten by large dogs with sharp, red and white teeth who consume my flesh, leaving only bones behind.
When the wind comes and blows,
the flesh immediately regenerates.
The dogs come back to eat again.
What is the cause of this suffering?"
Mùlián answered:
"In your previous life, you were the master of a celestial temple (shrine).
You constantly taught sentient beings to slaughter sheep and use the blood to sacrifice to the heavens.
You yourself ate the meat.
Therefore, today you repay it with your own flesh."
Another ghost said:
"My body is constantly covered all over with smeared excrement.
I also eat it.
What is the cause of this sin?"
Mùlián answered:
"In your previous life, you were a Póluómén (Brahmin).
You held wicked and heterodox views and were faithless.
When a practitioner begged for food, you took a bowl, filled it with excrement, put rice on top, and gave it to the practitioner.
The practitioner carried it back and ate the rice with his hand.
The excrement soiled his hand.
Therefore, today you endure such a sin."
Another ghost said:
"My belly is extremely large, like a jar.
My throat, hands, and feet are as thin as needles.
I cannot eat or drink.
What caused this suffering?"
Mùlián answered:
"In your previous life, you were the chief of a village.
You relied on your own power and nobility.
You freely indulged in food and drink and lightly mocked others.
You seized their food and drink, causing sentient beings to suffer hunger."
Another ghost said:
"I constantly head towards the latrine, wanting to eat the excrement.
But large groups of ghosts holding staffs drive me away, preventing me from approaching the toilet.
I am rotten inside, stinking, starved, and utterly helpless.
Why is this so?"
Mùlián answered:
"In your previous life, you were the master of a Buddhist temple.
Lay people offered supplies to the assembly of monks and prepared meals.
You used the coarse offerings to serve the visiting monks.
The fine (better) portions you ate yourself."
Another ghost said:
"My body is covered all over with regenerating tongues.
Axes come and chop the tongues.
They are cut off but immediately grow back, this happens ceaselessly.
Why is this so?"
Mùlián answered:
"In your previous life, you were a practitioner.
The assembly of monks assigned you to make honey drink (syrup).
The rock candy was in large chunks and difficult to dissolve.
You chopped it with an axe.
With a mind of theft, you ate one mouthful.
Because of this cause and condition, your tongue is now chopped."
Another ghost said:
"I constantly have seven hot iron balls going straight into my mouth.
Entering my belly, my five viscera are scorched and rotten.
They exit and then re-enter.
Why do I receive this sin?"
Mùlián answered:
"In your previous life, you were a Shāmí (novice monk).
Carrying fruit seeds and melon seeds, you went to your master’s place.
Out of respect for your master, you favored him and gave him seven pieces more than the others."
Another ghost said:
"I constantly have two hot iron wheels.
They are under my two armpits.
As they turn, my body is scorched and rotten.
Why is this so?"
Mùlián answered:
"In your previous life,
you were making cakes for the assembly of monks.
With a mind of theft, you took two strips of cloth and hid them under your armpits."
Another hungry ghost said:
"My testicles are extremely large, like a jar.
When walking, I carry them on my shoulder.
When stopping, I sit upon them, constantly suffering whether moving or resting.
Why is this so?"
Mùlián answered:
"In your previous life, you were the magistrate of the market.
You always used a light scale and a small measure when giving things out.
You used a heavy scale and a large measure when taking things in.
You constantly sought great profit for yourself and encroached upon others."
Another ghost said:
"I constantly have eyes on both shoulders.
My chest has a mouth and a nose.
I constantly have no head.
Why is this so?"
Mùlián answered:
"In your previous life, you were always a chief executioner.
When your disciples killed criminals,
you always felt joy.
You took a rope, tied a knot, and pulled tight (on the victim’s neck)."
Another ghost said:
"I constantly have hot iron needles.
They pierce in and out of my body, causing unbearable suffering.
Why is this so?"
Mùlián answered:
"In your previous life, you were a horse trainer.
Or perhaps an elephant trainer.
If a horse was difficult to control,
you used an iron needle to prick its foot.
Also, when an ox was slow, you also pricked it with a needle."
Another ghost said:
"Fire constantly emerges from my body, burning and vexing me.
Why is this so?"
Mùlián answered:
"In your previous life, you were a king’s consort (lady).
The king greatly favored and loved another consort.
You constantly generated jealousy and watched for an opportunity to harm her.
It happened that the king awoke and left his bed.
The beloved consort was still asleep and not yet dressed.
You immediately generated evil intent, just as cakes were being made.
There was hot sesame oil, and you immediately poured it onto her stomach.
Her stomach became rotten, and she died instantly."
Another ghost said:
"A whirlwind constantly spins my body around.
I cannot be free to go east or west as I wish.
My heart is constantly distressed and tormented.
Why is this so?"
Mùlián answered:
In your previous life, you were constantly a diviner (fortune teller).
Sometimes speaking truthfully, sometimes speaking falsely.
Confusing people's minds, preventing them from achieving their wishes."
Another ghost said:
"My body is constantly like a chunk of meat.
I have no feet, eyes, ears, nose, etc.
I am perpetually eaten by worms and birds.
The sinful suffering is unbearable.
For what cause and condition?"
He answered:
"In your previous life, you constantly gave others medicine to abort the fetuses of their children."
Another ghost said:
"I constantly have a hot iron cage.
It wraps around my body.
I am scorched, hot, and tormented.
Why do I endure this?"
Mùlián answered:
"In your previous life, you constantly used nets and snares to capture fish and birds."
Another ghost said:
"I cover my own head with something.
I am also constantly afraid that people will come and kill me.
My mind is constantly fearful and unbearable.
Why is this so?"
He answered:
"In your previous life, you engaged in sexual misconduct with external partners, constantly fearing that people would see you.
Or fearing the husband would catch, bind, beat, and kill you.
Or fearing that the governmental law would execute you in the marketplace.
The terror was continuous."
Furthermore, another ghost asked,
"Having received this body,
there is always a bronze jar on my shoulder filled with liquid copper.
I grasp a ladle and pour it onto my own head.
My entire body is scorched and rotten.
I undergo suffering thus, countless and immeasurable.
What crime or offense did I commit?"
He replied,
"In your previous life,
you left home to practice the Way and managed the monastic food and drink.
You privately set aside a jar of *sū* (ghee/cream) in another place.
When visiting *Dàorén* (practitioners) arrived, you did not give them any.
After they left, you took out the *sū* and gave it to the established monks.
This *sū* belonged to the *Zhāotí* Saṅgha; everyone had a share.
Although the share you hid and the share you gave were unequal,
it is due to this cause that you suffer this penalty."
Shìdì Huán'yīn was in the Pǔjí Jiǎngtáng
enjoying entertainment with the *Yùnǚ* (Jade Maidens).
At that time, a *Tiānzǐ* (Son of Heaven/deva) reported to Dìshì, saying,
"Qúyì (Gautama), you should know:
there is now an evil ghost upon your honored seat."
Now the *Sānshísān Tiān* (Thirty-three Heavens) were extremely angry; the ghost turned handsome, his countenance surpassing the ordinary.
Shìdì Huán'yīn then formed this thought:
"This ghost must be a spirit of marvelous power."
He went to where the ghost was, not far away,
and announced his own name and clan,
saying, "I am Shìdì Huán'yīn, the ruler of all *Tiān*."
The evil ghost turned ugly and repulsive
and gradually vanished.
In the past, there was a person in a foreign country who died.
The soul returned and whipped its own corpse.
People nearby asked,
"This person is already dead; why do you whip it again?"
The soul replied,
"This was my former body.
It committed evil for me.
It saw the scriptures and precepts but did not read them.
It committed theft, fraud, and violated other men's wives and women.
It was unfilial to parents and siblings.
It cherished wealth and refused to practice *Bùshī* (giving/charity).
Now, upon death, it caused me to fall into the evil paths.
The suffering, pain, and poison are beyond words.
That is why I have come to whip it."
In a past life, there was a Lion King
living in a deep mountain cave.
He constantly held this thought:
"I am the King among all beasts.
I have the strength to observe and protect all creatures."
In the mountains, there were two macaques
who had borne two children together.
The two macaques asked the Lion King,
"If Your Majesty can protect all beasts,
we now entrust these two children to you.
We wish to travel elsewhere to seek food and drink."
The Lion King immediately consented.
The macaques left their two children in his care and departed.
At that time, there was a Vulture King in the mountains.
His name was Lìjiàn.
While the Lion King slept,
he immediately seized the two macaque children and settled in a perilous spot.
The Lion King immediately woke up
and addressed the Vulture, saying,
"I earnestly beg you to release them and not cause me to break my promise
and feel shame."
The Vulture King replied,
"I can fly through the sky fearlessly, crossing your territory.
If you wish to protect these two children, you should sacrifice your body for me."
The Lion continued,
"If I sacrifice my body to protect these two children, it is like sacrificing dry grass.
If I protect my body and speak falsely, how can I be called a practitioner of the Way?"
Having spoken this verse,
he immediately went to a high place, intending to sacrifice his body.
The Vulture King replied again,
"To sacrifice your body for others ensures you receive unsurpassed joy.
I return the macaque children to you. I hope Your Majesty does not harm yourself."
The Lion King was born dwelling in deep
mountains and large valleys.
He had squared jaws, massive bones, and a body full of plump flesh.
His head was large, his eyes long, and his brows high and wide.
His mouth and nose were deep and squared, his teeth straight and sharp.
He extended a red and white tongue, and his paired ears were tall and prominent.
He had a long spine, a slender waist, and his belly was not visible.
He had six teeth, a long tail, and shining, glossy mane hair.
He knew his strength, and his fangs and claws were sharp.
With four feet gripping the earth, he rested securely in the rocky cave, shaking his tail and emitting sound.
If someone possesses such characteristics,
you should know they are a true Lion King.
In the morning, he leaves the cave, stretches, and yawns.
He looks around in the four directions and emits a thunderous roar.
This is for eleven reasons:
First, to destroy those who are not true lions but falsely pretend to be lions.
Second, to test his own bodily strength.
Third, to purify the dwelling place.
Fourth, to let his cubs know his location.
Fifth, to prevent fear in his pride (group).
Sixth, to awaken those who are sleeping.
Seventh, to prevent all other beasts from acting recklessly.
Eighth, to allow all beasts to come and depend on him.
Ninth, to tame the great fragrant elephants.
Tenth, to inform his children and offspring.
Eleventh, to adorn his dependents.
When the lion's roar is generally heard,
those in the water dive deep.
Those on land hide in caves.
Those flying high fall down.
Fragrant elephants in the stable break their chains, void their excrement, and flee in fear.
Even a jackal,
though it studies the lion for a hundred or a thousand years,
can ultimately not produce the lion's roar.
But if a lion cub is only three years old from birth, it can roar.
In the paths of Xiāngshān (Fragrant Mountain), there are lions;
flying birds and running beasts disappear, not daring to peek.
Among all sentient beings,
the lion is the foremost.
The Fó told Mùlián:
The Yǒngzhì Púsà
was formerly a Lion King during the time of Guāngmíng Fó.
I was a *Fànzhì* (Brahman) cultivating pure conduct.
At that time, the Lion King stood still in eight places early in the morning,
shook his body vigorously, and then gave a great, thunderous roar.
Running beasts knelt down and stayed put, while flying ones fell.
Only then did he get up.
He traversed the desolate mountains and marshes, observing his territory, searching for herds of beasts.
He encountered an Elephant King, killed it, and ate it.
A spleen bone lodged in his throat, and he died and then revived. He then spoke to a woodpecker,
"Help me pull out this bone.
Later, if I obtain food, I shall repay your kindness."
The woodpecker heard this, entered his mouth, and used all its strength to pull out the bone, managing to remove it.
The next day, the Lion King searched for food and slaughtered many beasts.
The woodpecker was nearby, seeking a little repayment for the kindness, but the lion did not reciprocate.
The Fó told Mùlián:
The Lion King at that time
replied to the woodpecker with this verse:
"I am the Lion King; killing is my livelihood.
Eating flesh and drinking blood is my daily meal.
Since you did not overestimate yourself in removing the danger from my fangs,
and managed to come out of my mouth, how can this kindness be forgotten?"
At that time, the woodpecker
again used this verse
to reply to the lion:
"Although I am a small bird, I recognize kindness and did not spare death (risked my life).
But Your Majesty does not recall the kindness, presuming your oath was burdensome.
If you could be slightly generous and grant me a little reward,
I would never regret losing my life, and I would not dare to criticize you."
Yet the Lion King ultimately did not repay the kindness,
and abandoned him and left.
The woodpecker thought to himself,
"My kindness was extremely great, yet I was treated lightly and scorned in return.
Now I must pursue him and seek an opportunity.
He who does not repay kindness shall ultimately not walk the world.
In every place, I will never leave him."
Then the Lion King again killed a herd of beasts and ate them freely as he wished.
Satiated, he slept, fearless of anything.
At that time, the woodpecker flew toward the lion.
Standing on his forehead, it used all its strength to peck out and destroy one of his eyes.
The lion awoke in shock, looked left and right, but saw no other beast.
He only saw the woodpecker alone in the tree.
Then the Lion King spoke to the woodpecker,
"Why have you now destroyed my eye?"
The woodpecker then replied with a verse:
"You received great kindness but did not repay it, and furthermore conceived a murderous intent.
Now, by leaving you one eye, how can this kindness be forgotten?
Though you are the King of Beasts, your conduct lacks reciprocity.
From this point, let us both rest. Do not create further enmity or confrontation."
The Lion King then was the Yǒngzhì Púsà of today.
The woodpecker at that time is the Mùjiānlián of today.
In the past, there were two *Bǐqiū* in the mountains.
They lived in solitude, practiced the Way, and attained spiritual powers (*shéntōng*).
Not far from them lived a lion (*shīzǐ*).
It bore two cubs and raised them until they were somewhat large.
When it wanted to go foraging,
it entrusted the cubs to the two Daoists.
It sought food near the cave.
Sometimes it returned to see them once every five days.
It stayed close and attached to the Daoists.
Then it left again to wander.
Days and months passed.
Later, the Daoists had both gone out and were not present.
A hunter encountered the lion and intended to shoot it.
The beast fled into the forest.
The hunter thought:
“This creature often depends on and attaches itself to the Daoists.
If I dress in the clothes of a Daoist,
then I will catch it.”
There were the *jiāshā* (kasaya) and religious robes left in the cave dwelling.
The hunter put them on and went to where the lion was.
The lion thought it was the Daoist.
Happily, it rushed toward him.
The hunter struck and killed it, skinned it, made a fur coat from the hide, and sold it.
The Daoists returned from their travels but did not see the lion or the cubs, and searched for them without success.
They focused their minds and observed, realizing it had been killed by the hunter.
They immediately used their spiritual powers (*shénzú*) to pursue him and seize the hide.
They used it as a sitting mat, constantly stroking it and chanting incantations (*zhòuyuàn*), wishing for the lion's liberation.
Before long, they sat in meditation again.
They observed to see which path it had taken.
And [they saw] it had been born as twin sons in the house of a great elder (*chángzhě*) in the Central Kingdom (*Zhōngguó*).
When they first entered the womb, the mother had not yet realized [she was pregnant].
The Daoists asked [the *chángzhě*]:
“What lack or thirst do you have?”
He replied: “My family is very wealthy, but we only lack sons.”
The Daoists told him:
“I can enable you to have sons.”
The *chángzhě* was greatly delighted and said: “I am truly blessed by your grace.”
The Daoists said:
“If you surely obtain sons, how will you repay this kindness?”
He replied: “When they grow up, they shall be given to the Daoists to be disciples.”
The Daoists chanted their blessing and left.
From this point, she realized she was pregnant.
Later, two identical sons were born.
When they reached eight years old, the Daoists came back to his house.
The children, due to their past affinity (*sùyuán*), naturally felt love and respect.
The Daoists spoke to the *chángzhě*:
“Do you remember the former agreement?”
The *chángzhě*, bound by his original vow, had no choice.
He therefore gave both sons to the Daoists.
The Daoists took them and made them *Shāmí* (Novices).
They practiced diligently, and before long, both also attained the Way.
They habitually sat on the hide, trying to meditate together.
They observed the spirit born from this hide.
They then realized it was the former hide of their own bodies.
Reflecting upon this chain of events, they went together before their master.
They bowed at his feet and expressed their thanks, saying:
“We have truly received great kindness.”
In a past existence, near the foot of Snow Mountain (*Xuěshān*),
there was a Lion, King of Beasts (*shīzǐ shòuwáng*).
He was the chief of five hundred lions.
Later, this Lion King grew old, sick, thin, and blind.
While walking ahead of the other lions, he fell into a dry well.
The five hundred lions all abandoned him and departed.
At that time, there was a jackal (*yěgān*) who saw the Lion King.
He thought this thought:
“The reason I am able to live securely and contentedly, fed with meat in this forest, is due to the Lion King.
Now that he has fallen into a crisis, how should I repay him?”
At that time, there was a flowing ditch nearby the well.
The *yěgān* immediately [said]:
“I will use my feet to open the channel.”
The water flowed in and filled the well, and the lion floated out.
Then the forest spirit (*línshén*) spoke
in verse (*jì yán*):
“Though one’s body is strong and mighty, one should make friends with the weak.
The small jackal was able to rescue the Lion King from the well crisis.”
The *Fó* (Buddha) said: “The Lion King was I myself.
The five hundred lions were the *bǐqiū*.
The jackal was *Ānán*.”
In a past existence, there were two beasts at the foot of Snow Mountain (*Xuěshān*).
The first was named Fine-Mane Lion (*Hǎomáo Shīzǐ*).
The second was named Fine-Tusk Tiger (*Hǎoyá Hǔ*).
They were good companions, licking each other while closing their eyes.
These two beasts constantly obtained fresh, good meat to eat.
Not far from them was a two-tongued jackal (*Liǎngshé Yěgān*).
He thought this thought:
“I will go to the two beasts and say:
‘Let me be your third companion.
Allow me to join you.’”
The lion and the tiger said:
“As you wish.” The *Liǎngshé Yěgān* ate the scraps of the two beasts and grew fat.
He then thought:
“This *Hǎomáo Shīzǐ* and *Hǎoyá Hǔ*,
being good companions, are deeply affectionate towards each other.
They close their eyes and lick each other and constantly eat good meat.
If they should fail to obtain food at times, they will certainly eat me.
I must first find a way to separate their hearts.”
He spoke to the lion, saying:
“The tiger has malicious intent toward you, Lion.
All the food you eat is thanks to my effort.”
The lion said:
“How do you know this?”
The *Liǎngshé Yěgān* replied:
“Tomorrow, when the tiger sees you and closes his eyes while licking your fur, you should know that is an evil sign.”
He then went and spoke to the tiger, saying:
“The lion has malicious intent toward you, saying:
‘All the food we eat is thanks to my effort.’”
The tiger said:
“How do you know this?”
He replied:
“Tomorrow, when he sees you and closes his eyes while licking your fur, you should know that is an evil sign.”
Among these two companions,
the tiger developed fearful thoughts.
Therefore, he went first to the lion and said:
“Have you developed malicious intent toward me?”
The lion said:
“Who told you this?”
He replied:
“The *Liǎngshé Yěgān*.”
*Hǎomáo* then asked:
“Have you also developed malicious intent toward me?”
The tiger said: “No.”
The tiger said to the lion:
“If you had such malicious words, we could not be good companions.”
*Hǎomáo* said:
“Since the *Liǎngshé Yěgān* spoke these words,
why would we not be happy to continue living together?”
He immediately spoke in verse:
“If you trust a wicked person, you will quickly separate and depart.
You will surely harbor sorrow, resentment, and hatred that never leaves your heart.
Generally, good companions are not troubled by the words of others.
If you want to cast aside those you distrust, believing others and separating,
then you will be consumed by them. Those who do not trust the two-tongued person
will return to harmony, speaking to each other what is in their hearts.
Pure in heart and soft in speech, this is how one should choose good companions.
Harmonious like water and milk. Now, this base little insect,
inherently evil since birth, possesses one head yet two tongues.”
After the tiger and the lion verified the facts,
they seized the *yěgān* together and tore him into two pieces.
Outside *Yánfútí*, in the eastern ocean,
there is a Lapis Lazuli Mountain (*Liúlí Shān*) named *Cháo*.
It is twenty *yóuxún* high and possesses various treasures.
In that mountain is a cave named *Zhǒngzhǒngsè*.
This was a place where a *Púsà* (Bodhisattva) resided in the past.
It is one *yóuxún* wide and six *yóuxún* high.
A poisonous snake lives within it, practicing *Shēngwén Cí* (Śrāvaka Compassion).
Furthermore, there is a cave named *Wúsǐ*.
It is equally high and wide.
This was a place where a *Púsà* resided in the past.
Within it is a horse practicing *Shēngwén Cí*.
Furthermore, there is a cave named *Shànzhù*.
It is equally high and wide.
Within this place where a *Púsà* resided in the past,
there is a sheep practicing *Shēngwén Cí*.
The mountain’s Tree Spirit (*Shùshén*) is named *Wúshèng*.
There is a *Luóchànǚ* (Rākṣasī) named *Shànhéng*.
Each has five hundred dependents surrounding them. These two women constantly make offerings to these three beasts.
Outside *Yánfútí*, in the southern ocean,
there is a Crystal Mountain (*Pōlí Shān*) twenty *yóuxún* high.
There is a cave named *Shàngsè*.
Its length, width, and height are likewise the same.
This was also a place where a *Púsà* resided in the past.
Within it is a monkey practicing *Shēngwén Cí*.
Furthermore, there is a cave named *Kǒushìyuàn*.
It is equally high and wide.
Within this place where a *Púsà* resided in the past,
there is a chicken practicing *Shēngwén Cí*.
Furthermore, there is a cave named *Fǎlín*.
It is equally high and wide.
Within this place where a *Púsà* resided in the past,
there is a dog practicing *Shēngwén Cí*.
Within it is a Fire God (*Huǒshén*).
There is a *Luóchànǚ* named *Yǎnjiàn*.
Each has five hundred dependents surrounding them.
These two women constantly make offerings to these three birds and beasts.
Outside *Yánfútí*, in the western ocean,
there is a Silver Mountain (*Yín Shān*) named *Pútíyuè*.
It is twenty *yóuxún* high.
Within it is a cave named *Jīngāng*.
It is equally high and wide.
Within this place where a *Púsà* resided in the past,
there is a pig practicing *Shēngwén Cí*.
Furthermore, there is a cave named *Xiānggōngdé*.
It is equally high and wide.
Within this place where a *Púsà* resided in the past,
there is a mouse practicing *Shēngwén Cí*.
Furthermore, there is a cave named *Gāogōngdé*.
It is equally high and wide.
Within this place where a *Púsà* resided in the past,
there is an ox practicing *Shēngwén Cí*.
The mountain’s Wind Spirit (*Fēngshén*) is named *Dòngfēng*.
There is a *Luóchànǚ* named *Wúhù*.
Each has five hundred dependents surrounding them.
These two women constantly make offerings to these three beasts.
Outside Yánfútí, in the northern sea.
There is a golden mountain named Gōngdéxiàng.
It is twenty *yóujùn* high.
Within it is a cave named Míngxīng.
One *yóujùn* wide.
Six *yóujùn* high.
Formerly, a Bódhisàttva dwelt within it.
There was a lion cultivating Śrāvaká-mercy.
Furthermore, there is a cave named Jìngdào.
Its height and width are also thus.
Formerly, a Bódhisàttva dwelt within it.
There was a rabbit cultivating Śrāvaká-mercy.
Furthermore, there is a cave named Xǐlè.
Its height and width are also thus.
Formerly, a Bódhisàttva dwelt within it.
There was a dragon cultivating Śrāvaká-mercy.
The mountain has a water spirit named Shuǐtiān.
There is a Ràkshasī named Xiūcánkuì.
Each has five hundred attendants.
These two women constantly make offerings to these three beasts.
These twelve beasts constantly travel within Yánfútí day and night.
Humans and deities respect them, and their merits are perfected.
They have already made deep and serious vows before the Buddhas.
For one day and one night, one beast is constantly allowed to travel and teach conversion.
The remaining eleven beasts remain settled and cultivate compassion.
They circulate and restart (in rotation).
On the first day of the seventh month, the rat first begins its travels.
Using the Śrāvakayāna, it converts and teaches all rat-bodied sentient beings.
Causing them to leave evil karma and persuading them to cultivate good deeds.
Following this order until the thirteenth day.
The rat returns to its travels.
This continues similarly until the end of the twelfth month and until the end of the twelve years.
Therefore, this land has much merit.
Even the animals are capable of being converted and taught.
For this reason, Bódhisàttvas from other directions,
should constantly revere this Buddha-world.
If there are *bǐqiū*, *bǐqiūní*, *yōupósāi*, or *yōupóyí*,
who wish to see these twelve beasts,
who wish to attain great wisdom, great concentration, and great spiritual power,
who wish to receive all existing canons and scriptures,
who wish to increase good Dharma.
This person should make a mountain using white earth.
Seven *chǐ* wide and twelve *chǐ* high.
Smear it with various perfumes and gold leaf.
The four sides of the leaf surrounding it should be twenty *chǐ* in circumference.
The *zhānpó* flowers scattered there should be held in a copper vessel.
Place various non-seasonal juices on the four sides.
Purely observing the precepts, wash and bathe three times daily.
Revere and believe in the Three Jewels.
Stand exactly three *zhàng* east of the mountain.
Recite this *zhòu* (mantra) and remain for fifteen days.
Then you will see the image of the new moon upon the mountain.
At that time, you will know you have seen the twelve beasts.
Having seen them, your wishes will be immediately granted as desired.
If one can practice asceticism, they will obtain it immediately.
The twelve beasts, the Bódhisàttvas and others, whom one sees with one's own eyes,
sometimes appear as images of deities, sometimes as images of ghosts, or as images of birds and beasts.
They travel throughout Yánfútí converting and teaching such sentient beings of various kinds.
If they tame and convert sentient beings among humans and deities,
this is not difficult.
But if they tame and convert sentient beings among animals, that is truly difficult.
The Buddha traveled alone, desiring tranquility.
He arrived and stayed beneath a precious tree in the Sāluó Forest of Bōlìluóyē in the kingdom of Jiāosàluó.
At that time, a herd of five hundred elephants
was led by an elephant king who was constantly kept at the back.
He always received turbid water and leftover grass.
Disgusted by his group, he came alone beneath the tree.
He saw the Buddha from afar.
He used his trunk to pull out grass, treading the ground to make it flat.
He used his trunk to hold water, sprinkled away the dust, and spread grass to form a seat.
He bent his knees and requested the Buddha to sit.
He made offerings for three months.
The Buddha knew the elephant's intent.
He immediately accepted the request,
and spoke a verse, saying:
"Alone and good, free from worry, like a solitary wild elephant, delighting in morality and practicing the discipline,
why need companions?"
At that time, the elephant king
retrieved good lotus roots, washed them cleanly,
and presented them to the World-Honored One.
This continued for three months.
There was an elephant king named Shànzhù.
His body was pure white, and he was settled evenly upon seven points.
He had the power to fly.
His head was red, and his body hair was variegated in color.
He had six slender, pointed tusks.
With eight thousand elephant kings as his attendants,
he dwelt beneath a Sāluó tree on Xiāngshān.
The Sāluó tree king had eight thousand bathing ponds.
Fifty *yóujùn* in breadth and length.
Their water was cool and refreshing, with embankments made of seven treasures.
Five-colored mixed flowers were gathered and interspersed within the ponds.
When the elephant king thought of entering the pond, eight thousand elephants arrived at his thought.
Some held parasols and fans.
Some chanted praises and led the way.
Some washed the king elephant's tail, back, thighs, and feet.
Some pulled up flower roots and gave them to the king to eat.
Some gathered flowers and scattered them upon the king.
The eight thousand elephants also washed and bathed, enjoying themselves together.
When they defecated and urinated,
the various Yèchā ghosts
moved them outside the mountain forest. Shìtíhuányīn's lowest mount elephant
is the one the Wheel-Turning Sagely King rides, named Xiàngbǎo.
Within Jīnbì Mountain there are eighty thousand rock caves.
Eighty thousand elephants rest and shelter within them.
Their body color is pure white.
Their heads have variegated colors.
Their mouths have large tusks.
Gold is inlaid between their teeth.
In past ages,
there was a solitary elephant
who gave birth to a calf.
Not long after falling to the ground,
its mother died.
Not far from there was the dwelling place of an immortal.
He possessed spiritual power,
was complete with merit, and held great compassion in his intention.
He saw the elephant calf from afar.
Its mother had just died, and it could barely lift its feet.
Wandering east and west, it was unable to survive on its own.
He immediately helped it return to his dwelling.
He fed it with water and fruit.
At that time, the elephant calf
was benevolent, harmonious, worthy, good, and exquisitely meritorious.
It delighted in virtuous principles.
Having attained peace and comfort, it had no worries.
At that time, the immortal lay down and rose up together with it.
Its body shape gradually grew, and its coat was glossy and vibrant.
It offered the immortal water, juice, and good fruits and melons.
Only then did it eat itself.
The immortal viewed it with compassion, observed its virtuous conduct, loved it like a son, and never tired of looking at it.
At that time, Tiāndìshì immediately had a thought.
"Now this immortal is devoted to this elephant calf and relies on it without tiring.
Perhaps I should make him grieve and feel sorrow separately."
Then Tiāndìshì manifested a test, transforming the elephant calf so that it suddenly died on the ground, with blood flowing forth.
When the immortal saw the elephant calf die, he was sorrowful, worried, and wept.
Other immortals heard of it and came to counsel and enlighten him.
But they could not remove his sorrow.
Then Tiāndìshì stayed in the empty sky,
and spoke a verse for the immortal.
Then Tiāndìshì revived the elephant calf.
The immortal was greatly delighted.
The immortal was the *héshàng* (monk) in a previous life.
The dead elephant calf was the disciple.
Tiāndìshì was my present body.
In past ages, there were three close friends:
an elephant, a monkey, and a *duò* bird, who dwelt relying on a *níjùlǜ* tree.
They said to each other,
"Since we all rely on this tree, we ought to respect each other."
The monkey and the *duò* bird jointly asked the elephant,
"How recent or distant is the time you remember about this matter?"
The elephant said,
"I remember when I was young, I walked by this tree and it reached the height of my belly."
The elephant and the *duò* bird asked the monkey.
The monkey replied,
"I remember when I was young, this tree reached only to my hand and head." The elephant then said to the monkey,
"You were born many years before me."
The elephant and the monkey jointly asked the *duò* bird.
The *duò* bird said,
"I remember that on the right side of Xuěshān there was a large *níjùlǜ* tree.
I ate a fruit from it, flew here, excreted it, and this tree immediately grew."
They said to each other,
"The *duò* bird was born the most years ago."
The elephant placed the monkey upon its head. The monkey
placed the *duò* bird upon its shoulder.
They traveled together among men.
From village to village.
From city to city.
They constantly spoke a verse, saying:
"If a person holds the Dharma, they will surely respect all elders.
They will have fame in the present world and be born in a good path in the future."
At that time, the *duò* bird preached such Dharma.
Everyone followed the Dharma teachings, and they spread widely.
"You who have left home life in my Dharma,
should respect one another."
Thus, the Buddha's Dharma spread.
"From now on, I permit you to follow the order of age, paying homage, greeting, and inquiring after one another."
At that time, the *bǐqiū* heard the Buddha's teaching.
The *bǐqiū* followed the order of age, paying homage and greeting one another.
The horse king was named Póluóxī.
His palace was located on Míngyuè Mountain within a great ocean island.
He had eight thousand horses as attendants.
If a Zhūnlún Shèngwáng appears in the world,
the smallest one is taken as the Mǎbǎo,
and provided for the King's carriage and imperial control.
There was a person from a distant region.
Leading a large ox.
Fat, strong, and powerful.
He sold it to a person in the city of Shèwèi.
The city person bought it intending to slaughter it.
While at the city gate, they encountered the Buddha.
The ox saw the Buddha from afar.
In its heart were sadness and joy.
It broke its tether and galloped away, unable to be restrained by people.
It went straight toward the Rúlái (Tathāgata), bending its two front legs.
It cried mournfully, tears running from its eyes, and spoke for itself, saying:
“Great Sage, difficult to meet, appearing only once in countless ages.
I only beg that you extend your vast compassion and rescue me with one glance.”
The Buddha said, “This is entirely acceptable.”
In a long-distant age, there was a Cakravartin King (Zhuanlún Wáng).
He ruled the four continents, possessed a thousand sons, and the Seven Treasures.
He governed with the Right Dharma (Zhèngfǎ), and the people were peaceful and secure.
Furthermore, he possessed Four Virtues.
He viewed the people as his children, and the people revered him as their father.
Śramaṇas (Shāmén), Brahmins (Fànzhì), elders (zhǎngzhě), and common folk had never suffered illness.
His virtue was proclaimed in the four domains and reached the ten directions.
The king went out to tour the four directions, and as he was returning toward the palace.
He met an old relative who was being detained by a creditor.
It was said, “He owes fifty ounces of gold and is bound to a tree.”
The king, along with his attendants and the Seven Treasures, stopped and did not proceed.
He wondered why this was happening.
He told them, saying:
“Release him and let him go; I shall repay you a hundred ounces.”
Immediately, the relative was released and returned home.
That relative repeatedly went to the palace gate seeking the gold but did not receive it.
The creditor had already hidden, and his whereabouts were unknown.
Consequently, [the creditor] remained in saṃsāra (shēngsǐ).
He wandered back and forth for countless kalpas (jié).
He did not repay what he owed until this present life.
He fell and was born in the body of this ox.
The creditor sold [the relative] for several thousand ounces of gold.
The Zhuanlún Wáng of that time is myself now.
The relative who owed the debt is this ox.
The Buddha, acting as the Sagely King (Shèng Wáng), guaranteed the debt payment.
In the end, he did not give it, and thus [the ox] has come seeking rescue.”
The Buddha told the ox owner,
“I will go begging for alms for you and repay double the price of the ox.”
The ox owner was unwilling, still wanting the ox.
The Buddha again spoke heavily:
“I will weigh the ox’s body, giving you gold corresponding to its weight.”
Still, he was unwilling to release it.
At that time, Śakra (Shì) and Brahmā (Fàn Tiān) all came down together.
They addressed the Buddha:
“Ten thousand hundred million ounces—we shall obtain it for you.”
They led the ox into the Jíhuán (Jetavana) monastery.
After seven days, its life ended, and it suddenly was born in the heavens.
It immediately recalled and recognized the merits and virtues of the Buddha.
It returned to the human world, scattered flowers as offerings, and repaid the kindness and virtue of the Buddha.
The Buddha preached the Sūtra (jīng) for it.
It immediately attained the immutable stage (bùtuì dì) of the Patience with the Non-Arising of Dharmas (wúshēng fǎ rěn).
Then it returned to the heavens.
In a past age, there was a certain wilderness.
A water buffalo king (Shuǐniú Wáng) resided there.
It roamed, eating grass and drinking spring water.
At that time, the Shuǐniú Wáng, with all its relatives and dependents,
traveled to a gathering place, and he alone was in the front.

His appearance was beautiful, his awesome spiritual power (wēishén) was magnificent, his fame and virtue were extraordinary, he was patient and mild (rěnrǔ héyǎ), and his movements were calm and dignified.
There was a monkey (míhóu) living beside the road.
It saw the Shuǐniú Wáng accompanied by his relatives.
Its heart harbored resentment and jealousy arose.
It immediately stirred up dust and threw tiles and stones.
It scattered and hurled them at [the buffalo], treating him with contempt, slander, and disgrace.
The water buffalo silently endured it and did not retaliate.
Not long after they had passed,
Another group of water buffaloes followed closely behind.
The monkey saw them and again cursed, stirred up dust, and threw stones at them.
The latter group of buffaloes,
seeing how the former buffalo king had silently accepted it and not argued, imitated him.
They endured the insult and did not harbor hatred.
After this group of dependents passed,
Not long after, a water buffalo calf (shuǐ dú) appeared.
It followed closely behind.
It was tracing the path of the herd.
Thereupon, the monkey chased it, cursing, slandering, and treating it lightly.
The water buffalo calf harbored resentment and was unhappy.
It saw how the previous group had endured the insult without hatred.
It also learned and imitated them.
Not far from the road, between a large clump of trees,
at that time, there was a Tree Spirit (Shù Shén) residing there.
He asked the Shuǐniú Wáng:
“Why, when you and your company saw this monkey shamelessly cursing you,
did you instead endure the insult and remain silent, giving no reply?”
The water buffalo replied:
“If he insults and slanders me, and I repay him,
then that person must retaliate, and thus injury and suffering (wǎng huàn) will arise.”
All the water buffaloes passed by.
Not long after, there were several Brahmins (Fànzhì).
A great gathering of people, immortals (xiānrén), and others came along the road.
At that time, that monkey also slandered and insulted
the Brahmins and their company.
They immediately seized him, stomped on him with their feet, and killed him.
Thereupon, the Shù Shén immediately recited a verse (jì), saying:
“Evil deeds do not decay; suffering will be encountered when the retribution ripens.
Now the evil deeds are full; the subsequent calamities will not rot away.”
The Buddha said,
“The Shuǐniú Wáng was precisely me.
When I was a Bodhisattva (Púsà), I fell due to a fault and became a king among water buffaloes.
I constantly practiced patience (rěnrǔ) and cultivated the Four Immeasurable Minds (Sì Děng Xīn) [loving-kindness, compassion, joy, and equanimity].
Through compassion, joy, and protection, I naturally attained Buddhahood.”
In the past, there was a man who owned a black ox.
Another ox owner, for the sake of wealth, proclaimed:
“Whose ox is stronger than mine?
If yours wins, I will forfeit my belongings.
If yours loses, you forfeit your belongings to me.”
At that time, the owner of the black ox replied, “Agreed.”
They then loaded heavy objects and tied the ox to the left side of the cart.
They mutually ridiculed and laughed, calling out,
“Black, crooked-horned one!”
They struck it with a staff and ordered it to pull the cart away.
When the ox heard this, it immediately lost its color and strength, and could not pull the heavy load up the slope.
At that time, the owner of the black ox greatly lost his possessions.
The person who won the possessions later proclaimed another challenge.
The black ox heard the sound and immediately told its owner,
“You should agree to the challenge.”
The owner said, “I cannot.”
“Why is that?”
“You wretched black ox, you caused me to lose a great amount of my belongings.
If we try again now, I will lose all my possessions.” The ox told its owner:
“Before, when we were in front of the crowd, you ridiculed my appearance.
When I heard the hateful names, I immediately lost my color and strength.
Therefore, I could not pull the heavy load up the slope.
Now, when you speak to me, do not use malicious words.
When standing before him, you should speak to me saying:
‘You are a good, great black ox, born auspicious and excellent, with wide and straight horns.’”
The owner accepted the ox’s words.
He immediately washed and scrubbed [the ox], smeared its horns, and placed a beautiful garland of flowers on it.
He tied it to the right side of the cart and spoke gentle, loving words:
“Great, auspicious black ox, wide-horned and powerful!
Pull this cart away!”
When the ox heard these gentle, loving words, it immediately regained its color and strength.
It pulled the heavy load up the slope.
At that time, the owner of the black ox recovered what he had lost previously, and moreover, gained three times that amount.
This ox owner, having gained a great benefit, was extremely delighted in his heart.
He immediately spoke a verse, saying:
“It carries heavy loads into deep ruts, and follows my words to go.
Therefore, one should speak gently and should not utter malicious words.
Gentle words possess color and strength, enabling this ox to pull heavy loads.
I gained great wealth; my body and mind are happy and joyful.”
The Buddha addressed the Bhikkhus (Bǐqiū):
“If even an animal, hearing words relating to its appearance,
loses its color and strength,
how much more so for a human being!”
In the past, there was a great Kālāma (Dà Jiāluóyuè) who used money as his profession (lending).
Two men borrowed ten thousand cash.
When the time came, they repaid it.
Later, the two men spoke to each other again:
“We should each borrow another hundred thousand cash.
Afterward, we will not repay it.”
An ox was tied up within a fence.
It spoke to the two men:
“In my previous life, because I owed my master one thousand cash and did not repay the debt,
I have been reborn as an ox three times, yet still the debt is not settled.
How much more so for you, who intend to take one hundred thousand—your sin will never be finished!”
The two men were astonished, and soon it was dawn.
The master came out.
The two men recounted the words of the ox.
The master immediately released it into the herd and never used it again.
He prayed and wished:
“May this ox, from this point forward, no longer receive this animal body.”
If there was any money left over, he gave it all away in charity (bùshī).
After the ox died, it was able to be born among humans.
In the past, a man had a donkey (lǘ) which he used to pull a cart.
It traveled several hundred *lǐ* (miles) per day.
He told his younger brother:
“Do not release the donkey or let it meet other donkeys.”
His brother found this strange and thought to himself:
“Wise men, meeting each other, are naturally joyful.
Flatterers, meeting each other, are also joyful.
Creatures of the same kind, meeting each other, are without exception joyful.”
Thus, the brother released the donkey and allowed it to meet others.
It did not bray or sniff others, nor did it eat.
When the older brother harnessed it later, it lay down and refused to move.
The older brother became greatly angry and clipped its mane and ears.
The donkey, having suffered pain, moved forward as before.
The donkey spoke to the master (dàjiā):
“Your brother released me and allowed me to meet an evil friend (è zhīshì).
I asked it why it was fat.
It replied:
‘I work for the potter (táo jiā gōng), carrying earth.
If I encounter a difficult road, I simply lie down and refuse to move.
The master then walks and carries the earth away on his shoulder.
He lets me eat by the roadside.
I get to eat good grass and, upon returning, I get hay and grain.
That is why I am fat.’
I asked why I was thin.
It replied:
‘You pull a cart, traveling five hundred *lǐ* every day.
Your food is coarse and lacking, that is why you are thin.’
I, being thin, assumed that if I acted lazily, I would become fat.
Instead, I was shaved and clipped, and I dare not lie down again.
I beg to be allowed to live.”
The master took pity on it and released it, granting it liberation (jiětuō).
The herd of oxen were naturally docile and good-natured.
Wherever they arrived,
they selected soft, fine grass to eat,
and chose cool, refreshing water to drink.
At that time, there was a donkey.
It immediately had this thought:
I will also imitate their eating and drinking.
It immediately entered the herd of oxen.
It pawed the ground with its front feet, disturbing the oxen.
It imitated their bellowing, but could not change its nature.
With its own voice, it declared, "I am also an ox!"
The horns of the oxen gored and killed it, and then they left.
The Buddha was in Shèwèi Guó.
In a past life, there was a dog.
It left its own house and went to another house to beg for food.
When it entered the other house, its body was inside the door, but its tail was outside the door.
At that time, the owner, a gùshì (householder), beat it and did not give it food.
The dog went to the assembly of officials and said:
This gùshì,
I went to his house to beg for food.
He did not give me food; instead, he beat me.
I did not violate the law of dogs.
The officials asked, "What law does a dog have?"
It replied:
When I am in my own house, I sit or lie down as I please.
When I go to another person’s house, my body enters inside the door, and my tail remains outside the door.
The officials said:
Summon the gùshì here.
They asked him:
Did you truly beat the dog and refuse it food?
He replied, "Indeed so."
The officials asked the dog:
How should this person be punished?
The dog said:
Give him the position of Great Gùshì of this Shèwèi city.
Why? It replied:
I was formerly the Great Gùshì in this Shèwèi city.
Because I created evil through body and speech, I received this dog body.
This person's wickedness is greater than mine. If this person gains power and influence,
he will certainly commit great evil and be made to enter the dìyù (hells),
where he will endure extreme suffering and vexation.
Formerly there was a kingdom
where grain and rice soared in price and the people starved.
At that time, there was a shāmén (monk) who entered the city for alms (pindola).
He obtained nothing.
Next, he reached the gate of a wealthy and powerful zhǎngzhě (elder).
He obtained coarse and poor quality rice.
Just as he was about to leave the city,
he met a butcher carrying a puppy, taking it home intending to kill it.
Seeing the shāmén, the butcher rejoiced, came forward, and performed a reverence.
The shāmén recited a benediction.
Knowing the puppy was there,
and that the man intended to kill it,
he intentionally asked the man what he was carrying.
He replied, "I am traveling empty-handed."
He asked again:
I have already seen it; please show it to me.
I wish to exchange the food for the puppy so that its life may be saved.
The man replied:
I cannot give it to you.
This happened three times, with earnest persuasion and pleading.
The man obstinately refused to comply with the request.
The shāmén then said, "You can at least show it to me."
The man immediately brought it out and showed it to the shāmén.
The shāmén lifted the rice, fed the puppy, stroked it, and recited a benediction:
Tears flowed from the puppy.
Your karma has caused you to lack freedom.
May your sins be eliminated and merit arise in life after life.
May you leave the body of a puppy and attain birth as a human,
meeting the Sānbǎo (Three Jewels).
The puppy, having received the food, immediately gave rise to a wholesome mind.
When its life ended, it was immediately born into the house of a powerful and wealthy Great Zhǎngzhě.
Just after being born and falling to the ground, it already possessed a mind of compassion.
At that time, that shāmén arrived at the Great Zhǎngzhě's gate for alms.
The zhǎngzhě’s son was then seven years old.
Seeing that shāmén, he remembered the former connection.
He immediately came forward, bowed, prostrated at the shāmén’s feet, and invited him in to offer provisions.
He returned and told his parents:
Now I wish to follow this Great Héshang (Reverend), faithfully receive the scriptures and precepts,
and become his disciple.
The parents, loving him dearly, were unwilling to grant permission.
The little boy wept and refused to eat or drink.
He said, "If you are unwilling to let me go, I will immediately die."
The parents then agreed.
He followed the master to study the Way.
He shaved off his beard and hair and donned the three religious robes.
He immediately attained sānmèi (samadhi) and established non-regression.
He enlightened and converted all beings to generate the aspiration for the Great Way.
The Buddha went to Shèwèi city, traveling for alms.
He came at that time to the house of Yīngwǔ Móláo Dōuluózǐ (Parrot Móláo's Son).
He happened upon the time when Yīngwǔ Móláo Dōuluózǐ was not home.
There was a white dog named Jù.
It sat on a fine cushion, eating polished rice and meat from a golden bowl.
The white dog saw the Shìzūn (World-Honored One) coming from afar.
Having seen him, it immediately barked.
The Shìzūn said:
Stop, white dog.
You must not make this sound.
You were formerly a reciter (Yín'é), yet now you have become a white dog.
The white dog became extremely angry.
It got down from the couch and cushion, went under the door threshold, lay down, and remained silent.
Later, Móláo Dōuluó saw this and asked the people nearby:
Who disturbed my dog and caused it grief?
Today, the shāmén Qútán (Gautama) came to the house for alms.
The dog barked at him.
Qútán said:
Stop, white dog.
You should not make this sound.
You were formerly a reciter.
The dog became angry and unhappy.
Yīngwǔ Móláo Dōuluózǐ cursed the Shìzūn from afar.
Slandering Him with rage, he went to the Gūdú Yuán (Jeta Grove).
Seeing Yīngwǔ Móláo Dōuluózǐ approaching from afar,
The Buddha instructed the bhīkṣus (monks):
This man, due to his anger, will perish and be reborn in nílí (hell).
At that time, Yīngwǔ Móláo Dōuluózǐ said to the Shìzūn:
Shāmén Qútán came to my house today for alms.
What fault did the white dog commit toward you that made it unhappy?
The Buddha said:
The white dog saw me and barked.
I said:
White dog, you should not make this sound.
You were formerly a reciter.
And the white dog became angry.
Qútán, what relation was this white dog originally to me?
The Buddha stopped Móláo and said, "There is no need to ask."
You might become distressed and unhappy.
This happened two or three times.
The Shìzūn said:
This white dog, Móláo, in its previous life,
was your father, named Dōuluó.
He became doubly enraged:
My father Dōuluó
always practiced charity and always served the fire (Fire Worship).
After his body perished, he was born in Fàntiān Shàng (the Brahma Heaven).
Why should he have been born among dogs?
Móláo, because of your high arrogance (Abhimāna),
your father Dōuluó also ended up like this later,
being born among wretched and evil dogs.
And He spoke the verse, saying:
Brahmins (Fànzhì) with high arrogance eventually take birth in the six realms (liùqù):
Among chickens, pigs, dogs, wild foxes, and donkeys, and in the dìyù (hells).
The Buddha said:
If you do not believe what I say,
you may return home and say to the white dog:
If you were truly my father Dōuluó in your former life,
then return to the couch and cushion and eat the polished rice and meat from the golden bowl.
You must show me the inherited wealth of my father
which you formerly hid and whose location I do not know.
Thereupon, Yīngwǔ Móláo Dōuluózǐ heard what the Shìzūn had said,
and reflected upon it thoroughly.
After returning home, he recounted the entire matter to the white dog.
At that moment, the white dog immediately returned to the couch and cushion and sat down.
It ate the polished rice and meat from the golden bowl.
It went to the place where it used to sleep, under the four legs of the couch.
It pawed the ground with its mouth and feet.
Thereupon, Yīngwǔ Móláo Dōuluózǐ obtained a great amount of wealth.
A joyful heart arose in him.
He placed his right knee on the ground, facing Jíshù Yuán (Jetavana).
He announced his name and clan, saying:
Truly, the Shāmén speaks truthfully and without fabrication.
After announcing this three times,
he departed Shèwèi city and went to Jíshù.
The Shìzūn saw him from afar and instructed the bhīkṣus:
Do you see Yīngwǔ Móláo Dōuluózǐ approaching?
Indeed, Shìzūn.
If, at this moment,
Dōuluózǐ were to die, he would be born in a good realm,
because he has generated a wholesome mind towards me.
Sentient beings, due to a wholesome mind,
when their bodies perish, are reborn in the good realms of the heavens.
At that time, Yīngwǔ Móláo Dōuluózǐ went to the Shìzūn’s place.
After concluding their greetings and exchange of courtesies, he said:
The words of the Buddha are without divergence (absolutely true).
There was an elder (zhǎngzhě) whose wealth was countless.
There was a vicious dog that always liked to bite people.
Ordinary people were not allowed to rashly enter his gate.
There was a Bhikṣu (bǐqiū).
He was intelligent, virtuous, wise, saintly, and difficult to reach or attain.
He entered his gate to beg for alms.
He happened to enter when the dog was lying outside, unaware of his entry.
When the elder served food, the dog woke up and then saw him.
It thought, "I was lying outside and didn't notice the Śramaṇa (shāmén) enter."
"Now that he is already sitting, what should I do?"
"If he eats alone, when he exits, I will surely bite and kill him."
"And eat the delicious food he has consumed in his belly."
"If he shares his food with me, only then will I spare him."
The Śramaṇa knew its thoughts.
He took one mouthful (chuǎi) for himself and gave one mouthful to the dog.
Goodness and kindness arose in the dog toward the Śramaṇa.
It went forward and licked his feet.
Afterwards, it went out the gate and lay down.
(Later,) a man whom it had previously bitten chopped off its head with a sword.
That dog was immediately reborn in the belly of the elder's (zhǎngzhě) wife.
After birth, it had a short life and soon died again.
It was reborn again in the house of another elder (zhǎngzhě) in that country.
When it was just over ten years old,
it saw a Śramaṇa (shāmén), went forward to welcome him, and paid homage.
It petitioned its parents to request the Śramaṇa to be its teacher.
Having offered provisions, it soon received the Sūtras (jīng) and precepts (jiè).
It further guided everyone in the household, both young and old, to recite the Sūtras and contemplate the Way (dào).
Thereupon, it informed its two parents and sought to become a Śramaṇa.
It did not receive the full ordination (jùzú).
It served and supported its Upādhyāya (héshang) day and night without slackening.
Only after the Upādhyāya (héshang) passed away did it receive the precepts and virtues.
Formerly, there were several hundred deer forming a herd.
Following the delicious grasses, they encroached close to human settlements.
When the king went out hunting, they scattered and fled.
There was one female deer (mǔlù).
Pregnant and traveling alone, she was pursued.
Hungry, exhausted, and having lost her companions,
she then gave birth to two fawns, left them, and went to seek food.
Distraught, frightened, and having lost her way, she fell into a hunter's trap (huò).
She cried sadly, wishing to get out, but could not escape.
The hunter heard the sound and immediately went to look.
Seeing the deer, he was delighted and immediately stepped forward intending to kill her.
The deer then kowtowed, begged for mercy, and explained herself.
"I just gave birth to two fawns; they are still small and ignorant."
"They have just opened their eyes, bewildered, and do not yet know east from west."
"I beg you to grant me a moment to temporarily return and see my fawns."
"I will show them water and grass so they may live."
"I will then return immediately to face death, not violating my vow of sincerity."
The hunter was astonished.
He immediately replied to the deer, saying:
"Even all people in this world rarely possess utmost sincerity."
"How much less a deer, escaping death—how could it possibly return?"
The deer replied again:
"If you permit it, my fawns will live."
"If you detain me, my fawns will perish."
She spoke a verse (gè) saying:
My body is a wild animal (shòu) that roams the forest thickets;
This humble creature clings to its body and life, thus cannot defy death.
Now I have fallen into your trap (huò), my fate is to approach the knife block;
I do not begrudge this rank, foul body, but only pity my two fawns.
The hunter found this extremely strange and unusual.
Yet, his heart still held greed.
He replied to the deer again, saying:
"Artful deceit is unsubstantial, treachery and cunning are hard to trust."
"Empty vanity has ten thousand forms, and slyness is not singular."
"Cherishing the body and fearing death, few are able to sacrifice their life."
"If even humans lack goodness, it is difficult to set a time limit (for return)."
"How much more a beast (shòu) — having left, how could it ever return?"
"I absolutely will not release you."
The deer wept again.
She replied with a verse (gè):
Although my body is a lowly beast, ignorant of benevolence (rén) and righteousness (yì);
How could I receive your compassion and grace, and then leave and never return?
I would rather submit to the pain of being cut up than exist through falsehood and deceit.
Grieving for my two helpless fawns, I beg for a brief interval.
Should there be wicked people in the world who cause discord among the Bhikṣu Saṅgha (bǐqiūsēng);
Who destroy stūpas (tǎ), ruin Buddhist temples (fósì), and kill Arhats (āluóhàn);
Who commit rebellion, harm parents, wives, children, or servants (núbì);
If I do not return, my sin shall be greater than all of these!
The hunter heard the deer’s words again.
His heart became even more awed.
He stepped back and sighed, saying:
"Alas, I live in the world, having been born as a human."
"I am ignorant, confused, and unenlightened, turning my back on grace and slighting righteousness (yì)."
"I injure and harm living beings, taking killing and hunting as my profession."
"I seek ill-gotten gains through treachery and deceit, and my greed is insatiable."
"I do not recognize impermanence (wúcháng) nor distinguish the Three Jewels (Sān Zūn)."
"What this deer says is superior to that of humans."
"Its sincere vow is profound, revealing ultimate loyalty."
He then stepped forward, untied the trap (huò), and let her go.
Thereupon, the deer returned to the place of her fawns.
She lowered her head, whined softly, and licked the fawns' bodies.
She felt both sorrow and joy.
And spoke a verse (gè) saying:
All unions of love and affection are brought together by dependent causation (yīnyuán);
Where there is meeting, there is separation; impermanence (wúcháng) makes duration difficult.
Now I, your mother, constantly fear for my own safety;
Life in this world is full of dread, and life is more fleeting than morning dew.
Thereupon, the doe led her two fawns.
She showed them good water and grass.
With streaming tears mixing together,
she spoke a verse (gè) of farewell:
This morning, as I traveled, I met misfortune and mistakenly fell into the hunter’s hands;
Immediately I should have been butchered, my body broken down into decay;
Thinking of you, I begged for mercy to come here, and now I must return to face death;
Pitying you, who will soon be orphans, strive hard to sustain your own lives.
Having spoken, the doe left and departed.
The two fawns cried sadly, shedding tears of longing.
They pursued her from behind, collapsing and then getting up again.
The mother looked back and commanded:
"You must return and not follow me."
"We must not allow both mother and children to lose their lives together."
"I am willing to bear the grief of my death."
"You do not yet understand that the world is impermanent (wúcháng) and that all relationships entail separation."
"I myself have poor fate, and you were born without aid."
"Why harbor sorrow? You only increase worry and suffering in vain."
"You should simply establish your will and complete your lives."
Thereupon, the mother spoke this verse (gè) for her fawns:
In previous lives, I generated greed and affection, and now affection sustains this body;
All births in the world must face death, and those who do not escape affliction will not finish their troubles.
Once the mind is controlled and separated from craving (tān), then comes great peace.
I would rather submit to death based on my spoken promise than survive through deception.
The fawns still cried, grieving and longing.
They followed each other until they reached the location of the trap (huò).
Searching east and west,
they saw the hunter lying beneath a tree.
The doe stood still.
She spoke a verse (gè) to awaken him:
The deer you previously released has now returned to face death;
Your grace and favor upon this lowly creature allowed me to bid farewell to my two fawns;
I led them to show them water and grass, and spoke to them of the suffering of impermanence (wúcháng);
Though dying ten thousand times, I have no regrets, recalling your kindness, I dared not betray it.
The hunter was suddenly roused and stood up in surprise.
The deer knelt toward him again.
She repeated a verse (gè) saying:
Your prior release of me—your virtue is heavier than heaven and earth;
This humble beast (shòu), covered by your compassion, came to fulfill its promise and approach death;
Moved by your benevolence (rén) and unforgettable grace, I dared not violate your decree;
Even in returning to repay you, I still cannot complete the measure of your kindness.
The hunter saw the deer’s absolute sincerity and willingness to die for righteousness (yì).
Her integrity was deeply sincere, and her compassionate action demonstrated loyalty.
Her release was met by evidence of her abandoning life to fulfill her oath.
The mother and fawns had followed each other, grieving and longing, and arrived together.
Compassion moved him to pity and grief.
He bowed his head and apologized, saying:
"Are you a celestial being or a deity (shénqí)? Your sincerity and righteousness (yì) are marvelous to this extent!"
"My heart is filled with awe and dread; how could I dare inflict any harm upon you?"
"I would rather kill my own vile self or harm my wife and children,"
"How could I bear to harbor even the slightest thought of harming this divine spirit?"
The hunter immediately released the deer and let her go.
The mother and fawns cried out with sorrow and joy, bleating gently.
They thanked the hunter with a verse (gè):
This lowly animal, living in the world, should have filled the kitchen butcher's block;
My life should have ended immediately in cooking and cutting, yet your great kindness allowed me to bid farewell to my two fawns;
Your divine benevolence (rén) greatly cherishes living things, and again we received release, pardon, and forgiveness;
The accumulated merit and blessing are immeasurable, not something that can be expressed by mouth.
The hunter fully reported this to the King (Wáng).
Everyone in the kingdom came to know of it.
They were universally moved by this compassion and sincerity.
The benevolent conduct of the beast (shòu) surpassed righteousness (yì).
Everyone was filled with solemn admiration.
For their sake, hunting and killing were stopped.
The deer returned, bleating to their herd and calling to their companions; they gathered and each settled in its place.
The Buddha (Fó) said:
"The deer at that time was myself."
"The two fawns were Luóyún and the mother of Zhūlì."
"The King (Guówáng) at that time was Shèlìfú."
"The hunter was Ānán."
Formerly, a King (Guówáng) traveled and hunted.
He built an enclosure and a pit to capture the herd of deer.
At that time, there was a Deer King (Lùwáng) leading hundreds of millions of deer.
They came in succession to eat the delicious grass and entered the enclosure.
The guards closed the gate.
They went and reported to the King (Wáng).
The King (Wáng) was greatly delighted.
The Deer King immediately knew this.
He thought to himself:
"The reason the herd of deer came here is because of me alone."
"I must devise a plan to save the lives of the multitude."
He immediately laid his body horizontally over the pit.
He allowed the herd of deer to tread on his back and exit.
Their hooves injured his back, completely stripping away the skin and flesh.
Only the bones remained.
Enduring the pain, he saved them until all had successfully exited.
Struggling, he climbed onto the bank and looked around in the four directions.
There was only one deer that did not know how to seek escape.
The Deer King called out, and it came and was able to exit.
Thereupon, the Deer King (Lùwáng) exhausted his life force and fell into the pit.
Luóyuè Qíshéjué Shān.
His body suffered from a wind ailment.
Qíyù Yīwáng compounded soothing medicine for him,
using thirty-two ingredients.
Daily, he consumed thirty-two liǎng.
At that time, Típódá always harbored jealousy.
His heart was proud and great, hoping to be equal to the Buddha.
Imitating the Buddha, he also consumed the drug, which spread through all his veins and channels.
His bodily strength became weak, and he suffered painfully, groaning and crying out.
The Shìzūn took pity on him and stroked his head with his hand.
The medicine took effect, the sickness was removed, and he recognized the Buddha's hand.
He said:
"Xīdá, since the world did not adopt your other arts, you have returned to studying the path of medicine?"
The Buddha said:
"Típódá, your harboring of evil intent is not limited to today.
Formerly, there was a city in Yánfú Tí named Bōluónài.
The king was named Fànmódá.
He was violent, cruel, and lacked compassion.
He dreamed he saw a beast.
Its body hair was golden, and the tips of the hairs shone with gold light.
He immediately summoned the hunters.
'I will fully tell you my dream,' he announced.
'You are to seek and capture it.
If you obtain its hide, I shall reward you heavily.
If you do not obtain it, I will execute and destroy your clan.'
At that time, the hunters were worried and confused, gathering to discuss a plan.
They jointly selected one person to go and seek it.
'If you do not return successfully, we shall still give provisions to your wife and children.'
That person thought to himself:
'I must abandon my life and body; then I can undertake this journey.'
He traversed perilous lands and departed.
After a long time, his body was exhausted.
The weather was hot, oppressive, and steaming; he felt like he was about to die.
Sad and distressed, he cried out:
'Who possesses compassion to save my life?'
There was a wild beast named Míngtuó.
Its body hair was golden, and it was known to be very compassionate.
It submerged itself in a cold spring and came to embrace him.
Once he regained a little strength, it led him to the water source.
It bathed him and picked fruits for him to eat.
Once his body was recovered,
he thought to himself:
'Now I see this beast, exactly the one the king seeks.
However, when I was near death, I relied on it to save my life.
I have not yet repaid this gratitude; how could I bring myself to harm it?
Yet, if I do not capture it,
those other hunters will certainly be executed.'
Thinking this, he was sorrowful.
Míngtuó asked, 'Why are you unhappy?'
He replied with what was in his heart.
Míngtuó said:
'Do not worry about this matter; my hide is easy to obtain.
I have given up countless bodies, yet have never truly created merit.
Now, by using my body's hide, I can save the lives of those many people.
If you choose to obtain it,
just flay the hide; do not immediately cut off my life.
I bestow this upon you, and I shall never regret it.'
The hunter flayed the hide.
Míngtuó immediately made a vow:
'Now I use my hide as a gift to this person.
I save their precious lives.
I offer this merit to all sentient beings,
so that I may achieve the Buddha Path and universally save everyone.'
Once this vow was made, the three thousand worlds shook six times.
After the hide was flayed and removed, his body was naked and raw, and blood streamed profusely.
Furthermore, there were eighty thousand kinds of flies and ants.
They gathered on his body, feeding upon it simultaneously.
Though he wished to move towards a cave, he feared harming them.
He endured the pain, holding himself firm, his body remaining still.
He died there.
Those flies and ants that fed on him, when they died, were born in heaven.
