The hunter carried the hide and presented it to the king.
The king saw it as marvelous, and always spread it out to sleep on.
His body and mind were peaceful, comfortable, and joyful.
Míngtuó, the beast, is now my present body (i.e., myself).
King Fànmódá is now Típódá.
The eighty thousand insects are those who, when I first achieved Buddhahood and began turning the Dharma Wheel,
achieved the Way among the eighty thousand heavenly beings."
There was a wild fox that went to beg food from a lion.
Since it always received leftovers, it persisted in going without stopping.
It happened that the lion was hungry and had not yet eaten.
It called the wild fox, sniffed it, seized it, and swallowed it.
Before dying, while still in the throat, the fox cried out:
"Great Master, save me!"
The lion thought:
"I raised you to be fat and furry so I could keep you in reserve for this purpose!
What else do you have to say?"
There was a woman who placed her baby in one spot.
A wolf seized the child and ran off.
People pursued it and said to the wolf:
"Why are you carrying away someone else's child?"
The wolf replied:
"This child's mother is my enemy.
For five hundred lifetimes, she always ate my children.
I likewise, for five hundred lifetimes, always killed her children.
If she can abandon the heart of old resentment,
I can also abandon it."
Then people spoke to the child's mother:
"You should abandon your heart of resentment."
The child's mother replied:
"I have now abandoned it."
The wolf looked at the child's mother.
Although she said she had abandoned it, her heart had not let go.
The wolf harmed the child and departed.
Formerly, there was a Fànzhì aged one hundred and twenty.
Since youth, he had not married a wife and had no lustful desires.
He lived quietly in the deep mountains, using reeds for his hut.
He used weeds for his mat, and relied on fruits and melons for sustenance.
He stored no wealth or treasures.
The king invited him, but he did not go, remaining upright and inactive.
For several thousand years, he enjoyed himself among the birds and beasts.
There were four kinds of beasts.
The first was a fox.
The second was a monkey.
The third was an otter.
The fourth was a rabbit.
These four beasts listened to the scriptures and discourses on precepts at the Daoist practitioner's place.
This continued for a long time.
All the fruits and melons used for food were consumed and finished.
Afterwards, the Daoist practitioner intended to leave.
These four great beasts were anxious, worried, and unhappy.
They discussed together, saying:
"We should each seek offerings for him."
The monkey fetched sweet fruits and presented them to the Daoist practitioner.
The fox also sought food, obtained a sack of dried rice and presented it to the Daoist practitioner.
The otter entered the water, caught a large fish, and presented it to the Daoist practitioner.
The rabbit contemplated:
"What should I use to make an offering to the Daoist practitioner?"
It thought to itself:
"I must offer my own body as an offering."
It went and gathered brushwood, kindled a fire, and made charcoal.
It went and reported to the Daoist practitioner, saying:
"Today, I am lacking.
Please let me become charcoal and enter the fire,
so that I may offer my body to the Daoist practitioner."
But the fire would not burn.
The Daoist practitioner was touched by its benevolence and righteousness.
Taking pity on it, he then remained (did not leave).
The Fànzhì at that time was Tíhéjié Fó.
The rabbit is my current body (i.e., myself).
The monkey is Shèlìfú.
The fox is Ānán.
The otter is Mùjiànlián.
The Buddha and the various Bhīqiū,
accepted the invitation of Shīzhì Póluómén.
Upon returning to Qíshé,
they washed their bowls by the river.
In the Ānluó forest, there was a monkey.
It traveled and saw a tree with ripe honey, yet without bees.
It came up to Ānán and requested a bowl.
Ānán did not give it.
The Buddha said, "Just give it."
The monkey received the bowl, filled it with honey, and offered it to the Shìzūn.
The Shìzūn did not accept it, instructing him to cleanse it with water.
The monkey did not understand.
It thought there might be insects inside.
It took the bowl to the water's edge and washed it.
The water washed the honey, and the monkey presented it back to the Buddha. The Buddha distributed it among the Sangha until all had received a share.
The monkey, joyful, leaped and danced, fell into a pit, and died.
It was reborn in the womb of Shīzhì's wife.
Later, a male child was born, handsome in appearance. The Buddha said:
"In the past, during the time of Jiāyè Fó,
there was a young Shāmen.
He saw an Āluóhàn leap across a river.
He spoke of him as an ordinary Bhīqiū, saying:
'You jump rapidly like a monkey.'
Afterward, for five hundred lifetimes, he was consistently reborn as a monkey."
in the kingdom of Mótuóluó (Mathurā). A hundred years later, on Yōulúmàntuó Shān,
on one side were five hundred Pratyekabuddhas.
On one side were five hundred immortals (Xiānrén).
On one side were five hundred monkeys.
The monkey leader went to the dwelling place of the Pratyekabuddhas and saw all the Pratyekabuddhas.
He conceived a joyful heart.
He took flowers and fruits from the trees and offered them to the Pratyekabuddhas.
He paid obeisance (zuòlǐ) and sat at the foot of the assembly.
He did this every day.
Later, all the Pratyekabuddhas entered Nirvāṇa.
The monkey continued his offerings as before.
He saw that the Pratyekabuddhas did not accept the offerings.
He then pulled their robes and grasped their feet, but they still did not move.
The monkey thought,
"They must all be dead."
He wept and grieved bitterly.
He then went to the place of the five hundred Xiānrén.
They had all gone into the midst of thorny thickets.
The monkey also went there.
The Xiānrén then went onto the ashes and dirt.
The monkey also went onto the ashes and dirt.
The Xiānrén subjected their bodies to the five fires.
The monkey also did the same.
When the Xiānrén hung themselves by climbing trees, the monkey
pushed their hands, causing them to fall to the ground.
He constantly taught and converted all the Xiānrén using the four dignified deportments.
After he had converted them,
he sat upright and practiced meditation in the presence of the Xiānrén.
He said to the Xiānrén,
"All of you must sit like this."
At that time, the five hundred Xiānrén followed him and practiced sitting meditation (zuòchán).
Although the Xiānrén had no teacher preaching the Dharma,
concerning the Thirty-Seven Factors Conducive to Enlightenment (Sānshíqǐ Pǐn Zhù Pútí Fǎ),
they contemplated, attained realization, and achieved the path of a Pratyekabuddha.
They all had this thought:
"I attained the Holy Path because of this monkey."
They immediately used incense, flowers, food, and drink to make offerings to the monkey.
When the monkey died, they cremated his body with fragrant wood.
The Buddha said to Ānán (Ānanda),
"This monkey is none other than Yōupōjíduō (Upagupta).
While in a lower realm, he created great benefits for many sentient beings.
A hundred years or more after my Nirvāṇa,
there will be superior affairs."
Formerly, when the Buddha was in Luōyuèzhī Guó (Rājagṛha),
he sent an Arhat named Xūmàn (Sumana).
He carried the Buddha's hair and nails to the southern mountains of Jìbīn Guó (Kashmir) to erect a stupa (Fótú).
Five hundred Arhats frequently resided in that monastery (sì).
Morning and evening, they burned incense, circumambulated the stupa, and paid obeisance.
At that time, there were five hundred monkeys in those mountains.
They saw the renunciants (dàorén) making offerings to the stupa and monastery.
They immediately went together to the edge of a deep ravine.
They carried dirt and stones on stretchers, imitating the building of a stupa (Fótú).
They erected wood to form a finial (chà) and tied worn-out banners to their heads.
They paid obeisance morning and evening, just like the dàorén.
At that time, the mountain waters suddenly surged and swelled.
The five hundred monkeys were drowned simultaneously.
Their spirits immediately were reborn in the second heaven, Trayastriṃśa (Dāolì Tiānshàng).
They had halls made of seven treasures, and clothing and food appeared naturally.
Each one thought to himself:
"From where did I come that I gained rebirth in heaven?"
They immediately used their divine eyes (tiānyǎn) to see their former forms:
the bodies of monkeys,
who had imitated the dàorén playfully constructing a stupa and monastery.
Although their bodies were drowned, their spirits gained rebirth in heaven.
"Now we must descend and repay the kindness of our former bodies."
Each one brought attendants, flowers, incense, and musical instruments and approached their former corpses.
They scattered flowers, burned incense, and circumambulated them seven times.
At that time, there were five hundred Brahmins (Póluómén) in the mountains.
They followed external teachings, held heterodox views (xiéjiàn), and did not believe in sin or merit.
They saw the celestial beings (tiānrén) scattering flowers, making music, and circumambulating the monkeys' corpses.
They were astonished and asked,
"Your celestial light and splendor are so magnificent.
Why do you humble yourselves to make offerings to these corpses?"
The celestial beings said,
"These corpses are our former bodies."
They fully recounted the former affair.
"It was through this small merit that we gained rebirth in heaven.
Therefore, we now scatter flowers to repay the kindness of our former bodies.
To playfully construct a stupa and monastery yields such merit.
If you were to wholeheartedly serve the Buddha,
that virtue would be hard to compare.
You hold heterodox views (xiéjiàn) and do not believe in the True Path (zhèngzhēn).
Though you labor diligently for a hundred kalpas, you will gain nothing.
It is better to go together to Jīshéjué Shān (Gṛdhrakūṭa Hill), pay obeisance, serve, and make offerings, thereby gaining unlimited merit."
They all joyfully went together to the place of the Buddha.
They paid obeisance with their five limbs (wǔtǐ) and scattered flowers as offerings.
The celestial beings reported to the Buddha,
"We were recently in the bodies of monkeys.
Thanks to the grace of the World-Honored One (Shìzūn),
we gained rebirth in heaven.
We regret not having seen the Buddha, and now we intentionally take refuge."
They reported again to the Buddha, saying,
"In our previous lives, what offenses did we commit that caused us to receive the body of a monkey?
Although we built the stupa and monastery, our bodies were drowned and swept away."
The Buddha told the celestial beings,
"You did not arise from nothing.
In a past life, there were five hundred young Brahmins (Póluómén) who traveled together and entered the mountains, seeking the way of the Xiānrén.
At that time, there was a Śramaṇa (Shāmén) on the mountain.
He intended to plaster and repair his vihāra (jīngshè) on the mountain.
He went down to the valley to fetch water, his body moving lightly as if flying.
The five hundred Brahmins arose with jealous intent and laughed at him in unison, saying,
'This Śramaṇa floats up and down swiftly, just like a monkey.
Why should he be considered remarkable?
If he does not stop fetching water like this,
when the mountain water comes, he will soon drown.'
The Buddha told the celestial beings,
'The Śramaṇa moving up and down swiftly at that time was myself.
The five hundred young Brahmins were the five hundred bodies of the monkeys.
Because of the offense they committed through playful laughter, they received that bodily retribution.'
The Buddha spoke a gāthā, saying:
'Playful laughter results in evil; weeping and lamenting receive the retribution.'
When the five hundred celestial beings heard the Buddha's words, they immediately attained the stages of the Path.
The five hundred Brahmins heard about the retribution for offenses and the reward for merits.
They sighed to themselves, saying,
'We have been studying the way of the Xiānrén for accumulated years.
Yet we have not received any fruits of practice.
It is not comparable to the monkeys who playfully created merit and gained rebirth in heaven.
The Buddha's virtue is truly profound.'
They bowed their heads at the Buddha's feet, requesting to become disciples.
The Buddha said,
'Welcome, Bhikṣus (Bǐqiū).'
They immediately became Śramaṇas, diligently advanced, and attained the Path.
Formerly, there was a dàorén.
He sat in meditation (zuòchán) beneath a tree and recited scriptures.
There was a monkey in the tree that imitated him.
Unaware, he fell from the tree and died.
He gained rebirth in heaven.
Formerly, there was a king who owned a monkey.
It frequently played with a maidservant without stopping.
A Brahmin (Fànzhì) told the king,
"You must separate this maidservant and the monkey."
The king replied,
"How can they get along so well that I should make them separate?"
Later, the maidservant came from outside, carrying a meal vessel and a large staff.
The monkey ran over and pulled the maidservant.
The maidservant, in anger, pushed him with her foot and struck him with the staff.
The monkey fell into the fire, burning his hairy coat.
He ran away and entered the dry firewood stack.
The fire spread to the houses and the palace.
The treasures and storage were all reduced to ashes.
Only then did the king understand the words of the Brahmin (Fànzhì).
Formerly, there was a rabbit king (tùwáng) roaming in the mountains.
He ate fruit and drank water together with his companions.
He practiced the Four Immeasurables (sìděngxīn): loving-kindness (cí), compassion (bēi), joyful sympathy (xǐ), and equanimity (hù).
He instructed all his dependents to be benevolent and harmonious and not commit any evil deeds.
"After completing this life, you will be reborn in human form.
You will then be able to receive the religious teachings."
At that time, all his dependents were joyful.
They followed the instructions and dared not disobey the command.
There was a Xiānrén residing among the forest trees.
He ate fruit, drank water, and cultivated the Path alone.
He never wandered about freely, but established the four sublime states (Sì Fànxíng).
Practicing loving-kindness, compassion, joyful sympathy, and equanimity, he recited scriptures and contemplated the Dao.
His voice was clear and eloquent, and his tone was harmonious and elegant; anyone who heard it was delighted.
At that time, the rabbit king went near him.
Listening to his scripture recitation, his heart leaped with joy and he felt no satiety.
Together with his dependents, he brought fruits and melons to make offerings to the dàorén.
Thus, days accumulated and months and years passed.
Then the winter cold arrived.
The Xiānrén desired to return to the human realm.
The rabbit king saw this and became anxious, sad, and unhappy.
His heart was full of attachment and regret, and he did not wish for the Xiānrén to leave.
He asked where he was going.
"Being here and seeing you every day is our joy.
We forget hunger and thirst, relying on you as parents.
We beg you to stay and not depart."
The Xiānrén replied,
"I have the Four Great Elements (sìdà) which I must carefully guard and protect.
Now that the winter cold has arrived, fruits and melons are gone.
The mountain water is frozen, and there is no cave where I can reside.
Therefore, I wish to leave and rely on a dwelling place among humans.
I will seek food by begging (fēnwèi) and stay temporarily in a vihāra (jīngshè).
After this cold winter has passed, I shall join you again.
Do not be distressed."
The rabbit king answered,
"We, your dependents, shall go and seek fruits.
We will search far and near and surely provide you with enough.
We beg you to condescend once, show compassion, and save us by staying.
If you leave, our sorrowful attachment might prevent us from sustaining ourselves.
Even if today we have no offerings,
I will offer my own body to serve the dàorén."
The dàorén saw this and was deeply moved with compassionate thoughts.
Pitying his sincere heart, he wondered what could be done.
The Xiānrén served the fire, and there were burning coals before him.
The rabbit king thought in his heart,
"The dàorén is doing this for me," and thus remained silent, lifted his entire body, and threw himself into the fire.
The fire was blazing fiercely; the dàorén intended to rescue him.
But he had already passed away and was reborn in Tuṣita Heaven (Dōushù Tiān).
In the body of a Bodhisattva (Púsà), his merit was especially honored and his majestic power was lofty.
The Xiānrén saw this.
"For the sake of virtue and the Path, he did not begrudge his body and life."
Pitying him and feeling sorrow, he also disciplined himself
by fasting and refusing food.
Immediately thereafter, his spirit transferred and dwelled in Tuṣita Heaven (Dōushuài Tiān).
The Buddha said,
"The rabbit king at that time was myself.
The Xiānrén was Dìngguāng Fó (Dīpaṃkara Buddha)."
In a past existence, there was a cat-weasel.
Hungry, thirsty, weak, and thin.
In a hole, it watched and sought a young rat.
When the young rat came out, [the cat-weasel] swiftly seized and swallowed it.
The young rat's body was small and entered the belly alive.
It ate its internal organs.
The cat-weasel became confused and distressed, running wildly east and west.
Consequently, it died.
Foolish mendicants are unskillful.
In protecting their bodies and minds, they see various women.
And grasp at the form and characteristics.
The Buddha said:
*Jiālántuó* is the name of a mountain rat.
At that time, the King of *Píshèlǐ*,
led various courtesans into the mountains to amuse themselves.
The King was weary and slept beneath a tree.
The courtesans scattered to the left and right, running and playing.
At that time, in a cave beneath the tree, there was a large venomous snake.
Hearing the King’s smell of wine, it came out, desiring to sting the King.
A rat in the tree came down from above, squeaking to awaken the King.
The snake immediately retreated.
The King awoke, then slept again.
The snake came out once more.
The rat again squeaked and came down to awaken the King.
The King rose and saw the great venomous snake.
He immediately felt shock and terror.
He sought the courtesans but could not see them.
The King reflected, saying:
"I have survived today.
It is due to the grace of this rat."
He pondered how to repay [the favor].
At that time, there was a village near the mountain.
He immediately commanded the villagers,
"From now on, all my stipulated offerings shall be dedicated to supporting the rat."
Because of this rat, this village was named *Jiālántuó*.
At that time, there was an elder in the village.
He possessed forty billion gold coins.
The King immediately granted him the rank of Elder.
Due to the name of the village, he was called Elder *Jiālántuó*.
Formerly, the family of an elder possessed a ghee jar.
Its lid on the high building was not secure.
A rat entered the ghee jar and ate day and night.
Its body grew large, and the ghee was thus exhausted.
The rat filled the jar and looked like the color of ghee.
Someone came to buy ghee.
At that time, the elder took the ghee and placed it over a fire.
The rat, being inside the jar, died within the jar.
It transformed back into ghee.
The elder sold it to the buyer.
When measuring it out by the pint or peck, the bones sank to the bottom.
The skull and leg bones separated and dissolved.
The Golden-Winged Bird has four kinds.
First is born from an egg.
Second is born from a womb.
Third is born from moisture.
Fourth is born by transformation.
All previously performed great generosity, yet their minds were arrogant and lofty, soaring above the void.
They caused suffering to sentient beings, and their minds harbored much hatred and conceit.
Thus they were born among these birds.
They possess wish-fulfilling jewels as their necklaces.
They exhibit ten thousand kinds of transformations, and there is nothing they cannot accomplish.
Their bodies are forty *lǐ* tall.
Their clothing is eighty *lǐ* wide.
The clothing is forty *lǐ* long.
It weighs two and a half *liǎng*.
They eat turtles, alligators, fish, and soft-shelled turtles as solid food, and use washing/bathing garments as delicate, smooth food.
They also have marriages.
The contact of two bodies forms the *yīn* and *yáng*.
Their lifespan is one *kalpa*, or sometimes less.
On the north shore of the Great Ocean, there is a tree named *Jiūluóchēnmó*, one hundred *yóuxún* high.
It casts shade fifty *yóuxún*. To the east of the tree is the palace of the egg-born Nāgas and the palace of the egg-born Garuḍas.
To the south of the tree is the palace of the womb-born Nāgas and the palace of the womb-born Garuḍas.
To the west of the tree is the palace of the moisture-born Nāgas and the palace of the moisture-born Garuḍas.
To the north of the tree is the palace of the transformation-born Nāgas and the palace of the transformation-born Garuḍas.
Each palace measures six thousand *yóuxún* in length and width.
Their ornamentation is as mentioned above.
If an egg-born Garuḍa flies down into the ocean and strikes the water with its wings,
the water immediately divides into two banks, two hundred *yóuxún* deep.

The bird seizes the egg-born Nāgas and eats them as it wishes. The womb-born, moisture-born, and transformation-born [Garuḍas] do likewise. There was a transformation-born Nāga’s son who observed the eight precepts during the three fast days.
At that time, a Garuḍa wished to seize and eat him.
It carried him in its beak up onto a great iron tree on the north side of Mount *Xūmí*.
It was 160,000 *lǐ* high.
The Garuḍa searched for his tail but could not find it.
The bird heard [the teaching] and also received the five precepts.
The King of the Garuḍas,
was named *Zhèngyīn*.
Among the feathered tribes, he enjoyed freedom and happiness.
In *Yánfútí*, he consumed one Nāga King and five hundred smaller Nāgas daily.
In the Four Continents, he ate further.
The daily number was also as above.
Turning in a cycle, starting again.
After eight thousand years, when the signs of death appeared,
the Nāgas spat poison, and he could not obtain food.
Tormented by hunger, frantic, he found no lasting peace.
He reached the Adamantine Mountain.
He went straight down from the Adamantine Mountain, from the edge of the great waters.
He reached the boundary of the Wind Wheel, was blown by the wind, and returned to the Adamantine Mountain.
He did this seven times, and then he died.
Because of his poison, the Ten Jewel Mountains caught fire simultaneously.
*Nántuó* Nāga King, fearing the burning of these mountains,
immediately sent down heavy rain, the drops like cartwheels.
The bird's flesh dissolved completely, only the heart remained.
The heart also went straight down seven times, as before, staying on the Adamantine Mountain.
*Nántuó* Nāga King took it and made it into a radiant pearl.
The Cakravartin obtained it as a wish-fulfilling jewel.
If a person contemplates the Buddha, their heart is likewise.
A thousand years.
Human face, bird body.
The son born subsequently killed its mother.
The son later studied and attained the fruit of Arhat.
Animals do not possess this wisdom, nor do they possess the concept of high or low status.
They do not incur the five deadly sins.
Near the Monkey River in *Píshèlǐ*, there was a garlic garden.
The *Tōuluónántuó* Bhikṣuṇī
lived not far from the garden.
The garden owner asked:
"Auntie, do you need garlic?"
The Bhikṣuṇī, together with the Śrāmaṇerikā and Śikṣamāṇā,
repeatedly went to ask for garlic.
Consequently, they finished it all.
The owner abandoned the garden and left.
The Buddha spoke of a previous life story.
Formerly, there was a Brāhmaṇa.
He was 120 years old, and his body was weak and thin.
His wife was incomparably beautiful.
They had many sons and daughters.
This Brāhmaṇa was deeply attached to his wife and his children.
He never abandoned them.
Because of this deep emotional attachment,
he eventually died and was reborn among the geese.
His body's feathers were entirely golden.
Due to previous causes of merit, he remembered his past life.
He thought, "By what means can I support these sons and daughters so they do not suffer poverty?"
Every day he came back and shed one feather before leaving at sunset.
The children saw this but did not know the cause.
They immediately discussed, saying:
"We should wait until he comes.
We should find a way to seize him and take all the golden feathers."
According to their plan, they plucked out all the golden feathers.
When the feathers were gone, white feathers grew instead.
The Buddha told the Bhikṣus:
"If you wish to know who the Brāhmaṇa who died and became a goose at that time was,
how could it be anyone else?
It is the garden owner.
His beautiful wife is the Bhikṣuṇī.
The sons and daughters are the Śikṣamāṇā and Śrāmaṇerikā nuns, etc."
The Buddha was in the Kingdom of *Bōluónài*.
In a forest swamp,
He revealed and taught the profound Dharma for various beings: devas, humans, and the four assemblies.
At that time, there was a flock of five hundred geese in the sky.
Hearing the Buddha's voice, they deeply cherished and loved it, circling and wishing to descend.
A hunter spread a net, and the geese fell into it.
They were killed by the hunter and reborn in the Trāyastriṃśa Heaven.
They appeared upon the knees of their parents like eight-year-old children.
They were incomparably handsome and magnificent, shining like mountains of gold.
They immediately reflected, saying:
"By what cause was I born here?"
They instantly recalled their past lives and the result of loving the Dharma.
They immediately gathered flowers and descended together to *Yánfútí*.
They went to the World-Honored One, bowed at his feet, and said:
"We received the sound of the Dharma and were born in this wonderful heaven.
We request that you instruct us again."
The Buddha preached the Four Noble Truths.
They attained *Sūtuóhuán*.
They then returned to heaven.
The King's consort ascended to the high tower.
She saw geese flying in the sky and desired their flesh.
She then informed the King.
The King dispatched hunters.
They carried nets and snares, scattering them to search and seek.
They immediately caught several dozen and kept them in a cage.
Among them were some who refused to eat.
The other geese said:
"We have now survived; what benefit is there in not eating?"
The one who was not eating said:
"Worry prevents me from eating."
After seven days, he became thin and weak, escaped through a hole in the cage, and flew away.
He spoke to the fat ones from afar, saying:
"You, being greedy for food, shall suffer pain later."
In the Buddha Land of *Émítuó*,
there are constantly various marvelous birds of mixed colors,
white swans, peacocks, parrots, *shèlì*, *Jiālíngpíngqié*, and the *Gòngmìng* birds.
Day and night, during the six periods, they utter harmonious and elegant sounds.
The sounds they speak [teach]:
The Five Faculties,
The Five Powers,
The Seven Factors of Enlightenment,
The Eightfold Noble Path,
And other such dharmas.
The sentient beings in that land, hearing these sounds,
all contemplate the Three Jewels.
Formerly, on Snow Mountain, there was a dove.
At that time, there was heavy rain and snow.
A person lost his way, met with calamity, and suffered hardship.
Hunger and cold arrived together, and his life was in imminent danger.
The dove flew seeking fire.
It gathered firewood for the person and lit it.
Once lit, [the dove] cast its body into the fire.
To give as alms to this starving person.
The Fó was walking in Qíhuán Lín during the late afternoon.
Shèlìfú followed him.
At that time, an eagle was chasing a dove.
The dove flew near the Fó.
The shadow of the Fó’s steps covered it.
The dove's body was calm and safe; its fear was immediately dispelled, and it ceased making any sound.
Afterward, Shèlìfú’s shadow reached it.
The dove immediately made a sound, trembling and afraid as before.
Shèlìfú spoke to the Fó, saying:
Both the Fó and I are free from the Three Poisons (sān dú).
When the Fó’s shadow covers the dove, the dove is not terrified.
When my shadow covers the dove, it trembles and fears as before.
The Fó said:
It is because you still retain habits (xí) of the Three Poisons.
Observe the past life causation (sù shì yīnyuán) of this dove: for how many lifetimes has it been a dove?
Shèlìfú immediately entered the Samādhi of Past Lives Knowledge (sùmìng zhì sānmèi).
He observed this dove.
For eight myriad great kalpas (dà jié) already, it has continually embodied the form of a dove.
Beyond that, I am unable to see.
The Fó said:
If you are unable to fully know the past,
try observing when this dove will be released (from the form of a dove).
Shèlìfú immediately entered the Samādhi of Vow Knowledge (yuàn zhì sānmèi).
He observed this dove.
It will not shed the dove body for eight myriad great kalpas (dà jié).
Beyond this, he did not know.
For great kalpas equal to the sands of the Gangā (Hénghé) River, it will continually assume the form of a dove.
Long ago, a wildfire burned a forest.
In the forest, there was a pheasant.
It diligently exerted its strength, flying back into the forest.
It sprinkled water on the forest, repeatedly flying back and forth, exhausted, yet not considering it hardship.
At that time, Tiāndì Shì came and asked it, saying:
What are you doing?
It replied:
I am saving this forest out of pity for the living beings.
This forest provides vast, cool, and joyous shelter and nourishment.
All my species and relatives rely entirely upon it.
Since I possess physical strength, how can I be negligent and fail to save it?
Tiāndì asked:
Since you are so diligent, how long will you continue?
The pheasant said:
I will continue until death.
Tiāndì said:
Who will bear witness for you?
It immediately made a self-vow:
If my heart is utterly sincere and my belief is not false, the fire shall immediately extinguish itself.
At that time, the Jìngjū Tiān knew of the pheasant’s vast vow (hóngshì).
They immediately extinguished the fire for it.
The forest remained lush from beginning to end and was not burned by the fire.
King Bōsīní Wáng had four chief ministers.
They were appointed as generals.
They gathered the four divisions of the army, intending to conquer a small state.
The four ministers saw the Fó and bowed their heads to his feet.
The Shìzūn asked them:
Where are you gentlemen going?
They replied fully concerning the matter.
We have established many things for this king, often fearing for our lives, and now we are about to attack and conquer.
The Shìzūn praised them, saying:
Excellent, virtuous ones.
This is how one repays kindness and demonstrates fidelity.
It is not only in this present life that you have served this king.
In a past life, in the kingdom of Shājié,
a host of crows gathered and rested in that country.
The Crow King was named Gānzhè.
He commanded eighty thousand crows.
The Crow King had a wife named Jiùlíní.
When she was pregnant, she had unusual food cravings (è shí) and sincerely reported to the King:
My body is slightly afflicted and desires fine, tender (meat).
I must eat the flesh of the Deer King to live; otherwise, I will die.
Thereupon, the Crow King heard her words and assembled the crowd of crows.
You must go to the kingdom of Shājié.
The King of Shājié possesses a great Deer King.
Named Xūjù.
I desire its meat.
Four crows responded to the call:
We are capable of taking this responsibility.
We will not begrudge our bodies or lives and will surely carry out this matter.
At that time, the four crows frequently came to the royal compound.
The prince of that kingdom saw the crows and was afraid.
He rushed back and reported to the King:
I saw four crows of such an appearance.
They repeatedly come to the deer park.
The King immediately ordered men to capture them.
The crow masters devised a method, setting up nets to capture the crows.
They successfully captured them and presented them alive to the King.
The King questioned the four crows and reprimanded them:
Why do you repeatedly come here?
Violating my boundaries?
The crows replied:
Indeed, Heavenly King (Tiānwáng), this is not what we wished for.
There is a king named Ānzhù.
His wife is carrying a child.
She desires the fine, tender deer meat of Xūjù.
That King sent us here.
We received the command of our sovereign.
The King was astonished and deemed it marvelous.
That they accepted the King’s command and formulated this plan,
sacrificing their bodies and lives, is truly extraordinary.
If one seeks ordinary people who possess such fidelity,
it is hard enough to find those who follow the command of a lord or father.
How much more so for birds and beasts?
The King informed the crows:
Today, I pardon your offense.
In the past, there was a crow named Jūqí that wandered among the thicket, giving birth to its young in a tree.
Jūqí and a monkey were close friends at that time.
In the thicket, there was a poisonous snake.
It waited until they were away.
It devoured Jūqí’s young, leaving no remnants.
Jūqí, having lost its young, cried out mournfully, not knowing what had happened.
It deeply pondered.
It realized the snake had devoured them.
When the monkey returned and saw this, it asked what the matter was.
It replied:
The snake devoured my young, completely consuming them all.
The monkey said:
I shall avenge this.
At that time, the poisonous snake was moving.
The monkey went forward and coiled around it.
The snake, enraged, wrapped itself around the monkey.
The monkey grasped its head and dragged it.
It dragged it to a stone, ground it until it shattered, and it died.
It threw the body away and returned.
Jūqí leaped for joy.
In a past lifetime,
there was a flock of chickens living near a hazel thicket.
A badger invaded and preyed on them, leaving only one hen.
A crow came and covered her, and together they produced one offspring.
When the offspring made a sound, the crow spoke a verse (gè), saying:
This child is not fully mine; its father is wild, its mother is of the village.
Born from their coupling, the child is neither crow nor chicken.
If it wishes to learn the father’s sound, yet it is born of a chicken.
If it wishes to learn the mother’s cry, its father is still a crow.
It learns the crow’s call but sounds like a chicken; it learns the chicken’s cry but makes the crow’s sound.
If it attempts to learn both crow and chicken, neither of the two will be successfully accomplished.
In an age long ago,
a eunuch (huángmén) died.
His body was discarded among ailanthus trees.
A magic fox (gǔ hú) and a crow,
came together to eat the flesh.
They praised each other mutually.
The crow said:
Your body is like a lion’s, your head is like an immortal’s (xiānrén).
Born from the King of Deer, beautiful indeed, like a fine flower!
The fox said:
Who is the venerable one in the tree, whose wisdom is paramount?
His brilliance illuminates the ten directions, like accumulated violet-gold.
At that time, a Great Immortal (dà xiānrén) was residing in quiet solitude.
Purely cultivating the Way.
He heard them and spoke a verse (gè), asking:
What you are doing I have observed for a long time; this deed is deceitful (liǎngshé).
Hiding yourselves among the trees, eating the flesh of a dead eunuch (huángmén).
You base and contemptible creatures, yet you proclaim yourselves like superior beings (shàngrén).
The crow said:
The lion and the peacock—they consume the flesh of birds.
How are you different, shaving your head and seeking alms in sequence?
There are four types of dragons (lóng):
First, egg-born (luǎnshēng).
Second, womb-born (tāishēng).
Third, moisture-born (shīshēng).
Fourth, transformation-born (huàshēng).
All of them previously had much resentment and rage; their minds were perverse and dishonest.
They practiced great generosity (bùshī), which is why they now assume this form.
Their palace is made of the Seven Treasures (qī bǎo); their body is forty *lǐ* tall.
Their robe is forty *lǐ* long,
and eighty *lǐ* wide.
It weighs two and a half *liǎng*.
Possessing spiritual power and freedom, they enjoy a hundred flavors of food and drink.
However, the last mouthful transforms into a toad (xiāmá).
If one transforms oneself and inspires one’s dependents to give rise to the Mind of the Way (dào xīn),
or gives a black robe to a beggar, they can cause all the dragons to arise and make offerings.
Sand does not rain upon their bodies, and they are free from various calamities, feeding on turtles, alligators, fish, and soft-shelled turtles.
They use (these creatures) as grasped food (chuǎi shí). Washing their clothes serves as a fine, smooth meal.
They also have marriages.
They touch bodies to achieve *yīn* and *yáng*.
Their lifespan is one kalpa (jié).
Some, however, have shorter lives.
Those exempt from being eaten by the Jīnchì Niǎo.
There are only sixteen kings:
One, Suōjié.
Two, Nántuó.
Three, Bánántuó.
Four, Yīnuópóluó.
Five, Tídóulàizhà.
Six, Shànjiàn.
Seven, Āxū.
Eight, Gāgōuluó.
Nine, Gāpíluó.
Ten, Āpōluó.
Eleven, Gānuó.
Twelve, Gōugānuó.
Thirteen, Ānòudá.
Fourteen, Shànzhù.
Fifteen, Yōushǎngjiāpōtóu.
Sixteen, Déchākā.
Sājiélóngwáng.
Resided in the deep northern sea beneath Mount Xūmí.
His palace and dwelling extended eighty thousand *yóujūn* in length and breadth.
The walls were made of seven treasures and were seven layers thick.
Balustrades and nets adorned it beautifully.
Gardens, groves, and bathing pools, where numerous birds sang in harmony.
Golden walls and silver gates.
The gates were two thousand four hundred *lǐ* high.
And two thousand two hundred *lǐ* wide.
The painted murals were exquisite and lovely.
They were constantly guarded and protected by five hundred *guǐshén*.
He was able to summon rain according to his wishes.
Which other dragons could not accomplish.
The abyss where he lived surged and flowed into the sea.
In the color of blue *liúlí*.
The Dragon King addressed the Buddha, saying:
"Since the beginning of the *jié*, I have resided in the Great Sea.
Since the time of Kūlóuqín Fó,
My wives and children within the Great Sea were very few.
Now, the dependents and family of the sea dragons are exceedingly numerous."
The Buddha informed the Dragon King:
"Those who renounced household life in the Buddhist teachings,
violated the precepts, committed wrong deeds, and did not abandon their broken precepts, mostly reincarnated among the dragons.
Having proper views, they did not fall into *dìyù*.
Beings of this kind, after their lifespan ended, all were reborn among the dragons."
The Buddha told the Dragon King:
"During the time of Kūlóuqín Fó,
ninety-eight billion people, both lay and monastic,
violated the prohibitions and precepts and were all reborn among the dragons.
During the time of Jūnàhánmóuní Fó,
eighty billion people, both lay and monastic,
destroyed the precepts and indulged their minds.
After their lifespan ended, all were reborn among the dragons.
During the time of Jiāshè Fó,
sixty-four billion people, both lay and monastic,
violated the precepts and were all reborn among the dragons.
During my time,
ninety-nine billion lay people,
who fought, disputed, slandered the scriptures and precepts, died and were reborn among the dragons.
Some have already been born.
Because of this reason,
the wives, children, and dependents of the dragons in the Great Sea are countless.
After my *níhuán*, there will be many wicked *Yōupósāi*.
Who violate and lose the prohibitions and precepts shall be reborn among the dragons.
Or fall into *dìyù*.
There was a powerful venomous dragon.
If it looked at a weak person with its eyes, that person died immediately.
If it breathed air upon a strong person, that person also died.
At that time, the dragon received the one-day precepts.
It renounced home life and entered the forest among the trees to meditate.
After sitting for a long time, it grew tired and fell asleep.
According to the dragon nature, when it slept, its form resembled a snake.
Of varied colors like the seven treasures.
A hunter saw it and exclaimed in surprise and joy:
"With this rare and hard-to-obtain skin,
I will offer it to the King.
Would it not be suitable to use it to decorate his boat?"
He immediately pressed its head down with a staff and used a knife to strip off its skin.
The dragon thought to itself:
"My power can overthrow a kingdom.
How can this small creature possibly hurt me?
Since I am now upholding the precepts, I shall not regard this body.
I must follow the Buddha's words and endure this.
It closed its eyes and did not look, and held its breath and did not exhale.
Pitying this man.
For the sake of upholding the precepts, it wholeheartedly endured the skinning and felt no remorse.
Having lost its skin, its raw red flesh lay on the ground.
The sun was scorching hot then, and it writhed on the earth.
It wanted to head toward the great water, but it saw many small insects coming to eat its body.
For the sake of upholding the precepts, it dared not move again.
It reflected and said:
"Now I bestow this body upon these insects.
For the sake of the Buddha Way.
I now give them flesh charity to fill their bodies.
Later, I shall give them Dharma charity to benefit their minds."
When its body dried up and its life ended, it was immediately reborn in the Dāolì Tiānshàng.
There were Dragon Kings.
The first was named Xīqì.
The second was named Dàxīqì.
The third was named Néngluó.
The fourth was named Wúliàngsè.
They addressed the World-Honored One, saying:
"In this sea, there are countless varieties of dragons.
There are four types of Golden-Winged Birds that constantly prey upon the dragons in the sea.
We pray that the Buddha protects us, so we may attain peace and tranquility, free from worry and fear."
The World-Honored One removed the dark robe from his body and said to the Sea Dragon King:
"You shall take this dark robe of the Tathāgata.
Divide it among all the dragons, so that it covers every one of them.
In the Great Sea, if a dragon possesses even a single thread of it,
the King of the Golden-Winged Birds will not be able to harm it.
The inconceivable and magnificent virtues established by the Buddha are indeed like this."
Then, the Sea Dragon King took the Buddha's robe and distributed it among the various Dragon Kings.
According to what they lacked, whether large or small, wide or narrow, it was naturally supplied to them.
Yet, the robe remained as it was, and could never be exhausted.
Thereupon, the Sea Dragon King announced to the other Dragon Kings:
"You must revere this robe as you revere the World-Honored One.
After Nirvāṇa, venerate the *shèlì*.
Everything necessary shall be used to serve the World-Honored One."
The Four Kings of the Golden-Winged Birds, hearing what the Buddha had established, were alarmed and fearful.
They quickly went to the Buddha's presence and bowed their heads at his feet.
"Why, World-Honored One, have you taken away our food?"
The Buddha said:
"There are entirely four kinds of food (livelihoods).
Which lead beings to three destinies.
What are the four?
First: using nets to hunt birds and beasts, injuring and harming flocks of animals, taking life unjustly, and using them as food and drink.
Second: holding and carrying weapons, swords, and spears to hack, stab, oppress, fight, shoot, and rob the property of others, and using it as food and drink.
Third: being stingy and greedy, flattering, violating prohibitions chaotically, holding false views, and deceiving cleverly to obtain food.
Fourth: claiming to be a teacher when one is not a teacher.
Claiming to be the World-Honored One when one is not the World-Honored One.
Following evil yet claiming to be righteous.
Claiming to have quiet resolve when one does not have quiet resolve.
Claiming to be pure when one is not pure.
Claiming to have *fànxíng* when one does not have *fànxíng*.
Making false claims about oneself and fraudulently seeking to obtain food.
These are the four kinds of food.
Which lead beings to the three evil destinies: *dìyù*, hungry ghosts, and animals.
The Dharma I teach excludes these four kinds of food.
One ought not to harm sentient beings in order to nourish one's body.
If you wish to protect your own body, you must protect others.
What ought not to be done, you must strictly refrain from doing."
At that time, the Four Kings of the Golden-Winged Birds,
each accompanied by a thousand dependents, addressed the Buddha, saying:
"Today, we take refuge in the Buddha, the Dharma, and the Assembly of Monastics (*Sēng*).
We confess and repent the past sins we have committed.
We shall uphold the prohibitions and precepts starting from this day.
We grant the gift of fearlessness to all Dragon Kings.
We shall protect the True Dharma until the Buddha's Dharma remains in the world.
We will not violate the Buddha's teachings until the Way and the Dharma are extinguished."
Formerly, in Yánfú Tí, there was a kingdom named Bōluónài.
Within it lived a man.
Who especially loved gold.
He tormented himself striving to find and obtain seven jars of gold.
He buried them in the earth and never used them for clothing or food.
He contracted a disease and died.
Since his greedy attachment was heavy,
he transformed and was reborn as a venomous snake.
It coiled around the jars of gold, and after dying, was reborn again, spending tens of thousands of years there.
Later, reflecting upon itself, it suddenly became aware and realized:
"It is precisely because of this gold that I suffer this evil retribution.
I must relinquish it and give charity to a field of merit (*fútián*), seeking a good destiny."
At that moment, it emerged by the roadside and saw a Bōluómén.
It then said:
"I have one jar of gold; I entrust you to feed the assembly of monastics (*Sēng*) with it.
If you do not do this for me, I will kill you."
The Bōluómén said:
"I can do this for you."
The snake brought out the gold and gave it to him.
He immediately took it and went to the *qiélán*.
He fully reported the matter to the *Sēng*.
Stating the snake's intention to hold an offering.
The *Sēng* agreed.
The gold was taken and handed to the Wéinà.
The Wéinà managed the preparations, and the date for the meal was approaching.
The Bōluómén took a small *āhàntí* and went to the snake's dwelling.
The snake was delighted to see him.
It immediately coiled up on top of the *āhàntí*.
The Bōluómén covered it with cloth and carried it toward the monastery.
Passersby saw this and gave many valuables, sending them to his home.
A separate day was set.
To invite the venerable and holy monastics to offer a meal.
When the gathering concluded.
The snake went forward to the *Sēngqiélán*, positioned itself in front of the *Sēng*, stood in the street.
It instructed the Bōluómén to walk past them sequentially and observe.
It used its own faith to observe those receiving the food.
Gazing intently without moving.
When the affair was finished, the snake cherished increased reverence and felt no satiety.
After the *Sēng* finished eating, they preached the Dharma again for the snake.
The snake then gave away all seven jars of gold, asking the Wéinà to take them and use them for offerings.
It immediately abandoned its evil form and was reborn in the Dāolì Heaven.
Formerly, there was a snake whose head and tail quarreled with each other.
The head said to the tail:
"I ought to be the greater one."
The tail said to the head:
"I ought to be the greater one."
The head said:
"I have ears that can hear.
I have eyes that can see.
I have a mouth that can eat.
When moving, I am in front.
Therefore, I should be the greater one.
You possess none of these abilities."
The tail said:
"I make you move forward.
That is why you are able to go.
If I coil my body three times around a tree,
and do not stop for three days, you will not be able to seek food.
You will be starved and near death."
The head said to the tail:
"Please let go of it, and I will acknowledge you as the greater one."
The tail heard his words and immediately let go.
The head then said to the tail:
"Since you are now the greater one, I permit you to walk first."
The tail walked in front.
Before traveling many steps, it fell into a pit of fire and died.
Formerly, there was a snake.
Which, along with a toad and a turtle, were close friends living together in one pond.
Afterward, the pond water dried up.
They were poor, hungry, distressed, and had nowhere to turn.
At that time, the snake sent the turtle to call the toad, saying:
If one encounters poverty, one loses the original mind, failing to consider the original righteousness, putting food first.
The toad (Háma) said:
"You use my voice to speak to the snake;
the toad will never come near you."
He addressed the Bhikṣus (Bǐqiū):
"Imagine in the great ocean there is a blind tortoise.
Its lifespan is immeasurable kalpas (jié).
Once every hundred years, it happens to raise its head.
Furthermore, there is a floating log which happens to have a single hole.
It drifts on the ocean waves, carried east and west by the wind.
When the blind tortoise emerges once every hundred years, it may happen upon this hole and reach the east side of the sea.
The floating log might sometimes drift to the west side of the sea; missing each other is also common.
Although they miss each other, sometimes they meet again.
Common people drift in the sea of the Five Destinations (Wǔ Qù);
returning to a human body is far more difficult than this."
The Buddha (Fó) and the Bhikṣus,
heading towards Vaiśālī (Píshèlǐ),
reached the Líyuè River (Líyuè Hé).
By the river bank were five hundred cowherds and five hundred fishermen.
The Buddha sat down not far from the river to rest.
At that time, the fishermen netted a fish.
Five hundred men pulling could not bring it out.
They then called upon the crowd of cowherds.
A thousand people combining their strength captured a great fish.
Its body had a hundred heads of various kinds.
Donkeys, horses, camels, tigers, wolves, pigs, dogs, apes, monkeys, foxes—creatures of this sort.
The crowd was extremely astonished and rushed to gather and look at it.
The World-Honored One (Shìzūn) immediately went to where the fish was,
and spoke to the fish, asking:
"Are you Kāpilī (Jiāpílǐ)?"
When asked three times in this manner, it replied each time, "Yes."
He asked again:
"Where are your followers whom you taught now?"
It replied:
"They have fallen into the Avīci Hell (Ābí Dìyù)."
Ānanda (Ānán) asked:
"Why is this hundred-headed fish now called Kāpilī?"
The Buddha said:
"In the time of Kasyapa Buddha (Jiāshè Fó), there was a Brahmin (Póluómén).
He begot a son
named Kāpilī (Jiāpílǐ).
He was intelligent and knowledgeable.
Among his kind, he was foremost in erudition.
Only compared to the Śramaṇas (Shāmén) was he not superior.
When his father was near death, he diligently commanded him:
'You must be careful not to discuss doctrines with the Śramaṇas of Kāśyapa.
Why is that?
The Śramaṇas' wisdom is profound; you will certainly not equal them.'
After his father died, his mother asked him:
'You were originally highly learned. Is there now anyone who surpasses you?'
He replied:
'The Śramaṇas are markedly superior to me.'
His mother asked again:
'How are they superior?'
He replied: 'If I have doubts and go ask the Buddha, he can resolve them.
But if they ask me, I cannot answer.'
His mother told him:
'Why do you not learn their Dharma?'
He replied:
'To respectfully learn their Dharma, one must become a Śramaṇa.
I am a layman (báiyī); how can I learn?'
His mother further instructed him:
'Falsely pretend to be a Śramaṇa; once you have learned and attained mastery, come back home.'
Obeying his mother's instruction, he became a Bhikṣu.
After a short period, he read and recited the Three Baskets (Sāncáng), thoroughly mastering the meaning of the principles.
His mother asked him:
'Have you attained superiority now?'
He replied:
'I am superior in scholastic learning, but not in seated meditation (zuòchán).
How do I know this?
When I ask those people, they can all differentiate and explain.
When those people ask me, I cannot know.
Because of this, I am not yet equal to them.'
His mother further instructed him:
'From now on, when you discuss doctrine,
if by chance you are inferior, then simply curse and insult them.'
Kāpilī said:
'Śramaṇas who have left home have no fault or transgression.
How can I curse them?'
She replied:
'Just curse them, and you will gain superiority.'
At that time, Kāpilī could not bear to disobey his mother.
The next day, he debated the principles again.
When he was shown to be deficient or cornered, he immediately cursed them, saying:
'You people are foolish and dull, recognizing nothing, worse than livestock!'
He used all the heads of the hundred beasts to compare them.
This was not done just once.
Because of this karmic retribution (guǒbào), he now suffers the body of a fish with a hundred heads."
Ānanda asked the Buddha:
"When will he be freed from this fish body?"
The Buddha told Ānanda:
"Even when the thousand Buddhas of this Bhadrakalpa (Xián Jié) have passed, he still will not be freed."
At that time, Ānanda and the assembly,
hearing what the Buddha had said,
all spoke together in unison, saying:
"One must not be incautious in the actions of body, mouth, and mind."
Then the fishermen and the cowherds, etc.,
all simultaneously joined their palms toward the Buddha,
requesting to leave home and purely cultivate the Brahmacarya (Fànxíng).
The Buddha said, "Welcome."
Their hair and beard fell away naturally, and the monastic robes appeared on their bodies.
He preached the subtle Dharma for them, and they achieved the fruit of Arhatship (Āluóhàn).
In the Southern Sea (Nánhǎi), there was a sudden surging of astonishing waves that flooded the land.
Three great fish flowed into a stream between small islands.
They said to one another:
"We are trapped here, and the water has not yet receded.
We ought to swim upstream and return to the great ocean."
They were then blocked by a sandbar and could not cross over.
The first fish used all its strength to leap over the island and managed to pass.
The next fish relied on the weeds and managed to pass.
The third fish’s strength was exhausted
and it was captured by a hunter.
The Buddha saw this and spoke a verse (sòng) saying:
"This day has passed, and life diminishes accordingly.
Like a fish in shallow water, what joy is there in this?"
In the Jiāluó Pond (Jiāluó Chí) there was a clam.
It heard the Buddha preaching the Dharma.
It immediately came out of the pond and went under the grass roots.
At that time, there was a cowherd.
He saw the great assembly surrounding the Buddha, listening to him preach the Dharma.
He went to the Buddha’s location.
Wanting to hear the Dharma, he poked the ground with his staff.
By mistake, he hit the clam's head.
The clam immediately died and was born in the Trāyastriṃśa Heaven (Dāolì Tiān).
He saw various celestial courtesans (jìnǚ) making merry sounds.
Immediately he reflected:
"I was previously an animal (chùshēng).
For what cause (yīnyuán) was I born into this celestial palace?"
He immediately used his divine eye (tiānyǎn) to observe.
Previously, by the pond, he had listened to the Buddha preach the Dharma.
By means of this merit (gōngdé), he attained this retribution (guǒbào).
At that time, the clam celestial being immediately mounted his palace
and went to the Buddha's location, bowing his head and touching the Buddha’s feet.
The Buddha preached the Dharma for him, and he attained the fruit of a Sotāpanna (Xūtuóhuán Guǒ).
Formerly, there was a great family (dàjiā) that harvested a thousand measures (hú) of grain.
They buried it deep in the earth.
The following spring, when the weather warmed, they opened it to take the seeds.
They saw no grain at all,
but there was one worm, as large as an ox basket (niú jǔ).
It had no hands, no feet, no head, and no eyes, like a dull lump of flesh.
The master and servants were all astonished.
They took it out and placed it on the flat ground.
They immediately asked:
"What are you?"
It said nothing in response.
They then used an iron awl to poke it in one spot.
It spoke, saying:
"If you want to know my name, take me and place me by the side of the great road.
There will naturally be someone who names me."
Thereupon, they carried it and placed it beside the road.
For three days, no one could name it.
Next, several hundred yellow horse carriages approached.
The clothing and attendants were all yellow.
They stopped the carriages and called out:
"Grain Thief! Why are you here in this place?"
It replied:
"I ate a man's grain, which is why I was placed here."
After speaking for a long time, they bid farewell and left.
The owner asked the Grain Thief (gǔzéi):
"Who was that just now?"
It replied:
"That was the essence spirit (jīng) of gold treasure.
It resides three hundred steps west of here, beneath a large tree.
There are a hundred stone jars full of gold there."
The owner immediately took several dozen men, went to dig, and immediately found the jars of gold.
The family was overjoyed, loaded it up in carts, and brought it home.
They kowtowed to the Grain Thief, saying:
"The gold we received today is due to the great kindness of the spirit (shén).
Would the spirit stay with us and return home so we can offer further sacrifices (gōngyǎng)?"
The Grain Thief said:
"The reason I ate your grain earlier and did not reveal my name
was so that you could receive this golden reward.
I must now travel on and spread blessings throughout the world.
I cannot stay here any longer."
Having finished speaking, it suddenly disappeared.
In the southeastern corner of the city of Wángshèchéng, there was a stagnant ditch.
The ditches and drains within the city were foul and filthy.
All feces and urine flowed into it.
The stench was unbearable to approach.
There was a great creature born within the stagnant ditch.
Its body was several *zhàng* long, and it had no hands or feet.
It wriggled, lowering and raising itself, playing in the stagnant water.
The observers numbered several thousand.
Ānán, while performing his alms round, saw it and went to look.
The creature immediately leaped and thrashed, causing waves to surge and swell.
[Ānán] fully informed the Buddha.
The Buddha and the various *bhikkhus* went together to the site of the pool.
When the crowd saw the Buddha,
they each thought:
"Today the Rúlái,
will surely speak to the assembly about the creature's origins and fate, resolving the doubts of the masses—how wonderful will that be!"
The Buddha said:
"After Wéiwèi Fó attained Nirvāṇa,
there was a stūpa temple at that time.
Five hundred *bhikkhus* passed through the temple.
The temple master saw them and was greatly delighted.
He invited them to stay and receive offerings for three months, and the assembly all accepted the invitation.
The temple master diligently provided food offerings, leaving nothing out.
Later, five hundred merchants, having entered the sea to gather treasures, returned and passed the stūpa temple.
They saw the five hundred *bhikkhus* diligently practicing the Way.
They all conceived the thought [of merit].
Joyfully, they discussed among themselves:
'A Field of Merit is rarely encountered; we should set up a humble offering.'
They then informed the temple master.
The temple master replied:
'My invitation for three months will be completed in five more days.
Then you may widely set up your offering.'
The merchants said:
'We must depart and cannot wait for the completion [of the three months].'
The five hundred merchants each donated one pearl.
They obtained five hundred *móní zhū*.
They entrusted these to the temple master.
They instructed the temple master, saying:
'When the day arrives, use our jewels to provide offerings to the Saṅgha.'
The *bhikkhu* said, 'Yes.'
He immediately accepted them all.
Afterwards, he conceived an evil thought,
scheming to take them entirely for himself.
Consequently, he did not provide the offering.
The Saṅgha assembly asked, saying:
'Master, the merchants formerly donated jewels; the offering should be prepared.
Have you already dispatched it?'
The temple master said:
'This was given to me only.
If you want to take [something from] me, my feces can be given to you.
If you do not leave immediately,
I will cut off your hands and feet and throw you into the cesspit.'
The assembly pitied his ignorance, remained silent, and departed.
Long, long ago in the past,
after the Rúlái, who appeared in the world, attained final extinction,
during the Semblance Dharma period, there was a *bhikkhu* who practiced sitting meditation.
He was alone in the forest and constantly troubled by mites and lice.
He immediately made an agreement with them:
'When I sit in meditation, you should remain silent.'
They concealed themselves and resided quietly; the lice followed the Dharma well.
At a later time,
a sand flea came to the side of the lice.
It asked:
'How is it that your body is now so plump and robust?'
The louse replied:
'The master we rely on constantly cultivates *chándìng*.
He instructed me regarding the times for eating and drinking.
I acted according to the Dharma, which is why I am fresh and plump.'
The flea said:
'I also wish to practice that method.'
The louse said, 'Do as you wish.'
The flea smelled the fragrance of blood and flesh and immediately began to eat and chew.
The *bhikkhu* suffered torment.
He immediately removed his clothes and burned them with fire.
The *bhikkhu* practicing meditation was Jiāyè Fó.
The sand flea was Típódádduō.
The louse was me."
"As for Yánluó Wáng:
Formerly, he was the King of the country of Píshā.
Because he fought against Wéituóshǐ Wáng,
and his military strength was inferior,
he therefore made a solemn vow:
'May I become the Master of the Hells.'
His eighteen ministers and aides, leading a host of one million, all had horns on their heads and were filled with anger and resentment.
They jointly established this vow, saying:
'In the future, we shall assist him in governing these sinners.'
The Píshā Wáng is now Yánluó.
The eighteen individuals are the various minor kings.
The host of one million are the various Ābàng.
[Yánluó] is subordinate to the Bǐshāmén Tiānwáng of the North.
South of Yánfútí there is a great Vajra Mountain.
Within it is the palace of Yánluó Wáng.
It is six thousand *yóuxún* in extent, and three times day and night, a great copper cauldron naturally appears before him.
If the cauldron enters the palace,
the King sees it and is terrified.
He leaves and exits outside the palace.
If the cauldron exits outside the palace, the King enters the palace.
There are great prison guards
who lay the King upon the hot cauldron.
They use iron hooks to tear open his mouth.
Molten copper is poured into him.
From his throat down, everything is scorched and rotten.
When the affair is finished, he returns to enjoy pleasure with his court ladies.
His various ministers who share in this retribution also experience the same.
There are three messengers:
the first is old age,
the second is sickness,
and the third is death.
If any sentient being commits evil through the three karmas,
when the body perishes and life ends, he should fall into hell.
The King asks, saying:
'Were you summoned by the heavenly messenger?'
The King says:
'Did you see the first messenger?
When you were among men,
did you see [a person] whose head was white, teeth had fallen out, and eyes looked dimly,
whose skin was loose, flesh wrinkled, back stooped, walking with a staff and groaning—did you see such a person?'
The sinner says, 'I saw him.'
The King says:
'Why did you not reflect upon yourself, [thinking]:
"I, too, shall become like this?"'
The sinner says:
'I was heedless at that time and failed to realize it myself.'
The King says:
'Now, I shall make you understand the suffering of heedlessness.
This fault belongs neither to parents, brothers, the Heavenly Emperor, ancestors, acquaintances, servants, nor *shāmen*.
You committed the evil yourself, and now you must bear the consequences yourself.'
He further asks: 'Did you see the second messenger?
When you were originally a human,
did you ever see someone desperately ill, lying upon a foul place of feces and urine,
requiring others for food and drink, aching in all his joints, weeping, groaning, and unable to speak?'
He replies, 'I saw him.'
The King asks:
'Why did you not reflect upon yourself?' He further asks: 'Did you perceive the third messenger?
Did you ever see a person die, their body ruined, life ended, and all faculties permanently extinguished,
their body stiff and straight like withered wood, abandoned among the mounds, and eaten by birds and beasts?'
He replies, 'I saw him.' Having spoken, [the King] hands him over to the prison guards to proceed to the great hells.
The eighteen minor kings are:
First, Jiāyán, who governs the Nílí (Hells).
Second, Qūzūn, who governs the Mountain of Knives.
Third, FèiShòu, who governs the Boiling Sand.
Fourth, FèiDiǎn, who governs the Boiling Feces.
Fifth, Jiāshì, who governs the Black Ears.
Sixth, Kuīsuō, who governs the Chariot of Fire.
Seventh, Tāngwèi, who governs the Cauldron of Boiling Water.
Eighth, Tiějiārán, who governs the Iron Bed.
Ninth, Èshēng, who governs the Kuī Mountain.
Tenth, [name missing], [who governs] the Cold Ice. Eleventh, Píjiā, who governs the Flaying of Skin.
Twelfth, Jìngtóu, who governs the Beasts.
Thirteenth, Tíbó, who governs the Weapons and Blades.
Fourteenth, Yídà, who governs the Iron Mill.
Fifteenth, Yuètóu, who governs the Ice Hells.
Sixteenth, Tiě [unclear], Seventeenth, Shēn, who governs the Maggots.
Eighteenth, Guānshēn, who governs the Molten Copper.
Píng Cháo Wáng.
He supervises the Great Ābí Dà Nílí. Second is
Jìn Píng Wáng.
He manages the Heavy Black Rope Hell. Third is
Tú Dū Wáng.
He manages the Pestle and Mortar Hell. Fourth is
Fǔ Tiān Wáng.
He manages the Gathering Hell. Fifth is
Shèng Dū Wáng.
He manages the Great Mountain Hell. Sixth is
Xuán Dū Wáng.
He manages the Fire City Hell. Seventh is
Guǎng Wǔ Wáng.
He primarily governs the Sword Tree Hell. Eighth is
Wǔ Yáng Wáng.
He supervises the Shouting Hell. Ninth is
Píng Yáng Wáng.
He primarily governs the Eight Paths Hell. Tenth is
Dū Yáng Wáng.
He manages the Thorn Tree Hell. Eleventh is
Xiāo Yáng Wáng.
He primarily governs the Boiling Ash Hell. Twelfth is
Tǐng Wèi Wáng.
He manages the Great Wailing Hell and the Small Wailing Hell. Thirteenth is
Guǎng Jìn Wáng.
He oversees the Great Ābí Yù. Fourteenth is
Gāo Dū Wáng.
He primarily governs the Iron Chariot Hell. Fifteenth is
Gōng Yáng Wáng.
He primarily governs the Iron Fire Hell. Sixteenth is
Píng Jiě Wáng.
He primarily governs the Boiling Excrement Hell. Seventeenth is
Zhù Yáng Wáng.
He primarily governs the Burning Hell. Eighteenth is
Píng Qiū Wáng.
He manages the Mí Lí Hell. Nineteenth is
Jiāo Shí Wáng.
He primarily governs the Mountain Stone Hell. Twentieth is
Láng Yé Wáng.
He primarily governs the Duō Huán Hell. Twenty-first is
Dū Guān Wáng.
He primarily governs the Nílí Hell. Twenty-second is
Xuán Xī Wáng.
He primarily governs the Flying Insect Hell. Twenty-third is
Tài Yī Wáng.
He primarily governs the Yáng Ā Hell. Twenty-fourth is
Hé Shí Wáng.
He primarily governs the Great Grinding Hell. Twenty-fifth is
Liáng Wú Wáng.
He primarily governs the Cold Snow Hell. Twenty-sixth is
Wú Yuán Wáng.
He primarily governs the Iron Pestle Hell. Twenty-seventh is
Zhèng Zhì Wáng.
He primarily governs the Iron Pillar Hell. Twenty-eighth is
Gāo Yuǎn Wáng.
He primarily governs the Pus and Blood Hell. Twenty-ninth is
Dū Jìn Wáng.
He primarily governs the Burning Stone Hell. Thirtieth is Yuán Dū Wáng.
He primarily governs the Iron Wheel Hell.
These are the thirty Hells (Nílí) of great bitter suffering.
The gods and spirits listen, examine, and keep a detailed record of sins and blessings, regardless of rank or status.
Six reports are submitted per month, and four reviews are conducted per year.
The days of the four reviews are all managed by the Eight Kings.
On the days of the Eight Kings, the Heavenly Kings tour and investigate in order to assess all those belonging to the heavenly people and their subordinates.
Those who have blessings have their lifespan increased; those who have sins have their allotted time reduced.
The determination of long or short life is fixed and not erroneous even by a hair's breadth.
Mortals are blindly ignorant and utterly unaware of this.
They fail to perform good deeds beforehand and are consequently taken and handed over to the hells.
The Five Officials are:
One: The Xiān Guān (Fresh Official), who prohibits killing.
Two: The Shuǐ Guān (Water Official), who prohibits theft.
Three: The Tiě Guān (Iron Official), who prohibits sexual misconduct.
Four: The Tǔ Guān (Earth Official), who prohibits slander/duplicity.
Five: The Tiān Guān (Heaven Official), who prohibits alcohol.
The east, west, and south sides of Yánluó Wáng’s city are lined with various hells.
There is light from the sun and moon, but it is not bright or clear.
Only the Black Ear Hell is not illuminated by the light.
When a person dies, the spirit is born into the intermediate state (Zhōngyīn).
The intermediate state means having already abandoned the dead state but not yet having reached the birth state.
The sinners ride on their intermediate body.
They enter the Nílí City.
The Nílí City is where the multitude of sinners dwell.
It is the place where they gather together before they receive their punishment.
Blown by the Skillful Wind, they receive large or small bodies according to the severity of their karma.
Blown by the Stinking Wind, the coarse and ugly forms of sinners are achieved.
Blown by the Fragrant Wind, the subtle bodies of the meritorious are achieved.
Those born in heaven or fallen into hell,
each have greeters.
When a person is sick and about to die,
their eyes naturally see the arrival of the greeters.
For those destined to be born in heaven, heavenly beings bring celestial robes and music to welcome them.
For those destined to be born elsewhere, their eyes see revered persons speaking wonderful words to them.
For those destined to fall into hell, their eyes see soldiers holding knives, shields, pikes, halberds, and ropes surrounding them.
What they see is different.
The mouth cannot speak.
Each obtains their karmic retribution according to the deeds they performed.
Heaven is without injustice or abuse.
It is impartial and without deviation.
They are governed by the net of Heaven according to what they have done.
The Eight Kings' Day (Bā Wáng Rì) is defined as follows:
It refers to the thirty-two ministerial subordinates of Tiāndì Shì (Śakra Devānām Indra).
The Four Guardian Great Kings, the Officials controlling Destiny, and the Officials controlling Records.
The Five Luó Great Kings, and the Eight Kings' messengers.
They all go out, spreading everywhere, and conduct their reviews.
They verify the memorials presented by the Four Kings on the 15th and 30th days.
They investigate and assess the good and evil deeds performed by the populace.
The Hell Kings also dispatch assistant ministers and lesser kings.
They all emerge simultaneously, and sins are immediately recorded.
On the Bā Wáng Rì (Eight Kings’ Day) before the fast,
if transgression occurs, but blessings are strong, there is help, peace, and no further calamity; the blessings are used for pardon.
If, upon reaching the day of the subsequent fast, the transgression is repeated,
those whose number of sins is numerous have their lifespan reduced, their names are listed, and their death date is determined.
On that year, month, day, and hour, they are confined and sent down to hell.
The Hell immediately receives the official document and dispatches a hell-demon holding the register of names to summon them.
The hell-demons are merciless; even if the death date has not yet arrived,
they forcefully push people to commit evil, causing their lifespan to be quickly exhausted.
Those with abundant blessings have their lifespan increased and their allotted time extended.
Heaven sends virtuous spirits to guard and protect their bodies.
They are removed from the list of those sent down to hell, and their sinful names are erased.
Death is removed, and rebirth is determined.
Later, they are born into heaven.
Question: What are the Hells?
Answer: They are the Cold, Hot, and Borderlands Hells.
There are countless types.
I shall now summarize them briefly.
Regarding the Cold Hells:
The Clearly Wailing,
the Unclearly Wailing,
and the Non-Wailing.
These three categories involve the worst forms of painful cries.
There are three types of Clearly Wailing Hells:
One: Āfútuó (Arbuda).
Two: Níluófútuó (Nirarbuda).
Three: Ābō Bā (Aṭaṭa).
In the Āfútuó Hell, due to the cold, sores resembling boils grow on the body.
In the Níluófútuó Hell, the wind blows the body up until it is swollen.
In the Ābō Bā Hell, extremely cold wind blows, peeling off the skin and flesh until nothing remains.
They all utter sharp, shuddering cries.
These three are clearly discernible.
Regarding the Unclearly Wailing Hells:
One: Āzhà Xiū Zhà Xiū (Ha ha ha).
Two: Yōubōluó (Utpala).
The Āzhà Xiū Zhà Xiū Hell is also blown by extremely cold wind.
The skin and flesh peel away, causing cries of Āzhà Xiū Zhà Xiū.
The Yōubōluó Hell involves extremely fierce cold wind which blows and peels the skin and flesh; iron lotus leaves inside the body wrap around the body itself.
It resembles the utpala flower.
They fall into this hell because they slandered the Sages and Worthies.
Regarding the Non-Wailing Hells:
One: Jūmóutuó (Kumuda).
Two: Xūjiàntí (Sugandhaka).
Three: Gāfēntuólí (Gundharaka).
Four: Gāpōtánmó (Padma).
Extremely cold wind blows, causing the body to swell fully.
In these four manifestations, they suffer and groan.
Because they slandered the Sages and Worthies, they fall into these four types of hells.
At all times, they endure immeasurable suffering.
These are all the Great Cold Hells.
They are located between the Four Continents,
lodged at the bottom of the Iron Ring Mountains (Tiě Wéi Shān).
They lie facing upwards, dwelling in the deep darkness.
Cold wind destroys their bodies.
They are consumed by great fires.
Like the burning of a bamboo grove.
Their cries and coughs clash with each other.
There are also other sentient beings who suffer within them.
All who slandered and disparaged the Sages and Worthies suffer such pain.
As the World-Honored One (Shìzūn) said in a verse:
There are hundreds of thousands of Níluófútuó and thirty-five Āfútuó—
the hells for those who destroy the Sages, the evil destinations for those with evil vows of mouth and mind.
These are called the Cold Hells.
Question: What are the Hot Hells?
Answer: One: Those with rulers governing them.
Two: Those with few rulers governing them.
Three: Those with no rulers governing them.
The governing involved in these three manifestations is torment and scourging.
Those with rulers are:
One: The Reviving Hell.
Two: The Walking Hell.
Three: The Black Rope Hell.
Regarding the Reviving Hell:
The prison guards use sharp knives and axes to slice, flay, chop, and cut the sinful beings, like chopping the tops of grasses.
Although the skin and flesh are dispersed, their karmic cause for punishment is not yet exhausted.
A cold wind blows, and they are revived to their former state.
Furthermore, because of their wicked deeds, iron claws grow on their hands, sharp like knives.
They each develop enmity and hatred, mutually striking and slicing one another.
Like reaping bamboo or reeds.
Because they listened to each other and bore hatred until death, they are reborn here.
Regarding the Black Rope Hell:
The sinners are splayed out on the ground.
They use black ropes to mark and measure them, then chop and cut.
They are born into that hell because they previously chopped and cut other sentient beings.
Furthermore, they use hot red copper.
Plates of it wrap the body, breaking bones, causing marrow and blood to flow.
They used whips and staves against sentient beings and monks
who were unmotivated yet wore clothes donated by the faithful; therefore, they are born in that place.
In the deepest darkness, they suffer the affliction of smoke inhalation.
They hang their bodies upside down, forcing them to inhale the smoke.
This is because they caused sentient beings dwelling in caves (by smoke) to suffer.
Those who travel to Dìyù
line up the sinful beings like butchers
and chop off their hands, feet, ears, noses, and heads.
They originally committed the crime of being a butcher (tú'ér), so they suffer this affliction.
Furthermore, on the hot iron ground, they drive iron fire carts.
The hell wardens (yùzú) ride them, glaring and roaring loudly.
They force them to run, because they previously used elephants and horses until they were exhausted; thus, they fall into this place.
Those who commit adultery with others' wives are driven up the Sword Tree (Jiànshù), naturally being burned by fire, and suffer such pain.
It is said that the hell wardens who govern Dìyù
are not burned by the fire due to their karmic actions.
Fewer govern Dìyù:
One is Zhònghé, Two is Dàkū, Three is Tiějiàn.
The Zhònghé Dìyù:
Sinful beings, fearing the hell wardens,
run in countless hundreds and thousands into the mountain passes.
Fire naturally springs up before and behind them.
The two mountains spontaneously come together like grinding stones.
Blood flows like a river, and bones and flesh are utterly pulverized.
This is because they previously enjoyed grinding up sentient beings.
Furthermore, a great iron mortar is burned by fire, and they pound them with a pestle.
After a hundred years, their lives do not end due to their sinful karma.
This is because they previously used mortars to pound and kill fleas, lice, and other pests.
The Dàkū Dìyù:
Great iron mountains are entirely burning, and in the four directions there is no place to go.
Wicked hell wardens, without compassion,
angrily say,
"Where do you intend to go?"
They use burning iron pestles to strike and break their heads.
This is because they previously caused suffering to the common people (wànmín); thus, they are born here.
The Zhì Dìyù:
The flames of great iron mountains clash together.
They are shoveled with iron shovels.
They are laid out and roasted all around; as soon as one side is cooked,
the shovel naturally turns, flipping them over.
This is because they previously impaled and stabbed people; thus, they are born here.
The Wújiàn Dìyù:
The iron ground burns all around, spanning a hundred yojanas (yóuxún) both horizontally and vertically.
The four gates are like a fortress, covered with thin copper plates, with continuous, successive flames.
All the sinful beings are piled up like firewood.
The flames encounter no obstruction, burning and rotting their bodies; they receive suffering without interruption.
This is because they killed their father or mother or an Arhat (Zhēnrén),
harbored malicious intent toward the Buddha, causing blood to flow,
disturbed the assembly of the Sangha (Sēngzhòng),
and performed the ten serious unwholesome deeds (shí bùshàn yè); thus, they are born here.
The Biāndì Dìyù:
They are located in homes, by the water, in the mountains, and in the wilderness.
They individually receive retribution for their wicked karma; this is called Biāndì Dìyù.
Outside the Four Continents (Sì Tiānxià), there are eighty thousand continents (tiānxià) surrounding them.
Outside the eighty thousand continents, there is a great ocean.
Outside the ocean, there is a great Vajra Mountain (Dà Jīngāng Shān).
Outside that mountain, there is another mountain also named Vajra (Jīngāng); in the space between the two mountains, the light of the sun, moon, gods, and heavens does not shine.
There are Eight Great Dìyù.
One is Xiǎng.
Two is Hēishéng.
Three is Chuíkuò.
Four is Jiàohuàn.
Five is Dà Jiàohuàn.
Six is Shāozhì.
Seven is Dà Shāozhì.
Eight is Wújiàn. Each of these Dìyù
has sixteen small Dìyù.
The sixteen of the Xiǎng Dìyù are:
One is Hēishā.
Two is Fèishǐ.
Three is Wǔbǎidīng.
Four is Jī.
Five is Kě.
Six is Yī Tóngfǔ.
